https://gothamist.com/news/queens-man-to.title: Queens man took girlfriend’s body to beach in a wagon, where it remained for 5 days
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-man-to.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-man-to.text:
A Queens man wheeled his girlfriend’s body in a wagon to the beach at Rockaway Community Park and buried her in a shallow grave, where she remained for five days before police found her, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Two days after the alleged killing on Oct. 19, the boyfriend, Rogelio Lozano-Garita, 26, called 911 to report Seraphina Pereira, 35, missing, according to the Queens district attorney's office. He told police that a box holding her belongings had been dropped off at his apartment building, along with a note from a surfer who he said had found her things on the beach.
Lozano-Garita, of Edgemere, was arraigned Wednesday on charges of second-degree murder, weapon possession, concealment of a human corpse and tampering with physical evidence in Pereira’s death, according to prosecutors. He pleaded not guilty, court records show. Police said he was taken into custody Monday.
A lawyer for Lozano-Garita did not return messages seeking comment.
Prosecutors said Lozano-Garita shot Pereira in the head sometime between 2 a.m. and 6 a.m. on Oct. 19 inside an apartment at 343 Beach 54th St. The city’s chief medical examiner ruled her death a homicide on Monday and found she had been shot in the head, neck and torso, officials said.
An NYPD K-9 unit searched the beach and Pereira’s remains were found just before 10 p.m. on Oct. 24 near a cricket field near Beach 58th Street and Almeda Avenue, about half a mile from her home, officials said.
The couple lived together in Edgemere with their two young children and Pereira’s child from a previous relationship, prosecutors said. Police said her home was in Ocean Bay Apartments, a complex that is part of the New York City Housing Authority.
In a statement, Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz said that, as alleged, Lozano-Garita “mercilessly killed his girlfriend,” the mother of his children, then tried to cover up the crime.
A judge ordered Lozano-Garita held without bail, court records show. He is due back in court Friday and faces up to 25 years to life in prison if convicted, according to the district attorney’s office.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Queens Leaders Urge Mamdani to Acquire African Burial Ground to Turn Into Memorial
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. this week sent letters to Mayor Zohran Mamdani and two government agencies demanding they intervene to transform a parking lot built on top of an African burial ground into a respectful memorial commemorating the sacred ground.
Richards, joined by eight Queens elected officials, asked Mamdani and the city to buy the lot and join a growing effort to turn the privately owned lot at 47-11 90th St. in Elmhurst into a memorial. It’s believed more than 300 freed slaves are buried there in a cemetery that dates to the early 19th Century.
“In unity with dozens of community leaders and local preservationists, we urge your administration to acquire the lot and transform it into a proper memorial to the nearly 300 individuals who are interred there,” he wrote to the mayor Tuesday.
In August, The City Reporter revealed that a limited liability corporation that owns the site had paved it over and was renting it out as a parking lot. It held cars and trucks towed under an NYPD effort to rid city streets of abandoned vehicles.
The account inspired a wave of outrage by officials and local leaders at what they saw as a disrespectful treatment of the site.
On Tuesday Donovan and the other elected officials also fired off missives to Lisa Kersavage, chair of the city Landmarks Preservation Commission, asking the agency to designate the site as landmarked, and another letter to Kathy Moser, commissioner of the state Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation department, asking her to consider placing the site on its registry of historic sites.
Those who signed on included the U.S. Rep. Grace Meng, Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, state Sen. Leroy Comrie, Assemblymembers Catalina Cruz and Larinda Hooks and City Councilmembers Shanel Thomas-Henry, Ty Hankerson and Shekar Krishnan, all Democrats.
In his letter to the mayor, Borough President Richards emphasized his ongoing conversations with City Hall about the fate of the site. On Wednesday City Hall did not respond to questions about the status of those talks.
The site dates to 1818 and was taken over by the founders of what would be St. Mark’s African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1828, the year after New York State abolished slavery. The church sold off the lot in the 1930s and it was for years the site of a factory.
In 2009 the factory owner sold it to 90 Queens LLC, a developer who planned to build luxury condos there. While digging a foundation, workers hit an iron coffin containing the remains of an African American woman believed to have died of smallpox around 1835. Subsequent archaeological exploration uncovered hundreds of other graves.
The Rev. Kimberly Detherage of St. Mark’s has called on Mayor Mamdani to get the city to buy the plot and back the creation of a memorial that would honor the individuals buried there. A local group, the Elmhurst History and Cemeteries Preservation Society, has a pending request for examination filed with the city’s landmarks preservation agency. On Wednesday the LPC did not immediately respond to questions about the status of that examination.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-exten.title: Mamdani extends NYC racial equity leader's term after Council pushes back on replacement
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-exten.author: Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-exten.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani will delay his plan to replace the chair of the city’s racial equity watchdog, who has emerged as a sharp critic of the administration. The move comes after pushback from the City Council.
Linda Tigani has led the Commission on Racial Equity since its inception in 2023, after it was formed by a ballot measure approved by voters.
In recent weeks, Tigani has said that Mamdani has been pushing to remove her. She has also condemned some of his policies, specifically his police commissioner Jessica Tisch’s strategy of cracking down on low-level offenses, which disproportionately affect Black and Latino New Yorkers.
“My job is to hold the city accountable,” she told Gothamist on Wednesday before holding a rally with supporters on the steps of City Hall. “We know that any movement in leadership would undermine that work.”
The commission recently won a lawsuit in which they argued that Mandani and his predecessor, Eric Adams, broke the law when they failed to release a plan to combat racial inequity by the legally-mandated deadline. Tigani has been fiercely critical of the Mamdani administration's decision to appeal the judge’s ruling.
The Mamdani administration released its plan in September.
In her interview with Gothamist, Tigani also cited last week’s town hall where New York Times journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones grilled Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels for failing to put forward a plan to integrate public schools.
“We had an education town hall where the chancellor could not give us any information or action plans on how he was planning to desegregate the schools and increase racial equity or close racial equity disparities,” she said.
Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who jointly appoint the chairperson of the commission, agreed Tigani will now serve through July 2027, both offices said.
The commission is charged with advancing the goals of racial equity in city government and increasing community input into the decision-making process.
At an unrelated press conference in Brooklyn on Wednesday, Mamdani thanked Tigani for her service, and said Christopher Alexander, executive director of the NAACP New York State Conference, should be the next chair — but not until next year.
“We're excited to work with the same council to put forward Christopher Alexander as the next commissioner to pick up the mantle that Linda is going to leave behind,” the mayor said.
Jack Lobel, a spokesperson for Menin, said the Council is currently vetting Alexander as Tigani’s replacement.
Wednesday’s announcement came after city lawmakers urged the mayor to keep Tigani.
On Tuesday, the City Council’s Black, Latino and Asian Caucus released a letter sent to Mamdani, urging him to retain Tigani. News of the plan to replace Tigani was first reported by the New York Times.
"At this consequential moment, continuity in CORE’s leadership is essential to advancing its mandate and delivering on the commitments our City has made to racial equity, accountability and justice,” they wrote.
Menin's spokesperson later issued a statement supporting Tigani, saying she had met with members of the caucus and had conveyed to Mamdani their view that “Ms. Tigani be allowed to remain in her position for an extended period.”
Bronx City Councilmember Althea Stevens said members of the mayor’s office had recently made clear to her and her colleagues that Mamdani wanted to oust Tigani as soon as her term ended.
“They were very direct that she needed to go,” she said, adding that the mayor’s team never gave them a “clear understanding” of why they wanted to remove Tigani.
Stevens and other members argued that Tigani had done a good job and that the decision to replace her was not the mayor’s alone.
“We wanted to make clear that this isn’t a mayor appointee. They came to us with a name, there was no discussion of how to do this together,” she said.
This story was updated with new information.

https://gothamist.com/news/woman-charged.title: Woman charged with federal hate crimes after allegedly stabbing 2 Jewish men in NYC
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-charged.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-charged.text:
A Russian woman is facing federal hate crime charges following the alleged stabbing of two Jewish men near Manhattan’s Diamond District earlier this month.
Federal prosecutors identified the woman as Anna Mochalova, a 32-year-old Russian national, and accused her of stabbing the men “with a sharp object that is consistent with being a needle.”
Mochalova allegedly stabbed the first victim around 5:50 p.m. on Oct. 21 while the man had been walking along West 47th Street between Fifth and Sixth avenues, according to the complaint. Federal prosecutors described the first man as having a beard and wearing clothes associated with the Orthodox Jewish community, including a black hat and tzitzit, the strings attached to the corners of a prayer shawl.
Prosecutors say Mochalova then approached another victim — also a Jewish man wearing a yarmulke — on the corner of Sixth Avenue and West 45th Street, just two blocks away from the first stabbing. She bumped into the man several times before stabbing him in the right forearm, prosecutors said.
Another person who was present at the scene during the second stabbing said Mochalova asked him if he was Jewish, and then apologized when he said he was not, according to prosecutors. She is is facing two hate crime charges, which each carry a maximum sentence of 10 years.
"Mochalova allegedly stabbed two men specifically because they were Jewish, an attack made all the more terrifying because the specific weapon used — and its potential contents — remain unknown pending further investigation," U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Jamie McDonald said in a statement.
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Mochalova’s actions struck fear “in an entire community.”
“A hate crime is a message written in violence, and this defendant’s message was loud and clear,” she said in a statement.
Attorney information for the accused was not made immediately available.

https://gothamist.com/news/ex-nypd-serge.title: Ex-NYPD sergeant sentenced to 4-12 years in deadly drunken Taconic crash
https://gothamist.com/news/ex-nypd-serge.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/ex-nypd-serge.text:
A former NYPD sergeant convicted of driving drunk the wrong way on the Taconic State Parkway and killing a Peekskill man was sentenced Wednesday to four to 12 years in prison, the state attorney general’s office said.
Tiffany Howell, 48, of Warwick, New York, pleaded guilty in August before Westchester County Judge Anne B. Bianchi to aggravated vehicular homicide and second-degree manslaughter in the January crash that killed Manuel Boitel, 61.
Howell’s driver’s license has been revoked, and she waived her right to appeal, New York Attorney General Letitia James said.
Boitel’s family said the punishment fell short. In a statement released through their attorney, the family members said they were was disappointed.
“It does not provide the measure of accountability the family had hoped for,” attorney Jonathan Roberts said.
Howell was driving south in the highway’s northbound lanes at more than 50 mph when she crashed head-on into Boitel’s car shortly before midnight on Jan. 22, prosecutors said. Her blood alcohol level was at least 0.18, more than twice the legal limit. Boitel was pronounced dead at a hospital shortly after midnight.
Earlier that night, Howell, an 18-year NYPD veteran, had helped organize a dinner and cigar event with an open bar in Scarsdale for the NYPD Holy Name Society, a Catholic fraternal group, according to social media posts.
The family is also suing the City of New York, the NYPD, the Holy Name Society and the cigar bar where the event was held.
In letters to the judge, Boitel’s wife and sons asked for no leniency. Marisol Boitel wrote that she met her husband when she was 18, married him at 20, and that he was driving home from work happy because he had the next two days off.
“She did not only kill him; she also killed my will to keep living, my dreams and our plans for now and for the future,” she wrote, asking for the maximum sentence.
His son, Marvin Boitel, wrote that his father had once wanted to become a police officer but chose safer work after becoming a father. Marvin Boitel ended his letter with something he said his father always told him: “Actions have consequences.”
Howell’s attorney, a Sergeants Benevolent Association lawyer, did not return calls seeking comment.
The attorney general’s Office of Special Investigation prosecuted the case. State law requires the office to investigate deaths that a police officer may have caused, whether the officer was on or off duty.

https://citylimits.org/11-year-old-boys-.title: 11-Year-Old Boy’s Death in Bronx NYCHA Fire is a ‘Horrific Reminder’ Of E-Bike Battery Dangers, Mayor Says
https://citylimits.org/11-year-old-boys-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/11-year-old-boys-.text:
Share This Article
The deadly blaze, which broke out early Wednesday at NYCHA’s Patterson Houses in the South Bronx, was started by an a lithium-ion battery on an electric bike, which was blocking the apartment’s exit, officials said.
This story has been updated since original publication.
A fire that killed an 11-year-old boy in a NYCHA apartment building in the Bronx was caused by a lithium-ion battery on an electric bike, officials said—renewing concerns about the potential dangers of such devices, which have contributed to hundreds of similar blazes across the city this year.
The fire broke out early Wednesday morning in the kitchen of an 11th-floor apartment at NYCHA’s Patterson Houses in Mott Haven. While FDNY crews arrived within four minutes, the e-bike that caused the blaze “was placed in the pathway of the exit door,” according to Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore, and “made it impossible for the residents to leave safely.”
Kristina Diaz, a resident of 35 years who also lives on the 11th floor and serves as the development’s captain of tenant patrol, described hearing neighbors banging on doors down the hall shortly before 1 a.m. on Wednesday, and said by the time she got to her front door, “the whole kitchen and living [room] was already smoky.”
She then watched firefighters break down the door of the blazed apartment, and described seeing one of the residents on the floor.
She said she received 72 calls in 18 minutes from fellow neighbors asking what happened, or inquiring about how they could help. “I don’t want nothing, just bring a candle for the little 11-year-old,” she told them.
Wednesday’s blaze is the second fire residents of Patterson Houses experienced this year, following an electrical fire that occurred in January and injured six.
Residents of the building expressed shock and grief. Florence Banks, 68, lives on the fifth floor and said she was watching TV when she heard firetrucks pull up to the building. She called her neighbor, and watched from the hallway windows as firefighters “were bringing people out, and pumping their chests.”
“I couldn’t take that,” she said. “I’m just shocked.”
Officials said the damage was contained to the apartment where the fire started. In addition to the boy who was killed, four others were critically injured, including two teenagers.
“Today is a horrific reminder of the danger that lithium-ion battery fires can pose,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a press conference outside Patterson Houses on Wednesday, where officials displayed the charred e-bike that ignited the blaze.
The city has seen more than 400 fires caused by lithium-ion batteries so far this year, officials said, up from 292 last year, and six New Yorkers have died in 2026 so far.
According to the FDNY, 22 of those fires this year took place in NYCHA buildings—up from 18 such fires in 2025, and 13 in 2024.
E-bikes have become increasingly popular in recent years, especially among residents who work as delivery drivers. But the batteries they run on can spark fires that are “extremely dangerous, because they spread fast and ferociously,” Bonsignore said.
“The battery cells go into thermal runaway, which makes a small fire turn into a very big fire, very very quickly,” she said.
Officials urged e-bike users to take precautions, including charging and storing the bikes outdoors whenever possible. If they do take their bike inside, they should keep it out of the way of any exit, including doors and windows, and should never charge it unsupervised.
“Buy certified batteries that come with nationally safety-certified testing laboratory approvals,” Bonsignore said. “If they are leaking, damaged, or smoking, do not use them, and do not buy off-market batteries, but use the manufacturer-recommended devices.”
NYCHA previously considered banning e-bikes from public housing properties, but officials said they recognized that many residents rely on them to get around, especially those doing app-based delivery work.
The housing authority’s current rules allow for no more than one e-bike to be charged in an apartment, and it must be kept away from means of egress, plugged into a wall, and someone over the age of 18 has to be “present and awake while the battery is charging,” said NYCHA CEO Lisa Bova-Hiatt.
“We need individuals to listen and follow the policy,” she added.
Mayor Mamdani told reporters Wednesday that further reforms will be under consideration.
“I think it is our responsibility to continually evaluate every option we have,” he said. “This is an issue that we have seen far too often.”

https://gothamist.com/news/after-being-b.title: After being booed at integration forum, NYC chancellor praised by school parent leaders
https://gothamist.com/news/after-being-b.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/after-being-b.text:
Less than a week after being booed by integration advocates at an explosive town hall, Chancellor Kamar Samuels got a warmer reception from a panel of parents Monday who serve on the Citywide Council on High Schools.
“I was shocked when the audience booed when you defended parent choice,” said Linda Quarles, a member of the council, a group made up of volunteer parents that advocate on behalf of all public high school students. She said fellow parents, especially those who support selective admissions, asked to “pass along their thanks.”
“There are communities who were definitely not represented at that event last week, and our families want you to know that,” Quarles added.
Fellow panel member Deborah Alexander noted that the city’s own surveys found that more than 40% of families who left New York City public schools cited a desire for more rigorous academic instruction as a reason for leaving.
Integration advocates want to reduce or eliminate selective admissions to the city's public schools, pointing to data showing those policies lead to schools that are disproportionately white, Asian and affluent. But other parents, including many on the high school council, support selective admissions, saying students deserve the more rigorous programs “screened” schools provide.
Samuels has said he does not favor selective admissions “screens” but wants to be responsive to communities, and is launching education working groups across the city.
Supporters of pro-integration policies feel emboldened by New York Times journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones’ deeply personal article on her daughter’s experience in public schools. Hannah-Jones has said selective admissions are tools of segregation.
Last week, Hannah-Jones grilled Samuels on the Mamdani administration’s plans to advance integration. Samuels demurred on specifics, saying he was committed to working with communities to develop policies. Members of the crowd jeered Samuels, saying they were disappointed with his answers.
But supporters of current admissions policies — many of whom serve on the council on high schools — say high-achieving students should be rewarded, and that any move toward integration should not result in fewer opportunities for the sharpest kids.
The stark differences between the two meetings hint at clashes to come as integration efforts regain the spotlight in the city's education debates. Past debates over integration have polarized communities, largely along racial lines.
A call for reform
The council, an advisory group, consists of elected parent leaders from around the city, including some members of the group Parents Leaders for Accelerated Curriculum and Education (PLACE). PLACE members have mobilized in the past to preserve selective admissions policies at top-performing schools as integration advocates have sought to dismantle those policies.
On Monday night, Samuels defended his participation in the town hall.
“Anyone should be able to ask the questions and the things that they prioritize, and so the fact that that’s where that conversation went is fine by me,” he said. “I have always in my work prior to being chancellor and as chancellor really committed to making sure that parent voice is a part of what is driving our system.”
Samuels said he personally supports reducing selective admissions but said policies have to be driven by communities. “I won’t always agree with everything our parents are saying,” he said, “but I do think it’s quite critical that we hear those voices.”
Communities across the city are mobilizing for a fight.
On Tuesday night, Adams administration alumni, former Schools Chancellor David Banks and his wife, former Deputy Mayor Sheena Wright, gathered several elected officials, civic and religious leaders to call for reforms to admissions to the city’s specialized high schools as part of a live taping for their podcast in Harlem.
While the specialized schools are just a small sliver of the overall system, they’ve become a shorthand for segregation in public schools.
Banks said he wanted to change admissions at five of the city’s eight specialized schools when he served as chancellor, but that then-Mayor Eric Adams told him no.
“He's a politician. I'm not casting any aspersions. But I want you to know the reason for it is this. And that's why. …He was not prepared to take that on as an issue. And quite frankly, he said, you know, Black and Hispanic communities may get a little upset. They talk about it at home, but they're not gonna do anything about it. The Asian community is very, very, very organized around this issue, and I don't blame them for that.”
Adams did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Last month, Banks acknowledged to Gothamist that promoting integration was not a priority during his tenure. He said he favored policies that aimed to boost academics across the board, especially overhauling literacy instruction. In recent weeks, Banks has become a vocal supporter of efforts to improve diversity in the specialized schools, which rely on a single test — the Specialized High Schools Admissions Test — to determine admissions.
Last spring, only three Black students scored high enough on the test to get into Stuyvesant High School, the crown jewel of the specialized schools. Overall, Black and Latino students made up roughly 10% of offers to the elite high schools, while Asian American students got 56.5% of offers, and white students got 23.5%.
Banks said last spring’s admissions numbers should be a rallying call to Black and Latino communities to activate on the issue.
“Tonight represents one of the first moments where the Black community and Latino community can begin to come together and say, ‘We have a voice in this as well,’” Banks said.
When the most recent admissions numbers for the specialized high schools were released in July, Mamdani called for improvements to elementary and middle schools to increase the pipeline of strong applicants.
“I will say that we know that a single test does not reflect the aptitude of students across the city. We know that Black and Latino students are excelling across the five boroughs, as are students in a wide variety of schools. We have to ensure that we're doing everything we can to deliver for those students at the earliest ages,” said Mamdani, who is an alum of Bronx High School of Science.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: How the Village Halloween Parade keeps its soul
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
It is a logistical fact that events tend to lose their soul as they scale up. More people means more problems, more expenses, more liability and higher expectations. To meet them, organizers generally must sacrifice some amount of quality, community and heart.
By all means, this should apply to the Village Halloween Parade, which began in 1974 as a roving get-together of like-minded puppeteers and artists and has since grown into one of the world's biggest Halloween parades. The annual event, which draws 50,000 participants and 2 million spectators, has become a city-sanctioned ordeal requiring street closures, crowd control and NYPD liaisons.
But even as New York City's artistic spirit has been flattened by rising rents and the drab preferences of those who pay them, the Village Halloween Parade has remained a beacon of creative expression, a mainstream, humanity-uniting delight that is still deeply weird.
It's managed the feat due to the dedication of Jeanne Fleming, a purple-haired octogenarian who's served as the parade’s director since 1980.
“ This is nothing like any other parade. This is really a march of spirit and creativity and imagination. So it doesn't work like anything else,” Fleming said from her red-linteled house at Rokeby, the Hudson Valley estate where she’s lived for 54 years. The parade is less than a week away, but she’s that rare artist who knows how to delegate, so at this point her plate is mostly full of what she calls “detail work,” like being on call in case of crisis, or managing the 100 or so emails she receives each hour.
“What happens is I download all the information into everybody's brains, and then I'm kind of free,” she said as a geriatric long-haired cat named Kitty lounged beneath photos of bygone parades piled next to her cluttered desktop.
Meanwhile, down the gravel path, in a cavernous barn, volunteers fix and finish puppets old and new.
This is the final “puppet-raising,” an October weekend fixture, when the greater puppet community descends on Rokeby to create, choreograph and practice the leading number, transforming the estate’s road into a stand-in for Sixth Avenue.
The process is led by Alex Kahn and Sophia Michahelles, who met and later married after working on the parade in 1998, and have lived in a house attached to the barn since 2007. Today they are leading a smattering of volunteers collaborating on various puppet-related tasks. Country singer Townes Van Zandt is crooning through the speakers and a woman is dancing with an enormous window-shaped puppet on a rod beneath the barn’s soaring rafters. Outside, others peacefully papier-mâché among winged clocks in the fading afternoon light. Everyone is at least somewhat covered in paint.
“People are so willing to do this because you're in an ensemble of 50 people, and we're all making this one tableau vivant together,” Kahn said. “And we're doing it not online and not through some mediated experience. It's happening here and now in physical space, and literally a million people are gonna see it.”
He’s standing in front of a mood board displaying various surreal printouts illustrating this year’s theme, Body and Soul, an exploration of the relationship between the physical and spirit worlds. That’s consistent with past years' cerebral themes, which utilize the puppets’ big performance not for sponsorship or pop culture mimicry but to “expand people's notion of what is possible for Halloween self-transformation,” Kahn said as various children wander in and out of the door connecting his home to the barn. “The parade is an invitation to think. It's an invitation to go deeper into some aspect of our collective mythology, and then make it visual and impactful for the crowd.”
Lake Simons, who’s been participating in puppet-raisings since 2001 and came up from Brooklyn to help prep, said “it becomes something that everyone's got their hands in and therefore it becomes more powerful. We all feel like, I participated in this magical event and my hand was a part of this.”
Indeed, there are more people interested in helping than the core Rokeby crew can accommodate, a fact they clearly feel bad about.
The volunteer power is vital as the Parade still runs on a shoestring budget. Thankfully rent at Rokeby is low, for some buildings nil, and many hands make lighter work of maintaining and bringing giant puppets to life.
As with money, many operational elements have not scaled along with the parade’s size and influence over the years, although there have been numerous small shifts: Parade progenitor Ralph Lee used to store the puppets in the shaft of a decommissioned West Beth elevator. Then for a time they lived in Fleming’s house, before eventually being moved to the barn. Fleming used to cook for all the volunteers herself; that job was eventually passed on to a longtime friend, then to the friend’s daughter.
Fleming still sees the Parade not as a job but an opportunity to create and maintain an annual moment that also serves as a throughline of meaning and belonging in many peoples’ lives.
“ I feel like what I do is I send a ping out into the universe, and then who responds?” she says. “There's one family, their mom died at 35. The kids are in their 20s now, and they come every year for her. They carry puppets and celebrate her life and who she was. There’s so much like that.”
People have gotten engaged and married at the parade. Some have even asked Fleming to imbue their dead grandmother’s spirit into puppets.
“Every kind of thing you could imagine. People just call up and say, ‘I wanna do this,’ and I say, yes, OK, now how do we make it happen? And that’s the game. That’s what’s fun. Being able to allow all these people to realize a dream that they have. That's what it's about for me.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Past Due: Why CUNY Adjuncts Can’t Get Paid On Time
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Aisha Baiocchi
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
Scores of adjunct professors at the City University of New York aren’t getting paid on time, CUNY officials acknowledged, in an ongoing problem that has frustrated the university’s part-time teaching workforce for several years.
Some CUNY adjuncts are owed sums north of $10,000.
“First paychecks don’t come through for a lot of people, and they’ve made that standard,” Rose Shelor Moulton, an adjunct at Hunter College, told The City Reporter. “But our first month of rent is still due.”
This semester, CUNY’s Professional Staff Congress said it has received 110 complaints of delayed pay. That’s actually an improvement: Using payroll data from the state teachers union, the PSC counted just over a thousand late paychecks in Spring 2025.
The delays are due to late additions to the payroll at individual colleges, CUNY said.
“CUNY values the dedication of its adjunct professors and has worked to improve the payroll process to reduce delays, including sending reminders to the campuses before payroll deadlines for the start of each semester, making it easier to provide advance pay to faculty who are hired at the last minute or paying them outside the normal payroll period,” spokesperson Noah Gardy said in a statement.
Adjuncts and union reps said the delays are baked into the university’s hiring practices.
Lynne Turner, a union vice president and an adjunct lecturer at LaGuardia Community College, said pay delays are one of the many consequences of what she called the university’s “employment model of extreme contingency.” Adjuncts are hired on a semester-to-semester basis, according to their union contract and CUNY standards.
“We are employed, re-employed, and then re-employed again,” Turner said. “Of course that comes with problems. Late paychecks are the tip of the iceberg.”
GET THE CUNY SCOOP: Subscribe to our new weekly newsletter covering the City University of New York
According to CUNY’s most recent human resources report, the university employs 11,000 part-time faculty, compared with just under 7,000 full-time faculty. CUNY reported that part-time labor makes up 52% of its instructional staff, higher than the national average of 40%, as reported in February by the College and University Professional Association for Human Resources.
Most CUNY part-time faculty must be rehired each semester. Adjunct pay can range from approximately $7,000 to $11,000 per course.
The PSC’s data analysis shows the vast majority of late paychecks go to employees at senior colleges: in Spring 2025 there were 984 late paychecks to senior colleges, and 25 to community colleges. Senior colleges receive the bulk of their funding from the state legislature, including for payroll.
Because of CUNY’s split funding model, the payments of senior college employees are processed through the state comptroller’s payroll system. This means paperwork has to go through an extra step, possibly one of the reasons for the systematic delays.
In a letter to PSC president James Davis, a senior CUNY administrator said the principal cause for the delays is late submission of paperwork by department chairs, and said the university is working on an improved communications plan to “remind chairpersons.”
Turner said “shifting the blame” to individual department leads ignored what he called the root cause of the issue: CUNY’s reliance on temporary contract labor.
Late paychecks are standard for adjuncts, Moulton said. She is also one of over 50 adjuncts who has joined a union grievance seeking outstanding pay for teaching so-called jumbo courses, which have more than 90 students.
When the union renegotiated its contract with the university in 2023, it increased wages for those teaching courses of 90 or more. Moulton says she is owed $13,000. Her colleague Jasmine Bayron, who teaches in the geography department, says she is owed nearly double that for three semesters of jumbo courses.
Moulton is on a costly payment plan to cover her child’s daycare, which she needed over the summer in order to stay on top of bills. Bayron has taken to grading high school advanced placement exams and tutoring students for the state Regents exam, on top of her regular course load.
Katelyn Peters, an adjunct who teaches at Borough of Manhattan Community College and Hunter, said unstable pay affects her ability to teach.
“There’s all these different programs to increase retention and graduation rates,” Peters said. “But I would think that if you take care of your teachers, the people who are delivering instruction, that’s going to help improve students’ academic experience a whole lot.”

https://gothamist.com/news/if-this-is-wh.title: 'If this is what you want': East Village board halts vote on Tompkins Square overhaul
https://gothamist.com/news/if-this-is-wh.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/if-this-is-wh.text:
An East Village community board tabled an anticipated vote on a controversial, multimillion-dollar update to Tompkins Square Park after park preservationists at the meeting loudly flexed their vocal muscles over the fate of iconic pull-up bars.
“If this is what you want for the last word, this is what it will be,” said Arnette Scott, the chair of Community Board 3, addressing a handful of participants who yelled through a parks department presentation Tuesday night. “Everyone will have another time to voice their opinion.”
The board put off the vote on the $10 million overhaul until next month, after the preservationists – particularly those looking to hold onto the park’s old-school recreational equipment – refused to be quiet.
“The only vote I’m having is if I’m gonna call the cops,” said Scott. “Calm it down.”
The stir comes after the community board’s parks committee earlier this month backed the parks department’s plan. The full board was set to review the plan on Tuesday, until it didn’t. The renovations include updates to the 1990s-era outdoor fitness area, the adjacent basketball courts, and the kids-only swimming pool.
The parks department has said the amenities need to be made more accessible to all users, the public infrastructure needs improvement and the fitness equipment needs to be safe. The agency has updated its original plan: The renovated gym's layout would be kept mostly the same, and new materials would be used.
Participants at the heart of the preservation fight told Gothamist that they love the pull-up bars the way they are. They held up signs in a school auditorium that read: “keep the bars,” “repair don’t destroy,” and “we like it DON’T TOUCH.”
Salo Coslovsky, an associate professor of urban planning at NYU and an opponent of wholesale changes, considered the delayed vote a win.
“I don’t know who they are,” Coslovsky said of the hecklers who led to the postponement. “But someone thought it was worth their time and energy to show up and scream.”

https://gothamist.com/news/60k-runners-2.title: 60K runners, 2.5 million fans: NYPD promises tight security for NYC Marathon
https://gothamist.com/news/60k-runners-2.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/60k-runners-2.text:
NYPD drones, dogs, horses and helicopters will join throngs of spectators to keep a close eye on this year’s New York City Marathon, according to Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch.
While Tisch said there are “no known specific credible threats” to this year’s race, security across the city on marathon day is historically tight. Thousands of officers will be posted along the route, joined by specialized units on land, in the harbor and in the air. Strategically placed blocker vehicles will restrict access to busy areas, while intelligence teams will monitor live-feed cameras throughout the five boroughs, Tisch added.
“As always, there will be assets you will see and assets you will not see,” Tisch said.
The 50th New York City Marathon will begin, as always, with waves of runners crossing the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from Staten Island to Brooklyn. The 26.2-mile course weaves through Sunset Park, Park Slope and Williamsburg before crossing the Queensboro Bridge into Manhattan, where it takes runners along the Upper East Side. The course briefly crosses into the South Bronx, then returns to bring runners to the finish line in Central Park.
Anyone planning to watch runners by the finish line should prepare for increased security measures. Tisch said police will search bags, but items like coolers, umbrellas, chairs and large backpacks are prohibited.
Tisch also said unauthorized drones are prohibited on marathon day, and the NYPD’s drone mitigation teams will be deployed throughout the day to identify and address any illegal drone activity.
City residents and visitors are encouraged to use public transportation on Sunday, as rolling closures along streets and bridges will cause heavy traffic.
The Verrazzano Bridge's upper level will close at 11 p.m. Saturday, and the lower level will shut down at 7 a.m. Sunday. The Queensboro Bridge will close at 6:30 a.m. Sunday. And the Pulaski Bridge will close at 7:15 a.m. Sunday. The Willis and Madison Avenue bridges will close at 7:30 a.m., Tisch said. All bridges will reopen once the last runners have passed through.
More than 60,000 runners will take to the streets on Sunday, including more than 29,000 New York residents and about 18,600 first-time marathoners, according to New York Road Runners.
About 2.5 million spectators are expected to descend on the city from all over the world, officials said.
Beyond the NYPD’s efforts, Tisch said spectators can provide valuable eyes and ears to help ensure a safe day.
“We ask everyone to stay alert; if you see something, please say something,” she said.

https://hellgatenyc.com/cb3-tompkins-cal.title: East Village Pull-Up Bar Preservationists Test the Limits of Democracy
https://hellgatenyc.com/cb3-tompkins-cal.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/cb3-tompkins-cal.text:
On Tuesday evening, a group of a few dozen demonstrators gathered at the calisthenics bars in Tompkins Square Park, and then marched together to a meeting of Manhattan's Community Board 3 on the Lower East Side. They carried signs bearing slogans like "No One Asked For This," and "Repair! Don't Destroy!" 
The demonstrators are pissed about the Parks Department's planned project to replace the basketball courts, pool, and, most controversially, the exercise bars. The work will make the park more accessible, safer for children, and less prone to flooding. It'll replace the above-ground pool with a larger, in-ground pool. It's expected to take about 18 months, during which parts of the park will be closed—an almost unbearable scenario for many vocal park users.
The community board meeting immediately turned rancorous, with a pro-bars advocate screaming at a board member to "get the fuck out of my fucking face." Board Chair Arnette Scott threatened to call the cops on multiple preservationists, who jeered through a presentation by a representative for the Parks Department. The beleaguered bureaucrat strained to be heard as he confirmed their plans still included replacing the bars with "high quality materials," and bringing the area up to "all applicable codes, including ones that have to do with approach by wheelchairs, and clearances for circulation and safety." 
Paul de Rienzo, a retired teacher who later told me he doesn't use the bars, caused such a scene that the Parks Department had to cut their presentation short without explaining what "underlying issues" they had found with the concrete below the basketball courts in their plans to add stormwater detention tanks. 
Watching the display, it was hard to decide whether I was becoming an arch liberal, ashamed that the crowd of crowing hippies and tatted software engineer "punks" couldn't act like respectable adults, or a burgeoning Stalinist realizing that bureaucrats should not be accountable to the public. At any rate, I discovered I hated to see New Yorkers make their voices heard, or at the very least thought a poor example of civic engagement was being set for the multiple children in attendance.
Other than the pull-up bar obsessives, the public comments consisted of neighbors decrying an affordable housing complex being built on Fifth Street, and others urging the board to reject a restaurant permit because the ventilation system would be too noisy.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: New Getty grant initiative supports museums’ accessibility and engagement efforts
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The Getty Foundation has launched a multi-year grant initiative to support 11 museums in the US and abroad with an initial $2.7m for projects that rethink how language, accessibility and community engagement can enrich visitors’ experiences The programme, dubbed New Interpretations, aims to move beyond traditional wall texts and labels, emphasising research, collaboration and tech-forward approaches.
The grantees include the Association for Art Museum Interpretation; the Australian Centre for the Moving Image; the Baltimore Museum of Art; the Denver Art Museum; the First Americans Museum; the Fowler Museum at UCLA; the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum; the Leeum Museum of Art, in partnership with M+; the Manchester Museum; the Queens Museum; and the Walker Art Center. Heather E. MacDonald, the senior programme officer of the Getty Foundation, tells The Art Newspaper that the foundation sought to partner with museums that have shown a commitment to visitor-centred research.
“We have an opportunity to support creative work that will serve as wonderful case studies for the field,” MacDonald says. “Because we are emphasising visitor research, evaluation and the dissemination of findings, we hope this work will reach peers and other organisations and create a ripple effect, with ideas being transmitted and scaled up.”
The Leeum Museum of Art in Seoul and M+ in Hong Kong will host some of the first public-facing projects under the initiative, including a major international gathering at M+ in December 2026 bringing together museum professionals to discuss new approaches to interpretation and visitor engagement in Asia.
The Walker Art Center in Minneapolis will continue developing visitor guides and wall texts in Spanish, Hmong and Somali, an initiative it began in 2024. The collaborative project involves consultation and partnerships with communities in the Twin Cities area that aim to ensure that interpretive texts reflect the languages and voices of the communities they are reaching.
The First Americans Museum in Oklahoma City will work with a fellow to conduct visitor surveys with a significant focus on Native American audiences, and will produce a report on how museums can ensure that Indigenous knowledge and authority inform exhibitions. The results will also help guide an exhibition on the bicentennial of the Indian Removal Act in 2030 that will present historical and contemporary perspectives.
The Denver Art Museum will commission a research firm to report on the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and its impact on visitors, alongside on-site surveys and panels. The project follows an essay published earlier this year by members of the museum’s interpretive team on the American Alliance of Museum’s website, “A Colossal Mirror: Museums as a Refuge for the Real in the Age of AI,” which outlines the museum’s broader position on AI, authenticity and institutions. Earlier this year, the museum removed a ChatGPT-generated illustration of a Buddhist statue following visitor backlash.
“I’m hoping we will see a continued commitment to a visitor-centred approach at museums, which, in some ways, is still an emerging field,” MacDonald says. “As with our other funding, we want to support work that is creative and experimental, but also rigorous and based in research. In this case, there is a real commitment to better understanding the needs and desires of visitors.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: ‘Encounter the unexpected’: Harry Houdini exhibition commemorates the famed illusionist on the centenary of his death
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Allison C. Meier
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The famed escape artist Harry Houdini dreamed of retiring to his library and spending the rest of his life writing about the many topics that filled its volumes: the history of conjuring, witchcraft, psychic phenomena and the drama of the stage.
“Every hour which I could spare from my professional work was given over to study in libraries, to interviews with retired magicians and collectors, and to browsing in old bookstores and antique shops where rare collections of programmes, newspapers and prints might be found,” he wrote in his 1908 book The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin. In the townhouse he shared with his wife, Bess, at 278 West 113th Street in Manhattan, ephemera and books were crammed into shelves and stacked in precarious piles.
On 31 October 1926, he died suddenly while on tour at the age of 52 from a ruptured appendix. The thousands of items he had devoted years to amassing were dispersed, with his magic collection going to the Library of Congress. The drama collection, after passing through a series of hands, arrived at the University of Texas at Austin in 1958, where it is held by the Harry Ransom Center.
“There was a misconception, even within the magic community, that what came to the Ransom Center was just an incredible collection of Houdini’s personal papers, not realising that there’s material on magic dating back hundreds of years that doesn’t exist anywhere else, and that had all come from Houdini, too,” says Eric Colleary, the centre’s curator of theatre and performing arts.
After he joined the Ransom Center in 2015, Colleary started noticing traces of Houdini’s collection everywhere, whether engravings of mechanical automata or theatrical playbills dating back to the 18th century that most others at the time treated as disposable. “He mentioned it in almost every interview he gave,” Colleary says. “He figured out ways to work it into letters that had nothing to do with his collection. It was really important to him.”
Colleary has now spent over a decade unravelling the depth of Houdini’s bibliophilia, an effort that has culminated in the Houdini’s Library exhibition at the Ransom Center (until 24 January 2027) and a book of the same name out now from Abbeville Press. The curator’s detective work to illuminate this lesser-known side of the legendary magician included tracking down a lost mahogany bookcase that had held his theatrical materials and examining Houdini’s typescript catalogue that is now at David Copperfield’s International Museum and Library of the Conjuring Arts in Las Vegas. The 53-page document is not exhaustive of Houdini’s holdings but shows his deep engagement with them through his personal annotations, including his frustration at some volumes. For an 1881 edition of Thomas Frost’s The Lives of the Conjurers, for instance, he remarked: “This book is a pack of mistakes and wilful errors from the start to the finish.”
It was his disappointment with that book in particular that propelled Houdini’s collecting with the aim of bringing together enough primary sources to write a better record of magical history. The desire for magic to be recognised as a serious academic area of study mirrored his advocacy for the professionalisation of magic, such as serving as an early president of the Society of American Magicians.
Houdini had little formal education. Born Ehrich Weiss in 1874 in Budapest, his family immigrated to the US in 1878. They settled in Appleton, Wisconsin, where there was no public library. Yet he had formative memories of the theological books kept by his father, a rabbi.
“One of the things his father instilled in him was that having a library was a gentlemanly thing to do. It was a way of demonstrating your knowledge and that you had access to it,” Colleary says. “But you also had to be able to use it.”
Always an autodidact—revealed by his shaky spelling, like “I bot…” written inside numerous covers—books were how he first learned about magic. Reading the memoirs of the French magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin inspired his adopted name. As the “Handcuff King” would later quip in an interview: “When I have come to a town, the police have tried to show me that their shackles could hold me, and have failed; the booksellers have tried to sell me many books, and have succeeded.”
On view at the Ransom Center are examples of his obsessive collecting from every angle related to magic and the stage, from Reginald Scot’s 1584 Discovery of Witchcraft—an exposé of the occult that also includes some of the first published information on sleight of hand—to broadsides advertising appearances of Henry “Box” Brown, whose great feat of illusion was escaping slavery by mailing himself in a wooden crate.
“Houdini felt very strongly that all of human knowledge was in books, and we just needed to be curious enough to go and look for it,” Colleary says. “Now with the internet, you’re so targeted and focused, you don’t get to stumble upon something you didn’t expect, and that was at the core of what Houdini loved about his collection: that ability to encounter the unexpected.”
- Houdini’s Library, Harry Ransom Center, Austin, Texas, until 24 January 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: UK art market growth lags behind competitors, new report finds
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Riah Pryor
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The UK art market has more than tripled in size over the past 30 years but has fallen behind the pace of growth seen by its principal competitors, with mounting regulation identified as one of the key potential barriers to growth.
A report published this week to mark the 30th anniversary of the British Art Market Federation (BAMF), authored by Arts Economics, found that the UK remained the world’s second-largest art market by sales value, growing from £2.6bn in 1996 to £8bn in 2025. The UK also continues to enjoy the dominant position in Europe, with its hold over 50% of the continent’s market share.
However, its recovery from successive economic shocks has been weaker than that of its major competitors. Since the market’s low point in 2009 following the global financial crisis, UK sales have risen by 17% to 2025, compared with 114% growth in the US and 51% globally.
"While celebrating three decades of growth and cultural contribution, our sector faces clear hurdles," says Thomas Christopherson, Chairman of BAMF, in a release accompanying the report, which was launched at a reception at Christie’s in London, on 27 October. "Over-complicated and excessive regulation continues to disproportionately impact the many small and micro businesses that form the backbone of the UK art market. If we are to maintain our competitive edge against major global peers, the heavy burden of compliance must be addressed so that our galleries and auction houses can continue to invest, expand, and thrive."
Given the report’s finding that 89% of UK art businesses reported annual sales below £1 million, the potential burden of regulatory obligations on small teams is evident.
Shifts in cross-border trade
Patterns of cross-border trade are also shifting. UK imports of art and antiques are down 45% from £4.1bn in 2015, to £2.2bn in 2025. UK exports, meanwhile, stand at £3.1bn in 2025, down 48% from £6bn recorded in 2015.
Beyond this contraction, the report notes a diversification of trading partners. In 2000, the United States dominated the UK’s export market, taking 72% of the total value, followed by Switzerland (14%), Japan (2%), and China, Australia and Qatar (1% each). The US remained the largest single destination in 2025, but its share had fallen to 35%, less than half its earlier level. Exports were by then spread across a far broader range of markets, with Switzerland (11%), France (10%) and the Netherlands (6%) among the leading recipients.
There were signs of resilience in the domestic market, however. UK public auction sales rose by 8% to £2.1bn, and the report underlines the sector’s wider economic importance, with the UK art market found to be supporting an estimated 53,290 jobs across 8,780 businesses and generating £1.5bn in tax revenue in 2025. It also underpins the livelihoods of an estimated 62,800 visual artists, according to the report.
Art dealers and auction houses spent an estimated £2bn on ancillary services and products in 2025, equivalent to around a quarter of their turnover.
"Our success is built on a long tradition of specialist skills and expertise in buying and selling art, the benefits of which support thousands of jobs, nurture specialist ancillary businesses, generate tax revenues, and contribute to Britain’s cultural life," said BAMF’s president, Anthony Browne, in the release.
This positive impact is also seemingly reaching beyond the capital. While London remains a major international hub, 65% of employer-registered art businesses are based elsewhere in the UK.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Painting by overlooked Abstract Expressionist Anna Walinska gets key role in television series Best Medicine
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Karen Chernick
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
“It’s not always an actor whose scene gets cut,” says Rosina Rubin, steward of the estate of her aunt, the Modernist painter Anna Walinska (1906-97). Sometimes, art cast to feature in films or television shows get cut from the final edit, too. Such was the case with an abstract black-and-white Walinska painting, The Earth Bears Witness (1956), which was due to appear in an HBO miniseries about the Watergate scandal a few years ago, White House Plumbers (2023), only to be edited out of the final version.
But Walinska’s expressive monochrome painting got a second chance and is now playing a key role in the second season of the series Best Medicine on Fox, which began last month. It hangs in the office of the lead character Martin Best (played by Josh Charles)—a hotshot surgeon from Boston who left the city to work in a small New England town. Like the doctor himself, the painting is a fish out of water. The non-figurative composition is an unexpected addition to the old-fashioned surroundings, which are adorned with fusty wood panelling and floral wallpaper.
“For season two of our show, the storyline required a redress of our doctor's office, to a more modern and sophisticated look,” says Diane Lederman, the production designer for Best Medicine, who got the idea to use the Walinska painting after seeing and admiring a print of it that hung in the show’s production offices. “For me, this painting epitomised cosmopolitan urbane style and culture, completely opposing the rural, provincial art pieces that previously decorated the walls of the set. This was the perfect piece."
On its surface, The Earth Bears Witness may exemplify a certain Abstract Expressionist sophistication. For Walinska herself, however, the painting held a deeper meaning. Created roughly a decade after the Holocaust, this was one of a series of works the artist painted in reference to it at a time when people were not readily articulating their feelings surrounding the Holocaust and museums were not yet commemorating it. It was not publicly shown for over 20 years and was first exhibited in 1979 at New York's Cathedral of St John the Divine, along with 92 other Walinska works created in response to the Holocaust.
“She kept doing Holocaust-related work, it never left her mind,” Rubin says of her aunt’s dedication to this subject matter, over the course of her seven-decade career. “It’s just kind of interesting because [the creators of Best Medicine] found this painting, they hung it up. They have no idea what its story is.”
The original meaning of the painting may have been lost in its translation to the small screen, but it is true to Walinska’s life in another, unexpected way. According to Rubin, her aunt habitually paid doctor’s bills with art (usually commissioned portraits, but other works as well). In fact, the eye doctor that Rubin currently sees took over her father’s practice and inherited some Walinskas that were once given in lieu of payment.
In the real world, outside of its cameo appearance in a Maine doctor’s office on Best Medicine, The Earth Bears Witness entered the permanent collection of the Arkansas Museum of Fine Arts in Little Rock in 2024, along with additional Walinska works. This museum accession follows a pattern of renewed interest in the modernist artist, who was successful in her lifetime but whose works were exhibited less frequently after her death. Within the past few years, her work has been presented at the American Art Fair and was also the subject of a 2023 solo commercial show of both early figural drawings and later abstractions at Graham Shay 1857.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: A brush with... Sung Tieu—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Ben Luke, David Clack, Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Sung Tieu’s work uses her own personal history to explore various conditions in contemporary society. Born in Hai Duong, Vietnam, in 1987, she now lives in Berlin.
This interface between her Vietnamese background and her present environment—in the broadest sense of the term—forms the structure for a wideranging, materially rich investigation of migration, labour and capitalism, Cold War and post-Cold War European society and culture, and post-colonial life more widely.
She explores these complex subjects with a language that acknowledges yet offers a critique of recent traditions in Western art, including Conceptual Art, Minimalism and Post-Minimalism.
This distinctive approach, allied to her ability to operate across diverse disciplines, forms and scales and her sensitivity to space and site, led to her being commissioned to respond to the German Pavilion in the 61st Venice Biennale.
She reflects at length on her work in Venice, discusses the balance of intimacy and investigative rigour in her work, and how she can be playful even when addressing deadly serious subject matter.
She discusses her early interest in Francisco de Goya’s Black Paintings, the enduring influence of Hanne Darboven, her response to Albrecht Dürer in her Venice exhibition, her close reading of Ocean Vong and Walter Benjamin, and the impact of the films of Ken Loach.
Plus, she gives insight into life in the studio and answers our usual questions, including the ultimate: what is art for?
- Sung Tieu: How is your day?, Emalin, Helmet Row, London, until 14 November
- Sung Tieu: Ruin, German Pavilion with Henrike Naumann, 61st Venice Biennale, until 22 November
- Sung Tieu, Inserzioni, Castello di Rivoli, Turin, Italy, now open
This podcast is sponsored by Bloomberg Connects, the arts and culture platform. Bloomberg Connects offers access to a vast range of international cultural organisations through a single click, with new guides being added regularly. They include several organisations in which Sung Tieu has shown her work, including MUMA, Caulfield East, Melbourne, Australia, Amant in Brooklyn, New York, and the Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin. There is also a dedicated guide to the German Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. On the guide to the German Pavilion, you can read a biography of Sung alongside her fellow exhibitor, the late Heinrike Naumann, and the curator of the pavilion, Kathleen Reinhardt. You can also see a range of installation photographs of the pavilion, including several images of Sung’s installation, which reflect the range of materials and concepts in her presentation. Also on Bloomberg Connects are dedicated guides to a number of other pavilions, including the British Pavilion, which in 2026 features a project by a former guest on A brush with… Lubaina Himid, as well as the overall guide to the Biennale Arte, which continues until 22 November.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Nowhere to Go: 68 NYC Parks Bathrooms Sit Closed — Some for More Than a Decade
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
A few blocks off the Belt Parkway in Gravesend, Brooklyn, a playground bathroom has been closed so long its doors no longer have handles.
A rusted latch box is bolted to the graffiti-tagged doors of the cube-like structure, which city records show has been shut since at least 2018 — three mayors ago. One local says she hasn’t seen it open in roughly 15 years.
“I come here often. I’ve never seen this bathroom open,” said Magdalena Maxine, who works at the Shoreview nursing home next to the playground.
The Gravesend bathroom is one of 68 Parks Department facilities currently closed, according to records obtained through a Freedom of Information Law request. Nine have been closed for at least nine years, the records show, and only three of those have a capital repair project scheduled, the data reveal.
Parks advocates and experts point to a combination of factors behind the city’s shuttered bathrooms, including chronic underfunding, state contracting laws that can complicate repairs and a lack of urgency from City Hall.
City Councilmember Ty Hankerson (D-Queens), who chairs the Council’s Committee on Parks and Recreation, said the closures are a serious inconvenience for parkgoers, particularly parents with young children.
“Bathrooms being closed during that time is not only a big inconvenience, but it forces people many times to unfortunately go outside,” Hankerson told The City Reporter.
A Parks Department spokesperson said Tuesday they needed more time to comment on repair plans for the long-shuttered washrooms.
Not all our news is this filthy.
Get all our headlines in your inbox every weekday morning.
The Cost of Comfort
Restoring just one of the city’s aging park bathrooms, known as comfort stations, can cost between $5 million and $7 million, a hefty price tag that could potentially consume an entire year’s $5 million capital allocation for an individual Council member.
In an effort to address the lack of public bathrooms, the administration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani in September began installing 17 modular public bathrooms across the five boroughs as part of a $4 million pilot aimed at expanding access to free facilities in busy public areas.
The units, selected through the city’s Economic Development Corporation, are open daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. and include accessible entrances, running-water sinks, flushing toilets, climate control and baby-changing stations. The company operating them, Throne Labs, handles cleaning and maintenance.
Unlike traditional park comfort stations, the self-contained units do not require connections to water, sewer or power infrastructure, allowing them to be installed more quickly and relocated as needed.
The rollout comes as the Mamdani administration also has struggled to develop a broader strategy for expanding public bathroom access.
The One Percent Solution
A citywide plan to build 2,120 public bathrooms by 2035 — doubling the existing network under legislation known as the Bathroom Bill — has been delayed, The City Reporter detailed in August.
At the time, Deputy Mayor Julia Kerson told City Council Speaker Julie Menin that she hopes to submit the plan by Nov. 1.
Parks advocates are eagerly awaiting that report and want the mayor to do more.
As a mayoral candidate, Mamdani promised to dedicate 1% of the city budget to the Parks Department. His initial proposed budget actually set aside just half of that.
The final budget allocated roughly $709 million to Parks, restoring some of the proposed cuts, but still several hundred million dollars short of the 1% target.
“For many, many years, parks have not been a priority for previous administrations,” Adam Ganser, executive director of New Yorkers for Parks, told The City Reporter.
A Parks Department spokesperson said the agency operates more than 700 restroom buildings containing over 1,400 individual restrooms, nearly all of which are open seven days a week, year-round, and free to the public.
A Parks Department spokesperson, Gregg McQueen, said the agency operates more than 700 restroom buildings, nearly all of which are open daily year-round, and that its in-house trades staff makes repairs when facilities go offline.
“Building and improving bathrooms is one of our priorities,” McQueen said, adding that the agency is on target to complete renovations or new construction at 14 restroom facilities this year.
The department is also working with the city’s Department of Design and Construction on a faster design-build process for new restrooms and participating in the administration’s modular bathroom pilot, he said.
But Parks does not have a dedicated budget for restroom repairs, according to the department. Instead, its in-house trades staff handles bathroom fixes as part of its broader building maintenance responsibilities.
Why So Expensive?
Meanwhile, the price tag for park bathroom construction has been climbing for years.
A 2019 investigation by THE CITY found that the typical Parks Department restroom — a no-frills rectangular structure with four walls, several toilets and a handful of sinks — cost taxpayers just under $3.6 million on average. That was nearly triple the $1.3 million average the agency spent in 2011.
It’s not just a money issue.
Adrian Benepe, the parks commissioner during the Bloomberg administration, said an antiquated state law has created a major obstacle for new construction.
Under New York’s Wicks Law, certain projects above specified cost thresholds must use separate contractors for plumbing, electrical, heating and general construction work. The law prohibits the use of a single general contractor.
Why hasn’t the law been adjusted? The city’s trade unions — who benefit from the bifurcated projects — have lobbied for years to keep it in place.
Park bathrooms face other hurdles.
Even relatively small bathroom renovations require reviews by community boards, the city’s Design Commission, lawyers, the comptroller’s office and budget officials.
“There are at least a dozen bureaucratic steps even a simple project has to go through,” Benepe said.
The city’s problems go beyond red tape.
Many of the park buildings housing public bathrooms date back nearly a century, to the Works Progress Administration era. They have aging plumbing and outdated fixtures.
Restoring them has also been hampered by a lack of dedicated capital funding, Benepe said. The department has historically had to seek money from individual City Council members and the borough presidents.
“I was once involved in a project to restore an old bathroom that was actually pre-1930s in Van Cortlandt Park,” Benepe recalled. “It took 10 years because of these delays and change orders and cost overruns.”
Benepe said the city needs to weigh whether some long-shuttered facilities are worth restoring or should be replaced altogether, particularly in areas with little foot traffic. In some cases, he said, buildings have been closed for “decades” and are effectively shells.
But he said the department cannot address the problem without more money, “hundreds of millions of dollars,” for both construction and ongoing maintenance.
And it’s not just repairs: The bathrooms need to be constantly cleaned and restocked with supplies.
In Gravesend, one mother said she couldn’t remember when the bathroom at Grady Playground was last open.
“We just go home to use the bathroom,” Gina Prokopets, who was at the play area with her three-year-old son, told The City Reporter last week.
“I don’t like to come here,” she said, noting the rundown equipment and alleged drug dealing in the area. “We usually choose a different location that’s further away.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Crash-Detecting System Rolling Out on More City Buses Navigating Crowded Streets
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Jose Martinez
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
The MTA is looking to significantly boost the number of buses in its fleet that alert drivers about would-be hazards while they’re behind the wheel.
With the number of collisions between buses and bicycles this year down 16% from the same time period in 2025, according to MTA data, the transportation authority plans to add up to 150 buses to the six equipped with collision-avoidance systems that it began testing in 2024.
Sensors outside the buses detect when a person or object is too close, with small panels to the left and right of the bus operator lighting up the outline of a pedestrian in orange or red lights, and occasionally beeping an added warning.
“This is a safety feature that we’ve piloted, it’s effective, our operators like it,” Frank Farrell, head of buses at the MTA, told The City Reporter. “They find it effective, so we want to move forward with putting it on more buses.”
The development is being rolled out as buses contend for space on the road with pedestrians and other forms of transportation.
“You got bicyclists, then you got the skateboarders and the motorcyclists and these battery-powered bikes,” said Donald Yates, a Transport Workers Union Local 100 vice president who represents Manhattan and Bronx bus drivers. “And the bus operator has to avoid all of it.”
To date, the MTA has put the safety devices to the test on just six buses, all from the Michael J. Quill Bus Depot in Manhattan and the Far Rockaway Depot in Queens. The authority last month issued a solicitation for a five-year contract to retrofit between 100 and 150 additional buses out of a fleet of close to 6,000 by sometime next year. Future bus orders could also come equipped with collision-detection systems.
The contract solicitation carries an estimated range of $1 million to $5 million and was issued after what MTA records describe as the “successful outcome” of a trial run that bus operators signed off on after Yates said they initially noted the sensors “didn’t pick up everything” during early testing phases.
“It’s really an obstacle course out here,” Yates said, adding that bus operators face a “shortening of the real estate we have to operate with” from the other forms of transportation on the road.
According to the MTA, buses and bicycles have collided 61 times so far in 2026, 26 fewer than during the same period in 2025, while there have been 84 physical contacts with pedestrians, one fewer than last year.
Since 2019, transit agency numbers show 275 instances of buses coming into contact with increasingly popular forms of micromobility.
The number of bus and micromobility vehicle collisions peaked at 65 in 2023, MTA numbers reveal, including 47 with e-scooters and 18 with e-bikes. So far this year, buses have collided 24 times with e-scooters or e-bikes, while there were 39 contacts in all of 2025.
Under Mayor Zohran Mamdani, City Hall has put the installation of bike lanes into high gear and micromobility has boomed, as well. For all of 2019, there were just four collisions involving e-scooters or e-bikes, according to MTA numbers.
“We definitely welcome [a collision-avoidance system] because it has everything to do with safety,” Yates said. “We want to embrace anything that avoids collisions, especially pedestrian collisions.”
The move to expand the use of sensors on buses also drew praise from Transportation Alternatives, which advocates on behalf of cyclists and pedestrians.
“Glad to see them scaling up a proven safety technology,” said Ben Furnas, the group’s executive director.
Buses on which the collision avoidance devices would be installed would also be equipped with an “Intelligent Pedestrian Turn Warning” system that has been in use for more than a decade on approximately 3,000 buses.
The turn-warning system essentially puts a voice on buses, with pedestrians hearing a warning at intersections. But the next-generation setup is designed to be slightly less vocal.
“This is a bit smarter where it only alerts when there is someone in the area,” Farrell said. “If there is nobody or any object or anything out there that could potentially come into contact, the bus will not put out that audible.”
More than 4,000 bus operators are also trained annually on simulators that are designed to mimic the conditions and challenges of New York City streets.
“Any action we can take to provide safer service and safe operation of our buses, we always look for,” Farrell said.
