https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Art Basel Qatar releases 2027 exhibitor list as renewed threat of war looms over Gulf
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Art Basel Qatar (ABQ), the Qatari state's finely orchestrated selling event in partnership with the Swiss fair giant, today announced the exhibitor list for its second edition, which will take place across the M7 and Doha Design District venues from 28 to 30 January 2027 (VIP preview days 26-27 January).
Eighty-two galleries plan to take part, a slight decrease from the 87 that showed in the inaugural edition. Among them are Sylvia Kouvali (London, Piraeus) bringing the kinetic art pioneer Liliane Lijn, and Gagosian, which will offer works by the art-world prankster Maurizio Catellan. Like the inaugural edition, almost half of participating galleries operate spaces in the Menasa (Middle East, North Africa and South Asia) region, including Marfa’ Projects from Beirut, whose stand will feature the Lebanese artist Stéphanie Saadé, and India’s Nature Morte, presenting the architecturally minded sculptor Ayesha Singh.
Each presentation will respond to the theme of “between”, which was chosen by the fair’s artistic director, the Iraqi curator Wassan Al-Khudhairi, who was the founding director of Doha’s Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art from 2007-12. She takes the reins from Wael Shawky, who curated the inaugural edition.
Who's returning—and who isn't
Exhibitor turnover is high from last year’s edition, with 35 galleries—or around 40%—not returning, including global dealerships like Hauser & Wirth, Pace, Almine Rech and Victoria Miro, as well as prominent regional spaces such as Gallery Isabelle from Dubai. Filling their places are 30 newcomers: Isla Flotante (Buenos Aires, São Paulo), Pilar Corrias (London) and Silverlens (Manila, New York) are among those taking part for the first time.
A full list of galleries exhibiting at Art Basel Qatar 2027—plus those not returning—can be found at the end of this article.
Vincenzo De Bellis, Art Basel’s global director of fairs, tells The Art Newspaper the high turnover is typical of ABQ’s format. “Across our global fairs, we see greater turnover in the sectors that are theme-led, and in Qatar that approach extends to the fair as a whole. Selection is closely tied to how galleries’ proposed solo presentations respond to each edition’s theme, so it is natural for the exhibitor list to change from year to year.”
Gallerists in the selection committee are: Lorenzo Fischi, Galleria Continua; Gordon VeneKlasen, VeneKlasen Gallery; Daniela Gareh, White Cube; Shireen Gandhy, Chemould Prescott Road; Sunny Rahbar, The Third Line; and Mohammed Hafiz, Athr.
Contingency plans
Like its competitors, Art Basel does not discuss motivations behind individual exhibitor applications, including whether some prospective applicants may have pulled out due to geopolitical tensions in the Arabian Gulf. Nonetheless, visitors planning their trip to Qatar next year will certainly be conscious of renewed bombardment in neighbouring Saudi Arabia earlier this month, and looming threats of the US and Israel resuming war with Iran. In late February, a few weeks after the conclusion of the first Art Basel Qatar, Iran launched missiles into Qatar, injuring 16 people, according to Qatari authorities at the time, and causing major disruptions to its airspace.
As a contingency plan, should the fair be postponed or considerably altered due to such circumstances, exhibitors will receive a refund of their participation fee or have the option to defer their participation to the following edition, currently planned for January 2028. Nonetheless, any last-minute drop outs will be subject to a standard penalty fee, similar to other Art Basel fairs.
While this uncertainty might deter some galleries, others will likely be incentivised by the unusually generous level of support provided to exhibitors via Art Basel's partnership with Qatar Sports Investments (QSI) and QC+, the commercial branch of Qatar Museums. This funds customs clearance, in-country transportation, consolidated storage and installation services, hotel accommodation for up to two staff members, and travel and hotel costs for exhibiting artists. In addition, from the 2027 edition Art Basel Qatar will also cover 50% of outbound shipping costs for unsold works, up to a maximum of $20,000 per gallery, further mitigating costs and risks for galleries.
Art Basel is also deepening its roots in Qatar by launching a year-round programme there to develop the country’s art market, including masterclasses and workshops designed to foster new collectors. "Our ambition extends well beyond the fair week: through our new year-round programme, we aim to deepen collector engagement between editions and contribute to the sustained growth of the regional art market," Art Basel's chief executive Noah Horowitz says in a statement.
Visitors to the second edition of ABQ will also get a chance to see the inaugural Rubaiya, a quadrennial exhibition in Doha, that will bring together more than 120 artists, including Saodat Ismailova and Rirkrit Tiravanija.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Fake or Fortune art historian donates major Anglo-Indian art collection to Tate
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
A UK collector has donated a significant collection of 50 works by artists who lived and worked in India during the 18th and 19th centuries to the Tate in London. The collection, given by the UK art historian Charles Greig, includes works by Indian artists, such as Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan, and European artists, including Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, along with British figures such as Thomas Daniell and William Daniell.
The works throw light on a “period of profound cultural, social and political change brought about by British colonialism in South Asia” says a Tate statement. Key pieces donated include three watercolours by Sita Ram who was instrumental in creating works known as “Company paintings”, watercolours created in a European style for foreign patrons. The British Library in London has a large collection of watercolours by Ram.
Greig says in a statement: “Most of the works were made in the vanished world before photography and they provide us with a visual record of our rich shared history from about 1770. Assembling this collection has been my life’s primary passion, but at no stage did I ever see myself as other than a temporary steward.”
Asked why Greig opted for Tate, a spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper: “Tate has long held a few key paintings related to Anglo-Indian history of the period, including Zoffany’s Colonel Mordant’s Cock Match (around 1784) and Indian landscapes by Thomas Daniell and William Hodges”. Greig recently appeared in an episode of the television series Fake or Fortune?, in which he assessed a portrait of an Indian woman by the 18th-century Scottish artist Katherine Read.
A free display of the works drawn from the Greig collection is due to open at Tate Britain in 2028.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: New Yorkers Want to Play Ball. The Toughest Game is Getting a Field.
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Haidee Chu, Carol Chen, Stephen Lurie | The Pudding, and Matt Daniels | The Pudding
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
When the playground at St. Vartan Park closed for renovations this spring, parents in Murray Hill rallied around one question: Where will the children go to play?
“We thought, well, at least we have the field next to it,” said Rebecca Webber, a 51-year-old mother from the neighborhood. “And every evening we would get sort of ushered off the field by an organization that had a permit.”
Across the East River, at Pier 5 of Brooklyn Bridge Park, a group of eight high school soccer players filmed a public plea addressed to Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Instagram.
“Mamdani! Three fields, three permits, this is crazy,” they said. “We just want to play and now we have to go home. … We propose that one field should be open at all times!”
At New York City’s hundreds of public ballfields and soccer pitches, casual pick-up players are feeling the squeeze as demand surges for organized games, practices and sports clinics. But even those with the persistence and resources to score a permit don’t feel like winners. League and club operators say they, too, are struggling to get enough field time as interest in recreational sports explodes.
The Parks Department permitted 48% more daily reservations for organized sports on public athletic fields in 2025 than a decade ago, according to public and internal Parks Department permit data obtained and analyzed by The City Reporter and data visualization site The Pudding. Nearly 1,850 organizations secured permits — roughly 310 more than in 2015.
The proliferation of recreational leagues and sports clinics has at times pitted older neighborhood teams against new entrants in a struggle for field time. In East Williamsburg, for example, longtime residents who’d been playing softball at Sternberg Park for five decades were surprised to learn last year that one of their weeknight league permits had been denied to make space for another group.
“Before, no one wanted this park. It was in bad conditions,” said Hector Perez, who moved to the neighborhood from Puerto Rico as a kid and now plays in the 55-and-up Los Abuelos league. In 2021, the Parks Department unveiled a new artificial turf field at Sternberg Park. That same year, Williamsburg ranked second citywide for new housing construction over the previous decade.
“And now, after the neighborhood’s been gentrified, everybody wants to play here,” he continued. “But we’ve been here the longest.”
On weekends, the park still throngs with cheers as the old-timers compete against one another, while free food is laid out for the crowd ringing the field, folding chairs galore.
“We’ve kept the spirit of baseball going — to not forget our culture — because this is all gentrified, and this is the little bit that we have left,” Perez said.
But amid the growing competition for fields, even the big leagues have struggled with permitting.
“It remains the single most frustrating aspect of this job,” said Tarek Pertew, founder and CEO of NYC Footy, the largest adult recreational soccer league and for-profit permit holder in the city.
It took Pertew three years to score a permit at Brooklyn Bridge Park when he started out in 2010, then another five years to break into Manhattan. Sixteen years later, Pertew said he’s still waiting on McCarren Park in Greenpoint, home to a football field and three baseball diamonds. His waitlist of would-be teams, in the meantime, continues to grow.
“There’s so much demand for this simple service,” Pertew continued. “And we can’t even come close to fulfilling that demand because of these restrictions.”
A Crowded Field
According to Parks Department data, the number of permitted field reservations has grown year over year at least since 2014 — until 2020, when the COVID pandemic forced New Yorkers indoors and demand plunged.
But as coronavirus restrictions began to loosen, permitted field usage didn’t just bounce back. It boomed.
Field usage continued to reach new highs, with 223,860 permitted reservations issued in 2025.
“COVID changed everything,” said Pertew, whose recreational soccer league service exploded with demand overnight. “There was this very natural biological reaction for people that wanted a physical and mental outlet with a social backdrop … It was the perfect combination of what people needed coming out of COVID.”
It was youth sports, however, that accounted for the majority of the permitted field usage during this time. Around 75% of all permitted field reservations every year since COVID, in fact, were issued for youth sports — noticeably more than the roughly 55% from a decade ago.
“In 2020, we started picking up momentum, and we started to see, ‘OK, people value it,’” Sherard Sullivan, 41, said on a recent afternoon at Jesse Owens Playground in Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant, where teenagers scrimmaged on one side of the soccer field and parents played with their toddlers on the other. A former teacher, Sullivan founded the non-profit S.S. Soccer Academy in 2015 to serve children from three to 14. “More people aligned with our vision.”
As popularity grew, so did the competition. Sometime around 2023, Sullivan recalled, his permit renewal at Jesse Owens, where he’d been running his program for three years, was denied. His academy’s field time was instead granted to a soccer club based in Williamsburg, he recalled.
“That was one of the hardest nights I ever had in my life. I couldn’t sleep,” said Sullivan. He’d made a commitment to his young athletes that he’d get them college-ready, he said, reminiscing on the way soccer had brought him from his home country of Trinidad and Tobago to New York City, where he played in college.
He continued: “I was really devastated, because all I thought about was all the different kids: What am I gonna tell them? What am I gonna do for them? I hit the ground running and luckily it was rectified.”
In 2024, the Parks Department modified permitting rules to give non-profit organizations like Sullivan’s priority. And youth groups, as is always the case, are prioritized over adults.
But that did little to help the Harlem Jets, a non-profit that has been serving youths for more than two decades.
“We live in Harlem. We’re from Harlem, but we’re forced to come to Randall’s Island because the fields in Harlem were being utilized by other people,” its founder and CEO, Jamel Wright, told The City Reporter while coaching football on the island. “We use any field we can get that we can get on, to be perfectly honest … There’s just a lot of utilization that needs to happen with limited options.”
Wright has always had trouble securing enough field time in Harlem, he said — even after the city unveiled a new artificial turf field last year at General Charles Young Playground.
“That’s part of why we purchased our own bus, so that our kids wouldn’t necessarily have to take the M35 bus,” Wright added. “This team has 30-something children on it. But what do you see here? Maybe 15, 20. That’s because they’re finding it to be problematic to get them from over there, over the bridge, to over here.”
Wright proposed a solution: The city, he suggested, should reserve field space for neighborhood youths during the afterschool hours until the early evening.
“After 8 p.m. every kid off the field — and grown-ups can play until they fall asleep,” he said.
Ken Conyers, director of citywide athletic permits for the Parks Department, said the agency has continued to refine its permitting systems and its scheduling practices to make sure facilities are used “fairly and efficiently.”
“As demand for permits has grown, we’ve worked hard to keep pace,” Conyers said. “Our goal is to make sure everyone who wants to take part in athletics and other permitted activities has a place to do so, and we’ll continue working with our communities to meet that need.”
Let There Be Light
As the fall yields to winter, however, shorter days will begin to eat into available field time.
That’s because just 5% of the city’s 5,850-something active athletic facilities are equipped with lights, according to Parks Department data.
This poses additional headaches especially for soccer, football and lacrosse organizers. These “rectangular ballfield” sports, as the Parks Department calls them, are prioritized in the fall and winter, as opposed to diamond sports like baseball, softball and cricket, which take precedence in the spring and summer.
“Once daylight loss pushes sunset earlier than 6:00 p.m., fields become effectively unusable for working adults unless they are lit,” Pertew, who operates NYC Footy, wrote in a letter to Parks Commissioner Tricia Shimamura in April.
In the letter, Pertew also urged the city to introduce temporary lighting to expand field access, while investing in permanent lighting infrastructure in areas where adult recreational sport is most in demand.
Pertew’s for-profit organization stands to benefit financially from increased field access, to be sure. By his estimate, however, one single lit field could add roughly 1,200 hours of play each year — offering more field time for not just NYC Footy, but to all park users.
Already, the Mamdani administration has experimented with the idea in partnership with NYC Footy over the summer, as the World Cup fueled fervor for soccer. For a little more than a month, the city kept the lights on overnight at one field in every borough, opening them up for pick-up play from 10:30 p.m. through 8 a.m. for adults.
Parks Commissioner Shimamura herself pointed to the pilot as a success when The City Reporter asked in the late summer how her department can make it easier for New Yorkers to access fields and permits.
“I don’t think we’ve exhausted all of the low-hanging fruit to create more access,” she said. “In the long term, we need more fields and more lights.”
The Parks Department extended the pilot earlier this month, granting one soccer field in each of the five boroughs extended night lights until 2 a.m.
Pertew’s attention, meanwhile, is now focused on St. Vartan Park in Midtown East, where parents, children and sports organizations alike feel squeezed for play time since the playground closure.
While the City Council already voted last year to fully fund the installation of field lights on the multipurpose field there, Pertew is now offering to cover the bill for temporary lighting while the upgrades are pending, he said, so that field access can be expanded for everyone in the neighborhood — so long as Footy can be permitted to play on the field for at least one day each week to cover the cost.
Youth sports could take over in the after-school hours till sunset, he envisioned, followed by community open field time, and adult leagues in the evening.
“If you do that, you are going to drastically minimize the complaints in the conflict because youth is benefitting, community’s benefitting, and the adults get more time as well,” Pertew said. “That is what lights can do.”
Webber, the Murray Hill parent, has missed the daily kids’ meetup at their local playground in the meantime — squirt gun fights and all, she said. She spent the summer exploring other playgrounds in the neighborhood with her son, who still occasionally plays pick-up with his friends at the St. Vartan field.
The children would occasionally sit along the sidelines while the adults played, she said, choosing a player to root for as though they were watching a professional match.
“It’s really cute, so I wouldn’t want to lose it entirely,” Webber said. “I think it’s just about balance, and it’s a really hard question: Who should get the park when and who should get it most, and how do we allocate this?”
This story was reported by Haidee Chu and Carol Chen of The City Reporter, based on original research and data analysis by Stephen Lurie and Matt Daniels of The Pudding. Katie Honan contributed.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: A Freedom of Information ‘Christmas Present’ Remains Unopened as City Delays Rollout
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Katie Honan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
The city is dragging its feet on a requirement for all city agencies to upload records requests and data to an online public portal, further delaying transparency from city agencies, good-government advocates said.
The bill, which was passed in the City Council last November, requires every municipal agency to opt into the city’s Open Records portal for data requests.
The updated bill formally requires every agency to participate in the portal and now will include Freedom of Information requests made to the City Council and the five borough presidents’ offices.
The law would make it easier to file data requests and provide more transparency on delays. Agencies would be required to upload responses within a certain time frame, allowing the requestor — oftentimes journalists — 14 days to publish a story without it being shared widely, according to Rachael Fauss, the senior policy advisor at the nonprofit Reinvent Albany.
She and other good-government advocates helped craft the bill and are now concerned because a report on its implementation due in June has still not been released.
“The law would absolutely put us on better footing to actually monitor the agencies and see what they’re actually doing on FOIL,” she said.
The bill, introduced by Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer, lapsed into law on Dec. 25, 2025 — “a Christmas present for the advocates who fought for it,” Fauss joked.
“If you get every agency on the open records portal to start proactively releasing records, you can get some better data about what the actual problems are,” she said.
“How do you know what the problems are if nobody’s looking systematically at them at the city level?”
‘Nothing’s Happening’
A spokesperson for the Department of Records and Information Services, Kenneth Cobb, said they planned to release the plan to Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Speaker Julie Menin in mid-November, but did not answer a question about its delay.
Brewer told The City Reporter the Council planned to hold a hearing on the law’s delay in January.
“Nothing’s happening,” she said of the initiatives the bill planned. She said she thought the Mamdani administration “should be better.”
New York City government is notoriously slow around Freedom of Information Law requests, often delaying for years before releasing information.
A 2025 analysis from Reinvent Albany found that the city government receives around 170,000 FOIL requests a year, and 16% were still open a year later. Data from the existing Open Records portal showed that response times were slowing, which they blamed on staffing issues.
Journalists often rely on the Freedom of Information Law to obtain schedules, emails, renderings, and any other data to inform their reporting — but the delays can often render the data useless once it finally arrives.
And it also can keep vital information from the public.
In September 2019, The City Reporter requested data and outside contracts related to a 911 system upgrade from the city’s technology agency.
Since then, the city’s Office of Technology and Innovation has extended the deadline 60 times. The latest projected response date is Dec. 1 of this year.
Noel Hidalgo, the executive director of BetaNYC, an open government advocacy group, said this law would ideally give everyone a better sense of how the city works.
“We’re in a moment in time where government information is one of the few things that you can actually trust,” he said. “FOIL is our last recourse in regard to transparency and operation.”

Marian Goodman Gallery in New York has hired curator Ebony L. Haynes as senior director, global head of curatorial affairs. Haynes, who will join the gallery in late November, is the first person to occupy the newly created role. She arrives from David Zwirner, where she is global head of curatorial projects. In 2020 Haynes was tapped by Zwirner to create and oversee TriBeCa outpost 52 Walker. Run by an all-Black staff, the space launched in 2021, and held seventeen exhibitions before undergoing a name change to David Zwirner Tribeca this past summer. Among the artists given solo shows at 52 Walker during its run were Sara Cwynar, Nicole Eisenman, Nikita Gale, Arthur Jafa, Bob Thompson, and Kandis Williams.
Before joining Zwirner, Haynes, who cocurated the 2024 Triennial at MOCA Toronto, was curator for the inaugural Fine Arts MFA exhibition for first-year students at the Rhode Island School of Design, Providence, and visiting curator and critic at the Yale School of Art in the Painting and Printmaking program. She also runs Black Art Sessions, an online “school” offering free professional practice classes to Black students around the world.
Marian Goodman also announced Rose Lord and Junette Teng as its new co-presidents. The pair will shape the gallery’s strategic direction and oversee its management team, which includes Haynes. Emily-Jane Kirwan, managing partner and head of sales, will leave the gallery to focus on cultural philanthropy after a fifteen-year tenure.
“Ebony is a natural fit for the Gallery,” said Teng in a statement. “She brings a strong curatorial vision, intellectual rigor, and deep engagement with artists, which aligns with our approach. Her appointment also reflects where we want to go next: expanding the ways we support our artists, creating new contexts for their work, and bringing a new perspective to our program.”
Asked by Artnews about her reasons for joining Goodman, Haynes was succinct. “How do I say this?” she said. “It’s Marian Goodman.”

https://gothamist.com/news/lithium-ion-b.title: Lithium-ion battery caused Bronx fire that killed boy, FDNY says
https://gothamist.com/news/lithium-ion-b.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/lithium-ion-b.text:
An e-bike’s lithium-ion battery caused a Bronx apartment fire that killed a boy and critically injured four other people early Wednesday, FDNY officials said.
Firefighters found an e-bike in the kitchen near the entrance of an 11th-floor apartment at the Patterson Houses, a public housing complex in Mott Haven, officials said. The blaze began around 12:50 a.m. and spread quickly throughout the home, according to officials.
“It was placed in a spot in the kitchen that made it impossible for the residents to leave safely,” Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said at a press conference Wednesday. “ We know lithium-ion batteries are everywhere, and we know how valuable they are to people's livelihoods, so we need to remind New Yorkers how to use them safely.”
FDNY officials said firefighters forced the apartment door open, then searched the apartment for victims before working to control the fire. They found one person immediately behind the door, then crawled past the flames to search for and rescue the rest of the occupants, according to officials.
All five people were rushed to a nearby hospital, where a the boy was pronounced dead. Officials have estimated his age at 10 or 11, but the FDNY told Gothamist the boy's exact age has not yet been confirmed.
The four other occupants, including two teenagers, remain in critical condition, officials said.
“I ask New Yorkers to join me in sending our deepest condolences to the family of the child who passed away, and in praying for a full and quick recovery for those who are currently battling to survive,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at the Wednesday press conference.
According to FDNY data, lithium-ion batteries have caused more than 400 fires across the city this year, resulting in 74 injuries and six deaths. That's compared to 292 fires last year, which caused 51 injuries, and just one death.
“Lithium-ion battery fires are extremely dangerous because they spread fast and ferociously,” Bonsignore said. “The battery cells go into thermal runaway, which makes a small fire turn into a very big fire very, very quickly.”
Bonsignore said lithium-ion batteries used to power micromobility devices should be charged and stored outside when possible. She said the devices should never block exits, doors or windows, and the batteries should never be charged when people are sleeping or not in the room. She also said New Yorkers should only buy batteries certified by national safety testing organizations like UL, and advised against using leaking, damaged or smoking batteries.
Lisa Bova-Hyatt, CEO of the New York City Housing Authority, said NYCHA is working to relocate and support the affected families and is assessing needed repairs in the apartment and the building.
NYCHA had previously proposed an e-bike ban at its complexes in 2022, but rescinded the proposal and instead implemented rules for keeping e-bikes in apartments after pushback from tenants and delivery riders. The rules state that residents may only charge one lithium-ion battery or device at a time, and an adult must be present and awake while it’s charging. The device must also be placed more than 5 feet from a heating source and must not block any entryways, according to the rules.
This story has been revised based on updated information from emergency officials.

Sculptor Ursula von Rydingsvard, known for her craggy, majestic wood forms carved from cedar, died at her home in New York on October 27 of Alzheimer’s disease. She was eighty-four. Over a career spanning five decades, von Rydingsvard transformed humble four-by-four chunks of wood into towering shapes whose puzzling bumps and hollows gave them the aura of ancient living beings. So committed was she to cedar that she eventually developed an allergy to it; she refused to abandon the material, instead working in a full protective suit. For von Rydingsvard, work was necessary “to survive,” she said in a 2019 interview, “because it’s a place to put my pain, my sadness.”
Ursula von Rydingsvard was born Ursula Karoliszyn, the fifth of seven children, in Deentsen, Germany, on July 26, 1942. The daughter of Polish and Ukrainian parents, she spent the early years of her life in displaced persons camps. The experience would profoundly shape her practice. “We stayed in barracks of raw wooden floors, raw wooden walls, and raw wooden ceilings,” she told Art21 in 2007. “Somewhere in my blood, I’m dipping into that source.”
When she was eight, the Karoliszyns immigrated to Plainville, Connecticut, where her father farmed and took on factory work, and her mother worked as a barmaid. At first, young Ursula seemed destined to follow in her mother’s footsteps, taking a job in the same tavern. “I did everything conscientiously,” she told Judith Richards in a 2011 oral-history interview for the Archives of American Art. “And I say that with regret. I wish I could have blown—the grid, the fenced-in psyche. But I am trying to still blow it, through my work.”
Eager to escape small-town life, she attended first the University of New Hampshire and then the University of Miami, studying painting and drawing. In 1969, she moved to California with her husband, Milton von Rydingsvard, who was pursuing a medical residency there. Four years later, he suffered a mental breakdown, and the pair divorced. Von Rydingsvard moved to New York with her young daughter and enrolled in Columbia University, where she earned her MFA. “I just felt like that was a place where my mind would finally have a chance,” she told Richards.
Just before arriving at the school, von Rydingsvard had turned from paper and canvas to sewn forms, having increasingly become interested in sculpture owing to its tactile nature. “You can’t grab a painting,” she told Artsy’s Tess Thackara in 2018. While at Columbia, she experimented with steel, but found the material too cold and unforgiving. Given some four-by-four cedar beams by painter Michael Mulhern, a classmate, she first used them to prop up other materials but soon found herself deeply attracted to the wood. “The cedar is like butter,” she told Even magazine in 2018. “It yields so easily; it doesn’t fight you.”
Using a pencil, von Rydingsvard marked the wooden slabs, then cut them with a handsaw, stacking, gluing, and chiseling them into monumental, glitching forms. The sculptures were frequently stained with graphite or chalk dust, whose force of presence was comparable to that of cliff or cave, capable of stunning the viewer into silence. A 1988 exhibition at New York’s Exit Art proved pivotal, with the Metropolitan Museum of Art purchasing Untitled (Seven Mountains), 1986–88, and the Brooklyn Museum acquiring Umarles (You Went and Died), 1987–88. By 1992, she had been the subject of a ten-year retrospective at Storm King Art Center in New York’s Hudson Valley, and been taken on by Galerie Lelong, which would represent her for the rest of her life.
“Von Rydingsvard uses wood to sensualize the material and to evoke feelings, textures, and things that seem impossibly remote from wood itself,” wrote Zachary Fine in a 2019 issue of Artforum. “By combining and rearranging fixed units of cedar to produce this range of evocations and effects, [she] effectively turns the units into words and wood into language.”
She continued to express herself in that same language throughout the ensuing decades. An emblematic recent work is “All the Children I Never Had,” 2018–23, which suggests a trio of escarpments marching resolutely forward despite some invisible weight dragging them down. Von Rydingsvard ultimately expanded her practice to include materials such as resin and bronze. The latter enduring material appeared in several public commissions, including the nineteen-foot-high Ona, 2013, outside Barclays Center in Brooklyn.
Von Rydingsvard earned numerous accolades over the course of her career, including a lifetime achievement award from the International Sculpture Center as well as a Joan Mitchell Award, an Academy Award from the American Academy of Arts and Letters, and fellowships from the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts. Her work is held in the collections of numerous major institutions, including the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City, Missouri; the Art Institute of Chicago; and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Whitney Museum of American Art, all in New York.
Von Rydingsvard’s second husband, Nobel Prize-winning neuroscientist Paul Greengard, died in 2019; her daughter, Ursula Anne von Rydingsvard, died in 2022. She is survived by two siblings, three grandchildren, and three step-grandchildren.
“I feel completely different in the world where I make my art,” she told the Creative Independent in 2018. “It’s so clear to me that this is what I was born to do.”

On elections day next week, ballots in Philadelphia will include a question to formalize the office for local arts and culture—Creative Philadelphia—into a permanent part of the city’s government.
The ballot’s Question 2 asks, “Shall the Philadelphia Home Rule Charter be amended to establish and define the functions of Creative Philadelphia, an office headed by the Chief Cultural Officer to promote the City’s arts, culture, and creative economy sector?”
Currently, Creative Philadelphia exists by way of an executive order. According to Broad Street Review, a creative office was established in 1986 under Mayor Wilson Goode, but was subsequently shuttered in 2004 by Mayor John Street. Michael Nutter, his successor, re-established the office, only to have his own successor, Jim Kenney, propose eliminating it in 2020 due to budget constraints. Instead, Kenney reduced its capacity and moved it under the Managing Director’s Office.
In 2024, Mayor Cherelle Parker rebranded the Office of Arts, Culture, and the Creative Economy as Creative Philadelphia, and turned its directorship into a cabinet position with a seat at the mayor’s table. Currently, that position is held by Valerie Gay.
Gay has been instrumental in getting Question 2 on the ballot. “It was a moral obligation for us to try to become permanent instead of starting over from scratch with every mayor,” she told Broad Street Review.
The measure, proposed by Councilmember Isaiah Thomas, would also allow the office to grow its staff from ten to fifteen. The Committee of Seventy, a nonpartisan civic leadership organization based in Philadelphia, reports that the city’s art community has a large economic impact but that public support for the arts is low. The city recently slashed its funding for the Philadelphia Cultural Fund from $5 million annually to $3.5 million.
“We’re part of civic infrastructure, just like other things,” Gay said. Without public funding, “only the folks who are able to pay should have access to arts and culture … If only the rich people can pay for art, what kind of society would we be?”

https://hyperallergic.com/documenta-16-n.title: Documenta 16 Names Four New Curatorial Team Members
https://hyperallergic.com/documenta-16-n.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/documenta-16-n.text:
Documenta 16 Names Four New Curatorial Team Members
The embattled German exhibition's latest appointments, artist Catherine Opie wins a Yale University award, and Dallas Art Fair partners with … a university?
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Documenta Appoints New Curatorial Team Members
Less than eight months away from the 16th edition of Documenta, the German contemporary arts festival has appointed four new curatorial team members: artist and musician Raven Chacon will serve as curator-at-Large, and Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus, and Noam Segal will be curatorial advisors.
The upcoming iteration, opening on June 12 in Kassel, promises to offer a space for “study, experimentation, and awakening, where artists hold right to expression alongside their artistic creation.” But artists and free speech advocates have argued that this stated mission jars with Documenta’s adoption of a controversial definition of antisemitism that includes criticism of Israel, raising serious questions about creative freedom. In a recent interview with the German newspaper Die Zeit, Artistic Director Naomi Beckwith revealed that some artists have already declined to participate in Documenta 16 over Germany's support of Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Chacon, Bonsu, Junghaus, and Segal will join Beckwith and the core curatorial team for the 16th edition — Carla Acevedo-Yates, Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, and Xiaoyu Weng — to help shape the program's artistic vision.

https://gothamist.com/news/15-year-old-b.title: 15-year-old Bronx boy fatally shot while walking to school, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/15-year-old-b.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/15-year-old-b.text:
A 15-year-old boy was shot and killed on his way to school in the Bronx on Thursday morning, police said.
The shooting happened around 9:30 a.m. near East 171st Street and Crotona Place, near Crotona Park, according to an NYPD spokesperson.
Officers who responded found the boy shot once in the abdomen and drove him in their patrol car to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.
Police later identified the boy as Javits Frimpong.
Authorities did not immediately describe any suspects, or say how many there were. Police have not said what led to the shooting.
According to the boy’s father, Thomas Frimpong, Javits was on his way to school at DreamYard Preparatory School.
Frimpong, 60, said the school called him Thursday morning to say Javits was not at school. Soon after, he said, the principal called to tell him his son had been shot.
“It’s not easy for me,” he said. “I’m here with him alone.”
Frimpong said he moved to New York from Ghana in 2000, while his son followed him here last year to live with him.
Whenever Frimpong came home, he said, Javits would come downstairs to open the door for him.
He described his son as a reserved boy who came home from school and stayed inside playing games on his phone.
"My son is always quiet, always," he said.
A few days before the shooting, two students fought with Javits at school and both were suspended, Frimpong said. He said the school told him his son was not to blame.
"I thought that was all," he said.
Frimpong said he called Javits' mother in Ghana to tell her what had happened. She and other relatives were "crying, crying, crying," he said.
Frimpong said police had not told him whether they had any suspects.
Relatives are on their way, he said, and the family will decide what comes next.
Neighbor Sherric Philips, 39, said she heard two shots in the morning.
“It was a pow pow,” she said. “It woke me up.”
The killing comes as shootings and murders are down this year in the 42nd Precinct, which covers the area. There have been 17 shootings in the precinct so far this year, compared with 27 last year at this time, according to NYPD data.
This is a developing story and has been updated with new information.

https://hyperallergic.com/how-edouard-ma.title: How Édouard Manet's Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity
https://hyperallergic.com/how-edouard-ma.author: Rebecca Schiffman
https://hyperallergic.com/how-edouard-ma.text:
How Édouard Manet's Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity
Long associated with witchcraft and bad luck, the black feline became an emblem of artistic rebellion and urban life in 19th-century Paris.
Every Halloween, black cats return as emblems of witchcraft, bad luck, and the supernatural. Their sinister reputations stretch back centuries: starting in the Middle Ages, people associated cats with heresy and sexual transgression, and their perceived affinity with witches intensified during the trials of Elizabeth Francis and Agnes Waterhouse and their cat Sathan between 1565-1579.
But after the Enlightenment, 19th-century French artists and writers began to reclaim the mysterious and devilish qualities foisted onto felines as desirable. Alongside a new bourgeois pet-keeping culture, where caring for animals became associated with progress and enlightenment, bohemian artists and intellectuals began incorporating black cats into their work. The black cat became a symbol of independence and nonconformity, reflecting changing attitudes toward individualism and self-expression amid industrialization and urbanization. French writer and diplomat François-René de Chateaubriand described the cat’s modern independence favorably, stating, “What I like about the cat is his character, independent and almost heartlessness […] The cat lives alone, he has no need of society.” These inherited qualities of eroticism and defiance also became synonymous with the emerging language of modern art.
No painting or artist makes this transformation more apparent than Édouard Manet’s “Olympia” (1863). Historians like T.J. Clark have long hailed it as a “founding monument of modern art,” updating Titian’s “Venus of Urbino” (1534) with a stark depiction of a contemporary prostitute, her Black maid, and a black cat. The work provoked outrage at the Paris Salon in 1865: its subject matter, combined with flattened forms, bold color contrasts, and use of black, clearly rejected academic conventions. Critics latched onto the wiry black cat, whose arched back and luminous eyes seemed to embody the painting’s perceived vulgarity by showing what Olympia’s hand covered.

https://hyperallergic.com/this-years-gay.title: This Year's Gay Halloween Celebrates Women's Rights and Wrongs
https://hyperallergic.com/this-years-gay.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/this-years-gay.text:
This Year's Gay Halloween Celebrates Women's Rights and Wrongs
From the Kelly Clarkson's mechanical bird fiasco to Carrie Bradshaw's Dior newsprint dress, Gay Halloween speaks to the staying power of women's iconic media moments.
With everything that's happened in the 1,000+ lifetimes jammed into 2026, I think we've all been waiting for Gay Halloween to rehash the year in popular culture. A recently named phenomenon for the chronically online, Gay Halloween is best described as the costume-based valorization of specific media moments, however iconic, niche, or overlooked they may be.
Against the grain of sexy cat costumes and run-of-the-mill superheroes, those blessed with ✨ the vision ✨ devote their resources and talents to fashioning a high-commitment outfit about some bullshit like the hyperpigmentation meme or the disco testicles stage prop from Kacey Musgraves's concert tour.
This year, I've noticed that a majority of Gay Halloween costumes pay homage to the real and fictional women carrying pop culture on their backs. That's not to say that there haven't been hat tips to the cyclosporiasis outbreak from Taylor Farms's lettuce, the hidden death rumors that emerged from Mitch McConnell's multi-week disappearance, or other 2026 happenings that were so absurd they became memes.
I'm just saying that for the most part, this year's Gay Halloween appears to be heavily influenced by the staying power of iconic women and their enduring impact across fashion history, viral interview clips, cringeworthy plot points, salacious scandals, and diva-defined media personas. And it gets really specific, too.

The Met and Swiss watchmaker Vacheron Constantin have unveiled three original works created during the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Vacheron Constantin Artisan Residency. The brand new program took place over the course of eighteen months, and emphasized preserving and reinterpreting traditional craft techniques. The three works of art produced in the residency are Vessel by Aspen Golann, Shaping Time by Ibrahim Said, and Ruined Splendour – BRONZE DIADEM by Joy Harvey. This is one of several collaborations between the Met and Vacheron Constantin.
The residency began in May 2025. In a press release, the watchmaker shared the residency is built on three key pillars: encouraging “the development of the widest range of artistic and craft skills so that they may evolve and thrive,” challenging and expanding “the norms of traditional craftsmanship by directing it towards new forms of expression,” and inspiring “future generations through the exchange of ideas and transmission of knowledge”
The three artists used the Met’s vast collection as a source of inspiration for their new works. Golan looked into the museum’s collection of American wooden furniture from the 17th to 19th centuries; Said studied an ancient Egyptian Lentoid bottle and a thousand year old Islamic water filter; while Harvey found inspiration in ancient jewelry from Greece, India and China.
“This artisan residency program is a collaborative initiative that embodies our mutual commitment to supporting artistic innovation and cultural dialogue,” said Max Hollein, The Met’s Marina Kellen French Director and Chief Executive Officer, in a statement. “It is a thrill to see how the three artisans, inspired by their engagement with The Met collection and Vacheron Constantin, have created works that breathe new life into traditional techniques, powerfully connecting the past and present.”

https://gothamist.com/news/trash-contain.title: Trash containers take over Brooklyn parking spaces as NYC gets garbage bags off sidewalks
https://gothamist.com/news/trash-contain.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/trash-contain.text:
Trash bag piles will soon be eradicated from a swath of Brooklyn as the city sanitation department installs hundreds of trash containers in parking spaces in some of the borough’s densest areas.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Sanitation Commissioner Gregory Anderson on Thursday announced that crews began installing more than 700 “Empire Bins” on streets across Downtown Brooklyn, Boerum Hill, Dumbo, Clinton Hill and the Navy Yard. The bins will be placed in front of buildings with more than 30 units, and officials said the rollout would be completed by the end of the fall.
Mamdani and Anderson installed the first of the bins during a news conference in Brooklyn Heights. The bins will be serviced by one of the city’s newly purchased garbage trucks, which lift and empty the trash containers.
“Every New Yorker deserves clean streets and sidewalks,” Mamdani said. “For too long, New Yorkers have had to walk past mountains of trash bags piled high on the curb that offer feasts for rats and stink up our streets. We’re changing that.”
The bins could replace around 768 of the area’s 23,795 on-street parking spaces, according to an analysis published by the sanitation department. More than 31% of households in the area where the bins are coming own at least one vehicle, according to city data.
The city already requires all buildings with nine or fewer units to use a smaller official NYC Bin to wheel out their trash to the curb. Buildings with 10 to 30 units can opt into the Empire Bin program.
By the end of this year’s rollout, trash bag piles will no longer be permitted across this swath of Brooklyn, which is home to 138,000 people. Recycling bags are still allowed to be put out on the curb.
Rat sightings in Harlem dropped after the bins were installed through a pilot program in the neighborhood, and officials say they'll drop across the five boroughs if the city's waste is fully containerized.
Previous Mayor Eric Adams introduced the bins to Brooklyn last September by ordering them to be installed outside school buildings. The new rollout marks the first time the street bins will be used for residential buildings in the borough, as well as the first time the containers have been deployed in such a dense area of the city.
“I cannot recall a time when New Yorkers have not had to dodge mountains of trash bags and rats on their own sidewalks — but now, I can proudly say that those days are numbered,” said City Councilmember Crystal Hudson, who pushed legislation that mandated the sanitation department continue the rollout after Adams’ departure.
Some neighborhoods could see 10% of their available parking spots swallowed up by the trash bins.
The city plans to continue the rollout next year by installing the bins in Hunts Point and University Heights in the Bronx. Empire Bins are also slated next year for Sunnyside in Queens, Manhattan's West Village, Prospect Heights in Brooklyn, and Staten Island's North Shore.
Clarence Gilliam, who was parking his car near the Brooklyn Navy Yard on Thursday, said he has no plans to give up driving even if the bins make it harder for him to find a parking spot.
“If it gets rid of the rats, it's a good thing, but make it easier for people to park," he said.

World Monuments Fund has raised $62 million, tripling its endowment and beating its fundraising goal eighteen months ahead of schedule. This will give the New York–based preservation organization a financial cushion to protect monuments around the world.
The organization’s endowment net assets are now expected to pass $100 million by 2028. The money raised will support everything from conservation training to protecting heritage sites threatened by war, climate change, and natural disasters. The fundraising drive launched less than a year ago, as part of WMF’s sixtieth-anniversary celebration.
WMF was founded in 1965 and has since worked to preserve more than 700 notable sites across 114 countries. Projects include conserving historic buildings and archaeological sites, training local craftspeople, and protecting and restoring cultural landmarks after natural disasters.
The Robert W. Wilson Charitable Trust was the main donor, with a $20 million challenge grant matching 50 cents for every dollar raised, up to $40 million. Other major contributions came from Suzanne Deal Booth, who gave $10 million to establish the Suzanne Deal Booth Institute for Heritage Preservation. Virginia James donated between $5 million and $10 million. Susan de Menil, Stephen Lash, Annabelle Selldorf, and Christian Louboutin are also on the list of notable donors.
“Cultural heritage is being lost to conflict, climate change, neglect, and urbanization faster than the world can respond,” Bénédicte de Montlaur, WMF’s president and CEO, said in a statement. “This campaign gives WMF the long-term resources to act with greater urgency and ambition.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/25/hegs.title: Hegseth Built a New Pentagon Office for Religion. Military Religious Leaders Wish He Hadn’t.
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/25/hegs.author: Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/25/hegs.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has extended a line for the military’s religious leaders to reach him directly — and current and former military chaplains say they don’t want it.
Hegseth announced the creation of a new Office of Religious Affairs on September 30, vowing that the office would give members of the armed forces’ chaplain corps access to him without “bureaucratic dilution.” It coincides with his openly Christian “Send Me” campaign, an online propaganda effort that the Pentagon launched over the summer promoting a biblical phrase widely understood as a vow to accept a divine mission.
“We should not be in the business of wrapping the state’s mission in one particular religion,” an active-duty Army captain serving as a non-Christian chaplain told The Intercept. But as Hegseth’s Pentagon increasingly pushes Christianity, the chaplain, who was granted anonymity because he feared retaliation from the Defense Department, said he and other non-Christian chaplains worry the new religious affairs office will be used to do just that.
Hegseth’s body bears an assortment of Christian and Crusader imagery, including a Jerusalem cross across his chest and the Latin phrase “Deus vult,” or “God wills it,” on his bicep — a battle cry associated with the medieval Crusades that has since been adopted by far-right extremists. His forearm bears a cross and sword referencing Matthew 10:34, in which Jesus declares that he came not to bring peace but a sword, alongside the Hebrew name for Jesus. In 2021, a fellow National Guard member flagged Hegseth as a potential security threat over his Deus vult tattoo, before Hegseth was removed from an assignment protecting Joe Biden’s inauguration.
As defense secretary, Hegseth has frequently turned to messaging that centers religion and vengeance while promoting the U.S. and Israel’s unpopular war in Iran. His “Send Me” campaign is built around Isaiah 6:8, a biblical verse commonly invoked by Christians as a call to serve God. During his 9/11 speech last month at the Pentagon, Hegseth said the “struggle against evil” that followed the attacks continues today and “will continue until Judgment Day,” before turning to the current war with Iran.
“Using specific scriptural language for a military campaign inappropriately frames state-sanctioned armed conflict and government service as a Christian religious crusade,” the chaplain said. “Once a mission is declared God’s will, every act inside it is sanctified in advance.”
The new Office of Religious Affairs, the chaplain said, could entrench this dynamic. While the Pentagon memo establishing the office says it cannot compel religious participation or diminish the free-exercise rights of service members of any faith or no faith, the office’s director will report directly to Hegseth and the deputy defense secretary, oversee the Armed Forces Chaplains Board, and work with the civilian religious organizations that endorse military chaplains. The office will also oversee efforts to assess spiritual fitness, spiritual readiness, and spiritual resilience across the force. This consolidated control, the chaplain warned, may make it difficult to maintain pluralism among the chaplain corps.
“Our chaplain corps must serve [non-Christian service members], not just the soldiers that share a faith with the SecDef,” the Army chaplain said. While it’s too early to know what that authority will mean for non-Christian chaplains, he wondered how it might change the ranks of the chaplaincy itself.
“Will this group begin accepting fewer and fewer non-Christian chaplains into our ranks?” he said. “Will we begin seeing fewer and fewer non-Christian chaplains be chosen for promotions?”
The concerns extend beyond the active-duty chaplain. Rev. Dr. Rebekah Savage, a former military chaplain who now helps oversee the Unitarian Universalist Association’s endorsement of clergy serving as military chaplains, said the organization was not consulted before the office was established.
“I am deeply concerned about how this office will serve the religious needs of the members of the service,” she said. “I can’t speak for others who are a part of the chaplaincy corps, but I know I am not alone.”
In response to questions about the new office from The Intercept, Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson wrote in a statement that the department “protects the constitutional right of every service member and civilian employee to practice their faith without coercion or discrimination. This is why Secretary Hegseth recently established the Office of Religious Affairs.” She said that prayer services and religious activities are always voluntary.
“The Christian faith is woven deeply into the fabric of our nation and shared by America’s wartime leaders like President George Washington, who prayed for his troops at Valley Forge, and President Franklin D. Roosevelt, who gifted Bibles to America soldiers during WW2 and encouraged them to read it,” Wilson added. “Despite the Left’s efforts to remove our Christian heritage from our great nation, Secretary Hegseth is among those who embrace it.”
In August, when “SEND ME” could still be dismissed as a string of social media posts, the Pentagon repeatedly declined to explain what the phrase meant or whether it represented a broader communications strategy.
As scholars of religion previously explained to The Intercept, the Pentagon’s use of the passage strips away part of the biblical story. Isaiah is not being sent to destroy God’s enemies; he is being sent to preach a warning to his own people. And the commission ends not in military triumph, but judgment. Cities are left empty, the land is devastated, and God’s own people suffer the destruction.
“Secretary Hegseth’s Send Me Tour is a military outreach and recruitment initiative focused on recognizing the Americans who volunteer to serve,” Wilson added in her statement. “We are grateful for the Americans—past, present, and future–who have raised their right hand and said, ‘Send Me.'”
Questions about the Pentagon’s treatment of minority religious traditions predate the new office.
In June, Savage joined 10 other religious endorsers in a letter to Hegseth objecting to revisions to the military’s Religious Affiliations Code list. The signatories said the changes removed or obscured the identities of several religious communities, including Unitarian Universalists, historically Black churches, and Wiccan and Pagan practitioners.
The endorsers warned that the changes could affect religious accommodations, access to clergy, and the distribution of chaplaincy resources.
“Classification is resource allocation,” they wrote.
Savage said the earlier changes, combined with the establishment of the Office of Religious Affairs, “calls the Department’s commitment to meeting the spiritual needs of all of its members into question.”
The active-duty Army chaplain questioned how the office’s stated religious-freedom protections would work in practice under a defense secretary who has increasingly incorporated Christian scripture into his public messaging.
“What oversight will exist to prevent religious bias?” he said. “When investments are made, will they be defining spiritual fitness by Christian, or by more pluralistic metrics?”
The same concerns extend to money. The office’s funding priorities include faith-based home school support for military families, faith-based suicide-reduction programs, and contracts with faith-based organizations.
“Will the Humanists, Muslims, Jews, Hindus, and other groups receive an equal, commensurate amount of support and funding for such programs?” the Army chaplain said. “Or will all or most of the funding go to Christian based organizations?”
Beyond institutional support, the chaplain said the Pentagon’s religious messaging could interfere with one of the central responsibilities of his profession: helping service members navigate questions of conscience, morality, and killing.
In reporting for Task & Purpose last month, this reporter examined how Army chaplains were preparing to address the moral and spiritual consequences of artificial intelligence in warfare. As one scholar of military ethics pointed out, moral injury can arise when service members feel responsible for actions that violate their values, even when they have little meaningful control over those decisions.
The Army chaplain raised a related concern: What happens when the military itself invokes religious authority to justify its mission?
“If my role as a chaplain is to advise soldiers and commanders of issues of morality and ethics, what can I say to them now?” he said. “How can I advise a commander on doing moral and ethical actions if the state has announced that their god has ordained their war?”
For service members who do not share the religious beliefs invoked by military leadership, the Army chaplain said, that tension could be especially difficult to reconcile.
“What can I say to a non-Christian soldier who is being ordered to kill his fellow man or risk dying himself for a god he does not believe in?” he said. “What do I tell a soldier who believes an action is immoral, but also believes that God commanded it?”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://hyperallergic.com/why-do-horror-.title: Why Do Horror Films Have Such a Hold on Our Imaginations?
https://hyperallergic.com/why-do-horror-.author: Matt Stromberg
https://hyperallergic.com/why-do-horror-.text:
Why Do Horror Films Have Such a Hold on Our Imaginations?
An exhibition at the Academy Museum explores the transgressive power of scary movies, channeling our deepest fears about life, death, and the unknown.
LOS ANGELES — Horror films may have historically been relegated to second-class status in the cinematic canon, viewed by some critics as vulgar fright fests that lack the gravitas of “serious” filmmaking. But there is no denying the captivating power they have exerted over audiences, channeling our deepest fears about life, death, the world around us, and the unknown onto the silver screen. Now on view through July at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles, The Horror Show takes a broad look at the history of the genre, exploring why scary movies have had such a hold on our imaginations — and prompting a reconsideration of their place in the filmic pantheon.
It all began with a single object: Dracula’s cape. That is, the original iconic cape worn by Bela Lugosi in Todd Browning’s Dracula (1931), which the Academy acquired from the Lugosi family in 2019. “It’s been a family heirloom for several generations,” Jessica Niebel, senior curator at the museum, told Hyperallergic. “We knew we wanted to highlight it in a special way.”
Once they had this cornerstone of the exhibition, curators began to assemble a wide range of material, including costumes, props, concept art, film posters, and scripts, from horror classics (The Shining, Psycho), contemporary masterpieces (Midsommar, Get Out) and underrated gems (Tales From the Hood, The Stuff). Centering both visual and narrative artistry, the curators drew heavily on the Academy Museum’s own robust collection, as well as objects and archival materials borrowed from dozens of lenders.

https://hyperallergic.com/hell-takes-the.title: Hell Takes the Form of State Repression in 1971’s “The Devils”
https://hyperallergic.com/hell-takes-the.author: Phillip Pyle
https://hyperallergic.com/hell-takes-the.text:
Hell Takes the Form of State Repression in 1971’s “The Devils”
Ken Russell’s film designed by Derek Jarman, newly released in a 4K restoration, mirrors the horrors unfolding outside our windows.
Before Derek Jarman became known for his anachronistic, queer film adaptations of the lives of Saint Sebastian, Caravaggio, Edward II, and even the Passion of Jesus, the English artist and activist worked as a set designer. This facet of Jarman, who died from AIDS-related illnesses in 1994, has recently come to the fore with the hyped release of the 4K restoration of Ken Russell's scandalous 1971 horror film The Devils, screening at the IFC Center, Brooklyn Academy of Music, and Nitehawk cinemas in New York in the coming weeks.
Adapted from Aldous Huxley's 1952 book The Devils of Loudun and John Whiting's 1961 play The Devils, the film is set in the castled town of Loudun, France, in 1634, in the aftermath of the Huguenot Rebellions against the French state's attempts to consolidate the power of the Crown and the Catholic Church. It opens with an image of a near-naked, genderqueer King Louis XIII performing on a half-shell on a theater stage à la Botticelli's “Venus” before shifting to Loudun, the site of a famous scandal wherein Ursuline nuns reportedly experienced bouts of demonic possession. The blame for this hysteria is strategically placed on a secular priest by the name of Urbain Grandier (played by a mustached Oliver Reed), who was subsequently tried and executed for his alleged crimes.
Grandier's entrapment by his enemies comes to comment on a larger evil that comes not from one poorly behaved individual but from the totalitarian powers that knock down the town's walls immediately following his burning at the stake.
"At the time that I made The Devils, I was a devout Catholic, and secure in my faith," Russell recalled in an interview in Sight and Sound in 1995, addressing the controversies surrounding the film's highly sexual depictions of nuns, priests, and even a fallen crucifix that becomes a sex object in a frenzied exorcism-cum-orgy.
“For myself, although I am not a political creature, I always viewed The Devils as my one political film. To me, it was about brainwashing, about the state taking over,” he added.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.title: Mamdani says he's 'confident' NYC will collect $500 million with pied-à-terre tax
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.author: Elizabeth Kim, David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he’s “confident” that New York City can collect $500 million through a new tax on pricey second homes, even as thousands of properties have been exempted.
“I know that there's a number of legal challenges, as there always are, when you seek to raise revenue to make a city a better place,” Mamdani said during an interview on Thursday with WNYC’s Brigid Bergin for the political pop-up show “Who’s Running This Place?”
The pied-à-terre tax, which the mayor touted as a fulfillment of his campaign pledge to tax the rich, is currently facing three separate legal challenges.
On Wednesday, city lawyers sparred with attorneys representing landlords who claim the tax's rollout caused “mass confusion” and should be restarted. In a separate complaint, billionaire casino mogul Steve Wynn and former Trump Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross say the state law discriminates against wealthy nonresidents.
The city’s Department of Finance granted more than 8,800 of the roughly 11,000 exemption applications, according to figures provided by City Hall. The exemptions mean fewer than 9,000 properties are subject to the tax. Those figures have led some experts to question whether the city will collect the $500 million Mamdani projected will come from the tax.
In April, city Comptroller Mark Levine estimated the tax would generate only up to $380 million from roughly 11,200 homes.
Attorney Ben Williams, who leads the property tax department at the law firm Rosenberg & Estis, noted that the city hasn’t budged from its projection despite the rising number of exempted properties.
“No matter what the numbers are, the city says, ‘We’re confident we’ll hit the $500 million,’” Williams said. “I am curious if they don’t hit the target, if they’ll just raise the tax rate in the future.”
During the roughly 30-minute interview, Mamdani also spoke about clashes between federal immigration agents and New Yorkers. Earlier this month, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal. The Marble Hill resident is currently being held at a federal jail in Brooklyn.
Mamdani said he was still having ongoing conversations with President Donald Trump and U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin.
“My demand to the president and to Secretary Mullin was not simply a demand around Oscar's case specifically,” the mayor said. “It was to end ICE operations in our city.”
The shooting marked a major escalation of Trump’s immigration crackdown in New York City. It also marked a turning point in the mayor’s relationship with the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. In response to scenes of police officers tussling with protesters, the DSA pressured Mamdani to fire Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch. The organization accused the NYPD of colluding with ICE.
In the interview, Mamdani said he and Tisch have spoken about ensuring that the city complies with its sanctuary laws, which limit cooperation and information sharing with federal immigration agents.
“That's something that we both take seriously and are delivering on,” Mamdani said.
The mayor also addressed the recent criticism over his education agenda and concerns that he has a racial blind spot when it comes to the Black community. His Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels was booed last week by parents and students who saw a lack of urgency in delivering plans to integrate the school system.
New York City has one of the most segregated school systems in the country. During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani promised to address the long-standing racial inequities. But 10 months into office, he has yet to articulate a clear plan and vision for K-12 education.
“One of the things that was most exciting to me in selecting our chancellor to be our chancellor was his distillation of his agenda as one to transform our city's public schools into ones that are safe, rigorous and integrated,” Mamdani said. “And that to me is a north star that we have to deliver on all of those fronts.”
He added that he did not begrudge New Yorkers frustrated with his administration.
The mayor, who has been campaigning with Gov. Kathy Hochul, had a few barbs for her Republican rival Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive. Blakeman has vowed to cancel the pied-à-terre tax as part of his campaign platform, arguing that the surcharge discourages investment in the city.
“What we're speaking about is, again, a surcharge on secondary homes worth more than $5 million, and the money that will come from that will be used to make our streets safer, our schools stronger,” Mamdani said.
He then added: “I know that that is still offensive to someone like Bruce Blakeman.”
In response to a clip of Blakeman attacking him, the mayor laughed and said, “He must have prepared for that one. He's been going at it in the mirror.”

https://gothamist.com/news/who-is-enforc.title: NYPD won't enforce NYC's bus fare while MTA security force is suspended
https://gothamist.com/news/who-is-enforc.author: Clayton Guse, Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/who-is-enforc.text:
This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani may be getting those free buses after all as enforcement of New York City’s $3 bus fare is on pause following a series of confrontations involving MTA agents.
The agency’s 350 fare enforcement agents — who don’t have the authority to make arrests — are on the bench after a pair of caught-on-camera confrontations.
And the NYPD says it has no plans to help.
That presents a vexing problem for MTA Chair Janno Lieber, whose agency is losing more than $300 million a year to farebeaters on the bus. The agency estimates roughly half of bus riders simply don’t pay and walk right past the driver, who is not required to intervene. Lieber has said the situation is untenable — and that the so-called EAGLE team of fare enforcers is necessary to correct rider behavior.
But Mamdani and the NYPD will not be coming to Lieber’s aid.
NYPD spokesperson Brad Weekes said “the NYPD has no plans to assist with EAGLE team enforcement in the future.”
Mamdani’s spokespeople have cited the EAGLE team controversy as further evidence of the need for his signature policy proposal of making the buses free. The mayor has yet to propose a way to replace the money the MTA collects from bus riders.
MTA spokesperson Tim Minton said the “NYPD is the agency responsible for law enforcement on subways and buses, and of course we are confident that will continue.”
The finger-pointing highlights an apparent change in policy. In 2024, the EAGLE team and NYPD under then-Mayor Eric Adams collaborated on bus fare enforcement.
Lieber said at a news conference Wednesday that the EAGLE team will pause pending an investigation while the agency ensures that enforcement agents are properly trained and that “everybody is playing by the rules.”
“I’m confident that we’re going to be able to come out the other side with an even better operation,” Lieber said.
MTA officials are now weighing whether or not the transit agency could equip EAGLE team members with body cameras. The MTA also plans to be more explicit with the riding public on how to file a complaint against a transit employee.
Lieber said the complaint system will be an item the MTA brings up at the end of its ongoing investigation of the EAGLE team. The agency is looking into the alleged assault of Brooklyn high school aide Kyle Taylor, who plans to sue the transit agency over a run-in with the EAGLE team earlier this month.
Video of the confrontation showed fare agents pinning Taylor against a bus shelter before shoving him to the ground in Brownsville. The alleged farebeater was taken away in an ambulance. Taylor said he had paid for his ride.
The agency is also looking into a second incident Lieber referenced when announcing the fare enforcement pause.
Gothamist obtained videos of that clash on Aug. 6, which show a man getting off the Bx39 bus at East Gun Hill and White Plains roads in the Bronx with an EAGLE officer close behind. The officer tackles the man to the pavement. Three more officers then try to restrain the passenger.
“Let go of my arm!” the man says, to which an EAGLE team officer responds “No.”
The videos do not show how the struggle began. The NYPD said no one was arrested in connection with the incident.
Lisa Daglian, executive director of the Permanent Citizens Advisory Committee to the MTA, described the pause as a “hiccup” to combating fare evasion, but that paying the fare is an important civic duty in New York City.
“There’s no doubt that we have to bring down fare evasion across the board,” she said. “Without the fares, we have a potential for seeing service reductions and a decrease in reliability, and those are things that nobody wants at all.”
Carol Chen contributed reporting to this column.
NYC transportation news this week
Why can’t the city fix Brooklyn's Ocean Parkway? Ocean Parkway was designed in the late 19th century as a peaceful, idyllic promenade stretching 5.5 miles from Prospect Park to Coney Island in Brooklyn, but these days, it’s a six-lane highway known for reckless driving. City data shows that over the last five years, seven people have been killed and 74 were seriously injured in crashes on Ocean Parkway. But state regulations prohibit Mayor Mamdani — whose administration has focused on redesigning dangerous thoroughfares — from implementing a sweeping redesign of the street. Like the West Side Highway and the FDR Drive, Ocean Parkway is technically run by the state. Any major changes to its layout must be overseen by the state transportation department, not the city.
The Midtown bus terminal rebuild is moving ahead. A new deck over a section of the Lincoln Tunnel entrance in Hell’s Kitchen will be used to store buses and supplies while crews tear down and rebuild the Midtown bus terminal, and once the project wraps, the space will be converted into a new park.
Brooklyn's Third Avenue will be redesigned. The city transportation department said a deadly stretch of Third Avenue in Brooklyn’s Sunset Park neighborhood will undergo a major overhaul that will replace traffic lanes in each direction with bike lanes and shorten the street's pedestrian crossings.
City folk head upstate to leaf peep. This year’s super El Niño is making the autumn foliage brighter and last longer, so the Metro-North has added more trains to and from the Hudson Valley to accommodate flocks of people hoping to spend a bucolic weekend peeping leaves outside the city.
The ban on permits for new street fairs continues. Mayor Mamdani’s administration is extending a decades-old moratorium on new street fairs through 2027, citing a likely increase in NYPD overtime. The city can reject applications for any street fair that did not take place in 2026, but fairs held this year are able to renew permits for next year.
An E-bike lithium-ion battery caused a Bronx fire that killed a 10-year-old. Four others were also critically injured. According to FDNY data, lithium-ion batteries have caused more than 400 fires across the city this year, resulting in 74 injuries and six deaths.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
Question from Tony in Hartsdale, New York
“What was behind Metro-North's decision to have its tickets expire at 4 a.m. on the day following their purchase?”
The MTA enacted this policy in January 2025 on the Metro-North and Long Island Rail Road as a way to ensure riders pay their fare. Instead of activating their digital tickets on their phones during the course of their ride, many riders would stash them for a later trip. The Citizens Budget Commission had estimated the commuter railroads were losing $46 million a year in skipped fares. Under the new policy, unactivated tickets bought on the MTA’s TrainTime app expire at 4 a.m. the next day. Riders can also be fined $8 if they’re caught activating their ticket after they board the train.
