https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/c.title: Confused NYPD Abandons East Village E-Bike Raid
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/c.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/c.text:
Eight bikes taking up the same space as a single private car. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Cops abandoned a hastily planned raid of a makeshift e-bike parking lot used by hundreds of delivery workers on Wednesday morning – prompting community leaders to call on Mayor Mamdani to create an infrastructure at the ad-hoc worker hub.
“We have an administration that says one thing about immigrants and the dignity of workers and then we have a police department that is left over from the last administration that seems to be totally different,” Community Board 3 District Manager Susan Stetzer told Streetsblog.
When Streetsblog arrived at 11th Street and First Avenue at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, workers had already re-organized the hundreds of bikes to be mostly on the south side of the block and out of the taxi relief areas in front of the Madina Masjid Islamic Council of America.
Cops from the local precinct showed up at around 9 a.m. The commanding officer of the Ninth Precinct, Deputy Inspector Pamela Jeronimo, claimed that the bikes parked neatly on the street in what would otherwise be space used by car drivers for the same purpose were in violation of “the law.”
“If they’re not on a bike rack, then that’s outside of the law. [Bikes] are blocking parking for cars,” she said. “These are violations. It’s just the way the law is written, I didn’t write it.”
There is actually nothing in the city’s vehicle and traffic code that prohibits bike users from parking against the curb in un-metered spots. Mopeds and scooters are allowed to park at an angle to the curb, in the same way the workers are parking their e-bikes.
When asked by Streetsblog why New Yorkers are able to park their private cars, but not their bikes, on the street for free, NYPD on the scene doubled down.
“You can’t store personal property on the street,” said Matt Russo, a managing attorney at the NYPD. “A bike is personal property and a car is not.” (You might want to let that sink in for a second.)
One passerby thought of it differently.
“I order delivery, these people have every right to be there, it’s never bothered me,” said Willaim Kelly, who lives near the delivery worker hub. “They’re both modes of transport, they [cops] should be encouraging people to use bikes and not drive cars.”
The area looked clean and orderly, thanks to weekly cleanups organized by the nearby community organization, Cafewal. The bike parking in the area isn’t concentrated to just that block; clusters of bikes spill over to the sidewalk on First Avenue, further west on 11th Street adjacent to a Citi Bike dock and further east in some free on-street parking for cars, but are mostly organized.
For around 45 minutes, the cops from the Ninth Precinct walked around looking at bikes and handed out fliers with directions for what to do if a bike is seized. Someone from the mayor’s office showed up who would not provide a name to Streetsblog or say why he was there, and suddenly, the officers abandoned the mission, got into their cars and left.
“I don’t think we’re doing any enforcement,” said Russo when Streetsblog asked why they were leaving without taking the bikes the officers said were parked illegally. “While this condition isn’t perfect, I think it’s in okay shape.”
The area exists as an informal hub for the community of delivery workers of African descent who make deliveries in the East Village. Most live outside the area and choose to park their bikes with their peers so they don’t get stolen. The app companies that employ these men as private-contractors are not required to provide them with bike storage, charging, or even spots to take breaks.
“What company gets to use the city streets to operate their business?” said Council Member Harvey Epstein (D-East Village) of the delivery app companies like DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub. “We think the burden’s on the app companies to find indoor locations for bikes to be placed. We’re working on legislative and policy solutions along with the mayor’s office to force those companies to take responsibility for the workers who are on the streets who have no place to go during the day and no place to put their bikes.”
Tensions in the neighborhood have been high over the bike parking. During the previous administration, a simple rage-bait article from the New York Post could get the NYPD to raid the area and take delivery workers’ bikes.
Back in March, Streetsblog reported that the Mamdani administration had changed that approach. Instead of sending the NYPD in response to the Post labelling the area a “junkyard,” it sent DSNY to help clean up— a welcome change, the advocates said at the time.
Epstein said he is happy that no bikes were taken and said the anticlimactic result of the raid can be attributed to the community coming together to help workers organize the bikes and keep the area clean.
“We have worked hard to do an education campaign,” he said. “I think the education campaign was successful.”
But still it doesn’t feel like the administration is looking for a real solution, Stetzer, the district manager said.
“The only work the city is doing right now is to figure out the enforcement. I don’t see anyone doing anything or talking to us about how to create infrastructure so that all this can be done legally and so the neighborhood doesn’t have to bear the burden,” she said.
Mayor Mamdani’s preliminary budget allocated $25 million to build secure bike parking in the city. DOT recently selected California-based Tranzito to build an initial 500 secure structures over the next five years, which the delivery workers would be able to use for a fee.
Those who showed up on Wednesday to observe and warn workers of the impending raid said they were confused about what the workers were supposed to do with their bikes, and that the NYPD had been teasing a raid all month and nothing happened.
“We ask if they can park here, but they don’t answer clearly,” said Diamy, who works at Cafewal and informed workers via Whatsapp group about the NYPD’s plans, and who didn’t want his last name published. Diamy said the bike parking has been a conflict since he started at Cafewal in 2024. He said the police first wanted to do the raid on Oct. 7, then they pushed it to Oct. 21, at which point some workers moved their bikes to racks in Union Square, where some were stolen.
The NYPD confirmed this timeline and told Streetsblog through a spokesperson that it “worked with advocates and local leaders to inform them of this enforcement action and is responding to the complaints from the community.”
Others who showed up to help workers saw the morning’s events as a sign that the community wants to find a solution to the parking issue that won’t hurt workers.
“There is definitely a stress on the block that people recognize but people are also very supportive of the workers,” said Shawn Garcia, a CB3 member and the executive director of Earth Matter. “Sometimes the narrative that is put out there is that the community is up in arms about it, but I think that’s not the case. It’s more nuanced than that.”
Still, landlords from nearby buildings on First Avenue are organizing a press conference on Thursday at noon at 180 First Ave. regarding the “ongoing concerns about bicycles and delivery workers congregating on East 11th Street,” according to an email sent to tenants in the area obtained by Streetsblog.
UPDATE: On Thursday morning the NYPD returned to the area and confiscated eight bikes that were parked next to the orange Jeep in the on-street parking spot, according to Diamy from Cafewal. It’s unclear what changed from Wednesday morning, when Streetsblog arrived on Thursday the bikes had already been removed and the NYPD was not present.

https://gothamist.com/news/person-killed.title: NJ state police fatally shot man in Moonachie, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/person-killed.author: Kaya Laterman
https://gothamist.com/news/person-killed.text:
A man died after a fatal shooting involving a New Jersey state trooper Wednesday night in Moonachie, officials said.
The New Jersey attorney general's office said it is investigating an incident in Bergen County where an adult male civilian was fatally wounded, according to prosecutors.
His identity, and the name of the New Jersey State Police trooper involved in the shooting, were not immediately released.
According to preliminary information, the shooting occurred on Gotham Parkway, near the intersection with West Commercial Avenue at approximately 5:15 p.m., according to prosecutors.
The circumstances surrounding the encounter are under investigation, officials said.
A spokesperson for the New Jersey State Police referred inquiries to the attorney general's office.
The attorney general is required by law to investigate a person's death that occurs during an encounter with a law enforcement official.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-.title: Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Reduced Mail Service
https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-.author: Ken B. Morales, Jen Fifield, Misty Harris
https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Rural Cuts: Delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, a ProPublica analysis found.
- Rejected Ballots: The rates of ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in areas affected by the cuts compared to the 2022 primary. That wasn’t the case elsewhere.
- Extraordinary Measures: Postal Service leaders say special procedures in place for the Nov. 3 election should prevent similar delays, but experts warn that mistakes are likely.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.
Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.
Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.
In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail.
But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.
Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.
The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.
In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.
Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.
Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.
“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”
Rates of Rejection Due to Late Ballots Were Higher in Counties with Reduced Mail Service
Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.
At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.
“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”
Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.
“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.'”
A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)
After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.
At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.
Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.
“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”
Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.
The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006.
When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)
The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.
Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.
The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.
Mail Services Have Been Cut in 16,000 More ZIP Codes Since the 2024 Election
A pilot program that reduced mail pickups to save money was paused in the lead-up to the 2024 election. The rollout has since resumed, and the changes have been made in five times as many ZIP codes for the 2026 midterms.
In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.
This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.
Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.
A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.
“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,'” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”
Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.
Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.
In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.
In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.
Has Mail Service Been Reduced in Your ZIP Code?
If the frequency of mail pickups has been reduced in your area, mail may take longer to send and receive, and the date on the postmark could be later than the day you dropped it off, which may matter for mail like ballots that is subject to a deadline.
In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.
“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”
In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.
Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.
Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.
Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.
Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.
The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.
ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)
Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.
“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.
Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.
A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.
In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.
Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.
In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.
“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

https://www.propublica.org/article/civil.title: Sexual Assaults on Campus No Longer Scrutinized as Closely Under Trump’s Education Department
https://www.propublica.org/article/civil.author: Jennifer Smith Richards, Jodi S. Cohen
https://www.propublica.org/article/civil.text:
The civil rights arm of the U.S. Department of Education has dramatically scaled back investigations involving schools and colleges since the second Trump administration began, even as complaints continue to pour in, a ProPublica analysis of newly obtained records found.
The analysis shows how severely the department’s Office for Civil Rights has retracted from its mission, launching an average of about 100 new investigations a month — 1,839 total from Inauguration Day in 2025 through July 2026. The OCR launched an average of 310 new investigations each month in 2024 during the Biden administration, according to data previously obtained by ProPublica.
Under President Donald Trump, the OCR abandoned the public-facing list of schools it was investigating and the reasons for those investigations, including claims of discrimination based on race, sex and disability. ProPublica sued the department to obtain internal case data. The government subsequently provided records of the OCR’s actions in the first 18 months of Trump’s return to power, and we are publishing the data so the public can search the cases.
Search for School Civil Rights Investigations
See where the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights under the Trump administration has launched investigations into alleged discrimination in schools and colleges or dismissed complaints without investigating. The table also includes complaints filed with the OCR during the Trump administration that the office has not yet decided to investigate.
The OCR uses “case opened” to record when complaints were received by the agency. “Investigation start date” indicates the date the agency initiated an investigation.
The decline in investigations is especially dramatic for cases involving sex discrimination. More than 200 new complaints were filed with the office related to schools’ handling of sexual violence — rape, assault and abuse. But the Trump administration launched investigations in only 29 of them, finding fault with a school district only once, according to the newly obtained data. It’s typical for there to be at least 60 sexual violence investigations opened each year.
The department addressed fewer of these cases despite continued concerns about the persistence of the problem — as demonstrated by the intense public scrutiny over how Cornell University addressed a student’s report of a 2024 gang rape.
Beyond that, the OCR launched only two investigations into discrimination based on sexual orientation.
“They’re barely doing anything to protect women and girls, including survivors of sexual violence,” said Shiwali Patel, an attorney who previously worked at the OCR and is now with the National Women’s Law Center. “They just don’t care about women and girls.”
The organization and more than 120 other advocacy, civil rights and education groups sent a letter on Tuesday to Congress’ ranking education committee leaders urging them to hold the OCR accountable for “its failure to enforce civil rights law and protect students from sexual violence.”
With OCR’s online database idle since Trump took office, the only way to know where the agency has launched investigations has been through selective department press releases, when OCR employees provided internal data to reporters or from schools and colleges that acknowledged that their institutions had become targets of the investigations.
The data ProPublica received as a result of our lawsuit can now fill that gap on the more than 1,800 civil rights investigations that the department initiated from Jan. 20, 2025, to July 29 of this year. The database also reflects the 24,000 new complaints logged through May and the nearly 17,000 new and old cases the department closed — almost always by dismissing them.
The agency is dismissing complaints more frequently than in prior years, the records show. And fewer than 700 cases opened by the administration were resolved with a finding of wrongdoing.
The data does not include investigations that had been opened before Trump retook power but that are pending decisions by OCR — a backlog of more than 10,000 cases.
In response to questions from ProPublica, an Education Department spokesperson blamed the Biden administration for leaving office with 19,000 unresolved cases, which the Trump administration has worked to address.
“Spare us the crocodile tears as the Trump Administration is working to restore OCR to its original purpose: enforcing the law to ensure all students can receive an education free from discrimination,” spokesperson Sabin Sidney wrote.
He added that the administration “treats any form of discrimination on the basis of race or sex as illegal.” And he criticized the prior administration for endorsing policies that allowed transgender girls and women to compete in women’s athletics and use women's restrooms.
The data disclosure comes as the administration is moving forward with efforts to shut down the department and move the OCR under the Department of Justice. Disability rights advocates and others have been critical of the move, while the administration says it will lead to more efficiency and do a better job protecting students’ rights. The majority of cases before the OCR involve students with disabilities, as has been the case historically.
In the early months of Trump’s second term, Education Secretary Linda McMahon fired hundreds of employees and closed seven regional OCR offices, leaving the department severely diminished. Its remaining civil rights workers have described untenable case loads and pressure to dismiss complaints.
The remaining attorneys “are navigating pure chaos,” said Rachel Gittleman, president of the American Federation of Government Employees Local 252, the union that represents OCR staff. “They are being asked to use the tools they have used for their entire careers not for good, not to protect students, but to harm students. You see it in the case dismissals, the cases that target trans students or people of color.”
In examining the new records, ProPublica found the extent to which the agency has shifted its focus, as the OCR places a new emphasis on complaints that men faced discrimination. The agency launched 172 investigations into alleged “discrimination against males,” compared with 104 cases of alleged “discrimination against females” in the period examined.
It also has investigated allegations that campus programs or scholarships excluded men. For example, it investigated a complaint against Skyline College in California that had been filed in 2023 but that President Joe Biden’s administration had not acted on, according to records from the university. The complaint alleged that Skyline discriminated against men by listing scholarships on its website that are exclusively for women and for promoting a program for women.
The civil rights office opened the investigation in mid-April, and two weeks later the community college agreed that it would remove the scholarships from its website and add language that the program was open to all students. A Skyline College spokesperson did not respond to questions from ProPublica.
At the same time, the agency chose to open fewer than 370 new investigations involving racial discrimination, even though about 5,000 complaints were filed.
Of those new investigations, about 11% involved allegations of discrimination against white students. Over the summer, the department announced investigations into five medical schools’ admissions policies.
“They are not allocating their resources to racial discrimination complaints, to sexual assault complaints, to the types of complaints that really often speak to systematic discrimination and problems,” said Johnathan Smith, managing director of education at the nonprofit National Center for Youth Law.
That organization also has sued the Education Department for similar information obtained by ProPublica; the lawsuit is pending.
Help Us Report on How the Department of Education Is Handling Civil Rights Cases
Have you recently filed a civil rights complaint or do you have a pending case? We need your help to get a full picture of how the dismantling of the Office for Civil Rights is affecting students, parents, school employees and their communities.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.title: Mexican Grand Prix qualifying: Lewis Hamilton takes pole – live
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.author: Philip Cornwall
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
Toto Wolff pleased for his old charge Hamilton and his current charge Russell.
Mexican Grand Prix qualifying: Lewis Hamilton takes pole – live
🏎️ F1 updates from 9pm GMT in Mexico City
 
🏎️ Giles Richards’ race scene-setter | And mail Philip
Sat 31 Oct 2026 18.39 EDT
First published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 16.00 EDT
Sat 31 Oct 2026 18.39 EDT
First published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 16.00 EDT
He wondered if this was his first pole in Mexico. When you have a record 105, it is easy to forget one: he won from pole in 2016.
There is life in Lewis Hamilton yet. When you heard him talking about racing into the 2030s, to race at an African Grand Prix in Rwanda, it felt inspiring but perhaps overoptimistic. But there he is.
The top 10
1 Lewis Hamilton 🇬🇧 Ferrari 1:16.514
 
2 George Russell 🇬🇧 Mercedes +0.009
 
3 Charles Leclerc 🇲🇨 Ferrari +0.119
 
4 Max Verstappen 🇳🇱 Red Bull +0.178
 
5 Kimi Antonelli 🇮🇹 Mercedes +0.193
 
6 Lando Norris 🇬🇧 McLaren +0.310
 
7 Isack Hadjar 🇫🇷 Red Bull +0.386
 
8 Liam Lawson 🇳🇿 Racing Bulls +0.515
 
9 Arvid Lindblad 🇬🇧 Racing Bulls +0.603
 
10 Pierre Gasly 🇫🇷 Alpine +0.639
And now Hamilton. “Wow. That feels great … So happy. Oh man, I’m lost for words. It’s been a really, really tough, challenging weekend … The engine issue we had yesterday … But it’s so close between us all … Wow. To have a pole here.” He is told he is the oldest driver to have a pole since Mario Andretti in 1982. “Where there’s a will, there’s a way. It’s all in the mind, honestly, for all of us … I love what I do … I dream about it. I have this amazing support around the world, these guys keeps me going, I hope they are happy today, and I hope I can deliver for them tomorrow.”
Now Russell, who is asked if he is happy. “I am, I am. It’s been a tricky few races for me and still struggling to get on top of this car, to be honest because it’s been a very difficult weekend until one lap in Q3. To almost get pole … it was very close in the end. I always know it’s in there.” His self-belief remains, despite all the frustrations.
“I was fighting with the car particularly in Q3 … There is such low downforce here.”
Leclerc speaks. “I just didn’t do a good job. The outlaps were difficult to put the tyres in the right window … A bit disappointed but to start third here is not too bad.”
So there was no false Ferrari qualifying dawn. And Russell took second – David Croft points out that the two drivers who need to win to keep the title race alive are one and two.
Lewis Hamilton takes pole!
Hamilton does it. After Verstappen locks up on 13th then backs off, the Briton gets his first Ferrari pole, his 105th overall.
Final seconds. Here comes Antonelli. Only fifth fastest.
George Russell +0.009 in second. Leclerc third +0.119.
Hamilton goes fastest! 1:16.514.
All going wrong for Hadjar. He misjudged the line coming into the pits. Bernie Collins says the Frenchman is all over the place mentally, complaining more than Gordon Ramsay in a Wimpy.
Bernie Collins eavesdropping on the drivers, saying their messages are full of uncertainty as to the best strategy.
Though Verstappen has that one-place penalty.
Turn 13 unlucky again for Hadjar but Verstappen gets second, +0.045.
Russell P3, Antonelli P4, then Norris beat Hamilton at +0.177.
Leclerc puts in a 1:16.647 for provisional pole. Hamilon +0.422, a middle sector mistake.
Q3 is go.
Karun Chandhok analyses Piastri’s lap. Kerb after kerb after kerb.
Yet Norris went fastest. Top 10: Nor, Ver, Lec, Ham, Rus, Had, Ant, Lin, Law and Gas.
Q2 eliminations – with Piastri out
Blimey. Out go Hulkenberg, Colapinto, Piastri, Bortoleto, Bearman and Sainz. McLaren saved a set of soft tyres but an aborted fast lap doomed Piastri.
Piastri out! He is 13th fastest!
Relief for Hamilton. Up in third, at a minuscule +0.077.
Norris shot up to third. Piastri is 10th. Hulkenberg at seventh is the big disruptor, a threat to Lawson, Hadjar and Piastri. And HAMILTON.
Drop zone is looking like Gasly, Bortoleto, Bearman, Colapinto, Sainz and HAMILTON.
Verstappen goes fastest, 1:16.876. Hulkenberg is sixth at present.
Hamilton into the pits. Down in the drop zone at present, as is Norris, who was on used tyres initially.
Lindblad is second at +0.191, ahead of Antonelli at +0.259 and Russell at +0.307.
Charles Leclerc gets a 1:16.944, while Hamilton goes off the track at turn 13 when on a flyer, which is causing a lot of problems.
Q2 is go.
Hadjar used another set of soft tyres, which explains his margin over Verstappen.
Something weird happened to Leclerc, a power surge. The spirits of the night?
Top 10: Ham, Had, Lec, Pia, Rus, Bor, Nor, Hul, Ant, Ver.
Q1 eliminations
Out go Albon, Alonso, Hirakawa, Stroll, Perez and Bottas. Hirakawa was about a second slower than Bearman but got a lot of sympathy on the team radio.
Hadjar has split the Ferraris! +0.044.
Ollie Bearman 10th fastest for Haas, his new teammate 19th.
Yellow cleared. Phew.
Yellow flags … Could settle things.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.title: Canelo Álvarez v Christian Mbilli: WBC super-middleweight championship – live
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.author: Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
Another assured round from Álvarez, whose jab is sharp, his counters precise and his movement economical, stepping out of range whenever Mbilli tries to mount an attack. It’s a masterclass in ring generalship from the wily vet, who appears to have his French foe completely figured out. Canelo enters the championship rounds with an yawning advantage on our card.
Mbilli is playing straight into Álvarez’s hands. The relentless pressure and workrate has all but vanished, allowing the 36-year-old Mexican to fight at his own pace. He’s stacking rounds now and it’s hard to see how the Frenchman can turn it around.
A spot of controversy in the eighth as Mbilli is docked a point for punching behind the head following complaints from Álvarez, who appears to have the referee’s ear. The Mexican is then granted another timeout, further disrupting the champion’s rhythm. Mbilli needs to become more assertive, but Hector Afu’s officiating is now bound to become a talking point in a fight that remains very much in the balance.
Here comes Canelo. The Mexican produces his best round of the fight, looking increasingly comfortable as his heavier, more eye-catching counters begin to take their toll. A crisp combination off the ropes, punctuated by a flush right uppercut that rocks Mbilli, leaves no doubt.
Mbilli takes the initiative, putting together combinations and keeping Álvarez occupied with a steady stream of punches. Both men find openings to the midsection, but neither has really shifted into top gear. It’s a tactical, closely contested fight so far, with the Frenchman’s greater activity giving him the edge on our card.
Another competitive round with Mbilli increasing his output and doing some good work to the body while Álvarez grows a little too comfortable on the defensive. Canelo is slipping punches and looking to land the occasional big counter, but he’s not throwing enough. Mbilli finishes strongly, his speed and volume beginning to pose serious questions for the Mexican. Álvarez shades it on our card, but the champion is making him work for everything.
Mbilli is finding his rhythm now, ripping off combinations and using his superior workrate to back Álvarez against the ropes. Canelo is showing his age at times, but his lead hand looks as sharp as it has in years and his footwork remains crisp as he repeatedly pirouettes out of danger. It’s an intriguing contrast in styles: Mbilli has the advantage in volume, while Álvarez is landing the cleaner, more accurate punches and doing his best to dictate the pace. Another close round.
Mbilli is throwing and landing more and appears to have found his footing after a slow start. Álvarez is mostly picking his spots and pot-shotting. This one could have gone either way but it says here the champion nicked it.
Álvarez holds his ground in the center of the ring early before circling Mbilli, looking the sharper and more composed fighter. The Mexican puts together a couple of crisp combinations, including a thudding left hook, while Mbilli is slow to get going. The Frenchman finally begins letting his hands go in the final 30 seconds, but he’ll need to increase his volume to trouble Canelo. CompuBox has Álvarez landing 10 of 24 punches to Mbilli’s seven of 43. A clear opening round for the challenger.
The waiting is over. The final instructions have been given by referee Hector Afu, the seconds are out and we’ll pick it up with round-by-round coverage from here!
Here come the fighters. First it’s Mbilli, entering first despite his status as the champion, wearing a black tee and red trunks. And now after an extended video introduction it’s time for Canelo. It’s a muted, pyrotechnic-free ringwalk by his theatrical standards as he enters surrounded by his team and the recording artist Tito Double P.
Anthem time at Kingdom Arena. First the national anthem of Saudi Arabia, in honor of our hosts. Then La Marseillaise, for Mbilli. Then Himno Nacional Mexicano, for Canelo. The fighters should be making their entrances any moment now.
Munguía, speaking through a translator, is candid about his struggles in the sixth round, admitting he got carried away after hurting Zon and left himself exposed.
Pues la verdad que me agarró, o sea, me agarró tirando golpes, lo agarré y me fui con todo. Entonces descuide descuidé y fue cuando me agarró este. Pues digo, es parte del trabajo, pero hay que aprender. Y hay que, pues, aprender a no descuidarnos.
Well, honestly, he caught me. I mean, he caught me while I was throwing punches. I caught him too, and I went all out. So I let my guard down, and that’s when he caught me. Like I said, it’s part of the job, but you have to learn from it. You have to learn not to let your guard down.
The Mexican gave himself a six or seven out of 10 for his performance.
No la la verdad que me siento muy bien. Muy contento. Honrado. Este contento para el trabajo. El desempeño este. Yo creo que digo se me complicó ahí un poquito en rival. Pero la verdad que me me siento muy bien. Casi ellos pudimos sacar el trabajo. Y yo creo que es parte del aprendizaje. Y hay que seguir trabajando mucho.
Honestly, I feel really good. Very happy. Honored. I’m pleased with the work – with the performance. Things got a bit complicated with the opponent, but, truly, I feel very good. We managed to get the job done, and I think it’s all part of the learning process. We just have to keep working hard.
Munguía has retained his WBA super-middleweight title by a 12-round unanimous decision. The three judges at ringside handed down scores of 116-112 and 117-111 (twice).
The 30-year-old Mexican entered the ring as roughly an 18-1 favorite with the bookmakers. Zon nearly made a mockery of those odds, coming within a whisker of stopping the Mexican champion in an extraordinary sixth round, but Munguía was dominant throughout the second half of the contest to wrap up a close but uncontroversial win.
We may have just witnessed the round of the year in Riyadh. Nikita Zon had Jaime Munguía on the brink of defeat in a white-knuckle sixth, rocking the Mexican champion with a barrage of punches that left him barely able to stay upright. But Munguía somehow weathered the storm and came roaring back, hurting a punched-out Zon in the closing stages as the two traded hellfire in a remarkable display of courage and violence.
There was controversy, too, when referee Tony Weeks stepped between the fighters as Munguía appeared close to being stopped, giving the champion precious seconds to recover. The intervention could prove decisive.
The numbers tell part of the story: Zon landed 28 of 65 punches to Munguía’s 18 of 54, with 43 of their combined 46 connections coming on power shots. An unforgettable three minutes.
Jaime Munguía is (finally) in the ring for the final preliminary bout of the night, defending his World Boxing Association super-middleweight title against unbeaten Russian challenger Nikita Zon.
The 30-year-old Mexican (46-2, 35 KOs) claimed the belt with a unanimous-decision victory over Armando Resendiz in May and now makes his first defense against Zon (12-0-1, 10 KOs), who is fighting outside his native Russia for the first time.
Munguía, who lost to Canelo Álvarez by unanimous decision in May 2024, will be looking to make a statement ahead of his compatriot’s appearance in the main event. The winner could move into position for a 168lb unification fight with whoever emerges victorious between Álvarez and Christian Mbilli later tonight.
While we wait (and wait, and wait) for the final undercard bout, a few choice quotes from Thursday’s final press conference in Riyadh, where Álvarez and Mbilli struck contrasting notes ahead of tonight’s WBC super-middleweight title fight.
For Álvarez, who is for the first time since 2022 after losing his undisputed championship to Terence Crawford last year, the message was one of unfinished business.
“After 20 years as a professional, I’m glad to be here,” the 36-year-old Mexican said. “I’m the challenger now, but always in my mind, I’m the champion.”
He added: “I don’t believe in shortcuts. I’m going straight for the champion because I already have the experience. I’ve been a champion for many years and I want to be a champion again.”
Mbilli, the unbeaten Cameroon-born Frenchman making his first defense of the full WBC title, was no less confident.
“I’m ready for this fight. I’m ready to shock the world,” the 31-year-old said. “I have a lot of respect for Canelo and I want to congratulate him, but on Saturday it’s going to be a different story. I’m coming for the win.”
Asked about his preparations, Mbilli offered a simple formula: “My training camp was perfect. My mind is ready for this fight. I don’t need to do anything special to win; I only need to be myself.”
The undercard is nearing its conclusion as we build towards tonight’s main event between Álvarez and Mbilli, with one preliminary bout remaining before the headliners make their ringwalks. Jaime Munguía is up next to defend his WBA super-middleweight title against Nikita Zon in a scheduled 12-round contest.
In the most recent bout, Rafael Espinoza retained his WBO featherweight title with a third-round TKO of Ricardo Blandon, who was unable to continue after suffering a cut caused by a punch. The unbeaten Mexican improved to 29-0 with 25 knockouts. It should be noted the stoppage felt awfully premature.
Earlier, Japan’s Reito Tsutsumi overwhelmed Raymundo Rojas with a series of heavy left hands to force a second-round stoppage at 2min 27sec, improving his professional record to 6-0.
On the non-televised card, Brayan Leon outpointed Hector Aguirre over eight rounds, while Emiliano Rojo stopped Flavius Biea in the fourth. Bek Nurmaganbet needed less than three minutes to dispatch Marcos Vazquez, dropping him twice before securing a first-round knockout with just three seconds to go.
Before that, Sultan Almohammed earned a unanimous decision over Erick Villegas, while Carl Jammes Martin edged David Picasso by split decision in a closely contested featherweight contest.
Hello and welcome Riyadh’s Kingdom Arena for tonight’s fight between Saúl “Canelo” Álvarez and Christian Mbilli from Riyadh, where one of boxing’s biggest names is attempting to reclaim his place atop the super-middleweight division in circumstances that are anything but ordinary.
For the first time since 2022, Álvarez enters the ring as a challenger. The 36-year-old Mexican superstar, who lost his undisputed championship to Terence Crawford 13 months ago, is seeking to regain the World Boxing Council title against the unbeaten, Cameroon-born Frenchman Mbilli, who has promised to “shock the world” in the biggest fight of his career.
But the backdrop is almost as compelling as the matchup itself. The contest is going ahead despite a wave of drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia that have forced the cancellation or postponement of other major events and raised questions about whether the fight could safely take place. After weeks of uncertainty, the fighters are here, the stage is set and the show, remarkably, goes on.
Stay with us for all the buildup, round-by-round coverage and reaction from Riyadh.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/3.title: Legal filing questions Trump’s claims of non-citizen voting in California
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/3.text:
Legal filing questions Trump’s claims of non-citizen voting in California
Data scientists find that many ‘likely non-citizens’ identified by the Trump administration were erroneously flagged.
A new court filing has cast further doubt on the accuracy of a list of “likely non-citizen” voters that the administration of United States President Donald Trump sent to the state of California ahead of the midterm elections.
On Saturday, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA), an advocacy group, submitted an analysis to the court conducted by two data scientists from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).
It found that more than four in every 10 names on the list were not on California’s voter rolls.
It also found that thousands of potentially eligible US citizens were incorrectly identified as ineligible to vote.
The Trump administration’s list, delivered to California in early October, had suggested that as many as 20,930 “likely non-citizens” were registered on the state’s voter rolls.
That list has formed the basis of a lawsuit, filed on October 15, that calls on California to sequester any ballots sent to those “likely non-citizens”, preventing them from being tallied as part of voting results.
The lawsuit is unfolding in the final days before Tuesday’s pivotal midterm elections, which will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local offices.
Trump has expressed fear that, if his Republican Party loses its majorities in the two chambers of Congress, he could be impeached.
The Republican leader also has a track record of spreading false information about elections, including that his defeat in the 2020 presidential race was the result of a “rigged” vote.
He has often targeted California in his criticism. The state – the most populous in the country – is considered a longtime left-wing stronghold. It will elect 52 seats to the 435-member House of Representatives in Tuesday’s elections.
Already, Trump has accused California of “cheating” in its June 2 primary elections, after several Republican candidates underperformed, including Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt.
Under the US Constitution’s Elections Clause, election administration falls solely to the states, though Congress may pass regulations governing voting.
Critics, including California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, have cited that fact in their rebuttal to Trump’s lawsuit.
All 50 states already prohibit non-citizen voting in federal elections and undertake measures to prevent voter fraud, which is considered exceedingly rare.
Other states that have received similar lists of “likely non-citizen” voters have also found significant errors in the Trump administration’s accounting. Nevada, for example, found that none of the names included on that list were non-citizen voters.
Such errors have raised concerns that eligible citizens would see their votes denied if the Trump administration wins its California lawsuit.
Still, the Trump administration has threatened state officials with prosecution over the potential for non-citizen voting.
It has also vigorously pursued its lawsuit through federal court. On Friday, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco rejected the complaint a second time, determining it unconstitutional.
“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the court majority wrote in its ruling.
In Saturday’s court filing, the data scientists from UCLA’s Voting Rights Project found that 8,880 names on the list were not listed anywhere in California’s current voter files, a proportion of 42 percent.
Many other names on the list were either confirmed as US citizens or may correspond to US citizens.
“This review proves, at least as a preponderance of the evidence, that demands of election officials under criminal and civil threats, endangers the voting rights of plaintiff CHIRLA’s members and clients,” the filing said.
It was co-signed by the Democratic candidate to succeed Newsom as governor, Xavier Becerra.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: Fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro é ‘discussão incontornável’ nos debates do G20, afirma analista internacional
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
O ministro das Relações Exteriores brasileiro, Mauro Vieira, participa nesta sexta-feira (30) de um encontro com o secretário do Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos, Marco Rubio, e com o chanceler argentino, Pablo Quirno, durante o G20, em Atlanta, na Geórgia (EUA). Está prevista uma conversa bilateral entre Vieira e Rubio.
A reunião acontece em um momento de tensionamento da relação entre os países. Os governos de Javier Milei e Donald Trump ajudaram Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) a fugir do país após derrota nas urnas.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Gustavo Menon, docente na Universidade Católica de Brasília (UCB) e no Prolam-USP, avalia que a reunião será marcada por um processo de esvaziamento de diversas pautas. “É uma cúpula conduzida pelos EUA a partir dessa atuação muito capitaneada pela nova administração de Trump. A título de referência, nessa reunião do G20 houve a descontinuidade de agendas importantes e uma série de restrições à delegação da África do Sul”, afirma.
“A pauta sobre a fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro aos EUA trata-se de uma discussão incontornável do ponto de vista das relações e dos diálogos que serão chefiados a partir dos próximos dias”, ressalta.
Menon também destaca que o contexto eleitoral brasileiro e a fuga de Flávio “agudizaram a tensão” de uma relação que já vinha sofrendo desgaste, diante da taxação de produtos brasileiros e outras sanções. “Estamos falando de pressões políticas a partir do Escudo das Américas, em que Marco Rubio se comporta como um verdadeiro xerife hemisférico. E essas pressões comerciais acabaram se conjugando com pressões políticas e militares, com a reformulação do plano de defesa dos EUA, em que eles voltam a conceber a América Latina como uma região de histórica influência”, avalia.
Nesse sentido, a vitória de Lula a partir da mobilização popular em defesa da democracia ganha outros contornos. “É uma resposta a esse avanço de projetos da extrema direita na região. A eleição brasileira é decisiva em nome da soberania, em nome da democracia na região”, defende.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: Nunes não teve compromisso com a democracia, diz vereadora sobre redução da frota de ônibus nas eleições
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
Uma Comissão Parlamentar de Inquérito (CPI) poderá ser aberta na Câmara dos Vereadores de São Paulo para investigar a intencionalidade do prefeito Ricardo Nunes (MDB) ao não respeitar a ordem de funcionamento total da frota de ônibus durante as eleições. Além da solicitação da CPI, foi protocolado um pedido de impeachment pela Bancada Feminista do Psol, que está em análise na Câmara.
O secretário municipal de Mobilidade Urbana e Transporte, Celso Jorge Caldeira, foi convidado para comparecer à Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) e responder questões referentes à falta de ônibus. Nunes admitiu que, no domingo (25), durante o segundo turno, 8 mil ônibus estavam em circulação. O número total da frota é de 12 mil.
Em entrevista ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, a covereadora Silvia Ferraro afirma que a situação é grave e que é preciso responsabilizar as pessoas que cometeram o “crime eleitoral” de impedir o direito ao voto. “Na nossa avaliação, o prefeito Ricardo Nunes tem responsabilidade, porque ele não se prestou a esse compromisso com a democracia. Ele agiu para favorecer o candidato dele, que era Flávio Bolsonaro. Nós já sabemos que os locais onde mais houve problemas com ônibus são regiões onde Lula teria mais votos. Há suspeita de que ele tenha agido de má-fé”, afirma.
Ferraro explica que, se ficar comprovado que Nunes retirou propositalmente os ônibus de circulação, ele poderá sofrer impeachment. “É um crime eleitoral e um crime contra a democracia. Isso que foi feito na cidade de São Paulo e também em Salvador não pode se repetir”, defende.
A vereadora explica que, neste momento, a Câmara analisa o pedido de impeachment e que, para instalação da CPI, serão necessárias 19 assinaturas. “Não será fácil, porque a base governista na Câmara age para proteger o prefeito e é maioria”, explica.

O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM, na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: BdF Entrevista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
O Congresso que tomará posse em 2027 contará com forte presença da extrema direita e deve ser uma pedra no sapato do quarto mandato do presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). Durante os anos de Lula 3, o presidente já precisou encarar alguns reveses. A tendência, contudo, é que esse tensionamento aumente, já que o PL, sigla que representa o bolsonarismo, elegeu 121 deputados e 29 senadores.
A fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) após perder as eleições, no entanto, pode modificar em alguma medida essa correlação de forças, já que a maioria dos quadros aliados desaprovou a atitude, em especial depois da carta golpista questionando o resultado do pleito.
Ao BdF Entrevista, a cientista política Daniela Constanzo afirma que, neste momento, a extrema direita está um pouco enfraquecida, impactada pelos acontecimentos e também porque os eleitos ainda não tomaram posse. Portanto, acredita que, tão logo o ano comece, isso poderá mudar.
“A oposição não tem poder de veto exatamente sozinha no Congresso, porque, pelas minhas contas, o bolsonarismo é 31% das cadeiras, mas ela tem um poder de veto muito importante no Senado, onde é metade das cadeiras”, pondera.
A analista destaca que, diante desse cenário, Lula já começou uma série de articulações com o Centrão, que teve uma leve redução de 50% para 45%, inclusive para pautar temas importantes antes de o ano terminar. “Quando ele foi eleito em 2022, ele tentou contornar o teto de gastos ainda em 2022, antes de tomar posse. Isso é importante porque o presidente chega com uma moral um pouco maior”, afirma.
De acordo com Constanzo, Lula não conseguirá fugir da dependência do Centrão para governar, e a concessão de ministérios a partidos da coalizão já não assegura a fidelidade irrestrita das bancadas no plenário. “O Centrão hoje tem as suas próprias emendas; as emendas são obrigatórias. Um ministério não significa tanto dinheiro, porque a maioria das despesas já é obrigatória do Executivo. Então acaba que o Congresso não tem tanto interesse em ter um ministério e já votar com o governo. Não adianta você dar um ministério e esperar que todos os votos daquele partido venham para você”, pontua, observando que o governo precisa negociar item por item. “Agora, cada pauta, você vai lá negociar com todo mundo. E o que isso significa? Que as pautas mais populares são mais aprovadas. A gente viu agora o fim da escala 6×1”, ressalta.
Em meio a esse cenário, o governo enfrentará algumas batalhas, como a aprovação da Tarifa Zero aos finais de semana, que é uma promessa de campanha, e as indicações de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), que precisam ser aprovadas pelo Senado. “A Tarifa Zero é um tema que vai ser muito disputado. Eu acho que só vai passar se tiver muita mobilização popular, como a gente viu na 6×1. Também tem a PEC da segurança, que o Lula também está querendo passar agora. Ele quer aproveitar esse momento, que é mais fácil de negociar e passar essa PEC, que também seria muito importante para o governo dele”, avalia.
Nesse sentido, Constanzo considera que o engajamento da sociedade nas discussões e a mobilização popular nas ruas terão papel de grande importância para garantir a governabilidade de Lula. “Eu acho que teve uma parte da população que saiu às ruas, puxada muito pelos jovens, e que também saiu às redes, vamos dizer assim. Teve essa mistura fundamental entre ruas e redes, que a gente viu acontecendo nesse segundo turno, que vai ser fundamental para o governo poder governar”, afirma. “O campo progressista aprendeu de novo que tem um poder de mobilização, e isso vai ser fundamental para poder pressionar no Congresso”, resume.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: Chanceler da Rússia diz que Zelensky precisará ir a Moscou se quiser se reunir com Putin
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
O ministro das Relações Exteriores da Rússia, Serguei Lavrov, afirmou nesta sexta-feira (30) que se o presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, quiser se reunir com o presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, ele terá que ir a Moscou.
“Se Zelensky quiser se encontrar com Putin, ele precisa vir a Moscou”, afirmou Lavrov, ao falar sobre a posição da Rússia sobre o local de possíveis conversas entre os dois líderes.
O ministro também acusou países europeus de tentarem interferir no processo de resolução do conflito ucraniano. Ele alegou que conversas telefônicas entre o presidente finlandês Alexander Stubb, o primeiro-ministro norueguês Jonas Gahr Støre e Putin causaram discórdia na Europa.
O ministro russo informou que entrou em contato com o secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio, em Atlanta.
De acordo com ele, sempre houve e sempre haverá problemas entre a Rússia e os Estados Unidos, mas Moscou acolhe com satisfação o interesse de Washington no diálogo.
Foi relatado que o chanceler russo e o secretário de Estado, Marco Rubio, discutiram a cooperação em fóruns multilaterais, incluindo a ONU, o G20 e a cúpula da APEC na China.
“Relações bilaterais e cooperação em fóruns multilaterais, incluindo a ONU, o G20 e a cúpula da APEC, que será realizada em breve, em novembro, em Shenzhen, na China”, disse o ministro em uma coletiva de imprensa.
A declaração aconteceu durante a reunião entre os ministros das Relações Exteriores do G20, que serve como preparação da cúpula do G20 entre chefes de Estado, prevista acontecer em Miami, em dezembro.
O chanceler russo afirmou também que Moscou apoia o objetivo dos Estados Unidos de despolitizar ao máximo as discussões no G20.
Lavrov se reúne com chanceler do Japão pela primeira vez em 5 anos
O ministro das Relações Exteriores da Rússia manteve conversações com o chanceler japonês pela primeira vez em cinco anos. De acordo com serviço de imprensa da diplomacia russa, a conversa entre Serguei Lavrov e Toshimitsu Motegi ocorreu a pedido do Japão e serviu para discutir as relações bilaterais entre os dois países.
“O lado russo enfatizou que, para retomar um diálogo interestatal pleno, Tóquio deve abandonar sua postura hostil”, diz o comunicado da chancelaria russa.
A última vez que os ministros das Relações Exteriores da Rússia e do Japão se reuniram pessoalmente foi em setembro de 2021, à margem da Assembleia Geral da ONU em Nova York.

Sculptor Alma Allen‘s contributions to this year’s US Pavilion at the Venice Biennale could be stranded in Italy due to a funding shortfall. Pavilion Commissioner Jenni Parido issued a call to donors seeking funds to cover the costs of dismantling and shipping the roughly thirty works comprising Allen’s exhibition “Call Me the Breeze,” after her nonprofit, the American Arts Conservancy (AAC), raised only $1.4 million of the necessary $2.5 million needed.
Parido told potential donors in a letter viewed by the Times, that the funding need was “urgent.” The Biennale is set to close on November 22, after which the sculptures’ fate is uncertain, as the US Pavilion has no storage space, and the Guggenheim Foundation, which owns the building, is unable to accommodate them. Though the State Department covered a fraction of the costs of mounting the pavilion, a spokesperson told the paper it was not responsible for fundraising and would “have no further comments regarding the 2026 Venice Biennale.”
The situation is the latest bump in what has been a rocky road for the US Pavilion, beginning with the ousting of the originally selected artist and curator, and continuing with the selection by the State Department of AAC founder Parido, previously the owner of a Tampa, Florida, pet-food store, as commissioner. Jeffrey Uslip, the director of a gallery in Bellport, Long Island, and a board member of the AAC, was tapped to curate the pavilion. Uslip subsequently approached Allen, an American sculptor living in Mexico, to produce an exhibition. Allen told the Times that neither Parido nor Uslip ever visited his studio to see his work before it was shipped over to Italy, and that by the time the Biennale opened to the public, he and Uslip were no longer speaking.
Allen told the Times he was unaware of the AAC’s funding issues. “I received only reimbursement for travel and my Airbnb, which was cheap,” he said in a statement.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: No G20, chanceleres dos EUA e Brasil se encontram pela primeira vez após fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Mauro Vieira, e o secretário de Estado dos Estados Unidos, Marco Rubio, tiveram um breve encontro nesta sexta-feira (30), durante a Cúpula de Chanceleres do G20 em Atlanta, no estado da Geórgia, nos Estados Unidos, e marcaram uma reunião bilateral para dezembro, às vésperas da reunião com os chefes de Estado do grupo.
É o primeiro encontro após o resultado das eleições, em meio às tensões diplomáticas entre Brasil e Estados Unidos pela demora de reconhecimento oficial da vitória do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva e do tratamento protetivo ao candidato derrotado do segundo turno, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), que fugiu.
O chanceler brasileiro e o secretário de Estado estadunidense conversaram rapidamente, após apertarem as mãos, durante a recepção de boas-vindas à Reunião de Ministros das Relações Exteriores do G20.
O empresário e advogado Simón Levy, aliado do presidente Donald Trump, disse que Rubio ajudou a planejar a fuga do bolsonarista. Flávio recebeu autorização do governo americano para permanecer por um ano no país.
O Itamaraty não solicitou um encontro reservado com Rubio. Segundo o g1, a diplomacia brasileira avalia que o caso do ex-candidato à Presidência deve ser tratado na esfera jurídica, após a apuração dos fatos.
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, chegou a insinuar, sem provas, que houve fraude nas eleições. Depois disse que falará com Lula. Questionado sobre quem, para ele, havia vencido as eleições no Brasil, ele respondeu que “não quero comentar isso agora”.
Durante o G20, Mauro Vieira também se reuniu com o chanceler indiano, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, e tinha encontros previstos com o representante britânico Ed Miliband e o alemão Johann Wadephul.
O evento, que reúne ministros das Relações Exteriores das maiores economias do mundo, é presidido por Rubio e prepara para a cúpula de líderes do bloco, que vai reunir chefes de Estado em dezembro. Tanto Trump quanto Lula são esperados na reunião.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: ‘As crianças em Gaza estão com a sua infância roubada’, alerta presidente da Fepal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
Setenta por cento das vítimas fatais do genocídio praticado por Israel em Gaza são mulheres e crianças. É o que aponta levantamento do Alto Comissariado das Nações Unidas para os Direitos Humanos.
Como é a vida das crianças hoje em Gaza? Com o massacre, uma infância sem escola sai às ruas para prestar pequenos serviços em troca de algum dinheiro para a família. É seu modo de tentar sobreviver no território destroçado.
Agora, com o mote “Toda criança tem o direito de ser criança”, está sendo lançada a campanha “A solidariedade entra em campo”, uma iniciativa da Associação dos Juízes e Juízas pela Democracia (AJD), com apoio da Federação Árabe-Palestina do Brasil (Fepal), do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST) e do Brasil de Fato. Sua meta é arrecadar 500 bolas de futebol para meninos e meninas palestinas.
Fátima Ali e Muna Ali Hajoj, as entrevistadas do podcast, descrevem o drama vivido em Gaza e nas prisões de Israel que, somente agora, começa a sensibilizar as lideranças do Ocidente. Enquanto isso, no Brasil, a mídia empresarial nega ou ameniza a limpeza étnica levada a cabo pelo governo de Benjamin Netanyahu e que já dura três longos anos.
O podcast De Fato é uma produção do Brasil de Fato RS em parceria com o SindBancários de Porto Alegre e Região.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: Eleições em Israel: ‘O que está em jogo é reconhecer a diversidade interna do país’, afirma jornalista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: Gabriela Carvalho
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
O primeiro-ministro de Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, foi derrotado nas urnas e perdeu a maioria do Parlamento. O grupo formado pelo Likud e seus aliados de direita, extrema direita e partidos religiosos conquistou 53 cadeiras, oito abaixo das 61 necessárias para governar. A oposição, liderada pelo ex-general Gadi Eisenkot, obteve 48.
Os partidos árabes conquistaram 19 das 120 cadeiras do Knesset, quase o dobro das dez obtidas em 2022. Não há, assim, maioria para definir o próximo governo. Netanyahu afirmou, sem apresentar provas, de que houve fraude nas urnas.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, a jornalista Flávia Gianini, especializada em política e economia internacional, destaca a gravidade das declarações de Netanyahu, que geram instabilidade ao processo eleitoral.
“A gente poderia fazer um paralelo de que fazer a contestação das eleições em Israel é o mesmo que aconteceu com Dilma aqui no Brasil, que acabou culminando com o impeachment dela. Mas acaba sendo um pouco mais profunda essa questão”, afirma.
Segundo a jornalista, a discussão sobre quem vai governar Israel pelos próximos anos passou a envolver a legitimidade da participação política dos cidadãos árabes-israelenses. “Quando Netanyahu contesta e acusa, sem provas, a corrupção dos partidos árabes, ele cria uma dificuldade na formação de maioria até pelo Eisenkot. Ele está questionando o processo democrático e a participação política dos árabes-israelenses”, explica.
Por outro lado, Gianini destaca o aumento da participação política de pouco mais de 40% para quase 80% entre os cidadãos árabes que moram em Gaza. “Essa organização chegou a 19 cadeiras, mas, para constituir maioria, será necessário negociar com esses partidos”, reforça, ao mencionar que o caminho para derrotar Netanyahu será o da coalizão. “Os eleitores árabes perceberam que a participação pode ter impactos concretos.”
A jornalista conta que “Eisenkot está disposto a negociar sobre as questões de segurança e os erros cometidos em 7 de outubro de 2023”, contudo, há limites e alguma resistência a negociar com países árabes, já que, embora oposição a Netanyahu, ele é sionista. “O único democrata progressista é Yair Golan”, reforça Flávia Gianini.
“O que está em jogo é bem mais amplo do que a disputa entre Netanyahu e Eisenkot. É a capacidade de Israel de reconhecer a diversidade interna e garantir que a cidadania política não seja condicionada à origem étnica e religiosa”, defende. “Eles estão descentralizando a discussão sobre como formar o governo para qual é a importância dos partidos árabes e o peso da participação árabe-israelense que vive em Israel e, principalmente, em Gaza”, frisa.
Na avaliação de Gianini, a situação de Netanyahu é muto delicada, já que ele passa por investigação de corrupção e erros de segurança com relação ao Nakba. “E gente nem vai falar sobre os crimes de guerra. Então ele não tem como recuar. Ele vai questionar as eleições”, ressalta.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Lula 4, com mais democracia e direitos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: A Cidade é Nossa
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
As urnas deram um recado contundente no último dia 25 de outubro, reelegendo Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva com mais de 64 milhões de votos para um inédito quarto mandato presidencial. Foi, talvez, a reviravolta política mais surpreendente da história recente do país: depois de passar 580 dias preso, de ter todas as condenações anuladas e retornar à Presidência da República, Lula protagonizou uma façanha política ao reverter o resultado de uma eleição em apenas três semanas, algo sem precedentes na história do Brasil, culminando em uma vitória acachapante.
Inúmeras análises foram publicadas a respeito dessas eleições nos últimos dias. Portanto, este texto não busca ser apenas mais uma delas. Nosso intuito é trazer um olhar voltado para o que está por vir. Mas, para isso, antes, precisamos nos deter sobre alguns dados eleitorais e fatos importantes deste segundo turno.
A campanha ganhou força de massas já nos primeiros dias, com pessoas se auto-organizando para convencer eleitores indecisos e aqueles que se abstiveram no primeiro turno. Cabe destacar a importância das grandes regiões metropolitanas, como Belém, Belo Horizonte, Brasília, Fortaleza, Manaus, Porto Alegre, Recife, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador e São Paulo, que concentraram parte significativa dos votos conquistados por Lula no segundo turno.
Além disso, o chamado “Exército do Lula” teve papel fundamental na campanha e representou uma das grandes novidades da disputa nas redes sociais. A capacidade de mobilização, articulação e produção de conteúdo por milhares de apoiadores demonstrou a força da organização popular no ambiente digital. Não por acaso, essa atuação foi alvo de sucessivas ameaças de censura por parte do ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, presidente do TSE. Essa experiência deixa uma lição importante para o governo Lula 4 e a esquerda brasileira: a comunicação não pode se limitar aos canais institucionais nem ficar refém da lógica da grande mídia. É preciso disputar a narrativa, dialogar diretamente com a população e fortalecer os canais de comunicação com o povo. O próprio presidente já sinalizou essa intenção ao afirmar que pretende promover uma mudança radical na comunicação do governo, passando a falar diretamente com as pessoas.
Outro fato relevante desta campanha de segundo turno foi o governo ter conseguido pautar, no Senado, a votação da PEC 221/2019, que inseriu na Constituição Federal (EC 141) o fim da escala 6×1, com a redução da jornada de trabalho de 44 para 40 horas semanais. Essa foi a maior conquista de direitos desde a promulgação da Constituição Federal de 1988, o que diz muito sobre a força da classe trabalhadora quando está unificada.
Ainda durante a campanha presidencial, no dia 21 de outubro, o presidente Lula sancionou o Prospera MEI, pacote de medidas que beneficiará até 17,6 milhões de pessoas que trabalham por conta própria com CNPJ. Na mesma data, o governo encaminhou ao Congresso a PEC da Tarifa Zero, que propõe a gratuidade no transporte público aos finais de semana. A medida pode beneficiar pelo menos 25 milhões de pessoas, considerando os dados de passageiros pagantes de 2022.
Vencida a batalha eleitoral, está em jogo agora a definição das medidas que serão adotadas pelo novo governo. Se lembrarmos bem, essa movimentação já deve começar nos dois meses finais do atual governo, com o processo de transição. E a pressão pela adoção de medidas impopulares será grande, como já demonstram os economistas alinhados ao mercado financeiro, que propõem ajustes de até R$ 450 bilhões nas contas públicas.
Para o povo brasileiro, que sobrevive do próprio trabalho e vive a economia real, e não dessa lorota fiscalista, a redução do custo de vida, considerando os aluguéis, o transporte público e os preços dos alimentos, combinada com o aumento do poder de compra, a geração de empregos e a elevação da renda do trabalho, constitui um conjunto de medidas fundamentais para a manutenção da vida digna. Para que isso aconteça, vamos ter que cobrar mais caro do andar de cima e manter a mobilização nas ruas e nas redes para pressionar o Congresso Nacional a aprovar essas medidas.
Portanto, a vitória eleitoral de Lula neste segundo turno abre um novo ciclo de possibilidades para a classe trabalhadora brasileira. Mas somente nossa capacidade de mobilização de massas e de organização de base poderá determinar nossa capacidade de moldar o futuro de acordo com os interesses da maioria.
* Pablo Bandeira é advogado popular e membro da coordenação nacional do MTD.
