https://taz.de/Quinn-Slobodian-ueber-Tru.title: Quinn Slobodian über Trump und Big Tech: „Wir müssen herausfinden, was wir stattdessen wollen“
https://taz.de/Quinn-Slobodian-ueber-Tru.author: Sebastian Moll
https://taz.de/Quinn-Slobodian-ueber-Tru.text:
Quinn Slobodian über Trump und Big Tech: „Wir müssen herausfinden, was wir stattdessen wollen“
Die US-Tech-Giganten sind mit dem MAGA-Staat verschmolzen. Doch diese Entwicklung könnte sich bald wieder umkehren, sagt der Wissenschaftler Quinn Slobodian.
taz: Herr Slobodian, Elon Musk hat den republikanischen Wahlkampf für die Midterms mit mehr als 400 Millionen Dollar unterstützt. Was verspricht er sich davon?
Quinn Slobodian: Ungünstige Gesetze und Vorschriften können das Geschäftsmodell von SpaceX erheblich beeinträchtigen. Das gilt beispielsweise für Genehmigungen von Raketenstarts, für die Erlaubnis, weitere Satelliten in niedrigeren Erdumlaufbahnen zu platzieren, für die Vergabe von Frequenzlizenzen oder für Musks Mobilfunkpläne. Darüber hinaus vertritt er immer wieder die Überzeugung, die Demokratische Partei sei von woken Sozialisten übernommen worden, die den Fortschritt der Zivilisation aufhalten würden – so, wie Musk diesen Fortschritt versteht.
ist Professor für Geschichte an der Boston University. Zu seinen bekanntesten Büchern gehören „Crack Up Capitalism“, eine Analyse des postneoliberalen Globalismus, und „Muskism“, ein Annäherungsversuch an die globale Wirtschaftsordnung im Zeitalter der Technologie-Giganten.
taz: Welche dieser beiden Erklärungen trifft seine tatsächlichen Motive besser?
Slobodian: Man kann das nicht voneinander trennen. Musk ist kein Intellektueller, sondern ein Kapitalist. Seine geschäftlichen Interessen sind zugleich seine geistigen. Ich glaube nicht, dass Musk lügt, wenn er seine Sorgen über das sogenannte „Woke-Mind-Virus“ äußert. Aber das liegt daran, dass er in dieser Art von Politik seine wirtschaftlichen Interessen gefährdet sieht.
taz: Wäre denn das Gesamtsystem des Muskismus, das Sie auch als „Symbiotischen Staat“ bezeichnen, gefährdet, wenn die Demokraten bei den Zwischenwahlen den Senat oder das Repräsentantenhaus zurückerobern?
Slobodian: SpaceX und Tesla gehören zu den zehn größten Unternehmen am US-Aktienmarkt. Die Gesundheit dieses Marktes hängt davon ab, dass Investoren Unternehmen wie die von Musk als vertrauenswürdige Anlageziele betrachten. Wenn die Demokraten gegen Musk vorgehen wollen – und es sieht so aus, als wollten sie das –, müssten sie deshalb sehr gezielt vorgehen und anderen Unternehmen glaubhaft versichern, dass sie nicht als Nächstes an der Reihe sind.
taz: Aber dann wäre das System, das Sie als Muskismus bezeichnen, doch nicht verändert?
Slobodian: Das stimmt. Ich verwende den Begriff Muskismus so, wie andere den Begriff Fordismus verwendet haben. Es geht um ein System der Gewinnerzielung und um die gesellschaftlichen Strukturen, die Zustimmung zu diesem System herstellen. Die Konzentration wirtschaftlicher Macht ist nicht auf Musk beschränkt. Viele der grundlegenden Dynamiken, die die Tech-Branche 2024 in die Arme von MAGA getrieben haben, bestehen weiterhin. Und ich habe bislang keine überzeugende Erklärung von demokratischen Politikern gehört, wie sie erreichen wollen, was ihnen schon damals nicht gelungen ist.
taz: Sie glauben also, dass das der symbiotische Staat – diese enge Verbindung zwischen Staat und Tech-Unternehmen – auf absehbare Zeit bestehen bleiben wird?
Slobodian: So weit würde ich nicht gehen. Der Begriff beschreibt den gegenwärtigen Zustand. Unter der Trump-Regierung wird diese Verbindung vertieft und beschleunigt. Aber es gibt durchaus Möglichkeiten, die US-Wirtschaft relativ schnell wieder breiter aufzustellen. Die Technologiebranche ist schließlich nicht die einzige Stärke der USA. Eine vernünftige demokratische Regierung würde versuchen, Investitionen wieder stärker in andere Bereiche zu lenken: in erneuerbare Energien, aber auch in traditionelle amerikanische Stärken wie Forschung und Entwicklung.
taz: Sie haben den wachsenden Unmut in der Bevölkerung erwähnt. Glauben Sie, dass die Bevölkerung inzwischen verstanden hat, wie dieses System der symbiotischen Verbindung von Staat und Technologieunternehmen funktioniert und welche Macht die großen Tech-Konzerne besitzen?
Slobodian: Ich denke schon. Als die Branche sich Ende 2022 mit der Einführung von ChatGPT auf das neue Wachstumsversprechen der generativen KI konzentrierte, änderte sich praktisch alles. Die Unternehmen konnten sich nicht mehr einfach auf Distanz zur Bundesregierung halten, so wie sie sich das in der Ära von Web 2.0 – der Ära der Plattformen – vorgestellt hatten.
taz: Wegen des enormen Bedarfes an Datenzentren.
Slobodian: Genau. Für die neue Entwicklung brauchen sie große Flächen, enorme Wassermengen, günstige Energie und die Beseitigung regulatorischer Hindernisse. In manchen Schätzungen ist von Investitionen in Höhe von bis zu 10 Billionen Dollar innerhalb des nächsten Jahrzehnts die Rede. So ein historisch beispielloses Vorhaben lässt sich nicht umsetzen, ohne dass die Bevölkerung darauf aufmerksam wird. Menschen aus unterschiedlichen politischen Lagern fragen sich: Was zum Teufel passiert hier eigentlich? Und was soll für mich dabei herausspringen? Die Unternehmen haben keine überzeugende Antwort darauf.
taz: Die Ausbreitung der Rechenzentren hat die Macht dieser symbiotischen Verbindung von Staat und Wirtschaft für die Menschen konkret erfahrbar gemacht, deshalb richtet sich ihr Ärger gegen das gesamte System?
Slobodian: Bislang richtet sich der Ärger der Menschen vor allem gegen die gewählten Politiker, weil sie den Ausbau zulassen.
taz: Sie sprechen in Ihrem Buch von den drei Rs, die dazu beitragen könnten, das System zu verändern – Regulation, Replacement (Ersetzung) und Reimagination. Das Wichtigste davon sei die „Reimagination“, also die Fähigkeit, sich etwas grundlegend Neues vorzustellen. Wie könnte man das gegenwärtige System neu denken?
Slobodian: Nehmen wir künstliche Intelligenz. Es werden gewaltige Summen in der Hoffnung ausgegeben, Arbeitskräfte einzusparen, was für diejenigen, die über die entsprechenden Werkzeuge verfügen, äußerst profitabel ist. Aber man kann sich – und solche Anwendungen existieren bereits – wesentlich bescheidenere Formen derselben Technologie vorstellen, die für gesellschaftlich produktive Zwecke eingesetzt werden.
taz: Zum Beispiel?
Slobodian: Ein Beispiel ist die Forschung, die mit dem Nobelpreis für Chemie ausgezeichnet wurde. Da wurde ein Modell entwickelt, das die unterschiedlichen Formen vorhersagen kann, die Proteine annehmen können. Das könnte wissenschaftliche Durchbrüche und die Entwicklung neuer Behandlungsmethoden für Krankheiten ermöglichen.
taz: Es ginge also darum, die Technologie für gemeinnützige Dinge und echten Fortschritt einzusetzen.
Slobodian: Ich halte es für gefährlich, wenn sich um technologische Neuerungen ein grundsätzliches Stigma als Arbeitsplatzkiller entwickelt. Disruptive Technologien erfordern eine neue gesellschaftliche Verständigung darüber, wie ihre Folgen verteilt und ausgeglichen werden. Es braucht neue Kompromisse, die auch die betroffenen Bevölkerungsgruppen berücksichtigen. Man muss den Menschen das Gefühl geben, dass sie an diesem Prozess beteiligt sind und ihn mitgestalten können.
taz: Das größte Problem am Muskismus ist also, dass die großen gesellschaftlichen Umwandlungen undemokratisch vorangetrieben werden?
Slobodian: Ja, das ist der Kern des Problems. Die Menschen müssen selbst entscheiden können, was in ihrem Leben wichtig ist und was nicht.
taz: In gewisser Weise geht es also darum, in diesem neuen technologischen Umfeld ein weniger zynisches, stärker am Menschen orientiertes Leben zu ermöglichen?
Slobodian: Die Entwicklung zwingt uns dazu, grundlegende Kategorien unseres gesellschaftlichen Lebens neu zu hinterfragen. Warum sollten wir uns eigentlich nicht darüber freuen, von Arbeit befreit zu werden? Aber das wäre für eine linke Zukunftsvision natürlich zu kurz gedacht. Es geht auch um die Würde der Arbeit. Insofern könnte eine neue Vorstellung von Gesellschaft tatsächlich darin bestehen, die Bedeutung von Arbeit neu zu denken. Für solche Überlegungen sollten wir offen sein.

Slobodian: Diese Verweigerung ist eine Chance. Sie ist nicht das Ende eines politischen Prozesses, sondern dessen Anfang. Bewegungen können entstehen, weil Menschen mit unterschiedlichen Hintergründen einen gemeinsamen Gegner erkennen und sich zunächst schlicht weigern, dessen Vorstellungen zu akzeptieren. https://taz.de/Praemenstruelle-dysphoris.title: Prämenstruelle dysphorische Störung: Zehn Jahre ohne Diagnose
https://taz.de/Praemenstruelle-dysphoris.author: Hannah Marlene Göschel
https://taz.de/Praemenstruelle-dysphoris.text:
Prämenstruelle dysphorische Störung: Zehn Jahre ohne Diagnose
Jeden Monat ist Leo wieder wütend, fühlt sich leer und muss ständig weinen. Sie versteht nicht, warum. Bis sie die Diagnose PMDS bekommt.
Leo fühlt sich wie ausgetauscht. Ihr inneres Gleichgewicht ist aus den Fugen geraten – mal wieder. Ein Gefühl, das sich jeden Monat von Neuem einstellt, immer in der Phase nach ihrem Eisprung und vor der Menstruation. In dieser Zeit ist Leo, die mit ihrem vollen Namen und ihrer Krankheitsgeschichte nicht in der Öffentlichkeit stehen will, oft angespannt. Sie ist wütend auf die Welt, fühlt sich leer, leidet unter Schlafstörungen.
In diesen zwei Wochen ihres Zyklus müsse sie ständig weinen und könne schlechter mit Konflikten umgehen, erzählt die 30-jährige Sozialpädagogin. Das spürt sie bis in jede Ecke ihres Alltags. „Manchmal kann ich wegen der Weinkrämpfe gar nicht arbeiten oder gehe wegen der starken Reizbarkeit viel mehr an die Decke, wenn ich mit meinem Freund streite“, sagt Leo. Seit sie 15 Jahre alt ist, kämpft Leo mit den Symptomen. Mittlerweile kennt sie den Grund: Leo hat PMDS – die prämenstruelle dysphorische Störung. Doch bis sie zu ihrer Diagnose kam, musste knapp ein Jahrzehnt vergehen.
Lange hatten viele Mediziner:innen die Störung nicht auf dem Schirm. Dabei sind Studien zufolge etwa 3 bis 8 Prozent aller menstruierenden Personen von PMDS betroffen. In Deutschland entspricht das etwa 450.000 bis 1,2 Millionen Menschen. Erst in den letzten Jahren ist Frauengesundheit stärker in den Fokus gerückt und mit ihr Untersuchungen zum Einfluss hormoneller Schwankungen auf den Körper sowie die Psyche. Die Forschung steht noch am Anfang.
Viele Ärzte nehmen die Symptome nicht ernst
Als Leo erzählt, dass sie so lange nicht wusste, was jeden Monat in ihr geschieht, schüttelt sie wütend den Kopf. Früher habe sie gedacht, sie hätte eine bipolare Störung. „Weil das immer so gewechselt hat. Mir ging es zwei Wochen super und dann hatte ich wieder diese Zeit, in der sich alles leer angefühlt hat oder ich total aggro war.“ Auf die Möglichkeit, PMDS zu haben, stößt sie erstmals über eine Webseite, die über das Syndrom aufklärt. „Ich habe die Symptome gelesen und gedacht: Das bin doch ich!“ Leo wendet sich an das Berliner Zentrum für Seelische Frauengesundheit, wo sie mit 25 endlich ihre Diagnose erhält.
Viele Patient:innen, die zu Stefanie Krüger kommen, haben solch einen langen Weg bis zu ihrer Diagnose hinter sich. Die Gynäkologin arbeitet in dem Berliner Zentrum. Es ist eines der wenigen, das sich auf hormonell bedingte psychische Veränderungen spezialisiert hat. Von vielen Ärzten werde die Erkrankung nicht ernst genommen. Viele ihrer Patientinnen hätten immer wieder gesagt bekommen: „Stell dich nicht so an“ oder „Da muss man durch als Frau, solche Symptome haben ja viele“. Zudem waren die Diagnosewerkzeuge schwach, die Erkrankung war also lange auch gar nicht offiziell gelistet.
Erst 2021 wurde die Störung in das aktuelle Klassifikationssystem für Krankheiten, das International Classification-System of Diseases (ICD-11), aufgenommen – als gynäkologische Erkrankung. „Die Symptome wie erhöhte Reizbarkeit, Schlafstörungen, Depressivität bis hin zur Suizidalität sind aber nun einmal psychisch“, erklärt Krüger.
Das Bewusstsein steigt
Welche Fachrichtung ist also verantwortlich? Die Frage ist nicht ganz leicht zu beantworten und stellt sich für mehrere Syndrome, bei der hormonelle Veränderungen, andere Organe beeinflussen. Zu lange lag die Zuständigkeit lediglich bei der Gynäkologie, interdisziplinäre Zusammenarbeit mit der für Hormone zuständigen Endokrinologie kam zu kurz. Generell wurden Studien und Forschung zu oft an westlichen Männern als Maß aller Dinge ausgerichtet.
Das ändert sich gerade: „Es gibt mehr Forschende, die sich mit Frauengesundheit beschäftigen, und auch mehr Gelder“, sagt Birgit Derntl, Leiterin der Arbeitsgruppe Psychische Gesundheit und Gehirnfunktion von Frauen an der Universität Tübingen. Auch das Forschungsministerium hat zuletzt verstärkt Forschungsprojekte zu geschlechtsspezifischen Themen gefördert, wie in diesem Jahr zu den Wechseljahren.
Die Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG), einer der größten Geldgeber hierzulande, zieht mit. Seit 2020 müssen Forschungsanträge die Relevanz des Geschlechts für das jeweilige Vorhaben darlegen. „Mittlerweile gibt es unter anderem deshalb mehr Bewusstsein für die Relevanz des Geschlechts unter Forschenden“, sagt die Psychologin.
Trotzdem gibt es auch heute noch Studien, bei denen das Geschlecht nicht erfasst oder in der Analyse nicht berücksichtigt wird. Ein Aufwärtstrend mit Abstrichen also. „Es ist eher ein Hinterherhinken, weil geschlechtssensible Forschung so lange vernachlässigt wurde“, sagt Derntl.
Ursachen ungeklärt
Die Ursachen von PMDS sind weitgehend ungeklärt. Klar ist jedoch, dass Leos Symptome daher kommen, dass das Gehirn von PMDS-Erkrankten Schwierigkeiten hat, sich an die monatliche Hormonschwankung anzupassen. Dabei sind frühe traumatische Erfahrungen einer von vielen Risikofaktoren. Auch nach großen hormonellen Veränderungen wie bei einer Schwangerschaft kann eine PMDS entstehen. Stress spielt ebenfalls eine Rolle; er verstärkt die Symptomatik, ist aber kein Auslöser.
Maria Kühne, Neurowissenschaftlerin an der Universität Magdeburg, forscht zu den Ursachen und zu Behandlungsmöglichkeiten von PMDS. Sie sagt: „Es gibt einige Faktoren im Nervensystem Betroffener, die zwar nicht alleinige Ursache sind, aber mit der PMDS-Symptomatik zusammenhängen.“ Eine wichtige Rolle spiele Allopregnanolon, das normalerweise beruhigend wirkt. Es ist ein Abbauprodukt des Hormons Progesteron, das nach dem Eisprung gebildet wird. Bei PMDS passe sich das Nervensystem weniger gut an die wechselnde Konzentration des Abbauprodukts an.
Auch das Serotoninsystem sei verändert. Serotonin ist ein Botenstoff im Gehirn, der unter anderem an der Regulation von Stimmung, Emotion, Schlaf und Wohlbefinden beteiligt ist. „Bei Betroffenen scheint mehr Serotonin aus dem Raum zwischen den Nervenzellen zurücktransportiert zu werden“, sagt Kühne. Außerdem funktioniere die Emotionsregulation in der zweiten Zyklushälfte weniger gut.
In Studien hat man die Gehirnaktivität untersucht und für verschiedene Bereiche Abweichungen festgestellt. „Dabei hat man gesehen, dass teilweise die Amygdala, das Emotionszentrum im Gehirn, überaktiv ist“, sagt Kühne. „Und der präfrontale Kortex, der dieses Emotionszentrum normalerweise herunterreguliert, macht das möglicherweise nicht genug.“ Das könne die erhöhte Reizbarkeit erklären.
Die extreme Erschöpfung, die viele PMDS-Betroffene erleben, hängt laut Kühne unter anderem mit einer veränderten Immunreaktion zusammen. „Marker im Immunsystem, die dem Körper signalisieren ‚Du bist krank. Du bleibst im Bett!‘ könnten bei PMDS verstärkt aktiviert sein“, sagt sie.
Behandlung für Betroffene
Weil das Gehirn bei PMDS nicht gut auf die hormonellen Schwankungen in der zweiten Zyklushälfte reagieren kann, sollen Betroffene ihren Lebensstil anpassen. Etwa indem sie in ihrer Ernährung auf alles verzichten, was hormonelle Schwankungen verstärken könnte. Dazu gehört zum Beispiel rotes Fleisch, das den Abbau von überschüssigem Östrogen verhindern kann. Auch Cardiotraining lindert die Symptome. Zu den medikamentösen Behandlungsmöglichkeiten gehören die Pille, Progesteron und Antidepressiva – Letztere sorgen für mehr verfügbares Serotonin. PMDS ist zwar nicht heilbar, aber bis zur Symptomfreiheit behandelbar.
Kühne forscht derzeit auch an einer neuen Behandlungsmöglichkeit. Bei dieser wird der Vagusnerv stimuliert, und zwar über Elektroden, die mit einer hörgerätähnlichen Konstruktion am Ohr befestigt werden. „Der Vagusnerv macht viel in Körper und Gehirn“, sagt Kühne. Er habe Einfluss auf das Emotionszentrum, auf die Immunreaktion, auf den Parasympathikus, das „Erholungssystem“ des Körpers. Die Forschung dazu steckt laut Kühne zwar noch in den Kinderschuhen. „Aber es gibt erste Hinweise darauf, dass PMDS-Symptome mit der Methode möglicherweise gelindert werden können.“ Und das, ohne die Pille oder Antidepressiva nehmen zu müssen, die Nebenwirkungen haben.
Zurzeit können die Kosten für eine Behandlung von PMDS nur über Umwege von gesetzlichen Krankenkassen übernommen werden. Denn PMDS steht nicht im ICD-10, und das neue Klassifikationssystem ICD-11 wird im deutschen Gesundheitssystem noch nicht angewandt.
Wie schwierig die Kostenübernahme teilweise ist, erlebt Stefanie Krüger ständig bei ihrer Arbeit im Berliner Zentrum. Oft müsse die Gynäkologin mit den Krankenkassen diskutieren, ob eine Behandlung nun übernommen werde. Antidepressiva würden meistens übernommen werden, aber bei der Pille hieße es oft, es ginge um Verhütung, „das sei ein Lifestyle-Präparat und kein Medikament“. Krüger sieht darin eine Stigmatisierung von PMDS im Gesundheitssystem.
Die Symptome einer PMDS und fehlende Unterstützung seien „eine ganz teuflische Kombination“, sagt Krüger. Eine Kombination, die auch das Risiko für andere psychische Erkrankungen erhöht. Etwa 20 Prozent der Betroffenen leiden auch an einer anderen psychischen Erkrankung, wie Depressionen, Panikstörungen oder auch ADHS. Auch Leo erzählt, dass sie eine Zeit lang unter Panikattacken gelitten hat.
Mithilfe von Psychotherapie hat Leo gelernt, besser mit den Symptomen umzugehen. Weil sich alles extremer anfühlt, muss sie mehr reflektieren – das habe auch etwas Gutes. Sie versucht herauszufinden: „Wo bin ich gestresst? Warum ist das gerade so stark? Was habe ich anders gemacht als sonst?“
Eine Behandlungsmethode, die ihr richtig gut hilft, hat sie aber noch nicht gefunden – und wünscht sich das sehr. „Ich erhoffe mir einfach bessere Hilfe für Betroffene“, sagt sie. Aus dem Grund hat sie dieses Jahr auch selbst angefangen, auf Instagram über das Syndrom aufzuklären. „Damit die eben nicht wie ich zehn Jahre lang denken, dass sie falsch sind.“ Die ersten Schritte dafür sind getan.

Neuer Substack-Boom: Wie eine Überdosis Brokkoli
In Deutschland gibt es eine neue Welle von Substack-Newslettern. Die sorgen wie das Gemüse für erfreuliche Abwechslung im sonst so tristen Mailordner.
Ich kann mich nicht erinnern, wann ich das letzte Mal eine persönliche Mail bekommen habe. In meinem privaten Mailordner sammeln sich Rechnungen, Werbung und Google Alerts.
Doch seit ein paar Jahren landen wieder erfreulichere Nachrichten darin. Tipps, welche Sachbücher ich lesen sollte, ein philosophisches Essay zu romantischer Liebe oder ein Rant gegen Promis, die statt Musik Parfüms auf den Markt bringen. Die interessanten Mails habe ich dem Substack-Boom zu verdanken.
Eine Plattform, über die Autor:innen ihre Newsletter (kostenlos oder gegen Bezahlung) verschicken können. Mittlerweile gibt’s auch eine App mit News-Feed, in dem sich Rezepte für Kürbissuppen an Urlaubsfotos und Gemälde ungesehener Künstlerinnen reihen. Und obwohl auch Rechte und Trolls die Plattform für sich entdeckt haben, ist es trotzdem noch ein netteres Instagram. Mit persönlichem Touch – aber ohne nervige Werbung.
Oder wie ein Substacker treffend schrieb: „Doomscrolling substack feels like overdosing on broccoli“. Die App hinterlässt einen also nicht so negativ wie jegliche Meta-Plattformen, sondern mit einem Gefühl, man hätte gerade etwas Schönes, vielleicht sogar Inspirierendes gesehen.
Zwischen Hobby und sechsstellig
Und auch wenn die meisten Texte keine journalistischen Standards erfüllen, entdecken die Autor:innen oft schneller Trends und gesellschaftliche Entwicklungen als der gemeine Journalist.
Bislang dominieren US-Amerikaner:innen die Plattform, doch auch in Deutschland setzt sich die Plattform immer stärker durch. In den letzten Wochen sind die Autorin Alice Hasters „In Between Things“, der Lektor Florian Kessler oder die Autor:in Hengameh Yaghoobifarah mit „Habibitus“ dazugekommen.
Dass der Trend bald aufhört und mein Postfach wieder nur aus Rechnungen besteht, muss ich nicht fürchten. Denn auch wenn das Newsletter-Schreiben für viele ein Hobby bleibt, das sie recht schnell wieder aufgeben, verdienen jetzt auch erste Autor:innen hierzulande einen sechsstelligen Betrag mit ihren Newslettern.

https://taz.de/BSW-Einspruch-gegen-Bunde.title: BSW-Einspruch gegen Bundestagswahl: Wagenknecht hofft auf ihr Weihnachtswunder
https://taz.de/BSW-Einspruch-gegen-Bunde.author: Rainer Rutz
https://taz.de/BSW-Einspruch-gegen-Bunde.text:
BSW-Einspruch gegen Bundestagswahl: Wagenknecht hofft auf ihr Weihnachtswunder
Das Bundesverfassungsgericht wird bis Jahresende über den Einspruch des BSW gegen das Bundestagswahlergebnis entscheiden. Das wird aber auch Zeit, schimpft Wagenknecht.
Es ist der Strohhalm, an den sich das BSW seit der vergeigten Bundestagswahl 2025 klammert: Bei einer flächendeckenden Neuauszählung der Stimmen könnte die damals denkbar knapp an der 5-Prozent-Hürde gescheiterte Wagenknecht-Partei nachträglich doch noch in den Bundestag einziehen – und endlich wieder bei den Großen mitspielen.
Nachdem der Bundestag eine vom BSW geforderte Neuauszählung vor gut einem Jahr abgelehnt hatte, zog die Partei im Februar mit einer knapp 180-seitige Wahlprüfungsbeschwerde vors Bundesverfassungsgericht. Passiert sei seither nichts, behauptet zumindest die Partei. Immerhin gibt es nun Licht am Ende des Tunnels: „Eine Entscheidung soll noch in diesem Jahr veröffentlicht werden“, sagt ein Sprecher des Gerichts zur taz. Zuerst hatte der Stern berichtet.
Das werde jetzt auch mal höchste Zeit, findet Parteigründerin Sahra Wagenknecht. Die angeblich skandalös lange Bearbeitungszeit der „Klage“ in Karlsruhe sei nicht nachvollziehbar. „Der Weg für eine Neuauszählung muss endlich freigemacht werden.“ Zumal es „unvorstellbar“ sei, „dass die Grünen oder die FDP ähnlich behandelt worden wären, wenn sie den Einzug in den Bundestag so knapp verpasst hätten wie wir“.
Nach dem amtlichen Endergebnis 2025 fehlten der Partei am Ende nur 9.500 Stimmen für den erneuten Einzug in den Bundestag. Bis heute steht für die Spitzen des BSW fest: Bei der Auszählung der Stimmen im Februar vergangenen Jahres kann es nicht mit rechten Dingen zugegangen sein. Das BSW habe ja schon unmittelbar nach der Wahl „auf fundierteste Weise Fehler nachgewiesen“, heißt es immer wieder. Da muss also noch mehr zu holen sein.
Der Traum von der Rückkehr auf die große Bühne
„Bei korrekter Auszählung der Bundestagswahl wären wir aller Voraussicht nach in den Bundestag eingezogen und hätten uns auch in den Ländern weiter etablieren können“, klagt der BSW-Vorstand auch aktuell wieder im Leitantrag für den anstehenden Bundesparteitag Ende November.
Klar ist: Für das jüngst in Bündnis Soziale Gerechtigkeit und Wirtschaftliche Vernunft umbenannte Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht ist das Thema letztlich zu einer Überlebenserzählung geworden. So hat es das BSW zwar im September in Sachsen-Anhalt mit fünf Abgeordneten in den Landtag geschafft. In Berlin und Mecklenburg-Vorpommern scheiterte es hingegen an der 5-Prozent-Hürde. Und Besserung ist nicht in Sicht, im Gegenteil.
2027 stehen fünf Landtagswahlen an, allesamt im Westen, bei allen fünf droht die Partei – wie schon in diesem Jahr in Baden-Württemberg und Rheinland-Pfalz – abzusaufen. Um bundespolitisch noch einmal einen Fuß auf den Boden zu kriegen, bräuchte es daher wieder eine große Bühne, eine größere jedenfalls als den Landtag von Sachsen-Anhalt, den Bundestag eben.
Wagenknecht und ihre Getreuen stellen gleichwohl wiederkehrend einen anderen Aspekt in den Vordergrund. Auf eine Neuauszählung, so die Botschaft, würde aus ihrer Sicht zwangsläufig der Sturz von Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) folgen. „Ziehen wir durch eine Neuauszählung in den Bundestag ein, verliert diese Regierung ihre Mehrheit“, stellt die Parteigründerin fest. Wenigstens hiermit läge sie auch richtig.
Keine mündliche Verhandlung in Sicht
Rechtsexpert:innen gehen unterdessen davon aus, dass es vor der Entscheidung in Karlsruhe in den kommenden Wochen keine mündliche Verhandlung der Wahlprüfungsbeschwerde mehr geben wird. Das Bundesverfassungsgericht will das auf taz-Nachfrage weder bestätigen noch dementieren. Man kommentiere Mutmaßungen über Beratungsdetails grundsätzlich nicht.
BSW-Bundeschef Fabio De Masi wittert mit Blick auf die wahrscheinlich ausfallende Verhandlung des Falls trotzdem schon den nächsten Skandal. Der Umstand, dass das Verfassungsgericht „bislang keinen Termin zur mündlichen Verhandlung hat ansetzen lassen“, deute „leider eher darauf hin, dass man unsere fundierte Beschwerde eher geräuschlos abwickeln möchte“, schreibt er auf X.
Tatsächlich werden die Chancen auf einen Erfolg der BSW-Beschwerde allgemein als gering eingestuft. Der Wagenknecht-Partei bliebe dann nur noch der Gang zum Europäischen Gerichtshof für Menschenrechte nach Straßburg. Das sei aktuell aber noch nicht entschieden, so ein Sprecher des Parteivorstands zur taz.

https://www.humanite.fr/sciences/dioxyde.author: Jérémie Bazart
https://www.humanite.fr/sciences/dioxyde.text:
Alors que se tient actuellement la COP17 sur la biodiversité en Arménie, des chercheurs allemands montrent que l’augmentation du CO₂ atmosphérique modifie la composition des protéines du blé. Une évolution qui pourrait affecter la qualité du pain et certaines sensibilités alimentaires.
L’une des questions abordées à Erevan, en Arménie, lors de la 17e conférence des Nations unies sur la biodiversité (COP17), qui se tient du 19 au 30 octobre, porte sur la préservation des espèces végétales et de leur diversité génétique face aux bouleversements environnementaux. Car les conséquences du changement climatique ne se limitent pas à la disparition d’espèces ou à la diminution des rendements agricoles. Elles pourraient également modifier la composition de notre alimentation, jusque dans la farine de blé. C’est ce que révèle une étude publiée par une équipe de chercheurs allemands1.
Le dioxyde de carbone (CO₂) est indispensable à la croissance des plantes, qui l’utilisent lors de la photosynthèse. Elles absorbent ce gaz présent dans l’atmosphère pour fabriquer, grâce à l’énergie lumineuse du soleil,...

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.title: Israel’s war on homes: From Hebron to Gaza and southern Lebanon
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.text:
“Around 12:30 at night, the Israeli army vehicles were at al-Jalda Square,” one Hebron resident told Al Jazeera. “They told us to leave our homes. We asked until when, and they said until further notice. We left with the clothes on our backs.”
Hours earlier on October 23, two Israeli soldiers had been killed by armed Palestinian men at a checkpoint near the city. Hebron, the occupied West Bank’s largest city, has been under Israeli siege ever since, with restrictions extending across a governorate of about 800,000 Palestinians.
A black X now marks the homes from which families have been forcibly expelled. Soldiers have moved into others, turning them into military outposts.
In just over a week, nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been displaced, according to UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, which called the measures collective punishment in violation of international law.
The current operation builds on years of demolitions. From 2009 up until the siege began on October 23, Israeli forces demolished 2,491 buildings and displaced 3,534 Palestinians in the Hebron governorate, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Across Area C and occupied East Jerusalem, the monthly average of demolitions since 2024 has been at least double that of the preceding 15 years.
Many demolitions are linked to Israel’s restrictive permit system. Palestinians struggle to obtain Israeli-issued building permits, leaving structures built without them vulnerable to demolition.
In Masafer Yatta, a cluster of 13 communities in the South Hebron Hills, Israeli authorities have demolished about 400 structures in 15 years, displacing 969 Palestinians. Nearly half were demolished since January 2025.
UNRWA’s West Bank director, Roland Friedrich, said the scenes in Hebron carry “alarming echoes” of the mass displacement in the northern occupied West Bank in early 2025, when Israeli military operations emptied the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps.
More than 34,000 Palestinian refugees from the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps remain displaced, according to UNRWA, more than a year after Israel’s “Iron Wall” operation began in January 2025. The operation destroyed more than half of the camps’ residential buildings.
OCHA’s demolition records capture only a fraction of that destruction. Between 2009 and October 2026, the agency recorded 1,399 buildings demolished in the Jenin and Tulkarem governorates, displacing 4,139 people. Those records mainly track demolitions carried out for lack of permits or as punishment, not buildings destroyed during military raids.
An investigation by the research group Forensic Architecture found evidence of deliberate, systematic destruction. Researchers verified more than 200 incidents involving the destruction of buildings and streets across four refugee camps, using armoured bulldozers, controlled demolitions and air attacks. They found that roads were widened through homes and gardens to create routes for military vehicles. The group concluded that Israel was applying tactics in the occupied West Bank similar to those it had used in Gaza.
In February 2025, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said Tulkarem and Jenin would come to resemble Jabalia and Shujayea, two of Gaza’s most devastated areas.
The raids have not stopped. Last week, Israeli forces detained four Palestinians in Tulkarem, and in the village of Burin, south of Nablus, troops converted several homes into military barracks, as they have in Hebron.
Near Jenin, the army has ordered the residents of an entire village to leave permanently. “I have sheep and cows. Our entire lives are tied to this land,” said farmer Jabri Yahya. “Last year they uprooted our olive trees, and this year they want to force us to leave. We don’t know where to go.”
In Gaza, the destruction is on a far larger scale. By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the UN Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).
Many families now shelter in tents, makeshift structures or damaged buildings, often without reliable water or sanitation.
Another winter brings new risks. Mohammed al-Jamal, 60, has been displaced several times since he fled his home in Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood. He now shares a worn-out tent on the beach with about 30 members of his extended family, patching it before every storm because they cannot afford a new tarpaulin. “We are living in the street, not in houses that protect us,” he said.
Across the Strip, the neighbourhoods families fled have been reduced to rubble. Google Maps satellite imagery updated in September shows the scale of the destruction across the besieged Gaza Strip, more than three years into Israel’s genocidal war.
Drag the sliders below to compare neighbourhoods before and after.
In southern Lebanon, a July 2026 assessment by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), based on satellite imagery from June 16, identified 31,259 buildings damaged or destroyed, mainly south of the Litani River.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded displacement of 333,144 people across Lebanon as of September 9.
Despite the ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon, Israeli forces continue to occupy parts of the south, and demolitions have left many residents unsure whether they can return.
Across Hebron, Jenin, Gaza and southern Lebanon, the destruction does more than displace people. It leaves them nothing to return to.
In Hebron, UN human rights chief Volker Turk warned that “threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods” raise "serious concerns of ethnic cleansing", and called for all those displaced to be allowed home.
For many families, the question is no longer when they will go home, but whether there will be a home to go back to.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Gaza doctors struggle with bereavement, overwork, trauma amid genocidal war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Gaza doctors struggle with bereavement, overwork, trauma amid genocidal war
Doctors and nurses struggle to cope with the horrors they endured during the height of the Gaza war.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza – Manar Fayyad, 29, an anaesthesiologist at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, has suffered severe psychological trauma since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
The turning point came when he discovered that a man lying before him in the operating room was his own brother Shadi, who was killed in an Israeli air strike on December 27, 2023.
He recalled the moment he was summoned into the operating room to administer anaesthesia to a critically injured man before emergency surgery.
“He died before I could reach him,” he said. “When I arrived in the operating room, I recognised the man’s clothes. I had a strange feeling, so I approached him and uncovered his face. To my shock, he was my brother Shadi, who was 34.”
Since then, the hospital has become inseparable from the traumatic memory, and he has been unable to continue to work, ultimately bringing his professional career to a premature end.
He continues to struggle with the psychological effects of the experience, trying to cope with it on his own without professional help. He has withdrawn from social life and avoids people and noise as he searches for peace since his brother died.
Sitting by the sea and writing offers him some solace, helping him express his pain and process what has happened. Yet he remains preoccupied with the idea of leaving Gaza, hoping that distance might free him from the reminders of that day.
Having lost his brother, his profession and much of his social life, Fayyad now faces a different battle: one against trauma that he is trying to confront alone.
Khaled Raafat, 29, a nurse in the emergency department at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, stepped away from work for an extended period after losing his wife, children, mother and several siblings in an Israeli air strike on his family home on October 18, 2023. He was at the hospital at the time, trying to save their lives of others injured that day.
“Learning that I had lost my family marked a painful turning point in my life,” Khaled told Al Jazeera. “I could no longer do my job in the same way. The hospital, once associated in my mind with my humanitarian duty, became a reminder of personal pain that was beyond what I could bear. It deeply affected my ability to continue my professional and social life.”
Raafat said he eventually decided to rebuild his life.
“I realised that life could not stop at the tragedy and that I had to find a way to carry on. I decided to work towards my psychological recovery, got married and started a new family in an attempt to regain stability and hope,” he said. “I then returned to work at the hospital.”
At least 1,700 medical personnel have been killed in Israeli attacks during the war while 83 healthcare workers remain in Israeli detention, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
These figures do not reveal the deep psychological burden borne by medical workers who have lost family, friends and colleagues and witnessed horrific injuries and death on a daily basis. They have also faced continued displacement, relentless pressure and have been overworked for years.
A study found that 41 percent reported losing family members and 46 percent had experienced both personal bereavement and displacement from their workplaces, according to a report on the strain on medical workers in Gaza published in the Public Library of Science.
At least 78 percent of healthcare workers in Gaza lacked access to mental health services, showing the gap between the trauma healthcare workers endure and their access to psychological care. It has meant that Gaza’s health system is struggling to retain its remaining staff and prevent them from leaving the medical field.
Although it is difficult to assess how many doctors, nurses and other medical workers have left Gaza and their jobs, official reports have acknowledged a “loss of human resources” and “diminished capacity in the healthcare system”.
To help halt this brain drain and protect healthcare workers who have experienced psychological trauma – probably most of those in Gaza, they need psychological and social support.
“They are caught between their professional duty to save lives and the pain of losing the people closest to them,” Munir al-Bursh, director general of Gaza’s Ministry of Health, told Al Jazeera. “They find themselves treating others’ wounds while struggling to heal their own.”
Working under constant pressure without adequate support or rest deepens exhaustion and threatens healthcare workers’ ability to continue, he said.
“Protecting medical personnel is not just about securing medicines and equipment. It also means safeguarding their mental health and giving them time to rest and recover. Those who save others also need someone to reach out and help them.”
The acute shortage of medical staff after the killings, detentions and injuries of many healthcare workers makes it difficult to give those who remain enough time to recover, he added. This is compounded by the continuing arrival of patients and wounded people, shortages of equipment and a lack of replacement staff.
The experiences of these doctors and nurses reveal the psychological toll of war on Gaza’s healthcare system. Those accustomed to confronting death and saving the wounded have sometimes found themselves facing it as bereaved family members rather than medical professionals. Caught between their duty to save others and their own grief, some have paid a profound psychological price with consequences for both their professional and personal lives.
Nurse Hiba al-Tawil, 39, witnessed her brother’s death in the intensive care unit at the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, where she worked.
“Losing my brother at my workplace was a difficult experience that had a profound psychological impact on me,” she told Al Jazeera. “Being in the intensive care unit afterwards reminded me of what had happened and made it harder to cope with the loss.”
She later transferred to another department. which helped ease the psychological pressure she was experiencing and allowed her to distance herself from the place where her brother died.
The psychological clinic at the hospital treats doctors and nurses struggling with trauma caused by bereavement and their experiences during the war. In some cases, these experiences can develop into severe psychological disorders that affect their everyday lives and ability to work.
Reham Abu Rokba, a psychologist at the complex, said treatment begins with assessing the patient’s psychological condition, diagnosing symptoms and determining their impact before developing a treatment plan.
For patients with post-traumatic stress disorder, treatment may include cognitive behavioural therapy, which helps them understand their psychological responses to traumatic events and regain their ability to cope.
Depending on the patient’s needs, treatment may involve about 12 individual sessions and, when necessary, medication.
Reham said that continued psychological support, appropriate treatment and adherence to the treatment plan can help ease symptoms and lead to improvements.
“Recovery requires time and ongoing participation in psychological support sessions,” she told Al Jazeera. “Providing the appropriate treatment and ensuring adherence to it can help alleviate symptoms and lead to tangible improvements in an individual’s mental wellbeing.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Police storm Portugal housing protest camp
Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square in Lisbon early on Sunday.
Police have used shields and batons to disperse housing protesters from a tent camp in Portugal’s capital, Lisbon, a week after similar operations drew criticism from protesters and rights groups.
Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square at about 4:30am (04:30 GMT) on Sunday, a day after thousands marched demanding the government withdraw a rental bill they say would deepen the country’s housing crisis.
Protesters had erected more than 50 tents following Saturday’s march through Lisbon. Police commander Iuri Rodrigues issued three warnings to remove the tents, saying they had been erected illegally and that anyone resisting their removal could face disobedience charges.
Hundreds of demonstrators shielding the camp were dispersed, while police also dismantled a smaller encampment in Porto’s Dom Joao I square.
Earlier, lawmaker Pedro Delgado Alves said Rossio Square was peaceful and that nothing justified “a police intervention involving force, physical violence or baton charges, the kind of scenes we witnessed last week”.
The intervention followed operations in the same squares the previous Sunday, when police arrested 25 people in Lisbon and six in Porto. Housing campaign group Casa para Viver said 60 people were injured across those operations, which police described as “proportionate”.
Rising housing costs
The protests reflect growing anger over housing costs across Europe, including demonstrations in Spain and opposition to government economic policies in France, Germany and Albania.
Portugal faces one of Europe’s severest housing affordability crises, with young people among the hardest hit. House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents on new leases have almost doubled.
The Bank of Portugal estimates a nationwide shortage of 300,000 homes, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.
Demonstrators want the minority centre-right government to scrap legislation that would make evictions easier and remove rent caps on new leases, saying it would worsen affordability and leave tenants more exposed.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: A Gulf non-aggression pact could be the path forward
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
A Gulf non-aggression pact could be the path forward
Oman is in a unique position to mediate talks on a security arrangement that could stabilise the region.
Proposing a non-aggression pact amid regional hostilities may seem premature. Yet agreements to stop war matter most when distrust is the deepest. The key question is whether regional governments can agree on rules that make their disagreements less destructive.
In a recent lecture at Cambridge University in the UK, Oman’s Foreign Minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, called for a non-aggression pact among all eight Gulf littoral states: the six members of the Gulf Cooperation Council along with Iraq and Iran. He described it as the essential prerequisite for an inclusive regional security architecture.
Could such a pact work? As Albusaidi conceded, it would be hard to achieve. But as another major escalation looms between Iran and the United States, the region urgently needs a diplomatic path forward.
Indeed, the ongoing conflict has proved so hard to resolve because the region’s security arrangements have remained underdeveloped, relying for too long on external powers. The way forward then can be an inclusive agreement.
Reviving the promise of 1976
The Omani proposal is anchored in a historic precedent. In November 1976, the foreign ministers of all eight Gulf littoral states met in Muscat to pursue collective security after Britain’s withdrawal from the region.
It remains the only time all eight have sat at one table. The Iranian Revolution, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran–Iraq war then pushed the region towards defensive arrangements that later hardened into exclusion.
For decades, Iran, in particular, was seen as a threat to the rest of the region. Yet, given that the country holds roughly half the Gulf coastline, any security architecture without it is structurally unsound.
It was not until 2019 that the idea of a regional security arrangement was revived. In May of that year, then Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif proposed a regional non-aggression pact with Gulf neighbours during a visit to Baghdad, which Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov endorsed.
That September, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani launched the Hormuz Peace Endeavour (HOPE) at the UN General Assembly, envisaging a non-aggression pact among Hormuz states. Gulf reactions were largely dismissive, citing Iranian support for armed groups threatening regional stability.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has revived the idea on the Arab side. In May, the Financial Times reported that Saudi Arabia was discussing a non-aggression framework with Iran, reportedly modelled on the Helsinki process between the US and Russia during the Cold War.
This month, Qatar’s defence minister called for GCC–Iran dialogue, joined by Turkiye and Pakistan, towards a non-aggression agreement.
Oman’s proposal comes as the latest iteration of this regional shift. Muscat is in a unique position to mediate given its history of acting as a mediator and its recent record of hosting US-Iran talks in 2025 and February 2026. It has access that few others have.
Concluding a pact that works
The strongest objection against a Gulf pact with Iran is simple: Why trust a state whose conduct has threatened the region’s security? Gulf concerns about Iranian actions are not misunderstandings. Oman itself formally protested to Iran after drone attacks targeting Musandam and Al Wusta in July.
Reassurance is therefore insufficient. Inclusion must mean obligation. Membership in a regional pact would have to bind Iran as much as any other signatory, providing a means to constrain threatening behaviour and address legitimate grievances.
A pact must rest on observable conduct, reciprocal restraint and consequences for violations. At minimum, it would need commitments against the threat or use of force, interference in internal affairs, attacks on civilian infrastructure and support for armed groups conducting cross-border attacks, alongside protection of navigation.
To reach a workable agreement, negotiations can adopt a gradual approach. Consultations among the eight countries could first identify minimum shared interests: territorial security, functioning ports, reliable energy exports, civilian protection and uninterrupted trade. Oman can facilitate, but each state would represent itself; Muscat’s channel to Tehran confers no mandate to negotiate for its neighbours.
Initial talks should yield limited, reciprocal measures: military hotlines, rules for maritime encounters, notification of exercises and rapid communication after attacks. An understanding about protecting energy facilities, desalination plants and commercial shipping would offer an early test of compliance.
Hormuz is the obvious starting point, though progress could be hard. Oman-Iran talks have already outlined a temporary navigation arrangement. However, as Albusaidi conceded, it cannot be implemented unless Washington and Tehran compromise, including by reversing wartime actions that halted maritime traffic. Any wider framework must respect international navigation rights.
Armed groups would be the hardest issue to resolve. Governments should undertake neither to direct nor materially support cross-border attacks by such actors, and demonstrate compliance through verifiable steps. Where control is contested, the pact would need procedures for establishing evidence and requiring corrective action.
Compliance with initial measures could open cooperation on maritime safety, environmental protection and emergency response. Serious violations should trigger investigation, urgent consultation and agreed diplomatic consequences, while the right of self-defence would remain intact.
A regional pact would not settle every conflict touching the Gulf. The United States and Israel, both parties to this year’s war on Iran, would remain outside it and Yemen’s war involves actors whose agendas a Gulf arrangement could not easily bind. But a framework need not end every war to be worth having. It need only make it harder for any of them to become a war among its signatories.
The pact’s credibility will depend on whether it changes conduct. Fewer or no attacks, functioning crisis channels and demonstrable respect for sovereignty will matter more than signatures.
Present hostilities make the task difficult, but they also expose the cost of postponing it. The first achievement would be modest but consequential: establishing that disagreement entitles no state to endanger another’s security.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Binance says 90% of losses from $6.3bn hack covered as FBI says North Korea behind attack
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has replaced 90% of the amount stolen after a record $6.3bn hack of its platform by a group the FBI identified as being backed by North Korea.
The remaining 10% of tokens are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday. Co-CEO Richard Teng said separately that the company was “committed to covering the remaining 10%” and that “users will not bear the financial impact of this incident”.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said on Sunday that some had resumed and would be rolled out in phases to ensure stability.
The announcement came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
“The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets”.
Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
Binance said it had set aside around $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses.
“Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.
The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said on X.
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Rubio says Trump administration did not help Bolsonaro flee Brazil to US
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Rubio says Trump administration did not help Bolsonaro flee Brazil to US
Trump says defeated presidential candidate, who faces investigation in Brazil, can stay in the US ‘as long as he wants’.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says President Donald Trump’s administration did not help Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro flee the country for the United States after losing a run-off to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Bolsonaro arrived in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday, a day after the US Department of State said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted US visas after his October 25 election loss, which bucked a trend of conservative electoral wins in Latin America.
Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion, and before leaving, he had been ordered to surrender his passport because police deemed him a flight risk.
“We didn’t facilitate anything,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday in Atlanta, Georgia, where diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies were gathered.
“We had word that he had arrived in the United States. He had previously held a visa, and the president made a decision to allow him to enter the country,” Rubio said.
He added that the US government was not “involved directly in any of the moves that were made”.
Rubio also said he had seen Brazil’s foreign minister, Mauro Vieira, in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday and he expected to see Brazilian officials again in November in France during a foreign ministers meeting.
Separately, Trump, who had previously called Brazil’s election “rigged”, voiced sympathy for Bolsonaro and said he could stay in the US indefinitely.
“I think he got treated very shabbily, very shabbily, so he can stay here as long as he wants,” the president told reporters at his Florida residence on Saturday.
The Reuters news agency reported that Bolsonaro was admitted to the US under humanitarian parole, a status that typically lasts for one year.
Trump’s comments suggested relations between the Western Hemisphere’s two largest democracies may remain strained for some time.
After Bolsonaro’s run-off loss, he fled Brazil to the US via Argentina and Ecuador on a journey that some US media outlets reported was partly arranged with the help of Jason Miller, a White House official.
Bolsonaro has refused to concede the Brazilian election and called the results fraudulent without providing evidence.
Since arriving in the US, he has claimed to be the true “leader” of Brazil and said he left the country because he was a victim of “persecution”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Canelo Alvarez defeats Christian Mbilli to reclaim WBC title in Riyadh
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Canelo Alvarez defeats Christian Mbilli to reclaim WBC title in Riyadh
Mexican boxing star wins 12-round decision to defeat the French fighter and regain the super middleweight belt.
Mexican veteran Saul “Canelo” Alvarez has delivered a commanding performance to defeat French fighter Christian Mbilli and regain his WBC super middleweight title in an emotional victory in Saudi Arabia.
Alvarez won a 12-round decision on Sunday in Riyadh after exerting his influence in the second half of a fight that went ahead despite the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis.
The 36-year-old Mexican was returning to the ring for the first time since he was beaten by American Terence Crawford in September 2025 in a loss that ended Alvarez’s reign as holder of the division’s four major titles.
He faced Mbilli, 31, who was elevated to titleholder in January, and the fight, which started off as a tight contest, turned into a convincing victory for Alvarez.
The judges scored the contest 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 in Alvarez’s favour.
The Mexican superstar struggled for words after receiving the belt.
“It’s so difficult to explain. It’s so difficult to explain,” Alvarez said in English. “It’s something unbelievable. It feels like my first title, now, after 20, 21 years as a professional. Sixteen years ago, I won my first title. Now I won the title again.”
Alvarez added another world title to a haul that stretches from light middleweight to light heavyweight in a 20-year career.
A host of other sporting events has been called off since the Houthis launched drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition that supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight against the Houthis.
Alvarez hinted at the security situation when he thanked his family “who are watching me from afar today for the first time”.
He was the more composed boxer in the opening round in Riyadh, but by round three, Mbilli was ripping off combinations and looking the more active of the two fighters.
The Frenchman took the initiative in round five although the bout remained a tactical battle.
Alvarez began showing his class and ringcraft in the sixth, easily winning the round, but it was in the seventh that he really pressed home his advantage, pinning Mbilli to the ropes and delivering a right uppercut that had the Frenchman rocking on his feet.
In the eighth, Mbilli had a point taken away for punching behind the head, and he seemed to lose more momentum from then on, allowing Alvarez to begin dictating the fight in the next round as the wily veteran pulled ahead of his younger opponent.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Golden State Valkyries defeat Atlanta Dream to capture first WNBA crown
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Golden State Valkyries defeat Atlanta Dream to capture first WNBA crown
Gabby Williams, named Most Valuable Player, sets records for most points (137) and most steals (18) in the WNBA Finals.
In a near-single-handed performance, Gabby Williams helped the Golden State Valkyries defeat the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in game seven of the Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA) Finals to give the West Coast franchise a championship in the second year of its existence.
Williams scored 28 of her game-high 30 points in the second half to force a turnaround and bag the Finals Most Valuable Player (MVP) award in San Francisco, California, on Saturday.
Kiah Stokes converted a Williams miss into a key hoop with 53 seconds left to the deafening cheers of “Ballhalla”, as the Valkyries’ home crowd is known at the Chase Center.
In what was mostly a defensive struggle, Williams made the difference in the end, including winning a jump ball over Allisha Gray with 8.3 seconds to go.
With the likes of former San Francisco Giants superstar Barry Bonds and multiple NBA title-winner Draymond Green of the Golden State Warriors rooting her on, Veronica Burton was fouled with 5.1 seconds remaining and produced the final points in the Valkyries’ storybook season.
On a night when the WNBA had its first game seven in a championship final series, strength in numbers was credited with propelling the second-year franchise to historic heights.
From owner Joe Lacob to coach Natalie Nakase and MVP Williams, one number stood out: 18,064.
“Ballhalla,” Lacob screamed into a microphone in tribute to the capacity crowd during the trophy ceremony.
Williams overcame a two-point first half to become the first player in WNBA postseason history to score 28 points in a half.
The Valkyries’ only All-Star, who was added as a free agent in the offseason, joined Lacob in thanking a crowd that has sold out every game in franchise history, setting league attendance records.
“Honestly, everyone here, not just the players and the staff. [Also] the community, the city, the [San Francisco] Bay [Area],” she gushed on court shortly after having been named the MVP.
“Y’all have been pouring into me all season. It’s a long season and y’all gave me energy.
“When the energy is this good and positive, it’s easy to come to work every day. That’s what I came here for.”
Playing 38 of the game’s 40 minutes, Williams saved enough energy to do a Stephen Curry impersonation on a go-ahead three-pointer with two minutes and 18 seconds (2:18) to go and later win a key jump ball, and Kiah Stokes converted a rare Williams late miss into a key hoop with 53 seconds left, sending the violet-clad crowd into a frenzy.
In the end, Nakase recognised the enormity of piecing together a bunch of players left unprotected in the expansion draft, a handful of international imports and one key free-agent signing into the league’s second-best regular-season record and a victory in the first-ever game seven in WNBA history.
“This is for all the people out there who are underrated, misunderstood. This is for all y’all,” she insisted from midcourt to her home fans and a national television audience as well. “This is proof: If you put all your heart and all your soul [into it], you can win championships.”
Rallying from a nine-point deficit in the third quarter, the Valkyries were tied at 53-all midway through the fourth after Gray connected on a short jumper for Atlanta with 5:14 to play.
Williams, after spearheading an earlier rally, came alive again. She hit two free throws with 3:34 to go and a driving hoop 32 seconds later as the teams exchanged baskets. She then buried arguably the most important shot in Valkyries’ history — a 31-footer to give Golden State the lead for good at 60-57 with 2:18 to go.
She added two free throws, and when Stokes tipped in her teammate’s miss in the final minute, Chase Center erupted as Golden State had a 64-57 advantage that it was able to protect through the end.
“We didn’t let anyone put a limit on us all year,” demanded Burton, who backed Williams with 10 points, 10 rebounds and five assists. “When you work hard, and you put your head down and drive, anything’s possible.”
Williams’s 30 points were her second-most in a playoff game, topped only by the 36 she had in game two of Golden State’s first-round series win over the Dallas Wings on September 30. She made 10 of her 23 field-goal attempts on Saturday when neither team shot well.
She set records for most points (137) and most steals (18) in a WNBA Finals. She also found time for four of Golden State’s eight blocks in the championship game.
Besides holding Dream star Angel Reese to eight points, Stokes had a game-high 13 rebounds for the Valkyries, who won despite making just five of their 20 three-point shots. The Golden State centre also had two blocks, giving her a WNBA Finals-record 19 en route to her fourth title.
Tiffany Hayes also aided the Golden State cause with 11 points.
Jordin Canada had 18 points and Gray 16 for Atlanta, which shot just 33.3 percent overall (23 of 69) and went 6-for-30 from beyond the arc.
“I’m just grateful I got to go to war with this group,” Reese, who led Atlanta with 12 rebounds, assured the media afterwards. “It’s tough in the moment, but we’ll be back.”
Dream coach Karl Smesko lamented what he called “a lot of little stretches” of subpar play, including a game-opening 5:19 in which Atlanta went scoreless, falling behind 8-0 while missing eight straight shots — four three-pointers and four shots from inside the arc that were all blocked — and tossing in four turnovers.
“It’s beyond frustrating that we didn’t accomplish what we set out to accomplish,” he admitted at his postgame news conference. “Those first five minutes … you can’t get those five minutes back.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: John Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
The home of 85-year-old Uta Frith does not exactly look like the latest front in the culture wars. Located in a serenely quiet corner of north-west London, it suggests a life still well lived, a set of deep interests and an idyllic kind of retirement. There are so many books that some are reachable only using a very tall ladder. The four hours I spend talking to her – and her husband Chris, an expert in schizophrenia – are an absolute pleasure. There is no sense of outrage or upset: even when I ask her about the stream of hostile and abusive emails she has recently received, she is relaxed and phlegmatic. “I tend to cope by just deleting them,” she says. “I don’t dwell on it.”
“It” is a reference to the controversy kicked up by her recently expressed views on a subject that sits at the heart of Frith’s academic career: what it is to be autistic, and who should or shouldn’t qualify for a diagnosis. Back in March, Dame Uta Frith – she was honoured with the title seven years ago – gave an interview to TES magazine (formerly the Times Educational Supplement) scattered with stark pronouncements. Among them was a claim that the so-called autistic spectrum has “gone on being more and more accommodating”, to the point that it “has come to its collapse”. Then, in August, she published a piece in the academic journal Psychological Medicine claiming autism was in dire danger of being turned from a “precise, clinical” term into a “vague, culturally amplified identity category”.
What she said has inevitably added to the cacophony of political and media noise about rising autism diagnoses. In the UK, there was a 787% increase between 1998 and 2018, with the rise greater for women than men, and the single biggest jump among adults; credible American stats have shown an increase across the whole population of 175% between 2011 and 2022, with the largest rise occurring among 26- to 34 year-olds (in both countries, childhood rates have also leapt up). Once, Frith agreed with the idea of a broad autistic spectrum; now, she has come to the conclusion that many people diagnosed as adults are so different from the autistic people whose condition becomes obvious in their early years and have learning disabilities that most of the former group do not merit the label “autistic” at all.
“Some of them, I think, are being wrongly influenced by social media to believe that they’re autistic, because it’s a possible way to explain your difficulties,” she tells me. “And then we have a subgroup of people who used to be called neurotic, who have all sorts of mental issues, including anxiety. And a kind of hypersensitivity.”
Over the summer, Frith did an interview with the Times’s Andrew Billen, in which she expressed opinions about the TV presenter and autism activist Chris Packham – who was diagnosed with what was then known as Asperger’s syndrome when he was 44 – which she says she did not expect to make it into print. “He cannot be autistic in my opinion,” Frith said. “It is just absolutely absurd to me that somebody who can communicate as brilliantly as he does – that is what I call a blatant contraindication.” The day after we meet, Packham is scheduled to pay Frith a visit with a BBC camera crew: as with just about everything she talks about, her feelings on this prospect are characteristically relaxed (I subsequently learn that they got on very well).
I have a 20-year-old autistic son, James, who also has learning disabilities – as well as an amazing talent for music – and now goes to a specialist further education college. When he was diagnosed 17 years ago, understanding and awareness of autism seemed to be moving in roughly the right direction. I could never have anticipated the way it has ballooned into a subject of such controversy, which puts me and millions of others in a worldwide community of people who now follow the news with a mixture of bafflement and dread.
On and on it goes. The word “overdiagnosis” is now common currency, partly because of the bestselling book The Age of Diagnosis by the neurologist Suzanne O’Sullivan, which claims that autistic people “with the greatest need are becoming invisible” and that there are questions to be asked about diagnoses that cause “more harm than good”. Donald Trump and his health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr look ahead to the absurd prospect of an autism “cure”. The rightwing press and its favoured politicians – whose loathing of any kind of diversity inevitably triggers a mistrust of neurodiversity – rage about how many neurodivergent young people are on disability benefits. Celebrities constantly lay claim to being on the spectrum. Meanwhile, there are real-world tragedies: Jason Arday, for instance, was not only a black Cambridge professor who ended his own life after relentless coverage of his allegedly specious claims about his life story and achievements. He was also autistic – which statistics show put him at a hugely increased risk of suicide.
In December last year, the then health secretary Wes Streeting commissioned three eminent academics to carry out what the government called an “independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism”. The result, published a few weeks ago, traced the increase in autism diagnoses to “socio-cultural changes in awareness [and] recognition”, and the fact that “diagnostic concepts have also broadened”. But in some people’s eyes, its authors had tried to have their cake and eat it. “If present trends continue we are clearly entering a phase in which the balance of risks is changing … towards an increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis,” they said. The review recommended much closer monitoring of privately run clinics that diagnose autism and ADHD. But it also said “we cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”.
Frith is at pains to stand well away from all this political and cultural hurly-burly, telling the story of her change of mind as a matter of careful thought and worry that, as so-called high-functioning people cast the popular understanding of autism in their image, the needs of more intensely autistic children and adults are in danger of being forgotten. A few minutes after we have talked about the common idea that autism can be a “superpower”, she says, “I have had emails from parents who say, ‘I no longer call my child autistic. When somebody asks, I say he’s intellectually impaired, and they will say, ‘Oh, all right.’ But if I say he’s autistic, they will expect things that are just … not likely.’”
Frith is one of the tiny cluster of people who came up with the understanding of autism now accepted across most of the world. In 1964, she came to London from Germany, and found her niche at the Institute of Psychiatry, connected to the famous Maudsley hospital. She had planned to study obsessive-compulsive disorder, but her head was turned by new research into what were then known as “psychotic” children.
She vividly remembers her first encounters with such kids, at the UK’s first dedicated school for autistic children, in Ealing, west London. “I was fascinated,” she tells me. “The astounding thing was that they could do things I would not expect children who were then called mentally retarded to do.” Like what? “Jigsaw puzzles, tests that would be given to very young children to measure their intelligence. They did pretty well, sometimes in a way that was completely unconventional – like completing the jigsaw with the picture on the underside.”
Frith ran experiments that showed the autistic minds tended to be more responsive to visual cues than words. In 1989, she also came up with the so-called theory of Weak Central Coherence: the idea that autistic people tend to fixate on detail rather than big, over-arching things such as stories and themes.
While all this was going on, she was also keeping the company of the psychiatrist Lorna Wing (who had an autistic daughter) and the psychologist Judith Gould – who would spend four years in the 1970s transforming the understanding of autism. Focusing on the London borough of Camberwell, they interviewed more than 900 teachers of children under 15 who, at one point or another, had needed either psychiatric treatment or attention from social care services. They then visited and closely observed every one of the 132 children those interviews suggested might be autistic, which eventually led to the conclusion that autism was a much more widespread and complex phenomenon than had been previously thought, best considered a “continuum” – or, as they were to later term it, a “spectrum”, a word intended to conjure up images of how light works, combining different colours into a single beam.
Autism, Wing said, ran “from the most profoundly physically and mentally retarded person … to the most able, highly intelligent person with social impairment in its subtlest form”. But what unified everyone on the spectrum was what she and Gould called the “Triad of Impairments”: problems with social skills, reciprocal (ie give-and-take) language and “social imagination”, most obviously evident in children not understanding the concept of pretending while they play. Though subsequent diagnostic criteria have changed – it is now accepted, for instance, that autism usually involves sensory issues including heightened or lowered sensitivity to sound, light, texture, heat and cold – these ideas are still at the heart of what most people think autism is, along with a tendency to deep obsessions, or what the autism vernacular calls “special interests”.
Frith says when the idea of a spectrum arrived, “I was more than happy. I was always worried about the sort of marginal cases, so that was one good thing. And the other was that we had more people to work with.”
The subsequent story of autism included Wing’s creation (in 1981) of the category known as Asperger syndrome: a term named after the work with a group of “little professors” of the Austrian psychologist Hans Asperger, now understood as a collaborator in the Nazi extermination of disabled children. Wing used the term to describe autistic people without language issues or learning disabilities. In 1994, it was included in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association and now on its fifth edition. But it was taken out in 2013, leaving “autistic spectrum disorder” as a single broad category, now broken down into three levels: “requiring support”, “requiring substantial support” and “requiring very substantial support”.
By then, Wing – who died in 2014 – and her colleagues’ work had led on to the idea of neurodiversity, and the activism of so-called autistic self-advocates. And as all this happened, Frith says she began to feel increasingly uneasy. “I suddenly realised, maybe 15, 20 years ago,” she says, “that I had talked completely differently about autistic people in the past compared with people who didn’t have learning disabilities and had been diagnosed more recently. I’d used completely different language and completely different arguments. And that seemed to me to be a sign of something not being quite right.”
She is sceptical about some concepts that are now taken for granted by many autistic people and autism specialists. A good example is “masking”: people – particularly women and girls – trying to cover up autistic traits through a painstaking process of copying which, in most accounts, after a day at work or school, leaves them feeling exhausted. “It’s a non-scientific concept, if ever there was one,” she says. “It’s completely unfalsifiable: if you could use the idea that you’re masking – ie you don’t have any symptoms to show … ”
But, I counter, people who mask say, “I have got symptoms to show. And I show them when I get home from school or work or when I’m on my own.”
“But that’s entirely subjective. It’s true that they have fatigue and exhaustion. These are the really important things to notice. But why believe that they are caused by masking?”
Because it’s such an effort, I reply.
“We all do that,” she says. “It’s acting, which is exhausting. But what does that have to do with autism?”
Well, I say, the deficits and impairments they’re concealing are stereotypically autistic. But what Frith craves, on this subject and many others, is scientific certainty. “The studies I’ve seen measure masking on a test with items on it like ‘I copy body language’. And I dismiss that as non-scientific because subjective experience is not reliable.” She is keen to emphasise there is usually a tentative element to what she thinks and says. “I’m not certain. I may be wrong. But I think we’re at a point where it’s useful to have a debate.”
Disagreement with Frith’s opinions has inevitably been led by some of those aforementioned self-advocates. Among them is Mary Doherty, an Irish anaesthetist who was diagnosed at 45 and has a son and daughter who are both also on the spectrum. She has memories from her schooldays of trying desperately to mask her differences, and failing. Now she is one of the founders of Autistic Doctors International, which promotes the idea that medics who are on the spectrum “bring a variety of strengths to healthcare, including an array of benefits for autistic patients”.
We spend 90 minutes talking on an outdoor cafe terrace near London’s Victoria station. Throughout the conversation, Doherty constantly stretches and loosens an elasticated hairband: an example, she says, of the “stimming”, or self-stimulatory behaviour, many autistic people use as a way to calm themselves. Frith and others, she says, are effectively averting their eyes from “the harm that’s done by invalidating people’s life experience. If you are autistic, understanding your autistic nature is life-changing. It’s so damaging to deny that to people, particularly people who are already at risk of mental health problems.”
Even if they have a blurry intersection, I suggest, there is a pretty obvious distinction between her kind of autism and more intense, “classic” varieties, which is part of what people are now arguing about. “It’s not a clear division, she retorts. “If you see me on a bad day … ” So does she feel a strong instinctive affinity with, say, an autistic person who is non-verbal and has learning disabilities? “Yes. And that was probably one of the biggest shocks to me in the earliest days of my advocacy journey.”
One big current argument, as she knows, is that when it comes to public services and healthcare, more confident, articulate autistic people will somehow get to the front of the relevant queues much more quickly than more intensely affected people (or their parents and carers). And as a consequence, people with more complex needs will get neglected. Maybe, in fact, that has been happening already.
In thousands of people’s everyday lives, the debate about supposed “overdiagnosis” – and whether certain people are now prioritised over others – is very real, not least at the proverbial school gates.
