One mother I speak to, who asks to remain anonymous, lives in the south-east with her partner and two children, one of whom is a girl with an intense kind of autism that seems to defy cliched categories: she is bright and intellectually curious, but also has profound sensory issues and difficulty navigating through the world that means she requires constant support at school.
She has recently heard that one in five of the children in her daughter’s year are reckoned to be autistic. “From day one, I just felt my child’s needs were lost and misunderstood because that word now applies to so many children.” A lot of kids, she says, “find modern school life very difficult. And people are seeking a diagnosis so their child is treated as an individual. I don’t blame them for that. But it isn’t helpful to the children who have a classically autistic inability to cope with those environments.”
She has one other concern. “When my daughter got her diagnosis, I would have described her as high-functioning because she was verbal and she could read and write. But that term has shifted very far, even from my child. It now seems to mean children who can do every sort of activity; it’s becoming unrecognisable. And you wonder: how wide can the spectrum be?”
Is there any way out of what feels like a polarised stalemate? One possible solution is offered by Frith’s one-time protege Simon Baron-Cohen, another autism expert who has felt the heat of cultural controversy, thanks to his theory that autism might be a byword for what he used to call “the extreme male brain”, low on empathising, but good at understanding systems and patterns (earlier this year, he said such language was no longer useful).
Baron-Cohen’s working life has been defined by autism since he began working at a trailblazing autism school called Family Tree in north London in the early 1980s. And he has seen plenty of past conflict about who should and shouldn’t be considered for particular diagnostic categories, not least when Asperger syndrome was first talked about.
He now thinks the catch-all term “autistic spectrum disorder” – or “autistic spectrum condition” – is proving to be increasingly problematic. “By removing the diagnosis of Asperger syndrome [from the diagnostic manual] and lumping all forms of autism together,” Baron-Cohen recently wrote, “we have ended up with individuals like Elon Musk calling himself autistic, and a child being called autistic who will never leave home or live independently and who has significant learning and language disabilities … So, in 2013, overnight, the prevalence of autism massively increased, as now both major subgroups of autism were folded together.”
I speak to Baron-Cohen – who is in his rooms at Trinity College, Cambridge – via Zoom. “The term ‘autism’ is too much of a sledgehammer,” he says. “It’s being used to cover too many things. So … I want to see subgroups.
We can call them type one, type two, type three, and we can decide. You know, type one is autism with an intellectual disability and a language delay. Type two is autism without an intellectual disability. But the reason why I’d be happy to see a proliferation of subgroups is the research that now shows most autistic people have at least six diagnoses: autism with ADHD, autism with dyslexia, autism with dyspraxia, autism with anxiety, autism with gastrointestinal pain, autism with or without epilepsy. I just think we need to start being more precise.”
I have one possible objection to that, to do with my son James. Most people who are familiar with the politics of autism will know there is often an awkward tension between articulate self-advocates and parents – like me – who have no choice but to speak on their children’s behalf. And woven through it, for me at least, is a nagging ambivalence. I sometimes worry that ideas of autism being a difference rather than a disability overlook James’s lived experience. On the other hand, because of the broad definition of autism, it’s really helpful for me to be able to say, “You know that thing Chris Packham’s got? This is my son’s version of that.” If we move to subtypes and he’s given the label type one – which is understood as lower functioning – that’s going to other him, and I don’t want that to happen.
“Nobody wants to be othered,” Baron-Cohen replies. “We want to make sure all subgroups are equal in terms of access to resources and cultural esteem. And we must never prejudge what someone is capable of.”
Two days after my chat with him, I go back to where the modern understanding of autism all started: the clump of buildings around the Maudsley, where I meet Francesca Happé, another Frith protege and professor of cognitive neuroscience at King’s College London, who is now pioneering research into how the condition is experienced by older people.
“Uta’s right that the most important things to know, to the extent that you can know anybody’s life trajectory, are about levels of language and speech and general intellectual functioning,” Happé says. “Within autism, they’re the most determinate things.”
But she clearly worries about categorisation and her sense that it may well not reflect people’s psychological complexity. “We tried it with Asperger’s: we had a go at, on the one hand, high-functioning, lots of language and no intellectual impairment, that type of autism – and then all the rest of autism. And it didn’t work – because everything blurs, and because people change.
“I’ve met people where, at first sight, I wouldn’t pick up anything. I meet them on another occasion when they’re more tired, and I can begin to see the mask almost literally slip. There’s a particular woman who came to stay with us, and my children could have diagnosed her within about half an hour when she was out of her comfort zone. You know, if she had a bad day, it was a disastrous day.”
Happé has a tentative solution to the overdiagnosis wars. “I would say there’s an argument for autism spectrum disorder as a medical diagnosis, and it must require support. If you don’t require support, then by all means you can say you have an autistic identity, but you don’t have autism spectrum disorder, because it’s not impairing you. What you need at the ground floor, before you get to the disorder level, is understanding: self-understanding, understanding from other people, reasonable accommodations. That’s level zero.”
Which brings us to perhaps the most important question of all: right now, amid all the hue and cry, what is it like to be autistic, particularly if some people might place you – rightly or wrongly – on the borderline? When I contact the National Autistic Society, they put me in touch with two women who roughly fit that description.
Hina Shaikh’s story is so fascinating, it probably deserves a book. She lives in Bradford and was diagnosed with autism four years ago, when she was 42. She was working in a car dealership, and made a successful sale to a man who turned out to be a social worker. “He just said, ‘I think you might be an undiagnosed autistic adult’, just like that. And I was taken aback: you thought of special needs children who weren’t living normal lives. But he started pointing out everything he had noticed: I didn’t make eye contact, I didn’t shake his hand, I didn’t do small talk. And he noticed how I had organised my desk, how all my pens were lined up.”
As she read up on autism, all this seemed to chime with her past history, and her profound unease about everyday social rituals. After her GP instigated a spell of form-filling, she found the average local wait for an NHS diagnosis was 18 months, and went instead to a private clinic in Shropshire. There, a consultant said, “If I had diagnosed you 15 or 20 years ago we would have called it Asperger’s. Now it’s all under one umbrella called autism. But yes, you are autistic.”
She still receives no support for her autism, but has since changed jobs and is now employed by a neurodiversity-friendly company that allows her to work from home. The big issue she spends her spare time on is the lack of autism awareness in her own community. “After I was diagnosed, I went on YouTube, trying to find something in Urdu that would explain autism to my mum. And there was nothing. In the Asian-Muslim community, with a lot of people, if a child is autistic, you take him or her to an Imam and an amulet or something is going to cure them.”
Her dad, she tells me, left the family home in his 50s (“He was one of those people who should have never got married – he couldn’t deal with family life”) and moved to Manchester. He died of Covid-19 in 2021, and she and her sister were given the keys to his flat, where they found apparent proof that Shaikh’s autism had genetic roots. “That’s when we realised he had special interests: there were 13 bikes there, and toolboxes, and collections of albums we couldn’t even have imagined.” They also found a pile of medical paperwork. “I realised they were his autism diagnosis. He’d been diagnosed in his late 50s, after he left.”
Shaikh likes Baron-Cohen’s idea of new autistic subtypes. “I think maybe they could have changed the name of Asperger’s because of its connotations, but they still needed to keep different criteria and different diagnoses. I’m gonna be very blunt now, but I am not like an autistic child who is having severe meltdowns, and who is really struggling socially and academically.”
Abigail Stow is 28. She was diagnosed in April and lives in Stevenage, where she works in the NHS, “booking, doing counselling appointments, answering emails, stuff like that”. As she grew up, she tells me, “I was very horrendously bullied, and it caused a lot of anxiety and depression, and at one point self-harm.” Even if she displayed some signs of autism, she got no extra help or support at school. Then, when she was 19, her stepdad heard a podcast about girls and autism. When she listened, she heard loud echoes of her own experience. “So I went to my GP, got booked in for an assessment, and they turned around to me and said, ‘You can’t possibly be autistic or ADHD because you’re giving me eye contact and you have a boyfriend, and you’re able to work.’ So I was like, I must just be weird.”
Nonetheless, she carried on reading about autism and became increasingly convinced she had autistic traits. “I was really struggling to hold down work. If places were busy, that really stressed me out. I’d wear noise-cancelling headphones if stuff was too noisy. And I really struggled to make friends and keep them.”
She has an autistic brother who got his diagnosis two years earlier (“School just thought he was an angry kid”) and two special interests: dogs and heavy metal. “When I’m obsessed with something,” she says, “it becomes my whole personality.”
She also freely talks about masking. “Work is very masky. I think people at work would probably describe me as outgoing and bubbly and chatty. And then I come home and I’m like, don’t even talk to me.”
When she was diagnosed – by a private company paid by the NHS – it was an epiphanic experience. “I cried. I could breathe again. It just felt so good, knowing I wasn’t crazy and I wasn’t wasting anyone’s time.”
I wonder how she feels if she sees people on, say, TikTok, laying claim to autism when they seem to show none of the signs? “It really depends. I don’t know … I feel like they’re almost trying to, like, cutify autism – like, ‘Oh, I’m a little bit autistic’ or, ‘I’m neuro-spicy, and I’ve got a touch of the tism.’ It just makes me cringe. But I also appreciate [that there are] some people like that who are autistic as well. It’s complicated.”
Back in north-west London, I ask Uta Frith what she thinks will happen next. “Things come in waves,” she says. “There are sometimes subgroups, then sometimes they’re put together again, and then it splits back up. You always have the splitters and the lumpers, don’t you?”
And we’re still in a lump phase, I suggest. “Yes. And the next one will be a split. It’s the pendulum swing.”
And why does she think that will happen?
“Just because the extension of the spectrum has gone too far. There are too many cases that were not anticipated to appear.”
Mary Doherty stands on the opposite side: she insists that what some people see as overdiagnosis is really just the birth pangs of a proper understanding of how many people are autistic. “Without the self-advocacy movement, when [autism] was just people who were obviously disabled, that picture was incomplete. I think we’re moving towards a much more holistic and complete version of what it means to be autistic.”
Is there a way through this ever more intense conflict? Simon Baron-Cohen has a different belief again: in accepting an extended spectrum, but moving into what he calls “precision diagnosis” and “support for whichever group you’re in. Because I see them as equally needy; it’s just that the needs are different.”
And all the time, yet another quintessentially 21st-century battle rumbles on. “I’d like the polarisation of views to change into a discussion where all sides start with the assumption of goodwill and we can actually talk about things without being afraid,” Francesca Happé says, somewhat optimistically. “But I would like that in all aspects of life.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘What’s our crime?’: A Palestinian family’s fight to get care for son injured by Hamas rocket
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Um Rukbeh
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
It was 7.30am on 7 October 2023 when a Hamas rocket exploded next to 7-year-old Kinaan Dadou. The rocket was aimed at the Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank but missed its mark by a few hundred metres, landing in front of Kinaan’s family home instead.
A piece of shrapnel struck Kinaan in the head. He stood rigid, his hands frozen to his sides, and screamed “Baba!” before collapsing to the ground. An Israeli soldier who passed by promised to call an ambulance. No help ever came. Kinaan’s parents rushed him to the hospital themselves, but it was six hours before a doctor arrived due to the chaos of the day. All the while, Kinaan’s brain was haemorrhaging.
It was the last time that Kinaan’s parents heard his voice.
Now 10 years old, Kinaan lies in a small bed in a persistent vegetative state. His limbs, pale and thin from atrophy, are covered with Mickey Mouse blankets. On the wall above his bed, his parents have taped pictures of Kinaan before the injury. The lively boy climbing trees and beaming into the camera bears little resemblance to the one below, whose one open eye moves listlessly across the bedroom. He is fed through a tube and breathes through a tracheostomy.
“I look at him and I ask him what he wants, what does he need? But he can’t respond, so I begin to cry. I think he’s in pain,” says Alaa Hassan Yakoub Dadou, Kinaan’s 47-year-old father, looking down at his son.
Kinaan’s case is unusual: a Palestinian child wounded by a Hamas rocket on the same day that about 1,200 people were killed in a Hamas-led attack on Israel. Three years on, Kinaan’s parents are still seeking help to pay for his treatment, finding themselves stranded between the Palestinian Authority (PA), which is responsible for healthcare in their area, and the Israeli authorities, who control virtually all facets of their lives.
The Dadou family live in the small village of Um Rukbeh, west of Bethlehem, a part of the occupied West Bank classified as “Area C”, where the Palestinian population lives under Israeli military rule.
The Palestinian Authority, which administers healthcare for Palestinians in Area C, gave some medical support for Kinaan early on – he underwent multiple brain surgeries and had a part of his skull removed – but his parents say it has refused to cover further specialist care and has been inconsistent in providing medication. Under Palestinian law, people with disabilities have the right to have at least 75% of their rehabilitation costs covered, while children also have the right to “obtain the highest possible standard of free healthcare services”.
Officials in the Palestinian ministry of health did not respond to questions.
Meanwhile, Israel, as an occupying power, also has certain obligations under international law to provide medical services, though it’s unclear if that extends specifically to Kinaan’s case. It has told a lawyer representing the family that Kinaan was injured in an area outside its jurisdiction, something the family questioned due to Israel’s de facto control over their daily lives. Israeli authorities control construction permits in Area C, including for bomb shelters, and dictate much of the family’s movement, complicating their efforts to get access to healthcare. Three months ago, they received a warning Israeli authorities would soon demolish their home.
The family has appealed to the Israeli government on humanitarian grounds. If they were Israeli and living in one of the increasing number of illegal settlements surrounding their home, the family says they would have had access to a bomb shelter and medical treatment.
“We’ve knocked on every door. The Arabs and the Israelis, it’s the same response. The Palestinian side says: ‘This isn’t our area.’ What’s our crime? That we happen to live among settlements? Neither side takes responsibility for us,” Alaa says.
Cogat – the Israeli body that oversees the Palestinian territories – did not respond to questions about Kinaan’s case.
Without outside help, the family has been unable to pay for the medical treatment that may improve their son’s condition. A specialist in Turkey said that, with an intensive recovery programme and further surgery, Kinaan’s condition could improve. But the cost of the treatment – about $250,000 (£190,000) – is far beyond what the family can afford.
“I pay 4,000 shekels [£950] per month just for his medication. I borrow from here and there, but it’s too much,” says Alaa. He used to work as a labourer in Israel, but has been out of work since Israel stopped issuing work permits to most Palestinians in the West Bank after the 7 October attack, leaving the family without income.
To save money, Kinaan’s mother, Woroud Dadou, has begun to perform some of the routine medical procedures herself. She changes her son’s breathing tube, saving the family £225 each month.
“I try to keep the tube as clean as possible so it lasts longer, but sometimes if I use the same one too long he begins to cough,” says Woroud, who adds she learned by watching doctors perform the procedures in hospital.
Alaa was told about a former colleague of his in Israel whose child was injured on 7 October. The child was flown to Germany for treatment and has since improved. He is happy for his colleague, but cannot help but wish Kinaan had access to the same treatment.
“If this was an Israeli child, even a settler child, do you think they’d have left him like this? He’d have been taken to the best hospitals. They would have done everything for him,” Alaa says.
“That’s what Israel does for its injured. It takes care of them. But when it comes to us, as a humanitarian case, it’s as though they’re saying: ‘Just give him his medicine until he dies.’”
Memories of Kinaan are scattered around the house. A little blue notebook is filled with his childlike scrawl as he practised letters: “pepper, cabbage, knight”. His parents are proud of his handwriting and said he dreamed of becoming a pilot when he grew up.
Though Kinaan is the middle child, he was the loudest of the three brothers. “Always putting them in order, like a little sergeant,” his father says, smiling. He recalls how, whenever he would come home from work, Kinaan would be waiting at the door, bringing his two siblings along to greet him.
Now only his wife greets him, and the sounds of play have mostly disappeared.
Kinaan appears to wake up, his face seemingly forming a smile as his father speaks. He keeps opening his mouth and pausing, as if about to speak, but no words come out. The room is silent, save for the sucking sound every time Kinaan takes a breath.
“We are realistic – we know he probably will never be the same as he was. But at least we want to relieve his suffering and relieve our guilt,” his father says. “It’s another kind of pain for a mother and a father, not knowing what exactly is hurting your child. That’s an enormous burden for a parent.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
The vast ‘snow yard’ in otherwise arid Rajasthan state attracts hundreds of tourists daily, but residents face severe health risks.
Kishangarh, India – As Bagharam Gurjar kneels to pull weeds from his maize field in western India’s Rajasthan state, the sound of his wife coughing nearby makes him restless.
“Everything gets ruined when dust settles on the soil,” says Gurjar, 53, barely looking up.
“May God make everything right,” replies his wife between bouts of chronic cough. “Otherwise, it becomes difficult to grow crops.”
The Gurjars are among nearly 5,000 people living in the vicinity of what has turned out to be one of the most unusual tourist destinations in India.
Their village, Bhogiyawas, is just 6km (4 miles) from Kishangarh, where a 300-acre (121-hectare) marble slurry dumping yard resembles a snow-clad landscape, attracting hundreds of tourists every day in an otherwise arid state.
Locally known as a “Snow Yard”, the landfill in Rajasthan’s Ajmer district is the largest of its kind in Asia. Its pristine white hills and slopes with water-filled pits provide a surreal backdrop for visitors, who get free entry to the site.
Newlyweds pose against the snowy backdrop or the blue artificial lake, while couples soon to get married organise pre-wedding photoshoots. Social media influencers throng the landfill to make reels. Music videos and movies are also frequently shot here.
“Everyone, right from my five-year-old niece to my mother, loves it very much. Their first impression was that this looks like Kashmir,” Salim Shahzada, a businessman from Uttar Pradesh state, told Al Jazeera, referring to Indian-administered Kashmir.
Shahzada said he had visited the place a couple of times and decided to bring his family along this time. But he had no idea about the health and environmental problems linked to the dumping yard.
“I do not have much knowledge about this place or its ill effects. I only know that this is where marble cutting waste is dumped and that the hill itself is made of this waste,” he said.
Kishangarh, a marble and granite hub, is home to nearly 1,200 processing units, with the total daily business estimated at more than 160 million rupees ($1.7m), providing jobs to about 25,000 people, according to the Federation of Indian Granite and Stone Industry.
Every day, nearly 1,000 tankers carry slurry from those units and empty roughly 5,500 tonnes of waste on the government-allotted dump site, which, for the people living nearby, has turned into a health hazard.
Gurjar said the yard has affected residents in at least six villages. “How many problems can I even tell you about? If there were just one or two, we could deal with them,” he said.
“But here, almost everything is going wrong because of the dumping yard. People like me are suffering from chest infections, dental problems and skin allergies. It does not matter whether they are children or elderly people; everyone is suffering.”
Gurjar said he and his wife are forced to take regular medicines for chest infections or skin problems.
Aditi Goyal, a general physician at Ajmer’s Ganga Narayan Hospital, said the residents of Kishangarh face several health risks, mainly respiratory and skin problems. She said the workers in the marble processing units are more vulnerable to chronic illnesses because of prolonged exposure to toxic dust.
“Over the last couple of years, cases of respiratory problems have increased significantly in this area because people are exposed to dust from the dumping yard,” Goyal told Al Jazeera.
“However, dust from industrial waste is not the only issue. People in Kishangarh, who are mostly farmers, also suffer from infections caused by dust coming from the soil,” she said, advising people to wear masks to protect themselves from dust.
The same dust settles on the fields, hardening the soil and making it difficult to grow crops.
A study led by Laxmi Kant Sharma, professor in the department of environmental science at the Central University of Rajasthan, found that the concentration of lead silicate in Kishangarh’s soil was several times higher than normal, indicating extreme contamination.
“Since the waste particles are smaller than 75 micrometres, they can spread far and wide, making the soil infertile,” the study said.
The study also found that the concentration of PM2.5 exceeds the limit of ambient air quality standards. “Several people may be suffering from silicosis. The government needs to take immediate action to prevent the situation from getting out of hand,” it said.
Ugam Singh, another resident of Bhogiyawas, remembers when things were different. The continuous dumping of slurry slowly changed the landscape and the lives of people in Kishangarh, says the 65-year-old.
“Nowadays, the situation has worsened to such an extent that even the groundwater is no longer fit for consumption,” Singh said.
“The fluoride levels in the water are so high that it tastes salty. My teeth have started decaying and my bones have become weak,” he added, pointing to his teeth, which appeared pale, pitted and worn.
Singh said the residents of villages surrounding the dump yard have complained to the authorities, including officials of the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board (RSPCB). But their requests fell on deaf ears.
“What I have come to understand is that it does not matter which government is in power. No one listens to the poor. To make the rich richer, the government sacrifices the interests of people like us. It feels as though our lives have no value,” Singh said.
“Even today all we want is for this marble slurry dumping to stop so that we can breathe freely again and our fields can become green and productive once again.”
Singh also claims that if residents of all the villages around the dumping yard were properly examined, almost every household would have someone suffering from respiratory problems such as asthma.
Last year, local environmentalist Drupad Malik filed a case before the National Green Tribunal over the harmful health and environmental effects of the Kishangarh dumping yard. The tribunal observed that unregulated dumping of marble slurry was contaminating groundwater and air. It directed the RSPCB to enforce monitoring, conduct sample inspections and penalise the marble processing units violating environmental norms.
Al Jazeera reached out to a senior official at the RSPCB’s regional office in Kishangarh, but she refused to speak on the matter.
Central University’s Sharma said the areas surrounding the Kishangarh dumping yard are unfit for human settlement. He said his research was shared with state authorities, but nothing was done to improve the environmental conditions in the area.
“There is a dire need to shift the dumping yard to another place where there is no human contact. This area has become extremely toxic and vulnerable to severe diseases. I am surprised that people are allowed to visit the site without masks and even have food there,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“I have forwarded several suggestions, including installing tile units, as [marble] slurry is used in tile manufacturing. This could, to some extent, help reduce pollution in Kishangarh,” he added.
Meanwhile, Ram Lal, a resident of Tokra village, about a 15-minute drive from Bhogiyawas, appealed to the government to find an alternative site for dumping the marble slurry.
“Kishangarh is full of slurry, and it is time to shift the dumping yard out of here to some other place where no one will suffer for at least two to three decades,” Lal told Al Jazeera.
“We also demand that free medical camps be set up to assess people whose health has declined because of the fine dust particles that have been flying in the air and settling here for years,” he said.
“No one from our village can afford it if someone develops a disease that costs thousands of rupees to treat.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat was torched in an arson attack. Should it be rebuilt?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Deborah Cole in Berlin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
One of the last structural relics of Adolf Hitler’s dictatorship was conceived to project indomitable power. Last month it was destroyed in a suspected arson attack. Will it, and should it, be rebuilt?
The historic Nazi mountaintop retreat known as the Eagle’s Nest is perched on an Alpine peak at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft), with stunning views over southern Germany and Austria. In German, its design is known as Überwältigungsarchitektur, intended to overwhelm and intimidate.
Now, despite the efforts of 200 firefighters battling through the night, only charred ruins remain of the former guest lodge, tourist magnet and remembrance site destroyed in the blaze which started on 23 October. It is closed indefinitely.
“Even if a British air force bomb had struck the building on 25 April 1945, as it did most of the other structures in what was then the ‘Führer’s no-go zone’ on the Obersalzberg near Berchtesgaden, Hitler’s former tea house … could scarcely have been more severely damaged than it was by the fire,” Munich’s Süddeutsche newspaper said.
The fire has triggered a debate about whether, and how, to rebuild at the toxic site for the next generation of visitors, while mitigating the never-quite-banished risk of creating a shrine for neo-Nazis.
While the places associated with Hitler’s victims, including the former concentration camps, are preserved in perpetuity, the question of how to treat the perpetrators’ artefacts remains fraught, particularly given the resurgence of the far right in Germany and in Europe more broadly.
Local authorities believe the fire was deliberately started by a 33-year-old suspect with a history of mental illness. The site, which is owned by the German state of Bavaria, attracts more than 300,000 people each year but was closed to visitors that day. No one was injured.
Bavarian state culture minister Markus Blume has said a commission of experts in heritage conservation, construction and Germany’s culture of Holocaust remembrance would be enlisted to help determine the future of the Eagle’s Nest.
Given the building’s inextricable links to the Nazi regime and its crimes, Blume said, “any reconstruction must do justice to this historical responsibility”.
The marvel of Alpine engineering, which took 3,800 workers just over a year to build, is known more prosaically in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, for the mountain it rests on.
After a coach ride on serpentine roads through five tunnels, visitors rode a brass-plated lift, built into the rock, for 41 seconds to reach its portal.
“The prestige project and the road leading to it cost about 30 million Reichsmarks, equivalent to about 130 million British pounds today,” said Nazi-era historian Felix Bohr, author of Before the Downfall: Hitler’s Years in the Wolf’s Lair, which is being published in the UK in November.
“Hitler loved architecture that made other people look small. He insisted on being involved in the planning and construction of propaganda buildings.”
The lodge was completed in 1938, and mainly used to welcome and impress state guests, diplomats and select foreign journalists.
Just a short distance down the mountain at the Obersalzberg complex was Hitler’s own residence, the Berghof, where he spent about a quarter of his 12 years in office.
“Important decisions about prosecution and crime, about war and genocide were taken there,” said Sven Keller, director of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, an educational facility at the site.
“The surrounding mountain scenery was used as a backdrop for the construction of Hitler’s ‘Führer’ image. It offered spectacular, awe-inspiring views, and demonstrated technical prowess to subjugate even this rough natural environment.”
Inside, it had many of the trappings of Nazi bling, including Untersberg marble donated by Mussolini, Venetian mirrors and plump green leather armchairs recalling an English country manor house.
Hitler is known to have visited the Eagle’s Nest only 14 times until 1939 and then never again due to the second world war’s outbreak, when the tea house no longer matched the warrior-statesman image he wished to project, Bohr said. Close associates including his companion Eva Braun still used it regularly, however.
After the war, Obersalzberg became a recreation centre for occupying US troops, but the last vestiges of the Berghof were torn down and hundreds of trees were planted in its place – a fateful decision that has served as a cautionary tale.
“The Americans and the Bavarian state tried to prevent it from becoming a pilgrimage site for old Nazis and Hitler admirers. It didn’t work. If anything, a hidden site in the woods is even more interesting and mysterious,” Keller said. Nazi swastikas were often found carved into the tree bark.
He said a 180-degree pivot toward clearly marking the site and exposing its history, including how it fit into the Nazi power apparatus, proved the healthier approach.
“Public accessibility creates transparency whereas barriers or fences encourage rumours and legends,” Keller said. “Today, a popular public trail crosses the site, and mundane activities such as hiking keep it from becoming a sacred space (for neo-Nazis).”
Keller said transparency should be the watchword going forward.
“I cannot imagine that those responsible would opt for [a] simple reproduction of Nazi architecture, but it also can’t be left as a ruin – those tend to be even more fascinating,” he said.
“Instead, we should find ways to integrate the material remains and new information and education, showing the temporal layers, including the use as a tourist destination since the 1950s. The fire added a new layer to the history to Obersalzberg, and this should be visible too.”
New political realities in Germany and Austria, where the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) and Freedom Party lead the respective national polls, will have to be taken into account as well, he said.
Bohr said that troubling context led him to oppose any reconstruction of the Eagle’s Nest. “Hitler’s megalomania should remain a ruin. My suggestion would be to secure the remaining structure as far as possible and to use it to convey the history of the site,” he said.
“Particularly in view of the strength of the AfD and the rise of right-wing extremism in Germany, the focus should be on coming to terms with Nazi ideology, not on restoring its stage sets.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Are the US midterms going to see a blue wave of Democrats winning seats – or a blue flood?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
He spoke admiringly of a senator’s posterior. He baselessly accused a Muslim candidate of being a terrorist. He boasted about his renovations of the White House. He quipped that his own supporters couldn’t afford a hamburger at his Mar-a-Lago club. Every now and then, he spoke about the cost of living, and other everyday concerns of voters.
Donald Trump has held dozens of campaign rallies before next week’s US midterm elections. The 80-year-old remains convinced that he can prove the doubters wrong again and help Republicans retain control of the US Congress. But it was five words he uttered at this summer’s Republican convention in Dallas that could seal his party’s fate: “Pretend I’m on the ticket.”
That plea was music to the ears of Democrats. It helped ensure that the midterms will deliver a national verdict on Trump’s second term in the White House. And opinion polls suggest that the judgment will be damning, piercing his aura of invincibility, reshaping the final two years of his presidency and setting the stage for a fierce battle to succeed him.
“Donald Trump nationalised these races, and now they’ll lose seats because of it,” said Michael Steele, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. “He made himself the referendum. Individual candidates wanted to run their individual races but he told them: ‘Put me on the ballot.’ He has political instincts for himself, but no political instincts for the party.”
Pain is the norm for White House incumbents when the midterms roll around. In 1994, Bill Clinton suffered a 54-seat setback in the House of Representatives; in 2010, Barack Obama lost 63; in 2018, Trump himself lost 40. He seems unlikely to defy history this time. Trump goes into the elections with the lowest approval rating of any president before the midterms since Harry Truman’s Democrats were crushed 80 years ago.
The coalition that in 2024 powered Trump to the greatest comeback in modern political history has suffered blow after blow: his failure to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files detailing ties of the elite to the child sex offender; the growth of datacentres in rural communities; an eight-month-old war in Iran that he promised would be over in weeks; a relentless rise in the cost of fuel and food.
The anger over Trump’s broken promises has been compounded by a whiff of corruption, and the perception that he is using the presidency to enrich himself and his family. He accepted a plane from Qatar to use as Air Force One, decorated the Oval Office in gold, demolished the White House East Wing to make way for a $400m ballroom and is planning a triumphal arch in Washington. His personal fortune meanwhile has surged – from $2.3bn in 2024 to $6.5bn, according to Forbes.
‘Much more macro than Maga’
With Republicans clinging to a paper-thin 218–214 margin in the House and 53–47 lead in the Senate, opinion polls indicate a rising “blue wave”. A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey gave Democrats an 11-point lead, 47% to 36%, on the generic congressional ballot, while Trump’s approval rating stood at 32%. Voters will also choose governors in 36 states and three US territories, and decide thousands of state legislative contests.
Tens of millions of early votes have already been cast, with habitual Republican turnout lagging behind Democratic participation in critical battlegrounds. So dire is the environment for Republicans that conservative Super Pacs backed by billionaire Elon Musk, who has poured $366m into saving Republican candidates, are being forced to dump emergency funds into strongholds like Kansas, Iowa and Texas.
Trump won the presidency in 2024 after promising to curb inflation and lower prices; instead, the opposite has happened. Across the country, voters are confronting an affordability crisis exacerbated by two defining choices of Trump’s second term: a sweeping regime of foreign tariffs and the fateful decision to launch airstrikes on Iran in February.
Chris Matthews, a political commentator and former presidential speechwriter and congressional aide, said: “He’s losing on cost of living and affordability. Older people on limited incomes are focusing on what it costs to live each month. It’s much more macro than Maga. No matter what he does for Maga people, the power of macroeconomics is much stronger and people are going to vote against him.”
The economic fallout of the Iran war, which Trump frequently downplays as a “little detour”, has reverberated across global energy markets. Diesel prices have soared, sending shock waves through agriculture and freight transport from the Central valley of California to the grain belts of Iowa and Ohio.
Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former official in the Clinton White House, points out that voters can directly attribute their economic misery to the president. “There’s a very clear line between his actions and the things people don’t like,” she said.
“It’s going to be the tariffs and it’s going to be the war: both self-inflicted wounds. He didn’t have to raise tariffs; that was his theory of the world, which turned out to be wrong. Bombing nuclear sites in Iran was one thing, but going to all-out war turned out to be a mistake. Voters connect his actions to things they don’t like.”
This frustration is fuelling an energetic mobilisation among Democratic candidates, particularly women running in districts that once seemed out of reach. Jessica Mackler, the president of Emilys List, which is backing 247 female candidates this cycle, notes that voters feel the economic system is actively stacked against them.
“Voters understand that the corruption coming out of Washington is directly linked to why they can’t get ahead, and why they find it so hard to make ends meet,” Mackler said. “Cost of living is a huge driver but voters are desperate for new leadership who have lived their pain and understand it.”
A ‘devastating referendum’ on Trump
For months, Republican strategists urged their candidates in tight suburban races to keep national politics at arm’s length, and focus on local accomplishments, perhaps hoping that Trump might quietly concentrate on his day job in Washington. Instead, the president has embarked on a whirlwind tour across the country, denouncing Democrats as “communists” while touting a strong economy, secure border and historic drop in violent crime.
But Steele, a co-host of the MS Now network’s the Weeknight, argues that core conservative voters feel increasingly betrayed by a president who promised to avoid foreign entanglements and bring down costs. “Donald Trump lied to his tribe … He said he wouldn’t engage us in foreign wars; we’re now turning the corner into a year of a war he started and people are saying: ‘I can’t even afford to put gas in my car.’”
Perhaps no development in the 2026 midterms is more alarming to Republican strategists than the dramatic erosion of support among Latino voters. In 2024, Trump made historic inroads with Latino men, sparking triumphant declarations of a permanent multiethnic, working-class coalition.
Yet no sooner had he taken the oath of office than he unleashed an aggressive, high-visibility deportation campaign featuring heavily armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in cities and agricultural hubs.
Larry Jacobs, founder and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “Donald Trump launched his radical deportation strategy and it has powerfully alienated the fastest-growing part of the electorate.
“A year ago, Republicans thought they had established a new Hispanic coalition that would guarantee five new seats in Texas alone. They may lose all of them. Economics is a driving factor, but opposition to Trump’s deportation policies has contributed massively to the magnitude of the defections.”
Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, notes that the Latino shift is visible across public polling and state-level data, saying: “Whether it’s a 15-point shift or a 30-point shift, it’s a big deal. Unless every piece of evidence we have is wrong, Latino voters are having serious buyers’ remorse.”
This dynamic is evident in Texas, where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative and former public school teacher who preaches a gospel of social justice, is taking on Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in the most expensive Senate race in history.
Paxton, a staunch Trump ally, has been bogged down by years of corruption allegations, personal scandal and securities fraud charges. Despite $300m in outside Republican spending, led by Musk, Talarico has a narrow lead in most polls.
Jacobs views Texas as a bellwether for the post-Trump Republican party. “If Paxton loses, it’s going to send a very powerful signal to future Republican leaders about how they handle immigration,” he said. “It proves that attacking the fastest-growing part of the electorate is political suicide. Texas is a devastating referendum on Donald Trump.”
A test for Democrats
While Democrats appear heavily favoured to pick up the four net seats required to capture the House of Representatives, their path to taking the Senate is a steeper climb. Yet because of Trump’s dismal approval ratings and the economic shock of the Iran war, the Senate battlefield has expanded into states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.
In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown is mounting a comeback bid against incumbent Republican Jon Husted. Brown, a grizzled populist with deep ties to organised labour, has capitalised on working-class anger over fuel prices and plant closures, as well as local opposition to datacentres. In a peculiar recurring feature of his rallies in the state, Trump has frequently veered off-script to praise Husted’s physique. (“His ass was like a big piece of muscle,” according to the president.)
In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers is up against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old doctor and former Detroit health director bidding to become the first Muslim senator in the US. Republicans have aggressively targeted El-Sayed over past foreign policy statements, while pro-Israel Super Pacs have poured millions of dollars into the state to defeat him. Trump has launched Islamophobic tirades, calling El-Sayed a “jihadist”.
Olsen said: “El-Sayed is the biggest test for progressives. If he wins stateside in an industrial heartland state like Michigan, progressives will argue they have the upper hand heading into 2028.”
However, Kamarck cautions against over-interpreting progressive strength. She insisted: “The progressives are a minuscule portion of the Democratic party. This is an overblown story. The moderates are winning the vast majority of these races across the country.”
In Maine, veteran Republican senator Susan Collins is fighting for her political life against Democrat Troy Jackson, a lumberjack and former president of the state senate. Collins has attempted to distance herself from Trump, appearing on the trail with independent former senator Joe Manchin, but Democrats have relentlessly hammered her votes for conservative supreme court justices and other Trump priorities.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is mounting a challenge to Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The contest has become embroiled in a legal dispute after the justice department sought to block certification of a possible Peltola victory. Her allies reportedly helped recruit a decoy candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement.
‘He’ll do anything’
Election integrity remains a broader national concern. Trump’s repeated, unsubstantiated claims of election fraud have prompted Democrats and voting-rights organisations to prepare legal teams and observers for disputes or federal interference. The administration says federal election monitors will follow the law, and has denied plans to send troops or immigration agents to polling stations.
Tara Setmayer, a co-founder and chief executive of the Seneca Project, a women-led political action committee, said: “I am extremely worried. We have seen what Donald Trump has done when he had guardrails; now he has none. He has power and people who are aligned with him in the attack on our election integrity in positions of power.
“This is a great concern to me because Trump is looking at the sun setting on his presidency and we all know that he is deathly afraid of being out of power. He’ll do anything to stay in power, even if that means creating another constitutional crisis to try to stop Congress from being seated. We cannot suffer from a lack of imagination of what these people are capable of.”
A Democratic victory in either chamber will effectively stall Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, leaving his administration to rely on executive orders. Hakeem Jeffries, who would likely become the first Black speaker of the House, has pledged to immediately unleash subpoena power to investigate administration corruption, foreign policy decisions in Iran, and the personal financial enrichment of the Trump family.
Jacobs said: “It’s going to be a fistfight. I’m not expecting major legislation to pass. I think there will be extensive investigations of Donald Trump and his cabinet, and that’s what we’re going to get for two years.”
Steele believes that a Democratic House will immediately assert control over federal purse strings. “Congress will freeze money on projects like tearing down the East Wing for Trump’s ballroom, and they’ll reassert oversight over the Kennedy Center,” he said, referring to the national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. “Trump is effectively a lame duck now. The rest of the country knows his time is coming to an end.”
Indeed, before the last vote is counted, attention will likely turn to the presidential contest in 2028. For Republicans, a crushing midterm loss could accelerate the race to a post-Trump future. JD Vance is currently positioned as the heir apparent to the Maga movement, but figures such as the senator Ted Cruz of Texas and the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, could also be in contention.
Steele commented: “Republicans need to recognise that the future of the party does not rest solely with the Maga base. It rests with winning back the suburban, moderate and Hispanic voters this administration has isolated.”
Under pressure from a restive base, Democrats will also be preparing for a sprawling contest to decide the future direction of their party – and how it can turn the page on the Trump era. The next Democratic presidential candidate is equally uncertain, with outgoing California governor Gavin Newsom, Georgia senator Jon Ossoff, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and even former vice-president and 2020 nominee Kamala Harris among those regularly mentioned.
Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “Voters are tired. When you combine high prices, the endless argument and the constant noise of Donald Trump, people want a change from the status quo.”
“On November 3, the voters are going to speak – and Donald Trump is not going to like what they have to say,” he predicted.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Piles of rubbish, power cuts and potholes: anger grows over Johannesburg’s run-down infrastructure
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
One week before the local elections in South Africa, the pavements and roads of the Johannesburg township Alexandra were filled with piles of rubbish, rotting in the heat. At the Jukskei River, its banks choked with rubble and litter, foul-smelling brown water flowed out of a culvert.
“We’ve got way too many challenges,” said Semadi Manganye, the chief executive of Alexandra Water Warriors, an environmental NGO that organises clean-ups of the river and plants trees on its banks. “If it’s not electricity, it’s water. If it’s not water, it’s waste.”
Manganye acknowledged the challenges of providing public services in a city whose population grew by 10% to 4.8 million between the 2011 and 2022 censuses. “I have an understanding of why they’re failing,” he said. “But we’ve got to mitigate against this – we knew that it was going to happen.”
On 4 November, up to 29 million South African voters will go to the polls for local elections amid deep discontent with the water cuts, power outages and potholes that plague the country’s 257 municipalities. Their problems are so deep that even the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has admitted: “Too many of our municipalities are failing to meet the needs and expectations of the people they are meant to serve.”
In the last financial year (2024-25), only 39 local governments, 15% of the total, received a “clean” audit from the country’s auditor general. Two-thirds are “financially distressed”, according to a parliamentary budget office report.
Nowhere are the problems more pressing than in Johannesburg, South Africa’s largest city and commercial capital. The city has been ruled by a series of unstable coalitions, with 10 changes of mayor in the past decade. Authorities have admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog. It is estimated that a quarter of the water bought by the municipal water body Johannesburg Water is lost to leaks.
At a public meeting in Rabie Ridge, a township in the city’s north-east, about 400 people berated the incumbent mayor, Dada Morero, and executives from Johannesburg’s electricity utility, City Power.
One person said she had had no power for six months. Another said her mother had been forced to turn to loan sharks after receiving energy bills as high as 6,000 rand a month when her monthly pension was 2,000 rand.
“If there is any organisation that is dysfunctional it is this organisation … it is failing,” one man said, drawing huge cheers from the audience.
Even some affluent northern suburbs are going without piped water for weeks at a time. After a month-long outage about six months ago, people in parts of Melville and Westdene have been unable to predict when they will get water since September.
“The word I’d use is desperate, because literally there’s been almost no water at all,” said Kate Spiller, a semi-retired management consultant. “During the day, there’s dribs and drabs. And then sometimes in the middle of night, my husband’s been able to fill a couple of five-litre bottles and then it’s gone dry again.”
Spiller and her husband drive 10 minutes almost daily to a mosque that has a borehole to fill up about a dozen five-litre bottles, which they use to take bucket showers. “It’s incapacitating … you’re always planning, you’re always thinking: ‘We need to get water, we’d better make a plan,’” she said.
“Overall, Johannesburg is providing the necessary services to our communities,” Morero said in an interview after the Rabie Ridge meeting. “Isolated areas where they don’t have [services], we are focusing on right now.”
He acknowledged parts of the inner city were without power, due to a “collapsed” substation, but blamed “vandalism” and criminals. “From time to time, with the JPMD [Johannesburg Metropolitan police department] we try to push back, but there are also syndicates who are also organised and affecting our infrastructure,” he said.
However, experts have said many city politicians and officials are themselves corrupt. An October report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime said: “Governance failure in the CoJ [city of Johannesburg] has given birth to a criminal ecosystem.”
“People in charge of the supply chain system can easily get backhanders,” said Rashid Seedat, a former city official and the executive director of the Gauteng City-Region Observatory, a research organisation.
“Of course, corruption is the metro police officer taking a bribe of 200 rand [and] a 200m rand tender. It’s across the board and endemic in the entire system and acceptable.”
The Democratic Alliance, South Africa’s second-largest political party, has mounted an energetic campaign in Johannesburg, under the 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor Helen Zille, to try to unseat the African National Congress (ANC) and its coalition partners, the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the populist Patriotic Alliance.
Zille, who is white, has previously caused controversy, particularly among black voters, including for tweets in 2017 that said colonialism was not completely negative. However, viral stunts that have drawn attention to Johannesburg’s infrastructure issues, such as Zille snorkelling in an enormous flooded pothole, have helped to put the DA ahead of the ANC in the polls (voters choose parties and councillors, who in turn elect the mayor).
The DA has polled between 29% and 36% in October, compared with 22% to 27% for the ANC, which is fielding three possible mayoral candidates amid factional infighting. However, this may not be enough for Zille to form a coalition, analysts say.
“In order to understand Joburg, you actually have to zoom out a bit and look at all of Gauteng [province],” said Ziyanda Stuurman of Africa Practice, a consultancy. “Over the last decade, and especially since 2021, there’s been this very clear working relationship between the ANC, EFF and ActionSA across the three municipalities [Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni].
“Once in-principle coalition arrangements are agreed to, you’ve seen the EFF back ANC and ActionSA mayors across all three cities and there’s been a negotiation keeping in mind all three.”
Stuurman said a coalition similar to recent ones could lead to five more years of decline in Johannesburg. “It’s been much more horse-trading than it actually has been about the city’s best interests.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: UN demands investigation after staffer’s death in Houthi custody in Yemen
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
UN demands investigation after staffer’s death in Houthi custody in Yemen
Mohammad el-Shami had been held since June 2024, when he and many other UN and NGO workers were accused of being spies.
The United Nations has demanded an investigation into the death of an employee in Houthi detention in Yemen.
Mohammad el-Shami, a staff member of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in Yemen, died more than a month ago, but his family was only recently informed, the UN said in a statement on Saturday.
The Houthis did not say how he died, but his family “deserve to know the truth”, said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk.
The human rights chief also demanded “full transparency” from the Houthi authorities and an “urgent, independent and thorough investigation” into el-Shami’s death.
El-Shami had been arbitrarily held in Houthi custody since June 2024, when he and more than 60 people working with the UN and other NGOs were detained and accused of being part of an “American-Israeli spy network”.
“I am also gravely concerned” for the seven other OHCHR personnel who were detained alongside el-Shami and are still being held, Turk said. “I appeal again for their immediate and unconditional release.”
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a separate statement on Saturday that he was “appalled” by el-Shami’s death and echoed Turk’s calls for an investigation.
The UN is “urgently seeking answers” from the group about the circumstances of his death, Guterres added.
El-Shami is the second UN staff member to die in Houthi detention, following the death of a World Food Programme staffer in February 2025.
A total of 72 UN staffers and NGO workers, including el-Shami, have been detained by the Houthis.
The UN paused operations in parts of Houthi-held Yemen in February 2025 over concerns for the safety of its employees.
The rebel group has previously paraded some detainees on television channels, presenting them as collaborators with Western intelligence agencies and Israel.
On October 6, the UN announced that a World Food Programme employee had been released after being “arbitrarily detained” by the Iran-backed group.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
Drought is affecting 78,000 families, and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, as El Nino is due to peak in late 2026.
Bolivia has declared a nationwide state of emergency to free up resources to deal with the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed the decree on Saturday, which also called for further deployments of rescue teams in areas of the country hard hit by flooding and drought.
El Nino will have “very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods”, Paz said, adding that Bolivia needs “the cooperation of all institutions”.
Drought is now affecting 78,000 families in six of Bolivia’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, according to a government report this week.
Bolivia is also prone to flooding. In December 2025, floods in the Santa Cruz region killed dozens of people.
Neighbouring Chile’s capital, Santiago, recorded the rainiest October ever, while wildfires in Peru killed at least 12 people last month.
El Nino, a global climate phenomenon that occurs roughly every two to seven years, is part of the planet’s natural weather cycle.
During this climate event, warming in the Pacific Ocean brings worldwide changes in winds, pressure, and rainfall patterns, often causing extreme weather.
El Nino’s intensity varies, and its impact changes based on geographic location, but this cycle could be the strongest in recorded history. It is due to peak at the end of 2026, but its impacts could continue well into 2027.
Scientists predict El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths globally, with the poorest countries worst impacted.
In early September, the World Meteorological Organization reported a nearly 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.title: Weltspartag | Viele wollen vorsorgen, doch oft fehlt es am Geld
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.author: Hermannus Pfeiffer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Weltspartag
Viele wollen vorsorgen, doch oft fehlt es am Geld
Im Schulterschluss mit der Bundesregierung macht die Finanzbranche mobil: Die Zukunft der Altersvorsorge liege an der Börse.
Sparen war gestern, heute wird investiert. So lautet die Botschaft der kommunalen Sparkassen in Deutschland. »Sparen bedeutet heute mehr, als Geld auf dem Sparbuch zurückzulegen«, sagte Ulrich Reuter, Präsident des Deutschen Sparkassen- und Giroverbandes (DSGV), während einer Videopressekonferenz anlässlich des Weltspartages am 31. Oktober, der vor über 100 Jahren von Sparkassen aus der Taufe gehoben worden war. »Es bedeutet auch, einen Teil des Ersparten langfristig zu investieren.« Doch beim langfristigen Sparen nutzen viele Menschen die Kapitalmärkte bislang kaum – zum Ärger der Finanzbranche, versteht sich.
Laut dem »Vermögensbarometer 2026« des Sparkassenverbandes halten immerhin 75 Prozent der Befragten regelmäßiges Sparen für wichtig oder sehr wichtig. Unter den 16- bis 29-Jährigen sind es sogar 83 Prozent. Deutliche Unterschiede zeigen sich beim Wertpapierbesitz: Während 36 Prozent der Männer Wertpapiere besitzen, sind es bei den Frauen 21 Prozent. Dadurch bleibe beim sogenannten Vermögensaufbau viel Potenzial ungenutzt, beklagt DSGV-Chef Reuter.
Das Narrativ, das Werbeabteilungen von Sparkassen und Banken verbreiten, ist einfach: Die zukünftigen Renten seien unsicher und in jedem Fall zu niedrig. Um den gewünschten Lebensstandard zu halten, reiche auch das klassische Sparen wegen der zu niedrigen Zinsen nicht mehr aus. Der propagierte Ausweg: in den Kapitalmarkt »investieren«. Konkret sollen die Verbraucher Geld in Aktien und ähnliche an Börsen gehandelten Wertpapiere anlegen. Diese böten Chancen auf eine höhere Rendite als das Sparbuch. Garantien dafür gebe es zwar nicht, aber wer nicht wagt ...
Die Parole lautet »Investieren statt Sparen«
Dabei verschweigen Finanzdienstleister ihr eigenes Interesse. Während sie bei klassischen Sparanlagen regelmäßig Zinsen an Kunden auszahlen müssen, kassieren sie bei »Investitionen« Provisionen und streichen unmittelbar Gewinne ein.
Assistiert wird das Narrativ »Investieren statt Sparen« von der schwarz-roten Bundesregierung. Zum Jahreswechsel löst das angesichts klammer Kassen großzügig vom Staat geförderte, aktienorientierte »Altersvorsorgedepot« die bisherige, auf Sicherheit bedachte Riester-Rente ab. Kürzlich hat der Bundestag außerdem das Frühstartrentengesetz beschlossen. Mit diesem schafft die Regierung Merz/Klingbeil den Einstieg in eine private Altersvorsorge schon im frühen Kindesalter von sechs Jahren.
Sparkassen, Banken und Finanzvertriebe wittern nun das große Geschäft. Marktbeobachter erwarten einen Ansturm besonders auf ETF-Produkte, die höhere Renditen bei geringen Kosten versprechen. Ein solcher »Exchange Traded Fund« ist ein börsengehandelter Fonds, der die Wertentwicklung eines Index nachbildet. Da Geldanlagen grundsätzlich breit gestreut werden sollten, legen viele ETFs das Geld ihrer Kunden in weltweit operierenden Indizes wie den MSCI World an. Hier dominieren aber US-amerikanische Aktiengesellschaften und Technologiekonzerne wie Amazon, Meta (früher Facebook) und Tesla des Donald-Trump-Vertrauten Elon Musk. »Wir stärken mit dem MSCI World nicht den heimischen Markt, sondern die USA«, kritisierte kürzlich der Vorstandsvorsitzende der Deutschen Vereinigung der Finanzberater, Thorsten Müller, das Altersvorsorgekonzept der Bundesregierung.
Dabei verschweigen Finanzdienstleister, dass selbst eine erfolgreiche Aktienanlage das individuelle Rentenloch nur selten stopfen wird. Langfristig kann sie in normalen Zeiten zwar eine Rendite von etwa acht Prozent im Jahr bringen – was im Alter genügen mag, wenn zeitlebens höhere Summen eingezahlt werden. Nur ein Teil der Bürger kann das.
Laut Statistischem Bundesamt ist Deutschland das Sparschwein Europas. Private Haushalte in Deutschland sparen anteilig mehr als in vielen anderen Industriestaaten. Mit 18,9 Prozent liegt die Bruttosparquote deutlich über dem Durchschnitt in der Europäischen Union von 14,3 Prozent und den USA mit 10,7 Prozent. Die Sparlust der Bundesbürger belastet allerdings die Volkswirtschaft erheblich, da Erspartes als kaufkräftige Nachfrage ausfällt. Zugleich erklärt die geringe Sparneigung der US-Konsumenten teilweise die höheren Wachstumsraten in den Vereinigten Staaten.
Mehr als jeder Fünfte kann nichts sparen
Nach einer repräsentativen Befragung, die im Auftrag des Bundesverbandes der Volksbanken und Raiffeisenbanken (BVR), aslo des genossenschaftlichen Sektors, zum Weltspartag durchgeführt wurde, sparen die Menschen in Deutschland durchschnittlich rund 200 Euro im Monat. Auch bei jungen Menschen ist die Renten-Botschaft der Politik angekommen. Jugendliche zwischen 14 und 19 Jahren legen der Befragung zufolge schon durchschnittlich rund 100 Euro im Monat zurück. »Das ist eine gute Voraussetzung für den langfristigen Vermögensaufbau und die private Altersvorsorge«, meint BVR-Präsidentin Marija Kolak.
Allerdings spiegeln solche Durchschnittswerte nur einen kleinen Teil der gesellschaftlichen Realität wider. Während etwa ein Fünftel der Befragten 20, 30 und mehr Prozent des monatlichen Netto-Einkommens auf die hohe Kante legt, »investiert« die Hälfte der Bürger nur unregelmäßig, wenn mal Geld übrig ist. Und bei 21 Prozent ist das nie der Fall. Mehr als jeder und jede Fünfte spart also höchstens – beim Konsum.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.title: Louvre Signs Deal with Unions, Ending Threat of Continued Strikes
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.author: Devorah Lauter
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.text:
As nationwide protests continue to loom across France, with the next action planned for Saturday, October 31, at least one social grievance has been addressed at the country’s top museum. On Thursday, the Louvre in Paris signed an agreement with unions who had threatened to strike for months, reports Le Figaro and AFP.
“The signature of the agreement amounts to a positive step for the Louvre,” a museum representative told AFP.
A few months after last year’s daytime robbery at the Louvre emptied the museum of over $100 million worth of its crown jewels, a broad coalition of French unions went on strike and, until this week’s deal, had pledged to continue protesting over poor working conditions, insufficient personnel, and the handling of museum renovations. The strikes began in December and forced the museum to close entirely for a total of four days and partially for another four days. Meanwhile, unions maintained an official “notice” to continue protests as needed, signaling they were not backing down and could block the museum at any time. All told, the dispute with unions is one of the longest face-offs of its kind for the Louvre.
As part of the new deal, the Louvre pledged to hire 50 new security personnel in 2027, or about 100 new hires in total by 2028, according to Le Quotidien de l’Art and other French reports. Additionally, the museum will improve pay for certain categories of workers, including a €50 ($56) monthly raise for security staff.
“The more of us there are carrying out our surveillance duties, the more we will deter criminals from targeting our institution,” Christian Galani, a representative of the French union CGT, told AFP.
The museum is in the throes of raising funds for an over one-billion-dollar renovation that will include security upgrades, the preservation of its aging infrastructure that has fallen into disrepair, and a separate, new entry and gallery dedicated to the Mona Lisa. However, there is disagreement about the cost and scope of the major renovation, and union representatives want a say in how it is handled. “We will quickly ask for a meeting on the management and prioritization of the construction works. We still have very little visibility on the safety and security plan announced in November 2025,” Alexis Fritche, leader of the CFDT-Culture union, told Le Quotidien de l’Art.
Following the crown jewel theft a year ago, Louvre president Laurence des Cars stepped down amid staff criticism that she used a top-down management style and ignored their concerns about the building’s disrepair and lack of personnel, while spending on projects they considered lavish. The arrival of the museum’s newly appointed president, Christophe Leribault, seems to have calmed some of those tensions.

Are Black Cats Modernity’s Icons?
How Manet transformed the misunderstood feline into an emblem of independent thinking; plus, Gay Halloween memes galore!
Centuries of superstition may be to blame for black cats facing among the lowest adoption outcomes at shelters across the US. But these mysterious, furry angels have shed at least part of their witchy stereotype in the modern era — thanks largely to 19th-century French artists, argues Rebecca Rebecca Schiffman, Hyperallergic associate editor. According to Schiffman, who makes a case for the black cat as a modern icon in art history in an essay perfectly timed for Hallows' Eve, painters such as Édouard Manet helped dark-furred felines come to symbolize a Belle Époque “appetite for provocation” and “refusal to be domesticated.”
On a related note, a big, heartfelt thanks to all who joined us at Hyperallergic’s Halloween party last night — you blew us all away with your commitment to the art costumes. (I’m looking at you, “Two Fridas” and “Saturn Devouring His Son.”) Look out for photos from the evening soon!
And in another tradition, Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar rounds up the spiciest Gay Halloween memes this year, a trend that holds a mirror up to our broader pop-culture moment. “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean we're dressed as Kelly Clarkson and an animatronic bird?”
—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor
How Édouard Manet’s Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity
Every Halloween, black cats return as emblems of witchcraft, bad luck, and the supernatural. Their sinister reputations stretch back centuries: starting in the Middle Ages, people associated cats with heresy and sexual transgression, and their perceived affinity with witches intensified during the trials of Elizabeth Francis and Agnes Waterhouse and their cat Sathan between 1565-1579.
But after the Enlightenment, 19th-century French artists and writers began to reclaim the mysterious and devilish qualities foisted onto felines as desirable.| Rebecca Schiffman
