https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.title: A Retrospective Introduces Francis Picabia to a New Generation—with Funhouse Mirrors and a Peep Show
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.author: Emily Watlington
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.text:
While midday crowds throng under a brilliant sky on Milan’s Piazza del Duomo, darkness gathers behind the windows of the nearby Palazzo Reale, where the vernissage for a major Francis Picabia retrospective has just begun. “Picabia. Open the Gates of Night” is curated by the artist’s great-granddaughter Anne Berest, who explained in her opening remarks that “to know [Picabia] is… to spend the night with him.” As if in a dream, the exhibition unfurls in a dusky twilight, low-lit galleries gathering works under associative themes that simulate an evening escapade with the playboy artist, evoking everything from ecstatic dance and nocturnal trysts to narcotic delirium and crepuscular epiphany.
Picabia (1879–1953) is one of the elusive figures of modern art, a Franco-Spanish painter and poet who moved freely between Impressionism, Fauvism, Orphism, Cubism, Machinism, and Dada, counting among his friends luminaries like Marcel Duchamp, Guillaume Apollinaire, Alfred Stieglitz, Erik Satie, and Gertrude Stein. Always pursuing a visual language for the forms that blossomed within his brain, Picabia believed in perpetual artistic evolution, an idea encoded in two of his oft-quoted aphorisms: “A conviction is a disease,” and, “If you want to have clean ideas, change them as often as you change your shirts.” In the exhibition, this heterodox ethos is manifest in the sheer stylistic variety of Picabia’s work, the walls a procession of representational compositions, geometric abstractions, mechanical diagrams, and syncretic paintings full of appropriated imagery.
“Picabia. Open the Gates of Night” makes psychoanalytic forays into the artist’s subconscious and daringly diagnoses his desires and disorders. The stage is set with a boyhood fixation—a gallery dedicated to “the Spanish Night,” also the title of a 1922 painting. Though Picabia was born and raised in France, his father was a Spaniard; during childhood visits to Seville, he witnessed Holy Week processionals, the rhythmic movements of Flamenco dancers, and the vital choreographies of the toreador. Emphasizing his “Andalusian blood,” the adult Picabia sublimated this self-exoticizing nostalgia into compositions on Spanish subjects. At the Palazzo Reale, an entire wall is punctuated by Picabia’s loose pencil and watercolor studies of the severe faces of Sevillian women, dark tresses piled high under lace mantillas. Across the room, a series of works showcases the persistence of dots—a common pattern on Flamenco dresses—across Picabia’s figural and abstract works, such as an untitled 1942 illustration of ballet dancers and his late geometric canvas Symbole (1950). Elsewhere in the room, comparison is drawn between photographs from the Picabia Family Archive of Andalusian architecture, with its lattice panels and arches, and the painted superpositions in Salicis, a 1929 work from his “Transparencies” series (1927–33) in which image planes interweave and interrupt one another as if in double-exposed photographs.
A later gallery, “Love Parade” (borrowing its title from a 1917 mechanomorphic painting), pathologizes Picabia’s lifelong libertinism as a response to the tragic loss of his mother at the age of seven. In their 2017 book Gabriële, the show’s curator and her sister Claire detail his all-male adolescence—he was raised by father, grandfather, and uncle—and observe that his family’s resulting nickname “les Quatre sans femme” (“the Four without a Woman”), might also be heard as “les quatre cents femmes” (“the Four Hundred Women”),” perhaps foreshadowing the vast number of lovers he courted over his lifetime.
Regardless of its roots, Picabia’s sexual drive was a galvanizing force in his work, from the machinic sketches à la Duchamp’s bachelor machine to erotic paintings such as Woman with the Bull (1940–41), which was collaged from found images of pin-up models. Picabia’s unchecked libido offers another interpretation for his “Transparencies,” which emerged at a time when, as the exhibition didactics euphemistically state, Picabia “lived through multiple loves simultaneously.”
Repeatedly, the wall texts underscore the idea that “every portrait is a self portrait.” There is a sense that the exhibition’s most significant revelation is neither synesthetic experiment nor vanguardist provocation but, merely and monumentally, Picabia himself. “Picabia. Open the Gates of Night” attempts to “escape chronology,” as Berest writes in her curatorial statement, setting aside the artistic canon and movement-based ideology in favor of character-study and lyric intuition. Despite their intrigue, these biographical reveries lose their place in history, splitting narrative threads and origin stories for bodies of work—including the “Transparencies” series—across the galleries. Rather than suggesting an overarching vision of the artist’s corpus and context, a dissolution into timeless simultaneity prevails.
Berest frames the exhibition as one for a “new generation,” the museum reimagined as a carnival or party. Within the decadent interiors of the Palazzo Reale, the exhibition operates theatrically as its own scintillating setpiece, the installation design completed by sparkling lights, funhouse mirrors, and a peep show that reveals some of Picabia’s more lascivious drawings. It’s almost as extravagant as the galas that Picabia hosted in the 1930s on the French Riviera, for which he orchestrated outrageous mise-en-scènes—zoo animals secured for “Une nuit à Singapore,” a grove of palms potted and arranged for “Un soir au Palm-Beach.” The exhibition addresses an audience for whom history has been superseded by the experiential, the embodied, and the personal. Perhaps this is as Picabia himself would have it. Another of his aphorisms, after all, celebrates the unbridled iconoclasm of an eternal present-tense: “Everything for today, nothing for yesterday, nothing for tomorrow.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/al.title: In Postwar Rural France, Alexander Calder Found Respite from Pressures of Fame and a Chance to Dream Big
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/al.author: Devorah Lauter
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/al.text:
If you’ve ever looked long and slow enough at Alexander Calder’s mobiles made of wire-suspended, leaf-like metal shapes painted solid colors, you likely know that they are as much about their sculptural form and silhouette as they are about the breathing air, light, shadow, and nature all around them. They shiver, drift, and play with the unpredictable whims of the surrounding atmosphere, making the invisible ether newly visible. Calder’s alternately delicate and massive sculptures are in communion with much larger forces around us.
At Hauser & Wirth in Paris, several of these sculptures are now on view (until December 19) in the exhibition titled “Calder: François Premier.” The show focuses on the late artist’s return to France from the US from 1953 to 1954 and includes a few mobiles that haven’t been seen in over 70 years: Les Granettes (1953) and The Putney Mobile (1954).
They are joined by an upstairs gallery full of bold, abstract, and figurative gouaches made between a small hamlet near Aix-en-Provence, called Les Granettes (where the 1953 mobile was made and named for), and a 17th-century home in Saché, another hamlet in the Loire Valley, now an artist residency. The more figurative gouaches include mysterious imagery such as pyramids, pulsing, planet-like orbs and even some camels.
“I seemed to develop something new,” Calder said of this sojourn to France after a 20-year absence. His “main” home and studio remained anchored in Roxbury, Connecticut, but he ultimately spent time living and working in Saché until his death in 1976.
“Calder’s return to France in 1953 is essential in understanding his late period. He was really emboldened and really inspired by being back,” Alexander S. C. Rower, his grandson and president of the Calder Foundation, says in a film screened at the gallery. “In really an unprecedented way, he was drawing directly on the metal: fabricating, welding, crafting the works into existence in full-scale, and that didn’t happen before. It was an extraordinary moment, with fantastic works of tremendous vocabulary.”
But what had brought Calder to the French countryside in the first place, and how did the place change how he worked?
To find out, ARTnews spoke with Rower, who was 13 when his grandfather died. After he completed a quick, “energetic reading” on me, which first mistakenly concluded I had been a sculptor in my youth but was amended to predict I would become one later, possibly in my 60s, Rower started with recounting Calder’s postwar story.
“The backstory is that during WWII, all of Calder’s friends were trying to come to America and be refugees,” he told me. Calder wrote to the State Department and successfully urged them to let in artists from Europe, such as Fernand Léger and André Masson. He eventually housed Masson and his young family, who all slept in Calder’s Connecticut barn-studio. After the war, Masson insisted Calder come to Aix-en-Provence, but it didn’t take much convincing. With his wife, Louisa, and their two daughters, Calder packed their things and joined their friends in southern France by 1953.
Later that year, the Calders discovered Saché in central France, where another friend (and later son-in-law) was living: the French-American journalist Jean Davidson. Calder soon bought a house in Saché on Davidson’s land, in exchange for three mobiles. From that moment on, “Saché just very naturally evolves into this hub. They have grandchildren there, and it becomes their homestead,” Rower said.
This conversation has been edited and condensed for concision and clarity.
ARTnews: What was special and inspiring about the French countryside to Calder, that might have led to the works we’re seeing here in Paris?
Alexander S. C. Rower: I wouldn’t say that France, or the countryside, was inspiring to him. He wasn’t making works related to what he was experiencing in the village and region. He was using being there to quiet his nervous system. He’s already a super famous guy when he shows up in 1953, and he has lots and lots of commissions. He’s this worldly character, and he needs to have quietude. That’s what Saché really deeply represents. It wasn’t the architecture, the chateaux in the region.
In Calder’s own words, he said he was trying to return to the ‘medieval‘—he’s talking about simple things, like going to this one place with a wood oven for baking bread, and another place that has this flock of goats and they’re making cheese. He liked the people that had maybe more challenges in life, but also had more authenticity, and he felt he was that way. He grew up with absolutely no money. His mom was a painter. His dad was a sculptor. He had to fend for himself. So the countryside in France, it’s still quite like that.
Did that simpler life away from it all change his work?
It definitely changed his work, but didn’t inspire his work. I’d say that he then had the chance with the big open skies to dream about bigger sculpture. He also was achieving success. By 1962, he found a big industrial iron works to execute his major works. He already had a smaller one in Connecticut that was making all the big works, and now he needed one in France, and the very biggest works were executed here in France. For that first group of works completed in 1963, they were all made for his own account. He commissioned seven outdoor sculptures, because he had enough money to make what he wanted to make.
What was his studio in France like?
The wagon shed, or remise, he converted to his studio was a very small space. A highly productive space. He made so many works there of the late period. Some of the 1950s, but mostly ’60s. Most of the sculpture made in the 1960s was made in that studio. Everything else before that was made in Connecticut, which was his number one studio.
When he arrived in France in 1953, he made four outdoor sculptures, standing mobiles that you put in your garden, one of which was Les Granettes (1953). He made lots of smaller works, but he didn’t make any big sculptures [in France that year].
And yet he started to think more about making large-scale works in Saché?
Saché is this little town where Henri de Balzac used to go and write, and it’s very flat. There’s nothing mountainous in the region, and the idea of monumental sculptures coming up out of the landscape is pretty obvious. It’s big sky country. Maybe the sky, you could say, was inspiring, because a big dynamic black form against the sky is terrific.
Why did you love about this place as a child?
Seeing Calder hard at work in France was a great pleasure. To go to the foundry, and see how he talked to the guys. He loved the guys that helped him execute his works. He wasn’t dismissive. He wasn’t offhand. He wasn’t at a distance. He was really connected with them. He gave them all gouaches and stuff. The welder was the guy he really liked. He’d come bring him a bottle of wine and talk about welding.
I wonder whether they kept any of those artworks he gave them.
They’ve all sold them. They’ve all come to market, and the grandchildren have sold them for education or whatever. Calder would have loved that. It’s just as it should be.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mo.title: MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Will Treat Their Holdings as One Collection in Unprecedented Alliance
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mo.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mo.text:
Six years ago, the director of Hong Kong’s M+ museum, Suhanya Raffel, told cultural strategist András Szántó, in an interview for the book The Future of the Museum, that in the years to come museums will need to “stand together and work to help one another to deliver a more sustainable baseline.” Collaboration, she went on, “will be a key aspect of the next chapter of museum work.” Her words seem to have been prophetic: on Friday morning in Hong Kong, M+, the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris announced a wide-ranging cultural alliance unprecedented in its scale. At the heart of the alliance is an agreement that the three institutions will treat their respective holdings as a shared collection, curated by staff spread across three continents.
“If we succeed,” Laurent Le Bon, the Pompidou’s president, told ARTnews in Paris, during a joint interview that also included Raffel and MoMA director Christophe Cherix, “we will be more than the sum of our parts, and I think that is something quite new.”
The combined holdings of MoMA and the Pompidou mean the total shared collection will number in the hundreds of thousands of objects, and the three institutions are also stewards of voluminous archives. The collection at M+, founded six years ago, numbers around 8,000 objects, but the museum has a definitive collection of contemporary Chinese art, much of it donated by Swiss businessman and former diplomat Uli Sigg. The Pompidou houses the largest modern art museum in Europe (its holdings are a national collection owned by the French state). The potential audience will be enormous: based on current figures, the museums will have a combined 10 million annual in-person visitors and 125 million online visitors.
The collection sharing will kick off with several initiatives. Beginning in late 2027, a selection of major works from M+’s collection will be installed on long-term loan in MoMA’s collection galleries, and in 2028, a long-term Centre Pompidou gallery will also open at MoMA, with similar, parallel plans in development at the other museums. (The Pompidou is currently closed for a five-year restoration of its building and is scheduled to reopen in 2030.)
As part of the alliance, the partner institutions will, over the next five years, co-organize an exhibition exploring the complex concept of “the contemporary,” which will include works from all three collections and be presented at all three institutions; curators at the Centre Pompidou and M+ will join MoMA’s C-MAP (Contemporary and Modern Art Perspectives), a cross-departmental research program founded in 2009 with the aim of exploring art histories outside North America and Western Europe.
Additionally, a joint steering committee, made up of the three museum directors along with department heads and curators from the three museums, will begin to work on such priorities as exhibitions and collection sharing, research, conservation, and professional development. The committee will meet monthly, and there will be one major in-person meeting a year, the first of which will take place next month at MoMA. (Subsequent annual meetings will rotate among the museums.)
To a certain extent, the alliance comes out of previous partnerships between M+ and the other two institutions. In February 2025, M+ and MoMA signed a memorandum of understanding that encompassed collection sharing, joint research, and curatorial exchanges. Earlier this year, M+ and the Centre Pompidou announced their own multiyear strategic partnership, which included plans for the Pompidou to inaugurate its renovated space with an exhibition of works from both museums’ collections, followed by a presentation of that show at M+.
	In the interview with ARTnews in Paris, the three directors acknowledged that the new cultural alliance grew out of the previous bilateral partnerships. They stressed, however, that it also grew out of the three institutions’ commonalities, such as cross-disciplinary collecting and a focus on the art of the present, as well as the lineage the museums form: nearly a century of collecting contemporary art, starting with MoMA’s founding in 1929 and continuing through the Pompidou’s opening in 1977 and M+’s in 2021. Raffel has acknowledged that Centre Pompidou was “one of the key institutions” that M+ “looked to that helped us guide the principles around building an institution like this for Asia.”
“We each have things that are absolutely unique in the world,” said Cherix. “Our first role is of course preservation. But how can we make those collections work harder for us and touch people well beyond the walls of our institutions?”
This alliance differs from past models such as traveling exhibitions, co-organized shows, and collaborations on specific projects, Cherix explained, in that it is a long-term commitment to building programs together from the ground up, one that will involve “bringing our teams much closer together.”
The new arrangement also aims to take advantage of economies of scale and to make things like shipping more sustainable. Raffel and Cherix pointed out that, for instance, sending parts of M+’s collection of contemporary Chinese art to MoMA for extended periods would not only allow those works to rotate through the MoMA galleries but also make them more easily available to other museums in the United States.
In a world in which museums want their collections to reflect global perspectives, sharing makes more sense than continuing to accumulate separately. “We can’t just keep collecting, so we are sharing instead,” said Raffel. This raises the bar for acquisitions: to be added to the shared collection, a work will, as Cherix put it, “need to have no equal” in any of the three collections.
“Even if we want to be devoted to the art of our time, we become a historical collection,” Cherix continued. “How can we reset that? I think this alliance gives us exactly the capacity to have a different scope, and a forward-looking vision.”
More museums have partnered in recent years to share collections, pool resources, and expand their audiences. The strategy has evolved from standard short-term exhibition loans to deeply integrated models that include joint acquisitions, shared private donations, regional networks, and long-term international exchanges. Joint acquisitions have become increasingly common since 2003, when the Whitney Museum, Tate, and the Centre Pompidou teamed up to purchase Bill Viola’s video installation Five Angels for the Millennium.
An arrangement somewhat similar to the MoMA–Pompidou–M+ model came in 2018, when Chinese Indonesian collector Budi Tek partnered with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) in a collection-sharing arrangement with Shanghai’s Yuz Museum, which Tek had founded. (China rejected attempts to make the Yuz Museum a public institution; Tek died in 2022.) In that case, a new foundation was formed to oversee the collection, which would live in China but otherwise travel between Los Angeles and Shanghai for temporary exhibitions. Works from LACMA’s collection, for example, traveled to the Yuz Museum in 2009 for the exhibition “In Production: Art and the Studio System,” while in 2021, 20 pieces from Tek’s collection went on display at LACMA for the exhibition “Legacies of Exchange.”
More recently, museums have agreed to be the joint stewards of certain collectors’ holdings. In 2022, around 100 works from the collection of Greek industrialist Dimitri Daskalopoulos became a shared gift to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. In 2024, three Los Angeles museums—the Hammer, LACMA, and the Museum of Contemporary Art—jointly received some 350 works owned by Jarl and Pamela Mohn. Those three institutions continue to add to that collection, called the Mohn Art Collective (MAC3).

Qatar condemns tanker attack in the Gulf as threat to global energy security
Qatar has condemned an attack on one of its tankers as a "dangerous escalation" that threatens global energy security and maritime navigation.
In a foreign ministry statement, Doha warned of the dangers posed by "reckless and irresponsible practices" of attacking tankers.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs affirms that the State of Qatar reserves its right to take all necessary measures – in accordance with the provisions of international law and the Charter of the United Nations – to protect its property, safeguard its interests, and ensure the safety of its ships and crews," said the Qatari foreign ministry.
Earlier, the Qatar Gas Transport Company Limited said its vessel was hit by “unidentified objects” while sailing in the Gulf on Friday.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.title: IA : pourquoi les géants de la tech plongent en bourse malgré des résultats records
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Pierric Marissal
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
Les investissements dans l’intelligence artificielle devraient s’élever à près de 2 700 milliards de dollars cette année dans le monde, plombant les résultats des géants de la Tech qui dévissent en bourse.
Pas facile d’expliquer à des actionnaires que malgré des résultats records, ils devront s’asseoir sur leurs dividendes à cause d’investissements qui creusent des trous béants dans la trésorerie. C’est ce qui est arrivé à Google, qui a perdu vendredi 30 octobre 500 milliards de dollars de capitalisation boursière en 24 heures, le plus gros plongeon boursier de son histoire.
C’est en effet la période des résultats trimestriels, et si les chiffres d’affaires dans la Tech sont en hausse, les 2 670 milliards de dollars investis en 2026 dans l’IA dans le monde, selon les dernières estimations de Garner, laissent les trésoreries en négatif : – 9 milliards sur le dernier trimestre pour Google. Les valorisations de Meta (Facebook) et Amazon qui ont publié des résultats guère plus brillants ont également fondu.
Au total, à la clôture du Nasdaq vendredi soir, le secteur de la Tech avait perdu 1 500 milliards de dollars, soit le PIB de la Turquie. Le décrochage a débuté jeudi 29, quand un constructeur de datacenter, CoreWeave, s’est effondré. Les marchés ont jugé son endettement, de plus de 50 milliards, bien trop excessif.
La palme de la chute revient à Intel, le fabricant de processeurs à destination des PC, qui a cédé 29 % de capitalisation. La pénurie de mémoire vive et de stockage, accaparés par les centres de données pour l’IA, a entraîné une chute des ventes d’ordinateurs et plombé les résultats de l’industriel étasunien. Les géants de la Tech empruntent désormais à plus de 15 %. « Argh » a réagi Elon Musk qui vient de boucler un nouvel emprunt de 40 milliards.

This is an entry from: Live: Iran says Hormuz could be reopened within two days if conditions met
Iran submits evidence of US-Israeli attacks on maritime infrastructure to IMO
1 November 2026 13:03 GMT
Iran said it has submitted evidence of US and Israeli attacks on its maritime infrastructure to the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
The dossier of evidence given by Tehran to the IMO includes documents and photographic evidence of sabotage on its maritime infrastructure.
An Iranian official said IMO member states will discuss the evidence at a council session taking place in London on 2-6 November.
The attacks on its maritime infrastructure, according to Iran, threaten the safety of international shipping and seafarers.
Iran's IRNA news agency reported that damage to maritime traffic control systems also increases the risk of accidents, and the destruction of rescue facilities undermines emergency response capabilities.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Michigan race: All you need to know about Abdul El-Sayed v Mike Rogers
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Michigan race: All you need to know about Abdul El-Sayed v Mike Rogers
Al Jazeera examines the crucial US Senate race in Michigan, including the candidates’ positions and largest spenders.
Dearborn, Michigan – Chadi Abdulrazek, an Arab American political activist who has been volunteering to help elect Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, says he’s spoken in recent days to journalists from Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom.
The United States Senate race between El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers is attracting national and international attention, reflecting the potent political symbolism that belies its outcome, which extends far beyond one seat in the upper chamber of Congress.
Supporters in each camp paint the contest as a crucial fight that could shape the political direction of the state and the nation for years.
Abdulrazek, a small business owner, said the election is a chance to hold Trump accountable for breaking his promises to pursue peace in the world and focus on the needs of Americans.
For Arab and Muslim communities that have been facing Islamophobic attacks as part of the Senate race, the vote is pivotal, he added.
“What’s on the line is they have to stand up for themselves and say, ‘We are part of this country, and we’re going to be voting, and we will actually make a change’,” Abdulrazek told Al Jazeera.
Here, Al Jazeera looks at the US Senate race in Michigan and why it has gained so much attention.
Who are the candidates?
El-Sayed is a public health advocate who previously led the health department in Detroit and Wayne County in southeast Michigan. He is 42.
If elected, the Democrat of Egyptian descent would become the first-ever Muslim US senator.
El-Sayed ran for governor in 2018 but fell short in the Democratic primary against eventual winner Gretchen Whitmer. The Democratic nominee has embraced progressive policies, especially Medicare for All – a plan to expand government-funded healthcare to everyone in the US.
Rogers is a 63-year-old former US Congress member and state legislator. The Republican nominee ran for the Senate in 2024 and narrowly lost to centrist Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin.
He is a close ally of Donald Trump, but has sought to create some distance between his campaign and the unpopular president.
For example, Rogers has supported Trump’s decision to join Israel in launching the war against Iran, while also calling for an end to the conflict.
The Republican candidate also backs tax cuts, increasing domestic energy production and deregulation.
Why is the race so important?
It will be difficult for Democrats to gain control of the Senate if they lose Michigan. The seat is currently held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters.
A Rogers win would hand the swing state Senate seat to Republicans for at least six years.
The race, however, is not just about the partisan math in the Senate. It is a test of the electoral viability of progressive ideas, including sharp criticism of Israel, in a swing state.
While the Senate has many progressive members, most come from coastal states considered Democratic strongholds.
A victory for El-Sayed in Michigan would show that his message can attract a winning coalition, which could influence how Democratic presidential candidates may go about their campaigning in 2028.
There is also the factor of El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, which had become the subject of near daily attacks by Rogers and Trump.
The race has raised questions about whether Michigan and the US are ready for a Muslim senator.
Why has Israel become a major issue in the race?
El-Sayed has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza, echoing the findings of major human rights organisations and United Nations investigators.
The Democrat has also linked wars, including the conflict in Iran and US aid to Israel, to domestic issues. He says that US taxpayer money is better spent on addressing issues at home, such as healthcare and crumbling infrastructure. Pro-Israel groups, namely the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), have spent tens of millions of dollars to help defeat El-Sayed.
AIPAC backed El-Sayed’s opponent Haley Stevens with more than $30m, making Israel policy one of the most discussed subjects in the election.
El-Sayed overcame the spending onslaught in the primaries, but Rogers – a staunch Israel supporter – has seized on the criticism of El-Sayed from pro-Israel advocates, including some Democrats.
Rogers – who has pledged unconditional support for Israel – has accused El-Sayed of caring more for Palestine than Michigan.
After a lull in spending in Michigan, AIPAC has returned to the race to back Rogers.
The pro-Israel lobby group’s election arm, United Democracy Project, has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on mailers against El-Sayed. According to The New York Times, it has funnelled $9m to a Republican group supporting Rogers.
Why is Haley Stevens back in the headlines?
It is uncommon for the candidate who lost a primary to be part of a major storyline in the general election, but Stevens has been making headlines days ahead of the vote after her fiance endorsed Rogers, citing El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Stevens, a Democrat in the US House of Representatives, has also criticised El-Sayed for his positions on Israel while saying she would still vote for the Democratic candidate.
The congresswoman’s repeated media appearances bashing El-Sayed have earned the scorn of some Democrats.
On Friday, El-Sayed and several Democratic-aligned groups and politicians responded to Stevens, saying that the party must focus on winning the Senate seat.
El-Sayed said in a statement that while “defeating Trump’s hand-picked candidate” should be the priority, “Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”
What are the voters saying?
Both Rogers and El-Sayed supporters interviewed by Al Jazeera have stressed the race’s importance.
Former Democratic Cynthia Johnson said the negative campaigning around El-Sayed’s religion and ethnicity makes the election especially crucial.
“What’s really at stake is life or death. Our children are being exposed to some very negative, nasty things,” Johnson told Al Jazeera.
“We have to vote like our lives depended on it because we have a person who’s in the White House right now who’s a maniac and we need as many people who are going to speak up as possible – people like Abdul.”
Outside a Trump rally on Sunday, Rogers supporter Rob Cortis expressed similar urgency.
“This election is so important. Our country is at stake. Our border is at stake. The future of our children in America is at stake,” Cortis told Al Jazeera.
“If it flips to communism, socialism or if it goes to Muslim rule America was never intended for that. America is intended to be a nation of Christians, showing the goodness of God.”
What are the polls saying?
Most recent polls have shown El-Sayed with a narrow lead over Rogers – ranging from four to seven percentage points.
However, polling in Michigan – a diverse state of more than 10 million people – has been unreliable over the past decades, often getting the results wrong by several percentage points.
The Cook Political Report has classified the race as a toss-up and both campaigns have warned their supporters that the result may come down to a few thousand votes.
Who is spending in the race?
With nearly $300m spent, Michigan’s Senate race is quickly becoming one of the most expensive in the country.
Political action committees (PACs) aligned with both major parties have been buying ads in support of their respective candidates.
On the Republican side, one of the largest spenders has been Senate Leadership Fund, whose largest donors include pro-Israel billionaire Miriam Adelson.
MAGA Inc and its subsidiary No Going Back, a pro-Trump group funded by the US president’s allies, including Adelson and Elon Musk, have also spent millions of dollars on the race.
Great Lakes Conservatives Fund (GLCF), a Michigan Republican PAC that AIPAC has backed in general elections, has also been a big spender, according to media reports.
The Senate Majority PAC (SMP) and an affiliated group called WINSENATE have been the largest spenders. SMP’s top funders include businessmen Eychaner Fred and Amos Hostetter Jr.
When is the election?
Early voting is underway across Michigan and hundreds of thousands of people have already cast their ballots.
Election day, Tuesday, November 3, will be the last day to vote. Polls in Michigan close at 8pm (01:00 GMT on Wednesday).
When will the result come out?
That depends on how close the race is. If it’s a tight contest, Michigan likely will not find out who won until Wednesday. In the primaries in August, when El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens, the Associated Press did not call the race until about 10am (15GMT) on the Wednesday after election day.
Likewise, Michigan was called for Trump in 2024 around 1pm (18:00 GMT) on the day after the election.
However, if one of the candidates acquires a commanding lead across the state, he could be projected as the winner hours after the polls close.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war
Tehran says it could reopen Hormuz in a shorter period if conditions are met, as Trump says the US still has several Iranian targets to ‘take care of’.
Iran’s Foreign Minister speaks to Al Jazeera about US proposals
Tehran, Iran – Ongoing contacts through mediators have provided a potential diplomatic opening between Iran and the United States, even as both sides express readiness for renewed military escalation.
After two days of Qatari-mediated talks, Iranian authorities have signalled that a deal remains possible provided that their demands are tangibly implemented. At the same time, they have doubled down on a willingness to expand attacks or even launch preemptive strikes if they deem war is inevitable.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”
His comments came as US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the talks were going “fine” but added that Iranian authorities were not “reliable”.
The Republican leader, who ordered attacks alongside Israel against Iran on February 28, has repeatedly raised prospects of once more hitting the country’s civilian infrastructure. In recent weeks, he has suggested that an attack could potentially take place after the November 3 midterm elections in the US.
“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida about further bombing Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Sequencing and timeline
The mediated talks in Tehran on Friday, and then in Qatar on Saturday, appear to have produced a new tangible result by shortening the period after which Iran’s proposal to partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz can be enforced.
Tehran had previously offered seven days, but that has now come down to two, Araghchi said in his interview with Al Jazeera.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said there are “indications” of US interest in a negotiated settlement, citing the continuing Qatar-mediated talks and US Vice President JD Vance’s recent outreach.
“However, Iran is seeking a series of concessions while the United States insists on progress on Iran’s nuclear programme before concessions are made,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore the central difficulty is sequencing and leverage. Each side wants the other to act first.”
Araghchi’s two-day offer indicates some flexibility over sequencing that could also allow both sides to claim an initial diplomatic achievement without immediately resolving their fundamental disagreements, according to Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.
“However, the military statements show the limits of this opening. Iran appears increasingly determined to prevent a repetition of previous scenarios in which negotiations or temporary ceasefires were followed by renewed military conflict,” he wrote on social media. “From Tehran’s perspective, the objective is to make another attack so costly and unpredictable that Washington would have to reconsider the option altogether.”
As the talks were ongoing on Saturday, the office of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he had a meeting earlier with top military commanders to demand “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for an immediate response “without geographical restriction” to any threat.
Targets would include “tangible and intangible” US and Israeli assets, Khamenei said. Iranian authorities have previously said if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is attacked again, seabed cables and infrastructure across the region could also become targets.
After Khamenei’s statement, commanders of the general staff of the armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the traditional army separately expressed readiness to launch missile, drone and other attacks in case of an escalation of conflict.
State media on Sunday also aired footage of missiles and drones being taken out of massive underground storage sites and deployed during the eight months of war so far.
The authorities also signalled that they expect more potential attacks from the US and Israel, including against Iran’s power grid.
Gholamreza Jalali, commander of the National Organization for Passive Defense, said during a speech on Sunday that they have identified 14 sectors most dependent on electricity that would need support if the war restarts, without naming any.
“Adopting preventive measures in the area of passive defence for the electricity grid is a fundamental principle that all authorities must follow up in their capacities,” he said, adding that officials were considering “network islanding” practices to create different segments that would not all be simultaneously affected by potential bombing.
‘Positive change in tone’
In and around the Strait of Hormuz, vessels continue to be attacked if they refuse to coordinate with the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the entity set up by Iranian authorities to enforce control and sovereignty in the critical waterway.
At least four tankers were identified as being hit on Friday and Saturday, although not all attacks are reported by vessels and monitors. According to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a vessel carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) was struck by three Iranian projectiles on Saturday about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran’s Lavan Island, deep into the Gulf.
Transit in the strait and surrounding waterways will not return to normal unless the US takes steps towards Iran’s conditions, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told state television during an interview on Saturday night.
For the sequencing to work, he said Tehran wants the US to lift its naval blockade that has halted oil exports and the majority of Iran’s trade, which used to be facilitated through its southern ports. The US must also issue waivers for oil sanctions, unfreeze Iran’s assets abroad, stop fighting on all regional fronts, including Lebanon, and recognise a bilateral Iran-Oman arrangement for Hormuz.
Rezaei said he has yet to respond to a letter addressed to him by Vance, although he said the missive indicated a “change in tone” that he described as “positive”.
Mostafa Najafi, a Tehran-based political analyst said to be linked with Rezaei, said if the conditions are not met, the letter is likely to go unanswered and negotiations – including on Iran’s nuclear programme – will not enter a higher level.
“It is unclear how willing Washington is to accept these demands. It is clear that not recognising rights emphasised by Iran will lead to the failure of the negotiations,” he wrote on X.
The US has also doubled down on the effectiveness of its Operation Economic Outcast involving the blockade, sanctions and pressure on overland trade and aviation.
A report by the US Treasury to inform Trump’s decision-making, which was publicised by news outlet Axios, said no new oil had been loaded onto tankers at Iran’s terminals since August 25. It also showed overseas crude deliveries were down, while Iran’s year-on-year inflation neared 90 percent in September and the national currency continued to dwindle.
The report said Iran’s economy was “crippled” by the combined measures, but did not argue that it was close to collapsing.
