https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Spirit of 1676: remembering the Native American cataclysm of King Philip’s war
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Rich Tenorio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Massachusetts is proud of its ties to the American Revolution. From Paul Revere’s Ride to the siege of Boston, the past year-plus has been devoted to celebrating 250 years of US independence. Yet during this time, the state, and New England in general, has given far less attention to an older, more complex remembrance: The 350th anniversary of King Philip’s war.
King Philip, or Metacom, was an Indigenous leader from the Pokanoket people. Alarmed by English colonists’ infringement of Indigenous rights, from seizing land to proselytizing, Metacom led an alliance of New England tribes – including the Pokanoket, Nipmuc and Narragansett – in an existential struggle for control of the region. He gave his name to the conflict, but paid with his life – as did many others, soldiers and civilians alike. With an estimated 800 dead on the colonial side, and three to five thousand Indigenous slain, the war claimed more deaths per capita than any other in colonial American or US history.
For the Indigenous, the price of defeat was steep. The victorious English sold many into slavery, and executed others on Boston Common. The war marked a turning point in relations between the ascending colonial presence and an increasingly diminished Indigenous population, whose ancestors had met for a peaceful Thanksgiving celebration just a half-century before.
Today, the conflict continues to reverberate. With November marking both National Native American History Month and the Thanksgiving holiday, and 2026 marking 250 years of American independence, historians are reflecting on the impact of King Philip’s war, 350 years later – a somber moment amid the Revolutionary hoopla.
“Recognizing the two anniversaries occur at the same time offers a moment to reflect why some things get much more attention than others,” says Christine De Lucia, an assistant professor of history at Williams College in western Massachusetts and the author of the 2018 book Memory Lands: King Philip’s War and the Place of Violence in the Northeast.
Mack Scott III, an assistant professor of critical Native American and Indigenous studies at Brown University, and a member of the Narragansett tribe, says, “The way we remember it, when we do talk about it, is through ideas that become part of the lore of a nation, that we don’t even associate with the war but are definitely internalized as a community, as a people, as a nation: ‘This is the process by which the land becomes the US, and the process has some sort of benevolence.’
“A lot of people believed that,” Scott says, “[for them] it was an almost undeniable natural process, almost inevitable, it was going to happen in this way. They don’t remember how violent the war was for New England. That was the thinking about those processes – it was a promised land. When you frame it almost in those senses – it was almost inexorable, undeniable, natural, divine, supposed to happen – the removal of Indigenous people, the death of Indigenous people becomes almost preordained, natural, something you expect to see. Today, Native peoples are almost back-of-mind for most Americans.”
The situation was much different in 17th-century New England.
Metacom’s father, Massasoit or Ousamequin, held a powerful position as the leader, or sachem, of the Pokanoket. (The tribe has been connected to the Wampanoag people, although there is some dispute over this.) It was Ousamequin who helped the starving Pilgrims survive their first winter at Plymouth in 1620-21, and it was Ousamequin who joined in on that first Thanksgiving meal of coexistence. Yet the ensuing decades had altered the landscape. Pathogens brought by English and earlier European explorers had decimated the Indigenous population. A continual influx of English colonists tipped the population balance in favor of the newcomers, who increasingly encroached on Native land.
“It was like a pot that had been boiling for a long, long time,” says Brad Lopes, the education and public programs manager for the Aquinnah Cultural Center, and a member of the Aquinnah Wampanoag tribe on the island of Martha’s Vineyard. “Our ancestors faced almost an existential crisis … The world they knew, that our ancestors knew, would never really be around any more.”
Metacom’s older brother, Wamsutta, had been raised to succeed their father as sachem. Instead, shortly after assuming the role, Wamsutta mysteriously died after meeting with the colonists, with the less experienced Metacom becoming the new sachem. The colonists soon compelled Metacom to accept a humiliating agreement that incensed the Pokanoket.
Eric Schultz, co-author of the 2017 book King Philip’s War: The History and Legacy of America’s Forgotten Conflict, says that Metacom faced a “very complex moment”, one that “his father and brother never faced before”,
In June 1675, war erupted with an Indigenous attack on Swansea, in what is today south-eastern Massachusetts.
Metacom’s forces were “very successful at the outset”, says bestselling author Michael Tougias, who co-wrote King Philip’s War with Schultz. “They quickly adapted hit-and-run tactics into ambushes. The English were reeling. I often thought, had all the tribes in New England united, they would have pushed the English back into a ring around Boston.” However, he adds, “because so many natives did not join, ending up with the English or wavering on the side, it eventually tips the balance.”
When Metacom led a force into the colony of New York to seek an alliance with the powerful Mohawk tribe, it backfired: the Mohawk preferred fur trading with English colonists, and attacked Metacom’s men. Another powerful tribe, the Narragansett of Rhode Island, did join the conflict on Metacom’s side, but they lost heavily in an engagement remembered by the colonists as the Great Swamp Fight, and by Indigenous as the Great Swamp Massacre. Several tribes – the Mohegan and the Pequot – fought alongside colonists. Other Indigenous people, who had converted to Christianity and were called “Praying Indians”, sided with the colonists but their loyalty was doubted. Colonial authorities relocated them to Deer Island in Boston Harbor; there, running low on supplies in the winter, hundreds died.
Although Indigenous forces committed their share of depredations, they were unprepared for the scale of colonial vengeance, in engagements such as the Great Swamp Fight and the Turners Falls Massacre, or for the determination of the English to press the war at all seasons.
“This is a war of attrition,” says Donald “Strong Turtle” Brown Jr, the official historian of the Pokanoket and a descendant of Metacom. “Indigenous people cannot sustain their warriors or plant in the field. They surrender because they’re starving, or dying from exposure to the elements.”
One colonial military leader – Benjamin Church – successfully adopted Indigenous military tactics. When an Indigenous man named John Alderman offered to locate Metacom, Church listened. On 12 August 1676, Alderman guided an expedition to Metacom and killed the Pokanoket sachem at the tribe’s stronghold of Mount Hope in present-day Rhode Island.
Metacom’s head was displayed on a stake outside Plymouth. His wife and son were sold into slavery, as were many other Indigenous people. The conflict did not end in all of New England upon Metacom’s death; in Maine, the Wabanaki continued fighting until 1678 and, unlike many of their counterparts, they got to remain on their land.
“The issues that were present during King Philip’s War do not go away by the time of the American Revolution and the advent of independence in the US,” Williams professor De Lucia says. “In some ways, they intensify – the theft of Native lands, US attempts to diminish Native sovereignty.”
Recent decades have witnessed increasing interest in Indigenous history – consider the inclusion of Native Americans in the recent Ken Burns documentary on the Revolution, or the land acknowledgments now de rigueur at some US institutions. That’s what makes it difficult to understand the relative dearth of attention to King Philip’s war.
Amid the many Revolutionary 250th celebrations in Massachusetts, there have been some local, regional and inter-tribal commemorations of the earlier war. It is harder to find evidence of larger-scale events. The offices of the governors of three New England states involved in the conflict – Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island – did not respond to separate inquiries as to whether their state held, or is planning to hold, a commemorative event.
Three hundred and fifty years later, several federally recognized Indigenous communities remain in New England: the Wampanoag in Massachusetts, and the Narragansett in Rhode Island. Metacom’s community, the Pokanoket of south-eastern Massachusetts and eastern Rhode Island, have not received federal recognition. But they have been recognized by other entities in tangible ways.
“Because we remember who we are and celebrate our history, Brown University [in 2024] returned 255 acres of our ancestral land – Mount Hope in Bristol – to the Pokanoket tribe,” says Metacom’s descendant Brown. “It’s one of the largest land-back grants to a non-federally recognized tribal [community], so we can secure our ancestral lands in perpetuity.”
And, Brown says, “Rhode Island General Assembly Senate Resolution S1034 last year officially acknowledges the Pokanoket tribe as the ancient and ongoing stewards of our ancestral land. The past does not erase us. Our story continues.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Dark money made darker’: funding labyrinth conceals donors to Republican campaigns
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jason Wilson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In the summer of 2024, a non-profit called the Green Dragon Coalition wired the last $20,000 of a $445,000 grant to a Super Pac. Its tax return for that year would describe the purpose of the transfer as “educational”.
The same day, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records, the Super Pac spent $8,000 attacking Celeste Maloy, the Republican congresswoman for Utah’s second district, four days before the primary that would decide whether she kept her seat. It had already spent more than $400,000 promoting her challenger, Colby Jenkins, who was running to her right with the endorsement of the rightwing Utah senator Mike Lee.
One man was involved at every stage, and his name is on the paperwork for the charity that raised the money, the non-profit that passed it on, the Super Pac that the non-profit donated to and the campaign this money eventually supported.
His name is Thomas Datwyler, and his businesses are mostly headquartered in a rented address in Hudson, Wisconsin, a town of 15,000 near the border with Minnesota. Datwyler operates at an industrial scale, acting as treasurer of more than 350 federal political committees in the current election cycle, including 115 congressional campaigns and 100 Super Pacs, and as an officer of more than two dozen non-profits.
The extent of Datwyler’s activities over several political cycles raises questions about the attitude of Republican campaigns and candidates to campaign finance in the run-up to the November midterm elections, and the evolution of so-called “dark money” electoral funding.
Across the 2024 and 2026 cycles, Super Pacs whose books Datwyler also keeps have spent more than $2m supporting 14 candidates that are also his clients, or attacking their opponents, according to FEC filings. In several of those races the money reached the Super Pac through charities and social welfare groups for which he is a treasurer.
Datwyler-tied groups have been funded by donors connected to the rightwing megadonor Leonard Leo, along with the Conservative Partnership Institute and the personal foundation of the Claremont Institute’s board chair, the Thomas Klingenstein Fund, among others.
Money raised from these conservative donors has gone into organisations that Datwyler runs the books for, and those organisations have passed money on to Super Pacs that spent in Republican primaries. Non-profit tax filings do not show which donors’ funds made up any particular onward transfer.
Along the way, the same firms are paid by both the campaigns and the groups that are legally required to be independent of campaigns in order to maintain their tax-exempt status. In Florida’s 19th district, a campaign and the supposedly independent Super Pac backing it share 14 vendors, according to FEC filings.
Federal law prohibits coordination between Pacs and campaign committees, but proving it is challenging. The FEC is a reluctant cop, and while Datwyler has attracted significant controversy and state-level investigations, what he does may not be illegal.
“Somebody in Datwyler’s position is well aware of where all the cracks and crevices in the system are, how to sort of exploit the rules in a way that maximises his clients’ ability to secretly influence elections,” says Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the non-profit Campaign Legal Center.
“There’s a reason why the same handful of people – and Datwyler’s probably the chief among them – tend to come up in connection with these dark money operations. It’s because they have the knowhow of how to do it. And they’re willing to be the public face on each of these entities.
“The actual donors providing the money don’t want to be publicly outed as the source of the outside money pouring into the race.”
Datwyler wrote to the Guardian that “AxCapital [where he is CEO] is grateful that so many clients entrust our team to facilitate their participation in the democratic process. As an industry leader, we have strict internal firewalls, strong safeguards, and robust policies to ensure full compliance with all laws, regulations, and requirements.”
The Green Dragon pipeline
The Green Dragon entities exemplify a pattern that recurs across Datwyler’s network.
The Green Dragon Coalition is a 501(c)4 social welfare non-profit, and one of three entities registered in Delaware in 2023 with sequential IRS employer numbers, all listing the same address in Hudson, Wisconsin. The other two were the Green Dragon Society, a 501(c)3 charity, and the Constitutional Conservatives Fund, a Super Pac.
Datwyler is treasurer of all three, and is the only officer that any of the organizations pay: the Green Dragon Coalition paid him $25,012 during the 2024 cycle and the Green Dragon Society paid him $29,066.
This is just a fraction of the compensation Datwyler has received across various arms of the political operation he works on. Tax filings indicate that he received at least $487,545 in the 2023-2024 cycle from non-profits. FEC filings indicate that during the last two election cycles at least $793,470 flowed to Datwyler directly, or to two Delaware-registered consultancies, 10Six Consulting and Same Day Processing, that share a Wisconsin address with the vast majority of his political and charity organizations.
Meanwhile, AxCapital, where Datwyler is CEO, brought in $4.9m across both cycles. AxCapital was created in a 2022 merger of HenryAlan and Datwyler’s 9Seven Consulting.
The Green Dragon Coalition’s $445,000 “educational” grant to the Constitutional Conservatives Fund in 2024 is recorded in the Pac’s FEC receipts in five payments between 15 March and 21 June 2024. In turn, the Pac spent $447,347 supporting Jenkins. Datwyler was also treasurer of Colby Jenkins for Congress, a role he had held since October 2023, and of the candidate’s joint fundraising committee. Datwyler is therefore keeping the books for the charity, the social welfare group, the Super Pac attacking the incumbent and the campaign it was attacking her on behalf of.
The Green Dragon Coalition’s 2024 revenue was $917,002, of which $750,000 – or about 82% – came from the Concord Fund, the Leonard Leo-network group formerly called the Judicial Crisis Network. The Green Dragon Society, a 501(c)3, also took $250,000 from Purple Action, a 501(c)4 whose officers include tech mogul and former Trump administration “crypto czar” David Sacks, and $200,000 from the Conservative Partnership Institute, and $90,000 each from “dark money” vectors DonorsTrust and Fidelity’s donor-advised fund. The Thomas D Klingenstein Fund gave the 501(c)3 $75,000 in 2023, before the 2024 payments to the Super Pac.
Lawson Bader, the president and CEO of DonorsTrust, said the organisation was “unfamiliar with the Constitutional Conservatives Fund, and the fact that the Green Dragon Coalition has an affiliated 501(c)4”. Grants from donor-advised funds to a 501(c)3 “cannot be used for political purposes”, he said, adding that DonorsTrust “would reconsider future grant recommendations made to organizations that violate the rules governing charitable activities”.
A Fidelity Charitable spokesperson said: “Use of Fidelity Charitable grants for political contributions or campaign activities is prohibited. The terms all non-profits receive when grant funds are issued to them include explicit language to that effect.”
These are not the only money flows from major conservative funders through Datwyler-connected entities.
In 2024 American Majority Action, a 501(c)4 founded by conservative activist Ned Ryun, gave Integrity Minnesota, for which Datwyler served as treasurer, $250,000 for “voter registration and activation plans”. (A 2020 Campaign for Accountability complaint asked the IRS and two state agencies to investigate whether Ryun’s groups spent more than half their money on politics, which would violate IRS laws governing 501(c)4 groups. Campaign for Accountability communications director Michael Clauw told the Guardian that the IRS did not respond to the complaint or take any action.)
American Majority Action did not respond to a request for comment.
Integrity Minnesota also received $50,000 that year from Restoration of America, which the Chicago Sun-Times reported in October 2024 was part of “a sprawling empire of organizations pushing far-right agendas and election denialism”, funded by at least $150m from shipping-supplies billionaire Richard Uihlein.
The Guardian contacted Restoration of America for comment.
And a separate Datwyler vehicle, Aurora Venture, received $300,000 from Ardleigh Impact Corp, a Delaware 501(c)4 with one director, no employees and no website, registered to the Springfield, Virginia, home of Staci Goede, a former Republican State Leadership Committee finance chief who is the treasurer of 26 federal political committees this cycle.
The Daily Beast reported on 16 May 2024 that Ardleigh had moved more than $2.5m to Republican Super Pacs within months of being formed, raising the suspicion that it may be a straw donor.
The Guardian contacted Goede for comment.
The money pipeline functions such that none of these organizations are named as donors in the FEC filings of the Super Pacs.
The Guardian contacted the Concord Fund, Thomas Klingenstein and the Conservative Partnership Institute for comment, and emailed Purple Action at an address that returned the message undelivered. None responded.
This cycle, the Green Dragon Coalition has put a further $177,500 into the same Super Pac in seven payments since 5 December 2025, the most recent on 21 April 2026. The Pac’s independent expenditures so far this cycle total $15,000 in support of Barry Moore, the Alabama congressman currently running to replace Tommy Tuberville, who is departing the US Senate to run for the Alabama governor’s seat.
The Guardian contacted Barry Moore for comment.
Elsewhere, the Pac’s expenditures have gone to organizations connected to Datwyler’s associates.
Its payments to L4 Consulting LLC total $164,809 across 13 installments between 2 January and 5 June 2026, with the disbursements booked as “PAC strategy consulting” and “fundraising consulting”. L4 is run by Dan Hauser, who is president of both Green Dragon entities and takes no salary from either.
Hauser was reported in October 2025 to have been a paid senior adviser to the Utah senator Mike Lee, another Datwyler client, during the same period. In the 2024 cycle, L4 took $207,560 from the same Super Pac. Green Dragon’s charity separately paid L4 $128,033 for “event production”.
The Guardian contacted Hauser for comment.
Ghosh, the campaign finance reformer, pointed out that while non-profits have to disclose donors to the IRS, with the exception of private foundations and some political non-profits, they do not have to disclose them to the public.
“So if the entire object is to conceal the sources of the money, the [501](c)4 on its own can accomplish that objective. The only thing the [501](c)3 layer adds is that [501](c)3 donations are tax deductible for the donor,” he said.
Ghosh added: “But that’s a little riskier because if they are using the [501](c)3 to first obtain a tax deduction and then that money is being used to influence elections, that’s one of the few things that federal tax law does prohibit.”
Either way, he said that “that’s a transparency nightmare. It becomes this problematic daisy chain where the [501](c)3 is sending money to the [501](c)4, theoretically not to support its political advocacy. But again, who can say exactly whether that’s happening or not? These are opaque entities. They are black boxes.”
Alyssa Bowen, executive director of True North Research, put the same structure more bluntly. “It’s like dark money made darker,” she said. “It’s almost like he’s running science experiments to find out all the ways you can conceal who’s donating.”
She said the charity layer carried a second advantage for the giver. “The Pacs are legally required to disclose your donors, but you’re not [required to do so] for a 501(c)3 or [501(c)]4. And then there’s also the tax benefits – donors receive tax benefits for donating to a 501(c)3,” she said. “So it’s twofold for these donors that are trying to make sure that they’re not held accountable for some of the more political spending that they do.”
Parallel pipelines
A similar pattern is visible across four other 2026 races. In each, Datwyler is treasurer of the campaign and of the Super Pac spending in that race, and in each he held both roles before the spending began.
The Love America Uphold Freedom Pac spent $248,091 for Catalina Lauf in Florida’s 19th district between 13 and 24 July 2026, which is all the independent spending it has ever made. It is registered at Datwyler’s own address, and amended its registration on 11 July to add the domain LAUFPAC.com, two days before the advertising started.
It shares 14 vendors with Lauf’s campaign, seven of them substantive digital firms, over overlapping periods – which engages the FEC’s common-vendor conduct standard independently of who the treasurer is.
The Guardian contacted the Lauf campaign for comment.
On shared vendors, Ghosh said this is “more pressing than just having a treasurer in common. The use of vendors in common for things like media production, placement – that’s exactly the kind of spending that would be the subject of prohibited coordination. If the vendors they’re using are actually taking what they learn from their work for the campaign clients and then utilising that information or passing that information to their Super Pac clients, that’s exactly what the law prohibits.”
The Defending Conservative Values Pac was registered on 9 May 2026 and spent $485,213 against Blake Moore, the incumbent Karianne Lisonbee is challenging, between 29 May and 20 June – again, 100% of its spending, and again in Utah’s second district. The Show Me Valor Pac was registered six weeks after Taylor Burks’ campaign, with Datwyler as treasurer, and spent $166,051 supporting him. The American Honor Pac spent $162,800 for David Flippo in Nevada’s second district; Datwyler is its treasurer, custodian of records and only named officer, and its entire 2026 income – $155,000 – came from Stephen Flippo.
The American Liberty Foundation is simultaneously the name of a 501(c)3, a 501(c)4 and a Super Pac, all with Datwyler as treasurer, the first two presided over by Raymond Yonkura, Jim Jordan’s chief of staff for nearly a decade. The Super Pac spent $294,021 for Jenny Costa Honeycutt in South Carolina’s first district in June 2026, funded by $355,000 from the social welfare arm, $250,000 from the Geo Group’s Pac and $250,000 from a group called Voice of the Children of Israel.
What those campaigns knew is the open question for True North’s Bowen. “It’s concerning that all of these organisations and entities are using him, because what do they know about his past?” Bowen said, referring to Datwyler. “Is that why they’re using him – or are they totally unaware?”
She was skeptical that one person could service so many committees properly. “It feels far-fetched that he could be doing a good job,” she said.
‘Stunning … inexplicable’
In the current electoral cycle, Datwyler has already attracted controversy.
The Delaware Republican party reportedly claims he went unresponsive and then left in January 2026 amid five straight months of negative federal cash balances, missing a filing deadline and drawing an FEC warning of “civil money penalties, an audit or legal enforcement action”; he says he resigned because the party had not paid him.
In Alabama he is the sole officer of a Pac registered to a rented mailbox that has reportedly drawn legal threats over its attack mailers. A former state senator, Dell Hill, reportedly said in April that he had launched the Pac, whose registration names only Datwyler. Datwyler reportedly said he was “strictly the accountant doing the books” and had “nothing to do with producing the ads”.
One of the Republican incumbents it targeted, the state representative Matt Simpson, lost his primary in May.
In a telephone conversation, Simpson said of Datwyler: “If he found loopholes to try to exploit for his purposes, then that’s the nature of the business that we’re in. You can’t lie, though. That’s the problem that I have with it.”
He gave the Guardian a copy of a later mailer in which the Pac said a false claim about Simpson’s positions “was a printing error”.
The Guardian contacted Phillip Pettus, another incumbent the Pac targeted, for comment.
A Texas campaign Datwyler keeps books for drew a watchdog complaint in May 2026, and Andy Ogles, whose campaign he still runs the books for, confirmed in 2024 that, at that time, the FBI was investigating his campaign finances.
The complaint has not moved because the FEC needs four votes to open an investigation and has had only two commissioners since October 2025. Donald Trump’s two nominees have sat with the Senate rules committee since 11 February with no further action.
In May this year, the Campaign Legal Center asked the commission to investigate Datwyler again, over a $250,000 payment to one of his Super Pacs from the private prison company Geo Group, ICE’s largest contractor.
Datwyler has not been charged with any offence, and several of the investigations closed without findings. His firm’s general counsel has called the allegations against him “baseless attacks”.
The incidents are part of a longer pattern of scandal and regulatory scrutiny.
To date, Datwyler has been named as a respondent in 24 complaints before the FEC. Two ended in penalties, both for conduct that predated his appointment as treasurer. The other 22 were dismissed or closed without a penalty, at least three of them after commissioners deadlocked 3-3.
In January 2023 the FEC fined Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign $15,080 for failing to promptly report contributions totalling $147,601 received between 14 and 30 April 2022, before the 3 May Ohio primary.
Datwyler’s successor as Mandel’s campaign treasurer, Elizabeth Curtis, wrote to the FEC about “the stunning number of inexplicable reporting errors made by Mr Datwyler … ignoring the FEC and potentially incurring significant fines without notifying the Committee”.
The Guardian contacted Curtis for comment via a consultancy website contact form.
In 2023, the FEC fined four campaigns for failing to file required notices of late contributions in the 2022 elections while Datwyler was their treasurer: Mandel’s Senate campaign ($15,080) and the House campaigns of Rodney Davis ($5,820), Ann Wagner ($3,560) and Joe Kent ($3,304), for a total of $27,764. Fines against the campaigns of Rich McCormick and Kyle Sinclair also named Datwyler as treasurer, for failures that predated his appointment.
Those were not the only cases. A Guardian review of FEC enforcement records found 13 cases in which a committee was penalised for failures that occurred, at least in part, while Datwyler was its treasurer, with penalties totalling $110,791. The largest came in April 2024, when Rodney Davis’s campaign agreed to pay $43,475, in a settlement Datwyler signed, after it failed to refund $479,783.82 in general-election contributions within the permitted time once Davis had lost his 2022 primary.
The largest penalties to name Datwyler concerned reporting from before he took over.
In March 2024, Mike Braun’s Senate campaign agreed to pay a $159,000 civil penalty over improperly reported loans from the 2018 race. The FEC’s file on the matter records that Datwyler became the campaign’s treasurer on 29 January 2019, after the period in question, and that the campaign blamed its former treasurer for the errors. Commissioners deadlocked 3-3 on a separate allegation, that the campaign had misreported receipts and disbursements.
A representative for Datwyler reportedly said he “served as treasurer at the time the issue was corrected, reviewed, and resolved, not at the time of the underlying activity”.
In July 2022 Jim Jordan’s campaign agreed to pay $60,000 for failing to accurately disclose $1.2m in receipts and disbursements in five reports covering late 2018 to mid-2020. The FEC’s referral lists Datwyler as its treasurer from 15 July 2020, and the campaign told the commission he had “identified hundreds of errors” in its earlier accounting and filed corrected reports.
He was the shared treasurer of Joe Kent’s 2022 congressional campaign and of a Super Pac backing it – an arrangement the Guardian examined in February 2025, when campaign finance experts questioned the campaign’s routing of more than $1m through a company they described as a possible shell.
Liberty Ohio
In December 2021 Mike Dowling, a former FirstEnergy executive defending himself in a shareholder lawsuit over the $60m scheme that secured passage of Ohio’s HB6 energy bailout, subpoenaed two dark-money groups at the centre of that scandal: Partners for Progress and Generation Now, the latter of which had pleaded guilty to racketeering that February.
He asked for their communications with a list of people and organisations that included Liberty Ohio Inc, a non-profit for which Datwyler was treasurer, as well as Datwyler himself and the group’s secretary, Scott Guthrie. The same list named Ohio’s governor and lieutenant governor and every current and former member of the state legislature. Neither Datwyler nor Liberty Ohio was served with a subpoena or was a party to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit settled in August 2022, with $180m paid to FirstEnergy by insurers to resolve the derivative claims, less $36m in court-awarded legal fees. The defendants admitted no liability or wrongdoing.
Both Datwyler and Guthrie were working at the time on Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign, with Datwyler as its treasurer and Guthrie as its manager. Mandel subsequently lost the 2022 Republican primary to JD Vance, who was subsequently elected Senator for Ohio, and then vice-president as Donald Trump’s running mate.
Committees for which Datwyler served as treasurer spent more than $7m across the race – more than $5.4m of it from the USA Freedom Fund, a Super Pac registered to his own post office box, which put $831,281 behind Mandel and a further $4.6m into attacking his three main rivals: $3m against Mike Gibbons, $1.5m against JD Vance and $36,530 against Jane Timken.
The Guardian can reveal other striking transactions involving Datwyler during that campaign. Between September 2021 and June 2022, Team Josh – the joint fundraising committee for Mandel’s campaign and his leadership Pac – transferred $1.1m in seven installments to the federal account of the Shelby county Republican party, a committee registered not in Ohio but at Datwyler’s post office box in Hudson, Wisconsin. The federal account of a second Ohio county party, Delaware, sent a further $362,458.
Those two transfers were the entire declared income of the Shelby county account, amounting to $1,471,200. It then spent $1,398,811 on independent expenditures supporting Mandel, amounting to 95 cents of every dollar it took in, and wound itself up that December. Datwyler was treasurer of all three committees, and of Mandel’s campaign.
The Guardian contacted Scott Guthrie for comment. An email to Josh Mandel was returned undelivered.
State-level enforcement
Twice, state authorities have probed Datwyler as opposed to his clients.
The most developed coordination allegation against him is in Tennessee. In 2024, the state’s registry of election finance referred a complaint to the attorney general over the Republican primary in the fourth senate district, where a dark-money Pac spent more than $600,000 to defeat the incumbent, Jon Lundberg. Datwyler was treasurer and officer of that Pac, East Tennessee Conservatives; he was also treasurer of the congressional campaign of Diana Harshbarger, whose son Bobby was the challenger.
The attorney general’s report found that Datwyler had helped Bobby Harshbarger set up his campaign in April, after being introduced by the congresswoman’s chief of staff. According to the report, Datwyler sent him guidance on appointing a treasurer, obtained a tax number for a bank account and opened a fundraising account with Republican donation processor WinRed, and that the Pac he ran then spent heavily against Lundberg.
Investigators could not reach a conclusion, mainly because Datwyler declined, through counsel, to be interviewed or to produce documents. Two registry members said he should be subpoenaed. “The system’s not working the way it needs to on the dark money side,” the registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said, “and I don’t know if we’ve got the tools to do anything for it.” Datwyler’s lawyer, Eric Brown, reportedly said that “news reports confirm that the AG report found no factual or legal basis to support the allegations of improper coordination”.
The registry dismissed the complaint in May 2025 at the request of Ken Yager, the Republican state senator who had filed it. “It’s just one of those where nobody was here to prosecute it,” Lawless said at the time.
The Guardian contacted Bobby Harshbarger for comment.
A second Tennessee complaint went further. Lawyers for the Civic Engagement Forum and Datwyler conceded to the registry that the group had operated as a political campaign committee and should have registered and disclosed its spending, and offered $2,500 to settle. The registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said the offer was not high enough. In July 2025, the registry deferred a decision and ordered the group to register and file its disclosure reports, and in September it accepted a revised offer of a $6,000 penalty and closed the case.
Datwyler reportedly told the attorney general’s investigators that he had no personal knowledge of the Citizen Engagement Forum, a second group named in the complaint.
In April 2024 Emily’s List asked the FEC to investigate an Arizona group with a Democratic-sounding name, the Turn AZ Blue Pac, which had disclosed neither its spending nor its donors and which was listed with Datwyler as its treasurer. Through a lawyer, Datwyler told the commission he “is not, nor has he ever been, the treasurer” of the group, and the FEC’s dismissal report records that he swore he had never heard of it before the complaint. The commission dismissed the case in April 2025.
That July, a Nevada leadership Pac formed to back the Republican Senate candidate Jim Marchant asked the justice department to investigate Datwyler for alleged wire fraud over a $500 cheque written from its account to his compliance firm, AxCapital, after he had stepped down as its treasurer. The complaint, written by the Republican election lawyer Dan Backer, alleged “a long history of running roughshod over federal campaign finance law”. It said Datwyler first described the payment as a bank error made through an online bill-pay system, then said he would refund it; the Pac’s own FEC filings record a $500 “compliance refund” from AxCapital on 22 April 2024. Eric Brown, general counsel of Axiom Strategies, which owns AxCapital, reportedly said the firm faced “baseless attacks” and that the letter was “nothing more than a stunt”. No charges have followed.
Backer told the Guardian this week that he believed the $500 was refunded “only after filing the [justice department] letter”; his letter is dated 26 July 2024. Asked whether the justice department had responded, he said: “Law enforcement agencies generally do not comment on pending investigations.” He said Datwyler had “cost the GOP vast sums of money” and was “just not cut out for this line of work at this level”, and that aggrieved former clients rarely act because “no one ever wants to spend the money or put their reputation out there, to sue or to file an FEC complaint”.
The Guardian also contacted the Tennessee complainant, the state representative Michele Reneau, and Emily’s List for comment. They did not respond.
In Maryland, Datwyler was listed as the treasurer of “Dan Cox for US Congress”, a committee registered in the name of a candidate who had not filed to run. In Ohio’s Mahoning valley, county party chairs of both parties could learn nothing about a group attacking local officials beyond his name on the treasurer designation.
In Texas, a Super Pac Datwyler kept books for reportedly spent almost everything it raised on credit card fees and nothing on campaigning, according to its own FEC filings.
Perhaps most notoriously, George Santos’s campaign named him treasurer in January 2023 and his lawyer told the FEC the appointment was unauthorised – a position the same lawyer later retracted, writing that he had lost confidence in his client’s account.
Santos, the New York Republican who fabricated most of his biography, was expelled from the House in December 2023 and sentenced to more than seven years in April 2025 for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. He served 84 days before Donald Trump commuted the sentence in October.
Secrecy
Datwyler is steadfast in maintaining secrecy on behalf of funders.
Asked in October 2024 about $200,000 that arrived at a Super Pac opposing Sheldon Whitehouse from his Wisconsin address, Datwyler said a Florida couple were the primary funders and declined to name them.
Occasionally, Datwyler’s denials have been undone by his own filings.
Asked in October 2025 about attack mailers in a Utah school board race, he said the address on them “is not associated with us at all”; hours later, the Pac filed state paperwork listing him as its primary officer.
Time after time, however, investigations that reached committees he kept have ended without action against him. Three executives of Navatek, a Hawaii defence contractor, pleaded guilty over schemes that included routing $150,000 of company money through a sham entity, the Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers, to 1820 Pac, a Super Pac backing Susan Collins for which Datwyler was treasurer. The Pac told the FEC the contribution was lawful. Commission lawyers later recommended finding that it had failed to refund the money once its source came to light, but the commissioners never voted on that, and in January 2025, with the statute of limitations running out, they dismissed the allegation against the Pac and Datwyler in his official capacity. The Pac’s FEC reports show no refund.
On Datwyler’s overall operation, Saurav Ghosh said: “What you’re describing is both incredibly common and incredibly problematic for our elections.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘We spend our days in silence’: fear and repression in Ohio as ICE terrorizes Haitian immigrants
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Stephen Starr in Springfield, Ohio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Michaelle Louis’s feet and legs are aching. She can barely walk.
Surrounded by corn fields and the distant hum of a busy highway, the native of Haiti and dozens of other activists are 23 miles into a 45-mile march from Springfield to Ohio’s statehouse in Columbus to demand better rights for Haitian immigrants.
But the pain she’s feeling now is nothing compared to the mental anguish and fear she was subjected to last summer.
In August, she spent five days huddling with her daughter and brother in the basement of her Springfield home. The family went without electricity during daylight hours out of fear that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers might come knocking on her door to deport them.
“I closed the curtains. I didn’t want anyone to know there was people living in our house,” she recalls.
“We spent our days in silence.”
For months, ICE has terrorized members of Springfield’s immigrant community, speeding after vehicles down normally placid streets and causing crashes. Chief among those being targeted are the city’s Haitian community, who began immigrating to the struggling town of 60,000 residents eight years ago to fill hundreds of open blue-collar jobs.
But a supreme court ruling allowing the Trump administration to end temporary protected status (TPS) for more than 350,000 Haitian nationals in July meant they could no longer work legally, and within days, dozens of ICE agents descended on Springfield. In September, Markwayne Mullin, the US homeland security secretary, said 380 people had been detained by ICE agents in Springfield.
Louis grew up in Haiti’s capital city Port-au-Prince, and says she came to Springfield in 2021 having entered the country legally through the southern US border. Her 31-year-old brother was murdered by a gang in Haiti in December 2018.
“I had so many threats from the gangs. I left three months after he was killed,” she recalls.
“It was very hard for my mom and dad to lose their son.”
It’s not only Haitians who feel harassed by federal immigration agents in Springfield. When ICE began patrolling city streets in August, resident Sean Moorman set about monitoring their activities and following their vehicles around town.
But that soon drew unwanted attention from arguably the most powerful federal law enforcement agency in the country today.
In a lawsuit filed on his behalf by the American Civil Liberties Union of Ohio against seven ICE officers last month, Moorman claimed agents swerved one of their vehicles towards his, “as if to ram him”, took photos of his car and used several of their vehicles to corner Moorman in his car, “making him fear for his life”.
Agents also allegedly drove by and photographed his home while his wife was inside.
Last month, a federal judge ordered ICE to stop “retaliatory action” against Moorman and granted a temporary restraining order against seven of its agents, all of whom remained unnamed.
But many of the ICE officers operating in Springfield at the time were moved out of state and the judicial order ran out on 18 September.
“It is disappointing, but unfortunately not surprising, that ICE chose to play a shell game by shuffling their officers around rather than allowing them to face accountability in court for their lawless actions,” says David Carey, managing legal director at the ACLU of Ohio and Moorman’s legal representative in the case against the ICE agents.
“We certainly disagree with the court’s decision to entertain that shell game, but the fact that the court had already entered and extended a temporary restraining order against these officers also sent the most important message: ICE does not have a blank check to violate first amendment rights.”
Moorman declined an interview with the Guardian, fearing further retaliation from ICE. His lawsuit was thrown out by a federal judge on 2 October.
ICE says it “is aware of the lawsuit filed by the ACLU in Ohio and is reviewing appropriate next steps in coordination with the Department of Justice”.
“Every day, [the Department of Homeland Security] is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe,” an ICE spokesperson said.
“Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
Around the country, ICE “watchers” such as Moorman have become essential in bringing to light the agency’s dangerous and often homicidal actions in their attempts to detain immigrants.
More than two dozen people have been shot by ICE officers, many in front of their children, since the beginning of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in February 2025. Among them are three US citizens who were shot dead in Minneapolis and Texas. Two of those people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were, like Moorman, monitoring the actions of Ice agents.
For Louis, the false statement Trump made during his presidential election campaign in September 2024 about immigrants in Springfield eating people’s pets hurt her the most.
“That opened my eyes. Until then, all I did was go to work and come home. I wasn’t that interested in community issues. I was helping people – Americans facing domestic violence. I served the nation; I served citizens,” she says.
Millions of immigrants from dozens of countries around the world have lost their ability to work legally in the US under the Trump administration. According to the Migration Policy Institute, ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have deported 980,000 people since the beginning of Trump’s second stint in office.
“And when you say I’m eating dogs and cats and I’m coming illegally, that’s something that’s shaken me. I was sleeping and now I woke up for my community.”
Louis says the three-day march across Ohio is to raise awareness for activists’ demands to end ICE’s detention of and use of ankle monitors on immigrants, for its agents to leave Springfield and for authorities to establish a permanent residency pathway for Haitians who have contributed to life in the US.
On day two of the march, as a large Amazon warehouse where dozens of Haitians were employed before the Trump crackdown comes into view, Louis talks about a Haitian woman she knows whose husband was recently deported to Haiti, where violence and political unrest has reigned for more than a decade.
“They had bought a house here [but] now they are moving back to Haiti,” she says.
“I think this is a method by ICE – take the man and the family will follow.”

Basketball der Frauen: Perfektes Spektakel
Das siebte Spiel der WNBA-Finals zwischen Atlanta Dream und den Golden State Valkyries wurde ein Festival der Rekorde. Das zeigt den Boom der Liga.
E s wurden wieder jede Menge Rekorde aufgestellt am späten Samstagnachmittag in San Francisco. Das alles entscheidende Spiel der WNBA Finals stand an: Game 7. Atlanta Dream zu Gast im „Ballhalla“ der Golden State Valkyries, dem Schwesterteam der Golden State Warriors aus der NBA. Das wäre auch schon der erste Rekord, der zu verzeichnen ist, denn noch nie zuvor wurde in der WNBA bei den Final Playoffs das siebte Spiel erreicht. Oder wie es vonseiten der Kommentatorinnen heißt: „the best two words in sports“.
Das mag aber vielleicht auch daran liegen, dass der Spielmodus „best out of 7“ für die Finalrunde der besten und am stärksten wachsenden Frauenbasketball-Liga der Welt erst vergangene Saison eingeführt wurde, wer weiß. Die Dreams und die Valkyries hatten sich nichtsdestotrotz bislang eine heiß umkämpfte Finalrunde geliefert. Und wohl auch eine unerwartet lange.
Das sechste Spiel jedenfalls, bei dem die Valkyries schon die Chance auf den Titelgewinn gehabt hätten, wurde in Atlanta trotz allem Hype an einem Donnerstagmittag um 12:30 Uhr angesetzt. Weil für abends in der Halle tatsächlich schon die NBA-Männer von den Atlanta Hawks spielen sollten. Die 17.000 Tickets für das WNBA-Spiel waren trotzdem binnen zwei Tagen ausverkauft. Weitere 1,5 Millionen Menschen schauten die Live-Übertragung im TV.
Die reguläre Saison hatte Atlanta Dream dieses Jahr sogar noch in einer 3.500-Zuschauer-Halle spielen müssen, erst kommende Saison sollen sie die NBA-Arena permanent mitnutzen können. Selbst die Liga-Organisatoren scheinen vom Boom überrumpelt.
Perfekte Spannung
Im Mittagsspiel glich Atlanta Dream schließlich in der Gesamtwertung zum 3:3 aus und machte die Spannung perfekt. Game 7 also, allerletztes Spiel der Saison, zwei Teams, die noch nie den Titel gewonnen haben, kämpfen darum. Eines davon, das Franchise aus San Francisco, spielte auch noch vergangenes Jahr seine erste Saison. Es ist jetzt schon ein weiterer Rekord, dass sie in ihrer zweiten Saison schon im Finale stehen. Beide Teams gelten als die abwehrstärksten der Liga. Das Setting ist so ausgelegt für noch mehr Rekorde. Die Arena ist selbstverständlich ausverkauft. Etwas mehr als 18.000 Zuschauer sind vor Ort, und dann ist auch noch Halloween, besser kann die Show nicht werden.
Es ist ein Finalspiel, wie man es sich nur wünschen kann. Und das exemplarisch steht für das Niveau und die Entwicklung, die die WNBA in den letzten Jahren durchgemacht hat.
Das ganze Spiel bleibt eng
Atlanta braucht ein paar Minuten auf dem gegnerischen Parkett, inmitten all der hell-violetten Fans aus Kalifornien, um die ersten Punkte zu erzielen. Ab da bleibt es das ganze Spiel über eng. Mit Superstars Angel Reese, Jordin Canada und Allisha Gray holt Atlanta Dream auf und die Walküren sogar ein, führt dann bis ins dritte Viertel. Auf der anderen Seite braucht es eine ganze Halbzeit, bis sich der Star des Matches herauskristallisiert und für weitere Rekorde sorgt: Gabby Williams. Mit gerade mal zwei Punkten in der ersten Halbzeit übernimmt sie nach der Pause fast komplett. Im dritten Viertel erzielt sie mit 15 Punkten sogar alleine mehr Treffer als Atlanta insgesamt.
Am Ende läuft Altlanta Dream die Zeit davon und Williams und die Golden State Valkyries sind nicht mehr zu bremsen. Sie gewinnen als jüngstes Franchise der WNBA-Geschichte mit 68 zu 63. Wieder ein Rekord. Und Gabby Williams, mit 30 Punkten, wird zu Recht zum MVP, der wertvollsten Spielerin, des Spiels erkoren. Außerdem ein Zeichen für die Qualität der WNBA inzwischen: Es gewinnt ein Team ohne die großen Stars wie Caitlin Clark oder Breanna Stewart. Es würde eine nicht wundern, wenn zur kommenden Saison weitere Rekorde aufgestellt werden.

Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://taz.de/Steinmeier-Nachfolge/!622.author: Lukas Wallraff
https://taz.de/Steinmeier-Nachfolge/!622.text:
Steinmeier-Nachfolge: Alles geklärt!
Nach einigem Hin und Her ganz einfach: Wie Merz und Söder am Tegernsee die Präsidenten-Frage lösen.
D eutschland kann durchatmen: Die leidige P-Frage ist gelöst. Nach einigen Überlegungen ist es am Ende doch ganz einfach, die Steinmeier-Nachfolge zu klären und die nächste Präsidentschaft einvernehmlich zwischen CDU und CSU zu regeln. Sie müssen es nur so machen:
Wie unter den Schwestern üblich, treffen sich Friedrich Merz und Markus Söder zu einem harmonischen Frühstück in Bayern, diesmal im Ferienhaus des Kanzlers am schönen Tegernsee.
Merz (öffnet die Tür): „Hallo, Markus.“
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Söder (tritt ein und setzt sich unaufgefordert an den Tisch): „Servus, Fritz! Wie geht’s? Schon die neueste Umfrage gesehen? CSU 37, CDU 18!“
Merz: „Schon gut. Setz dich erst mal. Ach so, du sitzt ja schon. Schau, ich hab dir extra Weißwürste gekocht.“
„Wohl eher verkocht, würde ich sagen! Die sind ja alle geplatzt wie deine Reformpläne. Meine Herren, Fritz. Du kriegst echt gar nix mehr gebacken.“
„Gehören die nicht so?“
„Nein. Aber wurscht, ich darf eh kein Fleisch mehr posten, weil ich ernster sein soll. Lass uns zur Sache kommen.“
„Zu welcher Sache? Brauchst du Senf?“
„Ja, und zwar deinen zu der Präsidentensache, die du seit Monaten vor dir herschiebst! Du musst das endlich entscheiden. Die Ilse nervt total.“
„Also, wenn hier einer schiebt, dann ja wohl eher du! Was sollte denn dieses Theater auf eurem Parteitag neulich? Aigner, Aigner, Ilse, Ilse, alle für Ilse! Ich kann’s nicht mehr hören.“
„Ja, eben, ich auch nicht, dann mach halt endlich!“
„Ilse aufstellen?“
„Ja, natürlich, ich kann die nicht mehr sehen, die muss weg aus Bayern, weil mich die Bayern nicht mehr sehen können und die Ilse viel beliebter ist. Am Ende haut die mich noch weg.“
„Aber wenn Ilse Präsidentin wird, kannst du doch nicht mehr Kanzler werden. Soll das dann der Wüst machen oder was?“
„Ach ja, stimmt! Oh Gott! Also lieber doch nicht die Ilse.“
„Tja, wer dann? Die Prien?“
„Zu links und norddeutsch!“
„Nein, zu rechts für die SPD.“
„Wer? Die kennt doch kein Mensch. Es muss jemand sein, der schon mal wichtig war und von allen respektiert wird.“
„Ich?“
„Der war gut. Die Merkel.“
„Nur über meine Leiche! Dann trete ich zurück.“
„Sehr gut! Ich ruf sie an.“

https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Filmstar-Elke.title: Nachruf auf Filmstar Elke Sommer: Eine polygotte Fränkin mischt Hollywood mit Aura auf
https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Filmstar-Elke.author: Jan Feddersen
https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Filmstar-Elke.text:
Nachruf auf Filmstar Elke Sommer: Eine polygotte Fränkin mischt Hollywood mit Aura auf
Bar jeder Vulgarität. Mit natürlichem Glamour machte Elke Sommer eine einmalige Karriere vom Schönheitswettbewerb in Viareggio bis ins Zentrum der US-Filmindustrie.
Ihre Karriere, die sich – alles in allem – in dem Begriff „Hollywoodschauspielerin“ bündelt, war ganz unwahrscheinlich. Weder hatte sie vor, Schauspielerin zu werden, noch irgendwann überhaupt als Künstlerin zu arbeiten. Anfang November 1940 in Berlin geboren, als Tochter einer Pfarrersfamilie, was nicht hieß, von allzu starker evangelischer Enge heimgesucht worden zu sein.
Aufgewachsen im fränkischen Erlangen, auf dem Weg zum Abitur kurz nach der Mittleren Reife ausgestiegen – um Dolmetscherin zu werden. Vielsprachig sich durch welche Welten auch immer bewegen zu wollen, das hatte die Note, sich von dem, was hinterm eigenen Horizont liegen könnte, nicht unangenehm irritieren zu lassen. Ende der 1950er, bei einem Familienurlaub an den Stränden der Toskana, nahm Elke Sommer an einem Schönheitswettbewerb teil und wurde, so geht die Legende, „Miss Viareggio“.
Der italienische Starregisseur Vittorio de Sica soll in einer Illustrierten Fotos von diesem Event gesehen haben – so kam sie zum Film mit dem Debüt „L’amico del giaguaro“. Film, das war das Business, das sie wesentlich bis in die siebziger Jahre mit ihren Rollen anreicherte: In Deutschland 1959 in der Verfilmung von B. Travens „Das Totenschiff“, kurz darauf in „Am Tag, als der Regen kam“, 1962 „Der Staatsanwalt und das Mädchen“.
Souveränes Sprechen
1963 spielte die Sommer erstmals in einer Hollywoodproduktion – Hintergründe über ihre erste Zeit erzählt sie in einem bemerkenswerten Gespräch mit dem Bayerischen Rundfunk 1963. Interessant, allein wegen der Art ihres souveränen Sprechens wegen. Sie spielte mit dem damals noch nicht sehr berühmten Paul Newman in „Der Preis“. Im Jahr darauf würdigte man die Deutsche als beste Nachwuchsschauspielerin mit einem „Golden Globe“ Award.
Elke Sommer war, nach Marlene Dietrich, die berühmteste Deutsche in den Hollywood-Castingkarteien. Sie galt als unkompliziert, freundlich und buchstäblich lebenslustig. Wovon ihre deutschen Kolleginnen träumten – Oh, wann ruft mich Hollywood? – lebte sie dortselbst. Sie hatte nicht das, was Deutschen in den USA gern nachgesagt wird: too weltschmerzy.
Dass sie als Figur für frivol, unzüchtig und allzu aufreizend galt, störte sie nicht. In einem Gespräch mit der Mallorca Zeitung vor acht Jahren sagte sie: „Die Leute wollten eben auch das in mir sehen, die vermeintliche Sexbombe – so idiotisch! Ich habe den Begriff immer gehasst, mein ganzes Leben. Was ist das überhaupt, sexy? Sexy ist so ein Scheißwort. Sexy ist gar nichts, tits and ass. Anziehend, erotisch ist etwas anderes. Das sind Bewegungen, Augen, die Aura, wie man mit jemanden umgeht.“
Dass in den noch übel sittendrakonischen 1960ern (nicht nur) hierzulande sie skandalisiert wurde, trug zum Erfolg auch ihres Business bei. Einen Zweiteiler („Bikini“) zu tragen, war ihr recht. Allzu freizügig? „Nein, dessen waren wir alle uns nicht bewusst. Für mich war der Zweiteiler nur Garderobe.“ Und die daueraufgeregten Kirchen, die öffentlich davon abrieten, Elke-Sommer-Filme im Kino anzugucken? „Wirklich? Ich bin Pfarrerstochter und selbst sehr gläubig.“
Komisches Traumpaar
In Hollywood spielte sie in einer Fülle von Filmen mit, in einem Teil der Pink-Panther-Reihe (an der Seite von Peter Sellers als trotteliger Kommissar Clouseau) namens „Der Schuss ins Dunkle“ (1964): Es war eine der komischsten Performances jener ja oft aufbrüchig stimmenden Jahre. Sommer war die eigentliche Attraktion dieses Films, ihr Talent, noch jeden Sprechschnipsel wie spontan geflachst klingen zu lassen, war enorm.
So groß wie Sommers Kunst, selbst knappste Textilausstattung wie das Natürlichste der Welt aussehen zu lassen, bar jeder Vulgarität. Filmisch möglicherweise ihr bestes Stück war 1966 „Heiße Katzen“, eine sensationell unterhaltsame, zugleich anmutige Trashproduktion bar aller Kunstansprüche. Eine James-Bond-Parodie, in der sie mit ihrer Kollegin Sylvia Koscina ein Killerbienenduo gibt, in dem nur so scheppert und knallt. Am Ende verrichtet eine Bombe im künstlichen Haarteil der einen ein kurioses Ende.
Echter Ruhm
Quentin Tarantino, der ein gläubiges Herz für die Nichtkunstreligionskinostreifen jener Jahre hat, würdigte diesen und andere Sommer-Filme in seinem Film „Once Upon A Time in Hollywood“ 2019: Mehr echter Ruhm geht für einen deutschen Filmstar nicht.
Ende der 1970er zog sie sich aus dem Big Business zurück, lebte als Malerin fortan in Erlangen und Los Angeles. Sie habe so viel gearbeitet, dass sie sich beide Lebensorte leisten könne – im Winter lebt es sich in Südkalifornien natürlich klimatisch leichter. Sommer war ein wenig vom Radar jener Regisseure geraten, die ein anderes deutsches Kino wollten, auch Fassbinder hatte sie nicht so recht auf dem Schirm.
Altersgemäße Rollen fanden sich auch nicht so recht. Vielleicht sollte auch nicht verstanden werden, dass Elke Sommer Glamour als Person mitbrachte. Wenige Monate nach dem Tod von Wolf Walther, Gefährte ihres Lebens und zweiter Ehemann, ist sie in Bel Air im Alter von 85 Jahren gestorben.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Binance restarts withdrawals after $6.3bn heist
The FBI says hackers from North Korea are responsible for the theft.
Binance has begun restoring customer withdrawals after hackers stole about $6.3bn in cryptocurrency in a record theft that United States authorities have blamed on North Korea.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange resumed some of its services on Sunday, following a suspension imposed after Thursday’s attack as the company investigated the breach and carried out security checks.
Binance said it had replaced approximately 95 percent of the affected assets. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X on Sunday.
Withdrawals are being restored in stages, with major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ether, along with some stablecoin services, being reopened.
The exchange warned that high demand could cause delays as services return, advising customers whose transactions fail to try again after a short wait.
It said further services would reopen as security checks were completed, while teams continued working with law enforcement and industry partners to trace and recover the stolen assets.
FBI blames North Korea
The FBI said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the theft, identifying the operation as cyber-activity it tracks under the name TraderTraitor.
Investigators had observed the attackers converting stolen assets primarily into ether, the cryptocurrency used on the Ethereum network, the agency said. It warned that further laundering was expected through decentralised finance platforms and instant cryptocurrency exchange services.
The FBI previously attributed the theft of approximately $1.5bn from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in February 2025 to the same actors.
Binance initially said a compromised employee laptop might have enabled the intrusion, but later reported that investigators had also uncovered additional points of breach.
The company said its investigation remained ongoing and that it would publish a detailed report once the inquiry was complete.

https://taz.de/Das-Detail-zum-Bundesliga.text:
Das Detail zum Bundesligaspieltag: In der Doppelrolle
Immer häufiger agieren als TV-Experten Promis wie Michael Ballack, die zugleich finanzielle Interessen im Spiel haben. Problematisiert wird das kaum.
Michael Ballack war voller Begeisterung über Lennart Karl: Dass „Lennarts Leistungskurve wieder klar nach oben zeigt“, befand er als TV-Experte für DAZN. Die Kritik vonseiten des Bayern-Sportdirektors Max Eberl sowie Uli Hoeneß sei „vom Zeitpunkt her unverständlich und inhaltlich zu hinterfragen“.
Dass er sich so ins Zeug legte, hatte allerdings einen schnöden Business-Grund: Michael Ballack ist zugleich Karls Berater. Da mag schon mal einiges durcheinandergehen. So konnte auch Eberl nicht ganz auseinanderhalten: „Hat er das als DAZN-Experte gesagt oder als Berater?“ Und: „Ehrlicherweise finde ich es schwierig, wenn man über die Medien jetzt so eine Diskussion führt.“
Heerscharen von Promi-Experten
Die aber gibt es immer häufiger, seit zig Streamingsender eine ganze Heerschar von Fußball-Promis beschäftigen, die öfters parallel finanzielle Interessen auf dem Rasen verfolgen. Problematisiert wird das kaum. Die vielleicht berühmteste Doppelrolle hatte diesen Sommer Jürgen Klopp inne, der als TV-Experte zur Männer-WM für Magenta im Dienst war, während er schon als Nachfolger von Julian Nagelsmann gehandelt wurde. Im TV konnte er sich selbst ausgiebig als Bessermacher präsentieren.
Ärger gab es auch um Matthias Sammer, der als Berater des BVB fungiert und gleichzeitig bei Amazon als TV-Experte BVB-Spiele kommentierte. Kurioserweise war es in diesem Fall Borussia Dortmund, das den Interessenkonflikt anprangerte, weil Sammer im TV gern mit dem Holzhammer über den BVB herzog („körperliche und geistige Nichtverfassung“).
Tatsächlich setzte Sammer daraufhin bei BVB-Partien aus. TV-Experte allerdings ist er weiterhin – und hält sich nicht zurück: Dortmunds Chancen vor dem Spitzenspiel seien, „als wenn ich jetzt mit meinem Knie einen Marathon laufen möchte“. Da hat man doch lieber einen so wohlmeinenden Berater wie Michael Ballack.

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: « Mary Cassatt. L’indépendante » au musée d’Orsay : la peintre impressionniste enfin exposée
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Maurice Ulrich
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Le musée d’Orsay attire la lumière sur une des grandes figures de l’impressionnisme, Mary Cassatt, peintre revendiquant son indépendance et militante des droits des femmes. Une exposition à découvrir jusqu'au 31 janvier.
Femme et américaine. A priori, c’était déjà deux fois trop. On échoue à imaginer ce qu’il fallut à Mary Cassatt (1844-1926), à qui le musée d’Orsay consacre une importante exposition, la première en France, d’audace et de force de caractère pour parvenir à s’imposer, au XIXe siècle, dans le milieu artistique parisien. Et pas n’importe lequel : celui des impressionnistes, soit la nouvelle peinture d’alors.
Ce qui laisse penser que, dès son arrivée dans ce qui était alors la capitale des arts, son ambition n’est pas de s’en tenir aux normes académiques d’une honnête peinture. Il s’agit bien de relever les défis de la modernité, comme elle va relever celui de son indépendance et celui du combat pour les droits des femmes, et, essentiellement, du droit de vote, aux...

https://taz.de/Nach-der-Knesset-Wahl-in-.author: Tamar Ziff
https://taz.de/Nach-der-Knesset-Wahl-in-.text:
Nach der Knesset-Wahl in Israel : Eine Brandmauer gegen den Netanjahu-Block
Die Regierungsbildung in Israel wird kompliziert. Das Offensichtliche muss ausgesprochen werden: Ohne die arabischen Parteien gibt es keinen Wandel.
D ie Knesset-Wahl der vergangenen Woche war in mehrfacher Hinsicht historisch. Eine Rekordzahl von Israelis ging wählen, und die arabischen Parteien Ra’am und Vereinigte Liste errangen zusammen 19 Sitze. Doch selbst als klar wurde, dass der Eisenkot-Block mit 48 Sitzen weit unter den für eine Koalition nötigen 61 lag, brachten die Parteiführungen das Offensichtliche nicht über die Lippen: Ohne eine Partnerschaft mit den arabischen Parteien ist kein Wandel möglich.
Einige führende Köpfe des Eisenkot-Blocks schließen die Zusammenarbeit mit arabischen Parteien mit der Begründung aus, sie strebten eine „zionistische“ Koalition an. Dabei ist Ra’am, eine arabisch-muslimische Partei, zionistischer als jede Partei des Netanjahu-Blocks. Sie respektiert die israelische Demokratie, hat einen jüdischen Politiker der Mitte angeworben, um die jüdisch-arabische Partnerschaft sichtbar zu machen, und fordert ausdrücklich, dass arabische Israelis freiwilligen Zivildienst leisten.
Allerdings zögert auch die Vereinigte Liste, sich einer Anti-Netanjahu-Koalition anzuschließen. Ihr Vorsitzender Yousef Jabareen erklärte vor der Wahl, seine Partei werde dem Eisenkot-Block nicht beitreten, sondern eine Minderheitsregierung nur von Abstimmung zu Abstimmung stützen. Das ist kein Angebot zur Zusammenarbeit, sondern ein Rezept für baldige Neuwahlen. Die würden aber nur Netanjahu nützen: Von 2019 bis 2022 gab es fünf Wahlen in drei Jahren, die die Parteien der Mitte und der Linken zersplitterten, während die Rechte sich radikalisierte und zusammenrückte. Das Ergebnis war die „Koalition des Grauens“.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Nach 17 Jahren Netanjahu und vier Jahren mit der schlimmsten Regierung in der Geschichte Israels stimmten in der vergangenen Woche Millionen jüdischer und arabischer Israelis für einen Wandel. Der Change-Block aus jüdischen und arabischen Parteien errang 67 Sitze, eine klare Mehrheit. Sie alle müssen jetzt erkennen, dass der notwendige historische Wandel nur durch Partnerschaft gelingen kann. Und zwar geschlossen gegen den Netanjahu-Block.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Yamaha pulls out of Qatar MotoGP over ‘situation in the Middle East’
MotoGP says Yamaha’s lack of participation at next weekend’s event in Lusail ‘carries sporting implications’.
Yamaha has withdrawn its MotoGP team from next weekend’s race in Qatar, citing “the situation in the Middle East”.
The Japanese manufacturer announced its decision shortly after the Malaysian Grand Prix on Sunday.
“Yamaha has not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions,” Yamaha said in a statement.
Among the racers on the MotoGP grid riding Yamaha bikes is France’s Fabio Quartararo, the 2021 world champion. Alex Rins of Spain is the other racer on the Yamaha team.
The sport’s governing body, the MotoGP Group, said it was “disappointed” by the decision and “Yamaha’s non-participation also carries sporting implications”.
“While we recognise the team is subject to a broader corporate policy restricting travel to the Middle East, we do not believe this decision reflects the extensive assurances provided to all championship stakeholders,” it said.
MotoGP said talks with the organisers in Qatar and safety advisers had not flagged any reasons to change plans for the event, which will run from Friday to November 8 at the Lusail International Circuit outside Qatar’s capital, Doha.
“We communicated that position, together with the latest available information, to all manufacturers and teams today and welcome the confirmation from the remainder of the grid that they will compete in Qatar, and we thank them for that commitment,” the MotoGP Group said.
The statements were released shortly after the Malaysian MotoGP in Sepang, after which there are just three races left in the season.
Ducati’s reigning seven-time world champion, Marc Marquez, won the race at Sepang and could clinch the title in Doha.
Qatar was subject to Iranian attacks from February to April after the United States and Israel began a war on Iran. On Friday, a Qatari liquefied natural gas tanker was hit by unidentified objects in the Gulf, and in September 2025, Israel carried out an air strike on Doha that killed and injured Hamas leaders.
Al Jazeera has requested a comment from the Qatar Motor and Motorcycle Federation.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Ciara Mageean, European 1500m gold medallist with Ireland, dies aged 34
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: AFP
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Irish middle-distance runner Ciara Mageean, who won European gold and competed at two Olympic Games, has died aged 34, her family announced on Sunday.
“At 6:30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones,” said a statement posted on the athlete’s Instagram account.
Mageean’s death comes only weeks after she married her long-term boyfriend in Belfast. She had been receiving treatment for bowel cancer, revealing her diagnosis in July 2025 and subsequently disclosing that the disease was at an advanced stage.
Originally from Portaferry in County Down, Northern Ireland, Mageean established herself as one of Ireland’s leading middle-distance runners, setting several national records.
She represented Ireland at the 2016 Rio Olympics and the Tokyo Games held in 2021. Her greatest sporting achievement came in 2024 when she claimed the 1500m title at the European Athletics Championships in Rome. But an achilles injury prevented her from competing at the Paris Olympics that year.
Mageean remained remarkably positive throughout her period of illness saying she was “continuing to find the joy in everyday” as she thanked people for their support following her diagnosis.
Speaking to the BBC in June, she said she was “grateful” for having a career “that many others didn’t get to have”.
Tributes have been paid to Mageean, who also won a European silver and bronze in the 1500m at the 2022 and 2016 events respectively and finished second in the event in the 2022 Commonwealth Games.
“The country has lost a hero,” the Olympic Federation of Ireland said in a statement. “Beyond the medals, records and sporting accolades, Ciara will be remembered for her warmth, courage and tremendous strength of character,” said Northern Ireland’s First Minister Michelle O’Neill.
Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin said he was “deeply saddened” by Mageean’s “untimely passing”.

https://taz.de/Mandat-der-UN-Mission-abg.title: Mandat der UN-Mission abgelaufen: Die Westsahara-Mission wird „liquidiert“
https://taz.de/Mandat-der-UN-Mission-abg.author: Dominic Johnson
https://taz.de/Mandat-der-UN-Mission-abg.text:
Mandat der UN-Mission abgelaufen: Die Westsahara-Mission wird „liquidiert“
Ein Veto Russlands im UN-Sicherheitsrat beendet die UN-Mission für die Westsahara. Seit 35 Jahren sollte sie ein Referendum vorbereiten, das nie kam.
Eine der ältesten UN-Missionen der Welt ist Geschichte. Das Mandat der „UN-Mission für das Referendum in der Westsahara“ (Minurso) ist am Samstag 31. Oktober abgelaufen, nachdem die Verlängerung ihres Mandats am Freitag im UN-Sicherheitsrat scheiterte.
Russland blockierte den von den USA vorgelegten Resolutionsentwurf zur Verlängerung mit seinem Veto, damit fiel der Entwurf durch. Im 15 Mitglieder zählenden Sicherheitsrat stimmten elf Länder dafür, China und zwei weitere Länder enthielten sich.
Der Resolutionstext hätte die Mission von Minurso zu Minuso umbenannt und den Bezug auf ein Referendum gestrichen. Er entspricht der US-Position, die Marokkos Souveränität über die Westsahara anerkennt, und nennt Marokkos Vorschlag einer begrenzten Autonomie für das Gebiet „die einzige“ Grundlage einer Lösung des Westsahara-Konflikts – statt, wie zuletzt, „eine“ Grundlage.
Die Position der USA und Marokko stößt auf scharfen Widerspruch Algeriens, das die Westsahara-Befreiungsbewegung Polisario auf ihrem Staatsgebiet beherbergt. Algerien ist militärisch mit Russland verbündet, Marokko mit den USA. Russland legte nach seinem Veto am Freitag einen eigenen Resolutionsentwurf vor, der die Minurso in ihrer bisherigen Form bewahrt hätte. Für diesen stimmten bloß Russland, China und Somalia. Die USA stimmten dagegen, elf Länder enthielten sich.
Seit 35 Jahren bleibt die UNO ohne Erfolg
Die Minurso umfasst derzeit 201 zivile und 158 militärische Mitarbeiter und steht seit 1991 in der Westsahara. Das einstige spanische Kolonialgebiet wurde nach Spaniens Rückzug 1975 unilateral von Marokko besetzt, die antikoloniale Befreiungsbewegung Polisario floh mit Teilen der Zivilbevölkerung nach Algerien und nahm von dort einen Guerillakampf auf.
1988 akzeptierten Marokko und die Polisario einen UN-Friedensplan, der die Entsendung einer UN-Beobachtermission vorsah, um einen Waffenstillstand zu überwachen sowie ein Referendum über den zukünftigen Status des Territoriums abzuhalten – Unabhängigkeit oder Integration nach Marokko. Stimmberechtigt wären „alle Sahrauis, die in dem 1974 von den spanischen Behörden organisierten Zensus genannt sind und 18 Jahre oder älter sind“, so die Vereinbarung von 1988.
Das waren schon damals bloß etwa 70.000 Menschen, und viele davon sind heute nicht mehr am Leben. Die damals geflohenen Sahrauis leben mit ihren Nachkommen in Polisario-regierten Flüchtlingslagern nahe der algerischen Stadt Tindouf. Nach Schätzungen leben heute rund 170.000 Sahrauis unter Polisario-Kontrolle in Algerien und rund 160.000 unter marokkanischer Kontrolle in der Westsahara.
Die Polisario beharrt auch nach fünfzig Jahren weiter auf der Umsetzung der Referendumsvereinbarung in ihrer ursprünglichen Form, beherrscht die Flüchtlingslager und kontrolliert innerhalb der Westsahara die unbesiedelte Wüste entlang der Grenze zu Mauretanien und Algerien. Marokko sieht die Westsahara als Teil seines historischen Territoriums, hat das Gebiet mit Hunderttausenden Siedlern in Besitz genommen und geht mit harter Hand gegen jedwede Unabhängigkeitsbestrebung vor.
Immer mehr Länder auf Marokkos Seite
Den 1991 vereinbarten Waffenstillstand kündigte die Polisario 2020 einseitig auf, seitdem kommt es immer wieder zu wechselseitigen Angriffen. Immer mehr Länder haben derweil Marokkos Position anerkannt. Die Afrikanische Union nahm Marokko 2017 wieder auf, die USA unter Donald Trump erkannten Marokkos Kontrolle der Westsahara 2020 an, später gefolgt von Frankreich und Spanien und weiteren Ländern, der UN-Sicherheitsrat erkannte 2025 Marokkos Autonomieplan an.
Die UN-Mission Minurso selbst stellte ihre Referendumsvorbereitungen in der Westsahara und damit die Grundlage ihrer Entsendung bereits vor zwanzig Jahren ein, und das Amt des UN-Sondergesandten für die Westsahara ist seit dem Rücktritt des ehemaligen deutschen Bundespräsidenten Horst Köhler 2019 vakant. Geleitet wurde die Minurso seit 2021 von einem russischen Diplomaten – er fällt nun ausgerechnet dem Veto seines eigenen Landes zum Opfer.
Nach dem Ende ihres Mandats packen die UN-Mitarbeiter in der Westsahara nun die Koffer. UN-Generalsekretär Antonio Guterres bestätigte am Sonntag, es beginne nun die „Liquidierung“ der Mission und rief beide Seiten zur Kooperation auf. Dies dürfte kein Problem darstellen. Marokko hat das Ende der UN-Präsenz begrüßt. Algerien und die Polisario haben das russische Veto begrüßt. Niemand außerhalb der UNO weint der Minurso eine Träne nach.
