Features
Marysia Paruzel’s fairy-tale photos make the case against Conceptual detachment
SVETLANA
Marysia Paruzel met Svetlana on Taskrabbit in the spring of 2024. Her first message said that she was also Eastern European, and an artist, and that she was looking for a model. She sent some links to her work. Svetlana never said why she agreed to the project. No one else on the app answered Marysia’s message. Svetlana later told her that the other profiles Marysia had found were likely run by people like Svetlana’s old boss, a New York native who used her own Social Security number to create a profile through which she manages jobs for over a dozen undocumented women across the city. Svetlana would come to her boss’s apartment to collect her wages in cash: twelve dollars an hour, half the fee advertised on Taskrabbit. Before Svetlana met Marysia, this woman was her only American friend. They’d smoke weed and listen to K-pop together. She took Svetlana to see a BLACKPINK movie. But once Svetlana began working for herself, she made enough money that she could in theory pay for her seven-year-old son to cross into the US via the Mexican border: ten thousand dollars.
Marysia is thirty-three. She lives in an old tenement building off the Bowery with her husband and three-year-old son. She left Warsaw for Germany as a teenager and has worked often in other people’s homes since then. In the States, she once spent a couple of months as a maid and nanny in a penthouse apartment overlooking One World Trade Center. Marysia would drink cold-pressed juices and eat cardamom buns from the fridge, use the heated toilet in the master bedroom, watch the sun set over the Statue of Liberty. She’d press a button to close a soundproof window curtain while the family’s two-year-old daughter screamed, “Bye-bye, helicopters!” She made forty dollars an hour. The parents were never there. “Not being seen,” Marysia told me, “is so relaxing.” She likes her photos to be the same way: to give the heavy, peaceful feeling of trespassing together into a space where you don’t belong, where you do a task and then you are gone.
The apartments Svetlana cleaned belonged to people in their thirties who didn’t seem to leave the house much—there was trash from Amazon and Uber Eats everywhere. Svetlana’s own apartment, in Brighton Beach, was clean, bright, big. She and her husband had a roommate, a Georgian man. For a long time, Svetlana’s husband lived off her income. It was an uneasy marriage. To get them green cards, Svetlana considered a sex change operation; as a gay couple from Russia, they’d qualify for asylum. She could still wear girls’ clothing: “No one would have to know what’s underneath.” From Svetlana’s window, you could see the Coney Island Ferris wheel: a wheel of fortune, in Marysia’s opinion—“very symbolic.”
For more than a year, Marysia took photos of Svetlana inside friends’ apartments and in public, across the city. Svetlana, Marysia told me, would tell her many stories about herself, all with the air of serious confession, all contradictory. At that time, the twelve posts on Svetlana’s Instagram grid included photos of daisies at night, pizza, blue jeans, a sleeping cat, and the opulently gilded moldings of a room in the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg, where she used to live. In the stories pinned to the top of her profile, there was lots of NYC: Times Square, a Korean rap concert, Korean barbecue, subway breakdancers. The stories she reposted from day to day were mostly memes relating to life in post-Soviet Eastern Europe. Or mom content, like a mother and son drinking milkshakes on Coney Island, captioned “My husband made me a little version of himself, so we can go on fun dates without him.” Svetlana had a fascination with American single moms, Marysia told me.
Marysia enjoys telling stories, also. Her photography seems to be in part a technique through which to meet and talk to other women, and sometimes their children, and then to talk to other people, like myself, about the stories she and her models generate while making pictures. I asked what she and her models talk about. She said, “Emo things.” The resulting photographs often remind me of Dorothea Lange’s, if Dorothea Lange were a teen girl on Tumblr doing a photo shoot with her girlfriends. They are documents of a collaborative narrative process somewhere between fantasy and reality. Svetlana’s pinafore in the photos, for instance, is a costume, a maid uniform Marysia bought in Chelsea. When Svetlana was actually cleaning, she’d wear pajamas, which didn’t work on camera. Svetlana, Marysia told me, is shy. But in front of Marysia’s camera, she wasn’t awkward. She moved slowly, struck poses. It wasn’t Marysia’s idea for her to eat grapes so seductively! An assertive, even difficult model, Svetlana liked to demand they stop so that she could have a cigarette. She looked good smoking. But usually Svetlana said: “No pictures.”
One day in November, a week after the 2024 election, Svetlana and Marysia drove to an old US Army installation on the Jersey coast. During the Cold War, Fort Hancock was one of the first lines of defense against Russian missile strikes; today, it’s part of a national park. It is a strange place. As Svetlana and Marysia walked along the abandoned beach, a man appeared to them. He was Polish, a fisherman. Marysia comes from a fishing family, too. The fish this man pulled ashore that day was gigantic, one inch over the legal limit. Marysia photographed Svetlana posing with the enchanted fish.
While they were taking photos that day, Svetlana asked Marysia whether she knew about “liminal spaces.” Like when you are in a place, she said, that should be full of people, but nobody is there. And this makes you feel like you shouldn’t be there, either, and that, maybe, you are not alive. She told Marysia that she’d deleted her Taskrabbit profile. Her husband had gotten a permit to drive commercial trucks cross-country. Svetlana wanted one too. They’d be able to do it together, taking turns at the wheel. And he wouldn’t be able to drink while driving. “You’re crazy,” Marysia told me she’d told Svetlana. “America is big and scary.” “Not as big and scary as Russia,” Svetlana responded.
As they were leaving the park, their car got stopped by park rangers. On the road up ahead, a man was apparently getting arrested for smoking weed. Weed is still illegal in national parks, and an offense can get you sent straight to federal court. Svetlana didn’t have papers. They watched the rangers put the man in handcuffs. Backlit by the orange sunset, it looked like an American western. Now Svetlana lives in Honolulu, with a new boyfriend. On her Instagram, photos of New York have been replaced with photos of Waikiki; in one of them, a rainbow arcs behind her. “The longer I look at this photo, the stranger it seems,” reads her caption.
WALMART
From January 2025 until this summer, Marysia and her family lived upstate. That winter, she discovered that a babysitter was secretly taking her son to hang out at the local Walmart. This Walmart was one of the only public places where people in the area could gather, especially when it was cold out. An informal preschool had sprung up between the overstocked shelves; on the linoleum floors crisscrossed by rubber-soled sales associates and wheelchairs and shopping carts, children, sometimes accompanied only by a slightly older sibling, ran around in a quasi-feral state. Marysia’s son had fallen under the spell of a rowdy three-year-old girl; he liked to tag along while she screamed “Bitch!” and “Motherfucker!” at shoppers. The workers at this re-wilded Walmart did not seem bothered by the mayhem. Marysia knows lots of other moms in the area. She photographed her friend Ellyn’s kids at Walmart with a babysitter character played by a woman named Sofi. Sofi set up camp with Bruna and Herman in an aisle lined by racks of discount sneakers; sprawled on a Bambi-printed blanket, they drew together in Sofi’s notebook. Then they wandered around the store, climbing in and out of printed-plastic wastebaskets and crates of rubber balls. Bruna wore her favorite outfit, a Princess Elsa costume, to the shoot.
Meanwhile, in the parking lot outside, a huge mountain of dirty snow was accumulating. When you have that much snow, it creates its own ecosystem, has its own temperature. It grew bigger and bigger, and would not melt, even in late spring. A large colony of seagulls congregated there, although (or because?) there was no sea nearby. Also, a parrot who had escaped from PetSmart.
Marysia enjoys occupying public space for extravagant reasons. As a teenager in Warsaw, she would go by herself to a mall called Blue City. She was always being shooed away by the shopgirls, who could tell she wasn’t there to spend any money. She was making time, not killing it. Marysia walked around Blue City looking at one object for sale and then another, imagining the life she might lead with each. Longing makes its own time and place, outside of life but right next to it. It is a technique much older than photography, but especially suited to it.
I am interested in Marysia’s work because it is romantic, which is to say that it is made by a loving, longing eye. The photos in the trilogy partially reproduced here—of cleaners, shoppers, and treasure hunters—are neither portraits nor “typologies” of people; they are fairy tales. Marysia’s Walmart is populated by fantastical creatures and bewitched artifacts: monstrous pillows shaped like marshmallow bunnies, a babysitter-lizard chimera, a robotic puppy being dragged around by a girl with a cheerful, eerie smile. These scenes look to me the way I imagine photographs might have looked to their very first audiences: like by-products of enchantment. I think of the silver, mist-shrouded subjects of daguerreotype portraits. As familiar as a beloved family photo, her photos are also as mysterious as magic.
Many artists and audiences seem to think that a clinical, alienating, ironic, evasive, or aesthetically empty eye makes work very highbrow. There is much great unloving art of exquisite formal intelligence, but there are just as many lazy gestures at “difficulty” that are far too easy on us. Art is easy when it does not require us to think, wonder, dream, or articulate for ourselves. My least favorite work by Christopher Williams, for example, is a beautiful photo that appeared on the April 2006 cover of this magazine. In Kodak Three Point Reflection Guide, © 1968 Eastman Kodak Company, 1968. (Meiko laughing), Vancouver, B.C., April 6, 2005, a smiling “stock” woman appears as a stupid object. This image may have packaged a charade of “criticality” into a luxury commodity, but it has nothing to do with the creation of new concepts or the revision of old ones. It reminds me of the obvious: what cameras or Walmart would like to do to me. It does not help me imagine what wild things I might do at Walmart, or with a camera.
Marysia’s photos are difficult, which is to say intelligent, because they generate non-predetermined reactions in the viewer that must be actively developed. When, like Svetlana, we look long enough to see that they are strange, we discover that there is something in them, and therefore in the world, that we may not yet understand. The ethnographer Kathleen Stewart: “What’s a concept but an active experiment with an event that’s already moving and composing on its own? What’s a conceptualization adequate to what’s thrown together in scenes, events, characters, aesthetics, forces, and situations?”1
HISTORY TREASURES
Marysia met Daniel at a Żabka convenience store in Warsaw in the summer of 2026. Żabkas are like Polish 7-Elevens; there’s one on every block. In Poland, all shops must close on Sundays, except for this one chain, which according to Marysia is exempted because it cut a deal with the Catholic Church. (They actually cut a deal with the postal service, but I like her version better.) Marysia’s friend who is a radical left-wing terrorist told her that Żabka is, moreover, a sect; all the employees go to evil religious camps together. “Of course, I fully believed him,” Marysia said. Daniel was working at Żabka as a cashier. Marysia liked his shaggy dyed black hair and his nonchalance. He delivered his lines—“Do you want a bag? Do you have a membership card?”—with a certain flair, as though merely acting the role of a cashier. He looked young, under the legal working age. When she returned the next week, he wasn’t there, nor the next. Eventually Marysia asked a woman cashier about that boy with black hair, when he might be back. “Oh no! What did he do?!” she demanded. Daniel was her son. He had only just turned fifteen and was not, in fact, an employee. He’d been covering her shifts at the store secretly, to help her out. Marysia gave her a handwritten letter explaining her new project—her printer was broken—and Daniel agreed to take some photos with her.
Marysia wanted to photograph Daniel playing with a wolf dog named Orion. Wolf dogs are a rare breed, a cross between German shepherds and Carpathian gray wolves first bred in Czechoslovakian military kennels in the 1950s to patrol the heavily forested borders of the Iron Curtain. It was a short-lived experiment. Though wolf dogs were, as had been hoped, physically superior to other breeds of working dog, they had also inherited the wolf’s temperament: Military dogs are meant to obey any officer in uniform, but a wolf dog is loyal only to the person who raised it. This wolf dog, who is well known in her neighborhood of Warsaw, belongs to a man from Belarus named Misha. After much probing by Marysia, Misha eventually revealed where he got this animal: from the very north of Russia—he didn’t want people to know his dog was Russian because of the war.
The photos of Daniel were inspired by a boy Marysia had met in the summer of 2022, a security guard working a night shift in the Soviet-era housing block where her mother lives, on the outskirts of Warsaw. When he wasn’t working as a guard, this boy said, he was either playing video games or going treasure-hunting in the forest just outside the city. He and his friends would take a metal detector and search for old coins, old jewelry, gold teeth. Most of the valuables buried in the forests of Poland, Marysia knew, belonged to Jews and other victims of the violence of the Second World War. There is a history of poor Poles looting killing sites; directly following the war, this was called the “Treblinka Gold Rush,” after the camp where much of Marysia’s father’s family was killed. The night guard was not unaware of this. He liked graveyards, he said. A World War II fan, he was “in search of history treasures.” Marysia had heard about this dark subculture, increasingly popular among teen boys in Poland—she thinks it is an indirect way of dealing with the trauma of the current war with Russia. The boy helped Marysia buy some weed, then disappeared. She did not see him again.
In Marysia’s photos, as in fairy tales, it is ordinary things that are being transformed. Everything and everyone is on the edge of becoming something or somebody else. There was a drought this summer in Europe: The soil dried out, came loose, was blown away to reveal all kinds of things. A whole mammoth skeleton appeared at the bottom of the Danube in Bulgaria. Lots of Nazi shipwrecks, too. In the forest, new material for treasure hunters. And out of the forest, into the city, came wild boars. These foraging boars are increasingly a big problem for the police, but Marysia loves when wild animals are in the streets or when domesticated animals are in the wild. It is a sign that things are not as they should be. She photographed Daniel with a herd of goats belonging to a teenage shepherd she knows who lives in the woods with his flock and his family in a makeshift structure, “his castle.” He doesn’t go to school, just tends to his animals. There are lots of things gone wild in the forests around Warsaw, like patches of marijuana, and a railroad that used to deliver bread to the city; now, there are trees growing into the steel tracks. For Marysia, the thing about the forest is that there is always something more—just a little deeper, a little farther—that we cannot see.
Daniel lives with his mother, grandmother, and sister on the outskirts of the city and has to walk through the forest to get to the mall, where he looks at clothes and records. He has a little dog. He likes Travis Scott. He wants to use one of Marysia’s photos for his first rap album. He is shy. At first, Daniel followed Marysia around in silence, listening to music through headphones even when they were taking photos. Svetlana posed in a socialist-realist style, like somebody who’d grown up seeing Soviet sculptures or reliefs on buildings, of workers captured in profile. Daniel’s poses, on the other hand, belong to a universal kind of boy: awkward, unaware of his body. “You know how boys are, they don’t like to talk about their emotions,” said Marysia. But when she told Daniel that Misha wanted to thank him, because he could see in the photos how much his dog had loved playing with him—Daniel shrugged. “I’m not surprised,” he said. “I had the best time ever, so I know he had a good time too.” Daniel is not at all like that night guard, Marysia said—not so dark. The bane of his existence is his annoying little sister. In Marysia’s favorite photos of Daniel, he stands with one sneaker on, one off. Daniel’s feet remind her of Caravaggio’s dirty feet. Caravaggio’s paintings are radical because they are painted with a loving eye; they are also, I think, some of the last great works about mothers and children, who soon disappeared from the history of high art. Daniel’s legs are so sunburned that his feet look pure white.
Olivia Kan-Sperling is articles editor at Artforum and the author of two novels.

Jeppe Ugelvig on the queen of consumer criticism
STYLE, BOTH AS A NOUN AND A VERB, seems to have largely eluded twenty-first-century art criticism. If style (n.), with which one names aesthetic networks and formal traditions, has been all but done away with as an art-historical concern, to style (v.) does not seem to register as a legitimate tactic for working critics. The reason for this is obvious enough: Style (n.) and style (v.) are both technologies of consumption, working to market aesthetics either by packaging them into compelling “-isms” or by matching the aesthetic vogues of the day. Critics, in the name of objectivity, have all but expelled “voice-y” writing from their craft, and would be hard-pressed to acknowledge the relation of their practice to the forces of crude commerce. “When it comes to contemporary art, ‘style’ is a bankrupt concept,” David Joselit asserted in a 2012 essay in Texte zur Kunst. Once central to the historian’s mandate to periodize art, style has become “not only conservative but practically meaningless” to the work of criticism: “more old-fashioned than obsessing about ‘medium’ or ‘postmedium.’”
But Joselit noted that the tactic of styling—the present participle of style (v.)—has been used by artists to much success: Fashioning artworks to “look like” bygone art styles, consumer debris, or plain advertising evidently carries both critical and commercial potential (Joselit’s essay centers 1990s art collective Bernadette Corporation, but also takes as examples the postmodern break of the 1970s, 1920s Dada, and nineteenth-century historicism). It is most unfortunate that art criticism has not followed suit. Reviews, press releases, and catalogue essays—all genres of value production—are evidently shaped by stylistic conventions, but in such texts, the lingo of promotion is rarely pursued to any aesthetic or critical effect. Situated somewhere between the highbrow pretensions of latter-day modernist art theory (which some would say has since further calcified into so-called International Art English) and the publicity demands of an ever-shrinking economy of coverage, art writing perpetually misses its own privileged window of opportunity, that is, to play self-reflexively with style (n.) (v.). This is a shame, because the genre, at this point a few centuries old, is the very product of the public encounter with style objects and style industries—artworks, art galleries, and museums, but also artists, brands, corporations, and other person-like entities. Even a great stylist of postwar American art like Andy Warhol is frequently “un-styled” by his tenured academic examiners, stripped of the very economies his work not only responded to but accrued meaning within.
Style (and its corollary, stylishness) is what modernist art à la Clement Greenberg tried to definitively expel. But art has never transcended style, nor have our eyes and sensibilities. Today, style inevitably means consumption—shopping for stuff. This is the humble if radical dictum of critic, columnist, essayist, educator, and sometime curator Rhonda Lieberman. Her high-intensity textual output, much of it published in these pages, became a mainstay of American art criticism at the turn of the millennium. Thirty-some years after she emerged in New York City armed to the teeth with Theory and casting its art society as the ambivalent subject of her fieldwork, the sociological obviousness of her claim—that art is an object of taste and must be dealt with accordingly—remains a provocation, not least to mandarins of the field still wedded to the doctrine of art’s aesthetic autonomy. So-called high art, she argued in 2007, is patterned and stylized like so much else, and may simply be understood as that which is lifted and falsely separated “from life, décor, and fashion.” Everything that is not “Art” is relegated to the category of “Stuff”: that “which mingles promiscuously with the viewer, leaks out of its frame physically and politically, looks good or bad with your couch.”
But style, Lieberman suggested, has in effect saturated all aspects of society—as she wrote in 2004, it is “no longer an occupational hazard restricted to fashionistas, drag queens and neurotics.” Rather, consumer culture has turned “everyone into a de facto esthete: Life becomes a style problem—with style solutions,” per a 2006 essay. Having never fully severed its ties to style, visual art—its making, selling, buying—is inevitably absorbed by accelerating style industries: by the totalitarian logics of shopping, marketing, glamour, celebrity, and entertainment. Art is not (quite) those things, but it covertly informs them and frequently steals from them in turn. To put it sociologically: Because art is a cultural practice whose specificity is revealed exactly by its distance from those activities it socially approximates, it must continuously deny these affiliations in order to maintain its distinctiveness. But all aesthetes are ultimately marked by style’s compulsive perfectionism—that “evil genie motivating great works of art and flawless outfits.”
As the intellectual representative of the style public, the critic’s utmost task is to recover the inflamed connection between art and style—indeed, between great works of art and flawless outfits. The sociologist Pierre Bourdieu began this work with his 1979 treatise, Distinction, in which he placed museumgoing and art-buying in a consumerist matrix alongside preferences in food and interior decor (though the writing was notably less stylish than that of his countryman Baudelaire, who according to Lieberman had already completed his theory of the “consumer-vampire of modernity” in his “The Painter of Modern Life” essay some hundred and twenty years earlier). Bourdieu showed how, in an advanced consumer society, style becomes a socially circulated commodity language, and how cultivating an aesthetic disposition—the usual hallmark of art appreciation—becomes the dominant mode of organizing the self and the world. This tendency to conceive of life itself in the crude terms of product culture is today encapsulated by that dreaded compound word, lifestyle, which since the time of Distinction’s publication has become a ubiquitous term.
Lieberman extended this sensibility to the mainstream art-publishing landscape of the fin-de-siècle United States, a relatively self-conscious period in the world’s first consumer republic, marked by the rise of Sex and the City as much as by the pop-cultural mainstreaming of French Theory. “Who has never felt flabby and shabby compared to a sleek glistening commodity?” she asked in “The Loser Thing,” published in Artforum in September 1992. A sprawling reflection on aesthetic apprenticeship as well as a substantial piece of criticism on several contemporary artists—David Diao, Sean Landers, and Cary Leibowitz, aka Candy Ass—the text ricochets between Nietzsche and Lynda Benglis, Samuel Beckett’s feet and Joan Rivers’s thighs in search of a theory of the self-as-professionalized commodity:
No one wants to be subject of the gaze, we all want to be fabulous objects. Late this century the lines between wanting to have, wanting to be, and wanting to seem like a commodity have gotten hopelessly collapsed. Under the combined misery complex of capital and fame, abjection—the plight of those who are insufficiently recognizable as commodities, for commodities, by commodities—is a national and personal emergency.
Warhol, Lieberman wrote, may have been the first artist to transvalue this abjection into “happy profitable outcomes” and embrace the “wannabe moment as the generative power of the work” and the artist’s own mythos. Diao, Landers, and Candy Ass approach the productive acting out of the “professional loser persona” more negatively, sublimating their own indignity, insecurity, and envy into zany artworks that retain the less-than-shiny traces of shame suffered by the struggling artist (as well as the struggling consumer, similarly aspiring to be some shiny thing). By comparing the professional logics of contemporary art with those of glamour industries of entertainment (which “institutionalizes the lack-in-being when it swerves back and attacks you with accusations that you’re not someone else”), Lieberman identified wannabehood as a generalized contemporary condition: the wish to acquire, embody, or resemble the “Special Stuff” one compulsively projects into the artist, celebrity, or commodity.
Four years earlier, while still a graduate student at Yale, Lieberman delivered a lecture titled “Lip-Synching for Life” at the CUNY symposium Shock ’88, organized by Catherine Liu in New York City. Remixing her canon of Continental philosophy and literature, Lieberman argued for the embodied, unconscious ventriloquizing of style (be it that of a pop song or of Foucault) as a core logic of contemporary life and language—a natural aesthetic consequence of “shock,” Walter Benjamin’s 1935 term for the modern subject’s reaction to perpetual sensory bombardment by consumer technologies. In Lieberman’s gloss, modernity itself is defined in terms of shopping, that is, by the endless adoption of already available modes—of art, ideas, and outfits. How to react to the noises of style but to ventriloquize its choir of canned voices?
This diagnosis also serves as a productive method for criticism. If style is everywhere, latent even in high theory, it must be dealt with by dressing up in it, performing it as yet another pop song, or by “testing out this rather disembodied and theoretical discourse in my lived experience,” as Lieberman put it in 2016. Her response was to lip-synch it, quite literally: At the CUNY symposium, she brought a boom box onto the conference stage and mimed the entire lecture to the recorded sound of her own voice. This embodied approach to philosophy in the heyday of consumer culture is the stuff not only of Tiqqun, but of Michèle Bernstein, Proust, Baudelaire, and Mallarmé (himself a prominent lip-syncher, who posed as various female style columnists in his fashion magazine of the 1870s, La Dernière Mode). Lieberman, a real-life Carrie Bradshaw (only Jewish, Proust-reading, and fluent in Derrida), would likewise play with the verbose and gossipy prose conventions of the female fashion writer. She found a perfectly vulgar stage for this performance in New York City’s overcrowded art world, where an avant-gardist mythos rubbed shoulders with what economist Thorstein Veblen, a century before her, had called “the leisure class.” As she explained in a 2016 conversation with Bruce Hainley and Sarah Lehrer-Graiwer, she was intent on “inserting myself onto the scene of interpretation—questioning any space outside—and destabilizing my effect on the reader (by rejecting either an ‘objective’ or merely ‘personal’ stance).”
THE HISTORICAL VALUE of Lieberman’s writing lies in the ease with which she personified the self-consciously voice-y female auteur, in her mastery of the feuilleton as literary genre, and in its popular dissemination. If she was “too late” (as she bemoans) to the party that was 1980s high theory in US academia, it is clear to the contemporary reader that she arrived at professional art writing right on time.
Artforum, once an ivory tower of highbrow criticism, was then being redefined by savvy editors with deep critical interest in—and social ties to—systems of style. Ingrid Sischy, conspiring with the critic-curator Germano Celant, was the first to explicitly privilege fashion in the magazine’s pages, placing an Issey Miyake dress on the cover in 1982; a monthly column on advertising by Glenn O’Brien soon followed, coyly titled “Like Art.” Jack Bankowsky radicalized her high/low media theory dialectic further, putting Lieberman in his first issue (September 1992) alongside a review of the New York International Auto Show (by artist and fashion photographer Collier Schorr) and an essay on the Rodney King tapes by critical theorist Avital Ronell. Two issues later, in November 1992, Lieberman debuted her sublimely titled column “Glamour Wounds”—capturing the bittersweet but common work injuries of the style citizen—with “The Chanel Superego,” a phenomenological review not of an exhibition, but of a Chanel boutique: “[A]s traumatic for me as seeing Madonna in person,” she began. “I was commanded to expel myself as a symbolic turd: constitutionally flawed, a heterogeneous element that had to be pressed out of my reality because it couldn’t coexist with all that senseless plenitude.” Next, in December, she offered a theoretical inversion of Veblen through the supermodels of the ’90s (“warrior-priestesses of consumer practice”). And in January of the following year, we got the consumerist subtext of her own biography via a deconstruction of the contentious Jew-WASP in relation to the commodity form, as told through Derrida and Barbra Streisand (“Shut out from total identification with the commodity, she is doomed to witness the trauma of their inarticulate power”).
As the privileged tool of capriciousness and insincerity, style destabilizes art, value, opinion, truth—even one’s sense of identity. For Lieberman, this became one of the most contentious issues of writing through the so-called multiculti ’90s. “Recently, many disgruntled consumers (of identity) are demanding that their identity should exist as some prepackaged product out there (affordable and accessible), so they can shop for it like a car or a pair of shoes,” she had argued already in “The Loser Thing.” “People appeal to representation as some kind of exalted consumer advocacy board that can restore a self-image that you never had (but believe you have lost), a personal Wonder product, at once totally attractive, totally recognized, and totally you.” Identity, style teaches us, is the place where the intensity of being someone is put in the crass terms of the commodity. “What would it be like, I imagined, if Barbie’s Jewish roots were to show?” Lieberman joked in a 1995 Artforum column, “The Other American Princess,” a prescient, barely satiric description of today’s actual toy shelves. “How about Hanukkah Barbie (with a little bush)? Nose-Bob Barb (with preop detachable beak)? Bat Mitzvah Barbie—stunning! Barbie looking for a Bargain… NOT!” Identity may be important as a social form, but, marked with the insignia of style, it is always highly suspect. This makes identity politically difficult, which is not to say that it is politically bankrupt.
Lieberman just as easily took on the more opaque (and much more vulgar) consumer sphere that is the art world, whose materialistic subtext she uncovered as a latter-day Diderot, through the crimes—and joys—of style. Her takes, entertaining, tragic, and always dialectical, are best summarized in one of her oft-repeated mantras: that art is “the most esteemed form of shopping in our culture today.” Her instinct rested on real enough data. From the ’90s until the financial crisis of 2008, the art world enjoyed an unprecedented global expansion, attracting the interest of both corporate culture and the financial class. This presented a test for art magazines, which were tasked with straddling ever more lucrative promotional opportunities with good old Critique. Artforum’s response under Bankowsky was Scene & Herd, later renamed Diaries, a digital reimagination of the society gossip column, targeting the globe-trotting art set and its relentless calendar of professional social fluff—fairs, biennial openings, press trips, galas. “I gloried in the prospect of . . . ‘performing’ the unavoidable bondage of art and publicity (in the print media’s dissolute final hours),” Bankowsky wrote in an Artforum essay in 2012. He was wise in sending his best, and smartest, art critics to reinvent the genre of style reportage, including Lieberman as well as her contemporary David Rimanelli, a pair “ideally poised to ‘out’ the art world with respect to its enabling ‘contradictions,’” Bankowsky recently reflected, because they existed “(precariously) between the institutionalized safe havens of tenure-track propriety and mass-magazine pure product.” Through her entries, we follow Lieberman to art openings in TriBeCa, evening sales at Christie’s, a book promo with Jean Baudrillard, and that most bizarre ritual, the collector’s “open house,” a bygone vogue of the Armory Show’s VIP offerings. “Who could resist gawking?” Lieberman—a self-described “yenta intrigued by other people’s stuff”—asked, rightfully, regarding the domiciles of the 1 percent. The scene
was set for Lieberman’s unforgiving appreciation of Manhattan’s conspicuous consumption, that central cultural logic of America.
IT WAS NEVER HER SUBJECTS PER SE that primarily interested Lieberman. (She made this confession in a postscript written for her anthology The Rhonda Lieberman Reader, edited by Lehrer-Graiwer and published in 2018; long out of print, it has been reissued this fall by the publishing unit I run, Viscose.) “[I]t’s writing. A subject—or in the Diaries, a situation—is a pretext for questions of voice, tone, point of view. How to locate myself on the scene of interpretation and include analysis and description of the many vectors in play?” But if these contradictions are the fuel of Lieberman’s practice, they also establish its limits. The criteriological position that she mastered so young became harder to maintain as the art world became ever more contradictory—namely, when critiques of these contradictions became consumable commodities in and of themselves. For years, it was rumored that a Web banner on Scene & Herd was Artforum’s most expensive ad placement because the column was by far the magazine’s most read, suggesting that self-reflexive gossip was more economically valuable than criticism itself (as well as a more powerful version of institutional critique). This put the style critic in an impossible double bind, which Lieberman began to feel acutely as the aughts came to a close.
In the anthology’s postscript, we find the author at her most vulnerable and brutally honest about the hopes and disappointments of the trade. Stranded between the conservatism of the academic ivory tower (whose professors are increasingly reduced to precarious service work for status-seeking elites) and the prostitution of art-world promotion, Lieberman identifies an anguish all too familiar to any working critic: the devaluing of true intellectual work. “This cognitive dissonance was distracting at the very least. When it didn’t throw me into despair, it ironized my relationship to Fine Ideas, which acquired this added, shall we say, perspective.” As the art world grew and melded further with corporate finance (“which glorifies those systems of power, more often than it questions them”), Lieberman increasingly retreated from professional art writing. Her last substantial essay, on dirty money in museum boards, was published by the New Republic in 2019 with the telling title “Painting Over the Dirty Truth.” A chilling piece of investigative art journalism that concludes with a particularly dystopian cocktail party at MoMA, it also reads as a breakup letter.
If consumerism does not deserve criticism, as many critics would still argue, contemporary art did not deserve Lieberman. Paradoxically, even as her cherished French canon has remained required reading in comp-lit and art history departments to this day, their style is less appreciated, and even more rarely imitated, in today’s cultures of professional art writing. In abandoning this admittedly historically marginal strategy of formal “styling,” criticism lost something—specifically, its ability to adequately tackle the aesthetic apparatuses of consumer capitalism, including its willful instrumentalization of our field for the purposes of ever more advanced forms of PR (laundering, for example, the reputation of “toxic philanthropists,” per Lieberman’s New Republic essay). Criticism is also simply worse, by which I mean less beautiful, as well as less knowledgeable of the beautiful. Even those daring writers with an interest in stylish critique or the critique of style (or both) do not usually get very far before the Overton window of form closes its snare around them (blame bad editors, or conservative professors), and the professional demands of contemporary writing—that is, semiautomated marketing—entirely take over.
The absolute relevance of Lieberman’s writing today is in its demonstration that there is a third way for art writing—one that transcends priggish objectivity and histrionics of hype, both of which are ultimately performances of the same banal condition: the industrial production of economic value. Styling, as Joselit reminded us, is best understood as “an opportunistic tool directed at claiming power in the present”—that goes as much for writers as it does for artists, advertisers, and politicians. There may be no exit from the misery complex that combines capital and fame, and therefore no exit from its markets of beauty. In order to question these markets they must first be made sensible; by embodying their logic, their abjection can be revealed. And the name for this method is style.
Jeppe Ugelvig is a New York–based critic and the founder of the publishing unit Viscose.

How a biennial about the crisis of spirituality mistook messaging for meaning
WE TAKE A NICE PLACE in the Margarethenhöhe, a garden city in the late Romantic style, faux cottages, lush rosebushes. White asparagus is still in season, potatoes are firm, there is hollandaise. I’d arrived that evening into Essen’s main station, a sketchy place full of loitering youth that I rushed to vacate. I am used to thinking about Berlin as rough and messy, while the West Germany of my mind is well-organized and prosperous. But there they always are, the West German cities, along the Leine, the Main, the Rhine, like anthills crawling with life, their infrastructure overburdened and their populations much more visibly diverse, perhaps also more divided, than those of their eastern counterparts. So much effort has gone into erasing the GDR that it’s the Federal Republic that now appears lost to time, in the shadow of the economic miracle of the 1960s.
The truth is that capital does not distribute by nation-state, but erratically, into pockets. Luckily for us, I suppose, the Margarethenhöhe is one of them. Established in the early twentieth century mainly for workers of the Krupp corporation (and named after its founder, Margarethe Krupp), it has turned into something of a bourgeois colony. The Krupps—later of Nazi affiliation—built their own estate nearby, its vast Neoclassical gardens extending down toward the Baldeneysee, a lake that is really a dammed-up part of the Ruhr River. It’s another world from Essen proper; you cross a bridge to get there, the terrain is hilly, the forest dark green at the height of summer. Another unprecedented heat wave threatens to pass 40°C by the end of our stay. Who else is here at the Stadthotel Margarethenhöhe? A large group of men, on an annual golf trip, I imagine. Elderly people, as though on a retreat, taking the waters (which?). Us, going to an art biennial.
Manifesta 16 opened during the fair in Basel, the week before our visit. The biennial’s recent Mediterranean editions—in Palermo, Italy, in 2018; Marseille in 2020; Barcelona in 2024—took on issues from migration to ecology, but they weren’t required to do much in terms of providing an experience of art. The audience would be swayed by the cities themselves, framed by the biennial as it opened up old palaces, libraries, and hotels, pointing to the magnificent facts of what was already there. The Ruhr Valley, in contrast, might be Europe’s vastest, most depressing suburb. Since the nineteenth century it has been referred to colloquially as der Pott—the pot—because it is a crater of coal mines and because of the smoke that would rise from factory chimneys. Later, this industry became a prime engine behind West Germany’s economic recovery, the population rising steeply in the decades after the war. By now the mines have closed, while just over five million people remain in what is conventionally acknowledged to be fraught and unlikable territory. Manifesta 16 attracted me, for one thing, because here the art would have to pull its own weight, and for another, because it had been assigned a topic uniquely suited to its disposition: not migration or ecology, but the crisis of spirituality.
Art—in the broadest sense—has been enlisted to this aim in the region at least once before, namely in the construction of hundreds of new churches during the spiritual low point of the immediate postwar period. This year’s Manifesta took place across twelve of these churches: in Essen, Duisburg, Bochum, and Gelsenkirchen, some renovated, others of highly sophisticated modernist ilk—some, as of late, deconsecrated. Included in the “Urban Vision” developed by Josep Bohigas, Manifesta 16’s “first creative mediator,” was a series of maps showing the region covered in yellow and purple circles that mark where the mines were and where the bombs fell (not even the Margarethenhöhe went unscathed). A swarm of little black dots shows the many places of worship built to accommodate the rising number of workers assisting the economic miracle, a network so dense that it was said that wherever you lived, you could walk to church in your house slippers. Many of these structures are beautiful and challenging, both as sculptural artifacts and as theological propositions. But as Bohigas concluded in his Vision, “far too many were built for a society that no longer exists,” and it is this problematic that prompted the biennial to repurpose them.
The biennial’s title, “This is not a church,” made clear that there would be no attempt to recycle the buildings’ religious purpose. Still, I had hoped the exhibition might offer structure for some of the purpose provided by religion—holding questions of the soul, of doubt; of human dignity and the end of the world. Here the unusual “intergenerational tandems” within the curatorial team (Michael Kurtz and Henry Meyric Hughes, René Block and Leonie Herweg, and Krzysztof Kościuczuk and Anda Rottenberg) might help uncover a new spiritual use value in the aesthetic, by staging an exchange between a generation that lost religion and one that never had it. In spite of having leafed through press materials suggesting young people would be using the spaces for sports, I assumed at the very least that the mood of the exhibition would attune to the spiritual program of the architecture. How could it not? It had obviously been a while since I’d visited an art biennial.
FROM A SUN-SOAKED TRAM STOP we venture into the city, climb out from underneath a roundabout: to one side, a century-old industrial complex converted into a cultural space, to the other, a steel-and-glass shopping center. The streets of central Essen are narrow in the old way, but the buildings are almost entirely postwar. Outside St. Gertrud, a renovated nineteenth-century church in the city center, is a tree-shaped metal structure, its branches formed from heavy-duty surveillance cameras welded together. I read that the 2021–26 work, by Halil Altındere, is titled Security Tree and “invites visitors to consider how surveillance shapes contemporary life,” and I read the object in the same way—read truly being the word, for its logic is semantic rather than sculptural; it contains only the message that the artist put there.
The biennial is full of works that do not pass as art so much as a kind of visual communication: some more or less banal idea—though certainly by journalistic measures “relevant” or “topical”—translated into form. This is the dead end of what might once have been “Conceptual art,” the legacy of our misunderstanding of which is the notion that art should be “about” something, which would render it important and understood to be engaged in a project of “criticality.” At St. Marien, a striking brick church in the north of Essen, Alicja Kwade supplies a nearly farcical example of the genre: A stack of smartphones cast in bronze makes a tower in the shape of a spiral, reminiscent, the wall text reminds us, of a strand of DNA. Get it? “While DNA has traditionally been understood as the carrier of identity . . . the phone appears as a contemporary form of self-description.” The text tries to pass the work off as “both familiar and unsettling,” but it is neither. Like Altındere’s, it is little more than a literalist gimmick.
Though with more subtlety, the same fault lines run through Merve Kaplan’s work for the biennial. It is exhibited at St. Bonifatius in Gelsenkirchen, where a concrete roof unfolds origami-like over the multigonal brick room lined at the top with stained-glass windows. Kaplan’s tiled tabletops in shades of brown hang behind the altar. This style of furniture is known locally as Gelsenkirchener Barock, and we are told it is common in “both German and migrant households”—that is to say, in every household. And not only here: Variations of the style are familiar from just about every provincial Kneipe in the country. Gelsenkirchen is among the poorest towns in Germany, its streets on a hot summer day surreal in their vacancy, out of a de Chirico, its population largely made up of workers from the now defunct mines, many descending from the mainly Turkish “guest workers” who arrived in the 1960s and ’70s. St. Bonifatius is one of three venues curated by Gürsoy Doğtaş dedicated to their history and culture. The idea is presumably that giving space to staples of working-class domesticity (Kaplan has arranged a brown carpet, slippers, and glasses across the raised floor of the sanctuary) would offer representation to a demographic presumably underrepresented in the presumably prestigious environment of a contemporary art show. There is, of course, an automatic effect to hanging the tabletop pieces in place of the crucifix, their undulating surfaces almost reminiscent of a kind of spiritual abstraction. But then the notion of representation—the supposed fixedness of the objects’ connotations—once again forgoes presence and materiality in favor of semantics.
We can say, as the accompanying text does, that the objects carry with them stories about migration and cultural difference, about gathering and community. Is it true? The great potential for art in postmodernism’s semantic turn lay in recognizing the profound instability of signifiers, but both in the Kaplan presentation and throughout the biennial, there is a tendency toward a pseudo-ethnographic method of using objects as a social index. In this I am reminded of the work of the late Henrike Naumann, whose installations of furniture fashionable in East Germany in the 1990s, too, can run the risk of seeming to provide mere scenography for a conversation that many people are keen to have, and which, I agree, is both culturally and politically pertinent. But the objects we are left with, to take both Kaplan and Naumann as examples, often fall short of what either a painting or sculpture can be—and, without the theater play itself, what of the pertinent conversation? As I stand before the altar at St. Bonifatius, the latter amounts to little more than a vague swelling of emotion supported by a statement of intent.
One common problem with this semantically driven way of working with art is that objects become conflated with the existence of the people with whom they are said to be associated, like words mistaken for the things themselves. At several venues, Manifesta 16 seems to be inviting segments of the local population to their own wake. The motive might be sympathetic, but the effect is sentimentalizing. Black grids make a kind of labyrinth out of the nave of St. Bonifatius, exhibiting the work of some twenty artists with migrant backgrounds who have been enlisted to “represent” this experience. The many paintings here tend to be allegorical, with an air of magical realism—think Niko Pirosmani or Frida Kahlo, small cartoonish figures appearing in their own dreams—but thanks to this en masse presentation, any artistic content is subordinated to the exhibition’s ethnographic impulses. A curatorial gesture meant to honor stops at declaring that these people were here, that they lived their lives, that they were—are—human.
AS THE FIRST DAY WANED, we withdrew into the greenery south of the Margarethenhöhe, went swimming in the Baldeneysee as people paddled by in canoes, and drank Riesling under striped yellow umbrellas. The one painting at St. Bonifatius that I liked was a small still life from 1968 by Yiannis Psychopedis, a Greek artist, depicting a Vicks inhaler and a glass bottle with a red label. The accompanying text would have it that the medication “appears as a metaphor for those bodies scarred by the [Greek] dictatorship.” But Vicks, as far as I know, treats a cold. I thought the painting indicated a secret: sober, devoid of personality, and yet intense, almost mystical in its insistence upon these two, to me, fairly mute objects. Who is more cynical? Me, so resentful of collective feeling that I am unable to imagine that other people do not also feel condescended to by the imperative? Or the conveners of this exhibition, who too willingly betray the secrets of artworks, sacrificing complexity to sentimentality? A light-blue sky reflecting in the water, we swam in the dusk, the Krupp villa behind us. In whatever this biennial is conveying about our collective crisis in spirituality, is the art an instrument or merely a symptom?
Founded in the early ’90s by Hedwig Fijen, the Dutch art historian who has been at the helm ever since, Manifesta first took place in Rotterdam in 1996. Europe had opened up toward the East; there was a sense that new things might be possible. In a grainy promotional video for the Rotterdam exhibition, one of its curators, Viktor Misiano of Moscow’s Contemporary Art Center, described the biennial as a new model of exhibition adequate to what he called an “age which is in-between betweenness” characterized by “the loss of clear paradigms.” Andrew Renton, another of the Manifesta 1 curators (and later head of the curating MFA at Goldsmiths), added that it “is not so much an accumulation of objects, but more the gathering together of people and the opening up of communication between one culture and another.” Manifesta, then, was conceived not as an exhibition in the traditional sense, but as a way of “using the exhibition as the starting point of something else, open up those lines of communication . . . and keep them open.”
As ubiquitous as this mode of exhibition-making has become, such statements suggest that 1996 was a very long time ago. European openness has frayed, with the return of Schengen border checks and the departure of Britain from the EU. It also might have been overstated to begin with: In 2006, Manifesta 6 was canceled because the post-paradigmatic order hadn’t quite arrived in Cyprus yet. In 2014, the year of Russia’s invasion of Crimea, the biennial went ahead in Saint Petersburg. What’s more, “in-between betweenness,” to the extent that it manifested, turned out to be a rather empty place. Freedom for markets, for consumers, for everywhere to be the same. What else? The center holds, but only because the whole structure is hollow, carries no weight.
In this sense, Manifesta’s development over the past three decades mirrors the trajectory of the style of architecture that came out of Rotterdam offices like MVRDV and OMA in the ’90s. This architectural paradigm, which has directly informed the biennial via its Urban Visions, was initially a thrilling break from corporate postmodernism. But it has grown over time into a form of New Pragmatism, less about the object—the building—than about communication, making a “starting point of something else”: a skateboard ramp, an urban garden, a bicycle bridge, a swimming spot. Rather than engaging with how something is made, or out of what, the strategy here is for architecture to perform as social prompt and media phenomenon; life in the city is subsumed by the experience economy, the nicer phrase for which usually involves the word “community.” It is an outcome of what Robert Venturi thought we could learn from Las Vegas, and it is the opposite of the ethos of formal integrity that underlies the postwar modernist church.
Perhaps this is why it is so difficult for this Manifesta to deal with the religious spaces that have been chosen as venues. See, once again, the latest Urban Vision, with its belief that architectural stunts can help us “relearn how to be together.” Bohigas’s report contains a series of speculative renderings of cross-shaped swimming pools and recreational gardens floating along the Ruhr, and introduces the notion of the Beachurch: the church as beach, a “non-hierarchical public space” where “diverse bodies converge” and “temporalities slow down.” We find such spaces outside of several of the churches, delineated by makeshift garden furniture, potted plants, and colorful bunting. They are invariably hideous, and their effect is infantilizing, though unfortunately the concept is not native to Manifesta 16—a great many museums are now equipped with beanbags and food trucks.
At St. Josef, the venue curated by Bohigas, the inside is wrapped in blue plastic—a spectacular sight, actually—and the floor covered with sand. The pews have been transformed into bleachers. Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s Wrapped Reichstag, 1995, suggested a building undergoing metamorphosis, marking it as a site where the chain of signification ruptures to give form, as in Psychopedis’s painting, to a secret. Thirty years later, it is the interior of St. Josef that seems to have been wiped out, as if a void of purpose were a valiant end in itself. I am reminded of Nicolas Bourriaud’s notion of relational aesthetics in which the mere fact of the encounter takes primacy over the quality of it. Kids will play football here, people will meet for coffee—so what? For art, even as social proposition, that seems like too low a bar.
IN DUISBURG’S KULTURKIRCHE LIEBFRAUEN, designed by Toni Hermanns and built between 1958 and 1971, we find one of the most striking architectural manifestations of negative theology imaginable. After the war, any proof of God’s existence had to be found in his absence, in the material and spiritual devastation people were living with. Here, light does not issue from the far end of the room, drawing us toward salvation, but is coolly diffused through side walls made of milky Plexiglas. Magnificent concrete walls rise at front and back; slate-gray, as if wet, and monumental in their austerity, they box us in. What in Adorno stands for the impossibility of faith, and in Simone Weil is its ultimate proof, is in this case both.
Architecturally, Liebfrauen forms a pair with St. Marien—the site of Kwade’s smartphone/DNA provocation—designed by Hans Schilling and completed in 1963. The pentagonal shape of the nave enacts a break with the familiar unidirectional layout, as the windowless sanctuary does in Duisburg, except what in Hermanns’s church verges on a form of punishment in Schilling’s offers compassion, if only by a hair. Here, the architecture distributes the congregation into a half circle, gathering them around the matter of their faith as a question rather than as an assertion. Still, St. Marien, too, is dark, gloomy—the more so since it has been out of use, the ceiling leaking, the walls stained with damp. The eighteen-meter-tall brick curve that encases the altar has a tremendous body, nearly ominous in its presence, that imparts an intuitive understanding—even amid the doubt—that what provides shelter necessarily does so through strength. There is no semantics, the buildings do not communicate; in both churches, it is the empty walls that seem to lay reality bare.
What would it look like to do something analogous with art? With his installation at St. Marien, Jason Dodge emerges as one of the few actors in this biennial who have kept the space not only in mind but in body. His untitled work consists of assorted materials strewn across the floor of the nave: sawdust, flowers, feathers, sheets of plastic or fabric, what I would call various forms of trash—materials that do not signify but matter. The composition slips in and out of deliberation, a tableau of buckets and plates concentrating energy, which the lighter detritus then loosens and disperses. As the church falls apart, its demolition imminent, the work acts as an acknowledgment of the life that exists within materials, of how intention and attention can come together to bring out the sense of meaning inherent to a place. Dodge’s installation is ephemeral and finely tuned—light like a fog, yet adding gravity to the room, situating the viewer within it. The maneuver is very simple: The artist was here and made an effort to remain open to what else is here, visible and invisible. This is a plain definition of what it now means to work in a spiritual way, a definition that emphasizes not transcendence or divinity, but mundanity, fragility, the real.
The kinds of statements Manifesta 16 is capable of making work best when semantically and ontologically uncluttered like Dodge’s, the objects integral to themselves and their immediate surroundings rather than message boards for history, news, and theory from elsewhere. Of the several works in which church pews are utilized as sculpture, Augustas Serapinas’s Pew Tower, 2026, is the most successful. It stands within the Markuskirche in Essen, a tenderly understated Protestant church with a square nave and a sharply tented roof. Daylight enters through colored-glass mosaics and reflects on dark wooden floorboards; Serapinas’s tower of repurposed planks serves as a viewing platform that allows us to come closer to the mosaics, and to see the room from above. Nothing is revealed, exactly, but the shift in perspective is enough to make the quiet room strange. There are stripes and scuffs on the floor below, where the pews used to be. Serapinas’s approach is remarkable for its objectivity.
In another pew experiment—Nasan Tur’s Elevation, 2026, at St. Gertrud in Essen—the benches are stood upright, crowding the altar like tall buildings. Their steep verticality is somehow threatening, in hubristic competition with the crucifix behind them, a tension further heightened by a red laser target moving across the wall (part of a work by Šejla Kamerić). But this sense of danger is apparently incidental. Rather, as we should have come to expect, turning the pews upright is meant to transform the traditionally hierarchical (i.e., bad) seating arrangement into a “collective structure shaped by many voices,” an idea literalized by people having been invited to carve their thoughts into the wood. One person wishes that their parents stay healthy; another that they get rid of their anxiety. Me: that I be spared such banalities. Here is another mindless invitation to participation out of a seeming fear of the artwork being allowed to exist for itself, without some form of justification or declaration of benevolence.
THE GREAT PROBLEM with this biennial, as with so many major exhibitions today, is that the art and its context are not in attunement with each other. For a curator not to take the venue seriously as an interlocutor is a fault that could overwhelm even very strong work. Perhaps the offending benches at St. Gertrud could have landed for me if some spatial sensitivity had been established from the moment I entered the church. But each work is in its own world, too busy surviving the mess to mind its environment. Just because a set of works is made in response to the same location does not mean that they will have any kind of energetic affinity between them, or with the space. And yet the biennial conforms to the institutional convention that asks artists to transform a site into a “theme” in their work, even as the same site is suddenly considered blank when it comes to the installation. This stubbornly cerebral procedure is misguided in any scenario, but in the context of venues as auratically charged as these it starts to become absurd.
It is in this way that the biennial fails to contend with the fact that churches—regardless of what is suggested by the Urban Vision’s Beachurch—are very much not spaces in which anything goes. The relevance and authority of the Church and its buildings derive precisely from its rules, its liturgy. Blasphemy is not the relevant term here, but when churches are transformed into basketball courts or club spaces, could we not at least speak of wastefulness, of missed opportunity? We are not dealing, after all, with disused factory buildings or abandoned parking lots. Is it necessary, is it healthy, is it reasonable to think of places such as these as so inherently empty of meaning that they could be filled with any kind of activity at all? The schmaltzy rhetoric around nearly all of the works evidences a great desire for purpose, meaning, even dogma, but such things do not tend to emerge from entertainment or leisure practices so much as from constraint and necessity.
That our attachment to freedom stands in the way of “relearning how to be together,” as Bohigas hoped the Beachurch would facilitate, is a very grave, very difficult problem. One of the main hurdles in dealing with it is the question of authority. Where individual agency is always primary, the customer is always right and authority is generally considered oppressive. But without authority, without authorship, there can be no trust: As a viewer, I simply do not believe in the curatorial voice that presents me with these works. The Church, one presumes, would have lessons to impart when it comes to countering incredulity, but then, unfortunately, “This is not a church.” As a consequence, in this biennial, there is pedagogy, good intentions, and goodwill, but no framework capable of conveying what must remain outside of language—despite the architecture of the venues being made for exactly that.
DUISBURG IS AT THE EDGE of the Pott, where the Ruhr meets the Rhine. It is beautiful in glimpses. As our last day comes to a close, we find a restaurant in a gracious park named for Immanuel Kant. In the middle of the park, visible from the terrace of the restaurant, is a museum dedicated to the work of modernist sculptor Wilhelm Lehmbruck, designed by the artist’s son Manfred in 1957. We pay the check and literally run around the closed museum, looking through all the windows. The art and the building combine into a single work of extraordinary coherence, which seems to understand something about the relationship of sculpture to architecture: that one strong artistic gesture must be met by another; that no space is blank; that artworks speak for themselves even if they don’t use language. We speed off in a taxi to catch a final Manifesta church before heading back to the Margarethenhöhe.
A few weeks later, I teach a class on art criticism to students at Frankfurt’s Goethe University, address: Theodor Adorno Platz 1. We talk a lot about the first-person perspective, which all the students have used in some way. Criticism is about transcending yourself, I tell them, about trying to speak outside of your individual perspective. I get the Chris Kraus of it all, but let’s ask ourselves: How interesting is it, actually, how hot it was, what you ate, how you felt when you got off the train?
They too have been to the Ruhr and generally found the experience agreeable. They appreciate the engagement with the guest workers, the urgency of representing their lives, and if they take issue with the biennial’s social program, it is only because it does not go far enough. Will the retired miners really come? How could they possibly relate to this art? Is the interest in migrant communities merely an afterthought, a way of ticking a box? Besides, what is the Church but a history of power and oppression? This inevitably makes me feel like a grump. But, if they are pro-Manifesta, I tell myself, at least I’m pro-art! Believe it or not, I wanted to enjoy myself—to write something literary, a rich and abstract narrative about my trip to the Ruhr: “How I Spent My Summer Vacation.” But then, the work generally has to be pretty good in order to live inside a story; critique trumps narrative.
One student nimbly applies an Adornian lens, arguing that the nonidentity thinking suggested by the title, “This is not a church,” cuts across the exhibition as a whole, giving it a productively dialectical character. I think of the shopping center at the big roundabout in Essen when I counter that the very idea of negative dialectics has been commodified, turned into a rhetorical gimmick, Adorno turning in his grave. Still, it makes sense that a student might read the exhibition in this way—read truly being the word—because that is how it was written. Haven’t we all been taught on the Adorno Platz of our collective mind—that place where cultural studies has turned the soul into an object of sociology—that this is what art is?
Kristian Vistrup Madsen is a writer and curator based in Stockholm.

“No art ever died for Kluge”: remembering a maverick who worked in every medium
Alexander
Kluge would cup his hands to form a radio
delighting the children, if frightening them a little
He coated the Spree with a thin film of silver
long before this was standard practice
for capturing moonlight
A giant of sleep, Kluge invented the swan
Friend to the drowned, he always made time
to address their parliaments
The night the donors emerged from the woods
demanding individual faces
Kluge braided his voice into a hundred small channels
averting violence just long enough for angels
to escape by train, wings carefully folded
Because mercury had no effect on him
Kluge restored weak negatives in his summerhouse
He would stand in the vapor and bring images up
out of the dark, like this one where leaves
impossibly detailed, change color and fall
if you angle it, Kluge called this “obstinancy”
A portmanteau of the space between
Es and regnet, where the subject is ambient
He’d draw a dry brush across the finished page
to blur it a little, though later this fell to assistants
like me: I’d set up a pair of microphones
among the empty books and canisters
and wait, often for centuries
HAL FOSTER: OBSTINATE ANGEL
IN 1995 ALEXANDER KLUGE moved out of his Munich studio. Kluge, who died last March at the age of ninety-four, came to miss it—it was where he had done most of his television interviews in the 1980s and early ’90s––so he asked his friend Thomas Demand to “bring the memory of that place back to him.”1 No photo of the humble room, which used to be a kitchen, existed, so Demand based his model on video from the interviews, and we see the extraordinary image that resulted here. A tiled floor leads down a narrow space toward tall windows that illuminate the room dimly. A simple table is covered in a green cloth and fitted with a plastic chair for an interviewer opposite two wooden chairs, one for an interviewee, one for a translator. On the table are two microphones, a glass, and a few books and folders. More books appear on the metal shelves that border the studio, along with stacks of film canisters, rows of notebooks, and boxes of outmoded media like Betamax cassettes. Outside in the wintry brightness stands a lone tree severely pruned.
Demand likens the photo to early modern paintings of Jerome that depict the saint at work on his Latin translation of the Bible, alone in his cell but accompanied by manuscripts. The Kluge studio was also a place of study and a site of transcription. A writer, philosopher, and lawyer, as well as an artist, filmmaker, and television producer, the great German polymath worked in many media and collaborated with countless people; though he is absent in the photo and now everywhere, he transmits still. “Kluge did not seem to exist in time—or he seemed to exist in several times at once,” Ben Lerner wrote in a recent elegy. “I don’t just mean that his staggering productivity in so many media would seem to require many lifetimes; I mean that he felt like a time traveler, like someone from the past and future simultaneously.”2 “If I had my way,” Kluge once remarked to Lerner, “I would move between speech, text, moving images, music, still—the work would always change, switch between them.”3
The Demand photo is a wonderful distillation of this time traveler and medium switcher. The Lerner poem is another brilliant constellation, to use a Benjaminian term that Kluge made his own and shared with others.4 Lerner was also a young friend to Kluge; his first book of poetry, The Lichtenberg Figures (2004), inspired the older man to write some of his sui generis prose pieces, which in turn inspired additional poems from Lerner. In part Lerner based Thomas, the mentor in his recent novel Transcription (2026), on Kluge, who thus continues to transmit through this channel as well. At the risk of heavy-handedness, I want to elaborate on a few ideas that his poem “Alexander” offers us.
Kluge would cup his hands to form a radio. In his universe almost anything could be a medium: cupped hands, the River Spree, weak negatives, a dry brush. And no art ever died for Kluge. “Cinema,” he wrote in Cinema Stories (2007), is “immortal and older than the arts of film.”5 Kluge cherished “the primitive diversity” of early cinema in particular, which assumed many popular forms before it became a standardized arm of the culture industry. “I am a good archaeologist,” Kluge liked to say; he meant media archaeologist too.6 He sought primitive diversity in his own practice.
A giant of sleep, Kluge invented the swan. The first phrase suggests the world of fable which is also that of his writing. The second phrase summons the tale of Lohengrin, the swan knight of the Holy Grail who was a guardian of the distressed. Certainly Kluge was a friend to the drowned, who always made time / to address their parliaments. Early on, in Public Sphere and Experience: Toward an Analysis of the Bourgeois and Proletarian Public Spheres (1972), Kluge explored, with his coauthor Oskar Negt, the social spaces that subaltern folk had managed to carve out of the bourgeois world. He also pursued this agenda in his fictions and films. As Lerner commented to Kluge, “I feel you are investigating what escapes official history—what’s beneath the level of perception or above it—too micro or macro.”7
Kluge braided his voice into a hundred small channels / averting violence just long enough for angels / to escape by train, wings carefully folded. Kluge welcomed the idea of angels; “just because they very rarely come into laboratories” didn’t mean “we cannot know anything” about them.8 In his braiding of media he aimed to open a portal through which they might enter and exit our world, an opening that Kluge also called “the devil’s blind spot.”9 For Kluge this spot appears when the devil naps; it leaves a door open, if not to the Messiah (as Benjamin wished), at least to the possibility of change. “Are these poorly organized angels,” Lerner asked Kluge, “a reason to hope—they are, after all, angels—or a reason to despair—they don’t get much done?”10 Kluge let the question hang, but certainly his angels are avatars neither of ruin, as in Benjamin, nor of terror, as in Rilke. Closer to the Klee versions, his unusual aides help us survive our everyday lives that are often dominated by “administration”—as Kluge, borrowing from his mentor Adorno, termed the postwar form of bureaucratic capitalism. As Lerner pointed out, his “prose can also be quite cold—it can mimic . . . the language of bureaucracy, of standardization.”11 Kluge worked against the administered world from within its idiolect as well.
Kluge restored weak negatives in his summerhouse / He would stand in the vapor and bring images up / out of the dark . . . / . . . Kluge called this “obstinancy” / A portmanteau of the space between / Es and regnet, where the subject is ambient. This summerhouse might be the counterpart of the dim studio reconstructed by Demand, a bright space where Kluge brought pictures of the past to light and held them in a portmanteau with other montaged images and texts. His practice was indeed one of “obstinacy” in the sense he developed with Negt, another friend of the drowned, in History and Obstinacy (2008). In his essential introduction to the English translation of this volume, Devin Fore glosses obstinacy as follows: “The word Eigensinn—rendered variously into English as ‘autonomy,’ ‘willfulness,’ ‘self-will,’ and, here, ‘obstinacy’—implies a degree of stubborn obtuseness, an imperviousness to directives from above. Hegel, for example, describes Eigensinn as ‘a freedom’ that is ‘enmeshed in servitude.’ Kluge, in contrast, describes Eigensinn as ‘the guerrilla warfare [Partisanentum] of the mind.’ Obstinacy is the underside of history.”12 In his poem Lerner suggests that this underside is all around us, as plain as rain (Es regnet means “it is raining”), but only if we seize it. Only then, only if we are obstinate in our own ways, can it provide the space where the subject is ambient, where we can persist and resist.
KLUGE, DEMAND, AND LERNER form a constellation of their own. All three view art as a heterochronic enterprise, in the belief that, as Kluge puts it in The Devil’s Blind Spot, “nothing is more instructive than a confusion of time frames.”13 All three combine fiction and nonfiction, treating this conventional distinction as null and void, not in order to confuse the fictive and the real (once a critical device, this confusion has become the bane of our lives) but to produce “real fictions”—to use the fictive to make the real, after a long period of capitalist derealization, feel real again.14 In this shared initiative they are not opposed to new media; Kluge was an early adopter of new technologies, including, at the end of his life, AI. Rather, they are concerned, as Lerner recently phrased it, to capture the “little pockets of possibility in media configurations that are difficult to foresee.”15 This can mean different things. At times they almost locate the human in technological failure, as though our most human quality today were the media glitch, the noise in our cybernetic world. At other times they treat the human as a medium in its own right (for example, the narrator in Transcription stores messages like a “human phone medium”) in a manner that returns the word to its old meaning of communication with the dead.16
In all these ways this trio points toward a posthumanist humanism, which in my view is an important project for the culture at large. At its center is an old concern of the Frankfurt School, of which Kluge was perhaps the last associate. In The Theory of the Novel (1916), Georg Lukács proposed the concept of “second nature,” which was then developed by Adorno and Benjamin. Not only had “man-made structures” overlaid the first order of nature, Lukács argued, but in doing so they constituted “a complex of senses—meanings—which have become rigid and strange, and which no longer awakens interiority.” For the young Lukács a bewitched humanity could only be “brought to life” by a great “metaphysical act of reawakening.”17 Almost a century later, in a conversation with Demand, Kluge drew on this idea. “Your images unfold,” he commented to the photographer, in a second nature where all “human abilities appear outside us and confront us” as alien.18 Rather than wait for an unlikely metaphysical reawakening, Kluge suggested, Demand probes this second nature, stirring the “residues of dead labor” and “human abilities” estranged there. So, in their different ways, do Kluge and Lerner.
Kluge and Demand also speculated about a “third nature,” by which they meant a world driven by systems and networks that now operate largely beyond human control. “If the public sphere, the arts, the relationship to people no longer grows with the complexity of society as a whole,” Kluge warned, “then third nature arises.” Yet it is not too late to intervene: “The core of your entire oeuvre,” he insisted to Demand, is “the way people oscillate between first, second, and third nature.” That switching—this opening––is also performed in the work of Kluge and Lerner; they show us how to go about it with wondrous effects. Again, not opposed to media, they develop their own mediations to poke at the petrifications of second and third nature. The sheer barrenness of the sculpted tree in the Demand photo suggests the difficulty of this project, but then no one said it would be easy.
A constellation is also a matter of influence, an original meaning of which is the flow of light from the stars. A constellation, that is, is also about “intergenerational artistic transmission.”19 One can imagine Demand and Lerner in the chairs opposite Kluge in his studio. He left behind work for them—for all of us––to do . . . later this fell to assistants / like me: I’d set up a pair of microphones / among the empty books and canisters / and wait, often for centuries.
Hal Foster’s Fail Better: Reckonings with Artists and Critics was published in 2025 by MIT Press.
