Earlier on Sunday, the Iranian army's spokesperson, Mohammad Akraminia, stressed that Iran’s war strategy has shifted from a “purely defensive stance to an offensive approach some time ago".
“Should a new war erupt, the geography of the conflict will not be confined to the West Asia region,” Akraminia told Iran state media. “Any potential future war could prove significantly longer than past conflicts.”
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to "take care of" one or two targets.
"We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, said Trump has not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran, and that the US would be open to a diplomatic solution.
The United Arab Emirates, meanwhile, said it hoped for a breakthrough between Iran and the US while preparing for the worst.
"We're hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough," diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president Anwar Gargash said during a conference in Manama.
"It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we're also, as we've shown before, braced for the worst."
Following a visit to Tehran this week by a Qatari delegation, Iran has dispatched envoys to the Gulf country to continue consultations as part of indirect negotiations with the US to end the war.
Earlier this week, US Senator Chris Murphy described Trump's plan to restart the war on Iran as "insane" and said it would lead to a "devastating escalation".
"You've heard a preview that it would be a short-duration plan. I'll just say this: their plan is insane," Murphy said, speaking at an event organised by the Middle East Institute in Washington, DC.
"It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law."
Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations and Appropriations committees, made the comments after American media reported that the US warned several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military offensive against Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The war began on 28 February with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Iran retaliated by targeting, among others, Gulf countries hosting US military bases.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Dining across the divide: ‘My family are all Trumpian, so I’ve had a lot of practice talking to people who are far right’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Erica Buist
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Sam, 29, central London
Occupation Compliance officer
 
Voting record Sam is American so can’t vote in the UK yet, but when she can she intends to vote Green
 
Amuse bouche She is an expert knitter. She started when she was five and makes socks, mittens, hat, jumpers – if you know Sam, she’s knitting you something
Roger, 80, north-west London
Occupation Retired accountant
 
Voting record Never Labour or Tory. He’s always voted for “outliers” such as the Greens, and now Reform
 
Amuse bouche In 1978, he was an internal auditor and was sent to Angola during the civil wargoing on. He bribed soldiers with cigarettes to let him get to the frontline because he “wanted to hear the guns”
For starters
Roger I got there early and had a pint of beer, and when Sam arrived we got on famously right from the start. We were both surprised at how much we had in common.
 
Sam I wasn’t very nervous – my family are all Trumpian, so I’ve had a lot of practice talking to people who are far right.
 
Roger I started with a beautiful dressed crab with two slices of soda bread and a chunk of butter. For main I had fish and chips, and we were too full for dessert.
 
Sam I really enjoyed the dressed crab, then I had a wild mushroom risotto with broccoli stems, and a Coke.
The big beef
Roger  I don’t like net zero – I think it’s all happening too quickly. We’re doing all of this electrification too early. I think we should use the resources we’ve got: continue to extract more oil and gas from the North Sea until it’s all gone, and then you can have your electric cars.
Sam I think the climate crisis is a big problem, and the number one priority to reduce the effects would be to stop producing CO2. It’s been proved that a decrease in beef production and an increase in plant consumption would really help.
 
Roger The way to fix the climate crisis is to control the population. I think the UK is dangerously overdependent on imports of people, as well as food, energy and other things. We should encourage local production, expand our fishing fleet and exploit North Sea fossil fuels until they’re exhausted.
 
Sam I pointed out that his desire to drill for more oil contradicts his opinion on self-sufficiency in food production because the more CO2 that is emitted into the atmosphere, the higher the temperature gets and the less water there is available for agriculture.
Sharing plate
Roger I am a xenophobe and proud of it. Nothing to apologise for, as it’s a natural human trait of risk awareness. I believe many of the terrorist outrages in the UK in the past 25 years have been perpetrated by foreigners, and a few by the offspring of foreigners.
 
Sam He talked a lot about banning Muslims. I grew up in a very white, Christian, Republican area of Colorado and I heard a lot of fear-based rhetoric. I had absolutely never met a Muslim person until I moved to Glasgow, and realised none of it was true. It seems like Roger’s operating from a place of fear.
For afters
Roger I think Nigel Farage accepting a £5m donation was OK, but failing to declare it is troubling. There was nothing to lose by declaring it.
 
Sam In the US there used to be a limit on how much a person could donate to a political campaign, and now there is absolutely no limit. I just feel that’s wrong. I don’t think one person should be able to have that much sway and that much buying power over an election. And that principle is the basis of my aversion to that, apart from the fact that it broke the rules.
Takeaways
Roger I think she’s a thoroughly charming, intelligent person. And she’s an immigrant, but I think it’s human to look for sameness before differences first, so the discussion was very amicable. I liked the fact that we could agree on so much, especially green stuff – apart from North Sea oil.
 
Sam The majority of Reform voters I’ve met are not particularly sophisticated or educated people, and I guess it’s bad of me to stereotype them like that, because he was an accountant and refined and well-spoken. We arranged to keep in contact.
Additional reporting: Kitty Drake
Roger and Sam ate at the Bull & Last, London NW5.

https://www.mediapart.fr/journal/culture.title: «L’esprit critique» expositions: de la biennale de Lyon à Vancouver
https://www.mediapart.fr/journal/culture.author: Joseph Confavreux
https://www.mediapart.fr/journal/culture.text:
« Passer d’un rêve à l’autre » en empruntant les traboules de Lyon et en se rendant d’un ancien atelier SNCF à un Musée des tissus aujourd’hui désaffecté, puis découvrir le travail, saisissant de précision, d’un des plus grands plasticiens canadiens.
« L’esprit critique » de ce jour se rend d’abord, en prenant le temps, à la biennale d’art contemporain de Lyon, dont la commissaire est cette fois l’Australienne Catherine Nichols, puis au Jeu de paume, qui consacre une exposition au travail de Stan Douglas, situé entre document et fiction, entre cinéma et photographie.
Biennale d’art contemporain de Lyon
La dix-huitième biennale d’art contemporain de Lyon, dont la première édition date de 1991, a ouvert le 19 septembre dernier et vous pourrez en visiter les différents lieux jusqu’à la mi-décembre si vous passez par l’ancienne capitale des Gaules.
Elle se déploie à la fois sur le site des « Grandes Locos », installé dans un ancien atelier SNCF, sur celui du musée d’Art contemporain mais aussi dans l’ancien Musée des tissus, ainsi que dans quelques points de l’agglomération lyonnaise, en particulier l’Institut d’art contemporain de Villeurbanne.
Avec ses 120 artistes de 42 nationalités différentes exposé·es et ses milliers de visiteurs et visiteuses, la biennale de Lyon s’est imposée comme une des principales à se tenir dans le monde, même si l’on pourra s’interroger, dans la discussion, sur les possibles limites de ce modèle des biennales d’art contemporain, qui se sont multipliées depuis deux décennies.
Le titre de cette biennale est « Passer d’un rêve à l’autre », le thème structurant en est l’économie, la commissaire est l’Australienne Catherine Nichols et la directrice artistique, Isabelle Bertolotti.
« Parallax. Stan Douglas »
« Parallax » est le nom donné à l’importante rétrospective que le musée du Jeu de paume, à Paris, consacre au plasticien, photographe et cinéaste canadien Stan Douglas.
Un titre qui désigne le déplacement apparent d’un objet selon la position du spectateur et qui, métaphoriquement, fait de ce phénomène optique le rappel que les récits et les perceptions ne sont jamais stabilisés ni achevés.
Cette idée est au cœur du travail de Stan Douglas, né en 1960 à Vancouver, où il continue de vivre et de travailler. Stan Douglas élabore des dispositifs complexes pour piéger les récits dominants, donner place aux histoires mineures et mettre en crise les processus à travers lesquels nous produisons et regardons les images.
À travers une trentaine d’œuvres permettant à la fois de saisir l’ampleur du travail de Stan Douglas et de ne pas surcharger et saturer une exposition fondée sur des œuvres dont la densité visuelle et réflexive exige du temps, le Jeu de paume propose un parcours à la fois intelligent et lisible dans une œuvre dont la complexité et l’abstraction ne versent jamais dans l’exercice de style, alors qu’il s’agit de créer des « images impossibles » dans lesquelles la technicité vient troubler la réalité.
Le commissariat de cette exposition est signé Gloria Moure et Marta Ponsa.
Avec :
- Guslagie Malanda, actrice et curatrice d’exposition indépendante ;
- Margot Nguyen, travailleuse de l’art indépendante ;
- Magali Lesauvage, journaliste indépendante.
« L’esprit critique » est un podcast enregistré et réalisé par les équipes de Gong, cette semaine par Corentin Dubois.

Otis College of Art and Design in LA Offers a Two-Year MFA Fine Arts Degree Program
Refine your artistic vision and join a diverse community at the first professional school of the arts in Los Angeles.
In the MFA Fine Arts program at Otis College of Art and Design, we believe artists thrive when they can explore a wide range of approaches in artmaking and all its related disciplines.
Our program provides an artistic learning environment where artists of different backgrounds and creative practices can flourish together. Our courses, studios, labs, and galleries are welcoming places where everyone in our community can develop as artists and as engaged participants in society.
MFA students have 24/7 access to individual working studios. They are also guaranteed at least one semester of a Graduate Teaching Internship or Graduate Assistantship. Students receive access to painting, sculpture, and lighting studios; state-of-the-art wood and metal shops; photography, video, film, printmaking, and ceramics labs. A mid-residency show, annual open studios, and a final thesis show offer ample opportunities for exhibition over the course of the two-year program.
Distinguished alumni include Carlos Almaraz, Alonzo Davis, Roberto Gil de Montes, Judithe Hernandez, Vita Kari, Alison Saar, Masami Teraoka, and Kent Twitchell.
The Einstein Visiting Artist Lecture Series at Otis College brings distinguished artists, designers, and creative thought leaders to campus to engage with students and the public. Past guests have included Doug Aitken, Kelly Akashi, Dawoud Bey, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, Theaster Gates, Trenton Doyle Hancock, Edgar Heap of Birds, Shirin Neshat, Hank Willis Thomas, Jeffrey Vallance, Kara Walker, Zoe Whitley, and Anicka Yi, among others.
Priority deadline for fall entry is January 15 and October 1 for spring. After these deadlines, applications will be accepted on a rolling basis as space remains available.
To apply, visit otis.edu

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: « Amilcar Cabral, pour un humanisme radical » : la Maison des mondes africains fait dialoguer la pensée du militant décolonial avec notre époque
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Clément Garcia
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
La Maison des mondes africains (MansA) célèbre la mémoire du dirigeant marxiste guinéen et cap-verdien Amilcar Cabral en convoquant le regard d’artistes contemporains. Et projette sur notre époque les combats précurseurs de cet intellectuel et militant encore trop méconnu.
« La lutte de libération est un acte de culture », écrivait le père de l’indépendance du Cap-Vert et de la Guinée-Bissau assassiné en 1973, deux ans avant l’émancipation du joug colonial portugais, par de faux frères d’armes alliés à la police politique de l’Estado Novo.
Pour Amilcar Cabral, la révolution n’était qu’un commencement, le chantier d’un pays à bâtir, d’une culture à affranchir. Il n’aura entrevu que les prémices du « programme majeur » qu’il comptait mettre sur pied dans les deux pays frères séparés par un bras d’Atlantique. À savoir l’unité binationale, la souveraineté économique et la décolonisation des esprits.
« Il y aurait un parallèle à faire avec Frantz Fanon », soutient Ângela Benoliel Coutinho, cocommissaire de l’exposition « Amilcar Cabral, pour un humanisme radical », accueillie à Paris par la Maison des mondes africains (MansA). « L’un comme l’autre ont insisté sur la nécessité de mener la révolution avec les populations, au plus près d’elles et de leurs besoins », poursuit-elle.

Thousands rally in New Delhi to demand India’s election chief resign
Hundreds of police, some carrying batons and shields, are deployed around the rally site.
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets in India’s capital, New Delhi, to demand the resignation of the election chief over changes to voter lists that opposition parties say favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
Indian National Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi led Sunday’s demonstration, the latest in more than a month of protests challenging the revision of electoral rolls and the conduct of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Opposition parties alleged the exercise, which removed more than 130 million names from voter lists, disproportionately affected Muslims and other minorities considered unlikely to support Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said voters whose names were wrongly removed may register again.
The BJP has accused opposition parties of undermining democracy by challenging legitimate electoral procedures. India’s next general election is due in 2029.
Officials ramped up security measures and announced traffic diversions before demonstrators marched from central New Delhi towards the historic Ramlila Maidan ground.
Hundreds of police, some carrying batons and shields, were deployed around the rally site alongside riot-control vehicles. Demonstrators waved Indian and party flags as opposition leaders travelled in an open-top jeep.
Health Minister Jagat Prakash Nadda dismissed the demonstration as a “carefully orchestrated drama”.
“What is unfolding today at Ramlila Maidan is not an act of respect for democracy,” he told the ANI news agency. “It is a calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy, all in the name of democracy.”
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party have staged near-daily demonstrations since late September, calling for Kumar to step down.
The protests began after Kumar’s two deputies raised concerns about revisions to voter lists, registration procedures and digital systems.
Analysts described the demonstrations and growing support for the opposition as Modi’s most serious political crisis since he took office in 2014.

Mitlaufen beim Hamburger Halbmarathon: Am Schluss lockt das Franzbrötchen
Dass gemeinsam Laufen gerade sehr beliebt ist, war jetzt beim Hamburger Halbmarathon zu zählen. So viele wollten dabei sein wie noch nie zuvor.
K eine Ahnung, wieso der Typ mit einer Körperhaltung wie ein Flitzebogen schon wieder vor mir herläuft. Sein Bauchnabel schöbe sich vor seinem restlichen Körper über die Ziellinie, die ist aber noch fast 15 Kilometer entfernt, als ich ihn zum dritten Mal überhole, mindestens. Na gut, trabe ich also erneut an ihm vorbei und noch mal und noch mal und denke irgendwann an Hase und Igel und dann geht es leicht bergab, die Elbe kommt in den Blick, wir lassen den Hamburger Fischmarkt rechts liegen und rennen Richtung Landungsbrücken, Speicherstadt, Hauptbahnhof, um die Alster und zum Fernsehturm über einen blauen Teppich ins Ziel.
Ein Halbmarathon. Ich laufe die 21,1 Kilometer an diesem Sonntag eine Stunde und 8 Minuten langsamer als die Siegerin Selly Simatinyang aus Kenia. Und zwei Minuten schneller als mein Neffe. Der war am Start an mir vorbeigelaufen und in der auf und ab wippenden Menge verschwunden.
Als mein Neffe, meine Freundin aus meiner allerersten WG und ich gegen 10.45 Uhr starten, sind bereits gut 12.000 Läuferinnen und Läufer auf der Strecke, lässt uns der Anheizer wissen und ruft „viel Spaß!“ und so ins Mikro. Beim Frühstück hatten wir erst über Fluch und Segen von KI diskutiert und dann über die Kleiderwahl: Langarmshirt? Windbraker? Regenjacke? Wintermantel? Regenschirm? Doch bloß ein T-Shirt?
Zusammen durch die Stadt laufen kann man auch in Hamburg immer häufiger. Demnächst zum Beispiel im Klövensteen, einem Waldgebiet, in dem neulich ein Wolf gesichtet wurde. Run to tree heißt der Lauf, bedeutet: Erst rennen und dann einen Weihnachtsbaum kaufen. Und im nächsten Sommer findet in Hamburg der Halbmarathon ausschließlich für Frauen statt.
ChatGPT hatte kurze Hose und ärmelloses T-Shirt vorgeschlagen, so eine KI weiß eben nicht, wie kalt kalter Wind ist. Und wir hatten uns gefragt, ob wir doch zusammen loslaufen können. Eigentlich gibt es Startblöcke, A bis G, nach Uhrzeiten gestaffelt, je nachdem wie schnell man so zu sein gedenkt. Als wir dann nach einem kurzen Fußmarsch quer über das Heiligengeistfeld am Millerntorstadion vorbei auf der Reeperbahn ankommen, verschwimmen wir sofort in der Menge, die sich anfühlt wie der Beginn einer Demo, und lassen uns einfach mitziehen.
Angemeldet hatten sich knapp 20.800 Leute, ein neuer Rekord für die 32. Ausgabe dieses Rennens, und damit war es der zweitgrößte reine Halbmarathon Deutschlands, wie der Veranstalter später mitteilt. Irgendeinen Superlativ braucht es halt immer. Die Anmeldezahlen machen aber auf jeden Fall deutlich, dass gemeinsam Laufen gerade sehr beliebt ist. Viele Laufevents melden Rekordanmeldezahlen. An diesem Sonntag in Hamburg sind schließlich 15.534 Leute wirklich gestartet.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Pappschilder zum Anfeuern
Eigentlich hätte das Rennen bereits Ende Juni stattfinden sollen. Wegen drohender Rekordhitze war es abgesagt worden. Viele Leute an der Strecke hatten ihre Anfeuer-Pappschilder eindeutig bereits im Sommer gemalt, so oft wie Wortspiele mit „heiß“, „hot“, „hotties“ oder so draufstanden.
Kurz vor dem Wiederholungstermin hatte der Deutsche Wetterdienst wieder gewarnt, nun vor Regen und Sturmböen. Hatte ich mir Juni noch schnell ein Cap gegen die Sonne gekauft, war ich nun losgerannt, um mir eine Regenjacke zu besorgen, weil mein Kollege mich fragte: „Du wohnst in Hamburg und hast keine Regenjacke?“ Ich laufe doch nicht im Regen, hatte ich geantwortet. Die Regenjacke liegt nun mit dem Cap unbenutzt im Schrank, Sonntagvormittag schien die Sonne.
An der letzten Getränkestation etwa zwei Kilometer vor dem Ziel sehe ich meinen Neffen wieder, ich stupse ihn von hinten an, als ich an ihm vorbeirenne, er blickt mich überrascht über den Rand seines Pappbechers an, zieht noch ein letztes Mal an mir vorbei, hat aber am Ende das Nachsehen.
Wir treffen uns alle in der riesigen Messehalle mit einer Medaille um den Hals am Franzbrötchenstand wieder. Schweißgeruch hängt in der Luft, Leute liegen dehnend auf dem Boden, ein Läufer fragt uns, wo denn der Bierstand sei. „Du hast blaue Lippen, geh mal schnell heim“, sagt mein Freund, den ich bei den Franzbrötchen treffe, und während die Letzten über die Ziellinie tröpfeln, ziehen wir von dannen. Ich gebe meinem Neffen noch eine Paprika fürs Abendessen mit, und meine Freundin schreibt später: „Meine Beine sind Zaunpfosten.“ Das wird nicht das letzte Mal gewesen sein.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/si.title: Sisi's 2030 exit plan would keep Egypt in the army's hands
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/si.author: Hesham Gaafar
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/si.text:
Sisi's 2030 exit plan would keep Egypt in the army's hands
At the Egyptian Military Academy's first graduation ceremony on 17 October, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi said what many Egyptians had stopped expecting to hear. He declared that 2030 will mark the end of his presidency, "if I live", and that the matter is "completely settled".
Most coverage stopped there, but the consequential part of the speech came next, when Sisi proposed a 30-month programme of more than 7,500 hours at the academy for doctorate holders aged between 40 and 50, from whom Egyptians would later choose their presidents, ministers and governors.
The armed forces would pay "whatever it costs", and a committee including the speaker of parliament and the ministers of higher education and justice would draft a law setting out the selection criteria.
Together, the two halves of the speech describe a president deciding where power will reside after him, rather than returning it to Egyptians. The answer is the military.
Every personalised regime faces the same dilemma, since naming a successor creates a rival while naming no one leaves the elite to fight over the vacuum. Sisi is trying to sidestep both. The 2019 amendments allow him to appoint a vice president, the route Sadat and Mubarak used to reach power, yet he has never used it.

Instead, he is institutionalising the gate rather than the heir, so that whoever governs next would have to pass through an institution owned and financed by the army.
The academy has been moving towards this role for years, running mandatory courses for newly appointed imams, teachers, judges and diplomats. In September, Sisi called it "a gateway to employment in the Egyptian state".
The new proposal climbs the final rung, from training those who are appointed to training those who rule. The defence minister appointed in February, Ashraf Salem Zaher, ran the academy until the day he took office.
The army's veto
The second element, the veto, is already written into the constitution. Sisi read aloud Article 200, which charges the armed forces with safeguarding "the constitution and democracy" and "the civilian nature of the state", saying he had insisted on it in 2014. In fact, that wording came with the 2019 amendments that extended his own rule.
He then promised that no "malicious person, traitor or criminal" would take charge "according to the text I have just read", and added that "what I don't say is more than what I say".
Whoever governs next would have to pass through an institution owned and financed by the army
The result is a soft filter that manufactures a preferred elite and a hard veto that lets the army decide who counts as a threat. "We will not prevent anyone," Sisi said, and the door is formally open, but guarded.
None of this requires touching the constitution, because Article 141 leaves "other conditions" for presidential candidates to be defined by law.
Ordinary legislation can require a doctorate, a set age range and an academy certificate, so the promise that the constitution "will not be touched" can be honoured to the letter while the rules of access to power change entirely.
With 30 of the remaining 43 months needed for training, the law must pass in 2027, the very year rumours had assigned to an amendment extending his rule.
The trigger lies inside the regime rather than on the street. In November 2025, parliamentary elections meant to be a formality became an open contest among the state's own agencies.
According to Hossam el-Hamalawy, citing Mada Masr reporting, the interior ministry's security apparatus, which backed the Nation's Future Party, clashed with General Intelligence and Military Intelligence, which backed rival loyalist parties.
Sisi intervened publicly, and the election authority annulled the results in 19 districts, with the courts later voiding many more.
Why now, and what for
On 29 September, in a meeting with the cabinet, governors and the heads of the army and police, Sisi spoke of attempts to set "the interior ministry against the judiciary, the army against someone else, the agencies against each other", and urged officials to stop hiding their opinions.
Two weeks later he declared the constitution untouchable, and three days after that he announced 2030.
The lesson of 2025 is that the unity of Egypt's security apparatus rests on a single arbiter rather than on its structure. Once he announces his departure, every agency starts positioning itself. The academy proposal tries to hand that arbitration to the army before he leaves, though it may provoke the very rivalry it seeks to contain.
Other pressures raised the cost of leaving succession open, including a campaign urging Sisi to rule until 2050 that revived talk of a presidency for life.
The IMF programme ends in December, while Egypt's financing needs are expected to stay high until close to 2030. A Saudi deposit worth more than $5bn fell due in October, and the war in Yemen has flared again, threatening Red Sea shipping.
In the same speech, Sisi pledged to defend Saudi Arabia "in accordance with the directives" of its rulers. For Gulf patrons and creditors, the message was that an army is available now and that Egypt will be predictable after 2030.
The deeper significance lies in what the proposal allows politics to be. For Sisi, the qualification to rule is knowing "what a state means", and no one who merely "says two well-arranged words" should imagine he can lead Egypt. In this view, politics is technical knowledge of the state, which only the state can certify.
The design leaves no role for parties, unions or social movements in producing leaders. In effect, the academy replaces parliament as the school of rulers, and legitimacy shifts from consent to competence certified by an institution issuing a diploma, rather than by voters judging performance.
A doctorate from a "reputable" university and 30 months of full-time training also form a class filter few dissidents, workers or provincial politicians could pass.
More than one way
One proposed exemption deserves particular attention. Sisi would exempt anyone with six years or more in government ministries, saying such experience qualifies them for "the responsibility of a state".
Since the programme cannot produce graduates before 2029, realistic candidates for 2030 are likely to come from this exempt pool of technocrats who owe Sisi their careers. The clause covers ministries but says nothing about the security agencies.
Such a successor would be weak by design, which may suit the military but also leaves room for the outgoing president.
The 2019 amendments bar more than two consecutive terms, not two in total; the transitional article granting Sisi his extra term is open to interpretation by a constitutional court whose president he selects; and if a successor resigns, elections follow within 90 days. None of this proves intent, but the pledge can be fulfilled in more than one way.
Sisi's record counsels caution, since he denied he would run in 2013 and then ran, and backed two four-year terms in 2017 before the 2019 amendments extended his rule. This pledge, though, is more specific than any before it, tied to a date, a committee, a budget and a timetable.
Parliamentary sources close to one of the security agencies told Mada Masr he does not want to repeat Mubarak's mistake of clinging to office. Reversing course would be costly, with a military now given a stake in the rules rather than the man.
The real test comes in 2027, not 2030, and it turns on who sits on the selection committee, whether the programme becomes a condition for candidacy, whether the exemption is widened to the security agencies and whether a vice president is finally appointed.
Egypt's presidents have seldom left office by choice. Sisi may choose to leave, but on terms that entrench, rather than end, the army's political role and replace representation with administration. The question for Egyptians is less whether he leaves in 2030 than whether anything he leaves behind will allow them to choose.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US elections | Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Chances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.
After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.
I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.
Now, it feels like anything can and will happen this week – from delayed results and slow counts to Donald Trump sending in the DC Comics Suicide Squad to your local polling place. That’s all we need, John Cena checking your ID before you vote.
It’s enough to make you crawl up into a ball and beg for mommy. But fear is a passive emotion, one that leaves a person paralyzed and incapable of action.
My preference is for the fully formed anger of the middle-aged curmudgeon. A shaken fist and a choice expletive is healthier than babbling for hours in your panic room. So, in lieu of a voter guide telling you how to fill out your ballot, here’s a list of all the most irritating, confounding and downright stupid things to scream about on Tuesday.
The Cheesecake Factory discourse
During a recent campaign stop, the former president Barack Obama compared the aesthetics of the recent Trump-led White House renovations with a Cheesecake Factory. Not only am I annoyed that this is even a talking point during a crucial campaign, I also resent the comparison being made. I’d rather eat at a Cheesecake Factory than the White House, any day of the week. I have to assume Bill Maher agrees with me.
The continued importance of Spencer Pratt
Here in California, the race everyone is talking about is a contest for Los Angeles mayor, a famous stepping stone to jobs as prestigious as “Ambassador to Country Chosen by Random Lottery Draw” or “Special Adviser to Herbalife”. It’s neck-and-neck between incumbent Karen Bass and the city councilperson Nithya Raman. The unfortunate twist in this daytime soap opera is that the reality show star they combined to defeat in the first round of voting this summer, Spencer Pratt, is still popular enough that his supporters could tip the scales toward one candidate or the other. The only thing I can think of that’s worse than Spencer Pratt as mayor of LA is Spencer Pratt deciding the next mayor of LA.
The curious case of the two Dan Sullivans
According to the New York Times, some Democrats figured out that the best way to unseat the senator Dan Sullivan was to force him to run against himself. Retired teacher Dan Sullivan was allegedly recruited to run for US Senate by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola, in the hopes of unseating … Dan Sullivan. (The Peltola campaign has denied any involvement in his candidacy.)
The Sullivan v Sullivan smackdown has the Republican party so worried that the justice department is suing to invalidate the results of the election if Sullivan (the senator) narrowly loses to Sullivan (the not-senator) or Peltola (the not-Sullivan).
I’m no fan of Dan Sullivan, but I’m not sure how I feel about Dan Sullivan either! This is the kind of goofy dirty trick that makes people hate politics. Who are you really fooling here? Old people? People who are too busy to read the fine print about which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent Alaskan senator? People with an acute case of Sullivantitis (a crippling disease that causes blindness to the name “Dan Sullivan”)? Can’t this country ever be normal?
Please don’t message me. I realize the answer is no. I just hope this election is more entertaining than The Undertaker v The Undertaker at WWF SummerSlam 1994. Unlike that match, this face-off of doppelgangers won’t involve Leslie Nielsen.
The continued push to close polling places
In an attempt to depress turnout amongst Democratic-leaning voters, red state election boards in states such as North Carolina are shutting polling places in blue areas. In North Carolina in particular, voting sites were shut on numerous college campuses, but that didn’t stop a group of predominantly students from organizing marches in excess of two hours so that they could maintain the franchise.
When I was a young man, the main tool crooked politicians had to keep people from voting was good, old-fashioned apathy. We should have changed the motto on the quarter from “E pluribus unum” to “They’re all bums, anyway.” In 2026, politicians have infuriated people to such a degree that they’ll walk miles just to vote.
It’s inspiring to see young people exercising their rights in the face of an actively hostile state government, but I find the notion of our nation’s leaders blatantly making it more onerous for citizens to vote absolutely abhorrent. I mean, the peer pressure is bad enough.
‘I voted’ stickers and selfies
I get why the stickers exist. An elaborate campaign of shame and embarrassment for those that didn’t bother to vote. I can’t think of two more powerful forces in my life than shame and embarrassment. They’re really the only two reasons I get out of bed these days, but I don’t have to like it.
Like a lollipop at the end of a haircut, the “I voted” sticker is the little treat at the end of a long period of interminable waiting. The only difference is, I don’t need to take a picture with my root beer-flavored Dum Dum. And I hate to be cynical here, but anyone who hasn’t planned on or even considered voting will not be swayed by a sticker.
As much as I despise people shirking their responsibility to democracy, I hate internet trends even more. Instead of wearing an “I voted” sticker on Tuesday, just slap it on your laptop. That way, anyone in your general vicinity will have to stop and double-check that there isn’t an election that day.
Donald Trump’s Mr America beauty pageant
This is Donald Trump’s last campaign of his risible political career. He has been a cancerous influence on our discourse since 2011, breaking traditions, norms, rules, and some priceless artifacts along the way.
I’m sure he’s getting nostalgic for the rush of election fervor – the ups and downs, the thrill of victory and the agony of not admitting defeat. These are some of the last campaign rallies he’ll ever lead, some of the final moments of political combat he’ll engage in in his lifetime.
Most of us would get wistful, maybe a tad somber. These days will never come again. Instead, the president is pondering the strength and power that emanates from various Republican buttocks.
Nothing, and I mean nothing, makes me bang my head against a wall this election cycle than my social media feed being littered with clips of Donald Trump sexualizing his colleagues.
- Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we know
Trump says latest talks ‘going fine’; while Iranian leaders say they favour diplomacy but are ready for maximum response if the US resumes war.
Iranian officials have been speaking with Qatari mediators about a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in the latest effort to find a diplomatic path out of the US-Israel war on Iran that has caused a serious global energy crisis.
But even amid signs of diplomatic progress, officials from both sides say they are ready for renewed military escalation.
President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly suggested the United States could attack Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, said the latest negotiations were “going fine”, but added that the US still had several Iranian targets to “take care of”.
Meanwhile, Araghchi has also said Iran’s military was more prepared than ever for renewed war, while the country’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened Iran would use “new weaponry” in response to any future attack.
Here’s what we know about the latest diplomatic efforts and the sharp rhetoric from both sides, and what it could mean for what lies ahead:
What is the status of talks?
Araghchi said on Saturday that an Iranian delegation, including one of his aides, travelled to Doha to meet Qatari mediators. Earlier, Qatari officials also travelled to Tehran for consultations.
The latest discussions in Doha centred on a plan that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, within two days and restart peace talks with the US, provided Washington meets a set of demands from Tehran, Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
Those demands include the lifting of recently imposed US sanctions, the reinstatement of oil waivers granted in June, a reduction in the US military presence in the region, recognition of new shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz designated by Iran and Oman, and an end to the conflict on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon, said Araghchi.
Qatari and Pakistani mediators were “continuing consultations regarding our conditions”, said the top Iranian diplomat.
Pakistan has been mediating between the US and Iran, with its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, visiting Tehran several times as part of the diplomatic efforts to end the war. Doha and Islamabad played key roles in the signing of the June memorandum of understanding (MoU) that collapsed in August.
Iran’s Rezaei said the US had “indicated its readiness” to accept its conditions, although Washington has not confirmed this.
On the US side, Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Qatar-led talks were ongoing, but said he was not aware of a timeframe for them.
“There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped,” said Rubio. “If there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it.”
Why has Iran noted a change in the US’s ‘tone’?
The renewed diplomatic activity comes after US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter earlier this week to Rezaei, reportedly seeking to gauge the prospects of restarting negotiations and averting another round of military escalation.
Rezaei confirmed on Saturday that he had read the letter, whose tone he said had “completely changed” compared with earlier correspondence from Trump.
Araghchi also said he had studied Vance’s letter, which he described positively.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned, “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”
What has Iran said about prospects for peace and war?
Iranian officials have said they are open to new peace talks if the US meets their conditions, but also ready to act more aggressively in any new military confrontation.
“I know that our armed forces are more prepared for war than any time before, and we are ready for any scenario,” Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
In the event of any new military threat from the US or Israel, Iran’s response would be “immediate” and “without geographical limitations”, according to a statement by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
Khamenei ordered commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.
Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Iran would use “new weaponry” in its response to any future attacks. He also said Iran’s government was weighing a change to its “nuclear doctrine”, which currently includes a ban on nuclear weapons.
Iran’s nuclear programme has been a major point of contention in the conflict with the US, and Trump has repeatedly said Iran must never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon. Tehran insists its nuclear programme is for civilian purposes.
What is the latest from Trump?
The US president has sent mixed signals about the status of peace talks. On Saturday, he said negotiations were “going fine” but added that they were “not very reliable”.
He also said the US military still needed to “take care of” several Iranian sites, singling out a suspected underground nuclear complex known as Pickaxe Mountain.
Trump added that the US could achieve its military objectives “very quickly” and was not in a hurry.
Previously, he threatened to renew attacks that would “finish off” Iran, while the US has reportedly warned its Gulf allies to prepare for a short, high-intensity round of conflict after the midterm elections.
Rubio said Trump had not yet decided on whether to carry out new strikes, but warned the US “can achieve military objectives if we seek to”.
How could Israel play into the calculation?
Israel, which joined the US in initiating the war against Iran in February, is preparing for another round of potential conflict right after the US midterm elections, according to a senior Israeli official cited by Israel’s Ynet News site.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel has a “historic, one-time opportunity … to remove the Iranian threat once and for all”. While Netanyahu’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority in recent legislative elections, the 77-year-old leader remains in office as caretaker until a new government is formed.
Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu’s threats complicate Iran’s calculus because Tehran fears “even a nuclear agreement with Washington may not end the threat of another Israeli attack”.
Brigadier-General Yadollah Javani, the deputy for political affairs of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Iranian forces are operating on the assumption that the US or Israel could strike at any moment.
What explains the parallel diplomatic efforts and war rhetoric?
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst with the Crisis Group, said Tehran is pursuing diplomacy while also “attempting to redefine” the military implications of another potential conflict.
“For now, diplomacy and military preparations are proceeding simultaneously,” he wrote in a post on X. “The emerging Iranian position seems to be that an agreement remains possible, but another war would be fought under different rules and on a much wider battlefield.”
He added, “Whether Washington takes these warnings as credible deterrence or further escalatory threats could significantly influence what happens next.”
Krieg said the November 3 elections give Iran an incentive to delay concessions to deny Trump a diplomatic victory. But that calculus could change afterwards when he has fewer domestic political restraints on military action.
“We could therefore reach a situation where Iran becomes more willing to compromise precisely when Washington becomes more willing to strike,” said Krieg.

https://taz.de/Erstes-deutsches-Frauenha.author: Marlene Thaler
https://taz.de/Erstes-deutsches-Frauenha.text:
Erstes deutsches Frauenhaus: Eine Villa für Frauen in Not
Vor 50 Jahren eröffnete das erste deutsche Frauenhaus in Berlin. Heute bieten ähnliche Einrichtungen jährlich Tausenden Frauen und Kindern Schutz.
D ie Feministinnen waren gerade dabei zu überlegen, wie sie Deutschlands erstes Frauenhaus einrichten und ausstatten wollten. Es war der 2. Oktober 1976, ein Monat noch bis zur Eröffnung. Den Oktober wollten sie nutzen, um sich möglichst gut vorzubereiten. Doch bereits an diesem Tag stand die erste Frau vor der Tür der Villa in Berlin-Grunewald. „Wir wurden von Anfang an überrannt und mussten alle organisatorischen Fragen im laufenden Betrieb klären“, erzählt Karin Kaltenberg-Wulf, eine der Gründerinnen, in einem Interview mit dem Verein Frauenhauskoordinierung.
Am 1. November 1976 wurde das erste deutsche Frauenhaus dann auch offiziell eröffnet. 50 Jahre ist das inzwischen her. Auf das erste Frauenhaus folgten weitere: in Köln noch im selben Jahr, im darauffolgenden auch in Hamburg und Bielefeld. Frauenhäuser sind deutschlandweit zu einem Zufluchtsort für diejenigen geworden, die unter häuslicher oder partnerschaftlicher Gewalt leiden oder von ihr bedroht sind.
Die Gründung in Berlin war ein Erfolg der autonomen Frauenhausbewegung. Sie entwickelte sich in vielen Großstädten im Zuge der internationalen Frauenbewegung der 70er Jahre. Karin Kaltenberg-Wulf bezeichnet sich als eine „Frauenbewegungsfrau der ersten Stunde“. Sie hatte mit Soziologinnen, Psychologinnen, Sozialarbeiterinnen und einer Rechtsanwältin mehrere Jahre für das Haus gekämpft. Die Idee kannten sie aus London, wo es 1976 bereits zahlreiche Frauenhäuser gab. Einige Frauen besuchten die Unterkünfte dort, sie berichteten von überfüllten Häusern, der Bedarf war offenbar da.
In der Berliner Villa gab es auf 660 Quadratmetern 12 Zimmer für die Bewohnerinnen mit bis zu 10 Stockbetten. Zu Hochzeiten lebten auch mal um die 15 Personen in einem 20 Quadratmeter großen Zimmer. Für die Kinder gab es einen Raum zum Spielen, einen Schularbeitsraum und einen Kindergarten. Die etwa 20 Mitarbeiterinnen des Hauses leisteten Tag und Nacht Telefondienste. Heute werden die Anschriften von Frauenhäusern geheim gehalten, um die Betroffenen zu schützen. Damals stand die Adresse des Frauenhauses in der Zeitung. Es folgten mehrere Brandanschläge, das Haus musste streng überwacht werden.
Karin Kaltenberg-Wulf erzählt, dass es im Frauenhaus keine Hierarchien geben sollte zwischen den Frauen. Doch die Initiatorinnen selbst hätten unbewusste Vorurteile mitgebracht, etwa dass häusliche Gewalt vor allem ein Problem sogenannter Unterschichtfrauen sei. „Eine der allerersten Bewohnerinnen war aber die Frau eines bekannten Staatsanwalts“, erzählt sie. Das habe gezeigt, „wie wenig wir wussten, was auf uns zukommen würde“.
der anstoß
Wie beginnt Veränderung? An dieser Stelle erzählen wir jede Woche von einem historischen Moment, der etwas angestoßen hat.
Das erste deutsche Frauenhaus gab es bis zum Jahr 2000, dann wurde es geschlossen, unter anderem, weil die Villa renoviert werden musste. 2022 wurde an ihrer Fassade eine Gedenktafel enthüllt. Sie erinnert an die Feministinnen, die das Haus „autonom, solidarisch und hierarchiefrei mit den Bewohnerinnen betrieben“. Tausende Frauen mit ihren Kindern hätten dort „Schutz, Anerkennung, Selbstbestimmung und Perspektive“ gefunden.
Heute gibt es in Berlin 10, bundesweit rund 400 Frauenhäuser. Im Jahr 2025 fanden dort nach Angaben der Frauenhauskoordinierung etwa 13.400 Frauen und 15.300 Kinder Schutz.

Morning update
Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,
If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:
*Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Hormuz could be reopened within two days if Washington agrees to a set of conditions, including the formal recognition of the new shipping route designated by Iran and Oman in the Strait of Hormuz.
*Iran is debating whether to maintain its longstanding ban on nuclear weapons if hostilities resume, though no decision has been taken on any change, Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei said.
*US President Donald Trump has said Iran wants to “make a deal” and that negotiations are “going fine”, but questioned Tehran's reliability.
*Iran's Foreign Ministry on Sunday designated Britain's Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as "terrorist" organisations, in retaliation for what it described as hostile actions by the British government.
*A Palestinian man died on Sunday morning from wounds sustained when Israeli occupation forces shot him in al-Musaddar village, in the central Gaza Strip, Wafa reported.
*Ebrahim Azizi, Chairman of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee of the Iranian Parliament, has said the country's armed forces will respond to any new threats with "an immediate and harsher reply than before".
*At least three civilians were wounded in two air raids by Saudi-led coalition forces on an oil facility in Bajil district in western Hodeidah governorate of Yemen.
* Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has set out four conditions for forming a new government, including recognising Hamas as a "terrorist" organisation.
*Lebanon's Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji has called for a complete Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territories, while urging Gulf states to support efforts to restore Lebanon's sovereignty.
* United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres says he is “appalled” by the death of UN staff member Mohammad el-Shami in Houthi custody in Yemen.
*The United States Central Command has said that as of 31 October, its forces have redirected 144 commercial vessels as part of its "ironclad" naval blockade against Iran.
* Ninety-four-year-old Margaret Owen has been arrested again under the Terrorism Act in the United Kingdom for defying the ban on Palestine Action, according to Defend Our Juries.
*Hundreds of Israelis took to the streets on Saturday to urge the opposition to ally with Arab parties to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has gone on the offensive against the minority group's leaders.
* Israeli forces carried out a large explosion in the town of Baraachit, in south Lebanon’s Bint Jbeil district, on Saturday evening.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘He’s a force’: Obama answers call to boost Democrats – and rattle Trump
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
That could have been awkward. Barack Obama, campaigning for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, acknowledged that his fellow Democrat has criticised some aspects of the Obama presidency.
“Yeah, Abdul didn’t agree with some things we wanted to do – that our administration was doing – when I was president,” he told a rally in Detroit. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” The crowd erupted in laughter. “I’d say about five times a day, she says, ‘You knucklehead. Why you do that?’”
It was an elegant attempt to bridge the gap between the old Democratic party and the new. The US midterm elections have brought anti-incumbent sentiment to the fore. Some candidates have actively shrugged off their party labels, eager to cast themselves as outsiders running against the Washington establishment.
Against that backdrop, who wants a 65-year-old former president who left office nearly a decade ago with his promise of hope and change still only partly realised? It seems that Democrats do.
“Yes, we can!” chanted the crowd this week inside an arena in suburban Atlanta, Georgia, reviving the cadence of an Obama 2008 campaign that now feels like an artefact from a vanished age.
With days to go before midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump’s second term, Democrats have turned to their most formidable orator for a series of blistering speeches in the campaign’s closing days.
America’s first Black president has mercilessly mocked Trump’s autocratic pretensions and derided his foreign policy misadventures in the Middle East.
“This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said in Georgia. “It’s the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it.”
For party strategists, the decision to deploy Obama in the campaign’s closing stretch was a calculated gamble. Unlike Trump, who has spent weeks staging grievance-filled rallies in traditional Republican strongholds, Obama maintained a selective public profile until the final weeks, allowing a new generation of Democratic candidates to establish their own identities before delivering a late burst of star power.
David Litt, a former Obama White House speechwriter, said: “What you’re seeing is him coming in to support a new generation of Democratic leaders who have emerged organically, rather than trying to be involved from day one. He still has both a credibility and an ability to drive turnout that, if you’re a candidate in a close race, you can absolutely benefit from – especially among young voters and Black voters.”
The former president possesses a rare currency in modern US politics, according to Litt: the ability to command attention, and unnerve his successor.
“Obama is good at getting attention, and attention is hard to get these days,” he continued. “The other thing is he continues to live in Trump’s head rent-free. Donald Trump is out there on the stump, and in theory, he should be talking about his accomplishments. Instead he’s relitigating his decisions involving ballroom renovations, because he can’t help but get triggered by a single sentence from a former president.”
That sentence came at a rally in Cleveland, Ohio, when Obama observed that Trump’s gold-encrusted renovations have left the White House looking as if “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”.
The comment triggered a mini-culture war in rightwing media – not because Obama had invoked a murderous Iraqi dictator, but because he had dared to suggest that a popular restaurant chain was a symbol of vulgar excess.
Trump waved his arms to mimic a lettuce leaf, accused Obama of snobbery and said: “Every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I’m not that choosy.” He defended his gilded White House decor and claimed Obama had left the executive mansion “deteriorated”.
Trump’s treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, a wealthy former hedge fund manager, even staged a photo-op outside a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, ordering a french-dip cheeseburger in an apparent attempt to rebut accusations of elitism and urging “the Martha’s Vineyard set” to sample the chain’s multi-page menu.
To Obama, the outcry merely proved his case. In Atlanta, he said: “They mobilised a whole-of-government response to a joke, not to inflation, but to a joke. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.”
For Litt, the Republican outrage betrayed a glaring double standard. “This is a party that spent years complaining, ‘Oh, you’re not allowed to say anything offensive any more,’” he said. “It turns out all these people who would die on the hill of allowing someone to use offensive language suddenly think [the] Cheesecake Factory is a line you just can’t cross.”
In rural east Tennessee, Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, scoffed at Republican attempts to portray Obama’s remarks as elite condescension toward working people.
He said: “They thought they were going to do this liberal elite stuff. I live in rural America. You’ve got this guy, Donald Trump, who presents himself like a mafioso, running our country like a mob – how can he enrich himself? There’s no accountability. You’re reminded of it every time you go to the grocery store, fill up your gas tank, turn on the TV and see that we’re bombing more places.”
Democrats have also mobilised former vice-president Kamala Harris for their midterm effort, while ex-president Bill Clinton campaigned with David Jolly, who is running for governor of Florida. But Obama has been unusually active in presidential, congressional and gubernatorial elections since he left the White House.
In 2024 he backed Harris in the final stretch of the presidential race, which Trump ultimately won. When Obama opened his presidential centre in Chicago in June, all living former presidents were in attendance – but Trump was not.
Yet within the broader Democratic coalition, Obama’s legacy remains complicated. For a younger generation of activists who came of age during Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns and the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the former president is remembered as much for his institutional constraints and moderate compromises as for his inspirational rhetoric.
Norman Solomon, a co-founder of the progressive group RootsAction, said: “It’s like a great oil painting. If you walk up to it and look real close, it’s not going to look so great. If you look too close at Obama’s record – the collapse on peacemaking in Palestine, tripling troops in Afghanistan, presiding over the greatest upward transfer of wealth in anybody’s lifetime – it does not look so great.
“Then he leaves the White House and jets off to an island owned by a billionaire [the Obamas spent a post-presidency vacation on private islands owned by the British billionaire Sir Richard Branson in 2017]. That is not solidarity.”
Solomon acknowledged, however, that in the immediate crisis of 2026, Obama’s tactical value is undeniable. “Almost anybody is going to look great compared to Trump. In Michigan, where there’s been resentment between African American and Arab American communities, it’s helpful for Obama to present a wiser outlook on what’s at stake.”
Other progressives welcome Obama back on the campaign trail, seeing his involvement not as a concession to the old order, but as evidence that the former president recognises how far the party has moved to the left.
Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, a group that grew out of Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign, said: “Obama hitting the campaign trail is a net positive because it’s strategic. He helps pull in key demographics including African American voters.
“But more broadly, I interpret Obama being on the campaign trail as a validation of the progressive movement’s momentum. He is the epitome of the establishment, and he is out there pounding the pavement for progressives, saying our agenda isn’t radical – it’s mainstream. It’s an affirmation of how powerful our movement has become.”
Geevarghese also highlighted Obama’s ability to shield minority candidates from xenophobic attacks. “Obama represents a candidate who overcame the opposition’s ‘othering’ – when they called him un-American and used his middle name, Hussein. In the case of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who is weathering some of those same attacks, having Obama on the trail validates his candidacy and bolsters him within the American mainstream.”
Since 2016, the DSA has grown from 6,000 members to over 130,000 nationwide, scoring high-profile mayoral victories with Zohran Mamdani in New York while looking to expand its congressional caucus.
Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the DSA, said: “Today, Obama appearing alongside progressive candidates shows where the decisive shift is happening. Voters want real results toward an alternative to the factors that produced Donald Trump. Barack Obama coming out and campaigning with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan shows a recognition of where voters are.”
Yet Obama, like Trump, remains a political unicorn: a figure who defies easy categorisation. That remains a strength. Nina Turner, a former Ohio state senator and prominent progressive voice, said: “President Obama, because of his uniqueness, transcends the anti-establishment movement.”
“He is still an extraordinarily positive figure among the Democratic base,” she added. “Even on the progressive side, for those of us who were disappointed with the ultimate analysis of his presidency – the drone wars, running on hope and change but not making a whole lot of change – he still has ‘that thing.’ He’s a force.”
“The critique of President Obama is he was very much establishment: he ran on hope and change, but didn’t make a whole lot of change,” said Turner. “People were hopeful, though, and it’s the hopeful portion of his candidacy that still looms large – even as people critique his presidency, particularly on the progressive side of the ledger. Overall him being out there will be good for Democrats of all generations.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/24/cent.title: The Spirit of “Party Unity, My Ass” Is Back and Coming for the DSA (and El-Sayed)
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/24/cent.author: Eoin Higgins
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/24/cent.text:
Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
The PUMA spirit is back. The 2008 Democratic Party protest movement, inflamed by what Hillary Clinton supporters viewed as Barack Obama stealing the nomination from their primary candidate, scorned his general election campaign and embraced the mantra “Party Unity, My Ass.”
This time, that energy is aimed at the candidates preferred by the Democratic Socialists of America.
DSA-aligned progressives have won a number of party primaries and are set to help Democrats take the majority in Congress. But once in power, they’re likely to make demands — the kinds of demands that could upend decades of carefully crafted donor-friendly policymaking.
For moderate Democrats, “party unity” is only a goal worth pursuing to bully the left wing of the party to fall in line with their preferred candidate. When it’s on them to step up and vote for someone who might have different goals, that’s another story completely, and some centrists are even hoping for Republicans to win the House this November if the alternative is an empowered DSA Democratic wing.
James Carville, the fossilized Cajun strategist who was part of exactly one successful national political campaign, Bill Clinton’s 1992 White House victory, said on The Bulwark podcast last Sunday that he’d prefer a tight GOP hold on Congress over a narrow Democratic majority.
“I would be disappointed if it comes in at 225 House seats,” Carville told host Bill Kristol. “I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats to win by five, because, if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA.”
To his credit, Kristol — who, in a sign of how people can change when they know which way the wind is blowing, spent the PUMA moment promoting Sarah Palin but is now a self-proclaimed Democrat — pushed back, saying he’d rather win.
Carville is the first of his cohort to explicitly call for a GOP victory rather than the left flank of the party getting more power, but he’s not the only centrist deprioritizing his party’s prospects in November.
Maine Gov. Janet Mills has yet to endorse the Democratic Party’s Senate nominee, Troy Jackson, after she lost to now-disgraced Graham Platner. (Mills and Jackson have a long and bitter history from state government, which may be playing a role here.)
Perhaps most consequentially, in Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has faced an uphill battle since winning his party’s grueling primary. He’s now focused on winning in the general election and becoming the first Muslim U.S. senator, but resistance to his candidacy remains a concern.
Much of the difficulty has come from members of his own party and other liberals. Their antipathy toward a candidate whose positions aren’t so out of step with other members of the caucus has raised questions about what exactly is so objectionable about him. El-Sayed may skew to the progressive side of the party, but he’s not a socialist and not a member of the DSA; his positions on domestic policy should place him companionably among the likes of Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s wing.
Until recently, most of the anger after El-Sayed’s primary in early August was confined to X and occasional cable news hits.
That changed on October 16, when two Michigan Democratic Party power players, David Kramer and Lon Johnson, urged voters in a Detroit News op-ed to leave El-Sayed’s place on the ballot blank — effectively handing the Senate seat over to Republican Mike Rogers, an election denier and a lockstep Trump ally.
The piece tied El-Sayed to extreme elements of Islam and suggested his opposition to Israel’s genocide, war crimes, and occupation was based in hatred for the Jewish diaspora.
“Our gravest concerns involve El-Sayed’s associations with figures who have excused or minimized terrorism, his reluctance to unequivocally condemn dangerous rhetoric, and his support of extreme policies,” Kramer and Johnson wrote. “At a time of rising antisemitism, Democrats deserve leadership that unequivocally rejects rhetoric threatening Jewish communities.”
Comedian Mike Drucker accurately described on Tuesday the centrist rejection of El-Sayed as less “blue no matter who” and more “blue unless brown.”
But Democratic leaders like Carville, Kramer, Johnson, and others are panicked beyond their obvious Islamophobia — they can see the writing on the wall goes well past Michigan. It’s a full-on existential crisis.
Former Intercept writer Jon Schwarz once opined on what he termed the iron law of institutions: “The people who control institutions care first and foremost about their power within the institution rather than the power of the institution itself.”
What we’re seeing now is the iron law’s white blood cells fighting a threat they don’t believe can be easily assimilated into the existing power structure. It’s a danger to their status and power.
Their attacks on the left are going to backfire, leaving the Democrats’ centrist wing even less empowered than before.
That outcome is ideal for the party, the base, and the country. For centrists, it’s a disaster — but if the way to stop their coming irrelevance is to vote for a progressive American Muslim who opposes genocide, they’re incapable of taking that step.
Ultimately, all their griping may not matter. El-Sayed is regularly polling slightly ahead of Rogers, and 95 percent of Michigan Democrats said they intend to vote for him. Much like Jackson in Maine, should he win, El-Sayed will be even less beholden to the elements of the party power structure who are so desperately trying to prove he needs them, rather than the other way around.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
