THE FACADE OF the McDonald’s on Sixth Avenue in Midtown Manhattan is covered in words, set in white Helvetica on a black background and arranged in an undulating pattern, an expanding ripple, like the whorl of a fingerprint: “Attraction, energy, EYE CATCHING, authentic, true, strong, flavour, responsibility.” This word cloud, a vapory section of a visual field that also encompasses an I ♥︎ NY gift shop, a pawnshop, an office building lobby, and the distant scrolling of Times Square, breaks up the more linear, gridded facades and curtain walls that surround it. “SECOND HOME, Reassuring, mothering, serenity, security, familiar, prospecting comfort.” Strings of adjectives and nouns float in space, some partially obscured by the building’s windows and signage: “alive, enlightening, shining.” “EXCITING, magic, energetic, inventive, dreams, inspiring.”
If parsed, the cloud almost condenses into a single list—an inventory of the kinds of things one might find inside the building, the text recalling that of a menu or a deli awning (“Beer, groceries, cigarettes . . .”). Unlike a menu, an awning, or a storefront sign, the language fills the visible surface area of the building completely. It can’t be scanned in a single line or column; it is contained by no frame other than the facade itself. The language drifts. “Pure, savoury.” “Harmonious, fresh, balanced, nourishing.” The items are not goods for sale but abstract terms, some of which could be elements of a description of what it is like to eat at McDonald’s, and others that are more like values that McDonald’s, the brand, might represent or actualize. The predicates swirl around, occasionally repeating themselves, unsettled, inexhaustible. They name nothing concrete. If there is a subject in this haze of predication, a subject of this text-portrait, it is nothing less than the total idea of McDonald’s.
The word cloud—which is what I will provisionally name the typographic form under consideration here—consists of specific, discrete concepts, rendered in clean, authoritative text, but leaves their relations indeterminate at the level of syntax. In fact, there is no syntax. The cloud is an impressionistic accumulation of themes, an array of correlations. The facade of the Avenue of the Americas McDonald’s looks like notes left on an office whiteboard after a brainstorming session: “McDonald’s is __________.” Or perhaps this cloud is a textual reduction of a larger discourse—words extracted from customer reviews? But the word cloud’s source text is as irrelevant as its effects are inconclusive: An atmospheric mass of linguistic elements situated next to one another, the cloud neither forms meaningful sequences (sentences, paragraphs) nor accomplishes the “pointing” effect of signage. It does not identify, like heraldry or a logo (the Golden Arches handle that). It is a kind of verbal aura or a semantic plasma. It does not really inform, but at the same time it is only barely decorative. Or it is decor that looks like information, recalling the data-visualization aesthetics and tag clouds of the early 2000s. This minimally styled data might be characterized as a set of tags that maps an experience. The data is verbal material for the identification of something more determinate that never quite arrives.
WORD CLOUDS ARE not ubiquitous features of our visual environment. But they are not terribly obscure, either. The window of an uptown juice and smoothie bar says, “Cheers to nature,” “positive,” “good,” “wellness,” “cure,” “watermelonade,” “freshness,” “serenity,” “kale delight,” “relaxation,” “peanut butter oatmeal,” “lifestyle,” “wheatgrass,” “wellness,” “whole greens,” “positive,” “protein supreme,” “healthy,” “organic,” “life.” The exterior of a Bushwick apartment building is latticed by the words “new,” “housing,” “social,” “avenue,” “street,” “future,” and “old city.” A Pepsi-themed wall at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey fills up with “play harder,” “go big,” “go home,” “football,” “strong,” “let’s go,” “dream,” “alive,” “we believe.” Nouns, verbs, adjectives, and slogans float uneasily near one another in different colors, fonts, and sizes.
Decorative word clouds seem to have peaked in popularity in the aughts and 2010s, but they remain in the commercial visual vernacular. They are installed in restaurants and cafés, but also in offices, gyms, hotels, shopping malls, and even in homes, as “Live Laugh Love” kitsch, small pieces of “word art” that celebrate their owner’s values and passions. Sometimes word clouds are big-budget supergraphics realized by design firms like Pentagram, but often they are produced cheaply and quickly by non-designers, or by anonymous Etsy merchants, or in-house at printing and signage companies.
These architectural word clouds may be cultural artifacts of what Rem Koolhaas, writing in 2001, called “junkspace”: the afterlife of urban modernization, a “fuzzy empire of blur,” an “endless frontline of display,” with its “superstrings of graphics,” “flamboyant yet unmemorable, like a screen saver.” Junkspace is characterized by formlessness, continuity, immersion, and accumulation. Inaugurated by the digital age, it lacks origin or history. It is “overdetermined and indeterminate at the same time.” Its forms are cloudy, soft-edged, provisional.
Koolhaas’s essay narrates both the irrelevance of modernism and the disappearance of architecture into communication. The question of what a building should say has long been a concern for architectural theory. Enlightenment-era critics wrote of an architecture parlante, a “speaking architecture” that would convey function and meaning through its form, establishing what sorts of things were to be done with it or inside of it. The idea was associated with visionary eighteenth-century architects like Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and Étienne-Louis Boullée—perhaps the most famous example is Ledoux’s Oikema, a proposal for a brothel shaped like a massive phallus.
As Denise Scott Brown and Robert Venturi argue in Learning from Las Vegas (1972), this path could only be taken so far. In the twentieth century, the rise of the automobile, the increasing pace and density of commercial development, and the growing functional differentiation of society in general contributed to an environment in which institutions, businesses, and commodities had to distinguish themselves from one another more efficiently. As the number and specialization of things demanding recognition increases, architecture becomes a less effective way to communicate. Since graphic communication is almost always faster, cheaper, and more immediately legible than purely architectural solutions, signage takes command. Architecture becomes attenuated, non-monumental, a mass medium. Industrial graphic design emerges, and along with it, new hybrids of word, image, and mark—graphic identities (custom rules governing a brand’s aesthetic); supergraphics (large-scale graphics applied to entire walls and buildings); LED screens (animated signage, video advertising, and live information displays)—that take on the role of spatial programming. A building becomes a “decorated shed,” a mere box with signs anchored to it, signs that, in some cases, conceal it entirely, reducing the actual structure to the verbal clustering that surrounds it. The McDonald’s building—its architecture—doesn’t speak. Instead, a speechlike word-image forms its surface. The writing is not just on the walls. In some sense, the writing is the walls.
What French anthropologist Marc Augé calls the “non-places” of contemporary modernity—airports, train stations, stadiums, malls, lobbies, facades—are apprehended less as buildings than as assemblages of large planar surfaces. When it comes to filling these surfaces, typographic treatments like word clouds offer some advantages over images. They can pick out products or concepts or experiences that have no obvious iconic representations, and they can present many of them at once. But ultimately the typographic texture doesn’t have to say much. It has to attract an eye that is already beset from all sides by attractions. Because we are taught that textures made of language hold the promise of information, this eye will take a moment longer to process the word cloud than it might an ornamental wallpaper or even an illustration. So fill a surface with words, more words and larger words than are necessary; fill a surface with something—anything—that achieves a minimal degree of individuation as well as commercial persuasion.
In junkspace, Koolhaas argues, formal strategies associated with modern art and design—abstraction, functionalism, fragmentation, radical juxtaposition—are hastily and unceremoniously redeployed in the ordinary language of commerce. The particular spatial affordances of language with which word clouds operate were also a significant concern of twentieth-century avant-garde art and literature. In the Cubist scenes painted by Pablo Picasso, Georges Braque, and Juan Gris, for instance, words or letters collected from newspapers, posters on café walls, or the lyrics of popular songs are dispersed over the canvas. Like word clouds, Cubist compositions use typography to model public and social spaces. Similarly, Gertrude Stein’s “text portraits” use repetition, disjunction, and syntactic play to make literature act like Cubist painting; these “word paintings” synthesize and compress data about a person into a defamiliarizing impression, one that can be received relatively quickly. This is an information-processing technique, a way of trying to show everything at once.
There is also concrete poetry—writing arranged in images or geometric forms—a tradition that can be traced to ancient instances of shaped poetry. Eugen Gomringer’s 1954 manifesto “From Line to Constellation” argues that poetry that unfolds in lines (and especially poetry that takes too long to do so) has no organic function in modern society. The concrete poem, on the other hand—the “constellation”—would restore poetry’s social value by imitating the cultural techniques of midcentury visual communication. It would be “perceived visually as a whole as well as in its parts.” It would be a “play-area” or a “cluster” instead of a series of lines. As Gomringer wrote in a 1960 text, “The Poem as Functional Object,” the concrete poem would be “as easily understood as signs in airports and traffic signs.”
The dispersion of words across architecture does something that does not really involve reading. It creates an atmosphere. It acts like a mood, an aroma, a murmur. Like its architectural, artistic, and literary precedents, the vernacular word cloud exists in the gap between what Vilém Flusser called “linear thinking,” or thinking that proceeds in a historical order of succession (alphabetic writing), and “surface thinking,” or thinking that follows a statistical order of distribution (technical imaging). Linear thinking deals with inscriptions that record past traces. Surface thinking deals with electronic interfaces, with screens that change in real time and algorithms that allow us to perceive all possible futures at once (within computational limits). In the unsettled space between the two, between the wall and the screen, the word cloud.
FOLLOW AVENUE OF THE AMERICAS six blocks up from the McDonald’s, past the “XYZ” buildings of Rockefeller Center, past Radio City Music Hall, and you will arrive at Eero Saarinen’s CBS Building (1965), also known as Black Rock (not to be confused with the BlackRock investment company). Like the McDonald’s, it is matte black. (Why are so many New York City McDonald’s black?) Jim Dine’s three headless Venus de Milos face it from across the avenue, and the black glass of the Museum of Modern Art reflects it from the opposite side of Fifty-Third Street. From 1966 until 1990, the building’s cafeteria wall was occupied by Gastrotypographicalassemblage, a word cloud conceived by Lou Dorfsman, CBS’s design chief, with typography by Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnese and additional design contributions from John Alcorn, Stanley Glaubach, and Nicholas Fasciano. Gastrotypographicalassemblage is an approximately eight-by-thirty-four-foot wooden mural composed mostly of culinary terms set in expressive three-dimensional typefaces. The words (foods, dishes, techniques, terms of art) are painted white, arranged at right angles, and studded with small sculptures (foods, cooking implements, containers), literary quotations (Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Alice B. Toklas), and a recipe for escargots à la bourguignon. A neon yellow EAT lies near the center. The effect of Gastrotypographicalassemblage is like that of a Surrealist rebus, mixing the likenesses of things with their words. A lemon sliced into a five-pointed star punctuates the word LEMON. A trio of ice cream cones perch atop the word OKRA. A donut is encircled by DOUGHNUT. Some of the elements are not likenesses but readymades, or the things themselves: a case of dried pasta, a set of pastry molds, a collection of aluminum cans. The language is a thick atmosphere around them.
Within the little history of word clouds, Gastrotypographicalassemblage is transitional, something between fine-art Combine and the latter-day commercial word cloud graphic. It has a solidity and craftsmanship that the McDonald’s facade obviously lacks. It contains literature, as well as an entire recipe. But the family resemblance is evident in form and in function. The piece is restaurant decor; it scans like a menu but does not actually enumerate things for sale; it fills an unornamented wall; it represents and accompanies an experience of consumption or conviviality or both. A species of relief, it is distinguished by its three-dimensionality from something quickly and inexpensively adhered to a wall. But neither is it entirely architectural. It is not part of the building.
Indeed, Gastrotypographicalassemblage stands in marked contrast to the building that housed it, a building whose exterior is the image of imagelessness: flat, geometric black. Saarinen’s facade consists of a faux-curtain wall of black windows filtered by dark granite piers, angled like a lenticular print, so that at a certain viewing angle, the curtain wall disappears behind the piers, which themselves, in turn, collapse to form what appears to be a single flat plane. There is very little language on the building—only some modest brass lettering recessed into the surface at the ground level.
Saarinen’s building contracts, solid and sober, its windows withdrawn from the sidewalk. The word cloud expands, filling an interior hall with text and picture. At this level, the two objects could not be more different. Yet both may be understood as constituents of a specific mass medium whose producers they were designed to serve: broadcast television. As Reinhold Martin has shown, television and the Manhattan curtain wall (first popularized by Mies van der Rohe) are components of the same mediatic process. The CBS Building, as black rectangle, as reticulated grid, as mute surface, echoes the television screen, which makes itself invisible and noiseless precisely in order to accommodate and transmit any number of possible audiovisual experiences. The word cloud unfolds the programmed cacophony of broadcast media itself, a condensation of speech, writing, and pictures.
Gastrotypographicalassemblage is now installed at the Culinary Institute of America in Hyde Park, New York. But a trace remains in the Black Rock lobby: another wall sculpture in white. This one is composed of the raised letters C, B, and S, cut up into rectangles and combined with stylized icons of media: a microphone, a record player, a book, and a Cubist guitar, lit by a hanging three-dimensional matrix of harsh LEDs. CBS left the building in 2024, and today the tenants are mostly legal and financial firms. On the ground floor, facing the Museum of Modern Art, is the Nusr-Et Steakhouse from the viral Turkish restaurateur known as Salt Bae. The hashtag #saltbae, in gold vinyl, is the largest text on Saarinen’s facade.
THREE BLOCKS NORTH and two blocks east of the CBS Building is 590 Madison Avenue, also known as the IBM Building. The current structure, which houses the watch store Bucherer, among other tenants, was built for IBM in 1983, but from 1938 to 1964 this site was occupied by the technology company’s headquarters and showroom. A ground-floor storefront called the Data Processing Center, designed by former MoMA curator Eliot Noyes, opened in 1954 to exhibit the “business machines” heralding the computer revolution. Passersby could gaze at the working computers and technicians inside, and could even rent computer time. Throughout the early 1960s, under the direction of Noyes, IBM was busily visualizing the coming information age, seeking to give computers a cultural form that would be legible to the public. It collaborated with A-list designers—Saarinen, Mies, Paul Rand, Marcel Breuer, Isamu Noguchi, Paul Rudolph, Egon Eiermann, and others—to develop systems and buildings that would become icons of postwar corporate modernism.
In 1964, at the New York World’s Fair, IBM presented “The Information Machine,” another Saarinen-designed building, which housed a twenty-two-channel film installation designed by Charles Eames. The building resembled an egg, an airship, and a cloud. Its concrete surface was covered in the raised IBM logo, repeated and staggered to create a continuous, dense field of text. Eames’s film installation, Think (1964), was described as “a machine” that, by giving viewers “a lot of information in a very short time,” encouraged them to “think” like a computer. Its twenty-two screens, displayed at various angles, bombarded audiences with montages of text, numbers, and images, like a rapid scroll through Instagram Reels. Designed to demystify digital information processing, Eames’s environment made computation into an immersive experience.
IBM’s early work in making computation visible would be eclipsed by developments in the graphical user interface, or GUI, which was pioneered at Xerox PARC and commercialized by Microsoft and Apple. Scientific research and the burgeoning field of data analysis had already required novel computational methods of display within industrially specialized contexts; GUIs made computers accessible to a broader public. But the personal computer created new design problems, which in turn yielded new algorithms for navigating ever-growing quantities of data. The social platforms of the early 2000s, such as del.icio.us and Flickr, were the first to introduce internet users to the “tag cloud,” a weighted list of metadata tags spread out across a browser window. Typographic variables like size, color, and weight corresponded to tag frequency or popularity. A “folksonomy” (folk taxonomy), the user-generated tag cloud served both as a navigational aid and as an overview of the platforms’ content.
In 2005, Jonathan Feinberg, an engineer working on a social bookmarking application at IBM Research, developed what he deemed a more visually pleasing tag cloud algorithm. “Wordle” was a simple Java applet that took any plain text input and transformed it into a dense, decorative composition, with limited use as a data visualization (text size proportional to word frequency). The tool had a brief but influential life as a website application. In a paper published in 2010, Feinberg wrote that over 1.4 million word clouds had been saved in the Wordle gallery, and that users of all technical levels had so far employed these word clouds as summaries or decorations in business presentations and Ph.D. theses, as illustrations in news articles and television broadcasts, and in elementary school classrooms. Feinberg refers to word clouds as “communicative artifacts.” Wordle users, he writes, “feel as though they have created something, that the created thing succeeds in representing something meaningful, and that it accurately reflects or intensifies the source text.” He compares these artifacts to poetry, which evokes “delight, surprise,” “recognition,” and “insight” by more “intentional” means. “A beautiful visualization gives pleasure as it reveals something essential,” the paper concludes.
Today’s internet users are increasingly unlikely to encounter word clouds. Contemporary social media platforms have abandoned dense lexical fields in favor of single- or multi-stream continuous content feeds (infinite scrolls) or thumbnail grids. Meanwhile, the field of data visualization prefers other, more precise kinds of presentation: charts, treemaps, network diagrams. But occasionally, as on the McDonald’s facade, word clouds surface in our built environment, like afterimages of the history of computational media. Outworn, the word cloud is an algorithmic artifact, but also something that points to the raw infrastructural operations that shape how we communicate and consume in the computationally mediated present. It literally—by way of the letter—visualizes the processes by which we cluster our impressions and perceive frequencies and collocations in the designed world, thereby making decisions and making meaning.
The contemporary city is mediated by our screens, which show us all of the calculably possible experiences we might have in it, often—with virtual maps, for example—all at once. These experiences—which include but are not limited to the ones we might have in stores and restaurants—are constantly being tagged and sorted by algorithms that both process and modulate user input according to their own internal parameters. Our experiences and our recordings of them (photographs, captions, videos), as well as the techno-social assemblages they compose with these distribution algorithms, do not easily end up as well-formed sentences or narratives; they are more like word-images, diagrams, rebuses, Cubist compositions. The language that they recirculate oscillates between over- and under-specification. We are more interested in vibes than in articulation. We track and label our experiences using forms of notation that are used to algorithmically deliver more of them. Inscription happens environmentally, ambiently, and it trains models that are themselves composed like clouds of words, latent spaces of particles near or far. Much like our machines, we scan our environment rather than reading it. We work with relations like proximity and connotation, it seems, more readily than we work with history, with linear succession and causality. Imaging is always happening around us, all at once. This all-at-once feeling is literalized in the word cloud. But the present does not favor literalization. This is why the word cloud, like architecture before it, may soon disappear.
Alec Mapes-Frances is a graphic designer and writer living in Manhattan.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/cuba-blockad.text:
The US Is Starving Cuba. Will It Invade Too?
Ten months into a US fuel blockade, Cuba’s hospitals, power grid, and economy are buckling, and the threat of invasion has become a midterm talking point in Florida. But the island hasn’t broken. That may make Washington more dangerous, not less.
On September 25, CBS News announced that it had obtained “exclusive new information” regarding potential US military action against Cuba. According to an Army Reserve memo reviewed by the network, the Pentagon was looking at the possibility of mobilizing police forces, medical personnel, and other units to support such an operation. Vague on details, the conveniently timed piece appeared suited to coincide with Donald Trump’s speech at the United Nations three days prior, where he asserted that his administration was seeking a “fundamental change in the situation” with the Cuban government, which is “failing like never before” and “will fall.”
The very night of its report, however, CBS published another article effectively walking it back, quoting a defense expert who claimed that the memo in question should be viewed as a routine planning exercise — one with electoral overtones. “It may be aligned with the interest in trying to inspire the South Florida vote to rally around the administration,” said Florida International University’s Brian Fonseca, “and not necessarily fall into the trap of mismanaged expectations.”
Nearly a month later, and with no invasion in sight, the Florida state government waded still further into pre-electoral waters, issuing an arrest warrant against former President Raúl Castro for his purported responsibility in the 1996 downing of two “Brothers to the Rescue” aircraft. Castro was the defense minister at the time. Essentially a copy-paste of a federal indictment unsealed in May, the announcement came some thirty years after the events in question but a mere two weeks before unusually competitive midterm elections, where even some safe GOP seats in Florida, like that of Cuban American hardliner Maria Elvira Salazar, are suddenly at risk.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Bulgarians vote in presidential run-off amid Black Sea tensions
Voters in Bulgaria weigh economic challenges and attacks on ships in a race marked by record low turnout.
Voting is under way in a Bulgarian presidential run-off marked by growing regional security threats and domestic economic concerns.
President Iliana Iotova, 61, led over former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, in the first round but fell short of the 50 percent threshold needed to win. The first round drew record low turnout. Only 23 percent of eligible voters cast a ballot, according to election officials.
Exit polls will be published after voting ends at 8pm (18:00 GMT) on Sunday, with a result expected on Monday.
The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in the past month, which have sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of Russia’s war on Ukraine.
About two dozen seafarers are feared dead, and the strikes have prompted the government to seek help from Bulgaria’s allies to bolster maritime security. On Wednesday, a Greek container ship sank after being hit by sea drones.
Both leading presidential candidates have condemned the attacks. Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who backs Iotova, said the strikes’ outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”. They have both called for a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president. She became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter and win a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine.
He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
Gyurov said he wants Bulgaria to be a reliable NATO ally able to stand for up its interests with strong diplomacy and a firm position.
A host of right-leaning political figures, among them ex-Prime Minister Boiko Borisov, have expressed support for Gyurov.

Museum über die Polizei: Eierlikör mitten am Tag
Christian Specht würde gerne mal in das Polizeimuseum in Berlin, aber auch er selbst kann alte Geschichten über sogenannte Kontakbeamte erzählen.
C hristian Specht, Jahrgang 1969, ist politisch engagiert und setzt sich für mehr Mitwirkungsmöglichkeiten von Menschen mit Beeinträchtigung in den Medien ein. Seit 2017 ist er der erste Mensch mit Beeinträchtigung im Vorstand der Lebenshilfe. Er hat ein Büro in der taz und zeichnet (un)regelmäßig den „Specht der Woche“.
Hier sieht man zwei Polizeiautos in einem Museum. Es gibt ein Museum oben beim Platz der Luftbrücke, die sogenannte „Polizeihistorische Sammlung“. Das Museum soll sehr interessant sein – das würde ich mir gerne mal angucken. Da hängen wohl auch tolle Plakate und es gibt alte Polizeiautos mit Gitter.
Ich komme da drauf, weil sie im RBB über das Polizeimuseum berichtet haben. Ich war da noch nie, aber ich hätte große Lust, mir das mit jemandem mal anzugucken. Auf dem Bild habe ich auch ein Funkgerät gezeichnet. Damals gab es in den Polizeiautos noch Funkgeräte. Aber die von damals haben sie irgendwann abgeschafft, heute sehen sie anders aus.
Früher anders ausgestattet
Taxis hatten früher auch solche Funkgeräte. Damals war die Polizei generell noch ganz anders ausgestattet. Heute, wenn ich die Polizei sehe, hat diese mehr Technik. Damals haben sie mit ihren Funkgeräten mit Antennen kommuniziert. Es gab sogenannte „Kontaktbeamte“ mit Umhängetaschen. Sie waren dafür da, dass man sie ansprechen konnte, wenn man irgendein Problem hatte.
Meine Oma hat damals an der Urbanstraße in Kreuzberg gewohnt; meine Mama und meine Schwester und ich übrigens auch. Daneben gab es ein kleines Polizeirevier, das aber später in den Bergmannkiez umzog. Als ich Kind war, und wenn diese Kontaktbeamten Glück hatten, wurden sie von Leuten eingeladen, zum Biertrinken – zumindest bei meiner Oma war das so; Eierlikör hat dieser Kontaktbeamte, der bei uns jeweils war, auch gerne getrunken – mitten am Tag. Heute machen die so etwas nicht mehr! Protokoll: Rahel Bueb

Araghchi says Hormuz could be reopened within two days if conditions met
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Hormuz could be reopened within two days if Washington agrees to a set of conditions, including the formal recognition of the new shipping route designated by Iran and Oman in the Strait of Hormuz.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi said other conditions include lifting the sanctions the US imposed on Iran after the collapse of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) in July; reducing the US military presence in the region; reinstating the oil waivers granted in June as part of the MoU; releasing frozen Iranian funds, including those held in Qatar; formally recognising the new shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz, set by Iran and Oman, and closing all other routes and ending the war on all fronts, particularly Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.
Araghchi told Al Jazeera that the plan currently under discussion is the one Iran originally presented at the beginning, known as the Iran seven-day plan, in which "we specified our condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz".
"Our Qatari friends asked to cut this time window from seven days to five days or less, and we worked on this idea during the Qatari delegation visit yesterday,” he said.
“We have now reached a plan that cuts the implementation time to two days. On day one, the US implements a set of measures. On day two, the Hormuz Strait will reopen, and navigation will be restored to what it used to be.”

Noah, 26
 The mechanics of how we have sex don’t matter to me. I still feel the same degree of pleasure
Sex with Nina is by far the best I’ve ever had. Our intimate life is incredibly communicative, but it wasn’t always that way. We were friends who lived in a house-share together, and decided to start a relationship. We hit an early roadblock – penetrative sex was very painful for her.
After that first time, we both shut down. We were each coming to it with our own worries. In the past, I felt anxiety about whether I was doing sex right, so I was left worrying that I had done it all wrong. Nina felt concerned that penetrative sex would feel better for me, and that without it our sex wouldn’t be good enough. We still tried penetrative sex for a bit, but it clearly wasn’t working. It started to feel ridiculous that we were even trying.
We had some productive conversations, and scribbled all our concerns down on a mind map. We looked it up, and Nina’s symptoms marry up with vaginismus, so we educated ourselves about that. We built our sex life organically from the ground up. We would kiss and grind on each other, and we knew that felt good.
Over time, she has seen how much I enjoy sex with her, which has eased her worries that I might crave anything else. The mechanics of how we have sex don’t matter to me. I still feel the same degree of pleasure the way we do it, and I am so happy to have Nina as my partner in life and in the bedroom.
Nowadays, I would say our sex life is quite mobile – we might both be on our backs or facing each other, and I might touch her from the front or wrap my arm around and touch her from behind. We can change it up more than other couples, because the positions of penetrative sex are more restrictive.
With previous sexual partners, I didn’t feel confident I was doing it right, because we stuck to the same formula we had seen in films. We didn’t play around and feed back about what felt good for us. But because Nina and I have built our sex life together, it’s created a place of comfortableness and love.
Nina, 23
 We tried penetrative sex but it really hurt me and I didn’t experience any pleasure
I’d only had one sexual encounter before Noah. I dated this guy for a few months. It was exclusively finger penetration, which I found incredibly painful. It was my first inkling that penetrative sex would be difficult. He didn’t communicate about what he was doing when he put his fingers inside me, and I didn’t feel comfortable with him at all.
When Noah and I slept together the first time we tried penetrative sex, but it was a complete disaster. It really hurt me and I didn’t experience any pleasure whatsoever – I may as well have been sticking something up my nose! I felt insecure – Noah had more sexual experience than me and I thought he might want someone who could have penetration and call things off – but he’s just a lovely, kind human.
As time went on, I started to realise he wasn’t going to end things and stopped worrying about it so much. I remember he joked: “It doesn’t really matter where the willy goes!” We have been together for three years now and he makes me feel entirely secure.
I know I should probably go to the doctor and find out why penetrative sex is so painful, but I just don’t feel the urge because there isn’t anything missing from our love life.
The bread and butter of our sex life is touching each other at the same time. I think nonpenetrative sex is more fluid and dynamic, and you are not limited by the positions of penis-in-vagina sex.
I find it frustrating when people define sex as penetrative. There are so many ways to have sex. In TV and film, you always see couples having penetration – I would like to see more straight nonpenetrative couples represented. I would define our sex life as full – fun, hot and loving.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/23/kohe.title: Bodycam: Cop Was Not in Danger When He Fired Shots That Killed 1-Year-Old Kohen Wiley
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/23/kohe.author: Liliana Segura, Radley Balko
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/23/kohe.text:
After the Mississippi attorney general cleared a white cop for firing into a car and killing a Black toddler in a Walmart parking lot, video footage released by the Mississippi Department of Public Safety has revealed the fullest picture to date of what happened.
The videos, provided to The Intercept in response to a public records request, come on the heels of leaked footage that exposed how a needlessly aggressive and reckless police confrontation of two suspected shoplifters led to 1-year-old Kohen Wiley’s violent death in his mother’s arms.
While the newly released videos include redacted versions of the previously leaked footage — including body camera footage for some of the officers, as well as Walmart surveillance video — the new footage reveals for the first time the body camera video belonging to the Senatobia police officer who fired the shots that killed Kohen Wiley: Sgt. Hunter Foster.
While the state concluded that the shooting was “justified” based on a probe by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, the videos show how police escalated a non-life-threatening situation — one that could have ended with a mere shoplifting charge — by pursuing Kohen’s mother, Vel’lesiya Wiley, and the driver, Latoya Ferrell, after they ran from the store and tried to drive away.
Foster’s body camera footage makes clear that he positioned himself in front of the vehicle, aimed his gun at the car, and fired the fatal shot into the passenger side window after the car was moving past him and posed no threat.
This is consistent with the conclusions of Dr. Roger Mitchell, a forensic pathologist hired by Kohen Wiley’s family, who determined in June that the fatal bullet was most likely fired into the side window, entering his small body on his right side and exiting his left.
The release also includes a 10-page, heavily redacted investigative report by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, which the state attorney general relied upon in concluding that the shooting was justified.
The report’s narrative is misleading: Its only description of the shooting is that one officer “discharged his firearm” after the car “sped toward the officers.” The report does not discuss the fact that the firing officer was beside the car when he first fired, which is clear in Foster’s body camera footage. The report also redacts Kohen Wiley’s cause of death.
Foster resigned from the Senatobia police department on Wednesday. Afterward, Foster’s lawyer told CNN, “The driver of the vehicle was attempting to kill those 5 officers, and Hunter Foster had no choice but to discharge his weapon.” (Neither Foster nor his lawyer responded to The Intercept’s requests for comment.)
Residents of Senatobia had called for months for the body camera footage and Walmart surveillance videos to be released. After the state attorney general announced that the police had been cleared, a spokesperson for the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, which houses the state’s Bureau of Investigations, told The Intercept that the videos would be released after the family had a chance to watch them.
Instead, as with the attorney general’s announcement, the family first saw the leaked videos on social media. By the time Kohen Wiley’s parents and grandparents met with state officials to view the videos on Thursday morning, most of the footage had been circulated online. At a press conference on Thursday afternoon, Kohen’s maternal grandmother, Veronica Roberson, called it “a slap in the face.”
Roberson said she’d been haunted by the word “justified” all week, slamming the idea that Foster fired the lethal shots because he feared for his life.
“You shot my grandbaby from the side of the car,” she said. “How are you in danger?”
“Get the Car!”
The incident began with what appeared to be a routine occurrence in retail outlets all over the country: a shoplifting allegation.
The earliest footage is from a Walmart security camera. An apparent Walmart employee dressed in a black hoodie is stationed by the store entrance when Wiley and Ferrell approach, carrying a child and a box of diapers. They pause at the door and appear to have a brief exchange with the Walmart employee before breaking into a run toward the parking lot.
In body camera footage, which begins moments later, the staffer in the hoodie appears in the doorway of a small security room, where other Walmart employees, three Senatobia police officers, and two Tate County sheriff’s deputies are gathered around a pair of computer monitors. According to the MBI report, the officers had been called to the store in response to a complaint that a man was sexually harassing customers.
The employee in the hoodie tells the cops and Walmart staffers that two people are running and gestures toward the store entrance.
Moments later, the five officers dash from the room and out into the parking lot, running toward a gray sedan. A sheriff’s deputy reaches the driver’s side door and puts his hand on the hood of the car while someone yells “stop.” The car backs up and starts to turn, but hits a parked SUV. Someone yells, “Stop the car!”
As the officers continue to run toward the car, it begins to move forward. At one point, two officers are directly in front of the vehicle, including Foster, the police sergeant identified as the shooter, who aims his gun at the front windshield.
The car starts to turn left, away from the three officers on the vehicle’s right side, and either narrowly misses or grazes Foster, who stumbles to the passenger side and aims his gun at the window. He then appears to fire three shots in rapid succession.
As the car pulls away, the officers continue their pursuit.
“Get the car! Get the car! Get the car!” one of them yells.
The gray sedan pauses briefly before taking off again.
The records released by state officials do not include any footage of what happened after the officers return to their vehicles. But the leaked footage, which was compiled into a nearly 7-minute long video, shows Foster pacing next to a police vehicle outside the nearby Highland Hills Medical Center an hour and 20 minutes after the shooting.
“I didn’t even see a fucking baby in her lap,” Foster says.
His colleague responds that nobody else did either: “All I saw was two females in the car.”
Reckless and Aggressive
As the leaked video began to circulate on social media on Tuesday, much of the attention focused on the moment the car moved toward Foster.
The Senatobia Police Department claimed from the start that the car drove toward officers and nearly hit one, suggesting the shots were fired in self-defense. Darkhorse Press, the independent Mississippi outlet that first published the leaked footage, even stated in a headline that the car “actually hit at least two officers.”
Among those who have repeated a version of this story is Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, who said the driver tried to “run over the policeman,” despite admitting that he had not actually watched the footage.
What the videos show is that the police officers themselves needlessly escalated a shoplifting incident into the scenario that they claim put them at risk. Almost immediately after being informed that two people were “running,” the five armed officers sprinted out to the parking lot, surrounded the car, and, at various points in the confrontation, drew their guns. They also positioned themselves in a way that cut off any escape route for the driver.
These are reckless, aggressive tactics in response to a minor shoplifting charge. They also violate best practices in policing.
Most departments today prohibit officers from standing in front of the possible escape route of a car when someone inside is suspected of only minor offenses. Many also require officers to get out of the way of a vehicle if it drives toward them. While most departments authorize a police officer to use deadly force if they “reasonably” believe it’s necessary to protect their or others’ lives, this generally does not excuse using lethal force if the “reasonable” fear arose from a cop’s own violation of department policy.
Policies and best practices, however, don’t establish the bounds of legal liability; they are related but separate. Under the landmark Supreme Court case Tennessee v. Garner, a police officer can use deadly force if he “has a good-faith belief that the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others.” The law is less clear about criminal liability when an officer’s own illegal or ill-advised actions caused the circumstances that led him to fear for his safety.
Other examples of self-defense law hold people criminally liable if their own actions put them in harm’s way. In general, those cases indicate that a person can’t argue self-defense after killing someone if they instigated the altercation that led to the killing — even if it was reasonable to deploy lethal force when they did.
By that standard, if an officer puts themselves in the path of a moving vehicle, they shouldn’t be able to justify lethal force by claiming to fear for their life because the vehicle was about to hit them. The law, however, isn’t crystal clear on this, and there’s at least some indication that the current Supreme Court may adopt a more lenient standard for police officers.
Moving Vehicle
Most police departments prohibit officers from shooting into moving vehicles unless someone inside poses a direct threat to the safety of others unrelated to use of the vehicle itself — for instance, if the person is armed and shooting at people. The reason is simple: Killing the driver of a moving car does not stop the car and can therefore exacerbate threats to public safety.
Like many other departments, the Senatobia police department’s policy contains vague language warning officers that firing into moving vehicles is dangerous to bystanders and unlikely to stop a car; it reads more like guidance than prohibition. One portion of the policy, however, is much clearer: Officers “will not” discharge firearms into a fleeing vehicle — with “will not” underlined for emphasis.
It seems clear from the leaked footage that Ferrell, the driver, maneuvered the car in what appeared to be an attempt to flee rather than to kill or injure officers. The video shows her at first trying to reverse away from police. After striking the SUV, however, she then appears to try to drive around and then between the officers. She then strikes another car while trying to drive away.
Foster’s actions aren’t consistent with any reasonable concept of self-defense. Footage shows that he fired at least three shots into the passenger side of the car. This was already apparent in the leaked body camera footage. It’s even clearer in the newly released video from Foster’s camera. By the time he fires the first of the three shots, he is clearly beside — not in front of — the car. By the time he fires the last shot, the car has passed him.
Even if Foster wanted to claim that he fired to disable the driver — and, again, his own department firmly prohibits shooting at a fleeing car — he fired through the passenger side window. He did so despite being told that there were two people inside, which means that whatever the driver was doing, he was also putting the other person at risk.
Ultimately, the videos depict a driver showing far more awareness for the officers’ safety from behind the wheel than Foster showed for the occupants of the car — or the surrounding bystanders.
Police policies should reflect how people behave in the real world, and people accused of stealing tend to flee. For armed officers to quickly escalate a shoplifting allegation puts everyone nearby at risk. Amid the frenzied response from the cops, Ferrell struck two other cars while attempting to escape. Anyone in or near those cars could have been injured or killed. Foster also fired his gun in a crowded parking lot. That, too, could have resulted in additional death or injury.
The police had other options. They could easily have written down the car’s license plate or obtained the plate number from the numerous surveillance tools at their disposal: their body camera footage, Walmart security footage, or one of the many Flock cameras nearby.
If they had to arrest the women, they could have done so later, at home and under less duress. They may not have caught Wiley or Ferrell red-handed with the alleged stolen goods, theoretically making a shoplifting prosecution more difficult. Creating an obstacle to prosecuting a shoplifting case, however, should be an easy tradeoff for not putting lives at risk.
Walmart’s Role
Finally, the leaked video footage raises important questions about Walmart’s role in Kohen Wiley’s death. The company has yet to publicly comment about the incident — and has not responded to repeated inquiries from The Intercept.
When the Walmart employee in the hoodie entered the room where officers were viewing security monitors, he told them that two people were fleeing the store. He did not say that one of them had a baby in her arms, even though surveillance footage showed Wiley carrying Kohen as she passed him. This would prove consequential, as Foster said in video footage that he had no idea there was a baby in the car.
Does Walmart policy require staff to tell police when a suspected shoplifter is accompanied by children? And how often does Walmart call on police for such minor crimes?
This isn’t the first time aggressive policing of shoplifting at a Walmart has resulted in the death of an unarmed person. Earlier this year, deputies shot suspected shoplifters in two separate incidents at Walmarts in Florida. When police tackled a fleeing shoplifter in Anchorage, Alaska, recently, he pulled a gun and shot two officers before they returned fire, killing him.
Over the last 10 years, police have also shot suspected shoplifters at Walmarts in Miami; Decatur and San Antonio, Texas; Tempe, Arizona; Colorado Springs, Colorado; Chester, South Carolina; and Lake Forest, California. Most of the suspects were armed, but gunfire erupted only after police confronted them for shoplifting.
Walmart seems to have wavered over the years between aggressive crackdowns on suspected shoplifters and more lenient policies that factor in whether the suspect has been accused before, the necessity of the items they’re accused of stealing, and the value of the stolen goods.
Like many national retailers, the company’s policy when it comes to its own employees is to avoid confrontations with suspected shoplifters. A previous lawsuit revealed that the company’s stated policy as of 2010 was “PUT PEOPLE FIRST” (all caps in original) and prioritized “the physical well-being of suspects, customers and Walmart associates.”
That policy means little if the store simply outsources enforcement to police who take a far more aggressive approach. Walmart itself has also been criticized by police groups, who claim that cost-saving reductions in staff have made the store a more attractive target for shoplifting, which then leads to more calls to police.
And in Senatobia, the last high-profile incident of police violence before Kohen Wiley was killed took place in 2025 — at the same Walmart parking lot.
Even the best policing policies are useless if they aren’t enforced. And officers are rarely prosecuted, period. Foster’s resignation is at least some form of accountability, but the insistence from state officials that police did nothing wrong means there will be little to stop similar killings from happening again.
This week, residents of Senatobia returned to the Walmart for a vigil in honor of Kohen Wiley, in the same place where a makeshift shrine once stood. A community gathering has also been scheduled next weekend to mark what would have been his second birthday.
At the press conference Thursday, family and activists vowed to keep fighting for justice. As with so much police violence, however, the most pressing question isn’t whether Foster himself is punished. It’s whether we’re willing to tolerate more deaths like that of Kohen Wiley — whether Senatobia, Walmart, and the state of Mississippi will do anything to make clear that a 1-year-old’s life is more important than a pack of diapers.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: V&A proposing significant cuts to its academy amid financial pressures
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Sarvy Geranpayeh
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) has drawn up plans to dismantle much of the V&A Academy, a significant part of its adult-learning programme, by the end of the year, The Art Newspaper has learned. Around 50% of the Academy’s staff may be cut and the future of flagship courses are under threat. Senior figures in other parts of the museum have also been asked to propose cuts to their teams, according to people familiar with the plans.
The V&A has offered adult courses for decades, drawing on its collections and curators in a tradition that goes back to the museum’s origins as a school of design. In 2016 it launched the Learning Academy to run much of its learning programmes. It was later renamed V&A Academy, which today runs expert-led courses, practical workshops and talks. Its courses are taught mainly at the V&A’s South Kensington site and online.
The proposals for cuts to the Academy, which sits within the museum’s commercial department, were communicated to staff on 5 October and justified by management on the grounds that the programme had failed to meet income expectations, according to people with direct knowledge of the discussions. The changes would see many of the Academy’s in-person courses at South Kensington brought to an end, including flagship courses relaunched this year in a ten-week format, with a hybrid option allowing students to attend in person or online.
The Academy’s African heritage programme and professional-development courses for museum-sector workers are among the activities expected to be retained. Selected on-demand and live online courses are also expected to continue.
The consultation period for staff to discuss the proposals with management and provide feedback is due to end today (26 October), according to people with knowledge of the matter that The Art Newspaper spoke to.
The Art Newspaper has spoken to current staff members and others with knowledge of the plans, all of whom asked not to be named for fear of repercussions. “Nobody had any inkling this was going to happen,” says one staff member. Another adds that the museum is “full of people who are feeling very demoralised”. If the proposals go ahead, the Academy will cease to operate in its current form by the end of the year, according to people with knowledge of the plans.
A V&A spokesperson said in a statement sent to The Art Newspaper: “We are currently reviewing the V&A Academy offer and the way in which this is delivered as part of wider efforts to streamline activity and identify efficiencies across our operations to ensure they are financially sustainable and deliver maximum impact. We are still in the consultation phase, and no final decisions have been made, but the current proposals will see us continue to deliver an adult learning programme." The spokesperson made clear that the V&A would not be able to comment further at this time.
The proposed restructuring is striking in light of the Academy’s recent reported performance. The V&A’s 2024–25 annual report says the Academy recorded sales of £1.2m, an increase of more than 22% on the previous year, while its contribution to the museum rose by more than 60% to £365,000.
The 2025–26 annual report does not provide a full breakdown of the Academy’s annual income, expenditure or profit. Instead, it describes the Academy’s hybrid learning strategy as “combining scalable online formats with high-impact in-person art history experiences”, saying the approach expanded the programme’s “reach and resilience” during its first full year and “consolidated” the growth achieved the previous year.
The report also records that the hybrid course Arts of Japan “contributed to V&A Academy’s biggest ever quarter in spring 2026, when total sales exceeded £400,000”.
At the time of writing, one of the Academy’s five flagship 10-week hybrid courses, A History of London: 1066–1666, was marked as sold out on the museum’s website. People familiar with the proposals say all five courses, including Arts of Japan and A History of London, are expected to be discontinued.
Cuts and strikes
The proposed cuts come after a series of challenges for the V&A in recent months, including allegations of racism reported byThe Art Newspaper in July and strikes over pay and working conditions in September. The disputes over conditions continue: on 19 October, the Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union and Prospect announced further strike action across all four V&A sites (South Kensington, East Museum, East Storehouse and Young V&A) on 29 and 30 October. However, statements sent to The Art Newspaper today from both unions said that their members have suspended strike action, to allow for further talks after an “improved offer” from the museum.
The V&A has also launched a voluntary exit scheme open to staff across the institution, which is expected to close on 26 October, according to people with knowledge of its terms. In response to The Art Newspaper’s October report on the voluntary exit scheme, a spokesperson said inflation, economic uncertainty and reduced visitor spending were contributing to financial pressures, while below-inflation government settlements would reduce funding in real terms over the coming years. The V&A’s 2025–26 annual report records a 30% rise in retail net sales to £15.7m.
The accounts show that the museum received £59.9m in government grant-in-aid during the year, up from £56.2m in 2024–25 and representing 42% of the group’s income. A further £5.2m was awarded through the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund to support essential work to protect the buildings at South Kensington and Young V&A.
The proposals to make cuts at the Academy come against the backdrop of a major expansion of the V&A’s estate, including the opening of V&A East Storehouse in May 2025 and V&A East Museum in April 2026. Some staff believe the South Kensington museum is bearing the cost of expenditure associated with the new east London sites. “We suspect that the South Kensington site is paying for the financial problems associated with V&A East,” says one staff member.
Prospect’s national secretary for heritage, Paula Lamont, tells The Art Newspaper in a statement: “Our members are concerned that the financial cost of opening new sites is falling on them, rather than being absorbed in other areas. Heaping more workload and pressure on an increasingly demoralised workforce is unsustainable and cannot be the answer.”
According to a report by Arts Professional, the PCS union has claimed that the institution is projecting cumulative operational deficits of £19m by 2030. The V&A did not address the figure when asked by The Art Newspaper. Its latest annual report rates the risk to longer-term financial sustainability as high. It says: “Mitigations through commercial growth and cost reduction have been identified and form a central tenet of the V&A’s new five-year strategy 2026-30.”
How many staff may be affected?
The terms offered to V&A Academy staff remain unclear, with concerns that those with less than two years’ service may not qualify for statutory redundancy pay under UK law. The Academy has around 17 permanent staff, but its courses also feature guest lecturers from across the museum and beyond. According to information available via the V&A’s website, for 12 of the Academy’s courses this autumn, five hybrid and seven online-only, there are around 100 lecturers and speakers besides Academy staff, from curators elsewhere in the V&A to freelance lecturers and visiting academics, suggesting the effects of any cuts could be felt far outside the Academy.
Staff are also concerned about proposed cuts to teams across the wider museum, believed to be around 10-15%, which are expected to affect curatorial roles. A former senior member of staff who witnessed the V&A’s 2021 post pandemic restructuring, when approximately 15–20% of staff were let go, says curatorial and conservation teams are not among the museum’s largest costs and are important to its ability to safeguard collections, attract donors and develop projects. Cutting expertise, they argue, risks undermining the very work that helps secure donations.
The proposals have also surprised some in light of the museum’s director, Tristram Hunt, having served in education-focused roles previously. A historian and former Labour MP, Hunt served as shadow education secretary and has a reputation for championing learning.
The V&A’s annual report describes its purpose as promoting public enjoyment and understanding of art, craft and design, including through study and research. Its founder, Henry Cole, placed education and public access at the heart of the museum’s mission, a legacy that the proposed changes risk undermining, according to people familiar with the plans.
“Henry Cole will be spinning in his grave,” says one.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/ai-bubble-la.title: Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/ai-bubble-la.author: Cory Doctorow, David Moscrop
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/ai-bubble-la.text:
Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.
Cory Doctorow talks to us about the internet, whether machines are conscious, why copyright maximalism won’t save us from ChatGPT, and why workers still have a chance to shape what comes next.
The artificial intelligence boom is fueled by an elite wager that software can supplant expensive human expertise. The tech industry and its investors are pumping hundreds of billions of dollars into the technology — Goldman Sachs forecasts that global AI-related investment will soon exceed $1 trillion. At the same time, government regulatory regimes are inadequate and consumer use cases often vague, misleading, or utterly counterproductive.
The economics of AI don’t make sense unless one factors in what its backers hope to gain: a way to displace workers. In his most recent book, The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI, Cory Doctorow explains how people have become tools of the machines and the capitalists who own them.
Doctorow recently spoke to Jacobin to discuss the rise of AI, the financial conjuring tricks behind the boom, the copyright fight, what it all means for workers — and why the answer to AI doomerism lies in building workers’ rights and public power.

https://www.humanite.fr/sports/basket/ba.title: Basket : la Française Gabby Williams soulève le trophée de la WNBA avec le titre de meilleure joueuse
https://www.humanite.fr/sports/basket/ba.author: Axel Nodinot
https://www.humanite.fr/sports/basket/ba.text:
La basketteuse française a remporté cette nuit le titre WNBA avec son équipe, les Golden State Valkyries, au terme d’une performance exceptionnelle qui lui a valu le titre de meilleure joueuse des finales.
Après la victoire, elle avait les larmes aux yeux, levés vers le panthéon du basket auquel son nom est désormais inscrit. Gabby Williams a brillé dans la nuit du 31 octobre au 1er novembre sur la plus haute marche possible : le match 7 décisif des finales WNBA, le championnat états-unien féminin de basket.
L’ultime partie de la saison devait départager ses Golden State Valkyries, équipe créée il y a seulement deux ans, et l’Atlanta Dream avec des stars telles qu’Angel Reese et Rhyne Howard.
Si la capitaine des Bleues n’a pas inscrit un point avant la fin du deuxième quart-temps, elle a ensuite fait le show dans le troisième, en attaquant la raquette mais surtout en prenant feu derrière la ligne à 3 points. Et, alors que les deux équipes étaient à égalité à trois minutes de la fin, elle a pris la lumière et assumé son statut d’ailière star en inscrivant plusieurs paniers importants, dont un énorme tir à 3 points, deux mètres derrière la ligne.
Une performance rare
Avec 30 points en un match, une performance rare dans le basket féminin, et 20 points de moyenne sur les sept matchs, Gabby Williams a été élue MVP – meilleure joueuse – des finales.
Une récompense de plus à côté du trophée suprême, le titre WNBA, qu’elle partage avec ses coéquipières et deux de ses compatriotes, Janelle Salaün et Aminata Gueye. Après la médaille d’argent décrochée à la Coupe du monde cet été, la Française est sur un nuage.
Avant de partir, une dernière chose…
Contrairement à 90% des médias français aujourd’hui, l’Humanité ne dépend ni de grands groupes ni de milliardaires. Cela signifie que :
- nous vous apportons des informations impartiales, sans compromis. Mais aussi que
- nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers dont bénéficient les autres médias.
L’information indépendante et de qualité a un coût. Payez-le.
Je veux en savoir plus
