https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.title: Photos: Youth-led rallies sweep Germany
https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.text:
In Pictures
Photos: Youth-led rallies sweep Germany
Tens of thousands take to the streets across Germany’s biggest cities to demand better education and lower living costs.
Large demonstrations have taken place across Germany, and some have descended into violence with police firing water cannon at people throwing Molotov cocktails.
Several police officers were injured on Saturday after tens of thousands of people joined youth-led protests across the country organised by the group “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z has got this).
The demonstrations, inspired by similar movements in France and Italy, remained largely peaceful during the day.
But tensions escalated in the evening as groups of young people refused to disperse. Violence was reported in major cities, including Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
“Gen Z regelt” said about 120,000 people took part in the protests, below the roughly 180,000 it had expected.

https://taz.de/Handke-am-Schauspiel-Koel.title: Handke am Schauspiel Köln: Abschiedsreif geschlagen
https://taz.de/Handke-am-Schauspiel-Koel.author: Björn Hayer
https://taz.de/Handke-am-Schauspiel-Koel.text:
Handke am Schauspiel Köln: Abschiedsreif geschlagen
Wiederentdeckt und hochaktuell: Das Schauspiel Köln bringt Peter Handkes „Kaspar“ auf die Bühne und zeigt, wie Faschismus in Sprache, Denken und Handeln kommt.
Aller Anfang ist schwer. Vor allem wenn man eine, genauer: die erste Sprache lernt, sind Fehler und Verdrehungen erwartbar. Kuriose Nonsens-Sätze wie „Aber der Stuhl ist ein Ekel, weil er kein Tisch ist“ oder „Der Besen ist ein Wort, das du auf ein Schuhband anwenden kannst“ – can happen! Je weiter man allerdings heranwächst, desto eher bilden sich Logik und Ordnung heraus.
Aus dem Kind wird ein Erwachsener. Davon erzählt Peter Handkes Stück „Kaspar“ von 1967, das just am Schauspiel Köln wiederaufgeführt wurde. Zunächst ein beschauliches Thema also. Denn allzu nett bleibt es weder im Text noch auf der Bühne. Sprache, so die Botschaft, führt nicht nur zur Autonomie, sie trägt nicht nur dazu bei, dass wir die Angst vor den Dingen verlieren, die wir zuvor nicht zu benennen imstande sind. Vielmehr führt sie auch zur Anpassung, bisweilen zur blinden Übernahme von Halbwissen und Fakes.
Bevor das Geschehen auf der Bühne – so viel sei jetzt schon gespoilert – kippt, geht es in Claudia Bauers Inszenierung aber tatsächlich zunächst humorvoll-beschwingt zu. Lose angebunden an die Geschichte von Kaspar Hauser, einem Jungen, der 1828 in Nürnberg ankam und wegen seiner vorigen Isolation über keinerlei kommunikative Fähigkeiten verfügte, blickt bei ihr eine Kasparin auf die Vergangenheit zurück.
Auf einer Videoprojektion richtet sie einen Geburtstagskuchen an und verfolgt in den kommenden beiden Stunden das Treiben auf der Bühne zumeist über den Fernseher. Dort stellt das Ensemble (unter anderem Rebekka Biener, Elias Eilinghoff, Andreas Grötzinger) zu Beginn die symbolische Geburt nach. Als würden sich dessen Mitglieder aus einer Vulva herauskämpfen, schieben sie die hintere, aus braunen Pappkartons zusammengesetzte Bühnenwand zur Seite. Sobald die clownesken, blau kostümierten Figuren dies gemeistert haben, fällt der rote Vorhang. Die Aussage: Ab jetzt ist alles Theater, und zwar nicht nur metaphorisch, das Leben selbst erweist sich als Theatrum mundi.
Reichlich Slapstick
Dafür braucht es den richtigen Text. Mal kommt er nur schwer über die Lippen, mal sprudelt regelrechtes Kauderwelsch aus den Darsteller:innen hervor. Hilfreich sind indessen die Telefonkabinen auf der linken Seite. Klingelt es dort, nimmt eine:r ab und spricht die Sätze in ein Kabelmikrofon. Begleitet wird das lustige Fernsprech-Theater von reichlich Slaspstick. Besonders lustig mutet der Auftritt eines Spielers als gigantisches Fellwesen an. Doch irgendwann kippt die bunte Zirkusshow. Die Wendungen erhalten einen merkwürdig bedrohlichen Charakter. „Der Krieg ist zwar ein Unglück, aber manchmal unvermeidbar“, erfahren wir, oder „Der Fremde ist anders“; „der Verbrecher ist Abschaum“.
Um die Indoktrination dieser gefährlichen Phrasen zu veranschaulichen, findet sich das Ensemble in einer Schulklasse zusammen. Einer deklamiert, die anderen ergänzen, ganz vorne gibt die Dirigentin den Rhythmus vor. Jene Farce spitzt sich durch das Stakkato eines Klaviers dramatisch zu. Die sich nun nach und nach aufstauende und entladende Gewalt wird überhaupt bestens getragen von den phänomenalen Live-Musikern Arpen Daks und Elisabeth Coudoux. Sie beherrschen die leisen Momente wie die ganz lauten. Zu Letzteren gehört beispielsweise eine Szene, in der die Gruppe mit Baseballschlägern auf eine der ihrigen in einem Schrank einprügeln. Wenig später torkelt sie blutüberströmt heraus und ballert, zynisch unterlegt mit Percussion, mit einem Gewehr herum.
Klingt nach Comic? Im häufig grellen Licht drängt sich diese Assoziation schnell auf. Die flippige Aufmachung markiert eine ironische Fallhöhe zwischen der Situationskomik und dem Entstehen faschistischer Strukturen. Ja, auch wenn die Figuren noch so sehr bekunden, höflich und selbstbestimmt zu sein, scheinen sie fremdbestimmt, gelenkt von einer Sprache, die Aggression und Ausgrenzung normalisiert. Wenn gegen Ende eine Frau alle anderen mit einer Fliegenklatsche verdrängt und daraufhin die Darsteller:innen Fotoaufsteller ihrer Gruppenmitglieder zersägen, steckt dahinter nichts anderes als ein sich entladender Hass.
Jene Aktualität ist gewiss schon in Handkes Werk, das wie all seine Stücke auf Psychologie und Handlung verzichtet und eher einem Bühnengedicht gleicht, angelegt. Die Herausforderung, die Monotonie der Satz-an-Satz-Ästhetik wiederum unterhaltsam und bildreich zu realisieren, meistert Claudia Bauer exzellent. Geradezu atemlos treibt sie das Ensemble an, das sich einmal auch in völliger Dekadenz ergehen darf. Dazu öffnet sich der Hintergrund und ein Wohnkubus mit Klingersteinoptik wird nach vorne geschoben. Während er sich dreht, feiern die Spieler:innen im Inneren. Sie masturbieren oder befriedigen einander oral.
„Aber niemand wird ohne Grund“, heißt es in einem der vielen Gesprächsfetzen, „abschiedsreif geschlagen“. Vergegenwärtigt man sich, dass Handke diese Wendungen am Vorabend der 68er-Revolte schrieb und dabei noch immer die unaufgearbeitete Nazi-Zeit vor Augen hatte, muten sie beklemmend an. Der Abgrund ist groß, allen inmitten dieses herrlich überdrehten Rauschs.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Palestinians in Lebanon suffering worsened by high energy prices, inflation
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Palestinians in Lebanon suffering worsened by high energy prices, inflation
As one of Lebanon’s most vulnerable communities, Palestinians are struggling to make ends meet.
Beirut, Lebanon — Osama Najjar is a Palestinian refugee living in the Beddawi refugee camp in Tripoli, Lebanon’s second-largest city, where he used to have a shop selling aluminium.
Palestinians are barred from working in specific professions in Lebanon, including medicine, law, engineering and pharmacy, meaning that owning a shop is a crucial economic lifeline for many, regardless of their education levels.
But Najjar, like other Palestinians in Lebanon, says the situation has grown increasingly difficult, as rising inflation and energy costs hit one of Lebanon’s most vulnerable communities particularly hard. With business stuttering and unable to keep up with his bills, he was forced to close his shop in early 2024. Since then, he has found work hard to come by.
“The whole Palestinian situation in the camps is tragic,” he said, citing high prices and rising electricity bills as two of his most recent concerns.
Palestinian discrimination
Palestinians first became refugees in Lebanon during the 1948 Nakba, when Zionist forces established the state of Israel. In the process, they destroyed more than 500 Palestinian towns, killed about 13,000 Palestinians, and turned 750,000 more into refugees who fled to camps in the occupied West Bank and neighbouring countries.
Of those, about 100,000 people went north to Lebanon, many of them promising themselves that they would return home one day. Many slept in informal settlements and tents at first, but as the years passed and hopes of an immediate return to their hometowns and villages faded, tents gave way to informal and often unregulated concrete structures.
In 1964, Lebanon passed a decree on foreign workers that required non-Lebanese nationals to obtain work permits. During the country’s civil war, which lasted from 1975 to 1990, a wide range of Palestinian political groups took part in the fighting. This legacy left behind ill will towards Palestinians from some segments of the Lebanese population.
In 2010, amendments were made to the Lebanese labour law that reduced certain permit fees and eased other restrictions for Palestinian labourers, but experts say implementation was limited. In 2021, the Ministry of Labour issued a decree that was supposed to ease restrictions on some professions, which led to political backlash.
In February 2026, the Lebanese government introduced an administrative mechanism that allows Palestinian nursing students to apply for employment sponsorship. However, experts say many of these legal changes do not alter the structural exclusion of Palestinians from the Lebanese labour force.
Today, UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, recognises 12 Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon. According to its Lebanon office, about 222,000 Palestinians resided in the country as of February 2025.
“Palestinians in Lebanon have been treated very differently in a very discriminatory way,” Elia Ayoub, a United Kingdom-based Palestinian-Lebanese researcher and podcaster, told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to the fact that Palestinians can study for but cannot work in many top professions in Lebanon. They are not allowed to own land, and are not politically represented in the country’s parliament.
“Lebanon has an ethno-sectarian system, but Palestinians are not [recognised] one of them,” he said.
Funding cuts
Despite long-running institutional and social discrimination, the situation for Palestinians in Lebanon has become particularly acute in recent months.
The country is yet to recover from 2019’s economic and banking crisis. But rising energy costs and domestic inflation have hit Palestinians particularly hard.
The Lebanese state provides only a few hours of electricity per day, leading most residents to rely on private generators or alternative energy providers. Meanwhile, the World Bank predicts Lebanon’s inflation could reach as high as 17.5 percent in 2026.
In such difficult times, many Palestinians turn to UNRWA for aid. But many countries cut funding to the agency in 2024 after Israel alleged, without providing evidence, that its employees took part in the October 7, 2023 attacks.
UNRWA fervently denied the accusations, and in recent years many states have reinstated funding to the group. Still, in July, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of a funding shortfall of about $100m.
In September, the group reported that it will likely face a minimum $200m financial deficit between the end of 2026 and the start of 2027.
Taking to boats
With no options for a dignified life at home, many Palestinians are risking their lives by trying to reach Europe by sea. In 2022, at least 86 people died on a boat that left Lebanon and sank off the coast of Syria. Many of the dead were Palestinians from the camps.
The number of vessels leaving Lebanese shores increased in the years following 2019, with Palestinians on board many of them. The number of boats attempting to cross the Mediterranean to Europe doubled between 2020 and 2021 and increased by 121 percent the following year, according to the Friedrich Naumann Foundation.
As the cost of living becomes increasingly unsustainable on Lebanese shores, there are fears that more Palestinians and other vulnerable communities in Lebanon could start taking to the seas with increased regularity.
In late October, the European Union approved a support mission to Lebanon that would help strengthen security forces, including “support [for] maritime security governance”.
Najjar said today, the camps are filled with talk of people boarding boats to travel to Turkiye and then on to Greece. Without any kind of economic relief on the horizon, Palestinians may continue to look for reprieve, no matter the risk.
“All of this is still because the situation for Palestinians in Lebanon is poor,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Why you should treat charisma as a red flag
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Alex Curmi
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Recently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round!”
It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. Disagreements on topics like these frequently damage relationships, alienate friends and estrange loved ones.
How did things get so bad? I believe the answer is, in part, that we’re constantly exposed to a novel form of charisma. As a psychiatrist, I’ve always been fascinated by this quality: the magnetism that brings out a deep sense of trust, loyalty or enthusiasm in others. The psychology of charisma tells us that it is not necessarily a magic, undefinable X-factor, but rather a set of skills and behaviours. Sometimes people have it naturally, sometimes people learn it.
I have some experience with this. When I started my podcast a few years ago, I struggled (as I still do) with my monotonous voice. All the content creation experts said the same thing: switch up the pitch, pace and volume of your speech to maximise audience engagement. Slick production is optional, charismatic communication is not. Storytelling, body language, moral outrage and more can be mastered to help would-be internet personalities put a spell on their audience.
It’s been a huge lesson for me to discover how difficult it can be to discuss big topics in the mental health space responsibly, even as a trained professional. It’s also become shockingly clear how easily someone can distort the truth on, say, antidepressants, psychotherapy or ADHD when they have no experience or knowledge in that area – as long as they come across confidently and convincingly.
The dangers of charisma are nothing new, of course. History is filled with examples of people using charm to advance their interests. Dictators, cult leaders and con artists are all proof that an otherwise reasonable person can succumb to a well-executed charm offensive.
The difference now is one of scale. The 2024 US election, for example, was widely described as the “podcast election”, as both candidates (Trump more successfully) consented to numerous softball interviews on the medium. They reached millions, not with policy, but with good vibes. And you don’t have to be a public figure to leverage charm in this way – any video with the right allure can go viral, regardless of that person’s intentions or expertise.
Why are we so easily taken in by charisma? Like many aspects of our psychology, we can understand it more clearly through the lens of our evolutionary past.
Our ancestors spent most of their time (approximately 94% of human history) as hunter-gatherers, living in nomadic tribes that may have consisted of as few as 20 people. Groups that small, pitted against the forces of nature, needed strong leadership. Like many animals, humans have status hierarchies. High-status hunter-gatherers likely had many of the traits we still associate with charisma today: great eye contact, body language that signalled certainty, a persuasive voice.
The difference being that, back then, you had the opportunity to observe your peers all day, every day: their flaws, their virtues, their competence, often while facing lethal danger. If a person was merely superficially charming, you found out quickly. Charisma would only win out if accompanied by other important qualities, including sound judgment, good character and wisdom.
That’s not the case now. Technology allows us to shield the unpalatable parts of ourselves much more easily, selecting only the best bits for public consumption. Our brains did not evolve to process handpicked slices of someone else’s behaviour, detached from the rest of their lives, so we’re vulnerable to being duped. One frightening example is that of Ruby Franke, the parenting vlogger with millions of subscribers who was jailed for child abuse after two of her six children were found beaten and malnourished.
We spend a lot of time worrying about how the minds of teenagers are warped by the online world. We’re keenly aware how prone they are to manipulation by seemingly impressive figures. What we fail to realise is, we’re all teenagers when it comes to the internet. Algorithmic social media has only been around for about 15 years, and we remain largely unconscious of how routinely it bypasses our better judgment. Is there any way to grow out of this newly acquired susceptibility?
The best form of defence against the excesses of charisma is critical thinking. We should regard it as being like a collective immune system, and it should be central to our culture and the way we educate our young people. They should be taught how to evaluate sources, interpret information and recognise bias. Similarly, separating confidence from substance ought to be considered a basic life skill. Looking at counter-arguments when we are emotionally pulled to someone’s perspective should be routine, and changing our mind when it is emotionally difficult should be celebrated.
It would also be helpful for the average person to learn the fundamentals of confident communication. Not only can this help you express yourself when you have something of real value to offer, but it also teaches you to see through a person who would happily use such tactics to deceive or seduce.
All told, charisma should actually be a red flag that encourages us to be more sceptical of an individual, not less. When someone can convincingly hold court on important topics like finance, healthcare or the Middle East, we should ask questions. What experience do they have? Do they have a history of dishonesty? What do they stand to gain from this view? What need in me might this person be speaking to? For my part, the next time I discuss something important, I will go easy on the pitch, pace and volume, and try to let the facts speak for themselves.
Alex Curmi is a psychiatrist and host of The Thinking Mind podcast.
Further reading
Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman (Penguin, £16.99)
The Age of Magical Overthinking by Amanda Montell (Thorsons, £12.99)
The Anxious Generation by Jonathan Haidt (Penguin, £12.99)

https://taz.de/Die-Wasserbilanz-des-Somm.title: Die Wasserbilanz des Sommers: Zu trocken und zu heiß
https://taz.de/Die-Wasserbilanz-des-Somm.author: Nick Reimer
https://taz.de/Die-Wasserbilanz-des-Somm.text:
Die Wasserbilanz des Sommers: Zu trocken und zu heiß
Die Wasserbilanz für Deutschland setzt neue Negativmaßstäbe. Damit sich die natürlichen Speicher auffüllen, ist langer, großflächiger Regen nötig.
Deutschland geht das Wasser aus: Nach Auswertung der Pegeldaten durch das Science-Media-Center wird das hydrologische Jahr 2025/26 in Deutschland neue Negativmaßstäbe setzen. Demnach war bereits der vergangene Winter außergewöhnlich trocken, bevor dann ein zu trockenes Frühjahr und ein weiterer Dürresommer folgten: Die hohen Temperaturen sorgten dafür, das Pflanzen mehr Wasser verdunsteten. Das hydrologische Jahr endete am 31. Oktober.
„Ein trockener Winter führte dazu, dass sich das Grundwasser nicht erholt hat“, erklärt Thorsten Wagener, Professor für hydrologische Systeme an der Universität Potsdam. Dies führe dazu, dass über die Flüsse weniger Wasser abfließen kann. „Durch den steigenden Einfluss des Klimawandels verlieren wir die natürlichen Schnee- und Gletscherspeicher in Gebirgsregionen“, so Wagener. Dadurch würden viele Flüsse einen wichtigen Teil des Abflussvolumens einbüßen. Der Abfluss des Rheins betrug an mehreren Pegeln nur 50 Prozent des vieljährigen Mittelwertes der Periode 1991 bis 2020. Aber auch Oder, Elbe, Mosel, Donau, Inn oder Lech erreichten Werte, die als „sehr niedrig“ oder „extrem niedrig“ eingestuft werden.
Die Folgen: „Im Oberlauf leidet oft die Ökologie an zu warmen und sauerstoffarmen Flüssen“, so Wagener. Diese Abschnitte seien wichtige Zufluchtsorte für Fische und andere Lebewesen. „Im Unterlauf leidet dann die Gesellschaft durch geringes Transportvermögen für die Schifffahrt oder verminderte Wasserentnahme für die Kühlung von Kraftwerken.“
Zum Grundwasserproblem gesellte sich im abgelaufenen hydrologischen Jahr die Niederschlagsarmut: Nach Daten des Deutschen Wetterdienstes DWD fielen im Frühjahr bundesweit im Durchschnitt lediglich 126 Liter auf den Quadratmeter – 68 Prozent weniger als im Durchschnitt der Jahre 1961 bis 1990. Das sorgte dafür, dass der Unterboden Anfang Juli bundesweit bis in eine Tiefe von 1,8 Meter unter Dürre litt.
Zu früh zu hohe Hitze
Zur ausgeprägten Dürre trugen die hohen Temperaturen bei: Um sich selbst herrunter zu kühlen, verdunsten Pflanzen mehr Wasser. Eine Buche etwa kann ihre Umgebung um bis zu fünf Grad herunterkühlen, wenn ausreichend Wasser vorhanden ist. Die erste Hitzewelle kam in diesem Jahr ungewöhnlich früh Ende Juni. Dabei wurde in der Brandenburger Lausitz mit 41,7 Grad ein neuer Höchstwert in Deutschland gemessen.
Um die natürlichen Speicher wieder aufzufüllen, seien jetzt „überdurchschnittlich lange und großflächige Niederschläge als sogenannter Landregen erforderlich“, erklärt Enno Nilson von der Bundesanstalt für Gewässerkunde (BfG). Allerdings ist nicht sicher, dass dieser auch komme: „Der vorausgegangene Winter war in dieser Hinsicht unterdurchschnittlich, was eine Vorbedingung für das Niedrigwasserjahr 2026 war“, so Nilson. Die Projektionen zum Klimawandel würden zeigen, dass es in absehbarer Zukunft aufs ganze Jahr gesehen in Deutschland viel weniger Wasser geben werde.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/serbia-elect.title: Serbia’s Students Changed How Serbians Think About Politics
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/serbia-elect.author: Nina Djukanović
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/serbia-elect.text:
Serbia’s Students Changed How Serbians Think About Politics
The election win for Serbia’s Student List reflects a deep desire for more democratic ways of doing politics. The test now is to see how the different forces within the movement can collaborate in changing the country’s institutions.
On Sunday, the largest and most sustained student movement in Europe reached its culmination. After two years of protesting and organizing, this fall Serbia’s students mounted an electoral challenge to former President Aleksandar Vučić, who was this time running to become prime minister. His plans were foiled, as the Student List won with over half of all votes, ending fourteen years of rule by Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
With the Serbian election process traditionally marked by irregularities, vote buying, pressure on public workers to vote for the ruling party, one-sided media coverage, and other efforts to manipulate the results, the students faced an enormous task. It was far from clear whether Vučić would concede and accept his defeat in case the students won. The tensions were high throughout voting day, and especially toward the evening, when the reports spread that the center of capital Belgrade was becoming filled with police, riot control vehicles, and pro-government thugs.
A deciding factor was the voter turnout, which reached 69 percent, up from 58.7 percent in 2023. Such a high turnout recalled the historic elections of September 2000 when Slobodan Milošević, an ultranationalist dictator responsible for many of the war crimes of the 1990s, was finally defeated. On Sunday, people lined up for hours at polling stations across Serbia and around the world, where the diaspora also participated. Many of the polling stations had people waiting from 5 or 6 a.m., before they opened. The student movement was also successful in mobilizing election observers who covered almost all of the polling stations, making any effort to manipulate the results much harder.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Museum acquisitions round-up: a Joan Jonas dance performance and a squirrelly readymade
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Anna Brady
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Squirrel (1960, edition 1969) by Meret Oppenheim
Detroit Institute of Arts
Meret Oppenheim’s playful Squirrel, an assisted readymade first created in 1960 and produced as an edition in 1969, is one of more than 2,000 Modern and contemporary works of art that have been donated to the Detroit Institute of Arts (DIA) by the estate of the property developer and art collector Gilbert B. Silverman and his wife Lila. The scope is enormous, reflecting the Silvermans’ eclectic tastes, ranging from decorative arts and jewellery to performance pieces and time-based media, though there is a particular focus on works by Fluxus artists from the 1960s and 70s such as Joseph Beuys, George Maciunas and Yoko Ono, among others. These items join 130 other Fluxus works that were given to the DIA by the Silvermans’ foundation in 2008.
Wind (1968) by Joan Jonas
The Gund at Kenyon College, Gambier, Ohio, and the Smithsonian’s Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Washington, DC
Wind is one of two works by the American performance artist Joan Jonas (born 1936) that have been jointly acquired by The Gund and Hirshhorn, using funds donated by Agnes Gund and the Joseph H. Hirshhorn Purchase Fund. Wind, a silent black-and-white film and one of Jonas’s first collaborations with dancers, shows a group of performers battling strong winds on a snowy beach. Playing with ideas of perception, reality and viewer participation, it features two performers wearing mirrored costumes. Mirrors are integral to the other acquired work, Mirror Pieces Installation II (1969/2014). This multimedia piece centres on mirrors that both reflect the viewer and a television playing another of Jonas’s filmed performances, Nudes with Mirrors (1969), showing a man donning and taking off a mirrored jacket in front of yet more mirrors held by other performers.
The Van Eeghen drawing book (17th century)
Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam
Although successful in his lifetime, the Dutch artist Rombout Uylenburgh (around 1580–around 1627) fell into relative obscurity after his death, and few of his works survive. However, the rediscovery of this book of around 30 drawings by Uylenburgh and his workshop significantly adds to his oeuvre. The book has been donated to the Rijksmuseum by the Van Eeghen family, which has owned it for more than three centuries, though it was only around 20 years ago that the link to Uylenburgh was made. The book includes fully worked biblical scenes alongside quicker informal sketches of, for example, birds and animals. Most books of drawings from the period have been broken up, the sheets sold off separately, so this is a rarity and, having barely been exposed to light, the colours remain remarkably fresh.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: An embattled Karen Bass is fighting tooth and nail to keep her mayorship in LA. It might be too late
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Charles M Blow in Watts, California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
At the end of 2022, the four largest US cities – New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Houston – all had Black mayors. It was a historic alignment made possible by the aftereffects of the Black Lives Matter civil rights movement and the unprecedented wave of protests following the killing of George Floyd in 2020.
Six years on, only one of those mayors remains: the embattled Karen Bass of Los Angeles, who is facing a strong challenge from a younger, even more progressive challenger. Bass’s opponent is Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, although the group is considering rescinding its endorsement over her refusal to explicitly embrace the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel.
As the sociopolitical zeitgeist has shifted away from Black lives to the death of democracy, and people now fixate on affordability the way they once did social justice, Black mayors have had to adjust to a new reality, one in which their presence alone isn’t palliative, where they are having to defend their positions against challengers from their own left, some of a younger generation less content with mainline Democratic principles.
Bass attributes part of the challenge Black mayors have faced to the country’s on-again, off-again relationship with Black people. “Every now and then we’re popular, but we go out of popularity very quickly,” Bass said on a recent Friday in Watts at Nickerson Gardens, a large housing development. “So those same people that had BLM flags in their yard and DEI and ‘Oh my God, I just discovered institutional racism and mass incarceration. How did that happen?’ are now like, ‘I’m done with it.’”
Over the course of three days, the Guardian visited with Bass and discussed the race with her and her team. The racial frustration she feels came through abundantly. But her campaign, pushed back on its heels, is digging in and fighting to survive a shifting political landscape.
The actor Anne-Marie Johnson, a Bass surrogate, described a general “malaise” among potential Bass electorate. Indeed, that was very much a recurrent sentiment in interviews with voters, coupled with a frustrated defense of her. As Sonia Hooper, a five-decade Nickerson Garden resident, said, some people have grown cold on the mayor because “everybody is struggling”. She continued: “People that wasn’t even struggling a couple of years ago, they’re struggling.” According to Hooper, some may have had higher expectations of Bass than she could deliver upon. “Everybody thought that the person in office was going to help them get to the income level they were supposed to be at.”
The California Association of Realtors reported on Friday that housing affordability dipped in Los Angeles, and in the third quarter of 2026, already near historic lows, it dipped again, with just 15% of households in the city able to afford to buy a median-priced home. That pressure is reflected in public opinion as a poll in April by Los Angeles Business Council Institute found that 87% of voters in the city said housing affordability was a serious problem, with 63% having considered leaving the city because of it.
So Bass is leaning into her legacy as a native Angeleno and leaning on her staunchest supporters – Black voters – while also wooing those wary of her opponent. A poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies/LA Times released on Wednesday shows that her strategy may be paying dividends. The poll showed Bass surging from an 11-point deficit to making the race a dead heat.
But Bass faces some very real hurdles. When asked why polls show that young people in the city, those who would have come of age during BLM, overwhelmingly support her opponent, Nithya Raman, Bass quickly provides a caveat: “They’re not young Black people.” She continues, “They’re predominantly white, some Latino. That’s the demographic of DSA.”
Bass then raises another frustration: “By the way, from some of those white people, young white people, I’ve been shocked at the racial insensitivity, shall I say, shocked.” Bass said that there were “very specific examples”, and she offered one.
When there was a proposal to run a Metro line under the historic Lafayette Square neighborhood, a predominantly upper-class Black community, Bass says that she pushed back on the proposal and talked about the historical significance of the neighborhood and how transportation infrastructure had historically been used to fracture Black communities.
“As I was speaking, to see a group of young folks do this while I was speaking” – Bass shows a thumbs down – “cut particularly deep because there were young white folks who consider themselves very progressive.” She continued: “But, when it comes to the displacement of Black people and brown people, all of a sudden not so progressive.” The board of Los Angeles county’s transit agency voted to move forward with the project believing that the tunneling wouldn’t damage structures in the neighborhood.
Some Black people in the city would take issue with Bass’s contention that the dissent doesn’t include Black people. In a phone interview, Melina Abdullah, co-founder of both Los Angeles Black Lives Matter and Black Lives Matter Grassroots, said of Bass’s mayoralty, “These last four years with her in office have not translated into collective advancement for Black people or any marginalized group.” Abdullah was a longtime friend of Bass’s and says the mayor even wrote her children’s college recommendations, but she has been a critic since Bass’s first run, particularly on her approach to policing.
Bass, like the other three big-city Black mayors in 2022, was of another generation and sensibility than Abdullah. None of the four was younger than 55 when they became mayor. Bass was 69. Each mayor increased police budgets and some increased the size of the forces. Bass is now campaigning on not only keeping the police chief: in December she asked the city council to increase the police budget and expand the force.
Abdullah calls this “a betrayal” of mayors who “were elected because of our protests” and “then betray the core fundamental ask of the protests”. Bass went from being the lead author and sponsor of the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, when she was in Congress, and having the city’s powerful police union, the Los Angeles Police Protective League, spending $2m on racially charged television ads attacking her in her first run, to now being endorsed by that police union, which has spent nearly $3m against Raman. On the issue of public safety, Bass has gone from insurgent to embellishment. “If she loses,” Abdullah says, “she earns that loss.”
This is a sore spot among some of her supporters. At a 25 October NAACP screening of the new documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem, the people who said that they were Bass voters also expressed trepidation. Adrienne Riley said that Bass’s decision to defend the police chief was problematic: “It appears that she’s toed the line. You’re with the people, but yet you won’t speak out against or fire this particular police chief.”
But Raman has made her own mistakes on policing and public safety, which have likely stoked Bass’s support. During a debate last week, Raman said, “This city used to be the gold standard in terms of non-cooperation with immigration enforcement, years ago under the era of Daryl Gates.” Gates is a controversial former LAPD chief who resigned in the wake of the 1992 LA riots, leaving a bitter legacy of racial tensions and police brutality. Raman has apologized for the statement, but Bass has glommed on to this costly gaffe as a rallying cry against a candidate she seeks to portray as too naive and insensitive to the city’s history to be trusted.
On one Sunday afternoon at Bass’s campaign headquarters, a strip mall storefront in Baldwin Hills at the corner of South Le Brea Avenue and Obama Boulevard, Gabrielle Woods, a loquacious 70-year-old, sits by the door icing an ankle she sprained rushing to a phone banking session.
Woods is a devout supporter of Bass’s, but even she confesses, “I don’t think she’s campaigning as well as she should.” Woods believes Bass spends too much time answering criticism and not enough touting her record. The Bass campaign trumpets actions on homelessness, fast-tracking more home building, falling crime rates and a comprehensive infrastructure plan. And, speaking of the advantage Raman has in the polls among younger voters, Woods concedes, “It’s hard to fight energy.”
Indeed, of the roughly 100 people in the room, most are like Woods: Black women, many of them appearing to be middle-aged. There is a smattering of younger people, some of whom appear to be staffing the event. One of the younger people is 26-year-old Diamond Brooks, a boxer and aspiring Olympian, who was brought to the event by a promoter. Brooks is a supporter of Bass’s, but a lukewarm one. He opts out of the phone banking and sits quietly on a cobalt blue sofa eating a Subway sandwich.
Woods believes Bass is suffering from an “anti-status quo-ism instead of an anti-Bass-ism”, and the Raman campaign might partly agree with that. A spokesperson for the Raman campaign said that what those young people believe is “that the status quo is broken, and that was true in 2020 as well”. The Raman campaign believes young people are drawn to her for two reasons: “an extension of this movement that was fed up with the political establishment” and a desire for a current change to make living more affordable and government more responsive.
Another stubborn issue that has dogged Bass is homelessness, one that she campaigned on fixing but has proven thorny, if not intractable. After driving down homelessness for two years, this year saw it tick back up, a change Bass blames on federal and state funding cuts.
It is an issue on which her passion is apparent. While talking in a seating area of the governor’s mansion on Saturday morning and then taking a driving tour of the Skid Row area of the city, Bass repeatedly refers to the homeless as “our people” because they are disproportionately Black. According to the Los Angeles homeless services authority, 50% of the people on Skid Row are Black, as are 34% of unhoused people in the city overall, but Black people comprise less than 9% of the city’s total population.
She touts Bass as an egalitarian leader. “She’s not particularly Black,” Woods says, underscoring that Bass isn’t governing as a Black mayor, but as a mayor who happens to be Black. But that might prove a complicated impression, as Bass leaned into the Black community for turnout as election day approaches.
Then there was Bass’s absence from the city when the devastating Palisades fires started – she was on a diplomatic trip to Ghana – and the slow pace at which displaced residents have been able to rebuild and return.
During the last mayoral debate, Bass offered an apology, saying: “I am so profoundly sorry that I was not in my city when my city needed me.” But Raman still hammered her for her absence and response to the fires, saying that she was in the emergency operations center during the fires as 60,000 residents of her district were evacuated. “The question that I heard over and over there, and across the entire city, was ‘Where is our mayor, where is our mayor?’”
Bass said that if she had it to do over again, “I sure as heck wouldn’t have gone”. But she is convinced that the withering criticism she received wasn’t only because her absence rankled Angelenos, but the racial dimension of where she was. “I think where I went had a lot to do with it,” she said. Bass said that Houston’s then mayor, Sylvester Turner, a Black man, had warned her: “Don’t go to Africa in your first term.”
In the end, Bass has settled into closing argument of both flashing alarm and guiding light: convincing voters that Raman is too much of a risk for the city to take, a candidate who doesn’t know or understand the city well enough to lead, while also convincing them that her policies are working but need more time to come into full fruition.
As Bass told the phone bank crowd about Raman: “It’s very hard to say that you want to be mayor of this city, and you’ve never heard of Rodney King.”

https://taz.de/Unterdrueckung-von-Medien.text:
Unterdrückung von Medien in Venezuela: Geldstrafen, Verhaftungen, Schließungen
Um die Demokratie in Venezuela wiederherzustellen, braucht es Meinungs- und Pressefreiheit. Doch noch gelten dort restriktive Gesetze.
Stellen Sie sich vor, Sie könnten weder aus den Medien noch aus den sozialen Netzwerken erfahren, dass die rechtsextreme Partei AfD nach den Wahlen im September in Sachsen-Anhalt zum ersten Mal den Vorsitz in einem deutschen Landtag übernommen hat. Oder dass Polizei oder Militär Sie auf der Straße festnimmt, nur weil Sie die Unpünktlichkeit der Bahn kritisieren. Oder dass Sie des Terrorismus bezichtigt werden, weil Sie an Massendemonstrationen zur Verteidigung demokratischer Werte teilgenommen haben.
Versetzen Sie sich nun in die Lage einer Journalistin, welcher der Zutritt zu Regierungspressekonferenzen regelmäßig verwehrt wird und die von Beamten statt Informationen von öffentlichem Interesse nur die Tür vor der Nase zugeschlagen bekommt.
Euromérica-Workshop
15 Journalist:innen aus 12 Ländern Lateinamerikas nehmen am Workshop „Euromérica“ der taz panterstiftung teil. Es geht um Chancen und Herausforderungen des EU-Mercosur-Abkommens und die lateinamerikanisch-europäischen Beziehungen. Am 5. 12. erscheint dazu eine Beilage in der taz, am 9. 12. gibt es einen öffentlichen Talk in der taz Kantine. Alle Texte finden Sie hier.
Eine Reporterin, die im schlimmsten Fall wegen „Anstiftung zum Hass“ kriminalisiert und vor Gericht gestellt wird und allein wegen der Ausübung ihres Berufs mit Freiheitsstrafen von maximal 20 Jahren rechnen muss – während das Medium, für das sie arbeitet, mit Geldstrafen belegt oder sein Erscheinen untersagt wird, weil es Inhalte verbreitet, die als Verstoß gegen ein Gesetz angesehen werden, das angeblich für „friedliches Zusammenleben und Toleranz“ erlassen wurde.
Und obwohl die Pressefreiheit auch in Europa zunehmend unter Druck gerät und dort inzwischen weniger Menschen dem öffentlichen Rundfunk und vermeintlichen „Mainstreammedien“ vertrauen, dürfte ein solches Szenario für europäische Bürger:innen kaum vorstellbar sein. Dort ist die Meinungsfreiheit als Säule der Demokratie ausdrücklich durch die Charta der Grundrechte der Europäischen Union geschützt. In Deutschland gilt sie als unverzichtbare Grundlage der politischen Debatte – und ihr „demokratiekonstitutiver Charakter“ wurde vom Bundesverfassungsgericht ausdrücklich bestätigt.
Repressionen gegen mehr als 400 Medien
Europäer:innen mögen die oben beschriebenen Umstände in Venezuela übertrieben erscheinen. Doch sie sind Realität in einem Land, das drei Jahrzehnte lang unter den Regierungen von Hugo Chávez (1999–2013) und Nicolás Maduro (2013–2026) den Verfall demokratischer Freiheiten erleben musste. Diese wurden schließlich in einem diktatorischen Apparat aus Unterdrückung bürgerlicher und politischer Rechte, Machtkonzentration, Verfolgung der Opposition sowie polizeilicher und militärischer Repression erstickt.
Moderatoren-Avatare und Nachrichten im Bus
Auf die Repressionen in ihrer Heimat reagieren Medien und Journalist:innen in Venezuela mit viel Kreativität: Um ihre Identität zu schützen, wurden etwa mithilfe von KI Moderatoren-Avatare mit venezolanischem Akzent geschaffen.
Die ernüchternde Bilanz der Meinungs- und Pressefreiheit im letzten Vierteljahrhundert in Venezuela sieht so aus: Mehr als 400 Medien, darunter Radio- und Fernsehsender, Printmedien und Onlineportale, wurden geschlossen, beschlagnahmt oder zur Einstellung ihres Betriebs gezwungen. Bis September 2026 blieben allein bei einem der zwei großen Internetanbieter fast 150 Domains gesperrt, von denen mehr als die Hälfte unabhängigen Medien sowie nationalen wie internationalen Nachrichtenportalen gehören. All diese Zahlen wurden von lokalen Organisationen akribisch dokumentiert.
Zwischen 2020 und 2024 wurden mehr als 20 Reporter- und Fotograf:innen unter dem Vorwurf des Terrorismus und der Bildung krimineller Vereinigungen inhaftiert. Rechtsgrundlage dafür ist das „Verfassungsgesetz gegen Hass, für friedliches Zusammenleben und Toleranz“. Es wurde 2017 als Instrument zur Kriminalisierung des Journalistenberufs und zur Förderung einer der schädlichsten Formen sozialer Kontrolle – der Zensur – erlassen und trieb viele venezolanische Journalist:innen ins Exil.
Restriktives „Anti-Hass“-Gesetz gilt bis heute
Während in Europa Zensur ausdrücklich verboten ist, wird sie in Venezuela durch digitale Sperren, Geldstrafen und behördliche Schließungen praktiziert. Zwar erkennt die Verfassung von 1999 die Meinungsfreiheit als Recht an, doch wurde sie Konzepten wie der „Stabilität des Staates“, dem „sozialen Frieden“ und der „kommunikativen Hegemonie“ untergeordnet.
Jetzt unterstützen!
Unterstützen Sie die taz panterstiftung und ihre internationalen Projekte mit einer Spende. Mehr erfahren
In der Logik des Chavismus ist ein Journalist kein Hüter einer pluralistischen Demokratie, der rechtlichen Schutz genießt, wie dies in der Europäischen Union der Fall ist, sondern ein der Regierung untergeordneter Akteur.
Wie es nun unter Interimspräsidentin Delcy Rodríguez weitergeht, muss sich noch zeigen. Das restriktive „Anti-Hass“-Gesetz von 2017 ist bis heute in Kraft. Laut Digitalrechte-Organisation VE Sin Filtro wurden Mitte September immerhin 17 Nachrichten-Webseiten und Medien entsperrt, die zuvor jahrelang zensiert worden waren. Doch viele andere werden noch blockiert – 188 Websites sollen weiterhin nicht erreichbar sein, darunter 79 Nachrichtenportale.
Es bleibt abzuwarten, ob die derzeitige Phase politischer und wirtschaftlicher Veränderungen, die durch die Entführung Maduros am 3. Januar 2026 in die USA ausgelöst wurde, zu einem Übergang in eine echte Demokratie führen kann. Venezuela könnte sich dafür an den Grundsätzen Europas zur Meinungsfreiheit orientieren – statt sich weiter von den USA bevormunden zu lassen. Deren Präsident Donald Trump hat bekanntermaßen auch ein schwieriges Verhältnis zur freien Presse.
Lisseth Boon Bartolozzi ist eine Investigativjournalistin aus Venezuela. Sie ist u. a. für die unabhängige Medienplatform Armando.Info tätig.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/food-workers.title: The Food Industry Is Rife With Worker Abuse
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/food-workers.author: Errol Schweizer
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/food-workers.text:
The Food Industry Is Rife With Worker Abuse
Food systems employ more workers than any other sector of the global economy — roughly 1.4 billion people. And few industries are more rife with worker abuse.
Two things in life are certain: everybody eats, and nothing explains capitalism better than food. A new report from the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food) presents a comprehensive analysis of the exploitation inherent in the global food system, and what needs to be done to change it.
More people work in food than any other sector of the global economy, yet the food system can only function through systemic exploitation. Addressing these contradictions gives us a blueprint for not only tackling the worst aspects of food production but a model for taking on the worst of capitalism in general.
Food systems employ more workers than any sector of the global economy. Roughly 1.4 billion people work in food systems — that’s two out of every five working people. Food workers face low pay, wage theft, forced and child labor, human trafficking, insecure work, discrimination, sexual violence, occupational health and safety risks, and exclusion from social protections. Nearly four hundred million food system workers earn below a living wage. Minimum wage protections are often weak or absent for food system workers, with farmworkers consistently ranked among workers most likely to live in poverty.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Arte Povera’s Marisa Merz honoured with trio of Turin shows
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Florence Hallett
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
A major survey celebrating Marisa Merz (1926-2019), Arte Povera’s only female artist, will open across three institutions in Turin this week. Marking 100 years since her birth, The Dance of the Hours will take place at the Castello di Rivoli Museo d’Arte Contemporanea; the Fondazione Merz; and the Galleria Civica d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Torino (GAM). It is reckoned to be an undertaking of such magnitude that it is unlikely ever to be repeated.
Though it will be by far the biggest exhibition ever dedicated to Marisa Merz, the project is not unprecedented. In 2005, the same three institutions joined forces to honour Mario Merz, her husband and collaborator, following his death in 2003.
Now, the centenary presents an opportunity for those institutions to explore the career and legacy of Marisa Merz, says Francesco Manacorda, the co-curator, along with Marianna Vecellio, of the exhibition at the Castello di Rivoli.
The artist’s estate, represented by Fondazione Merz, retains the majority of her works, which include sculpture, works on paper and documented actions, but the collaboration offers more than exceptional access, Manacorda says. “It’s really three different approaches, and this will give you three different Marisas, which is appropriate, because she created a mystery around herself, and hid herself behind it. There is a ‘polyphonic’ Marisa that it’s possible to bring out.”
The ten contemporary artists commissioned to respond to Merz at Castello di Rivoli are essential to this multi-voiced approach, Manacorda says. Contributions from artists such as Leonor Antunes, Thea Djordjadze and Lara Favaretto, and a film by Tacita Dean, will amount to “a piece of art history”,Manacorda says.
Despite achieving considerable acclaim, including a Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale in 2013, Merz tended, often deliberately, to slip from view. The details of her life prior to her marriage in 1960 are sketchy and so are the reasons for her decision in the mid-1980s to step back from solo shows. Theories range from a need to concentrate to a dislike of competition or attention. “Some people claim it was a feminist choice—she had a daughter, and she writes about the fact that she wanted to work with [her daughter] Beatrice when she was a toddler,” Manacorda says.
The domestic nature of Merz’s practice set her apart from her fellow poveristi and will provide the focus of the presentation at GAM. The family home was her studio, and her materials and techniques—from kitchen foil, staples and peas to sewing and knitting—were unassumingly homely.
Monstrous domesticity
“The home as a workspace was not a matter of practicality but of methodology,” says Beatrice Merz, who is now the president of Fondazione Merz, whose exhibition will explore process and transformation. “The home itself was an opportunity for making and working”.
Merz’s first major work was Living Sculpture (1966), a sprawling construction of aluminium foil, stapled together in a process that Merz said—surely with irony—was “as humble and modest as embroidery.” Now held by GAM, it was captured most memorably in photographs of her apartment, where its shiny tubes spilled like alien entrails from behind the television, almost engulfing the dining table. Made during hours at home caring for her daughter, Living Sculpture makes visible, and monstrous, maternal labour in a radical rejection of conventional domesticity. The sculpture frightened Beatrice as a child and in 1967 it featured in the avant-garde horror film Il Mostro Verde (the green monster).
The apartment was left intact following Merz’s death in 2019 and contains unknown quantities of works in progress, “some of which have never been seen, not even by Beatrice”, Manacorda says. The exhibition’s title was taken from one of many Post-it notes that Merz stuck around the apartment.
Even works that made it into the public sphere could lapse into obscurity. The focus of the Castello di Rivoli show is a reconstruction of E il Naufragar M’è Dolce In Questo Mare (roughly translated as “to be shipwrecked is sweet in such a sea”, a line borrowed from a Giacomo Leopardi poem). The work is a complex, multi-part installation that disappeared after its second outing at the Venice Biennale in 1980. Reconstructing it has been a process of recovery, with the arrangement of original elements, such as sheets of brown paper found in the apartment, being guided by photographs and an eyewitness account. Although if Merz were alive today “she would probably make it differently”, concedes Manacorda.
The provisional nature of much of Merz’s work and its inherent fragility makes its ongoing care particularly challenging. Conservation decisions are made on a case-by-case basis and in collaboration, Manacorda says. “The precarity that you perceive really is part of the work, but conservators and collectors are not necessarily ready to accept that fragility.”
• Marisa Merz: The Dance of the Hours, Castello di Rivoli Museo d’Arte Contemporanea, Fondazione Merz and Galleria Civica d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea, Turin, 29 October-4 April 2027

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Romeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with Shakespeare
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Romeo + Juliet is not the most renowned or beloved of Shakespeare’s plays, but it is perhaps the most foundational. The 16th-century tragedy, a story of love-addled teenagers and white-hot resentment, is often an English student’s first introduction to the bard’s oeuvre – more accessible and relatable to teens, with its plaintive lust and histrionic mood swings, than the more austere machinations in, say, Macbeth, Hamlet or Othello. And if Romeo + Juliet is the young person’s entry to Elizabethan English, perhaps no version of it is more worthy of the term “gateway drug” than Baz Luhrmann’s 1996 film version, which reimagined Verona’s family feud as a tropical gang war and launched an army of teenage crushes with the faces of Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes.
The maximalist interpretation of Shakespeare’s most lovelorn work, released 30 years ago this week (!), retains Elizabethan verse but announces its divergence from rigid classicism from the jump. Our scene is set in fair Verona beach by a news anchor via TV set, relaying the woe of two star-cross’d lovers before clips of civil strife. Fresh off his breakout success in 1992’s Strictly Ballroom, the Australian director boldly mapped the medieval story on to 90s tabloid fixations – grainy footage of violence in the streets, magazine headlines of capos and criminals, helicopter views of car chases and riots that recalled the media circus around the OJ Simpson chase two years prior. It is a movie that could have only been made in the 90s; Luhrmann’s vision of two warring families as rival gangs, replete with their own economic operations and marked territory, tapped into the era’s preoccupation with gangland as a source of transportive art, from movies to hip-hop, and as a conservative fixation for ideas on intrinsic criminality.
Luhrmann and his wife, costume designer Catherine Martin, reimagined Verona as a sun-scorched beach city, incorporating real locations – Mexico City’s famed Immaculate Heart of Mary Church and Chapultepec Palace, Veracruz’s Boca del Río – to convey an urban den of simultaneous reverence and decay. The Montagues, with their heedless hollering and open Hawaiian shirts, and the Capulets, urban cowboys in Cuban-heeled boots, nearly vibrate with loathing and brandish guns marked by Catholic iconography. Perhaps compensating for the at times impenetrable verse, Luhrmann cut and spliced and twirled the camera in a frenetic, at times literal firework display of manic energy. The film’s raucous shootouts and parties now read as an obvious precursor to Euphoria high school – these kids dressed up and showed out, popped ecstasy and ripped around town in souped-up cars. Watching a single scene, even the lovers’ infamous fish tank meet-cute, has the feel of chugging an energy drink.
As such, the blatantly youth-aimed film had plenty of detractors in its time. Critics dismissed it as vulgar and garish, but audiences turned out en masse; Romeo + Juliet made over $147m against a $14.5m budget, boosted in part by a period-defining soundtrack with needle drops from The Cardigans, Everclear, Radiohead and Garbage. (And of course, the song from that oft-replayed fish tank scene, Des’ree’s I’m Kissing You, became the ubiquitous soundtrack for couple-shipping montage videos on 2000s YouTube). By the time I first viewed the film in 2009 – like many, in high school English class, as part of my teacher’s bid to get us invested in Shakespeare – it was already considered a classic.
That my teacher’s bid worked is largely due to the performances of the film’s two luminous stars, both brimming with the type of uncut, untameable desire known only to youth. Romeo + Juliet, of course, was a movie about teenage obsession that sparked a million teenage obsessions with DiCaprio (including from yours truly, who cried in English class not over the lovers’ double suicide – soooo melodramatic of them! – but over the realization that youth is fleeting and I would never be with anyone so beautiful. Devastating!) But it is a 17-year-old Danes, in a role originally intended for a text-accurate 13-year-old Natalie Portman (correctly deemed too childlike next to a 21-year-old DiCaprio), that shines on a rewatch. Her beauty is wide-open and uncomplicated, her face shaded with feelings as fresh and fleeting as morning dew. When her face falls, upon realizing her lover’s suicide, you feel, too, the ear-ringing fall of one’s first galling disappointment, the lurch of a sickening comedown.
That is the genius of Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet: it is a feelings-first movie, a portrait of teenage melodrama where all emotions exist only at full volume. That’s true for the highs – when the lip-locked lovers careen across a pool, or when Harold Perrineau’s Mercutio enters the scene with a high-kick in full silver drag to Kym Mazelle’s Young Hearts Run Free – as with the lows. In Luhrmann’s vision, Mercutio’s death at the hands of John Leguizamo’s Tybalt, a devilish sharpshooter with a soul patch, lands as equally tragic and torturous as the lovers. Perrineau stumbles, processes and curses both houses with such fervor as a real hurricane swept into Veracruz, that the rest of the film feels muted without him. And still, Romeo’s agonized poisoning, which frankly puts DiCaprio’s more famous death in the North Atlantic to shame, lands as a timeless gut-punch. So much youthful idealism and beauty, wasted on such petty grievances.
Luhrmann’s masterpiece more than transcended the more straightforward Shakespeare adaptations of the era, such as Kenneth Branagh’s Much Ado About Nothing (1993) and Hamlet (1996), Trevor Nunn’s Twelfth Night (1996) and Michael Hoffman’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1999). It arguably inspired the many modernizations kicked off by the runaway success of 1999’s 10 Things I Hate About You and continued by Easy A and She’s the Man. It quite evidently inspired a recent Broadway revival, starring Rachel Zegler and Kit Connor, that borrowed the Romeo + Juliet styling and the film’s stir-crazy bombast. But nothing has quite captured the imagination, or imparted the hot blood coursing in Shakespeare’s literary characters, like those two cursed houses in Verona beach. Thirty years on, we are still waiting for the next truly great, pop culture-shifting Shakespeare moment.
- Romeo + Juliet is available to watch on Hulu and HBO Max in the US, and on Disney+ in the UK and Australia

https://taz.de/Wissenschaft-unter-Druck/.author: Annika Danielmeier
https://taz.de/Wissenschaft-unter-Druck/.text:
Wissenschaft unter Druck: „Wir müssen das Recht verteidigen“
Rund 200 Jurist:innen betonen in einer gemeinsamen Erklärung die Bedeutung des Rechtsstaats. Eine Mitinitiatorin erklärt, warum.
Beispiele dafür, wie die Rechtswissenschaft zunehmend unter Druck gerät, gibt es einige. Da wäre der Fall Frauke Brosius-Gersdorf, die neue Richterin am Bundesverfassungsgericht werden sollte, von der Union aber nicht mehr gewählt werden wollte, nachdem rechtskonservative bis rechtsextreme Medien eine Kampagne gegen die Kandidatin gefahren hatten.
Da wäre aber auch zum Beispiel der Versuch der AfD im Juni dieses Jahres, 14 Vorträge des studentischen Kongresses „Take back the future“ an der TU Berlin zu verhindern. Die AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt, die jüngst die dortige Landtagswahl gewonnen hat, will wiederum laut ihrem Wahlprogramm Richter:innen anweisen, mit „maximaler Härte“ vorzugehen und den „Strafrahmen voll auszuschöpfen“.
Eine Entwicklung, dem viele Strafrechtler:innen etwas entgegensetzen wollen. Rund 200 von ihnen haben sich deswegen mit einer Erklärung aus der Strafrechtswissenschaft zur Bedeutung von Rechtsstaat, Demokratie und Unabhängigkeit der Wissenschaft zu Wort gemeldet. Initiiert haben ihn die fünf Strafrechtsprofessorinnen Liane Wörner, Susanne Beck, Stefanie Bock, Katrin Höffler, Charlotte Schmitt-Leonardy und Georgia Stefanopoulou. An dem Text hätten aber noch mehr Leute mitgewirkt, das ist Wörner wichtig zu erwähnen.
„Wir sehen eine Entwicklung, in der das Recht sich eines Tages nicht mehr selbst erwehren könnte und wir es verteidigen müssen – die Weichen dafür müssen wir heute stellen“, sagt Wörner, Professorin für Strafrecht an der Universität Konstanz, der taz. Es sei ein schleichender, sich langsam verdichtender Prozess gewesen.
Strafrechtler:innen mit öffentlichem Appell
„Menschenwürde, Freiheit und Gleichheit, die umfassende Grundrechtsbindung aller staatlichen Gewalt, Gewaltenteilung, Gesetzmäßigkeit und Verhältnismäßigkeit staatlichen Strafens, die Unschuldsvermutung sowie die Unabhängigkeit der Justiz bilden grundlegende Voraussetzungen einer freiheitlichen Rechtsordnung“, heißt es in der Erklärung. Sie seien auch Maßstab von Forschung, Lehre und Praxis des Strafrechts.
Eine Gefährdung der Grundlagen zeige sich dort, wo die „Bindung staatlicher Gewalt an Gesetz und Recht relativiert wird, unabhängige Gerichte als politisch, ideologisch oder illegitim dargestellt und in ihrer Autorität untergraben werden, wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse pauschal delegitimiert oder politische Entscheidungen von Recht und empirischem Wissen entkoppelt werden“. Die Strafrechtswissenschaft dürfe dies nicht hinnehmen.
Inzwischen haben sich rund 200 Strafrechtler:innen der Erklärung angeschlossen. Die Erklärung sei ein Versuch, die Entwicklung zu stoppen, sagt Wörner. „Es geht unter anderem darum, Gerichte, Richterwahlen, wissenschaftliche Expertise zu schützen, bevor institutioneller Schaden eintritt, der dann vielleicht nicht mehr zu reparieren ist.“
Ähnliche Erklärung der Strafrechtswissenschaft
Vor einigen Wochen haben bereits rund 230 Jurist:innen aus dem Zivilrecht eine ähnliche Erklärung abgegeben, die „Hallesche Erklärung“. Dieser haben sich die Strafrechtler:innen nun angeschlossen: „Die Hallesche Erklärung aus der Zivilrechtswissenschaft hat in eindringlicher Weise daran erinnert, dass die Wissenschaft – gerade auch die Rechtswissenschaft – Verantwortung für die Grundlagen eines freiheitlichen, demokratischen und rechtsstaatlichen Gemeinwesens trägt.“ Deshalb möchten sie die „zentralen Anliegen aus der Perspektive der Strafrechtswissenschaft bekräftigen“, schreiben die Jurist:innen.
Die Bedeutung des Strafrechts für Demokratie und Rechtsstaat herauszustellen, sei ihnen wichtig. „Das Strafrecht erlaubt tiefe Eingriffe in die Menschenrechte, die ohne eine rechtsstaatliche Bindung leicht zu Instrumenten politischer, sozialer oder ideologischer Disziplinierung werden können“, so steht es in der Erklärung. Dann könnten für Personen Unterschiedliches gelten, „und das darf nicht sein“, sagt Wörner. „Wenn wir über das Strafrecht diskutieren, diskutieren wir letztlich auch über Fragen staatlicher Macht. Wir diskutieren über individuelle Freiheit.“

Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. Iranian lawmaker warns of 'harsher reply than before' to new threats
Ebrahim Azizi, Chairman of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee of the Iranian Parliament, has said the country's armed forces will respond to any new threats with "an immediate and harsher reply than before".
In a post on X, he wrote: “Leader's command is final and binding; we will respond to any threat with an immediate and harsher reply than before, and we will have no limitations in geography or target bank.”
“To any threat, we will deliver an immediate and even harsher response-with zero limits and an open bank of targets,” Azizi said.
