https://jacobin.com/2026/10/china-mievil.title: China Miéville’s The Rouse Is a Haunting Magnum Opus
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/china-mievil.author: Jon Repetti
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/china-mievil.text:
China Miéville’s The Rouse Is a Haunting Magnum Opus
The Rouse follows a secret British effort to weaponize ghosts amid the Cold War and decolonization. A supernatural spy thriller, a Marxist meditation on history, and a stylistic triumph, China Miéville’s novel is a masterwork two decades in the making.
China Miéville’s The Rouse is a book that should not exist, and yet here it is. It should be read cover to cover, and then immediately read a second time. For twenty-one years, Miéville wrote and rewrote it while publishing shorter works at an impressive pace: four novels; two novellas; a history of the Russian Revolution; a book-length essay on The Communist Manifesto; an out-of-left-field collaboration with Keanu Reeves; a children’s book with Zak Smith; countless articles and reviews. Each of these now seems like a stepping stone on Miéville’s path toward his great project.
Into The Rouse’s 1,200-plus pages have gone a lifetime of writing as well as a lifetime of reading — Miéville’s influences range from pulp horror to high modernism, from Marxist theory to esoterica. From the bones of this personal canon, he has developed the most ambitious and successful synthesis of genre fiction, formal experimentation, leftist political commitment, and metaphysical inquiry produced in English since Thomas Pynchon’s Gravity’s Rainbow.
The novel weaves together two main threads, both written in an extraordinarily close third person. One begins in 1970s London and concerns Maureen Towns, a downwardly mobile single mother to a reserved, awkward, and increasingly violent son named Ewan. Through Maur’s eyes, we see Ewan grow fascinated with guns in his adolescence, join the military when barely out of his teens, report “see[ing] stuff” during a deployment to Sarajevo, become involved with shadowy acronymous divisions, and then finally turn up dead in the woods outside his barracks. When his death is ruled a suicide despite the two bullet holes in his temple, Maur begins to investigate and soon joins forces with other parents of soldiers who perished under mysterious circumstances.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Pop-up tattoo studio opens at Amsterdam's Rembrandt House Museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Senay Boztas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
A young man in Amsterdam will become the lifelong owner of a free Rembrandt etching, thanks to a partnership between the Rembrandt House Museum and two Dutch tattoo studios.
In a collaboration entitled “The Poor Man’s Rembrandt Project”, tattoo artists are recreating one of Rembrandt’s most intricate etchings, The Descent from the Cross (1633), across a man’s entire back. The artwork will take 20 hours to create by a team of tattoo artists from the studios Schiffmacher & Veldhoen in Amsterdam and St. Catherina in Antwerp.
Members of the public can also book a session or drop in to the museum between 26 October-7 November to get a (smaller) Rembrandt tattoo, costing from €100 to €300, from the museum's temporary studio.
This is the second edition of the project; tattoo artists from Schiffmacher & Veldhoen first offered tattoos inspired by the Dutch master’s works in a pop-up studio at the museum in 2023.
The project is not a gimmick, according to the Rembrandt House Museum's director Milou Halbesma. “This is all about content,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “We are a museum of craftsmanship, and we are trying to throw open the craft of Rembrandt and his students as widely as possible. If you translate that to today, we have a number of world-famous Amsterdam creators… And this is a chance to get a tattoo from one of these masters.”
The tattoo artist Henk Schiffmacher says that the etching—one of a series by Rembrandt focusing on the people taking Christ’s body from the cross—was particularly suitable. “We looked at other Rembrandts but this was so dramatic,” he says. “The spine almost becomes part of the cross.”
He adds that a tattoo-based interpretation of the 17th-century Dutch master is also fitting. “Rembrandt was interested in sea farers, he was a collector, and there were so many different people in Amsterdam at the time, there would have been tattooed sailors,” he says.
Bo Kwakernaak, 28, and from Amersvoort, responded to a call on Instagram to provide his body as the canvas for the The Descent from the Cross tattoo. He currently has a partial reproduction of the etching on his back, created in around ten hours, and it will be completed during a late night opening at the museum on 7 November.
“I have always felt a connection with Rembrandt paintings,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “I’m not religious, but I’ve always been drawn to religious imagery. Here, it is the emotion in the faces, the feeling of grief. There is a whole story in one image.”
When the tattoo is completed, according to Schiffmacher, the pigment needs to ‘soften’ into the skin for a year before it will look its best. “This is an etching too but the skin is different from paper,” he says. “It is the only bit of art you can take to your grave.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Qatar LNG carrier struck by ‘unidentified objects’ in Gulf
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Qatar LNG carrier struck by ‘unidentified objects’ in Gulf
Qatar Gas Transport Company says no injuries or environmental damage.
A Qatari tanker has been hit by “unidentified objects” while sailing in the Gulf, the Qatar Gas Transport Company says, the latest attack on commercial shipping since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.
The attack on Friday evening struck the liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Mayeda, which belongs to the company, it said in a statement on Sunday.
None of the crew members was injured and no environmental damage was reported, it said.
The statement, published by the Qatar Stock Exchange, said the vessel is currently in a “safe condition, operational” and that the impact of the incident is being assessed.
The Qatar Gas Transport Company supplies Qatari ports and terminals with towage and marine support services.
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit since the start of the war, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and the UK Maritime Trade Operations.
Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz early on in the war, has repeatedly warned vessels attempting to pass through the vital waterway without its permission would face “destruction”.
The attacks have increased since the United States reimposed a blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
With at least 29 ships hit, October was the worst month of the war, ahead of the 20 attacks recorded in March.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: ‘Let’s take Alexa out into the garden and smash it with a shoe’: Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan take aim at Hollywood, AI ... and each other
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Tim Jonze
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
She has tackled Britain, conquered the world and even grappled with life itself. Now Philomena Cunk is back on our screens – looking as miserable and confused as ever – to take on her biggest subject yet: cinema.
Cinema, the iconically stupid presenter explains, is not just mankind’s greatest achievement but also a world where “men can be heroes, women can get off with heroes, and nobody ever goes to the toilet – unless you’re watching a specialist film from Japan”. So if you’ve ever wanted to know why “Citizen Ken” always has carrots in his pockets, where the word auteur comes from (“They felt they oughta get all the credit”) or how Benedict Cumberbatch reacts to the hardest-hitting questions of his career (such as “Who are you?”), this is quite literally the only place you’ll ever find the answers.
It has been 13 years since Diane Morgan and Charlie Brooker’s comic creation hit our screens, growing from an amusing segment on Brooker’s show Weekly Wipe into one of the most beloved figures on TV. To celebrate this new three-part series we’ve brought Morgan and Brooker together to chat about everything from defecating robots to dinner dates with Kanye West, and what it feels like to imagine a blue horse (there’s weirdly quite a lot about this).
It’s a busy time for them both. Brooker is preparing for the launch of Blackmere, his deadpan detective show due on Netflix early next year, which he says will be in the vein of Airplane! and The Naked Gun. “The title will end up annoying me and that’s all my own fault,” he says. “It’s how Americans say ‘Black Mirror’ and I thought: that’s actually a really good name for a policeman.” As for Morgan, she is on a roll at the moment: her sitcom Ann Droid, about a robotic care assistant, garnered rave reviews, and she recently survived five episodes of Prime Video’s Last One Laughing. “People thought Cunk would be good training for that because she never laughs,” she says. “What they don’t realise is that I do crack up during the interviews, they just cut those bits out.”
When we meet, Morgan has also just gone viral for chatting to J-Lo at the Stella McCartney show in Paris. So, before we get to anything else, what on earth were they chatting about?
Diane Morgan Well she’d just done a film with Brett Goldstein, so I told her that I used to do standup with him and that I enjoyed the film.
 
Charlie Brooker Is that the best you could do?
 
DM Well it’s something isn’t it? What should I have said? Asked her what she’s doing later?
Who’s the most unlikely person you’ve been in conversation with, Charlie?
  
CB Oh, I know the answer to this! It’s Kanye West. It was a couple of years ago. I actually had dinner with him. I don’t know if this is an anecdote for public consumption, really, but … it was quite a bizarre and sad occasion. I ended up thinking: “He’s not well.”
Why did you meet up? 
  
CB He wanted to meet because he’d seen a Black Mirror episode and liked it very much …
 
DM Was it one of the earlier funny ones?
 
CB [Deliberately ignoring her] I can tell you which one it was. It was called Metalhead. It’s got your mate Maxine Peake in it and a robot dog.
 
DM Honestly, how dead inside would you have to be to get a robot dog instead of a lovely little rescue dog?
 
CB But a robot pet wouldn’t die! That’s the reason I don’t have a pet in London, because I get very sad pre-emptively imagining that pet getting squashed.
 
DM When you say you “imagine” it, what do you mean? Because you told me once that you had that thing where you can’t see images in your mind [aphantasia]. So if I say: “Picture a blue horse”, everyone else pictures it but you can’t.
 
CB I think I can picture things. It’s just not like on telly where they have a flashback.
 
DM It is for me. It’s full surround sound, and so much detail.
 
CB [Closing his eyes] If I think of a blue horse, I don’t see it … It’s more like my brain is describing it to me.
 
DM That’s fascinating, isn’t it? The man who wrote Black Mirror can’t picture a blue horse! Whereas mine’s got reins on, it’s got facial expressions, it’s going … [Morgan blows an enormous raspberry while circling her head round in a convincingly horse-like manner].
 
CB OK, what’s it doing right now? Is it lifting its tail? Can you see its bum?
 
DM Well I can now. Now you’ve said that.
This is actually exactly the kind of material my editor asked for in this piece.
  
CB Did they say: “Can it be mainly about their psychic projections of horses?”
 
DM It is interesting, though. Have you been diagnosed with that or …
 
CB Diagnosed with what?
 
DM No imagination.
 
CB Critics might say I have, yes.
 
DM Do you have dreams?
 
CB I definitely see things in dreams and imagine that they’re real. Once I had a dream where a little circle appeared to signal a reel change, like when you’re watching an old film on TV. And the dream itself was about teachers at the school who were assassinating people. So fuck you with your “you can’t see anything in your mind’s eye” nonsense. I think our brains all have different operating systems, like Windows or Mac OS or Linux.
 
DM There’s actually a man who got to 40-odd and discovered he only had half a brain.
 
CB Was his name Jacob Rees-Mogg?
 
DM He was actually an accountant. And he’d been living totally fine with half a brain. They were like, how can this be? Because you think of all the areas of the brain, like, the hippocampus and, er, the other areas of the brain … I just think that’s incredible. That basically you don’t really need a brain. I actually think your brain’s more like an aerial. So we are actually in the cloud and we’re being livestreamed to the receptors in our skulls. And when you die, your body dies, but your consciousness just goes back to the cloud.
 
CB That’s beautiful, actually. What’s the point of that, though?
 
DM Well, what’s the point of anything? Don’t go pulling at that thread! Right, come on, let’s start!
Did you have any idea Philomena Cunk would be such an enduring character?
  
DM No, I was told by people on the programme that I would get a huge backlash because I wasn’t Charlie. They said brace yourself for a lot of shit on social media. Because people just want Charlie. Anything that isn’t Charlie is just people going: “Where’s Charlie, this is fucking shit!”
 
CB And now it’s the other way round!
Was Diane’s audition for Philomena Cunk the first time you met?
  
CB Yeah! Oh, actually, no! Because she’s got an anecdote about me being horrible at the Edinburgh festival.
 
DM Everyone in my family used to read your Guardian column. It started with my dad. He rarely laughed at anything, but he would be crying tears reading your column. And I’d be like: “What’s so funny?” So he’d read a bit of it and we’d all laugh, as a family, together. And then they started printing your photo.
 
CB And that ruined it for you?
 
DM It meant I recognised you at the Edinburgh festival. So I went over and was like: “You’re Charlie Brooker!” And you said: “Yeah, what do you want?” So I said: “I read your column, it’s really funny.” And you said: “So?”
 
CB Surely I was joking. Sometimes when people come up and say: “I really love Black Mirror”, I reply, “What’s wrong with you?” It’s just a joke!
 
DM Looking back, of course it was a joke. But I didn’t know that then. I was mortified. I thought: “He hates me!” and I was crushed. I couldn’t even think about him for years. When the auditions came up for Philomena, I knew I wanted it more than anything … but that Charlie hated me. Whereas actually you didn’t give a shit.
Philomena Cunk was supposed to be a posh character originally, right?
  
CB We used to get people going: “Oh you’re mocking working-class accents,” because of the Barry Shitpeas character. So the idea was to add an airhead, middle-class, yummy-mummy, Chelsea-tractor cupcake blogger to the show. Hence the name Philomena Cunk.
 
DM You’d never get someone called Philomena in Bolton – you’d get your head kicked in.
 
CB I was watching all the audition tapes and wasn’t quite sure who the character was.
 
DM Luckily I’d got the guts up to ask if I could do it in my own accent because I thought that was funnier.
 
CB When I saw you doing it in your flat, fucking depressed, unimpressed-with-everything tone, I was doubled over with laughter.
 
DM Ah, that’s so sweet … you’re forgiven for the Edinburgh thing now.
 
CB The strange thing about Cunk is she’s sort of weirdly in charge of things, even if she’s speaking to a professor or whatever …
 
DM We interviewed Michael Bay for this new series and the crew were a bit terrified of him because they’re big, big fans. But I wasn’t bothered. Because [whispers] I don’t really watch a lot of films. It actually helps that I don’t know or care who these experts are. Actually, I think we confused Michael Bay because I asked him how much he paid for his trainers and he thought I meant actual people who trained him. He said I was asking odd questions.
 
DM I often talk about my mate Paul, though, so that might get confusing.
There are lots of jokes about AI in these new episodes – mainly Cunk challenging experts by saying she’s asked AI. Do either of you use AI?
  
CB I use it when I’m somewhere I don’t know and want to find, say, a good barbecue restaurant that doesn’t serve pork. And then when you turn up it no longer exists. But other than that, no. I would never use it to help write something.
 
DM They’re trying to force it on you, aren’t they? But I won’t even let it do that [Mimics flicking something away].
 
CB I’m a bit annoyed that there’s new technology and I don’t like it. I think it’s more that I don’t like the people who are making it. Having said that, I think the idea that it’s going to take over the world and destroy us all is a bit far-fetched.
It has started speaking its own language, though, according to reports …
  
CB Yeah, but it’s just been fed on scraps of itself, hasn’t it? It’s a bit like when we started feeding cows on scraps of cow, and in the end they all got mad cow disease. So AI might look like it’s talking in some advanced language but actually all it’s saying is [sticks out tongue and waggles his head]: “Braaaappurgglefluuuurrrk!”
Did you ever think technology would advance this rapidly?
  
CB Not really. Our Alexa recently updated and started speaking in a very human voice, which really freaked my son out. It was like, “Hey, yeah man, we can do that if you like” … a bit uncanny valley. We’ve had to change its voice back to the previous setting. When really what we should be doing is taking it out into the garden and smashing it with a shoe.
Diane, you don’t use AI, but in a way you’ve written quite a pro-AI comedy with Ann Droid? 
  
DM Have I? Oh yeah. I suppose I have. [Anxiously] Is that what people are saying?
 
CB It’s what he’s saying, right now!
 
DM It wasn’t supposed to be a statement on anything. It was just supposed to be a funny show about a robot and an old woman. It’s different when it’s your own show. On another person’s show you just say the words and if it’s shit then it’s not your fault. But with this everything rests on you. I remember when I first had the idea. I pitched it to the BBC and then I suddenly thought: “Oh shit, they’re going to make me be the robot aren’t they?” And they did. So I spent a year freaking out about it. Because obviously if you’re on telly pretending to be a robot and it doesn’t go well then it’s going to look really daft isn’t it?
So you went to robot school …
  
DM I did! With a guy called Dan.
What did he teach you?
  
DM Never blink, mainly. He also taught you not to bob your head. To always walk like this [gets up and glides across the room in a chillingly robot-like manner].
Would you fancy robot school, Charlie?
  
CB Well I am quite stiff. I’ve got a very bad back. I’d quite like to be a robot, though. They don’t have to defecate.
Is that something they taught you at robot school?
  
DM No we didn’t cover that.
Did robot school require you to go full method with your character?
  
DM I mean, I practised at home. But I didn’t spend a day as a robot. My job’s not that weird.
What is the weirdest job you’ve ever had?
  
CB I know what Diane is going to say …
 
DM The worming tablets factory?
 
CB Yeah! Did you ever eat them?
 
DM Eat what? A worming tablet? Of course I didn’t. They’re for dogs. And I’m not a dog. Also, I’ve not got worms. You’ve not done horrible jobs like that, have you?
 
CB When I worked at CeX we had a lot of people coming in trying to sell stolen laptops. And a boss who would make us do things, like, one day I had to clear out the back room.
 
DM [Sarcastically] Oh, that sounds terrible.
 
CB It was! It was full of shit and a dead cat!
And look where you both are now!
  
DM I owe it all to Charlie! He totally made everything happen for me. All my subsequent career in comedy is down to him … I owe him everything!
 
CB Ah, that’s lovely. You’ve had to be really nice to me there and it’s all on tape!
Would you like to say anything nice back?
  
CB I’d say that Diane has naturally funny bones. And skin and eyes. She operates on a unique comic frequency – it’s rare to find a performer like that. She’s totally tuned in to the words which means in turn the writing room can tune into her. She elevates everything. Can I be sick now? I don’t like saying nice things.
Cunk on Cinema will air on BBC Two and iPlayer from 12 November.

https://taz.de/Jugendproteste-in-Deutsch.title: Jugendproteste in Deutschland: Die Wut ist berechtigt
https://taz.de/Jugendproteste-in-Deutsch.author: Timm Kühn
https://taz.de/Jugendproteste-in-Deutsch.text:
Jugendproteste in Deutschland : Die Wut ist berechtigt
Zehntausende junge Menschen gehen gegen hohe Preise, schlechte Bildung und Wehrpflicht auf die Straße. Auch Krawalle ändern nichts daran, dass das legitim ist.
E in Gespenst geht um in Europa und der Welt – das Gespenst einer wütenden Jugendbewegung. Nicht nur in Frankreich, auch in Italien, Spanien, Serbien, Albanien oder Indien gehen junge Menschen auf die Straße. Sie protestieren gegen Krieg und Aufrüstung, gegen miserable Zustände in den Schulen, die Wohnungsnot und soziale Ungleichheit. Kurz: gegen eine Politik, die ihnen zunehmend jede Vorstellung einer besseren Zukunft nimmt. An diesem Wochenende hat diese Protestbewegung auch Deutschland erreicht.
120.000 Teilnehmer:innen zählen die Organisator:innen der „Gen Z regelt“-Proteste bundesweit. Das sind zwar weniger als die 180.000, die sich angekündigt hatten – aber für das erste Auftreten der Bewegung ist das doch beachtlich. In 34 Städten gab es bunte und laute Proteste, die den Verlauf über friedlich blieben. Doch vielerorts trafen Demonstrierende auf eine martialisch auftretende Polizei, die Wasserwerfer und Räumpanzer auffuhr und damit die Stimmung der Kriminalisierung fortsetzte, die bereits die letzten Wochen den Diskurs bestimmte.
Und nein, auch dass es nach Ende der Demos – und gegen den Willen der Organisator:innen – vor allem in Frankfurt aber auch in Hamburg, Köln und Berlin zu teils heftigen Krawallen gekommen ist, ändert nichts an der Legitimität der Wut der Jugendlichen. Vielfach dürften die brennenden Mülltonnen sogar eine Folge dieser Gewaltdebatte gewesen sein: ein trotziger Versuch zu zeigen, dass man sich eben nicht vorschreiben lässt, wie man zu demonstrieren hat. Bei den auf den Protesten vielerorts den Ton angebenden sozialistischen Jugendgruppen kommen sicher auch Gefühle von Fomo (der Angst, etwas zu verpassen) mit Blick auf Frankreich dazu.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Vor alldem kommt aber das in der Generation real verbreitete Gefühl, verraten und verkauft zu werden. Junge Menschen leben in einer Welt, in der die Merz-Regierung mit offen vorgetragener Verachtung für arme Menschen die Bildungs- und Sozialsysteme dieses Landes kaputt spart. Sie blicken auf eine Zukunft auf einem brennenden Planeten, doch sie sehen, wie die fossile Wirtschaft einfach weitermacht wie bisher. Wie erst Flüssiggasterminals und jetzt Rechenzentren aus dem Boden gestampft werden, während eine Ex-Vorstandsvorsitzende eines fossilen Konzerns das Bundeswirtschaftsministerium leitet.
Und dann erklären Politiker:innen der Jugend unentwegt, ein kommender Krieg sei wahrscheinlich, sie könnten sich schon mal darauf einstellen. Weil aber nicht genügend Freiwillige in die Bundeswehr wollen, wird ziemlich offen die verpflichtende Wehrpflicht vorbereitet. Wie Krieg aussieht, sehen die jungen Leute dabei jeden Tag in ihren Livefeeds, wo die Bilder des auch mit deutschen Waffen begangenen Völkermords Israels in Gaza in Dauerschleife laufen, gefolgt von Szenen brutaler Polizeigewalt auf palästinasolidarischen Demos.
Es ist gut, dass sich nun zumindest Ansätze einer emanzipatorischen Gegenbewegung gegen die Gefühle von Hoffnungslosigkeit zeigen, die all das auslöst. Denn auf der anderen politischen Seite trägt diese Stimmung wohl entscheidend zum grassierenden Fremden- und Frauen*hass bei – also zu Wertesystemen, in denen man wenigstens noch durch die Abwertung anderer glaubt, etwas zu gelten. Doch dass die bürgerliche Mitte den demokratischen Impuls der Proteste versteht, darf bezweifelt werden.
Wahrscheinlicher ist, dass sich nun wieder alle in rassistisch aufgeladener Sprache auf die Bilder des geplünderten Snipes-Stores auf der Frankfurter Zeil stürzen. Bei rechten Politiker:innen und Medien ist das keine Überraschung. Aufhören muss aber die Moralpanik im linksliberalen Lager. Und zwar nicht, weil man geplünderte Läden gutheißen müsste. Es gibt gute Gründe für die Kritik, dass Krawallromantik der Sache mehr schadet als nützt. Aber im Zentrum sollte das politische Versagen stehen, das solche Proteste hervorbringt – nicht das Verhalten derjenigen, die offenbar nicht mehr wissen, wie sie sich sonst Gehör verschaffen sollen.
Das müssen sich im Übrigen auch die Organisator:innen der „Gen Z regelt“-Proteste sagen lassen, die sich in vorauseilendem Gehorsam von allem distanziert haben, was man ihnen irgendwie anlasten könnte. Dabei müssen sie verstehen, dass Deutschland 2026 nicht mehr dasselbe ist wie zur Zeit von Fridays for Future. Die Zeiten sind rauer geworden, und es ist absehbar, dass nur wenige Teile von Medien und Politik der Bewegung wohlwollend gegenüberstehen werden. Der Blick auf den Rest der Welt zeigt, dass „Gen Z regelt“ trotzdem etwas erreichen kann. Dafür muss die Bewegung aber Druck aufbauen – und darf sich nicht spalten lassen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Iran designates Britain's Royal Navy, RAF as 'terrorist' groups, report says
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Hilal Saki
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Iran designates Britain's Royal Navy, RAF as 'terrorist' groups, report says
Iran's Foreign Ministry on Sunday designated Britain's Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as "terrorist" organisations, in retaliation for what it described as hostile actions by the British government, including its designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a "terrorist organisation".
The ministry also designated Britain's foreign intelligence service, MI6, a "hostile group", saying the measures took effect on 1 November, according to Iran's Mehr News Agency.
The decision was taken under a resolution by Iran's Supreme National Security Council and followed Britain's designation of the IRGC under the State Threats Act 2026 on 13 July, the ministry said in a statement, Mehr reported.
Tehran also accused Britain of participating in the US-Israeli war against Iran by providing access to military and logistical bases and facilities under British jurisdiction.
The ministry said the measures were based on the principle of reciprocity and in accordance with international law, adding that the British government would be responsible for any consequences.
According to Mehr, the ministry condemned "Britain's anti-Iranian policies", saying they violated the principles of the United Nations Charter, including respect for national sovereignty and the prohibition of unlawful measures against other states.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/dockworkers-.text:
Dockworkers Worldwide Are About to Strike for Palestine
The second International Day of Action of Dockworkers, in solidarity with Palestine and against militarism, begins this Friday — and could be the largest worker action against war in history.
In 1984, while the global struggle against apartheid burned hot, union dockworkers in San Francisco refused to unload South African cargo to demonstrate their hostility to a white supremacist, fascist regime. In so doing they reaffirmed what Harry Bridges, the first president of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU), asserted when asked about what role organized workers should play in world affairs: “Interfere with the foreign policy of the country? Sure as hell! That’s our job, that’s our privilege, that’s our right, that’s our duty.”
Few workers believe that they have sufficient power to express political opinions at work, let alone insert themselves into global affairs by downing their tools. And yet, as revolutionary unionist “Big” Bill Haywood reminded, “If the workers are organized, all they have to do is to put their hands in their pockets and they have got the capitalist class whipped.”
Starting in 2023, the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions (PGFTU) called on workers and unions to “Stop Arming Israel.” In 2025, the PGFTU asked international workers to “organize days of rage and global solidarity in factories and workshops, in ports and airports, in the streets and public squares, in support of Palestine and its brave people.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: 2,500-year-old solar observatory identified in Mexico
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
An 11-year-long archaeological project at Teteles de Ávila Castillo, in Puebla’s Sierra Norte in east-central Mexico, may shed new light on ancient cultural interactions in Mesoamerica. Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) recently announced that the research team there has identified a 2,500-year-old solar observatory. It could be the region's first of its kind. Other findings include ceramic offerings, infant remains inside a ceramic vessel and numerous obsidian objects.
Teteles reflects the challenges of protecting archaeological heritage on privately owned land. Discovered in 1939, the nine-hectare site remained in private hands for decades, during which time it was looted and damaged. In 2007, its owner donated 3.5 hectares to INAH. Research began in 2015 with support from the civil association Tzoncóyotl, but the remaining land is still private property, limiting excavation there.
The site’s 16 pre-Hispanic pyramidal structures show several phases of occupation. “Teteles flourished during the Middle Preclassic period (900BC-600BC) but declined around AD100, possibly because nearby Cantona expanded,” Alberto Diez Barroso Repizo, Teteles’s archaeological project director, tells The Art Newspaper.
“Green obsidian beads found in offerings containing infant remains suggest connections with Teotihuacan,” Diez adds, “which controlled the Hidalgo quarry where the obsidian originated.” He says other human remains may have decayed because of harsh weather conditions, and the variety of obsidian objects could indicate that Teteles’s inhabitants produced and sold obsidian utensils. “Teteles lay along an active trade route, facilitating cultural exchange,” Diez says.
Even after the area was largely abandoned, ritual offerings continued to be placed at the site, suggesting that it may have become a pilgrimage destination. Diez links the offerings to the Totonac culture, which flourished in Mexico’s Sierra Norte region and along the northern Gulf Coast. “Totonac ceramic offerings and a sculpture fragment dating from AD600 to AD900 suggest that later groups may have regarded Teteles's former inhabitants as their ancestors,” he says, pointing to the possible origins of Totonac culture.
The structure identified as a solar observatory could point to early Maya-Huastec connections previously suggested by linguistic studies. “The observatory resembles E-Group complexes (structures associated with solar observations) at Maya sites like Uaxactún in Guatemala,” Diez says. “It is the first of its kind identified in northern Puebla, though La Venta's Olmec complex may be older.” He adds that its alignments could relate to the Mesoamerican agricultural calendar.
Diez also emphasises the astronomical significance of the site's main 12m-tall pyramid: “It may be aligned with Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky, associated with the beginning of the Mesoamerican calendar in February.” He notes that although scholars have studied this alignment in Mesopotamian and Egyptian structures, its significance in Mesoamerica remains underexplored.
The archaeologist Ivan Šprajc—an archaeoastronomy expert at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana (who was not involved in the project)—places Teteles within a broader tradition of earlier ceremonial complexes he has studied. “Previous archaeoastronomical studies using Lidar technology have documented similar and earlier complexes along the southern Gulf and Pacific coasts,” he says, “some dating to the late Early Preclassic period”, before 1000BC.
Šprajc is cautious about using the term “observatory”. “The common practice of referring to these complexes as observatories is not entirely justifiable,” he says. “Although they contain astronomical alignments, their primary functions were ceremonial or residential, and such alignments were commonly incorporated in very different types of structures throughout Mesoamerica.” He adds that solar alignments tied to the ceremonial agricultural cycle were common, though the calendar year's start shifted over time.
Further research, including comparative studies and artefact analysis, will certainly reveal more about these discoveries in the future. “Plans are underway to open the site and a museum to the public,” Diez says, although an exact timeline is pending.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on Brexit
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
The former chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued Britain’s future should be back in the European Union, saying Brexit has made the UK “poorer, weaker and less secure”.
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Andy Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.
Reeves, who was sacked as chancellor by Burnham, said in an article for the Sunday Times that no one who worked with her in the Treasury could be in doubt about her pro-European instincts. “I am proud of the progress we have already made in strengthening our relationship with the European Union. Brexit has made us poorer, weaker and less secure,” she said.
“There is a debate to be had about our future relationship with Europe, and I welcome Andy Burnham’s leadership in facing up to this. No one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were.”
The current focus for British negotiations is the EU summit later this month to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But the prime minister has made it clear he wants to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.
Burnham has said he believes there should be “honest discussion” about freedom of movement and that rejoining the single market could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.
In her article, Reeves said it was “incumbent on supporters of our re-entry to make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right”.
At his last cabinet meeting, Burnham warned individual ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, but said the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.
It follows reports that some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the possibility of a revised deal and its impact on migration.
Burnham has set out a two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will be within the scope of Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement. The process will formally kick off when the prime minister attends the European summit.
Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail.
As chancellor, Reeves was one of the first senior ministers to articulate that Brexit had damaged the British economy and its ability to grow. In her Mais lecture in March this year she said Brexit had “created profound uncertainty, raised new barriers to trade, and leaves Britain facing an additional danger today … The risk that we find ourselves stranded between powerful trading blocs, as globalisation retreats.”

https://taz.de/Dortmunds-Remis-gegen-Bay.title: Dortmunds Remis gegen Bayern: Es wächst etwas zusammen
https://taz.de/Dortmunds-Remis-gegen-Bay.author: Daniel Theweleit
https://taz.de/Dortmunds-Remis-gegen-Bay.text:
Dortmunds Remis gegen Bayern: Es wächst etwas zusammen
Die Bayern sind zwar noch besser, aber das 2:2 im Spitzenspiel zeigt: Dortmund rückt heran. Während es in München kriselt, wird der BVB immer stärker.
Die Erinnerungen an schlechtere Zeiten, an diese gruseligen Abende der Demütigung waren auch am Ende dieses Tages noch lebendig bei den Spielern von Borussia Dortmund. Regelmäßig sind sie schwer geschlagen aus München abgereist, was das 2:2 beim FC Bayern an diesem neunten Spieltag zu einem sehr süßen Erlebnis machte.
Der Kontrast zu den 0:5- oder 0:6-Demontagen, die sie hier schon erlitten haben, war enorm, nicht nur auf der Anzeigetafel. „Wir waren selbstbewusst. Wir hatten zwar Respekt, aber keine Ehrfurcht“, sagte Kapitan Nico Schlotterbeck. Und das hatte weniger mit irgendwelchen Psycho- oder Motivationstricks zu tun als mit dem neuen Qualitätsmerkmal dieses Fußballstandortes: nüchterne Facharbeit.
Auf die Frage nach der großen Widerstandskraft auch spät im Spiel, als Fabio Silva der Ausgleichstreffer gelang, sagte der Trainer Niko Kovac, man müsse eben „auch laufen können.“ Und zwar nicht nur, wenn es ums Verteidigen geht: „Viele denken ja, das Laufen nur defensiv bedeutet, aber man muss auch die offensiven Läufe machen. Das brauchst du auf diesem Niveau.“
Dass die Dortmunder in München weniger über ihre Verteidigungsarbeit sprechen mussten als über ihr Spiel mit Ball, gehört zu den großen Überraschungen dieses Auftritts beim Rekordmeister. „Ich sehe einen ganz klaren Trend, eine spielerische Entwicklung, und dabei gelingt es uns, eine spielerische Stabilität zu erhalten“, sagte Sportdirektor Ole Book.
„Gute Reaktion“
Dazu gehörte auch die Entscheidung, in München mit einem System anzutreten, das der BVB seit rund eineinhalb Jahren in der Bundesliga spielte: mit einer Viererkette. Joane Gadou entpuppte sich als brillanter Rechtsverteidiger. Links zeigte Daniel Svensson nicht zum ersten Mal, dass er gut darin ist, den eigentlich kaum zu bremsenden Michael Olise zu bekämpfen. Und Rückschläge lösen keinen Zusammenbruch mehr aus. „Wir haben immer eine gute Reaktion gezeigt“, sagte Schlotterbeck.
Das 1:0 durch Konrad Laimer nach einem Fehlpass von Felix Nmecha beantwortete der Revierklub mit vielen eigenen Angriffsversuchen sowie Serhou Guirassys 1:1. Und als die Bayern durch Dayot Upamecano abermals führten, mündete die energische Schlussphase des BVB in ein spätes 2:2 durch Fabio Silva. „Ich glaube, dass der Trainer und sein Team schon seit fast zwei Jahren daran arbeiten, an diesem Mindset, dass wir echt hart werden und eine Gewinnermentalität haben“, sagte der Sportdirektor Ole Book.
„Keep it simple“
Dem Fußball-Lehrer Kovac ist es mit seinem „Keep it simple“-Ansatz und auch dank seiner Beharrlichkeit gelungen, den Fokus auf erlernbare Aspekte des Spiels zu lenken, während in München gerade große Lebensfragen gestellt werden. Der viel zu frühe Tod des Vaters von Joshua Kimmich, die Erkrankung von Trainer Vincent Kompany, aber auch die Absencen von Jamal Musiala und immer mehr Verletzungen wichtiger Spieler, erschweren die Konzentration aufs Wesentliche.
„Wir sind gut, ich glaube, dass wir immer noch unterschätzt werden in Deutschland“, sagte Schlotterbeck, während der Münchner Kapitän Joshua Kimmich feststellte: „Unabhängig vom Ergebnis muss man sagen, dass wir gerade durch schwierige Wochen gehen.“ Auch weil sich Ismael Saibari und Serge Gnabry schwerer verletzt haben und auch Olise zehn Minuten vor dem Ende verletzt ausgewechselt werden musste.
„Genialer Schachzug“
Das ist die Ausgangslage, aus der die Bundesligaspitze sich dem zweiten Saisondrittel nähert. Harry Kane verschoss nach mehreren Tagen im Ballon d’Or-Fieber einen Elfmeter, während die Dortmunder unter der Woche die Viererkette übten und trotz eines misslungenen Abschlusstrainings an dieser Idee festhielten. „Niko hatte einen genialen Schachzug gehabt mit der Viererkette“, sagte Dortmunds Torhüter Gregor Kobel. Ein Sieg des Meisters wäre dennoch gut möglich gewesen und hätte schon zum Spielverlauf gepasst, dreimal trafen die Bayern Pfosten oder Latte. Aber die Entwicklungsrichtung spricht im Moment für den BVB.
Man muss zwar vorsichtig sein, weil auch künftig mit Rückschlägen gerechnet werden muss, eine missglückte Champions-League-Saison oder ein frühes Ausscheiden im DFB-Pokal sind weiterhin jederzeit möglich. Aber während sich in München immer neue Spieler verletzen und der Trainer sich selbst überfordert hat, werden in Dortmund gerade viele Spieler immer besser. Der Mittelfeldarbeiter Jobe Bellingham zum Beispiel, der zuletzt immer auf dem Feld blieb, wenn Felix Nmecha ausgewechselt wurde. Oder Carney Chukwuemeka, der nach einer schwachen ersten Saison in Dortmund schon als Fehleinkauf galt.
Wirklich bereichernd sind zudem der kluge Zentrumsstratege Joey Veerman und der schnelle Verteidiger Joane Gadou. Es wächst etwas zusammen. Die Bayern sind zwar schon noch besser als der BVB, aber die Ergebnisse eben nicht. „Wir können etwas reißen“, sagte Schlotterbeck. Was sich in den vergangenen Jahren noch anhörte wie eine vage Hoffnung, ist gerade dabei, zu einer Überzeugung zu werden, die auch in München Wirkung zeigt.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

Israel’s election campaign reflected the wide support for ethnic cleansing of Palestinians across mainstream politics. The electoral stalemate between government and opposition is unlikely to slow the radicalization of Israeli society.
Jewish and Arab voters with Israeli citizenship massively flocked to voting stations on Tuesday, October 27, for the elections to the Israeli parliament, the Knesset. These were the first elections since the formation, in 2022, of the most reactionary government in the Zionist state’s history. For the last four years, this far-right coalition joined Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and the neo-Nazi groups headed by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich together with ultra-Orthodox religious parties.
As polls had forecast, the ruling bloc led by incumbent Prime Minister Netanyahu and the opposition alliance led by the former Chief of the General Staff of Israel’s armed forces, Gadi Eisenkot, ended the race in what current estimates see as a tie. It may take a few days before definitive results are announced and several weeks of wheeling and dealing among Knesset factions before the shape of the next cabinet is known.
As has been amply emphasized, the most crucial particularity of the recent elections is that they were the first held since the Hamas-led operation of October 7, 2023 triggered the genocidal war launched by the Israeli army on Gaza, displacing its inhabitants and destroying its buildings wholesale. This has been accompanied with a dangerous and unprecedented escalation of Zionist settlers’ violence against the Palestinian population in the West Bank, clearly constituting a creeping campaign of ethnic cleansing akin to that witnessed in most of Palestine during the Nakba of 1948 and more recently in the Gaza Strip.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Houston cancer centre expands its art collection and curatorial ambitions
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
As more and more research indicates art can play an important role in health, healing and improving outcomes in medical spaces, the world’s largest cancer treatment centre is embarking on an ambitious expansion of its art collection, with plans to integrate contemporary works into new and renovated facilities as part of a broader effort to rethink the patient experience.
The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, considered one of the top cancer centres in the US, has long maintained a collection made up of classic, inoffensive “hospital art”, such as pleasant pastoral scenes. But in January 2025, it launched a contemporary art initiative focused on acquiring ambitious fine art. Since then, with the help of Jennifer Finkel, MD Anderson’s associate vice president for art experience, the institution has added nearly 300 works to a collection that already included approximately 9,000 objects.
The art initiative is part of a $2.9bn expansion across MD Anderson’s facilities in the Texas Medical Center in Houston, the largest medical complex in the world, alongside other regional and research developments scheduled for completion between 2027 and 2032. The construction projects provide an opportunity to commission site-specific works and build a collection that is integrated into the architecture, rather than simply hung on hospital walls.
“With all of the growth and new buildings, this is an opportunity to create a world-class art collection,” says Finkel, who previously held positions at Cleveland Clinic and Wake Forest University. “We're the number one cancer centre, and we deliver world-class care and research. Now it's time for our environment to really match.”
The initiative combines traditional acquisitions with site-specific commissions. Funding comes from a percent-for-art model based on construction costs, alongside philanthropic support and qualifying art donations. If 1% of the $2.9bn expansion were allocated to art, as is standard, that would amount to $29m, although the total budget for the art collection initiative has not been publicly disclosed.
The goal is to build the collection alongside the new facilities, “really integrating art into the fabric of the buildings and having this art collection be part of our culture and our in our DNA”, Finkel says.
“It's an opportunity to relook at the patient experience with art being a cornerstone of that, which is exciting,” she says. “As we renovate our older facilities, that's also an opportunity to bring new art and think about art and design cohesively in those older spaces as well.”
Art as a companion to treatment
A hospital presents particular challenges for a curator. Works displayed in waiting rooms, corridors and examination rooms may be encountered during some of the most difficult moments in a person's life, amid the uncertainty, disappointment and hope that accompany cancer treatment. The aim is to select art that can offer patients opportunities for reflection and distraction, while contributing to their emotional wellbeing, Finkel says.
Research into the effects of art and cultural engagement on health has grown in recent years, with studies examining how art in healthcare environments can support wellbeing and help reduce anxiety. For MD Anderson, the challenge is to translate those broader findings into decisions about individual works and the spaces in which they will be displayed.
“Is it uplifting? Is it hopeful? I really like art where you can get lost in something. It can be a little bit challenging, maybe, when you're decoding something. You can spend time with it—the art can reveal itself over time,” Finkel says.
That last consideration is particularly relevant for patients who return to the hospital frequently over weeks or months, and a work that initially seems familiar may offer a new perspective with repeated encounters.
“Thinking about art, when you look at something and you've probably looked at it 50 times, and it might be the 51st, you're like, ‘Oh, I didn't see that’,” Finkel says.
The selection process also takes into account the clinical context, the demographics of patients and the length of time they are likely to spend in a particular space. A corridor through which people pass quickly calls for different considerations from a waiting room where patients might sit for an hour or longer. Colour and imagery can also be sensitive issues: Finkel considers whether certain shades of red or imagery that is “too cellular” might be unsettling for someone undergoing cancer treatment.
“I really obsess about each artwork and how someone can respond,” Finkel says. “But at the end of the day, with good contemporary art, people bring what they're going to bring and see what they're going to see in it, and you can't control that. That's part of the beauty.”
The curatorial approach is informed by the people who will use each facility. When planning the collection for MD Anderson's new Colorectal Cancer Center, Finkel initially assumed that its patients would largely be older adults. She learned that one-third of patients were between the ages of 35 and 45, prompting her to reconsider the kinds of works that might resonate in the space.
Finkel is soon to begin work on the collection for a new dedicated prostate cancer clinic. Although its patients will predominantly be men, she is also keeping in mind their caregivers and other people who may accompany them.
The process begins before patients even reach a treatment room. Finkel considers the anxiety that can build during a hospital visit, from entering the parking garage to navigating waiting areas and undergoing examinations or procedures. “How can art be a companion on that journey?” she asks.
Wayfinding is another practical consideration. A particularly colourful print, for example, can help visitors recognise an elevator or exit in the sprawling medical complex, making a work of art a useful visual marker as well.
From local artists to site-specific commissions
Finkel says MD Anderson acquires much of the collection through commercial galleries and art fairs, with an emphasis on practising artists and diverse representation. She is also quick to support artists and dealers based in Houston, where MD Anderson's local expansion offers opportunities to connect the institution's collection with the city's contemporary art scene.
At this year's edition of Untitled Art Houston earlier this month, MD Anderson dedicated $20,000 to a new acquisitions prize. The selection committee chose works by Michelle Blade, represented by Night Gallery in Los Angeles, and Kelly Tapia-Chuning, represented by the Santa Fe gallery Kouri + Corrao. Other artists in the collection include Ping Zheng, represented by Houston's Seven Sisters; the Houston-based David Aylsworth, represented by Inman Gallery; and Mara Held, the daughter of the artist Al Held, who is also represented by Seven Sisters.
The initiative has also developed site-specific commissions that respond directly to their surroundings. One of the most recognisable works in the Colorectal Cancer Center is Carried by the Breeze, an installation by the local artist Shane Allbritton. Suspended above a waiting room, the sculpture comprises translucent leaves incorporating DNA-inspired patterns. The leaves move gently in the current from the air-conditioning system, reflecting light from a nearby window across the ceiling and walls.
The work was made using a specially selected plastic that is easier to clean and resistant to dust, illustrating how the demands of a clinical environment must shape the materials and construction of a commission. The project also carried personal significance for Allbritton's family: her mother, who was part of the family team that helped realise the artist's designs, was diagnosed with ovarian cancer.
“Anytime we can contribute to the comfort level of patients who are entering a space that may be filled with anxiety and uncertainty, it’s important to have environmental features that are comforting, that are handmade, that are creatively expressing something that gives them inspiration or hope,” Allbritton said in a video produced for the hospital.
“Artists want to be a part of this collection because there is that impact on someone's health,” Finkel says. “When they're going through probably one of the scariest times of their lives, and to be part of that, it's really impactful.”
Beyond the acquisition and display of works, MD Anderson encourages patients and visitors to engage with the collection. Works on display in facilities have wall labels, and the collection has its own focused interactive guide on the Bloomberg Connects app, allowing people to learn more about the art while they wait for treatment. Finkel says the hospital's partners at Bloomberg have relayed that they have been “astounded” by the level of engagement.
The plans extend beyond the visual arts. MD Anderson is developing a performing arts programme drawing on Houston's symphony, ballet and other cultural organisations. Finkel is also interested in establishing an artist-in-residence programme that could encompass visual artists, poets or musicians.
“It's not just about hanging the art,” Finkel says. “We’re thinking about those other levels that people can engage with the art while they're here.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Yemeni government forces seize strategic positions in al-Jawf
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Yemeni government forces seize strategic positions in al-Jawf
Weapons and ammunition depots are seized after a counteroffensive.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says its forces have recaptured military positions and strategic heights east of al-Hazm, the capital of the northern governorate of al-Jawf, while fighting continues to deepen the humanitarian crisis in the besieged city of Taiz.
The army’s media centre said in a post on X on Saturday that the 1st Emergency Brigade seized weapons and ammunition depots after wounding, killing and capturing Houthi fighters. It also said the attacks resulted in the destruction of armoured vehicles.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had thwarted advances by government forces in al-Jawf and neighbouring Marib.
Al-Jawf borders Saudi Arabia and lies alongside the Houthi-held governorates of Sanaa and Saada, making it a vital strategic front in the government’s campaign to regain territory. The fighting is part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, launched in October to reverse Houthi gains and restore government control over territory held by the group, which seized Sanaa in 2014.
Fighting has also continued around Taiz in southern Yemen with government forces saying they repelled Houthi attacks in al-Aqroudh, southeast of the city, and on the Tur al-Baha front in neighbouring Lahij governorate.
Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that two air strikes targeted an oil company facility in Bajil district in Hodeidah governorate.
Aid shortages deepen crisis
The fighting comes as the siege of Taiz strains hospitals and restricts deliveries of food, fuel and medical supplies. Although the Houthis do not control the city, they hold key routes in and out of it, limiting access to essential supplies and making it harder for civilians to leave amid reported sniper fire from the surrounding hillsides.
Videos published by Yemeni media showed what the outlets described as the first shipment of medical aid arriving from Marib to support wounded people, displaced families and other residents. Further shipments were reportedly held up by road closures.
More than 290,000 people have fled their homes since fighting escalated in August, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. The UN Population Fund said nearly 6,100 pregnant women were among those recently displaced, including 600 expected to give birth within two weeks of its briefing on Friday.
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that more than 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Yemen face worsening conditions as services are disrupted and food and fuel prices rise.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: As told to Rich Pelley
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
The first song I fell in love with
 
My father could sing really well – he was in a choir and had this coolness. He would walk around singing Love and Happiness by Al Green and, because he looked so much like him on the cover, I actually thought he was Al Green.
The first single I bought
 
Underlove by Melba Moore from Abraham & Straus, this department store in Long Island that had a mini record store inside. I later realised it was produced by Kashif, and I would fall in love with everything he produced.
The song I do at karaoke
 
I’d like to have a go at Everybody Wants to Rule the World or Shout by Tears for Fears.
The best song to play at a party
 
When someone throws down All I Do by Stevie Wonder, you can see it in people’s faces – this is a classic piece of soul music.
The song I inexplicably know every lyric to
 
It seems weird for an MC – I can tell you every drop and hi-hat, but lyrics have never been a big thing for me. When I play with Mos Def, Black Thought or Gorillaz, I’m amazed that they can seemingly remember the lyrics to every song on Earth. I can just about remember Top Billin’ by Audio Two.
The song I can no longer listen to
 
I don’t really fall out of love with songs. There are lots that get played too much, but at some point I usually grow back in love with them. I don’t want to name anyone in case they come and beat me up.
The song I secretly like
 
I’ll play These Dreams by Heart in my dressing room when I think no one else is listening. It reminds me of the big hair era.
The song that gets me up in the morning
 
I always try to start my day by saying: it’s going to be a lovely day. I even had Lovely Day by Bill Withers as my alarm, ready to go off at 6am.
The song that changed my life
 
I was living in the Bronx. My brothers would have mixtapes, but when I heard Planet Rock by Afrika Bambaataa and the Soulsonic Force, it made me really want to do this rap thing. I remember saying: “What the fuck is this?” and my mom telling me off for cursing.
The best song to have sex to
 
Any Barry White record. Or Let’s Get It On by Marvin Gaye. Have I ever tried making love to my own music? Hell no.
The song that makes me cry
 
I love the love Stevie Wonder gives the other person in I Love Every Little Thing About You – saying, basically, the only person I put before you is God, and nothing could top my love for you. I tear up when I hear that record.
The song I’d like played at my funeral
 
I Am I Be by De La Soul.
Stakes Is High, remixed by J Dilla and featuring Mos Def and Truth Enola, and Cabin in the Sky, the band’s ninth studio album, are both out now.

https://taz.de/Graphic-Novel-Neuerschein.title: Graphic Novel Neuerscheinungen: Von Malergenies, machtgierigen Wölfen und der Endlichkeit
https://taz.de/Graphic-Novel-Neuerschein.author: Ralph Trommer
https://taz.de/Graphic-Novel-Neuerschein.text:
Graphic Novel Neuerscheinungen: Von Malergenies, machtgierigen Wölfen und der Endlichkeit
Luc Jacamon erzählt über den Bösewicht im Kreml, Catherine Meurisse mit Dumas über Delacroix. Und Melanie Carolin Wigger über Freundschaft und Demenz.
Es begann damit, dass Vincent nicht mehr zum Stammtisch in die Pinte kam. Robert und Vincent sind im Rentenalter und seit ihrer Schulzeit miteinander befreundet. Also gewöhnt sich Robert an, seinen Freund einfach zu Hause abzuholen. Doch bald schafft es Vincent weder, sich für die Witterung passend anzuziehen, noch erinnert er sich daran, wie man Fahrrad fährt. Robert wird mit der Tatsache konfrontiert, dass sein Freund in ein Demenzheim ziehen muss.
Die 34 Jahre alte, in Bern lebende Schweizer Zeichnerin Melanie Carolin Wigger ist vielfältig unterwegs – als Illustratorin, Animatorin und Gamesdesignerin. In ihrem kürzlich im Berliner Avant-Verlag erschienenen Graphic-Novel-Debüt „Vincent“ widmet sie sich dem Thema Demenz. Angeregt von ihren Großvater, der ihr erzählte, dass ein guter Freund daran erkrankt war, begann sie sich dafür zu interessieren und arbeitete einige Monate in einer Einrichtung für Demenzkranke.
Ihr Buch spiegelt diese Recherche wider. Wigger erzählt auf unaufgeregte Weise von einer starken Freundschaft, die in eine schwierige Phase eingetreten ist. Robert muss verstehen, was mit seinem Freund passiert, und reagiert zunächst verwundert, dann zunehmend einfühlsam auf die Veränderungen in Vincents Wesen. Auch dessen Perspektive versucht die Zeichnerin aufzunehmen, wenn sie seitenfüllende Panels zeichnet, die in den Strudel seines Gehirns führen – Erinnerungen, Erlebtes und der Alltag im Heim werden durcheinandergewürfelt. Für die dauerhafte Verwirrung in Vincents Geist findet Wigger angemessene Bilder.
Die Bücher
Luc Jacamon: „Der Magier im Kreml“. Aus dem Französischen übersetzt von Resel Rebiersch. Schreiber und Leser, Hamburg 2026. 144 Seiten, Hardcover, 29,80 Euro
Melanie Carolin Wigger: „Vincent – Eine Geschichte über Freundschaft und Demenz“. Avant Verlag, Berlin 2026. 240 Seiten, Hardcover, 26 Euro
Catherine Meurisse: „Alexandre Dumas erzählt die Geschichte von Delacroix“. Aus dem Französischen von Lilian Pithan. Carlsen Verlag, Hamburg 2026. 140 Seiten, Hardcover. Der Erstauflage ist ein farbiger Kunstdruck beigelegt. 32 Euro
Die Autorin konzentriert sich in ihren mit Tusche und ausgewählten Aquarellfarben (Grautöne für die Gegenwart, Ockertöne für die Vergangenheit) gehaltenen Zeichnungen ganz auf ihre Charaktere. Auch Nebenfiguren stellt sie lebendig und pointiert dar. Ein gelungenes Debüt zu einem gesellschaftlich immer relevanter werdenden Thema.
Die Macht des Bösen
Spätestens mit Beginn des russischen Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine 2022 hat Putins Russland für viele sichtbar seine Maske fallen gelassen. Doch wie kam es zum Aufstieg eines niedrigrangigen KGB-Funktionärs zum wichtigsten Mann im Kreml? Der französische Zeichner Luc Jacamon, bekannt durch die Action-Serie „Der Killer“ (Text: Matz), wagt sich mit der Comicadaption des Roman-Bestsellers „Der Magier vom Kreml“ von Giuliano da Empoli (2022, auf Deutsch 2023 erschienen bei C.H. Beck) an ein brisantes wie zeitloses Thema.
Auch im gleichnamigen Comic, erschienen im Hamburger Verlag Schreiber & Leser, geht es um Wadim Baranow, einen fiktiven Berater Wladimir Putins, der dessen Weg zur Macht entscheidend begleitet. Unterstützt vom befreundeten Oligarchen Boris Beresowski, gelangt der aus dem Theater- und Medienmilieu stammende Unternehmer in den engsten Kreis um Putin, der zum neuen Präsidentschaftskandidaten aufgebaut wird und später als Präsident erste Probleme bekommen wird, als das Atom-U-Boot „Kursk“ auf Grund läuft.
Während die Zeichnungen sehr stimmungsvoll sind (vor allem in Naturszenen), ist Jacamons Adaption leider zu oberflächlich geraten. Der Protagonist, ein Beau ohne ausgeprägte Charakterzüge, bleibt – wie auch Putin selbst – blass, es bleibt unklar, was gerade ihn zum „Magier“ prädestiniert, welche Ideen entscheidend sind, um den neuen „Zaren“ (wie der Präsident fast durchgängig genannt wird) zu erschaffen.
Wadims „tragische“ Liebesgeschichte mit dem ach so erotischen Oligarchenliebchen Xenja ist an Klischeehaftigkeit kaum zu überbieten. Ebenso der raunende Ton der monologischen Dialoge und die wiederkehrende Allegorisierung des porträtierten Milieus mit (grausamen, einsamen) Wölfen oder (starken, russischen) Bären. Vielleicht eignet sich diese Graphic Novel als Einstieg ins Thema „Neorussischer Imperialismus“, tiefere Erkenntnisse lassen sich jedoch kaum finden.
Die Kunst der Erzählung
Die 1980 in Frankreich geborene Zeichnerin Catherine Meurisse war lange Mitglied der Redaktion der Satirezeitschrift Charlie Hebdo und konnte wie ihr Kollege Luz nur durch einen glücklichen Zufall dem islamistischen Attentat vom 7. Januar 2015 entkommen. In der Folge arbeitete sie an eigenen Buchprojekten, die sich teils mit autobiografischen Erlebnissen wie der Verarbeitung des Terroranschlags („Die Leichtigkeit“), aber auch häufig mit der französischen Kulturgeschichte auseinandersetzten.
„Olympia in Love“ von 2014 (Reprodukt Verlag, Berlin 2018) ist so ein Buch, in dem sie Edouard Manets Gemälde „Olympia“ von 1863 als Aufhänger für eine aberwitzige Comicgeschichte verwendete. Während die durchschnittlich gebildete französische Leserschaft ein solches Anspielungsfeuerwerk sofort versteht, setzt es bei deutschen Rezipienten allerdings ein gewisses Interesse an der französischen Kultur voraus.
Beim aktuellen Buch „Alexandre Dumas erzählt die Geschichte von Delacroix“ (Carlsen Verlag, Hamburg) verfliegen derlei Bedenken schnell. Meurisses leichtfüßige Erzählweise findet hier einen ebenbürtigen Partner. Der Text stammt von Alexandre Dumas („dem Älteren“, 1802–1870).
Der war im 19. Jahrhundert ein Bestsellerautor, schuf Klassiker wie „Die drei Musketiere“ und betrieb eine Schreibfabrik mit zahllosen Ghostwritern, die unter seinem Namen hunderte Feuilletonromane schrieben. Der Kunstliebhaber kannte nahezu die komplette Pariser Künstlerszene persönlich.
Plauderei über Delacroix
Mit dem Maler Eugène Delacroix (1798–1863) verband ihn eine Freundschaft. Ein Jahr nach dessen Tod, 1864, verfasste er anlässlich einer umfassenden Pariser Ausstellung seiner Gemälde eine Rede über den Weggefährten. In dieser „Plauderei über Delacroix und seine Werke“ ließ er dessen Karriere Revue passieren und in zahllosen Anekdoten sein Insiderwissen über die Pariser Kunstsalons einfließen. Der kurz danach publizierte Text dieser Rede ist die Grundlage zu Meurisses Buch.
Bereits 2004 illustrierte sie ihn für ihre (preisgekrönte) Hochschulabschlussarbeit, ergänzt um Comicbilder, in der etwa der beleibte Alexandre Dumas vor seine Zuhörer tritt und über Delacroix zu sprechen beginnt.
Die Rede selbst wird von der Künstlerin in handgeletterter Weise wiedergegeben, sodass Illustrationen und Text wie aus einem Guss wirken (das deutsche Lettering von Olav Kohrt lehnt sich an Meurisses Schrift an). Immer wieder werden Comicszenen eingestreut, die Dumas’ oft satirisch zugespitzte Anekdoten in bissiger Weise darstellen und durch eigene Einfälle ergänzen.
Meurisses Könnerschaft zeigt sich, wenn sie mit herrlich schrägen Figuren den damaligen Pariser Kunstbetrieb wie auch die Bourgeoisie aufs Korn nimmt. Dabei zitiert sie oft historische Karikaturen. So wird auch der Kampf zwischen der konservativen Malschule um Ingres (1780–1867), die Linien und Konturen betont, und Delacroix’ freierer Malweise plastisch vorgeführt.
Eigene originelle Setzungen
2019 griff Meurisse auf dieses Frühwerk zurück, kolorierte es und erweiterte es um seitenfüllende Aquarelle. Sie interpretiert berühmte Gemälde Delacroix’, erkundet die Wirkung der Farben, während zentrale Figuren schemenhaft bleiben. In eigenen Bildern arbeitet sie dem Erzähler Dumas zu, der genüsslich betont, wie Delacroix’ meisterhafter Umgang mit der Farbe die Kunstwelt düpierte, revolutionierte – und den Grundstein für den Impressionismus legte, der wenige Jahre später die Salons eroberten.
Natürlich wird auch Delacroix’ berühmtestes Gemälde angesprochen. „Die Freiheit führt das Volk“ (1830), eine Darstellung der Pariser Julirevolution von 1830, mit der Madeleine als Barrikadenführerin im Zentrum. Das ikonisch gewordene Werk, so weiß Dumas zu berichten, wurde zwar sogleich vom Staat angekauft, durfte aber jahrzehntelang wegen seines brisanten politischen Gehalts nicht öffentlich ausgestellt werden.
Catherine Meurisse hat mit ihren kongenial satirischen Comicszenen, ihrem lockeren Strich und mit bezaubernden Aquarellen der 160 Jahre jungen, hochamüsanten wie lehrreichen „Plauderei“ ihre Frische zurückgegeben und ihrerseits ein Gesamtkunstwerk geschaffen.
Mit der gelungenen Übersetzung von Lilian Pithan liegt Dumas’ fulminantes Porträt seines Künstlerfreundes erstmals auf Deutsch vor.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/france-eu-de.title: France’s Protests Fuel a Wider Fight Over Europe’s Future
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/france-eu-de.author: Harrison Stetler
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/france-eu-de.text:
France’s Protests Fuel a Wider Fight Over Europe’s Future
European authorities want France’s next government to cut welfare. It’s a stand for the same budget orthodoxies that have fueled current protests, and that have collapsed support for the liberal center ground.
The social unrest currently gripping France is in many ways a national phenomenon. Frustration with a stretched education system boiled over in the form of campus blockages and marches beginning late last month. By mid-October, students were joined by broader swaths of the population fed up with high gasoline prices, sticky inflation, and declining real wages.
There’s also little new in the violent police response that has shocked protesters and observers alike, both in France and abroad. Emmanuel Macron’s allies above all want to protect the president’s agenda of pro-business tax cuts, an often-elided factor in the country’s fiscal crisis. France’s state deficit is expected to reach 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026, the highest level in the eurozone, sending tremors in bond markets and leading to calls for drastic cuts to public services. On October 26, the government made its first overtures toward the students, hinting at the possible replacement of the reviled university selection platform Parcoursup, caps on classroom sizes, and state support for building renovations.
But shared European realities are also driving the anger. Spain’s recent demonstrations over the cost of housing pushed Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call snap elections for late November. Meanwhile, youth protests have disrupted cities in Italy, Belgium, and Greece, part of what some commentators are calling a “Gen Z” revolt against economic insecurity, the uncertainty surrounding the rise of artificial intelligence, and the withering political response to climate change.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Students stage protest performance over closure of Chicago's DePaul Art Museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Ruth Lopez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The closure in June of DePaul University’s esteemed DePaul Art Museum (DPAM) has rankled the arts community in Chicago. Students returning to campus this autumn responded to that loss with a communal piece of public protest art titled Waiting.
The format was simple: at 5pm on 8 October, a queue began to form at the front door of the shuttered museum. For the next hour, more than 100 people stood solemnly in the line stretching far down the sidewalk.
“The art department feels underfunded and forgotten by the administration,” said Ursula DeBray, a 22-year-old art student from Washington state. “Closing the museum felt like DePaul took ten steps backwards.”
This sentiment was shared by others who came to the protest hoping to convince the university's leadership to reconsider its decision to close the museum. “It’s showing that there was a community that got impacted by funding decisions,” said art student Jaret Ledford.
The DPAM had provided a cultural refuge for the campus community and surrounding neighbourhood of Lincoln Park, including educational and work-study opportunities. While the museum’s doors are now closed to the public, it remains minimally staffed to accommodate class visits and meet its obligation to a funded fellowship in museum studies.
The school responded to the protest the following day, saying in a statement: “DePaul University welcomes this peaceful demonstration in support of the arts in Chicago. The decision to stop operations at the DePaul Art Museum was a difficult one, as many institutions around the country are facing budgetary constraints. The arts are a critical part of DePaul’s community and academic offerings, and the university has no plans to sell the art collection or the building.”
The statement went on to say that university leadership was working with a faculty task force “to guide the next chapter of this space and collection” and expects to receive a report with recommendations from the group in December.
Most of the artists, students and faculty at the protest expressed frustration with the university’s partiality to sports. Just days before, the university had celebrated the groundbreaking for a $42m sports complex after demolishing four 1890s rowhouses. The building site is just around the corner from the museum, making the disparate spending decisions impossible to ignore.
“I don’t quite understand some of the funding priorities of academic institutions,” said Dana Boutin, an independent researcher and curator who held a handmade “I ❤️ DPAM” sign.
Boutin pointed out that another local college, the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC), recently sold the 19th-century home that once housed the Roger Brown Study Collection. Brown’s home and studio had been given to SAIC by the eponymous painter and collector in 1996, but its contents were later donated to the Wisconsin-based Art Preserve. Although the objects and art ended up in a more simpatico institution, SAIC had succeeded in dismantling a historic and culturally important experience for its art-school community.
“These are laboratories for students to learn and get professional experience,” Boutin said.
The mood in the queue at DPAM was wistful. Maybe it had something to do with the fact that the lights were still on in the museum, and that its collection will not be dispersed. DPAM’s director, Laura-Caroline de Lara, remains at the museum as the steward of its 4,000-piece collection. She said she has received many requests for external loans and is now in conversation with the Art Bridges Foundation about entering its collection-sharing programme.
