In Pictures
Photos: Thousands join India’s opposition rally against election chief
Protesters march in New Delhi demanding the election chief quit over voter roll changes seen as favouring Modi’s party.
Thousands have marched through New Delhi demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner over changes to voter lists that opposition parties say favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
Rahul Gandhi of the Indian National Congress led Sunday’s protest, the latest in more than a month of demonstrations accusing Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of overseeing a biased revision of electoral rolls.
Opposition leaders say the removal of more than 130 million names disproportionately affected Muslims and other minorities, who are less likely to back Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and says voters whose names were wrongly deleted can re-register.
The BJP has accused the opposition of undermining democracy by challenging legitimate procedures.
India’s next general election is scheduled for 2029.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Saturday Night Live: Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette fronts a scary good Halloween episode
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Zach Vasquez
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
A new, spooktacular episode of Saturday Night Live kicks off at a Halloween-themed amusement park, where visitors cross paths with confusing “Halloween guy” David S Pumpkins (Tom Hanks) and his skeleton pals (Mikey Day and Bobby Moynihan).
This seems like a copy-and-paste version of the previous Pumpkins sketches until Donald Trump (James Austin Johnson) jumps out to “[pause] SNL skit yet again.” He needles the live audience: “Aww, are you sad you don’t get to see your third David Pumpkin scene? I’ll save you three minutes; he keeps popping up and confusing people on the ride. The end!”
Trump acknowledges Hanks by noting what a great ass he has. “That’s something I’ve been doing lately, admiring men’s asses … they’re calling it gay dementia. Dementia short for da men should show me their butts.” Between that, the odd monosyllabic noises he has been making (“Probably soul trying to leave body”), and Tuesday’s midterms looking disastrous for Republicans, Trump is losing it even more than usual. He brings out support in the form of self-sabotaging allies, rapper Nicki Minaj (Saidah Belo-Osagie) and former press secretary Katie Zacharia (Veronika Slowikowska), the latter of whom tries to deliver the “Live from New York…” sign-off but ends up “whiff[ing] it”, leading Hanks and co to bring it home.
A much improved cold open, with Trump’s increasing dementia and looming political reckoning giving it much-needed narrative shape.
Inde Navarrette makes her hosting debut. The young breakout star assures the audience that she’s nothing like her character from the horror hit Obsession, even as she starts to slide into that character’s psycho speech patterns. She gets a dig in at preceding host Shane Gillis’s controversial jokes about women, noting that for her upcoming Marvel role she has to get in great shape, so “Every morning I put on my little whore outfit and I hit the gym.” Moving on, she invites the cast to come on stage and show off their Halloween costumes. Marcello Hernández is a (questionably) sexy TSA agent, Kam Patterson is Elizabeth Holmes (or, “the bad lady with the blood”), Jeremy Culhane dons a Wolverine getup in the hopes of being cast alongside Navarrette in the new X-Men film, and Grace Reiter and Slowikowska are a mechanical bird and an angry Kelly Clarkson, respectively.
The first sketch takes place on a Ghosts of the Queen Mary tour. The tour group is visited by the ghost of a wealthy heiress (Sarah Sherman) from the 1930s who is said to have hidden her diamonds somewhere on board. She reveals the treasure’s hiding place, but is interrupted by the spirits of two annoyingly chatty child siblings (Hernández, Navarrette). It’s a thin line between intentionally annoying and just annoying, and this crosses it almost right away.
A commercial for Delta Airlines introduces a new feature: Delta Disruptive, “a new section of the plane exclusively for crazy people”. From inconsiderate A-holes to out-and-out lunatics – including a guy screaming about how the plane is “made out of Israel” and a woman claiming other passengers aren’t real – it’s the perfect solution for domestic flights (especially those traveling within Florida).
The Uninterested Woman Game Show sees a woman be “upfront about not being interested in three bachelors, and they compete to react appropriately.” Said woman is Kelly (Belo-Osagie), a married lesbian who just wants to order a bagel at a deli, while the male contestants are an array of douchebags, including two white trash scumbags (Navarrette and Jane Wickline) and a sleazy gymbro (Sherman). Ashley Padilla steals the too-short sketch as the exasperated host.
The Inventor’s Wife is the latest Midnight Matinees short. Navarrette plays the widow of an eccentric, emotionally distant inventor. Touring his workshop after his funeral, she discovers his final invention, a cute robot helper named PD 44 made specifically for her. Neither she nor it can figure out what its purpose is, but they form a close bond nonetheless. Six years pass before she decides it’s time to start dating again, only to discover, upon bringing her new beau home, that PD 44 actually stands for Penis Destroyer 44, and that her husband did love her, albeit in a very twisted manner. A nice slow-burn story (replete with impressive animation and effects) that pays its tweeness off in gruesome fashion.
Behind the scenes of popular Mexican telenovela El Corazón No Siente, Navarrette and Hernández’s leads have to work a new Sprite drink into their scene as part of a product placement deal. Unfortunately, the sponsors are not pleased when the actors’ improv has them claiming that only perverts drink Sprite and attempting to use it to induce an abortion. Navarrette throws herself into this role with aplomb – literally, as she takes a couple of impressive dives over the set decoration. It’s good to see the show lean into her Mexican-American heritage.
On Weekend Update, Colin Jost picks back up on Trump’s recent obsession with men’s asses, noting that even JD Vance has commented on being jealous that his boss hasn’t complimented his butt, before asking: “What the hell is going on? Your party is about to lose the midterms; stop playing Smash or Pass with each other!” Michael Che earns awkward laughs and some gasps by reporting on Israel’s record election turnout, noting that it’s “Great to see, regardless if you’re on the right side, or the left side, or the geno-side.”
Apropos of the holiday, Update’s first guest is Pennywise the Clown (Ben Marshall). He’s there to discuss Gen Z wellness parties and spread a simple message to kids: “You don’t need to drink to have fun.” Acting more like a try-hard youth pastor than a child-murdering clown, he has moved on from trapping unsuspecting kids in the sewer to promoting his new startup: WeAllFloat.AI. The final moments are an intervention for Che following his recent stand-up special (or, per Pennywise, his latest “cry for help”). There’s a kernel of an idea here, but it’s pulled in too many directions.
We then get treated to the return of Moynihan as Update favorite Drunk Uncle. Ostensibly there to celebrate the Milwaukee Brewers’ first-ever championship victory (“My dream of a beer winning the World Series came true!”), it doesn’t take long for him to rant about everything under the sun: Mrs Met (“There’s only one gender!”), Elizabeth Holmes (“I believe her”), The Odyssey (“Helen of Troy was white!”), and more. Just as he begins breaking down, he’s joined by Brewers’ star players Christian Yelich (whom Moynihan hilariously confuses for Pete Davidson) and Brice Turang, and team manager Pat Murphy, carrying the World Series trophy in tow. It’s a deserved victory lap for all involved.
On Paw Patrol: Special Victims Unit, the furry first responders find themselves out of their depth when they have to investigate the brutal murder and mutilation of one of their own. Navarrette stumbles here, nearly breaking while delivering her lines. Not that it matters much since the cringeworthy sketch can’t end quickly enough.
A cool professor (Padilla) is enjoying a fun dinner out with students when their waiter accidentally drops a tray full of plates right on top of her head. She tries to play it off like nothing, even as she sits awash in broken china and food. Eventually, she admits that she’s in immense pain: “I can smell my blood, and I can feel my bones, and at one point I saw the Ninja Turtles walk in the room.” Things devolve from there, ending in a series of farts. Padilla was far and away the MVP of last season, but she hasn’t been given much standout material this season – until now. This is another showcase for her talents, namely her ability to milk pathetic pathos from the most juvenile of slapstick comedy. Also, good lord, does the knock she takes to the head here look legitimately painful!
Musical guest Gracie Abrams performs her second song of the night, followed by a clip of the late, great Patrick Stewart from when he hosted back in 1994, before the costumed curtain call. Although Navarrette was noticeably green at times, she was far and away the best host of the season thus far. Likewise, this is the best SNL has been since returning to air. One would hope the show can keep up the momentum, but given that next week sees a streamer hosting, that might be too much to hope for …

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: « Rien à voir » de Gaëlle Obiégly : l’art de voir ceux qu’on ne regarde pas
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Muriel Steinmetz
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Ses romans s’inscrivent dans des vies ordinaires et des objets mis au rebut, ce qui lui permet de réfracter, en toute complexité, un grand sujet d’ordre social dans tous les replis de l’intime.
Sa grand-mère Yvette, ancienne bonne à tout faire, lisait des romans en cachette, posés sur ses genoux. « Elle voyait des signes dans tout », nous dit Gaëlle Obiégly. Elle s’acharnait à les interpréter, « jusqu’à l’absurde, jusqu’à la rigolade ». Gaëlle Obiégly a grandi dans la Beauce, auprès de cette femme qui ne lui parlait jamais de ses livres. Les a-t-elle lus ? Y a-t-il, là, une filiation secrète ? Il s’agirait de déchiffrer le monde à partir de presque rien.
Les titres de ses romans désignent ce qui ne compte pas : N’être personne (Verticales, 2017), Totalement inconnu (Bourgois, 2022), Sans valeur (Bayard, 2024), Rien à voir (Verticales, 2026). « Je cherche le sens dans l’insignifiance. Le sens...

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.title: Israel intentionally released footage of Mossad operatives in Iran to provoke mass arrests, ex-chief says
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.text:
Israel intentionally released footage of Mossad operatives in Iran to provoke mass arrests, ex-chief says
Former Mossad chief David Barnea has said Israel intentionally released images of their covert operation in Iran during the June 2025 conflict to provoke mass arrests and make it harder for Iranian forces to find real Israeli agents.
“One of the reasons we immediately released an official video on the morning of Operation Rising Lion, with the Mossad logo, was to protect the agents who were there,” Barnea said, according to comments The Jerusalem Post reported on 25 October.
Barnea said the leak of the footage of Israeli operations in Iran was not just an attempt to showcase the Mossad’s reach but also a strategy to overwhelm Iranian counterintelligence, causing them to make mass arrests, making it more difficult to distinguish operatives from ordinary citizens.
“We wanted to make sure they arrested so many people in Iran that they wouldn’t be able to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and would eventually release everyone,” he said.
Barnea said Iranian authorities arrested 21,000 people during the operation.

“You have to imagine that when you arrest 21,000 people, even if you’ve caught an agent or two, eventually you have to release them because everyone’s story will be the same: I was walking down the street, I was driving a car, they arrested me,” he said.
Barnea added that many people arrested or executed on accusations of working for Israel had no connection to the Mossad.
“Some of the people being hanged in Iran on accusations of being Mossad agents, I have to ask who they are,” he said. “They tell me, ‘Listen, we don’t know either.’”
He described some of those executed as “just unfortunate people whom they decided were our agents, but who never worked for the Mossad, and probably never worked for any other intelligence organisation either”, according to the reported remarks.
The remarks made at the Priority Summit on 22 October to a private audience have sparked a sharp response from Trita Parsi.
Parsi, executive vice-president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, described it as an admission that Israel "used ordinary Iranians as tools to protect Mossad operatives" in the country.
“Rarely will you find a more crude admission of how Israel deliberately and carelessly put thousands of people it claimed it sought to liberate in harm’s way,” Parsi wrote on X.
Mass detentions
Israel launched Operation Rising Lion on 13 June 2025, during which they bombed Iran and killed senior military commanders as well as scientists.
After Iran retaliated with missile attacks on Israel, the 12-day war ended with a ceasefire.
On the first morning of the attacks, the Mossad released videos showing what it said were its agents operating inside Iran.
The footage included attacks on ballistic missile and air-defence targets, with the faces of those involved concealed.
Iranian police announced in August 2025 that they had detained about 21,000 people during the 12-day conflict.
Police spokesperson Saeed Montazer al-Mahdi said the arrests followed reports from members of the public and increased security measures.
More than 260 suspects were arrested on suspicion of espionage and 172 people were arrested for illegal filming, the police statement said.
Barnea’s comments come amid concerns over Iran’s use of espionage allegations to prosecute people following the conflict.
Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch said in September 2025 that Iranian authorities had arrested more than 20,000 people after the outbreak of hostilities with Israel.
Those targeted included journalists, human rights activists, social media users, members of ethnic and religious minorities, and foreigners.
Iranian authorities have said they were responding to genuine threats from Israeli intelligence and collaborators inside the country.
Tehran has repeatedly accused the Mossad of recruiting people to gather intelligence, carry out sabotage and assist military attacks.

https://taz.de/Zverev-an-der-Tennisspitz.title: Zverev an der Tennisspitze: Dramatischer Dreikampf
https://taz.de/Zverev-an-der-Tennisspitz.author: René Hamann
https://taz.de/Zverev-an-der-Tennisspitz.text:
Zverev an der Tennisspitze: Dramatischer Dreikampf
Der deutsche Tennisprofi Alexander Zverev ist die neue Nr. 1 der Welt. Nach der Halbfinalniederlage von Wien könnte das ein kurzes Vergnügen sein.
Jetzt hat er es doch geschafft. Seit diesem Montag ist Alexander Zverev auch offiziell die neue Nummer 1 im Herrentennis. Es hat ihn einige Mühen gekostet, es gehörte auch etwas Glück dazu, und die gute Gelegenheit, sozusagen die Gunst der Stunde. Und die hat er genutzt: Er ist in diesem abwechslungsreichen Tennisjahr stabil geblieben, ist an Ort und Stelle gewesen, wenn es darauf ankommt.
Zwei Grand Slams hat er in diesem Jahr gewonnen, erst Paris, dann New York, wo er nebenbei auch sein Corona-Dominik-Thiem-Trauma, das Verpatzen einer bequemen Führung im Finale, ablegen konnte. Und jetzt hat er es auf den Thron geschafft. Der Respekt sollte riesig sein – in der Wiener Stadthalle, die ihn nach dem Achtelfinale ausgiebig feierte, war er das auch.
Und doch wird auch die Kritik an ihm nicht so schnell verstummen, weder die sportliche, noch die persönliche. Seine juristischen Belange, einmal sei es noch gesagt, sind durchaus noch nicht abschließend geklärt – Stichwort häusliche Gewalt. Das wird ihm auch noch länger anhaften, egal, wie er sich außergerichtlich mit seinen Ex-Freundinnen geeinigt haben wird oder nicht.
Aber auch Boris Becker, Mentor, Kritiker, Vorbild und nicht zuletzt Vorläufer als letzte deutsche Nummer 1, hatte ja nie eine reine Weste, auch wenn dessen „Verfehlungen“ anders gelagert waren. Trotzdem nicht ohne: Steuerhinterziehung, Insolvenzverschleppung, Gefängnisstrafe; seine „Frauengeschichten“ waren zwar nie justiziabel, machten aus ihm aber auch keinen Ehrenmann.
Und doch bleibt Becker eine Ikone des „weißen Sports“. Vielleicht auch wegen seiner Fehler – deren sportliche Überwindung einen Teil der Faszination seiner Karriere ausmachten. Bei Zverev ist das anders: Er hat zu einer Stabilität gefunden, gleichzeitig lässt sich der Eindruck von Verdrängung nie abschütteln.
Zurück zum Sport
Kommen wir nun endlich zum Sportlichen. In Wien, beim diesjährigen ATP 500 in der Wiener Stadthalle, wusste Zverev erst zu überzeugen. In Runde 1 gegen den Qualifikanten Martín Landaluce (Spanien) wurde er überraschenderweise so richtig gefordert. Aber Zverev fiel eben nicht: Er blieb stabil, haute sich raus, gewann am Ende mit 7:5, 3:6, 7:6 (13:11).
Das entscheidende Spiel gegen den Niederländer Tallon Griekspoor, gegen den er auch schon mal verloren hat, war ebenfalls knapp, aber letztlich gewann er es souverän 6:4, 7:5. Das nächste Spiel war endlich so etwas wie ein Freilos, Zverev spielte trotz nahezu schlafloser Nacht, nachdem endlich feststand, dass er Montagmorgen als Nummer 1 der Welt aufwachen würde, einen perfekten ersten und einen dominanten zweiten Satz: 6:0, 6:2 gegen den bedauernswerten Arthur Fery aus Großbritannien.
Womit wir im Halbfinale wären und bei dem, was an sportlicher Kritik bei Sascha Zverev so schnell nicht verstummen wird. Gegen einen gleichwertigen Gegner kommt er oft mindestens in Schwierigkeiten. Dauerläufer Alex de Minaur aus Australien lief ihm am Ende in Grund und Boden und erreichte statt ihm das Finale von Wien (4:6, 6:1, 6:7 (4:7)).
Verfolger Alcaraz
Was mehrere lustige, vielleicht für Zverev sogar gute Seiteneffekte hatte. Zum Einen wich er damit dem wahren Duell mit dem anderen Gott des Gemetzels, dem Spanier Carlos Alcaraz, praktischerweise erst einmal aus. Zverev ist die Nummer 1, die wahre Nummer 1 ist vielleicht Sinner, der eine längere Verletzungspause genommen hat, oder eben Alcaraz, der ebenfalls noch ein Loch in seiner Punktesammlung auffüllen muss, weil er früher im Jahr eine Verletzungspause hatte.
Nächste Ironie: Die 500 Punkte von Wien hat Zverev verpasst; nach dem deutlich verlorenen Finale gegen Sinner 2025 verliert er sogar Punkte, weil es diesmal nur zum Halbfinale reichte. Sinner verliert 500, Alcaraz, 2025 nicht in Wien, kann 500 aufholen, wenn er nach Redaktionsschluss das Finale gegen de Minaur gewinnt, wovon die Tenniswelt ausgeht. Die Aufholjagd ist eröffnet, auch Sinner hat seine vorzeitige Rückkehr noch vor Jahresende bereits angekündigt.
Der wahre Showdown wird also in Australien stattfinden, beim Grand Slam im Januar. Die beiden Dominatoren der letzten Jahre laufen endlich wieder gleichzeitig auf; dazu läutet Altmeister Novak Djokovic vielleicht endlich sein letztes Jahr ein. Sascha Zverev indes wird sich beweisen müssen: Kann er „Sincaraz“ die Stirn bieten oder wird seine Amtszeit als Nummer 1 ein temporäres Phänomen bleiben und er als die Liz Truss des Herrentennis in die Geschichte eingehen?
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Why is Morocco celebrating the defeat of a UN resolution on Western Sahara?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Why is Morocco celebrating the defeat of a UN resolution on Western Sahara?
The mandate for UN mission that was tasked to monitor 1991 truce and hold referendum in disputed territory expires.
Morocco has welcomed the defeat of a US-drafted resolution which sought to extend the mandate of the UN mission in the disputed Western Sahara.
The mandate of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) expired on Saturday after a veto by Russia, leaving the future of the peacekeeping mission in limbo. In 1991, the UN established MINURSO to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future.
Morocco has considered Western Sahara its own territory since 1975, when Spain withdrew from the desert region in northwest Africa which is roughly the size of Britain. The Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
So, why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution? What does it mean for the future of the disputed region?
Here is what we know:
What happened at the UN Security Council?
On Friday, the US, which is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, proposed a resolution to support the principle of self-determination in the disputed Western Sahara.
Russia vetoed the resolution, despite support from 11 of the 15 council members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.
The US draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.
Last October, the UN Security Council adopted a resolution that offered genuine autonomy to Western Sahara. Under that plan, the territory would manage its internal affairs, but remain under Moroccan sovereignty.
The Security Council had already made the proposal a basis for negotiations last year and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.
Speaking after the vote, US ambassador Mike Waltz said it was truly unfortunate that in 2026 the veto was used to “preserve the letter R (in the Mission’s name) for referendum”.
He added that Washington’s proposal “would have moved the 50-year conflict forward” and added that the status quo is not acceptable.
Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.
“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.
Instead, Russia proposed renewing the existing mission without those changes. But that draft also failed to secure the nine votes needed for adoption, receiving two votes in favour, one against and 11 abstentions.
MINURSO’s mission has 155 military personnel and is set to cost $62m in the fiscal year that began in June, according to a UN report. But its mandate expired on Saturday.
How did Morocco and Algeria react to the failure of the UN mission?
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO, saying on Friday that UN personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days and that the Western Sahara issue should now be withdrawn from the Security Council’s consideration. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire.
According to a UN media statement, Morocco’s UN representative also questioned why Algeria’s delegate was giving the Security Council “lectures” on the Western Sahara.
“Let these people [in the Western Sahara] go back to Morocco,” he said, “let them go home”.
Algeria expressed regret on Saturday over the failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate. Its foreign ministry criticised what it described as the US draft’s excessive bias towards Morocco.
According to a UN media statement, Algeria’s delegate to the UN thanked Russia for its draft resolution and all other member nations “who have chosen not to associate themselves” with an egregious injustice and a flagrant attack on “the very foundation of our organisation”.
Algeria’s UN representative noted that the country has been a refuge for hundreds of thousands of Sahrawi people who have been denied their right to self-determination.
The “tragedy being endured by the Sahrawi people has oddly been diluted to the concept of refugee populations”, he added.
Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative at the UN, told reporters on Friday that he welcomed Russia’s veto because the US proposal would undermine Sahrawi self-determination.
What is the Western Sahara dispute all about?
The Polisario Front, the political and military representative, does not recognise Morocco’s annexation of the territory following Spain’s withdrawal in 1975. It has been seeking a UN-supervised referendum for self-determination.
In 1976, it declared the independent Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.
Decades of fighting drove at least 170,000 Indigenous people into refugee camps in Tindouf in neighbouring Algeria, which backs the Polisario Front.
The Polisario Front signed a UN-brokered ceasefire with Morocco in 1991. It called for a referendum within six months, but it was never held.
Morocco, which retains control of its lucrative phosphate and fishing resources in Western Sahara, claims historic and pre-colonial ties to the land and views the region as an integral part of its territory [“Greater Morocco”].
For decades, the US has provided military and diplomatic support to Morocco. But in 2020, Donald Trump recognised Moroccan sovereignty over the territory during his first term in office. Morocco soon established diplomatic ties with Israel as part of the so-called Abraham Accords.
The region is now the last United Nations-designated “non-self-governing territory” in Africa, where between 100,000 and 140,000 Moroccan military personnel are based.
Low-level fighting has also continued since the Polisario Front said it was resuming armed struggle in 2020.
Why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution?
MINURSO was set up to monitor the 1991 ceasefire and hold a referendum in Western Sahara. The expiry of its mandate will likely boost Morocco’s stance on the referendum question, though its autonomy proposal has already been adopted by the UN.
On Saturday, according to a video report by the Reuters news agency, a festive atmosphere prevailed in the streets of El Aaiun, the capital of Western Sahara.
In the central Mechoua Square, dozens of people were wearing melfas, the traditional Sahrawi women’s garments, and long robes known as darra, as they waved Moroccan flags and displayed portraits of Morocco’s King Mohammed VI.
Selim Balouati Lakhloufi, a historian and researcher based in Morocco, said that Morocco is pleased because “diplomatic developments at the United Nations are supporting its strategy regarding the [disputed Western] Sahara”.
“The support of powers such as the United States, France and the United Kingdom for Morocco’s autonomy proposal strengthens its international position and is gradually shifting the debate away from the right to self-determination and the possibility of independence toward a solution based on autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty,” he told Al Jazeera.
What does this mean for the future of the Western Sahara?
The collapse of MINURSO’s mandate could escalate the dispute in the Western Sahara, according to aid organisations.
Oxfam has warned that losing MINURSO’s “monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability”.
Lakhloufi said that the UN mission’s expiry is also unfavourable for Sahrawi independence aspirations.
Regarding the future of the Western Sahara, he said that Morocco will likely continue to consolidate its territorial, economic and administrative control, while the Polisario Front will face greater difficulties in securing international support.
“The proposal for autonomy could end up becoming the main framework for negotiations, pushing independence further and further out of reach,” he added.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: One person killed in shooting outside Magic City Classic football game in Alabama
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
One person was killed and eight others were wounded in a mass shooting outside Legion Field after the annual Magic City Classic football game on Saturday night, police in Birmingham, Alabama, said.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game, but the shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
He said he was “very grateful that more people weren’t injured.”
The circumstances of the shooting were unclear. Police spokesperson De’Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and transported to police headquarters for questioning, and “multiple weapons” had been found and secured.
Alabama State and Alabama A&M are historically Black universities and archrivals whose annual meeting has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, which Alabama A&M won 31-28. The event draws huge crowds to Birmingham every year.
“Everyone knows this is the largest event we have here in the city and it’s extremely taxing on our personnel,” said Pickett. “Other leaders in law enforcement recognize that and they quickly offered up support and we are grateful for that quick response.”

https://taz.de/Gen-Z-regelt-Demonstratio.title: „Gen Z regelt“-Demonstrationen: Eine Bühne für die Unzufriedenheit
https://taz.de/Gen-Z-regelt-Demonstratio.author: Amira Klute, Malte Steinmüller und David Muschenich
https://taz.de/Gen-Z-regelt-Demonstratio.text:
„Gen Z regelt“-Demonstrationen: Eine Bühne für die Unzufriedenheit
In Hamburg, Berlin und Erfurt bleiben die Proteste eher ruhig. Nur nach dem Ende der Kundgebungen werden mancherorts Böller oder Steine geworfen.
Da ist zum Beispiel Silvia Saß, 68, bunter Schal, die mit ihrem Mann gekommen ist. „Wir sind heute hier, weil wir Kinder und Enkelkinder haben, weil wir wollen, dass die jungen Leute ne ordentliche Bildung bekommen, dass sie ein lebenswertes Leben haben, damit keine Kinder in den Krieg ziehen müssen.“ Es sei ihre Verantwortung als Alte, die Anliegen der Jugend zu unterstützen.
Rund 10.000 Menschen folgten laut den Veranstaltenden dem Aufruf von „Gen Z regelt“, die Polizei sprach von 6.000 bis 7.000 Demonstrantinnen und Demonstranten, daunter auch ältere Semester. Die Sprecherin der Demo, die als Catalina, auftritt, zeigt sich zufrieden. „Es wurde geschafft, der generellen Unzufriedenheit eine Bühne zu bieten.“ Und das, obwohl der Hamburger Verfassungsschutz vor Linksextremen gewarnt und die Polizei Verwirrung gestiftet hatte: Es lege keine Demo unter dem Namen „Gen Z regelt“ vor, nur eine „Gegen Wehrpflicht“, sagte ein Sprecher Ende der Woche. Dann verschwand Hamburg von der „Gen Z regelt“ Webseite. Gab es Stress? Nein: „Das war viel weniger dramatisch, als es von außen wirkte“, sagte Lina Friedrich, Sprecherin von „Gen Z regelt“ Deutschland der taz. Man habe nur keine Kapazitäten gehabt, die Demo in Hamburg zu organisieren. Trotzdem rief man zur Teilnahme auf wie bei den anderen Städten.
Es spricht viel dafür, dass der Internationale Jugendverband, eine sozialistische Gruppe, an der Orga in Hamburg beteiligt war. Ihr Logo ist auf Flyern zu sehen, die verteilt werden. Doch in der Masse gehen sie eher unter – genau wie rote Schlauchschals, das Signature-Zeichen marxistisch-leninistischer Gruppen.
Hamburgs Luxusmeile verbarrikadiert
Die Einzelhändler rund um den Startpunkt der Demo in der Mönckebergstraße, Hamburgs Luxuseinkaufsmeile, verbarrikadierten sich vorsichtshalber. Patek Phillippe hatte sogar die Außenuhren eingepackt und an den Gucci-Stores schraubten Arbeiter noch bis kurz vor Start der Demo. Am Vormittag lösten sie dabei laut Bild-Zeitung versehentlich Alarm aus. Am Ende bleiben alle Läden unberührt. Ein paar Meter weiter Rufe: „Hoch die internationale Solidarität“. „Hoch, die was?“, fragt ein Jugendlicher, der sich durch die Menge schiebt. Er ist nicht der Einzige, der nicht alle Sprechhöre auswendig kennt. Es sind viele Menschen da, die noch nie auf einer Demo waren.
Zum Beispiel Tobias, 18, und Nikita, 19, die sich als Dragonball-Charaktere verkleidet haben. „Wir sind hier, weil wir einfach dabei sein wollen“, sagt Tobias. Sie hätten die Demos in Frankreich gesehen und fänden die Forderungen von „Gen Z regelt“ gut. Sie hofften auf Demos wie in Frankreich, aber friedlicher. Man dürfe sein Recht auf Demonstration nicht verspielen, sind sie sich einig. Wieso sie vorher noch auf keiner Demo waren? „Wir hatten noch nicht so viel Zeit“, sagt Nikita.
Die ersten Pyros werden kurz nach Start gezündet, dann der erste Böller in der Menge. Es knallt laut zwischen den Häusern und mehrere Menschen erschrecken sich sehr. Die Polizist*innen bleiben vergleichsweise zurückhaltend, was auch an der Masse der Menschen liegen mag. Kurz muss die Demo stoppen, darf aber sofort weiter. Aus dem Lauti fordert eine Rednerin das Ende der Merz-Regierung. Viele nennen die Kürzungen der Bundesregierung als Grund, auf die Demo gekommen zu sein. So auch Joana Mandlhate, 32. „It’s giving Zukunftsangst“ steht auf ihrem Schild. Sie arbeite im Marketing, erzählt sie, habe zwei Jobs und könne sich trotzdem keinen Urlaub leisten. „Ich bin genervt, dass gesagt wird, dass wir faul sind, ich kann gerade so meinen Lebensunterhalt bezahlen, lebe nicht auf großem Fuß“.
Böller auf die Polizei
Dann kommt die Demo an ihren Endpunkt. Es ist eine breite Straße, am Rand ist Baustelle. Es ist kurz unklar, was noch passiert, ein bisschen ungläubig: „War’s das jetzt?“ Dann fliegen Flaschen und Holzteile in Richtung Polizei,vor allem geworfen von jungen Männern, einige vermummt, aber nicht alle. Ein paar nehmen Baustellenabsperrungen und stapeln sie. Böller zünden in kleineren Abständen. Die Polizei rennt in die Demo, kesselt einen Teil, zieht sich aber wieder zurück. Sehr junge Menschen, viele Flinta drängen sie mit Antikriegs-Transpi an den Rand.
Um 17 Uhr wird die Versammlung vom Lauti aus aufgelöst, dann brennen Bauzäune. Die Polizei bleibt nicht länger am Rand, treibt die Menschen auseinander, geht rigoros gegen überwiegend sehr junge Menschen vor. Ein Sprecher sagt, es seien Böller auf Polizist*innen geworfen worden.
Am Ende der Hamburger Demo fährt ein Wasserwerfer auf die Straße. Pfefferspray liegt in der Luft, eine dicke schwarze Rauchsäule steigt in den Himmel, es riecht nach verbranntem Plastik. Doch der Wasserwerfer kommt nicht gegen Menschen zum Einsatz, er löscht nur die brennenden Bauzäune, die auf der Straße im Stadtteil St. Georg liegen, später noch ein paar brennende Mülleimer und Müllsäcke, die Beamte daraufhin mit Schaufeln aus dem Weg räumen.
Nach der Demo knallt es auch in Berlin
Ähnlich verläuft der Abend in Berlin: Nach der durchgängig friedlichen „Gen Z regelt“-Demonstration am Brandenburger Tor mit 5 000 Teilnehmenden startete eine weitere Demonstration, angemeldet unter dem Namen „Gen Z hat genug“. Aufgerufen hatte dazu nicht die Berliner Organisation von „Gen Z regelt“, sondern das Offene Rote Treffen Berlin (ORT). Dieser zweite Protest mit etwa 3.500 Teilnehmenden verlief nicht ohne Gewalt.
Schon zu Beginn geben sich die Teilnehmenden deutlich kämpferischer, rufen Parolen wie „Erst im Kommunismus sind wir frei“ und „Bullen-Schweine. Mörder. Lügner“. Auf der Demonstration wehen Flaggen von den sozialistischen Gruppen ORT, Young Struggle und SDAJ (Sozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterjugend). Immer wieder werfen Einzelpersonen Pyrotechnik in Richtung der Polizei. Später eskaliert der Protest. Die Polizist*innen halten den Demozug auf, können aber nicht alle Wege kontrollieren. Das führt zu Gerangel, Festnahmen und Polizeigewalt. Während einer Festnahme schlägt ein Polizist mehrfach mit der Faust auf einen am Boden liegenden Demonstranten. Selbst ein schätzungsweise 14-jähriger Junge wird mehrfach von der Polizei heftig geschubst.
Gegen 19 Uhr beendet der Veranstalter den Protest selbst. Bis die Versammlung aber tatsächlich vorbei ist, vergeht eine weitere Stunde mit teils gewaltsamen Räumungen. Mehrere Demonstrant*innen werden verletzt. Die Polizei sagt der taz, dass Beamte mit Steinen beworfen worden seien.
In Erfurt bleibt es friedlich
In keiner anderen ostdeutschen Stadt haben sich so viele für den „Gen Z“-Protest angemeldet wie in Thüringens Landeshauptstadt. Mehr als 10 000-mal wurde laut der Website für den Erfurter Domplatz auf „Ich bin dabei“ geklickt. Doch 15 Minuten vor Beginn ist dort wenig zu sehen. Ein Banner gegen Krieg, eine Palästina-Fahne, ein Dutzend junger Menschen, die etwas unschlüssig herumstehen. Aber tatsächlich stehen sie am falschen Ort.
Tatsächlich beginnt die Demo ein paar hundert Meter entfernt am Anger, einem anderen zentralen Platz in der Stadt. Dort bilden wenig später mehrere hundert Menschen einen Kreis um einen kleinen Lautsprecher. Durch ein damit verbundenes Mikrofon halten mehrere junge Menschen kurze Reden. Es geht um Leistungsdruck in Schulen, wie die Vermögensverteilung die Bildungschancen beeinflusst, Ausbeutung, Klimakrise, Rassismus und gegen Wehrpflicht.
Die meisten Zuhörer:innen sind ebenfalls eher jung. Auch aus den hinteren Reihen bekommen die Redner:innen oft Applaus, obwohl sie dort kaum zu verstehen sind. Der Lautsprecher ist zu klein. Die Polizei beobachtet die Kundgebung mit etwas Abstand. Es sind verhältnismäßig wenige Beamte zu sehen, ihre Schutzhelme baumeln entspannt an den Gürteln. Über dem Protest von Gen Z flattern Fahnen der kleinen Kaderpartei MLPD als auch der anarchistischen Gewerkschaft FAU. Zwischen zwei Redebeiträgen skandieren die Teilnehmer:innen: „Nie wieder Wehrpflicht!“
Wegen Reformationstag geschlossen
Am Rande des Angers, durch die Straßenbahnschienen vom Protest getrennt, grölen sechs Personen etwas Unverständliches und packen dann zwei Deutschlandflaggen aus. Ganz nüchtern wirken sie nicht. Nun werden aber die Polizeibeamt:innen aktiv, schnellen Schritts schieben sie sich zwischen die Kundgebung und die sechs mit den Deutschlandfahnen.
Wenig später zieht die „GenZ“-Demo los und skandiert eine Parole nach der anderen. „Ganz Erfurt hasst die AfD“, „Friedrich Merz, an die Front, werd doch selber weggebombt“, „Kein Gott, kein Staat, kein Patriarchat!“ Verbarrikadierte Schaufenster? Nicht in Erfurt. Die meisten Geschäfte haben wegen des Reformationstags geschlossen. Aber aus den Restaurants heraus beobachten Passant:innen die Hunderten Demonstrant:innen, teilweise winken sie.
Die Polizei geht in der Spitze von bis zu 1 900 Teilnehmer:innen aus. Ohne Zwischenstopp oder Zwischenfälle ziehen die bis zum Hauptbahnhof. Nach der Abschlusskundgebung ist in Erfurt alles sehr schnell vorbei.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
President Isaac Herzog must tap a candidate to form a new government after results are certified by November 10, with fraught negotiations likely to follow.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his coalition’s parliamentary majority following legislative elections on October 27.
But a bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu also failed to win a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving Israel without a clear path to a new government.
What’s ahead is likely weeks of political wrangling as Israel’s disparate factions weigh possible governing arrangements, including a unity government bringing rival factions together or a minority government reliant on outside support. If they fail to reach an agreement, Israel could head back to the polls.
Here’s what you should know:
What are the final results of Israel’s elections?
The pro-Netanyahu coalition won 53 seats:
- Likud – 27
- United Torah Judaism – 7
- Otzma Yehudit – 7
- Shas – 6
- Religious Zionism – 6
A bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats:
- Yashar – 21
- B’Yachad – 12
- The Democrats – 8
- Yisrael Beytenu – 7
Arab-led parties won 19 seats:
- Joint List – 11
- Ra’am – 8
That leaves all existing blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, meaning some parties would have to realign or join forces across bloc lines to form a new government.
What happens next?
Israel’s election results must be officially certified and presented to President Isaac Herzog by November 4.
The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10.
Herzog must task one incoming Knesset member with forming a new government by November 11. He is expected to make his decision with input from party leaders, selecting the candidate he believes has the best chance of building a coalition.
The candidate commissioned by Herzog has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of 14 days.
Who will Herzog nominate first to form a government?
He has not said yet, but the most likely candidates are Netanyahu or former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party received the most votes in the opposition bloc.
According to Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth media, Eisenkot may have an edge over Netanyahu as some Arab-led parties consider endorsing him in a bid to oust Netanyahu.
Herzog, for his part, has urged Israeli politicians to move away from rigid partisan stances and look for “creative solutions” that will lead to a new government and avoid a second round of elections.
Before the election, Herzog said he would do everything he could to spare the country another election cycle, even if that means pressing for a national unity government that brings together rivals Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Could the opposition bloc join forces with Arab-led parties?
It is unclear.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have previously ruled out partnering with the Arab-led parties.
Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, however, has said he believes they “can change their mind”, arguing that Netanyahu would do in their position.
“If Netanyahu had a similar problem, he would immediately invite Mansour Abbas”, the leader of Ra’am and “give him the role of a minister of interior”, Barak told France 24 on Friday.
Abbas himself has signalled a willingness to work the opposition camp, saying Eisenkot’s conditions would not pose an obstacle for his party, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
Yousef Jabareen from the Arab-led Joint List has also said that his party is ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”.
“The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Even if Arab-led parties do not formally join the opposition’s coalition, they could prop it up from outside by helping it pass a confidence vote in the Knesset.
Raluca Ganea, co-founder of Israeli civil society group Zazim, told Al Jazeera that a coalition between the opposition bloc and the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel “is the only path forward for Israeli democracy as a whole”.
What happens if no one can form a government?
If Herzog’s first candidate fails to form a government within the 42 days, the Israeli president has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
Even without a coalition commanding at least 61 seats, a candidate could still try to form a minority government by relying on outside support from smaller parties, including Arab-led parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
If none of these options succeed and deadlock persists, the Knesset would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days.
Who is in charge in the meantime?
Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
If the process drags out, that could leave Israel’s longest-serving prime minister in power for months more, even if he ultimately fails to become part of the next governing coalition.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘There’s a lot of hate’: rightwing racism stirs south Asian mobilization in Texas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Prachi Gupta
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Last winter, while Pooja Sethi was canvassing to become the Democratic candidate for the Texas house of representatives, she received a text from a staff member alerting her to a post on X. The Turning Point USA influencer Savanah Hernandez – a Trump supporter known for creating videos that target immigrants – had posted a photo of Sethi’s campaign banner with the caption: “Welcome to politics in Texas.”
The post went viral.
The responses were so vile, Sethi said, “that I called my team and I said I’m going to go home because I need to be with my son. I’m a little scared about what’s happening right now.” The far right even turned her name into a racist slogan: “Don’t Pooja my Texas.”
If elected, Sethi will become the first Asian Democratic woman and south Asian woman in the Texas legislature. “I didn’t run to have to sit here and combat anti-Indian hate. I didn’t know that this was going to be a thing,” said Sethi to a room of about 50 south Asians gathered at a private community listening session on anti-south Asian hate in Austin at the height of election season in October.
The event, which included Washington congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, was hosted by Indian American Impact, a nonpartisan group that supports south Asian candidates and voter engagement.
Across the country, anti-south Asian hate has spiked since Trump took office. According to the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), online rhetoric against south Asians surged by 240% between January 2024 and June 2026. In addition to citing xenophobia and racism, the report finds that economic resentment casting south Asians as “invaders” and “job thieves”, increased visibility in politics, and anti-migrant policies that include Trump’s prohibitive annual fee on H1-B visa applications, have contributed to the sharp rise in hate against south Asian communities of all faiths and nationalities.
Rightwing public officials too have ramped up the xenophobic and racist rhetoric ahead of the midterm election: in September, on X, the Department of Homeland Security posted an AI-generated image resembling a movie poster that featured a Sikh man facing off against a character that looked like Optimus Prime from Transformers. The caption read: “America for Americans. Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” The agency deleted the image amid backlash.
Days later, Bo French, the Republican candidate for the Texas railroad commission, posted a photo of a photo of what appeared to be majority south Asian American UT Austin students celebrating the school’s football win with the caption: “I heard UT graduation this year look like this, I didn’t believe it, the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”
This rhetoric stokes fear and translates into physical violence, says Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact. “There’s a lot of hate and discrimination that has been spreading for years on social media and online … but those things, they make it to the foreground.”
About a week after the DHS post, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed 17 times at a rest stop in Wyoming, deepening fears of violence within the Sikh community. In October – the day before Indian American Impact’s event in Austin – news broke of an attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, where a self-described white supremacist armed with a rifle and body armor had planned to “kill Indian people”.
Texas has become the “ground zero” for anti-south Asian hate, says Chanda Parbhoo, founder and executive director of nonpartisan voter engagement nonprofit South Asian American Voter Empowerment of Texas Education Fund (SAAVETX EF). According to 2021 US census estimates, more than 600,000 south Asians live in Texas – the second-largest population of south Asians in the country behind California. South Asians make up one of the state’s fastest growing ethnic groups.
Unlike California, however, Texas is a breeding ground for far-right policies that then travel to other state legislatures across the country.
Ahead of the 2026 midterms, Texas Republicans have built a platform on Islamophobia and attacks on migrants, issues that closely intersect with the attacks on south Asians writ large. In the last year, Texas attorney general Ken Paxton, who is currently tied in the Senate race against Democrat James Talarico, sued to shut down the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group. Paxton and Republican governor Greg Abbott deemed Cair a “ terrorist organization”, fabricated charges against a North Texas mosque, and launched an investigation into unsubstantiated claims of H1-B visa fraud – an inquiry that disproportionately targets Indian immigrants.
In the state legislature, Republican representative Brent Money launched a “Sharia Free Texas Caucus,” which has amassed nearly 40 members, following the creation of a national “Sharia Free America Caucus” started by Texas congressmen Keith Self and Chip Roy in 2025. According to a 2026 survey by Stop AAPI Hate Action, ICE deportations of south Asians are approximately 14 times higher under Trump’s second term – in July, Texas accounted for nearly a third of the nation’s ICE arrests, the largest share of any state in the country.
“The hate that’s happening right now is more than anything that I’ve seen. More than during 9/11,” said Texas state representative Salman Bhojani, who immigrated to Texas from Pakistan as a teenager. “This is not the Texas that I immigrated to.”
In 2022, Bhojani became one of the first Muslims and south Asians in the state legislature and arguably the most visible Muslim in Texas politics. At a re-election campaign fundraising event held two days before early voting began in Texas, Bhojani told the Guardian: “I get these calls a lot, like, every almost on a daily basis, where somebody is calling to say, “My dad was picked up by ICE, my brother was picked up by ICE, or my sister was walking on campus in a hijab and somebody pulled a knife on her.”
In Bhojani’s city of Euless, a white woman was sentenced to five years in prison for attempted murder after she tried to drown a three-year-old Muslim girl in 2024.
Bhojani launched the Religious Freedom Caucus to promote religious tolerance. “Today, Muslims are on the chopping block. Tomorrow maybe other communities – we cannot afford that. We need to stop it right now,” he said.
While south Asian communities have become a target, as a voting bloc, they remain largely overlooked by either party. “We are still underrepresented, overlooked, and we’re not getting the attention that we should probably receive for the powerhouse that we could be,” says Parbhoo.
This gap prompted SAAVETX EF to collaborate with the US Immigration Policy Center at University of California, San Diego, for a first-of-its-kind statewide survey, released on Wednesday. The Belonging Under Pressure: 2026 South Asian Community Survey of about 1,000 south Asian Texans confirmed what Parbhoo has observed from voter participation efforts on the ground: more than half – 57.5% – reported at least one experience of hate in Texas during the past year due to race, ethnicity, religion, or immigration background.
A majority felt politically disenfranchised: 63.7% of respondents said their community’s concerns are not well understood or not understood at all by elected officials, and 53.6% believe their community holds little to no political power.
But the survey also suggests that south Asians are motivated to vote. “Sometimes we see the lack of political agency lead to a lack of political participation,” said Tom Wong, associate professor of political science and director of the US Immigration Policy Center at UCSD. “But what we’re seeing in the poll is that there’s high motivation to vote – to mobilize, organize, and change who’s in office.”
Parhboo says that as of 26 October, one week into early voting, the total number of south Asian Texans who voted in 2022 has already been surpassed.
“People have talked about the rising Hispanic electorate turning Texas blue. But it isn’t any single community. It is a multiracial coalition that includes Asians,” said Wong. “Asian Americans can decide outcomes in tight races,” he said, including Michigan, Georgia, and North Carolina.
“I think that’s one of the major takeaways, and we are thinking it might happen in Texas.”
Beto O’Rourke, for example, lost the Senate election to Ted Cruz in 2018 by a margin of 2.6% – about 215,000 votes. The south Asian vote makes up that “margin of victory”, Parbhoo says.
Bhojani’s own race is further proof. In 2018, he was elected to the city council by only 37 votes. “These races are decided by razor-thin margins,” Bhojani said. “People don’t realize that in my city, 37 votes can make a difference.”

Gasspeicher nicht gut gefüllt: Zielverfehlung mit Ansage
Die deutschen Gasspeicher erreichen zum 1. November nicht den gesetzlich geforderten Füllstand. Die Bundesnetzagentur sieht darin kein Problem.
Die deutschen Gasspeicher erfüllen zum Stichtag 1. November die gesetzlichen Vorgaben nicht. Sie sind aktuell zu 61 Prozent gefüllt, gesetzlich vorgesehen sind 70 Prozent. Das geht aus den Zahlen der Initiative Energie Speichern (INES) hervor, in der 29 deutschen Gasspeicherbetreiber mit 47 Standorten organisiert sind. Sie repräsentieren mehr als 90 Prozent der deutschen Lagerkapazitäten.
Konsequenzen hat die Zielverfehlung nicht. Für die Überwachung der Füllstände ist die Bundesnetzagentur zuständig. Sie nehme die Entwicklung ernst, heißt es in der aktuellen Lageeinschätzung der Behörde. Gleichzeitig stellt sie klar: „Die Versorgungssicherheit ist gewährleistet.“ Dafür sei es nicht zwingend, dass die Füllstandsziele erreicht werden. „Für die Versorgungssicherheit entscheidend ist ein Zusammenspiel von Pipelineimporten, Speichern, LNG-Importen, Infrastruktur und Nachfrage“, heißt es weiter. „Auf dem Weltmarkt ist ausreichend Gas verfügbar, und es sind ausreichend Importmöglichkeiten vorhanden.“
Die Branche, Oppositionspolitiker:innen und Fachleute warnen seit Monaten davor, dass das gesetzliche Ziel nicht erreicht wird. Sollte der Winter sehr kalt und Gas knapp werden, steigen die Preise noch stärker an. Die zuständige Bundeswirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (CDU) hat sich lange dagegen gewehrt einzugreifen und darauf verwiesen, dass der Markt für genügend Gasvorräte sorgen würde. Erst Ende September hat sie eine Kehrtwende vollzogen und den Kauf von etwas zusätzlichem Gas angeordnet.
Ursache der niedrigen Füllstände sind Marktstörungen. Früher haben Händler:innen im Frühjahr und Sommer in großem Stil Gas gekauft und gelagert, weil sie es im Winter für mehr Geld verkaufen konnten. Seit dem russischen Angriffskrieg auf die Ukraine funktioniert dieser Mechanismus nicht mehr. Weil die Preise auch im Frühjahr und Sommer sehr hoch sind, lohnt sich der frühe Einkauf für Händler:innen nicht mehr. In diesem Jahr kamen verschärfend die hohen Energiepreise durch die Sperrung der Straße von Hormus infolge des Irankriegs hinzu. Die Speicher waren im Frühjahr außergewöhnlich leer, weshalb die Wiederbefüllung schwieriger war als in den Vorjahren.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US attorneys are freeing children from Trump’s ‘deportation machine’ with a new strategy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Alexandra Villarreal in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Migrant children stranded alone in prolonged Trump administration custody and targeted by whole-of-government efforts to deport them are starting to win release while they fight their cases – with a fresh legal strategy, the Guardian has found.
A growing army of attorneys across the US is racing around the clock like legal first responders to file petitions of habeas corpus in federal courts demanding freedom for their young clients.
Organizers of the new movement as well as pro-immigration advocates accuse the government of unconstitutional conduct and plain cruelty, keeping families apart and rushing small children into court without lawyers – to feed Donald Trump’s “deportation machine”.
Now they are hitting back with a rare habeas tactic and it is proving surprisingly successful amid the US president’s harsh crackdown that has swept up thousands of minors, according to leaders of the advocacy movement the Guardian first revealed in September.
Researchers estimate nearly all these cases end with a child’s release from federal custody. Some don’t even get as far as a court hearing before the administration backs down and lets the child go, likely in order to avoid having to explain their policy decisions to a judge.
Since Trump retook the White House, officials have taken to keeping children who crossed the US-Mexico border unaccompanied in prolonged custody instead of allowing them to be with relatives or other vetted sponsors stateside while their legal case plays out.
Immigration enforcement activity is also “creating” new unaccompanied children, after sweeping up migrant kids in the country’s interior and separating them from their caregivers.
As of September, more than 1,800 unaccompanied children have spent six months on average in federal custody, compared with an average of 44 days between 2015 and 2024.
“The government is violating the law, and the regulations, and their own policy sometimes in this area,” said Marie Silver, supervising attorney at the Immigration and Human Rights Clinic at Loyola University Chicago School of Law, which is co-managing the new initiative, called the Children’s Due Process Project.
But, Silver continued, “I think the core of what the judges are picking up on and really sort of incensed about is just the true, underlying constitutional problems here when we keep children from their family members for no reason.”
Leading advocates are countering by rallying an expanding band of lawyers, drawn from around a hundred legal organizations, law firms and solo practitioners across the US, who are representing children free of charge. They are swiftly filing habeas petitions to get as many children as possible released to loved ones before it’s too late and the administration bundles them onto deportation flights.
Habeas corpus petitions challenging unlawful imprisonment have become a staple for the many thousands of adults held within the US immigration detention system, the world’s largest. More than 91,000 such petitions have been filed since January 2025, according to a tracker run by ProPublica. Yet until recently, they were far less common for lone migrant children, who historically have been released to family members quickly after arriving in the US and entering federal custody.
In a report published this fall, the Washington DC-based Acacia Center for Justice identified just 33 total habeas petitions filed on behalf of these children before last year, most of them during Trump’s first term. They then tracked “a 3,500% increase in habeas filings” since January 2025, compared with the four years of the Biden administration.
Researchers found at least 72 habeas petitions involving unaccompanied children in government custody across 16 federal district court jurisdictions since the start of the second Trump administration. And, in cases where the outcome was clear, 98% ended with the child released.
“This is the most immediate way to help the kids who are currently being harmed,” said Becky Wolozin, senior attorney at the California-based National Center for Youth Law (NCYL), a co-manager of the Children’s Due Process Project.
Other co-managers include Acacia and The Door, a New York-based comprehensive youth development organization. Through the effort, these organizations are training attorneys and connecting them with young clients who desperately need help with the habeas process.
“Part of what we’re hoping with this project is essentially to build a bench of people who are ready, able and excited to bring these cases, so that more kids have access to this type of vital representation,” Wolozin said.
Children arriving in the US unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian fall under the care of the office of refugee resettlement (ORR), an agency that is part of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and that has typically filled a child welfare role.
US statute and regulations explicitly require that these kids be “promptly placed in the least restrictive setting that is in the best interest of the child”. And so authorities – until recently – put them in congregate shelters, foster care or secure facilities for as little time as possible while vetting prospective “sponsors” – oftentimes parents already in the US – who applied to take care of them after release.
Many of these children have survived abuse, neglect, trafficking, abandonment or other serious harms in their countries of origin or on the way to the US – tragedies that in turn may open the door for them to seek legal immigration pathways stateside.
But now, officials across executive agencies are coordinating efforts to make it much harder for children to receive legal protections before they are ordered deported, including by ending a federal contract that had funded attorneys for over 20,000 of them and plotting to have HHS attorneys represent them instead.
“The immigration judge works for the Trump administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable,” Democratic senators recently wrote in a letter to Robert F Kennedy Jr, the HHS secretary.
In practice the lack of legal representation manifests in cases such as that of a 12-year-old girl from a shelter appearing without a lawyer in the Santa Ana, California immigration court and receiving just one week to find counsel. When children like her are forced to return to court the following week, the chances are that judges will declare them “removable” and order their deportation, said Lindsay Toczylowski, CEO and co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center.
“She will join so many other children who have no fighting chance in these immigration courts, because this is what a deportation machine looks like – children alone, sitting on the other side of a computer screen, given impossible deadlines, handed useless lists of organizations that have been defunded and rushed toward life-altering orders they cannot understand,” Toczylowski said.
Among such examples are two siblings seeking asylum, ages nine and 13, who spent about six months in government custody and endured significant mental and emotional harms because of their separation from family. Officials knew within days of their arrival that the children’s mother was living in the US, ready to welcome them. Within a month, she had already gone through full federal security vetting protocols without raising any flags, said Matthew Johnson, citywide deputy director of immigrant justice at Legal Services NYC, in New York.
She moved to a more spacious apartment, checked out local schools and built bunk beds for her kids. “Still, her second bedroom sits empty,” the habeas petition his organization filed said, months into the children’s arrival. Weeks of delays piled up, including a technical glitch with a government portal and a government employee ghosting the mother.
“If this was a parking ticket, you would be really frustrated. If it’s your children, it’s inexcusable,” Johnson said. The government even suggested the siblings might pose a safety threat if released, despite there being “no conceivable basis to conclude that these nine- and 13-year-old children were dangerous”, Johnson said. By filing a petition of habeas corpus in federal court, attorneys effectively challenged the administration to justify the siblings’ prolonged time in transitional foster care, roughly 200 miles from their mother.
Just hours before a hearing in August where an official would have had to defend the government’s decision, the children suddenly received the green light to reunite with their parent in Rhode Island.
For their mother, “this was just a painful, and traumatic, and incomprehensible, and inexplicable saga”, Johnson said. “I think she just felt relief that this was over.”
And in another case, a teenager, identified by the initials EHCF in court filings, had lived in Massachusetts for six years before he was moved to ORR custody in Texas, where he was unable to speak to his mother on the phone for days to tell her what had happened.
After months being held against his will, first in San Antonio and then back in a different part of New England, in Connecticut, EHCF was diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, post traumatic stress disorder and attention deficit disorder, which the physician who evaluated him said was likely in part because of his “abrupt and prolonged removal from his family at the age of 15”.
Judge Vernon Oliver wrote in his decision granting the boy’s release: “The Court does not understand why E.H.C.F. is being separated from his mother.”
This is all part of what lawyers are describing as “a deportation assembly line depriving them [the children] of their rights”, where one-year-olds are defending themselves against government attorneys arguing for their removal from the US and some children are breaking down in tears during court, advocates said.
“The conclusion that I have and that other advocates have is that left to its own devices, this agency [ORR] will detain children indefinitely until they’re able to remove them. And so habeas petitions are necessary for that reason,” said Johnson His small team has accepted three referrals from the Children’s Due Process Project.
Meanwhile, Department of Justice and homeland security employees are expediting adjudications. Children’s asylum interviews have been scheduled just 24 hours in advance, sometimes to take place remotely and without notice to their attorneys, legal service organizations said in a lawsuit filed in October – also noting that immigration courts are rushing to complete children’s proceedings before the end of January at the latest. This is despite an enormous backlog of cases and widespread concerns that the fast-tracked decisions could hinder due process.
US district judge Brendan Hurson granted a temporary restraining order last week requiring the federal government to give unaccompanied children at least three weeks’ notice before an asylum interview and allow them to reschedule if needed. But that order only lasts until 13 November.
Amid these obstacles to family reunification and fair proceedings, habeas petitions have become a saving grace. And lawyers who hear about the Children’s Due Process Project are eager to sign up, advocates said.
“There’s just a huge need for the project,” said Beth Baltimore, interim managing director of The Door’s legal services center. “Kids were not getting out of custody. Family members are scared. Family members are targeted. It’s a really difficult process.”

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/amf/let.title: Lettre ouverte à David Lisnard, par les maires communistes et apparentés de l’Association des maires de France
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/amf/let.author: Tribunes
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/amf/let.text:
Les maires communistes et apparentés dénoncent l’instrumentalisation de l’Association des maires de France (AMF) au service des ambitions présidentielles de David Lisnard. Dans une lettre ouverte, ils l’appellent à se mettre en retrait de la présidence de l’association pour en préserver le pluralisme et l’indépendance.
Monsieur le Président,
Nous vous écrivons au nom de l’ensemble des maires communistes et apparentés du comité directeur et des maires et présidents d’intercommunalités adhérents de l’AMF de notre réseau au sein de la Coopérative des élus communistes républicains et citoyens.
Jusqu’ici le mandat de gestion paritaire paraissait clair : défendre les communes et rassembler les maires de toutes les sensibilités, au service de toute la population. L’AMF ne peut être un instrument de campagne lors d’une présidentielle.
Si nous ne partageons que peu de votre vision politique, vous avez su jusqu’ici mener l’AMF dans son esprit premier : l’intérêt général que nous devons servir comme élus locaux et l’unité républicaine malgré nos appartenances à des familles politiques différentes. À chaque débordement lors de votre mandat, nous avons su trouver les moyens collectifs pour maintenir l’association dans ses missions premières et chacun a pu exprimer ses positions.
Mais vos opinions personnelles ne fondent pas notre demande de retrait. C’est l’exercice de votre présidence aujourd’hui qui est en cause.
Lors de votre campagne vous défendez moins d’interventions publiques, davantage de « solidarités » privées et la privatisation de certains services. C’est votre liberté personnelle. À la tête de l’AMF, vous devez porter les positions arrêtées collectivement. Votre mandat est de défendre les services publics de proximité et les moyens des communes.
Les communes ne peuvent pas devenir la variable d’ajustement du recul de l’État. Elles risqueraient de devoir pallier seules aux hausses des besoins sociaux et financer davantage de soins, notamment dans leurs centres de santé. Les moyens correspondants ne sont pas garantis. Les habitants resteraient confrontés aux déserts médicaux et aux renoncements aux soins. De nouveaux désengagements de l’État imposeraient des choix lourds : réduire les services, augmenter les tarifs ou les impôts locaux, reporter les investissements.
Dans l’éducation, la mise en concurrence fragilise la mixité sociale et d’accentuer les inégalités territoriales. L’école doit rester un service public, gratuit et laïque, garantissant à chaque enfant les mêmes droits et les mêmes chances de réussite, indépendamment de son origine sociale ou de son lieu de résidence. Cette logique de compétition compliquerait également la prévision des effectifs et la planification des investissements nécessaires à la construction et à la rénovation des écoles. Elle déstabilisera l’organisation des cantines et du périscolaire, des services essentiels à l’égalité des chances et au quotidien des familles.
Nos exigences sont claires : l’accès de toutes et tous, des tarifs maîtrisés et la continuité des services. Les communes doivent en garantir l’équité et en garder le contrôle démocratique. La présidence de l’AMF ne peut servir un projet qui ferait payer aux communes et à leurs habitants le recul organisé des services publics.
Nous rejetons vos attaques contre les socialistes et vos propos sur les « délires écologistes, wokistes ou islamistes ». Les maires communistes, socialistes et écologistes ont toute leur place à l’AMF. Ils ont droit au même respect et à la même représentation que leurs collègues de droite, du centre ou sans étiquette.
La Coopérative vous a déjà alerté. André Laignel et Jean-François Debat l’ont fait à leur tour le 21 octobre. Vous vous étiez rendu à Limoges après l’incendie de la mairie. Ils vous écrivaient alors : « vos propos ont largement dépassé le cadre transpartisan qui est celui de l’AMF pour rejoindre davantage ceux du candidat à l’élection présidentielle ». Nous faisons nôtre cet avertissement. Respectez la gouvernance collective de l’AMF.
La solidarité avec les maires doit être sans faille. Ce mois d’octobre Bernard Baudoux, maire d’Aulnoye-Aymeries, dans le Nord, a été roué de coups par des colons israéliens. L’agression s’est produite à Taybeh, en Cisjordanie occupée, lors d’une visite aux côtés de diplomates européens. Le ministère français des Affaires étrangères l’a condamnée dans un communiqué. Nous vous demandons de la condamner publiquement et d’affirmer le soutien de l’AMF à notre collègue.
Plus de 60 maires vous ont écrit après vos propos sur le massacre du 17 octobre 1961. Des Algériennes et des Algériens manifestaient pacifiquement. La police française les a massacrés sous l’autorité du préfet Maurice Papon. Vous avez répondu : « j’en ai rien à foutre, j’en ai rien à cirer, j’étais pas né ». Ces mots sont indignes de vos responsabilités. Ne pas être né n’efface pas le devoir de mémoire. Les descendants de l’immigration algérienne n’ont pas à oublier leurs morts pour appartenir à la communauté nationale. Les travailleurs algériens ont aussi contribué à reconstruire notre pays.
Retirez ces propos. Présentez vos excuses aux familles. Respectez l’égale dignité de toutes les victimes. Nous demandons la pleine reconnaissance de la responsabilité de l’État, une commémoration nationale et la poursuite de l’ouverture des archives.
François Baroin a montré la voie en septembre 2016. Il soutenait alors un candidat à la primaire de la droite et du centre. Il s’est mis en réserve de l’expression et de la représentation publiques de l’AMF. Il avait eu le sens républicain des responsabilités. Suivez son exemple.
Mettez-vous en retrait de la présidence pendant votre campagne présidentielle. Les instances de l’AMF doivent en organiser la continuité. À défaut, retirez votre candidature à sa présidence lors du prochain congrès. Si vous la maintenez, nous voterons contre. Cette exigence d’indépendance vaut pour tout candidat, quelle que soit sa sensibilité politique.
Alors que notre pays subit un attentat raciste et xénophobe à Trappes, notre association et les élus de la République doivent incarner l’unité du peuple et l’apaisement.
Nous appelons les maires de droite et du centre à prendre leurs responsabilités. L’intérêt des communes doit l’emporter sur les logiques de parti.
Nous demandons la réunion rapide du bureau et du comité directeur. Des garanties publiques doivent séparer votre campagne de la communication, des moyens, des fichiers et des événements de l’AMF. L’élection résidentielle sera bientôt passée et les maires et élus locaux devront continuer à défendre ensemble la nation.
L’AMF appartient à tous les maires. Son unité et son indépendance doivent primer sur les ambitions personnelles.
Veuillez recevoir, Monsieur le Président, nos salutations les plus républicaines.
– Les maires communistes et apparentés membres du comité directeur, les maires et présidents d’intercommunalités du réseau de la Coopérative des élus communistes, républicains et citoyens adhérents de l’AMF
