https://taz.de/Neuer-Polizeiruf-110-aus-.title: Neuer „Polizeiruf 110“ aus Rostock: Tiefe Wasser sind kalt
https://taz.de/Neuer-Polizeiruf-110-aus-.author: Ambros Waibel
https://taz.de/Neuer-Polizeiruf-110-aus-.text:
Neuer „Polizeiruf 110“ aus Rostock: Tiefe Wasser sind kalt
Der „Polizeiruf“ aus Rostock taucht ins Prostitutionsmilieu ein, mit Zuhälterstempel in Tattooform, schlüssig und spannend. Eine Figur sticht heraus
S ie wissen nichts. Sie können mich nicht retten. Und sie werden mich nicht beschützen.“ Das sagt Natasha (Anastasiia Mazhara) den Kommissarinnen, die ihr eben kein Angebot machen können, das sie nicht ablehnen könnte.
Der neue „Polizeiruf“ aus Rostock spielt im Prostitutionsmilieu, das auch nur eine Unterabteilung der organisierten Kriminalität ist, deren Grenzen zur juristisch einwandfreien Realwirtschaft wiederum fließend sind.
In diesem Film steckt viel drin, manchmal auch zu viel an Plot und Nebenhandlungen. Jedenfalls für den gelegentlichen Zuschauer, der die über mehrere Folgen sich erstreckende Zeichnung der Hauptcharaktere nicht immer gleich nachvollziehen kann.
„Polizeiruf 110: Sie haben Namen“
Sonntag, 1. November im Ersten und ab 30. 10. in der Mediathek.
Aber Überforderung ist ja gut, man bekommt Lust, alte Folgen nachzuschauen. Die Personen bekommen Tiefe, manchmal auch ein wenig viel deutsche Schwere.
Ein deutscher Krimi
Aber vielleicht sind wir ja einfach so; und es wäre ein Irrtum, auf einem globalisierten Fernsehmarkt nicht das Eigene herauszustellen. „Sie haben Namen“ ist ein deutscher Krimi, auch wenn ihn Menschen aus Osteuropa, insbesondere die großartige Anastasiia Mazhara, prägen.
Die Wasser sind tief und kalt in diesem Land, die Leiche, die aus einem See geangelt wird, ist gut erhalten, eine minderjährige Prostituierte stellt sich heraus, totgefoltert, mit Zuhälterstempel in Tattooform.
Katrin König (Anneke Kim Sarnau) und Melly Böwe (Lina Beckmann) machen sich an die Arbeit. Sie wollen ein individuelles Schicksal und individuelle Verantwortung klären. Aber sie stoßen auf Strukturen in Form des diabolischen Oberstaatsanwalts Jan Jürgens.
Thorsten Merten ist vielleicht das darstellerische Hauptereignis in diesem „Polizeiruf“. Da stimmt bis zur sehr stimmigen Garderobe (Kostüm: Katja E. Waffenschmied) alles.
Und das Thema Prostitution, um das sich im Kern alles dreht? „Der erste und wichtigste Schritt wäre, Prostitution zu verbieten. Wir brauchen das nordische Modell“, sagt Julia Wege, Fachberaterin für den Dreh im Gespräch mit dem NDR.
Dem ist nichts hinzuzufügen; und es wird so kommen, früher oder später, je nachdem wie lange wir eben legale sexuelle Gewalt noch dulden wollen. Die Frau als Ware in der Prostitution, das alltägliche Gemetzel sexueller Gewalt, das hingenommen und gefördert wird, ist die Voraussetzung für Fälle wie Pelicot.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Life is full of suffering – but leaning into moments of pleasure can allow the nervous system to rest | Nadine Levy
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nadine Levy
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
There is a particular Buddhist story that reassured me I had found the right path.
The story goes that Prince Siddhartha Gautama was deep in spiritual practice – arduous, unforgiving practice. He had tried everything from breath-holding to extreme fasting. But none of it brought the freedom from suffering he sought.
As is sometimes the case in those moments, he was graced with a memory. He remembered being a child, sitting under the shade of a rose apple tree while his father worked nearby. As he sat there, free from preoccupation, his mind settled and his experience became infused with a deep sense of pleasure and ease.
This memory gestured at what later became a fundamental Buddhist idea: put simply, extreme self-denial is not the path to freedom. More radically, could it be that a certain kind of pleasure – a more refined pleasure – might help point the way?
I’ve always been intrigued by pleasure, its limits but also its invitation. The pleasure Siddhartha remembered was not wily or sneaky, waiting to trick him into attachment, but rather carried him towards freedom of heart.
Admittedly, the Buddha distinguished this kind of pleasure from sensual pleasures, which can become tangled with craving, acquisition and a mistaken belief that happiness lies in getting more.
But the point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure, but to lean into it when it naturally arises.
As humans, we are strangely adept at trying to elicit and extract pleasure, to plan for it and prolong it, but not so good at receiving it when it is right in front of us.
Stress can diminish our sensitivity to pleasure. Psychologists use the term “anhedonia” to describe the diminished capacity to anticipate or experience pleasure, a phenomenon associated with a range of mental health conditions.
As a teenager, I had a free-spirited friend who wholeheartedly called out, “I love bed!” before she went to sleep. We could hear her down the corridor.
I loved bed too; we all did. But would we admit it?
She noticed the sheets, the relief of placing a tired body down, the privilege of a pillow. Boy, she knew how to receive pleasure when it was being offered.
The Buddha observed that all experience is associated with a tonal quality – pleasant, painful or neutral. In Buddhism, we call this vedanā, or feeling tone. And then there is all the manhandling we do with feeling: judging it, willing it to stay, tweaking it.
When working with mindfulness students who are having a hard time, I often do a pleasure check.
I ask, sometimes provocatively, “What are you doing in your free time?” Then: “Are you able to read a good novel? Could you go for a massage or a meandering walk in the sun?” What I am really asking is: can you be with pleasure intentionally, even in the midst of suffering?
These conversations also make it plain that access to pleasure is not enjoyed equally. The time, safety and space necessary to notice and receive pleasure are impacted by our social and material circumstances. But when pleasure does arise amid turbulence, allowing it to register can offer the nervous system a chance to rest, even for a moment.
We feel this viscerally: a slower breath, a softening, a release. And if we are quiet, we might notice our minds relishing it – “How terrific, I love this.” Or as American novelist Kurt Vonnegut put it, “If this isn’t nice, I don’t know what is.”
Can we let pleasure simply hold our attention without trying to prolong it?
Pleasure arrives with different inflections. Some forms leave us aching for more. Others are more sublime, spiritual even – the kind the Buddha spoke of: the mind that gathers and settles. The simplicity of the breathing body. The sweetness of simply existing.
I once had a teacher who started meditation sessions with, “It feels good to be in the body.” It was a low bar for pleasure, but somehow I felt it.
Then there is the pleasure of living a life of non-harm, of treating ourselves and others with dignity, love and respect. Subtler still is the pleasure of laying down the burden, even for a moment, of having to be and do.
I remember marvelling that in my mother’s final weeks, days in the hospital could still brim with pleasure. Among the many unpleasant experiences, there was the sweetness of laughter, a leg massage, a feeling of togetherness, and a daughter’s recognition of the comfort and familiarity of being with her mum.
Each evening, I would think how strange it was that there was so much pleasure in despair.
And here receptivity was key. I suspect without it, I might have seen only what was painful and missed the pleasure braided through.
Every time I sit to meditate, I consciously luxuriate in the pleasure of breathing.
Of course, pleasure dissipates, and unpleasant and neutral sensations arrive too. Yet in Buddhist practice, these too are met with the same receptive attention: “Oh, this is unpleasant, and it will change.” Sometimes there is even a kind of pleasure in this honesty.
And, for the record, I still love bed.
- Dr Nadine Levy is a senior lecturer at the Nan Tien Institute. She coordinates its health and social wellbeing program and the graduate certificate in applied mindfulness

Alors que les campagnes de prévention des cancers exhortent chacun à prendre soin de sa santé, les contraintes imposées aux secteurs polluants s’allègent. Un paradoxe qui interroge la place des facteurs environnementaux dans l’apparition des maladies.
À chaque mois sa campagne de sensibilisation et de prévention des cancers : octobre avec Octobre rose, dédié à la sensibilisation et à la prévention du cancer du sein ; novembre avec le mouvement Movember, pour inciter les hommes à se soucier des cancers de la prostate ou des testicules ; janvier, dédié à la prévention du cancer de l’utérus ; février et la Journée mondiale contre le cancer ; mars avec Mars bleu, consacré au dépistage du cancer colorectal… La liste est très longue....

https://taz.de/Fluessiggas-Terminal-in-M.title: Flüssiggas-Terminal in Mexiko: Sind Wale Rechtssubjekte?
https://taz.de/Fluessiggas-Terminal-in-M.author: Diana Nava
https://taz.de/Fluessiggas-Terminal-in-M.text:
Flüssiggas-Terminal in Mexiko: Sind Wale Rechtssubjekte?
Im mexikanischen Bundesstaat Sonora klagen Aktivist:innen und Wissenschaftler:innen gegen ein LNG-Projekt, um die Wale im Meer zu schützen.
Als Erstes fragt Nora Cabrera am Telefon, ob ich glaube, dass es die Wale gutheißen würden, wenn ein LNG-Tanker durch ihren Lebensraum fährt? Die instinktive Antwort lautet: Nein. Komplizierter wird die Beantwortung, wenn man berücksichtigt, dass an der Entscheidung auch große Unternehmen und Regierungen beteiligt sind und Millionen von US-Dollar im Spiel sind.
Ein Wal kann nicht vor Gericht erscheinen. Er kann auch keine Anwälte beauftragen. Cabrera, eine junge Anwältin, möchte, dass diese Unmöglichkeit kein Nachteil mehr bedeutet.
Euromérica-Workshop
15 Journalist:innen aus 12 Ländern Lateinamerikas nehmen am Workshop „Euromérica“ der taz panterstiftung teil. Es geht um Chancen und Herausforderungen des EU-Mercosur-Abkommens und die lateinamerikanisch-europäischen Beziehungen. Am 5. 12. erscheint dazu eine Beilage in der taz, am 9. 12. gibt es einen öffentlichen Talk in der taz Kantine. Alle Texte finden Sie hier.
Es geht um das Saguaro-Projekt. Das US-amerikanische Unternehmen Mexico Pacific plant, in Puerto Libertad im Bundesstaat Sonora nahe der Grenze zu den USA einen Terminal für den Export von Flüssiggas (LNG) zu errichten. Die Anlage würde Gas aus Texas aufnehmen und es verflüssigen, um es dann zu verschiffen und nach Asien zu transportieren. Die Investition wird auf 15 Milliarden Dollar geschätzt. Das Projekt sollte ursprünglich in Kalifornien in den USA realisiert werden, doch strenge Umweltgesetze und gesellschaftlicher Widerstand verhinderten seine Umsetzung.
Im Golf von Kalifornien leben die meisten Wale
Texas verfügt über einen Gasüberschuss, und die Asiaten benötigen dieses Gas. Zwischen den Vorkommen und den Abnehmern liegt mexikanisches Territorium: das Land, durch das eine Gaspipeline verlaufen, und das Meer, über das der Brennstoff transportiert würde. Wirtschaftlich hat dieser Standort einen Vorteil, weil er die Reise nach Asien im Vergleich zu Projekten im Golf von Mexiko um elf Tage verkürzt und dabei den Panamakanal umgeht. Elf Tage weniger sind ein Grund zu investieren.
Doch der Golf von Kalifornien ist mehr als nur eine schnelle Transportroute: Dort leben fast 40 Prozent der Wale weltweit.
Rechtsanwältin Cabrera ist auch Leiterin der Organisation „Nuestro Futuro“ und Teil einer Koalition, die im September 2025 eine Klage einreichte, damit Mexiko die Wale als Rechtssubjekte anerkennt. Sie fordert, dass die Tiere um ihrer bloßen Existenz willen geschützt werden. Der Organisation ist es gelungen, den Bau des Projekts vorerst zu stoppen. Bislang handelt es sich aber nur um eine vorläufige Aussetzung, die nur so lange gilt, bis der Fall in der Hauptverhandlung entschieden wird.
Wir sind es gewohnt, ein Haus zu verteidigen, weil es einen Eigentümer hat, ein Auto, weil es ein Kennzeichen hat, eine Investition, weil sie auf Verträgen beruht. Bei Tieren hingegen suchen wir meist nach einem Nutzen, der ihr Recht auf Existenz untermauert. Dass sie etwa Tourist:innen anziehen oder Arbeitsplätze sichern. Als ob das bloße Dasein ein unzureichendes Argument wäre, welches man mit einer Rechnung untermauern müsste.
Zusammenstöße mit Schiffen oft tödlich
Die Lebensgrundlage der Wale wäre durch den steigenden Tankerverkehr in der Region jedenfalls in Gefahr: Eine von der Organisation „Equal Routes“ beauftragte Studie befürchtet eine Zunahme an Emissionen, des Unterwasserlärms und von Zusammenstößen mit Schiffen. Kollisionen mit diesen seien die häufigste Todesursache bei Walen, sagt Cabrera.
Jetzt unterstützen!
Unterstützen Sie die taz panterstiftung und ihre internationalen Projekte mit einer Spende. Mehr erfahren
Danach schrieben rund einhundert mexikanische und internationale Wissenschaftler einen offenen Brief, in dem sie die Produktion und den Transport von LNG im Golf als ein „direktes, existenzielles und inakzeptables“ Risiko bezeichneten. Neben Saguaro wiesen sie auch auf AMIGO GNL hin, ein weiteres LNG-Projekt in Guaymas, ebenfalls in Sonora. Sie forderten die Regierungen Mexikos und der Vereinigten Staaten auf, diese Vorhaben nicht umzusetzen.
Bei AMIGO GNL in Guaymas wären davon auch europäische Unternehmen betroffen. Der Rohstoffriese Gunvor mit Sitz in Genf hat etwa einen langfristigen Kaufvertrag unterzeichnet, um von dort jährlich 0,85 Millionen Tonnen LNG abzunehmen.
Sollten sie umgesetzt werden, wären die ökologischen Folgen der LNG-Projekte erheblich: Allein durch Saguaro würden jährlich mehr als 73 Millionen Tonnen Kohlendioxid entstehen. Das seien mehr als die jährlichen Emissionen von Schweden und Portugal zusammen, sagt Cabrera.
Wer trägt die Umweltkosten?
Für einen Investor lässt sich die Verzögerung eines Projekts in Geld bemessen. Für eine Fischergemeinde wiederum könnte dessen Umsetzung ihre gesamte Existenzgrundlage gefährden. Saguaro ist daher Teil einer größeren Debatte: Darüber, dass lateinamerikanische Länder größtenteils die Umweltkosten von Großprojekten tragen, deren Gewinne dann aber von den beteiligten Unternehmen über ihre Grenzen hinaus verteilt werden.
Investitionen lassen sich leicht mit einer Zahl ankündigen, die Schlagzeilen füllt. Aber was ist mit den Kosten und Risiken für die vor Ort lebenden Menschen und die betroffenen Tiere? Wer führt diese Rechnung? Und wie stark wiegen diese Aspekte bei seiner Umsetzung eines Projekts?
Mexico Pacific präsentiert Saguaro als Beitrag zur Energiesicherheit Asiens und zur Energiewende. Das Unternehmen argumentiert, dass Standort und Auslegung des Projekts die Emissionen im Vergleich zu anderen US-Exportrouten reduzieren würden. Doch welche Schäden gelten im Namen einer relativen Verbesserung als akzeptabel? Und wer ist befugt, das zu entscheiden?
Die Klage gegen das Projekt versucht, in dieses Ungleichgewicht eine Verpflichtung einzuführen: Bevor der Lebensraum der Wale verändert wird, muss es jemanden geben, der sie verteidigt und vor Gericht gehört wird. Doch ist die eingereichte Klage gegen Saguaro nur ein erster Schritt: Nun muss der Prozess auch gewonnen werden.
Diana Nava ist eine selbständige Wirtschaftsjournalistin aus Mexiko. Sie arbeitet u. a. für das digitale Finanzmedium REDD Intelligence.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Colorado community fights plan to use drones to spray weed killer
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Carey Gillam
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Soon, weed-killing chemicals will start falling from the sky over the Red Hill area of Boulder county, Colorado.
The wildland is known for its biodiversity, home to hundreds of important species and a concentration of rare environmental resources. It is a key habitat for beloved herds of elk and bighorn sheep, with farms and ranchland lying at its base.
But any day now, hundreds of acres of Red Hill are set to become the target for drone spraying of a chemical herbicide that some researchers warn come with concerns.
County officials say the plan is an effective and essential move that will wipe out invasive weeds and mitigate the risk of dangerous and costly wildfires that could use the unwanted vegetation as fuel.
They tout Boulder county as “ground zero” for research and testing of indaziflam - a relatively new herbicide developed by Bayer, the German chemical and pharmaceutical conglomerate, that has been approved for use across millions of acres of public lands as a tool for preserving native ecosystems.
But the drone spray project has prompted an outcry from many people living and working in the area as some scientists say the chemical comes with serious risks for vulnerable species and poses health dangers for people and animals, including through water that runs off the steep slope into rivers and creeks and into groundwater supplies for crop irrigation, though the chemical’s manufacturer denies that it is unsafe.
In June, two University of Colorado researchers added fuel to the community concerns, publishing a journal article highlighting risks to ecological and human health from indaziflam spraying and arguing that the cheatgrass issues cited as a basis for spraying are overblown. They cited prior published studies that raise concerns about genotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
“It really directly affects all residents downstream from this,” said Azuraye Wycoff, owner of Yellow Barn Farm, a regenerative agricultural operation tending to crops, sheep, pigs and other livestock located at the base of Red Hill. “There are a lot of people in our community who are really livid about it.”
Opponents fear the work could start this month.
Adding to the worries is evidence that the indaziflam product to be used, sold under the brand name Rejuvra, contains per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (Pfas), a class of chemicals linked to a range of health risks and known to persist in the environment. There have been years of ongoing federal and state actions to rein in Pfas contamination.
The drone plan for Boulder county is not new. Spraying over Red Hill was supposed to start last year but county officials paused the plan in the face of a backlash from community residents.The county plan includes mitigation measures aimed at protecting people and protected species, such as no-spray buffer zones around residential properties and measures to reduce chemical drift. But critics are not mollified.
They say particularly in a place like Boulder county, which boasts of its commitment to environmental health and sustainability, non-chemical measures should be pursued.
Overall, the county plan encompasses more than 2,000 acres (810 hectares) and extends beyond Red Hill. A group of local environmental advocates sued in 2024 to challenge the county’s broad plans. They alleged, among other things, that the drone spraying of terrain adjacent to homes, organic farms, trails and water features violated Fifra, a federal pesticide law, by contradicting labeling prohibitions of applications that will contact persons “directly or through drift”. But in a 9 October ruling, a district court judge ruled against the plaintiffs, dismissing their claims.
Now, with the drone spray plan for Red Hill revived, community members are scrambling to see whether they can find another way to delay the plan.
Opponents are pushing a “Delay the Spray” call for action to mobilize residents to contact the county. And two conservation groups have filed a notice of intent to bring a new lawsuit against Boulder county officials, this one alleging violations of the federal Endangered Species Act.
Even some Boulder City officials have questioned the wisdom of the spray strategy after recently completing a series of multiyear studies about the effects indaziflam could have on the area.
The city’s report warns of “regulatory testing that shows potentially serious health impacts to people and wildlife, and high toxicity to invertebrates”. The report cites published research showing indaziflam can have genotoxic effects, or effects on the genes and chromosomes, and notes that the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has identified concerns with the chemical as well. In a 2010 report, the EPA said indaziflam was “highly toxic” to fish, for instance. The agency also reported neurotoxicity seen in animal studies as well as effects on the liver, stomach and reproductive organs.
The city’s study findings also highlight particular concerns about the unintended consequences that spraying indaziflam could have on the viability of native seeds. Survival of native plants is critical to ecological balance, and indaziflam, which the city study found persists in the soil for years, could threaten that balance.
“Indaziflam is very effective at killing all seeds, with just a few minor exceptions,” said Brett KenCairn, a senior policy adviser for the city of Boulder on “climate and resilience”. KenCairn declined to offer an opinion on the county’s spray plan but said that, in the aftermath of wildfires, “we are desperately going to need that Indigenous seed bank”.
The city shared its report with Boulder county officials in September, but the county remains undeterred.
Protecting Boulder county’s “extraordinary” biodiversity and environmental health is at the core of the county’s approach to weed management, said a Boulder county spokesperson. The chemicals used in the spray plan “are specifically designed to target plant biology and have minimal impact on mammals”, including people, the spokesperson said. Drones are needed because of the rugged terrain that is “unsuitable” for other methods, she said.
Bayer did not respond to a request for comment. The company sold its indaziflam product Rejuvra in 2022 as part of an asset divestiture that led to the formation of a new company called Envu.
Envu, which now sells Rejuvra, said a wider base of evidence supports the safety and efficacy of the product.
“Cheatgrass and other invasive grasses pose a serious threat to western rangelands, damaging native ecosystems and increasing wildfire risk,” said Jennifer Poore, a spokesperson for Envu. “A substantial body of independent scientific research shows the importance of managing these invasive species and supports the effectiveness of indaziflam as one of the tools available to land managers.”
Bayer, and subsequently Envu, have marketed indaziflam for extensive use against invasive weeds, saying it will help the growth of perennial native vegetation, not harm it. In Boulder county, and elsewhere, a chief goal is to wipe out cheatgrass, a type of weed that researchers say pervades more than 50m acres amid the Rocky and Cascades mountains and the Sierra Nevada range. Cheatgrass can choke out native plants, leading to a loss of diversity and more intense and more frequent wildfires, according to government research.
The June paper from the University of Colorado researchers not only warned of potential environmental and human health effects of indaziflam, but pointed out that some published studies championing the use of indaziflam for spraying on public lands were written by people associated with Bayer.
“This adds indaziflam to the unfortunate list of products that have been promoted by commercial interests in the scientific literature without adequate disclosure,” researchers G Robert Brakenridge and Tim Seastedt wrote. “Tobacco, DDT and OxyContin are other examples.”
The concerns about indaziflam are disputed by Derek Sebastian, a scientist who worked for Bayer in the development and commercialization of indaziflam and now works for Envu as government relations and sales manager.
“There is an established body of peer-reviewed scientific research examining the use and efficacy of indaziflam, including its positive role in supporting biodiversity, fire prevention and preserving carbon sequestration,” Sebastian said.
Envu strongly rejects any allegations of undisclosed conflicts of interest, said Poore.
Ashley Stolzmann, a Boulder county commissioner and the lone opponent to the spray plan on the three-member board, said she is astonished that the plan is going forward in the face of evidence of harm and strong community opposition.
“I continue to oppose what we’re doing,” Stolzmann said. “The community never supported this.”
This story is co-published with the New Lede, a journalism project of the Environmental Working Group

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/journali.title: “Sous couvert d’objectivité” : le mythe de la neutralité journalistique
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/journali.author: Pierre Cazemajor,Caroline Constant
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/journali.text:
"Sous couvert d’objectivité" : le mythe de la neutralité journalistique
Publié le 1 novembre 2026
Face aux mouvements sociaux (retraites, gilets jaunes, lycéens...), le traitement médiatique dominant répète inlassablement le même refrain : la dramatisation des dégradations matérielles au détriment de l'analyse politique des revendications.
Entretien avec Pierre Casemajor, journaliste à l’Humanité et auteur du livre “Sous couvert d’objectivité”, dans lequel il décrypte l’illusion de la neutralité journalistique, le conditionnement sociologique des rédactions, les dérives du « journalisme de préfecture » ou la complaisance de “l’extrême centre médiatique” favorisant la montée de l’extrême droite.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The US founders made a grave error in granting presidents pardon power | James Rosen
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: James Rosen
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
From betraying Ukraine and dispatching masked agents who killed Americans to deporting US citizens and pulling out of accords controlling climate change and Iranian nuclear weapons, the list of Donald Trump’s abuses is long and growing still longer, seemingly by the day.
Looking back decades from now, historians will see that at the top of this shameful list is Trump’s utter abuse of his pardon power. It started on the first day of his second term, when he pardoned more than 1,500 insurrectionists who, on 6 January 2021, had stormed the US Capitol.
More recently, as documented in astonishing accounts by the New York Times, Wall Street Journal and 60 Minutes, Trump has overseen a robust pardons market in which friends or relatives of criminals offer to pay millions for presidential clemency.
Centuries before this unprecedented malfeasance, George Mason tried to warn us.
At the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, Mason cautioned the new country’s most powerful men – among them George Washington, James Madison, Benjamin Franklin and Alexander Hamilton – against the dangers of giving future American presidents too much power.
The risk was greatest, he told other delegates, in the absolute pardon power then being enshrined in our supreme law. Mason spoke out strongly against granting a president “power of pardoning because he may frequently pardon crimes which were advised by himself”.
The convention had dragged on for nearly four months in the oppressive summer heat of Philadelphia, the Constitution Hall windows closed against eavesdroppers, the delegates sweltering in their elaborate attire. Fifty-five men came to the gathering, but 16 had left, driven home to their manors by the heat and humidity.
Washington, who would become the newborn nation’s first president in 19 months, presided as Mason addressed his peers. It was as if he had a crystal ball displaying Trump’s cynical visage.
“It may happen, at some future day, that he will establish a monarchy and destroy the republic.”
Mason spoke on 15 September 1787, two days before the convention concluded. Perhaps they were too hot and exhausted to focus, but the delegates voted against limiting presidents’ pardon power. Even when Mason begged them at least to put treason beyond the pardon realm, they deferred.
Two years later, Mason delivered another forceful rebuke, this time at the Virginia Ratifying Convention.
“The president of the United States has the unrestrained power of granting pardons for treason, which may be sometimes exercised to screen from punishment those whom he had secretly instigated to commit the crime, and thereby prevent a discovery of his own guilt,” Mason said.
Mason’s effort, though, was doomed: James Madison, already known as “the father of the constitution” because of his contributions to it, told fellow Virginia delegates that even treason could be within the reach of clemency because presidents who protected it would face impeachment and possible removal from office.
As brilliant as Madison was, not quite 236 years later Trump has proven the fallacy of his logic. Despite being impeached twice, he was elected to a second term.
Mason would go down in history as one of only three delegates who refused to sign the Constitution. So strong was his opposition, he declared that “he would sooner chop off his right hand than put it to the Constitution as it now stands.”
Alexander Hamilton, who among the founders favored the strongest federal government, led the drive to quash limits on presidential pardon power. He and his allies cited a centuries-old British tradition called the “royal prerogative of mercy”, under which English kings and queens pardoned criminals.
This rationale, of course, was contradictory bordering on irrational – given that the delegates were fashioning a governing document to cement American independence from Britain and its monarchical government. And in subsequent centuries, British monarchs have pardoned far fewer criminals than US presidents.
While inflation and the war in Iran are the top issues voters cite in the forthcoming midterm elections, they have not forgotten January 6. Almost six years later, a large majority of Americans tell pollsters that Trump’s pardoning of violent insurrectionists was wrong.
There have been plenty of other bad presidential pardons, from Jimmy Carter protecting his wayward brother Billy to Joe Biden pardoning his son Hunter. Bill Clinton pardoned 140 people and commuted the sentences of 36 others on his last day in office, 20 January 2001, among them his brother and several large campaign donors. Gerald Ford’s pardon of Richard Nixon following his resignation over the Watergate scandal was widely criticized at the time, though historians have assessed it more kindly since then.
Trump’s pardon of the insurrectionists, however, stands alone because of his motivation: they used violence in a failed attempt to keep him in office after he had lost his re-election bid. No previous president had abused his pardon power to reward the subversion of US democracy.
- James Rosen is a former political reporter and Pentagon correspondent for McClatchy who has received awards from the National Press Club, Military Reporters and Editors, and the Society of Professional Journalists, which in 2021 named him top opinion columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Love the C word? You might be Australian. Hate it? You might be American
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Steve Dow
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
From Kath & Kim’s “pack of shunts” to Colin from Accounts’ call to “Go and trim your fuckin’ hooves for netball, cunt!”, the way Australian TV shows have incorporated creative vulgarities into their dialogue mirrors the way people like to swear – and linguistic researchers say younger generations of Australians in particular see once-taboo profanities as signifiers of cultural identity.
But a fondness for the C word in Australian TV doesn’t make Australians the world’s biggest swearers. Research published in 2025 by linguists Martin Schweinberger of the University of Queensland and Kate Burridge of Monash University showed the nationality that swore the most often online were Americans, followed by the British, with Australians ranking third.
However, Australia’s online swearing came second for breadth and creativity, with Britain topping this “better indicator” showing “richness of repertoire”, Schweinberger says. The Brits topped the list for many finely grained phrases that were “a little bit weird”, he says. “One was ‘knob-gobbler’. I thought, that’s beautiful.”
“Australians were [also] very creative in the number of forms they use [such as] bloody, crap, idiot, damn. Whereas Americans, when they use vulgarity, they focus on fuck and shit,” he says.
Overall, the British used “cunt” much more than Australians online, according to the study, but importantly the database used statistics collected in 2012 that did not include Australian blogs or social media posts. While Schweinberger agrees “cunt” has “lost its misogynistic meaning in Australia”, he adds: “I wouldn’t be sure about that in the US because they really shy away from it. It’s a very harsh word there.”
Lexicographer Amanda Laugesen, the director and chief editor of the Australian National Dictionary, says popular culture “does help to break down taboos”. “If you are hearing more of that in popular culture or online, it does help to shift the nature of what we think is acceptable.”
Kath & Kim pushed boundaries in 2003 on the ABC when Kim shouted, “Chardonnay, Chardonnay, you pack of shunts” – but by 2019, contestants on Australian versions of The Bachelor and Married at First Sight were uttering the word “cunt” without being censored in the edit.
“TV stations were playing on controversy,” Laugesen says. “They made a big deal about it in the commercials that somebody was going to say this word.”
Laugesen is about to release a second edition of Rooted: An Australian History of Bad Language, noting that since the book’s first publication in 2020 evidence has emerged of “young [Australian] people identifying the amelioration of the C word and the creative uses of the C word as being particularly Australian, which is fascinating”, citing the example of the portmanteau “shitcunt” for a particularly bad person.
Laugesen is referring to a 2025 thesis by Monash University PhD philosophy student Dylan Swayne Hughes which used online survey data and recorded commentary from 49 students and seven teachers across three Victorian high schools. In it, Hughes writes: “For some participants, cunt even seems to have undergone a process of enregisterment, becoming evaluated as a significant part of Australian culture and identity.”
“Some of the older feminists I’ve spoken to still felt that was a misogynistic word,” Laugesen says. “But as with many words, that baggage and meaning shifts across time, so it’s lost that kind of cultural meaning or even people thinking of it as a bodily descriptor. Now it’s really just an insult.”
Laugesen sees our broader use of swearing as a “performance of Australianness” arising from Australians’ self-perception as “more informal” and “anti-authority” compared to other predominantly English-speaking countries. Emerging from convicts, bushmen and “Digger” soldiers in the first world war, vulgar vernacular is celebrated in Australia today in phrases such as “I’m not here to fuck spiders” (meaning, “I don’t have time to waste”) or “cunning as a shithouse rat”, she says.
“Language is very much tied to ideas of Australian identity in a way that you wouldn’t say, I think, of the US or the UK,” she says. “There’s an argument to say, what else does Australia have in terms of an idea around itself, around the Australian character and Australian values? Language is one of those things we use to make up an idea of what is Australian.”
In 2027, Schweinberger and Burridge plan to publish new research drawn from the international corpus of English global linguistics project, which will show that among 14 English-speaking countries, New Zealanders swear most frequently face to face, closely followed by Ireland and Australia, with the UK and US behind at fifth and sixth.
Burridge says social swearing – in person – is a form of “verbal cuddling”, rooted in Australians’ love of banter and informality. “The main function of swearing is as a solidarity marker,” she says, noting the British-born Australian journalist Richard Twopeny’s observation in his 1883 book Town Life in Australia: “The lower-class colonial swears as naturally as he talks.”
“The English-speaking world is also becoming a lot more laid back now so there’s a blurring between public and private boundaries,” says Burridge. “But the lines have always been blurry in Australia.”
Laugesen predicts Australians’ “creativity with swear words will likely continue to flourish”, with school students now seeing “racist, sexist and homophobic slurs as much more taboo than traditional swear words”.
Social media “has become even more toxic”, however, with more abuse allowed by tech companies as free speech in the 2020s, with a lack of government regulation allowing “people to say pretty much anything online”.
But Laugesen says she would be “loathe to censor bad language”, noting taboos around swearing “have been used to close down voices and stop people from speaking out or challenging authorities”. She cites, as one example, the offensive language crimes that remain on the books in Australia, which are “disproportionately targeting Indigenous Australians”.
“The history of bad language has been entwined with what it has meant, and means to be, Australian,” she says.
“But all too often this has been defined along white, masculine lines. This is not to say we should reject our swearing reputation, but … we might want to think about what that says – and what we want it to say – about our values and identity.”
- Rooted: An Australian History of Bad Language by Amanda Laugesen is published by NewSouth in Australia, $34.99

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Tory Shepherd
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
AI is taking First Nations art and turning it into “Temu slop”, the Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales has said.
Scales, the chair of the National Gallery of Australia’s First Nations advisory group, said the technology is undermining the agency of First Nations artists and the authenticity of their work and represents a “a theft” of cultural knowledge.
Despite prime minister Anthony Albanese’s vow to protect Australian creatives from copyright theft, and the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, saying there are “no plans to weaken copyright protections”, AI has already been trained – without compensation –on the works of well known Australian artists including Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave.
But experts are particularly worried about the risks to Indigenous cultural and intellectual property (ICIP) and in a world where AI companies can hoover up anything that may be found online, including songs and paintings that include sacred and cultural knowledge. AI has altered work, removed names and then been sold, an act the peak body for Australian visual artists said was causing “cultural and economic harm”.
Searches on sites including Temu, Shein and Amazon reveal countless works described as Aboriginal paintings, as well as items such as coasters and stubby holders bearing Aboriginal-style designs, mostly without attribution to any artist.
“It’s in the name, it’s artificial,” Scales said.
“I’ve seen some works where I look at it and wonder if they’ve gone through a First Nations community or a person, or if it’s something generic that they’ve whipped up.
“It’s a theft of the agency of the artist. It rips the authenticity out of it, because it’s not been made by anyone who has the connection … the artist’s family lineage is not there, the lived experience is not there.”
Prof Kathy Bowrey, an intellectual property specialist from UNSW Law, said one in five creators already had problems with copyright infringement without AI. But she added the issues became even more complex when the creators were First Nations people, “partly because of lack of control over ownership and respect for Aboriginal culture”.
She gave an example of an organisation paying to use artwork or images of Aboriginal people themselves, then later using AI to “update” or repurpose those images without permission.
“The corporate client can pay you once and then make unauthorised Aboriginal derivative work and use the faces of the artists without consent,” she said.
“Not only do [the artists] not get the repeat business, but when they go to make new work they’re competing against an AI.”
The National Association for the Visual Arts (Nava) said Indigenous data sovereignty “recognises the right of First Nations peoples to exercise authority over their data, cultural material and knowledge”.
In a submission to the joint select committee inquiry on artificial intelligence, Nava pointed to work by the Wuthathi and Meriam lawyer Terri Janke, an international authority on Indigenous cultural and intellectual property, who has “documented AI scraping Indigenous art centre websites, removing artists’ names and altering their work”.
Janke has also warned of the broader risk of AI reproducing cultural knowledge without regard to its accuracy or appropriate use.
“Nava members have also raised concerns about AI-generated ‘Aboriginal-style’ images and designs that imitate community-specific techniques, stories, motifs and mark-making,” the submission said. “These images can be presented and sold as Indigenous or Indigenous-inspired work, spreading misinformation, causing cultural and economic harm and competing with work by First Nations artists.”
Bowrey and a colleague, creative technologies expert associate professor Oliver Bown, have proposed what they call a Copyright Plus framework, which would give creators more power over the use of their work through forcing AI companies to disclose their data sources and giving artists the right to say no to having their work scraped or mimicked. They have also proposed imposing a levy on AI companies to create a scheme to pay creative professionals and establish a cultural fund, and the use of takedown notices for fake content.
Bowrey said they wrote the draft policy based on the parameters of what the government has said so far.
A spokesperson for the attorney general said Australian creatives were “world class” and that the government was committed to supporting them.
“That’s why we’re continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on a range of options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation,” the spokesperson said.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: What does Olivia Colman's hot sex with a basket tell us about heteropessimism? | Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Apologies if this is too personal, but is there anything in your home that turns you on? A sleek standard lamp, say, or a sexy piece of kitchen kit? I’m casting an eye around here and wondering. I used to have the hots for my furry heated throw when it was sleek and glossy, but it’s so matted and grubby now, it gives me the ick. I still fancy the big kitchen cupboard, though. It is steely blue and so capacious, and its generous spice rack gives me a frisson every time I look inside.
I’m prompted to ask by the release of Wicker, the loopy erotic fable in which Olivia Colman’s fisherwoman enjoys a mutually supportive, sexually satisfying partnership with Alexander Skarsgård, whom the basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) has woven from wicker. I haven’t seen it yet, but the trailer is joyful and the premise is sending people – mostly women – wild.
The internet is full of horny comments about Skarsgård who, the fisherwoman’s neighbours gossip, is “strong as a tree and just as hard” (he’s certainly very pleasingly woven; a real statement piece). I also enjoyed an article in New York magazine, entitled What Would Happen If You Had Sex With a Wicker Dick?, in which an exceptionally game gynaecologist addresses this question with utmost seriousness, tackling splinters, lubrication and condom advisability, while also declaring, disarmingly: “But what do I know about wicker? Nothing.”
Unfortunately, I feel obliged to spoil everyone’s fun by wondering: what does it mean? Why has a film whose romantic (erotic) hero is plaited twigs sparked such enthusiasm? Have we all become basket cases? Because this wicker husband is no outlier: non-human romantic heroes have been wildly popular for a while.
At the more human-shaped end of things, romantasy has exploded (there’s wild excitement for romantasy queen Sarah J Maas’s latest), revealing a seemingly infinite appetite for stories about humans getting it on with goblins, elves, minotaurs and mothmen. Sentient object smut gets even wilder: I took an online quiz, guessing which objects of desire came from a real cultural product and which were made up, and completely flunked. There’s real erotica, I learned, about a front door, coronavirus, a garden rake, a coffee mug and Clippy the Microsoft Word paperclip (which does have very come-hither eyes).
So are humans sick of each other – and are women in particular sick of men? Depressing cautionary tales about everything from men’s reluctance to commit, to manosphere-enabled and excused misogyny have fuelled a climate of reported heterofatalism: exhausted disillusionment with the unequal burdens and trials of heterosexual relationships. Wicker features some pretty on-the-nose heteropessimism: married women have to wear giant thunking collars and the men mostly seem to be boorish lumps. So why not choose wicker? You don’t need to mankeep a woven spouse and they won’t add much to the domestic load – at most they need a quick wipe with a damp cloth and some furniture polish.
But hang on. Skarsgård may be part 70s coffee table, sure, but he’s all man: he’s man-shaped, fixes stuff, wears tweedy trousers and, of course, has a penis. Even the more out-there object erotica novels “overwhelmingly pair human women with male creatures and objects”, according to New York magazine. Unsurprising, maybe, when the latest ONS data indicates 93.7% of UK women identify as heterosexual. Reports of heterofatality may be exaggerated.
If anything, I see Wicker-mania and its ilk as indicative of a yearning escapism, a desire for life to be lighter, sexier and sillier. When everything is horrible, why not imagine, and enjoy, a world where – unlike this one – anything’s possible, including mutually satisfying relationships, gender equality and sex with macaroni cheese (also real, yes)?
Speaking of escapism, back to cheerier matters. If nothing at home is igniting your loins, what would you make a sexual partner out of other than flesh and blood? Wicker seems way too scratchy. I came up with a shortlist of cashmere and cake, but neither seem sufficiently sturdy.
Hmm, maybe Christmas cake, specifically, would work? It’s extremely durable and delicious, and if your fruity lover starts getting difficult, you could always keep them in check by biting a warning chunk off their edge. Yes, this could give Stir-up Sunday a whole new meaning.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

One distinguishing characteristic of the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez is the distance from the starting line to Turn 1. Then it’s right, left, right into another long straightaway, then some sharp turns before a shorter straightaway. Then they’ll veer left into a set of long, arcing curves, a short straight, a sharp right and then a near-hairpin turn before a complicated series of curves to take the drivers back to the starting line.
Another unique aspect – altitude. Denver is the Mile High City, but Mexico City is the Two Kilometer High City, which is considerably less catchy. Race engineers describe have to factor thin air into account.
The weather will be in the mid-20s Celsius, which in Fahrenheit is “pretty nice.” The track temperature will be approximately Venusian.

Lindblad, Gasly and Hulkenberg all moved up due to Liam Lawson’s disqualification from qualifying, which will place the Racing Bulls driver at the back of the grid, even behind Valtteri Bottas, whose engine overhaul incurred a 50-place penalty for an engine overhaul but in reality isn’t being punished at all because he was 21st in qualifying, anyway.
The other item of note on the grid: Ryo Hirakawa will make his F1 race debut on short notice, replacing Esteban Ocon after the lame-duck driver (to be replaced by Rafael Câmara next year) had a flareup with Haas management at a practice session. Hirakawa will start 18th after besting Lance Stroll, home-country hero Sergio Perez and Perez’s Cadillac teammate Bottas in qualifying.
That leads us to one moment of suspense: Can F1’s media team update its driver intro to include Hiwakawa? The video is best known for featuring Bottas’ mustache, Stroll smiling smugly as if daring his critics to keep talking, and a vivid look at the age difference between the graybeards (Bottas, eternal journeyman Nico Hülkenberg, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton and two-time champion Fernando Alonso) and fresh-faced youngsters such as Antonelli, Lindblad, Gabriel Bortoleto and Oliver Bearman.
I preferred last year’s video, if only because Alonso seemed to be doing a capable impression of The World’s Most Interesting Man.

There are still several ways Kimi Antonelli could be denied the F1 championship this year.
- George Russell could win all five remaining races while Antonelli picks up a total of just one point (10th place in any race).
- Lewis Hamilton could win all five remaining races while Antonelli picks up no points.
- Antonelli could decide to retire at age 20 and petition to retroactively forfeit his results from this year.
- AI agents could decide to shut down all the race computers for every F1 team in a bid to curb fuel consumption and Kim Kardashian’s screen time.
- Aliens could beam Antonelli back to his home planet.
- The entire year could be written off as Pamela Ewing’s dream, like the ninth season of the nighttime TV soap Dallas.
- Time travelers from the year 2053 may arrive in February 2026 and defeat Antonelli in several races in the new timeline.
Barring any of those scenarios, Antonelli will displace Sebastian Vettel as the youngest F1 champion in history. Barring an Antonelli catastrophe and a win by either Russell or Hamilton, that championship will be decided today.

Even as Formula One’s young gun Kimi Antonelli remains on course to claim his first world championship on Sunday it was the veteran, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton who gave a salutary reminder that there is very much fight left in the old dog yet as he claimed a spectacular pole position for the Mexico City Grand Prix.
Hamilton delivered a superb lap for Ferrari to secure his first pole for the team and just beat Mercedes’ George Russell into second. World champion in waiting Antonelli was in fourth place but remains in position to close out the title on Sunday, although Hamilton and Russell, who must win the race to have any hope of keeping the fight alive, have at least locked out the front row.
It was clearly a hugely emotional moment for Hamilton at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez to finally nail the top spot for Ferrari in his second season with the team, with the 41-year-old’s 105th pole also his first since 2023.
“Thank you so much, that’s been such a long time coming,” he said. “That feels good. I’m lost for words. My first pole with Ferrari. 105 poles, I like that number.
“Where there’s a will, there’s a way. It’s all in the mind. For sure, you might feel aches and pains, luckily I don’t, I do all those different things to keep myself young and fit. But I love what I do, and love is not gone.”

Iran warned on Sunday that any renewed war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of fighting, after President Donald Trump said he still had to "take care" of more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the US and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
Akraminia's remarks followed Trump's suggestion that the US could swiftly strike its remaining targets in Iran.

Ukrainekrieg : Optimismus ist fehl am Platz
Wer die Evakuierung aus Oleschky für ein Zeichen hält, dass Putin nun zu ernsthaften Friedensverhandlungen bereit wäre, ist komplett weltfremd.
H underte Menschen sind der Hölle in Oleschky am Wochenende entkommen. Die Evakuierung aus der ukrainischen, von russischen Truppen abgeriegelten Frontstadt ist geglückt. Das ist angesichts des alltäglichen Kriegsgrauens in der Ukraine zweifellos eine positive Nachricht.
Diejenigen, die jedoch glauben, aus der Mitwirkung Russlands an der Aktion weiterreichende Schlüsse auf eine Bereitschaft zu echten Friedensverhandlungen ziehen zu können, sind komplett wirklichkeitsfern oder unheilbar beratungsresistent – oder beides.
Kremlchef Wladimir Putin plötzlich mit menschlichem Antlitz? Von wegen! Hier lässt sich ein Mann vor allem mit Blick auf die Midterms in den USA am 3. November schamlos hofieren und abfeiern – sein Freund Donald Trump wird das zu schätzen wissen. Dabei ist Putin für die humanitäre Katastrophe in Oleschky wie für die gesamte Invasion der Ukraine der Hauptverantwortliche. Heuchlerischer und widerwärtiger geht es nicht.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Unlängst ließ Russlands Präsident die Öffentlichkeit zum wiederholten Mal an seinem profunden historischen Wissen teilhaben: Die Territorien im Osten der Ukraine seien russisches Land, die Bewohner*innen hätten ihrem Wunsch nach Zugehörigkeit zur Russischen Föderation in einem Referendum Ausdruck verliehen. Übersetzt heißt das: Moskau wird seinen Krieg in der Ukraine vorerst weiterführen, und zwar flächendeckend. Wie viele Menschen noch ihr Leben lassen müssen, spielt für den Kreml ohnehin keine Rolle, auch weitere Opfer unter den eigenen Landsleuten nicht.
Dennoch stellt sich die Frage, ob die „Aktion Oleschky“ als Blaupause für eine temporäre Waffenruhe auch andernorts in der Ukraine dienen könnte und Potenzial für mehr hätte – zum Beispiel im Hinblick auf einen Waffenstillstand. Darauf eine Antwort zu geben, wäre verfrüht. Fest hingegen steht: Optimismus in Bezug auf Russland ist absolut fehl am Platz und grenzenlos naiv.
Wie viel Lehrgeld, noch dazu auf Kosten der Menschen in der Ukraine, wollen die westlichen Staaten noch bezahlen?

Arsenal go top after narrow win at Liverpool
Arsenal record first win at Liverpool in 14 ttempts thanks to Kai Havertz goal
Arsenal went three points clear of Manchester City at the top of the English Premier League after a statement 1-0 win at Liverpool.
The Gunners had not won at Anfield since September 2012, when current coach Mikel Arteta captained the away side to a 2-0 victory, and had gone winless in their past 13 visits.
However, Kai Havertz turned home a low cross from Declan Rice after the home side were caught trying to play out from the back to silence the Kop on 16 minutes. The visitors withstood wave after wave of pressure from Andoni Iraola’s side thereafter.
Liverpool responded strongly with Florian Wirtz curling a free kick against the bar and Alexis Mac Allister heading a good chance over.
Arsenal weathered the storm, though, and defended superbly to keep Liverpool largely at arm’s length after the break, denying the home side a shot on target for the second meeting in succession.
Arteta’s side replaces Manchester City at the top with 24 points from nine games, with City on 21 after losing at home to Brighton and Hove Albion on Saturday.
Liverpool’s second league defeat of the season left them nine points behind Arsenal in fifth place.

Présents en masse dans les cortèges du samedi 31 octobre, les lycéens et étudiants comptent faire repartir leur mouvement social de plus belle, sûrs que leur pression contraindra l’exécutif à mieux satisfaire leurs revendications.
Ni les vacances scolaires, ni les annonces hiératiques du gouvernement, encore moins les gazages et coups de matraque ou les attaques contre le droit de manifester n’ont changé le cours des colères et des revendications. Les mobilisations lycéennes et étudiantes repartent de plus belle cette semaine.
Après une pause de quinze jours des cours et des blocages marquée par trois journées de manifestations monstres de convergences des luttes, toutes les organisations de jeunesse ont appelé, samedi 31 octobre, à reprendre le chemin de la mobilisation. Avec, en temps fort, le 5 novembre, journée intersyndicale et interprofessionnelle de grève et de manifestations pour les salaires, le service public, la jeunesse et les enjeux climatiques.
« Bien évidemment, nous soutiendrons dès lundi les blocages qui seront organisés par les lycéens, les lycéennes, étudiants, étudiantes. Mais lundi, on les invite à s’organiser en AG pour mieux bloquer mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi et autant qu’il faudra pour enfin gagner et avoir des conditions dignes dans ce pays », explique Ryad Rani,...

TOUCHDOWN! Raiders 21-23 Jets 9:59, 3rd quarter
- K Cousins to B Bowers for two yards
- Unbeaten Minnesota v Detroit; Jackson v Allen in Buffalo
- Email Graham here
 Updated 
Key events
It’s GOOD! Ravens 7-16 Bills 0:09, 2nd quarter
- T Bass 51 yard field goal
Allen motors out to the sideline who gives Tyler Bass an easy chance for another set of three points. Bass splits the uprights with ease.
Ravens 7-13 Bills 0:19, 2nd quarter
On 3rd and forever Buffalo are looking for a field goal. They call a timeout to assess their options.
Here are your scores on the doors at half-time. Except in Buffalo where rookie QB Joe Fagnano has just thrown an interception in quite possibly the weirdest game of the season. There have been two turnovers each already in a mad first-half. Buffalo have plenty of time now to extend their lead before the break.
- Baltimore Ravens 7-13 Buffalo Bills
- Tennessee Titans 13-14 Cincinnati Bengals
- Arizona Cardinals 3-14 Dallas Cowboys
- Minnesota Vikings 7-6 Detroit Lions
- Indianapolis Colts 0-28 Jacksonville Jaguars
- Las Vegas Raiders 14-23 New York Jets
- Cleveland Browns 6-20 Pittsburgh Steelers
- Atlanta Falcons 0-9 Tampa Bay Buccaneers
It’s GOOD! Vikings 7-6 Lions 0:05, 2nd quarter
- J Bates 37 yard field goal
As tight as it gets in Detroit. Second half is sure to be an absolute nerve shredder.
TOUCHDOWN! Titans 13-14 Bengals 12:51, 2nd quarter
- J Burrow to J Endries for one yard
PICK SIX! Colts 0-28 Jaguars 0:10, 2nd quarter
- R Lane 95 yard pick six
The rookie takes the interception almost the entire field for the score. Incredible.
TOUCHDOWN! Browns 6-20 Steelers 0:01, 2nd quarter
- P Freiermuth one yard rush
Easy does it for Pittsburgh.
Vikings 7-3 Lions 0:28, 2nd quarter
Three short completions leave the Lions at 4th and 1. The Vikings just refuse to let them have any easy gains. Ooo a neutral zone infraction from Minnesota does gift a 1st down. An unusual error allows Jared Goff to find a 14-yard pass to Jameson Williams. 35 yards to go.
PICK! Vikings 7-3 Lions 1:47, 2nd quarter
Kyler Murray is PICKED!!! Minnesota were moving nicely down field but the incredible turnover as the DB DJ Reed just snags it before it hits the turf. The Lions have 60 yards to travel.
TOUCHDOWN! Colts 0-21 Jaguars 1:51, 2nd quarter
- B Tuten 39 yard rush
Call it off.
SACK! Ravens 7-13 Bills 4:22, 2nd quarter
Baltimore’s defense force a three and out. Joe Fagnano back at the controls for the Ravens with 80 yards to travel. He delivers a short pass and 3rd down is quickly up. He is sacked again as the linebackers runs straight up the middle. Undrafted rookie in at QB and it the Ravens offensive line is giving him no help whatsoever.
SACK! Vikings 7-3 Lions 3:10, 2nd quarter
Andrew van Ginkel is making Jared Goff’s life a living hell right now. The Lions punt again after Van Ginkel records a third sack of Goff.
Vikings 7-3 Lions 5:06, 2nd quarter
Since the pick of Jared Goff the Vikings have punted twice and the Lions are back on offesnse at midfield.
It’s NO GOOD! Ravens 7-13 Bills 7:37, 2nd quarter
Doink. Tyler Loop hits the left upright as this madcap first half just gets madder. Baltimore having no luck right now as they are now running with their third-string quarterback rookie Joe Fagnano.
SACK! Ravens 7-13 Bills 7:49, 2nd quarter
Baltimore have an excellent chance of scoring with a short field after a 60 yard return on the kickoff from Rasheen Ali.
Rookie QB Joe Fagnano is in the game for the Ravens as Snoop Huntley has hurt a foot. The young passer throws a 15 yard strike and the Ravens are 1st and Goal. Landon Jackson delivers the sack on the next play. Welcome to the NFL.
This game is all over the place. Amazing.
It’s GOOD! Ravens 7-13 Bills 9:51, 2nd quarter
- T Bass 22 yard field goal
Another solid defensive effort from Baltimore is keeping the Ravens well in the fight. Can the offense respond?
TOUCHDOWN! Raiders 14-20 Jets 6:17, 2nd quarter
- G Smith to A Mitchell for 12 yards
Where is the defense in New York? Shootout is in session.
TOUCHDOWN! Cardinals 0-14 Cowboys 5:16, 2nd quarter
- D Prescott to R Flournoy for nine yards
TOUCHDOWN! Colts 0-14 Jaguars 7:14, 2nd quarter
- T Lawrence to N Boerkircher for 31 yards Cracking start for the home sides in total control.
Ravens 7-10 Bills 12:14, 2nd quarter
Scrap that. James Cook has now been ruled not short. 1st and Goal Buffalo.
Vikings 7-3 Lions 11:21, 2nd quarter
Detroit back on offense after a 3 and out from Minnesota. Only 92 yards for Jared Goff for travel after the brilliant punt. Good luck. Rather you than me.
Ravens 7-10 Bills 11:34, 2nd quarter
The Bills go for it on 4th and short. Josh Allen looks like he sneaks it but throws the lateral to James Cook. Cook reaches out and is ruled SHORT. Turnover on downs. How about that?! Huge stop from Baltimore.
FUMBLE! Ravens 7-10 Bills 14:01, 2nd quarter
Snoop Huntley is smashed and fumbles the ball to Buffalo. Josh Allen taking over in the red zone and gets five yards on a scramble. 15 yards to go.
PICK! Vikings 7-3 Lions 12:49, 2nd quarter
Jared Goff is intercepted by James Pierre who gets the ball to midfield for the Vikings. Cracking start from the best defense in the NFL. Would you expect anything less?
TOUCHDOWN! Raiders 14-13 Jets 10:44, 2nd quarter
- D Laube 95 yard kickoff return
A classic clanger from the Jets as they let Dylan Laube run almost the length of the field and instantly put the Raiders back on top.
TOUCHDOWN! Titans 13-7 Bengals 13:20, 1st quarter
- J Burrow to J Chase for 30 yards
Cincinnati on the board after a lovely deep ball to Ja’marr Chase.
- K Murray to J Jefferson for one yard
Minnesota take the lead after a 15 yard rush put the Vikings on the goal line. A short pass to their star receiver gets the job done on the 74-yard drive.
TOUCHDOWN! Raiders 7-13 Jets 10:56, 2nd quarter
- G Smith to I Williams for 18 yards
It’s GOOD! Browns 0-10 Steelers 14:05, 2nd quarter
- C Boswell 20 yard field goal
Pittsburgh’s red zone offense struggles, as it often does, as Aaron Rodgers throws a couple of balls away on 1st and 2nd and Goal. On 3rd Jaylen Warren is stuffed well short of the goal line. Chip shot is good but chance wasted for Pittsburgh.
Vikings 0-3 Lions 0:51, 1st quarter
Minnesota in the red zone after a 29-yard strike from Murray to TJ Hockenson. Wonderful shake and bake from the tight end to get into space.
TOUCHDOWN! Ravens 7-10 Bills 3:18, 1st quarter
- D Henry two yard rush
The Ravens are 1st and Goal and only three yards out after an 11 yard rush from Derrick Henry. That interception from the Baltimore defense is exactly what the doctor ordered and they have the score through Henry who rumbles through the middle. Boy did they need that.
It’s GOOD! Vikings 0-3 Lions 2:18, 1st quarter
- J Bates 25 yard field goal
Jared Goff is frustrated as he walks off but the Lions will be happy to have something on the board against the Vikings.
Brutal for the Baltimore Ravens who will be without quarterback Jackson for the remainder of the game against Buffalo.
… meanwhile the Ravens pick off Josh Allen! Game on!
TOUCHDOWN! Cardinals 0-7 Cowboys 2:33, 1st quarter
- Fumble return for touchdown
Dallas ahead as they chase getting to 4-4 on the season.
Ravens 0-10 Bills 4:17, 1st quarter
The Ravens quickly are forced to punt. Buffalo on top and then some with Lamar Jackson on the sidelines.
Vikings 0-0 Lions 4:27, 1st quarter
Andrew van Ginkel has his second sack of the day already in Detroit. The Lions think they have a touchdown to Amon-Ra St Brown but it is chalked off due to it being ruled incomplete. 2nd down and 25 yards to go for the Lions to draw first blood.
It’s GOOD! Ravens 0-10 Bills 12:51, 1st quarter
- T Bass 56 yard field goal
Slice of luck for Tyler Bass who hits a post and it still goes through. Meanwhile Lamar Jackson has injured the thumb on his throwing hand. Waiting to see if he will be able to return.
TOUCHDOWN! Browns 0-7 Steelers 7:57, 1st quarter
- R Dowdle nine yard rush
The big back gets the nod and fights into the end zone to give Pittsburgh an early lead in the battle for the AFC North.
TOUCHDOWN! Titans 10-0 Bengals 12:51, 1st quarter
- T Pollard 41 yard rush
Tennessee pick up where they left off from last week’s defeat using the skills of Tony Pollard. Another hat-trick this week might secure a much-needed win.
TOUCHDOWN! Raiders 7-3 Jets 7:23, 1st quarter
- K Cousins to B Bowers for 12 yards
TOUCHDOWN! Colts 0-7 Jaguars 5:30, 1st quarter
- T Lawrence to B Thomas for 12 yards
Great start for Jacksonville who are looking to put their disappointing loss in London to Houston behind them after their bye week.
Ravens 0-7 Bills 10:00, 1st quarter
Oh no. On the opening play for Lamar Jackson hits his hand on Greg Rousseau and is out of the game. Tyler Huntley in at QB as Jackson goes straight to the locker room. Bills bring up an early 3rd down.
SACK! Vikings 0-0 Lions 9:28, 1st quarter
The Lions are punting after a pair of sacks from Andrew van Ginkel and Eric Wilson. Minnesota take over from their 10-yard line.
- J Allen one yard rush
Wow. Khalil Shakir is in for the touchdown but it is ruled out as the receiver just put his foot out of bounds before being tackled into the end zone.
Buffalo have to go back to it on the one-yard line. Josh Allen goes for the sneak but goes way too wide to the left and the Ravens get the stop.
On 4th and Goal Allen goes again and is met by a huge mass of bodies. He rises above the sea of muscle and reaches the ball in for the score! Very strong start from Buffalo, they were not going to be denied.
Ravens 0-0 Bills 11:38, 1st quarter
No such problems for Josh Allen. Buffalo cruise to 1st and Goal on the back of 18 and 25-yard passes to Khalil Shakir.
Vikings 0-0 Lions 13:08, 1st quarter
Minnesota are finding some offensive production immediately against Detroit. A short pass from Kyler Murray to Ben Yurosek goes for 24 yards. Shortly after two incompletions and the Vikings miss a 57-yard field goal. Early chance for the Lions on the way.
Ravens 0-0 Bills 15:00, 1st quarter
Great to see Lamar Jackson going through his warmups. The NFL isn’t the same without his extraordinary talents. The Bills defense will likely be a little nervous as they sit comfortably as the worst in the NFL.
Fortunately for them Josh Allen will take over on offense for the Bills at the 40-yard line aster the Ravens boot it out of play to start. Oops.
Kick-offs on the way very shortly! Don’t want to jinx it but I am getting very good vibes that there are going to be some thrillers on the way. Blue 52, blue 52, hut … hut … HIKE!
One of the biggest surprises of the season has to be the Cleveland Browns and Pittsburgh Steelers juking it out at the top of the AFC North both on 5-2. I had both down to struggle mightily but strong defenses have kept the Ws flowing for both franchises.
The rivalry between the two is serious. Browns edge rusher Jared Verse caused a stir earlier this season when he criticised for the Steelers for playing dirty after Cleveland’s 27-24 win from week four.
“I don’t got no respect for anybody that plays too dirty, and that does too much extra shit after the game,” he said.
“I can’t wait until we see them again,” Verse added. “I’m going to put that one on the calendar. I can’t wait to get my hands on them again.”
Pittsburgh’s defensive lineman Cam Heyward fired back this week.
“Double teaming, sliding, chipping, are those not allowed in our game?” Heyward said. “Yeah, I got the bruises to prove it. But we don’t whine about it, baby. It’s part of the game. And so, I’m looking forward to this game. It’s gonna be a fun game.”
The Steelers are heavy home favourites but Verse leads a Browns defense with the power to spring a surprise.
Something has to give in Detroit today as the NFL’s best defense meet an offense scoring more than 30 points per game. Minnesota’s defensive coordinator Brian Flores has unbelievable stopping power at his disposal and will need to unleash all of it to stop the Lions’ impressive offense.
If the unbeaten Vikings do have any struggles in shutting down running back Jahmyr Gibbs and their strong receiving crew then it will be fascinating to see if Minnesota’s quarterback Kyler Murray can find some joy against a poor Lions defense. Murray and company have only nine offensive touchdowns so far but will have opportunities to flex their muscles today. Some more confidence and offensive production will certainly be needed in the postseason.
A pair of quarterback heavyweights?! Yes, just a bit. Lamar Jackson returns from a three-game absence for the Baltimore Ravens to face Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. Jackson’s two MVP awards play Allen’s one but Allen is very much the favourite to add to a second to his trophy cabinet after a scintillating start to the season.
After their own hot start with Jackson at the controls the Ravens have slumped to 4-3. Two defeats in succession leave Baltimore bottom of the AFC North. So they will be hoping Jackson can jump back in and stop the slide. Unfortunately the omens aren’t great. The Bills have beaten the Ravens on three straight occasions at home, the latest being last season’s thriller from the opening week as Buffalo scored 16 unanswered points in the final four minutes to overturn a 15-point deficit in their 41-40 victory.
Let’s hope for another epic today.
Hi and hello football fans! With Halloween in the rearview mirror and the season’s halfway point almost upon us the race to the playoffs is beginning to take shape. Who can overcome early struggles for a spot in January? Who will maintain their searing run to the postseason? Week eight might just provide a couple of answers in an exciting early window of eight games from 12pm CST/1pm EST/5pm GMT (home teams listed second):
- (4-3) Baltimore Ravens v Buffalo Bills (5-1)
- (1-6) Tennessee Titans v Cincinnati Bengals (4-2)
- (2-5) Arizona Cardinals v Dallas Cowboys (3-4)
- (6-0) Minnesota Vikings v Detroit Lions (4-2)
- (2-5) Indianapolis Colts v Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2)
- (3-4) Las Vegas Raiders v New York Jets (2-5)
- (5-2) Cleveland Browns v Pittsburgh Steelers (5-2)
- (3-4) Atlanta Falcons v Tampa Bay Buccaneers (2-5)
There is a potential classic between two QB heavyweights in the AFC as the Ravens take on the Bills, then the Browns and Steelers battle it out for top spot in the AFC North with the main event coming from the NFC North as the unbeaten Vikings take on the Lions in Detroit. It could be a very fun afternoon. Strap in!
