https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Ukraine blames Russia after air alert app sends out false warnings
Russian Emergencies Ministry also says its mobile app suffered a ‘massive cyberattack’, leading to ‘false information’.
Ukraine’s Air Force has said its air raid alert app sent erroneous messages after allegedly being hacked by Russia.
Fake alerts warning of nuclear and chemical threats to areas in and around Kyiv were sent on Sunday, along with warnings of potential street combat. An erroneous message also said Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed.
“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram on Sunday. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
SPRAVDI, Ukraine’s Centre for Strategic Communications, blamed Russia for the hack in a post on X.
The raid alert app is used across Ukraine to warn people in real time of incoming Russian air attacks. A separate app, specifically for the Ukrainian capital, was working normally, according to Kyiv authorities.
Hours later, early on Monday morning, Russia’s Emergencies Ministry said its mobile app had been hit by a “massive cyberattack”.
The ministry said on Telegram that the attack led to the spread of “false information”.
Russia’s and Ukraine’s announcements follow the end of a truce between the two countries in Kherson.
The localised ceasefire, which began on Tuesday and ended on Sunday, was the longest of the war so far.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.
The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.
The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Tens of thousands build 108 Buddhist stupas for Bhutan ‘mindfulness’ city
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Tens of thousands build 108 Buddhist stupas for Bhutan ‘mindfulness’ city
Bhutan is creating a ‘mindfulness’ city aimed at driving economic growth and persuading more young people to stay.
Tens of thousands of volunteers have taken part in building 108 Buddhist stupas in Bhutan’s new “mindfulness” city, as the Himalayan kingdom embarks on an ambitious project to boost economic growth.
The 15-metre-tall (50ft) stupas, sacred Buddhist monuments found across the Himalayas, were installed on Sunday along 12km (7.5 miles) of riverbank near the Indian border, at the site of the future Gelephu Mindfulness City.
More than 40,000 volunteers participated in building the structures as “a physical form of prayer made permanent in stone and earth”, after starting work after midnight, officials said. The number 108 is sacred in Buddhism, widely practised in Bhutan.
About 200,000 people attended the ceremony, or nearly a fourth of the population, officials told the AFP news agency.
“I was worried that raising 108 stupas in a single day might not succeed,” Bhutan’s King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck said in a speech at the ceremony.
“But everything went successfully, and for that, I am truly grateful.”
Bhutanese leaders hope that Gelephu Mindfulness City, conceived by the king and designed by Danish architects, will boost the country’s economy and persuade more young people to stay, attracting investment in sustainable business, green technology, education, tourism and financial services.
Bhutan is facing massive economic challenges, from rising unemployment and falling birth rates to the mass migration of skilled workers.
The city, currently a small town with a population of about 10,000, is in southern Bhutan, along the border with India, about 240km (150 miles) south of Thimphu, the nation’s capital.
The king established the special zone by royal charter in 2024, saying its purpose was to “create a vibrant economic hub”.
The landlocked Himalayan nation, with a population of just under 800,000 and wedged between China and India, is known for its policy of prioritising “Gross National Happiness” alongside economic growth.
“This occasion will be recorded in our history for generations to come,” said Nima Gyeltshen, 65, head of the Organisation for Youth Empowerment, which helps young Bhutanese find work.
Cryptocurrency ambitions
Analysts have questioned whether Bhutan can attract sufficient investment to realise its vision for the new city.
But Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, head of the ports-to-power conglomerate, joined the project as a founding member in January.
The site is set to be connected to India’s rail network in neighbouring Assam, with an international airport slated to open in 2029.
The project is also linked to Bhutan’s cryptocurrency ambitions, with the kingdom mining Bitcoin using surplus hydropower and pledging to use digital assets to support the city’s development.
Bishnu Maya Moktang, a resident who attended Sunday’s ceremony, said she was excited about the upcoming mindfulness city.
“I hope to live long enough to see it,” Moktang, 56, told AFP.
“My parents died young, and they would never see the city. I feel fortunate.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell sustained a neck injury and was taken to a local hospital after being injured during the fourth quarter of his team’s 19-15 victory over the Minnesota Vikings.
“Thoughts and prayers are with Jack and his family,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said after the game. “He’s being taken care of. We don’t have any new information. We’ll keep you updated as this thing goes. But we are thinking about him. We are thinking about him.”
The Lions later said that Campbell would be kept in hospital overnight.
“Jack Campbell is resting and will remain in a local hospital tonight, for continued evaluation and monitoring,” the Lions said in a statement. “The team will provide further updates as we have them.”
Jack Campbell, a first-team All-Pro last season, was injured while tackling Vikings tight end TJ Hockenson in the fourth quarter.
The 26-year-old lay motionless facing the ground and was surrounded by medical personnel for nine minutes while being strapped to a board. He did not signal to the Ford Field crowd as he was driven off on a cart toward the tunnel.
“He’s breathing, he’s alert when he left,” Dan Campbell told the Lions Radio Network.
Lions quarterback Jared Goff was shaken up while observing the situation.
“Jack’s deal was definitely scary,” Goff said. “It just brings you back to reality for a moment that he’s a husband and a father. Scary. We’re praying for him and hope he’s going to be alright. If anyone is tough enough to get through something like that, it’s going to be him.”
Campbell, a fourth-year pro, was credited with three tackles prior to the injury. He has 57 this season after a career-high 176 last season. The Lions picked him in the first round of the 2023 draft.

Nine die in ‘cataclysmic’ Florida business jet crash
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis tells reporters there appeared to be no casualties on the ground.
Nine people have died after a business jet crashed into a residential neighbourhood in South Florida, the United States.
All on board were killed in the crash, which US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described as a “horrific tragedy” in a post on X on Sunday.
Federal Aviation Administration staff were on their way to the crash site to support a National Transportation Safety Board investigation into the incident, Duffy said.
Disturbing recordings in the plane’s cockpit shortly before the crash, retained by LiveATC.net, captured the pilot talking about “manageable” ice issues, before later saying the plane was rapidly losing altitude.
Shortly after, the panicked crew said, “We’re going to crash into the ground”.
The plane was a Learjet 60 – a popular business jet – heading from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas. Austin-Bergstrom International airport confirmed that the plane was a private jet, but not who was on board.
Videos of the incident circulating online appear to show the jet striking the ground at high speed and on a sharp angle, followed by a huge explosion.
Footage of the aftermath appears to show flames flickering around debris and chunks of pavement, with people milling around the area.
The plane looked to have fallen just metres from homes and cars, but Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters that there appeared to be no casualties on the ground.
Speaking from the scene, DeSantis described the crash as “cataclysmic” and said the plane “looked like a missile going down, and left a big crater on the side of the road”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Israeli officials say results stand as Netanyahu claims election ‘stolen’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Israeli officials say results stand as Netanyahu claims election ‘stolen’
Election body says deadlocked result won’t be undermined even if foreign interference claims are found to be true.
The head of Israel’s elections commission has said the results of the country’s general election would still stand even if claims of foreign interference were substantiated.
“Our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole,” Central Elections Committee head Noam Sohlberg said in a video on Sunday, in which he appeared with the head of the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, and the attorney general.
Prime Minister Benyamin Netanyahu’s Likud party had questioned the results after saying, without providing evidence, that Arab-led parties, which made significant gains in Tuesday’s elections, “stole” the vote and accepted funding from Qatar to do it.
Qatar has rejected the allegations, calling it a disinformation campaign.
Also on Sunday, Israeli police released two out of three political activists arrested before Tuesday’s polls opened. They were carrying envelopes of cash, allegedly to bribe voters, police said.
One was released on unspecified conditions, while another was ordered to remain on house arrest.
Police said the suspects were connected to the Arab-led Ra’am party, which won eight seats.
Its leader, Mansour Abbas, denounced the arrests as undemocratic and “an attempt to influence the election results”.
‘Orchestrated and organised campaign’
Main opposition leader Eisenkot on Sunday accused Netanyahu of launching an “orchestrated and organised campaign to delegitimise the results”.
Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Arab parties, but a deadlock in Tuesday’s elections means siding with the parties could help him form a government.
Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s elections, while the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, won 48, meaning neither side can form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament alone.
Israel’s three Arab-led parties, including the Ra’am party, won a record 19 seats.
A coalition of Arab parties with Eisenkot would provide a comfortable majority of 67 in parliament. However, for many in Israel, the idea of siding with Arab parties is politically unpalatable.
The results are due to be officially certified this week, after which President Isaac Herzog must nominate a candidate to form a new government.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Why governors’ races are important in the 2026 US midterms
Historic turnover in this election will allow dozens of states to vote on significant changes in leadership.
Much of the attention ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections has fallen on the battle for control of the United States Congress.
But key state-level races are also unfolding, with far-reaching consequences for the country’s future.
This year, 36 US states will vote for their next governor, the most powerful elected official in state government.
An unusually high proportion of those races centre on open seats, with no incumbent governor on the ballot seeking re-election.
In 19 of the races, the current officeholder is either term-limited, like California Democrat Gavin Newsom, or voluntarily opted to not run again, like Iowa Republican Kim Reynolds.
This historic turnover creates the potential for several states to take on significant changes in leadership.
Here’s why these races matter:
A state’s chief executive
Governors serve as the chief executives of their states, overseeing government departments and agencies responsible for delivering public services.
Their powers vary by state. In general, governors propose budgets, appoint senior state officials, direct state agencies about how to enforce existing law, and issue executive orders.
They can also choose to sign into law bills passed by their state’s legislature — or veto them.
One of their most visible areas of influence is reproductive rights. Since the US Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that there is no constitutional right to abortion access, state governments have played a central role in determining whether the procedure is legal.
Each state can now regulate abortion within its boundaries, and some 13 state legislatures have passed complete or near-total abortion bans.
But the Guttmacher Institute, a US-based reproductive rights organisation, noted that about a dozen governors have issued executive orders to “mitigate” the harm done by such bans.
“By issuing executive orders, governors could quickly declare immediate protections for providers and patients,” the organisation said. “This was particularly helpful in states such as North Carolina, where the governor is supportive of abortion rights — but the legislature is not.”
Governors can also influence how US elections are administered.
In some states, governors appoint the officials responsible for overseeing elections, while in others, those officials are elected independently. Governors may also sign or veto legislation changing voting rules, giving them significant influence over election administration.
Challenging the US government
Governors also help shape how states respond to the federal government.
They may challenge federal policies in court or negotiate with Washington over funding and programme requirements.
State governments also play a major role in implementing federally funded programmes, making cooperation between governors and the White House important.
One example came after former US President Barack Obama’s landmark healthcare policy, the Affordable Care Act, passed the US Congress in 2010.
In the aftermath of its passage, many governors were in a position to decide whether their states adopted the Affordable Care Act’s expansion to Medicaid, an insurance programme for low-income households.
Some governors, like Steve Beshear of Kentucky and Earl Ray Tomblin of West Virginia, issued executive orders in 2013 to adopt Medicaid expansion without their legislatures’ approval.
Others, like Florida’s then-Governor Rick Scott, opposed Medicaid expansion and directed their state legislatures not to adopt it. Scott, who now serves as a US senator for the state, later dropped his opposition, but the Republican-led Florida legislature did not take up a bill to agree to the expansion.
Future presidential candidates
As their state’s chief executives, governors have a unique platform to showcase their political talents.
Many use the governor’s mansion to catapult to the nation’s highest office, the presidency.
At least 17 former US presidents – including Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton and George W Bush – were governors before they occupied the White House.
But some governors find their presidential ambitions thwarted by backlash to their state-level policies.
The Eagleton Institute of Politics estimates that only 53 percent of the presidential nominees who were previously governors were ultimately victorious in their races.
During the 2016 presidential election cycle, for instance, the governor of New Jersey at the time, Chris Christie, hoped to secure the Republican Party’s nomination.
He dropped out of the race in February of that year, however, amid criticism of several actions undertaken during his governorship.
His administration in New Jersey was still reeling from a scandal known as “Bridgegate”, which concerned accusations that a major roadway was closed to punish the mayor of a nearby city.
And some Republicans denounced the way Christie had greeted Obama, a Democrat, when he visited New Jersey during Hurricane Sandy in October 2012.
Setting the stage for 2028
This year’s midterm races are expected to set the stage for the presidential election in 2028.
Several outgoing governors are among the likely hopefuls. Newsom, who has served as California’s governor since 2019, is prevented from running for a third term this year.
Instead, he is widely speculated to be a frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 2028, having established himself as a vocal critic of Republican President Donald Trump.
Several other potential Democratic contenders are also locked in re-election campaigns this midterm cycle that could serve as previews for future presidential bids. They include Wes Moore of Maryland and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
UN warns of security risks in Western Sahara as peacekeeping mission ends
The mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place in the disputed region since a ceasefire in 1991.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of potential escalation of hostilities in the disputed Western Sahara region after the expiry of a 35-year-long peacekeeping mission.
“The Secretary-General said he remains concerned about the security situation throughout the territory and the risk of hostilities escalating,” his spokesperson, Stephane Dujarric, said in a statement on Sunday.
Guterres also confirmed the end of the peacekeeping mission on Sunday, after the UN Security Council (UNSC) failed to renew its mandate on Friday.
He urged all concerned “to exercise maximum restraint and to refrain from actions that could further increase tensions or undermine regional stability”.
November 1 marked the start of the “liquidation phase” of the peacekeeping mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, Guterres said.
The UN established the Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future.
Morocco has considered Western Sahara its territory since 1975, when Spain withdrew from the desert region in northwest Africa, roughly the size of Britain.
The Polisario Front, an Algeria-backed movement acting on behalf of the Indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
At the UNSC on Friday, the US proposed a resolution to support the principle of self-determination in the Western Sahara. Washington’s draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.
Russia vetoed the resolution, despite support from 11 of the 15 UNSC members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.
The council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.
“While MINURSO’s peacekeeping operations have concluded, the United Nations stands ready to continue supporting efforts to advance dialogue and pursue a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” Guterres said on Sunday.
‘Deep regret’
Morocco’s royal palace said the fact the mission was not renewed was a “significant development” in withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from the UNSC’s consideration.
On Saturday, Algeria’s Foreign Ministry, however, expressed “deep regret” over the non-renewal, blaming the “excessive bias” of the US towards Morocco’s position.
The Polisario Front said in a statement that it was “concerned at the deadlock in the Security Council meeting”.
Speaking after Friday’s vote, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said it was truly unfortunate that in 2026, the veto was used to “preserve the letter R [in the Mission’s name] for referendum”.
He added Washington’s proposal “would have moved the 50-year conflict forward” and that the status quo is unacceptable.
Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.
“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Ukraine and Russia say emergency air-raid warning systems hit by cyber-hacks – Europe live
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Frances Mao
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Belgian PM meeting with King to tender resignation
Belgium’s prime minister Bart De Wever is handing in his resignation this morning following failed attempts to pass a budget, local media are reporting.
De Wever has been trying to get budget cuts through, and failed in late-night coalition talks yesterday to secure a compromise.
He arrived at the Royal Palace in Brussels this morning to meet with King Philippe, Belgian media say.
However they report he may be instructed to try and secure a deal again, by a certain deadline.
In Kyiv, residents received a succession of unusual alerts late on Sunday night over the period of roughly an hour.
Typically, people can receive several alerts a day warning of incoming Russian drones or missiles; locals after four years of living in a warzone are used to their phones going off, often followed by sirens in the street.
But these messages warned of radically different threats- a nuclear radiation warning, a chemical attack and even an incident of street fighting in Kyiv.
One of the messages was also transmitted in Russian, a clear tell that something was potentially off.
The messages sent out were:
22:47: “Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv.”
22:48: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying” [This message was written in Russia]
22:49: “Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
22:49: “Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
23:53: An all clear is sent out
Ukrainian authorities within the hour had publicised messages on Telegram saying they believed the app system had been compromised.
The Air Force wrote on Telegram: “The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of key events in Europe.
Ukraine and Russia have reported corresponding cyber-hacks on their app warning systems overnight.
These are the mobile apps which send alerts and air-raid warnings, alerting citizens to when missiles and drones are incoming (and thus advising residents to seek shelter or go down to a bunker).
This appears to be the first breach of the app, on such a scale, during the war so far; directly immobilising one of the most important channels of communication authorities have to help advise citizens.
In the Ukraine hack, the app started spewing out alarming fake messages late on Sunday night – warning residents of a nuclear radiation threat in the capital Kyiv, a chemical attack, street fighting and also incoming Oreshnik hypersonic missiles, which Ukraine lacks interceptors for.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued clarification within the hour on Telegram, urging people to remain calm and disregard the messages, one of which was written in Russian.
Some hours later, Russian authorities said its warning app had been hacked and had to be taken offline. A Ukrainian hacker group has claimed to have sent fake alerts warning of nuclear warheads to users inside Russia.
Amid the cyber warfare overnight, both sides also carried out strikes, targeting energy sites like oil refineries. Strikes have been reported in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts a missile as fighting rages in Yemen’s al-Jawf
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts a missile as fighting rages in Yemen’s al-Jawf
Houthi-affiliated media report that seven people were wounded in strikes on the city of Hodeidah.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen says air defences intercepted a Houthi missile, while fighting continues to rage along key fronts between the armed group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile” targeting Saudi Arabia’s southern region, said coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki in a statement on Monday.
Earlier, he said defences destroyed a drone launched toward the southern region on Sunday evening.
Also on Monday, the Saudi Civil Defence authority issued and then lifted alerts warning of “potential danger” in the city of Abha, as well as the provinces of Khamis Mushait, Taif and Najran.
The authority warned residents against “filming, publishing or sharing information” related to missile and drone attacks.
In Yemen, a media outlet affiliated with the Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), reported that seven people were wounded in Saudi-led coalition air strikes on Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast.
Four people were wounded in the attacks on Ras Isa port dock, while three others suffered injuries in a strike on an oil company site in the governorate’s Bajil district, Houthi media reported.
There was no comment on the reports from the Saudi-led coalition.
Humanitarian crisis
The latest clashes come as Yemeni government forces keep up their campaign to regain positions from the Iran-aligned Houthis in the strategic northern governorate of al-Jawf.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Sunday evening that government forces conducted 1,272 “targeting operations” against Houthi fighters, fortifications and weapons supplies over 24 hours.
Operations are ongoing in al-Jawf, neighbouring Marib and al-Bayda to the south, added al-Nazili. Government forces killed roughly 500 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled nearly 170 vehicles, equipment or heavy weaponry.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.
In southwest Yemen, the Houthis continue to besiege the city of Taiz, blocking the entry of food, fuel and medical supplies, in what authorities warn is a mounting humanitarian crisis.
Taiz Governor Nabil Shamsan has called for urgent help for the city’s deteriorating health facilities. He said 120 health centres have stopped operating and another 66 are close to shutting down since the Houthis cut off supply routes to the city in early October.
Nour al-Din al-Mansouri, a member of the committee facilitating the work of the Taiz Siege Affairs Office, told Al Jazeera that at least 23 trucks were damaged or overturned in the past two weeks while seeking alternative routes to Taiz.
The city is Yemen’s third-largest and home to about one million of the country’s roughly 43 million people.
Full-scale fighting reignited in Yemen in September, when the Houthis made crucial gains that tightened their grip on the Red Sea coast.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a campaign called Operation Dawn of Yemen last month to regain Houthi-held sites and restore government control over other territories held by the group, which seized the capital Sanaa in 2014.

https://taz.de/E-Dienstwagen-fuer-die-Mo.title: E-Dienstwagen für die Mobilitätswende: Der DAX steht unter Strom
https://taz.de/E-Dienstwagen-fuer-die-Mo.author: Nanja Boenisch und Simon Poelchau
https://taz.de/E-Dienstwagen-fuer-die-Mo.text:
E-Dienstwagen für die Mobilitätswende: Der DAX steht unter Strom
Zwei Drittel der neu gekauften Autos in Deutschland sind Dienstwagen. Wie halten es die größten DAX-Konzerne mit der Elektrifizierung ihrer Fuhrparks?
Friedrich Merz gibt sich gerade alle Mühe, Deutschland international als unverbesserliche Verbrennernation dastehen zu lassen. Dabei wollen viele große deutsche Unternehmen mehr E-Autos in ihrer Dienstwagenflotte. Viele von ihnen haben sogar schon feste Regeln dafür.
Die taz hat die 40 DAX-Konzerne – also die größten und zahlungskräftigsten Unternehmen des deutschen Aktienmarktes – im September gefragt, wie sie es mit der Elektrifizierung ihrer Fuhrparks halten. Fünf von ihnen, darunter Vonovia und Airbus, ließen die Anfrage unbeantwortet oder machten keine Angaben, Fresenius Medical Care hat gar keine Dienstwagenflotte.
Bei 15 der übrigen 34 Unternehmen gilt die Regel, dass nur noch E-Dienstwagen bestellt werden dürfen – zumindest für Führungskräfte, in einigen Fällen für alle Mitarbeitenden. 16 Dax-Konzerne schließen Verbrenner nicht aus, bieten aber finanzielle oder organisatorische Vorteile für die Wahl eines E-Autos. Nur drei Unternehmen – BMW, Mercedes-Benz und der Versicherer Hannover Rück mit jedoch nur 7 Dienstwagen – antworteten, dass sie ihren Mitarbeitenden die Antriebsart ihres Dienstwagens nicht vorschreiben, und machten keine Angaben zu unverbindlichen Anreizen.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Soll die Mobilitätswende gelingen, müssen vor allem Unternehmen Elektroautos kaufen und sich von Verbrennern verabschieden. Denn auf sie entfällt ein Großteil der Neuzulassungen. Nur jeder dritte Neuwagen wird von einer Privatperson gekauft, zwei Drittel werden gewerblich genutzt. Bei den Oberklassewagen sind es sogar 80 Prozent. „Damit beeinflussen die Firmen auch den Gebrauchtwagenmarkt“, sagt Caroline Tiefenbach, Referentin für Klimaschutz im Verkehr bei der Deutschen Umwelthilfe (DUH). Was die Firmen jetzt neu kaufen, werde später als Gebrauchtwagen angeboten.
Mehr Förderung vom Staat
„Das ist wichtig, weil Firmen der Umstieg auf Elektroautos leichter fällt“, so Tiefenbach. Sie haben in der Regel mehr Kapital als Privatpersonen und können die Anschaffung leichter stemmen. Außerdem erhalten Unternehmen in den meisten EU-Ländern mehr Förderung vom Staat als Privatleute. Im Schnitt bekommen Unternehmen in der Staatengemeinschaft eine steuerliche Förderung von 6.032 Euro pro vollelektrischem Neuwagen, während es für Privatpersonen lediglich 332 Euro sind.
Tiefenbach sieht deswegen besonders kritisch, dass Frankreich und Deutschland in der EU schwächere CO2-Vorgaben für den Autoverkehr durchsetzen wollen. Denn Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron machen sich nicht nur für eine Aufweichung der CO2-Ziele stark, die Hersteller zum Bau klimafreundlicherer Autos anhalten sollen. Auch die Vorgaben für Dienstwagenflotten sollen verwässert werden. „Der Vorschlag der Kommission zu Unternehmensflotten sollte für mehr Flexibilität sorgen“, heißt es in dem vierseitigen Positionspapier, auf das sich Berlin und Paris jüngst geeinigt haben. Anstatt starre Vorgaben zu machen, sollten „realistische nationale Ziele“ für emissionsfreie und -arme Fahrzeuge festgelegt werden.
Dies richtet sich gegen den Vorschlag, den die EU-Kommission vergangenen Dezember machte. Das EU-Parlament legt im November seine Position zum sogenannten zum sogenannten Verbrenner-Aus fest, dann stehen auch die Kommissionsvorschläge zu Firmenwagen auf dem Programm. Demnach müssten die Mitgliedstaaten ab dem Jahr 2030 für einen Mindestanteil von E-Neuwagen in der Flotte großer Unternehmen sorgen. Laut den Plänen der EU-Kommission läge die Quote in Deutschland bei mindestens 54 Prozent reinen Elektrofahrzeugen und 83 Prozent inklusive Plug-in-Hybriden. Europaweit wären es 45 beziehungsweise 69 Prozent. Vor allem will die EU-Kommission ab 2028 steuerliche Anreize verbieten, die dazu führen, dass große Unternehmen weiterhin reine Verbrenner verkaufen.
„Spätestens dann muss die Bundesregierung das Dienstwagenprivileg streichen, für Großkonzerne genauso wie für alle anderen auch“, sagt DUH-Expertin Tiefenbach. Durch die in Deutschland geltende steuerliche Besserstellung privat genutzter Verbrennerdienstwagen entgingen dem Staat im vergangenen Jahr 4,2 Milliarden Euro.
DAX-Unternehmen weiter als die Bundesregierung
Das hinter dem Dienstwagenprivileg stehende Prinzip: Das Unternehmen stellt seinen Angestellten ein Auto, das diese auch privat nutzen dürfen. Auf diesen geldwerten Vorteil müssen sie kaum Steuern zahlen. Der Satz liegt beim Verbrenner bei nur 1 Prozent des Kaufpreises pro Monat – hinzu kommen 0,03 Prozent vom Listenpreis pro Kilometer des Arbeitsweges.
Während die Bundesregierung in Europa für den Verbrenner lobbyiert, sind die großen DAX-Unternehmen bereits weiter –zumindest, wenn es um ihre Dienstwagenflotten geht. Die meisten bemühen sich um die Elektrifizierung ihrer Fuhrparks, auch wenn die Antworten, die die taz auf ihre Anfrage im September erhalten hat, sehr unterschiedlich ausfielen.
So zahlen Adidas und Infineon ihren Mitarbeitenden einen Bonus, wenn sie einen CO2-armen Dienstwagen bestellen. Bei der Deutschen Bank, der Allianz, SAP und dem Digitalunternehmen Scout24 bekommen die Mitarbeitenden nur noch E-Autos. Von den 82 Dienstwagen bei Scout24 sind demnach 72 batterieelektrisch, bei SAP sind es 8.300 von 19.000, bei der Deutschen Bank 2.160 von 4.600 und bei der Allianz rund 120 von 200.
Scout24 will schon Ende 2026 bei 100 Prozent E-Autos ankommen. Siemens, Siemens Energy und Siemens Healthineers sowie die Allianz, die Nivea-Mutter Beiersdorf und der Pharmakonzern Merck wollen diese Marke spätestens 2030 knacken – also dann, wenn laut dem Vorschlag der EU-Kommission 54 Prozent erreicht sein müssten.
Der Reiz der Vorteile
Beiersdorf, der Triebwerkhersteller MTU Aero Engines und die BASF haben CO2-Obergrenzen für Dienstfahrzeuge. Bei Fresenius, Henkel, der Deutschen Telekom, dem Chemiekonzern Brenntag und dem Anlagenbauer GEA müssen Dienstwagen im Innendienst elektrisch sein – bestimmte Fahrzeuge im Außendienst dürfen noch fossil fahren, sollen aber nach und nach elektrifiziert werden. Der Pharmadienstleister Qiagen, Merck und das Bauunternehmen Hochtief unterstützen die Installation einer Wallbox am Wohnort der Beschäftigten, wenn sie einen E-Dienstwagen wählen. So schafft ein Vorteil den Reiz, um die Verkehrswende voranzubringen.
Ein durchschnittlicher E-Auto-Anteil über alle 40 DAX-Konzerne hinweg ließ sich auf Basis der Antworten nicht berechnen; nicht alle Unternehmen nannten konkrete Zahlen zur Größe des Fuhrparks und zur Zahl der Stromer. Immerhin: Von den 20 Firmen, die vergleichbare Antworten lieferten, sagte die Hälfte, dass schon mehr als 50 Prozent der Flotte vollelektrifiziert ist. Sie haben also schon jetzt fast den Wert erreicht, den die EU-Kommission in vier Jahren erreichen will.
Laut einer Studie der Initiative Klimaneutral waren 30 Prozent aller neu bestellten Dienstwagen in Deutschland im ersten Halbjahr 2026 batterieelektrisch. Und fast drei von vier E-Dienstwagen wurden von der VW-Gruppe, BMW oder Mercedes-Benz gebaut. Von den großen Autobauern also, die in Deutschland zuletzt vor allem mit Krise und Stellenabbau Schlagzeilen machten. Inzwischen haben die großen deutschen Marken beim E-Auto-Absatz Boden gutgemacht – allerdings werden die einträglichen Batterien noch zu selten hier produziert. Und insgesamt liegt die internationale Konkurrenz, vor allem aus China, im Bereich der Elektromobilität weiter vorn.
Dass die Bundesregierung die geplanten EU-Vorgaben für Dienstwagenflotten mit Hilfe aus Paris aufweichen will, hilft der heimischen Autoindustrie nicht weiter. Im Gegenteil: Eine schnelle Elektrifizierung der Konzernflotten könnte ein Job-Booster sein, hat eine Studie des Fraunhofer-Instituts für System- und Innovationsforschung im Auftrag des Verkehrsverbands T&E ergeben. Würden die EU-Flottenvorgaben mit sogenannten Made-in-Europe-Klauseln verbunden, könnte das 134.000 zusätzliche Jobs in Deutschland schaffen.
Neue Jobs und mehr Umsatz durch Made-in-Europe
Die Wertschöpfung der Autobauer könnte um 7,8 Milliarden Euro steigen. Allein bei Volkswagen könnten durch eine kluge Umsetzung der Brüsseler Ideen zwischen 14.000 bis 56.000 neue Jobs entstehen, da der Konzern einen Großteil seiner Autos auf dem europäischen Firmenwagenmarkt verkauft.
Auf strenge Made-in-Europe-Vorgaben bestand der französische Präsident. Mit ihnen will Macron den europäischen Markt vor globaler Konkurrenz schützen, etwa indem Steuervorteile nur noch für Produkte gewährt werden, wenn sie zum Großteil in der EU hergestellt werden. Dagegen steht Merz, der das Verbrenner-Aus aufweichen will. Es einigten sich nun Konservative, Sozialdemokraten und Liberale, den strengeren Kommissionsvorschlag für die Elektrifizierung von Dienstwagenflotten abzulehnen. So bleibt die Politik bei der Antriebswende hinter vielen großen Unternehmen zurück.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. https://www.middleeasteye.net/Aipac-is-n.title: Aipac is now a toxic brand. The Michigan Senate race is only one example
https://www.middleeasteye.net/Aipac-is-n.author: Mitchell Plitnick
https://www.middleeasteye.net/Aipac-is-n.text:
Aipac is now a toxic brand. The Michigan Senate race is only one example
“A lobby is like a night flower: it thrives in the dark and dies in the sun.” So said Steve Rosen, former foreign policy director of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) in a memo to a fellow staffer. Rosen would later be fired amid a major scandal involving espionage in passing classified US information to Israel.
Rosen was correct about the danger to a lobbying organisation that publicity poses. But in December 2021, Aipac decided to test that theory by creating two political action committees (Pacs) that enabled it to take part directly in political campaigns.
The results were mixed, and Aipac recently announced that it was closing one of the Pacs it had set up.
Aipac had been an advocacy organisation, promoting Israel’s interests, but it did not fund campaigns directly, nor did it endorse or fund political candidates.
In many ways, that made it more effective. It could do things like issue a congressional report card which rated every member of Congress’s support of Israel. Then other groups that were actual Pacs could use those reports to decide which candidates they should be contributing to.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Aipac’s non-profit status allows it to lobby Congress on behalf of Israel while claiming it acts strictly in support of the wishes of pro-Israel Americans. It thus avoids having to register as an agent of a foreign government.
Meanwhile, Aipac’s sister organisation, the American Israel Education Fund, which is registered as an education non-profit, refrains from direct lobbying but offers vacation tours to Israel for members of Congress, under the rubric of “education”.
This strategy was effective for decades. Aipac’s bipartisan reach was strong, and it was often remarked by a credulous media how Israel was, somehow, the one subject Democrats and Republicans could come together on.
Changing opinion
That began to change in recent years.
The reasons are complicated, but the result was that presidential and congressional candidates, mostly among Democrats, were suddenly accepting the idea that annual military aid to Israel, which had risen to $3.8bn annually, should be conditioned on Israel conforming to the requirements of United States law and adhering with United States policy.
It’s a mark of how successful Aipac had been that such obvious conditions, which were already mandated by US law, were considered controversial.
But a growing awareness of the conditions that Palestinians were living under in the West Bank and Gaza Strip was changing the minds of many of Israel’s liberal supporters.
Aipac decided to take the step of getting more directly involved in political campaigns to try to stifle the number of advocates for Palestine in Congress while the number of them was still very small.
They created two Pacs: Aipac-Pac could contribute directly to candidates’ campaigns; and the United for Democracy Project (UDP), a super Pac, which cannot directly fund campaigns, but can spend an unlimited amount on advertising and other public advocacy to support their chosen candidates.
Aipac has long been known for its lobbying, but now, its support for individual candidates could be tracked in a measurable way, making it the perfect symbol of money in politics.
Aipac was attacked for its influence in Washington and was more easily assailed than other lobbying groups because it advocated for the interests of a foreign country.
Aipac’s argument that it was an American group representing the interests of America’s pro-Israel community has worked for decades to protect the organisation from the limitations it would face as a registered agent of a foreign government.
But in the court of public opinion, that technical argument holds little weight. People understand that Aipac defends and promotes the interests of a foreign country.
Now that it was openly spending on campaigns and giving money to candidates, it could be caught up in the general distaste the American public has for the role of big money in politics.
And the Aipac name started becoming toxic. Much of this was led by Bernie Sanders, who was among the first to recognise how vulnerable Aipac was to this sort of public shaming.
Instead of impacting American politics with its newfound ability to spend great amounts of money, Aipac only further tarnished Israel’s once popular image in the United States.
This was especially true for Democrats, whom Israel, under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, had been alienating for years, even though most American Jews are Democrats.
Battleground state
The decline of Israel’s image and the toxicity of Aipac were most clearly on display in the election campaigns this year in the battleground state of Michigan.
In the upcoming election, Democrats have long been expected to win back the House of Representatives and now have a good chance of winning the Senate too. One of the key states in the election is Michigan.
The Republican candidate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, is a known quantity, a staunchly right-wing man whose candidacy is backed by big corporations, extremist Christian groups, and Donald Trump.
Mike Rogers’ campaign quietly asked Aipac to refrain from supporting Rogers. That is a mark of how toxic Aipac has become
Abdul El-Sayed became the Democratic nominee after overcoming huge obstacles related to his views on Israel and Palestine, the war on Iran, and, most of all, the simple fact of his being a Muslim.
He won a bruising primary against Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who had been an Aipac candidate for years.
Stevens defeated Andy Levin in 2022, with a great deal of help from Aipac. Levin, who comes from a Michigan political dynasty and is a prominent leader in his Jewish community, was a self-identified Zionist, but a liberal one who believed in a two-state solution.
But that was nothing compared to Aipac’s support for Stevens against El-Sayed.
In total, Stevens outspent El-Sayed in the campaign by a 12-to-one margin. Aipac and other pro-Israel groups spent more than $30m between their own advertising and donations to Stevens’ campaign.
Stevens kept a distance from some of the often vicious anti-Muslim rhetoric aimed at El-Sayed by her supporters, including Aipac. But she was not forceful in denouncing it, and this was noted and would only grow worse when El-Sayed faced a Republican.
El-Sayed eventually defeated Stevens in a closely contested primary. Even as she denied that her association with Aipac might have hurt her chances of winning, Stevens inadvertently hinted that it did.
“I think that there [were] a lot of people talking about it, and they didn’t love it because maybe they don’t understand what the group is. Aipac is a group of six million Jewish Americans… a lot of people are deeply frustrated that [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has failed to give us peace,” she said.
Over the weekend, a dramatic turn of events took place when the Michigan Democratic Party kicked Stevens out of its ranks, after she endorsed Michigan’s GOP Senate nominee, Mike Rogers - over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
"Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future," the state party’s chair, Curtis Hertel, said in a post Sunday on X.
Islamaphobic rhetoric
Meanwhile, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent turned up the Islamophobic rhetoric, consistently and falsely accusing El-Sayed of working with the Muslim Brotherhood, and of saying that the United States “deserved” the attacks of 11 September 2001.
Yet despite that level of mudslinging, Rogers’ campaign, soon after the primaries ended, quietly asked Aipac to refrain from supporting Rogers. That is a mark of how toxic Aipac has become.
Eventually, Rogers, whose base of support includes some of the most zealous and extreme supporters of Israel from the evangelical Christian community, publicly welcomed and received support from Aipac.
But his reluctance to initially accept Aipac money despite his very proud right-wing views shows how ubiquitous hostility toward Aipac is.
The saga of Abdul El-Sayed and the Michigan Senate race is only one example of the toxicity of Aipac’s brand. The widespread distaste for the group explains why it is pulling itself out of the game of direct financing of candidates.
Aipac will maintain the UDP super Pac, in the hope that it can continue to influence races quietly, with few people noticing that it is Aipac behind attack ads which often have nothing to do with Israel but serve to denigrate candidates who might have the slightest tendency toward advocacy for the rights of Palestinians.
But if UDP can also be dragged into the light, it - like Aipac-Pac - will also wither and die. Aipac works tirelessly to portray an apartheid regime that is committing genocide as a warm, friendly country. Like a lobby, that effort cannot withstand the sunlight, and even Aipac’s own officials know it.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.text:
Introduction: Crypto 'scammers on overdrive' as Binance customers pull billions from accounts after $6.3bn hack
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.
Crypto scammers are now in “overdrive”, the founder of crypto exchange Binance has warned, as customers pull billions in funds from the platform as it recovers from a record hack.
The platform was hit by a $6.3bn theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history. Experts identified North Korea as the probable culprit.
Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach but on Sunday announced it had begun a phased reopening.
By Sunday afternoon, the platform had processed $4.6bn in withdrawals and $1bn in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of about $3.6bn – 2.1% of its $171bn in total assets under management. (Those numbers were confirmed by the company in its latest proof of reserves snapshot – a full report is expected today.)
Changpeng Zhao, the founder of the platform and commonly known as CZ, has warned that scammers are now targeting those that are trying to pull their money from the platform. He wrote on X:
 Scammers on over drive now. Be careful.
His post was in response to a post which said:
 Some of you may have seen posts and screenshots circulating recently. Please be aware that these screenshots are fake and the information in them is false. For accurate and up-to-date information, always refer to our official channels and announcements.
The hack has spooked the market, with investors also pulling out funds from Bitcoin ETFs in the US, according to Nick Forster, chief executive of Derive.xyz, a crypto platform. He said:
 US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $643 million in net outflows on Friday, their first trading session following the hack.
  
BlackRock’s IBIT saw $233.7 million in outflows, while Fidelity’s FBTC lost $201 million, ARKB $129.5 million, GBTC $53.3 million and BITB $25.7 million. No fund recorded net inflows.
  
….We’re seeing a similar shift in options trading on Derive.xyz. In the first 12 hours following the hack, put options accounted for 68% of Bitcoin options premiums traded, compared with 43% in the preceding five days.
  
Trading activity also remained elevated, with approximately $55 million in daily Bitcoin options volume since the hack, compared with $34 million the day prior.
  
Traders have been moving quickly to protect themselves against further losses, with downside protection taking a much larger share of options activity.
He added that the odds of Bitcoin hitting the $100,000 level by the end of the year were now just 3.5%.
 Last Wednesday, Derive options were pricing a 6% probability of Bitcoin exceeding $100K by Christmas. That has now fallen to just 3.5%, or roughly a one-in-30 chance.
…Before the hack, our options market was pricing a 75% probability of Bitcoin finishing above $80,000 at Friday’s expiry. Instead, Bitcoin settled at $77,786.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Nuclear radiation in Russia, Ukraine? No, just hacked warning alerts
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Nuclear radiation in Russia, Ukraine? No, just hacked warning alerts
Warnings startle people in Ukraine, but authorities say they cleared up the confusion in under an hour.
Ukraine and Russia have accused each other of hacking into systems used to send out emergency alerts to citizens, raising fears of a new escalation of digital and psychological warfare tactics.
The systems’ apps sent out radiation alerts on Sunday and Monday to civilians before officials issued public clarifications.
The fake threats began on the same day as a localised ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Kherson region came to an end on Sunday. The truce, which the United States said was brokered by first lady Melania Trump, is the longest so far in Russia’s more than four-year war on Ukraine. The ceasefire lasted for six days, during which humanitarian aid and evacuations were allowed in the Russian-occupied town of Olekshy.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said many people in Ukraine now expect renewed fighting along the front lines.
Here’s what we know about the fake notifications:
What happened?
Ukraine’s Air Force said late on Sunday that users of its Air Alert app, which warns people of incoming air attacks, received fake warnings of nuclear and chemical threats to areas in and around Kyiv.
Users were also warned of potential street combat and told that Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed.
“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram.
“There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications blamed Russia. In a post on X, the agency pointed to the use of the Russian language in one of the fake messages. The Ukrainian government said a separate app created for the capital city was working normally.
The fake alerts came just after 10pm (20:00 GMT), startling a lot of people, Macalpine reported.
“Even the speakers here in the centre of the city rang out warnings of these attacks,” she said. “But most people here understood within at least half an hour that this was some kind of hacking attack.”
Hours later on Monday morning, similar announcements came from Russia’s Ministry of Civil Defence, Emergencies and Disaster Relief, which said its warnings app came under a “massive cyberattack” and wrongly warned users of imminent drone attacks. The ministry did not name any suspects but said the alerts spread “false information”.
Media reports said the hackers warned Russians that “nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [Ukrainian drones] had been launched on all regions” of the country. The alerts also instructed people to “urgently” stock up on food for three weeks and to hide.
Has this happened before?
This appears to be the first time either Ukraine’s or Russia’s official alert apps have been hacked.
However, cyberwarfare has long been a major part of the countries’ previous confrontations.
Russian hackers have attacked Ukraine’s election systems in the past and in January 2022 attacked Ukrainian government and banking sites. Cyberwarfare tactics have only intensified since February 2022 when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In late 2023, the Russian hacker group Sandworm took the private telecommunications network Kyivstar offline, disrupting notifications for days.
Ukrainian groups have also launched multiple cyberattacks on Russia.
The country’s volunteer-based IT Army of Ukraine was founded in the wake of Russia’s invasion specifically to engage in cyberwarfare against Russia and has reportedly targeted the Moscow Stock Exchange, Russia’s power grids and several government websites. In 2022, the Reuters news agency reported Ukrainian attackers used facial recognition software to scan the faces of dead Russian combatants and notified their families of their deaths.
Why is the threat of nuclear radiation in Ukraine significant?
Ukraine is particularly vulnerable because it has already suffered one nuclear disaster and it remains at risk due to fighting around another major nuclear plant.
In April 1986, the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, located in the then-Ukrainian Soviet Republic, exploded, releasing radioactive material. Scores of people died from the explosion itself, but thousands later developed severe health issues as a result, including thyroid cancer. Radiation was detected as far away as Sweden. It’s regarded as one of the two worst nuclear accidents in history along with the 2011 Fukushima disaster in Japan. Chornobyl remains a ghost town after its inhabitants were evacuated.
Ongoing fighting in the Ukrainian region of Zaporizhia has raised fears that the tragic story could repeat itself. Russia partly controls the region, including Enerhodar, where the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Europe’s largest nuclear energy facility, is located.
Both sides have repeatedly launched attacks on each other’s positions with Russia targeting the Ukrainian-held provincial capital, Zaporizhzhia, and Ukraine targeting Russian-held areas, including Enerhodar.
Last week, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the United Nations nuclear watchdog, said a welder working at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant was killed in a drone attack. The head of the agency, Rafael Grossi, called for “maximum military restraint” from both sides.

https://taz.de/Friedensgericht-in-Kolumb.title: Friedensgericht in Kolumbien: Keine Sicherheit, sondern ein Blutbad
https://taz.de/Friedensgericht-in-Kolumb.author: Katharina Wojczenko
https://taz.de/Friedensgericht-in-Kolumb.text:
Friedensgericht in Kolumbien: Keine Sicherheit, sondern ein Blutbad
In Kolumbien hat das Sondergericht für den Frieden die bislang hochrangigsten Militärs angeklagt. Der rechtsextremen Regierung gefällt das gar nicht.
Das kolumbianische Sondergericht für den Frieden hat am Freitag zwölf ehemalige Militärs und Polizisten wegen Kriegsverbrechen und Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit angeklagt. Es geht um eines der blutigsten Kapitel des Bürgerkriegs: die Militär- und Polizeioperationen in der Comuna 13 in Medellín.
Die bekanntesten Namen sind die Generäle Manuel Montoya und José Leonardo Gallego Castrillón. Montoya leitete damals die vierte Brigade der Armee und wurde später unter Präsident Alvaro Uribe Kommandant der Armee. Gallego Castrillón war Polizeichef der Metropolregion Medellín. Gegen beide Generäle ermittelt das Sondergericht für den Frieden in weiteren Verfahren wegen schweren Menschenrechtsverletzungen.
Medellín ist die zweitgrößte Stadt Kolumbiens. Die Comuna 13 ist Tourist*innen wegen der Freiluft-Rolltreppen und Graffiti-Touren bekannt. Doch sie war städtisches Kriegsgebiet und beherbergt das größte Massengrab Kolumbiens, La Escombrera.
In der Anklage geht es um die Zeit zwischen 2001 und 2004. Damals fanden mehrere Operationen von Militär und Polizei in der Comuna 13 statt. Die bekannteste und größte in der kolumbianischen Geschichte war die Operation Orion.
Mord, Vertreibung und Verschwindenlassen
Damals hatten sich mehrere Guerillagruppen, darunter die Farc, in den bergigen Vierteln der Comuna 13 einquartiert, die den Zugang zu strategischen, überregionalen Korridoren für den Drogenhandel sichern. Aufgabe des Staates war, die Kontrolle über die Territorien zurückzugewinnen, sagt Richter Gustavo Salazar. Er leitet zusammen mit Richter Óscar Parra die Ermittlungen. Das war auch das erklärte Ziel der Politik der sogenannten „demokratischen Sicherheit“ von Präsident Alvaro Uribe.
Die Folge war stattdessen ein Blutbad in der Zivilbevölkerung. Am Ende war die Guerilla in der Comuna 13 vernichtet – aber die Herrschaft der Paramilitärs begann. Für die Bewohner*innen bedeutete das: noch mehr Bedrohungen, Folter, Flucht, Verschwindenlassen und Morde als vorher.
In der mehr als 1.300 Seiten langen Anklageschrift legt das Sondergericht dar, wie die staatlichen Sicherheitskräfte, die örtlichen Paramilitärs oder beide zusammen schwere Verbrechen begingen. Es geht um 951 Straftaten, darunter Mord, Vertreibung, Verschwindenlassen, Verletzung, willkürliche Festnahmen und 891 Opfer.
Sicherheitskräfte und Paramilitärs gingen gemeinsam vor
Den Ex-Generälen Montoya und Gallego wird nicht zu Last gelegt, dass sie die Verbrechen selbst begingen – sondern dass sie sie nicht verhindert haben und die Zivilbevölkerung nicht vor ihren Untergebenen und den Paramilitärs schützten. Das Militär unterhielt mehrere Posten in Sichtweite der Paramilitärs – ohne sie zu bekämpfen.
Das Sondergericht hat Beweise gesammelt, wie Militär, Polizei und Geheimdienst mit den Paramilitärs zusammenarbeiteten. Sie tauschten Informationen aus, koordinierten sich in Kampfhandlungen, machten den Weg für Paramilitärs frei. Zudem gaben die Sicherheitskräfte den Paramilitärs zu verstehen, dass der Staat ihr Handeln nicht verfolgen werde. Ebenfalls belegt sind Zahlungen an Paramilitärs, die als Informanten und Führer arbeiteten, also angebliche Guerilleros und angebliche zivile Kollaborateure anzeigten.
Die Angeklagten haben zwei Wochen Zeit, ihre Verantwortung zu bekennen. Dann stehen ihnen beim Urteil die ermäßigten Strafen des Sondergerichts offen. Tun sie das nicht, drohen ihnen im Widerspruchsverfahren bis zu 20 Jahre Haft.
Allerdings ist der Rechtsweg in Gefahr: Die aktuelle Regierung des ultrarechten Präsidenten Abelardo de la Espriella, der den Friedensvertrag mit der Farc kategorisch ablehnt, mit dem das Sondergericht geschaffen wurde, hat mit dem Kongress das Budget des Gerichts massiv gekürzt. Außerdem hat ein Gesetzesvorschlag die erste Hürde genommen, um die Laufzeit des Sondergerichts um fünf Jahre zu verkürzen.
Verkündet wurde die Anklageschrift auf der Escombrera. Neben Presse waren Mütter, Töchter und andere Angehörige aus der Comuna 13 dort, die seit mehr als 20 Jahren nach ihren Lieben suchen – und dafür verleumdet, bedroht und verfolgt wurden. Sie äußerten große Sorge wegen der Attacken auf das Gericht.
Das Sondergericht soll die Verbrechen der beiden früheren Kriegsparteien, Staat und Guerilla, aufklären, bestrafen und für Wiedergutmachung bei den Opfern sorgen. Das Friedensabkommen hat Verfassungsrang. Kürzungen beim Gericht verlangen Verfassungsänderungen – und würden Kolumbien in Konflikt mit seinen internationalen rechtlichen Verpflichtungen bringen.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120358.title: Tarifkonflikt | Metaller-Warnstreiks angelaufen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120358.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Tarifkonflikt
Metaller-Warnstreiks angelaufen
In den Tarifverhandlungen der Elektro- und Metallindustrie fängt die IG Metall nach dem Ende der Friedenspflicht nun an, Druck aufzubauen.
Frankfurt am Main. In der deutschen Metall- und Elektroindustrie hat die erste Warnstreikrunde im aktuellen Tarifkonflikt begonnen. Dabei geht es um die Entgelte von rund 3,7 Millionen Beschäftigten in der größten deutschen Industriebranche.
Unmittelbar nach Ablauf der Friedenspflicht in der Nacht zum Sonntag legten die Beschäftigten in ersten Betrieben die Arbeit nieder, darunter die Nachtschicht beim Weißblechhersteller Thyssenkrupp Rasselstein in Andernach (Rheinland-Pfalz), Beschäftigte beim Mobilfunkzulieferer RF 360 Europe/Qualcomm in München, beim Alu-Guss-Unternehmen KSM Castings in Hildesheim und im Recycling- und Walzwerk Speira in Hamburg. In Nordrhein-Westfalen sollte es am Sonntagabend eine erste Aktion in Bielefeld geben. Und seit Mitternacht ist nach Angaben der Gewerkschaft unter anderem der Kranbauer Liebherr in Rostock von einem befristeten Ausstand betroffen.
Die IG Metall will die Proteste von Montag an auf das gesamte Bundesgebiet ausweiten. Das soll in den Tarifverhandlungen den Druck erhöhen. Betroffen von den zeitlich befristeten Ausständen sind wichtige Industriezweige wie Autobau, Maschinenbau, Elektronik und Metallerzeugung.
»Starke Warnstreiks« angekündigt
Die Gewerkschaft hat bei einer Laufzeit von zwölf Monaten 5 Prozent mehr Geld sowie die Sicherung von Jobs und Standorten gefordert. Die Arbeitgeber haben in der zweiten Verhandlungsrunde ein Angebot vorgelegt, das im kommenden Jahr eine Einmalzahlung und 2028 eine Stufenerhöhung von 1,3 Prozent im Juli 2028 vorsah. Begründet wurde die Offerte unterhalb der Inflation mit der schwierigen wirtschaftlichen Lage und den hohen Kostenbelastungen für die Industrie in Deutschland.
Die Gewerkschaftsvorsitzende Christiane Benner hatte »starke Warnstreiks« angekündigt, weil das »sogenannte Angebot« in den Betrieben nur »Unverständnis und Wut« ausgelöst habe. Es gehe darum, Kaufkraft und Zukunft für alle am Standort zu sichern. dpa/nd
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Is it true that … drinking alcohol warms you up?
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Kate Lloyd
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Hot toddies, red wine, a dram of whisky: alcohol has long been a go-to remedy for keeping warm. But while a drink might make you feel warmer, does it actually help? “There’s a perception of warmth, but in reality, it doesn’t occur,” says Winston Morgan, professor of toxicology, equity and inclusive practice at the University of East London.
Alcohol affects the body’s temperature-regulating system. Our core body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain that helps regulate how we respond to changes in temperature. When we get too hot, blood vessels near the surface of the skin widen, a process known as vasodilation. This allows more warm blood to flow close to the skin, where heat can escape into the surrounding air. When we get too cold, the opposite happens. The blood vessels narrow, or constrict, reducing blood flow to the skin and helping to conserve heat.
Alcohol interferes with this process. It causes blood vessels near the skin to widen, even when our core body temperature has not risen. More warm blood reaches the skin’s surface, which can make us feel hot, and even leave us reaching to take off clothing.
“You’re sending more blood to your skin, which gives you the sensation of feeling warmer,” says Morgan. “But actually you’re not. Your body’s just moving around the blood.”
In fact, by increasing blood flow to the skin, alcohol encourages heat to escape from the body, potentially lowering core temperature. That can increase the risk of hypothermia in sufficiently cold conditions, particularly if you start removing clothing.
“After some time, what actually happens is your core becomes cooler,” says Morgan. “So, in a cold environment, you don’t really want to be drinking a lot of alcohol.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks
Democrats slam Haley Stevens over her endorsement of a Republican candidate a day before the polls.
With one day to go before the United States midterm elections, campaigning has reached a fever pitch with Democratic and Republican leaders pulling out all the stops to mobilise voters.
Democrats are hoping to flip control of both chambers of Congress, which is currently controlled by US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are up for grabs on Tuesday. Voting will also be held to elect governors in 36 of the 50 US states.
With the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points of these elections, here’s where things stand as of Monday:
What’s happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?
In a dramatic political development on Sunday, Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens threw her support behind Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her own party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan – one of the most closely watched races of the US midterm elections. Stevens had lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August to El-Sayed.
Her announcement followed weeks of tension with El-Sayed over US support to Israel, which has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza. El-Sayed has opposed military support to Israel, arguing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed the US into the Iran war. Stevens has accused El-Sayed of anti-Semitism for his criticism of Israeli actions in Gaza.
El-Sayed said a vote for his rival Rogers “is going to be a vote for Donald Trump” as his campaign reportedly saw a fundraising surge after Stevens crossed party lines.
Democratic leaders have rallied behind El-Sayed, who has faced Islamophobic attacks during the campaign.
The chairman of the Democratic Party in Michigan criticised Stevens. “She does not speak for that larger community,” Curtis Hertel said in an interview with CNN.
The leader of the Democrats in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, slammed Stevens over her endorsement of the Republican candidate.
“This is a despicable betrayal from Representative Stevens,” he posted on X.
“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors.”
Meanwhile, the advocacy group Michigan Jews for Democracy has backed El-Sayed.
“Haley Stevens does not speak for Michigan’s Jewish community,” it said in a statement, which rejected her “attempt to divide our community” two days before the election.
While Democrats have been angered by Stevens’s action, Trump celebrated her decision.
During a rally in Iowa later on Sunday, the US president said he would “love” it if Stevens joined the Republican Party. “Haley said what few people are willing to say,” Trump added. “It’s a thing called bravery.”
The question now is whether Stevens’s endorsement could persuade some of her supporters to back Rogers or discourage them from voting altogether.
Polling suggested El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support, according to the Reuters news agency.
Judge dismisses Trump’s Alaska election lawsuit
Meanwhile, a federal judge has thrown out a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying a loss by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The administration has argued that a rival on the ballot with the same name could change the outcome.
Sullivan pledged to accept the election outcome, days after the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of the Senate race if he loses.
“I’m going to accept the election results,” Sullivan, an ally of Trump, told CNN on Sunday.
Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-up races that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in the upper chamber of the US Congress.
How many Americans have already voted?
This year, out of about 210 million registered voters, 54.5 million had voted early as of 10am US East Coast time (15:00 GMT) on Sunday, according to a University of Florida analysis. This includes 30 million in-person votes and 24 million mail-in ballots.
In the 2022 midterm elections, 46 million people voted early.
Early voting enthusiasm has been higher among Democrats this year with more than 11 million registered Democrats having voted early, compared with about 8 million registered Republicans, according to the university’s analysis.
Early voting has particularly surged in the state of Texas, a key battleground, where more than 7.7 million people have voted early.
According to an Associated Press polling analysis, in South Carolina, where Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, early voting has surged 83 percent compared with the same point in 2022. The state has open races for governor and US Senate this year.
Kansas, Michigan and Maine have also seen a surge in early voting.
Early turnout figures, however, don’t show which candidates voters have chosen or what the final results will be.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Margot Bonnéry
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
Le procès de l’affaire des « Dubaï Papers » s’ouvre ce lundi 2 novembre au tribunal de Paris. Treize personnes et trois sociétés sont accusées d’avoir fait disparaître 200 millions d’euros des radars du fisc, en les faisant transiter, via des sociétés offshore, sur des comptes bancaires dans le monde entier.
Huit ans après les révélations de L’Obs en collaboration avec la Cellule investigation de Radio France, l’affaire des « Dubaï Papers » arrive devant le tribunal correctionnel de Paris ce lundi 2 novembre. Treize personnes et trois sociétés seront jugées pendant un mois pour leur complicité présumée dans des faits de fraude fiscale, de blanchiment en bande organisée et d’association de malfaiteurs. Ils sont accusés d’avoir permis à plus de 322 contribuables...
