https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Chinese state TV continues Real Madrid blackout after Mbappe-Mao meme row
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Chinese state TV continues Real Madrid blackout after Mbappe-Mao meme row
Real Madrid vs Racing Santander is not broadcast on CCTV despite apologies from Mbappe, Real and La Liga.
Real Madrid’s Spanish football league match against Racing Santander has not been broadcast on Chinese state TV as La Liga continues to pay the price of the fallout from Kylian Mbappe’s remarks about the country’s former leader Mao Zedong.
Neither of the two sports channels on the Chinese state broadcaster CCTV aired Real Madrid’s match on Sunday after star forward Mbappe caused a furore in the Asian country, where millions follow the Spanish league.
The match kicked off at 15:15 GMT but was not broadcast on either of CCTV’s two sports channels, according to the AFP news agency.
None of the other matches from matchweek 11 of La Liga has been broadcast live on public television so far.
Mbappe referred to Mao as a “dictator” in a video from April that went viral recently. It resulted in the body overseeing CCTV saying it would halt broadcasts of the top Spanish league.
Mbappe, Real and La Liga later all apologised for his remarks, and China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it took the player’s apology “seriously”.
Al Jazeera has reached out to La Liga for a comment but had not received a response from the Spanish league by the time of publication.
La Liga matches were broadcast on Migu, a digital streaming service owned by the state-owned China Mobile telecommunications network, according to reports.
The broadcast included Barcelona’s 6-1 win over Alaves on Saturday, but the Racing Santander-Real Madrid match did not appear to be shown.
The China Media Group (CMG), which oversees CCTV, had said it suspended La Liga broadcasts on October 26, adding that apologies from La Liga, Mbappe and Real Madrid were “an absolute prerequisite” for moving past the furore.
The viral video showed Mbappe saying the funniest internet meme he had seen about himself was of his face photoshopped onto that of “some guy. I think he’s a Chinese dictator.”
This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao.
Mbappe later apologised for his “ill-judged” comments. La Liga said it “deeply” regretted them, and Real followed suit.
CCTV’s sports website later reported that CMG had acknowledged the apologies, but it remained unclear whether talks to defuse the situation have begun.
China is a huge market for European football. CCTV also carries matches from the English Premier League and the German, French and Italian top flights.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho said on Saturday that the club had “done our part” to put the controversy behind them.
It is taboo in China to crack jokes about Mao, who died in 1976 and whose policies are blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths.
Major Chinese brands cancelled sponsorship deals with Mbappe after his comments.
Various overseas sports leagues and players have found themselves in hot water for comments on topics that are politically sensitive to China.
China essentially cut ties with the NBA for several years from 2019 after then-Houston Rockets General Manager Daryl Morey tweeted his support for Hong Kong protesters.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Israel has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalition
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Julian Borger in Umm al-Fahm
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction.
Yousef Jabareen, the head of the Joint List, said he was ready to join forces with the “Change” bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.
Turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, 20% of the population) more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.
Jabareen said the first demand of the roughly 840,000 Palestinian Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.
“This has been an awful four years … in all areas of life: in terms of house demolition, criminal gangs within the Arab community without any [intervention] from the police; not allocating the needed resources for our municipalities, for our education, for our youth in general; racism in all areas of life – physical attacks against Arabs, the brutality of the police,” Jabareen told the Guardian in one of his first interviews since the election. “So this has been really a very dangerous period.”
He said the next few days would be critical. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government, with no single grouping commanding a clear claim on power.
Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving the Arab-Israeli parties as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
Eisenkot and his partners have pledged not to form a unity government with Netanyahu, but Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept conscription, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, have signalled it is ready to join an Eisenkot coalition. The Joint List has no intention of joining such a government, but Jabareen said the coalition was ready to keep it afloat from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset.
“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen said at his family home in the northern city of Umm al-Fahm. “As long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government.
“However, in order to use our political power to get rid of the extreme Netanyahu government, we said that we will consider the possibility of supporting from outside. This is an opportunity to change policies, to change attitudes, including towards the Arab community and towards the Palestinian people.
“This is really a historic moment and I hope that there will be partners within the opposition to go ahead with that. We are thinking that this could be the start of a change.”
Jabareen, 54, a former law professor and the leader of the socialist Hadash party, has yet to talk to Eisenkot since Tuesday’s elections, but he confirmed that informal discussions among opposition parties were under way.
Forming a new government was unlikely to be straightforward. The party leaders in the Change bloc have to agree on a candidate for prime minister. They would also have to accept partnership with Arab parties, either in coalition or from outside. The rightwing opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman, is said to be the most resistant. Joint List officials said it was unclear whether partnership with Palestinians really crossed Lieberman’s red lines, or whether he was just holding out for a top cabinet position.
Even before a new government could be formed, Jabareen argued, the 67 opponents of Netanyahu in the new Knesset could use their clear majority to wrest control of legislative power. “That would start by changing the speaker of the Knesset,” he said, adding that the opposition could also take control of the committee that oversees the legislative agenda.
“That could be very crucially important … even before we reach conclusions on the issue of a coalition and a new government,” he said, adding that one of the priorities of the new Knesset should be to repeal laws passed by the outgoing majority that infringed the independence of Israel’s judiciary.
To allow an opposition coalition to oust Netanyahu and function as a minority government, Jabareen made clear it would also have to address deep-seated inequality in Israeli society.
“We have suffered from systemic discrimination for years, so if Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally,” he said. “We also ask for a political horizon. We would like to see the war stopped and the resumption of negotiation with the Palestinian leadership. We would like to see a start of a change.”
The Joint List leader said he was concerned over what Netanyahu might do to keep his grip on power. The prime minister has already made allegations, without evidence, that the Arab parties had used Qatari funds illegally in the election campaign, which Jabareen dismissed as a bid to “delegitimise the political power of the Arab community” and “a dangerous incitement”.
One of Jabareen’s concerns was that the Israeli leader would join Donald Trump in the resumption of war on Iran as a pretext for putting off political transition.
“This is really a critical period,” he said. “There should be a clear voice from the opposition to go against any attempt by him to initiate war … or dictate a new military agenda in Israel.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: How the president’s party has fared in every US midterm election since 1946
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
How the president’s party has fared in every US midterm election since 1946
Only twice in the past 20 midterms has the president’s party gained House seats. Polls suggest 2026 won’t be the third.
On Tuesday, Americans head to the polls for the United States midterm elections, held halfway through a president’s four-year term. Voters will choose all 435 members of the US House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats. The voting will decide which party controls Congress for the next two years.
Although the president’s name won’t appear on the ballot, the vote is widely seen as a verdict on the presidency, and the president’s party almost always pays the price.
In 18 of the 20 midterms held from 1946 to 2022, voters took House seats away from the party in control of the White House. The average loss was 26 seats. Only Bill Clinton’s Democrats in 1998 and George W Bush’s Republicans in 2002 bucked the trend.
Political scientists call this the “presidential penalty”, or the “midterm penalty”. The president’s party tends to lose seats simply because it holds power as voters use the midterms to put a check on the White House.
The House: 18 losses in 20 midterms
The chart below shows how many House seats the president’s party has won or lost in each midterm since 1946 from Harry S Truman to Joe Biden.
Democratic presidents have suffered the biggest midterm defeats since 1946. On average, their party has lost about 29 House seats in a midterm, compared with about 23 under Republican presidents.
The largest loss came in 2010, two years after Barack Obama became the first African American elected president, when Democrats lost 64 House seats and Republicans took control of the chamber. The Democrats under Truman lost 56 seats in 1946, and under Clinton, they lost 54 in 1994, each time losing control of the House.
The worst Republican defeats came under Dwight D Eisenhower when the party lost 50 seats in 1958 and Gerald Ford when it lost 48 in 1974. Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018 cost Republicans 42 seats and control of the House.
Big losses often cost the president’s party its majority. In seven of the 20 midterms since 1946 (1946, 1954, 1994, 2006, 2010, 2018 and 2022), the House changed hands.
The Senate: 13 losses in 20 midterms
The president’s party has lost Senate seats in 13 of the 20 midterms since 1946 but lost control of the chamber in only six: 1946, 1954, 1986, 1994, 2006 and 2014.
Unlike the House of Representatives, where every seat is up for election every two years, only about a third of the Senate’s 100 seats are contested in each cycle because senators serve six-year terms and their elections are staggered. That means which states are voting can matter as much as the national mood.
Eisenhower’s Republicans suffered the biggest Senate loss in the period, giving up 13 seats in 1958. Truman’s Democrats lost 12 in 1946, and Obama’s Democrats lost nine in 2014, handing control of the chamber to Republicans.
At times, the two chambers have moved in opposite directions. In 1982, Ronald Reagan’s Republicans lost 26 House seats but gained one in the Senate. In 2018, Trump’s Republicans lost the House but added a Senate seat, and in 2022, Biden’s Democrats lost the House while gaining one seat in the Senate.
These split results show that a backlash against the president does not land evenly across Congress. A party can hold its ground on a favourable Senate map while losing competitive House districts.
What does it mean to lose the House or Senate?
Losing seats and losing control are not the same thing. Lyndon Johnson’s Democrats lost 47 House seats in 1966 but kept their majority. Twenty years later, Reagan’s Republicans lost only four House seats but lost the Senate after an eight-seat setback.
Control of the chambers decides who sets the agenda and passes legislation. A bill must pass both chambers before it reaches the president for his approval or veto, so an opposition majority in either can block the president’s plans.
A House majority can also mean a party is able to launch investigations and impeach a president while a Senate majority can reject the president’s nominees, including federal judges, who serve for life.
This year, Democrats need to gain three seats to win the House and four to win the Senate. A 50-50 split in the Senate would leave Republicans in control because Vice President JD Vance may cast tie-breaking votes.

https://taz.de/Die-Wahrheit/!6226342/.title: Die Wahrheit: „Friedhofsrave mit anschließender Blutorgie“
https://taz.de/Die-Wahrheit/!6226342/.author: Ernst Jordan
https://taz.de/Die-Wahrheit/!6226342/.text:
Die Wahrheit: „Friedhofsrave mit anschließender Blutorgie“
Wie kommerzialisiert man Reisen in den Tod? Das Wahrheit-Interview mit den Dark-Event-Forschern Unkel und Ark bringt Licht ins jenseitige Dunkel.
Wer zu den Koryphäen der deutschen Dark-Event-Forschung will, muss vorbei an künstlichen Spinnweben und echten Plastikskeletten. Finanziert durch einen großen Reiseveranstalter arbeiten im Hannoveraner Untergrund Professor Dieter Unkel und Doktor Detlef Ark an Erforschung und Entwicklung von Dark Events. Die Wahrheit hat exklusiv mit dem Duo gesprochen.
Prof. Unkel: Hereinspaziert – wenn Sie sich trauen! Ist Ihnen schon das flackernde Licht aufgefallen? Habe ich selbst programmiert.
taz: Ja, schön unangenehm.
Prof. Unkel: Darf ich Ihnen etwas zu trinken anbieten? Kaffee, Cola, Schwarztee, Blutorangensaft?
taz: Nein, danke. Lassen Sie uns lieber anfangen. Herr Prof. Unkel, Herr Dr. Ark, was sind Dark Events?
Dr. Ark: Kurz gesagt sind das alle organisierten Formen des Umgangs mit Sterben und Leid wie der Dia de los Muertos in Mexiko oder das alljährliche Hotdog-Wettessen in Rotenburg. Also eigentlich alles, was Mordsspaß macht.
taz: Und wie erforschen Sie diese Dark Events?
Dr. Ark: Zunächst mal identifizieren wir sie. Wo immer auch der Tod oder seine Ausschlachtung festlich ausgeschlachtet wird, untersuchen wir das als kulturelles und soziales Phänomen.
Prof. Unkel: Und kategorisieren es nach der Präsenz des Todes oder dem Ausmaß vorhandener Tabubrüche und zugelassener Öffentlichkeit. Aktuell konzentrieren wir uns vor allem auf den Aspekt der Kommerzialisierung.
taz: Das bedeutet?
Dr. Ark: Mit den Methoden der Tourismusforschung bringen wir dahingehend Licht ins Dunkel, wie man bestehende Dark Events besser erschließen oder neue Dark Events zum Leben erwecken kann.
taz: Wie sieht das in der Praxis aus?
Prof. Unkel: Den Dia de los Muertos zum Beispiel, bei dem sehr bunt, laut und fröhlich der Verstorbenen gedacht wird, gibt es schon seit altmexikanischen Zeiten. Aufbauend auf unsere Arbeit wird auf der Anreise nun eine Bloody Mary serviert und im Deluxe Paket gibt es eine Friedhofsparty.
Dr. Ark: Zudem gibt es nur dank unserer Potenzialanalysen jetzt Glamping auf Black-Metal-Festivals oder Kaffeefahrten zum Volkstrauertag. Bestehende Dark Events sind weiterhin das Tod- und Buttergeschäft.
taz: Anders als das Event Building, das Sie im Vorgespräch erwähnt haben?
Prof. Unkel: Das ist New Business, sozusagen. Unser Team sucht zum Beispiel weltweit alte Herrenhäuser. Dann schauen wir: Wen könnte man hier auf mysteriöse Weise umbringen? In welchem Zimmer sieht der Schimmelbefall schon besonders gruselig aus? Daraus stricken wir dann passende Horrorgeschichten und setzen ein Vermarktungskonzept auf.
taz: Also eher kleine, dunkle Eventualitäten?
Dr. Ark: I wo! Unsere letzten wirklich großen Coups waren Wal Timmy – da haben wir empfohlen, ihn besonders langsam sterben zu lassen, um in der Nebensaison die Hotels an der Küste zu füllen – und natürlich die Sonnenfinsternis! Wie kriegt man eine riesige Scheibe unauffällig in die Erdumlaufbahn, welche Forscher müssen bestochen werden? Da saßen wir seit 1999 dran.
taz: Was ist Ihr liebstes Dark Event?
Prof. Unkel: Die Beerdigung meiner Schwiegermutter. Nein, Spaß. Die Begehung der Via Dolorosa. Die haben die Franziskaner vor Jahrhunderten schon bewusst touristisch ausgebaut, sie ist praktisch ein Ur-Dark-Event.
Dr. Ark: So ein richtig schöner Friedhofsrave mit anschließender Blutorgie ist für mich immer noch ein feiner Spaß.
taz: Arbeiten Sie auch an weniger friedlichen Dark Events?
Prof. Unkel: Um Satans Willen. Das überlassen wir schön der Abteilung für Forschung und Entwicklung der Illuminaten. Die sitzen übrigens unter dem „Tor zur Hölle“, diesem Dauerbrenner in Turkmenistan. Hat die Regierung extra für Touris gesperrt. Ein bisschen zu sehr on Brand, aber das haben Sie nicht von mir.
taz: Juckt es Sie nicht in den Fingern, doch mal am bösen Rad zu drehen?
Dr. Ark: Doch, schon. Kriege müssen es ja nicht gleich sein, aber an einer Menschenjagd wie bei den „Sarajevo-Safaris“ sind wir schon dran.
Prof. Unkel: Und suchen Teilnehmer.
taz: Prof. Unkel, Dr. Ark, wir danken Ihnen für das Gespräch.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Clea Skopeliti, Federica Rossi and Wouter Massink
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Marine biologist Alice Barbarioli waits with her camera trained on the horizon. A few minutes earlier, the hydrophone beneath the Pelagos research vessel detected codas – the sequence of clicks sperm whales use to communicate.
The sperm whale reveals its head and dorsal fin as those onboard the vessel in the Pelagos sanctuary, a conservation area established to protect marine mammals in the north-western Mediterranean, rush to take photos and note the rhythm of its breathing. After a few minutes, the animal arches its back, and begins to head back into the depths of the sea. They wait to catch a glimpse of its tail.
Barbarioli, the lead researcher of the citizen-science expedition, organised by the Tethys Research Institute, immediately notices an injury on its left fluke: “Given how precise the mark is, it’s probably the result of a [vessel] collision,” she says.
Collisions have long been recognised as a leading human-induced cause of death for the Mediterranean’s endangered sperm and fin whales. Now, a Guardian investigation using data from the maritime intelligence firm Veson Nautical, has found that large passenger and cargo vessels operated by four companies – the Grimaldi Group, Corsica Ferries, Baleària and Moby Lines – have frequently travelled through a protected habitat that includes the Pelagos sanctuary at 15 knots (17mph) or above – speeds that almost always kill cetaceans in cases of a collision. Strikes are unlikely to kill when a vessel is travelling below 10 knots.
Slowing vessels is the most effective mitigation strategy when rerouteing isn’t possible, according to conservation NGO Oceancare.
The sea between Valencia and Genoa, which includes the Pelagos sanctuary, is a key cetacean habitat, home to about two-thirds of the Mediterranean’s fin whales and more than a fifth of its sperm whales. In July 2023, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) created the north-western Mediterranean Sea particularly sensitive sea area (PSSA). In a voluntary speed recommendation (VSR), it advised vessels weighing 300 gross tonnes and above to sail at 10 to 13 knots in the area to reduce the risk of fatal collisions.
Despite the IMO’s recommendation, the Guardian, using additional data from Global Fishing Watch, found that ships with IMO identification numbers spent more than 280,000 hours travelling at 15 knots and above through the PSSA in 2025. The data also showed that ships spent more than 6,000 hours travelling above 25 knots. It builds on previous analysis that found the voluntary recommendations were largely ineffective.
In 2022 and 2025, ferries owned by the Grimaldi Group, including Cruise Roma – at more than 250 metres, the world’s longest cruise ferry – dominated the top-20 list of vessels spending the most time at 15 knots or above in the habitat.
Speeding remained concentrated among a few operators in the PSSA in 2025, with just seven vessels – four Baleària fast ferries and three Grimaldi cruise ferries – responsible for 70% of the hours spent above 25 knot. Seven Grimaldi cruise ferries amounted to about 8% of all hours recorded for all vessels at 15 knots or above in 2025.
The Guardian spoke to six captains – five current and one former – who have sailed in the PSSA since its designation. The seafarers, still or previously at the helm of ships owned by Grimaldi Group and Moby Lines, say their companies have not introduced measures to encourage slow steaming after the IMO’s VSR.
“As long as it’s only a recommendation, nobody will reduce speed,” says one Grimaldi captain. “It would mean overhauling the whole commercial system. The ferries in the area travel at 25 [knots], especially the ones carrying tourists. They have schedules to follow.”
Grimaldi and Moby Lines were contacted for comment but did not respond.
Thomas Folegot, the CEO of maritime tech company Quiet-Oceans, says that while slow-moving container vessels could stand to slightly cut speeds in the PSSA, it was far more challenging for ferries: “For their business, it’s a killer. [Passengers] will fly to Corsica.”
Quiet-Oceans and Oceancare’s analysis found that 80% of the journeys by merchant ships in the PSSA in 2023 were at speeds above 10 knots.
Simone Panigada, president of the Tethys Research Institute and chair of a scientific committee dedicated to the conservation of cetaceans, says it is time to “move, progressively, from voluntary to mandatory” rules on reducing collision risk.
“A binding framework would create more level conditions for all operators, encouraging compliance among shipping companies and ensuring the adoption of these measures doesn’t rest solely on individual corporate decisions,” he says.
The International Whaling Commission (IWC) told the Guardian it has recorded six incidents since July 2023 in the PSSA: five near-miss events and one collision. It believes most strikes go unrecorded.
While the annual time spent travelling through the PSSA above the key threshold of 15 knots remained high in 2025, it represented an 11% reduction compared with 2022. The time above 25 knots also fell by about a third between 2022 and 2025.
These overall declines are probably caused by factors including altered shipping routes, says Olivia Watkins, associate director at Veson Nautical, who adds: “The PSSA recommendation is unlikely to be a significant cause of the year-on-year decline in the data results.”
Wei-Jun Mun, director of public policy at the World Shipping Council, says the industry is committed to PSSA’s protective measures, while noting slower navigation involved “commercial trade-offs and operational concerns”, including having to add ships to a service for schedule reliability.
A spokesperson for Corsica Ferries says the company supports Mediterranean marine megafauna research and ship-strike mitigation through measures including continuous monitoring, crew training and the development of whale alert tools. Researchers from programmes including conservation project Life Conceptu Maris monitor wildlife using its ships, it says.
The company says it instructs captains to navigate with particular caution through the PSSA, and to lower speeds to 10 to 13 knots, “while seeking to avoid possible negative impacts of reduced speeds”, including on manoeuvrability. It says its captains have reported a reduced capacity to avoid cetaceans that appear suddenly when navigating at reduced speeds.
A spokesperson for Baleària says it is “committed to the conservation of marine biodiversity” and actively working to mitigate the risk of collisions, including through crew training and the use of real-time monitoring systems to allow captains to adjust speed and course where necessary. Baleària says none of its fast ferries had recorded a collision with cetaceans.
Baleària adds that it participates in marine conservation programmes, including the Life Conceptu Maris and Life Intemares initiatives.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: RFK Jr is wrong about the Arab world
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
RFK Jr is wrong about the Arab world
The challenges in knowledge production in Arab societies cannot be blamed on some kind of innate incompetence or a single political group.
At a recent campaign rally in Michigan, United States Secretary of Health Robert F Kennedy Jr made remarks that have caused much controversy. He alleged that Muslim Arabs do not produce science and literature and do not win major awards because of the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood.
This was not merely a hasty and inaccurate assessment of the knowledge production of a specific demographic. It was a statement that reflects racist attitudes and misconceptions about an entire region and an entire religion. It is also easily refutable.
There are plenty of Muslim Arab scientists, thinkers and writers who have made major contributions over the past century. Some of them are Nobel laureates, such as novelist Naguib Mahfouz, diplomat Mohamed ElBaradei, journalist Tawakkol Karman, and scientists Ahmed Zewail, Moungi Bawendi and Omar Yaghi. Many others have not received a Western award but have nevertheless contributed significantly to their own countries and the world.
The Arab world does face challenges in knowledge production, but this does not prove an inherent deficit in its people or the overwhelming influence of a certain political group. Rather, it reflects historical and institutional conditions that impact this process.
A changing history of knowledge
Human civilisations have not been equal in knowledge production across history. Some have witnessed scientific and intellectual flourishing while others have faced decline and turmoil.
Downturns have not occurred because populations had suddenly lost their mental capacities but because the political, economic, cultural and institutional conditions that allow knowledge to thrive change over time.
In the case of the Islamic civilisation, its centres – from Baghdad and Damascus to Cairo and Cordoba – experienced a vast scientific and intellectual movement involving scholars, translators, philosophers, physicians and mathematicians from diverse religious and linguistic backgrounds for centuries. This prosperity was not isolated from the world; it was built on the translation, critique, development and interaction with Greek, Syriac, Indian and other bodies of knowledge.
Meanwhile, parts of Europe experienced significant backwardness in scientific education and development. However, Europe was not a monolith, nor were those centuries a homogeneous dark period. It also witnessed varying intellectual, institutional and scientific developments across different regions and timeframes.
European conditions then gradually changed: Educational institutions and universities evolved, networks for book and knowledge circulation expanded, and European scientific traditions interacted with scientific knowledge transferred from the Islamic world and elsewhere.
No one can claim, based on these historical disparities, that Europeans are inherently incapable of producing science or that their religion or ethnic origins preclude them from innovation. Serious historical interpretation focuses on institutions, economics, education, political patronage and knowledge networks rather than claims that certain populations lack innate abilities.
The exact same principle must apply to Arabs and Muslims today. Since Europe was able to change the conditions of knowledge production, it is illogical to assume that the contemporary reality of Arab and Islamic societies reflects fixed limits in their scientific or literary capacities.
Science is universal and not the racial or religious property of anyone. Decline is not a genetic destiny for any people, and prosperity is not an eternal privilege.
Today’s challenges
Rejecting RFK Jr’s generalisations does not mean denying the challenges facing scientific research in many Arab countries. There are serious questions concerning research and development funding, university independence, education quality, freedom of research and expression, institutional stability, the ability to attract and retain scientists, and links between knowledge and the economy and production. However, these questions are the beginning of scientific analysis, not the end.
A society that does not provide a researcher with a suitable laboratory, does not grant universities sufficient independence, does not allocate the necessary resources for research and does not ensure the continuity of scientific institutions cannot expect results comparable to those of a society that invests sustainably in these areas.
Furthermore, wars, conflicts, displacement, brain drain and weak scientific cooperation can disrupt the accumulation of knowledge, even when a society possesses qualified human capital. The capacity for thought and innovation is one thing, and the ability to translate them into sustainable scientific production is another. Between the two lies an entire system of socioeconomic conditions, institutions and policies.
Blaming the challenges contemporary Arab societies face on a single political group – in RFK Jr’s case, the Muslim Brotherhood – and presenting this as a comprehensive explanation for the state of science and literature among hundreds of millions of people falls short of serious historical or social analysis.
Scientific production is influenced by a set of intersecting variables: state structure, economic policies, education quality, research expenditures, academic freedom, stability, international relations and the capacity for knowledge circulation.
Certain political movements or intellectual trends might impact educational policies or the cultural climate in specific contexts. However, proving this impact requires evidence and comparative analysis, which RFK Jr would likely fail to produce, should he be asked to do so.
Moving from critiquing an institution or political movement to issuing a judgement on Arabs or Muslims in general is a form of racism, hatred and Islamophobia because it transitions from analysis to generalisation, and from seeking causes to reproducing stereotypes.
A meaningful response to RFK Jr
The problem with RFK Jr’s statement is not merely its factual inaccuracy regarding awards and their superficiality, but the logic upon which it is based: transforming historical disparities in knowledge production into broad judgements about peoples.
His words hold symbolic, intellectual and political significance, reflecting a hostile Orientalist stance towards Arab-Islamic and even Eastern heritage.
A serious response to these statements requires more than merely recalling past glories or listing Arab and Muslim scientists and thinkers; it requires turning the discussion into a project for the future.
In the Arab world, we need more independent universities capable of research, equipped laboratories, sustainable funding, an environment that permits critique and experimentation, policies that retain scientific talent and institutions that link education with the economy and innovation.
We also need a documented, critical rereading of the history of sciences in Islamic civilisation – one that studies both achievements and failures and examines how scientific concepts emerged, evolved and were transferred between civilisations.
A civilisation does not regain its stature by repeating that its ancestors were great but by building the institutions that allow new generations to produce new knowledge.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://taz.de/Bud-Spencer-Museum-in-Ber.title: Bud Spencer Museum in Berlin: Knall! Wumms! Klatsch!
https://taz.de/Bud-Spencer-Museum-in-Ber.author: Andreas Hergeth
https://taz.de/Bud-Spencer-Museum-in-Ber.text:
Bud Spencer Museum in Berlin: Knall! Wumms! Klatsch!
Wehmütig darf man eine Runde in dem Berliner Museum machen, das den Filmstar Bud Spencer würdigt. Das Museum schließt, es rechnet sich nicht mehr.
Was passt besser als ein alter Röhrenfernseher? Auf einem kleinen Grundig-Gerät flimmern Ausschnitte aus alten Filmen mit Bud Spencer und Terence Hill über den Bildschirm. Man darf die Tasten der acht Programmplätze drücken und immer gibt es eine andere Filmsequenz. Meist in miserabler Qualität, als ob hier alte VHS-Kassetten abgespielt würden, wie früher.
Willkommen im Bud Spencer Museum Berlin! Das residiert seit Juni 2021 an einer der besten Adressen im Osten Berlins: Unter den Linden, also da, wo sich die Touristenscharen tummeln. Dennoch geht dem Museum die Puste aus, die Betreiber sehen wirtschaftlich keine tragfähige Perspektive für eine Fortführung, es muss schließen.
An diesen Mittwoch Ende Oktober ist erstaunlich viel los. Die Nachricht, dass das Museum zumachen muss, hat die Medien auf den Plan gerufen. „Dadurch haben wir eine enorme Aufmerksamkeit bekommen“, sagt Michael Maass, CEO der Betreibergesellschaft, „was natürlich auch dem Museum hilft.“
Die Besonderheit
Das Bud Spencer Museum Berlin befindet sich seit 2021 in der bei Touristen aus aller Welt beliebten Flaniermeile Unter den Linden, unweit des Brandenburger Tors. Der Standortvorteil reicht aber nicht zum Überleben.
Das Zielpublikum
Ältere Fans, die mit den Filmen von Bud Spencer und Terence Hill aufgewachsen sind, und deren infiltrierter Nachwuchs. Einzeltickets kosten 15, für Kinder 8 Euro. Es gibt Familientickets für 35 Euro für jeweils zwei Erwachsene mit eigenen Kindern oder Enkeln.
Hindernisse auf dem Weg
Die Zeit: das Museum schließt zum 23. Dezember. Der Countdown läuft.
Schon auf dem Gehsteig grüßt eine Bud-Spencer-Figur in Lebensgröße. Drinnen massenhaft Kostüme und Requisiten (ein Auto, ein Motorrad) aus Filmen, original und nachgebaut, dazu Drehbücher, Filmplakate, Fotos und persönliche Erinnerungsstücke. Überall Bildschirme mit Ausschnitten aus Spielfilmen des Duos und von TV-Auftritten, auch aus deutschen Shows.
Bud Spencer war ein Hüne. Das zeigt die riesige Ritterrüstung aus der Filmkomödie „Hector, der Ritter ohne Furcht und Tadel“ von 1975 gleich hinterm Eingang, vis-à-vis gibt es Ausschnitte zu sehen. An einer Wand hängen Filmschwerter und das entsprechende Filmplakat.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
An jeder Ecke tönt es: Die Filme des schlagkräftigen Duos waren bekannt für ihre teils nervige, teils kultige Filmmusik und die Geräuscheffekte – Knall! Wumms! Klatsch! –, die ihre Schaukämpfe begleiteten. Ach, die ausufernden Schlägereien, bester Slapstick, ihr großes Markenzeichen. Immer die beiden gegen eine Übermacht von Ganoven. Zur Kunstform gereift sind diese Prügelorgien mit ihrem Wechsel zur Westernkomödie (auch so ein ausgestorbenes Genre) „Die rechte und die linke Hand des Teufels“.
Comichafte Übertreibung
Trotz comichafter Übertreibung in Filmen wie „Vier Fäuste für ein Halleluja“ von 1971 – der Film trug in der DDR den Titel „Der Kleine und der müde Joe“ –, wirkte das Ganze immer auch authentisch, was daran lag, dass alles aufwendig choreografiert und geprobt wurde. Für eine Minute Film wurden oft mehrere Tage benötigt – über QR-Code kann man sich das in der Ausstellung erzählen lassen. Auch, dass Spencer und Hill echte Athleten waren. Deshalb mussten sie nicht gedoubelt werden.
Und dann sind da die frühen Aufnahmen: Spencer, als Carlo Pedersoli in Neapel geboren, steigt in einem Film von 1949 aus dem Wasser, er hat eine Frau vor dem Ertrinken gerettet … die schwarz-weiße Sequenz zeigt einen jungen und athletischen Mann, der sich als Schwimmer auch bei den Olympischen Spielen einen Namen gemacht hatte, bevor er ins Schauspielfach wechselte. Spencer hatte eigentlich keine Ambitionen, Schauspieler zu werden – willigte aber ein, um Schulden tilgen zu können. Der Schuldschein ist hier im Original zu sehen.
Noch ohne seinen typischen Bart
In Badehose und noch ohne seinen typischen Bart ist der große, schlanke Mann kaum zu erkennen. Na ja, an seinen Gesichtszügen aber schon. „Das ist er!“, ruft eine Frau ihren beiden Freundinnen zu und lacht: „Der war in jungen Jahren richtig gut gebaut und hot. Und später ein richtig süßer Opa.“
In Vitrinen gibt es Zigaretten zu sehen, die Spencer in „Plattfuß am Nil“ rauchte, aber auch Filmpreise, dazu Schallplatten mit der Filmmusik, Comics und Merchandising wie Federmappen für Kinder. Und im Museumsshop gibt es Bohnen in Dosen, Gewürzmischungen, Bier, Tassen, Kalender, DVDs – immer mit dem Konterfei der beiden.
Ach, es gibt viel zu lernen über zwei Schauspieler, die Jahrzehnte lang in einem Atemzug genannt wurden. Über ihre Anfänge, die gemeinsame Karriere und was danach kam, als sich ihre Wege trennten. Beide drehten TV-Serien, meist erfolgreich. Lustig bis traurig die Werbespots, mit denen sich Spencer über Wasser hielt, als seine große Zeit vorbei war: Für eine Bank prügelt er sich durch die Stadt.
Hill lebt ja noch. Rührend die Szenen, die in der Ausstellung zu sehen sind, wie er auf dem alljährlichen Bud-Spencer-Festival in Cinecittà, der Filmstadt im Rom, mit vielen Künstler:innen an seinen Buddy von einst erinnert.
Da liegt Wehmut in der Luft. Und auch, weil das Bud Spencer Museum am 23. Dezember in diesem Jahr zum letzten Mal öffnen wird.
Aber ihre Filme laufen ja immer noch in Spartenkanälen im Fernsehen, und auch in Mediatheken. Und wer will, kann sich im digitalen Zeitalter ohnehin bis in alle Ewigkeit von Bud Spencer und Terence Hill belustigen lassen. Darauf ein Halleluja.

With an explainer here:
“We now seem to be entering the era of post-PiF takeover where Will Osula is officially considered crucial to our su̶r̶v̶i̶v̶a̶l̶ lower-mid-table hopes,” writes Chris Paraskevas. “That’s either a reflection of a sudden discovery of hidden talent in the lad *or* a desperate reflection of a disastrous transfer window under the David Hopkinson + MJ + Ross Wilson + PiF Rockstar Supergroup.
In any case I’m not too fussed about today’s defeat (any time Mary Waltz manages a comment, Everton beat us...it’s the Curse of the Waltz! and we can’t do anything to stop it)
At least our second-choice striker is fit and scoring (Dan Burn).”
I can’t get my head around how dull this Newcastle side is. There’s no player in the starting Xi I’m excited to see, who defenders will fear; it’s hard not to think Toure and Steur are performing miserably in training, otherwise why would they be getting so few minutes?
Jaissle tells Sky Elanga is improving physically and deserves to start today; he wants him and Osula to show their potential, and both have the speed to cause any defence problems. His team have to be ruthless in both boxes, using every opportunity to score, and if they do it should be a great result.
Moyes says Rohl is adaptable, likewise O’Brien, so moving them isn’t a problem. Every team knows every other team, so he’s not expecting any surprises.
Everton, meanwhile, wo’t be afraid to go long, with Barry contesting aerial balls and Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall and George looking to get in and around him. George, in particular, will be tasked with running at the newcastle defenders, while Dewsbury-Hall will look to prompt around the box, nudging balls in behind or shooting, and box-crash with make third-man runs. Otherwise, Barry will look to run off the centre-backs, who don’t have the pace to keep up, and look for one-touch close-range finishes.
So where is the game? Newcastle will, I think, look to defend pretty deep, partly because the lack pace at the back, but also because they want to create space to counter. Elanga is brilliant on the break, but Barnes can also run, likewise Willock, whose eye for a goal is excellent. I also think they’ll want Gonzalez to control the play, with Joelinton often ahead of the ball looking to win high turnovers – they’ll reckon he has the physicality to get after Garner – and also send their full-backs forward so the wingers can attack the box, with crosses and cut-backs directed at Osula.
“Your note about not expecting a goalfest doesn’t tell the half of it,” sighs Matt Burtz. “One thing I’ve learned from watching Everton over the last 15 years is that I can usually expect defensive solidity while at the same time experiencing a distinct lack of attacking prowess. The last time Everton scored 50+ goals in the league was 2018-19. Somehow they managed 62 league goals in 2016-17, which was, not coincidentally, Romelu Lukaku’s last season at Goodison, when he banged in 25. The last time they scored 70? You have to go back to their last league title, 1986-87, when they played 42 games. (They were also relegated in 1929-30 despite scoring 80 because they contrived to allow 92, so maybe free flowing football isn’t always the answer).”
Yup, since the Dogs of War days in the mid-90s, Everton have been dogged rather than inspired. It’s a long time since they were the School of Science, or as fun to watch as the 1984-85 champions.
Email! “Greetings from California,” begins Mary Waltz. “The day before America hopefully begins to end the Trump delusion half of our citizens have been under. And then there is my beloved Everton, who can’t seem to catch a break. I get suspending Grealish but we simply do not have the depth to replace his ability to generate attacking chances.”
I’m looking forward to seeing how Tyrique George gets on in his stead, though, and it also means there’s more chance Dibling gets a go. And ultimately, those lads are the future of Everton, not Grealish – though the may well miss him in the short term.
David Moyes, meanwhile, also makes two changes. Jarrad Branthwaite returns after two games missed following concussion protocol, so too Harrison Armstrong. I doubt the away following will be chuffed that it’s Hayden Hackney and Tyler Dibling dropping out, but to accommodate the changes, Merlin Rohl moves forward from right-back to right-wing, with Jake O’Brien moving out of the middle to fill his old spot.
The big news for Newcastle is that Anthony Elanga returns to the starting XI, for the first time since diddling his hamstring at Millwall nearly two months ago. He and Joelinton are the two changes to the side which lost at Everton last midweek, Jacob Ramsey and Jacob Murphy dropping to the bench. But equally important is the news that Osula is fit enough to start.
Teams!
Newcastle United (4-2-3-1-): Hornicek; Dedic, Schar, Burn, Hall; Joelinton, Gonzalez; Elanga, Willock, Barnes; Osula. Subs: Pope, Botman, Bamba, Wissa, Thiaw, Steur, Toure, Murphy, Ramsey.
Everton (4-2-3-1): Pickford; O’Brien, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko; Garner, Armstrong, Dewsbury-Hall; Rohl, Barry, George. Subs: Travers, Maitland-Niles, Dibling, Keane, Johnson, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Graham.
Referee: John Brooks (Melton Mowbray)
Preamble
Different people are motivated by different stimuli. Some of us need to feel secure to deliver our best work, struggling when put under pressure to perform, while others need provocation to get them going, indignance driving the desire to stop coasting in order to prove people wrong.
Chances are, Thierno Barry falls into the first category. He showed enough at Villarreal to persuade Everton to sign him but then struggled to settle into Premier League rhythm, subbed off 18 times in 21 league starts and beginning the other 17 games on the bench and returning a paltry eight goals. It was not an especially auspicious start.
As such, it was no surprise that Everton wanted to sign Folarin Balogun from Monaco – essentially, to go in front of Barry. But that move broke down on deadline day then Joshua Zirkzee, a desperate contingency, stayed at Manchester United – to what end is unclear – meaning, with Beto sold, Barry moved from second-choice to only choice.
Very quickly, crisis turned into fortune. Able to relax in the knowledge there were no options but him, so the chances of him being sub or subbed were minuscule, and no longer dealing with a newborn or playing with the shoulder problem that hampered his debut campaign, Barry looks a different player. He scored on the opening weekend of the season and most recently last Thursday, when Everton binned Newcastle from the League Cup – a contest which featured an affirming ruckus close to full-time. Having bagged seven in 11 appearances, he’s on a roll and will fancy himself to add to that tally this evening – though only bottom-placed Sunderland have managed fewer than his side’s eight league goals.
Newcastle, meantime, will hope to avoid a third Monday-night clattering of the season, already beaten 4-1 at Leeds and Coventry. There have been some good signs under Matthias Jaissle but also some absolute dross, the lack of physicality a particular issue and especially glaring given, until recently, that was a strong point.
Last weekend’s win at Palace, though, has earned a little respite and, with Will Osula given a start and scoring, they too have a centre-forward ready to go – or would have, had he not got injured, again. He’s unlikely to play tonight, exacerbating a pre-existing problem: only two clubs have created fewer than Newcastle’s 14 big chances and, with Jaissle so far unwilling to use the young attackers signed in the summer for anything other than late cameos, there’s no reason to expect things to change.
All of which is to say that this match, 12th v 14th, is unlikely to deliver a goalfest elevated by flowing football. But happily, different people are motivated by different stimuli, and it’s not possible to appreciate English football without enjoying aggression, intensity needle and incompetence – of which there will, without doubt, be plenty to enjoy.
Kick-off: 8pm GMT

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Trump focuses on Washington DC construction projects on eve of midterm election as Democrats climb in polls – live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Shrai Popat (now); Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
Trump focuses on Washington DC construction projects on eve of midterm election as Democrats climb in polls – live
President at reflecting pool in Washington DC to talk about various projects in final appearance before Americans head to polls to vote in crucial midterm election
Donald Trump talks about Reflecting Pool and his Washington DC construction projects on eve of midterms
Donald Trump has been speaking for nearly 20 minutes, and he’s yet to actually make any substantial reference to the midterm elections which will take place tomorrow – and will decide the makeup of Congress in his final two years in office.
Instead, the president is using the opportunity to talk about his construction and makeover projects throughout Washington DC, including on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
“It’s really a beautiful thing. It’s a work of art in many ways, but it was a work of art that never worked, but now it will work,” Trump said, while joking that the pool should be renamed after him.
Trump noted that he’d spent the last two weeks crisscossing the country, holding rallies on behalf of several embattled Republicans.
“America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote. I hope they’re ready to do the right thing,” he said, while downplaying the effects of the ongoing Iran war in a final plea to voters.
“I don’t know if you even call it a war because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. “Oil prices are plunging now. They’re plunging a record. Nobody’s ever seen a plunge like this, and they’ll be down. I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon.”
On the eve of the midterms, national average fuel prices have surged to $4.10 per gallon for gasoline – a $1.00 increase over last year – while diesel has climbed to $6.20 per gallon, nearly double its price a year ago.
Trump has now mentioned the upcoming elections, running through his greatest hits of talking points, and repeating several falsehoods in the process.
“These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up. There’s never been anything like what we’re seeing: jihadists and Muslim Brotherhood members,” he said, baselessly claiming (again) that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, is a member of the Islamist group.
Trump added that Democratic candidates are “all committed to the same radical agenda: open borders, raising your taxes by trillions of dollars, taking away your guns, transgender mutilation of your children, abolishing oil and natural gas, sending energy costs skyrocketing and opening the floodgates to millions of migrants from all over the world, hoping to get them to be able to vote”.

“It’s really a beautiful thing. It’s a work of art in many ways, but it was a work of art that never worked, but now it will work,” Trump said, while joking that the pool should be renamed after him.
As we bring you the latest polling and predictions ahead of Tuesday’s election, one notable shift is in Louisiana – where a Democrat hasn’t won a US Senate seat since 2008.
Now, Republican Julia Letlow, a Trump-backed congresswoman who beat the incumbent Bill Cassidy in her primary, will face Jamie Davis, a Democrat and third-generation farmer.
Sabato’s Crystal Ball has moved the Senate race in the Pelican state from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican” – a sign that the Davis might be diluting Letlow’s strength.
One of the country’s leading election forecasters, Crystal Ball also moved several of their “toss up” races to “leans Democratic”. This includes the key Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Texas and Ohio.
Meanwhile, the forecaster also moved the competitive Iowa Senate race from “toss up” to “leans Republican”. Here, Democrat Josh Turek is attempting to beat Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson to win the open seat in the Hawkeye state.
As I noted earlier, we’re due to hear from Donald Trump shortly, as he delivers a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington DC – just a day before voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
According to the press pool, the president is set to leave the White House shortly. We’ll bring you the latest as it gets started.
Vice-president JD Vance is rallying in Swanton, Ohio, ahead of tomorrow’s critical midterm elections.
Opening his remarks just now, he told a joke about his daughter wanting to donate two of her brother’s favorite toys to a Christmas toy drive.
“I realized, ladies and gentlemen, that I’ve got a little work to do, because a little girl who’s taking from her brothers … maybe she’s a Democrat.”
There was a mix of groans, boos and some laughs from the audience. Vance then merged into more bullish Republican territory, talking about his own humble beginnings and how great it is to be American.
A federal judge has dismissed criminal charges against two former FBI officials who were accused of lying about their involvement in the investigation into Hunter Biden, the son of former president Joe Biden.
Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said prosecutors failed to show probable cause that the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, had knowingly made false statements.
Faruqui also suggested prosecutors purposefully brought the charges at a sensitive time, just 10 days before the midterm elections.
The judge said during the hearing:
What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization. I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar.
The judge criticized federal prosecutors for rushing the prosecution and making “critical mistakes”. Faruqui said that some of the former officials’ statements were not actually false and others could be attributed to “honest mistakes of memory”.
On a Monday afternoon in late September, Donald Trump gathered Iowa Republicans in the Oval Office to make a big announcement: the firm Mesabi Metallics would invest $15bn to make the midwestern state the site of the largest steel mill in the country.
One month later, and just days before the midterm election, word has spread in the small town of Wever, population 142, that the mill will be built somewhere nearby. And that’s been about it – no shovels in the dirt, workers on a job site or machinery on the dirt roads leading down towards the Mississippi River.
Ask about the project in town, and the reaction isn’t enthusiasm, but skepticism.
“More jobs,” Missy Pollpeter, 52, said of the project’s potential as she dined at the Green Bay Bar and Grill, Wever’s only restaurant. “If they bring it here,” her husband, Mike Pollpeter, 60, said as he finished a burger.
On paper, a steel mill seems like a great development for a corner of Iowa that has a long history both of manufacturing and the disinvestment that has struck so much of the industrial midwest. According to the White House, the project would create 6,000 jobs during its construction and then 1,750 when it is complete, and generate $95bn in economic activity.
What people can’t get over is how the project was debuted, and who was announced it. The president made the plan public just over a month before tomorrow’s midterm elections, when Iowa will play a major role in determining if Democrats regain control of Congress amid Trump’s downbeat approval ratings. Wever itself lies in a congressional district that is viewed as the most competitive in the state.
And then there’s the fact that Trump has a history of making proclamations that don’t quite pan out.
Trump administration appeals California ballot case to supreme court
A day before the midterm elections, the justice department has asked the supreme court to force Califronia election officials to set aside 20,000 mail ballots, that the administration claims were submitted by noncitizens.
This is the government’s latest attempt to block the Golden state from processing the votes, after the justice department gave California officials just 48 hours to review the list and said it would sue the state if officials did not sequester ballots from those whose citizenship it could not confirm.
Last week, a federal judge declined to order California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people the Trump administration claimed were non-citizens, rebuffing a legally thin request from the justice department that appeared designed to cast doubt over the results of the midterms.
A reminder that there are more than 23 million registered voters in California and non-citizen voting is extremely rare.
As I noted earlier, the latest polling from the New York Times/Siena College shows Democrats leading in key Senate races ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. One of the major battlegrounds is the competition in Texas, where Democratic state representative James Talarico has a seven-point lead against Republican challenger Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden attorney general who has Donald Trump’s endorsement.
My colleague David Smith reports from Austin on Talarico’s meteoric rise, and how he stands a chance of winning a Senate seat that has eluded Democrats for almost 40 years.
In an interview with CNN, DebbieDingell, the Democratic congresswoman from Michigan, addressed the anger directed at Haley Stevens, her colleague, after the representative announced she would endorse Republican Mike Rogers in the state’s bitter US Senate race.
“I have been worried about her because I know it’s really hard to be in these kinds of circumstances. I talked to her multiple times last week,” Dingell said. “And I was shocked. I can’t lie about that.”
Various reports noted that just hours before Stevens made her announcement pulling her support for Abdul El-Sayed, she spoke to Dingell on the phone and assured her that she would still be backing the Democratic nominee in the upcoming election.
“I was very shocked at what she [Stevens] did, but the hate and the anger in this country right now is very scary and it’s coming from all sides,” Dingell added in the interview.
When asked specifically what was worrying Dingell about Stevens’ decision, the congresswoman said that it was clear “she has had some hurt feelings”.
Dingell added: “It’s very difficult to lose an election. There are many people that respect her. She was feeling torn. She has a very significant Jewish community that itself was torn on this issue. She’s had a lot of people saying many things to her.”
While Dingell said that she wouldn’t “speculate” about what changed for Stevens and why she ended up backing Rogers, she noted just how hard it has been to quiet the vocal frustration from within her party towards Stevens.
“I tried to get many of my colleagues to focus on tomorrow’s election because this is a distraction. It’s been a distraction for 10 days and focus on what the real issues are,” Dingell said. “But there are a lot of people that don’t understand what she did and are very, very angry and you’ve heard those words and seen those statements.”
She noted that the way the four-term congresswoman went out “has probably permanently hurt her” and her future within the Democratic party.
While Donald Trump will rally in Washington DC today, his vice-president, JD Vance, will be in Rome, New York, to stump for Republican House candidates in competitive races in the state.
This includes, Anthony Constantino, the sticker company exec and rapper trying to keep Elise Stefanik’s seat in Congress red, and Kailee Buller, who served as a senior official at the agriculture department and is trying to flip her district.
Vance will be joined by the president’s son, Donald Trump Jr, on the trail today, and the pair will head to Ohio later for another set of campaign events.
Chris Pappas is stopping himself from getting too excited ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election.
“I take nothing for granted,” said the four-term US representative and Democratic nominee for New Hampshire’s open Senate seat. “This is a very purple, competitive state. Elections are never in the bag here.”
The race to replace the retiring Democratic senator Jeanne Shaheen has emerged as a source of 11th hour anxiety for the party.
In their attempt to gain four seats and reclaim control of the Senate, Democrats can’t afford to lose one they already hold. But September polling showing Pappas virtually tied with his Republican opponent, former senator John Sununu, rattled party strategists and raised the prospect that New Hampshire could become an unexpected battleground.
The warning signs were striking in a state Donald Trump has lost in each of his three presidential bids.
While Pappas has regained a narrow advantage in most polls, and the Cook Political Report moved the race in early October from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat”, his closing message has focused heavily on tying Sununu to an unpopular president.
Trump’s approval rating sits at just 32% in the state, according to a recent University of New Hampshire poll, giving Democrats hope that voter frustration with the administration will ultimately benefit Pappas’s run.
“Sununu has spent most of the last year on team Trump, and now that we’re getting within range of the election, he’s recognizing how unpopular the president is,” Pappas said as he traveled the state in the final days on the trail, often joined by party heavyweights, like Arizona senator Mark Kelly and former vice-president Kamala Harris.
Sununu, however, has spent much of the campaign arguing that independence, not loyalty, defines his political record.
The former senator has emphasized his criticism of Trump’s trade war with Canada, which has affected several industries in the state, and in a recent campaign advertisement, he even claimed to have “never met” the president.
The former senator’s anti-Trump bona fides do have some roots. In 2024, he voiced his support or Nikki Haley in an op-ed during Republican primary campaign, and also branded Trump a “loser”.
El-Sayed campaign reports record-breaking fundraising day after Stevens pulls endorsement
Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign announced that it received $2.4m in donations on Sunday, the day that Haley Stevens announced she would now pull her support from the Democratic nominee and back Republican Mike Rogers.
El-Sayed’s campaign that the amount is a single-day fundraising record for his Senate bid. His staff also noted that more than 26,000 people contributed for the first time on Sunday.
In the four hours after Stevens defected on Sunday, Politico reported that El-Sayed’s campaign raised $1.2m, which was already its second-highest day of donations.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘We cannot move forward’: Savannah Guthrie shares new post seeking information in mother’s disappearance
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Savannah Guthrie has issued a new plea for help on the whereabouts of her 84-year-old mother, who authorities believe was abducted in February.
On Sunday, the Today show co-host shared a photo of an old drawing made by her daughter featuring an umbrella and the words: “I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
She also posted a photo of her mother, Nancy Guthrie, with the caption: “Found this old drawing from my daughter today. It says so much about how I feel. The world goes on, things appear ‘normal’ – as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids – but it’s not and it never will be.”
Guthrie added: “We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward. We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.
“Thank you to all those who have been kind and shown the best of humanity. Join us in praying without ceasing,” she continued.
Guthrie’s latest post on Instagram comes just three months after an earlier plea in which she urged “someone to come forward” with details on the whereabouts of her mother, who was reported missing from her home in Tucson, Arizona on 1 February.
“Someone knows something. Someone suspects something. Someone recognizes the writing in the ransom demand notes. Someone has noticed something different, strange, troubling or just unusual – perhaps with someone they deeply love,” Guthrie wrote in August, adding that her family’s offer of a $1m reward is still available.
Alongside drops of blood discovered on Guthrie’s porch, investigators also recovered DNA from a glove found 2 miles (3.21km) from her home.
The glove appeared to resemble one worn by a suspect seen in surveillance footage from the night of her disappearance. However, the glove was later discredited after it was discovered to have belonged to a restaurant worker, not the abductor involved in the case.
Savannah Guthrie has used her platform as a host of a national television show to raise awareness about her mother’s disappearance, frequently sharing updates and appeals for information.
The FBI, which has put up an additional $100,000 reward for conclusive information about Nancy Guthrie, is looking for a man approximately 5ft 9in to 5ft 10in tall with an average build.
In July, authorities released two ransom notes sent to a Tucson television station following Nancy Guthrie’s disappearance.
A ransom note sent on 2 February claimed Nancy Guthrie was unharmed but frightened. It also demanded $4m in cryptocurrency in exchange for her release. However, a second note, received four days later, claimed she had died soon after her abduction.
Authorities have yet to establish whether she is alive and no arrests have been made so far.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/eg.title: Egypt Requests Return of Mummified Remains Removed from View by Glasgow Museum
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/eg.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/eg.text:
Egypt has sought the return of ancient mummified remains from the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in Glasgow, which controversially removed those remains from its galleries last month.
The mummified head, which belonged to a man named Nekht who lived sometime between 1985 BCE and 1797 BCE, was taken off view in October. In its place then appeared a new sign: “We have removed human remains from this display as a mark of respect.”
Speaking to the Times of London at the time, a museum representative clarified that the curators felt that they did not have the consent required to continue to exhibiting the head. “In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals,” the representative said.
Though such a removal is in keeping with industry guidelines regarding mummified remains, the removal raised ire in Scotland, where one prominent politician accused the museum of “woke madness.”
Glasgow Life, the charity that manages the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, confirmed this week to ScottishNews.com that the institution had officially received a request for the repatriation of Nekht’s remains. “We have received a request in the last few days to repatriate the Nekht remains to Egypt,” a museum spokesperson said. “Glasgow has a well-established process for repatriation requests. We will follow this process to guide our next steps.”
According to ScottishNews.com, other remains in the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum’s collection have also been taken off view. Unless those remains also face repatriation requests, they will remain in a storage facility for now.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/na.title: London National Gallery Head Says Just Stop Oil Protests Targeting Artworks Were a ‘Sad Thing’: ‘The Pictures Are Not Guilty’
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/na.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/na.text:
Between 2022 and 2024, the National Gallery in London was the site of three of the most public-facing protests by Just Stop Oil, the environmental activist group that controversially splashed liquids across two van Gogh paintings and hammered at the display case of a Velázquez (without causing any lasting to the paintings themselves). The protests earned a mixture of admiration and condemnation, and the actions’ detractors now even include the National Gallery’s director, who addressed Just Stop Oil in a new Telegraph profile.
Gabriele Finaldi, the director of the National Gallery since 2015, called the Just Stop Oil protests “a sad thing” and seemed to suggest that the group’s activism was misguided.
“Those attacks were very shocking,” Finaldi said. “The pictures are not guilty. The activists were seeking front-page coverage for their cause. They know that to attack a painting gets you front-page coverage across the world, while breaking the windows of an insurance company probably doesn’t.”
Moreover, he added, “People may have legitimate reasons to promote a particular cause. What I would say is: ‘Don’t come to the National Gallery to do it.’”
The National Gallery was hardly the only museum that suffered an environmentalist protest involving an artwork between 2022 and 2024. But it is, in many ways, the museum is where the mini-movement began.
In 2022, two Just Stop Oil activists threw what appeared to be tomato soup at Vincent van Gogh’s Sunflowers (1889), one of the National Gallery’s many masterpieces, then proceeded to glue themselves to the work. Their protest was said at the time to have caused roughly £10,000 in damage, primarily to the work’s frame, and the two activists subsequently received prison sentences. In 2025, the group formally ceased its protests after the UK adopted a new climate policy.
In the months afterward after the initial 2022 demonstration, other activist groups picked up the cause, staging similar protests at venues ranging from the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., to the Louvre in Paris.
Finaldi’s Telegraph profile also saw him wade into another controversial issue: the increasingly vexed relationship between the National Gallery and the Tate museum network. In years past, a formal agreement has seen that the National Gallery’s presentations do not run past the year 1900 and that the Tate museums exclusively handle modern and contemporary art. (Both collections are managed by the British state.)
But with the National Gallery now at work on a significant expansion that would include space for art made after 1900, Finaldi has expressed frustration about the agreement and has sought to upend it.
	Noting that the “20th century is already present in the National Gallery’s collection,” he told the Telegraph, “We and the Tate are both part of the great national collection, and this would lead to a slight increase in the overlap of our collections. But we tell the stories in different ways, and the 20th century is quite a big century.”

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: How rebuilding old mosques is bringing Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims together in Punjab
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Cheena Kapoor
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Many Muslims saw their places of worship destroyed or abandoned during the sectarian violence of India’s partition in 1947. Now villagers of many faiths are coming together to revive them

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.

The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.

He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.

“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”

Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.

“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”

Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh, donated family land to build a mosque in her village. ‘There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,’ she says

Gajju Khan, who hopes to live long enough to see the mosque in his village completed

During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.

But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.

About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.

Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.

Jaspal Sharma says donating some of his land to build a mosque was a neighbourly duty

The new mosque in Malerkotla, Punjab, welcomes worshippers for evening prayers

“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”

For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.

“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.

Sadna Qasai, one of the many mosques in Punjab that fell into ruin after partition

“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.

Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.

Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.

Sikh men in Punjab’s villages have been coming together to fund and help build or revive old mosques

“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

On 2 April 1964, two days after the coup that overthrew Brazil’s leftwing president João Goulart, US president Lyndon B Johnson was the first foreign head of state to recognise the change of government. ‘Please accept my warmest good wishes on your installation as President of the United States of Brazil’. he wrote to Pascoal Ranieri Mazzilli, speaker of the Chamber of Deputies. Under pressure from the Brazilian military, the Congress had handed Mazzilli the presidency. Fifteen days after the coup Mazzilli was replaced by Field Marshal Humberto Castelo Branco, who installed a military dictatorship at the Planalto Palace in Brasília. With Washington’s blessing, it would last until 1985.
João Goulart had come to power in 1961 with plans to implement agrarian reform and nationalise strategic enterprises in several sectors (oil, energy, mining and telecommunications) that required the expropriation of US companies. He also pursued an independent foreign policy, opening trade with Maoist China in late 1961 and re-establishing diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union (Brazil had severed ties in 1947). The final straw for the US came when Goulart refused to support US policy towards Cuba.
The success of the 1964 coup owed much to the CIA and US Agency for International Development (USAID). During Brazil’s 1962 legislative election, they financed opposition politicians and political organisations, paving the way for military intervention. US ambassador Lincoln Gordon and his military attaché Colonel Vernon A Walters (a personal friend of Branco’s), were also key, monitoring preparations for months before the coup.
All that is now in the past, and since the beginning of the 21st century Brazil has been an emerging power. Already Latin America’s economic leader, it could soon become the world’s biggest agricultural exporter, ahead of the US.
