https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/08oceania.title: The South Pacific's struggle for climate justice
https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/08oceania.author: Eric Wittersheim
https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/08oceania.text:
‘If we save the Pacific, we will save the world,’ UN secretary-general António Guterres said in Tonga in August 2024. His acknowledgement that the Pacific archipelagos are on the front line of the coming climate disaster gave his remarks to the Pacific Islands Forum Summit a prophetic cast. But they also implied that it was the powerful, and especially industrial, nations that would save them – with the Pacific islanders, once under the yoke of the French, British and American empires, still consigned to the role of victims.
But these islanders have long since stopped waiting for the international community to wake up. The Pacific region is pioneering new ways of thinking about and pursuing climate justice. Its small island states are among the world’s lowest emitters of greenhouse gases (around 0.03%). the main cause of global climate disruption, whose impacts include ever-rising sea levels and worsening environmental disasters. Yet these states suffer the most brutal consequences: increasingly violent and frequent cyclones, prolonged droughts, flash floods, disrupted seasonal cycles, soil salinisation, coastal erosion and the destruction of coral ecosystems. All these phenomena directly affect housing, harvests, access to water and economic resources.
This structural injustice feeds deep anger. How can it be acceptable that peoples whose way of life is still largely based on subsistence farming and modest patterns of consumption developed over centuries of adapting to the environment should be the first victims of an industrial system created far away? Why should the inhabitants of Samoa, Vanuatu, Fiji and Kiribati pay the price for prosperity they have never benefited from? These questions challenge the foundations of the international order and justice itself.

Travelling through southern Albania on horseback in 1809, Lord Byron was so captivated by its mountains scored by rushing streams, its fertile plains and the hospitality of its inhabitants that he would later celebrate its unspoiled natural beauty in his poem Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage: ‘fairest in her features wild / Where nothing polish’d dares pollute her path’. When he reached Tepelena, on the Vjosa, the local ruler Ali Pasha, who later openly resisted Ottoman authority, gave him a lavish welcome.
In July 2021 Donald Trump’s daughter Ivanka and her husband Jared Kushner, touring the same region on a yacht owned by a friend, British financier Nathaniel Rothschild, called at Sazan. With its strategic position between the Bay of Vlorë and Strait of Otranto (connecting the Adriatic and Ionian), this island became a forward post for the Venetian and later the Ottoman empire. Occupied by Italy and Germany during the second world war, it was a Soviet submarine base from the mid-1950s until 1961, when Albania’s dictator Enver Hoxha severed ties with Moscow.
Across the bay is the Vjosa-Narta protected area, including the Narta lagoon, a stretch of coastline and the mouth of the Vjosa, one of Europe’s last wild rivers. Lying on a major migration route between Africa and Europe, Vjosa-Narta’s lakes, sand dunes, pine forests and beaches attract some 250 species of birds, including pink flamingos and pelicans.
When the Trump-Kushners stopped to refuel in the Albanian port of Durrës, they were joined by Albania’s prime minister Edi Rama who told them of his hopes for tourism-led development in his country. Ivanka had spotted a great business opportunity: building luxury resorts with private beaches on Sazan and the mainland coast. https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/06russia.author: Hélène Richard
https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/06russia.text:
Vladimir and Nikolai had always been close, even as their careers took different directions. Nikolai stayed at home in Volgograd, where he runs a small business supplying spare parts to local industry. Vladimir went to work in Moscow as a consultant to major foreign companies.
Twenty years ago, I’d joined the cousins in their search for their grandmother’s village near Saratov. Out of a population of 3,000 in the 1980s, barely a dozen people remained on the former collective farm. Though vegetation was slowly reclaiming the village, it still had a mayor, who every morning swept the old Soviet ‘red corner’, a former assembly hall with a parquet floor and a stage where the locals once put on plays.
Every two weeks, a post van made its way up a dirt track to deliver the mail and basic supplies. On our trip, the cousins had reminisced about their Soviet childhood as though it were a lost country. As we drank and laughed, their bond seemed unbreakable.
This spring I heard they’d fallen out, though from phone conversations I couldn’t tell why. Perhaps seeing them in person would change that, I thought. So I flew to Moscow, despite the threat of Ukrainian missiles and drones.
The city didn’t look like the capital of a country brought to its knees by Western sanctions. There was a time when you would hurry through its streets, head down. Now you could linger on its newly widened pavements, admiring the art nouveau façades of buildings you had barely noticed before.
Between 2015 and 2023, the city authorities renovated 14,000 residential blocks and 380 historic buildings. Since 2022 the redeveloped banks of the Moskva have been part of a 15km pedestrian route that goes from the new Moscow City business district past the Kremlin to Sokolniki Park in the northeast.
The war comes closer

https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/05poland.title: Poland's support for Ukraine wears thin
https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/05poland.author: Philippe Descamps & Filip Meyer
https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/05poland.text:
‘I hope I don’t live to see Ukraine join the EU, and I hope to live a long life’
Poland’s support for Ukraine wears thin
The prospect of Ukraine’s likely EU accession is becoming less popular with Poles, as farmers and truckers face price collapses. And with disputes over historical memory, too, mistrust is deepening.
In late May, in open fields dotted with pines and black oak, the wheat was growing tall and the first red beans were beginning to sprout. But Jerzy Płachta, a farmer in Pińczów, about 80km north of Krakow in Świętokrzyskie voivodeship, was worried. He told us, ‘I hope I don’t live to see Ukraine join the EU, and I hope to live a long life.’ His wife Renata, who manages their grain and legume farm, steered the conversation: ‘We have nothing against Ukrainians – they are integrating well. In 2022 we volunteered to take in refugees and donated money to charities that buy drones. We support them, but their country is a threat to Polish agriculture.’
Since Poland joined the EU in 2004, the Płachta family has been selling produce to French supermarket chains that operate in Poland – Auchan, Casino, Carrefour and Leclerc, which also imports goods into France. Płachta told us about their struggle to get to this point: ‘French companies require IFS Food Certification, a safety and quality standard with requirements that we need to meet. And to get EU subsidies we need to document how often we till the soil, comply with specific seed types and planting schedules and so on. We have more and more things to record in logs that inspectors review onsite every year.’ Until recently, it was worth the effort. ‘But since the war in Ukraine, prices have halved,’ Płachta said. ‘With the influx of Ukrainian products, we’ve had to cut costs and reduce staff. We had ten employees in 2014 and now we only have two. A third of the farms in Świętokrzyskie are in financial difficulty. Many are giving up.’ On his way back to the village, he paused in front of the construction site where he and his wife were building a house for one of their children. The project was a testament to their success, but it was tinged with sadness – Płachta was disappointed that his son preferred city life in Krakow to the countryside.
Marcin Biesaga’s farm lay a few kilometres away. (…)

Reform UK’s annual party conference, held during the first week of September under the sprawling steel canopy of Birmingham’s National Exhibition Centre (NEC), was a battle cry for British nationalism. Over two long days, the party worked through its central ideological obsessions: the left-liberal plot to destroy democracy; the spectre of Western civilisational decline; above all, immigration as an existential threat to the British way of life.

At the centre of proceedings stood Reform party leader Nigel Farage. His image – grinning, in a brilliant aqua blue suit and Union Jack socks – beamed out from the posters, TV screens and stalls that lined the conference hall walls.
The months leading up to the conference had not been easy for Reform. The party’s popularity, which reached record highs following a strong set of local election results in May, had slumped as a series of financial scandals chipped away at its support: Farage and his colleagues have been accused of receiving potentially illegal donations from foreign donors and are now under police investigation.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Getting ‘woo-woo’ in the desert: Los Angeles artist launches pirate radio station
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Hannah Sage Kay
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
In May 2020, the Los Angeles-based artist Ian James received a package from Wuhan, China. It was a radio transmitter he had ordered months prior from the e-commerce site Alibaba. The seller—concerned about the scarcity of toilet paper and N95 masks in the US due to Covid-19—padded the crate not with bubble wrap and packing chips, but with masks and toilet rolls. After a long delay at customs, James tells The Art Newspaper, the package arrived “on a wing and a prayer”.
James had ordered the transmitter to use for a New Age pirate radio station in the desert called KHLZ. Beginning this past Saturday (24 October), every day at sunset the secret radio station starts its programming. KHLZ will broadcast overnight between 5pm and 9am—after the FCC monitors turn in for the evening. “It will be this ghost radio station broadcasting as though someone is asleep at the switch,” James says.
In his art practice, James often examines the adoption of spiritual technologies by corporate enterprises and capitalist value systems. His new radio station serves as something of a foil to corporate economies and federal regulatory systems. It operates off the grid as an unlicensed, itinerant broadcast featuring music and compilations from a diverse array of spiritually intoned, New Age musicians from the 1970s to the present. This programming is “good for people’s mental and emotional well-being”, James says.
The impetus for this project began nearly 15 years ago. Starting in 2012, James ran a New Age programme on KCHUNG—an artist-led radio station in Los Angeles. But in 2019, he decided to establish his own station, including it in his solo exhibition in Santa Monica.
Titled The Harmony of the Noosphere, the show drew on the writings of the New Age writer and artist Jose Argüelles, who popularised the concept of the Noosphere: the third sphere surrounding the Earth that serves as a site of human consciousness and mental activity, growing in complexity as planetary consciousness evolves. “Utopic in its goals, the Noosphere’s construction is aided by technological innovations, yet hampered and disrupted by the capitalist machinations that produce and pervert these possibilities,” reads the exhibition statement.
This precisely is the complex relationship that lies at the centre of much of James’s work. The exhibition featured wall works with stock photo-type advertisements for spiritual technologies and a live-streamed meditation session. And there were three pyramid-shaped sculptures housing a transmitter and two speakers, enabling James to broadcast New Age mixes.
While the 2020 exhibition served as the first iteration of James’s radio station, he had always planned to transfer it to a mobile facility and broadcast in perpetuity. Now, six years later, James has officially launched his station in a retrofitted caravan-turned-broadcasting studio near Joshua Tree.
The caravan came into the artist’s possession at a fortuitous and unexpected time. It was given to his partner, the painter Patricia Fernandez, just after the onset of the pandemic. James started renovating it as the federal government began increasing unemployment benefits and sending stimulus checks. “I was getting $1,000 a week or something that I was putting into this radio-station project,” James recalls. “It was stupid and crazy.”
After discovering rat droppings and mould in the caravan’s walls, James completely gutted the interior and decided to cover every surface in a faux-Calacatta marble laminate, which similarly ornaments the three pyramid sculptures inside. Inspired by a glacial cave he had visited in Iceland, James wanted to create a cool (but not cold) space, one that through material specificity—in this case, the simulacra of the oldest continually quarried marble in Italy that has been used in spiritual and governmental sites since antiquity—communicated across generations without need for explanation.
“I was interested in the fact that this marble had a simulacrum made by the Formica corporation,” says James, adding that he liked the idea of using “this repeating pattern that probably came from some small section of marble that is in another building somewhere”.
In addition to serving as a broadcasting studio, the caravan houses a growing archive of materials pertaining to the vast culture of New Age practices. It includes every issue of a Michigan-based newsletter called Pyramid Power. It also features a collection of typewritten and Xeroxed newsletters about extraterrestrial contact and interdimensional communication called White Star, given to James by the Ufologist and New Age musician JD Emmanuel—a featured guest on the artist’s old show on KCHUNG.
Alongside cassettes that James sourced from eBay—previously sold at massage parlours, spas and mediation centres—he includes the veritable all-stars of New Age music. These are people like Kat Epple (a close friend and collaborator of Robert Rauschenberg) and Iasos, a jazz student at Stanford University in the late 1960s who claims he was contacted by two interdimensional beings.
Iasos believed the music the aliens shared with him would “help humanity ascend to a higher plane of being”, James says. Only with the growing availability of synthesisers in the early 1970s was Iasos able to re-create the sounds that he had heard. He called it Paradise Music.
James had previously interviewed both Epple and Iasos at KCHUNG. “Iasos was always thinking about how the music can raise people's vibrations,” James says, “and help humanity become more peaceful and empathetic towards each other.”
KHLZ is meant to be “a benevolent thing that people can listen to and participate in”, James says. He imagines that, given its location near Joshua Tree—though it will also stream online and occasionally travel for pop-up events—the station will serve as a meditative soundtrack for people while they do yoga, cook dinner, or “eat mushrooms and run around. As you've probably seen, there’s a lot of ways to be ‘woo-woo’, so the radio station is open to those possibilities.”

https://apache.be/2026/10/21/waarom-comm.title: Waarom het commissievoorzitter Mortier zelf aan wetenschappelijke integriteit ontbreekt
https://apache.be/2026/10/21/waarom-comm.author: Wouter Arrazola de Oñate
https://apache.be/2026/10/21/waarom-comm.text:
De uitspraken waarmee professor Freddy Mortier aan de UGent het racistische gedachtegoed van pseudowetenschapper Nathan Cofnas verdedigde, vormen een langgerekte keten van uiterst problematische ideeën en flagrante redeneerfouten. Dat de voorzitter van de commissie wetenschappelijke integriteit het bestaan van witte suprematie aan de universiteit op deze manier duldt, toont hoe vervreemd hij is van de kernwaarden van zijn eigen commissie.
“De stelling dat er erfelijke genetische verschillen bestaan tussen groepen huidskleur wat betreft intelligentie is perfect begrijpelijk. En ze is zinvol. Dat die uitspraak vals is, is nooit aangetoond.”
Dit waren de woorden van professor Freddy Mortier tijdens een proclamatieceremonie aan de Universiteit Gent. Hij is ethicus en voorzitter van de commissie wetenschappelijke integriteit. Het is een korte uitspraak, maar één die wel heel wat aparte schakels in de redeneerketen bevat.
Elke schakel moet sterk genoeg zijn om voldoende wetenschappelijk integer te zijn. Voorwaarden voor die integriteit zijn onder meer: eerlijkheid (zonder misleiding), zorgvuldigheid (methodologisch verantwoord), transparantie (ook over de beperkingen van de beschikbare evidentie), onafhankelijkheid (ook van persoonlijke belangen) / verantwoordelijkheid (ook voor de manier waarop onderzoeksresultaten worden verspreid en gebruikt). Let’s see.
Onbestaande categorieën
Laten we beginnen met het woord huidskleur. “Huidskleur” is een heel vage omschrijving, eigenlijk véél te vaag om wetenschappelijk te zijn. Want welke huidskleuren zouden we dan allemaal erkennen? Waar is die lijst? Daarop bestaat al geen antwoord. Zijn de “huidskleuren” keurig afgebakend en zijn ze makkelijk, éénduidig en reproduceerbaar te bepalen bij iemand? Neen, dat zijn ze zeker niet. Worden ze vooral bepaald door genen en DNA? Neen, zeker niet. (Zie hierover ook het recente stuk van een groep genetici in De Standaard).
Er is geen enkele combinatie van genen die zou coderen voor iets dat men “ras” is gaan noemen
Wat met “ras”? Wel, dat concept bestaat biologisch simpelweg niet. Er is geen enkele combinatie van genen die zou coderen voor iets dat men “ras” is gaan noemen. Daar toch genetische verschillen aan toewijzen is dus met zekerheid onmogelijk.
De volgende schakel in de redenering: intelligentie. Wat is dat eigenlijk? Het is iets dat sowieso verschilt van plaats tot plaats en in de tijd. Het omvat in ieder geval veel meer dan enkel cognitieve prestaties. Het begrip wordt niet door iedere groep mensen of door iedere samenleving hetzelfde ingevuld. Opnieuw dus iets dat veel té multifactorieel is om wetenschappelijk hele scherpe en duidelijke conclusies mee te kunnen trekken. Of om groepen mee te vergelijken.
IQ-testen zijn eigenlijk niet zo'n goede meetinstrumenten om het hele brede begrip te meten. Het is erg misleidend om de véél te grote sprong te maken van IQ-testen naar “intelligentie meten”. IQ-testen meten op hun best slechts een klein stukje van wat intelligentie allemaal inhoudt. En vooral om populaties met elkaar te vergelijken zijn ze geen goed instrument. Dat is geweten, wetenschap dus.
Van “national IQ-databases” die vaak gebruikt worden, is aangetoond dat deze methodologisch van erg lage kwaliteit zijn, en sterk beïnvloed door enkele mannen met sterke ideologische linken met witte-suprematie-netwerken. Ze worden veel gebruikt in publicaties in door leden van deze netwerken opgerichte journals, maar zijn té slecht om als wetenschap aanvaard te worden. Academici als professor Rebecca Sear hebben dit al meermaals aangekaart.
Beperkte rol van genen
Hoe meer we leren over genetica hoe meer we te weten komen welke relatief kleine rol genen eigenlijk spelen, en hoe sterk de invloed is van de omgeving waarin iemand leeft en de sociale determinanten. Voor wat betreft gezondheid wegen die laatste minstens dubbel zo zwaar door als genetica in het bepalen van iemands gezondheid.
Sociale en omgevingsfactoren (en andere) wegen veel zwaarder door dan een of andere combinatie van aminozuren in het DNA
Sommigen zitten met hun gedachtegoed nog dertig jaar terug in de tijd, toen men hoopte dat alles kon verklaard worden met de DNA-code. Dat is helemaal niet zo, en hoe meer we te weten komen, hoe duidelijker die onwaarheid wordt. Sociale en omgevingsfactoren (en andere) wegen veel zwaarder door dan een of andere combinatie van aminozuren in het DNA. Recent werd zelfs gevonden dat ons DNA blijkbaar wijzigt tijdens ons leven
Ruimschoots de zwakste schakel in de redeneringsketen staat in de laatste zin: “de valsheid ervan is nooit aangetoond”. Dit is een klassieke misleidingstactiek, bekend uit de debatkunde. Doen alsof dit de waarschijnlijkheid van de stelling vergroot of dat die stelling daardoor aan wetenschappelijkheid wint, is niet correct. Zo werkt wetenschap niet, zo werkt de wetenschappelijke integriteit niet. “Niet weerlegd” is iets heel anders dan “wetenschappelijk plausibel”. Dat iemand in die functie deze truc gebruikt, of zo’n grote redeneerfout maakt, daar moet men zich ernstige vragen bij stellen.
Oude machtsarchitectuur
De uitspraak van Freddy Mortier bevat dus een hele reeks aan aannames die allemaal op erg twijfelachtige basis rusten. Een voor een. Met veel onzekerheid. “Perfect begrijpelijk” en “zinvol” zijn daarentegen erg sterke kwaliteiten die men iets toeschrijft, zonder voldoende sterk bewijs of empirie. In tegendeel: de meerderheid van de aanwezige evidentie wijst in de andere richting. Dit kan men moeilijk “eerlijk, transparant of voorzichtig” noemen. Vraag dat internationaal maar eens na.
Welke onveiligheid houdt Mortier met zijn verdediging in stand voor de vele geviseerde studenten en werknemers van UGent?
Waar wel zekerheid over bestaat is dat tijdelijk onderzoeker Nathan Cofnas tot witte-suprematie-kringen behoort (zoals ook zijn baas professor Bouke de Vries en zijn collega Craig Willy). Dat hij in zijn blogs heel duidelijk aantoont wat zijn racistische bedoelingen zijn. Dat hij zijn eigen achtergrond superieur vindt. Dat hij gerichte aanvallen uitvoert op zwarte mensen, en niet op diens witte collega’s. Met dodelijke gevolgen.
De aanwezigheid van dit onjuist superioriteitsdenken aan de universiteit zo sterk verdedigen voldoet niet aan de integriteitsvoorwaarde “verantwoordelijkheid”. Met academische vrijheid heeft zoveel foutief redeneren ook helemaal niets meer te maken. Het zijn net zulke waanideeën die leiden tot de rechtvaardiging van genocides. Bewust gefabriceerde nepwetenschap om de overkoepelende machtsstructuur van witte suprematie — met haar verwoestende impact — te bestendigen. Ethisch kan men dit niet noemen.
Reproductie en genetica behoren eveneens tot het expertisedomein van public health. Veelzeggend is dat juist degenen die hierover het luidst spreken, over geen enkele expertise ter zake beschikken. Professor Mortier niet uitgezonderd.
Waarom vindt hij het dan toch zo belangrijk om meermaals zijn machtspositie te gebruiken om in de verdediging te schieten? Welke oude machtsarchitectuur wil hij daarmee verdedigen en behouden? Welke onveiligheid houdt hij daarmee in stand voor de vele geviseerde studenten en werknemers van UGent?
Universiteit Gent, als de verantwoordelijke “wetenschappelijke integriteit” zelf niet wetenschappelijk integer is, hoe kan je dan nog je internationale geloofwaardigheid behouden?

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/m.title: Mayor Mamdani: Trash Containerization Protects Sanitation Workers
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/m.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/m.text:
Mayor Mamdani sold the new containerized garbage collection as a godsend for Sanitation worker safety. Photo: Michael Appleton/Mayoral Photography Office
The city’s effort to move trash from bags on the sidewalk into bins on the street will make Sanitation jobs less physically taxing and less exposed to reckless driving, Mayor Mamdani and a union leader said on Thursday.
DSNY is expanding its “Empire Bins” waste collection program, which relies on side-loading collection trucks to lift and empty curbside containers. The trucks help mitigate the risks of a job that is among the most dangerous in the country.
“If we continue down this path of using these black trash bags, what we will see are continuations of injuries to workers who are doing their best to make the best city in the world the cleanest city in the world,” Mamdani said at a press conference in Brooklyn Heights. “I think we owe it to them to use every strategy we have to make their job a little safer and a little easier.”
Hizzoner and Sanitation Department officials installed the first residential Empire Bin in Brooklyn on a quiet block of the tony enclave on Thursday, after testing out the new initiative outside schools in the area’s Community District 2 over the last year.
Sanitation workers are exposed to a plethora of dangers on the job, from sharp objects in bags to drivers crashing into them as they haul piles of them across the street. Refuse and recyclable material collectors rank fifth for highest fatal work injuries, according the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The new mechanized side-loading trucks mitigate a lot of these issues, according to the head of the union representing Sanmen.
“They’re not in the back of the trucks where it could be hazardous, getting hit by cars from operating a conventional truck… and these mechanical arms, it’s much easier on their backs and shoulders, and it’s also safer,” Teamsters Local 831 President Dennis Schock said at the mayor’s press conference. “You know what? This is something that should be done and should happen all over the city.”
Crashes and serious injuries dropped 15 percent and 52 percent respectively after DSNY deployed the bins uptown, Streetsblog previously reported.
Containerized waste collection is commonplace in cities across the globe, from Buenos Aires to Barcelona, but the City that Never Sleeps has long lagged behind its peers.
Former Mayor Eric Adams set out to change that with the containerization efforts in the name of his obsession to curb the city’s rat population, and Mamdani put more city funding behind it after taking office this year.
“It is time that New York City follows the best practices of leading cities across the world,” Mamdani said. “For too long, we have allowed an exceptionalism in our politics to justify mediocrity that really isn’t acceptable.”
DSNY’s Empire Bin program is mandatory for residential buildings with 31 or more units, but optional for those with 10-30 apartments. The latter can also opt for wheelie bins that go on the sidewalk, which are already required for all smaller housing stock with up to nine units. DSNY plans to allow smaller building to share Empire Bins in the future.
The bins have been one of the few bright spots of the otherwise car-focused Adams administration. They reduced the amount of stinky garbage on the sidewalk and also cleared up space on the foot paths. All these benefits came at the low low cost of repurposing a mere 5 percent of the city’s three million — largely free — parking spaces, or about 150,000 spots, DSNY has estimated.
The agency plans to roll out 700 bins at residences by the end of the fall across the Brooklyn district, which in addition to the Heights also includes Downtown Brooklyn, DUMBO, Fulton Ferry, Vinegar Hill, Boerum Hill, Fort Greene and Clinton Hill.
Mamdani committed to expanding the program citywide by the end of 2031, two years after the end of his first term.
Next up in 2027 are Bronx Community Districts 2 around Hunts Point and 5 in Fordham Heights, Queens Community District 2 in Sunnyside, Manhattan Community District 2 in Greenwich Village, Brooklyn Community District 8 in Crown Heights, and Staten Island Community District 1 on the North Shore.
Kevin Duggan joined Streetsblog in October, 2022, after covering transportation for amNY. Duggan has been reporting on New York since 2018, starting at Vince DiMiceli’s Brooklyn Paper, where he covered southern Brooklyn neighborhoods and, later, Brownstone Brooklyn. He is on Bluesky at @kevinduggan.bsky.social and his email address is kevin@streetsblog.org.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Pressure Mounts on Mamdani Administration To Address Growing Number of Small Schools
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Michael Elsen-Rooney, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. This is part two of a three-part series. Here’s the first story. And sign up for Chalkbeat New York’s free email newsletter to be the first to know when the next story is published.
As a parent leader for more than a decade, Johanna Bjorken has heard plenty of stories about New York City schools struggling with low enrollment.
But Chalkbeat’s investigation last month into the decline of Murry Bergtraum High School for Business Careers — the city’s smallest traditional high school with roughly 90 students — struck a nerve.
Bjorken’s son goes to school just two floors above Murry Bergtraum in a shared building in Lower Manhattan where the students play on joint sports teams. Yet the schools feel worlds apart. While Bjorken’s son takes Advanced Placement Calculus, students at Murry Bergtraum last year had only one math teacher and two math courses, Algebra I and II. Despite having a per-student budget nearly twice the city average, Murry Bergtraum’s limited academic offerings force some students to attend night school to graduate.
“I was shocked to hear that students, some of whom may very well play volleyball or soccer with my child, have to go to night school for basic graduation requirements, and moreover, that the school’s situation has been known for many years with no action,” Bjorken wrote in a September letter to city officials.
Like school districts across the country, New York City is struggling with a small schools crisis after years of enrollment declines. What makes the city’s situation unique, however, is how many of its small high schools share buildings with each other: 72 of the city’s high schools with fewer than 250 students are on shared campuses, a Chalkbeat analysis found.
Ten months into his tenure, pressure is mounting on New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels to address the increasing number of small schools, which cluster the most vulnerable students in schools with the fewest academic opportunities. School leaders and experts say that long term, the city will need to close and merge underenrolled schools — a process that can be slow and politically unpopular. But many principals feel they can’t afford to wait for that process to play out and feel a sense of urgency to ensure their current students have access to high-quality programs and advanced courses. Now, a growing chorus is urging Samuels to help small schools on shared campuses pool their resources.
“On shared campuses like ours the system accidentally pits us against each other — right when we need to share resources the most,” said Amy Piller, the principal of Urban Assembly Maker Academy, the school Bjorken’s son attends on the Murry Bergtraum campus.
Samuels indicated at a town hall last week that he’s not crafting a citywide plan and instead is asking five working groups to devise blueprints for underenrolled schools in their districts. None of those working groups includes high schools, but Samuels told parent leaders this week that the Education Department is looking at creating “campus working groups” for high schools. City officials have not shared a timeline for this work. An Education Department spokesperson did not respond to questions about how, or whether, the city is helping schools in the same building share resources.
In the meantime, some principals on shared campuses have pooled course offerings, while others have not — but are looking for guidance and support from the Education Department as they’ve seen their rosters shrink.
“They kind of leave principals up to their own devices,” said Mike Sill, the secretary of the United Federation of Teachers.
Inside the Push To Reimagine NYC’s Shared High Schools
About two decades ago, the Bloomberg administration made a big bet that small schools would better serve vulnerable students by providing them with more individual attention and ensuring they didn’t slip through the cracks. The city shuttered dozens of troubled large high schools and opened scores of small new ones in their buildings.
Small schools boosted graduation rates and college enrollment, but they couldn’t provide the same variety of extracurricular or academic options as larger schools.
As enrollment declined, some schools banded together in an attempt to provide students with more opportunities. At the Theodore Roosevelt campus in The Bronx, the principals of its six co-located schools decided a decade ago to open advanced courses like calculus and statistics to the entire campus since none of the schools had enough students to fill the courses on their own.
“It’s challenging with scheduling,” said Michael Barakat, the principal of Bronx High School for Law and Community Service. “But what’s the alternative? Kids don’t have calculus? That’s crazy.”
At the Lehman High School campus in The Bronx, the principals of six small high schools in a sprawling building agreed in 2016 to align their bell schedules so they could open courses to everyone on the campus.
“We sat down and figured it out,” recalled John Powers, the former principal of Lehman High School, who retired in 2023. “It was something we all felt compelled to do.”
Some education leaders said the city can be more ambitious in helping small schools pool resources than just sharing courses.
With nearly half the city’s high school buildings sitting “underutilized,” it’s worth trying to figure out how to use the empty space for new programs or academies to benefit all the students in their building, said Kristin Kearns Jordan, the former CEO of Urban Assembly, a nonprofit that helps run roughly two dozen small New York City public high schools.
The city recently built STEAM centers in Brooklyn and The Bronx where nearby high schools can send students to get hands-on experiences in math and science. Those centers offer a model of what the city could build on shared campuses.
“The possibilities are endless,” Kearns Jordan said.
Several of the schools on the Murry Bergtraum campus are already thinking about those possibilities. In a letter to families last month, Piller, the Maker Academy principal, said her school is a finalist for a grant to transform an unused locker room on the campus’s top floor into a shared academic space for all of the schools on the campus.
“As enrollment patterns change across New York City, large shared campuses like ours have an opportunity to rethink what sharing a building can mean,” she wrote. Chalkbeat’s story on Murry Bergtram “names a problem. I want us to be part of designing what comes next.”
Schedule Clashes and Fragmented Leadership Complicate Resource-Sharing on Campuses
Pooling resources, however, is not without complications.
Besides having schools with different bell schedules, they may also have different grading policies. Some, for example, might focus on classwork and prioritize essays and projects, while others assign more homework and exams. Principals have to figure out how to split the costs of teachers covering shared classrooms. Further complicating matters, on many campuses, including Murry Bergtraum, schools in the same building report to different superintendents, meaning there’s no single leader responsible for the whole building.
Some education leaders hope a new position Samuels created — a supervising official overseeing all 11 high school superintendents — will help streamline decision-making for shared campuses.
Shael Polakow-Suransky, the president of Bank Street College of Education and a former deputy chancellor under Bloomberg, said sharing courses can work for advanced classes and electives, but it’s harder for core academic subjects where different schools may have specific — and clashing — approaches to instruction, behavior, or grading.
“The key is how much does that shared instructional work impede on the autonomy of each school on the campus to do its model effectively?” he said.
Sharing resources often only benefits a portion of students, too, such as those who seek out advanced courses. That’s part of why it can feel more like a “Band-Aid” than a systemic solution to the small schools problem, said Vivian Orlen, the former superintendent of Manhattan high schools.
Barakat, the Bronx principal, agreed that merging schools is the “logical next step.” But for now, he said, “I would hope that there are principals all over the place who are taking advantage of the opportunity to work with colleagues.”
Sophie Hayssen and Kae Petrin contributed data analysis.
Michael Elsen-Rooney is a reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Michael at melsen-rooney@chalkbeat.org.

https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/10brazil.title: Brazil has not yet given up
https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/10brazil.text:
On Sunday 25 October, Brazilians will decide between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, in an election with consequences for the entire continent. After coming first in the first round of the presidential election on 4 October, the third son of the far-right former president has seen his lead shrink. On the eve of the vote, the two candidates were neck and neck in the polls.
On the streets, Lula’s supporters are mobilising to bring about a comeback for the incumbent president: students, labor unions, grassroots activists and artists are holding a growing number of rallies against Flávio Bolsonaro. In São Paulo, gig-economy delivery workers have even led their own versions of the motorbike caravans popularised by Jair Bolsonaro and taken up by his son as part of his signature campaign style. They support Lula while demanding that his administration provide the social protections for which they are still waiting.
Four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s defeat, ‘Bolsonarism’ still has powerful means to reclaim the presidency. Despite Bolsonaro’s conviction for an attempted coup d’état, the alliances that fuelled his initial rise have not been broken. The agribusiness sector, evangelical churches and sections of the security forces remain key pillars of support — structures that the change in government in 2022 failed to eliminate.
In a country where nearly 60% of the population relies exclusively on social media for news, the Brazilian far right is highly organised. Its opponents accuse US tech platforms — most notably Meta (Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp) — of using their algorithms to favour Bolsonaro’s camp. Following a petition from Lula’s campaign team, the Supreme Federal Court demanded explanations from the company, as well as from Elon Musk’s X.
In the US, Bolsonarism relies on the support of the Donald Trump administration. During the 18 October debate, Lula denounced Eduardo Bolsonaro’s overtures to the US, which contributed to Washington imposing sanctions on Brazil intended to put pressure on its judicial system. This demonstrates a curious interpretation of ‘sovereignty’, a concept that the Brazilian far-right claims to champion.
The issue of sovereignty also plays out within national borders. In Brazil, 1% of landowners hold nearly half of all agricultural land. The landless movement continues its struggle for agrarian reform — a process that remains incomplete, largely due to resistance from major landowners. The economic weight of these landowners translates into political influence, most notably within Congress. Beneath the rhetoric surrounding national independence lies a fundamental question: who gets to decide how land is used, how resources are exploited and how wealth is distributed? Regardless of who wins on Sunday, those who control these assets will retain significant means to defend their own interests.
There remains one final question about this election: will the US administration recognise the results on Sunday night, should Lula secure a narrow victory?

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: Líder supremo do Irã adverte EUA e ordena resposta imediata das Forças Armadas a qualquer ameaça inimiga
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
O líder supremo do Irã, aiatolá Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, ordenou às Forças Armadas do país que respondam de forma imediata e sem restrições geográficas a qualquer novo ataque militar promovido pelos Estados Unidos ou por Israel. A determinação foi transmitida durante reunião com a alta cúpula militar iraniana e divulgada neste sábado (31).
Na mensagem, o líder supremo instruiu os comandantes das Forças Armadas, entre eles o chefe do Estado-Maior, Ali Abdollahi, e o chefe do Exército, Amir Hatami, a atualizar o mapa de alvos do país.
“Se os inimigos retomarem os ataques militares ou terroristas, serão as Forças Armadas da República Islâmica e a nação iraniana que determinarão o tempo e as condições para encerrá-los”, declarou Khamenei, orientando o enquadramento de todos os bens materiais e imateriais das forças adversárias como potenciais alvos de retaliação.
Paralelamente às advertências militares, o ministro das Relações Exteriores do Irã, Abbas Araghchi, classificou a tentativa da Casa Branca de abrir canais de diálogo por meio de uma carta enviada pelo vice-presidente dos EUA, JD Vance, como um “passo positivo”.
Conforme informou a agência Tasnim, uma delegação iraniana foi enviada a Doha para negociar por meio de mediadores do Catar, embora a imprensa local ressalte que não há previsão de encontros diretos entre diplomatas iranianos e estadunidenses neste momento.
Em manifestação publicada pela rede Al Jazeera, o porta-voz do Exército iraniano, Mohammad Akraminia, afirmou que uma eventual nova investida sob pressão de Israel expandirá o conflito. “Se o presidente dos Estados Unidos embarcar mais uma vez em uma aventura regional, as chamas da guerra sem dúvida engolfarão uma área geográfica muito mais ampla”, disse.
O governo iraniano condiciona o avanço das tratativas à suspensão das restrições navais no Estreito de Ormuz.

https://mondediplo.com/2026/10/01zlonger.text:
←
			Previous article : « In search of a new geopolitics »
	
		
		→
			Next article : « The United States’ decline is also (…) »
	
		
Archive selection
In October’s Le Monde diplomatique, Renaud Lambert argues that contrary to received wisdom, Beijing is benefiting from US global hegemony. ‘It sees Washington’s bad behaviour as still preferable to an intensified Sino-American rivalry that would disrupt trade flows.’ For now, China is in a strange position: ‘Its development model allows it to aspire to the status of the world’s leading power, but is built on structures that currently prevent it from getting there.’ Quoted in a piece last year, the influential Hong Kong banker Charles Li said: ‘I don’t think China wanted to be number one … Because there’s a responsibility coming from being number one. And that itself is not terribly Chinese … We want it to be number two, number three.’
Back in 2021, the director of Le Monde diplomatique’s Brazilian edition Silvio Caccia Bava warned that Jair Bolsonaro’s defeat in the 2022 election may not be the end of Bolsonarism. And indeed, one of his sons, Flávio, has taken up his father’s mantle — and placed first in the initial round of the presidential election this month. As Christophe Ventura writes in this month’s edition, the US tipped the scales to favour this outcome.
Settler attacks escalate in the West Bank, Albania pushes back against corruption in the tourism industry, and the nations of the South Pacific shift the climate conversation from pleas for help to questions of human rights and state responsibility. https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120358.title: Kurz vor US-Kongresswahlen | Trump bekräftigt Drohung gegen Iran
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120358.text:
- Politik
- Kurz vor US-Kongresswahlen
Trump bekräftigt Drohung gegen Iran
Die USA und Israel könnten den Krieg gegen den Iran bald wieder aufnehmen. Teheran warnt Washington vor einem langen Konflikt
Dubuque. Kurz vor den US-Kongresswahlen hat Präsident Donald Trump seine Drohung bekräftigt, die Angriffe gegen den Iran wieder aufzunehmen. »Der einzige Grund, warum ich mit dem Iran noch nicht fertig bin, ist, dass ich nett sein will«, sagte Trump am Sonntag vor Anhängern bei einer Wahlkampfveranstaltung im Bundesstaat Iowa. Er wolle »all diese Leben retten«. »Aber irgendwann werden wir ihnen einen harten Schlag versetzen müssen.«
Am Samstag hatte Trump vor Reportern gesagt, die diplomatischen Bemühungen um eine Verhandlungslösung zur Beendigung des Iran-Kriegs liefen »gut«. Gleichzeitig gebe es aber noch ein bis zwei mögliche Angriffsziele, um die sich die USA »kümmern« müssten, darunter einen mutmaßlichen Atomkomplex südlich von Teheran.
Am Sonntag berichtete das Nachrichtenportal »Axios« dann unter Berufung auf israelische und US-Regierungsbeamte, dass Trump und Israels Regierungschef Benjamin Netanjahu in einem Telefonat über mögliche neue Angriffe auf den Iran beraten hätten.
Die USA und Israel hatten den Iran-Krieg Ende Februar mit Angriffen auf Ziele im Iran begonnen. Teheran reagierte mit Angriffen auf US-Ziele in der Region und auf mehrere Golfstaaten.
Nach Trumps Drohungen warnte die iranische Armee vor einem länger andauernden bewaffneten Konflikt. »Ein möglicher zukünftiger Krieg könnte länger dauern als der vergangene Konflikt«, sagte Armeesprecher Mohammed Akraminia nach Angaben des Staatsfernsehens am Sonntag. Der US-Präsident würde nicht in der Lage sein, »den Zeitpunkt oder die Bedingungen seines Endes zu diktieren«, fügte der Armeesprecher hinzu.
Opposition warnt vor neuem Krieg
In Israel warnte Oppositionspolitiker Jair Golan eindringlich vor einem neuen Krieg mit Iran unter der Führung von Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanjahu gewarnt. Netanjahu fehle das Vertrauen der Öffentlichkeit, um eine solche militärische Auseinandersetzung zu führen, schrieb der Vorsitzende der linksliberalen Demokraten auf der Plattform X und forderte die rasche Bildung einer alternativen Regierung.
Die Wahrscheinlichkeit einer weiteren Konfrontation mit dem Iran steige, schrieb Golan weiter. Israel befinde sich inzwischen in einer Situation wiederkehrender militärischer Konfrontationen mit dem Iran. Israels Sicherheit dürfe nicht zum »Werkzeug in Netanjahus Kampf um sein politisches Überleben« werden. Agenturen/nd

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Zero passing yards, one win. Did the Bucs just reinvent the NFL in all the wrong ways?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
I don’t think I’m being cheeky when I say that passing is the most exciting part of football. A solid hit is nice, and a big run can thrill you, but this is a quarterback-centric game. When a QB is bad, teams usually lose and fans get bored. So, Sunday’s performance by Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers has me positively gobsmacked. I wouldn’t say their 16-0 win over the Atlanta Falcons was thrill-a-minute, but it certainly was historic. By completing a grand total of zero passes out of a paltry three attempts, Baker Mayfield led the Bucs to the first game with no passing offense since the Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 16-12 on 29 September 1974. If you are miraculously old enough to remember the NFL before the advent of the forward pass in 1906, first off, congratulations on being over 120 years of age. Please email me your full diet and exercise regimen. You’re probably on your feet (if standing is still something physically possible), cheering a bit of hard-nosed, classic football. The rest of us young whippersnappers still grinding through our first century are holding our noses.
Of course, Mayfield – a former No 1 overall pick – can throw. As recently as 2024 he threw for 41 touchdowns and 4,500 passing yards in a season. But Sunday’s game was played in pouring rain that led to farcical moments like this, and Tampa clearly decided that the ground game was the only way to go. That Tampa Bay could score at all, let alone 16 points, is a credit to Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell running as if their lives depended on it. Irving finished the day with 170 rushing yards and one touchdown, while Gainwell had 140. Combined, they rushed 52 times for 324 yards – the most ever in a single game for the Bucs. They more than made up for Mayfield’s borderline irrelevance in the pocket. Mayfield made himself useful blocking for his runners, but otherwise, I probably could have started at QB for the Buccaneers and the game would have been the same, other than the high likelihood of me suffering at least one gruesome injury.
“If I’m not going to throw the ball, I have to get active somehow,” Mayfield said after the game. He certainly was more valuable for his team than Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr, who had a game that would be front-page terrible if not for the historic passing futility on the other side. Penix went 8-24 with four interceptions. The field was wet and as slippery as a greased-up ferret with a sugar rush. But even a wet playing surface wasn’t enough to stop Tampa’s run game, or kicker Chase McLaughlin’s three field goals. Having said that, McLaughlin didn’t even need to make one – Atlanta were just that bad. Next week, the Falcons face the Bengals in Spain. If Atlanta play like this in Madrid, they’ll be the worst American export to Europe since David Hasselhoff’s first album.
MVP of the week
Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. We’ll start with the positives: Burrow threw five touchdowns, ran for another, racked up 462 passing yards and led his team back from 13 points down to a 43-36 overtime win on Sunday. On the downside, he threw three interceptions and all this came against the Titans. But Burrow gets MVP this week for a refusal to do anything dull. And the Bengals are off to their best start since the 2021 season, when they made the Super Bowl.
 
Video of the week
The Chiefs-Broncos game was absorbing until the final moments. The Chiefs, down 28-24, looked set to pull of a late victory when they have a first and goal on the Denver four-yard line with 35 seconds left. But stout Broncos defending and a sloppy penalty from the Chiefs when they thought they had scored the winning touchdown meant they had to score on the final play of the game. When Patrick Mahomes is under center in this type of situation, a Chiefs win is automatic. Not this time, though.
Stat of the week
259. That’s the number of career touchdown passes across the regular season and playoffs by Josh Allen for the Bills after his pair during his team’s victory over the Ravens on Sunday. In reaching that milestone, he broke the record set by Buffalo legend Jim Kelly. The victory moved the Bills to 6-1 and they now have the best record in the AFC. Sadly, the game was also marked by a thumb injury to the Ravens’ Lamar Jackson, which may end his season, a sad turn of events for one of the most thrilling players in the league.
Elsewhere around the league
The Vikings are undefeated no more. The Lions pulled out a thriller to end Minnesota’s hopes of a perfect season. Jared Goff found Jameson Williams for a score with 4:35 left in the game to squeak home 19-15. This was Detroit’s third straight victory, but they were also bit by losing linebacker Jack Campbell to a neck injury. Campbell had to be carted off the field on a backboard early in the fourth quarter, which put an undeniable damper on the post-victory celebrations. Instead of reveling in his late-game heroics, Goff was somber and reflective when speaking about Campbell. “That was definitely scary. He’s a husband and a father.”
There’s more heartbreak on display at AT&T Stadium this year than a Kazuo Ishiguro novel. The Dallas Cowboys looked to be in the driver’s seat against Arizona as the fourth quarter began. They led 24-10 and their defense was looking well-prepared to lock down a win. Except, folks, they weren’t. Arizona exploded for 20 points in the fourth, as Gardner Minshew took over from an underperforming Jacoby Brissett. Minshew marched the Cardinals down the field in 63 seconds late in the fourth to tie the game at 30-30. A simple Chad Ryland extra point would have been enough to win the game, but the PAT flew wide left. This was Ryland’s first extra-point miss in the last 58 tries. To overtime, they went. Ryland was able to rescue his no-good, very bad day by hitting a 42-yard field goal to finally clinch the comeback. The Cowboys are 3-5, and a brutal 1-3 at home as we near the halfway mark of the season. Lucky for Dallas that they play in a division where only one team is above .500.
Are the Rams back? Or are the Chargers just awful? Time will tell, but in the Battle of Los Angeles, it was the Rams who took care of business, 24-9. The game was close until a pivotal second-half period in which the Rams scored two touchdowns. The Chargers are 0-7. They’re the only team in the NFL who haven’t scored 100 points or more combined this season – 99 points for, versus 175 against. All this with alleged offensive mastermind Mike McDaniel at OC.
The Jacksonville Jaguars remain the most pleasant surprise in the NFL, destroying Indianapolis at home, 42-7. The Jags are top of the AFC South, above three teams with sub-.300 winning percentages. Trevor Lawrence was superb for Jacksonville, sporting a 153.3 RTG, 210 yards on 10/14 passing, and three touchdowns. The Jags’ defense forced three turnovers – two interceptions and a fumble – and only surrendered one pity touchdown in the third quarter. Jacksonville are at the top of a terrible division. Is there any reason to think they won’t stay there?
As someone who has dated both a woman from Cleveland and a woman from Pittsburgh (not at the same time), I can attest that Steelers/Browns is one of the most heated rivalries there is, primarily because Pittsburgh and Cleveland are cities with chips the size of dinner plates on their shoulders. Personally, I prefer the food in Pittsburgh (specifically the giant hot dog they sold at Pirates games that had pierogies on top), and so I was pulling for the Steelers on Sunday. They did not let me down. This was the 23rd-straight home win for the Steelers over the Browns. Pittsburgh sacked Deshaun Watson eight times. Eerily, the last time I did this column, Deshaun was sacked … eight times by the Jets in Week 5. Maybe next time I’m writing this, I’ll give the Browns a heads-up.
The Raiders pulled off another of the day’s improbable comebacks, scoring 24 points in the second half to beat the New York Jets 38-33. Las Vegas broke a four-game losing streak and are 4-4 on the year. Kirk Cousins threw for 247 yards on 19/26 passing and three touchdown passes, plus a TD run in the third quarter that he punctuated with a peculiar Arrested Development-style chicken dance that he called his “wellness celebration.” He said, “We do a lot of tissue work here. At my age, it’s especially helpful. ... So I said someday if I run a touchdown in, I’m going to give a shoutout to all the staff that works so hard to help us feel good and be one of the healthier teams in the league.” Cousins almost forgot to do this peculiar celly, but Brock Bowers reminded him. Perhaps the first and last time anyone will ever say “Hit them with the wellness celebration!” on an NFL field. Or at least I hope so.

https://taz.de/Faschisierung-und-digital.title: Faschisierung und digitale Boheme: Das nächste richtig große Ding
https://taz.de/Faschisierung-und-digital.author: Dirk Knipphals
https://taz.de/Faschisierung-und-digital.text:
Faschisierung und digitale Boheme : Das nächste richtig große Ding
Gibt es eine Verbindung zwischen digitaler Boheme und Faschisierung durch soziale Medien? Das neue Buch von Simon Strick kann in die Magengrube treffen.
D er Tod des Schriftstellers Joachim Lottmann kann einen dazu bringen, in die Archive des Internets hinabzusteigen. Die Plattform Wir höflichen Paparazzi, bei der Lottmann Protagonist war, Freund für die einen, Abgrenzungsfigur für die anderen; von diesem frühen sozialen Medium ausgehend die Zentrale Intelligenz Agentur – eine Zeit der Experimente, wie Textproduktion und Internet zusammen funktionieren können.
Eine Zeit auch, in der man bei dem Wort Mitte nicht an bröckelnde große Koalitionen dachte, sondern an Berlin-Mitte und dabei nicht nur an Flagship-Stores, sondern an Labor Berlin und Digitale Boheme. Lange her.
Wenn man das alles einmal wieder im Kopf hat, kann einen Simon Stricks Buch „Faschisierung. Fluchtlinien des Digitalen“ (Suhrkamp) übel in die Magengrube treffen. Was der Medienwissenschaftler beschreibt, ist eh schon brisant. Die Faschisierung kommt, so seine These, nicht von außen und auch nicht von extremistischen Rändern her in die Gesellschaft hinein, sondern sie steckt längst im Inneren, angetrieben durch die sozialen Medien nämlich, von ihren eskalierenden Tendenzen, die antagonistische Verkürzungen mit Resonanz belohnen.
Trump brauchte diese Tendenzen, so diese Lesart, nur in die politische Sphäre zu übertragen.
Mit Unschuld zelebriert
Wenn dieser Befund stimmt, muss man dann aber nicht auch noch einmal neu über die digitale Boheme nachdenken? Keineswegs in dem verkürzenden Sinn, dass sie als terrainsondierende Vorform des digitalen Sendens eine Art unfreiwilliger Vorläufer der gegenwärtigen autoritären Tendenzen wäre.
Aber womöglich analog zur avancierten Gentrifizierungsanalyse, nach der bohemistische Kader die Pioniere der Gentrifizierung darstellen, indem sie Wohnviertel attraktiv machen, bevor dann die kapitalstarken Investoren kommen. Nach dieser Lesart wäre die digitale Boheme also Pionier der Faschisierung gewesen? Also etwa: Erst suchte man in Berlin-Mitte das nächste große Ding, dann kamen Musk und Meta und räumten die Kapitalisierung ab.
Jedenfalls liest man einen Satz wie „die härteste Pointe und das rigorosere Urteil regierten“, mit dem Holm Friebe im Wikipedia-Eintrag zu den Höflichen Paparazzi zitiert wird, inzwischen mit ambivalenten Gefühlen. Stimmt wohl, dass das in den Nullerjahren mit viel Unschuld zelebriert wurde. Inzwischen machen Autokraten, Tech-Milliardäre und Trigger-Journalisten harte Pointen und rigorose Urteile aber erst zum richtig großen Ding.
Der Unterschied zur digitalen Boheme ist: In den Nullerjahren verband das Internet konkrete Personen miteinander, es gab analoge Rückkopplungen in Kneipen, ein realer sozialer Zusammenhang wurde gestiftet (dabei allerdings zwischen Teilnehmern und Zuschauern unterschieden). Das ist inzwischen sehr anders. Simon Strick beschreibt die sozialen Medien als sich längst verselbständigte Maschine, die die Öffentlichkeit formatiert und damit Realität setzt – und eigentlich weiß man das ja auch, man weiß nur nicht, wie man da wieder rauskommt.
Auf jeden Fall muss man wohl beizeiten Trauerarbeit über verlorene Unschuld leisten.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: These midterms could effectively end the Trump era – but neither side is yet ready for what comes next | Nesrine Malik
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nesrine Malik
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The stats and polling all suggest one thing: the Republicans are set for a hammering in the midterms. Donald Trump has the lowest approval rating of any US president going into a midterm election since Harry Truman. And it’s still dropping. The Democrats are projected to win by a margin of 11 percentage points, the largest swing by any party in almost 20 years. It is possible that the Democrats flip the Senate and secure a large majority in Congress. Those majorities would make a material difference, perhaps finally establishing oversight of the policies Trump has brought in during his second term: immigration enforcement, trade disputes, gutting the federal workforce, the Iran war, to say nothing of his own family’s corruption. The tide seems to be turning, and one question is on everyone’s mind: is the Trump era really ending?
“Nobody wants to jinx it,” wrote David Wallace-Wells of the New York Times, but: “All the signs we have suggest that, historic or not, these midterms are likely to mark the end of a political era.” What that gives way to is a much more complicated picture in which the US will be delivered from Trump himself, but remains a country riven and undermined by what he has unleashed. By the time he is gone, Trump will have been president for eight years, and a toxic force for more than 12. That is a long time even for a normal politician. Under one who shatters norms and forces himself into the centre of everything, Trump’s effect is as if he were president for decades.
He has already enacted policy that is nearly irreversible, things that can only be overturned with a huge amount of work and legislative wrangling and improbable bipartisan consensus. USAID is gone. Probably also gone are government departments effectively eliminated or incapacitated by Doge, the “department of government efficiency”. There are entire global tariff regimes and the executive and budgetary empowerments of ICE to deal with. And most difficult to unspool is a war with Iran that, despite its promised, imminent end, is looking to be an open-ended conflict. Even if the midterms augur a win for the Democrats in 2028, the country they will inherit will have been permanently shaped by Trump.
And that is still a big if. Trump is a singular figure who cohered an otherwise inchoate and disparate coalition, from white evangelical Christians to working-class Latinos to Silicon Valley billionaires. Maga is a movement that is bound up with Trump, and feels increasingly weakened by his incumbency. Like Brexit and other insurgent movements, the galvanising anti-establishment power is lost when you are the establishment and have been for quite a long time. Looking for new people to blame, new grievances to exploit, becomes less an exercise in rebellion, more in whining and negativity. But whoever comes after Trump as a candidate, even if it is the black hole of charisma that is JD Vance, may still find some success using the same general pitch. That combination of combativeness and fractiousness might still read as authentic and subversive to the base. It may even seem comparatively sharp and legible against the opaque generic blah-ness of the Democratic establishment.
And that Democratic establishment itself is reason to worry. It is a ways to go yet, but the Democrats themselves seem unable to go either back or forward decisively. The party’s old guard is spent, either gerontocratic or gerontocracy-adjacent. In the latter camp is Kamala Harris, whose last campaign summons not the hope of a fresh candidate in 2026, but an apparatchik who offers only continuity without gravitas. In the former, there is a cohort who now only project entitlement and the out-of-touch, glassy-eyed bloat of so many years of capital acquisition - Nancy Pelosi, Chuck Schumer, Hillary Clinton.
Only Barack Obama still enjoys some sprightly relevance, and has used it to back Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate who is making that break with the past in a journey that Obama has cast as a passing of the baton. “He’ll finish the job we started,” Obama has said.
But even as El-Sayed is on the verge of making history as the first Muslim senator in a state that is pivotal to the presidential race, he is either drawing lukewarm, reluctant endorsements from other senior Democrats or he is openly attacked, primarily on his position towards Israel, which he believes has committed genocide in Gaza and should be defunded. Only a few days out from the election, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who El-Sayed narrowly beat last August to clinch the candidacy, has been taking big swipes at El-Sayed and his comments on Israel, and demanding he disavow election ads not even run by him, but by a leftwing group that backed him. The result is an unseemly scuffle that resulted first in El-Sayed saying he did not want Stevens appearing with him at a party unity event held on Sunday, and culminated later that day with an extraordinarily disgraceful development: Stevens endorsed El Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Divesting from Israel has become a flashpoint that appears to be less about political and ideological positions than the emergence of a new orientation in the party that breaks from an old guard overtaken by rapid changes of attitude. This was encapsulated by a quote from David Kramer, a Democrat who chaired Stevens’s primary campaign: “There’s a lot of talk about it being a big tent party, but sometimes we worry the tent is maybe devolving into a circus and we’re going to be pushed out.” Kramer is also voting for Rogers for the Senate. And there you have it. Some Democrats would rather lose than win on the left’s terms and be pushed out.
All of this suggests a future in which Trump is no longer on the scene, but there is still enough residual momentum among Trump’s acolytes, and disarray within the Democratic party, to render a midterm surge a temporary setback for Trumpism, not the restoration of the old order or the beginnings of a new one.
We have been here before. In fact, it’s worse than that, we have been here before in vastly better circumstances for the Democrats. Trump’s loss in 2020 happened in a context where there was a strong and familiar Democratic candidate in Joe Biden, a pandemic that research found hit Trump’s support, and no big live crisis in the Middle East roiling domestic politics. The midterms may spell the end of a certain Trump era, but what follows may probably be a case of long-Trump: a Republican party still unable to plot a path without him, and a Democratic party still unable to locate what it stands for outside of opposing him.
- Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

https://taz.de/Kinder-fragen-die-taz-ant.title: Kinder fragen, die taz antwortet: Was ist gesünder, Marmelade oder Nutella?
https://taz.de/Kinder-fragen-die-taz-ant.author: Svende Depping
https://taz.de/Kinder-fragen-die-taz-ant.text:
Kinder fragen, die taz antwortet: Was ist gesünder, Marmelade oder Nutella?
Wir wollen von Kindern wissen, welche Fragen sie beschäftigen. Jede Woche beantworten wir eine. Diese Frage kommt von Suki, 5 Jahre alt.
Schauen wir uns erst einmal an, woraus Marmelade und Nutella eigentlich bestehen. Auf den Gläsern findest du eine Zutatenliste. Beim Nutella – und auch in vielen Marmeladen – steht an erster Stelle eine Zutat: Zucker. Das bedeutet, dass von keiner Zutat mehr darin ist als vom Zucker. Beim Nutella macht er sogar mehr als die Hälfte aus!
Zucker ist der Grund dafür, dass Nutella und Marmelade so süß sind. Leider kann viel Zucker uns auch sehr krank machen. Trotzdem rühren manche Lebensmittelhersteller viel Zucker in ihre Aufstriche. Weil das viele Leute lecker finden – aber auch, weil Zucker im Vergleich zu anderen Zutaten so billig ist.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Marmelade enthält außer Zucker hauptsächlich Früchte. Darin sind zum Beispiel gesunde Vitamine. Allerdings gehen einige der Vitamine kaputt, wenn die Früchte gekocht werden. Und das werden sie normalerweise, wenn aus ihnen Marmelade hergestellt wird.
Beim Nutella ist die zweite Zutat nach dem Zucker das Palmöl. Das ist, wie der Name es sagt, Öl von einer Ölpalme. Es enthält eine bestimmte Art von Fett, die ebenfalls als ungesund gilt. Danach kommen Haselnüsse, Magermilchpulver und Kakao – die enthalten auch Stoffe, die für unseren Körper gut sind. Schade, dass davon nur so wenige im Nutella stecken.
Es gibt Alternativen
Tja, und was ist nun gesünder? „Wenn ich mich zwischen Marmelade oder Nutella entscheiden müsste, würde ich wohl die Marmelade wählen, da Nutella zusätzlich zum Zucker noch sehr fettreich ist“, erklärt Lisa Hitschler. Sie untersucht für das Magazin Ökotest verschiedene Lebensmittel.
Was Lisa Hitschler noch gesagt hat: In vielen Marmeladen und auch im Nutella sind noch andere Stoffe, die nicht auf der Zutatenliste stehen. Sie gehören da gar nicht hinein. Beim Nutella ist das Mineralöl. Das könnte zum Beispiel von Erntemaschinen stammen. Das schmierige Öl ist eigentlich dazu da, dass die Maschinen gut funktionieren. Leider weiß man noch nicht, ob es unserem Körper schadet.
In manchen Marmeladen fanden Wissenschaftler*innen giftige Stoffe. Pestizide heißen die. Sie werden vor der Ernte auf die Früchte gesprüht, um sie zum Beispiel vor Insekten zu schützen. Auch sie können uns krank machen.
Und nun? „Unsere Tests zeigen, dass Bioprodukte weniger mit Pestiziden verunreinigt sind“, sagt Hitschler. Sie schlägt vor, statt Nutella und Marmelade lieber Nussmus oder Fruchtaufstriche mit wenig Zucker zu kaufen. Probier’s doch mal!

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: HRW calls on Zambia to halt post-election crackdown
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
HRW calls on Zambia to halt post-election crackdown
Opposition figures arrested and disappeared since President Hakainde Hichilema claimed August victory.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called on Zambia’s authorities to halt the vicious clampdown on the political opposition that was launched following President Hakainde Hichilema’s victory in disputed elections in August.
The rights group demanded in a report released on Sunday that the authorities put a stop to the intensifying crackdown.
It accused Zambia’s government of silencing government critics, with several members of the opposition, as well as journalists and lawyers, arrested and some having disappeared in recent months.
“The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices,” HRW said.
The group said that Zambian police and military “forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026”.
“Zambia’s government should break this dangerous cycle of repression,” added Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at HRW.
“The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces.”
Hichilema was sworn in for a second term as Zambia’s president following his victory in August. Critics have insisted that the election was marred by vote rigging.
As he was inaugurated at the National Heroes Stadium in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, his main rival Brian Mundubile was in detention, accused of treason after claiming the opposition had won the election.
Police raided Mundubile’s home the day after the August 13 elections. A former cabinet member, Mutotwe Kafwaya, was shot and killed during the operation.
HRW called on the Zambian authorities to institute an independent, impartial and thorough investigation into the matter.
About a dozen other opposition figures who have questioned the election results have been arrested.
Meanwhile, authorities suddenly closed the country’s courts two weeks after the election, a move that Zambian police stated was an “intelligence-led and preventive measure”, without providing details.
HRW noted that the closure prevents the opposition from filing legal challenges against the vote.

Houthis launched cross border raids on Saudi military posts, sources say
The Houthis have launched multiple cross-border raids into Saudi Arabia in recent months, in an expansion of the conflict beyond Yemen, a western and Arab official with direct knowledge of the raids told Middle East Eye.
The small-scale raids have targeted border posts in Saudi Arabia’s rugged, mountainous southwest. At least one raid occurred at the end of October, the officials told MEE.
The western official told MEE that the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, appear to have captured specific small arms that are known only to be used by Saudi border security forces.
The end-of-October cross-border raid was also observed on surveillance equipment, the official added.
The raids, which have not been publicly reported, would mark the first instance of Houthi cross-border attacks inside Saudi Arabia since the collapse of a ceasefire in Yemen.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Before the 2022 truce was signed, Saudi Arabia reported regular attempts by the Houthis to infiltrate the kingdom, as the Houthis conducted ground raids on border cities and army bases.
Mohammed al-Basha, a Yemen expert and founder of the Basha Report Risk Advisory, told MEE he was closely watching Houthi military activity at the Saudi border, where the group is “gradually expanding the range and intensity” of attacks.
“The initial phase involved long-range drones and short-range ballistic missiles. The second phase introduced short-range quadcopters that drop mortar munitions, as well as sniper operations,” he said.
Basha said it was “only a matter of time” before the Houthis returned to launching ground raids.
“I expect the initial operations to resemble the early years of the nearly 12-year Yemen war, when the Houthi fighters carried out hit-and-run attacks, captured coalition personnel, seized weapons and destroyed military equipment and vehicles before withdrawing,” added Basha, who is an associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute.
The Arab official told MEE that Egyptian, Pakistani and Turkish military assistance would likely be valuable along the kingdom’s southern border as a result of the raids.
Saudi Arabia’s Mecca Pact allies, Turkey and Pakistan, have said they plan to deploy forces, including air defence batteries, to the kingdom. Egypt’s parliament also approved the deployment of defensive forces to Saudi Arabia last week.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said on Saturday that Damascus is also thinking of joining the pact. The western official told MEE that some Syrian drone specialists had already arrived in Yemen to assist the Saudi-backed forces.
Houthi claims on southern Saudi Arabia
The Houthis’ cross-border attacks are unlikely to alter the military balance of power in Yemen, where Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are struggling to stem a Houthi offensive.
Reuters reported on Monday that the Houthis have advanced to within 50 miles of Aden port, which is the capital of the internationally recognised government. The group has also encircled Taiz.
The Houthis have launched hundreds of high-profile strikes on Saudi civilian infrastructure, including airports and energy installations. At least 24 people have been killed by the Houthi strikes. As a result, Riyadh was forced to cancel a high-profile investment forum.
But the cross-border raids have underscored the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia’s remote southern border and the difficulties of policing the vast terrain.
The attacks also reaffirm apprehension inside the kingdom that the Houthis have territorial ambitions.
While the Houthis have mainly fought inside Yemen, they have revisionist claims against Saudi Arabia, particularly against its three southern provinces of Asir, Jazan and Najran, which Yemen ceded to Saudi Arabia in the 1934 Treaty of Taif.
The Houthis originated in Yemen’s Saada governorate, the mountainous region south of the border with Saudi Arabia.
The movement takes its name from its founder, Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi and follows the Zaydi sect of Shia Islam. The Houthis recruit across Yemeni society, but their senior leadership claims Hashemite descent, which would link them to the Prophet Muhammad.
