https://gothamist.com/news/california-ma.title: California man was shot by a NJ detective in Moonachie, officials say
https://gothamist.com/news/california-ma.author: Kaya Laterman
https://gothamist.com/news/california-ma.text:
Prosecutors investigating a fatal shooting involving a New Jersey state police detective in Moonachie on Wednesday said the civilian who died had approached an undercover officer working in the area before being shot.
The New Jersey attorney general's office on Thursday identified the deceased as Roberto Castro-Quinonez, 30, of Bakersfield, California.
The identity of the officer involved in the fatal shooting has not been released.
According to preliminary information, at approximately 5:15 p.m., New Jersey state police detectives were conducting an investigation on Gotham Parkway, near the intersection with West Commercial Avenue. The detectives, operating in plain-clothes, were in the area as part of a criminal investigation, according to prosecutors.
While in that area, one of the detectives was approached by Castro-Quinonez. An interaction between the two men ensued, and a second detective arrived at the scene to assist, prosecutors said.
Shortly thereafter, one New Jersey state police detective discharged his weapon two times, striking Castro-Quinonez, officials said.
Officers attempted to perform medical aid, but Castro-Quinonez was pronounced deceased at 5:44 p.m., according to prosecutors.
The attorney general is required by law to investigate a person's death that occurs during an encounter with a law enforcement official.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://gothamist.com/news/the-nypd-is-c.title: The NYPD is confiscating e-bikes along a clogged East Village street
https://gothamist.com/news/the-nypd-is-c.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/the-nypd-is-c.text:
A tiff over parked e-bikes is escalating on a busy thoroughfare in the East Village.
An NYPD spokesperson said on Thursday that police confiscated 11 e-bikes parked along East 11th Street and First Avenue this week, where neighboring business owners and residents have been complaining for months about idle delivery bikes clogging sidewalks and curbs, sometimes by the hundreds.
The spokesperson said the e-bikes were removed because they had been parked illegally or out of concern over the bike’s lithium-ion batteries sparking fires. The department had given the owners three weeks’ warning before beginning the enforcement, and the owners will be able to retrieve their property, according to the NYPD.
Members of a newly formed coalition, the East Village Beautification Project, convened a group meeting on the block Thursday afternoon, against a backdrop of dozens of parked e-bikes, and urged the city to intervene further.
“Delivery workers deserve safe places to park and charge their bikes, but not at this location at the expense of everyone else who lives and works here," Christine Renzi, the coalition’s leader, said in a statement.
“If the city, local elected officials, and our local community board will not take this seriously, we will make sure they cannot keep looking the other way," she added.
Renzi said the coalition is advocating for bike parking to be dispersed along other nearby blocks – just as Citi Bike dock stations are distributed to multiple sites – so that the impact isn’t so concentrated.
But other community advocates worried that confiscating e-bikes would hurt immigrant New Yorkers.
“People are going to lose their means of livelihood with no warning and no education,” said Susan Stetzer, the district manager of an East Village community board, said at a meeting on Tuesday ahead of the enforcement.
A spokesperson from Cafewal, a community kitchen and local resource center, said many of the e-bikes are used by immigrants who frequent the site, and that the organization conducts weekly cleanups of the area. He said the drivers need a place to go, and would welcome more formal parking.
Mamadu Djalo, a delivery driver from Guinea-Bissau who spends time on the East Village block, said removing bikes affects drivers and their families.
“They're surviving on this delivery job, so there's nothing else to do,” Djalo said.
Djalo said that he didn’t object to spreading the parking to other areas, but added that the neighborhood is important to the workers, too.
“ We spend time together here,” Djalo said. “We are together like one family.”

https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorkers-e.title: New Yorkers enrolled in SNAP will get more money for fresh produce next year
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorkers-e.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorkers-e.text:
New Yorkers enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program will receive more money to use at farmers markets and farm stands next year, City Hall announced Thursday.
The changes are coming to the city’s Health Bucks program, one of several initiatives that lower the cost of healthy foods for low-income residents who often struggle to buy fresh fruits and vegetables.
SNAP recipients are already able to receive an additional $2 for every $2 spent purchasing certain fresh produce at more than 100 local greenmarkets across the five boroughs, but the city sets a daily cap of $10.
Starting in January, the cap will increase to $14.
The cost of increasing the daily cap in this program, which is partially funded by the city, is expected to reach $2.3 million in 2027, officials said.
It’s a change that Mayor Zohran Mamdani said “puts fresh produce within reach and makes groceries more affordable” for low-income residents.
“Every day, New Yorkers walk into a store hoping prices haven’t gone up again,” the mayor said in a statement on Thursday. “As food insecurity rises, far too many families are forced to skip the fruits and vegetables.”
Those who aren’t on SNAP can still receive Health Bucks from nonprofits and faith-based organizations that distribute the $2 coupons.
A full list of farmers markets and farmstands that accept Health Bucks can be found on the city’s website.

https://gothamist.com/news/you-cant-even.title: 'You can't even look out the window': Asbestos dust coats Brooklyn NYCHA building walls
https://gothamist.com/news/you-cant-even.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/you-cant-even.text:
Some residents of Brooklyn's Marcy Houses are balancing their personal health against the difficulties of relocating after a steam leak deposited asbestos-laden residue on the exterior walls of two adjoining buildings there, and covered many of their windows with the white dust.
Workers from the New York City Housing Authority and the city Department of Environmental Protection were at 502 and 504 Marcy Ave. — two of the 27 buildings in the sprawling Bedford-Stuyvesant complex — responding to the incident on Thursday. NYCHA officials said the steam came from an exhaust vent for an underground line that connects with mobile boilers. Part of the apparatus sticks up from the ground and is surrounded by a wooden safety barrier, which residents have been concerned about for some time.
Some told Gothamist they had seen the steam billowing up for weeks or longer, and that it had been leaving a white powder on their windows.
“The steam kept coming up, real white steam. It would cover the windows. We can't look out our kitchen window or the room window facing that way,” said Digna Torres, 75, whose apartment was along the affected exterior wall. “And all of a sudden, the windows got white. I mean white white. You can't even look out the window.”
NYCHA officials said in a statement the residue tested positive for asbestos, and that residents of 23 affected apartments — those along the exterior walls of the buildings — had been offered temporary relocations. Four have relocated, officials said.
Torres said she’s been stressed since getting the notice on Wednesday, but decided against leaving her apartment because she didn’t want to transport her three parakeets. On Thursday morning, she said she was waiting for workers to clean her windows.
“I'm worried,” she said. “My sons are like, ‘Mom, that's asbestos. That's no good. You could get cancer.’ And I said, "Oh, my God." Yeah, it’s bad. … Right now I just wanna know when they're coming so I could do what I have to do.”
Councilmember Chi Ossé said earlier this week that nine buildings were without heat due to the same issue. By Wednesday, NYCHA confirmed it had restored heat to 234 apartments across four of the buildings, and was working to install mobile boilers for the remaining five buildings.
Estalin De Leon, 45, also lives in the buildings but in an apartment facing the opposite direction, so her apartment is not one of those considered directly affected. She said the notices regarding the asbestos still left her nervous about the building’s safety.
“Of course — I was really scared,” she said in Spanish. “I sent my daughter to stay with my sister, and I stayed behind in case they needed to come and check the apartment, but they didn’t end up checking my apartment.”
During an appearance on the WNYC show “Who’s Running This Place” on Thursday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he didn’t have updates on the situation, but said serving NYCHA residents' needs is a top priority for his administration.
“ We are looking to address not only this specific issue in ensuring that we're taking care of the health and safety of those NYCHA residents, but also delivering more in investment and attention to NYCHA than we've seen in recent decades because these are working-class New Yorkers who are being pushed out of New York through a lack of habitable conditions," he said.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: New York’s Socrates Sculpture Park rebuilds for resilience and expands
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Hannah Sage Kay
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
When Superstorm Sandy hit New York City in 2012, Socrates Sculpture Park, located on the Queens riverfront, disappeared underwater. With a four-foot rise in sea level, water streamed from the park into the surrounding area, which was at that time comprised mostly of factories and the neighbouring Noguchi Museum.
Fourteen years later, the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation broke ground last month on the park’s seawall reconstruction. This work, which has been unfolding at riverfront parks across the city with funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, necessitates that much of Socrates’s five-acre campus remain closed until its completion next spring.
A former landfill and illegal dumping ground turned green space that supports artists in the production and presentation of public art, Socrates’s founding is described by executive director Shaun Leonardo as “a radical act of land transformation”. In this same spirit, Socrates will unveil on 31 October—during its annual Halloween Harvest Festival—the transformation of a largely abandoned storage area on the park’s southern edge into a revitalised landscape featuring a long-term installation of three monumental sculptures by the park’s founding artist Mark di Suvero.
Called The Point, this one-acre expansion, Leonardo says, is an opportunity to “connect Socrates’s future to its founding story” on the occasion of its 40th anniversary. Though this parcel has historically been a maintenance and storage location to support the creation and installation of work by Socrates artists—including Di Suvero who built many of his towering sculptures at the park in the 1980s and 90s—it has steadily grown dormant. Now, at age 93, he primarily lives on the West Coast, but the three soon-to-be-unveiled sculptures have lived on-site since their creation (1995 for the earliest, 2017 for the most recent). While they are comprised of steel I-beams, like much of his work, these sculptures are dynamic and meant to be engaged with: two include a swing; one of those also features a spinning titanium element.
Di Suvero’s “work feels like drawing in space and, through that lens, you really start to see how much he thought about it interacting in its environment”, Leonardo says.
Established in 1986 by a coalition of artists and community members, Socrates grew out of Di Suvero’s nearby studio located in a defunct brick warehouse. Having brought in a team to help install his works, he also shared his space with other sculptors and gave them access to his tools. Together, they looked at the neighbouring landfill and “saw an opportunity again to extend the work they were doing in the studio into a space to develop works in public view, and in deep connection with the neighbourhood,” Leonardo says.
With the establishment of a workforce development programme—whereby residents of the nearby Astoria Houses public housing complex were hired to both clear the land and help artists fabricate their projects—Socrates revitalised the landscape while creating, as Leonardo puts it, an “economic engine of an opportunity for individuals to build up a skill set not only in horticulture, but in fabrication, maintenance, community engagement and public event production, knowing that they could leave from Socrates to full employment elsewhere”. Though the programme had fallen dormant since the Covid-19 pandemic, Leonardo relaunched it this year with a pilot edition supported by the Ford Foundation and Urban Upbound.
The factories that formerly populated the neighbourhood have in recent years been replaced by residential high-rises that are just as vulnerable to the next storm as the park is, if not more so. “What’s unique about erosion of a landfill, as opposed to a natural landscape,” Leonardo says, is that “not only has the rock shoreline disappeared, but the coast is caving in as well because of what is being eroded from underneath.”
“We have taken it upon ourselves to think about our work as it relates to climate resilience as a responsibility to both people and place,” he adds. “Much of our landscaping system has been strategic in terms of not only soil rehabilitation but also flood mitigation and providing a better barrier to the neighbourhood.” That has included, for example, cultivating native plants and restoring the habitat for monarch butterflies along their migration route.
“In order for the community to thrive,” Leonardo says, “the art has to serve an additional purpose of giving to that community and being in reciprocal relationship with the land.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Dallas Art Fair scores new venue at football training facility
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The Dallas Art Fair will move to a new venue for the first time in its nearly two-decade history, relocating from downtown Dallas to an American football training facility on the campus of Southern Methodist University (SMU) for its 2027 edition. The fair, one of the leading independent commercial art fairs in the US, will take place 15-18 April at the university’s Armstrong Fieldhouse—an indoor training facility for SMU’s football team.
The move will give the fair more room to accommodate galleries and improve visitor experience, says fair director Kelly Cornell, while offering a fresh setting for an event that has outgrown its longtime home. “FIG has been an excellent home for us for the past 18 years, but it's also had its limitations in the sizing and amount of booths—those nitty-gritty details of producing a fair have been challenging,” Cornell says.
Since its inaugural edition in 2009, the Dallas Art Fair has occupied the Fashion Industry Gallery (FIG), a wholesale fashion market venue in downtown Dallas. FIG is owned by the local real-estate developer John Sughrue, who co-founded the fair with the curator Chris Byrne; Byrne left the organisation in 2017.
Earlier this year, FIG announced that it had extended its lease on the building until 2033, and local media reported that the fair would continue to be held there. Cornell says the organisation had been searching for a suitable alternative for nearly a decade, and that plans to relocate in 2027 came together quite quickly.
The Armstrong Fieldhouse offers a more flexible layout than FIG, where fair exhibitors had been split across two floors with limited visibility between them. The new venue will bring everyone together on one level playing field—literally—with higher ceilings and fewer physical obstructions to work around.
The fair will need to cover the playing surface, but Cornell says she intends to retain the field goals. “It’s an easy blank slate that we can load one story in and out,” she says. “The logistics were excellent, and then it took getting the university support and buy-in.”
The fair first became interested in the fieldhouse three years ago, Cornell says. The ushering in of SMU’s president, Jay Hartzell, and provost, Rachel Davis Mersey, in recent years have helped bring the university on board to partner with the fair.
The private university, nicknamed Southern Millionaire’s University, has more than 12,000 students. It is located in University Park, around five miles north of downtown Dallas, and borders Highland Park, an affluent neighbourhood that is home to many of the city’s art collectors. Cornell says the fair’s new location will be walkable for many visitors, and the partnership with SMU could bring good relationships with both the university’s board and students having their first experiences with commercial art.
The fair does not intend to expand dramatically in exhibitor numbers for its 2027 edition. It typically presents around 90 galleries (with the total closer to 100 in the years before the pandemic), but the limitations of FIG left little scope for growth. Now, the new venue is expected to give participating galleries greater flexibility to create larger installations and more immersive presentations.
The move will also allow the fair to improve circulation and introduce an upscale dining option on site. Other planned upgrades include higher walls, improved lighting and infrastructure, and more space for hospitality and sponsors.
“The intention is to continue to increase the quality of the fair and provide better space for our galleries,” Cornell says. “Twelve-foot walls, nicer infrastructure and lighting, being able to provide more hospitality and sponsor spaces within the footprint—the goal is to be the best fair of our size in the world.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: As protests in Georgia intensify again, a new private museum puts focus on the country’s artists
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Alexander Morrison
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Georgia’s art scene has been navigating a period of tension since a wave of protests rippled through the country in 2024, sparked by issues including the introduction of a law that critics say threatens freedom of expression. Two years on, as demonstrations continue, some much-needed good news for local artists has arrived with the launch of a new private museum dedicated to Georgian contemporary art.
The Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, around two hours’ drive east from Tbilisi, past fields, forts and mountains, is scheduled to open on 2 November. One of its core missions, according to the foundation’s creative director Nino Sulkhanishvili, is “to show the artists who aren’t given space in an institutional setting”, in some cases because of their political stances. “We decided to give the space to those who actually need it,” she says.
The institution has been built from scratch on 115 acres of land purchased by its founder, the shipping and logistics executive Jemal Inaishvili. It is housed in a hyper-modern two-storey building, its facade a series of blood-red slats encased in a silver-grey frame.
Along with the exhibition spaces and shop, there is a rooftop auditorium for performances and film screenings. “We wish to have many reasons to have good people come and celebrate,” Inaishvili says. The grounds also comprise sculptures, a five-star hotel and a winery. The estimated total cost is more than €25m, funded by Inaishvili and his family.
Inaishvili’s personal collection provides an anchor for the foundation’s programme. He has been amassing art for about 40 years: he thought of becoming a painter in his youth, he explains, and surrounded himself with artists. He recalls the incident that kickstarted his collecting: “It was around 1985 and we were drinking until late hours. The artist Irakli Sutidze was hosting us and I said: ‘I want to buy this work’”. From the mid-1990s onwards, contemporary art became his focus.
It was a time of challenge and opportunity, Inaishvili says: following Georgia’s independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, “the country was poor, and so there were not too many buyers, not too many collectors”. Today, he remains one of few major collectors in the country who is concentrated on the work of living artists—something he wishes to change through his foundation. About 10% of his collection is by international artists–including Ukrainians, whom he is keen to support, he says, “especially in this very, very difficult condition for their nation”.
The inaugural exhibition, Georgian Contemporary Art: Origins and Continuities, combines works from Inaishvili’s collection with loans to trace the development of Georgian art since the 1960s. It will show, for example, how “in the post-Stalin era, artists began to experiment with their autonomy”, Sulkhanishvili explains; and how, in the 1970s and 1980s, artists began to work together in conscious opposition to art sanctioned by the Soviets, with examples including the avant-garde collective Archivarius. It will also explore the work of artists like Misha Shengelia and Kote Sulaberidze, who incorporated dark humour into their work in the 1990s to express their experiences of a difficult time for many Georgians, marked by war and financial chaos.
Inaishvili says this whole story has never been told before. But “we’re not trying to show everything that was done during those times,” Sulkhanishvili says, adding that the exhibition will feature many works that have never been seen in public.
“I was trying to see, first of all, what is the definition of contemporary art in general—so how Modernism developed into Post-modernism and contemporary art,” he says. “I tried to fix that equation in Georgian art, which was difficult because everything was basically underground, unofficial practice.”
Georgia’s institutional art sector has only been developing in earnest, Sulkhanishvili says, since the early 2000s. This has been a complicated journey, defined by seismic political shifts including the current Georgian Dream government’s pivot away from Europe and towards Russia.
The adoption of the so-called “Russian law”—officially the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence—in spring 2024 ushered in new rules for organisations receiving foreign funding, which the NGO Human Rights Watch argued would “marginalise and stifle critical voices”. The move prompted crowds of creative workers to take to the streets and boycott public institutions. Disputed parliamentary results in October that year, and the Georgian government’s decision to suspend EU accession talks a month later, brought fresh, intensified protests.
These demonstrations have continued since. This month, amid outcry over a lawsuit brought by Georgian Dream that seeks to ban five opposition parties, a new campaign was launched, which is reportedly expected to culminate with a major rally on 28 November.
A critical role for independent organisations
The fractious relationship between artists and state institutions places emphasis on the role of independent organisations like the Kvareli Foundation. Inaishvili’s career has been primarily in the shipping and logistics sector; his current roles include chairman of the board of Tbilisi Dry Port. But he also served as a member of the Georgian parliament—for his home constituency of Batumi—and as the deputy chair of parliament in the early 2000s, during Mikheil Saakashvili’s presidency. Business, he says, has always been his main focus. “If I wanted to continue in politics, I would still be in it; I said, ‘thank you and goodbye’.”
Sulkhanishvili places emphasis not just on the foundation’s independence but also its location outside of Tbilisi, which, she says, already has a healthy ecosystem of commercial galleries as well as foundations such as Atinati.
“Our goal is to shift the focus from the capital,” she says. “Kakheti [the wider region in which Kvareli is located] is known for its hospitality, its wine, for its amazing food, for its amazing historical sites, but not specifically for contemporary art. This is something that’s never been brought before.” There are plans for a future residency programme at the institution.
Inaishvili says he wishes to help people—including the country’s wealthy and international visitors—to learn about Georgian contemporary art and perhaps inspire them to collect and patronise it, as he has been doing for four decades. “Georgian artists do not have enough support in my opinion,” he says. “We have to create the appetite.”
- Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, Georgia, opens on 2 November

https://citylimits.org/new-yorkers-have-.title: New Yorkers Have the Right to Vote in Their Own Language. Here’s What You Need to Know.
https://citylimits.org/new-yorkers-have-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-yorkers-have-.text:
Share This Article
“New York City, especially, has a lot of laws that regulate language access,” said Olivia Nuñez, NYC Campaign Finance Board community engagement director. “All New Yorkers have the right to vote and to get a ballot in their language.”
This story was produced in collaboration with Factchequeado. Lea la versión en español aquí.
New York City’s linguistic diversity is vast, with residents speaking just over 700 languages.
Language access in New York City elections is governed by a multi-layered framework of federal, state, and city laws, covering different segments of the non-English-speaking electorate. These laws cover a little more than a dozen languages—the most widely spoken ones.
“New York City, especially, has a lot of laws that regulate language access,” Olivia Nuñez, NYC Campaign Finance Board community engagement director, explained. “We actually have more laws in place of protection than even at the federal level does.”
In New York State, about 5.96 million people aged 5 and over spoke a language other than English at home in 2024, according to Census data. A New York City Campaign Finance Board report published that same year found that 16.4 percent of New York City citizens of voting age had limited English proficiency. In boroughs like Queens and the Bronx, this percentage is even higher, accounting for 20.7 and 19.5 percent of voting-age residents, respectively.
RELATED READING: In New York Governor’s Race, What Are Candidates Doing to Reach Spanish-Speaking Voters?
Several local agencies that provide services to non-English-speaking voters have trained and recruited hundreds of interpreters, who have been deployed to the city’s early voting sites (early voting kicked off on Saturday, and will run through Sunday, Nov. 1). A second, slightly larger team of interpreters is preparing to do the same on Election Day on Tuesday.
City Limits put together this guide to help New York voters understand their rights at the polls regarding language access.
The Voting Rights Act
In 1975, Congress amended the Voting Rights Act of 1965, adding protections to remove barriers that prevented people with limited English proficiency from voting in elections.
The amendment ordered regions with significant numbers of people who speak a language other than English at home to provide them with language assistance at the polls.
Under these provisions, eight New York counties—including Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and the Bronx—must provide interpretation services to voters in certain languages, including Spanish, at select poll sites.
The New York Voting Rights Act
New York State also has its own language access protections. In 2022, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the John. R. Lewis Voting Rights Act of New York, lowering the population thresholds (compared to federal rules) that require localities to offer multilingual voting assistance.
New York’s “2 Percent or 300-Individual Rule” requires local governments to translate election materials into languages other than English when this percentage of the population has limited English proficiency (LEP) skills, based on data from the American Community Survey. There’s additional criteria mandating translations when there are more than 4,000 LEP-eligible voters in a specific political subdivision.
Under the law, translated materials—like voter registration forms, notices, instructions and ballots themselves—must be of “equal quality” to English versions.
Additionally, when the language spoken by a “minority group” has been historically oral or unwritten, the state of New York is required to provide oral interpreters for translation.
NYC’s language access laws
New York City has also enacted its own laws to address its immense linguistic diversity, and complement federal and state protections.
The New York City Board of Elections (BOE)—which creates the city’s ballots, runs polling places, and counts the votes—provides translators at certain poll sites in the following languages, based on the neighborhood’s linguistic needs:
- Manhattan: Spanish and Chinese
- Brooklyn: Spanish, Chinese, Korean, Bengali, and Urdu
- Queens: Spanish, Chinese, Korean, Bengali, Tagalog, Hindi, and Punjabi
- The Bronx: Spanish
- Staten Island: Spanish and Chinese
Around 60 percent of BOE poll sites get language help for a covered language under either the federal or state Voting Rights Act, Deputy Executive Director Vincent Ignizio explained. There are 2,000 interpreter positions to fill for a full election, Ignizio added. 
The Campaign Finance Board (CFB), a nonpartisan city agency that administers the city’s campaign finance system and matching funds program, also conducts voter multilingual education, outreach, and engagement initiatives through NYC Votes.
Each year, the CFB publishes a Voter Analysis Report that looks at underrepresented areas of the city where people aren’t voting or taking part in elections, and designates these as “Priority Communities.” The board then builds strategies to engage these communities, which include voters under 30, naturalized foreign-born voters, voters with limited English proficiency (LEP), and voters with disabilities.
“CFB identified neighborhoods in the South Bronx, South Brooklyn, Northern Queens, and Central Queens as communities in need of targeted voter outreach because of the number of recently naturalized residents or residents that speak languages the CFB has not historically included in voter outreach,” explained CFB Assistant Press Secretary Jadel Munguia.
“These are areas that we see a lot of low voter turnout, and again, a high population of immigrants,” explained Lía Guzmán, a CFB neighborhood specialist for the Bronx, during a recent bilingual voter outreach workshop (in English and Spanish) in University Heights.
“We recognize that there are a lot of different barriers to voting, and we recognize that language is one of them, which is why we’ve done the work to make sure that our materials are available in 13 different languages, along with our website.”
CFB’s voter guides, which are mailed out across the city, are available in 13 languages: Arabic, Bengali, French, Haitian Creole, Hindi, Korean, Polish, Punjabi, Russian, Simplified Chinese, Spanish, Traditional Chinese, and Urdu.
“We really want to ensure that all New Yorkers have access to the information they need in the languages that they speak,” Nuñez said. “All New Yorkers have the right to vote and to get a ballot in their language.”
In 2018, New Yorkers voted yes to creating the NYC Civic Engagement Commission (CEC), designed to provide additional language interpretation for voters beginning in 2020.
CEC’s interpretation program was one of a small number of set responsibilities, and the language access requirement, by law, can’t duplicate what the BOE already does, requiring the CEC to focus on different languages and neighborhoods.
The Commission started providing interpretation services in 11 languages in neighborhoods with high concentrations of “citizens of voting age with limited English proficiency” or CVALEP, based on estimates from the American Community Survey, explained Dr. Sarah Sayeed, CEC’s chair.
In 2019, the BOE sued the city to block CEC translators, but the city ultimately won the case. “This was one not handed down,” recalled Murad Awawdeh, the president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition, who was involved in creating the Commission.
Later, the CEC expanded its services to 14 languages.
“The CEC created the Voter Language Assistance Program to ensure that anyone who speaks the … top 14 languages in New York City had the support that they needed when they got to a polling site, to have someone translate for them and help them understand their ballot better,” Awawdeh added.
Sayeed and Anila Cobo, director of the Voter Language Assistance Program, said they plan to operate at 100 unique polling places for the general election, and have a team of 240 interpreters ready.
You can find your polling site here. CEC’s poll sites map, which shows which locations offer translators, is available here.
If there’s no interpreter available at your poll site, you can be assisted by a “person of your choice”—as long as the person is not your employer, an agent of your employer, or an officer or agent of your union. The “voting helper” doesn’t have to be a U.S. citizen, a registered voter, or even an adult.
“If a ballot in their language isn’t available at their poll site, they can bring someone with them to support the translation,” Nuñez explained. “They really can bring anyone with them, and there are a lot of protections in place for New Yorkers to ensure that their voting rights are protected.”
Ignizio said that BOE maintains a reserve pool of poll workers and interpreters so they can deal with last-minute staffing issues. They also offer video interpretation. “Poll sites are equipped with a tablet that voters who need language assistance can use to connect with a remote interpreter, helping ensure that language assistance remains available even when an in-person interpreter is unavailable,” Ignizio added.
Unfortunately, there is no single public map or site that consolidates all BOE, CEC, federal, and state language access services for each polling place in New York.
If you need help voting and there’s no interpreter available, ask a poll site worker for assistance.
Voters who experience issues at the polls—like a poll worker saying they can’t bring their “person of choice” in to help them complete their ballots—can do the following:
- Call 311 and make a poll site complaint
- Call the Election Protection Hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683). Assistance is also available in Spanish at 888-VE-Y-VOTA (888- 839-8682)
- Contact the New York Attorney General Office’s voter protection hotline: 866-390-2992

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Photography as sculpture and an 800-page photobook on the Russia-Ukraine war: Deutsche Börse Prize nominees announced
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Simon Bainbridge
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The four artists shortlisted for the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2027 are Hoda Afshar, Lotus L. Kang, Sasha Kurmaz and Salvatore Vitale. All born in the early to mid-1980s (as were all but one of the judges), this edition's selected artists invite a generational reading. Having grown up during the transition from analogue to digital, they share a formative experience, reflected in their varied approaches to the materiality and authority of the image. The shortlist’s focus on recent and ongoing projects, without an historical-survey contender, also creates a heightened sense of discovery similar to the award’s early editions.
Afshar, born in Iran and now living in Australia, has been shortlisted for her exhibition Performing the Invisible which was on view at the Musée du Quai Branly–Jacques Chirac in Paris in 2025-26. Its central project, The Fold (2019-25), reworks a colonial photographic archive held by the French museum to question how veiled bodies have been represented and understood in the past.
Kang, a Canadian installation artist based in New York, is selected for the commission The face of desire is loss that was exhibited at the Bvlgari Pavilion during this year’s Venice Biennale, which combines sculpture and film with suspended lengths of unfixed photographic material that change with exposure to light and humidity.
Kurmaz is a Kyiv-based photographer known for his conceptual artist’s books. He is shortlisted for the photobook Red Horse (2025), published by Éditions Images Vevey, which assembles photographs, notes, drawings and found materials into an 800-page account of life following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Vitale’s exhibition Sabotage, shown at Photo Elysée in Lausanne this year, examines the human cost of the digital economy. Combining the Italian photographer’s pictures with films and images commissioned from workers in South Africa through the freelance website Upwork, he connects insecure online employment with the mining of materials that sustain our technological lives.
A selection of the artists’ works will be exhibited at the Photographers’ Gallery in London from 10 March to 6 June 2027 with the £30,000 prize winner announced on 29 April 2027.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Largest ever Piero della Francesca exhibition to open at London’s National Gallery
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The National Gallery in London will open the largest ever exhibition of works by the influential Italian Renaissance painter Piero della Francesca next autumn (2 October 2027-30 January 2028).
The show will include around 25 pictures and manuscripts including The Urbino Diptych-Portraits of Federico da Montefeltro and Battista Sforza (around 1472), travelling from the Gallerie degli Uffizi in Florence; the entire Pala di Perugia (Perugia Altarpiece, 1468), from the Galleria Nazionale dell’Umbria, Perugia; and the Virgin and Child Enthroned with Four Angels (around 1460–70), from the Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts.
Three works drawn from the gallery collection will be exhibition centrepieces: Baptism of Christ (probably about 1437–45), Saint Michael (1469), and The Nativity (early 1480s). A digital version of The Legend of the True Cross in the Bacci Chapel of the Basilica of San Francesco in Arezzo will also feature.
“By delineating the pillars of Piero’s art—a distillation of what makes a Piero a Piero—the exhibition will comprise seven interlocking building blocks of his art: colour, design, space, perspective, narrative, and light,” says a gallery statement.
Last year Piero della Francesca’s The Baptism of Christ (1437-45) was selected by three artists as a favourite work in the collection for the publication The National Gallery: Paintings, People, Portraits (Taschen).
The late artist David Hockney called it a “truly a magnificent picture”, while the sculptor Antony Gormley says its stillness suggests “another world free from pain and uncertainty”. The Venezuela-born, London-based artist Alvaro Barrington said: “There is a balance in The Baptism of Christ that allows one’s eyes and body to rest, to stay still, while at the same time one’s eyes move without struggle across the painting.”
Piero, who was also a mathematical theorist, was the first artist to write a treatise on perspective, De prospectiva pingendi (from a painting perspective, around 1474) which discussed, among other technical topics, creating an illusion of three-dimensional space on a flat surface. It also discusses techniques for painting faces.
The State Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg staged an exhibition of Piero della Francesca’s work in 2018, which was the largest to date at the time with just 11 works.
The National Gallery‘s exhibition is co-curated by Laura Llewellyn, the museum‘s curator of Italian paintings before 1500, and Machtelt Brüggen Israëls of the Rijksmuseum and the University of Amsterdam. Exhibition sponsors include the Intesa Sanpaolo bank and the philanthropist John J. Studzinski.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Rudi Fuchs, influential Dutch curator and former director of Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum, dies aged 84
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Stéphane Renault
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Rudi Fuchs, one of the most influential figures in the Dutch art world, died in Amsterdam on 25 October 2026, aged 84. “Throughout his working life, he dedicated himself to visual arts both at home and abroad,” his family said in a statement to the Dutch newspaper Het Parool.
Born in Eindhoven on 28 April 1942, Fuchs studied art history at Leiden University before becoming director of the Van Abbemuseum, in his home city, in 1975. He rose to international prominence in 1982 as the artistic director of Documenta 7 in Kassel, Germany, where he championed new painting, the show featuring established artists as well as young talents such as Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring.
In 1984, he became the artistic director of Castello di Rivoli, near Turin, Italy’s first museum devoted to contemporary art. Three years later, he took over the Gemeentemuseum Den Haag, now the Kunstmuseum Den Haag, which he directed until 1993. He then moved to Amsterdam to lead the Stedelijk Museum, remaining at its helm for a decade.
Alongside his museum career, Fuchs taught at the University of Amsterdam and wrote extensively on art. He authored studies of Dutch painting, the Saatchi Collection and artists including Jannis Kounellis and Donald Judd, as well as a book exploring the relationship between Anselm Kiefer and Rembrandt.
In 2016, the Stedelijk invited Fuchs back to curate Excitement, an exhibition that revisited his career through more than 100 works produced over the previous 50 years. Bringing together artists including Georg Baselitz, Jan Dibbets, Tracey Emin, Gilbert & George, Damien Hirst, Jannis Kounellis, Mario Merz, Piet Mondrian, Bruce Nauman and A.R. Penck, the exhibition offered an insight into acquisitions he had made that helped shape the museum’s collection.
“Hanging works of art close to one another highlights their singularity,” he wrote at the time. “Take the 1970s: there were so many radically different artistic movements that were—or appeared to be—in contradiction with one another. But if you looked at these works with an open mind, each one excelled in its own way. At least, that is how I perceived it. One could be biased—as many people were—or one could embrace this plurality as a source of richness, and adopt that particular vision of art. As early as 1980, Markus Lüpertz and Richard Long said to me: 'What matters is the quality of what our generation produces.'"
He continued: "There is no single 'right' way of doing things. There is such a thing as taste and personal preference—but that is an entirely different matter. In today’s world, no one is automatically the 'first.' In art, no one is the 'best.' That is what this exhibition is about—from my perspective, and using the works I have at my disposal.”
Paying tribute to his predecessor, Rein Wolfs, the Stedelijk’s director, said in a statement: “As director of the Haags Gemeentemuseum, he transformed the way Mondrian was perceived; and as director of the Stedelijk, he surprised audiences with unexpected juxtapositions and innovative modes of presentation. Fuchs brought a clear, uncompromising vision to Amsterdam, rooted in a fundamental belief in the autonomy of the artwork and the direct encounter between the viewer and the art. Through his acquisitions, presentations, and publications, Rudi made a significant contribution to the understanding of art; everything he did served as an encouragement to really look.”
- This article was originally published in The Art Newspaper France

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: ‘There’s so much of Scotland in them’: cuts to Edinburgh College of Art craft degrees spark backlash
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Debika Ray
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Edinburgh College of Art (ECA) is clashing with Scotland’s cultural sector over its decision to close its textiles, jewellery and silversmithing, and performance costume undergraduate degrees. The move has drawn criticism from staff, alumni, industry bodies and politicians, with questions raised over the college’s commitment to craft.
On 15 September, the University of Edinburgh, which the ECA merged with in 2011, announced it would stop admitting students to the three programmes, taught at its School of Design, from 2027. The closures are part of a broader overhaul through which the university reportedly intends to make £140m of cuts, with 1,800 jobs at risk. These wider plans, which have sparked strike action among staff over the past year and a half, will see more than 90 programmes close, with arts and humanities hardest hit.
A spokesperson for ECA says there will be no staff reductions as a result of the loss of the three craft degrees as the institution intends to fold their teaching faculty into the five other undergraduate courses that will remain in place at the School of Design: animation, fashion, graphic design, illustration and product design. It also plans to offer elective courses in these subjects to students across the university.
Critics argue, however, that the decision to lose the three courses will strip out specialist training and in-depth research in discrete skills-based disciplines that are integral to Scotland’s cultural identity, international reputation and economic future.
“Keeping heritage and cultural traditions alive”
The ECA originated in 1760 as the Trustees' Drawing Academy, formed to train designers for manufacturing, particularly for the textiles industry. Its staff have included the weaver Archie Brennan, who founded its tapestry department and taught there from 1962 to 1977, and also directed Edinburgh’s Dovecot Studios; and the noted jewellery artist Dorothy Hogg, who was the head of the college’s jewellery and silversmithing courses from 1985 to 2007. The range of voices raising concerns about the closures have pointed to the international reputation of the courses and their staff and alumni, their standing in their respective industries and their longstanding history within the institution. The textiles programme, for example, can trace its heritage back to the origins of the institution in 1760.
The ECA’s principal Juan Cruz tells The Art Newspaper that the decision to bring the three making courses to an end was “by no means a disinvestment in craft”, pointing to the university’s development of glass, ceramics and jewellery making facilities for students enrolled in art, design, architecture and landscape architecture degrees before the cuts were decided upon, as well as the launch in 2025 of an MA in craft. “The best way to protect disciplines is to make sure they evolve and remain relevant to students and industries,” he says.
But Irene Kernan, the director of national development agency Craft Scotland, says that the intense training, research and creative development that takes place on dedicated four-year degrees in these specific fields contributes to “keeping heritage and cultural traditions alive”. An ECA staff member interviewed by The Art Newspapr says: “Students couldn’t possibly develop their handling and knowledge of [these] materials or their mastery of technique through a few loosely positioned elective courses.”
Staff who spoke to The Art Newspaper also say these courses connect contemporary practice with Scotland’s craft heritage. Third-year textiles students grow flax on campus, then harvest, hand-process, spin and weave it into linen, a material with a long history in Scotland and potential as a sustainable alternative to polyester. ECA jewellery and silversmithing students work with the Edinburgh Assay Office—which tests and hallmarks works made from previous metals—as well as the city’s luxury jeweller Hamilton & Inches.
The courses also collaborate with National Museums Scotland (NMS). Elizabeth Goring, the institution’s former curator of modern jewellery, says the work of ECA alumni was fundamental to her work establishing the museum’s contemporary jewellery collection in 1984.
“You’ll find the work of numerous teachers and graduates in the NMS collections, which inform the way Scotland sees itself. ” she says. “There’s so much of Scotland in the work coming out of those courses—its landscape, materials and colours.” She points out that it’s a place where people can learn endangered skills such as metal-spinning. “Losing these degrees will have an enormous impact on Scotland’s recorded cultural heritage for perpetuity,” she says.
Broader financial strain
The spokesperson for the university, which reported a financial surplus of £44m in its annual report for the year up to 31 July 2025, cites insufficient demand, enrolment figures, costs and income as factors in the decision to make cuts across its programmes, though they were unable to provide specific figures for student take-up and matriculation for these three courses, nor the cut-off point or criteria applied to them to make the decision.
ECA staff The Art Newspaper spoke to say these three courses remained very popular—especially in comparison to many of the others closing. The university was not able to verify or confirm that figure or confirm the number of people currently studying on these three programmes.
Staff also expressed concern that the decision would draw talented prospective students from Scotland to universities elsewhere, since alternatives within the country are “limited”. The university confirmed that the overall number of Scottish-funded undergraduate places at ECA remains the same, now spread out across other programmes.
A petition launched by Craft Scotland calling for the decision to be reversed has attracted almost 18,000 signatures, and its open letter has drawn support from the Goldsmiths’ Company, Heritage Crafts, the European Crafts Alliance and Art Jewelry Forum USA and others.
On 29 September Q Manivannan, the Scottish Green Party’s spokesperson for arts and culture, lodged a motion in the Scottish parliament calling the decision “a serious misjudgement”. It has since been signed by 19 MSPs from six parties.
“I don’t think there has been any accurate assessment of how much GDP graduates from these programmes have brought Scotland or how devastating the economic losses will be as a result of them going away—especially at a time when you’re hearing so much about the importance of hand-on work that is AI resistant,” Manivannan said. Textiles, including tartan, Harris Tweed and cashmere, contributed £304m in gross value added (GVA) to the Scottish economy in 2018, according to government figures, which the industry aspires to increase to £540 million by 2030.
The film and TV industry has published its own open letter about the “pioneering” performance costume course, signed by high-profile figures including Hugh Bonneville, Rose Ayling Ellis and Brian Cox. It was organised by the ECA alumna and Emmy-nominated Downton Abbey costume designer Anna Mary Scott Robbins, who described the move as“short-sighted and misinformed”.
Steve Byrne, the chief executive of the NGO Traditional Arts and Culture Scotland—a signatory to Craft Scotland’s letter—is more circumspect. “I absolutely get the outcry, but giving all responsibility and accountability to universities is not necessarily right”. He points to the lack of crafts education at school level, and notes that in 2024 the UK government ratified the Unesco convention on the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage – which seeks to safeguard intergenerational practices, knowledge and skills – without dedicated funding. “There’s more of a public conversation needed outside academia about how we safeguard craft skills,” he adds.

https://www.propublica.org/article/hanfo.title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.
https://www.propublica.org/article/hanfo.author: Lizz Giordano, Brandon Block
https://www.propublica.org/article/hanfo.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Toxic Legacy: Workers got sick cleaning up radioactive waste at a former federal nuclear weapons site in Washington, and the state passed a law to make it easier to claim benefits.
- Litigating Workers’ Claims: The Department of Energy denies responsibility and has filed more than 500 legal appeals seeking to block state benefits being given to workers and their survivors.
- Millions Go to Lawyers: DOE has spent nearly $12 million on outside lawyers and expert testimony to fight state compensation claims.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana.
For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site, a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals. The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.
Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged, based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers.
Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.
By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.
As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life.
For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law, agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses. Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.
Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.
But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.
The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.
Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.
The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.
Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.
“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”
After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings.
“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.
The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”
The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.
In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes.
In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.
“We were always told that nothing is out here that’s going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you’re going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.
“But that’s not what happens.”
“Depleted and Disgusted”
The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.
The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.
The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.
In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”
But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.
Washington’s workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.
The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.
The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.
Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.
Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.
Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.
The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.
Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.
“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I’m worthless. I have no value.”
“When Does This End?”
State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.
“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that’s been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.
Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.
The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”
Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.
The DOE appealed. It hired a medical toxicologist, who reviewed Rouse’s medical records and testified that he did not have the disease he claimed, and brought in an industrial hygienist, who downplayed the exposure risks at Hanford. The DOE’s toxicologist testified that Rouse’s drinking was “the most significant, what we might term, ‘toxic exposure’ that’s described in the medical record.”
A group of three physicians and an industrial hygienist have collectively earned over $1.7 million testifying against Hanford workers since the presumption law’s passage, according to DOE invoices the newsrooms obtained by a federal records request. One of the DOE’s go-to expert witness doctors earned more than $200,000 from the DOE last year alone. He did not respond to multiple emails seeking comment.
A single law firm, Wallace, Mann, Capener, Bishop & Debney, handles all of the DOE’s appeals. In addition to the fees paid to expert witnesses, the department paid the firm nearly $10 million between 2018 and 2025. The law firm did not reply to multiple requests for comment.
In cases where the DOE has appealed the state’s approval of a claim since 2018, the agency that handles appeals has sided with workers nearly 9 times out of 10, according to state data.
Pollet, the state representative who sponsored the 2018 presumption bill, acknowledged that the law has fallen short of his expectation.
“This was supposed to have ended a decade ago,” he said about sick Hanford workers still awaiting back wages and medical care. “It’s even worse than it was 10 years ago.”
“I think their actions are not only despicable, but they are criminal,” he said of the DOE.
The state Department of Labor and Industries said it expected “to engage further with the DOE,” which could include putting the department on an improvement plan and monitoring its progress.
Another option state regulators have is to revoke the DOE’s ability to accept and pay out claims directly. According to the state Department of Labor and Industries, the contractors that employ Hanford workers on behalf of the DOE would then decide whether to join the state-managed fund or seek state approval to manage claims themselves. Doing so could limit the DOE’s power to appeal, but contractors would still have that right.
Brown, the state attorney general, said he wants to wait and see how the DOE’s appeals of claims play out in higher courts. He hopes that once the DOE’s losses start stacking up, it will slow the volume of its litigation.
Attorney Charlynn Hull said she thought the DOE’s approach might soften during the Biden administration. But Hull said she observed no change in the DOE’s behavior. Her firm, Smart Law, represents the majority of Hanford workers’ compensation claimants, including Rouse and Kersey.
One of the hardest things about the DOE’s appeals, Hull said, is the testifying that the children and spouses of dead workers must do.
“I think that it’s just, it’s tormenting to them, in many ways, to relive how awful that experience was, especially with the cancer-related death,” Hull said. “When does this end?”
Dying While Under Appeal
For Isidoro Mata Jr., it ended with his children draining fluid from his lungs through a tube doctors had surgically inserted into his chest.
Mata demolished buildings at Hanford for nearly 30 years. Court records show he was diagnosed in 2015 with thyroid cancer, one of the illnesses that Washington’s law ties to work at Hanford. Sara Chilcoat, his daughter, said he kept working as long as he could.
State claims managers approved Mata’s claim in 2019. The DOE appealed, arguing that “medical opinion supports denial of this claim as not related to the distinctive conditions of employment.” The appeal did not elaborate further. The state forced the DOE to pay his wages and the cost of his medications, Chilcoat said. But the DOE filed a separate motion to stop his benefits while the appeal was adjudicated.
In its motion, the DOE argued that it was likely to prevail in its appeal because a doctor who examined Mata in 2019 believed his cancer was unrelated to his work at Hanford, according to court records. The state found the doctor’s examination “lacking in objective findings.”
“He was fighting for his life while they were trying to do that,” Chilcoat said. “That makes me mad.”
Mata’s case file notes that he missed three meetings with DOE lawyers in 2020. The state attorney general’s office sent the appeals judge a letter in July explaining that Mata was unable to participate because of his chemotherapy treatments. The DOE, which did not respond to questions about Mata’s case, dropped its appeal in December.
Less than three months later, Mata died.

https://hyperallergic.com/moma-centre-po.title: MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Announce Novel Collection Alliance
https://hyperallergic.com/moma-centre-po.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/moma-centre-po.text:
MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Announce Novel Collection Alliance
The partnership between the museums will include intermuseum loans and joint exhibitions.
Leaders at Manhattan's Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), Paris's Centre Pompidou, and M+ in Hong Kong signed an agreement granting unprecedented access to each museum's holdings for increased viewership, more collaborative curation, and additional research.
The alliance emerges on the eve of M+'s fifth anniversary at its physical location in Hong Kong's West Kowloon Cultural District, and just one year into MoMA director Christophe Cherix's tenure. The agreement follows a wave of institutional resource pooling and joint acquisitions that swelled in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic as museums seek to reduce overhead costs while navigating major deficits. In another shakeup earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming merger with Ronald Lauder's Neue Galerie, which is set to commence in 2028.
“Museums must evolve to reflect the complexity of our world,” said M+ Museum Director Suhanya Raffel in a press statement on the alliance.
Previous collaborations between M+, home to the Sigg collection of contemporary Chinese art among thousands of other contemporary works from across Asia, and the other two museums foregrounded this agreement. The Hong Kong-based museum signed a memorandum of understanding with the MoMA in early 2025 that established shared curatorial, conservation, and scholarship objectives. And this spring, M+ and Centre Pompidou entered a strategic partnership to “strengthen the cultural dialogue” between their respective continents through joint exhibitions, collections sharing, and a funded fellowship.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.title: Movimento Luta nos Bairros Vilas e Favelas ocupa imóvel abandonado em Curitiba
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/10/.text:
O Movimento Luta nos Bairros Vilas e Favelas (MLB) ocupou um terreno com imóveis abandonados na Avenida Paraná, uma das principais vias do bairro Bacacheri, em Curitiba (PR). A ação teve início no último dia 29.
De acordo com o Movimento, a nova ocupação é uma reação ao déficit habitacional no Paraná. Estimativa da COHAPAR aponta um déficit de aproximadamente 463 mil domicílios urbanos e 21 mil rurais.
A ocupação leva o nome Zumbi e Dandara dos Palmares. “Em memória do grande herói e heroína do povo brasileiro, que não mediram esforços para construir um espaço livre da exploração e da escravidão”, diz a publicação na rede social Instagram, em que o Movimento anuncia a ação.
Na tarde deste sábado (31), uma publicação no perfil Curitiba Mil Graus atribui a autoria da ação ao Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST). Procurado pelo Brasil de Fato Paraná, o MST classificou a publicação como falsa.
“A publicação foi divulgada sem qualquer apuração ou preocupação com a verdade. Mais uma vez, vemos a necessidade urgente em haver regulação das redes sociais, para que canais que propaguem notícias falsas sejam responsabilizados pela desinformação que promovem”, destacou a assessoria de comunicação do Movimento.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-progressiv.title: NY progressives have found a way to vote for Hochul, with an asterisk
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-progressiv.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-progressiv.text:
Some progressive Democrats who are dragging their feet to the polls to vote for Gov. Kathy Hochul have landed on a solution: Follow Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s lead and vote for her on the Working Families Party ballot line.
Hochul, a moderate who’s facing a challenge from Republican Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, appears twice on the ballot: as a Democrat and as the pick of the progressive third party.
Michael Lange, a political analyst and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, said casting a vote on the WFP line is a way for fellow lefties to "have your cake and eat it, too.”
“ It's a way to show support for the left and the institutional left while also voting for a not-super-lefty-big-progressive Democrat,” Lange said.
That’s exactly what Corey Hillsey of Greenpoint did on a recent weekday morning during early voting.
“It sends a signal that we are looking for more change than what the Democratic Party brought us for the past 250 years,” said Hillsey, who identifies as a progressive Democrat and an enthusiastic supporter of the mayor, outside the McCarren Park polling site.
New York progressives have long cast ballots for the WFP, which supports causes like raising the minimum wage and universal healthcare, in an attempt to push centrist candidates further left. In 2020, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said she voted for the Biden-Harris ticket on the WFP line.
Hochul and Mamdani have struck up a powerful alliance in the 10 months since the mayor took office, launching a new free childcare program for 2-year-olds. The governor has also made a point of defending the mayor from allegations of antisemitism and personal attacks by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Mamdani is reciprocating that support by campaigning for the governor across the five boroughs.
The mayor is hugely popular in New York City – a recent Siena poll found he had a 69% approval rating. Hochul needs city voters to turn out for her in big numbers if she’s going to take a commanding lead against Blakeman.
When Mamdani cast his own ballot last Saturday, on the first day of early voting, he told reporters he voted for Hochul on the WFP line.
New York is one of a handful of states with fusion voting, a system where candidates can appear on the ballot lines of multiple parties. Parties must receive more than 2% of the total vote to keep their place on the ballot in future elections, and all votes are counted toward the total, regardless of the party line.
Blakeman appears on the Republican, Conservative and Vote Affordable party lines.
Many political observers credit the WFP with helping Hochul win four years ago when polls showed a tight race against Republican challenger Lee Zeldin. In the end, Hochul’s roughly 325,000-vote margin of victory included about 250,000 ballots cast on the WFP line.
Since then, the party has been critical of her rollbacks to state climate policy and her reluctance to raise taxes on the rich.
Earlier this year, the WFP flirted with backing her primary challenger, Lt. Gov. Antonio Delgado. But after a “rigorous and animated debate” at its statewide convention, the party chose not to endorse either candidate, depriving Delgado of much needed fuel for his insurgent campaign.
Now the WFP has thrown its weight behind Hochul in the general election.
“ We've been happy to work with the governor to actually deliver on universal childcare, on data center moratoriums, on a pretty extensive immigrant protection package,” WFP Deputy Director Cori Marquis said in an interview.
Marquis said choosing to vote for Hochul on the WFP line communicates that voters want to see more action on progressive priorities. It means backing “ the same candidate, but a stronger message,” she said.
While the WFP has worried about not meeting the 2% threshold in past cycles, Marquis said it's “less concerned” this year.
Lange, the political analyst and DSA member, said he planned to vote for Hochul on the WFP line. “I would say the vast majority of my peers would, too,” he said.
As for Hochul, she told a reporter from City & State she didn’t care whether people voted for her on the Democratic or WFP lines.
"OK by me,” the governor said while leaving a Brooklyn Pizza shop over the weekend. “As long as they vote."

https://gothamist.com/news/can-you-eat-t.title: Can you eat the mushrooms growing out of your bathroom ceiling?
https://gothamist.com/news/can-you-eat-t.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/can-you-eat-t.text:
Mushrooms growing from a water-damaged wall or ceiling are one of the more maddening indignities of New York City living. Your apartment is so moist that organic life is sprouting from the walls.
But if you’ve ever gazed at the inky caps and wondered whether they’re edible, we’re here to help. No, you shouldn't eat them.
“You definitely shouldn't eat mushrooms that grow in most places in your house,” said Ethan Crenson, president of the New York Mycological Society. "Because mushrooms can accumulate environmental pollutants, you probably shouldn't eat mushrooms that grow in most places in your house.”
The most common mushrooms growing out of the ceilings and walls in New York City apartments are the Coprinellus domesticus variety. The fungus is non-toxic, according to the New York Mycological Society, but the sight of the coin-sized caps curling out of a wall gives a home dystopian “The Last of Us” decor.
Experts describe the ceiling shrooms' flavor as indistinct and not worth tossing into a risotto. They aren’t edible or tasty, and could cause indigestion or diarrhea.
Greenpoint resident Daniel Moyer knows the mental torment that a mushroom in the ceiling can bring. A friend suggested he eat the 2-inch mushroom growing above the shower in his apartment. Moyer rejected the idea — the mushroom was its own bad trip, and he wanted it gone.
