https://theintercept.com/2026/10/26/mili.title: Pentagon Records Missed Almost Half of Troops’ Domestic Abuse Killings
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/26/mili.author: Daniel Johnson, Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/26/mili.text:
Angelina Resendiz’s voice on the phone was frantic. She was calling a friend from the barracks room of Jermiah Copeland, a fellow sailor at Naval Station Norfolk in Virginia. They had spent the evening together, kissing and drinking, and now Resendiz, 21, needed to leave.
It was the last time anyone would hear from her. When Resendiz’s friend arrived at the barracks 15 minutes later, the pair was nowhere to be found.
“The Navy failed her,” Resendiz’s mother, Esmerelda Castle, told The Intercept. After her daughter’s disappearance, friends and family spent a week scrambling to find Resendiz. Castle found the Navy’s reports in that time unclear, delayed, or downright false.
A first-of-its-kind Intercept investigation has found critical shortcomings in the U.S. military’s procedures for documenting and preserving records of homicides that result from domestic abuse, including intimate partner violence. The Pentagon’s mandated reports to Congress appear to substantially undercount these killings, omitting nearly half of cases.
In the six years before Copeland’s murder of Resendiz, the Pentagon recorded 41 domestic abuse-related homicides committed by service members. The Intercept identified nearly twice as many: at least 73 potential cases involving 79 victims — almost all of them women — during the same period. Reports for fiscal year 2025, when Resendiz was murdered, are due in November.
The Intercept examined publicly available news articles, obituaries, court records, memorials, and other data to investigate the specifics behind the Defense Department’s numbers. Reporters also used data obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request on Army noncombat fatalities to match names, because some news coverage did not mention the victims’ and alleged perpetrators’ military service.
A killing qualified for the dataset if it occurred in fiscal years 2019 to 2024; if the perpetrator was a member of the military at the time of the crime; and if the case involved a homicide. The database only includes cases where a victim of the violence had dated or was in a romantic relationship with the suspected perpetrator, and it includes multiple women living abroad who were foreign citizens dating American troops.
In the fiscal years since the second Trump administration took power, The Intercept found at least 10 service women or women working for the Defense Department have died from intimate partner and domestic violence, six of them killed by male co-workers. An additional 10 civilian women have been killed by male military personnel in intimate partner violence-related homicides during the same period.
A Pentagon spokesperson acknowledged The Intercept’s queries about the discrepancy in homicide rates but did not respond to detailed questions before publication.
“At this moment in our country’s history, I am afraid these numbers are going to increase even further,” said Jacquelyn Campbell, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Nursing who has been studying domestic violence in the military for decades. “We need primary prevention for everyone in the military and their partners.”
The findings come in the wake of President Donald Trump’s August announcement of a Military Spouse Commission, led by Jennifer Hegseth, the wife of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and other high-level military leaders. The commission’s mandate is to guide policy around issues affecting military families. Though intimate partner violence and spousal abuse have concerned military family advocates for decades and thousands of new cases are reported each year, the commission does not mention the issue as one of its areas of focus.
The Navy and DoD have said in public statements and communication with members of Congress and Castle that while “proper procedures were followed” following the death of Resendiz, they have identified several processes that require further review.
“What Are the Statistics?”
Copeland killed Resendiz on May 29, 2025. In the days after Resendiz’s disappearance, her friends filed missing person reports and called Castle in Texas, who in turn called the Navy. None of them knew that Resendiz was dead.
The Navy’s official timeline of events says it did not start investigating her disappearance as a crime until a missing person’s report was filed on the 31st, and that Castle did not reach out until that day. Phone records she shared with The Intercept and members of Congress show she started calling on the 29th.
“I was told she was found, and that the original missing person’s report was exaggerated,” Castle recalled. “I didn’t think for a second that the Navy would lie to me.
Technically, Resendiz had been found — a Navy chief searching for her had seen Resendiz’s body packed under the covers in Copeland’s bed around 10 a.m. on the day of her disappearance. They assumed she was asleep, according to evidence later revealed during trial. But as Castle tells it — including in a congressional inquiry she wrote requesting a deeper investigation— a Navy chief claimed on the phone to have spoken to her daughter in Copeland’s room.
She had been dead for hours.
“He had Angie wrapped up in a blanket on his bed,” said Castle. “It was against policy for her to be in the barracks. And they just turned their backs and left.”
Intimate partner violence in the military has long been a problem with unclear signs of progress. Killings in the 1990s on bases such as Fort Campbell made national headlines, leading Congress to establish the Defense Task Force on Domestic Violence in 2000.
Campbell, the nursing professor, was part of the effort, which issued over 200 suggestions for improvement by 2003. “Most of the recommendations we made a long time ago were never implemented,” she said. For one, she’d repeatedly requested better recordkeeping.
“One of the things I kept asking was, ‘What are the statistics on intimate partner homicide in the military?’ We could never get them,” Campbell said. “And in the military’s suicide reports, you cannot determine how many suicides were part of homicide–suicides, where a service member killed a civilian wife or partner before killing himself.”
This lack of clarity sounded familiar to Priscilla Rodriguez, who spent 10 years in the Marine Corps before working in strategic communications for the Navy.
Rodriguez experienced domestic violence that met the Defense Department’s criteria from her husband, an active-duty Marine at the time, according to documents reviewed by The Intercept. Her husband pleaded guilty to misdemeanor child abuse in civilian courts, and military legal authorities recommended domestic violence charges. “The command chose not to pursue military legal action,” Rodriguez said.
The Intercept’s analysis of the rates of domestic abuse reported in Pentagon data found intimate partner violence among married military couples was at least four times higher than the civilian rate. The Pentagon does not report the rate of abuse involving unmarried intimate partners, like Resendiz and Copeland.
Gaps like these make it difficult to have a thorough reckoning of the problem’s scale. “When accountability is inconsistent,” Rodriguez said, “it sends a message that abuse can and will remain hidden.”
“I Knew My Kid Was Not Coming Back”
Copeland kept Resendiz’s corpse hidden in his barracks room for four days, until June 2, 2025, when he put her body into a duffel bag and dumped it in a wooded area behind a nearby elementary school.
By then, he was being questioned by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service on her whereabouts, and Castle was still wondering about her daughter’s safety. She’d asked naval authorities to have her daughter give her a call, and when it never came, she contacted the base again.
A Navy official suggested her daughter may have gone AWOL.
“I didn’t believe that,” Castle said. “My kid is scared to miss work. She won’t take off.”
Castle flew to Virginia herself.
Resendiz had been dead for a week. Castle felt she wasn’t getting the information she needed after the Navy and local authorities had put out a statewide missing person’s alert. She requested that she be let into her daughter’s barracks room.
“I didn’t want anyone else touching her stuff,” Castle said. “It was how she left it. There was still paint out; she had started painting again. Her yoga mat was still out. She had planned on returning. I knew my kid was not coming back.”
She spent two more days in Virginia searching for her daughter, talking to local news, and asking naval authorities to give more updates.
“They didn’t declare her AWOL or dead,” Castle said. “They said she was duty status unknown. I was worried they were going to wash their hands of her.”
On June 7, Castle flew back to Texas. Police found Resendiz’s body in the duffel bag two days later.
A History of Violence
Jermiah Copeland was convicted of Resendiz’s murder on June 8, 2026. According to evidence entered into court records in his murder trial, he had also been accused of two instances of domestic violence, three sexual assaults, indecent recordings, and other crimes from during and before his Navy service.
“He had a history of violence against women starting in high school,” Castle said. “And was still allowed to join with the charges against him. Then he was accused of raping another service member, and he was transferred. There were no safeguards in place at the new command.”
The absence of safeguards against intimate partner violence in the military is part of a broader set of structural and cultural failings, experts told The Intercept.
“There are many disincentives for a couple, particularly when one or both partners are on active duty, to seek help,” Campbell said. “Active-duty women who were being abused told us: ‘If my commanding officer knew, I would never get the next promotion.’ There is considerable stigma, even for the victim. That makes the violence much more likely to escalate and makes it more likely that we eventually end up with homicides.”
Research indicates that the military’s hypermasculine culture and systematic mistreatment of women play a role in the increased risks of intimate partner violence. Some studies suggest that veterans offend at higher rates than those on active duty.
A previous Intercept investigation found active-duty Army women were more likely to be killed by fellow service members than by enemy combatants and had a higher per capita risk of homicide than their fellow male soldiers between the years 2011 and 2025.
More than 70 percent of the victims had an intimate relationship with the perpetrator at some point. Army women faced an intimate partner homicide rate at least three times higher than women nationally; controlling for those killed by service men and male veterans alone, it was double.
The military’s systems for identifying and responding to abuse, meanwhile, have come under repeated scrutiny. A 2021 Government Accountability Office report found the department “has not collected and reported accurate data for all domestic abuse allegations received,” leaving it unable to assess the scope of alleged abuse.
The same can be said for homicides.
Almost a third of the 79 victims The Intercept found were killed in murder–suicides. Firearms were used in over two-thirds of the fatalities. Twenty-five of the victims were service members. Multiple homicides involved corollary victims who were not partners, including children, who research shows make up a sizable amount of intimate partner violence-related deaths.
In response to The Intercept’s questions, the Department of Defense stated that data in its domestic abuse reports does not constitute estimates, as it is only using aggregated data from the Family Advocacy Program Central Registry, a database run by the DoD. It further stated it did not have any more information to share on the matter.
“Right now, unless an incident is reported to the Family Advocacy Program,” said Campbell, “nobody knows about it. Those reports are only the tip of the iceberg.”
Data tracking failures have had deadly consequences. The Air Force failed to submit the criminal history of a former service member convicted of assaulting his wife and stepson to a federal database that could have prevented him from purchasing firearms. In 2017, he killed 26 people in Sutherland Springs, Texas.
When Rodriguez reported her own abuse to the DoD, she felt that they didn’t consider the previous information they had available. Installation-level committees review reported allegations and determine whether they meet criteria to be input into the central registry. But the process is plagued with issues, experts who spoke to the Intercept revealed, from investigation procedures to data tracking.
“I was terrified to disclose the full extent of the abuse I was experiencing,” Rodriguez said. “What stands out to me now is that the Family Advocacy Program already had access to my husband’s history. Given that history, I believe the conversation should have been much broader than simply asking whether I wanted to report anything. I left that initial interaction without understanding what support existed or how I could safely leave.”
While navigating her own case, Rodriguez was also watching the same problem surface through her communications work for the Navy.
“Headlines I monitored involved active duty and Marine veterans accused of intimate partner homicide,” Rodriguez said. “At the same time, I reviewed serious incident reports that were elevated to senior leadership. … The narrative often indicated that intimate partner violence or domestic violence was a contributing or co-occurring factor.”
Navy criminal investigative data showed domestic violence-related deaths increasing as Rodriguez was trying to raise the issue in 2022. She tried to compile domestic violence awareness resources, but she recalled being told the need wasn’t there.
“I was told there was ‘no demand signal,’” Rodriguez said. “It felt completely disconnected from the reality my family and so many others were living.”
Castle feels that the knowledge of Copeland’s history of abuse could have saved her daughter’s life.
“No one knew anything about him,” Castle said. “The leadership created an environment that allowed him to harm women.”
Winnable Cases
Since her daughter’s murder, Castle has been at work pushing the Navy and Defense Department to strengthen their responses to intimate partner violence. Her work led to the Navy changing its policies in July on how it transfers sailors with allegations of sexual violence.
Her wins, including potential plans by the Navy to change how it classifies missing sailors, are the latest in a long string of limited efforts toward progress.
“Records are important,” said Castle. “With my daughter, they didn’t want to classify her case properly at first. For the military, if something isn’t in a database, it doesn’t exist.”
Following the high-profile 2020 murder of Army Spc. Vanessa Guillén at Fort Hood — and two years after domestic violence became classified as a crime under the Uniform Code of Military Justice — Congress gave independent military prosecutors the power to decide which cases to bring to trial.
Domestic violence prosecutions climbed, with charges brought in 359 cases last year alone, up from dozens of cases four years earlier. But Pentagon data identified at least 25,000 intimate partner and spouse abuse victims, and 37,000 cases, from 2021 to 2024.
And while domestic violence prosecutions increased, military prosecutions of sexual assault — often related to intimate partner violence — fell by almost 60 percent in the past five years, based on data from its annual sexual assault prevention reports. A 20 percent drop occurred from 2024–2025 alone, and The Intercept’s analysis of military court data shows the trend is continuing into 2026.
“In the Pete Hegseth era, sexual assault prosecutions have dropped significantly. Domestic violence is essentially filling that gap,” said Paul Newell, an Army veteran and activist who tracks military suicide, sexual assault, and domestic violence while engaging with members of Congress on the issue.
Newell thinks the trial counsel’s office is “going for what they feel are stronger, more winnable cases,” he said. “They’ll tell you that their conviction rates at trial are still high, which shows that really, they’re just getting rid of the bad cases,” he said. “But we’re not down 60 percent in sexual assaults happening.”
The Pentagon stated in response to The Intercept’s questions that it does not have any additional information to share on why prosecution rates for certain crimes are dropping.
The Intercept also discovered preferential treatment in trial outcomes: Analyzing over 650 military court cases with guilty verdicts from 2021 on, reporters found less senior Navy, Marine, and Army service members had higher chances of losing their benefits and received more jail time after being convicted for domestic violence. Senior ranks closest to retirement received the best conviction outcomes, even compared to those of the same rank as them who had fewer years in service.
Newell feels that these discrepancies give perpetrators increased power over their victims. “The justice system should not take time in service into consideration since that’s prioritizing the perpetrator. If the punishment for domestic violence is a discharge where you lose benefits, it should be applied equally.”
In April, Hegseth directed installation commanders to allow service members to request permission to carry privately owned firearms on bases while off duty. He framed the change as a way to protect service members from attacks on military installations.
Campbell disagrees.
“I have reviewed far too many domestic violence homicide records,” Campbell said. “It is clear to me that, in many cases, there might have been a fight, and somebody might have been hit, but nobody would have died if there had not been a gun right there.”
Rodriguez, who is now studying public health, is calling for recurring anonymous surveys using specific questions to measure the prevalence of intimate partner violence, standardized tracking, independent evaluation, and public reporting.
Castle is still mourning her daughter and still pushing the Navy to reveal the full details about the investigation into her death. To add to the insult, she remembered the shock she felt late last June, when the Navy sent Resendiz home to Texas in a casket. Naval officials had told Castle that everything was taken care of, she recalled, including cleaning the body.
The Navy acknowledges that it failed to clearly inform Castle of her daughter’s true state. She was returned to Texas in decay, her body crawling with maggots.
“There’s nothing that can be done for her,” said Castle. “That’s injustice, and that’s what drives me. None of these women volunteered to be violated in this way.”
How we analyzed the data
Reporters searched through multiple databases to identify the number of potential victims of intimate partner violence, using definitions provided by health and policy research alongside government organizations, comparing it to the last six years of available DoD reporting from 2019 through 2024. The case of a U.S. Air Force airman who kidnapped and murdered a Mennonite woman in 2020 didn’t meet criteria because evidence revealed no previous or current relationship. The case of a soldier who was convicted a year later of the murder of a woman in Texas did, as evidence indicated they had a relationship before the woman’s death.
Cases were broken down by the year of the offense, gender of the alleged perpetrator and victim, and branch of the perpetrator and victim, if applicable.
To analyze court data, reporters from The Intercept pulled all court cases pertaining to domestic violence from the years 2021 to 2026 from the websites of the Air Force, Navy/Marines, and U.S. Army. Navy/Marine data was only available starting in 2021.
Data included the offense type, rank of the accused, and whether the cases ended in acquittal, dismissal, or conviction. For those convicted, the analysis included the amount of jail time given and whether offenders received a punitive discharge, which costs them military retirement and other benefits.
Retirement eligibility was calculated based on pay information provided in court documents, which in the military is based on years served. Air Force data could not be used for this analysis due to a lack of documentation and apparent discrepancies between the number of cases reported to Congress and those available on the Air Force portal.
To obtain the number of cases the DoD is prosecuting for sexual assault, reporters utilized Annex B of the DoD’s Annual Report on Sexual Assault in the Military to calculate the number of unrestricted reports made to military authorities and the amount sent to the military justice system to begin the judicial process.
The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline offers 24-hour support for those experiencing suicidal thoughts or for those close to them, by chat, text, or telephone. Service members can dial 988 and press 1 to reach the Military and Veterans Crisis Line. Support is free and confidential.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

The false choices behind “cultural heritage”
ON NOVEMBER 5, 2022, two activists from the environmental group Futuro Vegetal entered the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid, paid the admission fee, and walked through the permanent collection galleries. Arriving at the rooms devoted to Francisco de Goya, they glued their hands to the frames of La maja desnuda (The Nude Maja), 1795–1800, and La maja vestida (The Clothed Maja), 1800–1807, two of the artist’s most emblematic works. On the wall between them they scrawled a figure: “+1,5°C,” a reference to the warming threshold set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, which commits signatory countries to keeping the rise in global average temperature from exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, the point beyond which the effects of climate change are projected to be especially severe and irreversible. The campaigners were responding to a UN report released the week before the protest, which warned that the world was on track to exceed that limit. Their stated aim wasn’t to damage the artwork but to draw attention to what they saw as a failure to meet the scale of the emergency. They were later arrested and charged with crimes against cultural heritage and public disorder. The Prado filed a complaint against them, seeking an exemplary punishment, even though the harm caused was minimal. The case is still pending, and if found guilty, the protesters could face up to three years in prison.
Not long after the demonstration, a well-known Spanish cultural journalist, alarmed by the action of these “agitators,” asked me at a press conference what could be done to prevent those “vandals” from continuing their “misdeeds.” “Let’s all try to bring down that one and a half degrees together,” I recall replying. “The problem will be solved, and we will live in a better world.” She did not appreciate the response. In her view, I was confusing art with politics—making the same error she attributed to the activists. “They have no reason to protest in a museum and put its paintings at risk,” she said, visibly annoyed. I understood that the reporter was pushing me not so much because she wanted my opinion on the action, but because she expected me, as a museum director, to take an unequivocal stance against it. In fact, I agreed with both the protesters’ cause and the setting they chose for their action. The episode was a symptom of the inability of institutions to respond to some of the most urgent problems of our time.
WHY ATTACK A PAINTING? It is clear that the activists wanted to expose the contradictions of an art system that organizes major exhibitions and debates on extractivism, racism, and identity, yet at the same time proves resistant to any direct political engagement with those very same issues. The protest laid bare how difficult it is for many museums to act politically from the symbolic place they occupy in society. To target cultural heritage is to strike out at a worldview that unhesitatingly protects its treasures, but not the lives that give them meaning.
The term heritage is most commonly used in the sense of a body of cultural traditions, but it originally referred to an inherited estate: something possessed by birthright, property passed down to an heir. The nation-state constructs heritage with the aim of distinguishing itself from other nation-states, creating a tension between inside and outside. Whoever remains outside becomes, in this logic, the radically different other, necessary for self-definition yet always perceived as a potential threat. When the balance between these two impulses breaks down, heritage becomes a locus of conflict.
The scientific utopia of the Enlightenment aspired to a form of total knowledge that would encompass all beings and things. Nineteenth-century European empires pursued this ambition through the systematic extraction of animal specimens and cultural objects from distant territories. In 1798, the Napoleonic army entered Egypt accompanied by 167 archaeologists and scientists tasked with securing material for the future Musée Napoléon, better known as the Louvre. This heterogeneous accumulation was subjected to classification, ordering, and hierarchization. Each artifact was isolated and reassigned: art with art, nature with nature, politics with politics. This body of learning was then divided into sealed disciplines. Once the items were in Europe, museums and academies determined what counted as art, what qualified as science, and what was relegated to superstition. At the center stood the white European subject. Other peoples were displaced to the margins, or expelled from history altogether.
Who sets these rules? Who decides that a canvas carries more weight than a tree or a forest? We might be told that there is no need to choose between a tree and a painting, that both can and should be protected. But we know that is not the case, and that, deep down, a choice has been made—and not by us. Exhibitions dealing with politics or ecology are welcomed as long as they remain confined to discourse. In fact, the Prado itself had, a few years earlier, in 2019, collaborated with the World Wildlife Fund on an environmental-awareness campaign titled “+1.5°C Lo Cambia Todo” (+1.5°C Changes Everything). It featured several famous paintings from the collection, which had been digitally altered to depict the catastrophic effects of floods, pollution, and so on. And yet, the moment a couple of young people glue their hands to a frame, alarms go off. What irritated my stressed journalist was not the subject of the protest itself, but the fact that it unfolded within those walls. She, like many others, was horrified by the idea of a “politicized” museum—which is rather absurd, since a museum is by its very nature political.
ON OCTOBER 25, 2025, the Fondation Cartier opened its new headquarters in Paris with an exhibition of nearly six hundred works from around the world, arranged in four thematic sections: “Machines d’architecture” (Architecture Machines), “Être nature” (Be Natural), “Making Things,” and “Un monde réel” (A Real World). The curators, Béatrice Grenier and Grazia Quaroni, sought to pay homage to the building’s history. It was constructed in 1855 to house visitors to that year’s Exposition Universelle. In 1887 it became Les Grands Magasins du Louvre, a department store that offered every kind of item (toys, clothing, furniture, and so on), the heterogeneity of its wares shaping the spirit of the place: Any object could find a home there, under a single principle—that of merchandise. The title of Grenier and Quaroni’s project, “Exposition générale,” referred directly to the slogan under which the store first welcomed the public.
The selection of works appeared, at first glance, well-judged and harmoniously arranged, and the issues the exhibition addressed seemed pertinent (relations between human and nonhuman, science fiction, utopian construction, and the many ways of inhabiting Earth). I am convinced that the Futuro Vegetal collective would have found nothing to object to, were it not for the fact that conflict was simply absent from the show. The display failed to produce any meaningful commotion in the viewer, since it appeared to have been designed above all to facilitate a smooth and agreeable visit. The space, renovated by Jean Nouvel, reinforced that impression, with diffuse lighting and industrial materials that recalled his design for Paris’s Musée du quai Branly, devoted to non-Western art. As in nineteenth-century fairs, the pieces here were presented as deterritorialized, without any specific context reflecting the conditions under which the artists produced them, nor the communities to which they were addressed. This was the case with the interior design scheme for one of Bolivian architect Freddy Mamani’s cholets, multiuse structures in a neo-Andean style that he has erected across the city of El Alto, where he lives and works. (The name is a portmanteau of chalet and cholo, a derogatory term in Bolivia for Indigenous or mestizo migrant workers.) The display here told us nothing about the economy and culture of El Alto, the cholo culture, or the complex political and social reality of Bolivia. Instead, Mamani’s work was reduced to a set of strident shapes and colors with parallels in urban scenes elsewhere on the planet, or identified with another colonial universal: Indigenous baroque. Every meaningful difference was flattened into a falsely monolithic idea of style.
As if unconsciously echoing the building’s commercial past, the exhibition evoked the logic of an art fair. Though the wall labels dutifully invoked extractivism, heteropatriarchy, and racism, the installation suggested, above all, a regime of collectible goods, with objects grouped like bazaar commodities. Nothing was for sale at “Exposition générale,” but the prevailing logic was decidedly commercial: the capacity to incite and regulate desire, displacing practices grounded in specific communities and cultures and sustained through shared social ties. The show failed to produce the transformative effect promised by the institution, refusing to conjure that luminous future the curators spoke of in some of the promotional material. Viewers encountered the violence of the present without disturbance. Yet as one stood in the exhibition, it was entirely possible to forget that Nazi banners once hung from the facades on that same stretch of the rue de Rivoli. Art operates here as an invitation to anesthesia.
Cartier’s new initiative joins those of the Fondation Louis Vuitton, in the Bois de Boulogne, or of the Bourse du Commerce, near Les Halles, in the ongoing substitution of the public by the private that has come to define the cultural landscape of the French capital. These enterprises present themselves as custodians of the common good, since they make their collections and educational programs available to the public. In practice, they tend to produce the opposite effect, instantiating a culture of consumption and luxury that is governed through particular exclusionary frameworks. As Athena Athanasiou reminds us, when a public entity becomes corporatized, this affects not only its content and practices, but also the very conditions of possibility for its own transformation.1 The public sphere allows for radical change because it rests on shared laws; the corporate one does not, since its goals and norms are set in advance by the firm.
“Exposition générale,” claimed to amplify silenced voices and to host critical engagements with the present. But the origin of the Fondation Cartier’s funding remains unexamined. So do the working conditions of those who maintain the space, such as cleaners and guards. The ambiguity of this inaugural project reveals a familiar logic within the contemporary art system. Debate is staged, but rarely at the level where it might unsettle structural frameworks, or at least acknowledge its inability to do so.
The system of contemporary art, increasingly privatized, increasingly globalized, and increasingly attentive to absorbing its own critique, repeats the imperial drive to accumulate in different guises. Ultimately, the artistic practices of the colonized are subsumed now, as they were in the nineteenth century, into a generalizing discourse that mobilizes them as evidence of a presumed lag in relation to the metropolitan center.
A museum’s identity is defined by its collection, its program, its governance, and its own history. These dimensions are profoundly interrelated. A public collection is not the same thing as one that serves a firm’s communication strategy. The political dimension of a museum or art center is not limited to the themes its curators choose to address; it also extends to an acknowledgment of the place museums occupy in society. Can we speak of “luminous futures” when they promote self-interest over solidarity? Can we talk about ecology while maintaining sponsorships from extractivist companies? In these cases, thematizing a legitimately pressing societal concern serves to ratify an organization and the power relations it rests on. Critical self-reflexivity is not enough, nor is the argument here that cultural venues should replace different collectives or social movements. What matters is that these spaces recognize their political role—one that is not merely rhetorical—and that the discourse they invite and the institutional objectives they pursue go hand in hand, without foreclosing one another.
AT THE THIRTY-FOURTH SÃO PAULO BIENAL, in 2021, the Makuxi artist Jaider Esbell’s work—a series of strikingly beautiful paintings grounded in the cosmogonies of his community—was widely considered a highlight. Collectors moved quickly to acquire his pieces.
Esbell was not merely an invited artist; he coordinated the participation of fellow Indigenous artists (among them Gustavo Caboco, Sueli Maxakali, Daiara Tukano, and Uýra), acting as a bridge-curator between Indigenous worldviews and the biennial’s own framework. He coined and defended the category of arte indígena contemporânea (AIC), understood not as a simple market label (i.e., one describing standard contemporary art, except made by Indigenous people) but as a cosmopolitical project in its own right, positioned outside the modern/antimodern genealogy of Western art historiography. Where the latter judges a work’s value by its rupture with what came before (novelty as the individual merit of the genius-author), AIC measures its own worth by its capacity to sustain and renew a collective bond with ancestors and nonhuman beings. There is no “originality” in the sense of invention ex nihilo, because nothing belongs exclusively to anyone, not even myth.
It is not that the land, its fruits, or objects, including art, belong to everyone as abstract entities; rather, the community itself is a web of relations that renews itself daily, an order in which belonging rests on living bonds, not on a static legal title. At the biennial, Esbell presented paintings of serpents and protective entities of his people. Although these were executed by Esbell himself, the stories they depict are held in common by everyone; they cannot be reduced to a “theme” within a collection or curatorial program, nor exchanged without the community’s agreement. The entities represented by the serpents and other beings are not decorative motifs; they are real beings with their own agency over the Makuxi people, guarantors of abundance and protection.
On November 2, 2021, at the height of Esbell’s recognition, he was found dead in his São Paulo apartment. The critic Will Furtado characterized his death as the result of “epistemic extractivism”: the idea that Western art circles, even as they celebrated his Indigenous thought, “consumed” him, subjecting him to a demand for production and representation that ultimately proved unsustainable. Whatever other dynamics underwrote this tragic outcome, the broad arc of Esbell’s story, the tension it frames between collective bodies of thought and private markets of ownership, raises a broader question: To whom does culture belong? To those who produce it, to those who interpret it, to the countries that claim it, or to those who find meaning in it? Heritage is not anyone’s property; it belongs to everyone, to those who have shaped it over time, across generations and beyond national borders, and to those who will inherit it in turn. Its safekeeping and direction cannot be determined unilaterally by any single group of actors, be it a board of trustees or political and religious authorities. Cultural organizations, private and public, bear an ethical and legal responsibility to protect their collections—not because they possess them, but because they are held in common.
The commons implies the constant negotiation of distinct ways of knowing and forms of authority. Given that every exchange involves unequal forces, the weight of a judgment or an opinion cannot be determined by the size or power of whoever puts it forward. The norms that shape this shared terrain are relational: They are redefined at every encounter. An object can function, in this case, simultaneously as a work of art, as a spiritual medium, or as a political instrument. Moreover, the slow time of the mutual agreement resists precarity and that same epistemic extractivism denounced by the biennial’s commentators.
The scale of major museum collections is telling. The British Museum in London holds more than eight million objects; the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, around two million; the Louvre in Paris, over half a million. Such figures are obscene. They point to a longer history in which plunder, destruction, and dispossession have been persistent conditions, even as these processes have often been reframed as acts of preservation. The rhetoric of trusteeship obscures the extraction that underpins it, while continuing to generate economic and political value for those who control this heritage, whether as a symbol of national prestige or as a source of revenue drawn from the cultural and tourism industries.
In recent decades, debates over the restitution of illegitimately acquired objects have multiplied. It is evident that what has been stolen must be given back. However, the process must be accompanied by remembrance and reparations. Returning artworks—or the promise to do so, often left unfulfilled—isn’t enough. The wounds inflicted must be made visible. This task must take into account new forms of extractivism and recognize that museums and cultural organizations have frequently provided the setting for these dynamics, legitimizing them. Such patterns are not democratic, since they prevent other cultures from unfolding, making visible, and defending their own modes of self-rule and their place in the world. They are, moreover, impoverishing, since they disregard other ways of inhabiting the planet and push us to accept false dichotomies whose consequences fall on those who do not accept them or for whom they make no sense.
Specialists and enthusiasts have marveled at the beauty of objects displayed in imperial museums. In recent decades, cultural institutions have begun to show some curiosity about their places of origin, and about the paths these objects traveled before reaching their display cases. Yet professional interest in the present-day realities of these countries and their citizens remains practically nonexistent, condemning them to have no voice and no place as subjects of history. To preserve only what is defined as “ours” is to ignore how deeply entangled all forms of heritage are. Histories of migration and displacement—whether chosen or imposed—shape the material and symbolic fabric of every monument, so that what is inherited is never a closed system, but an open field of exchange. Its meaning lies less in discrete objects than in the connections they sustain, which is why engaging with heritage means attending not only to the intellectual traditions from which it emerges, but also to past and future generations. Under these conditions, the notion of property tied to a bounded nation becomes untenable; what constitutes patrimony exceeds the limits of the state.
IN HER EXTRAORDINARY FILM A água é uma máquina do tempo (Water Is a Time Machine, 2024), the Afro-Brazilian artist Aline Motta recounts a childhood memory: Her white neighbor and best friend asked her mother, “Aline, will she get better soon?” The child is referring to the color of Aline’s skin.
Years later, Motta begins to delve into her biography and to translate it into film. On her white father’s side, she traces her lineage back several centuries; on her African maternal side, she can only go as far as her great-great-grandmother Francisca. Little is known about her. The archives are obstinate and silent, recording just her death from tuberculosis. “What kind of history is this that condemns a woman forever?” Motta asks. Faced with the impossibility of an official answer, she decides to reverse the direction of time. If Marty McFly, the protagonist of Back to the Future—a movie she loved as a child—could travel to the past in order to alter the present, why could she not do the same?
Western time is linear and progressive, organized in sequential order, a convenient temporality, since “what is past is past.” We tell ourselves that “mistakes” may have been made in distant eras, but that we now stand “on the right side of history.” Motta, by contrast, proposes a spiral conception of time, capable of moving backward and of “returning” us to the future, thereby unsettling dominant regimes of memory. Should inherited documents merely confirm narratives that perpetuate oppression? Or might heritage be understood as a field capable of activating what never was? The question is how to give form to silenced histories, to recover erased voices, and to imagine lives foreclosed by genocidal violence.
The history of the world is a shared history, rooted in affective and lived experience. Rethinking heritage from this perspective requires questioning not only the term itself but also its etymology. This is precisely what a group of thinkers, cultural practitioners, artists, and activists within the HF Île-de-France association has been doing since 2015. At their annual meeting they advocate for the transformation of the heritage days organized by European Union member states into matrimoine days—employing a medieval term that refers to an inheritance passed down from the mother, in contrast to patrimoine, inherited from the father—dedicated to the study and dissemination of women’s contributions to history. In Roman law, patrimonium and matrimonium were articulated as complementary regimes. The former referred to the wealth a man brought into marriage and transmitted from father to son, securing patrilineal descent, while matrimonium designated the woman’s role within the marital bond: reproduction, the body, and care for offspring. If “patrimony” secured wealth and male lineage, “matrimony” contributed the production of life. In the sixteenth century, this “good of the mother” gradually shifted into “the mother as a property,” and marriage became increasingly subject to forms of consumption and control by the husband. Yet the claim advanced by the HF movement remains pertinent in proposing another conception of historical inheritance—one that privileges not the individual, the isolated object, or the nation-state, but what belongs to all.
Embracing the memories of the tout-monde, which include the actions of humans and nonhumans, works of art, or therolinguistic expressions (to borrow a term from Ursula K. Le Guin), is key to understanding a common world. It implies recognizing that the suffering produced by systemic violence concerns all of us, and that this “all” can no longer be restricted to the human. The doings of the Earth community must be aligned with geological, climatic, vegetal, animal, and microbial temporalities. We are summoned by all forms of the living: from the whole world to the whole planet.
The center is the Earth, not the human species. Within this framework, the subject–object dialectic loses its validity, as does a historiography based exclusively on documents and artifacts. Things are not inert; they are animated presences. Can we still speak of “art” in the sense that has prevailed since the eighteenth century? Clearly not. What, then, constitutes our legacy? Monuments, relics, and archives will persist, but they will no longer occupy a privileged position. There is no single locus of meaning, only an archipelago of heterogeneous relations. This implies a radical reconfiguration of the ways in which we imagine, preserve, and transmit past and future. Within the notion of matrimoine, culture is not property but offering. One does not choose between a painting and a tree. Caring for one entails caring for the other.
Manuel Borja-Villel is the 2026 Chair of Spanish Culture and Civilization at New York University. He was director of the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía from 2008 to 2023.
Notes:
1. Athena Athanasiou, “La desposesión como epistemología de la criticalidad,” in Communismos por venir, ed. Pablo Martínez (MACBA, 2019): 127.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-bolson.title: Election Denial Is Now Normal for the Right Everywhere
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-bolson.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-bolson.text:
Election Denial Is Now Normal for the Right Everywhere
Refusing to concede and trying to overturn the election result isn’t just limited to Donald Trump anymore. This past week makes clear it’s now the playbook for every right-wing politician who loses an election.
The series of recent elections across the globe have been read as a stinging defeat for right-wing authoritarians, which they are. But maybe more notable is another element: that denial of and efforts to simply reverse unfavorable election results now seem to have become de rigueur for the transnational Right.
All four of the major elections taking place in the ten-day period from October 25 to November 3 have seen or are seeing efforts by right-wing politicians to cast doubt on results where they lost or are likely to, and to engineer a way to change them in their favor.
In Brazil, right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro — whose father is serving a twenty-seven-year prison sentence for trying to organize a coup when he lost the presidential election four years ago — responded to his own shock defeat by announcing a legal challenge to annul the result over the courts’ last-minute extension of voting hours (even though his own campaign had requested the extension). Flávio has now, Juan Guaidó–style, just declared himself the president from Miami, alleging election fraud (before, confusingly, almost immediately deleting the post and declaring himself the country’s rightful “leader” instead).

https://www.propublica.org/article/bird-.title: Bird Flu Is Raging on a Mink Farm. It Could Spark a Human Pandemic, Experts Say, but Officials Won’t Act.
https://www.propublica.org/article/bird-.author: Nat Lash, Julie Leopo
https://www.propublica.org/article/bird-.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Deadly Outbreak: A bird flu outbreak has been raging uncontrolled on a Utah mink farm for two months. Flu experts fear it could spark a devastating human pandemic.
- Government Failures: State officials didn’t order the mink to be killed, which other countries with outbreaks have done. They are prioritizing the financial interests of the fur trade.
- Silent Risks: Despite CDC guidance urging officials to monitor workers, they actively chose not to and declined to test workers — including one with a symptom experts said would warrant testing.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
The strain of bird flu that’s ripped through American barns for the last four years has killed two people who caught it from sick animals. But as far as anyone can tell, humans can’t spread it. The virus has remained a true “bird” flu, tailored to attach to avian cells, not invade human throats and noses, where coughing and sneezing reliably spew droplets.
Under the right conditions, however, that could change. A single mutation could give the bird flu a foothold in people and spark a pandemic that experts fear could be deadlier than COVID-19.
For that to happen, this bird flu would likely need to find an intermediate host — an animal vulnerable to viruses that infect both birds and humans. These animals would be crowded together, each infection raising the odds that a new strain could arise through mutation. Then, for that strain to jump across species, it would have to have access to humans and time to spread among them undetected.
That perfect petri dish exists right now, a ProPublica investigation found. For over two months, an outbreak of bird flu has raged uncontrolled on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur. Mink have lungs and airways that on a cellular level are remarkably similar to those of people; they have caught and spread other flus and infected some humans with COVID-19.
Instead of trying to stop the outbreak and prevent it from spilling into humans, state and federal officials have done little except try to keep its existence quiet, our investigation shows. The failure to act amounts to a cascade of missteps flu experts called “irresponsible” and “puzzling.” One called it “playing with fire.”
Utah agriculture officials learned in mid-August that mink were dying of bird flu on C&T Fenn Farms, about an hour’s drive south from Salt Lake City, according to communications released under the state’s public records law.
Had poultry been infected, the playbook would have been clear: The strain is so virulent that if a single chicken tests positive, the U.S. government requires farmers to kill the whole flock to protect other farms as well as public health. Poultry farmers are reimbursed for the loss.
But there are no federal rules for how to deal with sick mink.
Handling Utah’s response was state veterinarian Amanda Price, who sought help from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which takes the lead on bird flu outbreaks involving poultry and cows.
USDA officials said they didn’t regulate mink or have a vaccine that was approved to give them. And though officials with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention spoke with Price’s health department counterparts who were less involved with the outbreak, they never talked to her, and she never reached out.
The threat of spillover has been far from the minds of Utah officials, records and interviews show. Instead, front and center have been the interests of a business raising animals to skin for luxury pelts to ship overseas.
“It has been devastating,” Price told ProPublica of the outbreak and its impact on the farm’s owner. “This is his life’s work that he’s seeing be destroyed. I really hope that you understand the humanity behind this situation.”
Flu experts were unequivocal that the government should have ordered the farm to cull its mink, as other countries have done.
But Utah never seriously considered it. A fur trade representative warned Price that doing so would kill the business and, ultimately, the industry. Farms spend decades breeding mink to develop unique genetic lineages.
“There’s just not a lot of options out there other than kind of sitting and waiting and seeing what happens,” Price said, noting that USDA officials did not urge her to kill the mink or make her feel like bird flu in mink was any riskier than infections in other animals that have caught it, like ducks and cows.
Flu experts found that response surprising.
“Every other country that I’m aware of that has had H5N1 in fur farms, depopulation has happened pretty quickly,” said Tom Peacock, an avian influenza researcher at the Pirbright Institute. “The fact that the first instinct wasn’t just to depopulate and figure stuff out later is very concerning to me.”
And all the while, officials didn’t monitor the mink workers for symptoms, as guidance from the CDC urges.
Their exposure is significant: Mink sneeze. They escape. They attack. “The mink are fierce,” said a Spanish-speaking “minkero” who works on a nearby farm, showing the scars he got from the aggressive, solitary creatures. “You get scared because the fucking thing bites, and it claws at you.”
Right now in Washington state, officials are working to track down the contacts of a symptomatic person exposed to dairy cattle infected with bird flu. The patient is isolating at home. Utah public health officials used to do similar, proactive monitoring. But they stopped after complaints from their colleagues in the agriculture department that farmers were annoyed by it.
“Us doing active monitoring was making it so that farms didn’t want to work with them,” said Pamela Gomez Pinedo, a respiratory disease epidemiologist for Utah’s health department. As a result, public health workers had a “pretty difficult time” getting details from agriculture officials, she said.
As part of a 2025 agreement, the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food agreed to share information about bird flu outbreaks on farms — so long as the health officials didn’t do anything to track workers’ health.
“We will only do active monitoring in the case of evidence of human-to-human transmission,” Pinedo said in emails with a CDC epidemiologist. As the outbreak stretched to a month, CDC officials expressed concerns, asking how anyone would know if a worker had been infected if they weren’t getting tested.
Price said the state’s policy not to monitor workers is meant to allow farmers to decide whether to contact the health department, rather than “forcing it on them.” “If we started seeing people actively dying from this, obviously that would change how we respond to this,” she said.
A telltale sign of bird flu infection in humans is eye redness. It is present in over 90% of cases and is often the sole symptom a person displays.
Last Saturday, a ProPublica reporter tracked down two people who worked at the Utah mink farm. One had a visibly red eye.
The CDC explicitly urges testing for the symptom.
After ProPublica reached out to the farm, its owner, Chad Fenn, contacted the Utah County Health Department about the red eye, which had cleared up by Monday, he told ProPublica. He said the worker got dust in his eye; the department didn’t recommend testing.
“They’re not going to do anything,” Fenn said. “They said they don’t see that there’s a need.” He said the department recommended testing only if other symptoms, like a cough or sore throat, developed.
A half dozen flu experts had no shortage of adjectives to describe their disbelief at the government decisions not to cull the mink or monitor and test the workers.
“It’s amazing to me,” said Gail Hansen, a former Kansas state public health veterinarian and epidemiologist. “Utah doesn’t want to be the epicenter of the next human flu outbreak, right?”
Most of the new viruses that have shaken humanity in the past century have spilled over from animals. Ebolas likely came from fruit bats; HIV, from chimpanzees. The leading theory for COVID-19 is that it jumped from bats to humans via an intermediate host mammal such as a raccoon dog. And all the modern flu pandemics have been bird flu viruses that mutated to spread in humans.
ProPublica reported extensively on spillover in a 2023 series called “Roots of an Outbreak.” To prevent more deadly spillovers, experts worldwide urge governments to take a “one health” approach to viral threats, treating dangers to animals as dangers to humans.
That’s not happening in Utah, experts said after reviewing ProPublica’s findings. Both the state and federal government are to blame.
“There’s no leader of this ‘one health’ team to take charge,” said Erin Sorrell, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “That is going to allow the virus to continue to circulate, potentially adapt and potentially spill over into another host, whether it’s avian, mammalian or human.”
This strain of bird flu, which began ripping through American poultry farms in early 2022, has proved adept at jumping to other species. It took hold in cows in 2024 and since then has run rampant through dairies.
Yet federal guidance to prevent the spread into mink farms hasn’t considered cows a threat. Farmers are encouraged to keep wild birds from infiltrating their barns and avoid feeding them raw poultry. It has said nothing about feeding beef parts to mink, which farmers commonly do in summer months to encourage the animals to put on weight and grow.
Dairy cows, which are not “depopulated” if exposed to bird flu, can still be slaughtered with the meat sold to farms and humans even though researchers have found the virus in the tissues of sick cows. USDA officials have insisted that beef for human consumption is free of bird flu, in part because the virus concentrates itself in sections of the cow people don’t usually eat. Fenn said that the mink are routinely fed raw organs of livestock, including cows.
The genomic data from the samples of mink lungs and brains sent from Utah to a USDA lab shows that the mink were stricken with the same strain of the virus that has spread in dairy herds. Officials said they didn’t know whether contaminated beef was the way the mink got infected.
In mink, the dairy strain of bird flu may have found a much better host for mutating into a human flu, because mink airways have an abundance of the type of cell receptors in people’s throats and noses that are a common pathway for infection.
A 2024 study of the dairy strain of the bird flu found that a single mutation could switch the virus from preferring the bird-type receptors to human-type receptors. And in studies using ferrets, a close relative of mink, the virus acquired mutations that let it attack human-type cell receptors.
It’s not clear to scientists just how much of an evolutionary leap would be needed for this strain of bird flu to spread among humans, or whether mink are the host that would allow that leap to happen.
How this ultimately plays out “really depends on what happens with the virus,” said Meghan Davis, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
“We might get lucky, and a response that is not robust may not have dire consequences,” she said. “But we may get unlucky.”
There’s also a risk of something called “reassortment,” where another flu virus could infect the same cell as a bird flu virus and swap wide swaths of genetic code already adapted to humans.
When the outbreak in the mink farm started, there was very little seasonal flu it could mix with, but September saw one of the earliest starts to flu season on record, compared with November, when flu normally takes off.
“The most likely scenario for a pandemic is that we have a virus that reassorts with another virus,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. “Obviously, having this circulate amid human flu season is not great.”
Utah officials were far more responsive to the threat of spillover in 2020, when outbreaks of COVID-19 spread explosively on mink farms – including this very farm. They invited federal officials to the state to research how the virus adapted and moved.
Given mink’s reputation as escape artists, wildlife experts set up traps around infected farms. The traps frequently caught mink carrying COVID-19 that had originated in the nearby barns. The virus infected both escaped mink and wild mink they had come in contact with. Mink and farmworkers were frequently tested, tracking the way that the virus was spreading and mutating.
As other states and countries took the same measures, they identified humans infected by the mink with COVID-19 and, ultimately, human-to-human transmission.
There are no similar efforts now in Utah with bird flu.
A USDA spokesperson told ProPublica that it was more involved in 2020 because the virus that causes COVID-19 had “significant” potential to transmit between humans and animals and vice versa.
Scientists with the USDA sequenced and published bird flu genomic data from the first samples of dead mink. Those sequences didn’t show any particularly concerning mutations, experts and the CDC told ProPublica.
But in the past two months, experts said, the virus is sure to have continued mutating as it spread – it’s only a question of whether those mutations could confer some advantage in infecting humans as well.
“As long as it continues to go mink to mink, then it becomes more and more likely that it could jump to a human,” Hansen said.
Fenn said new samples were taken two weeks ago. Price said she is still waiting for the results.
John Korslund, a retired USDA official who helped coordinate the response to COVID-19 on mink farms several years prior, was one of several experts who said officials need to look closely at newer genetic samples to see how the virus is evolving.
“I really want to know what the virus has done, from when it started to today,” he said. “Are we getting accumulated mutations making the virus more dangerous?”
ProPublica began reporting on the outbreak late this summer after the USDA updated a bird flu dashboard that showed seven captive mink had tested positive in Utah. But neither the USDA nor state officials had said anything publicly, and, when asked, they wouldn’t discuss what was actually happening on the farm.
Communications obtained under the state’s public records law — first published by the Animal Welfare Institute and reported on by the Salt Lake Tribune — show Utah officials took pains to protect the farm’s privacy amid the outbreak. The state did not declare an emergency, because doing so, officials said, “may alert animal rights groups,” according to the messages.
Willy Lanier, a public health veterinarian with the state health department, told colleagues to keep the outbreak under “closer hold” than outbreaks of bird flu on poultry and dairy farms. Keeping the information confidential was consistent with state protocol, a spokesperson in his department said, adding that it was still shared with local health officials. But when ProPublica reached out to the spokesperson for the Utah County Health Department about a possible bird flu outbreak, she said, “That would be news to me.”
Price is so deferential to the family that owns the farm that she has not set foot on the property.
“I’m really the only one here at this facility that’s been dealing with the producer. They’re a very private bunch,” Price said. “A lot of what I’m going off of is what I’ve seen from Google Maps, what I’ve talked to the producer about, what I’ve talked to the vet about. I haven’t felt the need to go out there based on those conversations.”
She said she “became very comfortable” in conversations with the owner that the virus wouldn’t spread off the farm. It doesn’t have animals moving on and off over the course of the year like on a dairy or poultry farm; mink leave only when they’re slaughtered and skinned for pelts at the end of the year. She also said that she was confident the owner would recapture any escaped mink.
Short of a formal quarantine, Price gave the farm a “verbal hold” to not move any mink, or manure or carcasses, off the farm. “We haven’t seen spread off of this farm. We have not had additional cases in Utah that are linked to this, so thus far the verbal hold orders and the measures that have been taken look to be successful: There is not spread happening from this farm from this case.”
Price’s assertion didn’t allay the concerns of experts that ProPublica spoke with. When poultry test positive for this strain of bird flu, all nearby farms are quarantined and tested for the virus. But the approach in Utah relies on farms reporting cases or the public calling in reports of dead birds in the area.
“If you’re not looking for something, you won’t find it,” Sorrell said. “Unless you’re doing active surveillance, you can’t claim that you haven’t had cases.”
Fenn told ProPublica his conversations with state officials made him less worried about any kind of spread. When the outbreak started, Fenn said, he asked whether the bird flu could infect people.
“Right off the bat, the state people we reported to, they said you don’t need to worry too much,” Fenn said. “My guys wear masks every day. They have glasses they can wear,” Fenn said. “ Me? I don’t wear it at all. Never have, never will, because I’ve been doing it for 40 years.”
Fenn said he wished he could vaccinate the mink for bird flu to keep the rest of his animals from catching it and dying; Price asked the USDA about a vaccine that had been used to save endangered wild species but said she got nowhere with that request. The USDA told ProPublica its division responsible for protecting animal health has no “species-specific regulatory authority or dedicated programs” for vaccinating mink, depopulating them or paying owners back for such a culling.
Fenn told ProPublica he thinks concerns about mink as a particularly risky bird flu host are trumped up by anti-fur activists, the same forces that he believed were behind the reactions in Spain and Finland, which depopulated mink farms hit with bird flu. “Europeans are a little scared of everything,” he said. “They’re going to do what they’re going to do, and here in the United States, we’re going to do what we’re going to do.”
Price said she was aware that Finland and Spain had depopulated their fur farms when the same strain infected them. “I didn’t really look much further into it,” she said, explaining that she was interested in those cases only for lessons about how to handle the outbreak, but not the particular reasons those countries chose to depopulate the farms.
A USDA spokesperson said Congress would have to specifically fund a program to depopulate mink. (The program to cull poultry to stop the spread of bird flu has cost well over $1 billion since 2022.)
The events in Utah are a “clear warning sign” about the dangers of mink farms, said Neil Vora, executive director for the Preventing Pandemics at the Source Coalition.
“Fur farms are to produce pelts purely for luxury goods, to make fancy coats,” he said. “It’s absurd that we’re willing to gamble with the lives of millions of people just to keep an industry alive.”
The industry has struggled as American consumers increasingly reject fur. Though domestic farms peaked about a decade ago, selling luxury pelts that often ended up in China, foreign farms have sprung up, threatening the business.
While animal rights advocates have pushed for Congress to adopt legislation that would phase out the fur industry, buying out farmers over the course of a year to end the practice once and for all, winds in Congress are blowing the other direction. The Senate will soon weigh in on the latest Farm Bill, which now seeks to expand market opportunities for mink farmers by undoing a prohibition in federal law on subsidizing the fur trade.
The virus continues to spread on the Utah farm, said Fenn, though at a slower pace. Experts told ProPublica it still poses a risk.
“I would want a full on hazmat suit if I were on that farm,” Peacock said. “Or, preferably, I’d rather not to be on that farm.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Ministério do Trabalho recebe 4,3 mil denúncias de assédio eleitoral em três dias
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Iara Balduino
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego (MTE) recebeu aproximadamente 4,3 mil denúncias de assédio eleitoral no ambiente de trabalho apenas nos três primeiros dias de funcionamento de um canal específico para esse tipo de ocorrência.
O canal começou a funcionar no dia 28 de outubro, depois que diversas denúncias desse tipo de prática começaram a surgir tanto na internet como em órgãos competentes.
A maior parte dos casos foi no estado de São Paulo (1.325), seguida por Rio de Janeiro (354), Minas Gerais (345), Paraná (268) e Santa Catarina (259). A Região Sudeste concentrou 48,5% das ocorrências.
Segundo o MTE, as denúncias já estão sendo apuradas.
O que é o assédio eleitoral
Assédio eleitoral é quando um chefe ou superiores hierárquicos pressionam o trabalhador a votar ou deixar de votar em um determinado candidato.
Demitir um funcionário pela opção política dele também é considerado assédio e, se ficar provado que a dispensa ocorreu por esse motivo, a empresa pode ser obrigada a readmitir o empregado e pagar indenização por danos morais.
Como denunciar
Quem sofrer ou presenciar casos de assédio eleitoral no ambiente de trabalho deve fazer a denúncia nos canais do Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego (MTE) ou do Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT).
As denúncias são mantidas em sigilo e encaminhadas aos órgãos competentes.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Trump descarta encontro com Flávio, mas diz que ele pode ficar o quanto quiser
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, descartou se reunir com Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) após fuga dele para o país. Ao falar com jornalistas em sua residência na Flórida no sábado (31), ele disse que, apesar de não ter planos para o encontro, Flávio poderá ficar nos Estados Unidos pelo tempo que quiser.
Mais cedo, o secretário de Estado, Marco Rubio, afirmou que Washington não participou diretamente da fuga após sua derrota eleitoral de Flávio Bolsonaro. “O governo dos Estados Unidos não esteve diretamente envolvido” no percurso realizado pelo senador e ex-candidato, declarou, segundo informações da agência internacional AFP. A declaração foi dada durante coletiva de imprensa na Cúpula de Chanceleres do G20, em Atlanta, na Geórgia.
A afirmação, no entanto, é contrariada pela imprensa estadunidense. Os jornais The New York Times e The Wall Street Journal apontam que o avião que levou o político aos Estados Unidos foi fretado por Jason Miller, assessor de Trump. À AFP, o diretor da companhia aérea informou que o voo de Flávio foi pago por um intermediário a partir de uma conta bancária estadunidense.
Decisões da Justiça
Apesar da tentativa de afastar a responsabilidade direta de Washington, a acolhida oferecida ao parlamentar ocorre em meio ao descumprimento ostensivo de determinações da Justiça brasileira. Flávio Bolsonaro fugiu do Brasil descumprindo a ordem de retenção e entrega de passaportes emitida pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), em inquérito que apura crimes contra as instituições democráticas.
A rota de fuga teria sido articulada com o suporte de governos alinhados à extrema direita na região. O senador cruzou a fronteira por Puerto Iguazú, na Argentina do aliado Javier Milei, fez escala no Equador e desembarcou em Miami.
Horas após a chegada aos Estados Unidos, Flávio Bolsonaro divulgou uma carta golpista em que se autodeclarou “presidente eleito”, repetindo a tática adotada pelo opositor venezuelano Juan Guaidó.
Na Flórida, o candidato derrotado passou a integrar uma estrutura permanente de cooperação política da extrema direita contra as instituições brasileiras. O local já abrigava o ex-deputado Eduardo Bolsonaro, condenado pelo STF a quatro anos e dois meses de prisão, o ex-diretor da Abin Alexandre Ramagem, condenado a 16 anos por participação na trama golpista de 2022, e o influenciador Paulo Figueiredo.
*Com informações de AFP e Opera Mundi

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Ex-agente do Mossad teria ajudado Flávio Bolsonaro a fugir do Brasil, afirma jornal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Renato Santana
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Um ex-agente do Mossad, serviço de inteligência de Israel, teria acompanhado o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) na fuga do Brasil em direção à Argentina, de onde ele embarcou em um avião particular com destino aos Estados Unidos.
A informação foi divulgada em Israel neste domingo (1º) pelo jornal israelense The Jerusalem Post, com base em uma investigação da Polícia Federal (PF) brasileira obtida pela CNN Brasil.
Segundo a reportagem da emissora, o ex-integrante do serviço secreto israelense, que não teve a identidade revelada, chegou ao Brasil em 19 de outubro, seis dias antes do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais. Ele teria acompanhado Flávio Bolsonaro desde Brasília até a fronteira com a Argentina e viajado no mesmo veículo que o senador durante a travessia.
A investigação teria identificado dois veículos utilitários que cruzaram a Ponte Internacional Tancredo Neves, entre Foz do Iguaçu, no Paraná, e Puerto Iguazú, na província argentina de Misiones, na noite de 27 de outubro. Imagens de câmeras de segurança foram utilizadas para identificar os automóveis e reconstruir o deslocamento.
Flávio viajava em uma das vans, acompanhado pelo ex-agente do Mossad. Na segunda estavam sua mulher e as duas filhas. Os veículos eram conduzidos por um ex-vereador de Foz do Iguaçu e seu filho.
Operação Alba
A operação teria recebido o nome de Alba e começado a ser organizada ainda durante a campanha eleitoral, antes da derrota de Flávio Bolsonaro para Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), no segundo turno de 25 de outubro.
Depois de chegar à Argentina, Flávio e seus familiares embarcaram em um jato executivo Gulfstream G400, operado pela empresa argentina de fretamento Baires Fly. A aeronave fez uma escala em Guayaquil, no Equador, para reabastecimento, e pousou na manhã de quarta-feira (28) no aeroporto executivo de Opa-locka, próximo a Miami, na Flórida.
De acordo com apurações da imprensa brasileira e dos Estados Unidos, o avião teria sido providenciado por Jason Miller, estrategista político próximo ao presidente Donald Trump e integrante da estrutura de comunicação da Casa Branca. A informação sobre a participação de Miller também foi atribuída pelo jornal israelense ao The New York Times.
Outra informação publicada pelo jornal argentino Clarín aponta que Santiago Caputo, assessor próximo do presidente Javier Milei, teria se deslocado à região da fronteira para acompanhar a operação.

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/etudia.author: Caroline Constant

Des assemblées générales se sont déjà tenues dans plusieurs universités, et une centaine de lycées étaient bloqués ce lundi 2 novembre. Sabrine Kharbach, porte-parole de l’Union Étudiante fait le point sur les revendications et le mouvement.
Sabrine Kharbac est porte-parole de l’Union Étudiante, un des syndicats au cœur des actions des lycéens et étudiants. En ce jour de rentrée scolaire, l’étudiante à l’Université d’Aix-Marseille parle des revendications de la jeunesse, et des actions prévues jusqu’à la manifestation intersyndicale du jeudi 5 novembre.
Ce lundi 2 novembre a eu lieu la rentrée des classes. Que s’est-il passé sur les campus ?
Sabrine Kharbach
Porte-parole de l’Union Étudiante
L’Union Syndicale Lycéenne, l’Union Étudiante et l’intersyndicale de la jeunesse ont appelé à reprendre les blocus dès ce mardi et ce jeudi.
