https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.title: Militarisierung der Gesundheit | Linkes Gesundheitsforum: »Plötzlich waren Panzer auf den Ärzteblättern«
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.author: Ruta Dreyer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Militarisierung der Gesundheit
Linkes Gesundheitsforum: »Plötzlich waren Panzer auf den Ärzteblättern«
Auch in Krankenhäusern und Arztpraxen ist die Militarisierung sichtbar. Beschäftigte erinnern an ihre antimilitaristischen Kämpfe in den 80er Jahren.
»Die Aufgabe von uns soll es sein, die Drehscheibe zu bilden, die Leute wieder an die Front schickt«, beschreibt Kinderarzt Julius Poppel die Funktion von Ärzt*innen im Kriegsfall. Poppel ist Ko-Vorsitzender des Vereins demokratischer Ärzt*innen (VDÄÄ) und spricht auf dem »Gesundheitspolitischen Forum« über Militarisierung. »Wollt ihr das?«, fragt er seine Kolleg*innen.
Der VDÄÄ organisierte das Forum dieses Jahr bereits zum 40. Mal. Er versteht sich als kritische Alternative zu standespolitischen Ärzteverbänden. Von Freitag bis Sonntag haben sich in Berlin die Mitglieder sowie weitere gesundheitspolitische Akteure vernetzt. Diesjähriger Schwerpunkt waren Strategien linker Gesundheitspolitik.
Der Verein habe früh begonnen, sich mit der Militarisierung des Gesundheitswesens zu beschäftigen, berichtet VDÄÄ-Geschäftsführerin und Medizinsoziologin Nadja Rakowitz. »Weil wir gemerkt haben, dass die organisierte Ärzteschaft auf ihren Ärzteblättern plötzlich Panzer hatte.« Beispiele dieser Entwicklung gibt es zahlreiche – die Medizinische Hochschule Hannover hat eine Kooperation mit der Bundeswehr vereinbart, die Zahl wehrmedizinischer Fortbildungen nimmt zu und ein Rahmenplan des Berliner Senats fokussiert die Gesundheitsversorgung in Krisenzeiten. Krisen- und Kriegsmedizin werden dabei oft vermischt.
Aus der organisierten Ärzteschaft gebe es zwar teilweise Kritik an dieser Entwicklung, insgesamt aber viel Zustimmung, meint Poppel. Darum sei es wichtig, über die Fachwelt, wie durch Artikel in wissenschaftlichen Zeitschriften, Einfluss zu nehmen. Der VDÄÄ organisiert Veranstaltungen und schreibt Broschüren und Zeitschriften. Gleichzeitig sollten Ärzt*innen über den eigenen Berufsstand hinaus aktiv sein.
»So absurd und vielleicht rückständig es auch ist, hat die Ärzt*innenschaft doch eine gesellschaftliche Stimme, die respektiert wird«, meint Poppel zu »nd«. »Wenn eine Ärzteschaft sich hinstellt und sagt, wir werden keinen Krieg unterstützen, dann hat es wahrscheinlich eine gesellschaftliche Wucht. Und wenn man klarstellt: Egal, wie wir versorgen, es wird nicht ausreichend sein.«
Derzeit plant der VDÄÄ eine Kampagne, die sich zugleich gegen Militarisierung und Sozialstaatsabbau richtet. Idee ist, den Sozialabbau zum Ausgangspunkt zu machen – über diesen beklagten sich viel mehr Leute, meint Rakowitz. Der VDÄÄ will das in einen Zusammenhang mit der Militarisierung bringen. Rakowitz kritisiert: »Man kann einen Panzer kaufen, aber keine Grundschule bauen.«
Apotheken oder Buchhändler: an jeder Ecke eine Friedensbewegung
Bereits in den 80er Jahren organisierten sich Ärzt*innen in der anti-atomaren Friedensbewegung in Westdeutschland und der DDR. Beim 4. Medizinischen Kongress in Tübingen 1984 versammelten sich tausende Besucher*innen unter dem Motto »Unser Eid auf Leben verpflichtet zum Widerstand«.
Die Apothekerin Ulrike Faber aus dem Verein demokratischer Pharmazeutinnen und Pharmazeuten war damals selbst aktiv und berichtet: »Es gab an jeder Ecke eine Friedensbewegung. Ob das Buchhändler oder Apotheker oder die Kirchen waren, alle haben ausgehend von ihrer Situation und Profession auf das Thema gesetzt.« Das habe einen großen Einfluss gehabt. Allerdings sei die gesellschaftliche Stimmung damals positiver gegenüber der Bewegung gewesen.
Ein anderer Teilnehmer des Workshops berichtet, dass er mit dutzenden Ärzt*innen in weißen Kitteln vor der Ärztekammer demonstrierte, als sie aufgefordert wurde, im Kriegsfall Listen ihrer Mitglieder weiterzugeben. Als Teil eines Gesundheitsgesetzes für den Verteidigungsfall war dies 1981 in der Bundesrepublik vorgesehen. Durch Proteste konnte das Gesetz letztlich verhindert werden – die schwarz-rote Koalition plant zurzeit eine Neuauflage.
Für Kinderarzt Poppel ist klar: »Die Lösung muss Austausch, Diplomatie und Abrüstung sein, so wie das auch in den 80er Jahren der Fall war. Da sehe ich die Rolle der Ärzteschaft.«

https://taz.de/Klimakiller-Rechenzentren.title: Klimakiller Rechenzentren: Hohe CO₂-Emissionen durch Datenzentren in den USA
https://taz.de/Klimakiller-Rechenzentren.author: Kai Schöneberg
https://taz.de/Klimakiller-Rechenzentren.text:
Klimakiller Rechenzentren: Hohe CO₂-Emissionen durch Datenzentren in den USA
Der Strom für neue Computeranlagen in den USA kommt oft aus Gaskraftwerken. Die Emissionen steigen dadurch stark, zeigt eine Untersuchung.
Die fossile Energieerzeugung für neue Rechenzentren in den USA produziert fast so viel Treibhausgas wie Deutschland. Das ist das Ergebnis einer Untersuchung der renommierten US-Umweltorganisation Sierra Club. Danach soll die Energieerzeugung allein für die derzeit in den Vereinigten Staaten von 2025 bis 2030 geplanten Datenzentren 618 Millionen Tonnen CO2 verursachen. Deutschland verursachte im vergangenen Jahr 649 Millionen Tonnen. Die zusätzlichen Emissionen der geplanten Datenzentren würden den Ausstoß des gesamten US-Energiesektors bis 2030 um 42 Prozent in die Höhe schnellen lassen, analysiert Sierra Club – und so die gesamten Einsparungen von Treibhausgasemissionen im Energiesektor seit 2011 auffressen.
Der Energiehunger der Rechenzentren ist riesig, die Zahlen seien „nach wie vor unfassbar“, sagt Jeremy Fisher, Klima- und Energiechef des Sierra Club, laut Nachrichtenagentur Bloomberg. Wegen des großen Energiebedarfs der für KI-Anwendungen in den USA projektierten Rechenzentren und der überlasteten Netze werden vor Ort für sie eigens Gaskraftwerke errichtet, um sie mit Strom zu versorgen. Allein durch diese neuen Anlagen könnten die Emissionen bis 2030 laut Sierra Club um 460 Millionen Tonnen CO2 steigen – ungefähr so viel wie die jährlichen Emissionen Mexikos.
Nach Angaben der Energieberatungsfirma electricchoice.com sind gegenwärtig mehr als 4.500 Computerzentren in den USA in Betrieb, über 700 im Bau. Wegen ihres Ressourcenverbrauchs sind die fensterlosen, riesigen Anlagen vor den Midterm-Wahlen zu einem Top-Politikum geworden.
US-Präsident Donald Trump ist dafür. Die USA müssten ihren technologischen Vorsprung gegen China aufrechterhalten, forderte Trump. KI-Skeptiker verunglimpfte er als „Verschwörungstheoretiker“ und „Verräter“. 60 Prozent der Wähler lehnen den Bau der Einrichtungen in ihrer Region jedoch ab. Laut Umfragen sind 53 Prozent der US-Amerikaner „äußerst“ oder „sehr“ besorgt über die Auswirkungen der Datenzentren auf die Umwelt. Die demokratische Gouverneurin von New York, Kathy Hochul, hat inzwischen ein einjähriges Bauverbot für große Rechenzentren angeordnet, ähnlich ihr republikanischer Amtskollege Greg Abbott in Texas.
Datenfirmen schielen auf Reservate Indigener
Für große Kritik sorgten in Memphis drei Zentren der Firma SpaceXAI, eines KI-Unternehmens von Elon Musk. Der Bürgerrechtsverband NAACP protestierte gegen die Abgase der Gasgeneratoren zur Stromversorgung, die lokale und nationale Grenzwerte überschritten. Inzwischen hat das Unternehmen Abhilfe versprochen. Man wolle ein „guter Nachbar“ sein.
Auch die Flächenkonkurrenz zur Landwirtschaft und der enorme Wasserverbrauch der Rechenzentren führen zu Kritik. Anwohner klagen vielerorts gegen die Anlagen. Wie der Verband datacenterwatch.org ermittelte, haben die Proteste im zweiten Quartal 2026 mindestens 45 Projekte im Wert von 68 Milliarden US-Dollar blockiert oder verzögert, im ersten Quartal waren es sogar mindestens 75 Projekte.
Wie die New York Times berichtete, haben es Datenfirmen zunehmend auf indigene Reservate abgesehen, dünn besiedelte Regionen. Doch auch dort sind die Zentren umstritten. Laut dem Informationsdienst Native News Online von Anfang August haben die Cherokee nach mehrmonatiger Untersuchung ein Moratorium beschlossen. Es gebe „schwerwiegende Besorgnis“, was die Zentren dem Land, den Ressourcen und der kulturellen Lebensweise antun würden, erklärte Oberhäuptling Chuck Hoskin Jr.
Die Cherokee sind eines der größten indigenen Völker in den USA. Die Seminole haben sich ebenfalls für ein Moratorium ausgesprochen. Doch auch hier lockt der Profit durch die Datenzentren. Der Verband National Congress of American Indians forderte das Weiße Haus Ende 2025 auf, in die KI-Infrastruktur in Reservaten zu investieren.
Eine Studie der den Demokraten nahestehenden Brookings Institution kam zu dem Schluss, dass weniger neue Datenzentren die Nachfrage an Datenverarbeitung nicht verlangsamen würden. Man müsse gesetzliche Restriktionen für den Betrieb durchsetzen, vor allem mehr Transparenz bei der Planung. (mit Agenturen)

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.title: Ukraine-Krieg | Sechs Tage, die Hoffnung machen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.author: Bernhard Clasen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.text:
- Kommentare
- Ukraine-Krieg
Sechs Tage, die Hoffnung machen
Die sechstägige Feuerpause von Oleschky hat gezeigt, dass ein Waffenstillstand möglich ist, wenn beide Seiten wirklich wollen. Ein Kommentar.
Sechs Tage lang schwiegen die Waffen in Oleschky und Cherson. Jetzt spricht vieles dafür, dass der Krieg wieder zurückkehrt. Also alles wieder auf Anfang? Nein: Die sechstägige Waffenruhe – die längste seit Kriegsbeginn – war durchaus ein Erfolg. Sechs Tage ohne Krieg sind besser als null. Gut ein Viertel der Bevölkerung hat das Angebot angenommen, Oleschky in von Kiew kontrollierte ukrainische Gebiete zu verlassen.
Die sechs Tage haben auch gezeigt, dass ein Waffenstillstand funktioniert, wenn beide Seiten wirklich wollen. Deeskalation ist möglich. Und dieser Erfolg beflügelt die Menschenrechtsbeauftragten Russlands und der Ukraine Jana Lantratowa und Dmytro Ljubinez, ihre humanitäre Zusammenarbeit auszubauen. Um es konkreter zu sagen: weitere Menschenleben zu retten.
Natürlich gibt es Vorbehalte gegen Lantratowa. Im Gegensatz zu ihrem ukrainischen Gegenpart hat sie noch nie die eigenen Behörden kritisiert. Schöner wäre es, mit vertrauenswürdigen Akteuren zu verhandeln, wie etwa Amnesty International oder das Rote Kreuz. Doch reden muss man mit denen, die in die Entscheidungsprozesse eingebunden sind. Und deswegen führt kein Weg an Lantratowa vorbei. Regionale Waffenstillstände sind auch dann zu begrüßen, wenn wie jetzt vom britischen Sender Skynews exklusiv berichtet, die russische Armee in dieser Zeit ihre Positionen ausbauen soll. (Was on Lubinez verneint wird)
Die Erfahrung von Oleschky muss genutzt werden, um weitere Feuerpausen zu ermöglichen. Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj und der türkische Staatschef Recep Tayyip Erdoğan wollen an einem Schwarzmeer-Getreidekorridor arbeiten. Sollte dieser Wirklichkeit werden, wäre der Hafen von Odessa, mitten in der Stadt gelegen, von weiteren Luftangriffen verschont.
Und selbstverständlich muss auf oberster Ebene die Suche nach einem umfassenden Waffenstillstand weitergehen. Eine sofortige instabile Feuerpause ist besser als eine stabile Waffenruhe am Sankt-Nimmerleins-Tag. Die Menschen können nicht ewig warten.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Miles Starforth at St James' Park
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Jack Grealish will do well to get back into the Everton starting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.
Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against 10 men at St James’ Park after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.
And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.
Moyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game following a breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”
Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”
Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”
Newcastle fans had made their feelings about the 3-1 Carabao Cup defeat away to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.
Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.
Frustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.
Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.
Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.
Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.
By now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.
Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.
Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.
The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.
“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.

Staatskrise in Polen : Kampf um Deutungshoheit
In Polen eskaliert der Streit um das Verfassungsgericht und weitet sich zur Staatskrise aus. Von der Eskalation profitieren die Populisten.
J e schlimmer der Machtkampf um das Verfassungsgericht in Polen wird, desto besser für den polnischen Präsidenten Karol Nawrocki und die rechtsnationale Oppositionspartei PiS, die wie zum Hohn „Recht und Gerechtigkeit“ heißt. Beide – die Partei wie auch der PiS-nahe Präsident – eskalieren die Situation und tun so, als seien nicht sie die Schuldigen am verfassungswidrig besetzten Verfassungsgericht, sondern die aktuelle Mitte-links-Regierung unter Premier Donald Tusk.
Ihren vorläufigen Höhepunkt fand die Eskalation, als Präsident Nawrocki in der Nacht zum Samstag gegen ein Uhr mit seinen Bodyguards das polnische Verfassungsgericht stürmte und versuchte, die dort ausharrenden Richter zu nötigen, ihm die Schlüssel zum Gericht auszuhändigen. Der Ex-Boxer drückte dabei sogar die Vorsitzende Richterin gewaltsam beiseite.
Die seit 2023 regierende Mitte-links-Koalition unter Premier Donald Tusk versucht seit drei Jahren, den demokratischen Rechtsstaat wiederherzustellen. Dazu gehört auch das durch die PiS gekaperte Verfassungsgericht. 15 PiS-loyale Richter hatten dort Gesetze nicht mehr vorrangig auf ihre Verfassungsmäßigkeit geprüft, sondern auf ihre Vereinbarkeit mit dem Parteiinteresse der PiS.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Der Europäische Gerichtshof und der Europäische Gerichtshof für Menschenrechte sprachen deshalb 2025 dem polnischen Verfassungsgericht ab, den Anforderungen an ein unabhängiges und unparteiisches Gericht im Sinne des EU-Rechts zu genügen.
Die meisten Polen und Polinnen haben nie mit dem Verfassungsgericht zu tun und verstehen gar nicht, worum es bei der derzeitigen Eskalation überhaupt geht. Handelt es sich um einen „Staatsstreich“, wie die PiS immer wieder behauptet? Oder doch um die „Wiederherstellung des Rechtsstaats in Polen“, wie Premier Tusk betont?
Der Ausgang dieser Staatskrise ist keineswegs klar. Sie ist auch ein Kampf um die Deutungshoheit. Sollte sich die PiS mit ihrem Narrativ durchsetzen, wird die aktuelle Mitte-links-Koalition unter Donald Tusk mit einiger Wahrscheinlichkeit auch die Parlamentswahlen im nächsten Jahr verlieren.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.title: »Gen Z regelt« | Jugend voran!
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.author: Thomas Blum
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120359.text:
- Kultur
- »Gen Z regelt«
Jugend voran!
Die »Gen Z«-Demonstrationen waren politisch diffus und wurden teils gekapert. Und die brutal auftretende Polizei findet immer Gründe, zuzuschlagen.
Man wusste es vorher schon: Dass die jungen Demonstrant*innen theoretisch recht schwach auf der Brust sind, zeigte sich ja bereits an der Losung, die sie sich erfunden haben. »Gen Z regelt«: Ein Motto, das ohne Weiteres auch die FDP-Jugend für ihren nächsten wirtschaftspolitischen Stammtisch hätte wählen können. »Gen Z kuschelt« oder »Gen Z googelt« wäre vermutlich der passendere Slogan gewesen. Wer erwartet hatte, dass die Generation Tiktok, die ihre Lebenszeit bevorzugt zwischen Couch und Kühlschrank zubringt, während sie sich in narzisstischer Selbstbespiegelung übt und Kram bei Amazon oder Zalando bestellt, einen halbwegs überzeugenden und politisch nicht allzu verblödeten Protest zustande bekommt, wurde am Wochenende eines Besseren belehrt. Selbstverständlich kriegt die »Gen Z«, die selbst ihren Salat noch im Internet bestellt, gar nichts geregelt.
Doch das sollte einen nicht überraschen, denn auch die Boomer-, die Generation-X- und die Millennial-Langweiler haben zu ihrer jeweiligen Zeit nichts auf die Reihe bekommen beziehungsweise sich gründlich und auf jede erdenkliche Art und Weise blamiert: die Boomer mit ihrem K-Gruppen-Schwachsinn, der schleichend in New Age/Esoterik (Langhans) oder Hardcore-Karrierismus (Schröder/Fischer) übergegangen ist; die Generation X mit ihrem materialismusfeindlichen Popgeschwafel und ihrer Postmoderne; die Millennials mit ihrem eindimensionalen Identitätspolitik-Blödsinn und ihrem ultradogmatischen Kulturalismus-Baukasten.
Thomas Blum ist grundsätzlich nicht einverstanden mit der herrschenden sogenannten Realität. Vorerst wird er sie nicht ändern können, aber er kann sie zurechtweisen, sie ermahnen oder ihr, wenn es nötig wird, auch mal eins überziehen. Damit das Schlechte den Rückzug antritt. Wir sind mit seinem Kampf gegen die Realität solidarisch. Daher erscheint fortan montags an dieser Stelle »Die gute Kolumne«. Nur die beste Qualität für die besten Leser*innen! Die gesammelten Texte sind zu finden unter: dasnd.de/diegute
Es ist ja im Grunde alles komplett wurscht. Warum und wie sich als links und widerständig begreifende junge Menschen hierzulande auch protestieren wollen, am Ende kommen doch immer wieder die gleichen öden Latsch-Demonstrationen dabei heraus, auf denen die üblichen Politmacker und Dogmatiker ihre mit Buchstaben bemalten Bettlaken in die Höhe halten und die ranzigen Parolen aus Opas Mottenkiste skandieren.
Das passiert zuverlässig stets dann, wenn, wie jetzt an diesem Wochenende wieder geschehen, die diversen ML-Splittergruppen, stalinistischen Sektierer und in Megaphone brüllenden Pali-Soli-Dullis die sogenannten Schülerdemonstrationen in großem Stil unterwandern, eifrig ihre diversen Flaggen schwenken und jene Sprüche klopfen, die in den letzten 40 Jahren nicht gerade an Aktualität gewonnen haben: »Kohl/Schröder/Merkel/Scholz/Merz muss weg!«, »Hoch die internationale Solidarität!«, »Viva, viva Palästina!«, »Deutsche Waffen, deutsches Geld – morden mit in aller Welt!«
Politisch wirkt das alles so frisch und so geistreich wie eine Volkskammer-Rede von Günter Mittag. Und spätestens wenn die Latsch-Demo endet, wird dann einen Abend lang Revolution simuliert: Ein paar Ladengeschäfte werden »entglast«, mit Pyrotechnik wird ein bisschen hantiert und mit den Polizisten zwei Stunden lang »Fang mich doch, du Eierloch« gespielt.
Weitaus verstörender und schlimmer noch als die ebenso fade wie politisch konfuse Aufführung der »Gen Z«-Demonstranten (»Es geht bei uns echt voll um die Basic-Themen«) ist aber das Treiben der zur »Deeskalation« abkommandierten Polizeieinheiten, die – nicht nur was ihre Bekleidung und Nahkampf-Ausrüstung betrifft – im Lauf der Jahrzehnte jenen brutalen Paramilitärs immer ähnlicher wurden, die man früher nur aus dystopischen/postapokalyptischen Science-Fiction-Filmen kannte.
Heute sehen die Polizisten nicht nur so aus, als handele es sich bei ihnen um Spezialtruppen zur Aufstandsbekämpfung, sie verhalten sich auch so, als müssten sie in einem südamerikanischen Bürgerkriegsland die kommunistische Guerilla niederschlagen. Dabei sollten sie doch am vergangenen Wochenende ursprünglich bloß einen Abend lang eine Handvoll diffus an Sozialdemokratie interessierte Pubertierende bewachen, die einander Schulhofwitzigkeiten zurufen (»Merz, leck Eier!«). Was das gesamte Szenario so grotesk macht.
Am Samstagabend konnte man in Berlin und anderen deutschen Städten tatsächlich beobachten, wie bis an die Zähne bewaffnete Polizeibeamte völlig enthemmt mit Schlagstöcken auf gelangweilt herumstehende Abiturienten einschlugen, die sich versammelt hatten, um mit einer Himbeerlimo oder einem zuckerfreien Proteinriegel in der Hand für eine Schule, in die es nicht mehr reinregnet, und ein etwas kuschligeres Deutschland zu demonstrieren. Die politische Naivität und beängstigende Harmlosigkeit der jungen Demonstranten, denen der Bausparvertrag gewiss näher ist als Andreas Baader, war förmlich mit Händen zu greifen.
In die laufenden Kameras hinein riefen sie nicht etwa: »Alle Macht den Räten!« Sie forderten auch nicht die Ausrottung des Kapitalismus mitsamt seinen Wurzeln oder die unverzügliche öffentliche Hinrichtung des Arbeitgeberpräsidenten. Vielmehr sagten sie Sätze, im Vergleich zu denen einem selbst das Grundsatzprogramm der Jungen Liberalen vorkommt wie ein radikalanarchistisches Pamphlet: »Wir fühlen uns zurzeit nicht ganz so repräsentiert von der Regierung«, »es fehlt uns an Wertschätzung, es wäre schön, wenn man uns mehr zuhören würde« – »Wir wünschen uns eine Zukunftsperspektive« – »Wir wollen keinesfalls herumrandalieren«.
Ein Großteil der bürgerlichen Presse hatte zuvor eine Woche lang diese kreuzbraven Jungstaatsbürger geradezu rauschhaft als linksextreme Terrorbande denunziert und den Untergang des Abendlandes heraufbeschworen. Und dann, am Samstagabend, musste man fassungslos dabei zusehen, wie diese 15- bis 20-jährigen Buben oder Mädchen, die artig solche Kuschelsätze in die ihnen hingehaltenen Mikrofone sprachen, von der Polizei niedergeprügelt wurden, als hätte sie es mit gemeingefährlichen Bandenmitgliedern des mexikanischen Sinaloa-Kartells zu tun.
Ich bin mir nicht sicher, ob, um einer besseren Zukunft willen, der weiteren Militarisierung der Exekutive und der fortgesetzten Erweiterung der staatlichen Repressionsmaßnahmen nicht etwas entgegengesetzt werden sollte.
Sicher ist jedenfalls: Auch künftig »regelt« nicht die »Gen Z«, sondern wie immer im Kapitalismus »die Wirtschaft«.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

Côté malaisien, les efforts de conservation sont au contraire en train de porter leurs fruits.
Les images de leur sauvetage font le tour de monde. Dernier exemple en date samedi 17 octobre, à Hampangen, dans le Kalimantan central (une des cinq provinces de la partie indonésienne de Bornéo). Un mâle âgé de 20 ans a été anesthésié, son examen de santé complété, puis transporté vers un centre de réhabilitation. https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/gaza-.title: Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/gaza-.author: Abdallah al-Naami
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/gaza-.text:
Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
After finishing her homework, Fatima al-Bayouk went to play with her cousins outside her grandmother’s home in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, when an Israeli bullet struck her neck.
Moments later, the eight-year-old Palestinian girl returned home trembling, blood soaking her shirt. She screamed that her cousin had been shot, unaware that she had been hit herself.
The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries.
For her grandmother, Safia Abo Amra, Bayouk - the sole survivor of her immediate family in an earlier Israeli air strike - was far more than a granddaughter. She had become her closest companion and the centre of her life.
“Fatima was my best friend. We did everything together, cooking, going on walks; we even slept on the same mattress. I have seven sons and six daughters, yet Fatima was more precious to me than all of them,” Abo Amra told Middle East Eye.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Despite everything she had endured, Bayouk had brought joy back into her grandmother’s life. Her uncle Ahmad Abo Amra remembered her as a bright, cheerful girl whose smile lifted the spirits of those around her.
'My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her'
- Safia Abo Amra, Palestinian grandmother
“The best thing about Fatima was her smile that always brought joy to everyone around her. She was smart, responsible and loved happy occasions like weddings and family gatherings,” he said.
Her death reflects a wider pattern of indiscriminate Israeli gunfire that has become a daily threat to Palestinians across the Gaza Strip, particularly displaced families living near the so-called Yellow Line.
Israeli shooting from military positions, tanks and quadcopter drones has killed and wounded hundreds of civilians since the October 2025 ceasefire. It has also disrupted access to basic necessities and made everyday activities dangerous.
As Israel expands its control over more of the territory, families increasingly find themselves exposed to gunfire, with little protection and few places to seek safety.
A life cut short
For Bayouk’s family, her death was particularly devastating. She had already survived the loss of her immediate family in the early days of Israel’s genocide.
On 13 December 2023, an Israeli air strike targeted their home in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, killing her family. Bayouk survived and went to live with her grandmother in Deir al-Balah, where Abo Amra and other relatives tried to rebuild her life amid the devastation of the war.
'With her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren'
- Safia Abo Amro
“We did our best to provide everything Fatima needed and make her feel cared for and surrounded by people who love her,” Abo Amra said.
“I wanted to make up for the loss of her family, but with her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren.”
Education remained an important part of Bayouk’s life as she grew up in her grandmother’s home. Concerned for her safety, Abo Amra refused to send her to a UN school after hearing that Israeli stray bullets frequently reached the area. Instead, she paid monthly fees to enrol her in a local school.
“I walked Fatima to school every day. She was very smart and always did her homework before playing,” Abo Amra said.
Her death reopened the grandmother’s wounds.
“I was shocked and couldn't speak or move. Her death was twice as painful for me; it reminded me of my daughter and grandchildren who were killed at the beginning of the war,” Abo Amra said.
“My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her.”
Despite her young age, Bayouk left a lasting impression on those around her. She loved dressing up, particularly for family celebrations.
Her uncle Reda Abo Amra remembered how much she enjoyed choosing new clothes. The family had recently bought her winter clothes, but she never got the chance to wear them.
“She always liked to be well-dressed. We bought her new clothes for winter, but she was killed before she could wear them,” he told MEE.
Bayouk was not the first member of her family to be killed by Israeli gunfire. Six months before her death, her uncle Masoud Abo Amra, who was born with a mental disability, was shot in the neck while visiting his sister in Khan Younis.
“Masoud was Fatima's favourite uncle. She was devastated when she bid him farewell,” Ahmad said.
‘When the shooting starts, life stops’
For displaced families in Gaza, Israeli gunfire is not only a deadly threat but also a constant disruption to daily life.
Zaid al-Kafarna, 19, and his family of 10 were displaced from northern Gaza to the Um Duhair area, south of Deir al-Balah, days before the October 2025 ceasefire came into effect.
Kafarna said Israeli shooting was initially “occasional” and took place some distance from their tents. But it gradually became more frequent and moved closer to the camp. Over the past three months, he said, it had become a daily threat, frequently causing deaths, injuries and damage.
“I miraculously survived stray bullets several times. My friend and neighbour, Mohammad Aqel, was killed a few weeks ago by a stray bullet while he was preparing to return to northern Gaza,” Kafarna told MEE.
His mother, Shereen al-Kafarna, was recently wounded by an Israeli bullet while inside their tent. She described how the shooting brings life in the camp to a standstill.
“When the shooting starts, life stops in our camp. Neighbours warn each other. We leave everything and hold the children, then lie on the ground to avoid the bullets hitting around us. Everyone is terrified, especially the children,” she said.
The gunfire also disrupts Palestinians' efforts to secure basic necessities, including food and water.
“Sometimes while we are waiting in queues for water and food, Israeli tanks and quadcopter drones start shooting directly towards us,” Zaid said.
“Everyone panics. We lie on the ground at the side of the road, watching the aid trucks carrying our food and water drive away to escape the bullets. On those days, we don't have anything to eat or drink.”
Nowhere to go
The pattern of daily Israeli shootings near the Yellow Line, alongside the ongoing expansion of Israel’s buffer zone in Gaza, raised questions among families about whether the gunfire is as random as it appears.
Many believe that the shootings appear to form part of a military tactic to force Palestinian families out of their homes and tents, allowing Israel to expand its control over more territory through force.
In the year following the ceasefire, Israeli control over Gaza grew from 53 to 70 percent, reflecting what the Palestinians describe as a systematic policy of territorial expansion.
Families living near the Yellow Line said the threat of stray bullets had forced several others to leave their camps.
“Watching families leave our camp every day makes us feel even more afraid. We wish we could move away from the bullets, but we have nowhere to go,” Shereen told MEE.
“Even if we had somewhere to go, we can't afford the extremely expensive cost of transportation.”
With few options for escape, some families have resorted to building small sand barriers and digging trench-like holes inside and between their tents to shelter from the bullets.
Next to his tent, Shadi Siam dug a small trench to protect his family of five.
“I fear for my children's lives every time I hear Israeli stray bullets flying low,” Siam told MEE.
“My children wake up terrified, and I carry them to the hole where we all hide for two to five hours until the shooting stops,” he added.
“I don't know how I will protect them when the winter comes, and the hole becomes unusable.”

Schaeffler streicht Tausende Jobs und schließt Werke
Dortmund, Morbach, Berlin, Schwalbach: Schaeffler will vier deutsche Standorte schließen. Welche Werke und Bereiche trifft der Sparkurs noch?
Herzogenaurach. Der Auto- und Industriezulieferer Schaeffler verschärft mit einem weiteren Kostensenkungsprogramm und Tausenden Stellenstreichungen seinen Sparkurs erheblich. Das Unternehmen will in Europa weitere 3460 Stellen abbauen, davon 2660 in Deutschland, wie es in Herzogenaurach mitteilte. Zudem ist die Schließung von vier deutschen Standorten geplant.
Der MDax-Konzern begründete die weiteren Einschnitte mit der Automobilkrise in Europa, die weitere Gegenmaßnahmen und strukturelle Anpassungen erfordere.
Vier Standorte in Deutschland sollen geschlossen werden
Fünf Standorte, davon vier in Deutschland, sollen perspektivisch geschlossen werden. Dazu gehören laut Schaeffler das Werk in Dortmund mit aktuell 430 Beschäftigten sowie der Standort Morbach mit 160 Mitarbeitenden.
Zudem ist laut Schaeffler geplant, die Aktivitäten am Standort Berlin mit aktuell etwa 270 Beschäftigten einzustellen und den Standort Schwalbach aufzugeben. Ein Großteil der rund 385 Beschäftigten solle an den Schaeffler-Standort in Frankfurt am Main wechseln. Insgesamt seien rund 190 Stellen vom Abbau betroffen.
Darüber hinaus sei vorgesehen, die Aktivitäten im Werkzeugbau am Standort Höchstadt einzustellen und im Sondermaschinenbau an den Standorten Erlangen und Schweinfurt Anpassungen vorzunehmen. Ferner seien Kapazitäts- und Strukturanpassungen an weiteren Standorten in Deutschland – darunter Herzogenaurach, Bühl, Höchstadt, Nürnberg und Regensburg – geplant.
Scharfe Kritik der IG Metall
Die IG Metall und der Konzernbetriebsrat kritisierten das neuerliche Sparprogramm scharf. »Bei Schaeffler folge inzwischen ein Abbauprogramm auf das nächste, noch bevor die Folgen des vorherigen bewältigt sind«, sagte Thomas Höhn, Unternehmensbeauftragter der IG Metall für Schaeffler. »Das ist kein Zukunftskonzept für den Industriestandort Deutschland.« Bereits 2024 und 2025 hatte Schaeffler die Streichung mehrerer tausend Arbeitsplätze beschlossen. dpa/nd

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Cyclone Murasu makes landfall on India’s eastern coast
Severe cyclonic storm uproots trees and downs power lines, days after another cyclone battered the same region.
Cyclone Murasu has made landfall on India’s eastern coast, uprooting trees, toppling electricity poles and flooding low-lying areas in Andhra Pradesh. It is the second cyclone to strike the region in a week after Cyclone Arnab.
The severe cyclonic storm came ashore near Ongole in Prakasam district about 1am on Tuesday (19:30 GMT on Monday), according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).
The IMD warned of heavy to very heavy rain across several districts through the day.
No deaths or injuries have been reported so far, Prakhar Jain, the managing director of the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, told the Reuters news agency. He said some trees and electricity poles had been uprooted.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency reported extensive damage in Prakasam and Bapatla districts, where thousands of trees were felled, hundreds of power poles damaged and fishing boats wrecked. Standing crops were also hit, and many areas were underwater.
Authorities began evacuating people on Monday and planned to move about 30,000 people to safety in Andhra Pradesh, Jain said.
“This is the most dangerous cyclone we have witnessed in the last 14 years,” Krishnamma, a fisherman from Kothapatnam in Prakasam district, told PTI. He said about 400 families from his village had been moved out before the storm hit.
Indian Home Minister Amit Shah said on X that he had spoken to Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu about the cyclone’s impact.
“I assured him that the Central Government will provide all kinds of assistance and support,” Shah wrote, adding that national and state disaster response teams were already on the ground.
Murasu formed over the Bay of Bengal, which regularly spawns deadly storms on India’s east coast. It comes days after Cyclone Arnab caused heavy damage in Andhra Pradesh and neighbouring Odisha.
The IMD forecast that Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu to its south would be worst hit. Murasu is also causing heavy rain in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Odisha.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/death.title: ‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/death.author: MEE correspondent
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/death.text:
‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma
In October, as clashes reached Taghreed Abdulellah’s area, located about 30km from Yemen's Taiz city, the mother of three found herself unable to flee with her children, as battles had already broken out in their village.
She had no choice but to gather her children, aged four, seven and 10, in the hallway to protect them from potential blasts or shrapnel coming through the windows.
“Their father wasn’t at home; it was just them and me. The clashes were outside, and an explosion went off right near our home, leaving the children terrified and crying for hours,” Abdulellah told Middle East Eye.
“I couldn’t stop them from crying; in fact, I broke down and joined them at times.”
When the fighting quieted down, the children would stop crying, and some neighbours visited to boost their morale.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
However, as soon as the battles flared up again, the crying resumed.
“This continued for four days until the fierce battles moved away from our area. But my children’s lives have completely changed for the worse,” she explained.
“My children are always angry, and the two younger ones are now suffering from bedwetting, while the eldest constantly talks about losing his life and believes he will be killed at any moment, rather than thinking about his studies and future as he used to.”
Abdulellah’s children used to sleep in their own room, but since the fighting started, they do not dare to sleep alone. The whole family now sleeps in one room, with the two younger children sleeping in their mother’s arms.
“Nightmares terrify them every night, and during the day they refuse to leave the house because they feel they will be killed or injured if they go outside. So, they spend the entire day indoors,” Abdulellah said.
Battles in Taiz
Public schools across Taiz governorate, including Taiz city and rural areas, have been closed since 4 October, as it is unsafe for children to attend school.
It is also unsafe for children to play outside, as shelling and air strikes hit almost every district in the area.
Abdulellah believes it is unsafe for her children to go outside, yet she wants them to be able to so they can resume a normal life and heal from the psychological trauma they are facing.
“It is the first time in my life that I have seen my children feel so lost. They don’t want to play, they don’t want to study, and they only talk about the war. I am worried this will impact the rest of their lives even when normal life returns.”
On 4 October, Houthi forces advanced into large areas of Taiz governorate, taking control of most of the governorate and seizing all roads leading to Taiz city.
Battles are currently ongoing around Taiz city and in rural areas, as the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, attempt to push from Taiz toward Lahij governorate while also trying to take full control of Taiz city.
Saudi-led air strikes have targeted Houthi forces in the rural areas of Taiz and around Taiz city, which have also taken a heavy toll on children in those areas.
The World Health Organization has reported that 1,677 people were killed and more than 7,395 injured across Yemen between August and late October 2026 amid renewed clashes between government forces and Houthis.
The executive manager of the Taiz Human Rights Centre civil society organization, Mazen Aqlan, told MEE that 19 children were killed and 49 injured in Taiz governorate in October 2026.
Severe psychological impact
Odai, 13, is a child in Taiz city whose life has also completely changed. He used to spend his mornings at school and his afternoons playing with friends. But since 4 October, he has spent most of his days and nights scrolling through his phone, only leaving the house briefly to sit with friends and adults under a nearby tree.
The main issue, however, lies in the photos and videos he views on his mobile, along with the stories he hears from adults about what happened in 2015 when fighting reached their neighbourhood and civilians, including children, were killed or injured.
“Life isn’t easy, and death is close to everyone,” Odai told MEE. “We were focused on our studies and weren’t aware that a person could lose their life in a single minute. That is what happened to many people, both nowadays and during the last war.”
Odai, who is in the seventh grade, appears mature for his age, but the ongoing developments and the stories he hears have shifted his priorities from his education to thoughts of the afterlife, something that is not typical for a child his age.
When asked about his priorities and whether they should focus on his studies, he laughed and said: “Studying is important, but there is no guarantee we will stay alive until schools reopen. Death is closer to us than resuming our education.”
MEE spoke with Odai’s father, in his 50s, who preferred to remain anonymous. He confirmed that Odai was not like this until last month, when he heard a story about a child killed in the city and saw related photos and videos, leaving him deeply affected.
“We do our best to keep our children away from the fighting. We keep them at home and don’t allow them to venture outside, especially to far areas, but it is difficult to keep a child mentally stable in this environment,” Odai’s father told MEE.
“Mobile phones and the stories they hear from friends leave a severe psychological impact on children, especially when they see photos of killed children. That is out of our control.”
He added that such horrifying scenes impact even adults like himself, not just children. He believes the best solution is for local authorities and organisations to provide immediate psychological support during these difficult times.
“During wartime, everyone worries about the physical safety of their children, and only a few care about their psychological well-being - which is just as important, as its long-term impact can be devastating,” he said.
Gap between needs and support
The Taiz Human Rights Centre's Aqlan told MEE: “There are more than 100,000 children in Taiz governorate who have witnessed the horrors of war and been traumatised by its shells, explosions and tragedies. They are in urgent need of psychological care.”
He identified the group most in need of psychological support as the families who have lost loved ones, had their homes shelled, been displaced or have directly suffered from the consequences of the war.
In mid-September, prior to the recent escalation around Taiz city, the UN children's agency Unicef reported that over 57,000 children had been displaced in just a two-week period.
While the Taiz Human Rights Centre estimates that over 100,000 children need psychological support in the governorate, the UN reported earlier this year, before the recent military escalation, that 12.2 million children across the country were in need of humanitarian assistance.
The Social Affairs and Labour Office in Taiz governorate stated on Sunday that non-governmental humanitarian organisations operating in the governorate provided psychosocial support services to 719 children, while 219 boys and girls received psychological first aid sessions.
Future at risk
Psychologist Saba al-Sabri, who works with several institutions providing psychological support in Taiz, confirmed that clear behavioural changes in children have been observed over the past month.
“These behaviours include non-acceptance of others, grief over loss, continuous fear, nervousness, bedwetting, clinging to parents even during sleep, and a total loss of motivation to learn because they believe they will die or become disabled, all of which severely affect the children’s future,” Sabri told MEE.
She said that the counselling sessions provided by humanitarian initiatives and organisations remain far too few compared to the immense need that has persisted for over 11 years.
“These recent events have added new children to the list of those in need, making psychological support vital to preserving the next generation.”
Sabri pointed out that some parents do not realise the severity of psychological trauma on children, and instead focus solely on basic survival, which represents a disaster for the child.
“Ignoring a child’s feelings and failing to sit and communicate with them leaves a deep negative impact on their well-being.”
Most children currently do not leave their homes. Sabri noted that children are naturally energetic and need to play outside; depriving them of this heightens stress and nervousness, weakens their personality development and worsens their mood.
Abdulellah, the mother of the three children who witnessed the fighting and were traumatised, strongly believes in psychological treatment, but it remains inaccessible to them.
“If psychological treatment were available, I wouldn’t hesitate to take my children. But we are in a time of war, and it is hard to access such services since they are usually only available in the city.”

Merz will eine Frau an der Staatsspitze
Lange hat der Kanzler in der Debatte über die Nachfolge von Bundespräsident Steinmeier geschwiegen. Jetzt gibt er erstmals eine Richtung vor.
Berlin. Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) hat sich auf eine Frau als nächstes Staatsoberhaupt festgelegt. »Ich werde der Partei eine gemeinsame Kandidatin vorschlagen, eine Kandidatin der politischen Mitte«, sagte Merz nach Angaben aus CDU-Kreisen in der nicht-öffentlichen Kreisvorsitzendenkonferenz am Montag in Berlin. »Ich bin festgelegt, in der Frage, dass es eine Frau werden muss«, betonte er demnach. Merz’ Koalitionspartner SPD begrüßte die Festlegung des Bundeskanzlers.
Auch früher schon hatte der Kanzler Sympathien für die erstmalige Wahl einer Frau ins Bundespräsidentenamt bekundet, eine solch klare Festlegung aber vermieden. Namen nannte Merz den Angaben zufolge in der Sitzung nicht. Es wurde damit gerechnet, dass er die Kandidatin spätestens bei der CDU-Präsidiumssitzung am kommenden Montag präsentiert.
Aus der CDU werden Bundestagspräsidentin Julia Klöckner, Bildungsministerin Karin Prien, Ex-Parteichefin und -Verteidigungsministerin Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer und die hessische Fraktionsvorsitzende Ines Claus als mögliche Kandidatinnen genannt.
Die Schwesterpartei CSU hat bereits die bayerische Landtagspräsidentin Ilse Aigner für die Nachfolge von Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier vorgeschlagen. Aigner genießt Unterstützung auch bei CDU, SPD und Grünen. Die CDU-Spitze hatte aber bereits klargemacht, dass sie den Anspruch hat, eine eigene Kandidatin aufzustellen.
Die CDU ist die größte Partei in der Bundesversammlung, die am 30. Januar 2027 das nächste Staatsoberhaupt nach dem aktuellen Bundespräsidenten Frank-Walter Steinmeier wählen soll. CDU, SPD und CSU verfügen in dem Gremium über eine gemeinsame Mehrheit.
Die SPD begrüßte die Festlegung von Merz darauf, dass das nächste Staatsoberhaupt eine Frau werden soll. Parlamentsgeschäftsführer Dirk Wiese sagte der »Rheinischen Post«, er sei »gespannt« auf den Vorschlag von Merz. Wiese fuhr fort, er werbe seit Monaten dafür, »dass eine Frau das erste Amt im Staat übernimmt«. Dies sei »überfällig«. Es freue ihn daher, »dass Friedrich Merz diese Notwendigkeit nun auch anerkennt«. Agenturen/nd

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘The world is out of control’: how political strategist Claire Ainsley is challenging the left to take it back
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Gaby Hinsliff
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Do you ever feel as if life is spiralling out of control? As if the world’s problems are too big, or politicians too small, to get a grip on everything from rising prices to emergent threats such as AI?
If so, says the political strategist Claire Ainsley, you’re neither alone nor irrational. “It’s probably because you’ve got a lot to do, and the world is out of control,” she says cheerfully from her home in York, where she lives with her husband, an artist, and their two teenage children. But it is the politicians’ job to master fast-moving and complex events, she adds, and if conventional parties seem increasingly powerless to do anything about them, then populist alternatives will be only too ready with dangerously easy-sounding answers.
Her new book Control: How We Lost It and How to Take It Back argues that the centre-left can tackle that fatally undermining sense of impotence by rewiring government and putting people back in charge of their own lives. “We know the rightwing populists have an agenda that is dangerous and divisive. The question is what is being done to stop it,” says Ainsley, who served as Keir Starmer’s director of policy in opposition and is now a consultant for the Washington-based thinktank Progressive Policy Institute. “It’s that lack of leadership from centre-left politicians that people are crying out for.”
But there is also a more personal dimension to the public anxiety and sense of learned helplessness she describes. Ainsley appears to be a private and self-contained person, so I’m surprised when at the end of the book she says she wrote it partly for her younger self “who didn’t always feel in control”. What did she mean? “I definitely had difficulties when I was a teenager in the early 1990s. It has just struck me how much we talk about mental health problems now because we have a language for it – [myself] and my other female friends, we didn’t. But I don’t forget the young women we were, and how we felt.”
The politics of control is personal for many people, she argues, including teenagers now suffering an epidemic of mental health problems. Feeling that you have agency in life and can choose your own destiny matters, she writes, not just because it makes us feel more secure: it’s what motivates people to work hard, obey social norms or even vote. Why bother, if you think nothing you do makes any difference?
We’re speaking in the wake of doomsday warnings from AI researchers about the risk of their products wiping out humanity, a classic example of what she means by apparent political impotence. “There was no political voice immediately saying, ‘This is a problem and we’re going to take action in the following ways’ – not to tell people we’re in control of things we can’t be in control of, but to say, ‘We have a plan, we have a grip on this, and this is how we’re compelling the tech firms to take responsibility for what’s being created,’” says Ainsley, who writes in the book that parliamentary legislation isn’t moving fast enough to keep up and that big tech should be forced to fund research on AI safety.
But if strong leadership in the face of global threats is half of Ainsley’s answer, the more controversial half involves a renewed focus on social mobility, aspiration and encouraging individuals to take charge of their own lives. “It’s about taking the actions that say, ‘We’re a government that is going to back you to do well and is very comfortable with you making that progress,’ rather than what people associate with the Labour party, which is: we just want to redistribute wealth.”
In her 2018 book, The New Working Class: How to Win Hearts, Minds and Votes, Ainsley argued that politicians hadn’t kept pace with the fact that “working class” no longer just meant white men doing manual labour, but women and minorities often earning painfully little in precarious service sector jobs. That earned her a reputation for being ahead of the political curve. Starmer was intrigued enough to hire her in 2020 but she left after two years, disillusioned less with a boss she still admires than with Westminster itself. (Tellingly, one of the book’s chapters is titled The Myth of Political Control.)
“An enormous amount of effort goes on the business of the day – how to out-manoeuvre the other side – and there is much less of a focus than I think there needs to be on what happens for the rest of the country,” she says now. “Some of that is about the smallness of politics compared to how big the world has become. I think they focus on what they can control – who gets on the Today programme, who is selected as a candidate.” Starmer once publicly complained, as prime minister, of endlessly finding and pulling on levers that didn’t seem connected to anything. “The bigger argument I make in the book is that many of the means of power have been given away or drifted away over time. If you know what the right thing to do is, but your only means of doing that is to tax and spend more, you’re actually very limited,” says Ainsley, who believes that the net result is politicians making promises they can’t deliver while voters lose faith.
What surprised her most when working for Starmer was that even the then prime minister seemed curiously helpless against some of the pressures on him. “I do think Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer shared a level of integrity, of public service – they both would have wanted to do the right thing. Rishi Sunak has said himself that he did not feel saying ‘stop the boats’ repeatedly was the right thing to do because it offered a binary choice that he didn’t think was realistic. But he had to say it.”
Ainsley’s politics – she says she admired Sunak and Starmer in different ways – are interestingly eclectic. To the dismay of her mother, a longstanding organiser for the Labour party with a horror of “the Trots”, she became a revolutionary socialist at university – which lasted, she writes, until she got a job working for the Transport and General Workers Union, and realised how badly student politics fitted the reality of life on the factory floor. She moved on to run the Joseph Rowntree Foundation and it was while leading a research project there in 2015, aimed at giving people in poverty a voice, that she first got interested in the idea of control.
“One of the questions we asked was, ‘What do you feel in control of or not?’, and immigration came out starkly as something people didn’t feel in control of. There were also a number of other things that people didn’t feel in control of, but which people on higher incomes might, such as their mental health, education or the state of the local area.” The left still hasn’t fully absorbed why “take back control” was such a powerful slogan for Vote Leave during the Brexit referendum, she suggests.
In the decade since, she thinks repeated inflation spikes caused by events patently beyond British governments’ control – including wars in Ukraine and Iran – have merely compounded the sense of political impotence, not solely among the poor but increasingly among the once comfortable middle classes. “We’ve had this series of crises that people are now feeling is the new normal, and that buffer that governments might have provided feels like it doesn’t exist in people’s lives any more … It’s economic insecurity and probably cultural insecurity, people not feeling like their efforts are rewarded – if you look at the position of graduates at the moment, it’s a good example,” she says, pointing to high rates of unemployment among university leavers.
In her book, Ainsley details research suggesting populist narratives are more appealing to people who don’t feel in control of their own destinies, and that feeling part of a bigger rebel movement can increase feelings of agency. Rightwing populists in particular also benefit, she argues, from chaos and social unrest, which prompts authoritarian voters to look for someone to reassert control. To compete, leftwing politicians must show that “strong action is going to be taken by a strong leader”, but also that they’re giving power back to people over their own lives.
So how is Andy Burnham doing against those metrics? Though she says loyally that Starmer and his chancellor, Rachel Reeves, laid the foundations on which Burnham has built, Ainsley thinks their successor has had a “strong start”, citing a crackdown on people listening to music without headphones on public transport – which she believes gives people who would otherwise be fuming impotently more freedom to object. He has also promised to give the electorate breathing space from rising energy bills as a small, practical step that people understand. “They’ve got much clearer understanding of how people actually live their lives – it doesn’t feel abstract.”
But she worries about the dispiriting impact on middling earners of being dragged into paying higher-rate tax by the repeated freezing of tax thresholds in successive budgets, fuelling the sense that working hard doesn’t pay. So she advocates tax breaks for retraining or going on courses to improve your skills, in order to reward workers with ambitions to move up the ladder, plus long-term tax reforms to reduce the burden on working people and welfare reform to encourage work. “The left has got very fixed on redistribution, and while there might be a fairness argument for certain tax changes, if it doesn’t create an incentive for people to earn more, or go into work, then you get a society where people feel their efforts aren’t rewarded,” she says. “I want to see a centre left that believes in the politics of progress again.”
More unexpectedly, she points to rising levels of severe school absence as a sign that school isn’t working for some teenagers. “At a point where they are desiring independence and autonomy, we expect them to comply in school with many more rules and systems than adults. And at the same time in their online life, they’re allowed to make choices – as a gamer you can choose everything,” she says. “I think the disconnection between their online and offline lives, and the stresses that are on them in terms of the education system, are worth exploring.” Though she supports banning social media for under-16s, Ainsley thinks screens aren’t the only reason teenage mental health is suffering. “I don’t think we’ve examined properly what the pandemic did in terms of the harm it caused them. We’re now telling them they’re somehow deficient because they don’t want to socialise when as a state we told them not to, and not having fronted up to that responsibility is causing the most enormous damage.”
Adults should also be wary of transmitting their own anxiety over the state of the world to more naturally optimistic teenagers, she thinks. “The narrative of my generation is imposing an anxiety upon them, which I don’t think totally resonates when you listen to young people themselves.”
In the book, she argues that a left version of “taking back control” could involve encouraging individuals to take more responsibility for their own health, giving them access to the kind of targeted advice on diet and exercise that the rich buy in from personal trainers. But is she sure that people genuinely want more control, if in practice that means being responsible for things we don’t necessarily want to do? Ainsley concedes that she argued for a similar approach to healthcare while working for Starmer, but that the idea was dropped when it met resistance in focus groups. Still, she’s confident that it’s the way forward. “On the whole, people want to do things for themselves rather than have the state do things for them.”
Meanwhile, Ainsley believes that taking back control necessarily includes controlling Britain’s borders – a position considerably more popular with the public than within the Labour party. However, she would hold open the possibility of legal migrants earning the right to settle permanently. “I don’t think it’s only about migration, but I do think you need to be able to say as a nation that we can determine who comes in and who stays, and also have a path to citizenship,” she says, arguing that small boat crossings might represent only a small proportion of immigration, but that they’re “a visible reminder that the government is not in control”. If that sounds like a curiously rightwing take on control, last year YouGov found that 58% of Labour voters have a negative view of asylum seekers arriving on small boats, while only 9% disapprove of asylum seekers coming here legally.
Does she think it’s risky for Burnham publicly to reopen the debate over Brexit and freedom of movement? “The country is capable of having a sensible national debate about it. The risk is it takes a lot of oxygen out of determining where we ourselves want to go [as a country],” she says, arguing that rejoining the EU or single market isn’t in itself a fully fledged vision for Britain. “Unless they set that vision out … we’ll just go round in circles.”
When Ainsley started writing this book, Starmer was prime minister and she had no reason to think he wouldn’t still be when she published. When I ask if she was surprised he survived only two years, a long silence ensues. “It was clear it was going to be difficult for Keir to win back public confidence, but I was surprised at how the parliamentary party went about it,” she says, explaining that she was worried it would make Labour look as chaotic as the Tories. “I do feel Andy Burnham has bought some time for Labour to get itself on track.
“That said, MPs have to get fully behind Andy, and stay behind him. They absolutely do not have another go at this.” On that, at least, it’s hard to argue.
Control: How We Lost It and How to Take It Back by Claire Ainsley (Biteback Publishing, £20). To support the Guardian, order your copy for £18 at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Sudan’s displaced return to new challenges in war-battered Khartoum
The Sudanese was one of the first areas to be affected, and one of the worst hit, by the war between the SAF and the RSF.
Khartoum, Sudan – Mohamed Mahdi Makki Farah, 51, returned home near the Sudanese capital in August 2025 after the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) declared the entire state of Khartoum free of Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters. But it was not the end of his family’s struggles.
The 51-year-old had left his home in Jabal Awliya, south of Khartoum, for el-Fasher in North Darfur in June 2023.
He returned home to find it destroyed and ransacked, with even the household utensils stolen.
“Everything had been completely destroyed. Now we sleep on the floor, and some of us are living in rented houses,” Makki Farah told Al Jazeera. “We have not made any decision to repair our home because the costs are extremely high, and we have not been able to start.”
His years as a trader appeared to have been wasted, with his possessions gone and his business capital reduced to almost a third of its pre-war level because of the Sudanese pound’s depreciation.
The journey of displacement and return exhausted his remaining resources, while children’s medical expenses and the family’s daily needs added to their financial burden.
This meant he was unable to generate the funds needed to repair his home, so rent became an additional burden, while access to water, electricity and healthcare services is still difficult.
They had also lost important documents during the war and had to start from scratch to replace them.
“Everyone knows about the water and electricity problems; Khartoum is almost entirely in darkness now. As for healthcare, only government health centres are operating, thank God,” Makki Farah said.
The family’s experiences are those faced by millions of Sudanese families returning to their homes after years of displacement.
Fighting between the SAF and the RSF, which began in April 2023, continues, particularly in the southeast of the country. But large parts of Sudan are more stable after government victories, particularly around Khartoum. Sudanese displaced from these areas during early years of fighting are beginning to return home now that the situation has improved.
According to the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix report, as of September 30, approximately 5.27 million displaced Sudanese returned to their homes in nine states.
Of those, 82 percent had been internally displaced, while 18 percent had crossed the borders. Children accounted for about half of all returnees.
According to an assessment published by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in August 2026, approximately 2.5 million people had returned to their homes in Khartoum state.
But the agency warned that returning did not necessarily mean people had the conditions needed to rebuild their lives. Many found their homes damaged or uninhabitable, while work opportunities remained limited. Access to water and basic services was also inadequate due to damage to infrastructure during the war.
Many returnees are still renting as they cannot afford to repair their homes.
Abubakr Ishaq Hamed Ibrahim, 40, returned to Khartoum in February 2026 after being displaced to River Nile state in May 2023.
Like Makki Farah, he also found his home destroyed, with the furniture, bedding and basic household belongings they had accumulated over the years gone.
They had to move to Omdurman, neighbouring Khartoum, renting a home in the al-Thawra neighbourhood, but this became difficult to afford without a regular income.
“Our homes were looted and destroyed. We found nothing inside. Everything was wrecked, and we had no furniture, no bedding, nothing at all. We were unable to pay the rent for several months, and rents are quite expensive. We have been through extremely difficult conditions, and even now we have no stable source of income,” he said.
Before the war, Hamed Ibrahim had relied on self-employed work, but now depends on any casual work he can find.
His family had exhausted all their savings and borrowed money from family and friends to cover basics such as food, housing and school fees.
“Thank God, we are now doing casual jobs. The income is not enough to meet the cost of living and the daily burdens. We have exhausted all the money and savings we had, and we have borrowed money from individuals,” he said.
Things are slightly improving. His children have returned to school with support from relatives.
The family also receives in-kind assistance from organisations such as the World Food Programme, including supplies of sorghum (a cereal grain), flour, wheat, oil and sugar.
But overall, the situation in Khartoum remains dire for most residents. There have been fuel shortages and repeated power cuts in recent weeks, disrupting public transport. Fares have increased on some routes and commuters are often forced to wait hours for a bus. There are also long queues outside bakeries in some areas due to shortages of flour.
Families with limited resources, few employment opportunities and homes in need of costly repairs have been the worst affected.
On Saturday, Khartoum state authorities announced measures to address the transport crisis. Governor Ahmed Osman Hamza chaired a meeting that agreed to supply public transport services with fuel and give buses priority.
Government departments were also instructed to give residents lifts when travelling to and from work. Members of the Popular Resistance of Sudan, a coalition of SAF-aligned armed factions, help manage traffic in the capital.
Economic journalist and specialist Khalid Takes said the public transport crisis in Khartoum highlights a need for the state to take more responsibility for managing a centralised process, away from a reliance on private minibuses.
“No country has left the public transport sector entirely in the hands of the private sector, which relies on small vehicles,” he told Al Jazeera. “This results in ongoing costs for the state, both directly and indirectly, particularly in importing spare parts and fuel, which require foreign currency.”
Makki Farah says although he has managed to return to his home city of Khartoum, it is not enough to return his life to how it was before the war. He does not see a future in the capital for his family unless they receive more support.
“We have lost everything we had before the war. Now we need assistance because everything we need – housing, healthcare and education – has been destroyed,” he said.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ca.title: Can the world withstand another winter of war?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ca.author: Marco Carnelos
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ca.text:
Can the world withstand another winter of war?
Almost five years after the Russian invasion of Ukraine scrambled Europe’s energy map, another war has delivered a second shock.
Since the US-Israeli war on Iran began this past February, the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil normally flows, has been closed or contested, while Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian refineries has removed more fuel from an overstretched market.
Increased energy prices feed inflation, forcing central banks to tighten monetary policy, while fiscal anxiety pushes up sovereign bond yields, inflating debt service. The final squeeze arrives in supply chains and households, and then in the streets and at the ballot boxes.
In other words, it is a perfect storm - the mother of all perfect storms.
We are seeing a clear example of historian Adam Tooze’s polycrisis concept: a situation where multiple, distinct crises overlap, amplifying their collective effects.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The Iran war is the larger shock. Within days of its start, Brent crude jumped almost 19 percent to nearly $111 a barrel, from about $70 before the war. Washington called it “a very small price to pay” for security.
After some ups and downs over the summer, oil was at $117 late last month. The International Energy Agency has called it the worst energy crisis in history. Even EU chief Ursula von der Leyen, the queen of denial, acknowledged “a regional conflict with unintended consequences”.
Talks and periods of ceasefire have not normalised energy flows. The EU Commission has warned of a prolonged supply shock, which could involve forced cuts to fuel consumption before winter.
Weak point
To make a bad situation worse, the Houthis’ control over Yemen’s Red Sea shores has endangered another chokepoint, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, with serious repercussions for maritime logistics.
Compounding this, Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have pushed Moscow into unprecedented export bans at the worst possible time, with the Iran war having already drained inventories.
Europe no longer buys Russian diesel directly, but Russia’s former customers now compete for the same alternative cargoes. Hormuz drives most of the disruption, and the Russia-Ukraine war compounds it; together, they strike at the same weak point - a European continent that imports almost all of its fossil fuels.
Governments in Paris, Rome and elsewhere have less fiscal space to compensate the public - and the combination of austerity and inflation is historically combustible
The inevitable outcome has been inflation in the EU, which reached 3.8 percent in September, up from 3.2 percent in August - significantly higher than the rate of 2.6 percent a year prior. Food prices have also soared, fuelling widespread public anger in European cities.
The European Central Bank’s president, Christine Lagarde, warned this summer that “the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to play out”.
Raising interest rates against a supply shock does nothing for commodity supplies, but it increases financing costs at exactly the moment when governments are being asked to cushion households.
The bond market has noticed, with the yield on 30-year US Treasury bonds exceeding five percent this year, as national debt rose past $40 trillion and annual interest payments over $1 trillion for the first time.
In the UK, 30-year yields recently hit six percent, the first time a G7 member had faced such rates since the 2012 eurozone crisis.
France is at the epicentre of this crisis. Its bond yields stood at 4.85 percent in mid-October, near their highest levels in more than two decades, with EU officials urging Paris to present a credible budget.
French debt service is projected at about €59 billion ($66bn) this year, compared with roughly €30 billion for Germany, and Italy must roll over debt worth 17 percent of GDP in 2026.
Ratchet turning
This is not yet a replay of the 2011 economic crisis. Earlier in the war, analysts noted that Italian, Spanish and Greek yields stood below their 2022-23 peaks, because those countries had cut primary deficits.
It’s important to note that debt offices feel higher yields only as maturing paper is replaced - so the bill grows with every auction, rather than arriving all at once.
In economic jargon, it’s a ratchet, and each turn leaves less budgetary room for governments to offer the relief that angry households are demanding - even as these same governments continue to spend billions on arming Ukraine and launching unprecedented weapons procurement programmes.
Dire social consequences arrived last month. In France, hundreds of thousands of people joined demonstrations that began as student protests over education, and widened into cost-of-living grievances. In Belgium, police clashed with protesters in Brussels, while tens of thousands of people marched in Lisbon, Portugal, over living costs, low wages and housing. Large and violent demonstrations were also reported in Italy.
There does not seem to be a single Europe-wide movement, or at least not yet. Situations and demands differ by country, but ongoing economic shocks have served as an accelerant.
France’s presidential election and Italy’s general election are both due next year, while Spain faces a snap election this month. EU governments are weighing support for vulnerable households, but disputes over the €2 trillion EU budget risk blocking decisions.
With debt service rising, governments in Paris, Rome and elsewhere have less fiscal space to compensate the public - and the combination of austerity and inflation is historically combustible.
US midterms
The same energy shocks are now testing Donald Trump in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with the US president’s approval rating at a record low. About seven in 10 Americans say gasoline has become unaffordable, with the national average price above $4 a gallon for a record 158 days this year.
Trump’s partial or total defeat - losing only the House, or losing both the House and the Senate - could trigger another constitutional crisis, like the one that occurred on 6 January 2021, with Trump and his supporters refusing to accept a negative result.
This all seems like a single feedback loop, rather than separate crises. A war of choice against Iran, backed by a US naval blockade, disrupts the Gulf; the price is paid first by importers in Europe and Asia, and then by American drivers; central banks respond with higher rates; bond markets reprice the debts of the most exposed states; and governments with shrinking fiscal space face electorates that have lost patience.
The irony is that two crises aimed at inflicting a strategic defeat, and ideally regime change, in both Russia and Iran, have blown up in the faces of western liberal democracies, which are facing unbearable and dangerous costs.
While Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unsuccessfully tried to reduce US bond yields, further fuelling investors’ concerns, Trump has been scrambling to find a way to end the conflict in Ukraine, aiming to better focus on his war against Iran after the midterms. It is not clear yet whether Russia, Iran, and above all China will allow him such room for maneuver.
Several crucial issues must now be monitored closely for developments, including the outcome of Israel’s elections, which resulted in a deadlock last week; will the incoming government continue to bamboozle the US into waging an unnecessary war against Iran?
Ongoing European economic negotiations will also be vital to watch, alongside the outcome of Tuesday’s US midterm vote and the impacts on markets and investments. In addition, what happens next in relation to the chokepoints at Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb will be crucial: if commodity flows normalise, prices could drop within months, and the storm may lose its force.
If not, winter will be the next stress test - and it is fast approaching.

- Politik
