https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cats who filled our house with live mice
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Amy Fleming
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
This is a cat-and-mouse story in which the cats are the real pests. My old house, despite being next to rodent-filled woods, was blissfully mouse-free … until, during lockdown, we got two kittens, Mimi and Ruben. As soon as their fine motor skills were sufficiently sharpened, they started hunting. Thankfully, they weren’t into birds, but wood mice became their specialism. I suppose the dearth of mice indoors meant they had to catch them outside. The tabby twins would then bring their prey back to their lair (our house) and release them, still miraculously alive. Perhaps they thought mice would make fun pets.
You would know they had brought in a mouse when they sat guarding sections of ill-fitting skirting or gaps under cupboard doors, uttering odd “prittering” sounds. Cue us humans moving furniture and dashing about, getting down on our hands and knees, reduced to hunting the mice ourselves with upturned Tupperware boxes. If we caught them, we released them in the woods, locking our yowling cats inside so they couldn’t see exactly where. But some mice inevitably escaped into the fabric of the house.
I don’t blame the mice – they didn’t choose to invade us – but it was disgusting when the cupboard under the kitchen sink became smelly with mouse poo and wee, so I caught the culprits in humane traps loaded with peanut butter. I find mice adorable and on one occasion fell for a particularly plucky one who kept getting dragged back in after I’d released it. Rescuing it for the third time, I was so moved by its plight that I held it close on a piece of kitchen towel, in an attempt to bond with it. Instead of thanking me, it bit my finger and I had to get a tetanus booster. Bloody cats.
During what seemed like a nice, quiet time on the hunting front, the fridge began to stink, a faint smell of rotten-eggs gradually growing into a putrid stench. When I moved the fridge out to look behind it, I found the most horrific scene. There is a trough on the back of fridges to catch water that dribbles out, so it can evaporate. This trough had become a toilet for the confused mice, forced by my cats to live indoors. You couldn’t detach the trough, so it took hours to absorb the slimy liquid in endless wads of balled kitchen roll before I could scrub it. Thank God we no longer live next to woods.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
When will we know the US midterm election results?
The first results are expected on Tuesday as polls begin to close at 23:00 GMT. But final results might take days.
On Tuesday night, the United States – and many people around the world – will be following one of the country’s most closely contested midterm elections in recent years.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for grabs as Democrats hope to take control of both chambers from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.
Here is what we know about the results:
When will the first results come in?
The first results should be known on Tuesday after polls begin to close. Voting will end first in some jurisdictions on the East Coast at 6pm (23:00 GMT).
Results will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening, and some probably won’t be known until Wednesday or later in some races as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts.
But the first reported results won’t necessarily mean that a winner has been announced.
Election officials release vote counts as ballots are processed, and news organisations, like The Associated Press, then analyse them to determine how to call a race.
A closely contested race could take hours to call – or even days. It might not be clear for days whether the Republicans will retain control of Congress or Democrats secure a majority in either or both chambers.
What time do polls close in the US?
The first polling stations to close will be in parts of Indiana and Kentucky.
- 6pm Eastern Standard Time (EST) (23:00 GMT) – parts of Indiana and Kentucky
- 7pm EST (00:00 GMT) – most of Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, and the remaining parts of Indiana, Kentucky and most of New Hampshire
- 7:30pm EST (00:30 GMT on Wednesday) – North Carolina, Ohio, West Virginia
- 8pm EST (01:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, the remaining parts of New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Washington, DC, and parts of Florida, Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas
- 8:30pm EST (01:30 GMT on Wednesday) – Arkansas
- 9pm EST (02:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin, Wyoming, and the remaining parts of Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas
- 10pm EST (03:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Montana, Nevada, Utah, and parts of Idaho and Oregon
- 11pm EST (04:00 GMT on Wednesday) – California and Washington, and the remaining parts of Idaho and Oregon
- 12am EST (05:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Hawaii and most of Alaska
- 1am EST (06:00 GMT on Wednesday) – the remaining parts of Alaska, including the western Aleutian Islands
Which states could take longer to count votes?
- Alaska: The state uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote, extra rounds of counting are needed to determine the winner. And while in-person early and Election Day voting are reported on election night, the mail-in voting results are released in the following days. In 2024, about 75 percent of the votes were counted by the morning after the election with the remaining votes reported over the following days.
- California: The state carries out elections primarily by mail. Large batches of ballots come in and are verified days after the polls close, so close House races can take days or weeks to resolve.
- Arizona: In some counties, voters drop off mail-in ballots on Election Day. These ballots must undergo signature checks before being counted, which can delay results by several days in close races.
- Nevada: All registered voters are mailed ballots. Mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive up to four days later. Voters also have six days after Election Day to fix any signature problem, and this could delay results until the following week.
- Maine: Like Alaska, this state also uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote in a race with two candidates, ballots must be taken to Augusta, Maine’s capital, for further counting. This can delay final results.
- Washington: The state holds elections by mail. Ballots postmarked by Election Day can be counted in the following days, which can cause delays.
Which states could report results earlier?
Some of the states that could report results earlier include:
- Florida: Votes are usually counted quickly. In the 2024 general election, about 99 percent of the votes were counted by 10:51pm EST (03:51 GMT the next day), according to The Associated Press news agency.
- Ohio: Ohio tends to release all or almost all of its early and absentee voting results in the first results. The first results of the 2024 elections were reported starting at 7:36pm EST (00:36 GMT), six minutes after polls closed. By 11:03pm EST (04:03 GMT), 90 percent of the results had been reported.
- North Carolina: This East Coast state is also expected to release most of its results from mail-in voting in the first update of the night. In 2024, the state reached 90 percent of vote reporting at 11:36pm EST (04:36 GMT).
- Pennsylvania: In 2024, the first results came in as polls closed at 8pm EST (01:00 GMT). Half of the votes had been reported by 10:12pm EST (03:12 GMT), rising to 90 percent by 12:48am EST (05:48 GMT) the next day.
- Wisconsin: In 2024, 90 percent of the state voting results were released by 2:22am (07:22 GMT) on November 6.
So when will we know who won?
Many races could be called on election night, but it might take several days to know which party will control the House and Senate in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
If, for example, the US Senate race in Alaska requires a ranked-choice tabulation, the next round is scheduled for November 18.
So there is no specific deadline for knowing all the results. In races that are not close, news organisations are able to declare winners well before every ballot is counted while official certification takes place later. So quick reporting does not guarantee a fast race call.
In 2024, it took eight days to determine which party would control the House of Representatives.
What happens if results are challenged?
If a race is very close, a recount might be triggered automatically or if requested by a candidate, depending on state law.
Candidates also have the option of challenging the results in court, which could also delay the final result.
Trump has also raised questions about whether he would accept the midterm election results. When he was asked if he would respect the final outcome, he said; “I will if there are honest elections.”
But the US president cannot overturn congressional election results simply because he disagrees with them. Elections are administered and certified by individual states, and legal challenges must follow a process.
“All the states run elections. Courts accept that states run elections,” Democratic strategist Mali Smith told Al Jazeera.
Under the US Constitution, the House and Senate have the final authority to judge disputes over the elections of their own members.
Depending on the dispute, recounts and legal challenges could take days, weeks or longer to resolve.

https://taz.de/Hohe-Preise-fuer-Benzin-u.title: Hohe Preise für Benzin und Diesel: Reiche plant Spritpreisdeckel nur bei hohen Preissprüngen
https://taz.de/Hohe-Preise-fuer-Benzin-u.text:
Hohe Preise für Benzin und Diesel: Reiche plant Spritpreisdeckel nur bei hohen Preissprüngen
Die Bundeswirtschaftsministerin legt einen Gesetzentwurf für eine Preisobergrenze für Benzin und Diesel vor. Er soll am Mittwoch durchs Kabinett.
Bundeswirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (CDU) will einen Spritpreisdeckel nur bei extremen Preissteigerungen und unter hohen Hürden ermöglichen. Dies geht aus dem Referentenentwurf ihres Ministeriums für ein Kraftstoffhöchstpreisgesetz hervor, der der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters vorliegt. Nach vorläufiger Planung soll das Kabinett den Entwurf bereits am Mittwoch auf den Weg bringen. Demnach kann die Regierung erst dann Höchstpreise festlegen, wenn die Kraftstoffpreise in Deutschland drei Wochen in Folge um jeweils mehr als fünf Prozentpunkte stärker steigen als im Durchschnitt der übrigen EU-Staaten. Das gilt für Benzin und Diesel getrennt.
Steigen die Preise europaweit ähnlich stark, wäre demnach ein Preisdeckel auch bei kräftigen Preissprüngen in Deutschland nicht möglich. Das Wirtschaftsministerium bestätigte, dass sich die Vorlage in der Ressortabstimmung befinde. Details zur Vorlage, über die zuerst das „Handelsblatt“ berichtet hatte, wollte das Ministerium nicht nennen.
Dem Entwurf zufolge soll die Bundesregierung für einen Zeitraum von drei Monaten die Möglichkeit erhalten, Höchstpreise für Benzin und Diesel festzulegen. Danach soll die gesetzliche Ermächtigung automatisch auslaufen. Einem Reuters vorliegenden internen Zeitplan zufolge sollen Bundestag und Bundesrat das Gesetzesvorhaben noch vor Weihnachten verabschieden.
Für den Preisvergleich sollen dem Entwurf zufolge erstmals die Daten der zweiten vollständigen Januarwoche berücksichtigt werden. Grundlage sollen die wöchentlich von der EU-Kommission veröffentlichten Kraftstoffpreise ohne Steuern und Abgaben sein. Das Bundeskartellamt soll über seine Markttransparenzstelle wöchentlich prüfen, ob die Voraussetzungen für einen Eingriff erfüllt sind. Aber auch dann müsste die Bundesregierung eine Preisobergrenze nicht zwingend einführen.
Bundesländer können abweichen
Der Entwurf sieht eine regelmäßig aktualisierte Berechnungsformel für die Höchstpreise vor. Dabei müssen die tatsächlichen Marktbedingungen, Importkosten sowie angemessene Handels- und Vertriebsmargen berücksichtigt werden. Zu niedrige Höchstpreise könnten dazu führen, dass Kraftstofflieferungen nach Deutschland unwirtschaftlich würden und Versorgungsengpässe entstünden. Die Bundesregierung soll die Preisbegrenzung deshalb bei drohenden Versorgungsproblemen aussetzen können.
Die Bundesländer sollen zudem von bundesweiten Höchstpreisen nach oben oder unten abweichen dürfen, um regionale Unterschiede bei Beschaffungs- und Transportkosten zu berücksichtigen. Das soll auch für einzelne Landkreise oder Postleitzahlgebiete möglich sein. Ausnahmen könnten zudem für bestimmte Tankstellen etwa an Autobahnen oder auf Inseln gelten.
Eine von der SPD geforderte Übergewinnsteuer für Mineralölkonzerne wird in dem Gesetzentwurf als Alternative zum Spritpreisdeckel verworfen. Eine solche Steuer könne kurzfristig nicht rechtssicher ausgestaltet werden, entfalte keine unmittelbare Entlastungswirkung für Verbraucher und wirke sich negativ auf Investitionsanreize aus. Auch eine erneute befristete Senkung der Energiesteuer, der sogenannte Tankrabatt, komme wegen der angespannten Haushaltslage nicht infrage. (rtr)
Die Koalition aus CDU, CSU und SPD hatte Mitte September auf Drängen der Sozialdemokraten vereinbart, möglichst ab Januar 2027 einen Spritpreisdeckel einzuführen. Damit sollen die hohen Tankstellenpreise als Folge des Irankrieges gedämpft werden. Der Entwurf schafft zunächst nur die befristete Möglichkeit, bei außergewöhnlichen Preissteigerungen einzugreifen. Eine konkrete Entlastung in Cent je Liter ist nicht vorgesehen.
Seit Oktober gilt noch bis Ende des Jahres eine dreimonatige Senkung der Energiesteuer auf Kraftstoffe. Daraus ergibt sich einschließlich der geringeren Mehrwertsteuer eine rechnerische Entlastung von rund 17 Cent je Liter.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: A response to Andy Burnham: We need an apology and reparations

A response to Andy Burnham: We need an apology and reparations
It is good news the British PM is open to calls for an apology for slavery. But debt restructuring instead of reparations won’t do.
I read with interest the recent news that United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham is now open to calls for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans and chattel enslavement.
On the face of it, this is some good news. Only a full and formal apology can allow for the healing of wounds and the destruction of cultures caused by colonialism, chattel enslavement and other forms of oppression of peoples to begin.
The Reparations Commission of the Caribbean Community (CRC of CARICOM) has been requesting a dialogue on apology and reparations for some time without success. Indeed, previous such demands have been met with expressions of deep sorrow and regret, but never an apology or even a promise of one.
As a reminder, in 2015, British Prime Minister David Cameron rejected calls for slavery reparations. Instead, he announced a 25-million-pound UK-funded project to help construct a new prison in Jamaica, aiming to facilitate the deportation of Jamaican nationals serving long sentences in British prisons. The proposal caused much controversy.
I suspect that, now that King Charles III will address the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua on Tuesday amid civil society protests and calls for an apology and reparations, this promise has been squeezed out of the British prime minister before the event.
I have often been asked why a formal apology for the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans and chattel slavery in the Caribbean is so important to the reparations process, and what difference an apology can make in terms of acknowledgement, accountability, healing and repair.
As CARICOM’s Ten Point Plan for Reparatory Justice emphasises, an apology is a formal gesture of goodwill and will foster better relations between the states of Europe and the Caribbean. It would acknowledge a shared history and interconnectedness to be mobilised towards justice and mutual respect.
It would accept responsibility for these crimes, commit to non-repetition and pledge to repair the harms caused to the victims and their descendants. It would represent an ethical and legal acknowledgement of how present-day inequalities and racial injustices are rooted in the history of such criminal conduct; acts such as complicity in native genocide, the introduction and perpetuation of chattel slavery and violent oppressive colonisation.
An apology would then have to be followed by meaningful reparations actions. Those actions, however, cannot be reduced to what Burnham proposes: improved debt repayment conditions.
Here, it is important to remind ourselves of the debt Britain and other nations involved in enslavement have to repay.
Sir Arthur Lewis, considered the father of the modern Caribbean reparations movement, conceptualised the call for reparations within the framework of social and economic development.
In his book Labour in the West Indies: The Birth of a Workers’ Movement, published in 1939, Lewis insisted: “It is the British who by their action in past centuries are responsible for the presence in these islands of the majority of their inhabitants, whose ancestors as enslaved persons contributed millions to the wealth of Great Britain.” He further referenced the over 200 years of unpaid labour Britain extracted from millions of enslaved people in the Caribbean as “a debt that must be repaid – and which the British have yet to repay”.
The British have not yet acknowledged or attempted to repay their “black debt”. Indeed, they have denied responsibility for reparations, even in the face of quantitative and qualitative evidence of how they benefitted from chattel slavery.
Lewis’s economic development theories were grounded in the belief that the 20th-century economic transformation of the British colonies could not be realised without the coloniser acknowledging and honouring its “black debt”.
Statements in the Ten Point Plan, Ghana’s March 2026 United Nations Resolution and the UN Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination’s General Recommendation No 40 all express, in varying ways, that the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans and chattel enslavement really broke the world.
Together they created an unprecedented racialised regime of violence and governance that reduced Africans and their descendants to permanent, nonhuman property, barred them from civic life, and laid the blueprint for modern global power, economics, and enduring hierarchies of race and gender.
What we, the descendants now living with the legacies of chattel enslavement and colonial terror, want is a conversation on actual reparations: debt cancellation rooted in the reality of the lingering legacies of colonialism.
Confronting that “complicated history” of which the British prime minister speaks includes paying for the wrongs of chattel slavery. In fact, it is not complicated at all.
That conversation should also be about setting the record straight about abolition: enslaved people like Chief Takyi in Jamaica and the Black revolutionaries in Ayiti and elsewhere, not Britain, led the fight for abolition.
Former colonisers do not seem to agree that African jurisprudence always saw the trafficking and chattel enslavement as wrongful acts. But as far as former colonies and Africans are concerned, a crime does not rot; it is carried forward until justice is achieved.
The UK prime minister may intend to launch a new “drive on debt” for poor countries that would allow them to pay back under better conditions. But we reject the notion that a nation that profited from chattel slavery should not now be held responsible for its actions. We demand debt cancellation and monetary compensation. It is time for Britain to apologise and pay its debt.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://taz.de/Gruengasquote-fuer-fossil.title: Grüngasquote für fossile Heizungen: Teures Täuschungsmanöver
https://taz.de/Gruengasquote-fuer-fossil.author: Anja Krüger
https://taz.de/Gruengasquote-fuer-fossil.text:
Grüngasquote für fossile Heizungen : Teures Täuschungsmanöver
Die Bundesregierung hat eine Grüngasquote für Heizbrennstoffe eingeführt. Stattdessen sollte sie eine Abwrackprämie für fossile Heizungen anbieten.
U mwelt- und Verbraucherverbände warnen mit Nachdruck vor dem Irrweg, den die schwarz-rote Bundesregierung mit der Einführung der sogenannten Grüngasquote geht – und sie haben völlig recht. Diese Quote sieht vor, dass ab 2028 Gas und Öl für fossile Heizungen einen bestimmten Anteil angeblich klimafreundlicher Brennstoffe enthalten müssen, etwa Bio-Methan. Die „grünen“ Gase oder Öle verdienen diesen Namen aber nicht. Denn sie sind nicht so klimafreundlich, wie die Bezeichnung suggeriert, und sie führen zu erheblichen ökologischen Schäden, weil die erforderlichen Pflanzen in Monokulturen angebaut werden.
Die Einführung der „Grüngasquote“ fürs fossile Heizen ist eine üble Finte der schwarz-roten Bundesregierung bei der Abwicklung des Heizungsgesetzes der Ampel. Sie will den Eindruck erwecken, dass die Klimaziele eingehalten werden können, auch wenn der Betrieb von Gas- und Ölheizungen unbegrenzt möglich bleibt. Doch das wird die Grüngasquote nicht erreichen – schon weil sie für die Industrie als Großverbraucher nicht gilt. Zudem ist völlig ungewiss, woher die gewaltigen Mengen an „grünen“ Brennstoffen überhaupt kommen sollen. Sicher ist dagegen, dass sie sehr teuer sind.
Den Preis für dieses Täuschungsmanöver zahlen künftige Generationen, die mit den dramatischen Folgen der Erderhitzung klarkommen müssen. Verbraucher:innen werden schon in wenigen Jahren mit den absehbar immens steigenden Kosten fürs Heizen mit Gas oder Öl kämpfen. Besonders bitter ist das für Mieter:innen, die keinen Einfluss auf die Art ihres Heizens haben, und jene, die sich von der Regierung blenden lassen. Im ersten Halbjahr 2026 wurden, trotz Klimakrise und Warnungen etwa von Verbraucherschützer:innen, immer noch mehr als 130.000 neue Gasheizungen verkauft.

Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Dass angeblich grüne Brennstoffe keine Lösung sind, kann nur eins heißen: Die Bundesregierung muss sich korrigieren. Sie sollte eine Abwrackprämie für Öl- und Gasheizungen einführen, statt den Bürger:innen Sand in die Augen zu streuen.
