https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.title: Farm workers are falling sick in a Kenyan horticultural town. Were they poisoned by pesticides?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.author: Carlos Mureithi in Timau. Photographs by Edwin Ndeke
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text:
When Reuben Muriki fainted while doing a chore in the compound of his home near the horticultural town of Timau in central Kenya several years ago, it marked the start of a series of increasingly serious health episodes.
His joints became swollen, his skin became discoloured and he found breathing difficult. He was in and out of hospital, and was forced to quit his work as a pesticide sprayer at a flower farm. Doctors treated him for suspected tuberculosis in vain.
“He would often fall and completely lose consciousness,” his mother, Margaret Mwanjaro, said in their living room in Mukuri village.
Now 30, Muriki is unable to walk on his own. He speaks incoherently and quickly forgets things.
Mwanjaro, on whom Muriki relies for round-the-clock care, believes her son’s condition is a result of poisoning from the pesticides that he used to spray on the flower farm.
Timau, a small town of about 10,000 people, has for decades hosted horticultural companies that employ thousands of workers from the area. Many have fallen sick over the years, some dying young. Their relatives say pesticides are to blame.
Muriki is now one of 87 people seeking to join a court petition case against the Kenyan government and agrochemical companies challenging the sale of highly hazardous pesticides (HHPs).
Pesticide use has risen to record levels in Kenya, as farmers seek higher yields and improved food quality for local and export markets. In recent years, concerns have grown about the use of chemicals that pose severe risks, including some that are banned in the EU. Two UN agencies – the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Health Organization – have said HHPs present particularly high levels of acute or chronic hazards to health or the environment.
The petition accuses five agrochemical companies – Monsanto, Syngenta, Bayer, BASF and Nairobi-based Twiga Chemical Industries – of selling pesticides containing lethal active ingredients in Kenya.
It was filed in 2022 by the nonprofit African Centre for Corrective and Preventive Action and environmental and human rights lawyer Kelvin Kubai. Last November, the court allowed the petitioners to publish an advert inviting people allegedly affected by 11 pesticide ingredients to join the case to make it a class-action lawsuit. The court is expected to decide whether to enjoin them early next year.
“These are people our government has neglected, (and that) these companies and producers have neglected right at the point of sale,” said Kubai, who hails from Timau. “The Kenyan farmer – just like the American farmer, just like the European farmer – deserves to be protected.”
Those who responded had histories of symptoms associated with pesticide exposure, including skin, stomach and chest problems, dizziness and Parkinson’s disease, a condition that causes nerve cells in the brain to become damaged over time.
Scientists hired by the petitioners tested the 87 court case applicants for paraquat, a highly toxic chemical that has been used as a herbicide and has been associated with Parkinson’s disease, and glyphosate, a cancer-linked weed killer. Kubai said that in all 87 people, they found levels of both chemicals above permissible levels.
In Muriki’s case, the scientists found nearly 200 times the reference limit for paraquat and 48 times the reference limit for glyphosate in his urine sample.
“We were not able to find any other cause of the conditions [affecting Muriki], except his paraquat and glyphosate levels,” said Prof Zakayo Thaimuta, a pathologist who worked with the petitioners. Thaimuta noted that all 87 people had presented with at least three major medical conditions. The most common were Parkinson’s disease, throat inflammation and pulmonary fibrosis, a lung disease.
Research has pointed to a huge presence and use of HHPs in Kenya. A report released in April by Greenpeace found that nearly half (48) of the 141 active pesticide ingredients registered in the country last year were classified as HHPs.
Like her son, Mwanjaro also worked at a horticultural farm, performing tasks such as weeding and picking roses and other flowers in greenhouses for five years until 2017. She also developed health complications.
She described starting work early in the morning without wearing personal protective equipment, just a few hours after sprayers had applied chemicals on the flowers. “You’d feel the fumes getting into your throat,” she said.
Four years after she began working at a farm, she quit her job after developing blisters on her body and noticing that she was becoming weaker. Today, her other health conditions include worn nails, inflamed skin and constant coughing.
Responding to a request for comment, Bayer, which acquired Monsanto in 2016, said all its products were safe for humans and the environment if applied according to label instructions, and that it applied consistent safety standards worldwide.
A Syngenta spokesperson said all its products sold in Kenya followed the country’s regulatory standards and that it stood fully behind their safety and effectiveness when used according to labelled instructions.
The Pest Control Products Board, which regulates the importation, exportation, manufacture and use of pest control products in Kenya, declined to comment because the matter was in court. BASF and Twiga Chemical Industries did not respond to questions sent to them.
Acres upon acres of lush horticultural farms stretch as far as the eye can see around Timau. The farms, which mainly target the export market, have been an economic lifeline for generations of residents.
But in the town itself and its surrounding settlements, stories abound of farm workers falling seriously ill.
Alice Kagwiria lives in Mukuri’s neighbouring village of Riverside Kieni. One morning in 2013 she was on her way to a bus stop to report for work at a horticulture farm when she felt a sharp pain in her neck and back – as if something heavy had landed on her, she said. Shortly after, her hand went numb.
For 11 years, she said, she had worked without gloves in greenhouses for eight hours a day, five days a week, picking green peas and runner beans that colleagues had sprayed with pesticides.
With her hand impaired, the company assigned her “light duty” for a few months. The following year she was let go. Kagwiria, who now walks with a limp, pulled down a sock to show skin rashes that have emerged in the intervening years. She also has eye and stomach problems.
“Anybody considering a job at a horticulture farm should think twice,” she said outside her house. “You’re better off working somewhere that won’t cause you health problems.”
The impact is felt beyond Timau, in the wider Meru county, from where the horticultural industry attracts labour.
Stephen Muriungi lives in Ndunyu Barikui village, about 25 miles from Timau, and worked as a sprayer on a flower farm in the town for two-and-a-half years. In 2018 he started getting severe headaches that lasted hours. In time his legs weakened and he became unable to walk.
He recalled how, wearing an apron and gloves, he would use a sprayer to pump pesticides stored in a rucksack for hours at a time, the fumes often becoming unbearable.
“Those chemicals were very strong,” the 47-year-old said. “Even after removing clothes, your whole body would smell of chemicals.”
Today he is heavily incapacitated – he moves slowly, has stiff muscles and poor balance and struggles to hold spoons and cups because his hands shake – and relies on his family’s support as caregivers.
The sale and use of HHPs in Kenya has caused intense debate. Campaigners and health experts have called for bans and the use of safer alternatives.
Kubai said there was an “extreme urgency” to address the issue, and lamented that Kenya’s healthcare system lacked the capacity to provide comprehensive care for those affected. “We do not have the luxury of a healthcare system that can wholly rely on curative measures. We can only excel through preventive measures, and that means that our farmers ought to be protected,” he said.
Millicent Kanario, a food safety researcher, said some HHPs took years to break down and be eliminated from the environment, posing a high risk to biodiversity in addition to human health.
Kanairo, who co-authored a paper on agrochemical use in potato farming in central Kenya, said pesticide use is becoming “explosive” in the country and called for user education and strict government regulation. “Where we are headed to as a country, it’s quite dangerous,” she said.
One day this May, the cancer centre at Meru Teaching and Referral hospital was a hive of activity, with some patients waiting on seats to be attended by medics, and others lying on recliners while receiving chemotherapy.
Dr Stephen Chege, the clinical and radiation oncologist who heads the centre, said that in recent years it had received an increasing number of referrals from other hospitals of farmers and horticulture farm workers from the county. Among those referred, he has noticed increasing diagnoses of blood cancers and gastrointestinal cancers.
“The numbers are definitely going up,” he said. “So, the question we ask ourselves is: ‘Is it because of exposure?’”
A study carried out in Peru, whose findings were released in April, found a “robust spatial association” between environmental exposure to pesticides and increased incidence risks for cancer.
Campaigners on pesticides often draw attention to a quirk of the pesticide industry in Kenya: the presence of ingredients that are banned in the EU.
The April Greenpeace report found that nearly half (47%) of the registered pesticide active ingredients in Kenya were banned in the EU because of health and environmental risks.
Data obtained by Unearthed and Public Eye found that in 2024, EU companies sent export notifications – a requirement for companies in the region planning to export a banned pesticide – to the European Chemicals Agency to export 474 tonnes of pesticides to Kenya. This was despite the EU Commission’s commitment in 2020 to end the practice.
France and Belgium have implemented bans on exporting pesticides prohibited for use in the EU.
Eustace Gacanja, chief executive of the Kenya Organic Agriculture Network, which promotes organic agriculture, said the export to Kenya of products produced and banned in the EU was indicative of a “double standard” approach. “Of course, it means Kenya has weaker legislation, weaker laws,” he said. “But then, is it right that if it’s bad for the Europeans, it’s good for the Africans?”
Olof Björnsson, programme officer at Swedwatch, which promotes responsible business practices and together with KOAN conducted research on the exports, said: “Europe has a failed export and pesticide policy, and the Kenyan farmer is paying the cost for that failed policy.”
Harun Warui, project lead of the Route to Food Initiative, which has studied HHP use in Kenya, said PCPB needed to shift from risk-based regulation, which considers the likelihood of a pesticide to cause harm based on exposure levels, to hazard-based regulation, which the EU uses and which focuses on a pesticide’s intrinsic potential to cause harm.
“These are highly hazardous pesticides that should not be sold because of their impact on the environment and health,” he said.
Citing the risk-based and hazard-based systems, Bayer said the authorisation of pesticides in some African countries but not in the EU “does not say anything about its safety”, but instead reflected different regulatory approaches.
It said the assessments of many regulatory agencies around the world reflected the specific agronomic and climatic conditions in each country and the local needs of farmers.
The Syngenta spokesperson said that, when exporting products from Europe, the company respected the importing country’s sovereignty and direction and met all the international regulatory requirements.
The use of HHPs and exports of banned pesticides from the EU to Kenya have had a blowback effect. Horticulture produced in Kenya for export to Europe has faced more interceptions in recent years because some of it has been found to contain active ingredients that are restricted or banned in Europe, or chemicals that exceed limits. Kenya’s earnings from vegetable exports dropped by 68% from 2023 to 2025, largely attributed to EU pesticide regulations.
In Timau, families blighted by health complications are also having to deal with the consequences of economic inactivity.
“I can’t do much work,” said Mwanjaro, who is struggling to take care of herself and her son. “I can’t stand the pain.” She pointed to an empty pack of neurological medications on a table. “For five days now, I’ve lacked money to buy these for him.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/jarrar-pales.title: A Palestinian Prisoner on the Nightmare Behind Israeli Bars
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/jarrar-pales.author: Khalida Jarrar, Jacobin
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/jarrar-pales.text:
Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Born in Nablus in 1963, Khalida Jarrar is one of the foremost voices of the Palestinian left — feminist, secular, socialist — and one of the towering figures of the political prisoners’ movement. For more than a decade she led Addameer, the main Palestinian prisoner support organization. In 2006, voters elected her to the Palestinian Legislative Council, where she chaired the prisoners’ commission, and she later served on the national committee that prepared Palestine’s accession to the International Criminal Court. Today she is a researcher at the Muwatin Institute at Birzeit University, where she is conducting a pioneering study of the class and gender dimensions of the women prisoners’ movement since 1967.

She has paid for each of these roles with her own freedom. Israel has imprisoned her five times, for a total of more than six years behind bars. Almost every time, Israel held her under “administrative detention,” a system it inherited from British colonial emergency law. It allows indefinite imprisonment on the basis of a “secret file,” without charge, without trial, and without a lawyer able to contest what cannot be read.

In 2014, when the Israeli army ordered Jarrar’s expulsion from Ramallah to Jericho, she refused and lived for a month in a protest tent until the order fell. In 2015, twelve charges against her amounted to political acts: speeches, attending a book fair, and visiting a released prisoner. In 2021, during yet another detention, her daughter Suha, a thirty-one-year-old researcher, died suddenly — and Israel denied her mother a farewell.

Israeli forces arrested her for the fifth time in the early hours of December 26, 2023, the day before she was due to publicly present a study on Israel’s abuses against Palestinian prisoners during the genocide in Gaza. Thirteen months of administrative detention followed. She spent the last six in total isolation, in a cell two and a half meters by one, without a window or ventilation. Prison authorities moved her there days after Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, visited Damon Prison.

When she asked why, a guard replied: “You will not know the reason for your isolation, nor how long it will last.” She walked out on January 19, 2025, in the first prisoner exchange of the ceasefire.

The conversation below took place in English, in mid-August. Israel’s doctrine of destroying refugee camps is spreading from the northern West Bank to the gates of Jerusalem. Israel voted in legislative elections on October 27, and Palestinians face elections in November that many do not believe in. Against this backdrop, Jarrar talks about prisons and libraries, about imperialism and oxygen — and about what a person does, locked alone in a darkened cell, in order not to go mad.

Israel first arrested you on March 8, 1989 — International Women’s Day, at the height of the first intifada. In an essay, you begin the history of the prisoners’ movement not with a battle but with a song: the women of the 1936 revolt who, outside the British Mandate’s prisons, hid messages in coded syllables of folk songs. You also trace an unbroken legal line from British colonial emergency laws to today’s military courts — and Israel has detained around one million Palestinians since 1967, more than fifty thousand of them children. How do you explain that an emergency law older than the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is still, in 2026, putting people in cells without charge?

When we talk about the colonial system, we have to talk about the colonial system all over the world. In the case of Palestine, there is a direct continuity with the British system: the British Mandate governed through emergency laws — house demolitions, curfews, collective punishment, administrative detention. When Israel came, it continued that system, learned from it, developed it — and today it exports it across the whole world. We are talking about a system tied to all the capitalist and imperial systems.

Since 1967, around one million Palestinians have passed through Israeli prisons, including children and women. And the prison system is the same as under the mandate. In my research, I found that it is also very similar to the Irish experience and to the US system.

It is a colonial system that always seeks the same thing — to colonize, to settle. Within its liberal mechanism, it developed something I call “making it nice”: making violence presentable through the law, through emergency laws, through military orders. That is why administrative detention exists: they arrest anyone on the basis of a so-called secret file, and there are people who spend seven years like that, without anyone ever accusing them of anything.

This struggle against colonial emergency laws no longer belongs only to Palestinians — they have become a worldwide mechanism, and we have to fight them together. And when we turn to international humanitarian law, we find that Israel has violated it in its entirety: the right to life, the conventions on the treatment of prisoners, the right to a fair trial. There is a big question today about this system: Is international law for the weak or an excuse for the strong? I believe we need an international law for the victims, not for the colonial system — a global system in the service of the weak and of the victims to protect, in the end, humanity.

Israel holds more than 9,600 Palestinian political prisoners today, over 3,500 of them without charge and some 350 of them children. More than one hundred have died in custody. Israel bars the International Committee of the Red Cross from visiting, and a new law creates a special court for Palestinians, with the death penalty. You came out of six months of solitary confinement straight into freedom and said that conditions are the worst since 1967 — that Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, “treats prisoners as if they were not human.” What has changed?

In my last imprisonment, I spent thirteen months in administrative detention, six of them in isolation. Ben-Gvir’s policy uses the tools of punishment out loud, not under the table. And he is proud when he enters prisoners’ cells to threaten them. He is proud of the death penalty law — when the world is moving to abolish that punishment, because it is inhuman.

He has reopened cells and prisons that Israel had closed for decades. In Ramle there is an underground prison, the “Rakevet,” which Israel used from 1967 until the mid-1970s and then shut down, because it was too terrible. Ben-Gvir reopened it and put people from Gaza there. For Gaza’s prisoners, there is in fact a kind of administrative detention called the “unlawful combatants” law: six months, renewable for another six, and another six, with no one knowing until when.

From my own experience, I tell you: they treat you like an animal. They attack your humanity — they want you to feel that you are not a human being. I do not want to go into details about the food, the beatings, the strip searches, the punishments.

But imagine: six months in a cell two and a half meters by one, with no windows, in summer, full of humidity. For the first three months the light was always on; then they started switching it off during the day and keeping it on all night. There was no oxygen.

This punishment is revenge, because I did nothing but give some speeches about the political situation. Of course I am Palestinian, I am against the occupation, and I seek the freedom of my people, as I seek the freedom of all the peoples of the world — I believe in that connection. And anyone who lives under the capitalist system also knows the mechanisms that crush people: running to eat, running for a house, living only to survive. What they did to me is a small example of how this system, full of violence, treats people in an inhuman way.

Those who study incarceration — in Palestine and around the world — say that solitary confinement is not an extra degree of harshness: it is a distinct instrument that works by removing the collective Palestinian prisoners spent sixty years building. The question is not how you endured the pain — it is how you kept your political mind intact, your mental health, when they took away exactly the thing that makes it political. And one more: the late prisoner and writer Walid Daqqah wrote that the occupier had moved on from disciplining bodies to trying to dismantle consciousness itself. Is that what you felt they were trying to do to you?

Yes, of course — that is their aim. From the first moment I entered isolation, which is an extremely hard experience, I made two decisions. The first: how to make my body survive; the second: how to keep my mind working. Because their aim is for you to go mad, or to damage your thinking.

The body I saved with water — drinking water, the only thing I had. And sometimes they cut it off, as punishment: two or three days without water, without being able to shower. Sometimes they brought me a bottle; other times they “forgot” — because the essential thing is to negate you, to pretend you are not there. When the guards passed the door of my cell, they turned their faces away; they did not look at me.

The mind was the second battle. In those few meters, I walked all day long. I decided not to sleep during the day — only at night.

There were no books; there was nothing inside the cell. So I held discussions inside my head. I told myself: they want to destroy you, but you are part of a people fighting for its freedom, and you are part of the strugglers of the whole world — like Bobby Sands, like Angela Davis. You belong to those people.

And I worked. At Birzeit University, I am doing a major piece of research on the class and gender analysis of women prisoners from 1967 until today — I had already written parts of it. So I would discuss the research with myself.

And there is something else: what they did shows their fascism, but it does not make me a victim. I am not an individual; I believe in the collective experience. That is why when people tell me, “we want to write your story,” I answer: no. I write about the collective experience because we are part of a collective experience worldwide.

The root of the fascist capitalist system contains violence. Violence is part of its content — not freedom and democracy, which are the slogans they want to teach us. Lately I have gone back to reading Karl Marx’s Capital, the pages on the violence of the colonial systems, on how many people they killed.

That is how I governed myself inside: always believing that I am part of a whole, that I am not alone. Those were the words I used with myself: Khalida, you are not alone.

The activist Munther Amira tells this story: when Israeli authorities transferred him to a high-security prison, he found in the yard a thin, weakened man he barely recognized who called out his name. It was Marwan Barghouti. The next day, the prisoners were sitting in a circle listening to Barghouti give a lecture — because the guards had emptied the prison library, and the men had answered by teaching one another.

Barghouti pointed him to a chair: “It’s your turn. We want to hear about your nonviolent resistance.” And when they asked him what he thought of it, he replied: “Call it whatever you like, as long as you resist.” Later, Barghouti sent word, through his wife, that Amira should come back to prison for another six months, to give more lectures.

You did precisely this on the women’s side — and wrote it down: “We are transforming the prison into a school.” The censors let in Ghassan Kanafani, Maxim Gorky, and Davis — and never let in [Antonio] Gramsci. How does that world work, from the inside? And why does the jailer fear an Italian intellectual who has been dead for almost ninety years?

When Israel arrested me in 2015, there were twenty-three of us women in prison. Most were under eighteen, students — and some were facing heavy sentences: ten, fifteen years. I began to think that education was essential for them: so that they would not spend those ten years merely inside a cell.

We discussed how to do it: first a small school, then a university. Seven women finished their studies and, after their release, are now doing their master’s degrees.

We ran into two problems: first, there were no books; second, the official conditions required two women with master’s degrees to teach — and at that moment I was the only woman in the prison with a master’s. At that time it was still possible to discuss matters through the lawyers, and our families visited us — that ended after October 7, 2023.

And there was an opportunity: the prison for underage boys was next to ours, and the prison authorities decided to transfer the boys to other prisons. Through the women’s representative, we got them to leave us their library — with the official schoolbooks. They moved us into the boys’ section, and the books stayed.

But we thought: they may come and confiscate them at any moment. So we copied the books by hand, in full. We divided the responsibility — each woman copied a part. We had pencils and notebooks, and we began.

Through the lawyers we reached the Palestinian Ministry of Education, which agreed to recognize me officially as a teacher. We gave classes in which we tied study to life — theory with practice. And we succeeded: they took the exam and finished high school. Before my release, I chose two women, showed them how we worked, and prepared them to continue.

The dream of those serving life sentences was university — imprisoned men studied at university; the women, never. After my release, I went to discuss it with the minister of higher education. They told me: “three master’s holders are required.”

I answered: What are we to do, if women with master’s degrees are not in prison? It is the men who seem clever to you . . . [laughs] We agreed on a method to get around the problem.

And then Israel arrested me again. Do you know what the women told me? “We are sad that you are in prison again — but, in here, we are happy: we can continue our studies. And we like you.”

That is what Barghouti sent word to Amira for: come back, we want to continue the classes. The prisoners want their teachers back.

[Laughs.] We succeeded. At that time, the prison authorities allowed each woman three books a month, which our families brought in. The guards always searched them, and the censors always read them. And Gramsci they always confiscated; they never let Gramsci in.

I don’t know — it is a question I ask myself, not them: Are you afraid of Gramsci? He died so long ago. They let in Davis — alive, a critic of the prison system, an active voice for Palestine. The dead Italian, no.

Let us talk about the Palestinian political situation. The polls are brutal: around 80 percent of Palestinians want Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas gone. Barghouti leads every presidential poll from his cell; elections are due on November 28, and 60 percent do not believe they will take place.

In 2016, you said that elections within the existing framework “will solve nothing” — that the root lies in the Palestine National Council and the refoundation of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). Do you stand by that? And security coordination with Israel: Can the Palestinian Authority reform it, or only end it?

If we need elections, we need real elections — not elections that the European Union, the Americans, and the Israelis design to shape the system to what they want. They want, for example, a system without the political parties that did not accept the Oslo Accords. Look at what happened in the municipal elections: Israel interfered directly — they phoned people to say, “if you stand as a candidate, you will be arrested.” And they arrested many.

We need elections that give the Palestinian people the right to decide, not the United States, nor Israel, nor the European Union deciding for the Palestinians. And it is from that perspective that I believe in the refoundation of the PLO: through elections to the Palestine National Council, not to the Legislative Council. Today no free elections are possible: they interfere with the candidates, they want to shape the Palestinian system to their will. That is why I do not think it will go well.

Let me end with the paradox of this moment. The Palestinian cause has never been so popular in the West: for the first time in a quarter of a century, Americans sympathize more with Palestinians than with Israel; some 160 states recognize Palestine. Zohran Mamdani is mayor of New York City. Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar sit in Congress.

Abdul El-Sayed won a Senate primary in Michigan against $30 million of pro-Israel money. Catherine Connolly won Ireland’s presidency with Palestine at the heart of her campaign. Rima Hassan, born in a refugee camp, is a member of the European Parliament. And yet European arms and trade keep flowing, while British police arrest thousands under terrorism laws for holding a placard.

From Damon, you wrote in 2020 that these gestures of solidarity “empower us, prisoners, from within.” What do you ask of this elected generation abroad?

I dream of a new world. And I think the changes are coming: good changes. What you describe in the United States are changes at the root.

We have not yet reached the point where things collapse, but these accumulated changes become big changes. I think that, after the genocide, the world realized that this fascist genocide can also reach their own houses and their own cities.

That is why I believe, and I dream, that the world will change toward more justice, toward a real democracy, not this democracy. I dream, of course, of my people’s self-determination, of our freedom, without occupation. And I dream, for the whole world, of peace, real justice, and equality among all peoples.

And I hope that the socialist system will be the solution. I know that the practical experience, in some countries, did not work, but I believe in the ideas, and in how to make them live, because I believe in equality and in social justice.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-maga-e.title: A Midterm Rout Will Hurt the GOP, but Trumpism Will Endure
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-maga-e.author: Joseph G. Peschek
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-maga-e.text:
Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Observers across the spectrum expect Democrats to make significant gains in the upcoming midterms, in House and Senate races and beyond. There are good reasons to trust in their predictions. Nonpresidential elections in the US are increasingly “nationalized,” meaning that evaluations of presidential and national politics strongly influence down-ballot choices. And President Donald Trump, having behaved cruelly and erratically while presiding over a weak economy and an unpopular war with Iran, has not set Republicans up for success.

With inflation rates high, wages stagnant, and borrowing costs elevated, economic issues are central to the GOP’s current quandary. In a recent Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll, Trump’s economic approval rating stands at just 28 percent. By a three-to-one margin, respondents said the state of the economy was either not so good or poor. Forty-eight percent said they were financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025, the highest percentage saying this about any president in Post-ABC polls since 1986. On other issues, 65 percent said it was a mistake to take military action against Iran, and 68 percent disapproved of the way Trump has dealt with US allies. Tellingly, 56 percent said Trump had gone too far in deporting undocumented immigrants, compared with 48 percent in April 2025.

But whatever happens in November, Trump will hold office for two more years, and the politics he represents won’t evaporate when he exits. Anyone expecting a midterm rout and Trump’s departure in 2029 to restore the old normal — and for the old normal to be sufficient to prevent another far-right resurgence — needs to think again. Instead, we must reckon with the political force that has been unleashed in American life, the aftershocks of which will no doubt be felt for generations to come.

In my new book, Class, Power and the State in the Trump Era: A Critical Analysis (De Gruyter Brill, 2026), I try to sketch an early picture of Trumpism. Below I draw on it to describe what Trumpism is made of, how it changed between Trump’s two terms, and what that means for the Left.

One unmistakable aspect of Trumpism is brazen authoritarianism. This dimension is on full display right now, as Trump works diligently to undermine confidence in the electoral system. The Supreme Court checked his attempt to use the US Postal Service to restrict mail-in ballots in September. Since then, the administration has engaged in “systematically laying out unsubstantiated and false claims in an effort to sow doubts about the safety of the country’s decentralized election system,” as a New York Times analysis put it.

For example, as part of Trump’s big-lie campaign about illegal voting, the Justice Department claimed without evidence that twenty thousand people on California’s voter rolls were “likely noncitizens.” The department then charged twenty-eight California residents, all legal immigrants, with violating federal election laws. Despite Trump’s disinformation campaign, most Americans are confident the midterm elections will be conducted fairly, though seven in ten lack confidence that Trump will accept the results if Republicans lose.

Recent weeks have brought stepped-up repression against those Trump regards as enemies. Most notably, Department of Homeland Security officials raided the Washington home of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, the Somali American representative of Minnesota’s Fifth District, seizing her phone, passport, and other documents. Trump has long displayed a fixation on Omar, whom he has called “garbage,” and on Somali Americans, who reside in large numbers in Minnesota, especially in the Twin Cities area. Several days before the raid, Trump wrote on Truth Social, “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back.” According to several reports, those familiar with the probe believe that its goal is to revoke Omar’s citizenship and eventually deport her.

In my book, I characterize Trumpism as a distinct form of right-wing politics, blending (pseudo-)populism, nationalism, and authoritarianism with uninhibited, even predatory or patrimonial, pro-capitalist economic and social policies. While these political forms have existed in various shapes throughout American political history, they combined in new ways in the Trump era. Trumpism marked a departure from the pre-2016 Republican ideological consensus and signaled the arrival of an alternative form of right-wing politics, one that played out in other countries as well.The goal of the MAGA movement is to weaken rival forces and establish hegemony in American politics based on a reconfigured national-conservative bloc enjoying both popular and elite support. The attack on the election system and the raid on Omar’s home make sense in that light. A movement bent on dominating American politics has every reason to discredit the elections that could check its power and to punish the people it treats as enemies.

If these features were plainly evident in Trump’s first presidency, they only deepened their hold after he left office in 2021 and during his second presidency. From 2021 to 2025, between Trump’s two terms, Trumpism underwent four important shifts. First, Trump’s reactionary political worldview grew more radical, marked by an unremitting commitment to the stolen-2020-election lie, intensifying authoritarianism, vows of retribution, and hysterical rhetoric about the threat of socialism, communism, and the “radical Left.”

Second, the Trump campaign worked with right-wing think tanks to draw up blueprints for a second Trump administration. The purpose was to go beyond such traditional conservative objectives as cutting taxes and reducing spending to a wholesale assault on the administrative state that would give the president complete control over the executive branch. As Russell Vought, now Trump’s budget director, put it in 2023, “The president Day One will be a wrecking ball for the administrative state.” The best-known plan for a second Trump administration was the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025, released in 2023, of which Vought was a key architect.

Third, Trump and the MAGA movement aligned closely with the preoccupations of right-wing culture and political thought, such as Christian nationalism, anti-wokeness crusading, “pro-natalism,” and concerns about “civilizational erosion” that draw on the far-right great replacement theory. Such thinking is common among Trump 2.0 figures like JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, and Stephen Miller.

Fourth, after leaving office in 2021, Trump almost entirely abandoned the economic pseudo-populism aimed at the working class that was a prominent part of his 2016 campaign. Trump’s 2024 campaign openly courted Wall Street, Silicon Valley, and other parts of corporate America, such as oil and gas, tobacco, and the cryptocurrency industry, which he had previously called a scam.

Trump vowed to cut corporate tax rates, reduce environmental and other regulations, and support fossil fuel drilling. In May 2026, Trump was asked if “Americans’ financial situation” motivated him to make a deal with Iran. “Not even a little bit,” he replied. “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody. I think about one thing — we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon. That’s all.” He added, “Every American understands.”

But not every American understands. The war with Iran is unpopular, especially in the context of Americans’ domestic economic difficulties. Those difficulties are largely of the president’s own making.

Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted in July 2025, has been called “the most regressive tax and budget legislation in modern American history” by Yale scholars Patrick Sullivan and Jacob Hacker. The inflationary pressures squeezing the working class stem largely from misguided Trump policies, including the war on Iran, which has driven up the price of oil and oil-based products; across-the-board tariffs, which have raised prices of imported goods and inputs used in domestic production; and anti-immigration and deportation measures that have led to labor shortages in construction, agriculture, meatpacking, and other sectors.

So the conditions exist for a large-scale repudiation of Trump and the MAGA movement, which are increasingly authoritarian and even fascistic. As early as 1921, more than a year before the March on Rome, Antonio Gramsci theorized the cross-class, psychologically intense appeal of fascism, noting that fascism “has become an unleashing of elemental forces which cannot be restrained within the bourgeois system of economic and political governance.” The challenge for the Left is to construct a politics that can leash, redirect, and de-energize these “elemental forces” to forestall further drift toward authoritarianism and fascism, something centrist and corporate liberalism has been unable to do.

What does this mean for politics after the midterm elections? First, the Left needs educational efforts to counter McCarthyite attacks from the Right on progressive and socialist ideas so that they can be discussed rationally and without stigma. Second, it should build on the successful electoral work by the Democratic Socialists of America and other groups seen in the Zohran Mamdani campaign in New York and elsewhere. Third, it needs progressive populist economic plans that serve working-class interests and cut through right-wing pseudo-populism. Economist Isabella Weber’s proposals for strategic price controls, which have been discussed in Jacobin, are one starting point worth considering. Gains by the Left in areas such as these will help counter not just the remainder of the Trump 2.0 presidency but Trumpism as an increasingly malignant form of right-wing, antidemocratic capitalist politics.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.title: NYC Council takes key step toward Mamdani's promised Department of Community Safety
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.text:
The New York City Council will take a crucial step Friday toward creating a Department of Community Safety as lawmakers hold a hearing on one of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s top campaign initiatives: reimagining how the city handles violence prevention and responses to mental health emergencies.
While creating such an agency was one of Mamdani's key campaign promises, it’s one on which he has yet to fully deliver. Political experts who spoke to Gothamist said making good on the pledge is important for the mayor, especially because he’s faced tough criticism of his handling of policing issues.
“This is a promise he made during the campaign and he's under a lot of pressure from people who identify as progressives to do things with the police department, some of which he hasn't done,” said Joseph Viteritti, a longtime New York City politics watcher and Hunter College professor.
Mamdani promised an expansive city department that would boost a number of existing programs to curtail violence and address mental health issues in the city. The agency would also allow 911 dispatchers to send non-law enforcement professionals to more emergency and mental health calls, Mamdani said as a candidate.
Strong Council support
Councilmember Lincoln Restler, who represents neighborhoods including Brooklyn Heights, Greenpoint and Williamsburg, is the primary sponsor of a bill up for a hearing Friday that would create the standalone city agency. He said in an interview that he has the support of 34 cosponsors — a veto-proof majority — and that Speaker Julie Menin was helpful and cooperative in scheduling Friday’s hearing.
Restler echoed Mamdani’s campaign pledges when he described his vision of the agency in an interview earlier this week.
“ We ask the NYPD to respond to every issue under the sun,” Restler said, adding that the workload is, “distracting them from preventing and solving violent crime, their core purpose.”
But the department is also a response to a number of incidents where NYPD officers shot and killed people in the midst of mental health crises. That conversation reignited when NYPD officers shot Jabez Chakraborty just weeks after Mamdani took office. Authorities say Chakraborty was experiencing a mental health crisis when he grabbed a large knife and walked toward officers who responded to a 911 call at his Queens home. That followed several incidents in recent years where family members have called 911 for loved ones in distress, only for them to end up getting shot by police. Raul de la Cruz, who was diagnosed with schizophrenia, sued the city in 2024 after he was shot during a mental health crisis.
Restler said he wants the department to achieve three things. The first is to expand violence interruption and public safety work done by nonprofit workers who partner with the city’s Crisis Management System.
The second is to coordinate services — such as homeless and mental health services — from multiple city agencies so they can reach New Yorkers who need them.
Lastly, he hopes Department of Community Safety workers can provide real-time responses to emergency calls to deescalate situations on a 24/7 basis.
“It's a big and ambitious mandate, and we have a lot of conversations to be had with the mayor's team and the speaker's team to reach a consensus,” Restler said.
'Lot of pressure'
As a candidate, Mamdani’s primary focus was affordability, though he did float a number of public safety proposals, most of which he has yet to deliver.
Mamdani said he would have the NYPD scrap its gang database, disband the controversial Strategic Response Group and have officers focus on solving serious crimes.
As of now, the database and the Strategic Response Group are still active and the department has continued its crackdown on minor quality-of-life crimes and violations, which began under previous Mayor Eric Adams.
Mamdani also vowed to create the enormous Department of Community Safety to help free up police officers to focus on serious crimes.
Since taking office, Mamdani has signed an executive order to create the Office of Community Safety, a scaled-down version of the agency that he pitched on the campaign trail.
Viteritti, the Hunter College professor, said the pressure Mamdani faces from progressives to deliver the robust city agency will likely continue because of his campaign pledges.
“This is something [where] his feet are going to be held to the fire,” Viteritti said. “He's going to have to do something with it.”
Evan Roth Smith, a campaign consultant with Slingshot Strategies, said he expects the agency to focus on issues like homelessness and mental health emergencies.
If it works, Roth Smith said, it could be a big win for Mamdani because those issues may make New Yorkers feel anxious — but they may be hesitant to call the police about them.
“He could go to folks on the left and say, ‘I didn't just talk the talk, I walked the walk, and I introduced a new way of approaching public safety,’" Roth Smith said.
“And he can go to folks who are not to his left or who may be skeptical of him generally and say, ‘Look, I take seriously issues of homelessness or of emotionally disturbed people or public drug use and so on, and I want our street life to be healthier,’” he added.
Restler said the Department of Community Safety is partly about shifting away from what he called broken windows policing.
“I know the mayor is committed to that vision, and I'm hopeful that the policies of the NYPD will reflect those values in the months to come,” he said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Em meio a novos ataques contra Gaza, israelenses pedem união da oposição para tirar Netanyahu do poder
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Após o resultado das eleições parlamentares em Israel, que apontam para o enfraquecimento do atual governo, o primeiro-ministro Benjamin Netanyahu retoma a ofensiva bélica contra a Faixa de Gaza.
Os ataques deste domingo (1º) mataram oito pessoas, incluindo uma criança, segundo serviços de emergência e hospitais locais.
Cinco pessoas foram mortas em Khan Yunis e três na Cidade de Gaza, segundo um comunicado do serviço de defesa civil do território, que opera sob a autoridade do movimento islâmico Hamas, que controla Gaza.
Hospitais locais informaram ter recebido os corpos e vários feridos.
Desde o ataque do Hamas em 7 de outubro de 2023, a ofensiva de Israel contra Gaza deixou grande parte do território em ruínas e matou mais de 74,5 mil pessoas, segundo o Ministério da Saúde de Gaza, cujos números são considerados confiáveis pelas Nações Unidas.
Apelo por união
Enquanto Netanyahu segue com a guerra em Gaza, israelenses ocupam as ruas do país, no sábado (31), para pressionar a oposição do atual governo a se unir aos partidos árabes para retirar o primeiro-ministro do poder.
A apuração das eleições parlamentares de Israel foi concluída na sexta-feira (30) com um avanço histórico dos partidos de representação palestina e sem maioria definida para a formação do próximo governo. As duas listas de maioria árabe, Raam e Lista Unificada, conquistaram juntas 19 das 120 cadeiras do Knesset – parlamento israelense -, quase o dobro das dez obtidas em 2022, enquanto o bloco de Netanyahu perdeu a maioria parlamentar que sustentava seu governo.
Nenhum bloco conquistou maioria no parlamento israelense, informa a agência de notícias AFP. Os partidos de maioria judaica contrários a Netanyahu obtiveram 48 assentos. Apesar da derrota significativa do atual primeiro-ministro, o líder da oposição, Gadi Eisenkot, ainda não considera formar um bloco que una os partidos árabes para conter o avanço de Netanyahu.
Eisenkot declarou que aceitaria apenas formar um “governo sionista”, cujos integrantes se comprometam com o “reconhecimento de Israel como um Estado judeu, democrático e liberal” e considerem o Hamas uma “organização terrorista”, destacou que não deseja depender dos partidos árabes, mas também não descartou explicitamente o apoio deles.
Já o líder da Lista Unificada, Yusef Jabareen, afirmou à AFP que estaria disposto a apoiar Eisenkot no Parlamento sem integrar o governo.
Para os cidadãos palestinos de Israel, o crescimento da representação parlamentar pode ampliar as possibilidades de negociação sobre igualdade de direitos, combate à discriminação, segurança e investimentos nas comunidades. A transformação dessa presença em políticas concretas, entretanto, dependerá da composição do próximo governo e de suas prioridades.
*Com informações da AFP

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Estudantes ocupam ruas para celebrar vitória de Lula, denunciar violência política e apoiar indígenas.
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Uma semana após a vitória histórica de Lula (PT) nas eleições presidenciais, a União Nacional dos Estudantes (UNE) realiza, neste domingo (1º), a mobilização nacional intitulada “Brasil com S”. As manifestações acontecem em 11 estados do país e no Distrito Federal.
Os atos são uma resposta às declarações do candidato derrotado, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que questiona o resultado eleitoral. A mobilização, além de celebrar a vitória de Lula, também denuncia e condena os ataques sofridos pelos povos indígenas após o resultado das urnas. Segundo a Articulação dos Povos Indígenas do Brasil (Apib), ocorreram mais de 30 denúncias de violência contra indígenas desde a eleição.
Para Camila Moraes, secretária-geral da UNE, os acontecimentos registrados após o resultado eleitoral reforçam a necessidade de manter a mobilização permanente.
“Hoje também deve ser um dia de luta e denúncia aos ataques e ameaças que a extrema-direita segue representando ao povo brasileiro, como estamos vendo, com os ataques aos povos indígenas, trabalhadores e estudantes, numa clara intimidação política. Por isso, acho fundamental que sigamos em estado permanente de mobilização, ocupando as ruas e, principalmente, nos organizando politicamente”, afirmou ao Brasil de Fato.
Mobilização.
A presidenta da UNE, Bianca Borges, participa do ato na Praça Roosevelt, na capital paulista. Em publicação nas redes sociais, ela também ressaltou a importância da mobilização permanente para garantir a continuidade do governo Lula e condenou a violência contra os povos indígenas após o resultado eleitoral. “Nos reunimos também para denunciar os graves casos de violência política, inclusive contra comunidades indígenas”, afirmou.
A mobilização “Brasil com S” ocorre neste domingo em Maceió (AL), Manaus (AM), Goiânia (GO), Cuiabá (MT), São Luís (MA), Belém (PA), Recife (PE), Rio de Janeiro (RJ), Porto Alegre (RS) e São Paulo (SP), Brasília (DF) e Maringá (PR).

https://taz.de/Ausschreitungen-nach-Gen-.title: Ausschreitungen nach Gen-Z-Protesten: Und wieder als fremd markiert
https://taz.de/Ausschreitungen-nach-Gen-.author: Yağmur Ekim Çay
https://taz.de/Ausschreitungen-nach-Gen-.text:
Ausschreitungen nach Gen-Z-Protesten : Und wieder als fremd markiert
Unionspolitiker machen das „migrantische Millieu“ für Ausschreitungen in Frankfurt verantwortlich. Kein Wunder, dass sich die ständige Ausgrenzung in Wut verwandelt.
W ie lange bleibt man ein Migrant? Diese Frage müssen sich migrantisch gelesene Personen seit Jahrzehnten stellen. Laut den Aussagen von Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) und dem hessischen Innenminister Roman Poseck (CDU) ändert offenbar auch ein deutscher Pass nichts daran, dass man für immer Migrant bleibt.
Denn Dobrindt und Poseck machten eine für sie ganz selbstverständliche Unterscheidung: Diejenigen, die an den Ausschreitungen nach den Gen-Z-Protesten am Wochenende beteiligt gewesen seien, hätten zwar überwiegend die deutsche Staatsbürgerschaft, gehörten aber zu den „Chaoten aus dem migrantischen Milieu“.
Das ist letztlich das, was CDU-Politiker seit Jahren mit Begriffen wie „kleine Paschas“ oder einem „Problem im Stadtbild“ kommunizieren und mittlerweile noch offener aussprechen: Egal, in welcher Generation ihr seid und welchen Pass ihr habt, ihr gehört eben nicht dazu.
Der gute Migrant ist unsichtbar
Frankfurt ist eine migrantische Stadt. 58 Prozent der Bevölkerung haben eine Einwanderungsgeschichte. Hier hat man längst verstanden, dass man in einer Migrationsgesellschaft lebt und migrantische Menschen selbstverständlich zum „Stadtbild“ gehören. Noch absurder ist, dass Poseck diese Aussagen am Sonntag neben dem Frankfurter Oberbürgermeister Mike Josef trifft, der selbst eine Fluchtgeschichte hat.
Also, wer soll dieses „migrantische Milieu“ genau sein? Wer ist damit gemeint? Stellte man dies am Samstagabend bei Polizeikontrollen anhand des deutschen Passes, der Familiengeschichte oder der Hautfarbe fest? Und warum wird ein Großteil der Frankfurter Stadtgesellschaft unter Generalverdacht gestellt?
Für die jungen Menschen aus Frankfurt ist es ein weiterer Schlag ins Gesicht, wenn dabei vom „Ziel-Klientel“ gesprochen wird, das Rechtsbrüche begehe und teilweise gewaltbereit sei. Gemeint sind damit offenbar auch migrantische Menschen, die sich am Wochenende auf Frankfurts Einkaufsmeile, der Zeil, treffen und dort Spaß haben. Denn hier wird klar: Die guten Migrant:innen sind offenbar diejenigen, die in ihren Vierteln bleiben, unsichtbar sind und ihren Spaß woanders haben, damit die sogenannte Mehrheitsgesellschaft möglichst nicht mit ihnen konfrontiert ist.
Was in Frankfurt am Wochenende passiert ist, war teilweise brutal. Es ist erschreckend, wie Frankfurts Einkaufsmeile am Wochenende ausgesehen hat und, dass nun viele Ladenbesitzer mit finanziellen Konsequenzen rechnen müssen.
Als Antwort darauf will die hessische Polizei Männer aus dem „migrantischen Milieu“ noch stärker in den Fokus nehmen. Es ist längst bekannt, dass die Frankfurter Polizei ein Rechtsextremismusproblem hat. Dass es in Frankfurt nun aber noch mehr Racial Profiling geben wird, ist nicht nur juristisch fragwürdig. Es stellt sich auch die Frage, welches Problem damit gelöst werden soll.
Migration soll alles erklären
Diese stark diskriminierende Politik, rassistischen Aussagen sowie Kontrollen tragen gerade nicht dazu bei, dass sich junge migrantische Menschen als Teil dieser Gesellschaft fühlen. Im Gegenteil: Sie verstärken das Gefühl, ausgeschlossen und diskriminiert zu werden. Denn seit Jahren wird eine ganz klare politische Linie verfolgt: Möglichst viele gesellschaftliche Probleme, von fehlenden Zahnarztterminen bis hin zu Antisemitismus sollen sich offenbar ganz einfach mit Migration erklären lassen.
Dazu kommt, dass migrantische Menschen, die sich in den vergangenen Jahren an propalästinensischen Demonstrationen beteiligt haben, häufig pauschal kriminalisiert und ihre Anliegen ignoriert wurden. Man darf eben auch nicht vergessen, dass viele Jugendliche in Frankfurt damit aufgewachsen sind, dass vor sechs Jahren in Hanau ein Rechtsextremist neun Menschen ermordet hat. Die Ermordeten gehörten ebenfalls zu den Menschen, die heute wohl unter das fallen würden, was als „Zeil-Klientel“ bezeichnet wird.
An jenem Abend versuchte Vili Viorel Păun, die Polizei zu erreichen, blieb jedoch ohne Hilfe und starb. Für Hamza Kurtović hatte es tödliche Konsequenzen, dass der Notausgang in der Arena Bar verschlossen war. Was bei den Hinterbliebenen, aber auch bei vielen jungen Menschen nach all den Jahren hängen geblieben ist, ist die Erkenntnis: Ein Rassist kann sie ermorden, ohne dass die notwendigen Konsequenzen folgen und tatsächlich jemand Verantwortung übernimmt.
Es ist keine Überraschung, dass diese Menschen irgendwann das Gefühl verlieren, politisch repräsentiert zu werden. Wer sie ständig kriminalisiert und ihnen das Gefühl gibt, nicht dazuzugehören, sollte sich nicht darüber wundern, wenn sie sich irgendwann tatsächlich nicht mehr als Teil dieser Gesellschaft verstehen.

https://taz.de/Rauchschwaden-ueber-Suedo.title: Rauchschwaden über Südostasien: Indonesien verpestet seine Nachbarn – und sich selbst
https://taz.de/Rauchschwaden-ueber-Suedo.author: Sven Hansen
https://taz.de/Rauchschwaden-ueber-Suedo.text:
Rauchschwaden über Südostasien: Indonesien verpestet seine Nachbarn – und sich selbst
Seit Monaten raubt der Rauch von Indonesiens brennenden Wäldern den Menschen der Region den Atem und die Sicht. Präsident Prabowo hofft auf Regen.
Indonesien kämpft seit Juli mit schweren Wald-, Busch- und Torfbränden. Mehr als 19.000 Quadratkilometer sind bereits verbrannt, hauptsächlich im Süden Sumatras und in Kalimantan auf der Insel Borneo. Neben den Feuern macht vor allem deren Rauch Probleme. Er taucht viele Orte in gespenstisches Licht, verdunkelt auch in den Nachbarländern Singapur und Malaysia den Himmel und reduziert die Sicht zum Teil drastisch.
Vor allem wird den Menschen die Luft zum Atmen genommen. Vielerorts fällt der Schulunterricht aus, allein in Malaysia betraf dies 600.000 Kinder. In Indonesien mussten sich wegen des Smogs bis September 333.000 Personen in ärztliche Behandlung begeben, darunter 75.000 Kinder unter fünf Jahren. Nach Berechnungen des finnischen Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (Crea) starben in Indonesien allein im September 3.560 Menschen an der stark durch den Rauch erhöhten Luftverschmutzung. Insgesamt seien davon fast 58 Millionen Menschen betroffen.
Indonesiens Regierung rühmt sich, 72.000 Feuerwehrleute, Soldaten und Polizisten zur Brandbekämpfung mobilisiert zu haben. Zusätzliche 2.100 Ärzte würden sich in besonders betroffenen Regionen um die Gesundheit der Menschen kümmern. Darüber hinaus seien 5,3 Millionen Atemmasken verteilt worden.
Medienberichten zufolge experimentieren die Behörden auch mit einem Gemisch aus Trockeneis und Salz. Das wird aus 15 Flugzeugen in Wolken gesprüht und soll künstlichen Regen erzeugen. Das hat viel Medienaufmerksamkeit erzeugt, aber kaum Brände gelöscht oder die Luft verbessert.
Prabowos Beliebtheit verbrennt
Feuer und Rauch sind längst zu einem großen innen- wie außenpolitischen Problem für den seit zwei Jahren amtierenden Präsidenten Prabowo Subianto geworden. In den letzten Monaten haben sich seine Beliebtheitswerte in Umfragen halbiert.
Dabei gibt es in Indonesien regelmäßig Brände nach dem Ende der Regenzeit im April. Die Ursachen sind großflächige Rodungen des Regenwaldes, um Platz für Palmölplantagen zu schaffen, Brandrodungen durch Kleinbauern sowie die Entwässerung von Torfmooren. Doch so schlimm wie jetzt waren die Brände seit mindestens zehn Jahren nicht mehr. Mit ein Grund dafür ist der diesjährige El-Niño-Effekt, der zu außergewöhnlicher Trockenheit geführt hat.
Prabowos Regierung wird vorgeworfen, das Problem vernachlässigt zu haben und keine Strategie dagegen zu haben. Kritisiert wird, dass das jährliche Budget der Katastrophenschutzbehörde BNPB drastisch zusammengestrichen worden ist. In diesem Jahr betrug es mit umgerechnet 24,26 Millionen Euro nur noch 4 Prozent des Umfangs des Jahres 2020. Mitte Oktober hat Prabowo den Behördenleiter zudem wegen Korruption in dessen Umfeld gefeuert.
Forstminister Raja Juli Antoni räumte ein, dass die Brände zu 99 Prozent von Menschen verursacht sind. Sein Ministerium suspendierte zwar die Lizenzen von 32 Firmen, die Regenwald abholzen, um etwa Palmöl oder Kautschuk anbauen zu können. Doch laut der Umweltorganisation Walhi brennt es in den Konzessionsgebieten von 372 Unternehmen. Die Regierungen von Singapur und Malaysia drängen Jakarta, effektive Maßnahmen zu ergreifen. Doch löst dies in Indonesien nationalistische Reflexe aus. Laut Walhi haben 66 der mutmaßlich verantwortlichen Unternehmen Verbindungen zu Singapur und 27 zu Malaysia.
Demonstranten fordern Ausrufung des Notstands
In letzter Zeit gab es in Indonesien in mehreren Städten Demonstrationen gegen die Umweltkatastrophe. Gefordert wurde dabei außer der Bestrafung der für die Brände verantwortlichen Firmen immer wieder die Erklärung eines Notstands. Doch ausgerechnet der Ex-General Prabowo verweigert dies und sagt: „Ich vermute, die einzige Lösung ist Regen.“
Bei einem Notstand müsste Prabowo Haushaltsmittel zugunsten stärkerer Brandbekämpfung umschichten. Und das würde wohl vor allem das milliardenschwere Programm für kostenloses Schulessen betreffen. Das ist aber der populistische Teil in Prabowos ansonsten an der Elite ausgerichteten Regierungsprogramm. Das Versprechen kostenloser Essen ermöglicht ihm, sich volksnah zu geben, und dürfte zu seinem Wahlsieg beigetragen haben. Durch Korruption wie durch tausende Fälle von Lebensmittelvergiftungen ist das Programm inzwischen in Verruf geraten. Laut einer Umfrage fordern inzwischen mehr als 60 Prozent die Abschaffung des Programms.
Das katholische deutsche Hilfswerk Misereor verweist in einer Erklärung auf die Mitverantwortung des Konsumverhaltens in westlichen Industrieländer wegen der dortigen hohen Nachfrage an Palmöl. Es „steckt in vielen Produkten unseres großen Bedarfs, von Chips und Süßigkeiten bis zu Margarine, Seifen und Kosmetika“, sagt Indonesien-Referentin Christine Kögel. Beim Kauf sollte deshalb auf sozial- und umweltverträgliche Produktionsbedingungen geachtet werden.

https://taz.de/Digitalgipfel-In-diesen-B.title: Digitalgipfel der Bundesregierung: Wo Deutschland mit KI punkten könnte
https://taz.de/Digitalgipfel-In-diesen-B.author: Svenja Bergt
https://taz.de/Digitalgipfel-In-diesen-B.text:
Digitalgipfel der Bundesregierung: Wo Deutschland mit KI punkten könnte
Mit ihrem KI-Gipfel will die Bundesregierung für Schwung in der Branche sorgen. Expert:innen raten Deutschland allerdings von einem Wettrennen ab.
Auf dem Digitalgipfel der Bundesregierung haben Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (beide CDU) mehr Tempo in Sachen künstliche Intelligenz gefordert. „Wir müssen in Deutschland und Europa viel schneller darin werden, digitale Technologien zu entwickeln und zu nutzen“, sagte Merz am Montag vor nationalem und internationalem Branchenpublikum. „Kühne Entscheidungen für Energieinfrastruktur und Investitionen“ seien nötig, sagte Wildberger. Und: weniger Regulierung. Es brauche „weniger Verpflichtungen und mehr Platz, um Ideen zu testen und auszubauen“.
Einen bedeutenden Deal hatte die Bundesregierung bereits zwei Wochen zuvor bei ihrem Investorengipfel verkündet: Das Wirtschafts- und das Forschungsministerium haben eine Absichtserklärung mit Nvidia unterzeichnet. Nvidia ist der global wichtigste Hersteller von KI-Hochleistungschips und einer der am höchsten bewerteten börsennotierten Konzerne.
Der Bundesregierung zufolge soll die Kooperation vor allem dazu dienen, KI-Modelle für die industrielle Nutzung zu entwickeln. Einbezogen werden sollen dafür nicht nur große Konzerne, sondern auch kleine und mittlere Unternehmen sowie Forschungseinrichtungen. Die Kooperation solle die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit Deutschlands und die technologische Souveränität sichern. Merz erklärte nun auf dem Digitalgipfel, man wolle auch europäische Frontier-Modelle entwickeln. Frontier-Modelle sind die leistungsfähigsten KI-Modelle, die derzeit von Unternehmen wie Anthropic und OpenAI kommen.
USA und China vorn
Doch was diese großen, besonders leistungsfähigen Sprachmodelle angeht, dürfte ein Wettlauf für Deutschland und Europa schwierig werden. Momentan sind in dem Bereich die USA führend, dicht gefolgt von den chinesischen Anbietern. Zwar ist über das Projekt SOOFI ein europäisches Open-Source-KI-Modell in Planung. Doch um den Leistungsvorsprung etwa der USA einzuholen, fehlen Europa nicht nur die immensen Summen an Risikokapital, sondern auch die großen Datenmengen, über die die US-Unternehmen verfügen und die sie – teils legal, teils mindestens im Graubereich – für das Training ihrer KI-Modelle nutzen.
Expert:innen sehen daher das deutsche und europäische Potenzial nicht darin, in einen Wettlauf mit den USA und China einzusteigen. „Souveränität entsteht nicht, indem wir den größten Sprachmodellen hinterherlaufen und sie mit eigenen Daten nachtrainieren“, sagt Björn Ommer, Leiter der Computer Vision & Learning Group der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München laut Science Media Center. Eine vielversprechendere Strategie sei es, „in strategisch wichtigen, bislang unterrepräsentierten Feldern wie der physischen und industriellen KI die Infrastruktur und das Betriebssystem für die Wertschöpfung von morgen zu schaffen, die in der realen Welt einen Unterschied machen“.
Auch aus ökologischer Sicht könnte das von Vorteil sein: „Die Entwicklung eigener Frontier-Sprachmodelle ist ungleich ressourcenintensiver als die Entwicklung von Modellen für andere Modalitäten“, erklärt Ommer. Die Frontier-Modelle sind die leistungsfähigsten KI-Modelle von Unternehmen wie Anthropic und OpenAI. Der Ressourcenunterschied zeige sich nicht nur beim Training, sondern auch bei der Nutzung.
Die Ressourcenfrage
Der Ressourcenverbrauch, gerade in Bezug auf Wasser und Strom, sowie die Emissionen sind Punkte, die für immer größere Kritik an der Technologie sorgen: „Die Chipproduktion verbraucht Unmengen Strom und Wasser, produziert Millionen Tonnen CO₂ – und dazu kommt erst noch der Ressourcenverbrauch der Rechenzentren“, kritisierte Benjamin Stephan von der Umweltorganisation Greenpeace nach dem Nvidia-Deal.
In Deutschland wird der KI-Boom jedenfalls voraussichtlich zu niedrigeren Standards für Rechenzentren führen. So sieht die Rechenzentrumsstrategie der Bundesregierung einen deutlichen Ausbau der IT-Infrastruktur vor. Die Kapazitäten alleine für KI sollen sich bis 2030 vervierfachen. Gleichzeitig wird der Bundestag voraussichtlich in den kommenden Wochen das neue Energieeffizienzgesetz beschließen. Es enthält eine deutliche Abschwächung der Vorgaben für Betreiber von Rechenzentren, etwa was die Energieeffizienz angeht.
Investitionen in offene Modelle
Stefan Heumann, Geschäftsführer des Thinktanks Agora Digitale Transformation, hält es für sinnvoll, wenn sich die Bundesregierung bei ihren Ausgaben für KI auf Felder konzentriert, die im öffentlichen Interesse sind – und die von den Big-Tech-Konzernen vernachlässigt werden. „Zum Beispiel offene KI-Modelle, aber auch solche für die Verwaltung oder den Gesundheitssektor.“ Also Bereiche, wo zum Beispiel sensible Daten verarbeitet werden. Für solche Investitionen seien aber auf mittel- bis langfristige Sicht Umschichtungen im Haushalt nötig.
Denn einer aktuellen Analyse des Thinktanks zufolge speist sich weiterhin der größte Teil des Haushalts für das Digitalministerium aus dem Sondervermögen – laufe das aus, stünden das Ministerium und die Projekte an einer Klippe, so Heumann. Der Experte kritisiert die Bundesregierung: „Momentan ist viel KI im Schaufenster und wenig im Maschinenraum.“ So hat Agora die Posten im Bundeshaushalt nach Titeln analysiert: Demzufolge sind nur 0,15 Prozent des Kernhaushalts Ausgaben mit KI-Bezug.

https://taz.de/Von-Tierliebe-zum-Affenha.title: Von Tierliebe zum Affenhass: Wenn Kapstadts Paviane die Reichen zum Affen machen
https://taz.de/Von-Tierliebe-zum-Affenha.author: Stefan Hunglinger
https://taz.de/Von-Tierliebe-zum-Affenha.text:
Von Tierliebe zum Affenhass: Wenn Kapstadts Paviane die Reichen zum Affen machen
Weil Paviane Probleme mit dem Recht auf Eigentum haben, diskutiert das südafrikanische Kapstadt jetzt über einen teuren Plan für ein Affenmanagement.
E in Wort reicht aus, um in Kapstadt starke Gefühle hervorzurufen: Pavian. Dann werden die Augen des Gegenübers feucht oder – viel öfter – ziehen sich wütend zusammen.
Denn dass sich die einst bedrohte Population der Bärenpaviane (Papio ursinus) auf der Kaphalbinsel wieder erholt hat, ja prächtig gedeiht, freut nicht alle Capetonians. Wenn so ein großer Primat auf der Küchenanrichte sitzt, mit den Fingern in einer Chipstüte oder im Erdnussbutterglas, endet die ansonsten gepflegte Gastfreundschaft. Und wenn so ein haariger Verwandter die Autotür aufreißt, um sich das Sandwich und die Banane auf dem Beifahrersitz (links!) zu stibitzen, ist es vorbei mit der Tierliebe.
Kürzlich eskalierte der Affenhass, als der stadtbekannte Pavian Fluffy mehrfach mit Schrotkugeln beschossen und an der Wirbelsäule sowie den inneren Organen verletzt wurde. Videos zeigten, wie das Alpha-Männchen des Paviantrupps CT2 mühsam seine Hinterbeine nachzog. Fluffy musste eingeschläfert werden, er ist das jüngste Opfer eines alten Konflikts.
Paviane und Menschen leben schon seit 600.000 Jahren zusammen an der Südspitze des afrikanischen Kontinents, darauf deuten archäologische Funde hin. 1652 allerdings wurde Kapstadt, die „mother city“, zur ersten europäischen Siedlung in Südafrika, zunächst einfach als Zwischenstation für Schiffe auf der Route zwischen Europa und Asien.
Früher wurde auf Paviane ein Kopfgeld ausgesetzt
Zur Versorgung der ausgehungerten Seeleute legte man Gemüse- und Obstgärten an. Weil die Paviane aber schon damals Probleme mit dem Recht auf Eigentum hatten und regelmäßig die Beete plünderten, fingen und töteten die Siedler die Tiere zu Tausenden. Bis weit ins 20. Jahrhundert hinein wurde für tote Paviane ein Kopfgeld bezahlt, in manchen Provinzen Südafrikas gibt es bis heute keine Abschussbegrenzung.
In Kapstadt aber wurden die Tiere Ende der neunziger Jahre unter Schutz gestellt, die Population wuchs von etwa 360 Tschakma-Pavianen in 10 Trupps im Jahr 2000 auf mehr als 600 Tiere in 17 Trupps an. Gleichzeitig entstanden auf den tiefer gelegenen Flächen der Kaphalbinsel, auf denen die Affen natürlicherweise nach Fressen suchen, mehr und mehr vornehme Häuser.
Durch die neuen Küchen, Gärten und mit hochwertigen Resten gefüllten Mülltonnen erweiterte sich aus Paviansicht schlicht die Speisekarte. So argumentieren die Tierfreund:innen auf der Halbinsel. Weg mit den Viechern, fordern andere Anwohnende.
So ist aus den Konflikten Affe – Mensch und Affe – Wachhund mittlerweile auch ein handfester Mensch-Mensch-Konflikt erwachsen. Und Kapstadts Verwaltung hat sich lange nicht darum gekümmert. Der Cape Peninsula Baboon Management Action Plan soll nun, vor den südafrikanischen Kommunalwahlen am 4. November, Frieden schaffen. Zäune sollen installiert, 44 Tiere aus dem Waterfall- sowie 16 aus dem Seaforth-Trupp sollen in ein umzäuntes Gehege umgesiedelt werden. Bei starker Vermehrung sieht der Plan auch „tierschutzgerechte Tötungen“ vor. Eine von der Stadt unterstützte „Beratungsgruppe für Pavianfragen“ soll in Zukunft für den Interessenausgleich sorgen.
Der neue Pavianplan ist teuer
Wissenschaftler:innen sehen den Plan kritisch, der Tierschützer Chad Cupido sagt: „Wenn man in einem Gebiet lebt, in dem es Wildtiere gibt, dann muss man mit diesen Wildtieren zusammenleben.“
Der Pavianplan der liberalen Stadtregierung ist zudem teuer. 33 Millionen südafrikanische Rand, also etwa 1,8 Millionen Euro, werden über einen Zeitraum von drei Jahren für das Affenmanagement bereitgestellt, die tatsächlichen Kosten könnten weitaus höher liegen.
Wieder so viel Steuergeld für die Viertel mit Meerblick auf der Halbinsel? Ärmere und arme Capetonians verdrehen die Augen, wenn sie das Wort Pavian hören: Sollen die Reichen doch einfach das Fenster zumachen – und ein Schloss an ihre Mülltonne hängen.
