https://taz.de/Ein-Stueck-Frankreich-in-.title: Geschichte des Berliner Gendarmenmarktes: Die französischen Gründungen gingen schief
https://taz.de/Ein-Stueck-Frankreich-in-.author: Christian Walther
https://taz.de/Ein-Stueck-Frankreich-in-.text:
Geschichte des Berliner Gendarmenmarktes: Die französischen Gründungen gingen schief
Vor 250 Jahren wurde am Berliner Gendarmenmarkt ein französisches Theater eröffnet. In der DDR wollte Peter Hacks dort ein eigenes französisches Theater haben.
Es war, wie etwa der „Geschichte der Berliner Theater“ von 1899 zu entnehmen ist, Friedrich der Große, der den Befehl gab zum Bau eines Theaters. Ungefähr da, wo heute in Berlin das Konzerthaus steht, entstand ein Gebäude mit über tausend Plätzen. Der Ort lag außerhalb der Stadtmauern inmitten der Friedrichstadt, einem Zentrum hugenottischer Zuwanderung.
1685 hatte der Große Kurfürst mit dem Edikt von Potsdam den Zuzug der Flüchtlinge aus Frankreich kräftig befördert, ab 1688 wurde die Friedrichstadt als neue Vorstadt geplant und errichtet. Mittendrin ein Platz, auf dessen südlicher Seite eine deutsche Kirche errichtet wurde und eine französische auf der nördlichen. Beide Kirchen hatten zunächst noch keine Türme – die kamen erst 1785, zu ausschließlich dekorativen Zwecken. Ihre Kuppeln – französisch: Dôme – sorgten für die inzwischen etablierte Bezeichnung Deutscher und Französischer Dom.
Schon früher also war die heutige stadträumliche Figur – zwei Kirchen, ein Theater – auf dem Platz vollendet: „Prophete links, Prophete rechts – das Weltkind in der Mitten“, wie die Berliner in Aneignung eines Goethe-Wortes spotteten.
Berlin französisch machen
Obwohl die Berliner Hugenotten damals eine veritable Parallelgesellschaft errichten durften mit eigenen Schulen, Krankenhaus, Diakonie, Gericht, Friedhöfen und ungestörtem Gebrauch der französischen Sprache, gehörte das Theater nicht zu diesen Einrichtungen. Hier bestimmte allein der frankophile Friedrich II. So kam das Französisch auf die neue Bühne: Mit Pierre Corneilles Märtyrerstück „Polyeucte“ wurde sie am 22. April 1776 eröffnet.
Die in Ulm erscheinende Teutsche Chronik vermerkte am selben Tag missfällig, dass die Schauspieler auf dem Wege seien, „das ohnehin schon halb französische Berlin vollends ganz französisch zu machen“. Und das Blatt berichtete („Ein Kontrast“), dass „unser teutscher Kaiser Joseph neulich zum Leidwesen aller Französlinge in Wien das ganze französische Theater“ zurückgeschickt habe nach Paris.
Doch auch in Berlin war die Freude am neuen Haus mit seiner Giebelinschrift „Ridentur et corriguntur mores“ („Die Sitten mögen belacht und verbessert werden“) nur von kurzer Dauer. Zuerst hatte der Monarch den Intendanten angewiesen – wie Adalbert Behr und Alfred Hoffmann 1984 in ihrem Buch zum Schauspielhaus belegen – eine schon zuvor in Berlin tätige französische Schauspieltruppe zu entlassen und ein neues Ensemble einzustellen: Er solle „das schlechte Crop, so jetzt noch bei dem französischen Theater ist, je eher, je besser wegschaffen“ und durch „ordentliche und geschickte Leute“ ersetzen, denen gleich Verträge für vier bis sechs Jahre gegeben werden sollten.
Dann aber ließ er das Theater nach nur zwei Jahren, in denen dreimal die Woche Racine, Corneille und Voltaire gespielt worden war, aber auch Kinderballett und sogenannte Divertissements, schon wieder schließen. Der König teilte dem Intendanten mit, dass er die Schauspieler zu entlassen habe und auch selbst von der Gehaltsliste gestrichen sei: „Die gegenwärtigen Conjuncturen bereiten auf ernstere Szenen vor. Man kann sehr gut der komischen entbehren.“ Der König plante, Österreich den Krieg zu erklären.
Das Ende des Französischen Komödienhauses war besiegelt. Das Gebäude stand leer, wurde für die Pfropfenproduktion genutzt, nach einigen Jahren aber – am 5. Dezember 1786 – auf Geheiß des neuen Königs Friedrich Wilhelm II. wiedereröffnet und bald darauf als „Königliches Nationaltheater“ geführt. Hier sprach man Deutsch.
Wiederaufbau des Ensembles
200 Jahre nach Eröffnung des Französischen Komödienhauses, im Frühjahr 1976, beschließt die SED, den schon früher angekündigten Wiederaufbau des kriegszerstörten Ensembles auf dem Gendarmenmarkt, der zu DDR-Zeiten Platz der Akademie hieß, nun tatsächlich umzusetzen. Als Erstes lässt die DDR die Französische Kirche wiedererstehen – klammheimlich finanziert mit Steuermillionen aus dem Westen, abgesprochen zwischen Diakonie West, Kirche Ost und den DDR-Devisenbeschaffern unter Alexander Schalck-Golodkowski. 5,5 Milliarden DM werden hier im Laufe der Jahrzehnte bewegt, zum Nutzen der Kirchen und zum Freikauf von Gefangenen.
Objekt Nr. 26 in einem 100 Millionen DM schweren Sonderbauprogramm für die Rekonstruktion von Kirchen und den Bau von Gemeindezentren in den Neubauvierteln der DDR ist die Französische Friedrichstadtkirche.
Jetzt kommt Peter Hacks ins Spiel. Der lange in Ost wie West erfolgreiche Dramatiker („Ein Gespräch im Hause Stein über den abwesenden Herrn von Goethe“) will ein eigenes Haus. So wie Brecht eines hatte mit dem Theater am Schiffbauerdamm („Berliner Ensemble“). Und dafür schwebt ihm der eben neu entstandene Kirchsaal der Hugenotten vor.
Hacks, ebenso streitlustig wie umstritten, geht mit Unterstützung des Freundes und Theologen Walter Beltz – Hacks-Biograf Ronald Weber nennt ihn einen „Strohmann“ – auf die Hugenottengemeinde zu. Der von Beltz unterzeichnete, aber nach Webers Recherche auf Hacks' Schreibmaschine entstandene Brief an das „hochverehrte Konsistorium“ vom 12. März 82 schlägt der Gemeinde die Gründung eines Französischen Theaters vor, das sich vornimmt, „in seinem Wirken publikumsfreundlich und erfolgreich zu sein und sich jedes Zugeständnisses an spätbürgerliche Modernismen zu enthalten“.
Hacks, der Klassiker der DDR, will die französischen Klassiker spielen: Corneille, Racine und Molière, aber auch deutsche Klassik – Goethe – und natürlich reichlich Hacks selbst.
Die Gemeinde ist damals aber gar nicht Herr im eigenen Haus. Sie hatte die Ruine für 30 Jahre an den Bund der Evangelischen Kirchen der DDR übertragen und ihr damit die Begleitung des Wiederaufbaus angedient. Dennoch ist es die Gemeinde, die den Brief beantwortet. Eine gelegentliche Nutzung für Aufführungen erscheint dem Konsistorium durchaus denkbar. Doch hat man gravierende Bedenken wegen des absehbaren Konflikts zwischen Theaterbetrieb und kirchlichen Aktivitäten.
Eine feuchtfröhliche Stunde
Und die Gemeinde schiebt noch ein juristisches Argument gegen das Projekt vor: Die der Gemeinde einst „aufgrund landesherrlicher Hoheitsakte verliehenen Privilegien“ gestatteten ihr ausschließlich kirchliche und diakonische Aktivitäten – sie sei nicht befugt, die Trägerschaft für eine kulturelle Einrichtung zu übernehmen. Das war ein denkbar schwacher Einwand, betrieb die Gemeinde doch längst eine kulturelle Einrichtung, nämlich das Hugenottenmuseum.
Beim Bund der Evangelischen Kirchen gab es zunächst eine etwas größere Offenheit: „vielleicht braucht man ab und zu Träumer, die uns alle aus eingefahrenen Geleisen herauslocken. Ich halte es in der Tat für erwägenswert, der französischen Theaterkultur einen ständigen Platz zuzuweisen“, heißt es in einem kircheninternen Vermerk. Andere Kirchenmänner halten Gespräche mit Hacks allerdings für „ziemlich sinnlos“ oder den Antrag gar für das „Produkt einer etwas feuchtfröhlichen Stunde“.
Die Absage der Hugenottengemeinde vom 14. Juli 82 bleibt das letzte Wort in dieser Sache.
Die Trauerfeier für den Atheisten Peter Hacks findet am 4. September 2003 in der Französischen Friedrichstadtkirche statt. Unter den Gästen neben Beltz viele aus der DDR-Kulturszene: Volker Braun, Eberhard Esche, Christoph Hein, Klaus Höpcke, Hermann Kant, Wolfgang Kohlhaase, Werner Mittenzwei.
Auf den Prominentenfriedhof an der Chausseestraße wollte Hacks nicht. Dort liegt auch Heiner Müller, mit dem sich Hacks längst überworfen hatte. Sein Verleger Matthias Oehme zitiert seine Gründe: „Ich habe mir mit Heiner Müller nicht so viel zu erzählen, dass es für eine Ewigkeit reichen würde.“
Und so wird Hacks auf dem zweiten Friedhof der Hugenotten beigesetzt, in der Liesenstraße, nur wenige Meter entfernt von Theodor Fontane.

https://taz.de/Bildung-gegen-Hass/!62267.title: Bildung gegen Hass: Jüdische Akademie eröffnet
https://taz.de/Bildung-gegen-Hass/!62267.author: Yağmur Ekim Çay
https://taz.de/Bildung-gegen-Hass/!62267.text:
Bildung gegen Hass: Jüdische Akademie eröffnet
In Frankfurt eröffnet die Jüdische Akademie. Die Bildungseinrichtung soll gegen Antisemitismus wirken. Bei der Eröffnungsrede geht es auch um die Berliner Linke.
In Frankfurt am Main hat heute die Jüdische Akademie eröffnet. Laut dem Zentralrat der Juden ist es die erste überregionale außeruniversitäre jüdische Bildungseinrichtung seit der Schoah.
Die Idee einer Jüdischen Akademie ist vor mehr als 15 Jahren entstanden. Nun will die Akademie den wissenschaftlichen, philosophischen und kulturellen Austausch fördern. Laut dem Zentralrat der Juden sollen dort wichtige öffentliche Diskurse aufgegriffen und um die jüdische Perspektive bereichert werden. Damit wolle die Jüdische Akademie dazu beitragen, die Akzeptanz für religiöse und kulturelle Pluralität in Deutschland zu erhöhen.
Die Schwerpunkte der Jüdischen Akademie reichen vom Zusammenleben in einer modernen, demokratischen Gesellschaft über Debatten zu Religion und Tradition, Antisemitismus, Kunst und Ethik bis hin zu Fragen der Geschichte und Erinnerung. Mit Fortbildungen, Konferenzen, Tagungen und Seminaren will sich die Jüdische Akademie an die jüdische Gemeinschaft ebenso wie an Akteure aus Wissenschaft, Politik und Kultur sowie an die breite Öffentlichkeit richten.
Wer behaupte, Judenhass habe keinen Platz in der Gesellschaft, der verleugne die Realität, sagte der Präsident des Zentralrats der Juden, Josef Schuster bei der Eröffnung am Montag. „Der Hass hat sich diesen Platz längst genommen.“ Daher sei der Judenhass Feind der Aufklärung. Nur mit Bildung lasse sich etwas dagegen ausrichten. Es sei auch Aufgabe des Hauses, dem Judenhass die Stirn zu bieten, sagte Schuster. Ein weiterer Schwerpunkt soll laut Zentralrat aber auch die jüdische Tradition, Kultur und Geschichte sein.
„Hessen ist das jüdischste Bundesland Deutschlands und Frankfurt die jüdischste Stadt“, sagte Hessens Ministerpräsident Boris Rhein bei der Eröffnung am Montag. Die Jüdische Akademie schaffe einen Ort, an dem jüdisches Denken und jüdische Perspektiven unsere gemeinsame Zukunft mitgestalten. Damit knüpfe sie an die Tradition des Freien Jüdischen Lehrhauses und das Erbe jüdischer Denker wie Franz Rosenzweig oder Theodor W. Adorno an.
Kritik an Berlin auch in Frankfurt
Die Reden bei der Eröffnung drehten sich dabei auch um die aktuellen Debatten rund um die Linkspartei in Berlin. Dort wird seit den Wahlen in Berlin über Antisemitismus in Teilen der Partei diskutiert. So sagte Rhein in seiner Rede auch: In Berlin werde die Linke nicht trotz, sondern wegen ihres Antisemitismus gewählt. Mit solchen Leuten koaliere man nicht.
Kritik äußerte auch Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier. Auch er war beim Festakt zur Eröffnung der Jüdischen Akademie am Montag anwesend. „Judenhass bleibt Judenhass, egal von welcher Seite er kommt, egal welchen Motiven er folgt“, sagte Steinmeier. Man erlebe, dass Feinde der Demokratie an politischer Macht gewinnen. „Wo über Koalitionen verhandelt wird und Regierungen gebildet werden, muss das Bedingung sein. Antisemitismus darf nirgendwo in Deutschland Einfluss auf die Regierungsarbeit bekommen“, sagte Steinmeier bei der Eröffnung der Jüdischen Akademie und rief zu einer klaren Solidarität mit Jüdinnen und Juden in Deutschland auf. Judenhass müsse ohne Hintertür und Vorbehalt in die Schranken gewiesen werden. „Wer auf den Straßen ‚Tod den Juden‘ skandiert und die Auslöschung des jüdischen Staates fordert, darf in keiner Partei Verständnis und Applaus finden.“ Alle Parteien seien in der Pflicht, in ihrem gesamten Einflussbereich der Judenfeindschaft entgegenzutreten. Niemals dürfe die direkte, glaubwürdige, unzweideutige Abwehr des Antisemitismus infrage stehen.
Frankfurts Oberbürgermeister Mike Josef warnte bei dem Festakt ebenfalls davor, jüdisches Leben immer nur dann wahrzunehmen, wenn es bedroht werde. Die Jüdische Akademie sei Ausdruck der starken jüdischen Gemeinde in der Stadt. Sie werde „wie ein Wellenbrecher gegen die Springflut des Antisemitismus“ wirken, sagte er.
Der Neubau der Jüdischen Akademie an der Frankfurter Senckenberganlage zwischen Messeviertel, Unicampus und Westend hat rund 40 Millionen Euro gekostet. Auch der Bund, das Land Hessen und die Stadt Frankfurt haben den Bau nach den Plänen des Frankfurter Architekten Zvonko Turkali unterstützt.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Citizen Kim by Jonathan Van Meter review – Kardashian under the microscope
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Rebecca Nicholson
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
The magazine writer Jonathan Van Meter profiles very famous people for extremely glossy publications. He was responsible for the notorious 1990 interview in which supermodel Linda Evangelista said she wouldn’t wake up for less than $10,000 a day, and in recent years, he has interviewed Taylor Swift, Michelle Obama and Lady Gaga for American Vogue. In 2019, he wrote a cover story, also for Vogue, on Kim Kardashian, the reality TV star turned businesswoman turned criminal justice activist, and one of the most famous women in the world. In the lengthy acknowledgments to this book, he describes receiving a phonecall from her after the piece had been published. “There’s no better feeling in the world than when someone gets you,” she told him. He replied by telling her that he was going to write a book about her, “whether you like it or not!”
Spoiler alert: she liked it. And the concept underlying the book can be justified: Kim Kardashian really has transformed celebrity culture. Her family, broadcasting their lives for years, came to define contemporary reality television, beginning with Keeping Up With the Kardashians in 2007 and continuing to the present day with The Kardashians. She saw the potential in social media and used it to her advantage from its inception. Last year, her clothing line, Skims, was valued at $5bn (£3.75bn). Van Meter notes that despite her ubiquitous presence, there has been “a dearth of well-written profiles and shrewd cultural analysis” about the phenomenon of Kim K.
But what is promised and what is delivered are not exactly the same. Early on, Van Meter references Kant and the academic Timothy Morton, and later, he invokes Joan Didion’s writing on Hollywood. But any attempts at cultural analysis, shrewd or otherwise, quickly fall away in favour of a more traditional in-depth biography, its wheels greased by regular, intimate access to the Kardashians and many of Kim’s closest friends and colleagues.
Van Meter visits his subject often, at her many homes and places of work. They talk over snacks and coffee. Kim may be in her pyjamas or a bathrobe, having just got out of the shower. At one point, she does away with the formality of clothing entirely. “I looked up from my phone and she was entirely naked. Neither of us flinched,” he writes, describing a day spent with her at a photoshoot. This is intended to suggest candour, though inevitably it implies a lack of critical distance. At the end, in the acknowledgements, he thanks her for her “time, but more so, your trust”.
Van Meter notes that Kim does not like to dwell on the bad stuff, nor does she seem particularly inclined towards introspection. What more is there to say about her life that has not already been televised? Ironically, her views on the family’s show may be the most fascinating part of this book. Doing television has been good for them, she says, “because we’re not going to leave an episode unfinished” – by which she means that arguments are almost always resolved, because they have to be, for the shape of the TV narrative. Public and private are one and the same.
At its best, the book does expose some of the Kardashian family’s gothic underbelly. In 1995, Kim’s mother and father found themselves on opposing sides of the OJ Simpson murder trial (Kris Jenner supported her best friend Nicole Brown’s family during the trial, while her ex-husband, the late Robert Kardashian, was on Simpson’s legal team). For a while, Kim’s teenage boyfriend was TJ Jackson, nephew of Michael, whose own family lore is horrifying and unique. Her school days are likened to the movie Clueless, but there is a touch of Bret Easton Ellis in there, too.
There is some reflection on the sex tape that propelled Kim into the public eye (it has left her with “a lot to prove”, she says). Van Meter offers a pop-psychology analysis of why she seems to gravitate towards “lost boys”, and she talks about her marriage to Kanye West, albeit with respect and restraint. She describes a move away from a more materialistic worldview after being robbed at gunpoint in Paris, in 2016. The book ends with speculation that she might run for political office. “I am so flattered,” she responds, and leaves the prospect open.
There are moments of camp extravagance. One chapter begins, “Did the trouble start with not one, but two boob jobs?” Van Meter namedrops Anna Wintour, Oprah Winfrey and his own tennis coach. But elsewhere, the narrative swoons and fawns. Kim’s private jet is “a shade of nudey grey,” we learn. “Which is so me,” she says. It is also so this book. The Kardashian aura must be strong, because reading this evokes the same sensation as watching their show: it is seductive, hypnotic, but possessed of a sleight of hand that turns everything beige.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The US launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, hours after the vice-president, JD Vance, said he was optimistic that diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.
The strikes, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the cost of living.
Unnamed US officials cited by the WSJ and other outlets described the attacks as defensive in nature.
Trump was asked earlier on Monday whether he had considered resuming strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections and replied “no”.
Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island on Monday evening, according to Iranian state media, with local outlets describing their cause as unclear.
The strikes targeted surface-to-air missiles being used against US assets, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.
US Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Reuters news agency, but the WSJ described the attacks as part of a series of strikes carried out against the country in recent weeks that had not been made public.
The paper reported that the recent strikes had been carried out on a smaller scale and purposefully kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal any intent of resuming the military campaign against Iran.
The US has targeted Qeshm Island on multiple occasions throughout the war. Positioned in the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the island has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping in the waterway.
Despite attacks having ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting oil tankers, shipping containers and other vessels attempting to transit the waterway.
On Monday, Vance said he and Trump were optimistic about securing a deal with Iran, after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington.
“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effects on the US economy.
“There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”
However, he said the US might still “have to go after Pickaxe Mountain” – referring to a fortified underground site in central Iran that is suspected to be a nuclear facility – but said it would not be a “big deal” and could be done in “one hour”.
Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices as his administration touted renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices have caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.title: ARTnews, Art in America, and Hublot Host Dinner at New York Headquarters of Kid Super
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.text:
On Wednesday night, ARTnews, Art in America, and Hublot hosted a dinner at the New York headquarters of artist and fashion designer Kid Super (Colm Dillane).
Guests included collector and Brooklyn Museum trustee Carla Shen; Frank Suznjevic, president of Hublot Americas; ARTnews and Art in America editor-in-chief Sarah Douglas; Time to Drive festival founder Perri Dash; fashion designer Mobolaji Dawodu; collector Viljon Caka; Gazelli Art House senior director Haley Shaw; filmmaker Saam Farahmand; collector and commentator Jeff Magid; gallerist Adam Cohen; artist Jonathan Gardenhire; curator Anwarii Musa, and real estate developer Ben Levine.
PJ Monte of Monte’s Fine Foods, also known as the Sauce Boss, provided dinner.
In a conversation with Douglas, Dillane said he had first found the art world somewhat inaccessible, and he compared his entrée into it to the reception he got early on in fashion. “I was really an outsider [there] as well,” he said. “I got rejected three times from the official calendar [at Paris Fashion Week]…. [T]hey finally said yes. Once I broke into fashion, I realized that behind this wall there’s really interesting people who care about new ideas.”
Dillane gave attendees a tour of his 10,000-square-foot headquarters. The building includes a Hublot-sponsored rooftop soccer pitch, an art studio, a podcast studio, a store, and other spaces for all kinds of creative work. “When everyone got here, I couldn’t wait to tour them around the building,” Dillane told the guests. “This is my greatest work, and I think it encapsulates [my] whole practice.” Of the many creative avenues he has pursued, he said, “For me, all of these different mediums were pushing towards the same spirit…. There’s a mischievousness to it…. There’s bringing people together. I want to capture the feeling that I feel when I’m in New York, where anything feels possible.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force California to set aside ballots
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The supreme court on Monday ruled against the Trump administration and its attempts to force California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people that the justice department claims are non-citizens. The ruling follows several lower courts siding with California officials, who argued the federal government was seeking to interfere in state elections.
The court did not issue an explanation for its ruling, which is customary in cases that come to it on an emergency basis. There were no noted dissents from the justices.
California and the Trump administration have been in a legal standoff over the past few weeks following the justice department’s claim that 20,000 non-citizens were on the state’s voter rolls. The DoJ delivered a USB drive to Los Angeles and Sacramento election officials in mid-October with the names, giving only 48 hours for officials to review the list and threatening to sue if the ballots were not sequestered until those listed could verify their citizenship. Election officials refused, leading to a series of courtroom battles.
The justice department’s claims faced immediate pushback from state officials and voting rights groups, who questioned how the agency compiled the list and accused the Trump administration of a ploy to cast doubt over midterm elections. The justice department refused to provide details on its methodology and analysis from election officials found numerous suggestions the list contained inaccuracies.
“The Department of Justice has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” Dean Logan, Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, said in a statement after receiving the list.
The justice department did not immediately return a request for comment.
Top Democrats in California praised the ruling.
“After repeatedly losing in the lower courts, the highest court in the land firmly slapped down the Trump DoJ’s baseless attack on California’s electoral process – not even entertaining it,” Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement.
Rob Bonta, the state’s attorney general, said: “This latest decision should put an end to the administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders. But our work is not over.”
The justice department had threatened to prosecute election officials in California who counted ballots from those on the list, leading to widespread rebuke. A federal judge on Friday blocked the government from threatening such officials.
As the Trump administration pushed the list of alleged non-citizens, it also trumpeted arrests of dozens non-citizens who allegedly registered and voted in federal elections. Media was on hand for their arrests and videos and pictures of the moment were circulated.
But several of those charged have been legal permanent residents for decades and said they had no idea they were ineligible to vote. “It was staged and I’m the patsy … They wanted to make a scene,” Omar Muñoz, one of the people arrested, told the Guardian last month.
The fight between the Trump administration and California officials escalated over recent weeks and subsequent court rulings. The administration has threatened to prosecute election officials if they process ineligible non-citizen ballots, a move experts say would have no legal basis. The Trump administration has also opened a criminal investigation in California to pursue claims of non-citizen voting, as well as begun subpoenaing election officials.
US district judge David Carter previously rebuffed the administration’s request to segregate ballots in a ruling on 28 October. Carter, who was nominated to the bench by Bill Clinton, wrote in his decision about how the administration’s move to interfere in California’s vote was unusual and extreme.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote. The US court of appeals for the ninth circuit also rejected the Trump administration’s efforts over the weekend.
The Trump administration’s demands are part of a larger effort by the federal government to assert a greater role in overseeing elections and push claims of voter fraud committed by non-citizens. The justice department has made a similar demand to segregate ballots in Washington state, while also filing criminal charges against 28 green card holders in California that the DoJ accuses of fraudulently registering to vote and casting illegal ballots.
Trump has also made vague promises to issue a $1m reward to anyone whose reports of voter fraud lead to an arrest or conviction. Data and experts have shown that ineligible non-citizen voting is extremely rare.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Les the bare-handed beekeeper asked if he should put them on his face. I said: Sure!’ Holly Lynton’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Chris Broughton
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. He looks like something out of The Odyssey’

The jumping-off point for my Bare Handed series was a bird becoming trapped in the netting around the raspberry bushes in my backyard. It made me think of the problem humans have interacting with the natural world. How do we navigate obtaining food and the other things we need while still being good stewards of the land? I’d seen work by photographers demonstrating how Big Agriculture was destroying the environment. I wanted to find people who took a respectful approach, tried to work in tandem with it, but who might be in a fearful or dangerous situation.

I approached Les, the man in this picture, after speaking to the director of an exhibition space in Albuquerque, New Mexico, who had hired him to remove a feral beehive from his tree. I’d already tried to photograph another beekeeper who wore a full protective suit, but he might as well have been an astronaut. With Les, I was able to stay nearby and work with him over three days. The first couple involved straightforward documentary pictures of him tending his hives. Then, on the third day, his apprentice Amber showed up to help.

Les had the queen bee in a cage in his shirt pocket and asked Amber to take it out. Wherever the queen is, the rest of the colony will swarm. There’s a picture I made where Les and Amber are joined together by bees, and that was my “ah ha!” moment. Amber took out the queen and placed her in Les’s hand, which is where the bees went next. He looked at me with his hands full of bees and said: “Should I put them on my face?” I said: “Sure!”

Les slowly moved his hands up to his face. Bees don’t like hair, which is why they’re not in his beard or the top of his head. He closed his eyes for a few minutes, and I photographed. Afterwards, he said: “You know, I couldn’t hear anything but the buzzing.” I don’t think he’d ever done that before. People sometimes have their own ideas, which I just go with. One of the reasons I like spending some time with them is that when they’re engaged in work, it’s almost like watching a dance and waiting for the right gesture.

Les didn’t wear gloves when handling the bees. He said he needed to be able to feel them so he didn’t crush them, and that it was too hot to wear a suit. I wore a shirt that buttoned up tight at the wrists and tried wearing a beekeeper’s veil, too, but I abandoned that after finding it hard to focus through the mesh. I did get a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up.

I was using a medium-format analogue camera, and the bees were also landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see them. That was disconcerting, but Les advised me just to move slowly, as he did. That worked: I didn’t get stung.

For a while, the photograph of Amber and Les joined together by bees was the one I preferred. I was worried people would find the bees on his face over the top. The themes of the project were quickly reinforced when I photographed wolves in a sanctuary with their trainers, and then went out with a family of catfish noodlers in rural Oklahoma. “Noodling” involved them catching these fish with their bare hands – even though they can weigh 45kg and really fight back. I realised none of these people had any fear. They were all experts at whatever it was they were doing, and for them this was a spiritual, meditative practice. That became the focus for the series.

Before I started taking photography classes, I planned to be a psychologist and a writer. But what I love about photography is that you can create ambiguous narratives, a multilayered story in a single frame. A lot of my work references cultural memory. Rather than straight documentary, I’m aiming for something more mythic, and gestures that happen spontaneously can sometimes seem to reference a certain myth or biblical allusion. This photograph leans more towards Greek mythology, even if it doesn’t directly reference an exact story. Les isn’t Odysseus but, like him, he elects to hear rather than protect himself, which makes him feel like he’s a part of The Odyssey, somehow.

High point: High points occur when my photographs are both made and shown. When photographing, a high point is when everything aligns – the light, content, composition – and I create an unanticipated image that transcends the moment. One that elicits allusion, mystery and wonder. In terms of exhibitions or publications, it’s often what is recent. In the past few years, institutions as varied as the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City and Bristol Cathedral in England have exhibited my work. I’m thankful that institutions have enabled people from many different backgrounds and perspectives to see my photographs. Talking with viewers and hearing their reactions has been a real gift. My book Bare Handed, published by L’Artiere, was another high point.

Top tip: Right now, the quest for authenticity instead of artifice feels crucial, and what I’d urge photographers to undertake. I’d also say there is no such thing as too much curiosity (even though some people might make you think so). Don’t be afraid to change your mind about what you are working on, the meaning behind it or how to go about it. Reframing is what I like to call it. Follow your intuition. And find the joy in the practice of making work and being creative. Difficult moments will occur, and ones that feel like failures, but it’s the journey, not the end goal.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Punk-Rock Appeal of the Women’s Pro Baseball League
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: G’Ra Asim
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The new competitive circuit captures the energy and DIY spirit of punk, while promoting a surprisingly sturdy vision of civic belonging.

Ashton Lansdell of the Los Angeles Queens celebrates after scoring against the San Francisco Firebells in game two of the Women’s Pro Baseball League Championship.

Cultic ecstasy seizes my body. I leap to my feet from a sitting position and thrust my hands skyward like someone who got the Holy Ghost in church. Like a contagion, the same behavior ripples across the aisle I’m sitting in. About a quarter of the way across the crowded baseball stadium, the vector peters out. Either the people roughly 10 rows away don’t notice our spirited efforts to sustain a wave across the entire crowd, or they just don’t feel like participating.

“Those guys suck, dude,” our wave leader groans. “They need to get with the program!”

It’s no less than the sixth time that this person has hectored our section to start an ill-fated wave. To the chagrin of the visibly exasperated spectators around him, he has not lost hope.

I’m in the stands for game three of the Women’s Professional Baseball League’s best-of-five inaugural championship series. The Los Angeles Queens are up two games to none on the San Francisco Firebelles, and another Queens win will secure the championship. The WPBL website boasts that “for the first time in 70 years, the best women baseball players in the world are competing on a professional stage.” Players hail from across the United States and 11 other countries. The league’s first-ever regular season began a few weeks earlier on August 1, 2026. Each squad in the league played all the other teams five times, for a total of 15 regular season games in a triple round-robin format. For now, there are four teams in the WPBL, two of whom have already been eliminated: the Boston Hunters and the New York Heights. All the games are played in impartial Springfield, Illinois. Watching teams named aspirationally after major markets compete in the neutral territory of flyover country feels like a provisional unity of these States, in a way it’d be hard to approximate by other means.

I’ve taken a road trip from St. Louis, Missouri, where I live, to Springfield, which I’m not sure I’ve heard of before now. Despite the city’s claim to fame as the adult home of Abraham Lincoln, it wouldn’t have surprised me to find the Klan posted up in the stadium parking lot. Along with my intrepid companions Jesse and Doc, I bought tickets online the night before the game, but pickings were slim. Three successive seats in the same row weren’t available. We bought a pair that were right next to each other and a third ticket a few rows behind those two. Our plan was to barnstorm the end of one row and dare anyone to challenge our claim. A group of white fans to our left look like they want to. They gawk over their shoulders at us like schoolyard extras in a Ruby Bridges movie. I almost hear my antebellum-era ancestors assembling into a bluesy chorus of telltale woe and foreboding.

When we pulled into Springfield half an hour ago, my eyes settled on a chain restaurant I’d never seen before.

“Taco Gringo?” I blurted. “Sounds a little too White Power for my taste. Is it really a selling point that gringos are back there making the tacos?”

“I don’t think the gringos are making the tacos,” Doc had joked. “They’re probably just cracking the whip.”

Though most of my teenage years and young adulthood took place on the East Coast, I’m a native St. Louisan. The MLB’s St. Louis Cardinals are our dominant sports franchise, so naturally my earliest baseball memories were formed at Busch Stadium. I’ve had difficulty rooting for the home team since the police killing of Ferguson teenager Mike Brown in 2014. That year, social media was awash in clips of mobs clad in Cards regalia spitting and cursing at Black Lives Matter protesters. It’s likely that there’s some overlap between the folks at the ballpark with me now and those justice-averse Cardinals fans. But here, as supporters of a new league, it feels like we have a clean slate.

Well, sort of. I can’t help but suspect that some percentage of the enthusiasm that radiates throughout Robin Roberts Stadium today is traceable to the 2023 NCAA women’s college basketball final, in which Caitlin Clark’s Iowa Hawkeyes fell to Angel Reese’s LSU Tigers. The widely watched showdown between two highly marketable and racially polarizing players sparked a surge in public interest in women’s sports. There is no competitive storyline Americans relish more than a clash between a Great White Hope and what they perceive as an uppity Black antagonist, and apparently the fervor is gender neutral. That revelation doesn’t exactly brighten the forecast for our crumbling empire, but it does boost the overall flashbulb wattage of women’s sports.

Here at game three of the WPBL’s inaugural championship series, fans carry signs with slogans like “I drove 300 miles to be a part of HERSTORY.” There is a palpable shared sense that the one thing better than being on the right side of history is cheering history on while you’re sitting by its third base line.

A strict, masc-of-center auntie in her 50s or 60s seated to my right foretells the outcome of each at-bat.

“That’s an out!” she yells sometimes, leaning back in her seat with her arms crossed as a fly ball lingers over second base.

“That’s a hit,” she claims other times, as soon as she hears the crack of the bat.

Growing up a baseball fan in the 1990s Midwest, I tracked the traditional box score stats in the paper every morning before school. Before the Moneyball movement, baseball diehards assessed player performance via straightforward statistical categories like batting average, fielding percentage, and runs batted in. These were the numbers you would see on the back of a baseball card. Starting in the early 2000s, those traditional statistics were phased out in favor of advanced analytics. Where sportscasters once narrated home runs by bellowing things like, “Busting out the whooping stick!,” they instead began to pepper the broadcast with references to math nerd esoterica like launch angle, spin rate, and exit velocity.

Look, I love Neil deGrasse Tyson. Physics has its place. But I doubt I’m speaking only for myself when I say I tune into baseball games to watch swaggering leviathans swing clubs at projectiles and hammer them to the moon. The shift in how baseball is discussed and understood is a microcosm for how the digital age has muddied the distinction between information and meaning. I appreciate that the experts can contextualize the game with such an impressive volume of information. This stern auntie’s play-by-play—which more than compensates with passion for what it lacks in data—strikes me as far more meaningful. The subtext of her commentary is that she’s been waiting for a league like this one for most of her life, and she’s not going to take one iota of action for granted.

Typically, yearning for baseball’s salad days would mark me as retrograde. In this case, I’m quite sure appreciating WPBL for its contrasts with MLB makes me a part of the vanguard. That said, I hesitate to position the WPBL as somehow morally superior to other professional sports leagues. Women’s sports are more often instrumentalized as battlegrounds in the culture wars than treated as legitimate ends in themselves. Moralizing is boring, and watching some of Earth’s most talented and tenacious people push their bodies to their limits in the name of autumnal glory is a good time. At least as much as we need an endless hermeneutics of ball, we need an erotics of ball.

Being taken out to this ballgame and taken out to the crowd also feels more poignant at a cultural moment defined by atomization. When things like, say, the venerable practice of wearing headphones when listening to media in public have fallen out of favor, any symbiosis between strangers feels like a sign of great respect in our culture. That’s what makes me realize why being absorbed into a fandom that’s both salutary and scintillating is so comforting, so familiar. The WPBL is the new punk rock.

As a millennial pushing 40, I’ve been a punk rocker much longer than I wasn’t one. I’m in two actively recording and gigging bands right now; I threw my first house show in my parents’ basement to celebrate my 15th birthday. Punk is about building the reconciled world in miniature and making its qualities infectious. Organizing a scene in your town is a small insurrectionary act—lining up a single domino that might, and sometimes does, kick-start a massive cascade.

A lot of the viral content about being an aging punk or emo kid focuses on nostalgia, as if the upshot of belonging to a forward-thinking subculture is to perseverate on the past. But the skills and instincts that we honed in VFW halls, garages, and church basements are just as easily applicable to the pursuit of gender equity in professional sports. Why settle into being a mark for the contrived cash grabs of your local Emo Nite when you could sublimate your ennui and residual angst into supporting a likeminded subculture like the WPBL instead?

Everyone who spent their teens and 20s working for street teams, orchestrating circle pits and Walls of Death, and tucking show flyers under windshield wipers can channel their punk-rock past in helping to secure the WPBL’s future. In 2018, Vice published a satirical article asking, “What Kind of Punk Dude Over 30 Are You?” The article joked that thirtysomething punks have a limited menu of acceptable hobbies and interests that they can cultivate to stave off the creep of cultural irrelevance. As I ponder the high jinks I might get up to as an over-40 punk, WPBL zealotry presents a compelling case.

Punks are better known for throwing bricks than laying them, but jury-rigging alternative structures is a big part of what we do. Whether we’re debuting a zine, a new band, or a DIY show space, we’ve always taken a distinct pride in supporting something precisely because it’s fledgling yet fertile, burgeoning and brimming with promise. The slightly grating wave whisperer here at the game reminds me of the dutiful mosh mentors I grew up with in the punk scene. They trained members of the audience to pick up anyone who fell down while slam dancing, reminded us to choose opportune and safe moments for our stage dives, and urged us to pass the hat for touring acts even when there wasn’t much money to go around. A movement isn’t only held together by the headliners—it’s also sustained by the energized, anonymous folks who dole out unsolicited marching orders, and those who roll with them even as we roll our eyes.

As the innings accumulate, I’m brought back to the beer-soaked stages and sweat-streaked floors where I cut my teeth. The early days of a punk band’s ascent are traditionally viewed as innocent, less cynical, driven by a genuine love of the game. Likewise, since legal gambling is now largely coextensive with professional sports, watching professional baseball for its own sake is a return to a simpler time. Cheering and jeering abound, but no one here is screaming about their parlay, or frantically refreshing the FanDuel app.

Much like navigating the street parking outside a makeshift venue or house show, figuring out where to leave the whip near the stadium was a riddle. My friend Jesse ended up pulling her SUV onto a muddy strip of grass next to some train tracks nearby. The demand for women’s professional baseball for the moment outpaces the real estate set aside for its patrons. We figured Springfield was still adjusting to the influx of fans from other cities, and strict parking enforcement would be unlikely. On his way to the ticket line, a man in a Chambray shirt and jeans looked back at our car and grinned impishly.

“Looks like a parking spot to me!” he declared, flashing us a thumbs-up. A nascent iteration of the American pastime foments the same constructive lawlessness as Warped Tour or the Fest.

A newfangled women’s baseball league and a punk scene both recall the architectural principle of flex space—a term that describes any versatile, adaptable, lightly zoned area in a commercial building. Some rooms or settings are designed for specific purposes. The construction of the room circumscribes how the room can be used. By contrast, flex space is meant to be pliable enough that occupants can customize it to suit the fluctuating needs and aims of their business. The punk scene and the WPBL are both flex spaces where norms can shift in real time. They’re both underground pockets that can slip the generally totalizing yoke of unfettered capitalism. In these flex spaces, the conditions of possibility are developed and implemented on the fly.

This includes a temporary suspension of the “customer is always right” ethos that otherwise guides American commerce. Jesse ventures into the bowels of the stadium to brave the concession line in the third inning. By the top of the fifth, she still hasn’t returned. I hop out of my seat and pace the stadium corridors until I find her in line, where an interminable trail of sweaty, hungry WPBL supporters are being surprisingly civil about the slow, disorganized food service. Jesse herself mentions being on the verge of becoming hangry, but exercises some commendable and not totally characteristic restraint. It’s as if the entire concession line is down for the cause. They know the WPBL is an embryonic but well-intended enterprise that calls for a level of patience and indulgence that the more established sports institutions may not require.

The phrase “social construct” penetrated the mainstream during the height of what is now derisively described as Woke 1, those pathbreaking days from early 2014 to 2021 when American culture seemed more mutable and benevolent than it has felt since. Whenever I heard gender, sexuality, or race described as social constructs, I always wondered why we couldn’t consciously build some new, more humane structures from scratch. Where was the social construct factory? Who among us might put on their hard hat and start hammering out frameworks meant to shelter rather than subjugate? In the stands at a WPBL championship game, I feel that construction effort commence.

It turns out the crowd of murmuring, staring white folks in the section next to us were actually marveling at Doc’s service animal, a preternaturally adorable toy Australian shepherd. Dogs are the ultimate social lubricant. When paired with baseball, they form a diversion powerful enough to neutralize racial reticence.

“His name is Dodger,” Doc tells a middle-aged white couple behind us. “The energy here almost reminds me of Dodger Stadium.”

“You’ve been to Dodger Stadium?” the husband breathes, as if Doc had seen the gates of Valhalla. I don’t directly observe this conversation, since I was wary that eye contact with the couple behind us would prolong the engagement. So I imagine Doc adjusting her sunglasses and tossing her fabulous Afro as she says, “Yeah, I’m originally from LA. The Dodgers are my favorite team. Where are you guys from?”

“We’ve seen Bush Stadium and Wrigley Field,” goes the husband.

It’s not quite an Obama-era beer summit, but it is a quiet coalescence of coastal elites and heartland dwellers, a glimmer of baseball’s potential to patch up tattered social fabric. The moment recalls the words of legendary folk-punk troubadour Frank Turner. Addressing the crowd at an Amityville Music Hall solo show in 2025, he explained how and why a punk performance—like a WPBL game—is always more than meets the eye.

“If we all do our parts, we will achieve two things. The first of which is, we’ll make a cool noise. And arguably, that’s what this is all about. But the other thing we’ll do is demonstrate a point which is important to me. Which is that live music, rock ’n’ roll, folk music, punk rock—whatever name you wind up calling this—is not about raised pieces of flooring and backstage passes and tour buses and egos and all that stuff. It’s about bringing people together. It’s about a room full of strangers who leave as friends, a room full of strangers who achieve something together that’s more than the sum of their parts, thereby demonstrating to themselves and to the rest of the world that we can be a community if we choose to be one.”

Doc, Jesse, and I rocked up to the ballpark expecting the Los Angeles Queens to close out the series with a 3–0 sweep. San Francisco had other plans. They overpowered the Queens from the jump, racing out to a commanding seven-to-nothing lead in the second inning and not letting up. Attendance at the decisive victory of a best-of-five series would certainly be more historic, but San Francisco’s fighting spirit won the crowd over. We all needed reminding that no deficit is too daunting if you come out swinging. A few weeks later, a sitting president will casually fantasize aloud about sacrificing two major Californian cities to the war against Iran. For now, we’re galvanized by the collective exercise of manifesting a future where the San Francisco Firebelles’ smoking baseball bats are as American as smoking gun barrels.

During a seventh-inning stretch, the wave’s most vocal advocate finally sees his wish fulfilled. The wave breaks out on the side of the stadium opposite ours. Our section exults and keeps it going when it reaches us. As fireworks shimmer across the late-summer sky, the glass ceiling feels like a piñata visibly starting to give way, sprinkling rewards that will only multiply if we all keep swinging on target. I’m filled with enough goodwill and forbearance to consider stopping at Taco Gringo on the way home.

G'Ra Asim, a writer and musician, is an assistant professor of creative writing at Washington University in St. Louis. His latest book is 99 Problems Finding the 1: a love story (sort of).

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Where with a little bit of luck—and a ton of grassroots organizing—decency has a fighting chance.

You can see it in the polls, which show Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor running for governor, consistently ahead of Republican Zack Lahn, in a state where the outgoing incumbent, MAGA Republican Kim Reynolds, was reelected by a 19-point margin four years ago—and where Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris by over 13 points.

You can see it in Dubuque, where hundreds of protesters gathered for a No Kings rally before Trump’s visit to the state earlier this month. And in Sioux City, where 12 percent of the city’s residents are foreign-born, and in Des Moines, where thousands of demonstrators turned out at the State Capitol in the spring, and where the most recent protest, on October 17, was focused on encouraging early voting.

I first saw it for myself in late July in Guthrie Center, a town of about 1,500 people spread out along the South Raccoon River. This was the second day of RAGBRAI, the 53rd running of the Des Moines Register’s Annual Great Bicycle Ride Across Iowa. Invented by John Karras, a feature writer for the paper, and columnist Don Kaul, as a stratagem to get their employer to pay for a newsman’s holiday, the pair invited readers to join them for a weeklong bicycle jaunt across the state. Some 300 riders turned up back in 1973—of whom 114 stayed the distance.

This year there were 20,000 of us at the start in Onowa, a town that claims the widest Main Street in the country, but whose chief attraction these days is the Blackbird Bend Casino, operated by the Omaha tribe of Nebraska, and which boasts 350 electric slot machines—but no table games. After dipping our rear wheels in the waters of the Missouri River (the ceremonial start to every RAGBRAI) our route climbed over 3,500 feet, and 59.3 miles, to Harlan, where the temperature briefly hit triple digits. The road to Guthrie Center the next day brought an even greater number of hills—by the end of the day, several riders could be heard cursing whoever had assured them Iowa was flat—with the heat index reaching 110 degrees.

The Iowans on the ride were not surprised; indeed, many wore jerseys with the slogan “Iowa: Flat as a waffle.” But after pedaling under the blazing sun for hours between cornfields on one side of the road and soybeans on the other, without a stick of shade between them, it was a great relief to come into the shade and think about politics. The topic would have been on my mind anyway—I’d been given my first lessons in prairie populism by David Leshtz and Jeffrey Cox, co-editors of The Prairie Progressive, back in 2015 when the two of them were all in for Bernie Sanders. Jeff died in 2020, but Dave keeps up the fight, and it was partly his influence that made me say yes when a Vermont friend asked me if I’d ride RAGRAI with him. But I’d also brought along a native informant from Brooklyn.

I met Peter Hedges because we shared a physical therapist in Cobble Hill, and after weeks of groaning side by side every Thursday, we began to talk and discovered a shared passion for movies and left politics. Peter is a playwright and screenwriter by trade; when I asked him if he’d written anything I might have seen, he said “I wrote the screenplay for What’s Eating Gilbert Grape.” Turns out he wrote the novel, too. Peter was born and raised in West Des Moines, where he graduated from Valley High School. And that’s where the story gets interesting.

Because it turns out that Ashley Hinson, the Trump-endorsed candidate to replace retiring MAGA loyalist Joni Ernst, is also a graduate of Valley High. Back in the spring, a bipartisan group of Hinson’s former teachers joined with Valley High alumni to form Iowans for Decency, a PAC dedicated to marshaling local grassroots opposition to the Republican’s campaign—months before Josh Turek had even secured the Democratic nomination. Peter was already deeply involved, so when I asked him if he might want to come along on RAGBRAI, I didn’t have to twist his arm. “My brother rode RAGBRAI, and my cousin, and I always wanted to do it. But I never did.”

What I was thinking about in Guthrie Center—once my brain stopped boiling—and kept thinking about all the way to the finish line in Dubuque, was the way his fellow Iowans responded to Peter, who wore an “Iowans for Decency” jersey during the daytime, and a “What’s Eating Iowans?” purple T-shirt in the evening, when he’d turn up at the local high school to talk to the theater kids, or at the town library for the Iowans for Decency Listening Tour.

It wasn’t the issues that were surprising: the devastating effect of Trump’s tariffs on farm incomes, the price of gas and diesel, fear for their sons and daughters sent to fight Trump’s wars of choice, or the way, thanks to Big Ag dumping chemicals into the water table, Iowa has seen a sharp rise in cancer diagnoses (even while rates keep falling elsewhere in the country). What I kept hearing, and seeing, was some kind of limit being reached. It wasn’t exactly a prairie fire of populist enthusiasm—though Turek, who was politicized by his experience as a person with spina bifida navigating the American healthcare system, does describe himself as a “prairie populist.” (Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, describes his politics as “radical centrist populism.”)

But then, in a state that sent Tom Harkin to the House for five terms and then to the Senate for five more terms, the Democratic Party brand is still sufficiently toxic for Sand’s yard signs to use green and orange rather than blue; I saw hundreds of them as I rode east across the state, without any idea which party the candidate was in.

So while Iowa may lack the high-stakes ideological drama of Abdul El-Sayed’s race in Michigan, or the presidential potential of Jon Ossoff’s expected triumph in Georgia, I’m going to be keeping my eyes on Iowa, where with a little bit of luck—and a ton of grassroots organizing—decency has a fighting chance.

D.D. Guttenplan is a special correspondent for The Nation and the former host of The Nation Podcast. He served as editor of the magazine from 2019 to 2025 and, prior to that, as an editor at large and London correspondent. His books include American Radical: The Life and Times of I.F. Stone, The Nation: A Biography, and The Next Republic: The Rise of a New Radical Majority.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent asks why the media is obsessing over Obama’s Cheesecake Factory joke while largely ignoring allegations of Trump’s sexual assaults. Plus: Republicans prepare to cry election fraud.

Donald Trump and future wife Melania pose with Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

The president of the United States of America has been accused of rape. Again. The president of the United States has been accused of rape in a report issued by the Democrats of the House Judiciary Committee, as part of their ongoing investigation of Donald Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The president has been accused of raping two women, one when she was as young as 13, and sexually assaulting three more. They are among 11 women who provided evidence or testimony that Trump “abused, assaulted, and even raped numerous women alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.”

I have been made to understand that many people do not know about the Judiciary Comittee report—and the fact that five women have accused Trump of sexual assault while in or near the presence of noted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein. I have been made to understand that this is because the mainstream media finds former president Barack Obama’s comments about the [checks notes] Cheesecake Factory more worthy of their attention than the current president’s abuse of multiple women.

If asked, mainstream media types would no doubt argue that the lack of coverage of these latest rape allegations stems from the fact that previous rape allegations failed to “move the needle.” Trump’s sexual misconduct (both alleged and litigated) is “baked in” to people’s understanding of the man. People either won’t believe the charges or won’t care—or else they do believe the women and do care and vote accordingly—but everybody knows what he’s been accused of, generally speaking at least.

I find this line of argument unadulterated bollocks that reveals the deep failure of our mainstream media. It is news when the president is credibly accused of rape. It is important news. While I, too, don’t think these latest sexual assault accusations will materially change the national conversation about Trump or his presidency, that is not an excuse for ignoring, downplaying, or skipping over brutal allegations that he repeatedly assaulted women, including minors.

Journalists cannot decide what other people think is important. Their job is to illuminate what they think is in the public interest. I think reporting on rape allegations levied against the president of the United States is in the public interest. And since I think that, it really doesn’t matter if the public agrees with me.

With that in mind, I, unlike people who work for Bari Weiss, read the Judiciary report. Here are some of the allegations:

Next week, the Republicans are going to lose. I don’t know precisely which ones or by how much: I suspect that Democrats will retake the House; there’s certainly a chance they will retake the Senate. But no matter how things shake out, it’s very likely that the Republicans will emerge from the election with less political power than they went in with.

That’s not surprising. This is a midterm election, and the party in power in the White House usually loses seats in the midterms, just as a matter of course. And we can expect those losses to be exacerbated when the president in power is deeply unpopular, the economy is in the tank, and the country is engaged in a pointless war that it’s not even winning. The laws of political physics say the GOP is supposed to lose next week, and quite badly.

But the Republicans, at least the ones most devoted to the Trump cult, likely have no idea they are about to lose. That’s because Trump and the white-wing media have been feeding them a steady diet of lies, priming them to believe that the only way Democrats could win is if there is election fraud. Their reasons for doing this are clear: If Trump’s base thinks their loss is due to fraud, they will likely support the most antidemocratic measures Trump takes to hold on to power over the will of the people. If they really believe Trump, at least some of them will turn to violence to support his antidemocratic efforts.

A new study from The Washington Post illustrates the complete saturation of the white-wing media by this false electoral narrative.

Nearly 600 high-profile, right-wing social media accounts, podcasts and other online media have published more than 7,000 statements questioning the election’s integrity so far this year, a Washington Post analysis found. That messaging has, in particular, pushed overstated claims that noncitizens are on voter rolls and that mail-in ballots enable widespread fraud—themes that are twice as prevalent as they were during the 2024 election cycle, The Post’s analysis found.

Look, losing can be a shock in the best of times, but when you are priming your audience to think that a loss could happen only through massive cheating and fraud, and that audience has already shown an appetite for violence when it doesn’t get the electoral outcomes it would like, you are playing with fire.

Trump, of course, wants there to be a fire if his party loses. He needs it. He can’t challenge the election if most people agree that his party lost fair and square. He is trying to sow distrust in the system, because distrust is a crucial precondition to violent overthrow of the system.

One wouldn’t expect any particular candidate to tell their supporters, “Hey guys, we’ll probably get our ass kicked tomorrow, but let’s show up and rock the vote anyway.” Candidates need to engender a sense of hope, even if it’s false, until the end.

But one would expect the media to do the work of preparing people to confront reality. What’s the point of all this inane horse-race coverage if it’s not even going to prepare people for the reality of losing?

Unfortunately, the door swings both ways. There isn’t a nefarious conspiracy about how Trump rigged this election that I’d dismiss out of hand at this point. If the GOP pulls off a series of “close” victories in majority-minority precincts because votes didn’t materialize or vanished into thin air, I’m going to be ready to take to the streets myself.

There is no trust left in the electoral system, on either side. Republicans have been actively trying to undermine it, but I’m not sure what Democrats can do to restore it.

The Department of Justice preemptively sued Alaska to delay certification of the results in the Senate race there because there are two candidates running with the same name. The New York Times then Columbus’d the story, reporting that one of the candidates was likely a plant from the Democrats meant to cause confusion among Republican voters.

The thing is, the Times had trouble remembering the most important legal fact of the story: that all of this was litigated, in Alaska, in June, all the way up to the state Supreme Court. That’s what I wrote about. I explained that Republicans had already objected to the other guy with the same name as their incumbent and lost. I explained that the only reason the DOJ is bringing this up again, in October, is to cause confusion and sow distrust in the election, as well as ask for a remedy so antidemocratic that it cannot be allowed.

As I mentioned, the mainstream media is more concerned with President Obama’s comments about the Cheesecake Factory than with the credible rape allegations against Donald Trump. For those who somehow missed it, Obama said, “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Cheesecakegate has inspired a raft of terrible takes, but none worse than the one from the whole-ass editorial board of The Wall Street Journal, which blared: “Obama Goes Socialist, Scorns Cheesecake.” The editorial criticized Obama for, among other things, being condescending toward Middle America with his slam on the Cheesecake Factory.

That last point requires some explanation. The Cheesecake Factory was founded in Beverly Hills, California, which is about as far from “Middle America” as you can get without getting wet. While it now has franchises across the US, it’s mainly an overpriced mall hub that is most popular on the coasts. It’s essentially a diner for people who don’t have access to good diners and don’t mind paying an outrageous premium for diner food. Only a WSJ editor could think that this kind of high-end schlock represents “Middle America.”

I lived in Indiana for 13 months. The chain-store diner-food option was Steak ’N Shake. Applebee’s was another contender. In places I don’t feel safe driving through, the equivalent is Cracker Barrel. There is no place I know of where the Cheesecake Factory’s (shitty) cheesecake represents a thin slice of Americana.

In any event, Trump allegedly sexually assaulted five people while in or near the company of Jeffrey Epstein. Obama made a joke about interior design. If you cannot correctly order the relative political importance of each of those stories, you deserve to dine at the restaurant of your choice with Saddam Hussein in Hell.
