https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Eviction Kings Are Being Sued
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Thomas Birmingham
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Corporate landlord American Landmark admitted that its business model priced tenants out. Now, former tenants have filed a class-action lawsuit against the company.

In January of 2025, recalling the eviction that had made him homeless, Diron Kelly told me his corporate landlord had left him living through “a nightmare.”

He said American Landmark, owner of his Charlotte, North Carolina, apartment and some 30,000 others, had a “bully” business model—from raising his rent by some $400 while forcing him to pay fees for frivolous amenities to jumping at the chance to take him to court once his pockets ran dry. “They really messed everything up,” he said.

But starting last week, it’s now Kelly taking the real estate giant to court. On October 20, he filed a class-action lawsuit against the company in an attempt to prove that not only does its model—first revealed by The Nation and Type Investigations in a piece last year—violate North Carolina law but it has left thousands of similar “nightmares” in its wake.

At stake are the likely millions of dollars that the suit alleges American Landmark illegally coerced out of current and former tenants like Kelly.

The lawsuit, filed by Halperin Petersen & Mikkilineni LLP, the North Carolina Justice Center, and Kelly Guzzo, PLC in the US District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, focuses on a state that has been an epicenter in American Landmark’s network of mega-complexes throughout the South. When I traveled to Charlotte last year, I learned that American Landmark had filed evictions against at least 450 residents over a six-month period, and my interviews with dozens of American Landmark tenants revealed how the company had engineered a system to price Kelly and his neighbors out.

Even American Landmark CEO Joseph Lubeck admitted when I spoke to him that the company’s “modeling” assumes that 45 percent of existing tenants will “move out” after American Landmark takes over: “a number of people are not going to be able to afford what we do.”

Kelly’s case, which is seeking additional plaintiffs, asks for restitution for any tenant who has lived in one of American Landmark’s roughly 3,000 apartments in the state since October 20, 2022. “During their tenancies,” the complaint reads, “Defendants have charged Plaintiffs thousands of dollars in unlawful, deceptive, and unfair fees.”

When reached by e-mail, Lubeck wrote, “American Landmark strongly denies all of the specious claims in the suit, which is clearly an attempt to extort money and rooted in antisemitism, like your previous coverage.”

According to the complaint, American Landmark weaponized mandatory “junk” fees to arbitrarily raise its tenants’ monthly costs by upwards of $100 per month. Kelly’s attorneys claim that American Landmark universally implements these fees—described as a “profit center”—in its North Carolina homes.

In 2025, 18 American Landmark tenants told me their first bill from the company surpassed what they believed they should have owed—thanks to the mandatory fees. Though Lubeck acknowledged at the time that he was “sure there are cases where people don’t know what they sign,” he told me that the fees were “disclosed up front and in writing.” In his e-mailed comment on the lawsuit, he again emphasized that “we provide full and fair value for all our residents and for all services, all of which are clearly spelled out and explained in their contracts and welcome packages.”

These underhanded fee structures are an epidemic for modern renters. As private-equity firms and large conglomerates take over more and more US real estate, tenants are losing out on hundreds of millions of dollars through junk fees every year, according to the National Consumer Law Center (NCLC). These fees, especially in cities like Charlotte, disproportionately burden Black and brown tenants. But a 2025 NCLC report found that states have begun pushing back, with at least 20 adopting laws restricting junk fees in some form. In Minnesota, for example, landlords must include mandatory fees in the publicly advertised cost of their apartments.

In December 2025, the country’s largest property manager, Greystar, agreed to refund tenants $23 million after the Federal Trade Commission sued the company for advertising rentals at “deceptive prices” that “excluded several fixed, mandatory monthly fees.” Kelly’s class-action hopes to build on that national precedent.

“In Mecklenburg County alone, more than 50,000 families faced eviction last year,” Peter Gilbert, director of litigation at North Carolina Justice Center, said in a press release. “These deceptive and unlawful fees are one of the primary drivers of evictions as landlords squeeze tenants past their breaking point.”

Specifically, the complaint alleges that the fees violate North Carolina’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act. After American Landmark took over, Kelly and his neighbors soon received an approximately $100 monthly fee for cable and Internet. Though Kelly’s lease, the complaint alleges, describes this package as “additional rent,” the details are buried in one of many lease addendums, and the nonnegotiable cost far exceeds what tenants could find on the open market.

What’s more, American Landmark disconnects the service when tenants fall behind on payments and “continue to charge the Technology Fee even though the tenant is not receiving the service,” the complaint reads. Then, American Landmark “impose[s] a $75 or more fee to “reconnect” the services that they have disconnected.”

“In at least one month, Mr. Kelly was charged over $160 in Technology Fees and Reconnect Fees when his service was not connected,” the complaint reads.

The Nation and Type Investigation’s 2025 investigation found that the technology package was anathema among American Landmark tenants. For that piece, I spoke to Stephen Tuju, one of Kelly’s former neighbors, who e-mailed complaints about the surprise $75 reconnection fee to his property managers. The company inexplicably responded that it would “adjust” the fee to $25.

In my conversation with Lubeck last year, he confirmed that the company disconnects the technology package when tenants pay late. In Tuju’s case, “it’s possible someone made a mistake,” Lubeck said, but “everything is established and fair across the board.” But the new lawsuit alleges that not only does Kelly’s lease authorize only a $25 reconnection fee but that the company nonetheless habitually demands tenants pay $75 or more for it, as it did to Tuju.

Once Kelly fell behind on payments, he allegedly encountered a “cascade” of additional fees American Landmark contrives from the eviction filing process. Under North Carolina law, landlords can charge tenants for court filing and processing fees, as well as up to 15 percent of a tenant’s overdue balance to help cover the cost of eviction attorneys. But Kelly was allegedly once charged “approximately $1,000 in Attorney or Legal Fees on a balance of less than $2,000,” according to the complaint.

Twice in 2023, per the complaint, American Landmark pressured Kelly to pay legal fees associated with evictions the company had never even filed in court. Less than a year later, Kelly became homeless.

Kelly’s attorneys analyzed thousands of North Carolina court records and found that over 40 percent of the tenants American Landmark files evictions against will incur another eviction attempt in the future. Each new case brings new fees. “In 2025 alone,” the complaint alleges, “over fifty tenants went through this cycle four or more times.”

“That’s why I’m still trying to play catch-up,” said Christopher Dawkins, a tenant I met in Charlotte in 2025, of these legal fees. He told me American Landmark charged him around $300 for each of his four eviction cases. “I got kids, too. When you got a lot going on, every dollar counts.”

Not content to have just kicked Kelly out, American Landmark, the complaint alleges, is also violating the state’s Debt Collection Act: Kelly “continues to receive collections notices from a third-party debt collector acting on behalf of [American] Landmark attempting to collect all illegally charged fees.”

Most of Kelly’s supposed debt, the complaint reads, comes from an “early termination” fee. After the company evicted him, American Landmark charged Kelly nearly $3,000 as a penalty for leaving the company unable to collect rent from him through the rest of his now-voided lease agreement.

The complaint alleges that American Landmark tenants “are given no notice” of this “immoral, unethical, oppressive, and unscrupulous” fee “prior to their eviction.”

“I feel like they’re predatory,” Jeff Schuman, a tenant who was evicted in March 2025 from an American Landmark property in Jacksonville and was similarly hounded by a collections agency, told me last year. “They can put a person out on the street with no recourse. I was like, ‘I don’t have anywhere to go and have a small child.’ It was one of the worst experiences I’ve had in my life.”

The scale of the American Landmark eviction machine that chews up tenants like Kelly and Schuman far outpaces state and national norms. As The Nation and Type Investigations reported last year, in one six-month period, the company filed 82 evictions for every 100 units at one Charlotte complex, and after American Landmark bought Kelly’s building in 2022, the company began filing evictions four times more often than the previous owner.

Kelly’s attorneys found a similar pattern: Though landlords statewide filed 12 evictions per 100 units during the 2025–26 fiscal year, American Landmark on average filed 50.

“Red states are very landlordist,” Gil Rushinek, board chair of American Landmark’s parent company, said in a 2024 podcast. In addition to North Carolina, the company owns buildings in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia, all of which have Republican-controlled legislatures. “In free-market capitalism, there are few protections for the tenant. If you want to evict a tenant in New York, you will have a lot more of a challenge than evicting a tenant in Florida,” Rushinek continued. But North Carolina is the only American Landmark locale with a Democratic governor and attorney general, and the chief justice of the lawsuit’s district court was appointed by President Barack Obama.

The case now enters an uncertain period of months, if not years, of litigation. In addition to millions in damages, Kelly’s attorneys are asking for certification of each of their proposed classes of exploited tenants and a jury trial.

Were the lawsuit to yield a substantial payout, the impact could also reverberate internationally, because, as the Nation/Type Investigations 2025 investigation revealed, American Landmark is wholly owned by the Electra Group, an Israeli conglomerate with extensive ties to both illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

Since these ties were first reported, the Electra Group has remained on the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights database of over 200 companies that do business in the illegal settlements. Electra’s business is centered on making it easier for Israelis to commute to and from the settlements by constructing tunnels and roads and operating bus lines on stolen Palestinian land.

Meanwhile, “the IDF is a major client,” the CEO of another Electra subsidiary said on a 2024 earnings call, after the IDF had already killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. “We stand shoulder to shoulder with them in facing challenges and fulfilling missions. We are likely the only supplier that can say we’ve expanded our areas of deployment.… This is a great source of pride for us.” In a podcast appearance the same year, Rushinek described American Landmark as a “big winning card” for the conglomerate.

The class-action lawsuit, should it eventually force American Landmark into a settlement, could therefore result in a payout to tenants like Kelly of revenue that may otherwise have been funneled into the Electra operation that is playing an active role in the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.

But in the meantime, as of the filing of the complaint, Kelly still does not have a place of his own. American Landmark continues to haunt his life—through a belligerent collection agency and the eviction staining his record—despite their throwing him out of his apartment some 29 months ago.

It’s a vision of what may someday befall Paula Hindman, the case’s other named plaintiff.

She retired from decades of program directing at Piedmont Community College in 2022, just three months before American Landmark bought her building in Hillsborough. Eventually, “the fees at my apartment became so expensive that I went back to work part-time,” she said in a press release. She joined the ranks of the tenants I met over and over again when I traveled to Charlotte last year who were on the brink of being priced out for good. Most of them have since been evicted.

So it’s with Hindman and all of American Landmark’s current and future tenants in mind that the complaint is also seeking “injunctive relief,” a court order that would require American Landmark to permanently change its practices in the state. That means no more mysterious charges. No more collection agency calls.

No more North Carolina tenants wrung out to their last dollar.

Thomas Birmingham is the research fellow at In These Times and an investigative reporter based in New Haven, Connecticut.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Centrist Democrats Are Trying Hard to Lose the Midterms
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Wreckers like Haley Stevens are probably the GOP’s last hope of avoiding a wipeout on Tuesday.

Making political predictions is always a fool’s errand—particularly these days, when polls are becoming increasingly unreliable and sometimes even fraudulent. But there are still plenty of signs pointing to a strong Democratic Party victory in Tuesday’s midterms. Democrats appear to be in pole position to recapture the House of Representatives, and have a real chance to gain control of the Senate—something that seemed all but impossible until relatively recently.

We can tell which way the wind is blowing by the fact that Republican super PACs are bailing out of states like North Carolina—which was expected to be a marquee battleground this year but now seems all but lost to the GOP—and moving funds to bolster candidates in even redder states such as Texas and Iowa.

The Trump administration has also noticed how bad things are going, and is flailing accordingly. On Thursday, the White House announced that President Trump was canceling planned rallies in Kansas and Iowa, replacing them with tele-rallies. This news was telling on a number of levels. The very fact that Trump was headed to deep-red states like Kansas and Iowa was a sign of trouble. In more successful years such as 2016 and 2024, he ended his campaigns by going to genuine swing states such as Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania, even making daring jaunts into New York.

Then, on Friday morning, the White House suddenly reversed course and said Trump would be holding the rallies after all. Perhaps Trump was stung by the implication of his previous decision to cancel—it sent the message that Republicans didn’t want to be seen with an unpopular president, and that Trump himself wanted to avoid the stink of being part of a losing campaign—or perhaps this was simply yet another sign of the chaotic, strategy-free nature of Trump’s approach. Not surprisingly, pundits such as Nate Silver and David Wallace-Wells are predicting that we may be watching the beginning of the end of the Trump era.

The president is clearly off his game. When he was at the peak of his political power, Trump would focus on issues that had genuine salience: immigration, the economy, and foreign policy. To be sure, he’d often muddle this message with his personal grievances and gloating, but he still had a coherent agenda. But in 2026, as Jonathan Lemire notes in The Atlantic, Trump’s message has become unusually muddled:

This time around, Trump’s primary rationale for why voters should support the GOP, as best I can tell, is that the affordability crisis is a “hoax,” Bill Maher is a “loser,” and Senator Jon Husted of Ohio has a nice physique. That easy-to-mock message has been accompanied by a staggering number of missteps. Just for starters, he’s belittled the impact of his stalled war with Iran, sided with Russia as it continues to pummel Ukrainian cities, defended an attack ad from the GOP candidate for Ohio governor that repulsed other top Republicans, downplayed high energy prices while boasting that U.S. oil and gas companies are “making a freaking fortune,” embraced AI as the nation turns against it, obsessed over White House construction projects, and spent a lot of time talking about handsome men, Husted being just one.

Trump seems to be engaged not in a campaign of persuasion, but a massive public crack-up And he’s not the only one. Prominent GOP candidates like Ohio gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy and Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton are also melting down. Ramaswamy is still dealing with the fallout from his disgraceful ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton. The truly sordid nature of the ad became clear when it was revealed that Acton’s mother was homeless and deeply troubled, having lost custody of her children after she sided with a husband accused of abusing them. Ramaswamy first doubled down on the ad—but, on Thursday, he yielded to massive backlash and pulled it from the air. As for Ken Paxton, he’s being plagued by so many personal and ethics scandals that even stalwart Republicans such as political strategist Karl Rove won’t endorse him.

The one glimmer of hope Republicans have is that elite Democrats seem equally addicted to self-sabotage. Indeed, this election has often felt like a competition to see which party can inflict the most damage on itself.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has been dogged by the sore-loser behavior of centrist Democrats who can’t abide the fact he won the primary. In particular, his defeated rival Haley Stevens keeps trying to extract political concessions from El-Sayed rather than letting him unite the party against Republican Mike Rogers.

Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan, who lost to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in a bitter Democratic primary for Senate in August, has grown increasingly critical of him as the election draws near, injecting unusual intraparty tensions into the final days of a pivotal midterm contest.

While Ms. Stevens reiterated Wednesday night that she plans to vote for Dr. El-Sayed, she did so through seemingly gritted teeth in a televised interview just hours after her fiancé said that he would be voting for former Representative Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed’s Republican rival. She also called on Dr. El-Sayed to denounce an ad from an outside group that she has argued amounts to “fear-mongering about Israel,” and to take down an ad from his campaign featuring Tucker Carlson.

On Thursday, Stevens seemed to partially relent in her undermining of the Democratic nominee by agreeing to campaign with El-Sayed.

Stevens’s actions are rooted in the internal Democratic Party rift over Israel/Gaza. Stevens is strongly pro-Israel, notoriously saying that “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” And she has company when it comes to undermining El-Sayed. On Thursday, former House speaker Nancy Pelosi went on a podcast and said El-Sayed’s comments on Israel were “concerning.” She added, “This new person in Michigan, we’ll see if he gets elected to the Congress.”

What makes Stevens’s antics particularly despicable is the fact that El-Sayed, like other Muslim candidates, has been subjected to vicious Islamophobia by the Republicans. At a rally in Michigan on Sunday, Trump said, “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator. If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”

Writing in The New Republic, Perry Bacon rightly notes that Stevens’s behavior follows the pattern of centrist Democrats’ “attacking and undermining a compelling Muslim candidate who is also a target of the right.” In 2025, centrist Democrats similarly tried to kneecap Zohran Mamdani, both when he was running for mayor of New York and even after he won the party’s nomination. As Bacon points out, “A Democratic Party that won’t fully accept Muslim candidates isn’t a party that actually practices the principles of democracy, diversity, inclusion, pluralism, and multiculturalism that it preaches.”

Not all Democratic Party self-sabotage is ideological. Some of it is merely motivated by standard dirty tricks, as in the scandal engulfing Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s team worked to recruit a third-party candidate named Dan J. Sullivan so as to create confusion on the ballot with the current Republican governor, Dan S. Sullivan. John F. Kennedy’s campaign made the exact same maneuver in 1946 when he ran against a rival named Joseph Russo. The campaign found a ringer with the same name, and Kennedy sailed to victory.

Still, even if a dirty trick has a storied pedigree, it’s a dirty trick. Peltola might still win the election, but she’s surely alienated some voters.

The good news for the Democrats is that it’s hard to beat Donald Trump in a self-destruction competition. Trump ran in 2024 on a platform of avoiding more wars and focusing on fixing the economy. As president, he launched a disastrous war against Iran, which is creating a new affordability crisis. When it comes to shooting yourself in the foot, Trump remains undefeated.

Jeet Heer is a national affairs correspondent for The Nation and host of the weekly Nation podcast, The Time of Monsters. He also pens the monthly column “Morbid Symptoms.” The author of In Love with Art: Francoise Mouly’s Adventures in Comics with Art Spiegelman (2013) and Sweet Lechery: Reviews, Essays and Profiles (2014), Heer has written for numerous publications, including The New Yorker, The Paris Review, Virginia Quarterly Review, The American Prospect, The Guardian, The New Republic, and The Boston Globe.

Where with a little bit of luck—and a ton of grassroots organizing—decency has a fighting chance.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Bernie Sanders Is Leaving It All on the Field in the Final Days of the Midterms
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The senator is mounting a relentless, urgent campaign to stop Trump, elect progressives, and transform US politics.

Bernie Sanders speaks in support of Wisconsin Democratic congressional candidate Rebecca Cooke during a rally at the W.R. Davies Student Center on October 25, 2026 in Eau Claire, Wisconsin.

Eau Claire, Wisconsin—Bernie Sanders was up bright and early on a windswept, late October Sunday morning for the 17th stop on a month-long, nationwide campaign swing in anticipation of Tuesday’s midterm elections. But he wasn’t up any earlier than the overflow crowd that had come to see him in this western Wisconsin city of 69,421. By the time the independent senator from Vermont and two-time Democratic presidential candidate took the stage at the University of Wisconsin–Eau Claire student center, voters from the nation’s ultimate swing district had filled every seat and were crowding against the walls, sitting on the floor, and spilling into the hallways at the far end of the sprawling space. Amid the sustained applause that greeted his arrival, Sanders gestured to the back of the room and half-joked, “We’ve got to knock down the door there. We’ve got a lot of folks.”

That was it for small talk. The senator launched into an appeal for Rebecca Cooke, a 38-year-old Wisconsin congressional candidate whom he endorsed more than a year ago. Cooke welcomed Sanders with an introduction that hailed him as “our champion for the working class for decades” and “one of the last people in Congress that still has a spine, that is willing to stand up [to] special interests, and continues to put people first.”

“In my view, this is the most important midterm election in the modern history of our country, or maybe the history of our country,” Sanders told the crowd. “And what Rebecca’s race is about—and the reason that I am here—is that the time is long overdue for us to hold the most dangerous president in the history of the United States accountable. But it’s not only holding Trump accountable. It is an understanding, and I know Rebecca has campaigned on this relentlessly, [that it is possible] to create an economy that works for all people—not just the one percent.”

Democratic campaigns across the country have relied a good deal on surrogates this year, with much attention paid to late-stage campaign stops by former president Barack Obama, former vice president Kamala Harris, and potential 2028 presidential contenders such as New York US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California US Representative Ro Khanna, and former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg. But no one has done it with quite the consistent messaging and strategic focus that Sanders has brought to the campaign trail. The senator, whom polls frequently identify as the most popular sitting elected official in the United States, began talking about the midterms shortly after Trump’s second inauguration, and used his 2025 “Fighting Oligarchy” tour of Republican red districts and states to argue that the 2026 election would offer a historic opportunity to transform American politics, place checks and balances on the White House, and strike a blow for governance by the people rather than wealthy elites.

Now, with the November 3 elections just days away, and an onslaught of billionaire-funded spending to prop up the flailing Republican effort to keep control of Congress, Sanders has been relentlessly making his closing argument to voters nationwide. In the past few weeks, he has attracted thousands of organizers, activists, and curious voters to events from Maine to California, on a tenacious schedule that is every bit as ambitious in its goals as any candidate or party leader’s. He told the cheering crowd in Eau Claire that this is the moment to “revitalize American democracy” by replacing Trump-aligned Republicans like Wisconsin US Representative Derrick Van Orden with working-class Democrats such as Cooke.

Sanders delivered a similar message the night before in Duluth, Minnesota, where an even larger crowd packed a school gymnasium to hear his pitch for Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party US Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan—a progressive who, like another Sanders endorsee, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, beat a more politically cautious, AIPAC-aligned Democrat in the primaries and is now locked in a fall contest that could define control of the Senate. “I am so grateful that you’re on Team Peggy,” Flanagan said in her introduction of Sanders, “because the coach of our team is here!”

After making early endorsements of working-class candidates in House and Senate races—many of whom faced primary fights—Sanders has used digital platforms to participate in dozens of organizing calls, virtual canvass launches, and livestream conversations to ramp up support for Democratic contenders. And he has shown up, often repeatedly, for rallies with candidates such as Flanagan and Cooke. This unflagging, “all-hands-on-deck” energy has Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison describing the 85-year-old senator as the great progressive movement builder of our time.

“Bernie is shifting the ground, giving people hope,” says Ellison, who campaigned with Sanders and Flanagan in Duluth.

So far this month, Sanders has appeared at 20 major events in seven states. He’s been in Maine for Senate candidate Troy Jackson, in Florida for Senate candidate Angie Nixon, in Texas with Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar for that state’s Democratic ticket, in California for multiple congressional candidates (as well as for the campaign in support of an ambitious ballot proposal to tax billionaires) and—just this week—in Michigan for three major events with El-Sayed.

At these stops, which often take him far from the well-trodden paths of American politics, Sanders does more than deliver a standard stump speech. He asks people in the crowds to talk about the issues that matter to them, and then he launches into deep discussions about those issues—data centers and artificial intelligence, single-payer healthcare, how economic inequality threatens the health and well-being of low-income Americans, and the desperate need for the Democratic Party to abandon deference to corporate donors and deliver for working-class Americans. “I’m fighting the two-front war. The first of the two fights is ending Republican control of the House and the Senate, and holding Trump accountable. But the second issue is having the Democratic Party do what the American people want it to do,” Sanders explained in an interview in Eau Claire. “I think you heard an example of that today. This is not New York City. We’re in Eau Claire, Wisconsin. All over the country, people understand that we need bold action to address the needs of the working class, that we need to take on the oligarchs, that healthcare is a human right.”

Sanders hasn’t just been donating his time. He’s also been donating his money and his team. The senator has joined online fundraising appeals to raise more than $3 million for the grassroots campaigns of endorsed candidates in states across the country. He has dispatched full-time staffers to work on the ground in key states such as Minnesota, Florida, and Michigan. And he has transferred roughly $2.3 million from his own committee—including $1,250,000 to support El-Sayed, more than $300,000 to help Nixon in Florida, more than $300,000 to Flanagan’s Democratic Farmer Labor Party in Minnesota, $100,000 to Troy Jackson’s Maine Senate run, and thousands more to boost the Senate bids of Democrats Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Scott Colom in Mississippi and independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, and the congressional bids of Michigan Democrats Will Lawrence and Donavan McKinney—with an eye toward helping organize on-the-ground, in-person campaigns that counter the massive spending by billionaires and special-interest groups on television ads backing Republicans.

“Any progressive movement that’s going to be successful has got to have some people who are fulfilling the function that Bernie’s filling right now,” says Ellison. “A candidate like Abdul El-Sayed needs help. Bernie’s in a position to help. And he does help. He comes to it in a meaningful way, and brings people with him, and puts us in a position [to mount a stronger campaign] for somebody who is overtly talking about putting money in your pocket, getting money out of politics and Medicare for All. That’s a huge thing. That’s an enormous thing.”

For his part, Sanders says, “This is a debate about the very fabric of American society — whether we remain a democratic society or [become] an authoritarian society, where we engage in endless wars or not, where we have a government that vaguely represents the needs of working families or one that is totally owned by the oligarchs. So, yes, I worry very much about the future of this country if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate, and I’m doing everything I can to prevent it.”

And the best way to prevent it, he says, is by returning to the grassroots and campaigning face-to-face with people in places like Duluth and Eau Claire.

“What I have always believed is that, at the end of the day, the way you win elections is by grassroots activism,” says Sanders. “People like Rebecca are winning elections—she won the primary, and hopefully she’ll win the general—because of the grassroots support that she has. People going out, knocking on doors, talking to their neighbors. I know that sounds very old-fashioned. But I, a thousand times over, prefer to invest in that vision and work with those types of people, rather than putting stupid ads on television that cost a fortune.”

John Nichols is the executive editor of The Nation. He previously served as the magazine’s national affairs correspondent and Washington correspondent. Nichols has written, cowritten, or edited over a dozen books on topics ranging from histories of American socialism and the Democratic Party to analyses of US and global media systems. His latest, cowritten with Senator Bernie Sanders, is the New York Times bestseller It's OK to Be Angry About Capitalism.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Will the Progressive Insurgency in NY-17 Oust MAGA Loyalist Mike Lawler?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Joan Walsh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Local progressive groups have turned out a huge ground game to support Democratic nominee Cait Conley, despite her centrist leanings.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries with Cait Conley, Democratic candidate for NY-17, during an early voting rally on the first day of early voting for the midterm election in Peekskill, New York, on October 24, 2026.

“When you take on Mike Lawler, you take on organized labor,” Teamsters president Sean O’Brien told New York 17th Congressional District voters at a rally for Lawler in Westchester County last week. It was a false, even brazen claim: The state AFL-CIO backs the Republican Lawler’s Democratic challenger, Caitlin Conley. So do the Communications Workers of America, SEIU1199, local teachers’ unions, and many other labor groups who are, as usual, supporting the Democrat in the race.

That didn’t stop O’Brien. And he wasn’t chastened by the fact that Conley would be the first female special operations veteran from New York in the House of Representatives when he told her, condescendingly, it’s time “to put your helmet on and button your chin straps, it’s a full contact sport.”

Here’s the thing: Conley would seem to sleep with her helmet on. Given the reservations I’ve heard about her from progressive voters over the last year, the main one is that she can be reserved, not at all warm or fuzzy, and is by progressive standards a little bit hawkish. She comes off as the Army veteran she is. But in the district, no one doubts Conley’s bravery or readiness for battle. Conley snickers at the Teamster leader’s braggadocio in a phone call with me a few days later. “I love how people who never left the comfort of their couch after 9/11 want to talk about hard fights.” She regularly talks about how she vowed as a teenager to join the military after the 2001 attacks.

Lawler is a MAGA loyalist who has on occasion broken with the president. But in a district that voted for Kamala Harris two years ago, that may no longer be a winning record. So he plays up his differences with Trump, and his support from Democrats and union members, and he hopes he can get by Conley that way.

He may not. Conley beat two popular, progressive female rivals in the June primary, and some of those women’s supporters are still a little bitter over what they perceive as establishment Democrats’ behind-the-scenes support for the military veteran, who had no local political record, over two local politicos, Rockland County legislator Beth Davidson and Tarrytown Village Trustee Effie Phillips-Staley, who have served their communities legislatively for years. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries didn’t prove to be the biggest draw when he appeared in Peekskill with Conley October 24. A crowd of maybe 200 people, many of them union members, milled about along the Hudson River and applauded, especially when Conley introduced him as “Speaker Jeffries” (his fervent wish). But elsewhere that day, Peekskill was teeming with activism, as the many local groups who’ve emerged in the district used the next-to-last election-season weekend to gather, train volunteers and canvas.

The paradox of Conley’s race is that if she wins, the centrist will at least partly owe her victory to a progressive insurgency that came together after Lawler’s 2024 victory vowing to defeat him with a Democrat. Many didn’t get their chosen candidate in the June primary, but they’re still hard at work. As Phillips-Staley herself told me, “What we are all aligned on, from the left to the moderate within the Democratic party, is that Mike Lawler needs to go.”

Most polls show Democrats winning the House, but Conley’s race is important. New York cost Democrats the House in 2022, losing five blue seats, when the party nationwide only came up short by four. This year’s primaries saw a lot of lefty victories in the Manhattan area–three DSA members, plus reliable progressives Brad Lander and Micah Lasher–but they’ll all win next week. Upstate near Conley, centrist liberal incumbents Pat Ryan and Josh Riley look safe. It’s Conley, plus somewhat vulnerable Democratic centrists Tom Suozzi and Laura Gillen on Long Island, and an unlikely Democratic victor in Elise Stefanik’s former seat, Democrat Blake Gendebien, who will make Tuesday night interesting.

NY 17 is a diverse district, with multiracial, fairly Latino Peekskill, Sleepy Hollow, and Tarrytown; still pretty white segments of Rockland, Putnam, and Dutchess Counties, plus miles of Westchester cities and towns, some of which are still 1960s alabaster, but most are not. Roughly 20 percent of the district is Jewish, and Conley’s self-described “balance” on Israel—some consider her to be rabidly pro-Israel—is helping the Democrat with many voters, but not with the energetic pro-Palestine left. “This is where I have been consistent, and as someone who has been to war, the last thing I want to see is more human suffering,” she tells me. “I do believe we have to get to a two-state solution, where there’s equal safety, security, and sovereignty for Israel and Palestine. And that America should be pushing to deliver on that and not just give it lip service.” Although Conley has opposed some Democratic moves to limit sales of weaponry to Israel, she insists that she “will criticize the Netanyahu administration or any administration I believe is doing the wrong thing for Israel and America.”

About half of the district’s voters are either veterans, law enforcement officials, or public employees (Conley’s mother was a postal worker). Conley’s military experience, as well as her family’s public service, resonates with many voters in the area. A white progressive volunteer told me she found that Conley’s military service was a draw to some Latino voters, and Phillips-Staley, whose mother is from El Salvador, said she wasn’t surprised. “My dad was a military veteran, and Latino cultures can sometimes be a little conservative, and that’s fine.”

Conley says her military service is a cross-racial, cross-party draw. “I have shown that I’m willing to do the right thing for this country in our community, even when it’s hard, even when it’s dangerous, I’m willing to put my life on the line, to protect this country and fight for our future. And there is a degree of trust that comes with that,” Conley told me in our interview.

“I’ve had Republicans come up to me and say, ‘I’ve never voted for a Democrat, but I’m voting for you because you’re a veteran.’”

Even though I could find plenty of progressives in the district with reservations about Conley—hey, I write for The Nation—virtually everyone I met united behind her, post-primary. Some believe they are helping her most by focusing on the low-propensity voters, low-income and/or Latino, that the Conley campaign may miss as it focuses on getting registered Democrats back in line, plus adding some independents and Republicans. Other progressives are focused on winning back Democrats who’ve fallen for Lawler’s bipartisan shtick. Another key group of voters to reach will be those who’ve been alienated by the party’s shenanigans in recent congressional races.

A Democratic seat since 1986, New York 17 elected progressive Mondaire Jones in 2020. But redistricting put DCCC head Sean Patrick Maloney, the representative in New York 18, in the newly drawn 17 for 2022, pushing Jones out of the race. Jones wound up moving to and running in New York 10, a lower Manhattan and Brooklyn district, against Working Families Party’s Yuh-Line Niou, and both progressives lost to the self-funding Levi’s family tycoon and liberal lawyer Dan Goldman. Maloney, widely accused of ignoring his own race to raise money for Democrats in Europe that October, lost to Lawler by 1,800 votes. When Jones ran again in NY-17 in 2024, the party was split, Lawler had made inroads with Democrats, and, despite Kamala Harris winning the district at the top of the ticket, Jones lost to Lawler by a depressing 24,000 votes.

After what many in the district call “the Mondaire mess”—and to be fair, Jones didn’t mainly make the mess—local progressives came together in a coalition of roughly 35 groups, known as the CD 17 Community Coalition. “The DCCC had run these last two campaigns and lost,” says its director, Tina Volz-Bongar. CD 17 Community Coalition committed to building a ground game that the DCCC had failed to create. Local progressives, including 20 small Indivisible chapters plus local nonprofits, got organized in 2025 and have been meeting almost weekly since. “People say we live in a purple district, but that’s because Democrats don’t come out to vote,” Volz-Bongar adds. In fact, the district has a one-point Democratic voter registration advantage, and is rated a toss-up by The Cook Political Report. But judging by demographics, it should be bluer than it is. The diverse coalition behind Conley is trying to figure out why it’s not.

So on the same Saturday that Jeffries visited Peekskill, the CD 17 Community Coalition hosted “Free Democracy Donuts and Coffee” events at the city’s public and Section 8 housing complexes. Working Families Party members were out knocking doors. In addition, Canvassing Connectors, a deep-canvassing group based in Peekskill, partnered with Plus One, which focuses on voters linking up with friends and neighbors over meals, for an open house at a local café. Plus One has found it challenging to meet its gathering goals, cofounder Emily Simoness tells me. “But once people actually do the work, they are thrilled, and they’re reminded of our shared humanity, and that we have more in common than the algorithm might tell us,” she says. “I really feel like part of how we get back to being a civil society is by being in person together.”

Canvassing Connectors likewise emphasises longer-term relationships and in-person gatherings. “We’ve been telling people we canvass that ‘we’re gonna have a party,’” Canvassing Connectors cofounder Ellen Chapnick told me, when she invited me to join them at the café. “Well, this is the party!” Food and Water Action sponsored a Stop Data Centers rally just before Jeffries’s waterfront gathering. You couldn’t walk the streets of the small, quaint Peekskill downtown that bright Saturday without spotting someone working to elect Conley.

Conley says she’s grateful for all the help. Despite ideological differences, she didn’t perceive her primary as a bitter one. “We shared a lot more than we differed on. And how we make a positive impact on people’s lives has to be our focus.” True to her brand, Conley added that she wasn’t only focused on Democrats but making a place in her coalition for independents and Republicans. Phillips-Staley, endorsed by the Working Families Party, also said the female candidates made common cause before the primary was over. “We could have been a lot nastier to each other. But for the most part all the candidates got along pretty well. Because we understood—and we said it repeatedly during the primary—that the mission is to defeat Mike Lawler. What we said in many debates and in many forums is that we would all be running against him in the general.” And so they are. The WFP endorsed Conley once she won the primary.

Even this late in the game, the polls are too close to call. The last Emerson College poll had Conley up by two points, within the margin of error. The good news for the Democrat was that Lawler was on target to lose some of the Democratic support he won away from Mondaire Jones in 2024. That year, according to Emerson, 20 percent of Democrats supported Lawler; this year it’s down to 12 percent, while Conley is grabbing 10 percent of Republicans, and Jones just 4 percent “Had Democrats stayed on the side of the Democratic Party, Mike Lawler would not have won,” Phillips-Staley told me. She is nonetheless working hardest on unaligned, low-propensity Latino nonvoters.

Canvassing Connectors is focused on much the same voters as Phillips-Staley, especially Latinos. Ellen Chapnick is proud of “El Equipo,” the group’s Spanish-speaking canvassers, who can quickly turn out to help English speakers work with Spanish speaking voters. “You know, they’re used to having an experience where people knock on their door, ‘Oh, you don’t speak English. I’m so sorry. Well, here’s a Spanish language flyer,’” she told me. “That doesn’t work too well.They don’t feel like they have a voice. But we can have a 10-, 15-minute conversation with them in their own language, and often what happens is they’ll say, ‘Oh, you should talk to my children. You know, you should talk to my sister-in-law.’”

Chapnick was ecstatic when we met in Peekskill that Saturday: She had just met two Republicans who’d decided to vote for Conley. That hadn’t happened to many progressives while out knocking doors, though some told me they felt the campaign dynamics shifting, especially as Donald Trump stayed out on the trail (though not in New York), talking about the physique of Ohio Senator Jon Husted as well as GOP rapper Nicki Minaj while lying about inflation and the Iran War. Speaker Mike Johnson visited Lawler’s district a couple of days after Jeffries did, and insisted local and national polling is wrong.

“It feels like 2024 to us,” Johnson told a press gaggle in Rockland County’s Orangeburg October 26. “The polling is wrong. They are trying to suppress and depress Republican turnout in the elections. The polling has underestimated the Republican vote by an average of 4 percent. Don’t believe the polls. People are not responding to polls anymore in increasing numbers.” But Johnson also praised Lawler for supporting Trump’s One Big Ugly Bill, which gave tax cuts to the wealthy and will lead to Medicaid and SNAP cuts to lower-income and working-class District 17 residents.

Conley may win over some progressives with her pledge to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, an issue on which Jeffries joined her in Peekskill. “Every day Pete Hegseth is in that seat, we are less safe,” she told me.“This man is single-handedly destroying our military institutions and driving out our best military leaders. The man needs to go.” Jeffries, not known for ideological fire and brimstone, told the Peekskill crowd he plans to “run Pete Hegseth out of town” if and when Democrats take the House.

Meanwhile, Phillips-Staley keeps working for Conley. “I see Cait’s role, and the way her campaign is structured, is to try to keep those Democrats [who voted for Lawler in 2024] in line with the Democratic Party, to try to retain them, to deny him victory.”

But she adds, “Unfortunately, that kind of message doesn’t work with a progressive base, but what does work is the truth that Mike Lawler is catastrophic for our democracy, right? We keep hammering home to remind people that harm reduction is real, and we have to deny him power. Not only do I want to see Mike Lawler go, I want to see communities that have been disenfranchised by the Democratic Party, standing up, using their power and firing Mike Lawler. That’s why I’m in it.”

Joan Walsh, a national affairs correspondent for The Nation, is a coproducer of The Sit-In: Harry Belafonte Hosts The Tonight Show and the author of What’s the Matter With White People? Finding Our Way in the Next America. Her most recent book (with Nick Hanauer and Donald Cohen) is Corporate Bullsh*t: Exposing the Lies and Half-Truths That Protect Profit, Power and Wealth In America.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sasha Abramsky
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
It is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for voters to turn things around for American democracy.

A protester holds a sign in front of the City Hall in downtown Los Angeles, California, during the No Kings–Vote Early march on October 17, 2026.

With the mid-term elections just days away, Trump has been caroming around the country making increasingly frenzied, incoherent pleas for voters to support the GOP. When he’s not off on bizarre riffs about admiring the asses of sycophants and foul bromides about jihadists running for the Senate and immigrants burning down Paris, he continually tells his shrinking cohort of adoring fans, Pretend I’m on the ballot.

Trump’s—and the GOP’s—problem is that his narcissism, the classic blinkered narcissism of the authoritarian strongman, is standing in the way of their political radar. Encircled by his cultlike followers cheering his every inane, incoherent, antidemocratic sentence, Trump simply cannot fathom that the broader public is busily ditching him and scrubbing his sadistic, strongman spectacle, his gauche merch, and his potty mouth from the collective psyche. He cannot comprehend or internalize the dozens of polls that have shown that the public, by nearly two-to-one margins, rejects his persona and his cruel, destructive, political vision.

“Pretend I’m on the ballot” is as good an incentive as any attack ad that Democratic spin-doctors could have come up with for tens of millions of voters to head to the polls and cast votes up and down the ballot for Democrats. It makes Biden’s awkward embrace of the phrase “Bidenomics,” during a time of high inflation and economic angst, seem positively benign.

Trump has spent the past two years on a wrecking-ball mission against the American government, the American people, and America’s international relationships, while being cheered on by the GOP-led Congress, aided and abetted by GOP governors and state legislators, and supported by America’s opportunistic new tech-overlords. If there is any karma in the universe, Tuesday will be the GOP and the oligarchy’s day of reckoning.

Increasingly fascist in its outlooks and its methods, this regime—for it is that far more than a regular administration—has systematically undermined the rule of law and attacked pretty much every part of the Constitution apart from the Second Amendment; and, it has done so not just with GOP congressional and state-level blind-eyes but with their active connivance.

Trump’s regime has repeatedly gone after the press, and attempted to ban critical outlets from covering the White House and the Pentagon, pressured television broadcasters to take liberal late night comedians off-air, encouraged oligarchs to buy up media outlets and remake them as pliant supporters of Trumpism, strong-armed universities to fire staff and expel students it dislikes and to end “diversity” hiring and admissions policies (a code word for firing or demoting the Black and brown people in academia and their departments), arrested and deported students simply for writing essays and articles about Israel-Palestine that stand contrary to administration policy, and bullied white-shoe law firms into committing to hundreds of millions of dollars in pro bono services.

The Trump regime has destroyed USAID and, in the process, knowingly condemned untold millions of people around the world to disease and to death. It has yanked the welcome mat, that has been such a defining part of the American story, out from under the feet of hundreds of thousands of immigrants, asylum seekers, and refugees. In doing so, it has separated families, imprisoned hard-working immigrants in gulag-like conditions, and “rendered” tens of thousands of immigrants to third countries where they are often held indefinitely in violent prisons. It has sent masked agents of the state into American cities from Los Angeles to Chicago, Charlotte to Minneapolis, where they have gunned down immigrants and citizens alike, and has then dared to accuse those who were killed of being “terrorists” and “paid agitators.” It has dragged toddlers—literally children still in diapers—into immigration court without any legal counsel to argue their case for being allowed to stay in the US. And it has attempted to deport hundreds of unaccompanied child-immigrants back to clear-and-present danger on middle-of-the-night flights to countries such as Honduras and Guatemala —flights stopped only by the last-minute interventions of judges.

The regime has preached family values even while its leadership is entirely compromised by their apparent involvement in the Epstein scandal. Trump and Vance have denounced their political opponents as undermining the sanctity of the family even while they double down on Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramiswamy’s odious advertisement that essentially accuses the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, of lying about being raped by her stepfather when she was 12 years old.

Trump has perverted the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, and immigration agencies so as to target his critics, from ex-FBI director James Comey to Congress member Ilhan Omar, getting a prostrate DOJ and FBI to launch clearly politically motivated investigations, and using the full force of a mobilized state to serve his personal whims. He has publicly called for the execution of opponents whom he has labeled as treasonous and has mocked protesters at his rallies while they are being savagely beaten by his supporters. In his recent campaign appearances, where one protester after the next has been thumped, Trump has morphed into something closer to the lyncher in chief than the commander in chief.

This regime has launched an illegal war in Iran—one that has resulted in both entirely pointless loss of life and economic devastation, and that has elevated inflation in large parts of the world to a level deeply destructive of communal well-being; and Trump himself, in a fit of pique, has threatened to end a civilization, which is as close to an explicit nuclear threat as one can make without actually saying, “I’m going to drop a thermonuclear weapon on your sorry heads.” He has, in so doing, deliberately and explicitly injected the language of hyper-terrorism into American diplomacy. The regime has arrogated to itself the right to assassinate purported drug smugglers on the high seas, without providing any evidence as to the “smugglers’” guilt—and, notwithstanding that, even if they were smuggling drugs, no international law gives the US government the right to simply kill suspected criminals. It has kidnapped an overseas leader, (the perhaps unlamented) Nicolas Maduro of Venezuela, and is making war plans to attack Cuba. It has threatened to annex Danish territory and has, repeatedly, mocked Canadian sovereignty and pushed the idea of Canada’s becoming the 51st state. It has unilaterally renamed international waters after America and floated the notion of renaming entire oceans after Donald J. Trump.

This regime has sanctioned international organizations such as the International Criminal Court that have a mandate to investigate war crimes and crimes against humanity. And it has denigrated democratic allies, from Canada to the UK to Norway, often in the crudest possible terms, leaving America increasingly bereft of friends on the global stage. Just the other day Trump, angry that he wasn’t awarded a Nobel Peace Prize, lambasted Norway as a “shithouse country.” At the same time, Team Trump has cozied up to some of the most brutal countries and leaders on earth, overtly positioning the United States as a force not for global good and the spreading of democracy but as an autocracy intent only on strong-arming other peoples and countries into quiescence.

This summer, Trump’s regime, which fetishizes violence-for-the-sake-of-violence, converted the White House grounds into a cage-fighting arena as a birthday celebration for Trump and for the American Republic, and then floated the idea of livestreaming executions. It regularly broadcasts snuff movies showing the moment US weapons blow up fishing vessels in the Pacific and Caribbean.

Millions of Americans are suffering from the effects of the One Big Beautiful Bill, passed by Congress at Trump’s urging last year, as well as the insane tariffs unleashed on the world, and, by extension, on US consumers. Because of the legislation, they are losing access to health insurance—at the same moment that Robert Kennedy is dismantling the public health infrastructure—food stamps, and housing assistance; and, because of the tariffs and the Iran war, they are finding that basic consumer goods cost far more than they used to.

Trump’s response? He is positively giddy with delight that high oil prices mean high profits for US oil producers; and on tariffs he has simply doubled down, even in the face of opposition from the Supreme Court. While the public suffers economically, Trump is busy constructing a gaudy White House ballroom and replacing bathroom faucets, picture frames, and even curtain railings with tasteless gold ornamentation. There’s a “let them eat cake” quality to his actions, a blithe dismissal of the optics of all of this shiny gaucherie in a time of economic angst.

While most Americans are getting swept backward economically by a combination of soaring energy prices, rising interest rates, and the threat of AI taking their jobs, Trump and his inner circle are on a self-dealing binge that is, surely, the most egregious display of public corruption in US history. It makes Tammany Hall smell like roses. In the past two years, Trump’s net worth has increased by about $3 billion, much of it through his hawking of cryptocurrency to gullible fans as well as to wealthy businessmen who realize that it’s an easy way to grease the wheels and get access to Trump regarding their pet projects and political priorities.

Nothing is off-limits for this crew of Class A grifters: Trump’s negotiators with Russia are busy selling out Ukraine in exchange for oil deals that pad their pockets. Ex–DHS secretary Kristi Noem was, it is widely alleged, channeling lucrative advertising contracts to people close to her and her family. Trump himself saw nothing wrong with accepting a nearly half-billion-dollar airplane as a gift from the Qatari government. Melania saw nothing wrong with accepting tens of millions of dollars of promotional money from Amazon to promote her ludicrous biopic.

In April, Hungary’s electorate said sayonara to longtime autocratic leader Viktor Orbán. Last week, voters in Brazil kicked Flávio Bolsonaro and his Trumpy-fascist vision to the curb—after which Bolsonaro fled, his tail between his legs, to Florida. And voters in Serbia elected a student-led coalition, in the process sending packing strongman leader Aleksandar Vučić.

Meanwhile, in just a few days, voters here in the US will have our chance not just for a regular midterm reset but for a fundamental moral recalibration of this oh-so-damaged country and a thorough repudiation of Trump’s autocracy. Even with the hundreds of millions of dollars that Elon Musk has poured into the election to try to shore up GOP fortunes, there are now scores of House seats and about a dozen Senate seats that seem to be in play, with the Republicans playing defense even in ruby-red lands such as Mississippi and Texas.

The United States has a rare window open to begin to undo the extraordinary harm that Trump and his GOP acolytes have inflicted on it over the past two years. We have a chance to say “not in our names,” and to punish the political party that let this authoritarian, xenophobic, racist, grifting rot take root.

It is a once-in-a-generation opportunity. There is no moral margin for error.

Sasha Abramsky is the author of several books, including The American Way of Poverty, The House of Twenty Thousand Books, Little Wonder: The Fabulous Story of Lottie Dod, the World's First Female Sports Superstar, and Chaos Comes Calling: The Battle Against the Far-Right Takeover of Small-Town America. His latest book is American Carnage: How Trump, Musk, and DOGE Butchered the US Government.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Massachusetts May Be the First State to Repeal Recreational Weed
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Genevieve Morrison
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
It’s not only weed at stake. The whole legal apparatus that supports social equity marijuana businesses would disappear if ballot question 8 passes.

Sean Berte and Armani White were arrested for weed, then became cannabis entrepreneurs through Massachusetts’s social equity program.

Mike Marinaro was a passenger in his friend’s car in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 2008 when a cop ran the vehicle’s plates. Police officers then pulled Marinaro out of the car, searched it, and found weed. He took the rap.

Even though the charges against him were eventually dropped, his troubles were only starting. His infuriated parents kicked him out, leaving him homeless. He was arrested several more times for public intoxication “because it was like, well, you know, I guess I was arrested once. What does it matter?”

But for all the difficulty it caused him, that first marijuana-related arrest also made him eligible years later for a fast track to a commercial weed license through a Massachusetts program that offers resources to entrepreneurs who had run afoul of the pre-legalization law.

Marinaro was accepted into the program in 2020. And though he has raised $3.6 million to build a bespoke cannabis growing facility, he needs to raise more funds to get his business across the finish line. But now, as Massachusetts voters are tasked with a ballot question that would repeal the legalization of recreational cannabis, finding investors has become tough.

“It made it impossible,” Marinaro said. “I have three or four people right now that are like, ‘Yeah, we’re not touching it until after [ballot question] 8 passes.’”

Massachusetts question 8 would reverse the legalization of recreational marijuana, which passed by ballot question in 2016. Massachusetts would be the first state in the country to repeal recreational weed.

But it’s not only weed that’s at stake. The whole legal apparatus that supports business owners like Marinaro would disappear if the question passed.

The state’s social equity program is designed to offer free training and support for those involved in the illicit market before 2016 who were in some way “impacted by the War on Drugs” to enter the legal marijuana industry.

Massachusetts grants licenses for marijuana delivery solely to social equity applicants that own a majority stake of their business. Effectively, they have the state’s entire market to themselves.

For Devin Alexander, who was arrested in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 2011 for possessing a small amount of cannabis, this exclusive licensing seemed like a golden ticket. He decided to start a cannabis delivery company, Rolling ReLeaf, around the pandemic.

“I went from being a bartender to a CEO overnight, which was a huge leap,” Alexander said. “Covid really placed an emphasis on delivery, and you could get anything delivered to you besides cannabis at that time,so we saw it, you know, as the pathway.”

By 2024, the state sweetened the deal even more for applicants like Alexander, offering the first grants from its “social equity trust fund,” which collects revenue from Massachusetts’s marijuana tax and redistributes it to social equity marijuana businesses. The first three rounds of payments distributed $57.7 million through 425 grants.

Alexander said the first grant he received changed his life.

“The first one we got was for $500,000, and I, like, cried my eyes out,” Alexander said. “I was like, ‘Holy shit!’ Because it was just so fucking hard raising capital.”

If question 8 were to pass, the trust fund would go away with it.

“All of the resources going to social equity businesses are going to disappear, and then we’re not going to have an opportunity to undo many of the harms of the war on drugs,” said Ryan Dominguez, the executive director of the trade group Massachusetts Cannabis Coalition.

The federal rules around marijuana make the picture even more complex for business owners. The Trump administration implemented a partial rescheduling order that moved FDA-approved and state-licensed medical marijuana products from Schedule I to Schedule III. But the broader rescheduling effort remains tied up in federal administrative hearings and court challenges.

If full rescheduling were to happen, the federally recognized medical trade would expand at a time that the recreational market in Massachusetts would be contracting.

But a wider medical market wouldn’t recoup the financial losses that the recreational industry would suffer under repeal, according to Travis Ahern, who leads the cannabis regulatory agency in Massachusetts, the Cannabis Control Commission (CCC).

“We would not see that medical just takes over for adult use. There would be a significant revenue loss to the state of Massachusetts if the adult use simply went away,” Ahern said. “We would see impacts in those folks who are in our [social equity program].”

The question before voters makes it all the more important for the government to clear the air on the legality of weed.

“I think there are a lot of people waiting for a directive from the federal government right now, and that is not just the CCC,” Ahern said. “That is every law firm that represents these businesses. It’s every CPA who does the taxes for these businesses. It’s a lot of the municipalities as well.”

The main group backing the ballot question is the Coalition for a Healthy Massachusetts, which has raised $3.6 million over the past two years to repeal cannabis, most of which was raised by a Virginia based anti-drug advocacy group called Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM), according to political finance records.

The organization describes itself as “the science-based alliance holding Big Marijuana accountable in Congress, the courts, and communities across the country.” SAM did not respond to an e-mail request for an interview.

On the other side of the question, the Committee to Protect Cannabis Regulation has raised a total of $2.6 million. Dominguez said a lot of that money is likely coming from people with stakes in the marijuana industry.

“There’s a lot on the line for business owners as well as for the employees, so to try to save themselves, they have to invest in our ballot question,” Dominguez said.

And he’s confident about the industry’s odds of success. A UMass poll published on October 19 showed that 61 percent of voters would either “probably” or “definitely” vote no on the repeal.

Ulysses Youngblood, who owns a social equity cannabis company called Major Bloom in Worcester, Massachusetts, said he’s not worried about passage.

“I just don’t see it having a clear chance, so I’m still not losing sleep over it,” Youngblood said.

Dominguez worries, though, that if the repeal effort succeeds in Massachusetts, or even comes close, it would send a nationwide message.

“SAM is using Massachusetts as a training ground for other states,” Dominguez said. “It is the first battleground for potential repeal of a legalized cannabis market, and this is going to continue if we’re not able to defeat it here.”

Genevieve Morrison is a 2026 Puffin student writing fellow for The Nation. She studies politics and journalism at Boston College, where she also leads the independent student newspaper, The Heights.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: How the Serbian Student Movement Is a Victory for Organizing Power
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Ivana Nikolić Hughes
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
In Serbia, the students may have discovered a formula for rescuing democracy through nonviolence and commitment to collectivism. Students everywhere should take note.

When I first came to the United States, as a foreign exchange student from former Yugoslavia in 1994, I didn’t come only because I dreamed of studying science at some of the world’s best universities. To my 17-year-old self, being in the US meant arriving in the birthplace of democracy, a place where human rights and individual freedoms were sacrosanct. At the time, the country I had grown up in was not just falling apart but doing so violently. Combined with the earlier repressive decades of Tito’s Communist government, however gentler they may have been relative to what went on in the Soviet bloc, made coming to America about more than a hope of a better education or personal life.

The irony was not lost on me when I learned that the Serbian student movement, which had challenged the rule of Aleksandar Vučić, a strongman who ruled the country for 14 years, won a parliamentary snap election outright. Standing on the corner of Broadway and 72nd Street in New York City and reading the news with tears in my eyes, I absorbed that democracy had won in my homeland, just as my adopted country is struggling to hold on to its own hard-won democratic experiment, 250 years in the making. But perhaps the Serbian example, novel in a number of ways, can give hope not only to the people of Serbia, who have collectively suffered long enough, but to all who have watched in fear as democratic standards and ideals erode across the globe.

The first time Serbia had multiparty elections in December of 1990, still as part of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, my mother took me along to the polling station at my school, just across the street from our apartment building. Inside the voting booth, she handed me the pen (I was 14!), knowing how much I cared about the historic turn towards democracy.

That election was a huge leap for democracy in Serbia, although one that followed the playbook of existing democracies. What the Serbian student movement has just accomplished is arguably more significant. Students began protesting in November of 2024, following a tragic accident in Novi Sad, the second-largest city in the country, where the awning of a newly renovated train station collapsed, killing 14 people instantly and injuring three more, two of whom died in the coming weeks and months. The protesters saw the disaster as a symbol of overwhelming corruption at multiple levels, both in the way in which funds for infrastructure projects had been distributed, and in how accountability for the tragedy was sought. Their demands for justice and responsibility quickly turned into an indictment of Vučić’s one-man rule.

What happened over the next two years was extraordinary. Students set up blockades of universities across the country, which eventually led to the suspension of the entire educational system, including K-12, for many months. Peaceful protests took place in Belgrade and across the country, with students frequently walking tens and even hundreds of kilometers from different towns to attend such protests. Once they reached a city, they would be welcomed with open arms by citizens of all stripes. Videos and images of these arrivals were powerful not the least because they were reminiscent of the spirit of “liberation,” that came with the partisan army kicking the German occupying forces out of Serbian towns in the fall of 1944.

Three essential features of the student movement emerged over time. Although this was at times very challenging, the students kept the protests peaceful. Nonviolence was essential to garnering and maintaining the support of the population, which began backing the students in larger and larger numbers. Secondly, the movement from the very beginning had no leaders, among the students themselves or the existing opposition politicians. They understood that in an authoritarian system, individuals were uniquely vulnerable to intimidation, legal action, and personal attacks. By maintaining a level of anonymity for those calling the shots, as well as truly running a grassroots movement, the students ensured continuity of their efforts. Finally, when it came time to form the parliamentary list of 250 candidates, they didn’t nominate themselves or existing opposition politicians but rather people from all walks of life, including professors, engineers, journalists, economists, and even a former NBA basketball player, Dejan Bodiroga. The number of candidates on the student parliamentary list with a PhD is a staggering 160 out of the total 250. The candidates were selected through student assemblies (known as plenums), followed by broad consultations and collective decision-making.

Contrary to what some Western media outlets and politicians are saying, the student movement and the government it has selected are not choosing sides in the geopolitical sphere. Their platform clearly states that the new government will not issue sanctions on Russia (which wouldn’t impact anyone but Serbia itself), putting the questions of joining the European Union (EU) in the background, in the great tradition of Yugoslavia’s role in founding the Non-Aligned Movement. In fact, the party that explicitly called for aligning with the EU and NATO won just 3 percent of the vote. Significantly, the new government is also committing to banning all arms exports to nations in military conflicts, including Israel, Russia, and Ukraine. Such an anti-war stance is much needed in today’s conflict-mired world.

Student movements should be seen as the purest expression of our democratic ideals. One should not have to agree with whatever students may be protesting for to think that young people coming together to pursue something bigger than themselves ought to be viewed as positive. The future after all, is theirs.

In Serbia, the students may have discovered a formula not only for finding their own voice but for rescuing democracy through nonviolence, persistence, and commitment to collectivism. Students everywhere should take note.

Ivana Nikolić Hughes is president of the Nuclear Age Peace Foundation and a senior lecturer in Chemistry at Columbia University. Her research on ascertaining the radiological conditions in the Marshall Islands has been covered widely, including by the Los Angeles Times. She is a member of the Scientific Advisory Group to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.
