https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: How the Midterms Will Test Our Desire for  Real Accountability
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Faris
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Sure, a Democratic win next Tuesday would be a relief—but we still need to repudiate all facets of MAGA authoritarianism.

Prresident Donald Trump addresses a midterms rally in Mobile, Alabama.

By now there’s little left to say about what might happen in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats seem all but assured of taking the House of Representatives according to experts, but the outcome in the Senate could be anything from a modest Democratic gain of two or three seats to a heretofore unimaginable wave that leaves Democrats with 55 or 56 seats. This latter scenario would include wins in places like Kansas and South Carolina that weren’t even on the radar a few months ago.

Without diminishing the obvious importance of Democrats’ reclaiming control of Congress, the stakes of Tuesday’s elections are as much existential as they are practical. Substantive Democratic gains in reliably Republican states and districts would serve as confirmation that the breathtaking, two-year display of self-dealing, cruelty, and ineptitude we have just lived through carries a penalty larger than the standard thermostatic midterm backlash. If it doesn’t, Republicans will rightfully conclude that they can get away with just about anything, as long as their next president doesn’t start a stupid war.

After all, it’s not particularly earth-shattering that swing states like North Carolina would go blue this year. Wins there and in Maine, together with holds in purple states like Georgia and Michigan, wouldn’t suggest by themselves that a tectonic political shift is under way. They’re closer to the outcomes you’d expect in a normal, pre-Trump midterm election, when voter sentiment shifts against the party in power enough to give the out party the advantage in many competitive districts and states.

It is the Senate contests in more sharply Republican-leaning states like Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Alaska, as well as in House districts that Trump carried by double digits that are the real test of the American electorate’s tolerance for abusive authoritarianism and rank corruption. The outcomes there will serve as a measure of whether negative polarization is a force so strong and resilient that it has warped the ability of voters to make informed judgments and hold their representatives accountable.

In the House, Democrats can build a majority of 232 seats without winning a single seat in a district that Trump carried by 10 or more points in 2024. If you had asked anyone on the left in, say, April 2025 whether they would be happy with a 17-seat gain in the House and a 232–203 majority, they would have replied with an exuberant, justified yes—especially if they knew that Republicans would make the prospect even harder by ordering fresh, Supreme Court–assisted gerrymanders in a series of red states.

But here, as in the Senate, the test of whether America is truly rejecting Trumpism will be how many seats Democrats can win deep in Trump territory. Given the sheer level of depravity on display from the Trump administration, failing to win a significant number of the hardcore Trump districts now in play will be not just disappointing but soul-crushing.

It will be satisfying, for example, if Democrat Brian Poindexter wins Ohio’s seventh district, which Trump carried by 11.1 points in 2024 and where incumbent GOP Representative Max Miller has been credibly accused of horrific acts of domestic violence by multiple women. But the GOP candidate shouldn’t have to be a physically abusive, misogynist dirtbag for Republican-leaning voters to support a Democrat amid the rampant authoritarian corruption of today’s GOP. Trump’s dreadful policy record and consistently unconscionable conduct in office should be enough to warrant dismissal of any congressional Republican who spent the past two years obsequiously surrendering constitutional power to Trump and his MAGA putsch—which, to be clear, would be all GOP incumbents on Capitol Hill.

ICE’s reign of terror alone should be enough to persuade even committed Trump voters to change their minds. Trump’s masked federal agents have terrorized both big metropolitan areas and rural communities, violently seizing tens of thousands of undocumented immigrants, the vast majority of whom had committed no serious crimes. These public renditions, often carried about by sadists in a repressive apparatus funded more lavishly than the Manhattan Project and glorified by unapologetic white nationalists in the Department of Homeland Security, are a permanent stain on America’s pretensions to be governed by laws and not men. These vicious brownshirt raids have inflicted extraordinary trauma on immigrant families and communities, led to the unlawful detention of hundreds of American citizens, and caused the tragic deaths of innocent noncitizens as well as dissenting US citizens like Renée Nicole Good and Alex Pretti.

The blatant corruption of the president himself is also grounds for broad and deep repudiation of his party in a functional republic. Trump continues to nakedly manipulate the stock market by selling access to his market-moving social-media posts and then conducting thousands of transactions whose sheer brazenness makes the phrase “insider trading” seem like a polite euphemism.

Trump has also corrupted the president’s pardon power by effectively selling freedom to oligarchs and partisan allies and turned American foreign policy into a tool to enrich himself and his circle of oligarchs. For the crime of living in a blue state, he has withheld relief from people whose lives were destroyed by natural disasters, and he has not been subtle about it.

Even Republicans who support dramatically lower levels of immigration to the United States should oppose a secret police force whose members can commit violent crimes on camera in front of hundreds of witnesses and never face any kind of accountability. Even those who believe, for example, that facilitating Somali immigration to the United States was a mistake should be disgusted and chilled by the GOP’s racist, menacing rhetoric and actions against Somalis, including the preposterous raid on the home of Representation Ilhan Omar (D-MN).

Trump voters who agree with many of his economic and social policies should be able to see that a president’s exploiting his office for the enrichment of himself and his family is disqualifying. Diehard Republicans should likewise grasp that the abuse of federal money and power to punish the citizens of states who withheld their support from the ruling regime a recipe for the eventual dissolution of the republic—-as, on the other side of the ledger, are Trump’s repeated promises to bribe citizens who give the GOP their support in this election.

Pick your issue, and you’ll almost certainly find conduct that is an affront to human decency or the rule of law—-and usually both. There’s the vindictive and inhuman assault that the Trump administration has conducted against the small and vulnerable trans minority; the wanton, illegal air strikes against boats suspected of drug trafficking; the bizarre threats of violence against long-standing democratic allies like Canada and Denmark; and the illegal, unprovoked war against Iran that started with the murder of schoolchildren and the country’s head of state and has turned into a geopolitical and economic calamity. This is to say nothing of the myriad abuses and public fleecings carried out by Trump’s coterie of fanatical MAGA allies in and around his cabinet, from Elon Musk’s illegal DOGE reign of destruction to Russell Vought’s deep-state machinations to punish applicants for scientific grants who don’t toe the party line.

The Nation would have to build its own data center to host a full accounting of this administration’s misdeeds. The names of congressional Republicans up for election this year who have done anything at all to push back on this bacchanal of abuse and crime, on the other hand, could fit on the back of a cocktail napkin.

If the characterization of these threats as “existential” seems overblown, it bears reminding that we are in this position only because we flunked a very similar test two years ago. Whatever motivated someone to vote for the disgraced Trump in 2024, be it the price of eggs or resentment against the Biden administration’s immigration policy or even just the boredom of affluence, there should have been little doubt about what he intended to do with a second term. Throughout that election cycle, Trump barnstormed around the country loudly promising mass deportations, partisan vengeance, ruinous tariffs, and vindictive persecution. The Supreme Court even drove home the apocalyptic stakes of that year’s election by granting American presidents almost monarchical power in its stupendously wrongheaded executive immunity decision, Trump v. United States.

Rarely has the American electorate faced such a stark choice between the rule of law and the whims of an aspiring autocrat. And yet here we are. Living through the second Trump administration has been like feeling, in the memorable phrasing of New York Times columnist Michelle Goldberg, “the air go out of an entire social order.” That’s the net result of a sustained campaign of eager MAGA capitulation led by elites in tech, law, academia, the judiciary, and the media. So it’s down to the electorate, again, to do the job that those tasked with defending the Constitution could not.

Democratic wins in unexpected places like South Carolina, which Trump carried by 18 points in 2024 and where a gold-standard New York Times/Siena College poll on Wednesday found a tie between Republican Darline Graham Nordone and Democrat Annie Andrews, would send an unambiguous message to the forces of Trumpism: that there is actually a line and they have crossed it, and that another electoral walloping awaits them in two years if they continue to empower authoritarian impunity in Washington.

It’s true that even a resounding Democratic win on Tuesday may mean nothing more than that these awful people that we have now twice put in charge of the country have at long last alienated enough voters to be thrown out on their ear. It could also be the case that it was mostly inflation and spiraling energy costs putting some of these races in play, and they will snap back to being GOP strongholds in a year or two. Still, such losses would be unspinnable, even by the talented propagandists that populate the MAGA media universe.

On the other hand, modest gains or, God help us, a failure to capture either chamber of Congress would send an unambiguously grim message—that an electorally decisive plurality of the American people likes violent, corrupt authoritarianism, wants more of it, and indeed enjoys being governed by hapless gutter racists, lazy podcasters, and moneyed rapists. They’d also effectively be saying that they don’t care how incompetent and negligent their leaders are, so long as the libs are being owned and the right people are getting hurt.

David Faris is a professor of political science at Roosevelt University and the author of It’s Time to Fight Dirty: How Democrats Can Build a Lasting Majority in American Politics. His writing has appeared in Slate, The Week, The Washington Post, The New Republic, and Washington Monthly. You can find him on Bluesky at @davidfaris.bluesky.social.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Billionaires or Democracy
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Bonifaz, Christina Livingston
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The fight over the California billionaire wealth tax ballot initiative has been covered largely as a state tax and budget issue, but that is too narrow a lens. At its core, this fight over the health and well-being of millions of Californians is about democracy.

In a democracy, there is a simple principle: Voters decide, not the people with the most money. Today, that principle is under extraordinary strain. The 170 biggest-spending billionaire families have already contributed a record-breaking $1.7 billion to the 2026 midterm elections. Elon Musk, now the world’s first trillionaire, has spent more than $480 million to bend the outcome toward his own financial and political interests. Billionaires are deploying unprecedented sums to drown out the voices of ordinary voters, and they are proving a hard truth: We can have a government of, by, and for billionaires, or the people, but we cannot have both.

The fight over Prop 40—which would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net assets of billionaires to provide healthcare, as well as food assistance and education, to millions of Californians—is Exhibit A in the threat that runaway extreme wealth poses to our society. Californians overwhelmingly support taxing the ultrarich. So, instead of persuading voters differently, a handful of billionaires have spent the past year trying to stop them from voting at all.

§ First, they tried to price democracy out of reach, driving up the cost of signature collection to keep the Billionaire Tax Act off the ballot;

§ When that failed, they tried to buy the company collecting the signatures; and

§ When that failed, they bankrolled two poison-pill measures, Props 41 and 42, designed to confuse voters, undermine Prop 40, and shield their fortunes from taxation permanently.

Now they are flooding the airwaves with misinformation, pouring more than $429 million into anti-wealth-tax efforts—more than Musk spent in the 2024 presidential election that landed him influence to grow his wealth to trillionaire status. And as a recent report shows, the billionaires complaining about Prop 40’s one-time 5 percent tax have seen their wealth surge by an average of 65 percent during the past 20 months and have paid only 0.26 percent of their wealth in state income taxes over five recent years. But the opposition’s playbook has nothing to do with morality or the merits. It is about whether concentrated wealth can override the will of the majority and drown out our votes.

That is why this fight matters so much for California and the nation. For people who spend more than $330 million and barely notice, this is a pilot program. If it works, every billionaire in America learns the lesson: When voters want something you don’t, then you obstruct, confuse, and outspend them until they give up. We cannot let that become the playbook. And the stakes will only grow as artificial intelligence threatens to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of these very tech bros on a scale the world has never seen.

A democracy responsive to the many rather than the few requires policies that check the wealth and power of the ultra-wealthy, starting with taxing the largest fortunes. California voters have the first chance to show it can be done.

The question on the ballot in California is not just about taxes. It is about who governs. Let’s answer it clearly: The people do.

John Bonifaz is a constitutional attorney and the cofounder and president of Free Speech For People, a national nonprofit public interest organization dedicated to defending our democracy and our Constitution across the country.

Christina Livingston is executive director of the Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment Action (ACCE Action) and chair of the California Working Families Party. She has over two decades of experience organizing at the intersection of racial and economic justice.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: College Activists Push Back as North Carolina Republicans Seek Another House Seat
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Alice Scott
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
As part of a Trump-led gerrymandering effort, North Carolina GOP leaders redrew the state’s congressional district map in 2025 with the hopes of achieving an 11–3 majority.

Even though 2025 gerrymandering only affected two congressional districts, it has become something of a rallying cry for student activists across the state.

As the president of the College Democrats at Eastern Carolina University (ECU), Thomas Remington is used to hearing from people who aren’t politically engaged. After all, he is often talking to college students—a demographic that traditionally votes at one of the lowest rates of any group in the United States—ahead of an election known to generate less voter turnout than the presidential race.

But recently, Remington has heard something surprising from these self-described apolitical students.

“Students are saying, ‘I’m not all that politically engaged, but I remember when they gerrymandered,’” Remington said. “It’s been really interesting to see how many people know what the word ‘gerrymandering’ means now.”

The gerrymandering that these students are referencing is the redrawing of North Carolina’s congressional district map in 2025. In North Carolina, the redistricting aimed to give Republicans an additional seat in the US House of Representatives, which would secure an 11–3 majority over Democrats. The effort followed a Trump-led push for states to redraw congressional maps that would favor Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections.

The redistricting is one of many attempts that college activists across North Carolina say Republicans have taken to try to increase their majority in the House. But with the midterms just days away, those activists believe the attempts might be backfiring.

North Carolina currently has 14 seats in the House—10 Republicans and four Democrats. The state’s new congressional district map focuses on making District 1, currently represented by Democrat Don Davis, Republican.

To do this, leaders of the state’s GOP-controlled General Assembly moved six reliably Republican counties from District 3 to historically Democratic District 1. They also shifted four counties previously in District 1 to safely Republican District 3.

But Remington said this has made the District 3 race more contentious than Republicans anticipated.

ECU is located in District 3, which is currently represented by Republican Greg Murphy. The last time Murphy was up for reelection, in 2024, he didn’t even face a Democratic challenger.

“Now we’re telling people, with the makeup of the district, if we vote enough, we actually can flip this seat,” Remington said.

Indeed, the Center for Politics recently shifted NC-3 from “Safe Republican” to “Likely Republican,” according to a September 29 report. Early voting tracked by Vote Tracker, a project of the Civitas Center for Public Integrity at the John Locke Foundation, shows a strong performance from blue voters in District 3.

As of Tuesday, October 27, about 47,600 Democrats have early voted, while Republicans have cast around 29,500. In addition, 29,760 unaffiliated voters have cast ballots. This is taking place as voter turnout has surged across North Carolina—up by about 50 percent from the last midterm election cycle.

Remington said he has noticed particularly high turnout among students. “In 2024, we were fighting for every vote we could get to go to the polls. This time, a lot of people that we’re approaching are not only saying, ‘Yeah, I’m going to go vote,’ but, ‘I’ve already done it,’ and they flash us their sticker.”

In Pitt County, where ECU is located, Remington said young people are currently making up almost 8 percent of the electorate, almost double what it was in 2022. Though Democrats are historically more likely to vote early, Remington said he remains hopeful about the District 3 race.

“The Republicans have dropped six figures into District 3 to defend their incumbent,” Remington said. “We’re going to have to talk to as many prospective voters as we can. We truly think that we could be the difference makers in a surprise on election night.”

At Elizabeth City State University, students are watching the other congressional race affected by 2025 gerrymandering unfold. ECSU is located in Elizabeth City, in North Carolina’s First Congressional District.

Malachi Bass, the president of ECSU DEMS, said that 2025 redistricting has changed the way the organization has thought about voter mobilization efforts. He said the organization has been working since the beginning of the school year to register voters and encourage turnout. Bass said that ECSU DEMS is planted at busy locations on campus at least once a week, sharing voting information with students.

District 1 historically houses the state’s majority-Black counties. By shifting six reliably Republican counties out of District 3 and into District 1, the maps have a effect of diluting the political power and voting strength of communities of color. At ECSU, Bass said the gerrymandering has led to an outcry from students.

ECSU also lost its on-campus early voting site, which Bass said many students felt was another attempt to suppress their votes. The polling site had been used by Pasquotank County voters in general elections since 2020. But despite the impact of this loss and the gerrymandering of District 1, Bass said he doesn’t think voter turnout will be depleted.

“I feel like voter turnout will be very high,” Bass said. “A lot of us students are about business now. We really want change, and we really want to make a difference.”

Bass said he has seen a strong response from ECSU DEMS’ voter registration efforts. To promote civic engagement, students organized a march to the polls on October 27.

Bass said he remains confident about Democrats’ ability to maintain control of the district. In fact, Davis recently outpaced his Republican challenger, Laurie Buckhout, in third-quarter campaign finance reports, and the race is widely considered to be a toss-up at this point.

Even though 2025 gerrymandering only affected two congressional districts, it has become something of a rallying cry for student activists across the state. Micah Mangot, president of the UNC-Chapel Hill Young Democrats, said she has been talking to students frequently about last year’s redistricting as part of the organization’s voter education efforts ahead of the midterms.

Mangot said she has used the new voter maps as a way to encourage support for North Carolina State Supreme Court Justice Anita Earls, who is currently seeking reelection.

“People are getting more and more informed about the fact that our maps are incredibly rigged, and the only way to undo that is to elect Democratic justices to the state Supreme Court to undo the gerrymandering that has crippled this state,” Mangot said. “I think that people are able to make that connection in a much more salient way than they were previously when the maps weren’t as unbalanced.”

District 1 and 3 aren’t the only contentious Congressional races in North Carolina. The state’s 11th congressional district, which encompasses much of western North Carolina, is seeing an unexpectedly tight race between Democrat Jamie Ager and Republican Jennifer Balkcom.

Though NC-11 is a traditionally safe Republican seat, the race faced a massive political shake-up in August when incumbent Chuck Edwards abruptly withdrew from his reelection campaign. Edwards dropped out of the race after the House Ethics Committee recommended his censure for “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”

This has opened up an opportunity for Democrats to flip the seat. Seth Digh, president of Western Carolina University’s College Democrats chapter, said student voters scored a major win when election officials decided to approve an early voting location on WCU’s campus. However, Digh noted that the site was not granted without a fight.

It was previously announced that WCU would lose its on-campus early voting site. Instead, students who intended to vote early would have been sent to a location 1.53 miles from the center of campus. Digh said getting to that polling site took 40 minutes and required students to walk on the unprotected side of a four-lane highway.

After bipartisan pressure from WCU student organizations election officials reversed course, eventually agreeing to place a polling location at WCU’s Health and Human Services Building—which Digh notes is still removed from the University’s main campus, but is closer than the off-campus site.

With the on-campus polling site reinstated, Digh said he is seeing high voter turnout among students. Vote Tracker currently shows that over 59,300 Democratic voters have cast their ballots in the District 11 race. Democrats are outpacing Republican voters, who have cast about 43,400 ballots so far. However, unaffiliated voters are turning out the highest, with over 71,000 ballots cast.

“It is very clear that the Western site on campus, even at HHS [Health and Human Services], is doing ridiculous numbers,” Digh said. “While Democratic turnout is slightly lower, it’s still very high, and unaffiliated turnout is really high this year, especially for a midterm.”

Given this, Digh said he is hopeful about Ager’s candidacy, which he thinks appeals to many WCU students.

“We are still feeling the effects of Hurricane Helene, and that has become a huge divisive campaign issue in the NC11 congressional race,” Digh said. “Both Chuck Edwards and Jennifer Balkcom have had enough time to release funding that we know that they have more than enough control over to provide critical aid to the 15 westernmost North Carolina counties. You drive around here for long enough, you can feel that. You can feel that things are not affordable.”

Other campuses have not been so lucky in their polling site appeals. Earlier this year, state and local elections officials denied petitions for a primary and general election early voting site at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University’s campus in Greensboro.

The campus had an early voting site for the presidential election in 2024. But the campus didn’t have one in the last midterm election in 2022, so elections officials declined to open one for the 2026 midterm. The off-campus polling site is about a 40=minute walk from NC A&T.

But Xavier Jones, the political affairs director of NC A&T’s College Democrats chapter, said this decision, which he thinks “was meant to keep us down,” has ended up “just firing us up more.”

Last week, NC A&T’s College Democrats organized a march to the early voting site, which was attended by more than 300 students. Jones said the organization is also arranging a shuttle service that will pick A&T students up at a nearby church and drive them to the polls. The shuttle will make a stop to pick up students at the neighboring UNC-Greensboro campus.

Jones said the issues of gerrymandering and polling sites have been a reminder of students’ power in the midterms. He said he and the College Democrats are going to continue to pursue efforts to encourage voter turnout right up until Election Day.

“It’s just ridiculous the effort that these Republicans have put into stifling young voter turnout,” Jones said. “It’s about us as a voting bloc, as a community, as a demographic, the power we hold, and the power that I think we need to realize we’re coming into.”

Alice Scott is a 2026 Puffin student writing fellow for The Nation. She studies journalism at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and has reported for PBS NewsHour and published in Texas Highways magazine and the Austin American-Statesman.

https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.title: What Is Money?
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.author: Trevor Jackson
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.text:
In their new book, economists Arjun Jayadev and J.W. Mason examine the peculiar role money plays in shaping human life.

Despite using it every day, and spending a lot of time thinking and worrying about it, nobody can quite agree on what money is, or why it so often seems not to do what we want it to. Even economic theory, which you would expect to have the answers, cannot decide whether money doesn’t matter at all, or whether it’s essential to economic life. Most economists agree on what money is for: It is a unit of account, a medium of exchange, and a store of value. Most textbooks claim that it emerged from barter as a private-sector way of making transactions easier, and the total absence of historical or anthropological evidence for this claim has hardly slowed it down. Yet this is where the agreement ends and the problems begin. For many economists, money is “neutral,” meaning that it simply represents a true underlying value and has no power of its own to shape anything. Some, like the early-20th-century economists Irving Fisher and John Maynard Keynes, even spoke of a “money illusion” that fools people into confusing the face value of money with its actual ability to command goods and services, like believing that a dollar in 1875 is the same as a dollar today. It’s not an accident that economists contrast the “nominal” monetary economy with what they call the “real” economy. Money is somehow less than—or at least distinct from—material reality itself.

In their new book, simply titled Against Money, the economists Arjun Jayadev and J.W. Mason set out to show that confusion about money and the peculiar role it plays in shaping human life are the result of confusion within the field of economics. “Money values,” the authors assert, “do not reflect any real things or quantities already existing in the world.” But at the same time, many familiar economic concepts like inflation, gross domestic product, debt, and credit only exist as money values. How, then, do these ideas have power in the world? Recognizing the actual autonomy of money reveals the hidden forms of social authority and, with them, new possibilities for using the systems of money and credit to produce better social outcomes.

An essential preliminary fact about Against Money is that Jayadev and Mason are heterodox economists, and this book is both a presentation of heterodox ideas and an extended critique of what the authors call “mainstream economics.” This fact will certainly shape the book’s reception: Readers invested in mainstream economics will likely dismiss it out of hand; readers skeptical of the mainstream will likely read it with sympathy; and orthodox Marxists will reliably be annoyed by the book, because it aims for radical conclusions that are still expressed in the idiom of traditional economics.

Heterodox economists such as Jayadev and Mason—as well as their teachers, James Crotty and Axel Leijonhufvud—reject the interpretation of Keynes at the heart of neoclassical and neo-Keynesian economics, which is exemplified by leading mainstream economists like Paul Samuelson. While mainstream economists argue that Keynes’s work provides the policy tools to achieve growth and equilibrium, their heterodox counterparts insist that economies do not tend toward stability, efficiency, or equilibrium. For them, economies are at least as likely to end up with monopolies as with competition, and crises are likely to happen even when the systems are working as intended, not just when there’s an outburst of fraud or irrationality. These heterodox economists further argue that their conclusions don’t stem from a rejection of Keynes but from a closer reading of his work, as well as that of his contemporaries Joan Robinson and Pierro Sraffa, who argued that most economic models do not accurately reflect an underlying reality and are therefore of limited explanatory power.

Heterodoxy plays a special role in the field of economics. Heterodox economists often read and respond critically to mainstream economists, who generally don’t return the favor except in moments of crisis, when the poverty of economic theory and policy is revealed and mainstream economists decide to raid the ideas of their heterodox colleagues. One such example: After decades of ignoring Hyman Minsky, mainstream economists finally started to take his theory of financial fragility—the idea that crises can result even from the normal, legal workings of the financial system—seriously after the 2008 subprime-mortgage crisis. Or another: In the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic and vertiginous inflation, mainstream economists reluctantly began to listen to Isabella Weber’s arguments for price controls. Although Paul Krugman once dismissed her proposals as “truly stupid” (for which he later apologized), today Weber’s op-eds about “sellers’ inflation” appear regularly in places like The New York Times. Indeed, reality often weighs in on the heterodox side: To take but one example of sellers’ inflation, the three biggest egg producers in the United States just settled with the Department of Justice over their conspiracy to manipulate prices from 2022 to 2025.

This focus on both the limits of mainstream economics and the desire to change many of its presuppositions informs Against Money. Most mainstream economists, Jayadev and Mason note, operate on the assumption of monetary neutrality, meaning that there exists a world of nominal prices that can change without affecting the “real” economy, understood in terms of the people and resources employed making goods and services. Against Money wants to offer a different understanding of how money works. Money, the authors argue, does not float above the “real” economy but is itself real—a material and organizational economic force, separate from (and even independent of) the nonmonetary world, and that is capable of changing it as much as any other element of the economy.

For Jayadev and Mason, this argument has three implications: first, that “how easy it is to acquire money shapes real activity of production and social existence in general,” meaning that money is a motivator of economic activity and getting it allows other economic activities to happen. Second, that “money quantities do not reflect developments in an underlying real world,” meaning that incomes and wealth can change without anything new being made or exchanged. The obvious example here is paper-wealth accumulation: If the price of Tesla stock fluctuates just a few cents because Elon Musk tweeted something, his wealth balloons or contracts by billions of dollars despite no new goods or services being produced. Third, that “many economic quantities…are only meaningful in terms of money.” The “quantities” that the authors especially have in mind are debt, capital, interest, and prices: They seek to show that “debt is not simply a record of past consumption in excess of income; capital is not simply a mass of useful equipment and structures; the interest rate is not simply the price of stuff today in terms of stuff tomorrow.” Jayadev and Mason spend the rest of their time exploring these economic quantities and their relationship to money.

Their chapter on capital alone is worth the price of the book, because capital is one of the most fiendishly difficult concepts in economic thought. Borrowing from the economist John Hicks’s 1974 writings on the history of capital-theory controversies, it becomes possible to group economic thinkers into two camps when it comes to the concept. Some think that capital is a mass of physical stuff—all the factories, buildings, machines, and tools that go into economic production. Others think that capital is a fund, an eternal pool of money (probably the result of past savings and abstention from spending) that gets transmuted constantly into different physical manifestations, each of which are epiphenomenal.

Jayadev and Mason do deft work navigating the complexities of this argument, and they show persuasively that holding both ideas at once is more analytically useful than adhering to one side or the other. The physical-asset idea can only be expressed through monetary quantities, and in any event much of it consists of land values, not past investment decisions. To take just one example, they cite several critics of Thomas Piketty’s U-shaped inequality curve who have shown that the rise in wealth concentration since the 1970s has been driven not by savings or the accumulation of productive capacity, but by price inflation in real-estate assets. Yet this purely fundist view overlooks the fact that what turns money into more money is its role in the production process. So what’s important in distinguishing capital from other kinds of money (or other assets) is that someone uses it as a source of authority. Capital is both a special kind of money and a set of material possessions that allows some people to command other people to do certain things.

Jayadev and Mason also show that debt is the production of new money, not a redistribution of money across time. We might think that getting a loan today is about financing current consumption or investment with future income, and that a fixed quantity of money is moved from savers to borrowers by some neutral intermediary like a bank. But in reality, they argue, a loan is money newly created by the bank, and the price doesn’t involve time but rather flexibility: The recipient of the loan gets a kind of money they can use for essentially anything right now, while the holder of the debt gets a kind of money that allows them a claim on future social production. A mortgage, then, is not the exchange of an IOU on property for cash, but rather the exchange of differently time-structured IOUs for each other. And the bank is not just an intermediary matching borrowers and savers, but an independent power—one with the ability to make new economic activity happen (or not) based on its willingness and ability to lend.

Or take the interest rate. The conventional view is that interest is the price of time: To persuade people to part with their money for longer periods of time, you need to offer them a higher interest rate, so long-term loans tend to have higher rates than short-term ones. Except, as Jayadev and Mason observe, this isn’t the whole truth. Interest rates are also the price of money, depending on the supply and demand of loanable funds. And they are the price of risk, so that riskier borrowers tend to have to pay more. So how do these elements relate to each other, and which one “really” determines the rate of interest? Here again, the standard models lead us to confusion. In the real world, the interest rate is simply a monetary price: the price of exchanging a set of fixed future payments for a flexible payment today, so that interest is actually the price of flexible access to money.

And what about the price level? Everyone knows that the cost of living has gone up, and that the price world of, say, the 1960s is very different from the price world of today. Surely the fact that an egg remains an egg even if it costs 10 times as much reveals the gap between the monetary economy and the real one. Jayadev and Mason argue that there is no such thing as “the” price level, but rather a whole range of prices that move in different directions and at different speeds. No consensus procedure exists for how to average them, and different procedures can end up with radically different results. Again and again, the models of an abstract nonmonetary world lurking behind and prior to the monetary one are shown to be incoherent or inconsistent with reality.

In his 1769 essay “Value and Money,” the early French economist A.R.J. Turgot suggested that we can think of money as a language, and this is a helpful way to see what Jayadev and Mason are doing here. Some might argue that language is irrelevant to the physical world: The sounds we use to refer to cars, trees, or dogs don’t change their actual existence. Others might argue that we have no knowledge of the world separate from its linguistic expression. Against Money occupies a kind of middle ground, much like recognizing that there are some speech acts that make things happen (as when a judge pronounces “Guilty” or a couple says “I do”), and some concepts, like ontology or cocktail hour, exist only in language. So too are there some purely monetary phenomena and others that can profoundly affect material economic activity.

Unlike some heterodox critics, however, Jayadev and Mason don’t want us to see the monetary economy as fake—as mere numbers on paper—and valorize the underlying material economy instead. They are doing something more ambitious than that, but also more abstract: They want us to recognize the autonomy of the monetary economy and its disconnect from the world of things, and they want that recognition to become a source of power. Once we see that the monetary economy is subject to human manipulation, then we can argue that it should be manipulated toward more progressive and egalitarian ends.

Jayadev and Mason are persuasive in showing how frequently and deeply our mainstream economic concepts conceal political choices and obfuscation. Their book is surprisingly clear for a technical study of economics, but it is also, at times, more theoretical than practical in its arguments. Unless readers have already encountered the mainstream idea that money is neutral, the book’s critiques are likely to seem belabored or unnecessary. This is not, however, intended as a criticism: Like many heterodox economists, Jayadev and Mason are trying to transform the discipline from within, and so they’re speaking to their fellow practitioners as well. Against Money is a frontal assault on the monopoly that mainstream economics has attempted to establish over the study of the economy, and it succeeds in this intellectual goal. It is especially effective in its moments of clearest empirical revision: for instance, that the well-known rise in household debt relative to income after the 1980s was due not to more borrowing, but to stagnating wages and higher interest rates. Still, a mainstream economist could probably accept many of their arguments—that “capital” is analytically incoherent; that “GDP” is made up; that banks create money; that interest is the price of liquidity, not of time—and still conclude that none of it matters because the field’s earlier vision of the world has worked tolerably well in practice. Of course, we might dispute that assertion, but at least within the epistemic community of the economists themselves and the policymakers who heed them, mainstream economics is a dependable engine for piloting our way through the world, even if many of its core concepts make no sense.

Jayadev and Mason repeatedly gesture toward the ways in which recognizing the “progressive, creative, and transformative role of money” would be a first step toward changing our social relations and moving to a world less dominated by the control of money. But, they conclude, “this book is not a how-to guide…. We are not trying to smash up the temple and denounce the priests as frauds, understandable though the temptation may be. That is not the way out. Instead, we can turn our backs on the idols, push the curtain aside, and walk out into the sunshine.”

It’s an estimable goal, although it still leaves unexplained whether that sunshine should be curricular: If we taught a new generation of students in Econ 101 that money is not neutral, would we really have a different world? Or perhaps the point is to produce intellectual ammunition for the day when (or if) a Democratic administration takes office and is presented with the usual eisteddfod over “the debt.” But Jayadev and Mason know perfectly well that austerity is an expression of class conflict, not intellectual rigor, and that what the controllers of money have is power, not compelling or even accurate ideas.

All of this, however, is not intended to note a set of limitations in Against Money, but instead to observe that the book can be read as a challenge to the rest of us toiling in the field. To keep Turgot’s metaphor, Jayadev and Mason want us not only to be fluent in the language of money, but also to recognize that it’s a language in the first place. What would be revealed if economic historians examined the Great Depression or the stagflation of the 1970s through this account of money? What monetary principles should be followed by an Against Money–informed Federal Reserve? At its best, Jayadev and Mason’s book may have given us an intellectual promissory note that allows others to make payments in the future.

Trevor Jackson is an economic historian at the University of California at Berkeley. His latest book, The Insatiable Machine: How Capitalism Conquered the World, was published by W.W. Norton in 2026.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Ro Khanna Is Making FDR Great Again
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Harvey J. Kaye, Nomiki Konst
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The California Democrat is renewing the Democratic Party’s vital connection to Roosevelt’s New Deal and the Economic Bill of Rights.

Joining Senator Bernie Sanders at the Ballots Over Billionaires rally in Los Angeles on October 5, Representative Ro Khanna proudly stated: “We are New Deal Democrats, not corporate Democrats. We are New Deal Democrats, not neoliberal Democrats. We are New Deal Democrats, not Chuck Schumer Democrats.”

Have you been listening to Ro Khanna’s speeches? Standing on the shoulders of FDR, Khanna has taken hold of a century of American history and not only thrown a challenge to the Democratic Party leadership but also begun to stake a powerful claim to the party’s 2028 presidential nomination.

Just as then–New York Governor Franklin Roosevelt did in 1930 when he wrote in the lengthening shadows of the Great Depression and the rising threat of authoritarianism, “There is no question in my mind that it is time for the country to become fairly radical for a generation,” Khanna has made it clear that he, too, recognizes that to effectively confront and prevail against the authoritarian menace that threatens to destroy American democratic life today, Democrats must not only win elections but also pursue determined progressive—indeed, radical-democratic—action when they do.

Speaking at the National Press Club (NPC) this past April, Khanna decried the ever-increasing concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a “new Gilded Age” elite and the difficulties working people face to stay afloat. Drawing on not only the best of Franklin Roosevelt but also Harry Truman, A. Philip Randolph, and Martin Luther King Jr., he proceeded to project a “New Economic Patriotism.… A new deal for this era. A freedom budget for this century”—indeed, a “21C Marshall Plan” for middle- and working-class Americans. This new New Deal or Marshall Plan would include creating a Work for America program—modeled after FDR’s Works Progress Administration—to help rebuild the nation and guarantee jobs to those who need them; establishing a National Industrial Bank to “invest in the industries that will define the future” and direct such investments in particular to those cities whose economies were most devastated by deindustrialization; and enabling workers to not only more easily organize unions but also participate in “worker ownership” of the companies for which they work.

Most critically, the New Economic Patriotism would entail the enactment of an updated version of the Second Bill of Rights that Roosevelt himself first proposed in 1944—an Economic Bill of Rights for all Americans that would guarantee, among other things, a useful job at a living wage, universal healthcare, food security, a decent home, a good education, and opportunities for recreation—a set of rights that the corporate bosses and congressional conservatives of both parties vehemently and successfully opposed.

The NPC speech was just the beginning. Taking a page from FDR’s deep-listening tours of New York State to hear from farm and factory workers affected by the Great Depression, Khanna spent July crisscrossing his home state of Pennsylvania, connecting with Rust Belt workers on the left and right. Khanna’s bipartisan conversations have led to bipartisan alliances—introducing the Data Center Bill of Rights, requiring disclosure of water and power use and the projected effect on local utility rates before a permit is issued, keeping these facilities out of residential neighborhoods and off farmland, and giving a community standing to refuse one. Yes, listening tours are common in American politics. Bills that come out of them are not.

Then there is the question of whether Khanna can pass anything, which is where most bold agendas die. Khanna and Thomas Massie, a libertarian Republican, forced the Epstein Files Transparency Act to the floor over the objections of both parties’ leaders and the president—and it passed. Republicans voted for it because their own voters understood what was at stake, which was whether this country runs two systems of justice, one for working Americans and one for rich men who abused young girls for decades. Roosevelt did not assemble his majorities simply from people who already agreed with him. Neither did the organizers who built the industrial unions.

Addressing the August meeting of the Democratic National Committee in Texas, Khanna intensified the challenge he had issued to party leaders. After declaring himself a proud Democrat, he proceeded to remind them that their party once had a tradition of “fighting for economic democracy against oligarchy,” but in the course of the economic crises of the 1970s, it had not only wrongly turned its back on that tradition and embraced the politics of neoliberalism but also tragically turned away from America’s urban and rural working classes in favor of serving the interests of coastal professionals. “In short,” he said, “we stopped being the party of Main Street and became the party of Wall Street.” And notably, the often ideologically, identically, and geographically rift-ridden DNC membership responded to Khanna’s words with universal applause.

Bluntly stating, “I am tired of platitudes. I am tired of the consultant-crafted, focus-group-tested phrases about ‘affordability’ and ‘renewing the American dream’ without the specific policies to make them real,” Khanna avowed that he had come to Washington “to fight for a real agenda: Medicare for All. Tax the billionaires. No foreign wars”—and insisted that if the Democrats were doing that, they could “crack” Trump’s coalition.

Here, one is reminded of FDR’s words of 1938: “I have always believed, and I have frequently stated, that my party can succeed at the polls only so long as it continues to be the party of militant liberalism” (aka social democracy).

Declaring, “I am from the economic patriotism wing of the Democratic Party—the New Deal wing of the Democratic Party,” the wing of the party that believes “a national economic project is our path back from the wilderness,” Khanna warned, “We see that America is at a breaking point, and that if we do not offer a new economic bargain, we will break.” And on that note, he reiterated his call for both Medicare for All and an industrial development bank and proceeded to propose a program that he calls “A Home by 35,” which would enable young workers to purchase homes after seven years of employment by granting them low-interest loans with zero down payment (a program already available to veterans).

Preempting the question of “How do we pay for all this?” Khanna put it simply and rather courageously, given that he represents the congressional district that encompasses Silicon Valley: “Tax the billionaires. All 989 of them!” Moreover, expecting to hear accusations that he was calling for “class warfare,” he outright dismissed them by saying: “The billionaires have already been waging a class war.” In fact, he does not hesitate to name names and directly take them on, as he has with Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, and Mark Cuban—and when they come after him, we can readily imagine him quoting FDR’s response to the oligarchs of his day: “I welcome their hatred.”

Khanna closed his speech to the DNC with an FDR-like call to action: “This is the time for our generation of Democrats to answer history’s call. You and I have our moment to write this next chapter so that one day we will say we saved the country and did our part to build a more perfect union.”

Harvey J. Kaye, the Ben & Joyce Rosenberg Professor Emeritus of Democracy and Justice Studies at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay, is the author of The Fight for the Four Freedoms: What Made FDR and the Greatest Generation Truly Great.

Nomiki Konst was a member of the DNC Unity Reform Commission and a surrogate for Bernie Sanders's presidential campaigns.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Dispatch From Post-Election Israel
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Jo-Ann Mort
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
The real story in this election is the extraordinary and uplifting strength of the vote of Arab citizens in Israel.

The votes in Israel are still being counted. By the end of Wednesday, only half of the actual votes (not exit polls) had been counted. Nearly 80 percent of Israelis voted. While sitting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has the most votes, it will be impossible for him to garner enough allied votes to achieve the necessary majority of 61 in the 120-member Knesset. Essentially, by panicking, Netanyahu spread the word to the right wing to vote for him rather than any of the smaller right-wing parties allied with him, and he has left himself without the wings to fly. There’s a silver lining in this strategy—it means that regardless of what happens, far-right racists Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, currently powerful ministers in the sitting government, will not return to rule.

But the early election-night euphoria of the opposition, or change bloc, led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot has dissipated. Eisenkot’s second-place finish to Netanyahu deflates the center-left, to say the least, though he holds the ability to form a government by picking one of two options.

The first option would be politics as usual, choosing to form a “unity government” between parties in his bloc and Likud. Eisenkot has previously said he won’t do that. He may decide he has no choice. But he does have a choice—the second option. That would be to take the leap to drastically change the Israeli political map and include at least one of the two parties dominated by Arab citizens of Israel in a government.

The real story in this election is the extraordinary and uplifting strength of the vote of Arab citizens in Israel. They came out in massive numbers—so far doubling their previous records—with a belief in a democratic process that hasn’t worked for them previously, to vote against the extreme hatred directed at their communities under Netanyahu, as well as the devastation in Gaza and the ongoing cannibalization of the occupied Palestinian territories by the Netanyahu government. Indeed, their numbers account partially for the significant voter turnout overall.

Every Israeli who holds citizenship within the internationally recognized 1967 borders has a right to vote. This population is composed mostly of Palestinians who are descended from the pre-1948 population, many of whom live in the Galilee and northern Israel and vote for the Joint List, a secular left-wing alliance of three parties (whose leaders have said they will support a non-Netanyahu government from the sidelines), and Bedouins who mostly reside in southern Israel and vote for Ra’am, a moderate Islamic party whose leader engages with non-Islamic Israelis (and which was briefly in government when there was a non-Netanyahu government led by Bennett and Lapid). Ra’am’s number two in this election even included an Israeli Jewish Knesset member who is a former police official, intentionally running on this list to break the paradigm of Jewish-Arab division.

One Bedouin town in southern Israel reported that people waited in line for four hours to vote. They were all determined to demand their rightful place in Israel’s politics and to vote out the far-right, racist policies of the Netanyahu government. The Joint List doubled its representation.

Historically, Arab citizens—represented in this election by two different party lists—don’t usually hold the same right to government. They have been shunned by both the left- and right-wing Zionist parties because they are not part of the Zionist project. This election result could change all that. Or not. Ameer Fakhoury, a political sociologist and the academic director of the Center for the Study of Binationalism at the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute, put it this way to me: This vote could be the “beginning of political and moral repair…creating either equal belonging in a shared homeland, or the gradual ruin of both peoples.”

Gadi Eisenkot has always left an opening for himself to support a shared alliance. He crafted his preelection language carefully to take a historic leap. But whether he can hold his own bloc together is in question. His right flank, led by Avigdor Lieberman (whose votes also fell below expectations), has emphatically refused an alliance, while the left-wing party in the Eisenkot alliance, the Democrats, wholeheartedly supports the inclusion of the Arab-based parties.

Yair Golan, the Democrats’ leader, posted on social media the morning after the election:

Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel.… We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens. Now we need courage. We need leadership. We need to stop being afraid and start acting.

Eisenkot’s voters want this. An election-night survey conducted by Hebrew University’s aChord Center found that 61 percent of voters for the change-bloc parties (Yashar, Beyachad, the Democrats, and Yisrael Beytenu) want Gadi Eisenkot to form a government with Ra’am. Another 20 percent prefer new elections, 12 percent favor a rotation government with Netanyahu, and 7 percent prefer a government with the ultra-Orthodox parties.

The reality of numbers has been facing the center-left in Israel for a long time. This moment was inevitable. Netanyahu is a well-honed demagogue. He knows how to count. He knows that if he keeps demonizing the Arab citizens of Israel, he will make it more difficult for his opponents to form an alliance with them. Indeed, he demonizes to the point of inciting violence. Few may realize that the reason former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was murdered by a Jewish right-wing fanatic was not because he signed peace accords with the Palestinians but, according to his assailant, because he did so with the parliamentary support of Arab Knesset members. The opposition leader who provoked the crowds against Rabin at the time was none other than Netanyahu.

Meanwhile, the Israeli Jewish left itself has become more of a shared left, Jewish and Arab together. There is still a long way to go with this alliance, but the threads are there. One of the key civil society leaders in Israel, Rami Hod, who heads the Berl Katznelson Center and Foundation, a cornerstone think tank of the democratic left, put it this way: “An absolute majority of Israeli citizens voted today against the government of the massacre and the abandonment…. Today, Netanyahu took his ‘Arabs are flocking to the polls’ rhetoric and put it on steroids, with a repulsive, racist campaign. The parties of the change bloc face a simple choice: racism or leadership. They can either surrender to Netanyahu and the racism of Smotrich and Ben-Gvir—or they can swear in a government of their own, which includes the Arab voters.”

A third option—new elections, also something Netanyahu would enjoy exploiting—is simply a terrible idea. It reminds me of the poem by Bertolt Brecht: Instead of changing the government, simply elect another people. The reality is that, especially for the center-left in Israel (and the growing numbers of Haredi fundamentalist voters), the numbers are not there without an alliance between Jewish and Arab citizens.

Israeli democracy, as broken as it has become under Netanyahu’s too-long rule, can’t be fixed without accepting that instead of a future fueled by the Jewish supremacy and racism of the Netanyahu years, there is another way—but only by recognizing the legitimate rights of both Jews and Arabs—Israelis and Palestinians—living in one part of the world.

Jo-Ann Mort writes about Israel/Palestine for publications in the US and UK and on her Substack.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Ukraine: Time to End the War
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Robert L. Borosage, Katrina vanden Heuvel
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
For both Russia and Ukraine, the war has taken a staggering toll and poses an ever-greater danger of spreading.

It is long past time to bring the brutal war between Russia and Ukraine to an end. Now, just as both countries seem open to serious negotiations, Donald Trump perversely seems intent on giving peace a bad name.

Even as his amateur emissaries—real estate investors Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law—launched separate discussions with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Trump decided to tilt the board for Putin. He lashed out at Zelensky, saying Ukraine needed a new president. For domestic midterms consumption, he announced an “energy ceasefire” that neither combatant had heard of, temporarily approved the purchase of Russian diesel oil, and shelved the intensified sanctions contained in legislation he had signed. He delusionally claimed that “Russia, frankly, had been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” even as Russia’s attacks on Ukraine intensified. Witkoff risibly hailed Putin as a “humanitarian,” while salivating over economic deals that the United States could cut with Russia when the war ends. Trump embraced Putin’s suggestion of a tripartite summit—Putin, Xi, and Trump—to settle the war, although Trump said it should focus on nuclear weapons, not Ukraine.

Delivery of defensive Patriot missiles paid for by the Europeans has been mysteriously held up. And although Trump denied that he was responsible, Ukraine suffered sudden restrictions on its use of Starshield, the Starlink satellite program vital to providing early warning of Russian missile attacks, restrictions that Elon Musk claimed only the White House could order.

Not surprisingly, these actions spurred outrage in Europe and condemnation in the US, even echoed by some Republican senators. They also inevitably triggered the Trump derangement syndrome that muddles liberal analysis. The New York Times editorial page indicted Trump for “helping Mr. Putin wage war,” and called on the West to “continue to punish Mr. Putin, the oligarchs who support him, and Russia’s war-making economy,” ignoring the terrible price Ukrainians are paying. At stake, the Times intoned, is “whether the West can rally to protect democracy and innocent lives,” although the Times carefully noted that in this “defense of democracy,” only Ukraine should put troops and civilians at risk, and Europe should bear most of the cost.

Hillary Clinton weighed in, painting Trump once more as “a willing Putin puppet,” warning that “Putin’s not going to stop with Ukraine.” She charged that Trump wants to “divide the world: He gets the Western Hemisphere, Putin gets Russia and Europe, and Xi Jinping gets the rest of the world,” a fantasy that makes the unlikely assumption that Trump would accept the smallest piece of the world and ignores European and other nations that might have something to say about the division. In contrast, the popular liberal historian Heather Cox Richardson scorned Russia as a “minor economic player whose military is flailing at its attempt to absorb its neighbor,” charging that Trump is “openly embracing Putin and is working to destroy the strongest and most successful alliance in human history to cement that partnership, apparently with an eye to enriching himself.”

Trump’s scorn for our allies and solicitude for strongmen like Mr. Putin and Xi Jinping are notorious. And his brazen use of his office to enrich himself is contemptible. Offering bribes to Putin while undermining Zelensky is more likely to undermine than facilitate negotiations.

That said, the understandable fury at Trump’s antics should not blind us to reality. This is a war that needs to come to an end.

For both Russia and Ukraine, the war has taken a staggering toll. Russia has suffered an estimated 1.5 million casualties; Ukraine, 500,000. Both find it harder to replace the losses. A million Russians have fled the country, disproportionately the most educated and skilled of the young. Over 20 percent of the Ukrainian population has been displaced, with over 5 million leaving the country. The Russian Navy has been driven out of the Black Sea; the key Ukrainian port of Odesa, center of its grain trade, has been shut down. Ukraine, with 80 percent of its power generation and 90 percent of its food logistics infrastructure destroyed, faces a brutal winter. Russia is suffering far greater damage than Putin would have imagined. Recent attacks on its oil industry have shut down some 30 percent of its refining capacity.

With continued oil sales to China, India, and other countries, Russia has managed to avoid a recession. Ukraine’s economy has been devastated, its GDP down by a quarter since the war began, its survival utterly dependent on European assistance. The World Bank estimated the cost of rebuilding Ukraine to be $588 billion over a decade even before the most recent devastating Russian missile and drone attacks.

And the war poses an ever-greater danger of spreading. Ukrainian drones striking St. Petersburg have been reported as traveling through or being launched from NATO countries. European allies warn of an escalating Russian “hybrid war,” with suspicious drone sightings and arson at Starlink hubs. Germany has called the threat of Russian sabotage of troop facilities “significant.”

Riots are spreading across Europe, a reaction to rising economic pain significantly worsened by the sanctions that cut off Russian oil and the renewed European military buildup, topped by the soaring energy prices resulting from Trump’s Iranian debacle. Ukraine requires ever more aid just as European economic turmoil makes that ever more difficult.

The assumption in the European and American foreign policy commentariat that Putin is on his last legs, and that with renewed aid and weaponry Ukraine can win the war, is both fantasy and folly. Fantasy because it ignores the reality that Ukraine verges on collapse; folly because, were Putin facing defeat, it would increase the peril of a wider war that no rational person would risk. Nor does the hysteria that Putin will take on NATO after Ukraine make sense: Ukraine has exposed Russia’s weakness, not its strength, and inflicted a steep price for its aggression.

Polls show majorities in both Russia and Ukraine are open to peace negotiations. Both Putin and Zelensky have accepted the need for negotiations, and preliminary talks have begun.

With Russia occupying nearly 20 percent of Ukraine, any settlement will be painful. The inescapable reality is that Mark Milley, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, was right in 2022, after Ukraine had repelled the initial Russian invasion, when he urged Ukraine to “seize the moment” and negotiate. After all the casualties and destruction, the settlement will be worse now than it would have been then.

Still, we would be well advised not to allow Donald Trump’s biliousness to give peace a bad name. What’s needed instead is a global movement for ending the war. The European allies now bearing the brunt of the cost of sustaining Ukraine should help lead the negotiations, bringing expertise and experience to an American team that badly needs it. The countries that ignored US sanctions—China, India, and others—should join the push for a negotiated settlement.

Zelensky, first elected as a peace candidate, has led a courageous resistance. Now he needs even more courage to lead the country to a settlement before it is completely destroyed.

Robert L. Borosage is a leading progressive writer and activist.

Katrina vanden Heuvel is editor and publisher of The Nation, America’s leading source of progressive politics and culture. An expert on international affairs and US politics, she is an award-winning columnist and frequent contributor to The Guardian. Vanden Heuvel is the author of several books, including The Change I Believe In: Fighting for Progress in the Age of Obama, and co-author (with Stephen F. Cohen) of Voices of Glasnost: Interviews with Gorbachev’s Reformers.
