In her new book Side Effects, the Politico reporter shows that the impact of abortion bans goes far beyond reproductive health care.

In her new book “Side Effects,” the “Politico” reporter shows that the impact of abortion bans goes far beyond reproductive health care.

Alice Miranda Ollstein covers the politics of abortion as a reporter for Politico. But as she traveled the country reporting on the fallout from the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022, Ollstein began to hear another drumbeat in the background. “[O]ver the course of writing hundreds of articles, as I interviewed patients, doctors, pharmacists, researchers, and others impacted by the new restrictions, I saw how such laws were also eroding the quality and availability of health care—and not just reproductive health care,” Ollstein writes in her new book, Side Effects: How Abortion Bans Impact Everyone’s Health (published by The New Press this October).

In her book, Ollstein uncovers how the harmful consequences of abortion bans stretch well beyond miscarriage management, maternity care, and contraception, as well as, of course, delaying or outright denying care to those seeking abortions. Everyone from veterans suffering the effects of war to chronically ill patients seeking care for debilitating pain are affected by these laws. The Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision has sent ripple effects across the healthcare landscape, shaping where clinicians live, how they train, what drugs they prescribe, and how they conduct medical research. “No part of the healthcare system went untouched by Dobbs,” Ollstein told me. I interviewed her recently about the findings in her book, and as the midterms approach, I also took the opportunity to ask her about how abortion will affect the elections in November.

I’ve edited our conversation for clarity and length.

Amy Littlefield: Let’s start with an area of medicine impacted by Dobbs that is fully related to reproductive health care—contraception. How did banning abortion affect access to contraception?

Alice Miranda Ollstein: There are so many contradictory trends in the contraception space right now. You have, on the one hand, more demand than ever for contraception, including permanent contraception, because people are more afraid of an unintended pregnancy that they would not be able to terminate. On the other hand, there is reduced access. Some of that is due to the blurring of the line between what is an abortifacient and what is a contraceptive. There’s been a lot of misinformation about that, from official state government entities and circulating online. That has led to certain forms of contraception being excluded from government programs [and] government coverage. In some cases, universities that are state-run stopped providing certain forms of contraception because they were unsure if it would violate their new state abortion ban. A lot of it was in the immediate aftermath of Dobbs, but some of it still continues to this day.

AL: Let’s talk about some areas of healthcare that are less intuitively connected to abortion. How do abortion bans impede medical research, including into conditions totally unrelated to abortion?

AMO: One example is that the abortion pill mifepristone has a lot of potential, being studied in the United States and around the world, for treating certain cancers and all kinds of other conditions. I met a researcher in Florida who found that this medication had a miraculous impact on older veterans who had debilitating mental and physical impacts from Gulf War Syndrome, which is caused by being exposed to toxic chemicals in Operation Desert Storm. This medication that right now is only authorized for abortions made a huge difference for them, but because of state bans, that research got delayed and there were all these hurdles, and so veterans still cannot access this medication that could really help them. I met another researcher who was trying to study mifepristone’s impact on breast cancer, and she ended up abandoning the study altogether because she was based in a state with a near-total abortion ban and was afraid of losing access to the medication midway through the study.

AL: In the book you tell the story of Tara Rule, a New York woman who had debilitating cluster headaches, whose doctor balked at prescribing medication that could have alleviated her symptoms because the drug could cause birth defects. Can you talk about this trend?

AMO: I was really struck by the trend of people with chronic illnesses who were not pregnant, were not planning on being pregnant, in some cases physically could not get pregnant, and they were still being denied medication they really depend on because either that medication was a potential abortifacient or that medication could cause birth defects if you become pregnant while you’re taking it. What was wild to learn about is that this was happening [all] around the country right after Dobbs. It was happening in states with bans and in states with abortion protections. It was happening to people with lupus, Crohn’s, rheumatoid arthritis, Ehlers-Danlos. Sometimes it was the doctor who refused to prescribe it; sometimes it was a pharmacist who refused to fill it, and sometimes it was the insurer who refused to cover it. When Tara Rule was posting on social media about this, which went viral at the time, she started hearing from so many other people saying, ‘Hey, this happened to me, too.’

AL: Some stories of women dying while suffering miscarriages when providers delayed giving care have gotten lots of media attention. But there are other fatalities we have heard less about —like that of an Indiana woman who died when her ectopic pregnancy ruptured and she had to travel further for care because her local hospital’s labor unit had recently shut down. What does her death show about how hard it is to document deaths from abortion bans?

AMO: You’re seeing labor and delivery units around the country close, and a lot of that is economic, but in some instances the hospital themselves publicly say that the state abortion ban is a factor in losing doctors and not being able to maintain access. Doctors are also just more fearful and hesitant to treat pregnant women who are going through literally anything. Even if somebody comes in from a car accident, there’s just so much fear of accidentally seeming like you maybe caused an abortion, or you didn’t document it right. These delays can be deadly in some circumstances. It’s hard to prove causality, and I think that it’s especially challenging because the state entities that are supposed to make those determinations, these mortality maternal mortality review committees, their work has been made a lot harder by bans, and in certain states they have been censored. They’ve been fired and replaced. The reports have been delayed. I’m thinking in particular of Georgia, Texas, and Idaho. All had major disruptions of their maternal mortality review committees, and those are the committees that are supposed to go through every death during pregnancy, birth, and the postpartum period, and determine what caused it. That’s information that could save lives in the future.

AL: Another story from your book that has stayed with me is that of Samantha Casiano, who learned during her 20-week anatomy scan that her fetus had a lethal birth defect called anenchephaly. But she lived in Texas and couldn’t afford to leave her four kids to travel out of state for an abortion. Talk about her story and what it shows about the overall message of your book.

Even though the whole thesis of my book is that everyone is impacted in some way by abortion bans, some people are clearly more impacted than others, and low-income women of color are, in a lot of circumstances, being impacted the most. I reported on women in Texas who received diagnoses later in pregnancy that their fetus had a medical condition that was incompatible with life. The upper-middle-class white women I met had the financial resources, the job flexibility, the family support to leave the state and get an abortion in another state and come back. I’m not saying that they had it easy. It was very, very difficult emotionally and physically. But you compare that with what happened to Samantha Casiano, who did not have the financial resources to be able to leave the state, and she ended up carrying to term her fetus that had anencephaly, and it died in her arms four hours after birth, gasping for breath, turning purple. It was so traumatic for Samantha that when she testified in court about it as part of a lawsuit by the Center for Reproductive Rights, she actually vomited on the witness stand, just reliving that trauma. I really think about her and what differences class and other divisions can cause.

AL: One of the most compelling parts of the book is your reporting on how the Dobbs decision has politicized doctors in new ways. Can you talk about that?

AMO: A lot of abortion providers were already very politically active. They were part of lawsuits. They were outspoken. Often, they felt like they had to be. But what I saw happen after Dobbs is that all of these other doctors who never performed an abortion themselves—many of them didn’t even treat women of reproductive age—they saw the spillover effects on their own work and thought, “I really need to get involved.” I talked to neurologists, rheumatologists, oncologists, pediatricians, ER doctors, just across the medical system, and you had this happening at the individual level, where individuals were speaking out more, participating in some of these political campaigns, running for office themselves in some cases, joining lawsuits. But they also lobbied their medical societies, either state or national, to take stronger stands on access to abortion than those groups ever had in the past.

AL: How do you see abortion shaping the way that people vote this year?

AMO: There are four states where abortion is going to be directly on the ballot. That obviously brings it more top of mind in Idaho, Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia. But it’s been coming up in the Maine Senate race, where the Democratic challenger has been hammering Susan Collins over her vote to confirm the Supreme Court justices who overturned Roe, and that has become one of her bigger liabilities. There is polling [showing] that people do care about abortion as an issue, and they want candidates to talk about it, and they say they’re more likely to support a candidate who supports abortion access. But when people are asked to rank issues, it does not rank in the very top, along with things like being able to afford groceries, for instance. There are glimmers of signs that it is still a potent issue. I was interested to hear James Talarico in Texas give a pretty full-throated support for abortion rights, and that is in a tough race in a very conservative state. I don’t think he would have said that if he didn’t think it was a message that resonated with a lot of people.

Amy Littlefield is The Nation’s abortion access correspondent and a journalist who focuses on reproductive rights, healthcare, and religion. Her latest book is Killers of Roe: My Investigation Into the Mysterious Death of Abortion Rights (Hachette).

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sena Chang
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Republican-led efforts threatening young people’s rights to the ballot have sparked efforts to protect the youth vote across college campuses.

In response to increasing federal attempts to limit ballot access, lawmakers, students and college administrators are mobilizing to safeguard young people’s access to voting.

More than 80 percent of eligible voters aged 18 to 29 in key battleground states said that they “probably” or “definitely” plan to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a recent survey. Despite this enthusiasm, deep concerns remain that thousands of student voters may be thwarted from casting their ballot come November by an absence of polling sites on college campuses.

On October 15, the first day of in-person early voting in North Carolina, more than 100 students walked 40 minutes to the Guilford County Courthouse to cast their ballots after a Republican-majority state board of elections denied requests for early voting sites at two Greensboro universities.

The students, from North Carolina A&T State University, the largest historically Black university in the country, and the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, had access to on-campus early voting during the 2024 election. While dozens of students advocated for adding the two polling sites, the sites were ultimately denied in January, with the board citing low turnout.

“Honestly, it took me back to the same fight that our ancestors were fighting years and years ago in the ’60s,” North Carolina A&T senior Tatiana James, the president of the university’s NAACP chapter, told The Nation. “Today, it’s the same fight, it’s just dressed up differently.”

In 2024, the closest polling site on campus was located at the Dudley Memorial Building, which features a statue of the Greensboro Four—the four Black students from North Carolina A&T who staged a sit-in at a segregated Greensboro lunch counter during the civil rights movement in 1960. “That’s literally the history of A&T. That’s our significance,” James, who is currently mobilizing students on campus to vote early, said.

At North Carolina A&T and college campuses across the nation, Republican-led efforts that threaten young people’s rights to the ballot have sparked efforts to protect the youth vote across college campuses. In an analysis of 35 states offering in-person early voting in 2020, 74 percent of college campuses lacked in-person voting options on campus, and over half of American college students did not have any voting option on campus.

Threats to youth voting rights extend well beyond the absence of on-campus polling locations. Restrictive residency and voter-ID requirements disproportionately burden young voters, who often move frequently and may lack accepted identification, especially in states that do not accept student IDs. Young people also face a disproportionately high risk of provisional ballot rejections and late mail ballots. For first-time voters already juggling coursework, jobs, and navigating an unfamiliar electoral system, these barriers can make casting a ballot especially difficult, experts said.

“For the first time since the Voting Rights Act was passed in the 1960s, we have millions of Americans headed to the polls without clear federal protections to enforce voting rights,” Rebekah Caruthers, the CEO of the Fair Elections Center, told The Nation. She noted that such threats could disproportionately impact young voters, potentially affecting a significant segment of the electorate; nearly 50 million people between the ages of 18 and 29 are eligible to vote in November.

In Texas, the majority-Republican Tarrant County Commissioners Court cut the number of polling places by nearly a third, from 316 in the previous midterms to 224. This included the elimination of four early voting locations on college campuses, including two places at Tarrant County College campuses and another at the University of Texas at Arlington.

“If you combine the [UT Arlington] student population, the faculty, and the staff, that’s about a population of 60,000, and no polling locations except the closest one a mile and a half away,” Janet Mattern, the president of the League of Women Voters of Tarrant County, said. Mattern and her team are offering options for low-cost transportation to the polls in the county.

“If it happens in Tarrant County, it can happen in other places too,” Mattern said.

This April, New Hampshire joined 10 other states in eliminating student IDs as a form of identification. Washington voters aged 18 to 25 faced the highest rate of challenges to their mail-in ballots from 2020 to 2025, according to a recent study. And in Greensboro, North Carolina, the student polling site now located at the county courthouse is “still really inaccessible to students,” according to Olu Rouse, the cofounder and codirector of Protect Ours North Carolina.

“You have to cross multiple highways and main streets to get to the site by walking,” Rouse told The Nation. “For first-year students who do not have cars, this has always been a concern, and why we pushed so hard for an on-campus early voting site,” he said.

The threats facing young voters are not confined to the local level, experts warned. In Washington, Republican lawmakers have pushed to overhaul voter registration requirements through the SAVE America Act, which passed the House earlier this year. The proposed bill requires Americans to present proof of citizenship to election officials when registering to vote for the first time, whenever they update their registration following a change of name or address—measures that could disproportionately impact low-income youth and youth of color.

Although the bill has stalled in the Senate, similar measures have gained traction in state legislatures. Since 2024, 12 states have joined Arizona and Georgia by enacting laws similar to the SAVE Act.

The broader topic of voting rights has also reached the Supreme Court. In April, the justices ruled in Louisiana v. Callais that Louisiana’s effort to create a second majority-Black congressional district amounted to racial gerrymandering that was unconstitutional. The decision also narrowed the circumstances under which the Voting Rights Act can justify race-conscious redistricting.

“We saw it as the last attack, the last takedown of the Voting Rights Act,” Selasi Tagbor Morales, communications manager at the Alliance for Youth Action, said. “That was very much a decision that was a product of this administration,” she said.

These federal actions could have a chilling effect on young voters this November, Molly Metz, a first-year student at Penn State and the president of the university’s NextGen chapter, explained. Speaking in her personal capacity, Metz pointed to President Trump’s unfounded claims of voter fraud associated with mail-in voting and the administration’s rhetoric on election interference as possible deterrents to voting.

“I think a lot of people are also afraid to even go in person to vote,” Metz said. “It is a really scary thing to do in a climate where ICE might be there and monitor the polls, as has been threatened.” Though the administration has denied that it will send ICE agents to the polls, advocacy groups are remaining cautious.

In response to increasing federal attempts to limit ballot access, lawmakers, students, and college administrators are mobilizing to safeguard young people’s access to voting.

Last month, Senator Elizabeth Warren reintroduced the Youth Voting Rights Act of 2026, which, among other measures, would require on-campus polling stations, expand voter registration at public colleges and universities, and allow preregistration before young people turn 18. Representative Nikema Williams introduced similar legislation in the House last year.

“Young people have a constitutional right to vote, and no politician should be allowed to stand in their way. With Trump and Republicans pushing voter suppression policies and on-campus polling sites being shut down nationwide, we must act now to protect young voters ahead of the midterms,” Warren told The Nation. “The Youth Voting Rights Act will break down barriers to the ballot box and make sure young people have a fair say in the future of our country.”

These various obstacles put in the way of youth political participation collectively reveal a “constellation of abridgements of the right to vote on account of age,” said Yael Bromberg, the architect of the Youth Voting Rights Act and an American University law professor. “They may look like rollbacks to the availability of offering student identification where voter-ID requirements are in place, or continued inconsistencies with equal access to vote by mail,” Bromberg said.

At Bard College, new students stop at a voter registration booth before getting their room keys. Massive student-led outreach campaigns are also conducted, among a host of other efforts to mobilize young voters. “Colleges should not be neutral on democracy,” Jonathan Becker, the acting president of Bard College and co-editor of “Youth Voting Rights: Civil Rights, the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and the Fight for American Democracy on College Campuses” with Bromberg, said. “The foundations of American higher education are informed by a belief in engaged citizenship—that is a through line in American higher education since the revolution, and voting, as the most foundational of democratic rights, is one they should be supporting.”

One of the biggest barriers to youth voting has been a lack of information, according to Metz. “If the process becomes any bit difficult, it becomes increasingly harder to motivate people who may be on the fence about voting,” she said, pointing out that many students do not know how to start a mail-in ballot away from home or format their dorm addresses. “It’s an objectively confusing process, and it’s hard to blame them when the system is not really set up with college students in mind.” Approximately 40 percent of 18-to-24-year-olds in the nation are enrolled in college, and these young voters could help play a decisive role in closely contested states such as Maine and New Hampshire.

Ahead of the midterms, Alabama A&M student Kelvin Edwards is constantly sending e-mails urging voting as part of the campus’s civic engagement and voter registration team. A combination of tabling events, civic engagement game nights, and a planned “March for Midterms” is energizing a majority of students to show up to vote, according to Edwards.

“Groups like [NextGen America] are doing everything in their power to provide pathways [to voting],” Arianna Jones, the executive director of NextGen America, said. “The big thing for me is that young people take hold of their own futures and step into that power and recognize the fact that no one would be fighting this hard to take it away from them if it wasn’t worth it.”

Sena Chang is a student at Princeton University and a 2026 Puffin Writing Fellow for The Nation. Her work can be found in The Daily Princetonian, Teen Vogue, and LAist.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
“I doubt that Russia, China, or the United States has an army as victorious as the army of democracy of this country,” the president told his supporters.

On Sunday, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a record fourth term in office, defeating far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. After his victory was declared, Lula addressed a cheering crowd of supporters in São Paulo. Here are some excerpts from that speech, as translated by longtime Nation contributor Greg Grandin.

I wanted to thank the Brazilian people for their generosity, those who stayed with me through the length of this runoff. I want to thank the generosity of the young, who took to the streets to defend democracy. I want to thank the elderly. I know that many of them were urged on by their grandchildren to vote for me. People with cancer, people with limited mobility, with other kinds of illness. And you went to vote. It will be very important to assure them that their vote was worth it, that it will safeguard democracy in this country.

I want to thank society as a whole, which is the real winner of this election. This is an election in which we prevailed over outside interference, especially by digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate. We need to understand that crime in the digital world will be treated as crime in the real world. We can’t have monstrous, giant companies earning millions and billions, paying no taxes to this country, and trying to influence electoral results.

This election was a defeat for denialism, a defeat for lies. And I confess that every time there was a debate, I felt embarrassed, because I’ve debated with a lot of people. I’ve taken part in many elections. I meet every year with the G20, the BRICS, the G7. I meet every year with the leaders of the world. And we discuss the world’s main issues. But I never thought I’d come face to face with the genuine representative [Flávio Bolsonaro] of paramilitary power in this country. I never imagined someone could lie so much, so shamelessly, as if there weren’t a single cell of humanity inside him. It all seems fake….

I was stunned to see the enthusiasm of people singing the Independence Anthem…in a demonstration that this country does not accept being anyone’s backyard.…

This election taught me many lessons. I can assure you that we are going to change the way this country is governed. We’re going to have the people take a greater part in decision-making. And digital communication is going to get a very large place in my government.…

I won’t allow my words to be interpreted in bad faith. I won’t. I’ll say what I think and what I do. One of the things that motivated me most in these elections was not letting those people win so they could privatize our public health system.

Again, I will say that having won the election, we no longer have an adversary. I will govern for all Brazilians. In my coming term, I am going to focus on caring for our elderly, who are have given us life. Women will be treated with much more respect by Brazilian public policy. All religions will be respected on equal terms.…

Whatever anyone’s faith and spirituality, it is the responsibility of the secular state to guarantee full religious freedom, so that people can practice their faith fully. We will continue our revolution in Brazilian education. We will achieve universal full-time high school. We will universalize the student savings program so that no young man or woman drops out of school because they have to work. We’ll teach more math, more engineering. Because I don’t want to depend on Chinese or US artificial intelligence. I want to create a Brazilian one. We have to take advantage of the energy potential of a country that may have the greatest renewable energy capacity, to bring here the data centers we need, so that our data is stored in Brazil. ….

We will move Brazil from being a developing country to a developed one, through investment in the digital economy, the green economy, and the creative economy. This country will be built not by me—because many of the things I’m mentioning here I know little about—but by you. We will the people’s creative potential so as to stop being a peripheral country.… We are going to show the world how to handle climate policy. This year is the first time we’ve managed to reduce deforestation four years in a row….

This country is ready to be built. I won’t use the words “national unity,” because that phrase doesn’t always fit this country. But I want you to know: As far as it depends on me, this country will be civilized. This country has a Constitution. Nobody is obliged to like the president-elect, but he was elected to govern for everyone, based on respect for the Constitution and on his relationship with Congress.…

I want to say I have great pride. First, because I am the only president of the Republic, a metalworker without a university degree, elected four times democratically…. We had Roosevelt, who was elected four times, but he couldn’t finish his final term because he had a very serious illness. Now, I won’t want another term but I’m going to finish this term in full.… So I want to thank God, and thank you, the men and women of this country. These elections were about honor, nationalism, democracy and the future you want. I’ve never won an election in the first round, but I’ve never lost in the second. I’m 81 years old. The day after tomorrow, the 27th, I turn 81. And I want to make a commitment in front of the press and in front of you: I’m going to have the best term any president has had in this country’s history. You can be sure. I’ll dedicate 20, 24 hours a day to making this the country everyone dreams of. A country where people know they can go to sleep and wake up with peace of mind….

I doubt that Russia, China, or the United States has an army as victorious as the army of democracy of this country. A hug to the soldiers, men and women, of our army.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is the president of Brazil.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Benjamin Fogel
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
The Brazilian left has stopped the right-wing wave in Latin America. Now it has four years to work out a succession plan.

After three of the most intense weeks in the history of Brazilian politics, Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva will be president again. Though he lost the first round of the presidential election earlier this month, he went on to win a historic fourth term, finishing 4.4 million votes ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro, the crooked oldest son of former president and convicted coup plotter Jair (the final tally was 51.79 to 48.21 percent). If it wasn’t clear before, it is now: Lula is the greatest popular leader of his generation and one of history’s most gifted politicians.

Flávio has predictably refused to concede, but Lula’s margin of victory was twice as large as his 2022 margin over Jair—and unlike his father in 2022, Flávio does not have the power of the presidency to try to stop Lula from taking office. Some of his closest allies have already fled to Miami, and his brother Eduardo, a former federal deputy who exiled himself to Texas a few years ago, suggested on a podcast last week that Flávio should join him in the United States.

Flávio ran a weak second-round campaign, as scandal after scandal broke almost daily. Together, they tied him and his closest allies to organized crime, money laundering, social security fraud, the gambling lobby, and the largest banking fraud in Brazilian history. He also alienated many voters by acting as if he were already in government, announcing bizarre cabinet appointments and unpopular policies. During the debates, his attempts to first troll Lula and then to pose as a statesman both backfired.

Lula’s victory has not only stopped the wave of right-wing victories crashing across Latin America, but it also marks a major setback to Imperial Miami’s project for the region, encapsulated in the so-called Donroe Doctrine. Indeed, it is the most significant defeat for the far right internationally since Donald Trump won a second term in 2024. It was a victory against the odds: Lula won an astonishing 10 million–plus new votes in the runoff after losing to Flávio by 2.2 million votes on October 4 (47.03 percent to Lula’s 45.16). And he did it despite coordinated attempts to sabotage his campaign by Big Tech, the United States, the president of Brazil’s Electoral Court, elements of legacy media, and one of the most powerful online disinformation machines ever assembled.

The result will reverberate well beyond Brazil’s borders. The country has the largest economy and population in Latin America, and it has often been credited with the potential to become a major power—not only because it is blessed with critical minerals but also because it has the capacity to withstand bullying, tariffs, and economic warfare from the United States. That power is why even the right-wing governments of its neighbors—with the exception of the increasingly delusional Javier Milei—have already acknowledged Lula’s victory. Trump has so far stayed silent.

What, then, can the left elsewhere learn from Brazil? First, we now have an answer to the question I posed in a piece for Jacobin before the second round: whether “the politics of the street are enough to counter some of the effects of social disintegration.” The answer is a resounding yes: The politics of the street still matter.

The day before the October 25 runoff saw perhaps the two largest rallies in the history of Brazil: Close to a million people, myself included, joined Lula on Copacabana Beach in Rio, and likely well over a million occupied the entirety of Avenida Paulista, the main thoroughfare in São Paulo, the most populous city in the Americas. There were also significant rallies in all of Brazil’s other major cities, midsize cities, and even small towns. Getting people on the street doesn’t just provide an antidote to the virus of political despair; it can still mobilize voters.

Second, this is the first election I have witnessed in which the left won the online battle—despite Big Tech, particularly Meta, tilting the algorithm toward the far right. Credit for that goes mostly to a centralized online army—Lula’s Army—of 10.8 million people, organized through a WhatsApp channel in less than three weeks and commanded by the Julius Caesar of Brazilian social media, Minas Gerais Federal Deputy André Janones. The general not only turned the algorithm against the far right but also reclaimed symbols of Brazil such as the national football team’s jersey (by sending his followers on missions like posting a selfie on Instagram on a Saturday at 9 am wearing it) and made the trademarked “L” hand sign for Lula.

In this war, Janones had help from a new generation of Brazilian left-wing politicians who launched their own offensives on social media. Among them were Homeless Workers’ Movement leader Guilherme Boulos, who also serves in Lula’s cabinet as minister for the presidency; Brazil’s Marxist-Leninist answer to Hasan Piker, Pernambuco Federal Deputy Jones Manoel; and the 21-year-old Minas Gerais Workers’ Party Federal Deputy Ana Elisa Silva.

The contrast with the right is instructive. Bolsonarismo’s Militant Digital Party—as political scientist Marcos Nobre describes it, drawing on the work of Paolo Gerbaudo—is largely organic and decentralized, led by a host of political entrepreneurs who run their own online pyramid schemes (as the philosopher Rodrigo Nunes outlines in his new book Anatomy of Disintegration). It operates largely out of public view, through covert networks and individualized algorithms, and is flush with dirty money from the online gambling industry, organized crime, and various other scams.

According to Nobre, it has a hard-line base of around 25 percent of voters and has swallowed up the old rent-seeking parties of the centrão (big center) by way of a conventional party apparatus. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party is now the dominant force in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. Those gains have come not at the expense of the left, which actually increased its representation in Congress, but of old-school authoritarian, center-right, and slightly more democratic machine parties.

The left took the opposite approach. By centralizing communications and messaging, it reached not only undecideds but also those who abstained in the first round or cast null ballots, and even more than a few Flávio supporters. The result was a historic jump in turnout. The upshot is that if the left is to launch a digital counterattack against the far right, it needs to centralize communications and create a welcoming online space for alienated and isolated people looking to do more than shout into the void.

While Lula is a generational leader produced by a world-historic movement of the working class—and Janones is a digital commander who could only have emerged in Brazil—this victory still offers invaluable lessons for a left that wants not just to play defense against the far right but to go on the counterattack, combining the politics of the street with a centralized online army.

None of this will make Lula’s job easy. Governing Brazil with a Congress controlled by the far right will be an enormous task, and we can expect repeated attempts, backed by the United States, to contest the results. After all, Jair Bolsonaro was convicted of plotting a failed coup after the last election—a plot that, among other things, would have involved the assassination of Lula.

Benjamin Fogel is the head of publications at the Alameda Institute and a contributing editor at Jacobin.

In Serbia, the students may have discovered a formula for rescuing democracy through nonviolence and commitment to collectivism. Students everywhere should take note.

The real story in this election is the extraordinary and uplifting strength of the vote of Arab citizens in Israel.

For both Russia and Ukraine, the war has taken a staggering toll and poses an ever-greater danger of spreading.

“I doubt that Russia, China, or the United States has an army as victorious as the army of democracy of this country,” the president told his supporters.

The bad habits Emmanuel Macron will pass on to his successor.

The Alaska case is a red flag that Trump has no intention of accepting the results of an election that Republicans lose.

Donald Trump speaks at a rally for GOP candidates in Wasilla, Alaska.

The Democrats have a legitimate chance to retake the Senate next week. The Cook Political Report rates 13 of the open Senate seats as favoring Democrats, giving them a possible total of 47 seats. It rates seven additional races as “toss-ups.” If Democrats win four of those races, they’ll control the chamber.

I don’t actually believe any polls, anywhere, anymore, because repeated polling failures during the Trump era have left me scarred for life. But for the sake of preelection argument, we have to pretend that these pollsters have professional skills and aren’t engaged in a terroristic plot to weaponize hope.

One of the toss-up states is Alaska, where Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan is facing a fierce challenge from former Democratic representative Mary Peltola. The race could be definitive in determining control of the Senate. The seven states rated as toss-ups are: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas. Let’s say Democrats win in Michigan and Ohio. Let’s say they split Maine and Texas—Susan Collins hangs on but James Talarico pulls through, or vice versa. Alaska could easily be the fourth seat Democrats need to take control of the Senate. It’s that important. (If you tell me Democrat Adam Hamilton is going to beat incumbent Republican Roger Marshall in Kansas, then I’m going to tell you Democrats are gonna run the entire table and Trump will need nukes to maintain control.)

I don’t need the pollster-industrial complex to tell me that Alaska is close, because Republicans are doing what they always do when elections get close: They’re trying to steal it. Last week, the Department of Justice, at the personal order of Donald Trump, filed a lawsuit to try to prevent Alaska from certifying the result of the Senate election, but only if the Republican loses.

Trump and the Republican Party have engaged in numerous forms of electoral skulduggery, including trying to gerrymander their way to one-party rule, trying to purge the voter rolls of eligible citizens, and threatening to unleash an army of election thugs wearing ICE clothing to intimidate voters at the polls. In such a corrupted world, it’s tempting to think of this Alaska lawsuit as more of the same, just another attack on democracy from an administration willing to burn the whole system down to be king of the ashes.

But the Alaska lawsuit is different from everything that’s come before, and a dangerous harbinger of what is to come. That’s because everything Trump has done up to this point has been aimed at preventing or suppressing the vote. He’s been trying to stop people from voting in the first place. This Alaska thing is trying to prevent votes that have already been cast and tabulated from counting. The lawsuit contemplates the Republican’s losing—it literally takes effect only if the GOP candidate loses—and then making that loss not matter. That is a dangerous escalation that should alert people that the Trump administration has no intention of accepting the results of an election in which the Republicans lose.

If it weren’t so obviously antidemocratic, this case would present an interesting legal issue. Alaska has ranked-choice voting, so there are actually four people running for Senate in Alaska: Sullivan, Peltola, a Republican named Gerald Heikes, and a candidate with no party affiliation named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Yeah, there are two men with the same name running for the same office. That’s not a coincidence. Moreover, it’s probably a dirty trick. Daniel J. Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher who recently registered as a Republican and then, even more recently, switched his affiliation to “undeclared.” He has given money to Mary Peltola in the past. Even if most people know the difference between the incumbent Dan S. and the schoolteacher Daniel J., if there are even some people who rank Daniel J. over or instead of Dan S.—people are allowed to rank a total of four candidates—it could matter.

Daniel J. claims that his candidacy is not a plant or a trick inspired by Democrats. But just because he says it, doesn’t mean I have to believe it. I was born at night, but not last night.

After Daniel J. won enough votes during the primary to get on the November ballot, Republicans moved to have him kicked off. That case was litigated all the way up to the Supreme Court of Alaska, which ruled in favor of Daniel J. The lawsuit launched by the DOJ last week challenges that ruling.

The most important thing to know about that state Supreme Court case is that it happened in June. If the Trump administration had a problem with the ruling, it could have filed its appeal over the summer and had this all worked out by now. But it didn’t. It filed its appeal in October, days before the election, to make sure to cause maximum confusion and uncertainty in the election. Attorney General Todd Blanche claims that there was nothing nefarious about the timing of the administration’s appeal, but, again, I wasn’t born last night. Everybody can or should be able to see that the DOJ is trying to interfere with the election.

The other reason the DOJ’s delayed timing matters has to do with the remedy it’s requesting. Pending its appeal (which now cannot be resolved before the election), the DOJ is asking the court to force Alaska to delay certification of the results should Daniel J. Sullivan secure enough votes to influence the outcome of the election. This is the most dangerous part of what Blanche and Trump are doing. They’re effectively asking the court to rule that all votes cast for Daniel J. are suspect, based entirely on the theory that anybody who votes for Daniel J. meant to vote for the incumbent, Dan S.

We know that logic is wrong. There will be some people who honestly want to vote for Daniel J., especially as their second choice. He is, after all, probably a secret Democrat. If I were an Alaska voter, I would rank Peltola as my first choice and Daniel J. as my second, not because I am confused and not because I am trying to participate in a scam; I would legitimately want a retired probably-Democrat schoolteacher to represent me in the Senate over a Trumper like Dan S. Casting my vote aside, or awarding it to a guy I never intended to vote for, because the Republican Party thinks it knows what I meant to do is ludicrously antidemocratic. It can’t be allowed.

Indeed, I know that courts do not allow this kind of remedy, because I am old enough to remember the 2000 election in Florida. I remember the infamous “butterfly ballot” in Palm Beach county. For those lucky enough not to remember one of the dumbest episodes in the history of American civics: The presidential ballot design in Palm Beach county (pictured here) likely caused confusion for people who wanted to vote for Democrat Al Gore against Republican George W. Bush. An analysis of the election results showed that over 2,000 registered Democrats voted for Republican bigot Pat Buchanan (running as a third-party candidate) instead of Al Gore. Those 2,000 votes were more than Bush’s margin of victory over Gore in Florida; if people who probably tried to vote for Gore had successfully voted for Gore, Gore would have won Florida and the White House, and (most likely) the entire freaking world would be different.

You know what the courts said to Democrats who complained? Tough nooggies. They said there was nothing they could do. They couldn’t just give Gore all of Buchanan’s votes in Palm Beach. They couldn’t just assume that the voters who mistakenly voted for Buchanan actually made a mistake. For all the litigation that erupted after the 2000 election, the butterfly ballot was not part of Bush v. Gore. You can argue about whether election officials correctly counted votes that were cast, but you can’t argue that voters cast a ballot in error so those votes should be awarded to another candidate.

That said, the current Supreme Court is even more nakedly partisan than the one that decided Bush v. Gore. I don’t think this Supreme Court will give all of Daniel J.’s votes to Dan S. I don’t think this Supreme Court will allow Republicans to engineer a new election in Alaska if the current one doesn’t go the way Republicans would like. But I can’t be sure. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito seem to be so deep in the cult of the Republican Party that they will vote for whatever the administration wants. If the Alaska race turns out to be the deciding seat, who knows what the rest of the Republicans on the Supreme Court will do?

Still, my biggest worry isn’t what the Supreme Court will do in Alaska. My real worry is what this means the Trump administration is prepared to do across all states. It’s trying to stop certification of results in an election the Republicans haven’t even lost yet, so what the hell do you think the administration will do when Republicans actually start losing some of these races? Every loss will be litigated on the thinnest theory of Republican supremacy, and that opens the door to Supreme Court shenanigans every day from the close of the polls to the induction of the new Senate, which JD Vance might not even be willing to oversee properly. And during every one of these legal fights, the potential for Trump to take extralegal means to assure power, including the destruction of physical ballots he doesn’t like, increases significantly.

The Alaska lawsuit proves that Trump will contest ballots that are validly and legally cast, and Todd Blanche will do whatever Trump tells him to do. I don’t think anybody is truly prepared for how dirty Trump is going to play.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/obituary-hue.author: David Bacon

When I came back from a solidarity work brigade in Cuba in the 1970s, I landed in New York City with no place to sleep. I called Lori Huerta, a friend from California, and daughter of Dolores Huerta (1930–2026), cofounder of the United Farm Workers (UFW). Not only did I get space on the floor of the NYC grape boycott headquarters, but Dolores and her partner, Richard, César Chávez’s brother, took us out to eat. Over pizza I enthused about the island. I had stars in my eyes, for both Cuba and Dolores, and still do. I went to work for the UFW as an organizer a few months later.

Over the years, long after I had left the UFW and worked for other unions and then as a photojournalist, I would see Dolores again and again. Going to Watsonville to cover the organizing drives of strawberry workers or to Salinas for the strikes in the vegetable fields, I knew she’d be there. It was a profound experience to watch her in union contract negotiations — this diminutive woman facing off against the beefy growers across the table — and see the sense of power it gave workers. For Dolores and Eliseo Medina, another of my teachers, being a good organizer was the bottom line — doing what the workers needed.

María Elena Durazo, who came from a farmworker family to head the Los Angeles Labor Federation and now sits in the legislature, remembered, “In that world of rural California, it was the grape strike and the boycotts that taught us that the only way to end poverty and injustice was to organize together. It was the United Farm Workers who taught us that, and Dolores was the best teacher among many good ones.”

Returning from Iraq, where I photographed workers after the 2003 US invasion, I took her picture in the front line of marchers against the war. When we were in Sacramento trying to stop the anti-immigrant, anti–affirmative action, anti-bilingual initiatives, she was the first to speak out.

There was often tension in the UFW about radical politics, and being called a “red” was sometimes the route out the door. Fear of saying anything that could lead to getting fired enabled César Chávez to exert such power that even otherwise aggressive and militant organizers and workers, like Dolores, didn’t challenge him, whether about sexual abuse or political purges. Abuse is a fact in other unions I’ve belonged to, and progressive leaders have stayed quiet there too. We have to confront this system of male supremacy directly, and I know she believed this.

Her relationship with the Democratic Party was complicated. She supported some movements for political independence in the 1990s while also campaigning for mainstream Democrats. As the union’s political director, she got the California legislature to pass a union recognition bill far better than the National Labor Relations Act, as well as pesticide protections and overtime that don’t even exist in other states. Randy Villegas, our hope for breaking the MAGA stranglehold on the southern San Joaquin Valley, is someone she’s had her eye on for years. You could call her a realist.

Four years ago I walked with Dolores from Poplar to Delano, California, in honor of Larry Itliong, who started the 1965 grape strike and boycott there. She was ninety-one then, and I had a hard time keeping up. She sent me a note afterward that ended, “Sí Se Puede con El Rojo Tocino.” It was a beautiful joke.

“Sí Se Puede” are three words we all use now, but she invented this confident way of saying “Yes We Can!” “Tocino” was the nickname the union gave me in the years I worked as an organizer — it means “bacon,” my last name. And calling me “El Rojo,” or “The Red,” in this way honored my politics.

So when she called me El Rojo Tocino, I thought, “What a compliment!” I hope I live up to it.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-ice-mi.author: Eric Blanc

All signs point toward a resounding rebuke of Donald Trump in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats have opened up a commanding lead in national polls, Trump’s popularity has sunk to historic lows, and even many of his former supporters are turning against him.

There are plenty of reasons for this collapse, from rising prices to Trump’s disastrous war with Iran. But we shouldn’t forget what was arguably the single most important turning point of his presidency: the defeat of his militarized assault on Minneapolis.

In January, Trump’s administration set out to terrorize immigrants, crush resistance, and establish the precedent that federal forces could occupy American cities against the wishes of their residents and elected officials. Instead, it encountered a mass movement whose courage and discipline forced Washington into a humiliating retreat.

The political fallout was immediate. By late January, a Reuters poll found Trump’s overall approval had fallen to 38 percent, matching its lowest point of his second term to date. His approval on immigration, previously his strongest political asset, had sunk to 39 percent. Minneapolis had helped turn Trump’s signature political strength into a liability.

In retrospect, this outcome can seem inevitable. Surely Trump’s attacks were so excessive, his agents so brutal, and the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti so shocking that a national backlash was bound to follow?

But nothing was predetermined. Indeed, there’s compelling evidence that Trump and his advisers had a plan with a real chance of working: provoke Minnesota into a social explosion, whose grassroots violence and property destruction would serve as a pretext for polarizing the country and escalating Trump’s crackdown on dissent and democracy nationwide.

Similar strategies have worked for authoritarian governments in other times and places. In Minneapolis, the trap failed because of the movement’s exceptionally high level of organization and nonviolent discipline.

It’s clear that ICE, under administration orders, was consciously provoking the people of Minneapolis this past winter. Thousands of heavily armed, poorly trained federal agents flooded the Twin Cities. Masked officers conducted aggressive raids, detained residents, confronted legal observers, and deployed chemical weapons against protesters. On January 7, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and killed Renée Good, a thirty-seven-year-old mother. And rather than de-escalate, Washington doubled down.

On January 13, Trump warned Minnesota that a “DAY OF RECKONING & RETRIBUTION” was coming. Two days later, he threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act unless Minnesota officials stopped the supposed “professional agitators and insurrectionists” confronting ICE.

Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem confirmed that military intervention had been discussed. And by January 18, the Pentagon had placed roughly 1,500 active-duty soldiers on prepare-to-deploy orders. The administration was preparing the ground for deploying the military.

Nor do we have to guess how some White House officials hoped events would unfold. On January 17, Zeteo reported that two administration officials acknowledged that figures inside the White House would welcome significant violence by Minneapolis protesters. One senior official said they “would not mind it” if such violence provided a pretext for invoking the Insurrection Act.

In other words, widespread disorder wouldn’t have been a setback for Trump’s strategy. It could have provided exactly the excuse he needed.

The logic was straightforward: Provoke confrontations through extraordinary federal aggression. Wait for enraged protesters and community members to retaliate with widespread violence or property destruction. Then portray the movement as an anarchic threat to public safety, rally Americans around the need for order, and justify an unprecedented expansion of federal military power.

Recent revelations make the administration’s methods even more disturbing. As Wired reported this week, federal investigators infiltrated activist organizations and communications networks on an extraordinary scale. Attorney Kevin Riach, representing one of fifteen Minnesota activists facing federal charges, has argued in court that undercover agents participated in organizing groups while seeking to entice participants into criminal activity.

The strategy was hardly irrational. Research shows that property destruction, even on a limited scale, can sharply undermine public support for protests. It would not have taken much for Trump to transform a confrontation about federal repression into a national argument about supposedly violent leftists and blue-city disorder.

Imagine the aftermath of Good’s killing had Minneapolis descended into sustained rioting, widespread vandalism, and attacks on ICE or local police. How long before the national conversation shifted away from the shooting itself toward whether Trump should restore order and whether movements should oppose property destruction and violence?

Trump’s central miscalculation wasn’t underestimating the anger his agents would generate. It was choosing to stage this provocation in one of the most deeply organized progressive metropolitan areas in the United States.

Minnesota has a rich, decades-long tradition of labor, immigrant-rights, and religious organizing. Groups including Unidos MN, ISAIAH, Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 26, and the Twin Cities teachers’ unions had spent years developing relationships, training leaders, winning reforms, and building the capacity to act together. As SEIU Local 26 President Greg Nammacher explained, their January resistance would not have succeeded without years of preparation: “We would not have met it if we had not built a capacity beforehand.”

These organizations saw clearly that a violent confrontation on Trump’s terms was one the movement was likely to lose. As JaNaé Bates Imari, co–executive director of the faith-based organization ISAIAH, explained in an interview on The Dig:

Part of what is happening in Minnesota is a needling by the federal government to try to get us to respond in a particular way. And Minnesotans across the spectrum have said we will not take the bait . . . . No one [is] confused about who the peacekeepers are in the midst of what’s taking place.

Crucially, organizers went beyond merely preaching restraint by building the organizational capacity to turn restraint into a collective practice.

Unidos developed mass trainings for legal observation of ICE operations, ultimately training approximately thirty thousand people. ISAIAH trained hundreds of clergy, while allied groups trained thousands in nonviolent civil disobedience. Neighborhood Signal chats sprang up. Residents organized to document immigration raids, distribute whistles, support families sheltering at home, and mobilize neighbors.

There were genuine pressures toward escalation. Some protesters threw objects at officers, and instances of vandalism occurred. After witnessing federal violence, not everyone agreed about the limits of confrontation.

But breaking with unstrategic leftist norms about a “diversity of tactics,” the movement’s leading organizations had developed the relationships and legitimacy needed to establish collective norms about disciplined nonviolent mass action. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that protesters confronted a suspicious flag-burner and that participants in organizing chats rebuked and expelled people proposing violence.

By cultivating shared expectations, training participants, challenging provocations, and giving people effective alternatives, the Minneapolis movement provided opponents of ICE with something more powerful to do than express their fury.

On January 23, an estimated 75,000 or more people marched through downtown Minneapolis in subzero weather during the Day of Truth and Freedom strike action. According to organizers, roughly a thousand businesses, overwhelmingly small businesses, participated in the work stoppage.

The movement’s militant resistance and discipline helped keep the attention on federal agents’ terrorization of Minneapolis’s undocumented community, as well as the heroism of two innocent Americans who decided to stand up for their neighbors.

Renée Good and Alex Pretti were ordinary people who resisted injustice and paid with their lives. But their deaths alone would not necessarily have been enough to defeat the administration’s offensive. Because without an organized movement committed to preventing mass violence and property destruction, their killings could have become entangled in a debate over which side was responsible for the disorder. Instead, Trump lost control of events and the narrative.

We don’t have to rely entirely on hypothetical scenarios to see what might have happened otherwise.

France’s growing protests this fall against the cost of living and the government have recently provided a troubling counterexample. What began with high school students protesting deteriorating educational conditions in September grew into a broader movement drawing in unions, Yellow Vests, and other groups demanding economic and political change.

But on October 17, huge demonstrations across the country were accompanied by extensive violence and destruction. Shops were looted in Paris, public buildings attacked, and Marseille’s city hall vandalized.

Remarkably, Le Monde reported that the government had deployed only about sixty thousand police nationwide — tens of thousands fewer than normal — even though intelligence services had warned of a high risk of violence and looting.

Before October 17, much of the national discussion had focused on police repression and the legitimacy of the protesters’ grievances. Afterward the government seized the opportunity to recast the confrontation as a battle against disorder. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu attacked the radical-left La France Insoumise, while politicians on the Right demanded harsher policing.

The events on October 17 were a gift to the right. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen received the most positive assessments of any major political figure’s response. And an Ipsos survey found that 55 percent of French respondents believed the leftist party La France Insoumise had contributed to the tensions and violence.

As historian Luca Provenzano has argued, allowing disorder to spread can itself be a highly effective state strategy. During France’s May 1968 upheaval, for example, authorities shifted from highly visible repression toward a more restrained police posture that created space for student escalation. A subsequent Interior Ministry assessment concluded that protesters’ excesses had helped restore support for order. The Right went on to win a sweeping electoral victory.

Whether the French government deliberately allowed the October 2026 violence to unfold is not yet established. But the danger doesn’t depend on proving a grand conspiracy. A state can benefit from disorder whether it consciously encourages it or simply takes advantage when it erupts. That’s precisely the trap Minneapolis avoided.

Of course, Trumpism is far from defeated. We don’t know exactly how badly MAGA will lose on Tuesday, and even a decisive electoral rebuke won’t automatically stop his political prosecutions, authoritarian ambitions, or continued mass deportations.

Trump could still try to manipulate or reject unfavorable election results, whether next week or in 2028. He could again seek to provoke widespread disorder and use the ensuing fear to justify repression.

To defeat Trumpism nationwide and to transform our country, we’ll need big, durable, welcoming organizations, new recruits beyond the ranks of existing college-educated activists, trusted leaders, and the ability to launch rapid, disciplined nonviolent action when necessary.

The best way to honor Renée Good and Alex Pretti — and to thank the people of Minneapolis for their courage and sacrifice — is to learn from what they achieved. Mass nonviolent resistance doesn’t happen automatically. It has to be organized. And when it is, even the most powerful government on earth can be forced to retreat.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/imperialism-.author: Max B. Sawicky
