It is common for mainstream news outlets and political commentators in the United States to describe socialists as “very liberal” or simply “progressive,” or to puzzle over how to draw ideological lines between democratic socialists and others on the broad Left. There are, in fact, serious differences — differences that socialists would do well to sharpen and articulate for the public. At the same time, as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) grows by leaps and bounds, some commentators prefer to highlight those DSA positions that are furthest from common agreement.

I have previously tried to distinguish between socialists and liberals when it comes to domestic economic policy. But what about foreign policy? Here I propose a socialist agenda for this field. Again, one of my objectives is to show how a socialist approach would differ from a liberal one when it comes to US relations with other countries.

As socialists work their way into positions of governing power in the United States in the form of urban mobilizations and the growth of the Squad and the DSA-allied bloc in Congress, we could expect the organs of “national security” to be among the last to open up. Historically, they have enjoyed considerable autonomy and have been the least susceptible to democratic accountability. The ease with which presidents of both parties have launched armed hostilities against other countries without the approval of the Congress, rumored to be a constitutional prerogative, has become notorious. Still, with growing political power will come opportunities for the Left to play a serious role in foreign policy.

There was a moment in the 1970s when the fabled Church Committee exposed an endless series of dirty deeds committed by the Central Intelligence Agency, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and others. That exposé was in 1975–76, and Senator Frank Church hailed from Idaho — these days as far right as a state can get.

Going back further, there was a moment in 1956 when a Republican president, Dwight D. Eisenhower, blocked US support for British and French imperialist machinations against Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal, which was surely Egypt’s right. Other than these anomalies, however, US-led Western imperialism has enjoyed free rein since World War II.

The basic dilemma for the Left is that the good deeds we might hope for our government to perform with the aid of its military would be the responsibility of a state that gives no sign of interest in beneficent acts. A libertarian friend impressed upon me the inevitability that any intervention by the (capitalist) state would be poisoned by craven, ulterior motives.

My thesis is that the overriding ulterior motive in US foreign policy since World War II has been world hegemony, enshrined in the infamous George Kennan “X Article,” which has superseded narrower economic concerns. It is this to which the quasi-autonomous institutions of US national security have been dedicated, hastening to fill the gaps left by the dissolution of the British and French empires.

Liberalism is compromised by sympathy for the hegemonic imperative. One notorious example was given by President Bill Clinton’s secretary of state, Madeleine Albright, who referred to the United States as “the indispensable nation.” In other words, hegemony was essential.

Another Democratic foreign policy maven and former human rights activist Samantha Power played the genocide card in her celebrated book, A Problem from Hell, to argue for a more interventionist US foreign policy. But when hell settled over Gaza and Ms Power had a chance to say something, her response to the carnage in 2024 was to send tents.

The Biden administration fiddled while Gaza was being blown to smithereens. It also dithered on the revival of Barack Obama’s deal with Iran, which likely made it easier for Donald Trump to initiate hostilities with the country when he returned to office. Of course, under the George W. Bush administration, we had the flaming lies about “weapons of mass destruction” (WMDs) in Iraq, now being replayed in absurdist form by President Trump with regard to Iran. Meanwhile, the US withdrawal from Iraq has left that field open to our supposed enemy, Iran. Nobody said foreign policy had to make sense.

The narrower, default stance on the Left has been blanket opposition to military intervention by the United States or its allies. The posture of liberal pro-interventionists is to exaggerate the horrors of a failure to intervene. These justifications have usually been spurious. Historically, every assault by a great power is justified by claims, usually fallacious, of a prior injury or of an overriding humanitarian purpose.

Complicating the picture, there are ways a powerful nation can commit aggression against a weaker one without resorting to military means. One has been the predatory use of indebtedness, about which much has been written. Another is the imposition of sanctions on the movement of capital and trade goods. The current weapon of choice is the tariff, not to mention the actual, lethal use of force by the United States and Israel currently on display in the Middle East. The effectiveness of sanctions and tariffs is open to question. And now the Trump administration is discovering in Iran that even its military might cannot always wrest concessions from a recalcitrant government.

Socialists, given the opportunity, would at the very least place a high bar before any proposals for US military intervention. We must reject the default to liberal excuses that skirt the underlying motivations for aggression. We saw many of these in the debates about Iraq: The Bush administration would not competently prosecute the war. The search for WMDs should have been allowed to continue. We failed to gain the cooperation of allies. Bush failed to get the proper approval from Congress.

Now the critique of choice is that “President Trump has no plan”; we also see efforts to use the spike in gas prices to score political points. We should be wary of putative anti-Trump voices with thin critiques of the Iran attacks. The issue is not the lack of an end game, Israeli connivance in the war, the shifting excuses for objectives, or the carnival of MAGA national security leaders.

And Trump does in fact have a plan: it is to flex, blow things up, kill people, and pose as the second coming of Douglas MacArthur. It may seem to boil down to the president’s deranged personality and feeble intellect, but the fact is that the US foreign policy establishment, guiding both parties, has had Iran in its sights for decades, ever since the rise of Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh in the 1950s and later the fall of the US puppet regime led by the shah.

War-skeptical liberals hoping for criticism of Trump’s Iran adventure from less militaristic US allies have been disappointed by the repetition of the bankrupt mantra that Iran must be blocked from possession of nuclear weapons. The allies have also been weak in their criticism of the machinations of Trump and the Israeli state in the Middle East, much like centrist or corporate Democrats in the United States.

One theory for US aggression that is bandied around is the notion that the international reserve currency status of the dollar would be endangered by oil exporters such as Iraq or Iran. But world trade is already conducted in a variety of currencies, not just the dollar, and this will increasingly be the case as the rest of the world — particularly the People’s Republic of China — continues to grow economically compared to the United States. Nations with large stocks of dollars also face the dilemma that if the dollar declines in value, which would happen if they tried to reduce their holdings in favor of another currency, their own wealth would take a hit.

Reductive economic explanations have plagued left-wing foreign policy debates more broadly for a long time. Back in the day, it was suggested that the Vietnam War was about the quest for control of rubber exports from Southeast Asia. In Kosovo, there was talk of vast mineral resources for which Western powers lusted. With Afghanistan, it was said that a pipeline was really what was at issue.

Now everything is supposed to be about oil. This may be so for Trump himself, but we know he is ignorant. The relevance of oil can be exaggerated. First, the world is weaning itself off fossil fuels, since wind, solar, and even nuclear can be more economical and secure. Second, the United States itself is a net exporter of fossil fuel. Third, much oil extraction sits uneasily on a knife-edge of profitability: a limited shift in its world price puts the higher-cost extraction operations out of business, which naturally limits investment. And fourth, investment in new extraction takes time and is prey to large, up-front, fixed costs that become sunk costs. Investment in oil and gas extraction is discouraged by the obstacles and uncertainties noted above; it can’t be turned on and off like a spigot.

This classic economic explanation for US aggression has been given new life by Trump’s nakedly acquisitive Venezuelan venture. We should not doubt that commercial opportunities existed in all of the targets of US interventions, including opportunities for fossil fuel exploitation. But the politics of hegemony, behind which stand the broad interests of capital, looms above them all. This basic analytical framework distinguishes socialists from liberals.

Today Donald Trump seems to have reduced the overarching, historic priority of Western imperialist hegemony, strongly founded in economic factors, to his personal dominance, wealth, and unrestrained freedom of action. We still lack a comprehensive story that explains the current regime, other than loose talk about nutty billionaires who want to go to Mars. Perhaps their influence, along with that of crypto bros, Gulf monarchs, and Israel’s rampages, exercise more leverage on Trump and US foreign policy than ordinarily understood.

We could imagine exceptions to default anti-interventionism. The big one now is Ukraine. Nobody proposes to send North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) troops up against Russians in Ukraine, but other types of assistance have been supported. I won’t try to resolve the Ukraine aid debate here, except to claim that there is a legitimate anti-Russian-imperialist rationale for aid. Socialists will probably remain divided on this question. There is a thin line between sending Ukraine missiles and sending US soldiers to fight alongside Ukrainians. (I don’t doubt the latter is also in progress, sub rosa, in the form of quasi-official trainers and operators.)

The broader issue is the fate of Europe, threatened on one side by the Russian Federation and on the other by Trump’s disdain for the NATO alliance. Europe is the chief redoubt of social democracy in the world, with all its faults, in sharp contrast to neofascist trends in Russia, India, Turkey, Hungary, Israel, the Philippines, and the United States itself. The fixation of the Left on NATO tends to gloss over this fact. Europe might also be considered a preferable rival for US hegemony; it would certainly be an improvement over Trumpist governance.

The other elephant in the room is Israel. By now the case for a liberal, much less a socialist, Zionism is dead. There can be no arguing about a death toll of seventy-thousand-plus, with a count that grows with new atrocities every day. The political collapse of Labor Zionism opens the way for a recovery of the history of Bundism, celebrated in the fabulous new book by Molly Crabapple.

A common theme for Ukraine, Palestine, and Iran is the right of a people to self-determination. This is a principle socialists ought to keep at the forefront; it was good enough for V. I. Lenin. Socialists have always been pioneers in the furtherance of democratic rights in capitalist countries, and democratic rights in domestic affairs logically extend to democracy in foreign policy — hence national self-determination. We may not like how some nations exercise such rights, but we often regret how other individuals exercise their freedoms, too. That doesn’t mean we are against freedom.

If an imperial hegemon is going to be meddling in affairs outside its borders, it should be limited to sending money and material assistance where it is needed, without conditions. In Ukraine, we could say that nation’s right to self-determination overrides concerns over the dangers of US-centric hegemony. In any case, the chief beneficiary of support for Ukraine is Europe.

An implication of the right of nations to self-determination, which in principle would logically, unavoidably apply to Israel, is the rightful sovereignty of nations. The dark side of sovereignty is the implied freedom of national governments to commit crimes against their own residents. There can also be a collision of national self-determinations, again vividly illustrated in Israel versus Palestine, so the principle cannot be an absolute one. But it can’t be ignored either. Israel has arguably forfeited its right to self-determination, just as could have been said of Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.

One good rationale for the rights of nations and peoples (among which I would include Palestine) to be free from aggression is for the sake of world peace. I would designate peace the second socialist principle for foreign policy. Socialists like peace; the working class always bears the greatest costs of war.

Once military force is put to the side, the other sorts of economic aggression can be dealt with by diplomacy. Setting aside how Trump’s addled mind conceives of them, tariffs are ideally a device to more fairly apportion high value-added manufacturing, which every country seeks, among nations. So too can disagreements that lead to sanctions be resolved, short of the use of force.

Predatory international lending can be reformed. Debts can be relieved and payments rescheduled on more bearable terms, or canceled outright. Support for international institutions of diplomacy and aid such as the United Nations, which Trump is trying to supplant with his “Board of Peace,” can be strengthened. Most of this is consistent with a liberal perspective, but that doesn’t make it useless.

Regarding tariffs, liberals tend to swing against the working class in favor of a mythical “free trade.” For socialists, tariffs ought to serve a fair trade agenda that assists economic development in the poorer nations and promotes economic sustainability, especially with respect to climate change.

One debatable off-ramp from foreign policy liberalism is the so-called realist school in international relations. In recent years, the most visible public faces of this thinking have been John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt, mostly for their bracing criticism of Israel and the Zionist lobby. Yet underlying “realism” is a chauvinistic, foundational prioritizing of US national security — hence it is not a suitable framework for socialists.

The realists do tend to have better arguments than liberals, as the latter are caught between the impulse to do good deeds and the realities of national power. The realists’ skepticism and hardheadedness about military adventurism have been more persuasive. This restraint could prove to be reversed, however, in the case of escalated conflict with China, which is an unambiguous rival to the United States for superpower status.

International working-class solidarity is my proposal for a third basic socialist principle of foreign policy. But that idea is bedeviled in the near term by the reality that presently workers rely on their own governments for security. In that light, the straightforward posture is to stand for national self-determination, which means noninterventionism and peace.

Liberals tend to be animated by a desire to see the government right wrongs elsewhere. Consequently, they are suckered by appeals for humanitarian interventions. They are also reluctant to call a crackpot excuse an outright falsehood motivated by bad intentions. And out of patriotic reservations, they gloss over foreign policies rooted in exploitative economic schemes. They have yet to figure out the disastrous trend, not least for Jews themselves, in Zionism. (Some on the Right have, it seems: former US Ambassador to South Africa Patrick Gaspard pointed out that there was no resignation from the Biden administration over Gaza equivalent to the recent protest by the MAGA neofascist Joe Kent.)

In this respect, socialists, going against stereotype, are often much more realistic about government and politicians. Liberals are the dreamers, and US foreign policy is the nightmare from which we all have to wake up.

The three basic socialist principles of national self-determination, peace, and international working-class solidarity offer a way out. The liberal, on the other hand, is caught between patriotic hopes for humanitarian interventionism, invariably dashed, and a desire for peace; they also fail to reckon with the relevance of trade policy to working-class interests. Incidentally, trade policy could conceivably benefit workers in the countries of our trade partners by upholding labor-rights components of trade agreements, a purpose for which liberals are usually asleep at the wheel.

It seems possible that socialist principles for foreign policy would even have some currency among Trump voters. The divisions among them over the Iran war are well known. Their neo-isolationism dovetails with socialist opposition to the hegemonic imperative, not to mention “forever wars.” Neither is the Democrats’ embrace of free trade doing them any good among working-class Trump voters.

The biggest obstacle to a peace-oriented foreign policy is the susceptibility of voters of all political types to paranoia. For that, a ready antidote is at hand: the manifest, recent failures of bipartisan-cum-Trumpian foreign policy in Libya, Syria, Iraq, and Iran. Aside from the usual, scandalous neglect of ongoing genocides in Africa and Palestine, the key fact undermining the usual US foreign policy nostrums is that its adventurism has failed in its own terms.

https://hellgatenyc.com/renewables-publi.title: What if NYC Just Built Its Own Renewable Energy Infrastructure?
https://hellgatenyc.com/renewables-publi.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/renewables-publi.text:
New York City's renewable energy buildout continues at a snail's pace. As of 2025, 90 percent of the power we use in the city comes from non-renewable power sources like fossil fuels burned at local power plants, while peaker plants burning fossil fuels continue to line the city's waterfront, spewing nitrogen oxide and other particulates into the city's neighborhoods during the hottest days of summer. The City has set a goal of relying on 100 percent renewable energy by 2040, but that looks increasingly unlikely, even with the long-awaited Champlain Hudson Power Express line bringing hydroelectricity in from Québec. New York's massive wind power projects are in the crosshairs of the Trump administration, and Governor Kathy Hochul has embraced an "all-of-the-above approach" to energy: approving a fossil fuel pipeline and pursuing a dramatic—and controversial—expansion of nuclear capacity in the state. 
But there has been one bright spot amidst all the climate and energy backsliding—New York City has been building out its solar power infrastructure far faster than expected, with the city expected to smash a 2030 goal for 100 megawatts of solar four years early. Solar power, unlike wind turbines, nuclear energy, or hydroelectricity, is cheap to build, and is done with no collateral consequences for nearby communities.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.title: Trump Vows to Send Election “Monitors” to Maine After Far-Right Conspiracies Spread
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.author: Noah Hurowitz
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.text:
With voters set to cast ballots in two critical races that could help determine control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, fears of potential voter suppression are running high in Maine.
Officials in the state have prepared for months against the possibility of election interference from federal officials, and the state remains on high alert in the run-up to the general election on November 3.
Training materials for law enforcement officials in the state, obtained by The Intercept through a public records request, were updated this year for the elections to include explicit references to federal statutes barring armed federal agents from polling sites.
In an interview with the New York Times this week, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the inclusion of such references was a direct defense in response to the fearmongering around election integrity from President Donald Trump and his administration.
“This is the first time ever that we have had to engage in scenario planning to safeguard against potential federal interference in elections,” Bellows said. “It seems like the federal government is now adversarial to the states.”
Bellows’s office offered up the training slideshow, which cites a U.S. law that bars armed civil or military officers from posting at voting sites, to law enforcement personnel in the run-up to Maine’s primary election in June and again in the lead-up to the general election on November 5.
Nationwide, Democratic officials have expressed fears that the Trump Administration might weaponize U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or other federal agencies to undermine the rights of voters. In New York, state Attorney General Letitia James issued a reminder to voters that federal officials may not “police the polls,” and the Arkansas chapter of the NAACP called out the assignment of federal election monitors to two counties in the state as potential intimidation.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, has sounded the alarm about the alleged scourge of non-citizens on the voter rolls, sending agents from the FBI and ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations division to probe alleged fraud. A handful of people in California, New York, and North Carolina have been indicted for allegedly voting as non-citizens, but a review of similar cases by the Washington Post found that such cases were often the result of honest mistakes.
In Maine, worries about federal interventions at polling places flared when — following a slew of social media videos from Trump allies suggesting that fraud is already taking place among the state’s Somali American community — a local outlet reported that the Department of Justice would be sending election monitors to the state.
Jon Fetherston, a journalist with the far-right Maine Wire, which is funded by conservative megadonor Leonard Leo, was seen following people in and around an early voting site at Lewiston City Hall and aggressively questioning them. (The Maine Wire did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
Critics said the moves were tantamount to voter harassment, but Maine Wire editor-in-chief Steve Robinson later defended them as an act of election transparency. Robinson, who has led a crusade against what he alleges to be a network of fraud in the state’s Somali American community, questioned the role of interpreters tasked with helping “jobless Somali bums” cast their ballots.
In the wake of the Maine Wire controversy in Lewiston, Bellows confirmed to the Maine Morning Star that a wave of federal election monitors would be headed to polling sites in Lewiston and Portland.
The Department of Justice on Tuesday confirmed to The Intercept that it intends to send election monitors to Maine for Election Day, but did not elaborate or respond to specific questions about where the monitors were to be sent.
“We will have around 1,000 monitors in counties throughout the United States, but we will not share the full list until Election Day,” a Justice Department spokesperson told The Intercept in an email Tuesday. “All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate.”
Robinson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Collins Takes Right-Wing Bait
With Maine a key battleground state for control of Congress — Democratic challenger Troy Jackson is seeking to topple long-serving GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and the Democratic House candidate Matt Dunlap is seeking to best former Gov. Paul LePage in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District — temperatures are running high in the state.
Progressives in Maine worry that even without a robust federal presence at voting places — whether monitors are armed or not — activist campaigns like the one undertaken by the Maine Wire journalists could pose a potential threat to voters’ rights.
“Basically, if you were walking into City Hall and you were Black, you could expect to have this guy come up to you with his phone and ask you all sorts of rude and obviously racist questions,” said Ben Chin, co-director of the progressive Maine People’s Alliance. “We’re trying to encourage everyone to come out to vote, but it makes sense why that might give people pause. You hear a guy like that is outside a polling location, it’s reasonable to wonder, ‘Should I go down there right now?’”
In a statement to The Intercept, Bellows said the state and the city of Lewiston were taking steps to ensure that voters could cast a ballot free of harassment.
“We have received complaints about the intrusive filming, photography, and harassment of voters in the City of Lewiston by political operatives,” Bellows told The Intercept in a statement. “All voters should be able to exercise their right to vote without feeling watched, questioned, or harassed, and we take these allegations seriously, particularly when it appears that voters were targeted for no other reason than their race or ethnicity. We understand the City of Lewiston has taken steps to address the problem, and we will continue to monitor the situation.”
Collins, meanwhile, took the Maine Wire’s reporting seriously after Fetherston asked the senator at a campaign event about the role of interpreters, which he and the Maine Wire cast as “electioneering.”
“I’m unaware of those allegations, but certainly only Americans should be voting in American elections,” Collins said. “And it is troubling to me if people are being accompanied into voting booths and handling ballots in a way that is not sanctioned by law.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/yeme.title: The Incredible Shrinking Superpower
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/yeme.author: Juan Cole
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/yeme.text:
The Limits of American Might
The failure of Tel Aviv and Washington to achieve their war aims in Iran has resulted in the most dramatic American retreat from a region since the U.S. flight from Vietnam in 1975. This startling American defeat — after a generation of forever war failures and stalemates — has been thrown into broad relief by the resumption of another regional conflict that has received far less attention than the Trump administration’s sputtering war with Tehran. This fall, the forces that most Americans know as “the Houthis” have conducted a blitzkrieg in their native Yemen and have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure with missiles and drones. In doing so, they have put a spotlight on the limits of American power, and the shrinking U.S. military footprint, in the Middle East.
The long-standing conflict between Saudi Arabia and northern Yemen’s Ansarullah, or “Helpers of God,” led by the Houthi clan, heated up again in July 2026, when Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa International Airport to prevent a Houthi delegation from landing on its return from the funeral in Iran for slain Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The Ansarullah government launched its own attacks and, in October, managed briefly to close Saudi Arabia’s own airport. The renewed war has now expanded into a regional conflict, with Pakistan, Türkiye, and, recently, Egypt pledging to defend the kingdom from attack, though none of these regional powers appear eager to conduct operations in Yemen itself. Notably absent from the current conflict is Saudi Arabia’s most powerful ally, the United States, since President Donald Trump has repeatedly declined to intervene on behalf of his Saudi allies.
The typical U.S. press framing of Ansarullah as an “Iran-backed militia” is inaccurate, since the movement has local, Arab nationalist reasons for its actions and is a full-scale government that rules some 80 percent of Yemen’s population. Still, it does receive surreptitious technical and military support from Iran, though nothing like the hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech armaments — from kits turning 2,000-pound “dumb” bombs into precision munitions to advanced air-to-air missiles — that the U.S. provides the Saudis. Ironically, Trump’s war on Iran, fought in conjunction with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, weakened the Saudis and exposed their vulnerabilities to military attack by Iranian drones and missiles, impelling them to seek a symbolic win over a less formidable enemy in neighboring Yemen. But the weaknesses exposed by Iran’s drones helped encourage a vigorous Ansarullah rejoinder.
The Incredible Shrinking Superpower
The American refusal to join Saudi Arabia’s war signals a profound degradation in U.S. capabilities and standing in the Middle East. The U.S. military had, for decades, dominated the region from a network of about 20 major bases. The U.S. Navy operated out of the headquarters of the Fifth Fleet in Manama, Bahrain. The U.S. Air Force flew missions from the massive al-Udeid Air Base in Qatar, which housed 10,000 U.S. personnel. Thousands of ground troops were barracked in Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Jordan. The Pentagon admitted that “Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict. In addition, dozens of U.S. aircraft were destroyed or damaged during OEF.”
The naval base at Manama, one of America’s most important naval facilities and headquarters of the Navy’s Fifth Fleet, was destroyed by Iranian strikes. (Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao admitted last month that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”) The loss of Manama led to supply shortages and poor morale aboard the USS Lincoln and other ships patrolling the Strait of Hormuz, bedeviling Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.
The CIA offices at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh were annihilated. Iran struck al-Udeid’s evacuated Combined Air Operations Center in Qatar, from which the Pentagon had directed its strikes on enemies as diverse as the Taliban and ISIL over recent decades, and rendered this facility inoperable. All U.S. troops were also withdrawn from Iraq, a process accelerated by the inability of U.S. missile interceptors to protect them from attacks by Iran and allied Shiite militias there.
Iran’s deployment of swarms of Shahed drones caused the United States and Israel to use up much of their stock of interceptors, which are time-consuming and expensive to replace. A basic Shahed costs as little as $20,000, though new hardened versions are more expensive — whereas a Patriot interceptor costs $4 million. One reason the Trump administration may be reluctant to intervene in Yemen is that if the U.S. cannot fly missions from al-Udeid, and cannot be sure any new fighter-jet fleets stationed in the region will be safe from Iran, given the paucity of interceptors, the Pentagon will have a limited ability to rescue any U.S. pilots shot down over Yemen.
America’s Profound Weakness in the Middle East
Saudi Arabia launched a war against the ascendant Ansarullah in 2015 when the latter staged a coup in the capital of Sanaa. The Ansarullah movement is rooted in Yemen’s Zaidi Shiism, though it is more radical than traditional Zaidism. (Zaidi Shiism differs substantially from Iranian Shiism, having no ayatollahs and having relatively good relations with Sunnis.)
About a third of Yemenis are Zaidis, who predominate in the north of the country, and many have long resented the dominance of their politics and culture by neighboring, oil-rich, Sunni Saudi Arabia, whose official ideology is hard-line Wahhabism, a puritanical form of Islam that insists on a literal interpretation of the Quran. Wahhabi proselytizing among the Shia enraged the Houthi clan and their followers began rebelling against the government of military dictator Ali Abdullah Saleh in 2004. But when he was deposed by popular demonstrations during the Arab Spring in 2012, Saleh gradually allied with the Houthis, and by 2015 about half the Yemeni military rallied to their side, along with some major Sunni tribes.
In response to the Houthis’ rise, a Saudi-led coalition that included the United Arab Emirates began bombing Yemen in 2015. Until 2022, the U.S, then militarily dominant in the region, provided the Saudis with strategic advice, weaponry, and in-air refueling for their fighter jets in the Yemen war, though Riyadh’s tendency to bomb civilian infrastructure rather than confining themselves to military targets caused tension between the two allies. While the Saudis and their coalition pushed the Houthis out of much of the south of the country, including Aden, they were unable to dislodge them from the north. The Saudis implicitly acknowledged their failure with a United Nations-brokered truce in April 2022, which largely held until this past summer.
The Forever Wars Effect
America’s forever wars against Middle Eastern countries that decline to accept the Israel project or American corporate neocolonialism helped reignite the Saudi–Yemeni conflict. Iran is the last major state in the region that rejects Israel and is off-limits to U.S. corporate investment, a stance that inspires much of Washington’s animus. Netanyahu was therefore easily able to persuade Trump, as a privileged visitor to the White House Situation Room, to attack Iran in February.
The glib expectation of Netanyahu and of his Mossad chief at that time, David Barnea, that the Islamic Republic would crumble if Israel murdered Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and around 50 other high-ranking regime figures proved wishful thinking. The notion that Iran was vulnerable to a tightened petroleum blockade was turned on its head by the hard-liners who ascended to power after Khamenei’s death. Largely veterans of the grueling eight-year Iran–Iraq War of the 1980s, the country’s new leaders pursued a policy of “de-basing” toward the United States, taking out its main regional military facilities.
In addition, Iran launched precision strikes at the energy facilities of their Arab Gulf neighbors who had hosted those American bases. They struck Kuwait’s national petroleum company and its fields and refineries. They took out 17 percent of the production of Qatar’s Ras Laffan natural gas facility, even though Doha had good relations with Tehran and had mediated for Iran. Tehran also struck ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, using missiles and drones, scaring the major shipping insurers into withdrawing their contracts. Few shipping magnates would risk cargoes worth billions of dollars without insurance.
Iran threw the world into an energy crisis reminiscent of the 1970s, which would have been even more devastating had China not released oil from its vast private and public petroleum reserves and cut its oil imports from 11.5 million barrels a day to under 9 million barrels a day, a move partially enabled by its turn to electric vehicles, which saved it 1.5 million barrels a day. High gasoline and diesel prices hurt Asia more than the United States, but prices rose globally. A third of the world’s helium, essential for cooling computer chips in the production process, comes from the Gulf, and that supply was also interrupted, increasing the price of electronics.
By successfully striking Saudi Arabia, Iran demonstrated that the kingdom’s ability to protect itself is imperfect and its infrastructure is vulnerable. By blockading the Strait of Hormuz in a way that the United States had difficulty undoing, Iran demonstrated the vulnerability of key world maritime arteries, something Ansarullah had already highlighted by striking at shipping in the Red Sea to protest the Gaza genocide.
Blockade for Blockade
When the Saudis bombed Sanaa’s airport in July 2026, Ansarullah’s leadership appears to have decided that Riyadh posed an ongoing existential danger to their state and sought to strangle the Yemeni economy, just as Israel had done to Gaza. Moreover, they sensed that the kingdom could be rolled back in the wake of the failure of the Israeli–U.S. war on Iran. Just as Iran had weakened the Gulf Arab states with its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis believed they could seriously degrade the Saudi economy by blocking Riyadh’s shipping through the Bab al-Mandab, “the Strait of Tears,” between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi exports through the Strait of Hormuz had fallen substantially. The kingdom did, however, have an escape valve: its East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Ships loading at Yanbu then headed for Saudi Arabia’s major Asian markets through the Bab al-Mandab. If Ansarullah could make the tanker captains fearful of this transit, they could reduce Saudi Arabia’s income even further. The Houthi spokesperson, Muhammad Abd al-Salam, warned that the prohibition of Saudi shipping was only the first step in a tit-for-tat strategy of “blockade for blockade.” The idea wasn’t original. The Saudis and the U.S. had often attempted to blockade petroleum imports to northern Yemen during the seven-year Saudi–Yemeni War.
In the subsequent three months, Ansarullah deployed missiles and drones constructed from Iranian models by military engineers trained by the old nationalist government of Ali Abdullah Saleh, many of whom had joined the Ansarullah military, in what has been called a Yemeni “military industrial complex.”
Just as the kingdom’s interceptors had proven unable to prevent Iranian strikes on targets such as the CIA section of the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, they sometimes failed to halt the barrage of Yemeni missiles and drones. Refineries and oil installations, even the headquarters of the state oil giant, Saudi Aramco, in Dhahran, were hit. In October, Ansarullah closed Riyadh’s International Airport, just as the Saudis had attempted to close that of Sanaa in July. Ansarullah also surged out of their mountain strongholds and made a major push to Yemen’s southwest coast, taking the strategic port of Mocha overlooking the Bab al-Mandab. They also moved on Taiz, an inland industrial city of nearly 1 million inhabitants, one of the last major population centers not already under their control, in a campaign that tested the ability of the small Saudi-backed government of Rashad al-Alimi in Aden to resist it.
Highlanders and Oil Sheikhs
Just as the Vietnam War was one conflict among many fought in the Third World during the Cold War between the U.S. and the Soviet Union, so the Saudi–Yemeni War of 2026 is part of the larger struggle between the U.S. and Israel and Iran. Still, just as Vietnam was more about Vietnamese anticolonialism, nationalism, and sovereignty than about Communism and the ownership of the means of production, so the Saudi–Yemeni War is about Yemeni autonomy more than it is about the loose Houthi alliance with Iran. The conflict is not primarily between Zaidism and Wahhabism, though religious tensions are part of the story, but is far more rooted in a struggle between desperately poor Yemeni highlanders and fabulously wealthy Saudi sheikhs.
The plutocratic Saudi ruling elite is closely tied to Washington and has secret dealings with the Israelis, with whom it shares a distrust of the poverty-stricken Palestinian resistance, and views Ansarullah as cat’s paws of Iran in the Arabian Peninsula and as radical republicans trying to overthrow the region’s oil monarchies in favor of populism. For its part, Ansarullah are Arab nationalists, anti-American, and seek to use oil resources for populist purposes. And they have been willing to attack Israel to defend the Palestinians of Gaza from genocide.
Last week, Ansarullah battered targets across Saudi Arabia, prompting a further pullback from the region by Washington. The Yemeni forces attacked King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. An Ansarullah spokesperson said the group also targeted the Saudi defense ministry in the capital, Riyadh, along with an Aramco site in Yanbu, and an airport in the southern city of Abha. Reports also emerged of an attack on another Aramco oil field.
“Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure,” wrote State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott in an October 21 post on X, after the wave of attacks, ordering “non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members” out of Saudi Arabia.
It’s just the latest evidence of the most significant regional retreat by the U.S. in half a century and evidence of profound American military decline. The outcome of their war with the Saudis will not determine the issue of the U.S.–Israeli contest with Iran, but the very ability of Ansarullah to prosecute it points to the profound weakening of the American posture in the Middle East.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

https://hellgatenyc.com/kine-musubi-hawa.title: Get Made-to-Order Musubi at This Nifty UWS Hawaiian Spot
https://hellgatenyc.com/kine-musubi-hawa.author: Scott Lynch
https://hellgatenyc.com/kine-musubi-hawa.text:
name:Kine Musubi;address:128 West 72nd Street, New York, New York, 10023;longitude:-73.98006188650736;latitude:40.77775034166158;website:https://www.kinemusubi.com/;picks:Spam Lakika, Ebi Opae, Tofu Mauka;
Chi Ian Chan spent his first 30 years in O'ahu, Hawaii, growing up in Honolulu's Chinatown. And he's quick to tell you that he never surfed a day in his life (he prefers skateboarding). Four years ago, he left his native island for Manhattan—specifically, Hell's Kitchen—to be with his now-wife and business partner Lizzy Han.
Chan loves his new home, but he told Hell Gate that the thing he missed the most about life in the South Pacific was musubi, the classic Hawaiian rice-and-Spam snack that's ubiquitous in Honolulu, but shockingly difficult to find here.
"There was no musubi in New York that satisfied my cravings," he said, "so I made my own." Chan started selling it over a Facebook neighborhood group. That led to a series of Sunday musubi pop-ups at an Upper West Side sushi restaurant, and then, upping his commitment in May of 2025, to signing a lease for a slender space on prime West 72nd Street. After sixteen months of waiting on permits and for construction to be completed, the neighborhood now boasts the city's only musubi shop, Kine Musubi.

https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.title: Meet ProPublica’s 2026 Class of Emerging Reporters
https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.author: Talia Buford
https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.text:
ProPublica’s Emerging Reporters Program provides support and mentorships to college students who are pursuing careers in investigative journalism and need additional training and financial support to help advance their goals.
Participants receive a $9,000 stipend, a trip to the annual NICAR investigative journalism conference, occasional training and presentations by speakers. They’ll also be paired one-on-one with ProPublica journalists who can help counsel them on stories, build their connections in the industry and expose them to the varied paths that careers in investigative journalism can take. Past Emerging Reporters have gone on to work at The New York Times, The Associated Press, Fresnoland, Capital B, The Tributary and other outlets.
Our goal is to encourage the next generation of journalists who seek to shine a light on abuses of power and produce stories with moral force that provoke change. In choosing the class, we look for students who demonstrate an early dedication to journalism as a career, through internships, work at local news outlets or work at campus publications. And where those opportunities — which are often unpaid — aren’t accessible, we look for other ways the student has shown an eagerness and a drive to learn the craft.
This year’s class of exceptional student journalists are from schools in Illinois, Texas, Nebraska, Iowa and New York.
Meet our 2026 class:
Annisyn Krebs-Carr (she/her)
Annisyn Krebs-Carr is a senior at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign studying journalism and animal sciences. She is a reporter for Illinois Public Media Student Newsroom, where she reports on the ongoing housing crisis in Champaign-Urbana. Previously, she served as the arts and entertainment editor at The Daily Illini, the independent newspaper at the university. She is now the managing editor and oversees content produced by the entire newsroom. In 2026, she interned for St. Louis Public Radio and formed relationships with the investigative reporters at NPR’s Midwest Newsroom. This is where she developed a deeper appreciation for investigative journalism. As she continues her journalism career, she wants to focus on how the criminal justice system has failed, and continues to fail, Black people. She also wants to explore how environmental racism has impacted lower-income communities. After graduation, she hopes to work in a public media newsroom and report on local stories while honing her investigative journalism skills. Long term, Annisyn hopes to build a dedicated career as an investigative journalist in public media.
Jessica Meza (she/her)
Jessica Meza is a senior at the University of Nebraska, Lincoln studying journalism, advertising and public relations. Jessica works across mediums, including in data visualizations, video, print and social media, with an emphasis on audio reporting. Jessica hopes to begin her career in investigative, in-depth reporting, focusing on marginalized communities. She hopes to use her reporting to amplify the voice of people facing hidden injustices in her community. Other interests include housing, immigration and food reporting. Jessica currently works at Nebraska Public Media as a reporting intern. She previously interned at NPR’s Midwest Newsroom and, as the Hortencia Zavala Foundation intern, wrote for The Fulcrum and the Latino News Network. In 2025, she was part of the team at Nebraska News Service that was awarded a regional Society of Professional Journalists Mark of Excellence Award for its investigative project on missing and murdered marginalized women.
Lajward Zahra (she/her)
Lajward Zahra is a senior English major at Rice University in Houston, originally from El Paso, Texas. Her reporting focuses on politics, immigration and the environment, particularly in Texas. She is a 2026 writing fellow at The Nation and has written for the magazine since 2023. She previously interned with the Houston Chronicle editorial board in summer 2025, reporting and writing on local and state politics, including the Texas Republican Party convention, among other issues. Lajward’s freelance work has also appeared in publications including The American Prospect, Teen Vogue, Business Insider, Rewire News Group and Scalawag. She was a 2024 Asian American Journalists Association Voices fellow.
Thai Theodoro (she/her)
Originally from Brazil, Thai Theodoro studies political science with a concentration in Latin American studies at Grinnell College in Iowa. Now in her senior year, she is the managing editor of The Scarlet & Black, Grinnell’s independent student newspaper. Thai has interned at The Boston Globe, the Des Moines Register and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, and her reporting has been published in dozens of newspapers across the country. She is a member of the New York Times Corps and a former participant in the National Association of Hispanic Journalists’ Student Project. Thai is passionate about telling untold stories, pursuing investigative reporting with the power to challenge the status quo, using the three languages she speaks to reach underrepresented communities, and, of course, writing the occasional quirky story.
Tsehai Alfred (she/her)
Tsehai Alfred is a senior at Columbia University studying English. She is the 150th editor-in-chief and president of the Columbia Daily Spectator, the campus newspaper, and is also an intern on CNN’s criminal justice team. Over the summer, she was a Dow Jones News Fund intern at VTDigger, an accountability-focused newsroom in Vermont, investigating the troubled integration of AI into healthcare, a struggling dairy farming industry, and soaring police use-of-force payouts. Previously, she has interned at City & State New York, covering the 2025 mayoral race and city council; at PBS News as a Gwen Ifill Journalism Fellow; and at her local news outlet, the Virgin Islands Consortium. Her reporting interests include local government, economic inequality, and political and corporate accountability.

https://apache.be/2026/10/28/buitenspori.title: Buitensporig politieoptreden bij vreedzaam protest in Antwerpen: wie beschermt de kwetsbaren?
https://apache.be/2026/10/28/buitenspori.author: Abel Meers
https://apache.be/2026/10/28/buitenspori.text:
Het Antwerpse De Coninckplein gaat dezer dagen onophoudelijk over de tongen; het vormt het brandpunt van het debat over overlast en veiligheid in onze wijk, in onze stad. Midden oktober was dit plein het toneel voor een vreedzame betoging tegen de nieuwe ‘claimersmaatregel’ van waarnemend burgemeester Els van Doesburg (N-VA). De reactie van de politie was disproportioneel.
“Ik heb pijn! Waarom doen jullie dit? Jullie beschermen just niemand. Iedereen is bang van jullie!” schreeuwde een jongen, zijn gezicht bebloed, donderdagavond (15/10) uit tegen de undercoveragent die hem enkele minuten daarvoor had toegetakeld. Zittend op de dorpel van een koffiebar wat verderop wist hij in enkele zinnen de essentie van de avond te vatten. Daarna werd hij per ambulance afgevoerd om gehecht te worden in het ZNA Cadix.
Deze maatregel past in een politiek van symptoombestrijding; de maatschappelijke ellende in een stad los je niet op met willekeurige arrestaties
Ik was die avond aanwezig op het De Coninckplein bij het burgerprotest tegen de omstreden nieuwe maatregel. Die laat de politie toe om gekende daklozen, thuislozen en mensen met een verslavingsproblematiek voor maximaal twaalf uur bestuurlijk op te pakken, in het kader van de “strijd tegen overlast” in de Seefhoek.
Die preventieve arrestaties konden aanvankelijk zonder aanleiding gebeuren, wat op 12 oktober werd bijgesteld. Sindsdien moet er een ‘claimerfeit’ aan voorafgaan, of de voorbereiding ervan. De politie van Antwerpen heeft sinds 1 oktober al 615 van dit soort bestuurlijke arrestaties uitgevoerd.
Dat de uitdagingen in Antwerpen-Noord reëel zijn en maatregelen absoluut nodig zijn, staat buiten kijf. Maar de stigmatisering die dit beleid met zich meebrengt, is allesbehalve de oplossing. Het past in een politiek van symptoombestrijding; de maatschappelijke ellende in een stad los je niet op met willekeurige arrestaties.
Muur van blauw
Wie objectief naar de menigte op het protest keek, zag dan ook geen relschoppers. Het publiek bestond uit bezorgde buurtbewoners, medewerkers uit de daklozenopvang, eerstelijnshulp en zorgverleners. Zelfs de omliggende cafés stroomden vol met sympathisanten. Toch voelde de politie zich genoodzaakt dit vreedzame protest op te wachten met een buitensporige muur van blauw: acht arrestatiebusjes, bewapende eenheden, agenten in burger en een handvol reguliere agenten.
Waarnemend burgemeester Els Van Doesburg (N-VA) benadrukt in de media te pas en te onpas dat de politie altijd éérst inzet op dialoog en de-escalatie. Het bemiddelingsteam was inderdaad aanwezig en kwam ons vooraf melden dat we een halfuur gedoogd werden, waarna we verzocht zouden worden uit elkaar te gaan. Na dertig minuten doken onaangekondigd agenten in burger op die de groep hardhandig uit elkaar dreven. Vier mensen werden opgepakt. Twee mensen geraakten gewond door het politiegeweld. Eén jongeman kreeg daarbij zulke zware klappen in het gezicht dat hij bloedend per ambulance moest worden afgevoerd. Hij houdt er wellicht een litteken als levenslang aandenken aan over.
De aanwezigen waren bezorgde buurtbewoners, medewerkers uit de daklozenopvang, eerstelijnshulp en zorgverleners
Toen ik het bemiddelingsteam nadien vroeg waarom er niet, zoals ons was gezegd, eerst werd gevraagd om te vertrekken, kregen we nul op het rekest. “Wij moeten in de eerste plaats de veiligheid van onze eigen mensen garanderen”, klonk het. Op mijn repliek dat ik me zélf ronduit onveilig voelde door de disproportionele politiemacht op straat, viel een stilte. Mijn weg naar huis was versperd door agenten met wapenstok en schild. Op de vraag hoe ik dan veilig naar huis kon, antwoordde een van hen: “Probeer maar, we zullen eens zien wat er gebeurt als je langs daar loopt.”
Deze disproportionaliteit lijkt helaas structureel. Dat uitte zich niet alleen op die avond, maar weerspiegelt zich in alledaagse situaties op exact dit plein. Mijn broer werd hier onlangs tijdens een interviewopdracht voor de universiteit zonder enige aanleiding geviseerd en om zijn identiteitskaart gevraagd. Wie deed hij kwaad? Net als buurtbewoner Erik, die − als ik de VRT NWS reportage over het protest mag geloven − al vier keer zonder duidelijke reden werd gecontroleerd. Waarom mocht dit protest, georganiseerd en gedragen door onze wijk zélf, niet in dialoog doorgaan?
Dat deze alledaagse intimidatie snel kan omslaan in fysiek geweld, ondervonden velen van ons al tijdens een eerdere, vreedzame betoging van de Antwerpse Coalitie voor Palestina. Omdat ik op de Suikerrui “niet snel genoeg achteruit stapte”, kreeg ik toen zonder waarschuwing een matrak in mijn nek. Even later kwam een vriend met pepperspray in de ogen naast me schuilen voor het waterkanon. Die avond brak mijn vertrouwen in de politie, maar nog veel meer mijn vertrouwen in de politiek. Zeker wanneer Els van Doesburg kort daarna live op televisie de feiten op het terrein stelselmatig verdraaide om het hardhandige politieoptreden te verantwoorden.
Disproportioneel optreden
Ik schrijf dit stuk vanuit een comfortabele positie: ik ben een witte man, ik ken mijn rechten en heb de middelen en het platform om dit disproportionele optreden aan te kaarten. Ik doe dat bewust, omdat de publieke opinie zich vaak moet baseren op officiële politieverslagen die niet altijd stroken met de feiten op het terrein.
Als ordediensten zich al zo intimiderend opstellen tegenover geprivilegieerde burgers, studenten en hulpverleners, wat betekent dat dan voor de mensen in de marge?
De vraag die mij na donderdagavond het meest bezighoudt is deze: als ordediensten zich al zo intimiderend opstellen tegenover geprivilegieerde burgers, studenten en hulpverleners op een doodnormale donderdag, wat betekent dat dan voor de mensen in de marge? Wat betekent die 'claimersmaatregel' voor de verslaafde of de thuisloze die ‘s nachts op dit plein door diezelfde eenheden wordt benaderd?
Antwerpen-Noord is een buurt met uitdagingen die vragen om maatschappelijke en menselijke oplossingen. Repressie is geen zorg. Een stad – een samenleving – die de dialoog met haar eigen hulpverleners en buurtbewoners vervangt door groteske intimidatie, creëert geen veiligheid. Ze creëert wantrouwen, en verliest uiteindelijk haar menselijkheid.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/bite.title: Prosecutors Want to Keep a Man in Prison for His Wife’s Murder — Despite Judge Saying Their Evidence is Junk
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/bite.author: Liliana Segura, Jordan Smith
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/bite.text:
Alabama attorney Larry Grissett was checking Facebook in late September when he saw a news story about a man he represented in a murder trial more than 40 years ago. According to the article, a federal judge had just vacated the conviction of that client, Charles McCrory.
Grissett was stunned. He later summed up his reaction: “Vindication.”
McCrory was 26 years old when he was accused of brutally killing his wife in the small town of Andalusia. He insisted he was innocent — and Grissett believed him. There was no evidence connecting McCrory to the crime; prosecutors seized on a supposed bite mark found on his wife’s body, which a state expert claimed to match to McCrory’s teeth.
Grissett was never convinced by the so-called bite mark. At McCrory’s 1985 trial, he said, Grissett’s own dentist sat through the expert testimony and found it preposterous. “He says, ‘There’s no way that guy can say that,’ Grissett recalled. “I mean, anybody with common sense would know that.”
In a September 21 ruling describing the case against McCrory as “thin,” Trump-appointed Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., zeroed in on this junk forensic science. Not only would the alleged bite mark not be allowed into evidence today, Huffaker wrote, bite-mark analysis itself “is grossly unreliable and unsupported by relevant scientific bodies. It amounts to nothing more than rank speculation.”
Unless the state moves to retry him within the next six months, Huffaker concluded, McCrory must be released from prison.
The ruling was not only momentous for McCrory, who has insisted on his innocence for more than four decades, but it also marked a new victory in the long legal battle against junk forensics — and the discredited discipline of bite-mark analysis specifically.
Yet more than a month after the decision, McCrory remains behind bars with no sense of when he might walk out. Although his lawyers asked the court to free him on bond pending the state’s decision to release or retry him, the Alabama attorney general’s office filed a motion last week asking Huffaker to reconsider his order overturning the conviction. The state’s appeals will likely drag out McCrory’s ordeal through the holidays and into next year.
In a statement, McCrory’s current legal team praised Huffaker’s “explicit acknowledgment that criminal convictions based on discredited bitemark evidence cannot stand.” Mark Loudon-Brown, senior attorney at the Southern Center for Human Rights, and Chris Fabricant, director of strategic litigation for the Innocence Project, said they are “grateful for the decision and look forward to continuing our fight to bring Mr. McCrory home.”
In 2022, The Intercept published a lengthy investigation into McCrory’s case, detailing the flaws in the state’s conviction. The case attracted additional media coverage, highlighting the problem of junk forensic science. Despite the glaring problems with the evidence against McCrory, Alabama courts have routinely rejected his appeals and in 2023, the state’s parole board denied McCrory release.
Julie Bond McCrory’s body was found inside her home in Andalusia on May 31, 1985. Her head was bashed in, and she’d been repeatedly stabbed in the chest. The couple’s son Chad, then 3 years old, was found unharmed in his bed. Police quickly pointed to McCrory as their only suspect: He and Julie were separated, and McCrory had been having an affair. At trial, the theory seemed to be that he’d savagely murdered Julie to be free from her.
The police investigation was cursory at best. Detectives found no physical evidence to connect McCrory to the bloody crime. Meanwhile, they ignored some evidence altogether, including two windows in Julie’s bedroom that were found open, but which investigators failed to dust for fingerprints. Police also failed to consider an alternate suspect, a man who worked at an excavating company bordering the McCrorys’ backyard and who, just weeks after Julie’s murder, committed a home invasion rape of another local woman. He was convicted and sent to prison for that crime.
Ultimately, the state latched onto a single piece of physical evidence against McCrory: a pair of small indentations on the back of Julie’s right arm, which prosecutors concluded was a bite mark made by McCrory’s teeth.
To sell this theory, the state employed famed forensic dentist Richard Souviron, a star prosecution witness in the recent and sensational trial of serial killer Ted Bundy. Although Souviron initially said he couldn’t definitively link the two marks on Julie’s arm to McCrory’s teeth, at trial he was unequivocal that they matched.
Bite-mark analysis is based on a two-pronged foundation. First, that the shape and arrangement of our teeth are unique, like DNA, and second, that skin is a suitable substrate for recording this uniqueness. As it turns out, there’s no science backing either assertion. In fact, research into the discipline has routinely found the opposite — that human dentition is not unique and that skin, with its malleability, is a terrible medium for accurately recording any injury. This makes bite-mark analysis a random and entirely speculative practice.
Still, after taking center stage at the Bundy trial, bite-mark analysis took off in the 1980s and ’90s and, despite not having any basis in actual science, made its way into courtrooms around the country, turning forensic dentists like Souviron into newsmaking, swashbuckling crime fighters.
In the years that followed, however, bite-mark analysis was increasingly called into question and ultimately exposed as junk science, a subjective pattern-matching practice that has led to dozens of wrongful convictions. At least four of those, including McCrory’s, are cases in which Souviron served as the prosecution’s expert.
In 2019, Souviron recanted his testimony in McCrory’s case, providing an affidavit to Fabricant and Loudon-Brown, who presented it at a 2021 evidentiary hearing in Andalusia. “As a forensic odontologist I no longer believe the individualized teeth marks comparison testimony I offered in his case was reliable or proper,” Souviron wrote. “I no longer believe, as I did at the time of trial, that there is a valid scientific basis for concluding that the injury found on the skin of the victim in this case, assuming that the injury is in fact teeth marks, could be ‘matched’ or otherwise connected to a specific individual, such as Mr. McCrory.”
Despite the fact that their key witness had disavowed the evidence they used to send McCrory to prison for life, prosecutors fought to preserve their conviction. At the 2021 hearing, they insisted that McCrory was guilty, based on the same evidence they presented at trial. They recast the supposed bite mark as “teeth marks,” implying that, while bite-mark analysis may be discredited, the study of “teeth marks” is a separate and valid discipline. Even if Souviron had not testified for the state, they argued, jurors could have looked at photos of the marks on Julie’s body and the dental molds taken from McCrory and decided for themselves that McCrory inflicted the wounds.
Covington County Circuit Court Judge Lex Short, who presided over the hearing, agreed with the prosecutor. So did the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals, which upheld his ruling in favor of the state. But Huffaker did not.
Huffaker took exception to the notion that analyzing “teeth marks” is somehow separate from bite-mark analysis. It is clear, he wrote, “that bitemark identification is based on analysis of individual teeth markings.”
But “most importantly, the state court unreasonably determined that, even without Dr. Souviron’s expert testimony, a reasonable jury could compare the bitemark evidence with McCrory’s dentition themselves and find that it belonged to McCrory,” Huffaker wrote. “This finding blinks reality in light of the evidence presented by McCrory at the postconviction evidentiary hearing.” In a footnote, he added that “if an expert could not testify about bitemark identification because it is junk science, a jury should not have been allowed to consider it either.”
McCrory is not the only person who is still fighting for his freedom decades after being convicted based on discredited junk science. Last year, Chris Duncan was declared innocent nearly 30 years after being sent to Louisiana’s death row based on bogus bite-mark evidence. He was released one day before Thanksgiving. In his case, a video showed the state’s supposed bite-mark expert manufacturing the evidence that was used to convict Duncan.
As in McCrory’s case, Louisiana prosecutors have nevertheless continued to insist their case against Duncan is solid. And as in McCrory’s case, this has not gone over well with some judges. Earlier this year, Louisiana Supreme Court Chief Judge John Weimer wrote that bite-mark evidence “should be discarded and no longer have a place in the realm of forensic science.”
“Long ago, some who were thought to have the best and brightest minds of that time endorsed ‘trial by water’ as a means of determining a person’s guilt or innocence. We now look back at those practices as asinine and absurd, since those who fell victim to those practices often did not survive, regardless of whether they were found guilty or innocent,” Weimer wrote. “Thankfully, as scientific knowledge evolved, there was a realization that these practices had no basis whatsoever in logic, reason, or the search for truth, and the practices were discarded.”
As the holidays approach, McCrory’s family remains hopeful that he will soon walk out of prison. His son Chad, who is now in his 40s, has attended a dozen parole hearings with the hope of one day seeing his father released.
Grissett, McCrory’s former lawyer, reached out to Chad to share his hope that McCrory will finally come home. While memories have faded in the tight-knit community of Andalusia, many people remember McCrory’s case, he said.
“Everybody sees this was junk science,” Grissett said. “You don’t have to be a scientist to understand that.”
It’s “sad that it’s taken this long,” Grissett said. It haunts him that “somebody’s still out there who murdered this lady. And I’m afraid that they’re not gonna look into that.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
