https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n44-a.author: Frédéric Loore, Roger Job
https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n44-a.text:
Pronostic vital engagé
Soins palliatifs à domicile
« On ne parvient plus à remplir notre mission ! » C’est le cri d’alarme des équipes de soins palliatifs à domicile en région bruxelloise. Entre sous-financement, crise globale du système de santé et attentisme politique, le secteur est au bord de la rupture. Les conséquences sont concrètes : les soignants s’épuisent et des patients meurent sans l’accompagnement garanti par la loi.
Plus tôt dans la journée, Noë (iel), « infi » spécialisé en soins palliatifs, faisait encore des blagues auxquelles riait sa patiente, une septuagénaire d’origine marocaine, flanquée de ses deux filles. Toutes trois réfugiées au premier étage climatisé d’un immeuble vétuste, proche de la gare du Midi à Bruxelles, elles s’efforçaient d’oublier à la fois la canicule et les pinces du « crabe » occupé à tisonner les intestins de la vieille Berbère. Cette dernière, la main parcheminée agrippée à celle de Noë, égrenait les ingrédients de sa meilleure recette de couscous, espérant se distraire de sa douleur lancinante.
À présent, Noë, qui travaille pour l’asbl Sémiramis, se tient au chevet de Lucas (prénom d’emprunt), 25 ans. Changement radical de décor et d’atmosphère, devenus soudain cliniques. Dans la pièce qui jouxte le vestibule d’une maison de maitre, située dans le très chic quartier du Châtelain, le mobilier de décoration a fait place à un lit médicalisé. Couché sur les draps écrus, l’ainé d’une fratrie de trois enfants. Sa figure de porcelaine est recouverte d’un peu de mort. Sans doute parce qu’il tient à la regarder en face.

https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n44-a.text:
Photos à la carte
Clichés d’identité
Chaque pays impose ses propres règles pour les clichés d’identité. Un casse-tête pour ce magasin photo bruxellois qui accueille une clientèle internationale.
Derrière le comptoir du magasin de photo Les Années Lumière, implanté au cœur du quartier européen à Schuman, Juliette Velissariou feuillette son grimoire : une farde énorme, avec des centaines de pages aux bords jaunis et déchirés. Il répertorie les règles propres à chaque pays pour la réalisation de photos d’identité.
« C’est bien ce qu’il me semblait », sourit-elle en scrutant la feuille dédiée au Kirghizistan. Au centre de cette page, trois points d’interrogation. « C’est la première fois que je dois faire la photo d’identité d’une personne du Kirghizistan. Bon, vu qu’on n’a pas d’information, on prend la photo belge par défaut, c’est-à-dire une image de 3,5 cm sur 4,5 cm, sur un fond blanc avec le visage dégagé et une expression neutre. C’est une photo assez standard, donc, la plupart du temps, ça passe. »
Les pays d’Asie centrale sont très peu représentés dans la clientèle de la boutique. Ce sont généralement plutôt des citoyens issus des 27 pays membres de l’Union européenne qui viennent se faire tirer le portrait. Néanmoins, avoir son pays qui siège au Parlement européen n’empêche pas le flou dans les règles à appliquer. « Je n’ai jamais pu avoir de règles précises pour les photos d’identité italiennes, alors on les a devinées, admet Benoît De Cuyper, patron des Années Lumière. On a déjà dû refaire plusieurs fois une photo, car elle était refusée. L’Italie avait modifié les règles sans rien …

https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n44-a.text:
Bienvenue en Belgique, où les escalators sont en panne
Les « escalators » sont des escaliers roulants qui, parfois, ne roulent plus. Ou ne roulent pas. Dans un article du Knack, le journaliste Stijn Tormans s’interroge : ces pannes qui nous accueillent dès l’aéroport de Zaventem seraient-elles une spécialité belge ?
« J’adore les escalators, disait le comique américain Mitch Hedberg. Un escalator ne casse jamais. Quand il est en panne, il devient temporairement un escalier. C’est pourquoi on ne devrait jamais voir de panneau “escalator en panne”, mais simplement “escalier temporaire – veuillez excuser la commodité”. »
Soyons clairs : c’est une blague. Elle a fait rire le monde entier, sauf nous. Ici, c’est une réalité. Il y a quelque temps, un panneau « escalier fixe » était placardé à côté d’un escalator cassé dans la station de prémétro Elisabeth, à Anvers.
La fréquence à laquelle ces installations sont en panne dans notre cher pays est tout bonnement effrayante : nous souffrons d’une forme inquiétante de maladie de l’escalator. On s’en rend véritablement compte quand on revient, comme c’est mon cas, d’Hawaï, par exemple, où les escalators fonctionnent normalement. La toute première chose que j’ai vue à mon retour à Zaventem, c’était une enfilade de voyageurs haletants qui trainaient leurs valises le long du tristement célèbre escalator cassé de l’aéroport. Bienvenue en Belgique. Sur le trajet jusque chez moi, j’en ai encore repéré trois. En grimpant à grandes enjambées le dernier, je me suis demandé si ce pouvait être une manigance des pouvoirs publics visant à amener tout le monde à faire de l’exercice.
J’ai aussi pensé au pays si souvent décrié dont je revenais, les États-Unis, où fut inventé l’escalier mécanique, au XIXe siècle. Aujourd’hui encore, tant d’années …

Les quatre fers en l’air
Où enterrer mon cheval ?
Cinq cimetières animaliers existent en Belgique. Un seul accueille les dépouilles d’équidés, ce qui le rend unique en Europe. Un cheval, ça s’enterre comment ?
Depuis 1993, environ 3 000 animaux de compagnie ont été enterrés à Liège au sein du cimetière animalier Le Paradis des Animaux. Chats, chiens, lapins et même une poule y ont trouvé le sommeil éternel. « On a déjà enterré un poisson rouge », relate Marie-France Geys, l’une des bénévoles qui s’occupent du cimetière.
Ce qui fait la particularité de ce lieu, ce n’est pas la présence des arêtes de Bubulle en son sol, mais bien celle d’une dizaine de carcasses d’équidés. Le site liégeois est le seul à proposer l’inhumation des chevaux et des ânes en Europe. « On a des chevaux français, hollandais, allemands… On nous a même déjà téléphoné d’Angleterre, mais on a dû refuser », dévoile-t-elle.
Lorsque son conjoint Robert Brose, le fondateur du cimetière, était encore en vie, Marie-France Geys l’accompagnait en camionnette pour aller chercher les dépouilles équines. « Il fallait faire vite, car si on attend trop longtemps, le corps gonfle. Il peut même doubler de volume, ce qui le rend impossible à transporter. »
Les deux premiers chevaux à avoir été inhumés, Grany et Rina, l’ont été en 1994 et ont la particularité d’avoir été ensevelis debout, dans un cercueil confectionné sur mesure. Ceux qui leur ont succédé, Blue Belle, …

https://www.propublica.org/article/depor.title: A Texas Cop Signed on to Help ICE Deport His Neighbors. It Tore the Town Apart.
https://www.propublica.org/article/depor.author: Francesca D’Annunzio, McKenzie Funk, Kirsten Luce
https://www.propublica.org/article/depor.text:
Reporting Highlights
- The Shadow Surge: In January 2025, President Donald Trump revived a troubled ICE program that deputizes cops as deportation officers. Over 29,000 local officers nationwide have enlisted.
- After the Flood: Ingram, Texas, was rebuilding from a historic flood when its Police Department signed on with ICE. Within a year, cops would hand over the equivalent of 10% of the town.
- Cop on the Ground: The local face of the national immigration crackdown became Officer Jaron Alexander. After suggesting ICE’s program to his chief, he grapples daily with the consequences.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
The new patrol officer parked his black Dodge Charger outside a house off Main Street and approached on foot. A Mexican ballad was playing. Someone had called in a noise complaint, claiming it sounded as if people were fighting.
But as the officer, Jaron Alexander, got closer, he found nothing of the sort. A middle-aged woman greeted him as her daughter, Joanna Martinez, petite and visibly pregnant, looked on. “What kind of party are you all having?” she remembers him asking. Behind her were three generations of an extended family. They were celebrating a 3-month-old’s baptism over pozole verde, horchata and beers.
Alexander ran some IDs and found no issues. The music wasn’t even that loud, he thought. He told them to have a good night, and then he left.
That encounter, in early October last year, was the first of many that Alexander and Martinez would have in tiny Ingram, Texas, a 1.5-square-mile town of 1,900 people beside the Guadalupe River. But it was the only one before Ingram signed an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that would roil the town and tear Martinez’s family apart.
“Her and I, at the beginning, I felt like we were running into each other all the time,” Alexander told us, in one of eight conversations over four months that offer a rare window into the thoughts of one of the local police officers on the front lines of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.
In a town as small as Ingram, drivable in five minutes end to end, more run-ins were probably inevitable. Later that October, Alexander pulled over a work truck for rolling through a stop sign, and soon there Martinez was, demanding that he let her friends go rather than let immigration take them. He didn’t. He pulled over another driver in November who turned out to be her cousin, the father of the baby they celebrated at the baptism party. Alexander handed him over to immigration agents as well.
He pulled over Martinez herself a few weeks before she was due to give birth, she says, surprising her when he knew her name and the type of car she typically drove. He warned her that the car’s window tint was illegal and let her go. After that, he says, he caught a glimpse of her and her husband and their newborn daughter in the toy aisle at Walmart. Martinez told us she doesn’t think it was even her that day — her baby girl was then just days old, and she couldn’t imagine running errands with her so soon. But in Alexander’s memory, she was shopping for Christmas presents, just like him.
Alexander, who is in his mid-30s, with dirty blond hair already turning gray, says he didn’t come back to Ingram to help deport his neighbors. In his telling, he just ended up making it part of his job. The town was where he started his law-enforcement career years earlier, before he took a better-paying position with the county, as a sheriff’s deputy. But things recently started to fall apart, first in his marriage, next at the sheriff’s office: A 185-page internal investigation found that he had an affair before his divorce was final and used a county vehicle to carry it out, then lied about it all. He says the investigator called him an “embarrassment to the profession.” The sheriff’s office fired him. (Alexander said at the time, and again to us, that he did not have the affair.)
Ingram’s Police Department took him back just when its new chief — its eighth in five years — was under pressure from the City Council to do more: more traffic stops, more citations, more arrests, more numbers. Alexander says he told the chief that the sheriff’s office had a deal with ICE and that Ingram should look into it; maybe it could help the department grow. “Blame me,” he eventually told people. “It’s my fault in a way.”
Donald Trump had retaken the presidency with a promise to carry out “the largest deportation in the history of our country.” America was still figuring out what that meant. Finding and expelling up to 4% of the U.S. population — the 14 million residents who are estimated to be undocumented — wasn’t something a few thousand ICE agents could do on their own.
Underway in Chicago that fall, and soon in Minneapolis, was one version of how the administration could try to do it: masked agents from across the federal government surging into a liberal city to round up immigrants, beating back — even killing — the citizens who tried to stand in their path.
But a quieter kind of surge was spreading across the country at the same time. In September 2025, ICE announced new incentives for a partnership program known as 287(g). The program’s most aggressive form, the so-called task force model, which Ingram opted in to, enlists local police officers as deputy immigration agents, and the new incentives included a $100,000 vehicle stipend, a $7,500 equipment stipend for every participating officer, quarterly performance bonuses and funding to help cover officer salaries and overtime. “By joining forces with ICE,” the announcement read, “you’re not just gaining access to these unprecedented reimbursement opportunities — you’re becoming part of a national effort to ensure the safety of every American family.”
Alexander completed an online course with ICE a few weeks after the baptism party, qualifying him for time-and-a-half pay whenever he helped the agency pick up immigrants. Here in the Texas Hill Country, he soon became the local face of the national crackdown.
Ingram was just starting to recover from its worst natural disaster in a century, the flood that summer that killed at least 139 people up and down the Guadalupe River, including 25 girls at Camp Mystic. In the riverbed, towering bald cypress trees now stood at a lean, their branches swept back by a 30-foot surge of water and mud, their trunks still plastered with debris. As construction workers rebuilding the community traveled to their jobsites via Junction Highway, Ingram’s five-lane main thoroughfare, a black Charger began stopping them before they could get there.
Within three months of the baptism party, Alexander and Ingram’s other patrol officer had delivered at least 70 people to immigration agents, picking off what the police chief called a “dumbfounding” number of undocumented drivers. Within a year, they would hand over the equivalent of 10% of Ingram to ICE.
The weight of what Alexander was doing started to settle on him after Christmas. He says he was out patrolling as one of his new ICE handlers, a man in a ball cap and dark glasses, hovered nearby in an unmarked SUV. Around lunchtime, Alexander followed two Latino men in a 2008 GMC truck for several blocks before stopping them, they recall him saying, for failing to signal a turn.
A young man sat in the passenger seat. Alexander checked his papers along with the driver’s and determined that both were undocumented. The agent in the unmarked SUV rolled up behind them. Alexander realized who the man in the passenger seat was only after Martinez arrived in tears. It was her husband, Ulices Macias, the father of her newborn daughter.
“I don’t normally do this,” Martinez recalls Alexander telling her, “but I’m going to open up the car. I’m going to take the handcuffs off him.” He let the family have a moment together. In a video taken by Martinez’s younger sister, Alexander stood by, expressionless, as Martinez embraced Macias by the rear door of the Charger. He watched Macias cradle his 2-week-old baby girl, swaddled in a white blanket, and hug Martinez’s 4-year-old son, his stepson.
Then the ICE agent put the handcuffs back on Martinez’s husband, wrapped a chain around his waist and led him away. Alexander says Martinez threw herself to the ground and sobbed.
Images of the family he broke up shortly after Christmas would intrude on Alexander’s thoughts for months, he told us. But it didn’t keep him from doing his job. His next shift came a few days after he handed over Macias, and he was back in the Charger, back to stopping cars on Junction Highway.
“Mini Guanajuato”
Alexander says he didn’t always want to be a police officer. He describes himself as “kind of a chameleon.” He grew up in nearby Harper, tried a few different colleges without graduating and spent his 20s cycling though jobs in freight logistics, pest control and insurance.
Still seeking his calling, he arranged a ride-along with a police officer outside Austin. What sold him on policing was the suburban officer’s power to enforce the law as he saw fit. That day, they pulled over a woman who had a warrant out for her arrest. She was coming back from the store with children and groceries in the back seat.
“You can use your discretion,” Alexander recalls the officer telling him. Wouldn’t they be doing more harm if they took her? What would the kids do without their mother? And wouldn’t it all create more paperwork? The officer let her go. Alexander imagined himself making the same kinds of judgment calls. In 2021, he enrolled in the police academy.
Even before the floods, tensions were rising in Ingram. Hundreds of Mexican immigrants and their families had settled there in recent decades as an increasingly militarized border made it harder for seasonal ranch hands and other workers to cross back and forth. Latinos would come to make up 45% of its population, and some residents began affectionately calling Ingram “mini Guanajuato,” after the central Mexican state where many have roots. Yet when Alexander returned, Ingram’s City Council still consisted of six white men.
A council faction led by Claud Jordan, now the town’s mayor, and Rocky Hawkins, now the mayor pro tem, came to power in November 2020, in a revolt against a new sewer project. They abolished Ingram’s city administrator position and took direct control of the Police Department, cycling through chief after chief. Five former city employees say Hawkins regularly used racist slurs for Mexicans. Four say that he pressured the city to go after Latinos through code enforcement or targeted patrols, and two say that Jordan did, too. One of the employees recalls Hawkins complaining that Mexicans were “taking over Ingram.” (Hawkins and Jordan each declined to speak on the record or address detailed questions we sent them by email. In a brief text-message exchange, Hawkins said that none of it was right but declined to offer any specific concerns.)
These were the men the new chief, Dustin Breshears, had to answer to as ICE revived the task force program, which had been shut down for a dozen years until the day Trump returned to office in January 2025. ICE, under President Barack Obama, had phased out the program after some of the first sheriffs to participate in it, including Joe Arpaio of Maricopa County, Arizona, used it to disproportionately target Latinos in their communities. Investigations by the Department of Justice found that deputies in the task force program pulled over Latino drivers at up to nine times the rate of other drivers and that some retaliated violently against people who accused them of racial profiling. But now, under Trump, any law-enforcement agency, no matter how troubled or small, was encouraged to sign up.
Breshears began appearing at City Council meetings armed with statistics: number of arrests since the last meeting, number of traffic stops, number of cleared cases from the backlog of hundreds he inherited — and number of what he called “deportations.” (He later explained this was his imprecise shorthand for “immigration-related enforcement activities.”) At the council’s October 2025 meeting, held a couple of weeks after Alexander showed up at the Martinez family’s baptism party, Breshears reported a remarkable 162 traffic stops by Ingram’s two patrol officers — Alexander and Christian Perez, who was 25 — in just 20 days. (Perez declined to comment.) The officers made more stops in two months than the department had made in the entire previous year. The City Council gave Breshears an $18,000 raise.
Before Breshears arrived and Alexander returned in August 2025, the weekly blotter in The West Kerr Current, the local newspaper, documented the humdrum of community policing: loose dogs, neighborhood disputes, code violations. Then, suddenly, it was filled with drivers stopped for defective brake lights, damaged license plates, cracked windshields, illegal window tints or other unspecified “equipment violations.”
Breshears and Alexander strongly deny targeting Latinos. “It’s honestly not what’s happening,” Breshears says, noting that his half brother, wife and daughters have Mexican heritage. Ingram’s traffic stops were simply up across the board, he says, so more Latinos were getting stopped. He shared statistics showing that stops of Latinos were proportional to their share of the population.
Alexander, who on top of his roughly $70,000 base salary was now logging dozens of hours per month for ICE, told us the same. “I don’t care who’s in the car,” he says. “I really don’t.”
“El Charger Negro”
As the ICE program took hold in Ingram, warnings about Alexander and his black Charger — the department has several — spread through the Hill Country and far beyond. Groups on Facebook and WhatsApp seemed to track his every move. The Charger was outside Rita’s taco shop. The Charger was near Dollar General. The Charger was parked by the church. A member of one particularly active Facebook group texted him screenshots, and he scrolled through blurry photos of himself looming behind work trucks or leaning over car windows.
Many Latino motorists trying to reach worksites up the Guadalupe began driving an extra 90 minutes each day to avoid the section of Junction Highway that Alexander patrolled. Ranch hands began sleeping at their employers’ properties in nearby Hunt, coming to town only when they knew — or hoped — that Ingram’s officers would be off duty. Residents were rattled the day a Customs and Border Protection helicopter hovered above town and the elementary school went into lockdown as the police hunted for a Mexican man who had run from one of Alexander’s traffic stops.
Workers Driving Between Kerrville and Hunt Add an Extra 90 Minutes to Their Daily Commute to Avoid Traffic Stops in Ingram
One family notarized guardianship papers, in case the parents were detained and the children left behind. One woman swore Alexander showed up outside a memorial service and asked people for IDs. Another woman said he detained her and her husband when they returned home from church. Parties dwindled. Invite lists shrank. People began to move away, to Kerrville and San Antonio, and Alexander’s reputation reached as far as La Ceja, a village in the mountains of central Mexico, where an elderly resident said he and his neighbors were familiar with the Texas town’s police. “El Charger negro,” he said, with a knowing nod. He estimated that some 20 or 30 people in the village were recent deportees from Ingram.
Alexander’s fortunes seemed to rise as the Martinez family’s fell. With her husband gone, Joanna Martinez couldn’t afford payments on the trailer they shared. She and their infant and her 4-year-old son moved back into her childhood bedroom in her mother’s crowded home, where several relatives and their children also lived. She tried to stay connected with her husband, Macias, via WhatsApp calls while working as much as she could as a house cleaner to keep afloat. “I can’t lock myself up in my room and just cry,” Martinez says.
Winter for Martinez and her family brought a string of dark incidents. The January arrest of her cousin near the carwash as she drove to pick up her children from school. A canceled baby shower for her older sister, Jazmin, over a rumor that the Charger planned to show up. Another cousin, himself the father of a newborn, stopped and taken right in front of her mother’s house as Martinez watched.
A half dozen of the attendees from the October baptism party would soon be gone from Ingram, after being detained and deported or leaving to join relatives who had been. Some people had gotten wind that Alexander was making money off his enforcement. When a Spanish-language Facebook page shared a photo of him questioning the passenger of a beige Ford pickup, someone posted an animated image in the comments: a stack of green dollar bills growing taller and taller in an endless loop.
Alexander received his first ICE payments in early December. In January, as the country’s attention turned to the violent immigration crackdown in Minneapolis, he was often spending three or four hours a day and sometimes entire shifts working on behalf of the federal agency. By the time federal authorities announced a drawdown in Minneapolis on Feb. 12, Alexander had already made $3,264.46 from his task force hours, according to his pay stubs.
Ingram was by then one of more than 750 task force model partners around the country, up from not quite 500 when it signed up in October. At least 43 million U.S. residents, according to an analysis of ICE records by the legal data firm Titus Consulting, already lived in a county with an active task force agreement. Alexander was one of thousands of deputized officers in Texas alone.
In interviews, Alexander described the immigration system he was enforcing as “skewed” and “weird,” but he saw himself as largely separate from these concerns. “If you’re taking federal money to do a job,” he says, “I think you should do the job.”
Still, he seemed to struggle with the contradictions of his role. He told us he sometimes shared his lunch with the people he detained and that he let them hold on to their phones to call loved ones from the rear seat of the Charger. He handcuffed them with their hands in the front rather than the back so they could use their hands.
Martinez told us about a moment when she watched him detain one of her cousins. He allowed the man’s wife and children to hug him goodbye and waited until his 7-year-old daughter wasn’t looking to handcuff him. To Martinez, it seemed as if Alexander was trying to prove to her that he wasn’t a bad person. “But I’m not going to fall for it,” she says.
There was a protest in Ingram the following day against Trump’s mass deportations. Martinez decided to go. As she stood among a few dozen protesters waving a handmade sign with the name “J. Alexander” circled and crossed out, she saw him drive by again and again.
A few weeks later, Katie Winer, the leader of the group that staged the protest, was following the Charger after Alexander detained another immigrant in a traffic stop. He approached her car and threatened to arrest her if she followed him in the future, on charges of interfering with public duties. But he also seemed to want to talk, and she recorded him as they discussed what was going on in Ingram. “I think you guys are making a bigger deal of it than they are,” he said of the people he handed over to ICE. The only outliers were “loudmouths” like Martinez and “her little crew.”
Winer interjected that Martinez’s husband was the family’s breadwinner, and it was Alexander’s actions that tore them apart.
“My actions did not,” Alexander said. “His actions did. I made a traffic stop. He was here illegally. That’s not my fault.”
Still, Alexander’s uncertainty seemed to be growing. In March, another of Martinez’s cousins confronted him outside the taco shop, pressing him about Macias as she filmed with her phone.
“If I’m being 100% honest,” he said, “I don’t enjoy when families are separated, like with the Joanna situation. That kind of fucked me up.”
“I Voted to Get the Bad Guys Out”
A month later, as Ingram’s handoffs to ICE surpassed 100 people, another video of Alexander circulated among a small group of community members. It showed an evening traffic stop, at least the fifth stop Alexander made that day. He had followed a silver Ford F-250 from the highway until it pulled into the gravel driveway of a mobile home. There, the man in the passenger seat, a landscaper named Victor Ramirez Hernandez, tried to hurry inside. Alexander grabbed him before he could get there.
The truck’s driver pulled out his phone and began filming. “Why are you arresting him?” he asked.
“I’m not,” Alexander answered, struggling to place handcuffs on Ramirez as he squirmed. “I’m detaining him.” Then he wrapped his hands around the laborer’s chest, lifted him off the ground and slammed him down on the driveway. “I played nice with you, and now I’m done,” he said. He straddled Ramirez and cuffed his hands behind his back.
“He’s bleeding because you hit him,” the driver said evenly. They argued back and forth.
“You’re an idiot,” Alexander said, his face reddening. “Shut up. The more you talk it’s just making you look stupider.” (Alexander declined to comment on this incident. Breshears, who reviewed body-camera footage, says Alexander’s use of force was justified to control a potentially dangerous situation.)
Acrimony pulsed through Ingram that spring. In the Latino community, family members and neighbors accused one another of snitching, which Alexander says did happen. Young women accused one another of having affairs with him, which he denies, insisting that people just misinterpreted his attempts to be kind. “I’m friendly with the people that I meet,” he says, “especially when they’re friendly to me.”
One subject of these rumors was Martinez. She and her older sister scoffed at them. “He’s taken our whole family at this point,” Jazmin says. “And she’s going to sleep with him? It’s really annoying.” But some in the community, even cousins, stopped speaking with her. “It’s like ‘Hunger Games,’” Martinez says.
As Latinos fled and avoided Ingram, the daily takeout orders at one Mexican restaurant on the edge of town dropped to 50 from 200. A corner store catering to immigrants lost around half its revenue and most of its Latino regulars. Landlords in a mobile-home park just outside town struggled to find tenants.
But it wasn’t just Ingram’s Latino community that was reeling. For Ingram’s non-Hispanic business owners, including many Republicans in a county that voted 77% for Trump in the 2024 election, the immigration crackdown was becoming an outrage. It was taking people they worked with and knew well. It was interfering with flood reconstruction. It was hurting the local economy.
The owner of a heavily damaged strip mall on the western edge of town, Steve Edelstein, lamented the loss of two workers who were helping him rebuild. “Technically local law enforcement is doing their job,” he told a reporter for The West Kerr Current, emphasizing that he supported Trump. “But it isn’t helping the community.” A manager overseeing the rebuilding of Ingram’s Little League field, which was washed away in the flood, made an angry call to the city after two of his workers were picked up, Breshears says. A contractor helping rebuild Hunt’s destroyed post office had his crew reduced to eight workers from 30 — causing what should have been a four-day job to stretch to two weeks.
Among the people who called Jordan, the mayor, to complain was his onetime high school classmate Neal Secor, who describes himself as “one of the most conservative guys you’ll ever meet.” His family business, a cluster of rental cabins called Waltonia on the River, was nearly destroyed by the flood. He was struggling to rebuild. He says that in the spring, in two separate stops, the Ingram police detained four of his workers and handed them over to ICE — the second set as they returned from a job repairing the docks at a nearby youth camp, a favor Secor was trying to do for a neighbor.
Secor says Jordan’s defense was simple: You voted for this. They’d all voted for this.
“Let me tell you something,” Secor says he told Jordan. “I didn’t vote for this. I voted to get the bad guys out.” The two employees detained coming back from the youth camp were like family, his friends and co-workers for over a decade. “There’s still a lot of bad guys here,” he continued. “These guys aren’t them.”
Secor recalls Jordan saying that Ingram’s officers were just following the law. But, Secor wondered, why was it that he could drive 85 every day on the 75-mile-an-hour interstate and police officers just let him pass? He told Jordan he’d put 175,000 miles on his truck and never been pulled over. “It’s a matter of what laws you want to pick and choose,” he recalls telling the mayor. “We all break laws every day if you really want to get down to it.”
“God Wanted Me to Meet You”
On an unpaved side street in the Ingram hills in April, Alexander again faced a decision over whether to separate a young family. This time he had more of a choice; ICE had yet to arrive. A woman named Norma Luján took his hand and said she was praying for him.
Luján, 61, runs a successful housecleaning company based in Ingram. She had heard of Alexander long before she confronted him. She had seen him in the Charger, too: on the side of Junction Highway as she made her way to jobs at vacation homes or youth camps up in Hunt. On the side of the highway on the way back. In her rearview mirror for four excruciating minutes one afternoon as her “girls,” as she called her crew, held their breath and sank into their seats, protected by the tint of her car’s windows and the fact that a license-plate reader would show it was registered to her, a Texas-born U.S. citizen.
In January, at the carwash, Alexander had helped a sheriff’s deputy take one of Luján’s best employees into custody. The woman, Cinthya Carranza, was a single mother and asylum seeker from Guanajuato — and Joanna Martinez’s cousin. Carranza was on her way to get her children from school after she and Luján spent the day cleaning houses. Later that day, Luján saw a Facebook post showing a familiar face in a mug shot: Carranza’s. Luján broke into tears. To her, the arrest was a signal event. The Charger had mostly stopped men up to that point. This was the moment she understood that no one was safe.
Luján started losing workers in droves after Carranza was taken — some to traffic stops, most for fear of having to drive through Ingram. Her crew of 30 people dropped to fewer than 10. She worried for her business, but she worried more, she said, for her workers, the lives they had made in Ingram and the relationships she had built with them. They invited her to parties and baptisms, surprised her with presents on her birthday. She often led them in prayer. “I love them,” she says. She promised she would try to protect them.
When Luján’s employee Maria called that April afternoon to say the officer in the Charger was outside her house, detaining her husband as he returned from work, Luján jumped into action. Maria (who asked to be identified by her middle name because she is undocumented) was eight months pregnant and already terrified that she would have to give birth alone. Alexander had taken her brother a week earlier. Now Maria was hiding behind the curtains of her home, sneaking peeks outside, hoping Alexander would let her husband go.
“Cálmate” — calm down — Luján told herself as she approached the Charger. “Cálmate.” She took a deep breath. She says Alexander was sitting in the driver’s seat with the door propped open, staring at a tablet computer.
“Look, his wife has had a complicated pregnancy,” she told him. (This was true.) “She’s in the hospital.” (For that lie, Luján says, she later prayed for forgiveness.)
Then Luján reached out and grabbed Alexander’s hand. “I pray for your being, for your soul,” she recalls telling him as she cried. “I want you to think about what you’re doing. Feel it. Feel it, please.” She squeezed his hand. “I need you to look inside your heart,” she continued, “and let him go.”
Alexander didn’t react at first, in Luján’s telling. “God wanted me to meet you,” she said. He met her gaze.
“I’m that guy that everyone talks about on Facebook,” she recalls him finally saying. “If you think I don’t lose any sleep, you’re wrong.”
Luján pushed through the lump in her throat to speak. “I’m going to pray for you every night,” she promised him. She says Alexander squeezed her hand back, then pulled away. He walked off to make a call. She couldn’t make out much of what he said. It was quiet, save for the sound of Luján’s sobs and the pebbles from the unpaved road crunching beneath the officer’s feet.
Then he returned to the Charger. “Get him out of the car,” Luján recalls him saying. “Hurry up.”
“God bless you,” Luján said. “God will repay you for this.”
Alexander says he doesn’t remember the details of his interaction with Luján, but he confirms that he let Maria’s husband go, calling it a matter of “human decency.” He knew how hard it was to raise children. “A woman needs rest,” he says. “She needs help.” Maria’s husband “needs to be there helping out.”
At first, nothing seemed to change. Over the next two months, as the Hill Country prepared to welcome summer tourists and campers back after the devastation of the floods, Alexander worked around 100 task force hours, earning close to $5,000 from ICE.
But the next time he ran into Joanna Martinez, he seemed to be having misgivings. It was early June, and he was eight months into the ICE program. He had pulled over another of her family friends on Junction Highway, a person she had known since childhood. Martinez got a phone call and rushed to the scene, as she had so many times before. “I don’t feel good about this,” she recalls him saying when she arrived. “I signed up to be a cop, not an ICE agent.” (Alexander says he remembers that they talked and that he could have said something like that.)
Later that month, he pulled over a young man from Honduras who was on his way to a soccer game with his cousin, a 12-year-old with developmental disabilities. The boy’s father says he and his wife hid across the street watching it all happen, too terrified to step out and claim their son. The parents sent a friend from church, but she was not a legal guardian. Alexander says he had no choice but to hand the boy over to ICE, adding though that if he was one of the parents, he would see it differently. “If I’m in that position, there’s no way I’m letting my kid go,” he told us. “I’m probably fighting someone.”
Within a couple of weeks, Alexander’s task force hours dropped by about 40%, according to his pay stubs. It remains unclear if he tried to step back from immigration work or whether the number of undocumented drivers in Ingram had simply dwindled because of all he had already done.
According to Chief Breshears, Ingram had logged 194 “immigration-related incidents” as of this August. Whether every handover led to a deportation, Breshears couldn’t say. Alexander says he doesn’t know how many of the 194 are people he stopped. But he says he has now let at least 10 people go — many, though not all of them, mothers of young children.
Alexander sees this, and his relationship to the Martinez family, as evidence of his humanity, despite what people say about him. “For context, I’ve deported like six of their family members, and they’re still friendly to me,” he says. “So I’m not the monster they make me out to be.”
On July 16, the skies over Ingram opened again, dropping nearly 19 inches of rain in a single day, and the Guadalupe again overtopped its banks, again destroying businesses and homes. In the predawn darkness in the early hours of the emergency, Alexander began racing toward Ingram in his black Charger to help. He had barely left his house when surging floodwaters consumed the vehicle, destroying the Charger’s engine block. A driver in a pickup truck took him back home, and that’s where he stayed until the storm receded.
“One Free Pass”
Alexander remains only one cog in a deportation machine for which the federal government has now earmarked $240 billion. Today more than 1,900 agencies in at least 30 states have signed up for ICE’s task force model, with more than 29,000 deputized officers. With their help, ICE recently hit a record of immigration arrests, totaling more than 50,000 in August.
On Sept. 11, Alexander met one of us at a taco spot on Junction Highway. Ingram had changed in the year since his return. Whole neighborhoods had emptied out, and residents noticed fewer drivers on the streets. In part because of the money from ICE, the Police Department had hired two additional officers. As a Mexican ballad played over the speakers, Alexander warned against making too much of the leniency he showed to families like Maria’s. “It’s like one free pass, I guess,” he said: If he encountered her husband again during a traffic stop, he would probably hand him over to ICE. He just thought letting the father-to-be go was the right call at the time. “I mean, don’t you?” he asked.
He said he hadn’t made all that much money working with ICE. But city records show that his earnings from the agency already totaled $18,793.25 in nine months, more than a quarter of his base salary. “I think it’s skewed a little bit,” he said, looking at the pay stubs we had gathered.
Alexander said it was hard for him to be out in public anymore. He can’t escape being recognized in Ingram and Kerrville. Sometimes he catches Latinos staring at him, then walking away, visibly uncomfortable. So he tries to do his shopping and errands in another town 30 minutes away.
He blamed the Facebook groups. They had created a climate of “unreasonable fear” in Ingram. “What do they think I’m going to do right now?” he asked, seated at his table in the taco shop. A steady stream of customers, many of them white, approached a counter staffed by two young Mexican sisters. He said their father used to hide out in Hunt to avoid being pulled over in town. Some of their co-workers had quit months before, too uncomfortable to serve Alexander when he came in for breakfast. But when the taco shop owner sees him, he said, she hugs him.
“I know the status of everybody in this room,” he said. He suggested everyone who worked there was undocumented. Whether they disappeared or were allowed to stay was up to him. And today, at least, he was just there for breakfast.
“They’re fine, right?”

https://apache.be/2026/10/27/schaduw-van.title: De schaduw van Didier Reynders boven een assisenproces
https://apache.be/2026/10/27/schaduw-van.author: Walter De Smedt
https://apache.be/2026/10/27/schaduw-van.text:
Wat heeft de gevallen Belgische toppoliticus Didier Reynders te maken met het assisenproces tegen Nicolas Ullens? Op 29 maart 2023 reed Nicolas Ullens de Schooten zijn stiefmoeder, barones Myriam 'Mimi' Lechien, klem en schoot vervolgens zesmaal, waarna Myriam Lechien overleed. Vader Ullens werd verwond.
Nicolas Ullens ging zich daarop aangeven bij de politie en bekende de feiten. De feiten zelf vormden op het assisenproces bijgevolg geen probleem. Wel is er de vraag of Ullens met voorbedachtheid had gehandeld, in welk geval het dus niet om doodslag maar om moord zou gaan. Een moord wordt zwaarder bestraft dan doodslag.
Op het eerste gezicht is dit een dramatische afloop van een familiale aangelegenheid. Maar de actualiteit – gelekte gesprekken tussen Reynders en een door hem benoemde topman binnen de Belgische Staatsveiligheid – leert dat er elementen spelen die mogelijk een antwoord kunnen geven op de vraag of er voorbedachtheid in het spel was dan wel of Ullens “ontplofte”.
De volgende vraag is dan of die elementen ook effectief werden onderzocht, of er op de assisenzitting over werd gepleit en of er bij de beoordeling rekening mee werd gehouden. Is het onderzoek naar de feiten voldoende gevoerd? En is het zogenoemde “moraliteitsonderzoek” – het onderzoek naar het verleden en de ingesteldheid van de verdachte – volledig gevoerd of vertoont het lacunes?
Voorbedachtheid
De jury en de beroepsrechters beslisten samen dat er sprake was van voorbedachtheid en veroordeelden Nicolas Ullens voor moord. De vaststelling dat de beroepsrechters daarbij meestemden werd initieel aangevochten, maar door het Hof van Cassatie terecht goedgekeurd. De wet voorziet immers dat bij een krappe meerderheid (zeven van de vijf stemmen) de rechters moeten tussenkomen. (Terzijde: dat neemt niet weg dat deze wettelijke voorziening eigenlijk het principe dat het volk de schuldvraag beoordeelt onderuithaalt.)
Op het proces werd voornamelijk naar de verspilling van het familiefortuin door de stiefmoeder en het gebrek aan aandacht door de vader gewezen
Voorbedachtheid (of voorbedachten rade) is in het strafrecht het plegen van een misdrijf na een kalme overweging en met een gepland besluit, in plaats van in een blinde opwelling. Als het dat laatste was, wat bracht Ullens dan tot zo’n blinde opwelling.
Op het proces werd voornamelijk naar de verspilling van het familiefortuin door de stiefmoeder en het gebrek aan aandacht door de vader gewezen. Er zijn echter heel wat andere elementen die de gewezen agent van de Staatsveiligheid in een toestand kunnen hebben gebracht die door professor Philippe de Timary, hoofd van de afdeling psychiatrie van de Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, werd uiteengezet.
De arts getuigde op het proces dat Nicolas Ullens op het moment van de schietpartij vermoedelijk een “dissociatieve” episode doormaakte. Een dissociatieve periode is een toestand waarin de normale, samenhangende functies van je brein − zoals bewustzijn, geheugen, identiteit, emoties en waarneming − tijdelijk verstoord of losgekoppeld raken. Wanneer iemand een misdrijf pleegt (zoals slagen of doodslag) nadat hij zelf werd uitgelokt door zwaar, onmiddellijk en onrechtmatig fysiek of psychisch geweld dat zijn vrije wil aantast, kan dat dienen als een verschoningsgrond of leiden tot strafvermindering.
Andere elementen
Als agent van de Staatsveiligheid deed Ullens onderzoek naar mogelijk beïnvloeding en corruptie door Didier Reynders en zijn entourage, voornamelijk zijn rechterhand Jean-Claude Fontinoy. Hij maakte er ook interne nota's over. Ullens deed ook aangifte bij het Vast Comité I dat de inlichtingendiensten controleert. Hij getuigde daar binnen de Belgische Staatsveiligheid te zijn tegengewerkt en gepest.
In een interview in Humo (18/05/2021) legde Nicolas Ullens in dat verband erg bezwarende verklaringen af:
Reynders en Fontinoy hebben een putsch op de Staatsveiligheid uitgevoerd: ze benoemden een derde topman, Hugues Brulin, terwijl de Staatsveiligheid sinds 1830 werd bestuurd door een tweespan: de administrateurgeneraal en zijn adjunct. Brulin kwam rechtstreeks van het kabinet-Reynders. Daarmee overtraden ze de regel dat een staflid van de Staatsveiligheid een magistraat hoort te zijn. Mijn diensthoofd, Frank J, was ook een MR-man. Frank J. en Brulin hebben me het leven onmogelijk gemaakt en de economische afdeling van de Staatsveiligheid, waar ik werkte, opgedoekt. Frank J. heeft me ook aangemaand om op te houden met het onderzoek naar Kazachgate, het dossier van een parlementaire onderzoekscommissie. Uiteindelijk heb ik me tot het Comité I gewend, dat toezicht houdt op de inlichtingendiensten. De toenmalige voorzitter, Guy Rapaille, een man van socialistische signatuur, heeft me niet bepaald gesteund: hij heeft geprobeerd me in diskrediet te brengen. Maar de ergste was de chef van de Dienst Enquêtes van Comité I, Frank Franceus, de oud-kabinetschef van Geert Bourgeois (N-VA, red.). Toen ik mijn verklaringen ging ondertekenen, zei hij: 'Meneer Ullens, als u dit tekent, brengt u niet alleen uzelf, maar ook uw vrouw en uw vier kinderen in gevaar.'
Bedreigd
Over de mogelijke bedreiging door de chef van de enquêtedienst I aan het adres van Nicolas Ullens werd een strafonderzoek gevoerd. Daarin kwam een belangrijke getuige terug op voordien schriftelijk weergegeven elementen die de klacht ondersteunden. Het onderzoek door het comité I zelf, kreeg evenmin gevolg.
Er waren ook andere bedreigingen. Die werden duidelijk en bovendien openbaar door meerdere artikelen en een boek van onderzoeksjournalisten.
Apache bracht er, soms samen met Humo, verschillende artikelen over:
Daarnaast werd het boek van de Franstalige onderzoeksjournalist Philippe Engels, De clan Reynders, in april 2021 gepubliceerd. Het onderzoekt de nauwe banden tussen politiek en het bedrijfsleven en volgt de loopbaan van MR-politicus Didier Reynders en zijn naaste medewerker Jean-Claude Fontinoy. Engels beschrijft daarin onder meer hoe private firma's zijn bevoordeeld, hoe NMBS-personeel zou zijn ingezet voor verkiezingscampagnes, en hoe de samenwerking achter de schermen verliep.
Vooral de verwijzingen naar de mogelijke betrokkenheid van Russische spelers en spionage openen de deur naar een geheel andere wereld. De mogelijke bedreigingen door externe personen en diensten, is een opdracht van de Staatsveiligheid. De vraag of Ullens zich ook daardoor bedreigd voelde is, gezien wat er in die wereld allemaal mogelijk is, niet onbelangrijk.
Gewapend
Een ander element dat als bezwarend kan worden gezien, is de vaststelling dat Nicolas Ullens gewapend was op het moment van de feiten. Was dat om zich te verdedigen tegen mogelijke bedreigingen? Wat daarover door onderzoeksjournalisten werd geschreven ondersteunt deze stelling. Ullens had immers al geruime tijd steeds zijn wapen bij. Nadat Nicolas Ullens geschoten had, stapte vader Ullens de wagen uit en riep “Dood mij ook” of “Schiet me nu ook maar dood”.
Nicolas Ullens was gewapend op het moment van de feiten. Was dat om zich te verdedigen tegen mogelijke bedreigingen?
De gespannen verhouding tussen vader en zoon was danig aangewakkerd door het bezoek van vader Ullens aan Didier Reynders. Vader Ullens had Reynders zijn verontschuldigingen aangeboden voor de beweringen van zijn zoon aan het adres van de gevallen toppoliticus. Werd daarover gesproken tijden het gesprek onmiddellijk voorafgaand aan de feiten? Speelde ook deze frustratie mee?
Al op 19 januari 2017, jaren voor de feiten, schreef Ullens een brief aan de directeur operaties van de Staatsveiligheid, Christiane Delvoye. Daarin komt hij terug op het verwijt dat zijn chef hem maakte omdat hij een examen voor het gebruik van zijn dienstwapen niet zou hebben afgelegd. Ullens antwoordde daarop dat hij de nodige schietoefeningen wel degelijk had gevolgd.
Daarbij verwijst hij expliciet naar het gevaar dat uitgaat van het fameuze Kazachse trio – een dossier waarin ook Didier Reynders opduikt − “en de verleiding die zou kunnen bestaan om een lastige getuige in dat dossier te laten verdwijnen”.
In de brief heeft Ullens het over “het feit dat de zaak rond het ‘Kazachse trio’ – een kwestie waarover ik tussen 2008 en 2015 veertien verslagen heb geschreven – op dramatische wijze opnieuw is opgedoken” en over “de banden met de georganiseerde misdaad en buitenlandse inlichtingendiensten die bekendstaan om hun gewelddadigheid binnen onze instelling ruimschoots gedocumenteerd zijn”.
Kazachgate
De voormalige justitieministers Stefaan De Clerck (CD&V) en Koen Geens (CD&V) slaagden erin de fameuze afkoopwet door het parlement te jagen. Daardoor kon het strafonderzoek in meerdere grootschalige fraudezaken worden stil gelegd en konden de daders door een enkele betaling van een “uitgebreide minnelijke schikking” aan een veroordeling ontsnappen.
Dat gebeurde onder meer in het onderzoek naar Kazachgate en bij de fameuze diamantdossiers. Omdat parlementairen zich bij de voorbereiding van de afkoopwet bedrogen voelden, werd er een parlementaire onderzoekscommissie in het leven geroepen. Die leerde dat bij de eerder genoemde dossiers zeer ernstige “disfuncties” speelden. Er werd “gelobbyd” zowel bij ministers, parlementairen als parketmagistraten. Bovendien werd de afkoopwet toegepast nog voor hij was gestemd en ongeacht de terechte kritiek van de Hoge Raad voor de Justitie. Er waren ook ernstige en samenlopende aanwijzingen van corruptie.
De bewering van Ullens dat hij door de chef van de enquêtedienst Frank Franceus werd bedreigd roept vragen op
De bewering van Ullens dat hij door de chef van de enquêtedienst Frank Franceus werd bedreigd roept eveneens vragen op. Frank Franceus, de oud-kabinetschef van Geert Bourgeois, werd door het Comité I immers aangesteld als expert bij de audit over de werking van de Staatsveiligheid. Hoe kon een expert nadien chef van de enquêtedienst van het Comité I worden?
Soortgelijke vragen werden ook gesteld bij de benoeming van Franceus in de Hoge Raad voor Justitie. De Hoge Raad voor Justitie is een onafhankelijk orgaan dat de selectie van te benoemen magistraten doet maar ook onderzoeken voert naar mogelijke “disfuncties” binnen justitie.
Bij de oprichting van het orgaan werd voorzien dat zowel vertegenwoordigers van de magistratuur, academici als politici maar ook leden van het middenveld een plek konden krijgen.
Hoe kon Franceus benoemd worden als vertegenwoordiger van het middenveld? Hij was immers tegelijk chef van de enquêtedienst van het Vast Comité I. Dat is geen particuliere organisatie maar een overheidsinstelling.
Bij de invulling van mandaten wordt bovendien gekeken naar het beroepsverleden van de kandidaten, minstens nagegaan of er geen “onverenigbaarheden” zijn die de uitoefening van het mandaat kunnen bemoeilijken. Als chef enquêtes van het Comité I mag Franceus naar de organieke wet op het comité I geen onderzoeken doen naar de werking van de magistratuur vermits dat uitdrukkelijk uit de onderzoeksbevoegdheid van de comités is uitgesloten.
Als voorzitter van de onderzoekscommissie heeft hij daartoe uitdrukkelijk wél de opdracht en is het zelfs de essentie van zijn taak. Frank Franceus verenigde dus op het ogenblik van zijn benoeming twee bevoegdheden die volgens de wet onverenigbaar zijn. Ook feitelijk zijn de twee opdrachten niet te verzoenen. Als chef enquêtes moest hij de opdrachten van de magistraten uitvoeren. Als voorzitter van de onderzoekscommissie moet hij onderzoeken of in die opdrachten “disfuncties” te vinden zijn. Hij was dus tegelijk uitvoerder en controleur. Hoe verkreeg Franceus beide benoemingen? Voor wie reed hij?
Didier Reynders
De bewering van Nicolas Ullens dat Reynders en Fontinoy een putsch op de Staatsveiligheid hadden uitgevoerd en zij daarbij Hugues Brulin benoemden, wordt intussen bevestigd door een gelekt document. Daarin schrijft Brulin onder meer dat hij zijn “job heeft volbracht” en de “krankzinnige Ullens” werd tegengewerkt en uit de dienst werd verwijderd.
Ullens verklaarde dat door de inmenging en de bedreigingen zijn leven onmogelijk werd gemaakt
Werd daar rekening mee gehouden? Een gerechtelijk onderzoek gebeurt zowel ten laste als ter ontlasting. De onderzoeksrechter moet daarbij “alle maatregelen nemen die de rechtscolleges in staat stellen met kennis van zaken te oordelen”.
De vraag of dat wel is gebeurd is terecht. Zowel de door de politie gekraakte berichten tussen Brulin en Reynders als de brief van Ullens waarin hij op de bedreigingen wijst zitten in het dossier. De verklaringen van Ullens in Humo zijn voor iedereen leesbaar. Daarin verklaarde Ullens dat door de inmenging en de bedreigingen zijn leven onmogelijk werd gemaakt.
Vanzelfsprekend is het proces-Ullens niet het proces van Didier Reynders. Maar een verdachte heeft wel het recht om alle elementen die een verklaring kunnen geven voor zijn daad aan het onderzoek toe te voegen. Zowel het parket als de onderzoeksrechter moeten dat volgens de vereisten van het “eerlijk proces” zelfs ambtshalve doen.
Dissociatieve periode
Dat brengt ons terug bij de vraag of Nicolas Ullens met voorbedachtheid handelde of op het ogenblik van de feiten in een dissociatieve toestand verkeerde
Tijdens het proces werd vooral naar de verstoorde relatie met de stiefmoeder en de vader gekeken. Maar zoals hiervoor aangegeven zijn er heel wat andere gegevens voorhanden die aantonen dat Ullens binnen Staatsveiligheid werd tegengewerkt en gepest en dat hij sinds 2017 door zijn onderzoeken naar voornamelijk de invloed van het Russisch crimineel milieu werd bedreigd.
Die bedreigingen moeten ernstig worden genomen. Bovendien werden die bedreigingen in de eigen dienst aangewend om de onderzoeken naar in de dossiers betrokken politieke mandatarissen te stoppen.
Tijdens het proces kwamen die feiten niet voldoende aan bod. Ze zijn belangrijk om de vraag te beantwoorden of Ullens met voorbedachtheid handelde, want ze bepaalden mee de toestand waarin Ullens werd gebracht. Dat vader Ullens bij Didier Reynders bovendien zijn verontschuldigingen had aanboden voor de door zijn zoon gevoerde onderzoeken kan daarbij de druppel zijn geweest.

In Israël drukt de darktechsector zijn stempel op de verkiezingen. Hele legers van AI-gestuurde bots worden in de strijd geworpen om kiezers te beïnvloeden. https://projects.propublica.org/american.title: Search More Than 500 Cases of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
https://projects.propublica.org/american.author: Nicole Foy, Ruth Talbot, Cengiz Yar, Bianca Fortis, Mariam Elba, Kahlie Wray
https://projects.propublica.org/american.text:
ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes
corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms. Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.
Experts have long warned that immigration dragnets will inevitably result not only in the erosion of rights for immigrants but also for citizens. Since the start of this Trump administration, we've watched those warnings come true.
So we have once again done what the government won’t: We have tallied and cataloged every case we can find of an immigration agent reportedly detaining a citizen during the current administration — more than 500 cases from Inauguration Day through Oct. 21, 2026.
We compiled our list by scouring social media, court records and local media, and we included an incident only if we could find at least two sources for it. We asked the Department of Homeland Security about each incident, and we searched for any federal criminal charges that were brought in relation to each incident. (DHS has repeatedly said it is not arresting U.S. citizens.)
Since the government itself does not track these cases, our list is almost certainly an undercount. Below, we're showing you every case we found — the reality that the administration denies — along with the receipts. Read more about how we reported this project.

Santa Maria, California.
A citizen riding a bike was tasered, injured and handcuffed after colliding with an ICE vehicle in Long Beach, California. Video footage shows the ICE vehicle driving the wrong way down a one-way street then swerving toward the cyclist. DHS denied hitting the citizen and accused him of smashing the vehicle’s mirror, which is not captured on available video.
One citizen was injured and detained by ICE agents who were looking for someone who matched his description in Evanston, Illinois. A responding Evanston police officer said one agent had blood on his hands and the citizen was taken to the hospital. DHS claimed the man didn’t cooperate with “lawful commands” and agents detained him until he identified himself.
A citizen leaving a coffee shop in Annapolis, Maryland, was handcuffed, denied a phone call and held for almost two hours. DHS said it took the citizen to another location to interview him because “agitators” had gathered.
A citizen mother of four was detained in Lafayette, Louisiana, at a local law enforcement checkpoint outside her apartment, then transferred to ICE custody and booked into a detention facility before her attorney won her release. ICE and the local law enforcement agency that detained her still dispute her citizenship.
Jeury Concepcion, a 19-year-old citizen, was walking in front of a barbershop in the Bronx when three masked agents tackled him, mistaking him for someone else. The teen said that they released him far from home with his head bloodied, and that an agent apologized to him. A DHS statement said agents temporarily detained the teen to safely finish their questioning. A video associated with this incident appears in our main story.
A citizen was accused of assaulting an officer during the arrest of her husband in Asbury Park, New Jersey. She was detained for eight hours in Delaney Hall, an ICE detention facility, before being released without any known charges. Videos showed her 9-year-old daughter and toddler left crying alone in her vehicle, with ICE agents standing guard until family arrived to pick them up.
A 25-year-old citizen from Denver, Colorado, was detained and deported after a traffic stop in Fredericksburg, Texas, when he was unable to provide identification or proof of citizenship. He was held without access to his phone or a lawyer for several days before he agreed to leave the country. He was allowed to cross back into the U.S. using his Colorado birth certificate in August.

https://citylimits.org/in-harlem-public-.title: In Harlem, Public Housing Residents Knock on Doors With Congressional Candidate Avila Chevalier
https://citylimits.org/in-harlem-public-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/in-harlem-public-.text:
Share This Article
“There’s a lot that needs to be done in our community,” said Barbara Williams, a 78-year-old activist and NYCHA Polo Grounds Towers resident. DSA candidate Avila Chevalier, who ousted the district’s longtime incumbent in June, “seems to be that person, from what she says and what I’ve read about her, that’s going to do the job.”
This story was produced in collaboration with Factchequeado. Lea la versión en español aquí.
Barbara Williams, a 78-year-old community activist and public housing resident of Polo Grounds Towers in Harlem, spent Saturday afternoon knocking on neighbors’ doors with congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier—who’s poised for a victory in the race to represent New York’s 13th District.
Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist endorsed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, achieved a major political victory by winning June’s primary elections (and ousting the five-time incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat, the first Dominican American to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives).
She’ll face Republican challenger Jomo Manuel Williams in next week’s general election (early voting is underway now). Manuel Williams, who ran for City Council in 2021 and the presidency in 2008, did not respond to City Limits’ attempts to contact him. 
“I’m out here today to make sure that residents are registered to vote,” Barbara Williams, a resident of Polo Grounds Towers since 1988, told City Limits.
For over a decade, she’s been a member of Community Voices Heard Power (CVHP), a political advocacy group that advances policies that promote racial and economic justice—and endorses candidates who will do the same.
The group, which works closely with New York Housing Authority (NYCHA) residents and tenant leaders, announced its endorsement for Avila Chevalier to represent the district, which includes Harlem, Hamilton Heights, Washington Heights, and areas in the North-West Bronx.
Half of the district’s residents identify as Hispanic, according to Census data, and nearly a quarter are Black.
Williams, along with about 50 public housing residents and community members, gathered at Polo Grounds Towers with Avila Chevalier for a “Get Out The Vote” event organized by CVHP on Saturday, which was the last day New Yorkers could register to vote for the general election on Nov. 3.
There, Avila Chevalier spoke to residents about her ideas to preserve public housing, and also visited their homes to hear about the day-to-day issues they face—various states of disrepair caused by NYCHA’s $78 billion maintenance backlog.
“There’s a lot that needs to be done in our community,” Williams said, adding that Avila Chevalier “seems to be that person, from what she says and what I’ve read about her, that’s going to do the job.”
One of the first homes Avila Chevalier visited belonged to Mary Andrews, an 82-year-old resident who pointed out chipping tiles, damaged drywall, and mold-stained cracks in the ceiling in her bathroom. Andrews, who said she recently suffered a stroke, worries about inhaling mold, and that repairs are slow to come.
Another resident described recurring plumbing issues that include her bathtub flooding with water.
“So often, we talk about these structural issues in very abstract ways but when you put a person’s story to it, it becomes more urgent,” Avila Chevalier told City Limits.
“To be able to champion this issue in Congress, it’s important for me to be able to say I met Ms. Andrews, and she showed me the condition of her bathroom,” she said. “For people who are living with the consequences of this day in and day out, it is already urgent, and that needs to be reflected in the institutions that have the power to change.”
When making endorsements, CVHP leaders say they seek out candidates who prioritize housing and low-income communities. The organization offers political support, education, training, and endorsements to candidates in New York City, Westchester, and two counties in the Hudson Valley.
This election season, the group invited over 50 candidates across 25 races to apply for its endorsement, and of those, the group endorsed six candidates for the general election.
In the city, those candidates are Avila Chevalier, former City Councilmember Diana Ayala, who’s running to represent Assembly District 68 in East Harlem, and Grace Lee, an assemblymember running for State Senate to represent Lower Manhattan’s District 27.
CVHP considers several factors before extending an endorsement, according to the group’s executive director Juanita Lewis. Those include a candidates’ strategies for engaging people on the ground, as well as their electability and willingness to collaborate on policies that support low- and working-class communities.
It also includes in-person interviews between candidates and CVHP staff—”folks who ask tough questions,” Lewis said.
Candidates are how they plan to persuade colleagues in Congress to support legislation that would benefit public housing residents—especially in New York City, which owns the largest public housing stock in the country—and how familiar they are with their campaign’s funding.
“All of our members have experience around being one or two paychecks away from wondering how they’re going to pay rent,” Lewis said. “We want to get into the policy piece. That’s the biggest reason we wanted you in office.”
Lewis said the group’s members especially resonated with Avila Chevalier’s focus on preserving public housing, funding urgent repairs, and improving community safety.
One of those members is Darique Warren, who moved into Polo Grounds Towers in 1999, at 11 years old. At the time, he said, residents were proud of the development, but as conditions deteriorated, he noticed his neighbors becoming despondent. He cited problems like broken intercoms and doors, among other security features.
“Today the main thing is encouraging people to vote and reminding people why it’s important,” Warren told City Limits. “We want to come to politicians and not just say we’re hurting, but that you can please do this, that and the third for us.”
Warren said he’s drawn to Avila Chevalier’s ideas for funding NYCHA, which include support for the Green New Deal for Public Housing Act, which would invest up to $234 billion over 10 years to transition all of the country’s public housing stock into zero-carbon homes. The act was proposed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY), Rep. Delia Ramirez (IL), and Sen. Bernie Sanders (VT), and incumbent Espaillat is a co-sponsor of the legislation, too.
Avila Chevalier is opposed to NYCHA’s efforts to convert its properties to Section 8, bringing in private management companies to take on operations of developments while paying for extensive repairs, including money the housing authority can’t access on its own.
“She’s mentioned using state and city funding, preserving housing, and collaborating with coalitions as the voice of this constituency,” Warren said. “We intend to maintain a positive relationship with her and her team, and I see it as a two way street.”
For other CVHP members, Lewis explained that the “the biggest question that came up around public housing for our folks is around the protection and preservation of it, and what that looks like.”
“If you’re saying housing is an important part of your agenda, you can’t forget this huge stock of housing,” Lewis said of NYCHA.
“Public housing is home to workers, caretakers, people that make the city and the country run,” she added. “It’s time for that new story and narrative around public housing.”
Lewis also said Avila Chevalier’s “excitement about wanting to come and door knock with us in public housing, come to town halls to hear the thoughts people are having around public housing, are some interesting ways she could be a champion for public housing in Congress.”
Residents at Polo Grounds Towers recognized and expressed support for Avila Chevalier as she walked through the hallways doorknocking, and she described those moments as “really surreal.”
“There’s so much excitement,” she told City Limits. “For so much of the campaign you have your head down doing the work, and then you have those moments where you kind of realize we are breaking through, and we are building the people power necessary to wage in Congress.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: The beautiful, shocking work of artist Hoda Afshar: ‘I don’t take freedom of speech for granted’
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Dee Jefferson
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
When Hoda Afshar was a teenager, coming of age in theocratic and authoritarian Iran in the 1990s, she and her friends were repeatedly arrested and physically punished by the “morality police”, for wearing their hijabs incorrectly in public and for attending underground parties. “They used to put a few of us in small solitary confinement cells together for a night or two, it was very common for my generation to experience that,” she says.
“We are part of the nasl-e sukhteh, or ‘burned generation’; the generation born after the 1979 revolution, who had to pay the price for many of the transformations and changes that happened.”
These formative experiences left the artist with an ongoing sensitivity to injustice, and an interest in incarceration, marginalisation and state violence. They have also amplified her appreciation of the rights and freedoms she now enjoys as a citizen of Australia, where she migrated in 2007, then as a lapsed photojournalist and emerging artist. “I grew up under a system that didn’t give me freedom of speech, or equal rights as a woman, so I don’t take it for granted,” she says.
But it has also made her more sensitive to Australia’s human rights and social justice failures: “Australia claims beautiful values. It is the country of a ‘fair go’, that wants everything equal for everybody. But rights are not distributed equally.”
“From the beginning, I was very excited to be able to critique authority; to be a responsible citizen in a society where we can fight for change,” she adds.
This combination of lived experience and strongly held values has resulted in some of the most vivid, urgent and achingly beautiful works of Australian art seen in the last decade – several of which are brought together in a/part, her new exhibition at the University of Melbourne’s Buxton Contemporary
The show brings together three projects that deal with what she calls “states of exception”, a term coined by the Italian political theorist Giorgio Agamben for “sites where the laws that are applied to normal citizens don’t apply or can be broken,” Afshar says.
For each project, she has created video and photographic portraits that foreground the humanity of her subjects, while interrogating the narratives that underpin each state of exception; the ways of depicting a marginalised person or group that make it possible to accept their disenfranchisement.
Best known among these works is Remain, the 2018 work Afshar made with the Kurdish Iranian journalist and author Behrouz Boochani and a group of refugee men detained on Manus Island as part of Australia’s offshore immigration detention system. Shot on a tiny island near Manus, the two-channel video marries the beguilingly beautiful aesthetic of the tropical paradise with poetry, Kurdish song and personal testimony to express the humanity of its subjects – and the depth of their suffering.
“The intention was to create a new visual language that can impact people about this issue, because we have become absolutely immune to images of suffering from the refugee crisis,” Afshar told me back when Remain debuted in 2018. Almost a decade later, it is her most exhibited work in Australia and abroad.
Code Black/Riot, showing at Buxton for the first time since its debut at the Sydney Biennale in March, is an immersive video installation and series of portraits focusing on Indigenous youth in detention shot in far north Queensland.
Created with Boochani and Kuku Yalandji/Waanji/Yidinji/Gugu Yimithirr artist Vernon Ah Kee, the video features former detainees and staff from a youth detention centre, talking about living and working within a dehumanising system.
The former staff talk about the rainbow-coloured system of “codes” used to identify security and safety issues, and the practice of “night mode”, in which children are locked in their cells, in pitch dark, for days at a time. The children describe beatings from guards, solitary confinement, and a seemingly endless cycle of arrests, incarceration and probation.
To protect the identities of her young subjects, Afshar shot them in tight closeup, focusing on bodies and the lower halves of faces, highlighting the tension in the children’s bodies and mouths as they share harrowing experiences.
The studio-based interviews are intercut with footage of the young people: navigating Cairns at night amid revelling locals and tourists, floating in rivers and waterholes, perching in trees and bouncing on trampolines.
“It was very important not to depict them as broken,” Afshar says of the children; their photographic portraits show them in playful and defiant poses, using hands, flowers, face paint and clothing to obscure their faces.
As in Remain, beauty is juxtaposed with violence; the humanity of the narrators is contrasted with the inhumanity of the systems they are trapped in.
Her 2021 project Agonistes, spotlighting prominent Australian whistleblowers such as the former Australian army lawyer David McBride, explores a different “state of exception”: government employees who breach confidentiality agreements to speak up about witnessing wrongdoing, and are prosecuted and imprisoned as a result.
“These people all made a sacrifice; they had to choose between the law and the public, and they chose the public, believing that if the public knows what is happening, things will change,” says Afshar. “They lose everything because they believe in the values that the society claims to have.”
A fourth work, Shafaq, premiering in a/part, is more personal. Made during a camping trip on Larrakia country in the Northern Territory in July, it reflects her anxiety as the US resumed bombing Iran’s south, where her family lives. Shafaq is “a conversation across distance to my family members”, she says.
The last year has been difficult, with career highs marred by grief and anxiety over the bombing of her homeland. “Seeing places that you grew up in being demolished like that, it’s like part of your body and identity is being erased by it too. It’s a kind of pain I didn’t know till that moment,” she says.
The way Iran has been portrayed internationally has left her sceptical of documentary modes of storytelling. “Our struggles and our movements are often hijacked and used for other political purposes and ends,” she says. “I wanted to rethink what documentary means, to allow for interpretation; to never present an image with concrete messaging or didacticism.”
The end goal of her art, she says, is to bring people together. “For me, it’s not about east or west, right or left, or these binaries that keep us endlessly separated and fighting with each other. I don’t belong to anyone’s camps … What I care about is human life and human dignity.”
- Hoda Afshar’s a/part is on at Buxton Contemporary, the University of Melbourne, until 24 April 2027. Entry is free

https://hellgatenyc.com/chantz-rivera-wa.title: He Did It! He Walked From the Bronx to San Francisco!
https://hellgatenyc.com/chantz-rivera-wa.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/chantz-rivera-wa.text:
On Tuesday, more than 2,500 miles and 149 days after he began walking on foot across the country, Bronxite Chantz Rivera made it to San Francisco. 
He left his dishwashing job in May with the goal of getting to the Pacific Ocean. Before that, he had only left the five boroughs twice in his life.
"The inspiration behind the trip was just free will, you know," Rivera told us last month from Ely, Nevada. "Just gotta experience life, be free." 
Late capitalism has drastically lowered the stakes for this kind of cross-country, identity-seeking journey. You have a $50,000 Sprinter van, an email job, and an Instagram account—we're supposed to give a shit? 
In contrast, Rivera's trip seemed ill-planned, spur-of-the-moment, mildly dangerous. That is to say: He left for the right reasons, and he has both the discipline to endure thousands of miles across this country's often-hostile highways and the uncynical heart to appreciate it all.   
Despite having been stopped by the police and having his stuff stolen the moment he walked into California, Rivera was in good spirits when we spoke to him on Wednesday evening.
This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.
