https://gothamist.com/news/a-violent-hat.title: A violent hate crime claimed one NYC man's marathon dream. A year later, he's taking it back.
https://gothamist.com/news/a-violent-hat.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/a-violent-hat.text:
When Daniel Cho crosses the finish line of this year’s New York City Marathon, he’ll join more than 18,000 first-time runners to do so.
But this time last year, he was part of a very different statistic.
Cho was standing on the platform of the Bowery J/Z train station at around 4 p.m. on Oct. 29, 2025. He was on his way to collect a racing t-shirt for his first-ever marathon from a non-profit group he was helping to raise money for low-income Asian youths.
A stranger approached him on the platform and punched him in the face, shouting a racist slur. Cho ended up on the train tracks.
“I turned around to look if there was a train coming. [The tunnel] was pitch black, and so I said, ‘OK, get it together, and you're gonna be able to figure it out,’” Cho said.
He climbed back onto the platform, called 911, and gave the police a detailed description that helped them quickly catch his assailant. But in an instant, Cho, 46, became one of more than 29,800 people who would experience a serious physical assault somewhere in the city in 2025.
The arrest of his perpetrator was only the beginning of Cho’s mental and physical journey toward recovery. With multiple fractures to his right cheekbone, nerve damage along his eye socket and only four days to go before the race, doctors told him to cancel his marathon bid.
In the months that followed, he’d endure surgery to install a titanium plate in his face, log hours of work with a therapist to overcome lingering post-traumatic stress disorder, and shuttle to acupuncture treatments to tackle persistent numbness.
In early spring, Cho decided he was ready to run again — and hoped to take another shot at New York City’s iconic race.
“ Both marathon training and recovery from violence, or just a crime, ask for the same things: resilience, motivation, mental fortitude,” he said. “So I've been able to redefine that strength.”
While many of the city’s major violent crimes have declined significantly this year, felony assaults — the kind of attacks that leave people with serious injuries — have remained confoundingly high. According to the most recent NYPD data, there have been 165 more felony assaults reported citywide this year than the same time period last year, bucking the decreases in other kinds of offenses.
The same man who punched Cho was allegedly involved in four other anti-Asian attacks that same day, according to Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. So far this year there have been 548 felony assaults in transit, up from 490 at this time last year; an 11% increase.
The MTA declined to comment on Cho’s attack or on the spike in assaults on its system.
Cho, who works for the New York City Campaign Finance Board, was originally running the marathon to raise money for Apex for Youth: a nonprofit headquartered in Manhattan’s Chinatown that provides resources and mentorship to young Asian Americans from low-income backgrounds. Now, he said, he is also running to raise awareness about the prevalence of similar attacks, to spread hope to other survivors, and to reclaim his sense of safety and community in the city he loves.
“I was running for kids who are learning to trust this city to nurture and protect their futures. And then I had to learn to trust the city again myself with every commute, with every subway ride,” he said.
Cho’s message to other survivors is to treat recovery like marathon training: a long process with ups and downs, twists and turns, progress and setbacks.
“Find your own healing journey,” he said. “Don’t be afraid to tell your story…and my last thing is, create space for that intentional rest.”
On marathon day, Cho said he is most looking forward to “taking it all in,” “finding joy in the struggle,” and seeing his wife and two kids at mile 14. He said the race provides a unique opportunity for people from all walks of life to find common ground with strangers.
“ New York is a place for everyone, like nowhere else in the world, and the city belongs to all of us,” he said. “Hopefully we can lift each other up.”
This story has been updated to clarify the item Cho was collecting and the nature of his attack.

https://gothamist.com/news/pre-k-busing-.title: Pre-K busing in downtown Jersey City's hitting a crisis point, parents say
https://gothamist.com/news/pre-k-busing-.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/pre-k-busing-.text:
A decadelong economic boom has transformed Jersey City’s Paulus Hook neighborhood into one of the most desirable in the city. But the influx of new families has led to chronic and often chaotic overcrowding at P.S. 16, the elementary school that serves the area.
Toddlers in the school’s Pre-K program have to be bused throughout the city because the building has no room for them. District leaders have said for years that busing pre-K students to other city schools was a temporary solution. But next year, all of the kindergartners at the school — which serves students through the fifth grade — will be bused to other locations as well. The issue has become a constant complaint from frustrated parents speaking at school board and City Council meetings, and it’s become a key issue in Jersey City’s pivotal and crowded school board election.
The school is situated amid brownstones, boutiques and brunch spots, but space is scarce in the area, and any building plan would need to be run by state officials who are grappling with even worse overcrowding in other cities.
That leaves Jersey City leaders weighing options no one likes — including the prospect of shuffling kids around further with redistricting. Jersey City often has worse traffic than Manhattan and local parents say during pickup they often wait in the cold without any sense of when their toddlers will be dropped off.
“ If it was a rainy day, we would be out in the rain. We're out in the sun. We've been out in the snow,” said Renee Perna, who has a pre-K student and a first grader at P.S. 16, also known as the Cornelia F. Bradford School. “ If your 18-month-old had an older sibling getting on the bus, you'd be out here with your infant waiting for the bus.”
For now, parents and officials say, students are left competing for space and attention in classrooms never intended to accommodate so many at once.
“My son is going be in a classroom with something like 35 students next year, and he's been in crowded classes since kindergarten,” said Patrick Carr, the father of a P.S. 16 fifth grader. “He started kindergarten with 30, 31 kids. At this point, kindergartens are upwards of 35 to 40.”
Rapid growth
About 68,000 new housing units have been approved in Jersey City since 2015, then-Mayor Steve Fulop said last year.
Much of that growth has been centered downtown and along the city’s waterfront, the areas served by P.S. 16. Enrollment roughly tripled from 430 students in the 2015-2016 school year, to 1,144 in the 2025-2026 school year.
That’s a drastic change for a school that still operates out of a brick building that opened more than a century ago, when Paulus Hook was far less desirable.
“ It was the poorest section of the city at the time it was built,” Norma Fernandez, the superintendent of Jersey City Public Schools, said.. “It was named after Cornelia Bradford, who was an activist in the community who really fought to educate the children of the lowest working classes.”
Today, Fernandez said, P.S. 16 serves the district's wealthiest and most highly educated families. It’s the only school in the district that doesn’t receive federal assistance funding. And it’s one of the most highly rated, highly sought-after schools in Jersey City.
But just 13 new classrooms have been added to the area, all inside an annex for P.S. 16 that opened in 2021 and was designed to accommodate the school's pre-K students. Fernandez said, by the time it opened, enrollment had grown so much that the space was needed for older grades instead.
The busing dilemma
Parents walk their 3- and 4-year-olds to P.S. 16 every morning to load the kids onto buses that line multiple city blocks, while older students play in the school’s courtyard.
Sometimes cars are parked in bus zones from the night before, so the buses have to double park and disrupt traffic, which is typically at a standstill during rush hour downtown. Parents complain that drivers don’t always respect bus stop signs and crosswalks, even after the city added crossing guards to the area.
Perna describes the scene as “mayhem.” She said the evenings can be worse, because of the uncertainty around when the buses bringing kids back to P.S. 16 will show up.
“ In winter when you've got the snow and the ice, and we're out here waiting, and nobody's updating us,” Perna said.
The Danforth Early Childhood Center in the Greenville neighborhood is the main destination for P.S. 16’s pre-K students. The drive can take 30 minutes or more.
Fernandez said pre-K students are bused instead of older grades because state regulations on class sizes and facilities mean pre-K takes up more space. And she said the resources inside P.S. 16 are better suited for older kids.
“ P.S. 16 has a beautiful auditorium, has a pool,” Fernandez said. “Those are facilities that are put to better use by the older students.”
Carr said he’s sympathetic to the situation district leaders are facing.
“This is a problem that's created by the city ultimately,” Carr said. “ The city is the entity that is permitting all the construction, and the school district just has to cope.”
A small portion of P.S. 16’s kindergartners are already being bused as well, to P.S. 3, about 10 minutes away. Fernandez said she wanted to have all of P.S. 16’s kindergartners bused this school year, but that idea was delayed to the coming year after pushback from parents.
New school unlikely
Most school officials, city leaders and parents who’ve spoken publicly about the overcrowding agree the best solution would be building a new school downtown.
The New Jersey Schools Development Authority typically leads school construction in Jersey City and 30 other districts. But the SDA is chronically underfunded and dedicates its resources based on the needs of the most overcrowded districts, like Elizabeth, Plainfield and Hoboken. Even in the decade where Jersey City P.S. 16 saw explosive growth, enrollment in the district as a whole had shrunk by roughly 2,000 students.
The authority opened new elementary schools for the district in 2016 and 2017, and plans to expand another by 2030, but none have been in the downtown area.
The SDA has long-term plans to replace one of Jersey City’s elementary schools with a new building. It’s unclear which school will get the upgrade — the SDA has identified 20 Jersey City school buildings built before 1950 that need to be replaced. P.S. 16 is one of them.
We're just not at the top of [the state's] list, and so that leaves us having to look for creative ways to get a school.
Mike Yaple, a spokesperson for the New Jersey Department of Education, said state officials are aware of the overcrowding at P.S. 16, but the current long-range facilities plan for Jersey City Public Schools — a document maintained by the district and approved by the state — does not call for a new school downtown. He said district leaders could ask the state to update the plan, but any project would still depend on funding and available sites.
P.S. 16 parents have urged school leaders to update the long-range facilities plan. Fernandez said a new demographics study the district launched this year is the first step toward doing so and said she’s hopeful it will be complete by December.
Leaning on developers
Eleana Little, who represents the ward that includes Paulus Hook on the Jersey City Council, said municipal leaders aren’t waiting for a change at the state level.
“ We're just not at the top of their list, and so that leaves us having to look for creative ways to get a school,” Little said.
The P.S. 16 Annex was built without state money, after the city negotiated with a developer to have the space set aside for a school as part of a community benefits agreement. Fernandez said as part of the deal, the developer sold the space to the school district for $1.
“ Fitting the building to our needs, it's a reasonable cost that we can absorb,” Fernandez said. “Building is not a reasonable cost we can absorb.”
Little said that model is the most realistic path to another school downtown.
“ Every developer that comes and wants to build a high-rise, I ask, ‘Could you do a school at this site? What would it look like with a school?’” Little said.
A proposed residential high-rise the city approved in 2020 included plans to build an elementary school to serve 300 students. But the developer scrapped the project in 2022, according to Jersey Digs.
Little said the 111 First Street project, which is still in its early planning stages, has potential to include a new school. She said Keshav Poddar, the city’s former deputy mayor for housing, had been leading negotiations with the developer. Poddar resigned earlier this month, and Little said she is concerned his departure could hurt the chance for new classroom space.
A spokesperson said Mayor James Solomon, who previously represented downtown on the Council, is committed to addressing P.S. 16’s overcrowding.
“The administration has worked closely and collaboratively with Jersey City Public Schools to explore a range of potential solutions, including options that would require additional investment and others that could be implemented at little or no additional cost,” spokesperson Kimberly Wallace-Scalcione said in a statement.
Pricey leases and looming redistricting
With dim prospects for a new school in the near-term, city leaders have said they are working with the school district to find vacant commercial space downtown that could be leased and converted to classrooms.
Fernandez said city leaders have brought potential lease options to the district to consider, but “it's not doable at this time because we do not have the funds to refit these facilities to make a school out of it or enter into a multi-year contract for the rental of space.”
If no space opens up downtown, busing at P.S. 16 is all but certain to continue. But an even more dramatic and permanent option looms for school officials — redistricting the designated zones that feed into each of the city’s schools.
Fernandez said the most likely outcome of redistricting would be a shrinking of the area that sends students to P.S. 16. That would leave some current P.S. 16 families permanently reassigned to schools further away.
“ I'm not sure if parents who bought in that area thinking that their child would attend this school would be as happy attending another school with a more diverse population,” Fernandez said.
Little said the district would have tough decisions to make if it decides to redistrict, because of Jersey City’s tricky geography.
“ You can't just draw a line as the crow flies to the nearest school necessarily because, for example, there's a cliff in the way,” Little said.
Fernandez said no decisions on redistricting will be made until after the ongoing demographic study is done.

https://apache.be/2026/10/22/iedereen-ve.title: Iedereen veroordeelt de rellen. Et alors?
https://apache.be/2026/10/22/iedereen-ve.author: Seppe De Meulder
https://apache.be/2026/10/22/iedereen-ve.text:
Ook wie vanop een afstand naar de rellen in Frankrijk kijkt, moet vaststellen: dit is niet normaal. Alleen stel je tegelijkertijd vast dat de morele verontwaardiging gekoppeld aan grotere repressie helemaal niet het krachtige antwoord is dat het pretendeert te zijn. Dat het eerder een uiting is van de onmacht die mee aan de basis ligt van het probleem.
“Heb je dit gezien? Dat is toch niet meer normaal?” We zijn in een brasserie in Dendermonde waar we iets eten in het midden van onze fietstocht. De man achter de toog toont ons een filmpje op Instagram van de rellen in Frankrijk. Ik weet niet goed wat ik moet zeggen, echt normaal is het inderdaad niet te noemen, die beelden van een stadhuis dat in brand staat.
Kranten en duidingsprogramma’s brengen vooral sensationele beelden gekoppeld aan een zekere morele verontwaardiging
Wanneer ik thuis ben, doe ik dus wat er van een brave burger in een democratisch bestel verwacht wordt. Ik laat de sociale media voor wat ze zijn en ga in de kwaliteitsmedia op zoek naar duiding en analyse die me kunnen doen begrijpen wat er aan de hand is. Maar wat ik in de kranten lees en de duidingsprogramma’s op televisie zie, verschilt eigenlijk niet zo veel van wat de sympathieke barman uit Dendermonde me toonde. Ik zie vooral sensationele beelden gekoppeld aan een zekere morele verontwaardiging.
Ja, vaak wordt er wel een onderscheid gemaakt tussen de brave, geweldloze betogers en zogenaamde casseurs. Hier en daar wordt er toch ook nog een beetje ingegaan op de eisen van de geweldloze betogers, maar een bijzonder groot deel van de berichtgeving wordt toch ingenomen door mensen die zeggen hoe erg ze de rellen afkeuren en waarom ze die afkeuren.
Nu denk ik zelf ook niet dat de kwesties waarvoor mensen protesteren worden opgelost door een winkel te plunderen. Als het nodig is om dat te veroordelen zodat er geluisterd wordt naar wat daarna komt, wil ik dat ook wel doen. Het probleem is alleen dat het herleiden van wat een publiek debat zou moeten zijn tot het performatief uiten van dit soort oordelen de afstand die nodig is om tot inzicht te komen in de weg staat.
Vergeten verlichtingsdenken
Het exponent daarvan was de passage van Mia Doornaert in De Afspraak. “Het is een Franse gewoonte om eerst alles af te breken zonder enig idee van wat er moet komen”, zo foeterde ze. “Dat is al begonnen met de Franse Revolutie.” In al haar boosheid over de vernielingen was ze even vergeten dat aan de Franse revolutie zoiets als de Verlichting voorafging, met toch wel een redelijk intense discussie over wat erna moest plaatsvinden. Een discussie waar ideeën uit voort zijn gekomen met een blijvende invloed op onze samenleving.
Wanneer de onvrede geen politieke vertaling kan krijgen, zal het geweld alleen maar toenemen
In al haar blinde afkeer begon Doornaert zelfs spoken te zien. De Palestijnse vlag die opduikt in de protesten, beschreef ze als “het cement van een monsterverbond tussen uiterst links en harde Islamkernen”. En even later had ze het over “een islamogauchistisch front, een vijfde colonne dat het land in de rug kan schieten”. Voor de duidelijkheid: er bestaat niet zoiets als islamogauchisme. Het enige wat bestaat, is het racistische herleiden van groepen mensen tot hun religie of afkomst en een links dat terecht weigert dit te doen.
Maar de term − die trouwens doet denken aan judeo-bolsjevisme waar de nazis over spraken − wordt wel gretig overgenomen door minister van Defensie Theo Francken (N-VA), die pleit voor de heroprichting van de rijkswacht. Nu wil het toeval dat er in Frankrijk al zo’n militaire politie-eenheid bestaat. En “het opschalen van geweld” waar Francken voor pleit, lijkt net de omvang van de rellen te doen toenemen. Maar in een opgefokt debat waarin wie niet harder wil optreden ervan verdacht wordt goed te praten, krijgen dit soort voorstellen wel een aura van redelijkheid.
De afkeer van het geweld wordt trouwens en passant ook misbruikt om politieke tegenstanders de mond te snoeren. Terwijl vandaag dankzij Mediapart naar buiten komt dat de Franse regering tegen alle bewijs in opdracht gaf aan de inlichtingendiensten te beweren dat La France insoumise achter de rellen zat, blijft men ook in ons land vanuit N-VA consequent ongegronde uitspraken doen over de vermeende linken tussen de PVDA en geweld hier bij ons. Maar de realiteit is dat wanneer de onvrede geen politieke vertaling kan krijgen, het geweld alleen maar zal toenemen.
Politieke crisis
Wars van alle morele oordelen moet wie even uitzoomt namelijk concluderen dat niet alleen Frankrijk, maar heel Europa een politieke crisis doormaakt. Of het nu gaat over sociale problemen, de ecologische crisis of de toekomst van het internationaal recht: de gevestigde politiek lijkt nog nauwelijks antwoorden te hebben die tegemoetkomen aan de ernst van de problemen waarmee ze geconfronteerd wordt. Wat al te zeer ontbreekt in het publieke debat is een sociologische verbeeldingskracht die in staat is om de handelingen van individuen te zien binnen die context.
Morele verontwaardiging gekoppeld aan grotere repressie is een uiting van de onmacht die mee aan de basis ligt van het probleem
Natuurlijk zijn er verschillende reacties mogelijk. Sommige mensen engageren zich en komen in verzet. Anderen staren angstig naar hun schermen en hopen dat extreemrechtse partijen hen zullen kunnen beschermen door al wat anders is uit te sluiten. Sommigen blijven onverschillig zolang zij niet geraakt worden. Sommigen vluchten in de ontkenning, anderen in drank en drugs. De meesten van ons zitten ergens tussen dat alles in en proberen ondertussen vooral ook een normaal leven te leiden. En ja, een minderheid gaat vanuit verschillende beweegredenen over tot plunderingen en het in brand steken van gebouwen.
Ook vanop een afstand bekeken moet je vaststellen: dit is niet normaal. Alleen stel je tegelijkertijd vast dat de morele verontwaardiging gekoppeld aan grotere repressie helemaal niet het krachtige antwoord is dat het pretendeert te zijn. Dat het eerder een uiting is van de onmacht die mee aan de basis ligt van het probleem. De werkelijk krachtige reactie die nodig is, is een politiek antwoord.
Maar dan moet je dus wel je blik even verruimen en naast het geweld van de Franse Revolutie ook het Verlichtingsdenken willen zien. Dan moet je ook willen zien hoe de belofte van vrijheid, gelijkheid en solidariteit voor velen een lege doos lijkt. En dan moet er opnieuw ruimte komen voor politiek debat dat zich ver voorbij het gehakketak richt op de vraag of we de samenleving anders kunnen inrichten om die belofte te realiseren.

Cartooning for Peace presents a educational tool to facilitate discussions on the key issues surrounding the deployment of artificial intelligence, always with humour and… intelligence!
The spectacular success of the ChatGPT conversational robot, launched at the end of 2022, has revealed a glimpse of the possibilities offered by artificial intelligence (AI): for better or for worse? This technological advance raises vast ethical, legal, political, economic and environmental questions… Human questions, in short, since it is disrupting every sphere of our lives. https://gothamist.com/news/woman-stabbed.title: Woman stabbed in neck while jogging in Brooklyn is in critical condition, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-stabbed.author: Amanda Rozon
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-stabbed.text:
A woman who went out for a jog Friday evening is in critical condition, police said, after being stabbed in the neck and left on a waterfront trail in Brooklyn's Bath Beach neighborhood.
Just after 8 p.m. officials said they received a call regarding a person stabbed on a bike path near Bay Parkway and Cropsey Avenue in Bath Beach.
Police found the 28-year-old woman with a stab wound to the neck and transported her to NYU Langone where she was listed in critical condition as of 9:30 Saturday morning.
No arrests have been made and authorities were not able to give a description of a suspect.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-greatest-a.title: The Greatest Art Costumes From Hyperallergic's Halloween Party
https://hyperallergic.com/the-greatest-a.author: Hyperallergic
https://hyperallergic.com/the-greatest-a.text:
The Greatest Art Costumes From Hyperallergic's Halloween Party
From “Las Dos Fridas” to a walking Eva Hesse sculpture, Hyperallergic members, readers, friends, and artists brought the spirit of the season to our second annual costume contest.
A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even the most obvious ones!) walk into a bar ... That’s a Hyperallergic Halloween, baby!
On Wednesday evening, October 28, almost 200 of our members, readers, artists, supporters, and their enthusiastic friends rolled into Oberon in Brooklyn for our annual art costume party. Winners in several categories ranging from “Best in Show” to “Most Likely to Get Censored in Florida” brought out the art-history nerd within them, materializing into both immediately recognizable icons — Roy Lichtenstein's “Drowning Girls” and Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” — and admirably obscure references (oh, she was an Eva Hesse rope sculpture?!).
We’re so grateful to our absurdly smart, creative, and crafty community for their commitment to the bit. And a big shout-out to Zac Thompson for their incredible photographs, which will help us relive the night for many moons, or at least as we wait impatiently for next year ... 🌝
Best in Show
Best in Show winners Emilio Rojas and Chico Raro as Pedro Lemebel and Francisco Casa Silva of Las Yeguas del Apocalipsis’s “Las Dos Fridas” (1989). No bribing was necessary to convince the panel.
Most Esoteric
Zoë Lescaze and Michael Rossi made every part of their costumes from scratch — yes, including the chair — to dress as lesser-known characters from Francisco Goya's Los caprichos (1797–98) series. The couple was among the winners of the "Most Esoteric" award, naturally.
Most Likely to Get Censored in Florida
Richard Prince's "Wayward Nurse" (2005), part of the artist's series critiquing the sexualization of nurses on pulp-fiction book covers, would not fly in the Sunshine State in 2026!
Most Likely to Get Acquired by a Museum Unironically
Curators and staff from the Heckscher Museum of Art in Huntington, New York, recreated a painting from the institution's own collection: George Grosz's antifascist "Eclipse of the Sun" (1926).
People's Choice
Melissa Brown and Marie Lorenz won over the crowd as none other than the infamously botched “Ecce Homo” aka “Beast Jesus” and its author, restorer Cecilia Giménez Zueco!
Hyperallergic Co-founders Veken Gueyikian and Hrag Vartanian with one of this year's costume contest judges, Nicholas D. Lowry, president of Swann Auction Galleries. Veken is Kazimir Malevich’s “Black Square” (1915), and Vartanian is a 17th-century Dutch still life painting — check out the skull! (Memento mori, very Halloween-coded.)
Our wonderful costume contest judges! Left to right: New York Democratic Congressional candidate Claire Valdez, artist Jia Sung as the Spirit of Spirit Airlines (aka what everyone used to take to get to Art Basel Miami Beach), critic Aruna D’Souza in sleek black feathers, and Nicholas D. Lowry as a fashionable pumpkin in plaid.
Hyperallergic Staff Writer Anna Lee as Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” (c. 1665) — an art-history classic, made otherworldly by photographer Zac Thompson’s expert double exposure.
These guests brought Museo del Prado right to your doorstep as a rather gory version of Francisco Goya's “Saturn Devouring His Son” (1820–23). Body horror!
Artist Coco Fusco donned one of the fabulous works in Marisol's wearable wooden sculpture "Three Women with Umbrella" (1965–66). Who says Pop art is dead?
If we had a “Cutest” category this year, this pawesome group would have taken the gold! Left to right: Will Swanson, Dwai, Cosette Patterson, Lauren Blaser, Shelby Roller, Sophia Tedesco, and Daniela Alonso as Cassius Marcellus Coolidge’s “A Friend in Need” (1903).
Emily Dotsikas of Alma Communications as Roy Lichtenstein’s “Drawing Girl” (1963). Brad, who?
Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara addresses the crowd after a very competitive contest. Just don't ask him what his costume is!
Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Rest Energy” (1980). There’s nothing scarier than a multi-year situationship, except maybe literally putting your heart in the hands of your lover.
Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar went as Snoopy for the fourth year in a row, a costume she calls her “magnum opus.”
“I made this Snoopy costume with stuff that I already had at home — the ears, spot, and tail were from an old black tee; I painted an old beauty blender black and used it as Snoopy's nose,” Nayyar shared. “My love of this cartoon beagle is well-known and documented. I'm already a crazy dog lady, but there's something about Snoopy's cheeky attitude and ridiculous antics that flips the script on the ‘man's best friend’ marker, which I find really liberating and inspirational.”
Writer Clara Maria Apostolatos (right) and her partner joined forces, quite literally, to embody Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Relation in Time” (1977).
What still life is complete without its peckish butterfly? Houry Geudelekian and Hyperallergic Co-founder and Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian make a perfect pair.
Us: “What are you?”
Artist Danielle De Jesus: “I'm a broke MFA student!”
Just brilliant, down to the Whitney Museum artist lifetime pass!
Hyperallergic contributors Julie Schneider (middle) as a Keith Haring subway drawing and Daniela Mayer (far right) as an AI girlfriend, with Felix Moody as water and Brian Henderson as Candy Warhol (not pictured: candy corn costume).
Artists Jesse Lambert as Ray Johnson and Linda Ganjian as Eva Hesse's rope sculpture "No title" (1970). Is this what they mean by a two-person show?
Writer Jennifer Samet of Hyperallergic's beloved “Beer With a Painter” column arrived as the ultimate tastemaker: Peggy Guggenheim.
Cheryl Hageman, deputy director of MTA Arts & Design, as a painting from Georgia O'Keeffe's Sky Above Clouds (1960–77) series.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Art Toronto reflects Canadian art community’s focus on sustaining domestic ecosystem
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Hadani Ditmars
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
There is something strangely comforting about this year’s edition of Art Toronto (until 1 November), Canada’s biggest art fair. In spite of the vast 20,000 sq. ft of space it inhabits at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, there is a sense of warmth and grounding in Canadian landscapes made manifest in the installation that welcomes visitors to the art fair’s 27th iteration: Untitled (Watching) (1996) by the late Lynn Donoghue and the first of her Caribou Tarp series to be shown in public, installed here on top of a pile of dirt.
Inspired by the artist’s time in Alberta in the mid 1990s, when she encountered discarded caribou antlers scattered across the tundra, the work speaks to one of the overarching themes at the fair this year, of a return to natural roots. But this Art Toronto is also about uniting the often-scattered Canadian art landscape and, as per the title of one series of talks at the fair, “Building a Stronger Arts Ecosystem”.
These are trying times for Canadian artists and galleries, hammered by a trade war with the US and larger macro-economic forces such as inflation, war and related fuel costs. Happily, though the fair’s new director Emily Jean Alexander tells The Art Newspaper that this year’s Art Toronto is “only down in capacity by 5%”, while some other international art fairs have pared back their exhibitor numbers more drastically. She says there are far fewer US galleries this year than in past editions, while 80% of the 105 exhibitors are Canadian. A commercial gallery from New Brunswick is participating for the first time, alongside dozens from British Columbia, Québec and Ontario. There is a pervasive tariffs-be-damned, “elbows up” sense of artistic solidarity afoot and, Alexander says, a renewed commitment to creating a sustainable art market in Canada.
There is a nostalgic, McLuhanesque installation on the convention centre’s ground floor (presented with Art Toronto’s sister fair, Artist Project) by the Ottawa-based former software engineer Rich Loen. Titled Databells (2025), it connects a collection of bells with statistics ranging from the whimsical (the number of female orgasms per minute) to the digital (the number of TikTok videos played globally per minute) to the serious (amount of carbon dioxide removed from the earth’s atmosphere). The installation’s church and door bells chime at numerically precise intervals, creating a balm for our information-overloaded minds and sparking a meditative state akin to a Balinese temple. It is the perfect hybrid analogue-digital cleanse before the throng of Art Toronto’s main floor.
As visitors ascend into the fair, they can contemplate Kathy Slade’s monumental tapestry Sinking in the West (2023), presented by Mónica Reyes Gallery, which considers recurrence, time and landscape. Turning the corner, visitors will find the McMichael Canadian Art Collection stand; the Kleinburg, Ontario-based museum is currently closed for an expansion and renovation. At the fair it is showing off a recent acquisition, My First Medicine Teacher, a large-scale painting by the Métis artist Christi Belcourt.
Nearby, the Toronto-based Nicholas Metivier Gallery has two stands: one featuring a selection of works by gallery artists, the other showcasing four decades of work by the Canadian photographer Edward Burtynsky. The solo stand includes two new photographs from the artist’s forthcoming project, Mining: For the Future. Burtynsky tells The Art Newspaper that he got his start in aerial photography in Western Australia two decades ago and he returned there last year to revisit a subject he has explored since the mid 1980s. The textural, painterly images in vibrant colours reveal both the brutality and beauty of mining materials such as lithium, copper and cobalt that are needed for components in the technologies that will enable a more sustainable future.
Another highlight of the fair, on the stand of Montreal’s Galerie Nicolas Robert, is Ascension (for Bakers) by the artist Sameer Farooq. An extension of his ongoing Flatbread Library, a long-term research project centred on the political and social significance of the tandoor, the new work connects the forms of collected bakeware with the Buddhist stupa reliquary. The appetising installation features a gathering of vessels, bread forms and tools that honour bakers as sculptors, tracing how ideas, objects and food move across cultures.
Next to it is the Vancouver-based gallery Wil Aballe, whose stand includes a work that has been attracting curatorial interest: Karin Jones’s The Bond (dress) (2023) is a mixed-media take on Queen Victoria’s wedding gown re-imagined with blonde hair extensions as a brilliant expression of the politics of adornment and beauty within contemporary material culture.
Additional eye-catching installations at the fair include Douglas Scholes’s (This is) What happens when a thing is maintained (?) (2024), a large-scale sculpture made from beeswax (presented by Galerie Robertson Arès), and the Montréal-based artist Karine Giboulo’s whimsical environment Joy is a Resistant Bacteria (The Living Room) (2026), presented by Art Mûr. Taken together, they convey a sense of the power of the organic overcoming the antiseptic aesthetics of the digital.
The booth of Toronto’s Nia Centre for the Arts, Canada’s first professional Black arts centre, features the wonderful painting Califia by the Congolese Canadian artist Heritier Bilaka, paying homage to the warrior Queen Nzinga. (Concurrently with Art Toronto, Nia is hosting A Black Art Fair at its headquarters on Oakwood Avenue.)
The Vancouver-based gallery Ceremonial Art is showing works by five artists on its booth, including a remarkable woodblock print by the Tofino-based artist Marika Swan. Titled Embraced in Interdependence, it is both a rare example of West Coast Indigenous art in Toronto and a neat metaphor for the current socio-political climate in Canada and at the art fair.
A nearby stand is devoted to Portfolio, a nonprofit run by a collective of Vancouver artists and dedicated to helping emerging artists via scholarships funded from a percentage of their sales. Among others, the organisation is showing new paintings by Angela Grossman and new works from the Predator series by Lawrence Paul Yuxweluptun—who will open a solo exhibition at the Art Gallery of Ontario in February 2027.
A few booths away, Vancouver’s Equinox Gallery is showing early paintings by the late artist Gathie Falk, mid-century prints from the Fred Herzog archive and a work by Sonny Assu that playfully subverts the colonial landscapes of Emily Carr by overlaying them with Kwakwaka'wakw formline designs.
During the fair’s gala preview on Thursday (29 October), benefiting the McMichael Canadian Art Collection, it was revealed that the federal and provincial governments would provide C$50m ($35.7m) each in funding for a new wing to be designed by Hariri Pontarini Architects. In a video marking the occasion, Canada’s first lady, Diana Fox Carney, proclaimed: “The world needs more Canada.” At this year’s Art Toronto, there is plenty to go around.
- Art Toronto, until 1 November, Metro Toronto Convention Centre

https://hyperallergic.com/10-years-later.title: 10 Years Later, Magenta Plains Is Still Embracing the Unexpected
https://hyperallergic.com/10-years-later.author: Aaron Short
https://hyperallergic.com/10-years-later.text:
10 Years Later, Magenta Plains Is Still Embracing the Unexpected
An anniversary exhibition spotlights the artists who’ve made the gallery one of Lower Manhattan’s most adventurous success stories.
Olivia Smith had a thriving career running Exhibition A on the Upper East Side, a company that sells original contemporary art editions, when artists Chris Dorland and David Deutsch approached her in 2015 about opening a gallery on the Lower East Side.
Smith had worked with hundreds of artists producing limited edition prints, but she had never managed a commercial gallery or negotiated with museums before. Still, she felt a kinship with Dorland and Deutsch, who found a ground-floor storefront on Allen Street and needed help programming it. First they had to agree on a name, as long as it wasn’t their own on the door.
“We wanted something expansive and open-ended,” Smith told Hyperallergic. “We felt Magenta Plains represented a place, but we didn’t know what that place was that we were building yet.”
A decade later, Magenta Plains has helped define what the Downtown contemporary art scene can offer the world. The gallery, which outgrew its original location and currently occupies a 4,500-square-foot space at 149 Canal Street, has featured groundbreaking technology-influenced installations, sculptures, and paintings, selections of which are on display in its 10 Year Anniversary show, up through October 31.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Works from US pavilion at Venice Biennale could be stuck in limbo due to fundraising shortfall
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Elena Goukassian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
With a little less than a month left of this year’s Venice Biennale, the US pavilion is in the news again—this time not for aesthetic but financial reasons. According to Zachary Small of The New York Times, the non-profit responsible for the pavilion has sounded the alarm that it needs to raise $1m or it will not be able to ship Alma Allen’s hulking sculptures back to the US.
“We are facing an urgent funding need associated with the final deinstallation and safe return of the artworks to the United States,” Jenni Parido, the director of the American Arts Conservancy (AAC), wrote in a plea to donors. She added that the organisation had only been able to raise $1.4m out of the $2.5m total needed for the pavilion.
While the State Department provided its usual $375,000 grant for the US pavilion this year, the rest was left up to Parido—a former pet-store owner with little background in art outside of a degree in graphic design—and her brand-new non-profit to raise. (Parido is a friend of the director of the State Department’s Art in Embassies programme, Erin Scavino—a former contestant on Donald Trump’s television programme The Apprentice.)
The funding shortfall comes even as this year’s US pavilion was lauded for costing much less money than usual. (The 2024 pavilion's budget was $5m, and in 2022 the pavilion cost $7m.) The AAC did most of its fundraising via private events with donors including the fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger and the art collector (and former US Navy secretary) John Phelan.
“Budgeting normally is very careful,” Katy Siegel, an art historian who co-curated the 2017 US Pavilion, told the Times. “Maybe there is no oversight now. This is crazy.” She added that finding space in Venice to store Allen’s sculptures—some of which weigh almost a ton—would be very difficult.
As for the Mexico-based Allen, he told the Times that he was unaware of the AAC’s financial woes. “I received only reimbursement for travel and my Airbnb,” he said, “which was cheap.”

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-unemployme.title: NY unemployment recipients brace for delays during system upgrade
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-unemployme.author: Jon Campbell, Carol Chen
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-unemployme.text:
Nearly everyone who interacts with New York’s decades-old unemployment benefits system agrees it’s in need of a major makeover.
That’s why advocates for those receiving benefits are largely pleased that the state Department of Labor is beginning an overhaul of the system on Monday. It’s a painstaking process that will require the state to migrate more than 5 billion business records to a new apparatus in a move that promises to make the byzantine apparatus more user-friendly.
But the massive changeover comes with a major snag: The state will shut down the entire unemployment system for several days. It’s a dramatic move that means tens of thousands of people could see their payments delayed for at least a week.
Jean Stevens, director of the benefits law project for Volunteers of Legal Service, a Manhattan-based nonprofit that offers free legal advice to those navigating the unemployment system, said the temporary pause is “a huge concern for most of the people we’re talking with.”
“They're really struggling to get by and they really rely on these benefits,” Stevens said. “They really need them to pay their bills, to pay for gas, to put food on the table. So every week is really important to them.”
About 106,000 people claimed unemployment benefits totaling $67.6 million for the week ending Oct. 17, according to state Department of Labor data. Of those, 50,206 — or 47% — were from New York City.
It’s easy to see why the unemployment system needs an upgrade.
The interface is outdated, doesn’t work on smartphones and is only active during certain hours of the day. Calls to the help line are known to drop during peak hours. In certain instances, businesses are required to fax — yes, fax — information in. And the technology on the system dates back to the 1970s and 1980s, with some functions requiring a key punch — a long obsolete data processing tool — to operate.
The new system is expected to fix all of that and be easier to use, allowing people to certify for benefits on their phone or tablet with a more modern interface. It’ll also include a feature that will allow anyone to check the status of their claim without having to call in. State Labor Commissioner Roberta Reardon calls it the “pizza tracker.”
The whole thing has cost the state about $188 million to build and implement, according to the Department of Labor.
The upgrade has been in process since at least 2017 and has had significant fits and starts. Most notably, it was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic — a period of time that saw the unemployment system grind to a near-halt under the weight of more than 1 million claims for benefits in March and April 2020.
“The build has taken a very long time, but we are ready,” Reardon told Gothamist. “And when we go live, this will be a significant upgrade. This is the largest transition of [an unemployment insurance] system ever in the United States.”
The shutdown is scheduled to begin at 5 p.m. Monday and last for nine to 12 days, according to the state Department of Labor.
The state is encouraging people to file for their weekly unemployment benefits before the Monday shutdown to avoid a delay in payment, at least for the first week. The pause will not result in anyone losing their benefits; they can certify for back payments after the new system comes online.
”If you're already collecting and you certify before 5 p.m. on Nov. 2, that claim will be processed as usual and your money will land in your bank account probably by the end of that week,” Reardon said.
But those who rely on the payments say that even a temporary delay could force them to make difficult financial decisions in a time where they’re struggling to find work.
After a short-term pain, there's going to be a long-term gain.
Magaly Irizarry, who has been collecting unemployment since May, said a delay will “affect me tremendously” because she’s relying on the benefits to meet her credit card and mortgage payments. She said she’ll try to certify before the shutdown to avoid that.
“I think they should have another way of us getting our payment,” said Irizarry, who spoke with Gothamist at the Bronx Workforce1 Career Center. “They should have another way of us certifying.”
Kenneth Johnson, who was at the Bronx career center and has just begun receiving unemployment benefits, said the shutdown could mean he pays his bills late.
“I won’t be able to certify right then and there,” he said. “If there's a bill that's due, it’ll just have to wait until I get the money.”
Reardon said the Department of Labor considered migrating to the new system in parts. That move would’ve required a series of shorter shutdowns, rather than one longer one. But ultimately, Reardon said the all-at-once approach was determined to be the best option.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she, too, questioned whether the shutdown was necessary. But she said she’s convinced it’s “the only way we can do the proper transition from the old system to the new.”
”We know it's not ideal, but this has been a many, many, many year process to try and take this antiquated system out of the '60s and '70s and to make it more efficient and better for our recipients,” Hochul told Gothamist Wednesday. “After a short-term pain, there's going to be a long-term gain.”
Hochul said the Department of Labor has assured her the outage won’t be any longer than 12 days, and possibly even shorter.
“We have to do it right,” the governor continued.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-when-it-c.title: Opinion: When it Comes to Closing Rikers, Justice Delayed is Justice Denied
https://citylimits.org/opinion-when-it-c.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-when-it-c.text:
Share This Article
“If construction stalls, Chinatown would have a large construction site for a few more years. In the meantime, more families would endure the demeaning trip to Rikers, and more legally innocent people would be subjected to the hellish process of getting to court from Rikers.”
The first time I visited Rikers Island I was in my early 20s, traveling with my mother to visit my younger brother. The trip from the Lower East Side was grueling—from the train, to another train, to a bus, to the Department of Correction (DOC) visitor center, to wait for yet another bus to take us to the jail my brother was at—one of 10 on Rikers.
On top of the trip that felt deliberately exhausting, the way we were treated when we got there sent a clear message that the powers-that-be thought people on that island, and the people who love them, deserved isolation and harsh punishment.
That struck me as wrong in a few ways. First, more than 80 percent of people on Rikers aren’t even convicted. They’re just awaiting their day in court, which most of them could do from home if they could afford to pay bail. Second, people heal with the support of their community, and we are all better off when people coming back from Rikers—whatever they have done or not done—maintain their connections to family.
Furthermore, whatever pre-judgement has been passed on people who are in jail, there are New Yorkers who love them and will make it our business to see them. Why should we be punished in the process?
I’ve traveled to Rikers many times over the years to visit family members, usually while they were struggling through mental health and substance use challenges. That place never gets any better. That’s why I am so excited to see New York City deliver on the historic promised of closing “Torture Island.”
But it’s not just closing the buildings that’s important to me—it’s ending our over-reliance on incarceration and transitioning to a borough-based jail system designed to treat people like people. At the same time, I’m worried that misguided and at times misleading opposition from a few advocacy groups could stall completion of the Manhattan jail, and extend the existence of Rikers. That would be a result that serves no one.
I have lived in lower Manhattan for more than 45 years, and have long been active in my community, from working with young people with disabilities, to chairing my community board, to fighting for racial justice. I know my neighbors are dealing with many challenges, and I know that we share some very tight spaces.
Large construction projects always have impacts in the community, and the city should do what they can to minimize those impacts. That includes using sound barriers and avoiding loud work during late night and early morning hours, paying the cost of independent monitoring, and providing support for local businesses. Another way the city can minimize the impacts of construction is by finishing projects as swiftly as possible, including the redesigned jail that is in progress to replace The Tombs.
Unfortunately, a proposal to move this jail to another site flies in the face of that goal. Starting a brand new land use approval and design process on any site, even a few blocks away, would delay completion (and therefore, the closure of Rikers) by years, and leave a huge vacant site on White Street for who knows how long.
An added complication with the proposed alternate site is that the federal government owns it, and there is no clear path or timeline for them to turn it over to the city. On top of all that, the suggested site isn’t next to the relevant courthouse, like the current site is (and The Tombs was). So detained people would be shuttled to court in vans, instead of escorted through an enclosed walkway—a worse result for them, and for local traffic.
For all of these reasons, Mayor Zohran Mamdani must stick with the plan to rebuild the Manhattan jail on the site of the previous one, next to the courthouse, where construction has already started, and work to complete the project sooner than the 2032 projected timeline.
Given how impractical and improbable a site relocation is, the most likely impact of entertaining that proposal is to prolong rather than stop the current construction. The same is true of a recent lawsuit—more delay, but no tangible benefit that I can see for Chinatown residents or the mass of New Yorkers.
If construction stalls, Chinatown would have a large construction site for a few more years. In the meantime, more families would endure the demeaning trip to Rikers, and more legally innocent people would be subjected to the hellish process of getting to court from Rikers (commonly known as ‘bullpen therapy’).
The jail’s price tag would also climb, not because of any improvements to the design, but just to shell out more money to a construction company. I would much rather see those extra dollars invested in the many needs my community has. I sincerely hope that lower Manhattan residents can come together to direct our efforts toward that goal. Closing Rikers can and should be an investment in all New Yorkers.
Alysha Lewis is a community activist and former chair of Community Board 3.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/30/texa.title: The Rise of the Christian Left in Texas
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/30/texa.author: Alain Stephens
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/30/texa.text:
Alain Stephens is an investigative reporter covering gun violence, arms trafficking, and federal law enforcement.
“Why do you wanna have a pep rally when people are hurting?”
That was the question Rev. Frederick Douglass Haynes III posed at a September food drive in South Dallas, where volunteers were collecting groceries for struggling families. Across town, Republicans were holding a midterm convention. Haynes, a longtime Baptist pastor and Democratic congressional nominee, was introducing James Talarico, the party’s candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas.
A month later, speaking at a Dallas megachurch, Talarico offered his own interpretation of Christian duty.
“I try to love my neighbor through public policy,” the Presbyterian seminarian told the congregation. “I’m trying to make my neighbor’s life easier, better, less stressful.”
Both men are making a deceptively simple argument in some of the staunchly staunch red-as-hell, Republican territory in America, one that might transcend the conventional wisdom about national campaigns and the millions poured into competing campaign war chests: When far-right policy translates into actual pain, at what point does intervening become a spiritual obligation?
Amid the big-ticket ad buys, fundraising appeals, and armies of political consultants, Talarico and Haynes are tapping into a political tradition that has long sustained communities across the South: showing up.
At Haynes’s Friendship-West Baptist Church, the ministry extends to legal services, immigration advocacy, counseling, economic justice, and food policy. It is an example of how churches often form the connective tissue of communities suffering under economic and political strain.
That strain is measurable. Texas is home to four of the nation’s 10 most financially distressed major cities, including Houston, which ranks second nationwide, according to a 2026 analysis. Feeding America estimates that nearly 1 in 5 Texans experienced food insecurity in 2024. Meanwhile, federal analysts project that changes to Medicaid eligibility enacted last year will increase the number of uninsured Americans by 7.5 million by 2034.
While Democratic Party leaders publicly debate how to punish Donald Trump politically, allege corruption, or navigate the ideological divide between moderates and democratic socialists, a different argument is emerging from Southern pulpits.
The Underground Church
From Quaker abolitionists to the Social Gospel’s challenge to industrial exploitation, progressive religious institutions have helped drive some of America’s most consequential political transformations. Christian farmworker ministries supported migrant laborers before joining the United Farm Workers’ California grape boycotts in the 1960s. And while Black churches overwhelmingly led, sustained, and suffered the brunt of violence in the fight for equal civil rights in this country, a handful of white denominations joined them.
Of course, churches also defended slavery, segregation, and exploitation. The blunt reality is that throughout American history, Christianity has always been political and has been used to justify a wide variety of competing political ends.
But Republicans have deftly exploited the perception that they alone speak for American Christians. The Trump administration has readily embraced religious iconography, from evangelical leaders praying over the president in the Oval Office to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s frequent invocations of the medieval Crusades.
There is no way around the fact that Republicans have built a formidable religious coalition, particularly among white evangelicals. Last year, the nonprofit, nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute, or PRRI, found a majority of Republicans qualified as either Christian nationalist adherents or sympathizers in 2025, compared with 17 percent of Democrats.
But Republicans don’t have a monopoly on Christian voters. Pew Research Center polling this month found 73 percent of white evangelical Protestant registered voters preferred Republican House candidates, while 74 percent of Black Protestants and 59 percent of Hispanic Catholics preferred Democrats. None of that is particularly surprising on the surface.
Nor is this some newly discovered religious awakening. According to PRRI’s Census of American Religion, which was published in April, 57 percent of Democrats identified as Christian in 2025, a significant drop from 70 percent in 2013. The white Christian left isn’t necessarily growing, but it’s far from insignificant. Much of it has simply been politically overlooked.
It’s a perception the GOP has routinely capitalized on, often spending a great deal of their election campaigns attacking opponents on religious ground.
On Sunday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott cravenly tarred his Democratic gubernatorial challenger, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, as supporting “Sharia law,” citing an endorsement from a Muslim advocacy group’s political affiliate.
Perhaps ironically, Hinojosa is, and has been on the record, a Catholic — same as Abbott.
“My faith is my moral compass,” Hinojosa told the National Catholic Register in September. “It grounds me in purpose and gives me the courage to do what is right regardless of obstacles or consequences.”
Faith Without Works Is a Dead End
For those who have spent years watching their faith become synonymous with a politics they don’t recognize, frustration may finally be giving way to something else: a determination to be heard.
There are signs that this long-overlooked religious tradition is finding a more public voice. An August study by PRRI documented progressive Christians organizing against Christian nationalism in eight states, including Texas and Louisiana, channeling local meetings, religious discussions, and community networks into political action. Elsewhere, hundreds of members of the clergy have joined protests against immigration enforcement, and some have been trained in direct action and civil resistance. While the movement may not be growing in numbers, its willingness to challenge political power is increasingly visible.
As retired Texas Rev. Kathleene Card, who has thrown her support behind Talarico, told the Houston Chronicle, “faith should influence how people respond to poverty, human rights, the environment, and the well-being of their community.”
Whether any of this will translate into winning on Tuesday is still an open question. An October Fox News poll put Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton at 49 percent apiece among likely voters, but newer polls show Talarico with a small lead. Abbott led Hinojosa by 5 percentage points in that Fox poll, and most polls in the race show the governor with a slim lead.
No matter the result, the Texas campaigns offer a different, more nuanced way of understanding political persuasion. They also challenge a long-standing assumption among national Democrats: that their voters are a monolith, moved by the same issues, values, and appeals.
Across rural America and the South, voters may be growing weary of manufactured arguments and hypothetical doomsday prophecies, with research showing that political advertising, as it stands, has little effect on changing minds at all.
There is something to be said for people willing to put boots on the ground, to do the work instead of endlessly debating how to begin and whether it matters, in the name of service.
It’s a moral code not too dissimilar to a Western: When confronted with injustice, you stand for what’s right, even if you stand alone and are ridiculed for what you believe. It’s a mode of Christianity that harkens back to Abraham Lincoln (and maybe even John Brown.)
That might be a more enduring political proposition than many Democrats’ feigned, helpless aggrievance to the latest Republican spectacle. Campaigns come and go; so do their promises, if they existed in the first place. But the obligation to one’s neighbors remains.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
