https://gothamist.com/news/influential-b.title: Influential Brooklyn developer illegally raised rents despite tax break, lawsuit claims
https://gothamist.com/news/influential-b.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/influential-b.text:
The influential, multibillion-dollar real estate firm Two Trees won a rare concession in this year’s state budget when lawmakers extended an expired tax break program to cover exactly one project: the company’s latest waterfront development in Williamsburg.
Now, a new class-action lawsuit accuses the developer of swindling the public by skirting rules that govern that same tax break program and illegally raising rents at one of its buildings in Fort Greene.
The complaint over rent increases at 300 Ashland Place is the latest such litigation filed by the law firm Newman Ferrara in coordination with the nonprofit Housing Rights Initiative. In recent years, the two have teamed up to target the leasing practices of some of the city’s largest landlords and most politically connected developers, including A&E Real Estate, private equity giant Blackstone and the real estate firm owned by former New York Gov. Elliot Spitzer.
The lawsuit filed Friday focuses on what Housing Rights Initiative Executive Director Aaron Carr called a frequently flouted aspect of state tax and rent stabilization rules.
In exchange for the valuable property tax break known as 421a, landlords must keep apartments — even high-cost, luxury units — rent-stabilized and adhere to state rent regulations that limit rent increases to a percentage set by a city panel. The lawsuit claims Two Trees violated the law when the company applied increases to the full “legal rent” of apartments when tenants renewed their leases, rather than the discounted “preferential rent” that tenants initially agreed to pay.
The lawsuit lays out a sleight-of-hand tactic, citing the example of a 20th-floor apartment in the Fort Greene building.
The legal rent for the apartment is $3,990, according to a listing included in the complaint. Two Trees advertised the unit with two months free, effectively bringing the monthly price down to $3,325. But when it came time to renew the lease, the company applied a rent increase to the $3,990 figure rather than the lower “preferential rent.” Such an increase would amount to a potential 20% rent hike, the lawsuit states.
Carr said a hike that high on the stabilized unit, and six others included in the complaint, violates state law given that the city’s Rent Guidelines Board has not approved an increase higher than 3.25% since 2021. Two Trees, the lawsuit claims, used the tactic to increase rents by more $30 million over the past five years.
“When landlords pocket taxpayer subsidies while legally overcharging tenants, they are cheating the public twice,” he said in an interview. “Once through the rent they steal, and again through the tax dollars they collect.”
In a written statement, Two Trees Managing Director David Lombino called the lawsuit “entirely without merit.”
“Frivolous litigation like this drives up the already extraordinary cost of building and operating housing in New York City,” he said. “Ultimately, those costs are borne by all New Yorkers, making it even harder to address our housing shortage. We intend to vigorously defend against these claims.”
The 379-unit complex opened in 2016 and features apartments priced up to $7,455 in the case of a two-bedroom leased in July. A 26th-floor one-bedroom available earlier this month was listed on the building website for $4,925.
Carr said property owners frequently advertise concessions to attract tenants before increasing their rent at renewal.
“So the landlord can wait for the rental market to heat up before pulling the concession or simply eliminate it at the first renewal, knowing that once a tenant has moved in the severe housing shortage makes it incredibly difficult and expensive to move again,” he said.
Housing Rights Initiative's investigations and frequent litigation have made it a thorn in the side of real estate firms and their allies, who say the organization and its attorneys have honed in on a technicality to squeeze landlords.
Seth Glasser, a partner at real estate investment firm Marcus Millichap, likened the overcharge complaint to annoying penalties assessed to tennis players who step just over the line when serving.
“These are foot faults.” said Glasser, who hosts an industry-focused podcast. “The penalty is so much worse than the infraction.”
Two Trees owns and manages more than 4,000 apartments in a portfolio worth $4 billion, according to its website. The company is constructing another 1,200-unit project called River Ring on the Williamsburg waterfront. In May, state lawmakers extended the 421a program to cover the project, even though the developers will not finish construction by a 2031 tax break deadline.
The 421a exemption requires the city to levy taxes on properties at a lower amount based on their assessed value before a development project adds new apartments, amenities and other improvements, leading to millions of dollars in savings over a period of at least 25 years. Lawmakers let the program expire in 2022 amid disputes over whether the tax break incentivized housing affordable to low-income New Yorkers. In 2024, Gov. Kathy Hochul and legislators approved a new tax break with deeper affordability and higher wage requirements derided by developers as too costly.
Councilmember Crystal Hudson represents the Brooklyn district that includes Fort Greene, where the Ashland Place building is located. She said she helped notify tenants of the Housing Rights Initiative investigation by sending mailers to residents.
“Everyone has to be held to the same standard,” Hudson said. “It’s intentionally confusing to potential tenants and they often think it's a great deal to take up front.”
But, she said, the arrangement can come back to hurt them financially in the long run.
Hudson criticized the state’s housing agency, the Division of Homes and Community Renewal, for not enforcing the tax break rules and instead leaving the job to a nonprofit watchdog and a private law firm.
Division of Homes and Community Renewal spokesperson Charni Sochet declined to comment on ongoing litigation.
Sochet said the agency is “committed to protecting the rights of rent-regulated tenants by enforcing and administering state law as enacted and as interpreted by courts.”
This story has been updated with more information.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/30/b.title: Brooklyn Crash Victim’s EMT Twin Sister Calls Out City, DSNY for Reckless Driving
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/30/b.author: Sam Brule
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/30/b.text:
The victim, Siobhan Lynch, right, with her identical twin, Shannon on their 30th birthday — their last together.
A woman whose sister was killed earlier this week by a Department of Sanitation truck driver holds the driver and city responsible for the fatal crash — and plans to sue them over the tragedy, which she called “not an accident.”
“As someone who responds to emergencies on the daily, it was not an accident. The autopsy report says it was from blunt force trauma. Clearly, that’s 1,000s of pounds of pressure that hit her. So how fast were you turning?” Shannon Lynch said in an interview on Thursday, the day after the driver of a DSNY dump truck struck and killed her 30-year-old twin sister Siobhan at the corner of Cropsey Avenue and Bay Parkway in Brooklyn.
“These sanitation workers are getting away with too much. I want this man in jail. I want him arrested,” she said. “You killed my sister. You took the only person that I have away from me.”
Shannon, who works as an emergency medical technician, said Siobhan was hyper-vigilant about crossing the street because of her sister’s line of work. She told Streetsblog she sees Sanitation Department drivers speed and run red lights “all the time.”
“They do run a lot of red lights. I see it all the time. I don’t know why they do that. They are not an emergency vehicle. You are picking up trash,” Lynch said.
Siobhan was crossing Bay Parkway from Bensonhurst Park to the southeast corner of Bay Parkway and Cropsey Avenue when the DSNY driver turned right from Cropsey Avenue onto Bay Parkway and crushed her, causing severe body trauma.
Lynch described Siobhan as a beloved aunt who helped care for her sister’s kids, often accompanying them at the very intersection where she was killed.
“My sister always went over there because her boyfriend lived there, and she would take my kids to the park across the street there all the time,” the grieving sibling said.
“She was always careful crossing the street, like she — I made sure she was careful crossing the street because she was with my children, you know. And even on her own, you know, she would cross. She would make sure. She would wait. She wouldn’t jaywalk. She wouldn’t. She was like, ‘No, no, no,’ you know. So I, I don’t, I don’t know how this could happen,” Lynch said.
A source who reviewed the video said both the driver and pedestrian had the light. DSNY declined to comment on the details of the incident.
“This is a terrible tragedy, and our thoughts are with the family of the victim. DSNY is assisting NYPD with their ongoing investigation,” Deputy Commissioner Joshua Goodman said in a statement.
The intersection of Cropsey Avenue and Bay Parkway is one of the worst in the city, sluicing impatient drivers on both of the wide, two-way roadways onto or from the Belt Parkway, itself one of the most dangerous highways in the city.
In 2025, there were 30 reported crashes at just that intersection, injuring 21 people, including five pedestrians. Since 2021, there have been at least 106 reported crashes, injuring 77 people, including three cyclists and 18 pedestrians, according to city stats. (There are likely many more victims, but city crash data has not been updated since early June, for reasons that have never been explained by the Mamdani administration.)
In a 2025 presentation in support of a recently installed bus lane on Cropsey, the city Department of Transportation pointed out that the entire stretch of Bay Parkway, including Cropsey Avenue, is a “Vision Zero Priority Corridor” because 25 people were killed or seriously injured between 2019 and 2023.
Friends of Shannon Lynch started a GoFundMeto help her cover childcare costs.
Sam Brule is a senior at The New School. He’s previously worked at the New School Free Press, the Sopris Sun in Colorado, and most recently amNY. When he’s not writing, he works as a bike messenger.
Tickets are still on sale to see the War on Cars Podcast live and Clarence Eckerson's "Close Encounters of the 34th Avenue Kind" in one night. Plus the news.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: The High School Hunt: A Guide to NYC’s Complex Admissions Process
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Amy Zimmer, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
Applying to high school in New York City is daunting: Eighth graders can choose from 700 programs in 400 schools across the five boroughs.
Last year, of roughly 68,000 eighth graders who submitted applications, 58% of those were offered a seat in their top choice; 82% received one of their top three choices.
There’s still time left to build your list — and you add as many schools as you’d like. Applications are due Dec. 4, with offers expected to be sent after 3 p.m. on March 3, 2027.
Some families have already spent months researching their options. Others might not know where to begin.
Here’s a guide to help with the basics. (And here are tips on how to dive into a school’s data.)
NYC high schools broken down by the numbers
Even though the application process is citywide, there are still roughly 20 large comprehensive high schools that guarantee spots for students who live within a certain geographic zone around their campuses. Another six give priority to students living in their zone. (You can find out if you are zoned for any schools through the city’s MySchools platform.)
That said, New York City schools have a larger share of selective schools than other districts across the nation. Nearly 130 programs screen students based on seventh grade GPAs in core subjects. Another 30 also use essays and interviews.
Screened schools sort students into groups for priority, with those in group 1 earning a GPA in the top 15% of their class or an average of at least 94.67 in their core courses last year.
More than 75 programs require auditions or art portfolios. Nearly 50 programs have a specific language requirement.
About 80 schools are open enrollment, meaning they have no priorities and are just based on your lottery number. (See below about lottery numbers.)
The vast majority of programs — about 400 — use the Education Option, or Ed. Opt., admissions method to create balanced classes, targeting a third of its seats for those in the high category (with a seventh grade average of 89.24 or higher), the middle category (78.67 to 89.24), and the low category (an average below 78.67).
Eight schools base admissions solely on the Specialized High School Admissions Test, or SHSAT, and the application process for these schools, along with the audition process for LaGuardia High School of Music and Art and Performing Arts, is completely separate from the rest of the application process. And if you get into one of these schools, you will also get an offer to another school through the regular admissions process.
Finding your lottery number
Before you build your application, you should know your Education Department-assigned random number, or lottery number. You can find it by signing into your NYC MySchools account, which is the portal through which you will submit your application.
When you click “edit profile,” you can scroll down to find the 32-character hexadecimal string of numbers and letters. The first two digits or letters are the most helpful, with priority moving from 0-9 and then from A-F.
A random number beginning with 0 means an applicant will have a relatively high priority; an applicant whose random number starts with an F will have the lowest priority.
The random number is essentially used as a tiebreaker when there are more applicants per seat in a given priority group.
If you don’t know how to log in to MySchools, reach out to your child’s guidance counselor.
Some students have higher priority at certain schools
Nearly 60 schools — 35 of which are screened programs — are part of the city’s “Diversity in Admissions” program, setting aside a portion of seats for students from low-income families, English language learners, or other underrepresented groups. When you find your lottery number in MySchools, it should also tell you whether you are eligible for these seats.
Schools also set aside a certain number of seats for students with disabilities. That means that applications from students with individualized education programs, or IEPs, who spend at least 20% of their week receiving special education instruction, are considered in a different pool than general education students.
How to understand your chances of getting into a particular school
MySchools includes last year’s applicant-to-offer ratio for general education students as well as for students with disabilities. For example, Eleanor Roosevelt High School, a coveted school on the Upper East Side that gives priority to families living in Manhattan, had 30 applications per seat for general education students and four applications per seat for students with disabilities.
MySchools also has a helpful tool illustrating your odds: Once your MySchools account is active — and shows your “tiered” groups for screened schools, ED Opt group, random number, and any other priority designations — you will be able to search schools and see a graphic with three bars, showing whether you have a high, medium, or low chance of getting into a particular program.
A parent-created search platform called NYC-SIFT, the Search Information Finder Tool, can also show your chances once you input your information. The SIFT tool includes a trove of other data and school tour information.
(You will not, however, be able to see your chances for schools that require essays, exams, or other additional measures.)
Make sure to create a balanced list
Education Department officials advise students to rank schools in order of preference.
You can list an unlimited number of schools on your application, but make sure your list is balanced with not only “reach” schools, where your odds might be slim, but also with some schools that you have a higher likelihood of getting a seat. In fact, before you submit your application, the Education Department will flag your application if you only include screened schools.
About 3% of last year’s applicants were placed in schools that were not on their list, according to Education Department data.
Also, if you don’t get your top choice through the regular admissions process, you will be on the waiting list for all of the schools you listed above the school where you received an offer.
What else to consider
It helps to decide what it’s important to your eighth grader. Is a short commute or a one-seat subway ride important? Is access to certain academics important, such as advanced math or theater? Do you want a school with a more traditional approach to academics or one that focuses more on project-based learning? What about clubs and sports teams? How important is homework load? Do you want a large school that has an array of courses and extracurricular activities or a smaller one that might have more personalized attention but not have a full array of activities?
Some of these questions can only be answered by touring a school. While it can be challenging to make time for tours — some are during the school day, some are at night or on weekends — it’s important to see at least some of your top choices and get a feel for the building, commute, and neighborhood.
What’s so special about the specialized high schools?
For the city’s eight schools that require the specialized high school admission test, or SHSAT, students must register to take the exam by Oct. 30. The test will be administered in middle schools and K-8 schools during the school day on Nov. 18. Other students can take the exam at central Education Department locations on Nov. 14 or Nov. 15.
Last year, about 26,100 eighth graders took the SHSAT, and about 4,000 test takers received offers.
Because the eight schools — often seen as a ticket to elite universities and a way into the middle class — admit relatively few Black and Latino students, many integration advocates have pushed for changes to the admissions process.
But research reveals some of the effects of attending these schools might be overblown. One study, looking at specialized high school graduates between 1994 and 2013, found no evidence that those students were more likely to enroll in college, complete college, or attend an especially elite institution than comparable students from other high schools. Another study found that students who just made the cutoff for Brooklyn Tech were actually 2 percentage points less likely to graduate from a four-year college.
Amy Zimmer is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat New York. Contact Amy at azimmer@chalkbeat.org. Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Underappreciated artists from the Chelsea Hotel are finally getting their due
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Sarah Cascone
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Since its opening in 1884, New York’s Hotel Chelsea has been famed as a hotbed of creativity—a seedy yet alluring beacon drawing artists, musicians and bohemians of all kinds. While the luminaries associated with the place (Mark Twain, Janis Joplin, Andy Warhol) are well known, less famous residents are only now beginning to gain recognition.
Among the more recently “discovered” artists who once called the Chelsea home are the late Bettina (1927-2021), Ching Ho Cheng (1946-89), Bernard Childs (1910-85), Herbert Gentry (1919-2003), Nicola L. (1932-2018) and Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020). Many of their relatives still live in the building; some feel their presence to this day.
“It’s happened many times, Ching contacting me,” Cheng’s sister, Sybao Cheng-Wilson, tells The Art Newspaper. She moved into the Chelsea in the 1980s to take care of her brother, who was dying of Aids. For years after Cheng’s death, the bathroom light bulb would flicker on his birthday, 26 December; Cheng-Wilson became convinced it was his way of checking in on her.
For her part, Cheng-Wilson became dedicated to preserving her brother’s legacy. She held onto both his art and the apartment where he made it. She even raised her daughter at the Chelsea, despite its notorious reputation as a hedonistic haven.
Judith Childs and her artist husband moved into the Chelsea in 1966. “My parents were a little horrified by the whole building,” she recalls. “It was not an elegant hotel.” Childs still lives in the first-floor apartment she and Bernard once shared, surrounded by his soft-hued geometric abstractions that seem to glow from within.
In September, these works—imbued with an almost cosmic fluidity—were the subject of a solo stand at New York’s Armory Show with the Shanghai- and New York-based gallery Bank. The 1970s canvases—priced between $14,000 and $55,000—stood out amid the more than 200 exhibitors at the fair; they hung above a fuzzy, cantaloupe-coloured carpet that enhanced the works’ warm, luminous quality.
Showing an essentially forgotten artist like Childs was a bit of a risk for Bank founder Mathieu Borysevicz. “He’s been off the map for so long,” says the gallerist, who just began working with Childs’s estate. The artist’s work was featured in Documenta in 1959; that same year, he had a solo show at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. But Childs’s previous dealer, Jason McCoy Gallery, last gave the artist an in-person solo show in 2013; the gallery itself closed in 2024.
Borysevicz already had experience helping artists from the storied hotel emerge from the shadows, having worked with the Cheng estate since 2021.
Over Cheng’s short but prolific career, the artist developed four major bodies of work, beginning with psychedelic paintings inspired by Tibetan spiritualism before experimenting with airbrushed gouache, graphite on torn paper and rusted surfaces made using iron and copper oxide on paper. The artist, who appeared in last year’s Sixties Surreal at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art, will have his first major retrospective in September 2027 at the Addison Gallery of American Art in Andover, Massachusetts.
Cheng had moved into the Chelsea in 1976, where he befriended Childs. Judith and Cheng-Wilson have stayed close over the years, united by their shared devotion to preserving and promoting their late loved ones’ work. It was Cheng-Wilson who introduced Judith to Borysevicz.
Another friend of Childs, from his time in Paris in the 1950s, was Herbert Gentry—an African American painter known for his jazz-inspired abstractions. He arrived at the hotel in the late 1960s; Gentry’s second wife, the artist Mary Anne Rose, joined him in 1978. She still lives at the Chelsea and now oversees his estate.
“Herbert’s work is so distinctive stylistically, but he was also foundational in bridging what was happening in North America and Europe,” says Gentry’s dealer, Jeffrey Lee of the New York gallery Ryan Lee. By December, the artist will have work simultaneously in museum group shows in Alabama, Germany and Martinique, plus a solo show at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, Sweden.
But not all Hotel Chelsea artists have family members on the premises to safeguard their legacies. When the reclusive Bettina died in 2021, management quickly began clearing out her apartment. The unit was nearly bursting with the conceptual artist’s life’s work, to the point where Bettina slept in a lawn chair in the hallway, as memorably captured in the 2022 documentary Dreaming Walls: Inside the Chelsea Hotel. That would have been the end of the story had Bettina not connected with the Moroccan artist Yto Barrada in her final years.
Barrada fervently believed in the value of Bettina’s work, and its need to be saved from the dumpsters and shared with the world. Before Bettina’s death, Barrada presented the older artist’s sculptures at the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council Arts Center on Governors Island, leading to an appearance in Greater New York 2021 at MoMA PS1. When Bettina died, it was Barrada who saved the contents of her apartment from the trash. The estate, which Barrada oversees with the assistance of Anna McCormick-Goodhart, is now represented by Ulrik in New York; a solo show at the Ruth Foundation for the Arts in Milwaukee closed in April.
“There is a lot to sort and sift through, and it leaves wonderful traces of the history of the making of her works, of her travels, of the people in her life—it’s very densely layered,” McCormick-Goodhart says.
In her later years, Bettina—whose work encompasses photography, printmaking, painting, sculpture, textile and commercial design—was known largely for her eccentricities. But she also planned an ambitious, albeit unrealised, exhibition to show her neighbours’ art. A series of typed index cards from the 1980s reveal the artist list and potential venues for The Chelsea Hotel: Artists at Work. The exhibition would have featured the works of Cheng, Childs, Gentry and Rose, among other residents.
Another artist in this heady milieu was Nicola L. A documentary film-maker, who turned her own lens on her home of nearly 30 years for the 2014 film Doors Ajar at the Chelsea Hotel, Nicola L. is best known for her “functional sculptures”—anthropomorphic furniture shaped like a massive foot, the silhouette of a head and other body parts. In a critique of the objectification of women’s bodies, some mimic the female form, but they somehow avoid feeling overly sexualised.
Nicola L. was largely overlooked until London’s Tate Modern included her work in a broader view of international Pop art for its 2015 exhibition The World Goes Pop. Nicola L.’s first institutional solo show took place in 2017 at New York’s SculptureCenter; the London gallery Alison Jacques began representing her estate after the artist’s death in 2018. A retrospective, When the Earth Turned the Other Way, closed earlier this month at Belgium’s Museum of Contemporary Art in Antwerp, and the travelling museum show I Am the Last Woman Object wrapped up a European tour in March.
Nicola L. was the catalyst behind the Chelsea Hotel residents’ successful fight to keep their apartments after new ownership embarked on an 11-year renovation project to transform the property into a high-end hotel—where rates start at around $500 per night. It was at her urging that the residents banded together to successfully protect their rent-stabilised tenancy.
“The Chelsea was a safe haven for these artists,” says Christophe Lanzenberg, Nicola L.’s son. “The Chelsea allowed them to thrive and stay in New York, instead of getting kicked out of places where rents were coming up.”
Today, there are 42 families still living at the Chelsea. (One artist, Gerald DeCock, is facing eviction at the end of February after 31 years in residence.) Over the years, those remaining have forged tight bonds.
When Childs died, Gentry sent Rose downstairs to keep Judith company. Rose and Nicola L. shared a Long Island City studio for years. As Nicola L.’s health began to decline due to Alzheimer’s, Rose and Judith kept a close watch. They let her sons know when their mother could no longer live alone.
Though its heyday as a refuge for free-spirited artists is long past, the hotel is still deeply connected to its creative history, including artists who checked out decades ago. The lobby, stairwells and hallways are filled with works of art, some said to have been given to the longtime manager Stanley Bard (1934-2017) in lieu of rent. A new Japanese restaurant, Teruko, opened in the basement last year featuring paintings by its namesake, Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020), who lived at the Chelsea from 1957 to 1960, during her marriage to Sam Francis (1923-94).
“I was a baby when she was just coming out of art school, juggling having a newborn and continuing to paint. Her studio was actually in the apartment,” says Yokoi’s daughter, Kayo Malik. But when the couple hosted parties for friends like Mark Rothko and Al Leslie, Francis would have Yokoi put her paintings away, hiding her work.
At the Teruko restaurant, the artist’s pieces are displayed in the dining room, enjoyed and appreciated by guests gathering to share a meal—“a full circle moment”, Malik says. The artist is also the subject of a solo show, Seasons, at New York’s Hollis Taggart (until 25 November). And the gallery is bringing one of Yokoi’s Hotel Chelsea-era works, Untitled (1959), to the ADAA Fair at New York’s Park Avenue Armory (12-16 November); there, it will be on offer at a two-person presentation with the artist Michael West (1908-91). Meanwhile in Los Angeles, the artist has a solo show currently on view at James Fuentes Gallery (until 7 November).
Yokoi eventually moved to Switzerland after separating from Francis. Determined to show her work, she opened two dedicated museums in her native Japan, enjoying a long career across three continents. But Malik still feels close ties to her first home at the Chelsea, that formative chapter in Yokoi’s life, and its vibrant artist community.
“The hotel has had an incredible life,” Malik says.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.title: Mamdani says Trump will 'immediately' grant visa to Ghanaian mom of slain Bronx teen
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.author: Christian Santana, Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.text:
President Donald Trump has agreed to grant an immediate travel visa to the mother of Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old boy originally from Ghana who was shot and killed on his way to school in the Bronx earlier this week, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday.
“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani posted on X. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.
Frimpong was shot around 9:30 a.m. on Thursday near Crotona Park in the Bronx, according to police.
Officers who responded found Frimpong with a gunshot to his abdomen, and drove him to St. Barnabas Hospital in their patrol car, where he was pronounced dead, police said.
Authorities still have not named or described any suspects, or said what led to the shooting.
Frimpong’s father, Thomas Frimpong, told Gothamist that his son came to the United States from Ghana to live with him last year.
In a post on X on Saturday, Ghanaian Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa thanked Mamdani and said he had assigned officials from his ministry to assist Frimpong's mother — whom he identified as Doris Adu Gyamfi — with the visa application process. He added that the administration of Ghanaian President John Mahama would pay the full cost of her travels and "stands ready to contribute towards a dignifying funeral."
Groups representing the Ghanaian diaspora are calling for answers about Frimpong’s killing, as well as greater engagement from city leaders.
The Ghana Diaspora Public Affairs Collective says that although the Bronx has been a haven for Ghanaians, there have been other violent acts affecting members of the diaspora in the borough.
An elderly Ghanaian husband and wife were beaten and robbed at gunpoint while waiting for a bus on Gun Hill Road just days before Frimpong was shot, the group said. And in January, a 53-year-old Ghanaian man was fatally stabbed while walking to work, according to the group.
"These are separate incidents, and there is no established evidence that they were connected or motivated by the victims' Ghanaian identity," the group said in a statement. "Together, however, they have intensified concerns about safety among Ghanaian families who have built their lives in the Bronx. GHPAC calls on city leaders to engage directly with the community, listen to its concerns, and ensure victims and their families have access to appropriate support."
Sam Raskin, a spokesperson for Mamdani, said the mayor called the Frimpongs on Friday. Raskin also said the Office of Community Safety funded and coordinated the deployment of grief counselors, outreach specialists and other resources to the neighborhood.
“This is a devastation that doesn't just affect this family,” Mamdani said in an interview posted to social media on Friday. “It devastates a community. This child was only here for a year. It devastates a diaspora; it devastates an entire neighborhood.”
In a statement on Friday, Ablakwa said he had spoken to Thomas Frimpong directly and "conveyed the condolences of the government and people of Ghana."
"On my instructions, officials of our Permanent Mission in New York have visited the family and coordinating with local authorities," Ablakwa's statement read. "The Foreign Ministry will work tirelessly with US authorities to ensure justice is secured."
This story has been updated with new information.

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/israel-elect.title: Only Israel’s Palestinians Vote Against Genocide
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/israel-elect.author: Matan Kaminer
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/israel-elect.text:
Only Israel’s Palestinians Vote Against Genocide
The “most consequential election in Israel’s history” has not changed the country’s unbearably bleak outlook. But the Palestinian minority has come out in force for solidarity and justice.
It was heralded by many as “the most consequential election in Israeli history,” and by rights it should have been. Under Benjamin Netanyahu’s outgoing far-right government, Israel plunged into a severe constitutional crisis, suffered the worst military setback in its history, carried out a genocide in Gaza and two failed wars in Iran, and become the most hated country in the world.
And yet, as Haaretz editor Aluf Benn noted in his postmortem, Israeli Jewish voters proved themselves imperturbable. Support for aggression throughout the region remains nearly universal among Jewish voters, who have once again sorted themselves again into pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs on a basis that, while reflecting real class divisions, is expressed in familiar culture-war terms, producing yet another frustrating stalemate.
There is, however, one dramatic exception to this uncanny stasis: Israel’s Palestinian minority, which responded to unprecedented levels of racist incitement with the highest turnout on record.
Of over eight hundred thousand votes cast by Palestinian citizens, 37 percent went to the Islamist United Arab List (UAL, also known as Ra’am), and 51 percent to the Joint List, which unites communists, left-liberals and independents. As a result, nineteen out of 120 seats in the Knesset, which are allocated proportionally, have gone to Israel’s only two non-Zionist parties, each of which also has one Jewish representative. (Support for these parties among Jews is numerically insignificant, though hundreds of Jewish academics signed a petition in support of the Joint List.)
In stark contrast to the violence and malaise that have gripped Israel’s Palestinian community following the rise of state-tolerated organized crime, the contest between the two parties was peaceful and restrained. This is all the more remarkable given the clear ideological divide between them.
The Joint List couples the demand for civic equality for Palestinian citizens with a clear rejection of Israel’s annihilationist policy in Gaza and its ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Meanwhile, the UAL — a prominent member of the original Joint List — has turned to a sectoral strategy modeled on that of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Following his 2021 split from the Joint List, UAL leader Mansour Abbas courted Netanyahu and then served as a junior partner in the government that briefly ousted him in 2021–22.
This time around, the anti-Netanyahu bloc has drawn the bar for cooperation at a level meant to exclude even the UAL. Its leader du jour, Lieutenant General Gadi Eisenkot, clarified that any party seeking to join him in government would have to declare Hamas — which still is hanging onto power in Gaza — a “terrorist organization which must be annihilated.”
As Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, Eisenkot elaborated the infamous “Dahiya doctrine,” which recommends mass killing of civilians in areas dominated by hostile forces. In the current context, his shibboleth cannot be read as anything but a demand for active consent to ongoing genocide.
The hostility of the Zionist opposition to any form of solidarity with Gaza was driven home when all its parties, including the liberal Democrats, backed an election board decision to bar Joint List candidate Sami Abu-Shehadeh from running on the basis of a vaguely celebratory article written on October 7 and subsequently repudiated. (Genocidal expressions by right-wing candidates, it goes without saying, were not censured in the same way.)
Against Abstention
Given the depth of the racist rejectionism Palestinian citizens have suffered from both Zionist blocs and the eager complicity of both in colonial violence, a turn to abstention would not be unexpected. But Israel’s Palestinian citizens do not have the luxury of ignoring the differences between these blocs, small as they may be.
Thus, Netanyahu’s finance minister and West Bank “viceroy” Bezalel Smotrich has empowered settler militias to carry out a campaign of ethnic cleansing that might be halted, if not reversed, under an Eisenkot administration. His ghoulish national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has made a fetish out of torturing and executing Palestinian prisoners.
High Palestinian turnout has severely weakened extreme-right parties led by the two and prevented two others from crossing the representation threshold, depriving Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority. Voters are justified in hoping a new government will dial back its ferocity on both fronts as well as tackling organized crime more seriously. For Palestinians, these are questions of life and death, if not of imminent decolonization.
Under these complex circumstances, voters have rewarded the Joint List for striking a balance between principle and pragmatism. Sociologist Maha Sabbah-Karkabi, who will be joining the Knesset as a Joint List representative, stressed the importance of Palestinians’ show of collective power. “By fully utilizing their electoral potential,” she told me, they “have repositioned themselves at the center of Israel’s political landscape.”
However, Sabbah-Karkabi added, the Joint List now confronts a “climate of delegitimization of Arab political participation coming from different parts of the political spectrum,” rendering the question of influencing government policy “much more complicated.”
Delegitimization has come swiftly from Netanyahu’s propaganda organs, which quickly coined the felicitous oxymoron “ballot box terrorism” while weakly claiming Qatari interference on the Joint List’s behalf. (Netanyahu’s advisers, of course, are the ones who have worked for Qatar.) But while Eisenkot and most of his allies obstinately continue to refuse any alliance with Palestinian parties, the Democrats are finally beginning to peel away from this boneheaded consensus.
For the Joint List, the situation presents opportunities as well as risks. Sabbah-Karkabi and Amjad Shbita, general secretary of the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality (the largest of the Joint List’s components), agree that seeing Netanyahu and his far-right government replaced is an urgent priority. Unlike the UAL’s deputies, however, they are also committed to Palestinian national solidarity across borders. The electorate has endorsed this commitment in no uncertain terms.
The ball is now in the court of Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc. To avoid a return election, he will have to break one of two campaign promises: not to enter a coalition with Netanyahu, and to avoid relying on “Arab votes.” If he reneges on the former vow — perhaps under cover of a new war with Iran, conveniently started by Donald Trump and Netanyahu in the coming weeks — he will gift the latter with a renewed sheen of invincibility and the international legitimacy he has done so much to lose.
To end Netanyahu’s rule, Eisenkot would have to break the racist taboo on negotiation with the Palestinian public’s representatives. Though it will not join an Eisenkot government, Shbita told me, the Joint List would be willing to provide it with a parliamentary safety net, preventing Netanyahu from getting another shot at power by bringing the government down with a vote of no confidence.
Even if Eisenkot lacks the courage to negotiate such an agreement, Shbita added, “we would consider enabling a minority government by not voting it down until Netanyahu’s departure from the political scene becomes a certainty.”
Following the “most consequential election in its history,” the political scene in Israel continues to look unbearably bleak. Progressives elsewhere have no reason to let up the pressure for broad sanctions and a total arms embargo. Nevertheless, they can take inspiration from the many Palestinian (and a few Jewish) citizens of Israel, who by voting for the Joint List have expressed their steadfastness — sumoud — in the struggle for democracy, justice, and peace.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Why LCD Soundsystem's 'New York, I Love You' is still the city's most honest anthem
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Nearly 20 years ago, LCD Soundsystem vocalist James Murphy bemoaned the state of New York City over a slow-moving piano: “Like a rat in a cage/ Pulling minimum wage / New York, I love you / But you’re bringing me down,” he sings in a spoken-word cadence. He laments the city’s power-hungry leaders and its general unaffordability crescendo. Then the climax hits right after he admits, “But you’re still the one pool where I’d happily drown.”
“New York, I Love You but You’re Bringing Me Down” might have been released in 2007 as the subdued final track on LCD Soundsystem’s otherwise punchy second album, “Sound of Silver,” but Murphy’s biting honesty still feels pertinent. His lyrics are defined by their contradictions, making the song an alluring choice even for film and television music supervisors looking to concisely convey that torn feeling. It has played in New York City dramas such as “Gossip Girl” and “Succession,” and even the Los Angeles-set series “Nobody Wants This,” which recently used it as the soundtrack for an explosive kiss between a will-they-won’t-they couple.
But the most apt on-screen use of “New York, I Love You” might be during a montage of the city’s sparkling skyline and busy streets early in the new film “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which stars John Turturro as an aging criminal struggling to find his place in a society that left him behind. The montage establishes the story’s setting, but the song sets its tone: Like Murphy, Turturro’s character is attached to a lifestyle that is no longer viable.
“That’s a very human feeling,” the film’s music supervisor, Dan Wilcox, told Gothamist. “It’s nostalgia wrapped up in fear of change, wrapped up in all these different things. No matter what generation of New Yorker you are, you’ve probably felt that way.”
You might have even felt that way from far across the ocean, as suggested by the “New York, I Love You” covers by Scottish singer KT Tunstall and the British-Australian rock band The Last Dinner Party. But the song resonates even more with those who have lived in New York, who have fallen in love with its towering spires and underground bustle while becoming increasingly aware of its skyrocketing prices and flattening culture.
“New York, I love you, but you’re freaking me out / There’s a ton of the twist, but we’re fresh out of shout,” Murphy sings. “Like a death in the hall, that you hear through your wall / New York, I love you, but you’re freaking me out.”
Indie rock and folk singer-songwriter Sharon Van Etten performed the song live in 2018 as part of a New York-themed edition of BBC Proms, a classical music concert series staged in London each summer. At the time, Van Etten, who grew up in New Jersey, had lived in Brooklyn for nearly 15 years but was about to move to Los Angeles. She told Gothamist that although she wasn’t very familiar with the song before conductor Jules Buckley suggested she cover it, its weight hit her as she processed her impending move.
“It is intense to revisit this [BBC Proms] video,” Van Etten said on a recent afternoon. “Because I can see that I was trying not to cry, and [I can sense] the wheel spinning inside, knowing that I was about to say goodbye to New York for that chapter.”
Van Etten, who was backed by a full orchestra as she sang at Royal Albert Hall, put her own spin on the song: “ I feel like you can hear the smile in the way he's performing it,” she said of Murphy singing the explosive climax, whereas “when I finally got to that point where it was supposed to be exploding, I was more saddened and angsty about it because I had all these unspoken decisions I was making in my mind.”
But still, Van Etten connected with Murphy’s overall sentiment: She both loved New York and found it incredibly difficult to live in. She felt at home in its creative community while recognizing that most of her friends were struggling to make rent; the only way she could afford her own apartment was by leaving it to go on tour. She found it difficult to watch small businesses come and go so rapidly. “New York, I Love You” reminded her of what her good friend Kyp Malone (of TV on the Radio) once told her about how he processed the city’s change.
“I remember he told me, famously, ‘Civilizations throughout time rise and fall. New York is no different,’” she said. The mantra shaped her own approach to the city: “I think communities change. Scenes change. For someone coming in and finding their circle, it’s different for them than it was for me. It’s [about] being at peace with that.” (Malone’s wise words also helped inspire one of Van Etten’s biggest hits, “Seventeen.”)
Murphy, who declined an interview, appears to reach a sense of acceptance toward the end of “New York, I Love You.” He might never know how he feels about the city but recognizes that its constantly evolving ways of life still suit other people: “For those who think it still exists / Maybe I’m wrong and maybe you’re right / Maybe I’m wrong and maybe you’re right,” he sings, repeating variations of the line.
LCD Soundsystem performed “New York, I Love You” at the end of their 2011 farewell show at Madison Square Garden. But that wasn’t the end of the band — LCD Soundsystem reunited in 2015 and will embark on their sixth consecutive New York City residency beginning Nov. 19 — nor was it the end of Murphy’s evolution in the city. The man shaped by his scrappy Williamsburg roots went on to open a Michelin-starred wine bar in the same neighborhood. He might have risen in rank, but the song — which derides Michael Bloomberg as a “mild billionaire mayor … convinced he’s a king” — stayed true to its humble origins. Stereogum's Managing Editor Chris DeVille credited its longevity to the continued resonance of that social commentary.
“The Brooklyn world that [Murphy] was coming from kind of feels like a microcosm of the changes that have happened everywhere,” DeVille said. “It makes sense on a broader level when you’re mourning an America that seems to be going away.”
Toward the end of “The Only Living Pickpocket,” Turturro’s character comes to realize that his best years — and, in an intertwined fate, those of the New York he loves — are over. But he doesn’t mourn this truth. He simply accepts it.
Wilcox, the music supervisor, wanted to bookend the pickpocket’s story with another song channeling the notion that New York is still great, even when it isn’t. He landed on cabaret singer Bobby Short’s live rendition of “I Happen to Like New York,” which was recorded at the Café Carlyle roughly 40 years after Cole Porter wrote it for the 1930 musical “The New Yorkers.”
Short sings, “When I have to give the world my last farewell/ And the undertaker starts to ring my funeral bell / I don’t want to go to heaven, don’t want to go to hell / I happen to like New York / I happen to like New York.”
You can imagine Murphy, however tongue in cheek, one day singing the very same.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Chris Ofili brings story of Laure—the Black model painted by Manet—in from the margins at Turin exhibition
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The UK artist Chris Ofili is rewriting the canon in a new show launching in Italy, giving one of Édouard Manet’s most famous figures—Laure, the Black model depicted in Manet’s Olympia (1863)—her own place in art history.
For the latest edition of Beyond the Collection curatorial initiative at the Pinacoteca Agnelli in Turin (30 October-4 April 2027), Ofili presents new works inspired by Laure including a large-scale painting, a watercolour and a series of drawings.
“[The exhibition] means questioning who has written our history and the exclusions involved,” said Sarah Cosulich, the director of the Pinacoteca Agnelli, at a press briefing. “Art historians rewrite history in their own way but Ofili brings this imaginative approach,” the exhibition curator Pietro Rigolo tells The Art Newspaper (Rigolo is also chief curator and head of collection at Pinacoteca Agnelli).
Among the works on view is Manet’s Portrait of Laure (La Négresse), around 1862, which is drawn from the Pinacoteca Agnelli's collection and has been renamed (the piece was originally entitled La Négresse).
“Ofili starts with this idea of giving back to this woman her name and her identity, giving her a story and presence,” Rigolo says. “Nobody has objected to the name change [of the work],” he adds.
Ofili’s large-scale painting, Saint Laure (2026), is the same size as Manet’s Olympia, in which Laure brings flowers to a nude, reclining Parisian courtesan. In his piece, Ofili turns Olympia’s body into a desert landscape which runs along the base of the work, shifting “Laure from the margins to the centre”, an exhibition statement says.
For the work, “Ofili looks to Italian and religious art—in particular depictions of angelic figures and artists such as Giotto and Fra Angelico (Beato Angelico)—and he also looked to an Italian movie called Io Capitano [2023],” Rigolo adds. Io Capitano follows two young Senegalese cousins on their journey from West Africa to Italy. “There is a debate in Italy about migration—this [Ofili] project is grounded in what is happening in Italy now,” Rigolo says, referencing the ongoing political issue polarising European countries. Ofili bases his depiction of Laure in particular on the film’s unnamed character known as “woman in the desert”.
Ofili’s new works also draw on the research of Denise Murrell, a curator-at-large at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Murrell has reshaped the role of the Black female figure in Modern art in her studies, as in the exhibition Posing Modernity: The Black Model from Manet and Matisse to Today, which opened at Columbia’s Wallach Art Gallery in 2018. “From the outset, Ofili said he wanted to involve Murrell [who contributes to a scholarly booklet accompanying the show],” Rigolo says.
The new season of exhibitions at the Pinacoteca Agnelli also include a retrospective dedicated to the 20th-century Greek-Italian painter and polymath Alberto Savinio, the brother of Giorgio de Chirico who played a fundamental role in the development of Metaphysical art (30 October-4 April 2027).
Next year, Ofili’s largest solo exhibition in London since his Tate Britain show in 2010 will open at the Hayward Gallery (7 September-9 January 2028). It will survey three decades of his practice and feature key works from the 1990s alongside his latest paintings.
- Laure. Chris Ofili & Édouard Manet, Pinacoteca Agnelli, Turin, Italy, until 4 April 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: After seven years, Hirshhorn Museum opens Hiroshi Sugimoto-designed sculpture garden
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Angelica Hankins
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
When the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden opened in 1974 in Washington, DC, The New York Times called it “the capital’s newest cultural treasure”. Likening the Hirshhorn to a René Magritte picture, reporters drew out the “juxtaposition of man and nature with architecture”, the seamless melding of light and form, indoors and out, that sets apart its collection of Modern and contemporary art.
On 31 October, the Hirshhorn is scheduled to unveil a new cultural treasure: its $68m renovated sculpture garden. The project has been years in the making, designed by the Japanese artist Hiroshi Sugimoto—who also redesigned the museum’s lobby in 2018. The reorganised 1.3-acre space, with its 30,000 new plants and trees, draws on the architect Gordon Bunshaft’s original design. This is part of a broader transformation at the museum, including renovations to the plaza and building infrastructure.
Featuring 60 works—21 of them from the 1974 installation—the renovated garden includes five entrances, east and west overlooks and an underground passageway of stainless steel. Sugimoto describes its mirrored finish as “reflecting the garden and the people moving through it, an experience in itself—one that is continually transformed by the interplay of light, nature and the visitors”.
I decided a Japanese dry-stone wall would serve as a symbolic link between the ancient and the modern Hiroshi Sugimoto
The walkways and alcoves are delineated using stacked-stone walls, each hand-selected and arranged by the artist. “Bunshaft was deeply influenced by the stone gardens of medieval Japan,” Sugimoto tells The Art Newspaper. “Inspired by this, I decided a Japanese dry-stone wall would serve as a symbolic link between the ancient and the modern, providing the perfect backdrop for the museum’s Modernist sculptures.”
The garden’s opening follows years of controversy. Sugimoto’s early vision for the space was met with criticism. In 2021, Charles A. Birnbaum (the president and chief executive of the Cultural Landscape Foundation) said that the stacked-stone plan “fundamentally disrupts” the garden’s Modernist design and the “artistic intent” of Bunshaft and the landscape architect Lester Collins.
Adjustments to Sugimoto’s initial design were made five years ago, according to the Hirshhorn, after a public consultation process as well as meetings with the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts. In 2022, the museum hosted a groundbreaking ceremony with Jill Biden. “I was amazed by the backlash,” Sugimoto said at the time.
Today, Birnbaum stresses that the Hirshhorn’s “landscape architecture is an art form” and urges the museum to “afford it the same curatorial oversight, care and respect as the rest of the material collection”.
A sense of calm
Sugimoto’s practice is meditative, rooted in a close study of the natural world. “There is an 11th-century Japanese garden manual, Sakuteiki, which tells us to ‘listen to the voices of the stones’,” he says. Each stone has its own character, weight and direction. He adds: “My task is not simply to place it, but to discover where it already wants to be; precision comes from listening carefully enough to find that inevitable position.”
This sense of balance is felt throughout the garden. With benches for quiet reflection and shaded, out-of-the-way recesses, the lawns encourage deep focus, an attentiveness to and a delight in the play of forms. “It’s not just about looking at art,” says Aaron Seeto, the Hirshhorn’s deputy director, “but about looking at it as the garden itself is changing.”
Sculpture in the space is arranged chronologically. The east garden includes a cast of Auguste Rodin’s poignant The Burghers of Calais (1884-89), its six figures weighed down and their necks bound in a darkened procession. Nearby is Henri Matisse’s The Backs I-IV (1909-31), a series of abstracted nudes in bronze relief, their angular silhouettes catching the light.
Henry Moore’s King and Queen (1952-53) is one of five works by the artist on view. It depicts a pair of seated figures, their faces abstracted, the curve of their shoulders liquid smooth. “Joseph Hirshhorn was one of Moore’s closest friends and one of the most significant collectors of his work,” says Godfrey Worsdale, the director of the Henry Moore Foundation. (Joseph Hirshhorn owned 55 sculptures by Moore, and Hirshhorn’s fourth marriage took place before a cast of the artist’s Upright Motive No. 1: Glenkiln Cross.) Worsdale applauds the renovated garden for offering “unfettered access to Moore’s work for new generations”.
In the west garden, home to new commissions, stands Yoshitomo Nara’s Sentinels of Stillness series (2025)—three monumental heads, fashioned from aluminium and coated in brilliant white paint. Following the Tōhoku earthquake and nuclear disaster in 2011, Nara found himself unable to paint and instead took to sculpting. The physicality of modelling clay served as a kind of healing for him.
Liz Larner’s 6 (2010-11), meanwhile, is a cuboid of stainless steel in deep ochre, lavender and white—the tendril-like lines seeming to expand and contract as if suspended in air. The work is a kind of “variable in space”, says Larner, who is absorbed by the mathematical concept of x (the unknown). Following in the tradition of the Surrealist artist Meret Oppenheim, Larner explores the indefinable, “the variable of a variable, the changing perspectives that don’t ossify”.
Comparably fluid is Raven Halfmoon’s Dancing at Dusk (2024), a neighbouring work of cream, coppery-red and slate-grey travertine. Halfmoon, a citizen of the Caddo Nation, gestures to violence and strength, pairing the themes in a work of banded-stone—her first in the medium—trimmed with a line of crosses. There is a kind of solemnity to the piece, the composite visage resolute, meeting the world as it is.
That pathos carries over to KAWS’s 14ft bronze SHELTER (2026), reminiscent of a mother and child—their eyes crossed out, their modelling soft, even tender. It is a warm embrace, the two encircled by an overhanging elm tree.
There is a stillness to the Hirshhorn’s new garden space, a sense of calm in the otherwise fast-moving capital city. “I hope people will experience a different sense of time in the garden,” Sugimoto says. “The sculptures, stones, trees, water and the changing light all exist on different clocks. The garden allows us to slow our own clock enough to become aware of these differences.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Behind a Van Gogh picture: the stories revealed on the reverse
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The backs of Van Gogh paintings can reveal hidden stories. Daubigny’s Garden, at Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum, is a picture with a tale to tell. Painted in Auvers-sur-Oise, a village just northwest of Paris, it depicts the garden of the artist Charles-François Daubigny, whom Van Gogh greatly admired.
A photograph of the reverse reveals two horizontal red stripes woven into the material of Daubigny’s Garden (June 1890), running close to the top and bottom of the picture. For this work, Van Gogh did not paint on conventional canvas, but on a striped kitchen towel (this household linen is known in French as torchon).
As the Van Gogh Museum’s web entry on the picture explains, the artist "had probably run out of canvas temporarily and reached for whatever was available”. Most likely he simply obtained the square of towelling from the kitchen of the inn where he was staying, the Auberge Ravoux.
Daubigny’s Garden was to prove the start of a more ambitious project. On 17 June 1890, Vincent wrote to his brother Theo to say that he had just completed “a small study” of Daubigny’s house and garden—the work on a kitchen towel. This inspired him with the “idea of doing a more important canvas”.
The following month, after receiving canvas supplies from Theo, he made two ambitious “double square” landscapes with a wider view of Daubigny’s garden. One is at the Hiroshima Museum of Art and the other is in the Rudolf Staechelin foundation collection in Switzerland.
Labelling the back
The stretcher of the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden is plastered with small labels recording the exhibitions where the painting was once displayed. Such labels were frequently used in the mid-20th century, although they are much less common nowadays.
Altogether Daubigny’s Garden has been lent to a total of 105 exhibitions since 1896. The labels record 17 of these venues.
Among the exhibitions which do not have labels were three in what may seem a surprising location: Indonesia. It was then very unusual for works by Van Gogh to be lent for shows outside Europe and North America. Indonesia was a Dutch colony at the time, which helps to explain the loans.
In 1938-39, Daubigny’s Garden, along with 13 other Van Goghs, was sent by the artist’s nephew (V.W. van Gogh) to shows in the capital Batavia (now Jakarta), Surabaya and Bandung.
The final Indonesian exhibition closed in January 1939, just a few months before the outbreak of the Second World War in September (which later led to the Japanese invasion of Indonesia in early 1942).
A label on the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden records its next journey. The painting, with the other Van Goghs, was sent directly from Indonesia to San Francisco, where it was included in a display of Masterworks of Five Centuries as part of the Golden Gate International Exposition world’s fair. The Indonesian exhibition had closed on 31 January, and the show in San Francisco opened on 18 February.
The San Francisco show eventually closed on 29 October 1939, a month after the outbreak of the war. It was then too risky to return the Van Gogh paintings to the Netherlands. The 14 pictures, including Daubigny’s Garden, were hastily formed into a North American travelling exhibition.
Labels on the back of Daubigny’s Garden record its subsequent stops at the Toledo Museum of Art, the Art Association of Montreal (now the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts), the Syracuse Museum of Fine Arts (now the Everson Museum of Art) and New York’s Museum of Modern Art.
The wartime show would end up touring in no fewer than 39 cities across North America in 1939-45, bringing Van Gogh to a huge number of people during these difficult years.
Other Van Gogh news
Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum last week opened Whistler: Dandy and Disruptor (until 10 January 2027), a version of which was shown earlier at Tate Britain, where it closed on 27 September. Van Gogh was a great admirer of James McNeill Whistler. In addition to the Amsterdam presentation, the Mesdag Collection in The Hague has a smaller show, Whistler: Loving the Netherlands, revealing the American artist’s links to the Dutch art scene.
A Van Gogh sketch done at Auvers-sur-Oise sold at Christie’s Paris for €230,400 (including fees) on 23 October. The first side is a complicated series of partly overlapping images (some at different angles), entitled Still Life: Can, Books, Wineglass, Bread and Arum, Sketch of Two Women and a Girl. On the reverse is a smaller drawing, Couple Walking (June-July 1890).

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Hong Kong’s M+ Museum launches alliance with Centre Pompidou and MoMA as part of fifth anniversary celebrations—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Benjamin Sutton
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
In the five years since it opened, the M+ Museum in Hong Kong has become one of the foremost contemporary art institutions in Asia, presenting landmark shows devoted to Yayoi Kusama, I.M. Pei, Lee Bul and others, and welcoming more than 2.5 million visitors annually for the past three years in a row. The museum is celebrating its fifth anniversary over the next month and beyond. It is also embarking on a new cultural alliance with the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Centre Pompidou in Paris. For a new episode of the In Focus podcast, our editor-in-chief spoke to Paulo Pong the chairman of the board of M+ and a board member of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, about the plans.
The new cultural alliance “brings together three leading collecting institutions united by a shared commitment to supporting artistic innovation and expanding public engagement through research and exchange,” Suhanya Raffel, the museum director at M+, said in a statement. “As Asia’s global museum of contemporary visual culture, M+ brings perspectives from Hong Kong and our region to this dialogue. We hope to create new opportunities for artists and audiences, shape a more cooperative and sustainable future for museums, and reimagine how cultural narratives resonate around the world.”
In the new podcast episode, Pong discussed the current and upcoming exhibitions and special programmes at the museum, from the recently opened exhibition Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia (until 4 April 2027) to the M+ Restored Festival (1 November-27 December), which showcases nine restored Hong Kong New Wave films.
Next year, the museum will take a comprehensive view of its local avant-garde and cultural scene from the 1970s up to the present in the landmark exhibition Hong Kong: Here and Beyond 2027 (13 March 2027-8 August 2027), unveil the latest presentation of its M+ Sigg Collection (opening 4 September 2027) and host an important Do Ho Suh exhibition (opening 25 September 2027).
In a further signal of M+’s institutional leadership in Greater China and beyond, Pong discusses the upcoming Public Conversation: 2026 Culture for the Planet Summit, taking place on 6 November and addressing the importance of sustainability within cultural activities and organisations. The museum is also launching, in November, the M+ Academy initiative, which seeks to support existing and emerging museum professionals. The goal of the academy is to provide resources, mentorship, connections and opportunities to cultural workers, helping to broaden the professional pipeline for museums and other arts organisations.
“Five years ago, M+ opened with an ambitious vision: to create a museum rooted in Hong Kong and engaged with the world,” Pong added in a statement. “More than 12.5 million visits later, we can see how strongly that vision has resonated. This anniversary is an opportunity to thank the people who made it possible, from our museum team and supporters to the visitors who have made M+ part of their lives.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
