https://theintercept.com/2026/11/01/marc.title: The CIA Is Resorting to an Open Casting Call for Would-Be Cuban Assets
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/01/marc.author: Séamus Malekafzali
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/01/marc.text:
Imperial ambitions are ever-shifting under President Donald Trump. Greenland, Venezuela, Iran, and Cuba are oftentimes spoken about as one continuous train of complete victories and soon-to-be-complete-victories. With the midterms fast approaching, and the date for an apparent telegraphed return to the Iran war on its heels, talk of easily overthrowing regimes has returned, if it ever truly left.
At a rally in Florida last Friday, Trump laid out his grand vision, which he promised would come to pass once the Islamic Republic is neutralized as a threat to the world: “We’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the descendant of Cuban immigrants who left under President Fulgencio Batista (though Rubio later tried to claim his parents fled Castro, who came to power three years later), has long put overthrowing the Communist government in Havana at the top of his agenda, with the hope of replicating the relative ease of kidnapping Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January. Rubio turned some heads last Friday when he publicly posted on X that those seeking “to create positive change in Cuba” could “seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA.”
The post was widely met with bewilderment (Bloomberg’s White House correspondent wrote: “Checked like four times that this was real”), but U.S. officials and members of Congress also shared the post, elevating the public call for collaboration. Recruiting in public might come across as strange and out of character to a public that imagines the CIA recruiting secret agents and informants through clandestine channels or hidden websites, as the agency had done to try and recruit agents inside Iran under Bush and Obama.
But public appeals of this kind are not wholly new. Under the Biden administration, the CIA recruited collaborators inside Russia via a public Telegram channel, as well as publishing videos on social media hoping to recruit Chinese, Iranian, and North Korean assets.
This kind of overt recruitment stems from the difficulties Western intelligence agencies face against adversaries who have built sophisticated surveillance networks of their own. A CIA official told ABC News in May 2025, “in today’s world of [universal technical surveillance], we can’t recruit sources the same way that we did 20 years ago, probably the same way you did 10 years ago.” This has not only affected intelligence operations targeting Beijing, but also Tehran and Havana, where both the U.S. and Israel’s lack of on-the-ground connections and limited official presence has led the CIA and the Mossad to try to recruit willing informants online.
While these limitations may govern the particulars of this strategy, those in power in their respective countries may not see it as evidence of constraints, but instead as evidence of the power of their new strategy: boasting about their national power, rather than keeping it behind closed doors where it supposedly remains useless. After all, what is the use of a deterrent if nobody knows it was you?
The scale of these public appeals, despite having started under Biden, has exploded under the second Trump term, but these moves were arguably preceded by Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to bring the Mossad’s operations much more into the public sphere. The Israeli prime minister’s bragging about numerous cyberattacks targeting Iran’s nuclear program in the late 2010s began to precipitate a shift in public discussion of the Mossad’s work, with many Netanyahu allies, like then-Justice Minister Ayelet Shaked, praising the fact that Iran could now “know it is exposed and that Israel can reach anywhere in the Islamic Republic.” A former deputy director of the Mossad said after the unveiling of Iran’s stolen nuclear archive that Netanyahu’s move “goes against our nature,” and that “the prime minister insisted on publicizing this.”
Netanyahu’s pick in 2021 for the director of the Mossad, David Barnea, has been credited with institutionalizing that change, shifting the secretive intelligence agency’s operations toward appealing to larger masses, and reportedly concerning Mossad veterans who were shocked by the publicizing of agents inside Iran. Casting Israel as a superpower capable of exerting its power anywhere has become a popular refrain under Netanyahu. In an interview with “60 Minutes,” one Mossad officer said of the 2024 pager attacks in Lebanon, which injured more than 2,000 people, that “they are walking proof of our superiority all around the Middle East,” with another officer saying the operation’s complexity and success demonstrated “the world is our stage.”
The U.S. has also gotten in the habit of flexing its superpower status under Trump, declaring the nation’s intent to conquer places like Greenland and Canada, to steal the natural resources of Venezuela and Iran to fill American coffers, and to openly and unabashedly place the Western Hemisphere under a Washingtonian protectorate known as the “Donroe Doctrine.” Rubio declared in Greece in early October, speaking in terms of civilizational battle against the backdrop of the Acropolis, that “we choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power.”
Openly siccing the CIA on foreign adversaries and ICE on domestic ones has been part of that strategy of embracing imperial fervor at home and abroad. Erik Prince, the founder of Blackwater and a private security contractor who remains influential in Trump world, said he was “jealous” of the pager attacks and publicly urged the CIA to take a lesson from the Mossad, saying “we should be getting those kinds of results.”
While both countries have openly sought deep intelligence penetration in adversarial nations, there are limitations to the power of clandestine and overt operations, even by superpowers and wannabes. While the CIA asserted its power in May by openly having its director meet with Cuban officials in Havana to demand “fundamental changes” in return for relief from economic strangulation, the agency’s history of attempts to overthrow the Communist Cuban government are as storied as they are unsuccessful. Earlier hopes for Iran to be as quick and as clean as taking control of Venezuela’s government were dashed early on in the conflict, with the war that was supposed to only take a few weeks now all but certain to extend past the midterm elections for another devastating round.
Even if the war with Iran ends so easily that American ships are able to go through Cuba on the way back ready for more, both outside analysts and even internal U.S. intelligence assessments do not see as easy a way to overthrow the Communist state. The New York Times reported in August that American intelligence sources indicate it could be a situation closer to Iran, where even if Raúl Castro (who has held no official position in the country since 2021) were captured, “few pragmatic officials” are likely to take power in his stead.
While Cuba’s military lacks the kind of advanced equipment Iran has, and shows of readiness (like with Venezuela) are no indication of a country’s actual willingness to fight a protracted campaign, Cuba’s military structure is similar to Iran’s in that it is based on decentralization and redundancies in leadership. In addition, Cuba has a political power structure that, also similar to Iran, is not actually based around a single individual, despite popular claims to the contrary.
Despite Trump’s constant bluster about the miracle of being able to take out Maduro without a single American death, the brazenness of that operation, and the openness with which the negotiations with Iran have been deceptive, appear to have had lessons for the Cuban leadership. President Miguel Díaz-Canel said in June: “All these elements create a lot of distrust in the Cuban people when it comes to conducting any type of negotiation. We continue to express our willingness for dialogue, but it has to be a dialogue between equals, without pressure and with respect for our sovereignty.” American officials have yet to internalize that sentiment. Discussing Cuba in March, Trump joyfully mused: “Whether I free it, take it, I think, I could do anything I want with it.” At the time, he was saying similar things about Iran.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://gothamist.com/news/democrats-ear.title: Democrats' early voting lead in NJ keeps growing ahead of Election Day
https://gothamist.com/news/democrats-ear.author: Mike Hayes
https://gothamist.com/news/democrats-ear.text:
Early voting turnout in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District has swamped 2024 totals ahead of next week’s midterm election, giving Democrats a key advantage in their attempt to take the seat back from Republicans. And unlike previous years, high Democratic turnout over Republicans has been sustained throughout the early voting period.
In the last general election, Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. was slightly behind Democratic challenger Sue Altman in the early vote by about 4,000 ballots heading into Election Day based on the number of votes cast by registered Democrats. He easily overcame that deficit and cruised to a 5-point victory.
This year, Kean and the Republicans find themselves in a far bigger hole after five days of early in-person voting in the state’s most competitive congressional race. Kean is facing off against first-time Democratic candidate Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot and healthcare executive.
As of Thursday, nearly 54,000 Democrats have voted in the district compared to about 28,000 Republicans, according to early voting data from the state’s Division of Elections. The preliminary totals include vote-by-mail ballots. The high turnout has given Democrats a more than 25,000 vote advantage in the district so far.
“Rebecca is taking nothing for granted and will be out across the district earning every last vote," Bennett campaign spokesperson Carly Jones said. Kean’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Early totals do not reflect whom voters cast their ballots for, but are instead a tally of which party they are registered with, hinting at which candidate they may support.
The Democratic swell builds on New Jersey's 2025 gubernatorial race between Democrat Mikie Sherrill and Republican Jack Ciattarelli. Democrats outvoted Republicans in the district by about 10,000 votes after a handful of in-person early voting days. Gov. Sherrill went on to carry the district by about 2 points.
“The early voting [turnout] is something I've never seen before in my life,” said state Sen. Jon Bramnick, a Republican from Westfield. “ Republicans better duck for cover.”
Statewide, Democrats are outvoting Republicans early by more than 323,000 votes.
Bramnick said Kean’s anemic numbers reflect an “anti-Trump” sentiment that has swept through New Jersey. A Fairleigh Dickinson University poll this week found the president’s job approval rating now stands at just 29% in the Garden State. The poll also found that just 10% of voters support Trump’s MAGA movement.
“I like Tom, but this race is about the Republican brand,” Bramnick said. “Unfortunately, the Republican brand is Trump, Trump and Trump. And until we change the brand in places like New Jersey, we're going to continue to lose race after race after race in any type of competitive district.”
Other Republicans were more confident in Kean’s ability to eke out a win.
“Democrats have done a very good job of getting people out to vote early and vote by mail, and then on Election Day, not that good,” said state Sen. Joe Pennacchio, the deputy Republican leader.
But sustained Democratic turnout during early voting points to what may be a larger shift in New Jersey’s electorate.
Since early voting started in New Jersey during the COVID-19 pandemic, Republicans have typically closed the gap after Democrats gained an initial early lead, according to Dan Cassino, a politics professor at Fairleigh Dickinson University.
“ New Jersey has nine days of in-person early voting every year, starting last Saturday, going through next Sunday, and we expect that on the first couple of days, Democrats do better, and the rest of it, Republicans tend to do better,” Cassino said.
For example, on the Monday after the first weekend of early voting in 2025, Republicans outvoted Democrats by about 2%.
But that’s not happening this year. Democrats outvoted Republicans across the state by 16% on Monday Oct. 26, the third day of early voting this election cycle. And that trend continued through Wednesday, the most recent day early voting numbers were available.
“Early voting just isn't helping Republicans the way it has in the past,” Cassino said.
Republican state Sen. Declan O’Scanlon said he still believes in Kean’s chances, even if the two-time incumbent is the state’s most “vulnerable” Republican this midterm election.
“ I think Tom stands a shot at pulling it out,” he said.
Though O’Scanlon agreed with Bramnick that ”sentiment doesn't favor Republicans this cycle.”
“ It never does in midterms when a Republican president's in, just as it doesn't favor Democrats when a Democrat is in the presidency,” he said.
Van Drew in trouble?
Democrats’ advantage has some political watchdogs wondering if South Jersey Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew might be more vulnerable than previously expected in the state’s 2nd Congressional district.
He is currently facing off against Democrat Zack Mullock, the small-town Cape May mayor from the Jersey Shore.
Mullock has received an injection of support in the final days of the campaign. A super PAC tied to Democratic opposition research firm American Bridge 21st Century spent a reported $1.5 million in the week of the race on an ad attacking Van Drew.
On Tuesday, Sherrill said on WNYC’s “Ask The Governor” that she plans to campaign for Mullock.
”He is a great candidate,” she said. “That's been a tough district. But the early numbers we're seeing in the early vote numbers are really looking good. I'm very excited about that race.”
With five days to go until the election, of the 80,000-plus early votes cast in Van Drew’s district, more than 40,000 Democrats have voted early compared to roughly 26,000 Republicans, including vote-by-mail ballots.
This would give Democrats more than a 17% advantage, slightly eclipsing the percentage that Van Drew won by in 2024.
“It certainly puts Zack Mullock in a much more competitive space than anybody would have thought from him a week ago, a month ago, six months ago,” said Micah Rasmussen, director of Rider University's Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics.

https://www.propublica.org/article/midte.title: Trump Has Tried to Exert More Control Over Elections. Here Are the Key Findings From Our Reporting.
https://www.propublica.org/article/midte.text:
Ahead of next week’s midterm elections, President Donald Trump has systematically demolished institutional guardrails that prevented him from overturning the 2020 presidential election, ProPublica’s reporting has shown.
Trump has empowered his loyalists to try to transform the voting process. He launched an unprecedented — and largely unsuccessful — effort to find noncitizen voters. And he tried to restrict mail-in voting.
Our reporters have spent much of this year covering Trump’s efforts to exert more federal control over elections. Here are five takeaways from their reporting.
1. The Trump administration has sought greater federal control over elections.
In April, Doug Bock Clark and Jen Fifield reported on Trump’s efforts to “take over” the midterm elections, detailing how the administration has discarded or diminished endeavors across the federal government to protect the voting process or block foreign interference. Those efforts have included cutting staff on election-related teams at federal law enforcement agencies and finding ways to exert greater federal control over voting.
Our reporting led by Peter Elkind revealed that the Trump administration harnessed Homeland Security Investigations’ personnel, technology and legal authority to try to back up Trump’s unproven claim that illegal voting by noncitizens is tilting elections toward Democrats. Administration officials insisted the effort spearheaded by HSI was producing meaningful results. Our analysis of Justice Department data found, as of May, 41 alleged noncitizens were charged with voting illegally or other election-related crimes. Earlier this month, CBS reported 156 people have been charged since the beginning of the second Trump administration.
“Paper Trail” Podcast
Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “Paper Trail.”
As part of that effort, the Justice Department has demanded states turn over unredacted voter rolls, which contain confidential information on millions of Americans and have historically been managed by states. Since September 2025, the department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for the confidential data. Wary of federal overreach, state officials — including some Republicans — have fought back, and so far every DOJ lawsuit that’s been decided by a federal judge has been dismissed. (The Trump administration has appealed most of its losses to federal appeals courts and has said it will consider taking its fight to the Supreme Court. A Justice Department spokesperson said its “attorneys are skilled, principled advocates who argue every case honestly and in good faith.”)
In a March executive order, Trump instructed the U.S. Postal Service to create new regulations for mail voting. The rules would have put the Postal Service in the unprecedented role of deciding whether to send or deny the delivery of voters’ mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court in September blocked the rules, at least until after November.
The Trump administration has said its actions will make U.S. elections fairer and more secure — and keep those prohibited from voting, such as noncitizens, from doing so. Spokespeople for the DOJ and Department of Homeland Security emphasized that their departments are focused on ensuring elections are free and fair, and that they are working closely with the states to achieve those goals. Contentions to the contrary, they say, are false.
2. Trump has pushed out career officials — and is coordinating with a conservative grassroots organization to transform elections.
At least 75 nonpartisan career officials who’d held roles at federal agencies related to election integrity and safety have been fired or left the government.
Two dozen Trump appointees — including many from the election-denial movement — have been hired. Ahead of the midterms, current and former government officials and election security experts have expressed concerns that once-fringe actors who’ve espoused debunked conspiracy theories about elections are now in positions to control the narrative around the voting process. (A DHS spokesperson said it hires “experts with diverse backgrounds who go through a rigorous vetting process.”)
At least 25 administration appointees have close ties to Cleta Mitchell, a lawyer who leads Election Integrity Network, a grassroots conservative group focused on transforming America’s voting system. This month, Clark profiled Mitchell — and detailed how, despite not holding a formal role in the White House, she’s played a key role in shaping the Trump administration’s elections agenda. The White House has appointed her associates to help hunt for noncitizen voters and investigate accusations of voting fraud in 2020. (Mitchell declined multiple requests to speak with ProPublica, but wrote in an email: “You’re my opponent. … You’re never going to write in any objective, non-judgmental way about the election integrity movement.”)
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
Mitchell, who played a role in helping Trump challenge his loss in the 2020 presidential election, has been leading efforts to pass state and federal iterations of the SAVE Act. The 2026 version of the bill, known as the SAVE America Act, would require voters nationwide to provide proof of citizenship to register and present a photo ID to vote, and would compel states to turn over their voter rolls to DHS. Trump has repeatedly called the measure his top legislative priority, but it has been blocked in the Senate.
In July, Trump also pushed out the remaining members of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission, a four-member board designed to be evenly split between Republicans and Democrats that sets standards for state voting systems. (At the time, a White House official wouldn’t confirm the moves but said the president “reserves the right to remove individuals that may not be totally aligned with the important task of securing America’s elections and ensuring every legal vote is counted.”)
3. Trump officials asked a cybersecurity agency to secretly acquire a voting machine — and hack it.
A few months into Trump’s second term, political appointees at DHS asked its Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure a voting machine, hack it and report the findings so they could be given to the White House, two former administration officials with knowledge of the request told Clark and Andy Mannix.
CISA employees told the political appointees their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. (One of Trump’s first actions when he returned to the White House was to dismantle the agency’s election security work.)
Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems. Since CISA became an agency in 2018, it has come to provide crucial support to thousands of local election officials grappling with increasingly sophisticated attacks.
But some state election officials said CISA provided them with little help as they planned for the 2026 midterms. And other state authorities told Clark and Mannix that they no longer trusted the agency and feared it had been compromised by the Trump administration. (A DHS spokesperson told us in April the “claim that DHS has a broken partnership with states and made our elections less secure is simply false.”)
DHS did not respond to questions for our October investigation, but a DHS spokesperson previously told ProPublica that the changes at CISA were in response to “a ballooning budget concealing a dangerous departure from its statutory mission,” which included “electioneering instead of defending America’s critical infrastructure.” A White House spokesperson declined an interview request but said, “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”
4. The White House floated an idea that would’ve shut down virtually all mail-in voting.
The White House initially proposed a change for the Postal Service that would’ve been even more disruptive than the rule the Supreme Court rejected in September.
As Fifield and Elkind reported, the Trump administration suggested all ballots be delivered through certified mail, meaning voters would need to be home to sign for delivery of their ballots. The Trump administration dropped this plan after the USPS said it would be too difficult to execute. It instead proceeded with the executive order that would’ve forced postal workers to serve as gatekeepers, deciding which ballots would be delivered and which wouldn’t.
In an emailed statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied the administration had interfered improperly with the Postal Service, an independent agency whose governance structure is specifically designed to protect it from political influence.
The Supreme Court’s order in September means that voting by mail can proceed as planned for the midterms, with states left to decide the rules for mail-in ballots.
5. The Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have led to delays and more rejected ballots in rural areas.
Amid the increased attention on the Postal Service’s role in elections, a ProPublica analysis found that delays resulting from the agency’s cost-cutting measures in recent years have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas.
The Postal Service has consolidated processing of first-class mail into regional hubs, and the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from those processing plants. The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and pushed back postmarking, an official mark confirming an envelope has been received by the Postal Service.
Across five states where the best data was available — Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon — the delays during this year’s primary elections have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024.
Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts in place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: New book charts American artist’s lifelong devotion to the South Seas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Christoph Irmscher
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
This is a book about a love affair, one that ran so deep it yielded thousands of watercolours, hundreds of oil paintings and three illustrated books. The painter Robert Lee Eskridge (1891-1975) first visited the South Seas in May 1927, when his ship pulled into the harbour of Papeete, Tahiti. Seeking respite from the grey skies and bone-chilling winters of Chicago, he was instantly smitten and kept returning to the South Seas, eventually making his home in Honolulu, Hawai’i.
Little in Eskridge’s early life had predicted that infatuation. Born in Philadelphia, he attended the Art Institute of Chicago, studied in Paris with the Cubist painter André Lhote, and travelled across Europe for three years. His style, fusing Art Deco patterns with a form of relaxed realism, won him gigs as an illustrator and artist, culminating in a high-profile commission to produce murals for the lobby of the newly rebuilt Palmer House hotel in Chicago. On the eve of his departure for Tahiti, he chose Marco Polo as his subject. (The murals were painted over in 1966.)
Honouring rich traditions
Falling in love with the South Seas is not a unique experience. Names like Herman Melville, Robert Louis Stevenson and Paul Gauguin conjure lush tropical forests, foam-crested waves lapping pristine beaches, and carefree Islanders performing hula dances: a vision inevitably darkened by the damages wrought by colonialism. The Islanders Eskridge painted, unlike Gauguin’s, are not immobilised by the artist’s desire to project meaning into them. They are walking, working, dancing, fishing and making music, living fully in the present even as they honour their rich traditions.
Eskridge’s enthusiasm for Islander culture finds a perfect match in biographer Cook’s enthusiasm for Eskridge. While the more lyrically effusive passages in this volume might not appeal to everyone, the lavish illustrations drawn from multiple collections and the excellent captions help us understand the breadth, range and sophistication of a supremely adaptable painter who deserves to be better known. (Regrettably, some images—of the lost Chicago murals, for example—are AI-produced).
Eskridge’s paintings, whether they show bustling street scenes or re-create rituals he witnessed, vibrate with life. As a young man, he was entranced with Sandro Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (around 1485, in the Uffizi Gallery), and that painting’s revelatory spirit lingers on in Eskridge’s bright, luminous colours or in the way he arranges groups of people around a central figure or an activity.
His training under Lhote shapes the cascading abstract forms Eskridge uses in the background of works such as Stone Fishing (around 1930, Gallery Hawaiiana). In this ancient Polynesian fishing practice, men use ropes with stones to herd leaping fish into shallower waters—a communal effort as well as an occasion for individual daring, represented here beautifully by the young man in the middle, who jumps to grab a fish from the air. A later masterpiece is Hilo Wharf (around 1949, Honolulu Museum of Art), a harbour scene, in which Eskridge blends shirtless workers and the bodies of gigantic tuna fish, some already packed up, into an intense drama of shapes, colour and movement.
Since Eskridge treated the Islanders and their culture with respect, they accepted him as one of their own
Since Eskridge treated the Islanders and their culture with respect, they accepted him as one of their own, Cook tells us. They even asked Eskridge to represent them at the Chicago World’s Fair in 1933. Invitations followed to provide Hawaiian-themed murals for the McCoy Pavilion in Honolulu’s Ala Moana Park and, later, to design clothes for the Hawai’ian label Paradise Sportswear.
Always one to defy expectations, Eskridge, at age 64, married Helen Gebhardt and settled in Olympia, Washington. But the Islands kept calling. He died in April 1975 at a hotel in Honolulu named, appropriately, Hale-kulani, “house befitting heaven”.
• C.J. Cook, Robert Lee Eskridge, South Pacific Dreams Publishing, 344pp, 509 col. illust., $59.95 (hb), published 11 August
• Christoph Irmscher is a critic and biographer

https://citylimits.org/los-neoyorquinos-.title: Los neoyorquinos tienen derecho a votar en su propio idioma. Esto es lo que debes saber.
https://citylimits.org/los-neoyorquinos-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/los-neoyorquinos-.text:
Share This Article
“La ciudad de Nueva York, en particular, cuenta con numerosas leyes que regulan el acceso en diferentes idiomas”, afirmó Olivia Núñez, de la Junta de Finanzas de Campañas Electorales de Nueva York. “Todos los neoyorquinos tienen derecho a votar y a recibir una papeleta electoral en su idioma”.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 29 de octubre. Traducido por Daniel Parra. Read the English version here.
Este reportaje se produjo en colaboración con Factchequeado.
La diversidad lingüística de la ciudad de Nueva York es enorme, ya que sus residentes hablan algo más de 700 idiomas.
El acceso a otros idiomas en las elecciones de la ciudad de Nueva York se rige por un marco normativo de varios niveles, compuesto por leyes federales, estatales y municipales, que abarca a diferentes segmentos del electorado que no habla inglés. Estas leyes cubren algo más de una docena de idiomas, siendo estos los más hablados.
“La ciudad de Nueva York, en particular, cuenta con numerosas leyes que regulan el acceso en diferentes idiomas”, explicó Olivia Núñez, directora de participación comunitaria de la Junta de Finanzas de Campañas Electorales de Nueva York (en inglés, New York City Campaign Finance Board o CFB). “De hecho, contamos con más leyes de protección que las que existen incluso a nivel federal”.
En el estado de Nueva York, alrededor de 5,96 millones de personas mayores de 5 años hablan un idioma distinto del inglés en casa en 2024, según datos del censo. Un informe de la Junta de Finanzas de Campañas Electorales de Nueva York, publicado ese mismo año, reveló que el 16,4 por ciento de los ciudadanos de la ciudad de Nueva York en edad de votar tenía un dominio limitado del inglés. En distritos como Queens y el Bronx, este porcentaje es aún mayor, ya que representa el 20,7 por ciento y el 19,5 por ciento de los residentes en edad de votar, respectivamente.
Varias agencias locales que prestan servicios a los votantes que no hablan inglés han capacitado y reclutado a cientos de intérpretes, quienes han sido asignados a los centros de votación anticipada de la ciudad (la votación anticipada comenzó el sábado y se prolongará hasta el domingo 1 de noviembre). Un segundo equipo de intérpretes, ligeramente más numeroso, se está preparando para hacer lo mismo el martes, día de las elecciones.
City Limits ha elaborado esta guía para ayudar a los votantes de Nueva York a entender sus derechos en las urnas en lo que respecta al acceso lingüístico.
Ley de Derecho al Voto
En 1975, el Congreso modificó la Ley de Derecho al Voto de 1965, añadiendo medidas de protección para eliminar las barreras que impedían votar en las elecciones a las personas con un dominio limitado del inglés.
La enmienda obligaba a las regiones con un número significativo de personas que hablan un idioma distinto del inglés en casa a proporcionarles asistencia lingüística en los puntos de votación.
En virtud de estas disposiciones, ocho condados de Nueva York —entre ellos Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens y el Bronx— deben proporcionar servicios de interpretación a los votantes en determinados idiomas, incluido el español, en algunos lugares de votación seleccionados.
Ley de Derecho al Voto de Nueva York
El estado de Nueva York también cuenta con sus propias medidas de protección del acceso lingüístico. En 2022, la gobernadora Kathy Hochul firmó la Ley John. R. Lewis sobre el Derecho al Voto de Nueva York, con lo que se redujeron los umbrales de población (en comparación con la normativa federal) que obligan a las localidades a ofrecer asistencia electoral multilingüe.
La “regla del 2 por ciento o de las 300 personas” de Nueva York exige a los gobiernos locales que traduzcan los materiales electorales a idiomas distintos del inglés cuando este porcentaje de la población tenga un dominio limitado del inglés (LEP), según los datos de la encuesta sobre la comunidad estadounidense (ACS, por sus siglas en inglés). Existen criterios adicionales que exigen traducciones cuando hay más de 4.000 votantes que cumplen los requisitos de LEP en una subdivisión política específica.
Según la ley, los materiales traducidos —como los formularios de inscripción en el censo electoral, los avisos, las instrucciones y las propias papeletas— deben ser de “igual calidad” que las versiones en inglés.
Además, cuando el idioma hablado por un «grupo minoritario» ha sido históricamente oral o no escrito, el estado de Nueva York está obligado a proporcionar intérpretes orales para la traducción.
Leyes de acceso lingüístico de la ciudad de Nueva York
La ciudad de Nueva York también ha promulgado sus propias leyes para abordar su inmensa diversidad lingüística y complementar las protecciones federales y estatales.
La Junta Electoral de la Ciudad de Nueva York (BOE por sus siglas en inglés), que elabora las papeletas electorales de la ciudad, gestiona los colegios electorales y cuenta los votos, proporciona traductores en determinados lugares de votación en los siguientes idiomas, en función de las necesidades lingüísticas del barrio:
- Manhattan: español y chino
- Brooklyn: español, chino, coreano, bengalí y urdu
- Queens: español, chino, coreano, bengalí, tagalo, hindi y punjabi
- El Bronx: español
- Staten Island: español y chino
Alrededor del 60 por ciento de los colegios electorales de la BOE cuentan con asistencia lingüística para alguna de las lenguas amparadas por la Ley de Derecho al Voto, ya sea a nivel federal o estatal, explicó el director ejecutivo adjunto, Vincent Ignizio. Hay 2.000 puestos de intérprete que cubrir para unas elecciones generales, añadió Ignizio.
La Junta de Finanzas de Campañas Electorales de Nueva York (CFB), un organismo municipal no partidista que administra el sistema de financiación de campañas y el programa de fondos de contrapartida de la ciudad, también lleva a cabo iniciativas multilingües de educación, divulgación y participación de los votantes a través de NYC Votes.
Cada año, CFB publica un informe de análisis del electorado que examina las zonas de la ciudad con menor representación, donde la gente no vota ni participa en las elecciones, y las designa como “comunidades prioritarias”. A partir de ahí, la junta elabora estrategias para involucrar a estas comunidades, entre las que se incluyen los votantes menores de 30 años, los votantes naturalizados nacidos en el extranjero, los votantes con dominio limitado del inglés (LEP) y los votantes con discapacidad.
“CFB identificó barrios del sur del Bronx, el sur de Brooklyn, el norte de Queens y el centro de Queens como comunidades que necesitan una campaña de divulgación electoral específica debido al número de residentes recién naturalizados o de residentes que hablan idiomas que la CFB no ha incluido históricamente en sus campañas de divulgación electoral”, explicó Jadel Munguia, subsecretaria de prensa de la CFB.
“Se trata de zonas en las que observamos una baja participación electoral y, de nuevo, una elevada población de inmigrantes”, explicó Lía Guzmán, especialista en barrios de la CFB para el Bronx, durante un reciente taller bilingüe de sensibilización electoral (en inglés y español) celebrado en University Heights.
“Somos conscientes de que existen muchos obstáculos diferentes para votar, y reconocemos que el idioma es uno de ellos; por eso nos hemos esforzado para garantizar que nuestros materiales están disponibles en 13 idiomas distintos, al igual que nuestra página web”.
Las guías electorales de la CFB, que se envían por correo a toda la ciudad, están disponibles en 13 idiomas: árabe, bengalí, francés, criollo haitiano, hindi, coreano, polaco, punjabi, ruso, chino simplificado, español, chino tradicional y urdu.
“Queremos asegurarnos de verdad de que todos los neoyorquinos tengan acceso a la información que necesitan en los idiomas que hablan”, afirmó Núñez. “Todos los neoyorquinos tienen derecho a votar y a recibir una papeleta en su idioma”.
En 2018, los neoyorquinos votaron a favor de la creación de la Comisión de Participación Cívica de la Ciudad de Nueva York ((en inglés, New York City Civic Engagement Commission o CEC), cuyo objetivo es proporcionar servicios adicionales de interpretación lingüística a los votantes a partir de 2020.
El programa de interpretación de CEC era una de las pocas responsabilidades que se le habían asignado y, por ley, el requisito de acceso lingüístico no puede duplicar lo que ya hace la Junta Electoral (BOE), lo que obliga a la CEC a centrarse en otros idiomas y barrios.
La Comisión comenzó a ofrecer servicios de interpretación en 11 idiomas en barrios con una alta concentración de “ciudadanos en edad de votar con dominio limitado del inglés” (CVALEP por sus siglas en inglés), según las estimaciones de la encuesta sobre la comunidad estadounidense (ACS), explicó la Dra. Sarah Sayeed, presidenta de la CEC.
En 2019, la Junta Electoral (BOE) demandó a la alcaldía para impedir la intervención de los traductores de la CEC, pero la alcaldía acabó ganando el caso. “Este fue uno de los casos que no se resolvió”, recordó Murad Awawdeh, presidente y director ejecutivo de la Coalición de Inmigración de Nueva York, quien participó en la creación de la comisión.
Posteriormente, CEC amplió sus servicios a 14 idiomas.
“CEC creó el programa de asistencia lingüística para los votantes con el fin de garantizar que cualquier persona que hablara los… 14 idiomas más hablados en la ciudad de Nueva York contará con el apoyo que necesitará al llegar a un lugar de votación, para que alguien le tradujera y le ayudará a comprender mejor su papeleta”, añadió Awawdeh.
Sayeed y Anila Cobo, directora del programa de asistencia lingüística para los votantes, afirmaron que tienen previsto prestar servicio en 100 lugares de votación distintos para las elecciones generales y que cuentan con un equipo de 240 intérpretes preparados.
Puedes consultar dónde se encuentra tu sitio de votación aquí. El mapa de sitios de votación de CEC, que indica en qué lugares hay traductores disponibles, está disponible aquí.
Si no hay ningún intérprete disponible en tu sitio de votación, puedes recibir ayuda de una “persona de tu elección”, siempre y cuando dicha persona no sea tu jefe, un representante de tu jefe ni un dirigente o representante de tu sindicato. La “persona de tu elección” que te ayuda a votar no tiene por qué ser ciudadano estadounidense, votante inscrito ni siquiera mayor de edad.
“Si en su lugar de votación no hay disponible una papeleta en su idioma, los votantes pueden traer a alguien con ellos para que les ayude con la traducción”, explicó Nuñez. “Realmente pueden traer a cualquier persona, y existen numerosas medidas de protección para garantizar que se respete el derecho al voto de los neoyorquinos”.
Ignizio señaló que la Junta Electoral (BOE) cuenta con una reserva de personal electoral e intérpretes para hacer frente a problemas de personal de última hora. También ofrecen interpretación por vídeo. “Los lugares de votación están equipados con una tablet que los votantes que necesiten asistencia lingüística pueden utilizar para conectarse con un intérprete a distancia, lo que ayuda a garantizar que la asistencia lingüística esté disponible incluso cuando no haya un intérprete presencial”, añadió Ignizio.
Lamentablemente, no existe un único mapa o sitio web público que recopile todos los servicios de acceso lingüístico de la Junta Electoral (BOE), la Comisión Electoral del Condado (CEC), el Gobierno federal y el estatal para cada lugar de votación en Nueva York.
Si necesitas ayuda para votar y no hay ningún intérprete disponible, pide ayuda a un miembro del personal del centro de votación.
Los votantes que tengan problemas en los centros de votación —como que un miembro del personal les diga que no pueden traer a su “persona de confianza” para que les ayude a rellenar las papeletas— pueden hacer lo siguiente:
- Llamar al 311 y presentar una queja sobre el centro de votación
- Llamar a la línea directa de protección electoral al 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683). También hay asistencia disponible en español en el 888-VE-Y-VOTA (888-839-8682)
- Ponerse en contacto con la línea directa de protección al votante de la Fiscalía General de Nueva York: 866-390-2992
Para ponerse en contacto con el reportero de esta noticia, escriba a [email protected]. Para contactar a la editora, escriba a [email protected].

https://hellgatenyc.com/southern-bk-midt.title: A Pre-Election Trip to Battleground Southern Brooklyn
https://hellgatenyc.com/southern-bk-midt.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/southern-bk-midt.text:
On Thursday afternoon, state Assembly candidate Chris McCreight knocked on doors inside the dilapidated Coney Island Sites 4 & 5 NYCHA housing with a list of Democratic voters who had not already voted early. The narrow hallways were littered with plaster and paint that had fallen from the ceiling. 
"These are some of the worst conditions we have," said McCreight, who's running against Republican incumbent Alec Brook-Krasny to represent parts of Coney Island and Bay Ridge. 
He would know. McCreight has long been part of the Democratic power structure in Bay Ridge. He's currently a senior advisor to Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso, and was previously chief of staff to Councilmember Justin Brannan for eight years. This is his second time running to represent this Assembly district, having lost to Brook-Krasny by five points in 2024.
Though Democrats, including ones McCreight works for, have long represented the area, there's been a swing to the right in recent years. That rightward shift is in a way encapsulated in the career of Brook-Krasny, an immigrant from Russia who switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party in 2022, when he won the southern Brooklyn Assembly seat. (He had quite the colorful career as a Democratic legislator before then.) 
But now, in this potential "blue wave" midterm year, McCreight is one of four Democrats in southern Brooklyn who are trying to flip Republican seats. He sees the entire environment this election cycle as far different from 2024, with voters way more focused on his own race and local issues than when he shared the ticket with the presidential race.

https://apache.be/2026/10/26/hoe-servisc.author: Simon Clément
https://apache.be/2026/10/26/hoe-servisc.text:
Wie vandaag de faculteit Filosofie in het Servische Novi Sad binnentreedt, merkt nog weinig van de blokkade die er maandenlang standhield. De Studentenlijst groeide hier uit tot de grote volksbeweging tegen de regering en de overheidscorruptie die afgelopen zondag (25/10) de verkiezingen won. Verdwijnen Vučić en zijn aanhangers na de nederlaag van dit weekend helemaal van het toneel?
Gejuich op de straten en pleinen in Servië gisteren (25/10): de Studentenlijst, die al twee jaar lang tegen het beleid van president Aleksandar Vučić protesteerde, heeft de parlementsverkiezingen gewonnen.
Deze lente trok fotograaf Simon Clément naar Servië om er de lokale verkiezingen te volgen, toen de studentenbeweging zich voor het eerst als politieke partij positioneerde.
Deze fotoreportage werd in juni 2026 gepubliceerd in Apache Magazine.
Op 1 november 2024 stortte een pas vernieuwd afdak van het treinstation in Novi Sad volledig in na een renovatie, waarop de regering nalatigheid verweten werd. Zestien mensen kwamen om het leven.
“De eerste dag was er een van shock. Iedereen stuurde sms’jes naar hun geliefden om te vragen of ze veilig waren”, herinnert Jelena Kleut zich, hoogleraar mediastudies aan de faculteit waar de studenten in opstand kwamen. “De tweede dag kwam de leugen.”
President Aleksandar Vučić verklaarde daags na de ramp dat de overheid de overkapping nog niet had aangepakt – iets wat verklaringen van betrokken ingenieurs en beelden van de burgemeester en minister van Transport die het net gerenoveerde station inhuldigden, onmiddellijk tegenspraken. “En dus braken er op de derde dag protesten uit”, vertelt Kleut.
Op de nationale dag van de studenten zei de huidige minister van Informatie, Boris Bratina, nog dat “de politie het recht heeft om studenten te slaan en zelfs te doden”
Meer dan twintigduizend mensen verzamelden zich aan het station van de kleine stad om hun woede te uiten over het feit dat de overheid de verantwoordelijkheid voor de ramp zo vlotjes van zich afschoof. In amper een jaar tijd groeide het aantal manifestanten tot 160.000 à 300.000.
“Samen met duizenden anderen waren we aan het wachten op de studenten alsof we wachtten op Tito, de voormalige Joegoslavische leider”, zegt de oudere Marica geëmotioneerd.
Anderhalf jaar na de ramp aan het stationsgebouw ligt het puin er nog steeds bij alsof het gisteren gebeurd is, slechts omringd met enkele hekken, talloze brieven, herdenkingsbordjes en verwelkte bloemen.
Sinds de Servische Progressieve Partij (SNS) van Vučić in 2014 de macht overnam, glijdt het land alsmaar meer af naar een dictatuur. “In Servië is werkelijk iedereen intussen getroffen of benadeeld door zijn beleid”, hekelt student literatuur Marco.
“Wanneer er zoveel politieke gevangenen zijn, onafhankelijke journalistiek zwaar onder druk staat en de rechterlijke macht haar autonomie verliest, kun je Servië moeilijk nog een democratie noemen”, meent Kleut. “Ze zijn het pad aan het effenen voor een complete machtsovername na de volgende nationale verkiezingen. De strijd is nog lang niet voorbij.”
Medeplichtige van Milošević
In de eerste jaren van zijn politieke carrière was Vučić minister van Informatie onder het nationalistische bewind van Slobodan Milošević. Hij was medeverantwoordelijk voor het ontkennen, verbergen en goedpraten van Servische wreedheden in Bosnië, Kosovo en Servië zelf. Kritische journalisten golden als buitenlandse spionnen, terwijl gedode burgers als terroristen werden omschreven.
Onafhankelijke media konden nog maar moeilijk overleven. Die zorgwekkende trend van intimidatie duurt ook onder de huidige minister van Informatie, Boris Bratina, voort. Op 4 april, Dan studenata of nationale dag van de studenten, zei hij nog dat “de politie het recht heeft om studenten te slaan en zelfs te doden”.
Vooral de demonstraties en campagnes tegen de geplande lithiummijnen inspireerden de huidige studentenbeweging
In zijn jaarverslag van 2025 spreekt Human Rights Watch van onwettig gebruik van geweld tegen demonstranten, intimidatie, inbreuk op de privacywetgeving en onmenselijke omstandigheden in de gevangenissen.
Het beleg van Belgrado
Voor Serviërs is protest niets nieuws. In het laatste decennium alleen al lijkt er elk jaar wel een kleine of grote protestgolf over het land te spoelen. In 2016 tegen vermeende verkiezingsfraude, in 2018 de “Een van de vijf miljoen”-protesten, toen Aleksandar Vučić zei dat zelfs als er vijf miljoen mensen op straat zouden komen, hij niets zou veranderen.
Maar vooral de demonstraties en campagnes tegen de geplande lithiummijnen inspireerden de huidige studentenbeweging. In 2024 trokken meer dan 100.000 mensen de straten op tegen de geplande mijnen.
Er werden treinsporen geblokkeerd en net als de studentenbeweging genoot het protest heel wat steun bij de bevolking, zelfs bij de SNS-achterban. Door de massale druk werd het mijnproject tijdelijk stop-
gezet, tot ongenoegen van de EU, die het als strategisch belangrijk ziet.
“Eten, protesteren, plenum en slapen. En dat vijf maanden lang”
“Al die ervaring heeft de studentenbeweging geërfd en getild naar een nieuwe protestbeweging”, vertelt student Milica Klajn. Ze organiseerden bijna dagelijks wakes om slachtoffers van de ramp in het treinstation te herdenken. Terwijl het dodental klom, blokkeerden de studenten eerst 14, dan 15 en uiteindelijk 16 minuten lang de straat in alle stilte.
In december viel een knokploeg kunststudenten uit Belgrado aan. “Ik ging meteen naar mijn faculteit omdat ik hoorde dat er een plenum was (een open vergadering waarin op gedecentraliseerde manier wordt gedebatteerd, red.). Daar besloten we om onmiddellijk ook onze faculteit te bezetten”, zegt Tatjana, een student biologie in Belgrado. Al snel volgden andere universiteiten en faculteiten over het hele land.
Ook buiten de traditioneel politiek actieve faculteiten groeide de mobilisatie: in Novi Sad daagden meer dan 3.000 studenten op voor het eerste plenum van de ingenieursfaculteit. “Ik hoop echt dat onze blokkades een verschil hebben gemaakt. Ik heb er zo veel voor gegeven, ik leefde er praktisch. Eten, protesteren, plenum en slapen. En dat vijf maanden lang”, zegt Milica met een zucht.
Vervroegde verkiezingen
Zelfs gewelddadige ontzettingen en een lange zomervakantie kregen de geest niet meer in de fles. “Vučić dacht echt dat deze beweging, net als eerdere protestgolven, gewoon zou uitdoven. Maar doordat hij ons bleef aanvallen in de media, maakte hij ons juist nog strijdvaardiger”, zegt Tatjana lachend. Tot op vandaag staat het plenum centraal in de horizontale manier van organiseren van de studenten.
Ondertussen hebben ook burgers het concept overgenomen. In Novi Sad komen sympathiserende groepen periodiek bijeen en bespreken zij zowel hoe ze hun lokale buurt kunnen verbeteren als hoe ze de protesten kunnen ondersteunen. Hoewel deze aanpak zorgt voor brede betrokkenheid, brengt ze ook vertraging met zich mee: het kostte de studenten maanden om te beslissen om als politieke partij voort te doen.
Tot grote verbazing werd er gehoor gegeven aan de eis tot vervroegde nationale verkiezingen, die er voor het einde van 2026 moeten komen. Volgens sommige peilingen genieten de studenten alvast van een meerderheid: zo’n 58% van de bevolking zou op hen stemmen.
Met als eerste cruciale tussenstop de lokale verkiezingen in ongeveer tien districten, die de lakmoesproef zijn voor zowel Vučić als de studenten. Maar ze zijn op hun hoede. “Want eerlijk verlopen de verkiezingen in Servië allerminst”, stelt Tatjana.
Waar blijft Europa?
Het verbaast de studenten dan ook wel dat er bijzonder weinig steun uit Europa komt. “Vroeger had ik een geïdealiseerd beeld van Europa”, geeft Tatjana toe.
“Ondertussen vertrouw ik die instituties niet meer. Al te vaak primeren strategische belangen op mensenrechten. Het lijkt alsof ze een andere taal spreken als het gaat over Oekraïne en Rusland dan wanneer het Israël en Palestina betreft. Europa wil nog steeds ons lithium voor goedkope batterijen in militaire drones.”
“Ze zetten wel druk, maar lang niet genoeg”, vertelt Kleut. “In het voorjaar vroegen negen Europese parlementariërs Vučić nog om de mensenrechten te respecteren. De EU ziet dat Vučić de controle verliest, en maakt zich tegelijkertijd zorgen over toekomstige lithiumaanvoer. De EU vreest dat als de banden met Vučić worden doorgesneden, hij zich volledig tot Rusland en China zal wenden. Dan verlies je elk middel van druk en invloed. De studenten blijven wat op afstand van die grotere vraagstukken over de EU. Maar je kan zulke beslissingen niet blijven uitstellen.”
Als de toren valt
Tijana Nešić (63) was een van de duizenden vrijwillige observatoren die de lokale verkiezingen hebben gemonitord. Ze ging eind maart naar Kula, wat in het Servisch ‘toren’ betekent, een klein stadje met net geen 50.000 inwoners. Hier hebben de studenten ervoor gekozen om zelf deel te nemen aan de lokale verkiezingen, terwijl ze in andere steden de bevolking aanmoedigen om op de oppositie te stemmen.
Voor haar vertrek verklaarde Tijana: “Als we Kula winnen, valt de rest als een kaartenhuis in elkaar.” Wellicht is ze een van de oudste studenten die aan de protesten deelnamen. Tijana besloot op latere leeftijd terug te studeren en belandde zo midden in de studentenprotesten. “Wat de studenten vooral doen met hun protesten is de bevolking weer verenigen, en dat is net de grote angst van Vučić. Het geeft ons opnieuw hoop, ik zie het ook bij mensen van mijn generatie”, getuigt ze.
Biologiestudent Tatjana: “Vučić heeft ons alleen maar strijdvaardiger gemaakt”
En dat is voelbaar in Kula zelf. “De enige manier waarop Vučić de verkiezingen hier wint, is door ze te stelen”, meent Dayin, inwoner van Kula. Dat wantrouwen is verre van ongegrond. Enkele dagen voor de verkiezingen eind maart duiken er plots heel wat nieuwe bewoners op in de stad.
“’s Nachts lopen er mannen met maskers rond om mensen te intimideren en op een avond weerklonken schoten. Twee weken geleden werden we zelfs met de dood bedreigd”, vertelt Vladica Klajić, een student die opkomt bij de verkiezingen.
“Normaal stellen de lokale verkiezingen helemaal niets voor. Maar de voorbije twee weken is de president al twee keer campagne komen voeren en waren er bezoeken van ministers in elk naburig dorp. In de media is dit het enige waar ze het over hebben.”
Op de verkiezingsdag rijden grote bussen rond zonder nummerplaten en een grote groep motoren baant zich een weg door de stad naar de stembussen. Rond de middag verlaat een gemaskerde knokploeg het lokale voetbalstadion. Ze vallen omstanders, onder wie journalisten, aan met stokken en keren terug naar het stadion, waar ze politiebescherming genieten.
Klokslag 23.00 uur bindt Vučić er geen doekjes om: zijn SNS-partij heeft in Kula gewonnen. Nochtans zijn de meeste stemmen op dat moment nog niet aangekomen in het stadhuis om geteld te worden. Uiteindelijk behalen de studenten de hoogste score, maar geen meerderheid – die is voor de SNS en haar coalitiepartners.
“We hebben voor onszelf uitgemaakt dat we nu kalm moeten blijven en ons moeten focussen op de nationale verkiezingen. Het feit dat ze zoveel energie hebben gestoken om in Kula te winnen, toont duidelijk dat ze aan het panikeren zijn”, vindt Vladica. “Dat is het teken dat we goed bezig zijn.”
Ondanks hun eerste nederlaag op lokaal niveau heeft de Studentenlijst de parlementsverkiezingen gisteren (25/10) gewonnen. De partij werd gevormd door universiteitsstudenten, maar geen van hen stond daadwerkelijk op de lijst. De kandidaten waren weinig bekende experts, sporters, boeren en kunstenaars. Deze fotoreportage werd in juni 2026 gepubliceerd in Apache Magazine, voor de nationale verkiezingen.

https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/br.text:
Cartooning for Peace / Brazil alert: Brazilian cartoonist Gilmar, also known on social media as ‘Cartunista Das Cavernas’, is the target of online death threats	
14 october 2026
Since July 2026, Cartunista Das Cavernas has been receiving death threats on Facebook because of his editorial cartoons. These messages, which have become increasingly violent, have turned into explicit death threats. The cartoonist has received these threats via private messages, but also in the comments on his posts. One user even went so far as to post a doctored photo of the cartoonist, in which he is depicted with a bullet in his head. The cartoonist has filed a complaint with the São Paulo State Police for threats and verbal abuse.
Cartooning for Peace, which is closely monitoring the ongoing legal proceedings, expresses its concern over the death threats against the Brazilian cartoonist Cartunista Das Cavernas and strongly condemns the attacks and acts of intimidation against the Brazilian press, particularly in the context of the upcoming elections.

Benjamin Paul on the emancipatory dimension of nostalgia
IN 1688 THE ALSATIAN PHYSICIAN Johannes Hofer coined the neologism nostalgia, joining the Greek words nóstos (return, homecoming) and álgos (pain), to designate a pathological expression of homesickness. By the 1960s, however, nostalgia had shed its spatial connotations to take on a temporal dimension, thus linking the feeling of loss inherent to homesickness with a sentimental yearning for the past. Amid the rapid social and technological reorderings of the twentieth century, nostalgia became anathema in particular to modernists and Marxists, who considered the idealization of bygone eras antithetical to their notions of radical reform and progress. Writing in 1962 in the essay “Those Twenties,” Theodor W. Adorno called both the romantic longing for the alleged sexual libertinism of the Roaring Twenties and the glorification of the innovations of the avant-garde “something immeasurably mendacious.” Fredric Jameson went even further, concluding, in 1969, that “nostalgia as a political motivation is most frequently associated with fascism.” Hence, in his landmark 1984 essay, “Postmodernism, or The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism,” he delivered a devastating diagnosis that the postmodern condition suffered from a “nostalgia mode,” the obsession with previous eras recycled in pastiches without any real connection to the complexities and ambiguities of history.
Jameson’s examples focused on architecture and film, but in 1981 Benjamin H. D. Buchloh identified an analogous phenomenon in contemporary painting, remarking that the primary function of Georg Baselitz, Markus Lüpertz, and other German neo-expressionist artists’ “attempt to resurrect figuration, representation, and traditional modes of production” was the “confirmation of the hieratics of ideological domination.” Nearly twenty years later, in a 2000 article on William Kentridge, Rosalind Krauss was at pains to dissociate the artist from any accusation of nostalgia, which she described as “a kind of retro-fashionableness that produces the historical itself as a form of spectacle,” despite Kentridge’s own acknowledgment of a nostalgia “inherent” to his practice.
Nostalgia is no longer what it used to be, however. Its reputation has changed. The condemnations of nostalgia—even if it is still leveraged toward regressive ideologies in the US and abroad—have their own old-timey ring about them; an unshakable belief in the progress of a better future seems, by now, an antiquated belief itself. The future, one beleaguered by tech oligarchs, Trumps, and climate contrarians, appears just as drained of revolutionary dimension as the nostalgic siphoning of the past. “Capitalist realism” is the term Mark Fisher coined to describe the depressing conviction that, despite its obvious flaws, capitalism is the only viable and realistic political-economic system, a theory that takes as its point of departure a sloganized quip attributed to Jameson: “It’s easier to imagine the end of the world than to imagine the end of capitalism.” As Fisher stated in an interview in his 2018 essay collection, K-Punk: “Capitalism’s victory has not consisted in it confidently claiming the future, but in denying that the future is possible. All we can expect, we have been led to believe, is more of the same.” What remains, then, is nostalgia for the future—a longing not so much for the past as for the hopeful attitude of a historical moment when art and culture still felt vitally entangled with radical politics.
Zineb Sedira’s Tate Britain commission “When Words Fall Silent, Cinema Speaks . . . ,” which opened in May and runs until January 2027, epitomizes this future nostalgia: not a misty-eyed glorification of the past, but a multilayered expression of longing for a time that had no demand for nostalgia because the future still seemed up for grabs. In other words, a nostalgia for a lack of nostalgia. Upon entering the neoclassical Duveen Galleries at Tate Britain, visitors find themselves in a meticulously re-created Algerian-Parisian café circa 1969, complete with a fully stocked bar, tables and chairs, the daily menu, and music from a jukebox. Among the knickknacks, postcards, record covers, and liquor ads pinned to the wall are framed photographs of Algerian independence leader Ahmed Ben Bella, Frantz Fanon, James Baldwin, and counterfeit Cuban pesos donning the face of Che Guevara. This immersive environment invites visitors to step back into the stylish public sphere of the postcolonial café, an inclusive center of political and social activities, in which bohemian lifestyle, cool design, and charismatic intellectuals combined in forging a revolutionary consciousness.
Sedira suggests in the other sections of the long hall of the Duveen Galleries that art, and in particular cinema, mattered a great deal in this process. She installed an impromptu movie theater with a ticket booth, an homage to the Cinémathèque Algérienne, the hub for the cultural and political intelligentsia of Algiers, where avant-garde films were screened, including classics of the struggle of resistance such as Algérie en flammes (Algeria in Flames), directed by René Vautier in 1958, and The Battle of Algiers (1966) by the Italian director Gillo Pontecorvo. There is a so-called Ciné Pop, a truck filled with film equipment used to screen movies in the countryside, originally of the colonial government and, after independence, of the revolutionary one, and a Scopitone, a type of jukebox designed in the late 1950s for music videos but that in this case shows excerpts from Agnès Varda’s avant-garde classic Salut les Cubains (1963).
Unlike the café in the central space of the Duveen Galleries, however, these other installations are no longer immersive. Rather than plunging visitors into the revolutionary lifestyle of the ’60s, they call for critical reflection, thus building a bridge to our contemporary condition. The impromptu movie theater shows Sedira’s interview with Boudjemaâ Karèche, who led the Cinémathèque Algérienne during its prime, and later lost his vision; in the interview, Sedira refers to this as a “premonition” of the decline of the Cinémathèque, which “has dried out, due to the brutal civil war of the ’90s, the rise of Islamism, the attacks and assassinations on intellectuals and artists, many now exiled. Culture is no longer a priority.” The Ciné Pop screens a recent interview with Ahmed Bedjaoui, the filmmaker and scholar of Algerian cinema, who pointedly remarks about the time: “Everyone was socialist. You had to be foolish not to be. And equally foolish to remain so.”
For all of Sedira’s efforts toward creating a transportive environment, the installations still seem a bit dwarfed by the vast Duveen Galleries, thereby dislocating the immersive effect, even of the café. It is precisely this contrast that brings into sharp relief the implications of the surrounding architecture. Added to the Tate in 1937 at a time when the British Empire was losing its grip over the colonies, the Duveen Galleries are a monument to nostalgia, albeit for the imperialist ambitions of an era of the United Kingdom that implanted such neoclassical structures in its colonies as expressions of power. This setting not only confronts the Algerian struggle for independence with the legacy of colonialism, but also points to a nostalgia of an entirely different kind: namely, the reactionary longing for the past of a kingdom that refuses to relinquish power, then as now, bearing Brexit in mind.
The retentive, conservative nostalgia of the gallery architecture lands with acute friction with the nostalgia deployed by Sedira, thus juxtaposing restorative with reflective nostalgias. Svetlana Boym made this distinction in her 2001 book The Future of Nostalgia: between a reactionary yearning for a past uncomplicated by prevalent struggles and conflicts—exemplified by the Duveen Galleries and described by Adorno and Jameson—and a more critical, reflective reconsideration that “opens up a multitude of potentialities, nonteleological possibilities of historic development.” By creating a plurality of temporal layers and horizons, Sedira produces precisely such a reflective environment, forming a nostalgia that collides the past into the present and even the future. “Some utopian dreams are unfulfilled,” Sedira said in a recent interview. “So we need to look back—and learn.” Sedira’s installation thus encourages critical deliberations on both the successes and the failures of the Algerian independence movement. But it does so while maintaining a strong feeling of nostalgia and longing for the desire for change and the future that the postcolonial struggle embodied.
Like Sedira, Matt Saunders’s obsession is cinema—perhaps for its abilities to immerse the viewer in the past with the most fidelity. For his exhibition “On an Overgrown Path” at Marian Goodman Gallery in New York, on view this summer, Saunders conjured a similar future nostalgia, copying sequences and stills from avant-garde cinema in multiple mediated formats. Among the works on view was a portrait of the actress Hertha Thiele, who starred in Kuhle Wampe (1932), the classic film about class struggle in the Weimar Republic cowritten by Bertolt Brecht, and Mädchen in Uniform (1931), a pioneering depiction of lesbian love in mainstream cinema. There were two pictures of the actress Barbara Sukowa playing the leader of the German Revolution of 1918–19 in Margarethe von Trotta’s Rosa Luxemburg (1986) and an entire series dedicated to an androgynous-looking Jane Birkin in the Serge Gainsbourg movie Je t’aime moi non plus (1976). The show also contained depictions of filmmaker Rainer Werner Fassbinder, alongside those of Warhol Superstar Candy Darling and Magdalena Montezuma, known for her roles in the films of Werner Schroeter. Though drawn from vastly different contexts, all the figures in the show participated in the creation of films that combined progressive content with innovative form; that depicted gender and sexuality in a free and uninhibited manner; and that were glamorous—their avant-garde ethos never compromising their popular appeal. It is precisely these ideals of modernism—based on the seemingly outdated conviction that true progress and a better future can arise from a reconciliation of inventive aesthetics with radical politics—for which Saunders himself is nostalgic and for which he wants to evoke nostalgia in others.
But Saunders’s re-creations of film stills don’t look anything like the originals. They are worn and blurred, as if to emphasize their distance—temporal and physical—from our present moment. In one work, Ingrid Caven, 2026, taken from Schroeter’s 1972 film, The Death of Maria Malibran, the titular German actress shines forth from behind a film resembling a veil marked by smears and patches of opacity. Any details of her face are lost; no subtle color transition and no sense of her physical complexion persist in an image in which the lack of focus matches the sexual ambiguity of the androgynous actor. By simply looking at Ingrid Caven, there is no way of discerning Saunders’s process: The picture is basically a cameraless photographic print, not unlike a photogram. Saunders produced a negative by imagining what the original might have looked like and then painted it on translucent voile before projecting it, in the darkroom, onto light-sensitive paper. Because of the erratic behavior of the liquid paint on the nonabsorbent voile, the resulting distortions and blurring are as much a product of Saunders’s hand as they are the functions of chance, the aesthetics of which were central to the modernism so many of his subjects evoke. He then adds marks of wet color on the print, hence the final picture also has a painterly dimension, forever obscuring both how it was produced and what exactly it is—a photograph, photogram, painting, print, or something else entirely.
Saunders has little control over the faint appearance of his images, in which a figure like Caven occupies an indefinite realm, somewhere between disappearing and emerging from behind a scrim. The resulting blend of imminent accessibility and unbridgeable distance, at once pointing to the future and the past, is responsible for the picture’s gloomy atmosphere: Caven is conjured in all her glamour, but only as an absent presence and unfulfilled promise. Saunders’s ghostly subjects do not seem to populate his compositions so much as haunt them with the memory of unrealized futures—not unlike what Jacques Derrida called hauntology in Spectres de Marx (1993), a neologism he invented to describe how seemingly suppressed utopian concepts of the past disrupt a linear understanding of time by their enduring influence on the present. The ongoing surfacing of the past, and the vestiges of lost possibilities in the present, make the broken time of hauntology so very melancholy.
Both Sedira and Saunders thus refuse to give up on the desire for desire. They long for alternatives that might open up what Fisher called the “closed horizons of capitalist realism.” Sedira looks to the integral role of culture in the struggle for independence as a model and ideal; her re-creations activate the past in order to stage its unrealized potential. In Saunders’s ghostly evocations, the past’s hopes for the future remain effective, if only as a virtuality and object of longing. Together these artists share a nostalgia for the future. “A ghost never dies,” Derrida observed of the communist ideal. “It remains always to come and to come-back.”
Benjamin Paul is an art historian and critic living in New York and Berlin. He teaches Italian Renaissance art at Rutgers University.
