How was it that, by the ’70s, this timeless approach could suddenly seem like a novel invention?
FOR MANY YEARS, Donald Judd occupied a peculiar place in architectural culture. He was undeniably a cult figure—architects admired him obsessively, and several decades of “Minimalist” architecture bore his distinctive imprint. And yet his own architecture sat uneasily with the discipline’s definition of serious work; across his entire career, Judd never designed and built a structure from scratch. He altered buildings, repaired them, combined them, and put them to new uses—often to beautiful and ingenious effect—but the architectural profession has historically treated the ground-up building as the purest expression of authorship. Only by beginning from a tabula rasa could an architect make every decision, design every detail, and fully express their singular architectural intelligence.
But it is amazing what an accelerating climate emergency, combined with a global economy jolted by cascading crises, can do to a profession’s sense of purpose. These days, the blank slate looks not only extravagant but indefensible, while reusing what is already there—the preferred term of art is “adaptive reuse”—both claims the moral high ground and makes an increasingly persuasive business case. Work once relegated to the lesser category of renovation has moved decisively toward the center of the field. In 2021, Google agreed to pay $2.1 billion for the enormous former St. John’s freight terminal in New York, transformed by COOKFOX into a 1.3-million-square-foot headquarters. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, whose signature glass-and-steel towers helped define the corporate International Style, now treats adaptive reuse as a distinct area of practice, pitching clients that “it can be a bold architectural statement not to build anew but to transform.” By 2024, more than half of all billings by members of the American Institute of Architects came from renovation and reuse projects. The real-estate industry stalwart Urban Land Institute titled a 2025 report simply: What’s Old Is New: The Business Case for Adaptive Reuse.
Judd’s architectural work, meanwhile, has undergone its own transformation. The process began in 2013, when the Judd Foundation opened his former home and studio at 101 Spring Street to the public for the first time after a three-year restoration, allowing visitors to experience the remarkable environment Judd had assembled there: careful alterations to the original 1870 cast-iron building, his own furniture alongside pieces he had collected, and works of art permanently installed throughout. Since 2018, the foundation’s Marfa Restoration Plan has extended that effort across the Texas town where Judd began buying property in 1973. The Chinati Foundation has done the same at the former Fort D. A. Russell, the decommissioned Army base at the edge of Marfa that Judd, with support from Dia, began transforming into a vast museum complex in 1978.
Between them, the two organizations now care for twenty-six buildings on which Judd worked in Marfa, ranging from an architecture studio in a former bank and an art studio in a former Safeway to a 1920s house converted to display his early paintings, alongside a motley collection of ice plants, warehouses, offices, and former military buildings—several still in the midst of renovation when Judd died in 1994. This body of work now has federal recognition as well, through National Register historic-district designations in 2022 and 2025 spanning central Marfa, Chinati, and the complex known as the Block. His restored Architecture Office, itself a converted turn-of-the-century commercial storefront, opened to the public in September 2025; this fall, Chinati began a comprehensive restoration of the artillery sheds and the one hundred aluminum works they contain.
The coincidence is striking: Just as renovation and restoration have moved from architectural afterthought to the professional mainstream, buildings have begun to be recognized as a significant part of Judd’s oeuvre. And having long admired his pure geometries, his precise detailing, and his crisp industrial sensibility, architects are now only too happy to claim him as an early pioneer of adaptive reuse, borrowing his authority to legitimize a mode of practice the profession once treated as secondary. But that flattering retrospective can obscure as much as it reveals, making a highly particular practice look like an early version of today’s trend. The question is not whether Judd anticipated adaptive reuse, but what he was trying to make possible by working this way in the first place.
THE ANSWER BEGINS IN SOHO, where, in the late ’60s, Judd was swept into a fierce struggle over the future of what was then known as New York’s Cast Iron District. The neighborhood’s nineteenth-century commercial lofts were losing the manufacturing uses for which they had been built; artists were moving into them illegally as studios and homes. The city itself was not quite sure what to make of the transition: Planners still regarded the district as an important source of industrial jobs even as vacant lofts were filling with artists using them in new ways still prohibited by the laws on the books. In those same years, Robert Moses’s proposed Lower Manhattan Expressway promised one brutally modern solution to the problem of obsolescence: Much of this aging industrial fabric would simply disappear beneath a new artery linking the Holland Tunnel to the bridges across the East River.
Judd and his wife, Julie Finch, bought 101 Spring Street in 1968. Designed by Nicholas Whyte, a New York architect who specialized in cast iron, and completed in 1870, the five-story commercial building had passed through a succession of manufacturing and retail uses, housing the Empire Embroidery company at the time Judd and Finch acquired it. Over the next several years, Judd renovated the building as a place to live and work, gradually installing his own artworks and those of others throughout. The following year, he and Finch helped found Artists Against the Expressway, with Finch serving as chair. The building itself also entered the preservation campaign’s orbit: By fall 1970, Friends of Cast Iron Architecture was including 101 Spring Street on its walking tours, eventually awarding a commendation to Judd and Finch for the “preservation and renewal” of the building. And in February 1973 Judd wrote Mayor John Lindsay urging designation of the neighborhood as a historic district.
The transformation of 101 Spring thus unfolded inside a much larger fight over what should happen to buildings whose original purpose had disappeared. New zoning introduced in 1971 allowed certified artists to live legally in qualifying manufacturing lofts. Two years later, the city created the SoHo–Cast Iron Historic District, protecting the inherited architectural fabric from wholesale demolition. The city had decided that these buildings would endure, in other words, but not by remaining unchanged; they would become useful in a different way. What was happening in SoHo resonated well beyond New York City. It helped crystallize a new model of architectural preservation then emerging nationally. Preservation had traditionally focused only on exceptional buildings, and protected them by more or less freezing them in place. SoHo suggested something different: Whole districts of otherwise ordinary buildings could possess collective historical value, and that value was not incompatible with new growth and new use.
In 1971, the National Trust for Historic Preservation published urban historian Myra Fraser Harrison’s Adaptive Use of Historic Structures, a practical series of case studies examining how existing buildings could be reorganized around new economic, cultural, and institutional functions while retaining their historical character. That December, Architectural Record devoted an entire special issue, “New Life for Old Buildings: The Architect’s Renewed Commitment to Preservation,” to the same expanding field. In December 1973, Progressive Architecture editor in chief John Morris Dixon could call adaptive reuse “an admirable preservation strategy” in what appears to be the earliest appearance of the now-ubiquitous phrase in the American architectural press. The following year, Giorgio Cavaglieri—a New York architect who had spent a decade documenting and advocating for SoHo’s cast-iron fabric—published the foundational article “Design in Adaptive Reuse” in Historic Preservation. By then adaptive reuse was no longer merely a tactic for saving old buildings. Architects had begun to understand the encounter between inherited fabric and new use as an urgent design problem in its own right.
There is an acute historical irony here. Adapting an existing building to new needs is arguably one of the oldest building practices in human history. Archaeological evidence clearly shows that since large permanent settlements began to appear nearly ten millennia ago, most buildings simply outlived any one particular purpose, gradually accumulating alterations and new uses over time. Houses were rebuilt over the remains of earlier houses, incorporating old walls and materials into new construction; basilicas became churches and churches became mosques; obsolete city walls and fortifications became boulevards and promenades.
How was it that, by the ’70s, this timeless approach could suddenly seem like a novel invention? Only because the profound dislocations of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries had obscured millennia of ordinary building practice. Industrial modernity produced buildings at unprecedented speed while also accelerating the rate at which the technologies, industries, and infrastructures that gave them purpose became obsolete. It also changed the economics of building itself. A hand-carved stone block or carefully fitted timber joint embodied enough skilled labor to make reuse self-evidently prudent; rolled-steel beams factory-made by the thousands or cheap concrete poured by the ton belonged to a world in which replacement increasingly seemed more attractive than repair. Modern architecture, meanwhile, made rupture with the past one of its founding ambitions: New forms, materials, and ways of living were meant to answer the transformed technological and social conditions of the present; the inherited city was something to overcome. By the postwar decades, clearing what existed and beginning again had become a normal response to the presence of buildings—and sometimes whole neighborhoods—that no longer seemed to work. Adaptive reuse only needed a name once replacement had become normal.
IN MARFA, the scale of Judd’s experiment changed. He first visited the town in the early ’70s, and in 1973 began acquiring property there, starting with two large former Army buildings, built as World War I–era airplane hangars. The following year, he added the adjacent former quartermaster’s office, which became his house. Over the next several years, the site, which he eventually referred to simply as the Block, absorbed an increasingly heterogeneous set of uses: spaces for living and working, for making and installing art, Judd’s vast library, accommodations for entertaining friends and hosting guests. At the Block, Judd did not begin with a single, fixed concept of use and then shape these buildings to fit; he salvaged a motley assortment of structures and gradually decided what he could do with them.
The same openness shaped the way Judd thought about materials in these renovations. Wanting privacy, he began enclosing the Block with a wall built of adobe bricks salvaged from buildings being demolished elsewhere in Marfa, including two run-down, abandoned hotels. Judd realized he would have to make new adobe on-site once that supply ran out, but by the time he arrived, the knowledge required to make and build with it had largely disappeared from Texas. Judd looked across the border to Mexico, where the craft survived, and hired (legally) two adoberos to come to Marfa and do the work.
In 1978, with backing from the Dia Art Foundation, Judd expanded this approach to the former Fort D. A. Russell on the edge of town. Here, he had the opportunity to work across three hundred and forty acres of abandoned military infrastructure. Initially known simply as the Marfa Project, the undertaking was renamed the Art Museum of the Pecos in 1984 and became the Chinati Foundation in 1986; Judd held its first public open house the following year. Over time, the site accommodated a huge range of uses: art installations, fabrication, storage, administration, and housing for staff, guests, and artists-in-residence. Judd’s work extended to the landscape itself: He collaborated with soil conservation specialists to reseed parts of the site with native grasses, treating ecological restoration as part of the larger project.
At the heart of the property were two low-slung reinforced-concrete artillery sheds dating from the late ’30s. Beginning around 1980, Judd replaced their garage doors with large spans of glass, opening the interiors to raking desert light. He also experimented with placing different artworks inside, including early installations of the large John Chamberlain sculptures now in downtown Marfa, before eventually deciding to fabricate new pieces specifically for the spaces. The first of his one hundred works in mill aluminum was installed in 1982; the installation process continued through 1986. As the works themselves took shape, Judd continued altering the buildings around them, adding huge vaulted roofs in 1984–85 that significantly changed the sheds’ presence in the surrounding landscape. This idea came from Judd’s encounters with another kind of vernacular architecture: Driving through the nearby town of Valentine, Judd noticed a large prefabricated metal vault in use as an agricultural building and began looking into employing something similar. He eventually settled on a product called the Wonder Building, Model 6222, a prefabricated steel-arch system descended from the logic of the Quonset hut—the ubiquitous wartime structure formed from a semicircular shell of corrugated steel—but engineered to span large spaces without an internal frame. Cheap, fast, and radically adaptable, Wonder Buildings could work as almost anything: barns, factories, warehouses, supermarkets, gymnasiums, aircraft hangars, fallout shelters. The company advertised its system as the “most practical, lowest cost way to cover or enclose vast areas.”
This is the harder pragmatism running through Marfa. At the Block, Judd revived a labor-intensive regional building technique that depended on specialized craft knowledge; at the artillery sheds, he ordered a standardized industrial system designed for speed, economy, and generic utility. Tradition had no inherent moral advantage over industry, but neither did new technology automatically supersede what was already there. Judd’s concern was what could be made to work in a particular situation.
By the late ’80s and early ’90s, this had become Judd’s ordinary way of extending his activities through Marfa. In 1989 he bought the former Marfa National Bank and turned it into an architecture studio; the following year he acquired the Glascock Building across the street, using its ground floor as an architecture office and the floor above for guests. Other houses, shops, storage buildings, and commercial properties were folded into his activities as needs arose. These were not overlooked architectural treasures waiting to be rediscovered. Many were marginal structures, long abandoned and often in questionable shape, whose conventional market value was close to nothing.
In 1992, while arranging insurance for Judd’s Marfa properties, his bookkeeper and assistant Jeff Kopie proposed leaving three small buildings then under renovation off the policy altogether, noting their minimal value. The idea is almost comical to anyone familiar with present-day Marfa, where Judd’s buildings not only are among the town’s most carefully maintained and culturally valuable properties but helped catalyze a broader regeneration whose visual language—crisp stucco walls, raw steel, expanses of plate glass, smooth concrete with immaculately sharp edges—now repeats across galleries, hotels, shops, and private homes. Marfa’s recent (and remarkable) gentrification can obscure the fact that market value was never the point. Judd’s fundamental concern was use value: not what a building was worth, but how it could be put to work.
Marfa, then, offers less an aesthetic than an approach: a radical pragmatism. Judd did not begin by deciding what architecture ought to look like, what materials ought to be used, or how faithfully an existing building ought to be preserved. He treated inherited conditions as facts: sometimes worth keeping, sometimes worth changing, sometimes useful precisely because they could accommodate something they had never been intended to support. Adobe bricks, military sheds, off-the-shelf construction systems, abandoned commercial buildings—there is no consistent material or formal doctrine connecting them. The consistency lies instead in the repeated act of judgment: Work with what is there, see what happens, alter what needs altering, keep on doing that until the arrangement holds.
OVER THE COURSE OF THE ’80s, Judd’s architectural work began to attract increasing attention. He became a sought-after speaker on the academic circuit, accepting invitations to lecture at elite institutions like Yale’s School of Architecture and Harvard’s Graduate School of Design. In 1989, the Westfälischer Kunstverein in Münster mounted the first major exhibition devoted to his architecture, which was widely reviewed in the European press. With this greater recognition came new opportunities to practice architecture in a far more conventional sense: ground-up buildings, major institutional clients, large budgets—and, inevitably, the complications of coordinating with consultants, answering to developers, and collaborating with other architects.
In 1986, Progressive Insurance chairman Peter Lewis hired Frank Gehry to lead a vast waterfront redevelopment for Cleveland. An avid art collector himself, Lewis, with Gehry’s encouragement, invited Judd, Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen, Richard Serra, and Carl Andre to participate in the design of what he envisioned not only as an unprecedented combination of contemporary art and architecture—a kind of Medici Florence for our time—but, as he put it in his confident invitation to Judd, “one of the most exciting and unique projects ever.” Judd worked on the project for roughly two years, developing a series of proposals that responded closely to the city’s historical Beaux Arts plan, its aging railroad infrastructure, its new highways, and its older civic buildings.
There seemed to be no dimension of the project’s context that Judd was unwilling to take seriously. The program swelled to include a modern art museum, a hotel, a health club, and eventually a proposal for the first home of the newly founded Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Judd gamely designed each one, treating the increasingly improbable mixture with characteristic literalness: Each function occupied its own pristine rectangular volume, carefully calibrated in scale and placement to its surroundings, with the whole arranged in a rigorous linear sequence that looked, in Judd’s surviving plans, almost like a row of his signature boxes balanced along the gentle curve of the Lake Erie waterfront. But the world was deprived of this Minimalist presentation of Little Richard when the project foundered at the end of the decade amid financial obstacles and the difficulties of coordinating its all-star cast.
Then, in 1990, shortly after winning the competition for what became the much-admired Kunsthaus Bregenz in Austria, Peter Zumthor invited Judd to contribute a building to the museum campus. That collaboration soon collapsed amid an acrimonious dispute over architectural control between two unusually strong authorial personalities, but Judd’s continued exposure in Europe led to another architectural invitation in 1992, this one by a large Swiss architecture firm, to collaborate on the design for the Peter Merian Haus. This enormous mixed-use development was to be built over a rail depot and would become the largest single building in Basel, requiring half a billion Swiss francs in investment capital. Judd attacked the problem volumetrically, proposing major changes to the building’s massing and roofline. But this design was unequivocally rejected; the building’s volume, Judd was told, had already been fixed “according to market development.” This meant that his freedom began and ended at the facade, but Judd stayed with the project, trying to use variations in glass color and finish to recover some relationship between the building’s surface and the different functions within. He died in February 1994 while the facade design was still being resolved; whatever survives there of Judd’s intentions emerged from a process he did not live to finish.
What Judd himself made of these experiences is hard to know, although one of his last lectures on architecture offers a clue. Speaking in 1993 at the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth, Texas, Judd had this to say:
Ten years ago I wrote that Louis Kahn was the last good architect. He died in 1974. He is the last good architect known to an international public. There are architects who are capable who are known locally. But as I’ve written before, all internationally known architects are either mediocre or fantastically bad. The best, the least mediocre, unfortunately, is Tadao Ando, the better of whose work derives from Kahn, the plain modular rectangles made of concrete framed by verticals and, less clear even in Kahn, the geometric cuts and sections. The exception internationally is Christopher Alexander, who is known for his handsome books of sensible statements, but not through buildings. Therefore, the internationally public discussion of architecture, the known history of architecture since Kahn died, is a false history of architecture.
To anyone accustomed to the usual genealogies of either Judd or late-twentieth-century architecture, his choice of Alexander might have been startling. An eccentric Berkeley professor trained in both mathematics and architecture, Alexander spent much of his career arguing that the best design did not come from the genius of a singular author but emerged slowly through a feedback loop between ongoing use, local knowledge, and repeated adjustment: what, in his 1977 book A Pattern Language, he memorably called “patient piecemeal growth.” Judd had most of Alexander’s books in his library, and a note he jotted down the year before his lecture sounds strikingly Alexanderian: “In previous civilizations ways of making things slowly accumulated, developed, according to practicality, according to definite or vague meaning, slowly to something coherent and unique.”
But here Judd, like Alexander himself, was swimming dead against the increasingly glamorous current of high architecture. Later in the decade, Alexander would enjoy something of a renaissance as software programmers seized on his idea of the “pattern language” as a way of organizing shared solutions to recurring problems; that lineage would help produce the first wiki and, eventually, Wikipedia. Architecture, meanwhile, was heading in almost exactly the opposite direction, toward the spectacular building and the architect as global celebrity. This culture reached its apotheosis a few years later with Gehry’s Guggenheim Bilbao. The premise of the Bilbao effect could hardly have been further from Alexander’s: Make one extraordinary building by one extraordinary architect, and the city will change around it.
THERE IS A REAL UNEVENNESS to Judd’s architecture. Some of the buildings in Marfa are extraordinarily refined; others are rough, provisional, at times barely finished. The degree of intervention varies wildly, as does the level of architectural ambition. Judged one by one, in other words, Judd’s architectural corpus can look inconsistent. But Judd was not always trying to make a great building; often he was trying to make a larger situation work, and the building was only one part of it. The “good building” may be the stock-in-trade of both architectural criticism and architectural history, but for Judd it is probably the wrong unit of analysis.
A more useful unit might be the institution—not simply in the familiar art-world sense of a museum or foundation, but as a social form, in Georg Simmel’s sense: a durable structure through which people enter into particular kinds of relationships and specific patterns of interaction. Perhaps this has been hard to see because so many of the artists, architects, critics, and theorists of recent decades have been trained to approach institutions primarily through questions of power and subject formation, in a broadly Foucauldian key. Legitimate questions, certainly, but they tend to ask only what institutions do to us. Judd’s work suggests another line of inquiry: What new forms of life can an institution make possible?
At the Block, the answer could be disarmingly ordinary. In the south room of the East Building, Judd placed an Arts and Crafts dining set among some of his best-known sculptures from the ’60s. This is the part of Judd’s practice that has, for decades, made art historians and curators uncomfortable; it’s usually explained away through formal affinities between the furniture and sculpture or, more recently, through the language of relational aesthetics and social practice, as though the very act of eating beside art could itself become an aesthetic event. But for Judd, this was precisely not “dinner in the gallery.” A dinner staged in a gallery as an artwork remains legible as transgression: Dinner is happening where dinner does not belong. Such a gesture works by leaving the institution itself conceptually intact; all its force depends on a stable, almost cartoonishly clear idea of what belongs and what does not.
Judd’s proposition was much stranger, and ultimately much more radical: Build an environment in which dinner could simply be dinner. A gallery, after all, is an institution before it is an organization. Its rules barely need stating: You enter, circulate, look, do not touch, perhaps sit briefly, and leave. The exhibition eventually closes; the works depart; another exhibition takes their place. Judd spent decades altering those protocols at the most fundamental level of operation. What if the art did not leave? What if the gallery was also someone’s house? What if people ate, slept, worked, read, and entertained among the art? What if maintaining the buildings became part of maintaining the institution itself? At some point, the experiment ceases to require quotation marks. “Dinner in the gallery” becomes dinner. The institution is no longer an object of critique, but a medium of construction.
It was architecture that Judd used to give those arrangements duration. Across Marfa, he repeatedly established a new set of conditions, lived with them, changed them, and (sometimes, but not always) decided that they should hold. The artillery sheds are one particularly vivid example: Their present relation of art, light, building, and landscape is so perfectly calibrated as to feel almost inevitable, but it emerged only after years of tinkering and alteration. The same logic runs through the Block, the downtown properties, and Chinati at large. Much ink has been spilled over Judd’s commitment to permanent installation in Marfa, but the architecture makes clear that permanence was never a matter of fixing an arrangement once and for all. “Permanence,” in this sense, does not mean freezing a perfect arrangement in advance. It means establishing a framework stable enough to sustain practices through time without determining them completely. That helps explain why proximity mattered so much to Judd. Maintenance, adjustment, repair, use, and observation were not aftercare; they were a fundamental part of the work itself. A practice based on continuing judgment becomes difficult to scale precisely because so much of its intelligence can never be standardized or even articulated in advance.
Seen this way, Judd’s current relevance is much more than simply reminding us that old buildings can be imaginatively transformed. Adaptive reuse was not his project, let alone his style—it was the material practice through which he could construct new arrangements from conditions that already existed. This is why formal affinities between his work and other architecture, however seductive—the “Minimalist” sensibility, the “Marfa Modern” aesthetic—lead toward a category error. Extracted from circumstance, even the most Judd-like spatial and material moves become just a repertoire of motifs. In his hands, their coherence lay elsewhere, in their responsiveness to the situations that generated them.
ADAPTIVE REUSE BEGINS, by definition, inside a world the architect did not create. The building already has materials, dimensions, defects, histories, neighbors, owners, previous uses, and established patterns of maintenance or neglect. Someone has already spent money on it; someone may still depend on it; someone else will have to live with whatever happens next. It will almost certainly change again. Working under those conditions makes it harder to sustain one of architecture’s most convenient fictions: that architectural agency begins when the architect arrives and ends when construction is complete.
That is where Judd’s example becomes larger than Judd. His buildings gradually became part of systems that sustained ways of living, working, making, encountering, maintaining. Architecture did not merely house those systems or establish their public face; it helped make them durable. As today’s cultural institutions are increasingly asked to function as classrooms, workplaces, meeting grounds, and forms of public infrastructure, they face a very Juddian problem: The question is less what image they project than what kinds of collective life they can actually sustain.
Over the past half-century, art has become exceptionally sophisticated at exposing institutions, criticizing them, and revealing the forms of power embedded within them. It has been less interested in the more difficult, more constructive question of how worthwhile institutions are actually made. Judd’s answer was never tidy, certainly not universal, and, in all its idiosyncrasies, perhaps not even transferable. But it was concrete: Buy the building. Keep what works. Change what does not. Put it to use. Maintain it. Reconsider it. Let relationships accumulate until they acquire a form that can last. Once adaptive reuse is understood as a form of institution-building, it is no longer merely a building type, an aesthetic, or a sustainability strategy. It becomes a way for architecture to participate in the formation of society over time.
Julian Rose directs the program in Alternative Materials at rearc institute.

https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.title: Advocatenkosten voor deontologische raad wegen op journalistiek
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.author: Steven Vanden Bussche
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.text:
Journalisten en media worden geconfronteerd met dure advocatenbureaus die mensen bijstaan tijdens de behandeling van deontologische klachten voor de Raad voor de Journalistiek. Die verregaande juridisering jaagt journalisten en media, klein én groot, op kosten terwijl hun verzekering hiervoor niet tussenkomst.
Eind vorig jaar onthulde Apache hoe twee Belgen verdienen aan een omstreden Congolese belasting op het gebruik van een mobiele telefoon. Journalist Thibault Coigniez achterhaalde hoe de Antwerpse diamantair Philippe Heilmann en de Brusselse zakenman Jérôme Spaey met hun bedrijf 5C Energy een lucratief contract sloten met de Congolese overheid. Het contract zelf blijft tot op heden een Congolees staatsgeheim.
Heilmann was niet opgezet met de publicatie. De Antwerpse diamantair werd nochtans tijdig gecontacteerd voor een weerwoord, zijn reactie werd in het artikel verwerkt en ook nog eens integraal gepubliceerd onderaan het artikel.
De Raad stelde geen inbreuken vast op het principe van waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving, maar jaagde Apache wel op kosten
Begin 2026 eisten advocaten Olivier Sasserath en Herman Croux verregaande aanpassingen aan het stuk. Via een ingebrekestelling dreigden Heilmanns advocaten met een schadeclaim. De diamantair diende ook een klacht in bij de Raad voor de Journalistiek, die zich buigt over het deontologisch handelen van journalisten en media. Het bedrijf 5C Energy stuurde tot slot een Recht van antwoord dat Apache, hoewel er geen juridische verplichting was, integraal publiceerde.
Aangezien Heilmann geld veil had om het gespecialiseerde Brusselse advocatenbureau MVVP op Apache af te sturen, zag de redactie zich genoodzaakt ook een advocaat te raadplegen. Na heen-en-weer geschrijf tussen advocaten en een hoorzitting, besliste de Raad voor de Journalistiek om de klacht van tafel te vegen. De Raad stelde geen inbreuken vast op het principe van waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving, maar jaagde Apache wel op kosten.
Doe een gift op BE55 5230 8045 8444 (met vermelding ‘STOP SLAPP’) of via onze giftenpagina.
Geen alleenstaand geval
Eerder dit jaar diende een gepensioneerde politieman via zijn advocaat klacht in tegen Humo en een journalist. De politieman werd eind jaren 90 van het Dutroux-onderzoek gehaald. In een commentaarstuk wees journalist Douglas De Coninck erop dat de agent destijds een verband zag tussen de bende rond Dutroux en twee Franse gangsters die opdoken in het onderzoek naar de Bende van Nijvel. De journalist handelde onafhankelijk, meende de Raad, en had geen “kwaadaardige bedoelingen” zoals de voormalige politieman opwierp.
Freddy Kempeneer, hoofdredacteur van Persinfo.be, een nieuwssite die regionaal nieuws uit het Pajottenland, de Zennevallei en de Denderstreek brengt, werd dan weer verrast door de aanwezigheid van een advocaat tijdens de hoorzitting. De klager, een schepen die zonder omgevingsvergunning verbouwingswerken liet uitvoeren, bracht Kempeneers niet op de hoogte dat een advocaat zijn belangen zou verdedigen.
“Ik voelde me daardoor benadeeld, te meer er ook geen beroepsmogelijkheid is tegen uitspraken van de Raad”, zegt Kempeneer. “Had ik dat geweten, dan zou ik me ook laten bijstaan door een advocaat. Dat die advocaat daar plots stond, was voor mij ook intimiderend.” De klacht bleek grotendeels ongegrond, op een feitelijk element en te weinig responstijd voor wederhoor na.
Er zijn het afgelopen anderhalf jaar nog meer voorbeelden gepasseerd waarbij advocaten de klagers bijstonden, maar finaal bot vingen bij de Raad: bij een klacht van een opgepakte verdachte crypto-oplichter over berichtgeving bij HLN en een gesanctioneerde deurwaarder bij opiniesite Doorbraak.be.
Niet gedekt door verzekering
Charlotte Michils, algemeen secretaris van de Vlaamse Vereniging van Journalisten (VVJ) merkt op dat een procedure voor de Raad voor de Journalistiek laagdrempelig en gratis is. De zaak komt pas voor de Raad wanneer er geen minnelijke schikking getroffen kan worden.
Karl van den Broeck: “Voor die éne zaak moest Apache ruim 5.000 euro ophoesten, terwijl het dossier feitelijk onderbouwd was en op een deontologisch correcte manier afgewerkt”
“Als de ene partij een advocaat in de arm neemt, is het niet onlogisch dat ook de andere partij dat overweegt”, zegt Michils. “De aanwezigheid van een juridisch professional brengt immers de nodige techniciteit in het dossier waardoor het meer tijd en middelen vergt om je te verdedigen. Voor minder kapitaalkrachtige partijen kan dat een probleem zijn.”
Omdat de Raad van de Journalistiek geen schadevergoedingen toekent, dekt een verzekering burgerlijke aansprakelijkheid ‘beroep en uitbating’ juridisch advies en bijstand bij de Raad voor de Journalistiek niet.
“Dat zorgde ervoor dat Apache voor die éne zaak ruim 5.000 euro moest ophoesten, terwijl het dossier feitelijk onderbouwd was en op een deontologisch correcte manier afgewerkt”, zegt Karl van den Broeck, hoofdredacteur van Apache. “We betreuren die manier van werken en maken ons daarover ook zorgen.”

https://apache.be/2026/10/23/westerse-do.title: De westerse doempolitiek moet transformeren naar moedpolitiek
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/westerse-do.author: Arne Geybels
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/westerse-do.text:
Na een kurkdroge zomer met hitterecords, is de kou eindelijk gearriveerd. Normaal is het tijd om te cocoonen en te vertragen. Helaas lijken we dit niet te mogen – de zondagsrust is op sterven na dood. En staat onze feed nooit stil, onze gsm nooit af en consumeren we meer dan we kunnen verteren. Een ware overdaad zonder einde, die de beeldspraak van een zondvloed oproept.
In 1524 voorspelde de astroloog Johannes Stöffler een zondvloed. Wie het kon, bouwde een ark. De vloed bleef echter uit. Vijfhonderd jaar later zien we techmiljardairs bunkers bouwen in Nieuw-Zeeland en op Hawaï, terwijl ze ons waarschuwen dat AI de mensheid kan uitroeien. Het einde der tijden is terug van nooit weggeweest.
Vandaag verkopen AI-labs het verhaal dat enkel zij de ondergang kunnen voorkomen, en dus onbelemmerd moeten doorgaan
Angst die zich projecteert op een onzekere toekomst of ‘eindtijdangst’ is zo oud als beschaving zelf. Rond 1200 voor Christus stortte de bronstijdwereld in. Ugarit brandde, het Hettitische rijk verdween, handelsroutes vielen weg. Wie erbij was, moet gedacht hebben dat de wereld ophield. De wereld hield niet op, maar het handelssysteem transformeerde. Veel autonome Fenicische steden overleefden deze ineenstorting, omdat ze niet van één paleis afhingen maar van handel en netwerken. In de brokstukken werd het alfabet en ijzer verspreid.
Na de Zwarte Dood, die een derde van Europa wegvaagde, verdwenen de lonen niet. Integendeel, ze stegen, en het feodalisme kende zijn eerste cruciale scheuren.
En ook de millenniumbug bleek uiteindelijk onschuldig omdat er hard was gewerkt aan het voorkomen van problemen én omdat consultants de dreiging ervan bewust hadden opgeklopt om er een fortuin aan te verdienen. Apocalyptische verhalen en opgeklopte angst zijn zelden neutraal of rationeel, maar wel al te vaak instrumenteel.
De middeleeuwse kerk verkocht aflaten tegen de angst voor het vagevuur. De IT-consultants van 1999 verdienden aan de angst dat computers op 1 januari 2000 zouden vastlopen. Vandaag verkopen AI-labs het verhaal dat enkel zij de ondergang kunnen voorkomen, en dus onbelemmerd moeten doorgaan. Wie de apocalyps voorspelt én bezit, wil vooral geen democratisch toezicht maar een hemels mandaat.
End times fascism
Naomi Klein en Astra Taylor noemden dat onlangs end times fascism in hun gelijknamige boek. Ze beschrijven daarin een elite die het vermeende, toekomstige maatschappelijke instorten al heeft ingecalculeerd en kiest voor ontsnapping in plaats van herstel. Net zoals een binaire machine heeft deze tech elite duidelijk geen menselijke moed en zijn ze zich niet bewust van het belang van gezonde frictie, tegenspraak en tegenmacht.
Econoom en auteur Yanis Varoufakis liet dan weer zien waarom angst zo goed past bij technofeodalisme. Want wie bang is, sluit zich aan, betaalt en past zich aan. Angst maakt de mens voorspelbaar of om het meer in zijn jargon te verwoorden: een horige.
Onder het huidige doemdenken (en doemscrollen) zit nog iets anders. Elke generatie voelt haar tijd als uniek en versneld. De middeleeuwse kroniekschrijver, de negentiende-eeuwse persoon voor wie de trein de ruimte “vernietigde” of de telegraaf de communicatie versnelde ervaarden allemaal wat wij nu ook voelen: de perceptie van versnelling. Elke dag is er iets nieuws: een nieuwe doorbraak en een nieuwe calamiteit. Wie de tijd niet meer neemt om te vertragen en te verteren, ervaart elke nieuwigheid als breuk, en een breuk lijkt altijd op het einde.
Zaaien, wachten, oogsten
Ondertussen is doem voor veel mensen geen toekomstscenario maar realiteit. Voor Gaza, Soedan en de Sahel is de breuk al decennia daar. Het dominante doemverhaal hier daarentegen is een westers en klassengebonden luxeproduct dat ons aangesmeerd wordt. En we slikken het als zoete broodjes.
Wie de tijd niet meer neemt om te vertragen en te verteren, ervaart elke nieuwigheid als breuk, en een breuk lijkt altijd op het einde
Dat betekent niet dat de risico's of problematieken verzonnen zijn. Klimaatontwrichting, een nieuwe wereldorde en machtsconcentratie zijn reëel. Maar we dienen ons bewust te zijn van wie het verhaal erover schrijft en hoe we met angst en met een veranderde wereld omgaan. Na de ineenstorting van de bronstijd overleefden niet de bunkerbouwers, maar de gemeenschappen die water, handel en kennis bleven delen. Zij die niet meegingen in de waan(zin) van de dag.
We kunnen een zekere toekomst niet garanderen, maar we moeten wel weigeren dat angst ons regeert. Want blijvend versnellen, wat de psychosomatische reactie is op angst, leidt uiteindelijk tot burn-out en accidenten. En dat zijn zaken die enkel lucratief zijn voor wie kapitaliseert op spreekwoordelijke pleisters op de wonde: supplementen en optimalisatietools, verzekeringen, of andere industrieën die niet verdienen aan de oorzaak, maar aan het gevolg. Een versneld lichaam is een klant. Een lichaam dat tijd krijgt, is een burger.
De bunkerbouwer koopt zekerheid en betaalt met zijn rust. Wie kanalen graaft, kent geen garantie, maar wel een ritme: zaaien, wachten, oogsten. Dat ritme is geen luxe maar moed en het is de voorwaarde om te gedijen.

https://apache.be/2026/10/23/klimaatvera.title: Klimaatverandering maakte hittegolf zeker in steden nog dodelijker
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/klimaatvera.author: Steven Vanden Bussche
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/klimaatvera.text:
Afgelopen zomer stierven in Europese steden meer dan 50.000 mensen door de hitte. Bijna twee op de drie van die sterfgevallen waren toe te schrijven aan de klimaatverandering. Britse wetenschappers brachten de hittedoden van de voorbije kwarteeuw in kaart. Ze publiceerden gedetailleerde ramingen voor 824 Europese steden, telkens met en zonder de invloed van de klimaatverandering.
Een groot deel van Vlaanderen verslikte zich vorige zondag (18/10) allicht in de koffie. Na een “wekenlange stilte” verkoos Annick De Ridder (N-VA) om in de gratis krant De Zondag “elke kritiek” op haar beleid te “pareren”.
Op de vraag of ze wakker ligt van de klimaatcrisis, antwoordde de Vlaamse minister van Mobiliteit en Openbare Werken laconiek: “Nee, ik lig daar niet wakker van. Ik ben een vooruitgangsoptimist. Dankzij onze innovatieve bedrijven zullen wij ook deze omslag maken.”
De Ridders kijkt vult de politieke stilte van premier Bart De Wever (N-VA). Hoewel afgelopen zomer zowat 3.000 Belgen meer stierven dan normaal, overal in Europa het ene na het andere hitterecord sneuvelde, én half oktober 60.000 mensen op straat kwamen voor een doortastend klimaatbeleid, houdt de premier de lippen stijf op elkaar wat betreft het klimaat.
Klimaatverandering duidelijke oorzaak
Wetenschappers van Imperial College London en London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) publiceren vandaag (23/10) twee onderzoeksrapporten over hittedoden in het vakblad Nature Health.
De grote oversterfte is duidelijk gelinkt aan de aanhoudende hittegolven van afgelopen zomer, stellen ze. Die hittegolven zijn op hun beurt een waarneembaar gevolg van de klimaatverandering. Door de klimaatverandering komen hittegolven niet alleen vaker voor, ze duren ook langer en zijn intenser. Oudere mensen en mensen met een zwakkere gezondheid zijn de eerste slachtoffers.
De grote oversterfte is duidelijk gelinkt aan de aanhoudende hittegolven van afgelopen zomer
De twee studies zijn gebaseerd op complexe klimaatmodellen. Die koppelen de dagelijkse temperatuurmetingen aan gedocumenteerde sterfgevallen in verschillende leeftijdsgroepen. Daarbij houden ze rekening met factoren zoals geografie, bevolkingsdichtheid of de socio-economische situatie.
Op die manier konden de wetenschappers inschatten hoeveel mensen per dag stierven bij bepaalde temperaturen. Daardoor kunnen ze uiteindelijk ook becijferen hoeveel hittedoden er zouden zijn zonder de gevolgen van klimaatverandering.
In de eerste studie staan steden centraal. Die zijn interessant vanwege de grote bevolkingsdichtheid en het fenomeen van het hitte-eilandeffect. Afgelopen zomer betaalden de grote steden in Zuid- en West-Europa de grootste tol voor de hete temperaturen.
Parijs registreerde naar schatting het hoogste aantal hittegerelateerde doden, gevolgd door Rome, Londen en Madrid. Als we kijken naar het aantal doden per aantal inwoners domineren Italiaanse steden de statistieken en zit België in de middenmoot.
Pierre Masselot, statisticus en epidemioloog (LSHTM): "Toenemende hitte zal voor iedereen in Europa een probleem worden"
Noord-Europese steden zouden volgens de schattingen verhoudingsgewijs minder hittedoden kennen. Toch ligt het aandeel hittedoden in de totale sterftecijfers er hoog.
“De toenemende hitte zal voor vrijwel iedereen in Europa een probleem worden”, vat Pierre Masselot het probleem samen. Masselot is statisticus en epidemioloog aan de LSHTM en een van de onderzoeksleiders.
De naar schatting 50.000 hittedoden van afgelopen zomer in Europa, waarvan ruim twee derde toe te schrijven is aan de gevolgen van klimaatverandering, zijn een triest hoogtepunt deze eeuw. Dat blijkt uit de tweede studie.
De wetenschappers becijferden het aantal hittegerelateerde sterfgevallen in steden gedurende de afgelopen kwarteeuw, telkens voor de maanden juni, juli en augustus. Ze becijferden ook hoeveel hittedoden er zouden zijn zonder klimaatopwarming.
Dit artikel maakt deel uit van een project over hittegolven, gecoördineerd door het Urban Journalism Network en met steun van Journalismfund Europe.
Auteur: Peter Aldhous (Centre for Collaborative Investigative Journalism)
Grafische vormgeving: David Meidinger
Coördinatie: Hendrik Lehmann, Gaby Khazalová

https://gothamist.com/news/november-has-.title: November has 3 meteor showers and the best chance to see Uranus
https://gothamist.com/news/november-has-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/november-has-.text:
Every week in November has a dazzling night sky headliner for fall stargazers.
“November has meteor showers that tend to be a favorite,” said Jackie Faherty, astrophysicist at the American Museum of Natural History. “This month is a good time to see planets, especially Saturn and Jupiter.”
Shooting stars
On Nov. 4-5, the Southern Taurids will peak with about five meteors per hour. That number might sound small, but the meteors are exceptionally bright, slow-moving and long-lasting. The shower often produces fireballs, which are as luminous as some of the brightest celestial objects. During the peak, there will be a crescent moon, which means skies will be darker and more ideal for spotting the streaking lights.
“Even in the city, some of these meteors will be bright enough that you'll be able to see them,” said Bart Fried, a member of the American Astronomical Society.
The Northern Taurids peak about a week later, on Nov. 12-13, yielding the same display of dazzling light as the Southern Taurids. During that evening, viewing conditions are good because of the low light from the crescent moon.
“These are bright enough that if you catch it anywhere in your field of view, your eyes snap right to it,” Fried said. “Don't worry about having to stare in the right spot. There is no right spot.”
The third and final meteor shower of the month, the Leonids, peaks Nov. 17-18 with around 15 shooting stars per hour. The moon will be at about half its illumination, which will make the sky brighter, but not impossible to see a meteor. Stargazers should head to darker spots in the city, such as Floyd Bennett Field.
“ Your best viewing for the Leonids will be from midnight until dawn after the moon sets,” Fried said.
Supermoon
The moon will appear up to 14% larger and 30% brighter on Nov. 23-24. The phenomenon is called a supermoon, when the moon is at or near its closest position to Earth in its oval-shaped orbit. When at this point, also called perigee, it appears larger and brighter.
A supermoon comes about three to five times per year. The next supermoon, which lands on Christmas Eve, will be the brightest, largest and final one of the year.
The planets
It will be possible to spot half of the planets in the solar system with the naked eye.
Jupiter, appearing in the southeast section of sky, is currently the brightest planet. For most of the month, Mars will be close to the gas giant. New Yorkers can see the red planet in the evening skies starting this month.
Golden-hued Saturn is also visible in the southern section of the sky. For views of the rings, stargazers will need binoculars or a telescope.
While looking for the rings, it’s a good time to find Uranus. The greenish-blue dot is the coldest planet in the solar system, and the second-farthest from the sun. The average temperature is about -320 degrees Fahrenheit. The seventh planet from the sun will be at opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s at its closest distance to Earth on its roughly 84-year orbit around the sun.
Fried recommends using a planetarium app in order to locate Uranus before pointing a telescope or binoculars at the sky. At around midnight, the ice giant will be at its highest point in the sky, right overhead.
“With a 4-inch telescope, you can find Uranus with no problem,” Fried said. “It’s reasonably bright. It’s not visible to the naked eye, but it is visible in binoculars if you know where to find it.”
Early risers can catch a glimpse of Venus, which was the brightest object in the night sky during the summer. At this time of year, the solar system's hottest planet is referred to as the morning star.
Fall Constellations
As the weather cools, the constellations are continuing to shift with the seasons. This month, Orion the Hunter shines prominently along with his two dogs, Canis Minor and Canis Major.
Despite the city’s formidable light pollution, these constellations are easily discernible from the dissonance. Orion has a famous line of three stars that form his belt. Sirius, the dog star, is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. The star is part of Canis Major.
Right near Orion, the bright stars of Gemini are also visible, Castor and Pollux.
“Gemini is a really good constellation to look for right now,” Faherty said. “You can see Castor and Pollux from New York City high in your sky towards the zenith.”

https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.title: ‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographs
https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.author: Gautam Malkani
https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.text:
Can photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?
Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.
Each issue has a particular theme. Earlier this month, the magazine featured photographs that have changed how we view masculinity – from a 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando in a white T-shirt to a paparazzi shot of David Beckham in a sarong and a bare-chested Vladimir Putin on horseback. Previous issues have focused on photographs that have reshaped sport, forced people to confront the reality of the climate crisis and upended the world of fashion.
Beyond the impact each image had back when it first came out, they still feel powerful and affecting today – reminding us how great photography can command a kind of reverence and stillness in the viewer. “Working on these issues, you realise that there’s something about the power of the images that’s elemental,” says Rebecca Liu, a commissioning editor on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine. “Some photos imprint upon us before we even can think about them. They just immediately hit our bloodstream.”
The first special issue featured protest images that have prompted social or political change. It was initially conceived as a one-off feature in 2022 amid protests in the US that year against the overturning of Roe v Wade and demonstrations against police brutality. But the feature resonated so strongly with readers that it spawned an occasional series.
That regularity means the process of putting the issues together is now fine-tuned, though not without its own drama and headaches. “Sometimes on the day of going to print we’re waiting on two or three final things to be confirmed,” says Rebecca. “It’s a massive act of organisation and coordination and a real collective effort with a lot of moving parts.”
Selecting which pictures to include involves tapping the collective minds of picture editors and journalists on the magazine and across the Guardian. Different colleagues will have different criteria. How to weigh up a photograph’s social or political impact against its technical importance to the medium? Should it be an image that, in itself, has changed the world or a photograph of a world-shifting moment?
“Everyone working on the magazine has a different take on it,” says Louis Siroy, the magazine’s deputy picture editor. “Some editors will ask how a particular photograph shaped society; what does it mean? Whereas I might be asking what are the important photographs or photographers that fit into that theme or category.”
For example, the first special issue about protest photography didn’t just include the famous image of a protestor standing in front of a tank in Tiananmen Square, it also included a less famous but equally powerful photograph of a boy sitting on the shoulders of relatives above the sea of soldiers’ helmets. Taken by the photographer Dario Mitidieri, the image was suggested by Louis. “That to me is a great photograph, and I was trying to bring something that wasn’t necessarily the image people are familiar with,” he says. “Hopefully these selections inspire people to value and appreciate the breadth and power of great photographs.”
By drawing on colleagues’ different perspectives and experience, each special issue sheds unique light on its theme. “So while the selection can’t possibly be comprehensive and definitive, it’s still authoritative,” says Rebecca.
Other images included in the initial protest photography issue include the famous picture of US athletes John Carlos and Tommie Smith raising their fists in a black power salute during a medal ceremony at the 1968 Olympics. There are also several photographs of protesters facing off against riot police or soldiers, including a powerful image of a young girl in Santiago, Chile, during a 2016 demonstration marking the anniversary of the country’s 1973 military coup.
One of the most time-consuming challenges involves obtaining the rights to publish the images. “Some of the greatest challenges involve finding the right copyright holder for some lesser-known photographs,” says Caroline Hunter, the magazine’s picture editor.
Even well-known photographs can present hurdles. “Sometimes you have to get permission from the subject of the photo as well as from the photographer, particularly when it comes to photos of celebrities or fashion,” explains Louis. “It can get really hard to track down the person you need. For instance, the masculinity special featured a famous second world war photo of a US aeroplane gunner that was taken by the photographer Horace Bristol, who is now deceased. It took some time to contact the photographer’s son Henri in California and explain the context in which we wanted to use the photo. And even when dealing with well-known photographers, it still involves negotiating the rights for editorial use rather than commercial use.”
Another challenge that can arise is the quality of the photographs. “We have to ensure the image is large enough or good enough quality to reproduce, especially for very old images that previously existed only as prints,” says Caroline. “Works by famous and art photographers often have specific rules around usage, so it’s important to ensure that we keep within their guidelines. We had a really good response from photographers after our recent photo special marking America at 250. I think this was because there were so many great, iconic images from seminal photographers.”
The team also has to decide the best layout for the print and digital editions – which images to give prominence to, how they might best fit together, and the range of black-and-white and colour images. Maggie Murphy, the magazine’s art director, experiments with different layouts, sometimes on a screen, sometimes with printouts strewn across the desks.
As well as the images, a huge amount of work goes into the words. Each special issue includes a short guest-written essay, and each photograph has an extended caption about that particular picture’s significance or backstory.
The journalists who are commissioned to write these captions undertake extensive research. For example, the masculinity issue includes a famous 1970 advertisement depicting a pregnant man, for which the journalist tracked down the original campaign’s photographer, who is now 98. “I encourage original interviews and research wherever possible,” says Rebecca. “We want the words to illuminate something about the picture and for people to learn things. That’s not something you necessarily have to do for a 150-word caption, but we want to do it because the editorial component is so important to us at the Guardian.”
Researching the captions also reveals something about the nature of photography. “It really shows the importance of not just taking an image at face value,” says Rebecca. “I’m always surprised by what you discover when you look into things. You might find a complicated backstory behind the person who is photographed – perhaps their ambivalence about being pictured, for instance.”
The same applies to the thought that goes into the introductory essays. The novelist Anne Enright wrote perceptively about how women are captured on camera, for better or for worse, in her introduction to an issue that featured photographs that have changed the way society sees women. “As you look at a Kardashian selfie, consider how many rules had to be broken to get her to this moment of self-commodification,” writes Enright.
The masculinity issue contains an accompanying essay by the poet and novelist Luke Kennard, who reflects on how the images seem to capture extremes of masculinity, with little in between: “To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men… Even the bang average is barely represented.”
Rebecca noticed that gap in representation back when the team was initially selecting which photographs to include in the issue. “I remember thinking, where are the other male bodies? It was difficult to find any – at least with the quality and artistry that we look for in these stories. You’d Google the words ‘dad bod’ and you’d just get screenshots of Seth Rogen and grainy paparazzi shots of celebrities on the beach.”
The team is very mindful of the power of images to subtly reinforce or subvert people’s preconceptions. “Working on these issues makes us reflect on how much we subconsciously absorb images,” says Rebecca. “And how they feed into our imaginations.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/nyc-public-s.title: Lord of Bench Is Fighting for Your Right to Sit
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/nyc-public-s.author: Liza Featherstone
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/nyc-public-s.text:
Lord of Bench Is Fighting for Your Right to Sit
Many Manhattan real estate developers have a legal obligation to keep space outside their high-rise buildings open to all — yet refuse. We spoke to Lord of Bench, an activist who is taking them on to reclaim public space for the public.
A plaza just outside 780 Third Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, brimming with well-tended flowers in warm weather and furnished with elegant stone benches, looks like an inviting place to sit down and enjoy a slice of pizza. Or at least Wade Phillips certainly thought so.
Phillips, a hospitality and security worker, used to take his breaks in that plaza every day. (“Wade Phillips” isn’t his real name, but a nom de guerre, or what its user refers to as “my please-don’t-fire-me name”). He describes himself as “kind of a Good Will Hunting guy,” referring to the Matt Damon character in Gus Van Sant’s 1997 movie about a self-taught working-class genius who has survived an abusive childhood. “I don’t really have a family,” says Phillips, “I’ve had kind of a rough road.”
For the past few decades, working in Manhattan, sometimes living with roommates, parks like this have been a respite where he’s been grateful to “go sit somewhere and breathe.” Such spaces provide a sense of peace for free for anyone who needs to rest a spell.
Last year, he was working on Forty-Eighth Street, taking his breaks almost every day on a bench in the especially idyllic plaza at 780 Third Avenue. “From the day I had my interview there,” he says, “till the day I left, it was, like, my spot.” On one occasion, Phillips had been having a rough night at work, and it was the anniversary of his father’s death. He needed some time to himself on the bench. A security guard appeared immediately and told Phillips he couldn’t be there. “I just need ten minutes,” Phillips told the guard, who was unmoved and insisted he move along.
Grumpily acceding to the guard’s demand, Philips crossed the street and saw an enormous sign carved into the stone bench in question. It read, “Welcome.”
“Everyone has their breaking point,” he says, “and that was it for me.” Phillips emphasized, “It doesn’t just say ‘Welcome.’ It’s carved in.” That moment, he says, is “when this whole thing started.”
Phillips, a meticulous and detail-oriented researcher who majored in finance in college, hit the city records and learned that the public has a legal right to use that space. 780 Third Avenue and nearly six hundred other spaces like it in New York City have a somewhat complicated legal status: they are POPS, or “privately owned public spaces.”
In Midtown Manhattan especially, real estate developers often, in order to be able to add height to their building that is outside what the zoning laws would typically permit for that neighborhood, reach an agreement with the city to “trade floor space in the sky for floor space down below,” as Philips explains. Buildings may also provide POPS in exchange for other types of zoning variances, but in Midtown, height is the most common. Individual agreements vary, but they all specify the building’s obligations to the public: exact square footage; whether the owner must provide chairs, tables, or benches for public use; whether there must be trees or plants.
Privately owned public spaces throughout New York City comprise more than 3.8 million square feet of space for public leisure. The practice of allowing developers to skirt some zoning rules in exchange for providing public space has been around since 1961, but in 2017, New York City Council passed Local Law 116 to strengthen the city’s oversight of these agreements, requiring annual reporting on the POPS by the relevant agencies — the Department of Buildings and Department of City Planning — and, crucially, requiring signage indicating that the public has access to the area.
But POPS violations, in which the public are denied access to these spaces by the companies who received the legal clearance to build additional floors, are common. Much of the real estate industry bitterly resents having to provide any public goods despite having legally agreed to do so. They prefer to take up space in our skies without providing anything in return.
Phillips, particularly incensed after carrying out his legal research and learning he was in the right to sit on the bench, went back to 780 Third Avenue the next day and told the security guard that the plaza was a public park. He says the building employee insulted him and threatened to have him arrested. “I was like, ‘Okay, game on.’”
Phillips filmed these interactions and gave the guard many opportunities to change his tune before finally going live with the whole imbroglio. Thus was born the Instagram account @780_lord_of_bench, which now has 64.7K followers, including Joe Rogan and Sarah Jessica Parker. And more importantly, ordinary New Yorkers, who now file complaints about POPS abuses, attend Phillips’s celebratory POPS events — part protest, part party, calling attention to the right to public leisure in those spaces — and donate to his Patreon to support his advocacy.
He now monitors POPS throughout Midtown. On a beautiful October evening, I meet Phillips just across the street from Radio City Music Hall for a tour of some of offending properties along Sixth Avenue and an introduction to some of the notorious security regimes featured in his videos.
The outdoor tables of a restaurant, Double Knot, protrude — illegally, according to Phillips — onto the POPS at 1251 Sixth Avenue, managed by the Hines Group and owned by Mitsui Fudosan America, a real estate developer that continues to dodge a fine despite public complaints and a violation issued by the city for allowing a restaurant in a place designated as a public plaza with obvious signage.
Nearby, at 1221 Sixth, property of The Rockefeller Group, which owns and manages some six million square feet of office space in Midtown Manhattan, a sunken plaza — also a POPS — has at times been blocked off on weekends. Due to complaints and advocacy by Phillips and his followers, the Department of Buildings has served Rockefeller with a violation on this issue, but they remain determined to skirt the law when they can. A sign barring the public from the lower plaza that is used on weekends sits nearby. And just two days earlier, security on the same property attempted to remove Phillips for filming on the property, though he was not breaking any of the posted rules about the plaza’s use.
In fact, as we walk from one plaza to another, I remark that Phillips seems scrupulous about following the rules of these plazas. “That’s my whole leverage,” he grins.” That’s my whole thing, is [that] I’m going to document that I’m being completely a normal guy.” The message of all his videos and advocacy is one of following the rules, and in the comments, he often pushes back when his followers urge some kind of civil disobedience. The ethos of his Instagram account and all his interactions with building personnel seems to be that the public should be respectful of these public spaces by observing the rules, and that the owners should do the same. “The issue is when they start to put their own rules into effect” and refuse to abide by their own agreements with the public, he says.
Since Phillips began making these videos, security follows him around when he is in these spaces. The evening of my visit, as we sit in the sunken plaza, a security guard watches us carefully and keeps talking into his phone. Just two days earlier, at the same spot, Phillips was removed by security.
Walking north, Phillips shows me another POPS, this one at 31 West Fifty-Second Street where, until he made videos about it, the handicapped access ramp was blocked off. It’s open, for now. Another offending restaurant on the same property has reduced its outdoor table intrusion to just one, which Phillips thinks is acceptable even if it might technically be out of line. “It’s a give-and-take,” he says, “because obviously nothing is ever perfect,” pointing out that it might be hard for an owner to completely forbid a tenant to use outside space that they’d assumed was part of the deal when they rented the space.
Phillips is not someone who has a hard time seeing the viewpoint of others, especially those in the same industry as him. “As a security guy, I work with a lot of these types of guys,” he says. “They kind of get the ego thing when they work in a building like this.” But they are not actually enforcing the law. Rather, they are enforcing the desires of a corporation uninterested in holding up their end of the bargain to the public.
Phillips says building owners are getting more fines and being issued more violations in response to his complaints. Phillips’s advocacy has engaged city officials, including the Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani, who was appointed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani in January and has met with Phillips and toured the offending sites. Phillips calls Tigani “a great, great asset.” Phillips would like to see the city strengthen enforcement and streamline the process for responding to complaints; at present, it’s hampered by the fact that multiple agencies are involved (exactly the kind of problem Mamdani’s Commission on Government Efficiency [COGE] has been trying to fix). He’d also like to see city council legislation to increase the fines on repeat offenders.
Phillips also holds dance parties, concerts, and most recently, a well-attended Halloween flash dance party and costume contest in the POPS, spreading the word about the violations but also reclaiming these public spaces for public joy. For the Halloween party, Phillips himself showed up in full king regalia, including a crown and scepter — the Lord of Bench, crowned as such.
While the response to his project is satisfying so far, Phillips would like to see the real estate industry comply more fully, and he thinks Mayor Mamdani’s attention on the issue would help significantly. “This is the one issue I cannot believe he has not said a word on since the moment it started,” Phillips says, noting with some annoyance that many content creators “with far less following, with far less reach” have been in conversation with the mayor. “I’m not one of the crazy guys out here!” says Phillips. “We need his voice on this.”
Phillips’s project — fighting for public control of space against real estate oligarchs who want to take it away — seems closely aligned with Mamdani’s own. Both have been fighting for the working class to quite literally have a place in the city: a bench, an apartment, a park, a soccer field, a night at the opera. Both insist that New York is for everybody.
Phillips, for his part, does not frame his crusade in ideological terms. “This is an issue that transcends everything,” he says. “Doesn’t matter if you’re left, right, green. Everybody’s gonna sit on a bench.”

https://gothamist.com/news/runners-and-t.title: Runners, and throngs of spectators, kick off the five-borough New York City Marathon
https://gothamist.com/news/runners-and-t.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/runners-and-t.text:
The New York City marathon kicked off on Sunday morning with partly cloudy skies and brisk temperatures in the high 40s.
As the first waves of runners got started on Staten Island, across the Verrazano Bridge – the first of five bridges along the 26.2 mile route to the Central Park finish line – a crowd of cheering supporters gathered in Bay Ridge.
Sarah Agrusa, a New Yorker who’s a performer with the touring production of Mamma Mia!, is supporting her boyfriend, Ryan Wong, who’s running the race for the first time.
“I'm planning to hit mile 9, 15, 17, 19 and then the finish line,” she told Gothamist. “It's beautiful weather out here, so I'm excited to see everyone run.”
The couple’s dachshund, Ollie, will join her along the route. “He'll hang out in the backpack once it gets a little busier. But he's excited, I think, to support his dad,” she said.
This year marks the 50th anniversary of the marathon’s five borough course.
Some 60,000 runners are expected to participate in the big race, which snakes through Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx before ending near 67th Street in Central Park. Another 2 million spectators are expected to be cheering them on along.
There are a number of major bridge and road closures for the big race. You can find them all here.
