https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.title: NYC Council to scrutinize snow removal plans as winter approaches
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.text:
The leaves are still falling, but New York City lawmakers are already talking about clearing snow.
The City Council’s sanitation committee will take a closer look at how the city prepares for winter storms and snow removal on Monday, after two major winter storms buried streets and sidewalks earlier this year and lingering low temperatures kept piles of snow frozen for weeks.
Lawmakers will also consider a bill requiring the city’s Department of Sanitation to keep and publish snowplowing records on its PlowNYC website. Right now, the site lets New Yorkers see the last time their block was cleared of snow, but it doesn’t keep historical data.
In a memo supporting the bill, primary sponsor Councilmember Ty Hankerson said the legislation would give New Yorkers greater transparency during and after snowstorms.
“Snow plows are often a contentious issue, with accusations that certain parts of New York receive many more snow plows than others,” Hankerson wrote. “As the City navigates this issue, it must do so with all of the relevant data publicly available to everyone.”
The hearing comes as federal forecasters predict a warmer-than-average winter in New York City, partly due to El Niño, a weather pattern linked to warming Pacific Ocean waters. But meteorologists have said a major snowstorm is still possible.
Last winter was particularly brutal, bringing prolonged cold and heavy snowfall to the city.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Ministério da Educação quer que PF e AGU apurem denúncias de violência política durante e após eleições
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Ministério da Educação (MEC) está reunindo denúncias de violência política ocorrida durante e após as eleições 2026. Relatos feitos à Ouvidoria do órgão ou enviados a universidades e institutos federais serão encaminhados à Polícia Federal (PF) e à Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU).
A medida foi tomada diante de ameaças contra universidades federais, estudantes e docentes circularem nas redes sociais logo após o primeiro turno das eleições, ocorrido em 4 de outubro. Nesse momento, o ministério solicitou investigação da PF e também acionou a AGU para a adoção das medidas jurídicas cabíveis.
Em nota à imprensa, o MEC informou que foram pedidas providências “diante da gravidade das ameaças de violência e de destruição patrimonial, além da utilização de símbolos nazistas contra as universidades federais, estudantes e docentes reportadas.”
A pasta informou que, como os processos de investigação ainda estão em andamento, novas denúncias serão adicionadas ao processo.
“O MEC reforça que as instituições de ensino devem ser, por essência, espaços plurais, de tolerância, diálogo e respeito à diversidade de ideias”, diz a nota.
O ministério destacou ainda que repudia qualquer tipo de ameaça, ofensa ou discriminação no ambiente estudantil e acadêmico, independentemente de sua motivação.
“A Constituição Federal garante o direito à liberdade de expressão e de pensamento, princípios fundamentais para a consolidação da democracia brasileira”, destaca o informe.
Caso em apuração
A Universidade Federal de Pernambuco (UFPE) foi alvo de um incêndio de grandes proporções no dia 7 de outubro. O fogo na sede da Diretoria de Inovação e Empreendedorismo (Dine), que integra o Núcleo de Inovação Tecnológica da universidade, começou por volta das 20h.
Durante a semana do incêndio, circularam uma série de prints de mensagens com ameaças de ataques contra universidades públicas em Pernambuco em grupos bolsonaristas. A PF apura o caso.
Expulsão em Maringá
No último sábado (31), a UniCesumar, universidade privada sediada em Maringá, no noroeste do Paraná, informou, em comunicado, que expulsou estudantes do curso de Medicina envolvidos na divulgação de mensagens discriminatórias contra bolsistas e com referências ao nazismo. Segundo a instituição, a decisão foi tomada após a conclusão de uma sindicância interna. As mensagens circularam em um grupo de WhatsApp da turma no domingo (25), após o resultado eleitoral.
“A Comissão de Sindicância recomendou e a Reitoria da UniCesumar decidiu pela aplicação de medidas disciplinares em relação aos alunos envolvidos, nos termos do Regimento Interno da universidade. As medidas disciplinares foram: advertências, suspensões e desligamentos do quadro discente da instituição, de acordo com a gravidade de cada conduta apurada”, informa o comunicado publicado no Instagram da universidade.
A UniCesumar não especificou quantos estudantes foram responsabilizados pelas mensagens discriminatórias. A instituição também declarou repudiar qualquer tipo de preconceito e informou que o Núcleo de Apoio ao Estudante de Medicina (NAEME) está à disposição dos alunos para oferecer acolhimento, orientação e suporte. O atendimento pode ser feito pelos telefones (44) 99122-3957 e (44) 3027-6360, ramal 2870.
Os comentários ofensivos desqualificavam estudantes que ingressaram no curso de Medicina por meio de programas sociais. Uma das mensagens dizia: “Quem paga trabalhou e tem 15 mil por mês para pagar >>>>>>> Quem passou numa provinha”.
Outras mensagens recorriam a expressões e imagens associadas ao nazismo para intimidar os bolsistas. Um estudante compartilhou uma fotografia do Exército nazista acompanhada de referências ao “leite cru”, expressão que se popularizou em grupos na internet ligados à defesa da supremacia branca.
O Ministério Público Federal (MPF) abriu uma investigação para apurar o caso. O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) também se manifestou publicamente e ressaltou o compromisso da profissão com a humanidade.
“Tais atitudes ferem diretamente os princípios fundamentais do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina, segundo os quais o estudante deve estar a serviço da saúde do ser humano e da coletividade, exercendo suas atividades sem discriminação de qualquer natureza.”

https://gothamist.com/news/the-best-day-.title: 'The best day of the year': Inside Clinton Hill's 'mile nine' NYC marathon party
https://gothamist.com/news/the-best-day-.author: Stephanie Keith
https://gothamist.com/news/the-best-day-.text:
For Danielle Strle, Marathon Sunday in New York City is “the best day of the year.”
Strle, 45, chief product officer for the satirical news site The Onion, came dressed as a banana to cheer people on as they dashed by.
She was among thousands of revelers packed into the brownstone-lined streets of Brooklyn's Clinton Hill, near mile nine of the 26.2-mile route, for one of the city's most exuberant marathon watch parties.
Strle said the "Mile Nine" party along Lafayette Avenue in Clinton Hill has been going on for 23 years. And she's been part of it since the beginning.
"We kind of started it by accident," she said.
In the early days, locals would pass out bodega sandwiches. Now, "we’ve upgraded to a grill. We have waffles. We have egg sandwiches. We have coffee. We’ve got orange juice," she said. "We’ve just gotten bigger and bigger every year."
"Nobody was having parties on the end of the block when we started doing this," she added. "It’s the best block for the marathon party spectator scene."
This year's marathon kicked off the morning after Halloween and many revelers appeared to show up in their Halloween costumes from the night before. Strle was one of many dressed up like the potassium-rich snack favored by endurance athletes.
Some 60,000 runners participated in the race, which winds through all five boroughs before finishing in Central Park.
A few blocks down the marathon route, another party convened around Emmanuel Baptist Church. Around 11 a.m., the church choir came out to serenade the runners, while a grill had been set up to serve barbecue.
On Sunday, nearly all the runners lagged far behind Andreas Almgren of Sweden and Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya, the men's and women's winners, who both finished the marathon in just over two hours.
But winning was hardly the point for most participants, and certainly not for the spectators cheering them on.
“It’s a real triumph of the human spirit,” said Strle.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Falta uma semana para o Enem 2026; veja horários e o que levar
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Alex Rodrigues
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Com a proximidade do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem), no próximo domingo (8), os mais de 5 milhões de inscritos devem estar atentos às orientações do Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep).
No primeiro dia do exame, além da redação, serão aplicadas as provas de linguagens, códigos e suas tecnologias, e ciências humanas e suas tecnologias.
Já no segundo dia, no domingo, 15 de novembro, os participantes responderão às questões de ciências da natureza e suas tecnologias, matemática e suas tecnologias.
Ao todo, são 45 questões em cada área do conhecimento. Confira as principais dicas do Inep e saiba o que é obrigatório, aconselhável, permitido e proibido no exame:
Horários
Abertura dos portões: 12 horas (meio-dia)
Fechamento dos portões: 13 horas
Início das provas: 13h30
Término das provas: 19h no dia 8; e 18h30 no dia 15
O Enem segue o horário de Brasília. Os participantes com tempo adicional terão, no primeiro domingo, até as 20 horas para concluir a prova, e até as 19h30 no dia 15.
O limite de tempo também será estendido em duas horas para os candidatos que farão a videoprova em Libras.
Identificação
A apresentação de documento oficial com foto é obrigatória. São válidos os seguintes documentos:
Documentos físicos:
RG,
passaporte,
Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH), e
Carteira de Trabalho (impressa e emitida após 27/01/1997) ou identidade profissional expedida por conselho de classe.
Estrangeiros podem apresentar o passaporte, Carteira de Registro Nacional Migratório (CRNM), documento provisório de Registro Nacional Migratório ou documento de identificação oficial emitido por país-membro do Mercosul.
Documentos digitais:
e-Título,
CNH Digital,
RG Digital,
Identidade Digital (CIN).
Os documentos devem ser apresentados exclusivamente dentro dos aplicativos oficiais ou no aplicativo Gov.br. Capturas de tela ou fotos não serão aceitas.
Também não são aceitos documentos não listados no edital do exame, tais como Boletim de Ocorrência, certidões de nascimento, casamento, título de eleitor impresso, carteira de estudante, certificado de residência, crachás e cópias (mesmo que autenticadas).
O que levar
Obrigatório: caneta esferográfica de tinta preta com o corpo de material transparente e documento de identificação válido (físico ou digital)
Recomendado: Cartão de Confirmação de Inscrição e Declaração de Comparecimento impressa (para quem precisa comprovar presença no trabalho), que terão que ser guardados no envelope porta-objeto que o chefe de sala fornecerá antes do ingresso na sala.
Lanches e itens pessoais: Alimentos e medicamentos são permitidos, mas passarão por vistoria do fiscal.
Antes de entrar na sala, o candidato receberá um envelope porta-objetos para guardar todos os itens proibidos. O envelope deverá ser colocado embaixo da carteira, lacrado e identificado, com aparelhos eletrônicos, como o telefone celular, desligados.
Itens Proibidos
Serão eliminados os participantes que, ao ingressar na sala de provas, estiverem levando consigo, fora do envelope porta-objetos, qualquer um dos seguintes itens:
Impressos: cartão de confirmação de inscrição ou Declaração de Comparecimento impressa.
Eletrônicos: celulares, relógios (digitais ou analógicos), fones de ouvido, chaves com alarme, garrafas digitais e cigarros eletrônicos, que devem estar desligados, com alarmes desativados e guardados no envelope porta-objetos.
Materiais de estudo e vestuário: Lápis, borracha, corretivo, lapiseira, réguas, livros, anotações, óculos escuros e chapéus/bonés não podem ser usados durante a prova.
Comunicação: É proibido estabelecer ou tentar estabelecer qualquer tipo de comunicação externa ou interna, assim como gravar ou fotografar a aplicação do exame. Também é proibido registrar ou divulgar, por meio de imagem ou som, a realização da prova ou qualquer material usado no exame.
Obrigações
São obrigações do participante do Enem:
submeter-se à identificação sempre que solicitado;
aguardar pela autorização para começar o exame;
submeter-se à revista eletrônica, a qualquer momento, por meio do uso de detector de metais; e
permitir que seu lanche, medicamentos, artigos religiosos e materiais próprios necessários à realização da prova sejam vistoriados quando solicitado.
Reaplicação
Participantes afetados por problemas logísticos durante as provas ou acometidos por doenças infectocontagiosas na semana anterior ao exame poderão pedir a reaplicação das provas. Os pedidos serão julgados individualmente pelo Inep.
Problemas logísticos: desastres naturais que comprometam a estrutura do local, falta de energia elétrica que prejudique a visibilidade ou erros de execução do procedimento de aplicação que causem comprovado prejuízo ao candidato;
Doenças infectocontagiosas: tuberculose, coqueluche, difteria, doença invasiva por Haemophilus influenzae, doença meningocócica e outras meningites, varíola, varíola dos macacos (monkeypox), Influenza humana A e B, poliomielite por poliovírus selvagem, sarampo, rubéola, varicela e covid-19.
Atenção
A partir das 13h (horário de Brasília), a ida ao banheiro será permitida, desde que o participante seja acompanhado pelo fiscal. Neste caso, ele deve fechar sua prova e deixá-la com a capa voltada para cima antes de deixar a sala.
Quando autorizado, antes de iniciar a prova, verifique se o Caderno de Questões contém a quantidade de perguntas indicadas no Cartão-Resposta e se não há qualquer defeito gráfico que impossibilite ou atrapalhe a resolução da prova.
As respostas às questões objetivas, bem como a redação, devem ser escritas com caneta esferográfica de tinta preta.
Entregue ao chefe de sala o Cartão-Reposta/Folha de Redação e a Folha de Rascunho ao deixar em definitivo a sala de provas.
Os gabaritos das provas objetivas serão divulgados no portal do Inep, na seção Provas e Gabaritos, até o 10° dia útil após o segundo dia de aplicação das provas.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Suspended Nurse Ordered Back to Work at Kings County Hospital Amid Union Standoff
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
A Kings County Hospital Center nurse practitioner who claims she was suspended in retaliation for union organizing was ordered to report back to work after three weeks away from the bedside, after the city hospital’s system apparently decided to put its misconduct investigation on ice.
The nurse, Sarah Dowd, and her union, the New York State Nurses Association, confirmed that she would return to work Nov. 2 and receive full back pay. NYC Health + Hospitals had been investigating claims of misconduct by Dowd stemming from an allegation that she improperly pulled nurses from their jobs last month to discuss union business. Dowd, who works in the intensive care unit, flatly denied those allegations.
Dowd received written notice of her return to work on Thursday, the day after her first disciplinary hearing with Kings County’s labor relations department, where she arrived flanked by about a dozen colleagues who crowded the lobby of the building in support.
A spokesperson for H+H did not respond to The City Reporter’s requests for comment about the status of its investigation.
“This was total bullshit and I think that we proved that,” Dowd said of Kings County’s claims that her union discussions interfered with patient care. “Now we’re going to go back to doing the work of making sure the hospital is following its contractual obligations, and state law, around safe staffing.”
Health + Hospitals suspended Dowd on Oct. 9, alleging that days earlier she had pulled as many as 10 nurses from their posts to attend a union meeting on the hospital’s campus. Dowd, who was on her day off on Oct. 6, the day of the alleged misconduct, flatly denies claims that she had taken colleagues away from their duties. She said she was in the hospital that day in her capacity as a union official talking to nurses about staffing issues that have plagued Kings County for months, a practice known as “rounding.”
The hospital’s claims, and the union’s objections, were laid out in internal communications between officials from both sides that were included in a formal complaint that NYSNA submitted to the state labor board on Oct. 22.
MORE: A 27-Hour Wait for a Hospital Bed? Why Delays Are Growing at NY Hospitals
The controversy dates to Oct. 6, when Dowd was in the hospital’s medical-surgical unit following up on reports of excessive “floating,” when en hospital administrators assign nurses to multiple departments per shift to make up for staffing shortages.
Dowd said she had “rounded” her own unit and others at the hospital “countless” times without incident in her capacity as the vice president of Kings County’s local bargaining unit — essentially the union local covering nursing staff at the hospital. But H+H claimed that Dowd improperly pulled nurses from their posts in order to discuss union business.
Issues surrounding nurse-to-patient ratios have been a flashpoint of the healthcare labor movement in recent years. It was a major point of contention during the weekslong strike by 15,000 nurses at three private hospital systems in New York this past winter.
Adam Marcus, a Kings County pediatric psychiatry nurse and union official, said that with Dowd’s situation now behind them the union will continue to push hospital leadership to improve staffing.
“Our work isn’t over,” said Marcus.

https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.author: Ryan Devereaux
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.text:
Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors.
“People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said.
Fifteen days later, her fears were realized.
ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors.
The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said.
The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted.
“The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.”
Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites.
“Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.”
Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing.
In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.”
The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio, that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental.)
Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.”
Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary.
“When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.”
U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.”
James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field.
While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.
Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.”
“Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.”
In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands.
Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations.
When DHS uses this authority, it typically waives dozens of laws at a time. That was the case in 2019 when the department set its sights on Organ Pipe. A waiver issued by then-acting Secretary Kevin K. McAleenan set aside more than 40 of the nation’s most stringent environmental and cultural resource protection laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and others. Also on that list was the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, the landmark 1990 law that acknowledged the nation’s long history of desecrating Native American burials and required that ancestral remains and cultural objects be returned to tribes.
In an internal 2019 report obtained by The Washington Post, park service officials identified nearly two dozen archaeological sites in Organ Pipe as at risk of damage or total destruction by government contractors.
Of particular significance is a desert oasis known as Quitobaquito Springs. Less than 200 feet from the international border, the springs provide one of the only reliable sources of groundwater and shade for miles around, and they were a longtime gathering place, grazing site and home for O’odham families.
“Archaeological evidence of human presence at Quitobaquito extends back thousands of years, at least to Archaic times,” the survey found, adding that the springs represent the “only known Hia C-ed O’odham village site in the United States.”
A park service report in 2024 noted that a cemetery at Quitobaquito holds the remains of at least two families, including Eiler’s, and 34 graves. Throughout the region, remains of 5,500 ancestors that were displaced have been made available for return to the Tohono O’odham Nation, according to ProPublica’s NAGPRA database.
“This sort of incident has happened numerous times across our homeland, and it’s always alarming to hear about a case from an O’odham point of view,” said David Martínez, a professor of American Indian and transborder studies at the University of Arizona and a member of the Hia-Ced O’odham and Akimel O’odham tribes, as well as the Gila River Indian Community.
“Those remains shouldn’t have been disturbed in the first place,” he said. “While there are protocols existing today to properly care for these remains, ultimately, whatever either the government or the corporate world is pursuing to build, we know that at some juncture that construction will continue, and it always leaves us feeling, I think, a little hollow.”
Today, Quitobaquito lies in the shadow of the border wall erected during Trump’s first term. Its construction required detonating explosives in the national monument, blasting apart an area called Monument Hill and outraging tribal leaders. According to Eiler, the remains recovered in September were not found at the springs, though government work crews are working in close proximity to the site.
This year, DHS hired Sundt Construction, an Arizona-based company, to build a second wall in the monument. The $443 million contract was finalized in May. (Sundt directed questions concerning the discovery of human remains on its job site to CBP.)
According to CBP, the 2019 waiver for Organ Pipe is still in effect, years after completion of the project that prompted it. A second waiver, exempting DHS from many of the same laws and applying to the national monument as well as a wildlife refuge to the west, was issued by Homeland Security’s then-Secretary Kristi Noem last year.
“Unfortunately, there is no end date to the effectiveness of the waivers,” said Dinah Bear, a Tucson-based lawyer who served for 25 years as a senior attorney in the White House’s Council on Environmental Quality under both Democratic and Republican administrations. What’s more, she added, “there’s nothing in the statutory language that ties the waivers to a particular project.”
The Department of Homeland Security’s waiver powers have been central to a high-profile legal fight over the department’s efforts to build a border wall through Big Bend National Park in West Texas, with a federal judge overseeing the case recently ordering a temporary halt to the project.
Borderlands advocates in Arizona are hoping for similar interventions. In Congress, Grijalva is preparing legislation to void existing waivers that have allowed DHS to disregard laws designed to protect tribal sovereignty, sacred sites and environmentally sensitive lands.
In the meantime, construction on the border continues. For Eiler, it’s not just the destruction in Organ Pipe that’s troubling. She sees the disturbance of tribal graves resulting from wall construction as reflective of a wider pattern of destruction across the border.
“It’s sad because it’s not only happening down there,” she said. “It’s happening all over the United States, and nobody’s saying much about it.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: In two minds: duality of Viktor&Rolf's design ideology on show in Milan exhibition
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: The Art Newspaper
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For their couture show of Spring Summer 2024, the Dutch designers Viktor&Rolf sent out 28 all-black looks that were both polished and raw, silly and serious, chaotic and controlled. One of them, a deconstructed glittering tulle ballgown layered over a sleek, blush-coloured corset and crinoline, will be on show in Milan until 22 November in the gallery space above the city’s famed concept store, 10 Corso Como.
The exhibition, called Spectrum, and brought together by Alessio de’Navasques, professor of fashion archives at the Sapienza University of Rome, will include 20 haute couture outfits from three decades of the designers’ career. Shown as ten pairs, the exhibition will create dialogue between the pieces, reflecting the duality that underpins both their own partnership and their design ideology. In Viktor&Rolf World, everything comes in twos.
The couple met in the late 1980s, at college in Arnhem, and established their own fashion house in Paris in 1993. Though they created ready-to-wear for a number of years, their flamboyance and experimentalism has always been better suited to haute couture, to which they dedicated themselves from 2015. “Our work is like a laboratory, a place to experiment and develop ideas,” they say. Though their central focus is always fashion—its codes, structures and aesthetics—there’s no denying that a gallery is as well, or even better, suited to their conceptual, sculptural works as a catwalk.

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-should-el.title: MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes, watchdog writes
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-should-el.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-should-el.text:
In less than four years, the MTA could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue, according to a new analysis from the Citizens Budget Commission, which recommends cutting the workforce to close the gap.
The budget watchdog recommends sweeping job cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete. The budget commission suggested the MTA allow its trains to run with just one worker, instead of two.
Train lines that have new computer-based signals, like the L and the 7, are already fully automated, as are the announcements on the trains. While the conductor opens and closes the train doors, the operator has few other duties, which include hitting a button every 20 seconds to signal they are alert. The budget commission cited the operator’s limited responsibilities as a sign the job could be cut with no impact to service.
Eliminating operator jobs on the L and 7 lines could save $36.5 million a year, according to the report. If the agency moved to phase out two people operating trains across the system, it could save $500 million a year.
The agency is in the process of installing new signals on other lines like the A, C, E, F, G, M and R lines. For now, those lines still require two people to run the trains.
The suggestion from the Citizens Budget Commission comes at a sensitive time as Transport Workers Union Local 100 negotiates a contract with the MTA for its 40,000 subway and bus workers. The MTA is expected to release its financial plan for next year in the coming weeks, which will include a 4% fare and toll increase. The board will vote on that plan in December.
“The same recommendations have been coming down for dozens of years, so there's nothing new about it,” said Transport Workers Union of America President John Samuelsen. “It's essentially a recommendation to balance alleged deficits that the MTA has off the backs of working people.”
Last year, the state legislature tried to enshrine a requirement of two MTA workers on each train into law, but Gov. Kathy Hochul vetoed the bill, leaving open the possibility that one-person train operations could happen in the future.
“Legislatively mandated staffing prevents the MTA from modernizing — as technology and best practices continue to improve — and realizing the efficiency and financial benefits,” the Citizens Budget Commission's report argues.
The Citizens Budget Commission acknowledges the MTA has become more efficient in recent years, saving a reported $576 million this year through what the agency calls “operating efficiencies.” But the report argues that without cutting labor and healthcare costs, the MTA faces a $300 million budget gap next year that will grow to $900 million by 2030. The budget commission estimates its recommended reforms could save $2.5 billion annually.
Other recommendations include streamlining fare collection on the commuter railroads by checking tickets prior to boarding, reducing the need for someone to walk through the train. The Citizens Budget Commission argues cutting more than 1,000 jobs on Metro-North and the Long Island Rail Road could save $380 million annually.
The report also recommended MTA retirees pay more in healthcare premiums, which could bring in an additional $315 million a year.
Samuelsen countered that many laborers, ironworkers, track workers, and crane operators in the MTA get paid less than their peers in the private sector, but accept that because of the generous retirement benefits.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/r.title: Report: NYPD’s Dangerous Increase In High-Speed Pursuits Did Not Decrease Crime
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/r.author: Sammy Sussman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/r.text:
The NYPD’s decision to increase high-speed vehicle pursuits under Mayor Eric Adams led to more crashes, injuries and deaths — and didn’t even drive down crime, according to a new study.
The department increased its pursuits 25-fold in 2022, as Streetsblog previously reported, from around eight pursuits per month to 200. The increase had no tangible impact on crime beyond larger national trends — but it did cause roughly 675 more collisions, 355 additional injuries and seven additional fatalities, according to the researchers.
“It’s a lot of innocent lives,” said Justin Nix, a professor at the University of Nebraska at Omaha and co-author of the study, “The Fast and the Spurious — A Causal Evaluation of NYPD’s Pursuit Policy, 2022–2025.”
“One-third of the people who are getting injured or killed are other people — drivers, pedestrians — who didn’t even decide to flee [police].”
The researchers used city crime statistics to look at the effects of the increase, and subsequent decrease, in pursuits. They focused on three specific categories of crimes — collisions, robberies and gun violence — while factoring in national trends. Their analysis found one immediate effect: crashes increased and then decreased, as did resulting injuries and deaths, based on changes in agency policy.
But the researchers saw no noticeable changes in robberies and gun violence.
“Pursuit escalation produced clear and attributable collision harms while providing no credible evidence of crime reduction,” Nix wrote with his co-author John Hall.
The researchers used a value-of-life analysis — a common, if macabre, method of criminological data analysis that essentially puts a price tag on injuries, deaths and property damage – to calculate at what point the toll of increased pursuits would be mitigated by decreases in crime.
Ultimately, they found that New York’s crime levels were nowhere near the level needed for the new pursuit policies to justify the overwhelming costs in terms of collisions, injuries and deaths. Instead, they found that the NYPD unleashed costly harms on city residents in exchange for purely imaginary crime-reduction benefits — in other words, the top brass’s decision to increase these pursuits came at a shocking net loss to public safety.
“Agencies should require affirmative evidence of crime-prevention benefits before expanding pursuit authority,” the authors wrote in implicit criticism of the NYPD after studying their actions from 2022 to 2025.
The study noted that the initial decision to increase pursuits was made unofficially, seemingly in late 2022.
“People thinking they can take off on us? Those days are over,” Chief of Department John Chell told reporters at the time — an indication that he had ordered his cops to be more aggressive with their cars.
By August 2023, then-Chief of Department Jeffrey Maddrey released a memo formalizing the department’s pursuit policy, which remained just vague enough to maintain the Chell-initiated trend: pursuits could continue for non-violent crimes, but they should be terminated when “the risks to uniformed members of the service and the public outweigh the danger to the community if suspect is not immediately apprehended.”
Police leaders across the country often argue that pursuits serve as a crime deterrent. But previous research has found that roughly 30 percent of police pursuits end without a successful apprehension. And suspects choosing to flee police are overwhelmingly young, male, intoxicated and unlicensed — characteristics associated with a “weakened deterrence perception” and “impaired risk assessment.”
Under fire as chases rose dramatically under Chell and Maddrey, the NYPD revealed in 2024 that around two-thirds of its pursuits began as simple car stops for traffic offenses — and 25 percent of the 2,278 chases “resulted in some combination of a collision, property damage, or physical harm,” the NYPD told Streetsblog.
Around a dozen of the pursuits resulted in fatalities — including Amanda Servedio, who was killed in Astoria in 2024 by a driver who was not suspected of a violent crime fled the cops.
Commissioner Jessica Tisch reversed the Chell-Maddrey initiative and codified NYPD policy in 2025, restricting chases to serious crimes, discouraging pursuits near schools and playgrounds and shielding cops from criticism or discipline if they chose to terminate a pursuit because of safety concerns. The department’s pursuit numbers quickly declined, though they remain slightly higher than where they were before the 2022 escalation.
Nix noted that this quick reversal was abnormal, and it allowed researchers to study how pursuits affected crime numbers both as pursuit numbers went up and as they came back down — making the statistically significant changes in crashes, and the lack of change in crime numbers, even more apparent.
“If we observed an effect,” Nix said, “we would obviously expect to see the opposite when the policy changed again.”
The NYPD did not respond to multiple messages seeking comment for this story.
Sammy Sussman joined Streetsblog in May 2026 as law enforcement reporter after successful stints at New York Focus and The New York Times. In 2019, he interned on a team that won a Pulitzer.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Fifth generation Indian weaver launches luxury cashmere brand
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: The Art Newspaper
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Mujtaba Kadri’s family has produced cashmere for five generations and his atelier in Srinagar, the largest city in Kashmir, is just 50m away from where his great-grandfather had his own. “I’ve been involved since I was a child,” Kadri says. His spinners and weavers are still based exclusively in Srinagar, mostly women working from home. Hand spinning creates a slightly uneven texture in the fibre, which leaves tiny air pockets once it is woven. It is this that makes the fabric both very light and incredibly warm.
Kadri studied at university in Mumbai but returned immediately to his home city, albeit with a more international outlook. “Our cashmere is the finest quality, which means its micron count is always below 14.5,” Kadri says. “I knew it had potential in foreign markets.” He went on to work with Carolina Herrera, Oscar de la Renta and Marni, making custom-ordered textiles. Later, he met Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, and collaborated closely with their label, The Row, when they launched their home line.
He is now launching the Kadri brand, using his own name, in outlets including London’s Dover Street Market. On sale will be scarves, blankets and other home and fashion accessories. “I’ve wanted to do this for a long time,” he says. Designs are developed in a small Paris studio where the creative team includes colour specialist Maeva Elfassi. “Colour can be the element that cashmere brands get wrong,” Kadri says.
Hand-woven cashmere is expensive due to the rare raw materials, from a special breed of goats in the Jankan region, and its time-consuming production. A shawl, which sells for $1,000, will go through 12 processes, undertaken by a number of artisans, and takes 40 days to make. “It really is slow fashion,” Kadri says. But more importantly, for him, it is a way to sustain a community where weaving has always been a way of life.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/w.title: Would A One-Way Conversion Fix Brooklyn’s Grand Street Or Make It Worse?
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/w.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/w.text:
Two cyclists on a tandem bike are forced into traffic on Grand Street. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Grand in name only.
The frequently blocked Grand Street bike lane in Brooklyn is one of the worst in the city — but advocates are raising early concerns that a nascent proposal by the city could be worse than the current dysfunction.
The Department of Transportation has been soliciting feedback for a plan to convert Grand Street into a one-way eastbound street and nearby Metropolitan Avenue, also currently two-way, into one-way westbound with a new protected bike lane.
Street safety advocates in the area worry that converting the currently two-way streets to one-way will create two faster roadways, thanks to having two traffic lanes in one direction. A conversion without traffic calming on side streets, parking reform, a road diet and maintaining two-way bike infrastructure wouldn’t improve anything, one advocate said.
“I think the most likely outcome with a one-way is two travel lanes on both streets,” said Brent Bovenzi, an organizer with North Brooklyn Open Streets who lived on Grand Street for four years. “That would encourage more speeding, especially at night. And Grand Street has so many bars. I just don’t see how that’s going to make the street safer.”
The idea of a one-way conversion of the two busy truck routes was first discussed formally at a Street Improvements Workshop in 2023. Industrial and manufacturing businesses in the area, who are represented by Evergreen Inc., want two-lane traffic on both streets, teeing up a future conflict with street safety advocates. Both streets are designated “local truck routes,” meaning trucks use them to get to inter-borough destinations.
“Both of those streets actually have manufacturers and industrial businesses directly on them. But more broadly those streets are truck routes,” said Leah Archibald, the executive director of Evergreen. “This really affects all of the businesses in the area because they do rely on trucks in and trucks out.”
Grand Street is a bustling commercial corridor. There are copious bars, coffee shops, grocery stores, clothing stores and gyms. Those who live in the area can pretty much get anything done on the street. One study suggests that two-way traffic could contribute to that vibrancy.
The study, conducted in 2017 by the Transportation Research Board, found that multi-lane, one-way streets have higher rates of traffic collisions and contribute to “degradation and erosion of community.”
Another 2019 study by researchers at Penn State and ETH Zurich found that two-way streets offer more redundancy to drivers which could come in handy if routes are blocked, and that two-way streets with prohibited left turns can be even more efficient. One-way networks, the study finds, are only the best option in “a few” scenarios because “they force vehicles to travel the longest distances on average.”
Grand Street’s high concentration of businesses means many will want a voice in the design process. Storefront businesses on the corridor between Union and Bushwick avenues are represented by the Grand Street BID, which is supporting a one-way conversion idea, for now.
“We’re really focused on safety and streets that work for everyone in East Williamsburg,” said Francesca Bruce, the Grand Street BID’s executive director. “I think that we are cautiously optimistic. We support [a one-way conversion] in theory because we haven’t necessarily seen a feasible alternative that accounts for all users.”
Eyes on Grand Street
All stakeholders Streetsblog spoke with said that Grand Street’s current design leaves much to be desired.
“Everyone agrees that what we have now is suboptimal,” said Archibald.
The eastbound side has concrete barriers, but breaks in the protection allow trucks and cars to double park, trapping cyclists in.
And the westbound side’s parking protected design is frequently blocked by construction and is much narrower than the new bike lanes that the DOT has been installing in Manhattan.
“It’s almost impossible to go from Union Avenue to Bushwick Avenue without having to leave the bike lane at some point,” said Bovenzi.
The further east, the worse it gets, with the lane essentially disappearing past Bushwick Avenue due to the industrial businesses using it as an extension of their garages.
Grand Street is not only a mess for cyclists, but bus riders on the Q59 and Q54 routes are forced to crawl through traffic.
The city has classified both Grand Street and Metropolitan Avenue as “Vision Zero Priority Corridors,” which means they are especially dangerous. In 2025, there were 103 reported crashes on the Grand Street corridor DOT is studying, injuring 26 cyclists and eight pedestrians. On the corresponding stretch of Metropolitan, there were 50 reported crashes injuring two cyclists and five pedestrians.
Looking ahead
Bovenzi said that everything he has seen so far makes him worried that the DOT will still prioritize vehicle movement with its new plans. “The outreach crews, the teams from DOT that were on Grand and Metropolitan, they talked a lot more about improvements to traffic congestion than anything else,” he said.
He also noted that because of the density of restaurants on Grand, many delivery workers are riding up and down the corridor at all hours. If the bike lane was changed to one-way, it would likely encourage “salmoning,” or riding the wrong direction, from workers picking up food and those commuting from further east in Bushwick to Manhattan.
“If you move one of the bike lanes all the way to Metropolitan Avenue [four blocks away], people are not going to do that. People are going to salmon,” Bovenzi said. “You’re going to make it harder for delivery stuff. You’re going to make harder for any commuters that are beyond the L train commuting shed too, which is a whole lot of people.”
The DOT collected about 1,500 responses via a survey, which closed on Sept. 30, and got another 200 responses on a feedback map. The DOT also conducted focus groups, did on-street outreach and had feedback sessions with local stakeholders, a spokesperson told Streetsblog. The agency is now analyzing the results of the outreach and has not yet proposed any formal plan.
“DOT is working closely with the community to develop a proposed redesign of Grand Street and Metropolitan Avenue that improves safety and better protects New Yorkers on these streets, while providing more space for New Yorkers on all modes of transportation,” said spokesperson Will Livingston. “We are currently reviewing the feedback we’ve collected, and we look forward to sharing our findings in the coming months.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: A Van Gogh hidden away for over 50 years and a vibrant Cezanne harlequin: our pick of the November auctions
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Vincent van Gogh, Châtaigniers
en fleurs (1890)
Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection Evening Auction, Sotheby’s, 18 November
Estimate: in the region of $180m
Vincent van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (blossoming chestnut trees) during the final weeks of his life, having just moved to the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise after spending the previous year in a psychiatric asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. Initially he took to painting with a renewed optimism at his surroundings and work. The painting at hand depicts flowering chestnut trees blooming into a blue sky, with women passing through with parasols and Japanese-inspired dress. Châtaigniers en fleurs is expected to fetch in the region of $180m, Sotheby’s says. The artist’s current record at auction is $117.2m, set by Christie’s New York in November 2022 during the Paul Allen sale with Verger avec cyprès (orchard with cypresses, 1888). Châtaigniers en fleurs has not been seen in public since entering the Argentinian Blaquier-Arrieta collection in 1975.
Paul Cezanne, Arlequin (1888-90)
Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection Evening Auction, Sotheby’s, 18 November
Estimate: Around $120m
Arlequin is a rare appearance on the market of one of Paul Cezanne’s paintings from his harlequin series, modelled on his son, Paul, and inspired by Mardi Gras parades from the artist’s childhood in Aix-en-Provence, France. It is one of only four such examples, according to Sotheby’s. When the painting was unveiled at Sotheby’s in London, it was the first time it had been seen in public since 1975, when it was acquired by the sugar magnates Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. Before it entered their collection in Argentina, it belonged to legendary dealers like Ambroise Vollard, Paul Durand-Ruel and Paul Rosenberg. It also hung for two decades at Merton Hall in Cambridge, the then-family home of the British branch of the Rothschild family. Another version of the painting is part of the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. If it exceeds its estimate, Arlequin could set an artist record at auction. The most valuable Cezanne to sell at auction was a view of his beloved Sainte-Victoire mountain, for $137.79m, at Christie’s New York in 2022 during the sale of Paul Allen’s collection.
Man Ray, Le Baiser (around 1930)
Collection Roger Therond, Christie’s, Paris, 13 November
Estimate: €250,000 to €350,000
Man Ray’s Le Baiser (the kiss) comes from the collection of Roger Therond, the journalist and longtime editor of Paris Match, whose holdings included photographs by some of the leading artists of inter-war Paris. Therond was particularly drawn to Man Ray, whom he nicknamed “the Frenzied One”. In Le Baiser, two figures are captured in ambiguous poses, leaving the relationship between the two sitters deliberately unclear. According to Christie’s, Therond encouraged his children to look at the photograph from a distance and imagine different possibilities and circumstances for the subjects. The sitter on the left side is the American photographer Lee Miller, who began her career as a fashion model and later worked as a correspondent for Vogue during the Second World War. Miller was one of the first journalists to arrive at the Dachau concentration camp after its liberation in 1945, and recorded some of the most haunting photographic evidence of the Holocaust. She famously posed for a photo while bathing in Adolf Hitler’s personal bathtub at his Munich apartment.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.title: Czech Archaeologists Rediscover Long-Lost Tombs of Ancient Egyptian High Officials
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.text:
Czech archaeologists working at Saqqara have re-excavated a group of tombs belonging to high priests and senior officials of Egypt’s Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BCE). The news was first reported by Ahram Online following an announcement by the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.
Located 20 miles south of Cairo, the Saqqara archaeological site was the main necropolis for the ancient Egyptian city of Memphis, which was founded around 3100 BCE and abandoned in the 7th century CE. The excavations were made as part of a project by the Czech Institute of Egyptology to locate, excavate, and document tombs partially explored in the 19th century and buried again over time.
These tombs were first discovered by the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette, founder of the Egyptian Antiquities Service, between 1858 and 1860. During those years, Mariette identified approximately 160 tombs in the area dating to the Old Kingdom. However, his excavations focused largely on major artifacts while leaving other parts of the tombs unexplored and inadequately documented.
Among the chief monuments investigated by the Czech mission are the tombs of a man called Sabu and his son Ptahshepses, both of whom were high-ranking officials associated with the cult of Ptah at Memphis. The team also excavated and documented previously unknown parts of the tombs, including an offering chapel belonging to Sabu’s wife, Ikhetnefert, which was never found by Mariette.
Located north of the tomb of his son, Sabu’s tomb has exterior walls mimicking the facades of royal palaces, reflecting his high standing. Inside, researchers found well-preserved reliefs depicting Sabu and Ptahshepses overseeing processions of offering bearers.
Ikhetnefert’s chapel contains a false door decorated with scenes of Ikhetnefert with her husband and their two sons, Peahshepses and Raneferef. According to Miroslav Bárta, head of the Czech team, it is one of team’s most important discoveries, providing new insight into the family and its relationships.
The mission also succeeded in locating the tomb of Ptahshepses through a combination of satellite imagery and field surveys. Here, the archaeologists found the untouched remains of his mummy inside a limestone sarcophagus. Their subsequent analysis indicated that he was over 60 when he died, making him exceptionally long-lived for his time.
According to surviving written sources, Ptahshepses held senior positions under four Fifth Dynasty kings: Sahure, Neferirkare, Raneferef, and Nyuserre. He was the first non-royal to marry an Egyptian princess, Khamaat, daughter of King Userkaf, the founder of the Fifth Dynasty.
In a statement, Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that the significance of the Czech mission’s renewed investigation lies in its study and documentation of these monuments using modern scientific methods, which are revealing new information about the religious beliefs and social lives of Old Kingdom officials.

https://gothamist.com/news/stabbing-of-b.title: Stabbing of Brooklyn runner believed to be ‘random attack,’ NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/stabbing-of-b.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/stabbing-of-b.text:
NYPD detectives believe the stabbing of a young woman who was jogging along a running path in Brooklyn was a random attack, the department’s chief of detectives said Monday.
An unknown attacker stabbed Katie Suarez, 28, in the neck as she was running on the path on Shore Parkway near Bay 17th Friday evening. She was critically injured in the attack and remains hospitalized. No arrests have been made.
“As of right now, it appears it was a random attack,” Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny told reporters. “ Nobody else would've known that she was running there at that particular time.”
On the night of the attack, Suarez was doing her usual routine, Kenny said. She left work at a nearby bank at about 6:35 p.m., changed into athletic gear, met up with her mother who took her work outfit, and then set off for her run.
Her father had also just left work and was planning to meet up with both of them at a nearby Wendy’s restaurant and give them a ride home after Suarez finished her jog, Kenny said. At about 7:56 p.m., her father called Suarez to find out when she would arrive, and she told him she was about half a mile away and would be there soon.
When she didn’t arrive on time, the father set off to look for her on the path. At 8:16 p.m., he found her unconscious under a tree, bleeding from the neck, Kenny said.
The path where she was attacked is a stretch of running and biking track that is not covered by surveillance cameras, Kenny added. The path runs along the water from a pier in Bay Ridge to a large shopping center in Bath Beach. It’s often crowded with runners, bikers and fishermen.
Police are trying to recover any surveillance footage that may have been recorded by a food cart that was parked near the crime scene, Kenny said. Police are asking any drivers who may have passed through the area on the Belt Parkway around that time to contact them in case they have dashcam footage of the attacker.
Police are offering a reward of $10,000 for anyone who comes forward with information about the stabbing that leads to the attacker’s arrest.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Chanceler da Venezuela se reúne com Marco Rubio pela primeira vez desde o ataque de 3 de janeiro
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Leonardo Fernandes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Nomeado para o cargo há menos de uma semana, o novo chanceler da Venezuela, Oliver Blanco, reuniu-se nesta segunda-feira (2) com o secretário de Estado dos Estados Unidos, Marco Rubio, em Washington. O encontro ocorreu na sede do Departamento de Estado e é o primeiro entre os chefes da diplomacia dos dois países desde o ataque militar estadunidense contra o país sul-americano em 3 de janeiro deste ano, que resultou no sequestro do presidente Nicolás Maduro e da primeira-dama Cilia Flores.
Blanco assumiu o cargo no dia 29 de outubro, por indicação da presidenta em exercício, Delcy Rodríguez, e em substituição a Félix Plasencia, que foi designado para dirigir a área de Assuntos Internacionais da Presidência. Antes de assumir a chancelaria, Blanco exercia a função de vice-ministro de Relações Exteriores e Comércio Internacional e já foi assessor de lideranças vinculadas ao Ação Democrática, partido de oposição.
Durante o encontro, Rubio e Blanco posaram juntos diante das bandeiras nacionais dos dois países, mas não ofereceram declarações. A agenda em Washington faz parte de um movimento de aproximação diplomática entre as duas nações.
No dia 30 de outubro, o chanceler venezuelano esteve reunido em Caracas com o encarregado de negócios dos Estados Unidos, John Barrett, momento em que reafirmou a disposição do governo venezuelano para manter um diálogo soberano e voltado à cooperação mútua.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-man-i-love.title: “The Man I Love” Wants Us to Do More Than Mourn
https://hyperallergic.com/the-man-i-love.author: Eileen G’Sell
https://hyperallergic.com/the-man-i-love.text:
“The Man I Love” Wants Us to Do More Than Mourn
Ira Sachs resists the attention economy, using objects and people to tell a moving story of 1980s New York amid the HIV/AIDS crisis.
In a scene that might be this century’s most faithful depiction of 1980s bohemian New York, a ragtag ensemble crowds around a cluttered dining room table. A mishmash of stemware gleams below the revelers, each importuned to perform a few bars of a song. One self-consciously croons “Someone’s in the Kitchen with Dinah,” another vibratos a Jehovah’s Witness spiritual, while yet another gamely stumbles through the verses of “How Are Things in Glocca Morra?” from Finian’s Rainbow (1968). As gloriously languid as it is insistently idiosyncratic, the tableau readily summons nostalgia for those who remember and those who do not alike. There are no screens; there are no smartphones. There are instead people singing — shyly, joyfully — as though sharing the secret to the universe.
And they are singing, knowing full well that some in the room might not last the year.
A cinematic elegy that urges you to live, Ira Sachs’s The Man I Love is an AIDS movie that isn’t — a movie set in the thick of the pandemic that not only never mentions the illness by name, but entirely dodges the genre’s clichés: no lesion reveal, no tidy redemption, no funeral filled with festive friends. Instead, the film enjoins us to embrace the vitality of the era so as to more potently suffer its imminent loss.
The Man I Love follows “theatre artist” Jimmy George (Rami Malek), a veteran of a downtown performance troupe, as he co-writes a new production and becomes enamored of a young Englishman named Vincent (Luther Ford) who moves into the downstairs unit of their weathered prewar building. Jimmy’s partner Dennis (Tom Sturridge) tolerates the burgeoning affair, but is duly irked by Vincent’s awkward attempts to ingratiate himself into their extensive queer network.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-s.title: 100,000 California State Workers Struck Last Month
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-s.author: Kari Thompson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-s.text:
100,000 California State Workers Struck Last Month
State employees with SEIU Local 1000 recently went on a one-day strike across California. It was the first walkout in the history of the union, which represents about 100,000 workers ranging from accountants to custodians to nurses.
State workers went on a one-day unfair labor practice strike across California on October 21, with picket lines in Sacramento, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and other cities. They’re demanding better pay, affordable health care coverage, and flexibility to work from home.
This was the first strike in the history of Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, which represents about one hundred thousand government employees, ranging from accountants to custodians to nurses at state offices, hospitals, and prisons.
They have been working without a contract since July 1. Some five thousand employees were excluded from striking.
Governor Gavin Newsom’s “return-to-office” mandate went into effect this past summer. It requires workers to be in the office four days per week — even though workers report there isn’t enough space for all of them.
Workers argue the return-to-office policy compounds the lack of pay increases. Being forced back into the office is “more than just a pay cut,” said Jonah Paul, who works for the Employment Development Department in Sacramento. ”It’s a huge reduction in quality of life.
“Telework is a stopgap for a lot of problems our society is not willing to address,” Paul said: “The cost of childcare and insane commutes. Telework becomes a catch-all solution for a grueling life.”
Zero Raise
Last year, Local 1000 agreed to a pay freeze to help the state meet a budget shortfall. This summer, however, workers were supposed to see raises. But they got zilch.
The union is asking for a 20 percent raise over three years to catch up, especially given increased state revenue over the past two years.
Though Local 1000 and the state have met several times to negotiate a new contract, the union says CalHR, the bargaining representative for the state, has not been negotiating in good faith. It filed unfair labor practice charges with the state Public Employment Relations Board against CalHR for delaying negotiations and failing to respond to proposals.
“When I first started working for the state ten years ago, for the most part CalHR would throw us a bone,” said Steward Giovanni Martinez, a state worker in Sacramento. “This is the worst bargaining cycle I’ve witnessed. They don’t want to budge on a lot of stuff. Newsom takes us for granted, and the people he’s appointed in CalHR are the same way.”
Under previous leadership, the union kicked in $1 million to help Newsom fight a recall campaign in 2021. Members question why a governor they supported doesn’t have their backs now.
Strike Schools
Members of Local 1000 have been organizing over the past few months to increase membership numbers. Activists have been approaching nonmembers at their own worksites to ask them personally to join the union and calling others on the phone.
Stewards did their best to increase communications across the membership, though they were hampered by limited updates from the official Bargaining Unit Negotiating Committee.
Paul said that three years ago, the local offered “strike schools” to members, but these were more about discouraging members from planning for a strike. This time, he said, strike schools emphasized that the decision to strike was one for members to make, building membership numbers along with enthusiasm for walking out together.
In a strike authorization vote held from September 9 to October 7, 96 percent voted “yes” to walk out.
On the final day of the vote, the union held informational pickets to encourage participation in the vote. One picket happened to be next door to a building where Newsom was giving a speech.
With just a half-hour’s notice, stewards and other union leaders managed to get members together to cover every entrance of the building and make enough noise that Newsom had to comment on it during his event.
Despite this pressure from members, there was no last-minute deal to avert the strike, as happened ten years ago under Governor Jerry Brown.
“For a lot of folks this is their first strike — this is mine,” Martinez said. “We didn’t want to walk off the job — we have a good relationship with our supervisors — but we had no choice.”
World’s Fourth-Largest Economy
Strike participation appeared strong, with thousands of workers joining rallies and marches in cities across the state. Striking workers in the state’s capitol shut down multiple blocks with a march from CalHR headquarters to the capitol building.
“I was up on the truck with our president and a few other folks, leading people to different rally points,” said Emily Ingram, a Department of Education worker in Sacramento. “All you could see in every direction was more people. It was a pretty powerful feeling.”
In Los Angeles, hundreds of workers rallied outside a state building. Arielle Mangabat-Lowe, who works at the Department of Toxic Substances Control, said she was surprised how many people showed up, after prior actions had only a few dozen participants. She reflected that it can be hard as an organizer to put so much work into the union without knowing whether other members will participate.
But being with others at the strike rally boosted her spirits. “The state of California is a terrifying employer — it’s the world’s fourth-largest economy. We showed up today anyways,” she said. “It’s cool to feel like you have a voice, especially in these times.”
“As someone who has been trying to get folks to join up, I think a lot of state workers are fired up,” said Martinez. “The energy is here. Where we go with it, that’s up to us as members and our leadership.”
The union continued to pressure CalHR after the strike. On October 27, about twenty members disrupted a CalHR event in Sacramento, distributing flyers and shouting a message to the crowd demanding that the state stop intimidating members and bargain fairly.
The two sides met for contract mediation on October 30, but they did not reach a deal. “We are continuing to prepare for another strike if needed,” Ingram said ahead of that meeting.

The Vilcek Foundation has announced the twelve recipients of its 2026 grants, totaling $212,000. Founded in 2000 by Czechoslovakian immigrants Jan and Marica Vilcek, the New York–based nonprofit to date has awarded more than $9.6 million in prizes to individuals and over $7.6 million in grants to organizations in its drive to promote the arts and sciences and bring attention to the contributions of immigrants to American society.
The dozen nonprofit organizations making up this years’ cohort of grantees were chosen from among nearly two thousand open-call applicants—representing a 46 percent increase over the inaugural, 2025 cycle. Winners were selected based on level of innovation, depth of community engagement, and the potential for lasting impact.
“Immigrants are essential to the fabric of the United States, yet their contributions are often overlooked or undervalued,” said Vilcek Foundation president Rick Kinsel in a statement. “The Vilcek Foundation is proud to partner with organizations that elevate immigrant voices and drive tangible impact within their local communities.” Kinsel noted that this year, the organization extended the geographic reach of its grantmaking, “with recipients in eight new states, bringing us closer to supporting local, regional, and national nonprofits enacting meaningful change across the country.”
A full list of winners is below:
- Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts, Omaha, NE ($20,000)
- Radio Boise, Boise, ID, ($20,000)
- Brattleboro Museum & Art Center, Brattleboro, VT ($20,000)
- City of Asylum/Detroit ($5,000)

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Race Has Been Defined Islamophobia. Will It Be Determined By It?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.text:
As Abdul El-Sayed’s one-time primary opponent attempts to redirect closing arguments in the Michigan Senate contest to the topics of Israel and antisemitism, the Democratic nominee has entered the final stretch of the midterms against a barrage of bigoted attacks over his own race and religion.
President Donald Trump called him a “jihadist.” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. went on a racist rant against Arabs. According to Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, a mailer went out showing El-Sayed’s face next to the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers.
“They are running the most bigoted, hateful, Islamophobic campaign I’ve ever seen,” McMorrow told a local TV outlet. McMorrow, who ran for the Democratic Senate nomination but dropped out before the August primary, is taking a far different tack than Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democratic primary runner-up who has spent the race’s final days painting El-Sayed as an angry antisemite and crossed party lines Sunday to endorse Republican contender Mike Rogers.
Rogers has sought to portray El-Sayed as anti-American and repeatedly tried to tie his opponent to the Muslim Brotherhood. He insists the attacks have nothing to do with faith. But that is exactly how many observers see them, including Muslim Republicans who have been disgusted by the rhetoric.
As the election draws to a close, the Islamophobic attacks have taken a backseat to Stevens’s claims of antisemitism — most prominently concerning a PAC ad that connected high grocery prices to U.S. spending on Israeli military aid — and a personal feud between the former primary opponents. And some of El-Sayed’s allies worry that the Muslim and Arab-baiting attacks will work. One recent poll found that 38 percent of Michigan voters said they would be less likely to vote for a Muslim candidate.
Michigan’s Muslim and Arab organizers have not been taking the attacks lying down, however. In interviews last month, two prominent leaders in Dearborn’s Arab American community described widespread excitement over the opportunity to vote for the man who would be the first Muslim in the U.S. Senate.
“It very much feels like when President Obama was running and his whole campaign was around like hope. That’s what it feels like,” Layla Elabed, the organizing director at Arab Americans for Progress, told the Intercept on October 8.
Elabed, the sister of Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., was one of the key movers in the Uncommitted movement, which urged Michigan voters to withhold their votes from Joe Biden during the 2024 primary in protest of his support for Israel’s war on Gaza. The movement succeeded in making a statement, but also drew criticism from centrist Democrats for allegedly fracturing party unity.
Elabed’s current group is an evolution of the Uncommitted movement. Its canvassers have been knocking on doors to turn out support for El-Sayed and other candidates.
“I don’t think many people in Dearborn are surprised by Haley Stevens,” Elabed told The Intercept on Monday. “Arab American Democrats in Michigan have been sounding the alarm about her for years, warning our fellow Democrats about a pattern of putting political interests ahead of the people she was elected to represent.”
She believes the same coalition that came together for Uncommitted could help push El-Sayed over the top this election.
“Abdul has been able to really take a stand on all the issues that were really important to anti-war voters and anti-genocide voters,” she said. “It’s not a coincidence that that same coalition, that same base of Democratic voters are now all coming out to support us.”
Hers is not the only group seeking to mobilize Muslim and Arab voters, who make up a sizable slice of the Michigan electorate. The Arab American Political Action Committee has also endorsed El-Sayed. Its president, Osama Siblani, said there is widespread enthusiasm for El-Sayed in areas with dense Arab populations such as Dearborn.
Siblani compared El-Sayed’s potential victory to John F. Kennedy’s pathbreaking election as the first Catholic president.
“First of all, he’s qualified. Second of all, he’s saying the right things, he has a good agenda,” Siblani. “His opponent is an asshole. In addition to all of this, he is breaking the ceiling for our community and for other communities. That is a plus.”
The goal of the Arab and Muslim-baiting attacks from El-Sayed’s enemies is clear, according to Nazita Lajevardi, an associate professor of political science at the University of Michigan.
“Islamophobia is a tried and true strategy for garnering a candidate support and swaying the vote,” she said.
Yet it is also possible that the attacks on El-Sayed’s identity will lead to greater turnout in places like Dearborn, she said.
“I think scholarship would tell us that when political elites discriminate, that it does mobilize people into action. Past scholarship would say yes, it would, but it’s an open question,” she said.
Elabed agreed that the attacks are nothing new. “We’ve watched it play out time and time again,” she told The Intercept. Stevens’s about-face isn’t a major development, she said, “It’s that the rest of the Democratic Party is finally seeing what our communities have been saying all along. We weren’t wrong. We just weren’t being listened to.”
Siblani expressed a similar sentiment on Monday. “I’m not surprised, I’m disgusted,” he wrote of Stevens in a text message, attaching an emoji of a person vomiting.
Stevens’s choice to jump ship for the Rogers campaign appears to have galvanized El-Sayed’s base. His campaign announced a one-day fundraising record after his fellow Democrat pulled her endorsement on Sunday.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

du site ou de l’application
