https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.title: “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day
https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.author: Jen Fifield, Peter Elkind
https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.text:
As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.
Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.
The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.
The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.
Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.
“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”
“Paper Trail” Podcast
Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “Paper Trail.”
In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”
The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”
Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.
Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.
Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:
1. Will There Be Federal Interference?
An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.
Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.
He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.
“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.
It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.
Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.
“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”
A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”
It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”
2. What Effect Will Noncitizen Voter Challenges Have?
The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.
Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.
On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”
This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.
In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.
Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”
A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation plan” that would interfere with legal voting.
Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”
In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”
Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”
Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”
Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.
A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.
“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.
3. Will There Be Problems at the Polls?
States often change laws and rules related to voting.
Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.
A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.
Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.
Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.
Every election features some issues with voting equipment.
So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.
ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.
4. How Secure Will the Election Be?
Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.
Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”
In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.
Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.
Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.
“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he said.
5. Where Will Postelection Challenges Come From?
Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.
Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.
Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.
Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.
“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.
In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)
Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.
Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.
“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Collectors Cristina Chacón and Diego Uribe to open contemporary art space in Miami
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Colombian collectors and philanthropists Cristina Chacón and Diego Uribe will open DC Lab, a new contemporary art space on Miami’s Bird Road, expanding their nonprofit DC Art Foundation.
The admission-free, 9,000-sq.-ft space will host projects by international galleries that do not have a permanent presence in Miami, alongside research and public programming. Opening just in time for Miami Art Week on 29 November, DC Lab will present the first major survey in Miami of the Cuban artist Carlos Garaicoa, the foundation’s current artist in residence.
Based in Miami, Bogotá and Madrid, longtime partners Chacón and Uribe view collecting as a means of supporting the art community. “For us, collecting has always been more than acquiring works and has focused on a commitment to contributing to the cultural ecosystem,” Uribe tells The Art Newspaper.
The couple’s collection includes more than 500 Modern and contemporary works from around the globe, and they support institutions in Miami and beyond. At the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, they sit on the chairman’s council and the American and Latin American acquisitions boards. They also serve on the Museo Reina Sofía’s international patronage board and on the boards of Bogotá’s Museo de Arte Moderno and Miami’s Coral Gables Museum.
In 2021, the couple founded the DC Art Foundation to support artists and connect Miami’s art scene with the international community beyond Miami Art Week. Since 2022, the foundation has run a residency programme for mid-career and established artists.
“The foundation was a vehicle for the residency programme we fund at a private residence,” Uribe says. “The intention is to bring to Miami artists that activate the community, promoting local and international exchange.” Past residents include the Spanish textile artist Sonia Navarro and the Colombian artist Miler Lagos.
DC Lab will include exhibition and education spaces as well as a library. “This is a laboratory where experimental ideas and projects can happen in the city,” Uribe says. “We created a novel residency model that provides international galleries with space to present mid-career and established artists new to Miami, potentially inspiring them to settle here.”
Chacón adds that while international galleries often participate in Art Basel Miami Beach and its various satellite fairs, DC Lab will enable more in-depth projects. It will also strengthen the foundation’s community-centred work. “In our residency programme, artists commit to an educational activity, and we often organise talks,” she says. “But this new venue allows for deeper community engagement.”
The opening exhibition at DC Lab, co-presented with Italy’s Galleria Continua and Mor Charpentier (based in Paris and Bogotá), links the new venue to the residency. “While the residency programme runs independently from DC Lab, Garaicoa’s residency was especially fitting for the opening,” Chacón says.
Garaicoa—known for addressing cultural and political issues through architecture, urbanism and history—will present works from his November residency as well as other recent projects. “My residency work relates to Miami, its architecture and growth,” he says, “reflecting how politics and language coexist in architecture.”
Passion is the key driver for Chacón and Uribe’s new space. “We are not trying to be a museum,” Uribe says. “We continue being a private foundation supporting the local community.”
Chacón adds: “For us, art is an incurable disease that lifts the soul.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Donald Trump Has Lost It
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Donald Trump Has Lost It
At one of his final midterm rallies, the president showed just what a spent political force he has become—and what little grip on reality he still has.
Dubuque, Iowa—“It’s pure fricking genius.”
Donald Trump was, of course, describing himself—or rather his rhetorical stump style, which had been trained on the crowd of MAGA faithful assembled here at Dubuque’s Five Flags Center for more than an hour. He’d been complaining about how his wife, Melania, wants him to be less demonstrative at the rally podium—less dancing, no more impersonations of female weightlifters getting bested by transgender competitors. The first lady, Trump protested, wants him to be “more presidential,” which prompted him to do an impersonation of a typical campaign stiff: “Ladies and gentlemen of Iowa, it is a great honor to be with you this evening.” (The impression came across a good deal like House Speaker Mike Johnson, who did a cameo turn at the podium during Trump’s performance.)
Trump then gleefully went through a series of weird angular gesticulations to simulate his slantwise narrative style—the string of non sequitur grievances and resentful old-rich-guy refrains that he dubbed “the weave” during the 2024 campaign. But that descriptor has graduated, midway through his second term, into the work of a maestro.
This was one of the last Trump rallies in the 2026 midterm cycle—which is to say, one of the last Trump rallies we will ever need to care about, given that the president is hurtling toward lame-duck status. The president’s stylings on the stump had revolutionized American politics a decade ago. Now, like a good Midwest county fair touring band, Trump had revived many of his oldest MAGA hits. He laid into the “sick people” on the press risers at the back of the room, insisting that “they are the biggest threat to our country.” He railed against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, dubbing him a “jihadist” and “Communist” and proudly explaining why he’s repeatedly given his first name as “Mohammed.” (It’s something he does for “certain reasons,” he said, in a strained effort to make gutter bigotry sound somehow cagey, before gleefully announcing that he does it “because I’m the president.”) He lobbed kindred racist attacks against Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar, whom his Justice Department has targeted with a bogus authoritarian raid and investigation, as well as Somali immigrants; like any washed-up anti-woke comic, he said, “I hope I don’t say anything too controversial” to set up his pet anti-Somali refrain: “We don’t want them here.” There were also extended riffs, even now, about Joe Biden’s cognitive failings, the de rigueur reminder that Trump has “aced” three cognitive exams himself, and some talk about Kamala Harris’s woeful turn as overseer of immigration policy at the White House—all key issues for him and essentially nobody else.
It was hard to see how any of this translates into fricking genius, though. I was in the upper levels of the stadium, and several of my seatmates were straining to make out just what Trump was talking about—especially when he went into digressive genius mode, dilating on optimal flagpole design and golf masters as models for political achievement (yes, really).
Last week, the GOP briefly canceled the rally in favor of a virtual gathering, which would ostensibly be a bigger draw (an objective that makes zero sense for an event meant to generate excitement and boost turnout for state and local politicians). Then the party reversed course, perhaps understanding how weak the move would make Trump look. Five Flags is a small facility—it boasts ads in the corridors for a February performance of a Pink Floyd Tribute band, “Think Floyd”—and it was reasonably full, despite the event’s bait-and-switch scheduling..
Trump came on stage 90 minutes late—long after all the GOP candidates in this suddenly purplish battleground state had delivered their own versions of the stiff-politician election-eve pitches. During the protracted stretch of dead air, the crowd began to get restive and bored; the playlist of classic rock standards began repeating, and at one point, people began swaying their phones in flashlight mode in time to Sinead O’Connor’s “Nothing Compares 2 U”—a singularly odd spectacle after the state’s gubernatorial GOP nominee, Zach Lahn, inveighed against the depraved and murderous character of liberal culture warfare; this was, after all, a performer best known for tearing a photo of the pope in half on live television. There was a palpable mood of the agitprop starting to lose interest in itself.
A very different brand of Kulturkampf was announced, in any event, ahead of Trump’s appearance. There was a video of white-jumpsuit Vegas-era Elvis—a performer the crowd had already heard at least a half-dozen times over on the soundtrack—delivering a demented medley of “Dixie” and “The Battle Hymn of the Republic.” Near the end of the mashup, the camera lingered uncomfortably on a Black flautist in the Elvis ensemble delivering the closing strains of “Dixie.” A nearby diehard MAGA supporter must have noted my goggle-eyed expression and volunteered, “That was really weird.”
Not as weird as the next video entry: the 2024 rally chestnut called “God Made Trump,” delivered as a riff on radio Paul Harvey’s address “God Made a Farmer,” but shot through with the militant messianic imagery of the New Apostolic Reformation. The video starts with an AI-manipulated version of Harvey’s voice announcing “On June 14, 1946, God looked down on his planned paradise and said, ‘I need a caretaker,’” and goes rapidly downhill from there, depicting Trump as an axe-wielding mortal foe of wolves, vipers, the deep state, and the fake news.
It all made for an abrupt shift of tone from the autopilot classic rock playlist, but it didn’t really come anywhere near a closing campaign argument. Iowa is facing many pressing economic and political challenges—from the soaring price of diesel and fertilizer in the wake of Trump’s war in Iran to overlapping crises in cancer and water quality to the declining standing of the state’s formerly distinguished public education system. Senate GOP nominee Ashley Hinson has belatedly positioned herself as an opponent of the Iran War, after voting in favor of it seven times in the House, in order to stay competitive with her upstart Democratic rival, state Representative Josh Turek. Lahn has broken ranks with deregulatory Republican orthodoxy to demand investigations into the cancer and water crises.
Trump, not surprisingly, didn’t mention any of these problems, or GOP proposals to address them; his prescription for electoral victory in Iowa appeared to be Worship me harder. So he stayed firmly and gleefully within his comfort zone of deriding Democrats as “lunatics” hell-bent on spreading communism and forcing sex changes on the children of unwitting God-fearing parents. He made desultory promises that gas prices would come down shortly after the midterms—presumably by resuming the same large-scale attacks on Iran that have already caused those prices to skyrocket while completely failing to defeat the Islamic Republic. He reprised his bribery pledge of $5,000 to every voter who will preserve and expand the GOP majorities in Congress. But he relied mostly on more video footage to drive home the theme of the GOP 2026 campaign: “craziness versus common sense.” One scattershot set of supercuts sought to dramatize the socialist orthodoxy and transgender fetishes of the Democrats, while another highlighted the alleged open-border excesses of the Biden White House, and dwelled on lurid details of murders and sexual attacks from undocumented immigrants. By the time the second video kicked in, people in my section and many on the main floor began to leave. They’d seen this show before—and besides, they could watch Fox News in the comfort of their home, without having to see Elvis hymn the Confederacy or Donald Trump cosplay as Jesus.

Crossings: Laura Pannack’s award-winning images of South African youth – in pictures
The British visual artist and photographer Laura Pannack has been named the winner of the inaugural Tom Stoddart award for excellence 2025. A collaboration between Gost Books and the Ian Parry photojournalism grant, the award supports photographers engaged in long-form documentary work. South Africa has one of the world’s highest levels of social inequality and a rapidly growing youth population; Pannack’s project Crossings looks at the journey to and from school and its physical and psychological challenges for young people

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-opens-heap.title: NY opens HEAP applications to help pay for heating costs
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-opens-heap.author: Louis C. Hochman
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-opens-heap.text:
The state has opened applications for the regular Home Energy Assistance Program, which can help provide up to $1,086 to low- and middle-income households for help with heating costs.
The benefits can pay for fuel, or for heating and cooling equipment. Specific benefit amounts can vary based on factors including income, household size, heating source and whether a family includes a vulnerable member. A family of five could make up to $7,948 per month and qualify for assistance.
The state increased the benefit amount this year in response to rising costs of heating oil and kerosene, state officials said in announcing the program. The benefit for heat with oil, kerosene, or propane has been increased by $90 to $990. The amount for heat with wood, pellets, and coal has increased by $65 to $700.
Applications opened Monday for people not automatically enrolled in the program because of their enrollment in other social benefit programs.
Applications can be submitted online or through the mail, or at at departments of social service. New York City residents can apply through the Access HRA portal.
State officials urge those seeking benefits to apply as soon as possible, as they’re awarded on a first-come, first-serve basis, and are only awarded until funding runs out. Payments are made directly to vendors for the expenses.
The state will also open applications for emergency HEAP benefits — for people in danger or running of out of fuel or having services shut off — on Jan. 4.
In October, the state opened applications for the Heating Equipment Clean and Tune benefit, to help both with the cleaning of primary heating equipment as well as chimney cleaning, minor repairs and installation of carbon monoxide detectors or programmable thermostats. Benefits for that program can be up to $500.
Older adults can contact Offices for the Aging or the NY Connects helpline at 1-800-342-9871 for help applying and navigating benefits.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Após inauguração incompleta às vésperas das eleições, Tarcísio adia entrega de novo trecho da Linha 6-Laranja em SP
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governo Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), em São Paulo, adiou a entrega das estações Brasilândia e Itaberaba-Hospital Vila Penteado, que compõem o segundo trecho da Linha 6-Laranja do Metrô na zona norte da capital paulista.
As duas paradas haviam sido prometidas pelo governador para o mês de outubro durante a inauguração do primeiro segmento da linha, realizada em 2 de julho, no limite do prazo estipulado pela legislação eleitoral para a participação de candidatos à reeleição em entregas de obras públicas. Apesar do descumprimento do prazo anunciado, a concessionária Linha Uni e a Agência de Transporte do Estado de São Paulo (Artesp) não definiram uma nova data para a abertura das estações.
De acordo com o diretor sindical Junior Luiz Barbosa Neto, do Sindicato dos Trabalhadores em Empresas Ferroviárias da Zona Central do Brasil, “ao invés de esperar a conclusão de um trecho funcional para a população, optou-se por abrir algumas estações justamente para usar isso na eleição, e criou um fato político consumado antes do período eleitoral, mas transferiu o gargalo real para a conclusão das obras”.
Em nota, a Artesp limitou-se a informar que a conclusão do trecho possui “previsão de operação até o final deste ano”, alegando que alterações no cronograma são permitidas mediante análise regulatória. A concessionária declarou que não tinha acréscimos ao posicionamento do órgão regulador.
Crítica sindical ao oportunismo eleitoral
Sem informações oficiais sobre os motivos operacionais do adiamento, o Sindicato dos Metroviários de São Paulo contesta a gestão do cronograma e aponta a utilização política das entregas sobre trilhos.
O secretário-geral do Sindicato dos Metroviários de São Paulo, Bernardo Figueiredo de Lima, destaca a falta de transparência técnica e a repetição de expedientes de apelo eleitoral no transporte público. “O governo Tarcísio, assim como o governo anterior, tem o costume de anunciar expansões na linha metroviária nos anos eleitorais, e a maioria delas não se confirma”, disse.
“Provavelmente essa é mais uma promessa frustrada do governo Tarcísio com a motivação de ganhar as eleições”, completou o dirigente sindical Bernardo.
A avaliação do sindicato soma-se aos questionamentos apresentados desde a abertura parcial da linha. Em julho, a entidade já havia criticado a aceleração artificial dos prazos promovida pela gestão estadual às vésperas do período de campanha.
Para o sindicalista Junior, o prazo de outubro divulgado pela gestão estadual já era “artificial” e os custos decorrentes desses sucessivos aditamentos e remanejamentos de cronograma acabam recaindo sobre a população.
“Esse prazo de outubro já era artificial, já se sabia que não se conseguiria entregar Brasilândia e Itaberaba nesse período. O governo Tarcísio assumiu um adicional bilionário somente para acelerar o cronograma e entregar o primeiro trecho antes da eleição, mas a ação política fala mais alto e a população é quem sempre sofre”, disse Junior.
Histórico de obras inacabadas
A entrega realizada em julho abriu seis das 15 estações previstas para a Linha 6-Laranja em regime de “operação assistida”, funcionando apenas de segunda a sexta-feira, das 10h às 15h, sem cobrança de tarifa e sem integração.
Especialistas em mobilidade urbana e usuários apontam que a inauguração às pressas serviu prioritariamente como plataforma de propaganda política, sem resolver o deslocamento diário da classe trabalhadora nos horários de pico.
Na ocasião da inauguração, o especialista em mobilidade urbana Rafael Calabria destacou que a abertura parcial caracterizou-se como uma estratégia eleitoral. “Na prática, a linha não está inaugurada ainda. Ela está em uma operação controlada que eles chamam operação assistida”, disse.
Anunciada em 2008 durante o governo José Serra (PSDB) e iniciada em 2015 na gestão Geraldo Alckmin (PSB), a construção da Linha 6-Laranja acumula paralisações decorrentes das investigações da Operação Lava Jato envolvendo as antigas empreiteiras responsáveis.
O empreendimento é estruturado como a primeira Parceria Público-Privada (PPP) integral do metrô paulista, com contrato de R$ 19 bilhões por 30 anos, concedido à empresa espanhola Acciona. A conclusão integral das 15 estações, ligando a Brasilândia à estação São Joaquim no centro da capital, está prometida apenas para outubro de 2027.

https://hyperallergic.com/how-former-the.title: How Former Theater Kid James Talarico Stands Up for the Arts in Texas
https://hyperallergic.com/how-former-the.author: Shahrzad Rasekh
https://hyperallergic.com/how-former-the.text:
How Former Theater Kid James Talarico Stands Up for the Arts in Texas
As Republicans exert an ever-tightening grip on creative freedom in the state, the Democratic Senate hopeful stands out for his track record on arts funding.
Every United States election season, a few candidates capture national attention. This year, one of those names is Democrat James Talarico, who is running for Senate against Republican Ken Paxton. A former theater kid turned language arts teacher now serving his fourth term in the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico would become the first Democrat elected US Senator since the 1980s if he wins.
Talarico has largely built his platform tackling education, a tough battle in a state that has seen eight school district takeovers since 2020. Among the bills he has co-authored is one that focuses on fine arts funding for public schools. Over the past years, the Texas arts scene has sat at the nexus between funding cuts and censorship.
First brought up in 2023 and subsequently reintroduced in 2025, the bill would have been the first of its kind in Texas, had it passed.
“This means hundreds of millions of dollars in new funding for music, dance, art, and theater programs! It’s a game changer,” Talarico, who has an endorsement from the Actors’ Equity Association, wrote on X in 2023. Hyperallergic has contacted Talarico’s campaign for comment.
Before earning his degrees in government and education, Talarico participated in his high school’s theater program, playing two leading roles: Danny Zuko in Grease and Aslan in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.
“Research shows fine arts programs improve student achievement, graduation rates, and mental health,” Talarico continued in his post. “I know it did for me when I was growing up.”
Austin-based artist Jean-Pierre Verdijo told Hyperallergic that he’s intrigued by Talarico’s overall message, which he views as focused on fair governance as opposed to fighting another party.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/patrick-stew.title: Captain Picard Was a Socialist, and So Was Patrick Stewart
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/patrick-stew.author: Alexander Deley
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/patrick-stew.text:
Captain Picard Was a Socialist, and So Was Patrick Stewart
Patrick Stewart, who died last week at the age of 86, was a committed socialist from the start. That conviction ran through his greatest role: Jean-Luc Picard, a leader who used reason and compassion rather than force.
For those of us who grew up watching Star Trek: The Next Generation, Patrick Stewart’s death last week was an enormous loss. Stewart was an actor of extraordinary talent, commanding every scene he appeared in while bringing emotional depth to even the most imposing characters. Equally comfortable with Shakespearean tragedy, science fiction, and comedy, Stewart could do it all. There was also something about his premature baldness that aged him — adding to his already impressive natural gravitas — but also gave him an ageless quality over the decades. Whether he was performing Shakespeare onstage or appearing in sci-fi shlock like the naked-space-vampire thriller Lifeforce (1985), he always fully embodied the characters that he played.
Best remembered for his portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was also something exceedingly rare among Hollywood’s biggest stars: an unapologetic, lifelong socialist. He never hesitated to make his political convictions known, even among the industry’s wealthy elite: “There’s nothing more fun than being at a dinner party in Beverly Hills, surrounded by elegant people, and telling them you’re a socialist.”
A Socialist from the Start
Much of Stewart’s radical political perspective emerged at an early age. Born in 1940, he grew up poor in Yorkshire, England, the youngest of three brothers. Stewart’s mother worked in a textile factory, while his father worked several working-class jobs, including as a day laborer and postman, never coming to terms with the post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) he suffered from after his experiences during World War II.
Stewart’s father would often subject his wife to domestic violence. Witnessing his mother’s exploitation at work and abuse at home profoundly shaped Stewart’s politics. Rather than accepting these injustices as inevitable, he committed himself to fighting them. Stewart said he became a socialist at the age of five. Later in life, he became an outspoken campaigner against domestic violence, drawing on the experiences that had so blighted his childhood:
I’ve been a witness to unfairness in society all my life. To the conditions under which my mother worked all her life, working in an industrial weaving shed in the north of England. And it has been this feature of unfairness that has motivated me in all of my political thinking.
Stewart also discovered from a young age, with the encouragement of his grammar school English teacher, that he had a wonderful talent for acting. Indeed, at the age of ten, that very teacher gave the young Patrick a copy of Macbeth and told him to get up on stage and perform. Stewart was a natural. He continued to act throughout his school career, often working alongside friend Brian Blessed, who would also go on to an impressive dramatic career of his own. Stewart and Blessed later received grants to attend the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. Stewart was reportedly the first person who was neither a graduate of Oxford nor Cambridge to receive a grant from West Riding Council.
Stewart began his professional career in 1959 with a production of Cyrano de Bergerac in Bristol. In 1966, he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he worked alongside actors such as Ben Kingsley. In 1967, he also made his on-screen debut, landing a one-off bit part in the long-running UK soap opera Coronation Street.
He subsequently appeared in Shakespearean plays and BBC dramas, including turns playing Vladimir Lenin in Fall of Eagles (1974) and the KGB mastermind Karla in the critically acclaimed adaptations of John le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1979) and Smiley’s People (1982). It also paved the way for a number of bit parts in films. These included John Boorman’s Excalibur (1981) and David Lynch’s Dune (1984), where his character Gurney Halleck memorably charges into battle cradling a pug.
Even as his screen career developed, Stewart maintained a deep commitment to the theater, encouraged by his lifelong friend and fellow Shakespearean powerhouse actor, Ian McKellen. Indeed, Stewart’s longtime connection to the theater and to Shakespeare proved to be key in his landing the role that would propel him to global fame.
The Making of Captain Picard
When Stewart was cast as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation (1987–1994), he drew on his years of Shakespearean training to develop the starship captain. As he put it, “There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that reminds me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean-Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in Henry IV, which is about brave men.”
This proved to be a stroke of genius, with Picard immediately becoming a fan favorite. Picard’s assured and wise but commanding demeanor alongside his philosophical bent proved to be the very ideal representation of who one would want to have exploring the cosmos on behalf of humanity. The show is considered by many to be the greatest iteration of Star Trek, and it is likely the version that hewed most firmly to series creator Gene Roddenberry’s famously left-wing politics, politics shared by Stewart. His singular performance helped make the show a success, and it made Stewart a household name and transformed him into an international star.
To viewers like me, who grew up watching The Next Generation, Picard represented the ideal father figure, something he himself never had. Yes, Picard had a quiet authority — Stewart said his own father could command any room he walked into — but Picard was also a man of deep kindness, intelligence, and compassion with a strong aversion to violence. His mission was one of peace, and though the USS Enterprise often found itself in peril, Picard was almost always able to negotiate a nonviolent way out. Picard embodied a vision of authority based not on domination but on cooperation, reason, and mutual respect. It was a vision compatible with Stewart’s socialism — a commitment to humanity over the barbarism of domination and violence.
The Humanity of Jean-Luc Picard
Perhaps Stewart’s most powerful exploration of these themes came in the two-part Next Generation episode “The Best of Both Worlds.” Over the course of the two episodes, the Enterprise encounters the Borg, a monstrous cybernetic collective that absorbs other civilizations into a single hive mind — an unsettling vision of the individual entirely subordinated to a larger power. Captured and assimilated by the Borg, Picard is eventually rescued by his crew. But the experience leaves him profoundly traumatized, forcing him to struggle with the lasting consequences of having his humanity stripped away.
Throughout the rest of the series, whenever Picard has further encounters with the Borg, he must struggle with his own belief in the sanctity of all life in the universe, versus resentment and the desire for revenge. Stewart’s portrayal of Picard’s anguish may have drawn on his own experience of childhood trauma growing up in a violent household — he had certainly spoken about the lasting psychological damage caused by his father’s abuse.
Picard’s subsequent encounters with the Borg repeatedly tested his commitment to compassion over revenge. His struggle to resist violence, even against those who had harmed him, remains one of the series’ most affecting expressions of its humanistic ideals.
Stewart also became a fierce defender of science fiction as a genre, recognizing its ability to explore complex moral, ethical, and philosophical questions. He once reportedly walked off a Good Morning America promotional appearance after learning that producers intended to ridicule the show and science fiction as a whole. The series of course was wildly successful, not only reviving the Star Trek franchise but spawning four feature films, each time with Stewart reprising his starring role.
This respect for science fiction and genre entertainment was also probably what helped guide Stewart to his other most iconic role: Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise. Beginning with the Bryan Singer adaptation X-Men (2000), Stewart played the psychically powered founder of, and mentor to, the X-Men across several films. Working alongside old friend Ian McKellen (in the roll of the antagonist of the series, Magneto), the films, much like the comics they were based on, explored the conflicting philosophies of the two men in a wider metaphor for the civil rights movement. Stewart’s Xavier sought equality and coexistence between humans and superpowered mutants, while McKellen’s Magneto favored a more militant response to persecution, a conflict often interpreted as an allegory of the contrasting political approaches associated with Martin Luther King Jr and Malcolm X.
Despite some unwieldy scripts, Stewart and McKellen brought Shakespearean gravitas to their roles, making the ideological conflict between Xavier and Magneto genuinely compelling. The two would also reunite onstage in 2009 for a celebrated performance of Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, a lifelong ambition for the pair.
A Lifelong Commitment to Justice
Off-screen, Stewart used his newfound fame to champion causes that mattered to him. He campaigned against domestic violence and championed women’s rights, trade unions, animal welfare, and greater recognition of PTSD among veterans. He also opposed Brexit and spoke out against right-wing demagogues, including Donald Trump. A resounding belief in fairness, ingrained in him from an early age, remained his guiding light.
Stewart also revealed a gift for comedy, gleefully parodying his own dignified persona in appearances on Extras and the animated program Family Guy as well as a legendary turn hosting Saturday Night Live in 1994. Stewart continued to work right up until his death: his final film arriving in theaters this winter will see him reprise the part of Charles Xavier one last time.
He will be remembered not just as one of the finest actors of his generation but also as a committed socialist who believed that compassion, equality, and solidarity were principles worth fighting for.
For those of us who grew up watching Jean-Luc Picard, he offered something equally valuable: an example of leadership rooted not in intimidation or force but in intelligence, cooperation, and respect for others. It was a vision of humanity worth aspiring to, both on earth and among the stars.

FAD Magazine reports that a previously unknown drawing of the Bloomsbury artist Vanessa Bell by the Scottish painter Duncan Grant, also a member of the Bloomsbury Group, has been discovered at Charleston, the former home and studio of Bell and Grant in East Sussex, England. The portrait is thought to be his last drawing of Bell, made around the time of her death.
The drawing was found among family papers as preparations were being made for Tate Britain’s exhibition “Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury,” opening November 12, which explores the relationship between the two artists, who were friends, collaborators, and lovers. The family has donated the work to Charleston. Made in pencil and biro, the drawing shows Bell’s head in profile, turned slightly away with her eyes closed.
The work is dated April 14, 1961, though Bell died seven days earlier, on April 7, at age eighty-one. She was buried in the churchyard of St. Peter’s in Firle, a short distance from Charleston, on April 12. According to a Charleston press release, Darren Clarke, head of collections and research at Charleston, believes the discrepancy in timing may be explained by Grant’s practice in later life of retrospectively dating works.
“We know that in Duncan’s later years he and friends spent a great deal of time going back through the huge body of work in his studio, identifying and dating pictures so that they could be recorded, exhibited, and sold,” Clarke said. “Those dates are not always reliable. What seems very likely here is that Duncan knew this drawing had been made around Vanessa’s death and later added a date from memory. He got remarkably close, but apparently not quite close enough. Everything about the drawing itself—its viewpoint, its intimacy, and its extraordinary economy—suggests someone sitting quietly beside Vanessa’s bed and drawing the face he had known for half a century.”
Grant’s drawing will not be shown as part of Tate Britain’s exhibition, but it is expected to be represented in the catalogue by a small reproduction.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/ferg.title: Fergie Chambers Faces Extradition to U.S. Despite Never Being Indicted, Says Lawyer
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/ferg.author: Timothy Pratt
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/ferg.text:
The Trump administration’s extradition case against millionaire left-wing donor James “Fergie” Chambers, detained in Spain since July, ran into an apparent hurdle when two witnesses called before a federal grand jury announced their intention last week to refuse to testify.
Several observers familiar with the case said the grand jury is likely related to the extradition effort.
The refusal of the grand jury witnesses to testify takes on added importance because the U.S. is pursuing Chambers’s extradition based on a criminal complaint, not an indictment, according to his Spanish lawyers. The criminal affidavit, signed by a single FBI agent, includes three charges related to his support for pro-Palestine causes.
The distinction, critics of the extradition case say, highlights how the case is hung on one agent’s complaint, which remains under seal, rather than a grand jury investigation to determine if the state had sufficient evidence to indict Chambers.
“The complaint is not only vague and weak, it’s not normal,” said Aitor Martínez, one of Chambers’s Spain-based lawyers. “In 20 years of practice, I’ve never seen a U.S. extradition request based on a criminal complaint.”
Martínez pointed to a statement from a summary of the complaint contained in an international arrest order reviewed by The Intercept and directed at Spanish authorities that says, “If Chambers’ extradition to the US is granted, another charging document called an indictment will be sought from a federal grand jury.”
Xavier de Janon, the executive director of the U.S.-based National Lawyers Guild and who is not working directly on the Chambers case, said, “Seeking an extradition without there being an indictment puts the cart before the horse.”
“If he is extradited under a criminal complaint,” said de Janon, “he can’t even fully challenge the charges, because he hasn’t been indicted.”
The State Department referred questions to the Department of Justice, which declined to comment.
Two of the three charges underpinning the extradition request against Chambers — riot and incitement to riot — are related to allegations that he helped fund a late-2023 protest in Merrimack, New Hampshire, against an Israeli weapons manufacturer, according to the summary of the complaint contained in the arrest order. The summary says Chambers provided funds for demonstrators used to purchase materials such as smoke bombs and to help cover protesters’ legal fees.
The third charge is international money laundering related to more than $7 million he transferred to bank accounts in Tunisia, where he was living in 2024. The Trump administration, according to the international arrest order, says the money was used to fund Hamas, which is a proscribed terror group in the U.S. The order does not say he is charged with material support for terrorism.
Chambers’s family and supporters and multiple representatives of Club Africain, a Tunisian soccer club, have said the money was used to pay the club’s debts and related expenditures such as training grounds. The club’s fan base has long supported Palestinians.
Grand Jury Refusal
Two women who participated in the 2023 protest against a factory operated by the Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems recently announced their intentions not to cooperate with a November 4 grand jury hearing where they have been summoned as witnesses.
“If they are being summoned now, this suggests that the grand jury seems to be linked to Chambers’s case,” said Martínez, his lawyer. “It seems like a fishing expedition against him.”
Kira Kelley, an attorney for the two women, said, “Context clues suggest this is about Fergie.”
If the pair don’t answer questions from a federal prosector before the New Hampshire federal grand jury, they could risk a possible jail sentence for contempt.
Nonetheless, the two women — Bridget Shergalis and Sophie Ross — shared a statement with The Grayzone Thursday announcing their intention to refuse to testify. In an interview on the same day with The Intercept, the women recounted being under investigation for a year over the protest and being threatened with felony charges that carried potential sentences of decades in prison.
Shergalis and Ross said they turned down several deals for their cooperation. By the end of the ordeal, they were found guilty of misdemeanor offenses and received 60-day jail sentences.
Following that experience, said Ross, the pair decided to reject the subpoena to testify before a grand jury.
“It was an easy decision for both of us,” Ross said.
Shergalis and Ross are slated to testify on Wednesday, at which time they plan to assert their Fifth Amendment rights and decline to answer any questions from the federal prosecutor.
At that point, a hearing before a judge may be scheduled, to determine whether to hold Shergalis and Ross in civil contempt, which could result in up to 18 months of prison, according to Kelley.
Martínez, who also worked on WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange’s defense team, said the decision by Shergalis and Ross recalled that of Chelsea Manning, who twice refused to testify against Assange before a grand jury, serving time in prison in both instances.
“It’s like Chelsea Manning, years later,” he said.
Shergalis and Ross decided to go public with their plans after speaking with organizers behind the recently-launched NSPM-7 Defendants Union, a nationwide project for protesters targeted by the Trump administration’s efforts to criminalize dissent as laid out in last year’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7. The document, part of a broader effort to paint left-wing activism as terrorism, directs the FBI to go after “violent and terroristic activities” associated with “anti-fascism.”
The NSPM-7 Defendants Union is centered around signing a pledge to follow practices such as not cooperating with law enforcement, adopting collective legal strategy when possible, and publicly announcing those strategies — a goal that runs against the secrecy surrounding federal indictments.
While secrecy benefits prosecutors before a grand jury, said Shergalis, “It’s good for all of us to be as transparent as possible.”
Shergalis, Ross, and Chambers have each signed the pledge, and the grand jury decision appears to be the first public test case of the union’s ideas.
“We should celebrate people across the country deciding to assert their legal rights boldly against the federal government and its NSPM-7 policy,” said de Janon, of the National Lawyers Guild. “We’re seeing NSPM-7 result in unprecedented levels of prosecution against protesters.”
“This Is Bad Faith”
Meanwhile, Chambers remains imprisoned in Madrid, as the Spanish courts decide whether to grant the U.S. extradition request or not.
Chambers has applied for asylum in Spain and, if his application is granted, he would be released and the U.S. extradition request would be denied. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course.
A self-described communist and anti-imperialist, Chambers is heir of the Cox family, owners of Atlanta-based telecom giant Cox Enterprises. As part of a settlement in which his family severed ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to them in mid-2023 worth about $250 million.
Since then, he has been funding an estimated 100 humanitarian and left-wing projects in 20 countries, according to his partner, actress and activist Stella Schnabel, including aid projects in the Occupied Gaza Strip.
As for the Trump administration’s case, Martínez, the Spanish attorney, underscored how the criminal complaint against Chambers raises charges related to the protest against the New Hampshire factory for Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer, but leaves out how federal prosecution efforts ended up with minor convictions for Shergalis, Ross, and other activists.
“The people who carried out the acts received a minor sentence,” he said. “They leave this out. This is bad faith.”
“Why don’t they tell this to Spain?” he said. “It’s likely that Spain won’t turn someone over based on actions that got 60-day sentences.”
Martínez said Chambers’s opposition to the Israeli genocide in Gaza is the real reason behind the case. “I believe this is part of the persecution against pro-Palestine protest. The U.S. has even sanctioned the International Criminal Court because of this.”
Of Chambers’s case, Martínez said, “This is one more attack.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Documenta 16 hires four new curators
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The curatorial team for Documenta 16 is expanding with the announcement of four new appointments. The new team members are the composer and installation artist Raven Chacon, who was named curator-at-large, alongside the curators and art historians Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus and Noam Segal, who were appointed curatorial advisers.
The next edition of the influential quinquennial contemporary art exhibition, which will take place next year (12 June-19 September) in Kassel, is led by Naomi Beckwith, the deputy director and chief curator of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.
Her team of four women curators—Carla Acevedo-Yates, Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, and Xiaoyu Weng—will develop the exhibition, publications and programming for the upcoming edition.
Chacon unveiled the two-mile-long land art installation Repellent Fence at the US/Mexico border in 2015; in 2022, he became the first Indigenous artist to be awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Bonsu is senior curator of international art, Africa, and diaspora at Tate Modern, where he co-curated Nigerian Modernism in 2025.
Junghaus was the founding director of Gallery8 – Roma Contemporary Art Space in Budapest (2013–2017) and launched the European Roma Institute for Arts and Culture in Berlin in 2017. Segal serves as the LG Electronics associate curator at the Guggenheim Museum in New York and was previously the director of curatorial research in the Master’s programme for curatorial practice at the School of Visual Arts, New York.
According to an online statement, “the [Documenta 16] exhibition and programmes will honour artists as they navigate a world in turmoil, developing strategies and new possibilities for living together amid planetary indeterminacy. Improvisation, experimentation, and collective learning will open new paths.”
The last edition of Documenta in 2022 sparked controversy after two antisemitic images were found in the work People’s Justice (2000), by the Indonesian artist collective, Taring Padi. The work was removed from show and, in the following days, Documenta posted a statement that was attributed to the Jakarta-based collective ruangrupa, who curated the exhibition. It read in part: “We acknowledge that this was our error.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Haley Stevens’s Betrayal Is a Fiasco for the Democratic Establishment
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer

Haley Stevens’s Betrayal Is a Fiasco for the Democratic Establishment
Centrist, pro-Israel Democrats helped Stevens undermine Abdul El-Sayed for months. Now they are reaping the consequences.
Michigan Representative Haley Stevens likes to tell the world what she’s dreaming about. Sometimes, she even overshares a little bit, as in her notorious December 2023 statement that “Israel comes to me in my dreams.”
On Saturday, Stevens dipped into her well of nocturnal visions in a bid to calm the waters she’d started churning up over her clear antipathy toward Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Michigan Senate nominee who defeated Stevens in a bitter primary in August. Responding to concerns that she might break with her party and endorse El-Sayed’s Republican rival, Mike Rogers, Stevens reportedly texted a Michigan Democrat, “I am voting straight Dem!!!! I had a dream last night we won. And I believe he will win! P.S. it was a happy dream.” She reportedly said much the same thing to multiple friends and congressional colleagues up until early Sunday morning—until, without warning, she appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church and announced that she was endorsing him.
The drama of Stevens’s life over the last few weeks has been a battle between these competing dreams. Her pro-Israel politics were in tension with her partisan identity after she lost the primary in August to El-Sayed, who is strongly critical of Israel. AIPAC spent more than $30 million supporting Stevens. After her loss, AIPAC and allied groups such as the United Democracy Project have continued to pour tens of millions of dollars into the effort to defeat El-Sayed, although the full spending on the race hasn’t yet been tabulated. Stevens, meanwhile, kept insisting that her dream of a Democratic Senate outweighed her dreams of Israel, even as she demanded that El-Sayed denounce anti-Israel ads he had nothing to do with. (El-Sayed complied.)
Now we know which dream ultimately won out. When Stevens made her announcement, one of the people in the background was Abigail Ronson, described by Drop Site News as not only a Rogers spokesperson but also “a registered foreign agent for the state of Israel.” Not surprisingly, AIPAC repeatedly posted celebratory retweets of Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers.
Stevens has a personal connection to Zionism as well. Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, is strongly pro-Israel and a megadonor to both political parties. He has donated more than $24,000 to the campaign of Maine Republican Susan Collins. Last week, Turkish announced that he is voting for Rogers. (A friend of Stevens told The Washington Post on Sunday that Turkish had been “really working her over” to endorse Rogers, including by saying that she was betraying Jewish voters by backing El-Sayed.)
In declaring her own support for Rogers, Stevens claimed, “Who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and it is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.” This claim is absurd, since El-Sayed has not been running a hateful campaign, while Rogers and other Republicans have targeted the Democrats with vile Islamophobia. In fact, after welcoming the support of Stevens, Rogers referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist.”
The journalist Ray Wert, who is married to Mallory McMorrow, who was also bested by El-Sayed in Michigan’s Democratic senatorial primary, offered some insights into Stevens in a long post on X.com that emphasized her personal flakiness and speculated on the role her fiancé might have played in the decision. According to Wert:
I’ve known Haley Stevens for a long time. Until now, she has always had staff to protect her, prop her up, and keep her safe from her own irrational behavior. What we’re seeing now? This is just raw, unfiltered Haley. 
The Haley who flip-flops and goes from thought to thought without rhyme or reason. The Haley that calls you at 3 AM to yell at you, and then calls you back at 5 AM oblivious to the fact that she even spoke with you at 3 AM. The Haley who bends to the last and loudest voice that tells her something. 
More often than not that last voice is now her fiancé. And…that appears to potentially be a really troubling relationship.
This account of Stevens’s personal instability is plausible enough, and other emerging accounts reinforce this narrative. So too will the train wreck of an interview that Stevens gave to CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Sunday night, in which she appeared erratic in the extreme and failed to give any coherent reason for her last-minute endorsement of Rogers.
But Stevens’s personality is only part of the story. Donald Trump is also weird, but his weirdness is amplified and given direction by his ideology as well as pressure from those around him.
In Stevens’s case, hardline pro-Israel ideology is key to understanding her decision. Danielle O’Byrne, a political strategist who has worked for Stevens as well as Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, wrote bluntly about the ideological dimensions of Stevens’s actions:
In 2022, I worked for Haley Stevens’ campaign. Over my time working there I quickly learned that she was bought and sold by AIPAC. A Democrat from the middle of America, obsessed with foreign interests and willing to sell herself and us out for it. We won that race by 20 points. With over $10 million in outside spending by AIPAC to oust another Jewish Democratic member, @andylevin, all because he wasn’t kowtowing to them.
It’s precisely because Stevens was a fierce pro-Israel warrior that she had the support of the Democratic Party establishment. In the primaries, she was the preferred candidate of Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader. After she lost the primary, Stevens started making comments that were clearly designed to sabotage El-Sayed. But this didn’t put her beyond the pale, since other party leaders such as former House speaker Nancy Pelosi and Neera Tanden (head of the Center for American Progress) were saying much the same thing.
In retrospect, centrist Democrats such as Pelosi and Tanden were playing a dangerous game. They were clearly intent on reducing El-Sayed’s margin without fatally wounding his campaign. The goal was to make sure that even if El-Sayed won, they could argue that he underperformed because his version of progressive politics—particularly when it came to Israel—was too extreme, thus making it easier to ideologically discipline him in office.
Stevens was playing the same game, but on Sunday, she went too far by actually endorsing Rogers. This robbed establishment Democrats of their plausible deniability in hamstringing the El-Sayed campaign.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Stevens also made herself toxic among Democrats. She still has a few defenders, such as Todd Richman, head of Democratic Majority for Israel. But her longtime chief of staff Justin German has quit and says many of his colleagues are also resigning. Party leaders—notably Schumer, Pelosi, and Tanden—who previously supported Stevens are now decrying what Schumer described as a “despicable betrayal.”
But the lamentations of these powerful centrist Democrats ring hollow. They sound like Dr. Frankenstein wringing his hands over the havoc wreaked by the monster he created. The monster, of course, deserves punishment—and there is already a move to expel Stevens from the Democratic Party’s congressional caucus—but so do the doctors.
The best-case scenario for the Democrats might be that they win a large enough supermajority that they can afford to expel a few wreckers within the party, not just Stevens but also Senator John Fetterman.
But Stevens is merely a symptom of a deeper problem. Even as voters are becoming more wary of the US alliance with Israel, Democratic Party elites are top-heavy with figures closely aligned to the pro-Israel lobby. Any reckoning with the Stevens fiasco has to also include radically weakening this lobby.

https://gothamist.com/news/heres-what-dr.title: Here’s what drove NYC gas prices higher and whether relief is on the way
https://gothamist.com/news/heres-what-dr.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/heres-what-dr.text:
The cost of living is top of mind for most New Yorkers — and the price of gas this year is playing a big part.
After the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran starting in February, global gas prices rose as the geopolitical makeup of the Middle East created a strain on oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz. That passage typically carries more than 20% of the world’s oil trade.
The conflict is impacting New York, which already pays more for gas compared to states like Texas and Louisiana, located closer to oil production and refineries.
But according to Patrick De Haan, who leads petroleum analysis at the gas price monitoring platform GasBuddy, New Yorkers can expect gas prices to lower in the coming weeks as the winter season approaches. The big caveat: The Trump administration doesn’t ramp up attacks on Iran after the midterm elections.
“ Generally, we do see gas prices fall most years in the autumn. [It’s] a combination of Americans that start to stay closer to home and aren't driving as much in colder weather now that the summer is kind of behind us,” De Haan said. “As well as a seasonal switch over to cheaper winter gasoline, which happens every year in September.”
According to the platform’s own data, New York City’s average gas price in the last week — based on a survey of more than 1000 stations — is $4.37 per gallon. A year ago, the city's average price was $3.10 per gallon.
This year has been nothing but ordinary for diesel prices as well. De Haan said targeted airstrikes over the summer of oil refineries in Russia by Ukraine in the ongoing war between the two European nations have peaked diesel prices.
“ Diesel prices in the last month have set new records in just about every U.S. state,” he added.
The underlying effect of higher diesel prices on the everyday New Yorker — who relies on public transportation — is on the MTA’s balance sheet.
Transit agencies like the MTA typically ink longer-term fuel contracts and lock in pricing for months at a time to supply their buses or a crop of their diesel-powered work repair trains. While the influx in global diesel prices might not affect the transit agency now, De Haan said a future with prices staying high could.
“The higher cost of diesel will eventually likely cause these agencies to have some imbalances in their budget and whether or not they raise fares or they somehow find revenue to offset that somewhere else is up to the respective agency,” De Haan said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A ex-presidenta da Argentina Cristina Kirchner afirmou que pretende disputar as eleições presidenciais de 2027, caso consiga reverter a inabilitação perpétua para exercer cargos públicos imposta pela Justiça do país. “Quando eu recuperar meus direitos políticos, por que não?”, respondeu em entrevista ao jornal estadunidense The Washington Post, publicada nesta segunda-feira (2).
Foi a primeira entrevista de Kirchner a um veículo internacional desde a condenação, classificada por ela como um caso de lawfare — uso político do Judiciário para tirar adversários da disputa eleitoral. A conversa ocorreu no apartamento da rua San José, em Buenos Aires, onde ela cumpre prisão domiciliar desde junho de 2025.
Proibida de entrar nos Estados Unidos (EUA), a ex-presidenta também previu uma derrota de Donald Trump e dos republicanos nas eleições de meio de mandato desta terça-feira (3) e disse esperar que o resultado impulsione uma onda progressista. “Paradoxalmente, o homem que fez de tudo para ajudar governos de direita a vencer na América Latina vai perder as eleições em seu próprio país”, declarou.
Aos 73 anos, Kirchner foi condenada a seis anos de prisão e à inabilitação perpétua no caso conhecido como Vialidad, sobre a contratação de obras públicas na província de Santa Cruz durante seu governo. Ela foi absolvida da acusação de chefiar uma organização criminosa. A sentença, de 2022, foi confirmada pela Suprema Corte de Justiça da Argentina em junho de 2025, poucos dias depois de ela anunciar que seria candidata a deputada provincial, coincidência que a defesa e aliados apontam como sinal da motivação política do processo.
“Digam-me onde coloquei o dinheiro. Porque, sinceramente, se eu tivesse roubado, não estaria presa. Estaria livre, porque teria conseguido comprar o sistema judicial argentino, porque eles são corruptos”, disse Kirchner.
Sem possibilidade de novos recursos na Justiça argentina, a defesa levou o caso ao Comitê de Direitos Humanos da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU), alegando violação do devido processo legal e de direitos fundamentais. Segundo os advogados, ela foi responsabilizada por atos de seu chefe de gabinete e de ministros, e a defesa não teve acesso a provas-chave. O comitê não tem poder para anular decisões de tribunais nacionais, mas a Argentina, como signatária do Pacto Internacional sobre Direitos Civis e Políticos, tem a obrigação de respeitar seus padrões.
Rotina na prisão
Kirchner pode receber visitas apenas quatro horas por semana, em dois dias, com no máximo três pessoas por vez. Ela usa celular, mas teme ser monitorada. Lula, que passou 580 dias preso antes de ter as condenações anuladas, foi o primeiro líder internacional a visitá-la depois da prisão. “Ele me disse: ‘Faça exercício e não fique deprimida’”, contou.
“Mas eu não tenho o direito de ficar deprimida nem de me atormentar diante do sofrimento dos outros. Eu sei por que estou aqui: pelo que represento, pelo governo que construímos e por minha recusa em me submeter aos poderes estabelecidos”, completou a ex-presidenta.
Disputa com Milei
Kirchner segue na presidência do Partido Justicialista, fundado por Juan Domingo Perón e Eva Perón, e na liderança da Fuerza Patria, maior bloco de oposição no Congresso argentino. Segundo o Washington Post, pesquisas recentes mostram a aprovação dela ligeiramente acima da de Milei, ambas na faixa dos 30%. O presidente deve tentar a reeleição em 2027, e a oposição ainda não tem candidatura unificada. Horas antes da publicação da entrevista, o governador da província de Buenos Aires, Axel Kicillof, disse a assessores que está disposto a disputar prévias com ela ou com o ex-ministro da Economia Sergio Massa.
A ex-presidenta reconheceu que o peronismo contribuiu para a própria derrota em 2023. No governo de Alberto Fernández, que teve Kirchner como vice, a inflação anual chegou a 211% e a pobreza, a 40%. “Houve uma ruptura na cultura do trabalho”, admitiu.
A inflação caiu sob Milei, mas a pobreza voltou a subir neste ano, assim como o desemprego, e a aprovação do presidente de extrema direita despencou ao menor patamar desde a posse. “Agora muitos argentinos estão frustrados porque suas vidas não melhoraram, seu dinheiro não dura até o fim do mês e eles veem um governo que não só não faz nada pelos pobres, como os ataca ativamente”, criticou Kirchner. Para ela, quando Milei e outros líderes de direita não cumprirem suas promessas, a mesma raiva antissistema que os levou ao poder vai se voltar contra eles.
Segundo a ex-presidenta, o desafio do campo progressista não é apenas recuperar o poder, mas entender a raiva que levou eleitores a apostar em quem promete derrubar o sistema e apresentar propostas que a população acredite serem viáveis, sobretudo para os problemas econômicos do dia a dia e o endividamento das famílias. “É possível governar racionalmente uma sociedade em que 50% acham que os outros 50% precisam desaparecer?”, questionou.
‘O povo sempre volta’
A previsão sobre os EUA atinge diretamente o governo argentino. Em outubro, em discurso em um jantar de uma associação hispânica em Washington, Milei pediu que o aliado saísse vitorioso do pleito. “É importante, não só para os Estados Unidos, mas para todo o Ocidente […] que o presidente Trump saia fortalecido das eleições de novembro; não podemos ceder um centímetro na nossa reconquista do hemisfério”, afirmou o argentino.
Nas eleições de meio de mandato, estão em disputa as 435 cadeiras da Câmara dos Representantes e um terço do Senado. Os republicanos controlam hoje as duas Casas, com 53 das 100 cadeiras do Senado e 218 da Câmara, contra 214 dos democratas. As pesquisas nacionais mostram os republicanos atrás dos democratas. Uma derrota no Congresso pode limitar o poder de Trump nos dois últimos anos de mandato.
“A história não se escreve em linha reta. Há avanços e retrocessos. Mas o povo sempre volta”, concluiu Kirchner.
