https://taz.de/Pflegereform-und-Finanzlo.title: Pflegereform und Finanzlöcher: Protest allein löst das Problem nicht
https://taz.de/Pflegereform-und-Finanzlo.author: Barbara Dribbusch
https://taz.de/Pflegereform-und-Finanzlo.text:
Pflegereform und Finanzlöcher : Protest allein löst das Problem nicht
Die Pflegekassen müssen sparen – dafür braucht es Maßstäbe. Pflegende Angehörige müssen geschützt werden, Künftige Erb:innen hingegen nicht.
F ast könnte man Mitleid bekommen mit Carsten Linnemann (CDU). Auf Facebook fleht der CDU-Bundesgesundheitsminister in einem Video um Unterstützung für sein Pflege-Spargesetz. Es wirkt verzweifelt: „Ich freu mich über Vorschläge, wie wir das System zukunftsfest machen. Ich freue mich, wenn ihr mitmacht“, sagt Linnemann, von dem es heißt, dass ihm das Amt des Gesundheitsministers vom Bundeskanzler aufgezwungen worden sein soll.
Linnemann steht unter Druck. Es ist ein finanzielles Problem, wenn vor 20 Jahren zwei Millionen Pflegebedürftige Leistungen aus der Pflegeversicherung bekamen und es jetzt sechs Millionen sind. Ohne Reformen fehlen der gesetzlichen, der sogenannten Sozialen Pflegeversicherung (SPV) im kommenden Jahr fast 8 Milliarden Euro, im Jahr 2030 dann 17 Milliarden Euro.
Protest allein kann das Finanzierungsproblem leider nicht lösen, das weniger durch politischen Kürzungswillen als durch die Zunahme der Leistungsempfänger:innen entstanden ist. Selbst wenn man die Einnahmebasis verbreitern und etwa eine Art Finanzausgleich zwischen privater und gesetzlicher Pflegekasse einrichten könnte, würde das nicht reichen, die Pflegekassen zu stabilisieren.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Es führt also kein Weg an einer Spardebatte vorbei. Das Pflegeneuordnungsgesetz (PNOG), das an diesem Donnerstag erstmals in den Bundestag kommt, soll ein Anfang sein. Doch die Empörung darüber zeigt, welche Fehler gemacht wurden.
Ungenaue Einstufung in die Pflegegrade
Die Pflegekassen sind ein System, hinter dem sich sehr unterschiedliche Schicksale verbergen. Eine Ehefrau, die ihren demenzkranken, inkontinenten, verhaltensauffälligen, immobilen 75-jährigen Ehemann, Pflegegrad 4, schon seit Jahren zu Hause pflegt und beaufsichtigt, bringt Opfer, die Nichtbetroffene kaum ermessen können.
Etwas anders sieht es im Haushalt eines alten Ehepaares aus, wo die Frau, Pflegegrad 3, zwar etwas Hilfe im Alltag braucht, aber gut orientiert ist und mit dem Rollator noch mobil. Die fast 600 Euro Pflegegeld im Monat fließen dort ins allgemeine Haushaltsbudget ein.
Details in den Fähigkeiten und im Verhalten eines Pflegebedürftigen, in der Wohn- und Familiensituation, können darüber entscheiden, ob der Alltag noch einigermaßen entspannt ist oder hohe Opfer vom Umfeld verlangt.
Wobei die Einstufung in die fünf Pflegegrade Unschärfen birgt: Sie erfolgt aufgrund der Selbstauskunft in einem einzigen Gespräch vor Ort mit einer Gutachter:in. Es werden Tätigkeiten des Alltags abgefragt und ob man diese noch „selbständig“, „überwiegend selbständig“, „überwiegend unselbständig“ oder „unselbständig“ ausführen kann. Die Auskünfte können unterschiedlich ausfallen, und oft gibt es Neid, wenn etwa einer Antragstellerin ein Pflegegrad 3 zugestanden wird, der genauso gebrechlichen Nachbarin aber nur Grad 2.
Abschaffung der „Verhinderungspflege“ ist fatal
Aus Gründen der Ersparnis die Schwellen für die Pflegegrade etwas heraufzusetzen, wie es das Pflegeneuordnungsgesetz vorsieht, ist zwar unschön, aber noch relativ vertretbar. Die beiden höchsten Pflegegrade 4 und 5 sind von dieser Anhebung ausgenommen, und das ist gut so.
Man darf es nicht verschweigen: Leider gibt es Missbrauch. Leicht kann ein Pflegehaushalt in der „Verhinderungspflege“ mehr als 3.500 Euro pro Jahr kassieren, wenn nur irgendeine Bekannte als „Ersatzpflegeperson“ für vermeintliche Ausfallzeiten angegeben wird, obwohl diese Pflege gar nicht stattfand. Dieser Missbrauch ist kein Kavaliersdelikt, sondern eine Sauerei, denn er beschädigt die Akzeptanz des Systems.
Mit dem Hinweis auf häufigen Missbrauch soll die „Verhinderungspflege“ abgeschafft beziehungsweise umgewandelt werden. Das ist fatal für hunderttausende pflegende Angehörige. Etwa für die Mutter des schwerstbehinderten Kindes, die das Geld braucht, um Ersatzpflege mit vertrauten Personen zu finanzieren, weil das Förderzentrum lange Ferien hat und sie ihren Teilzeitjob aber nicht einfach unterbrechen kann. Pflegende Angehörige müssen zudem auch selbst mal Freizeit haben, zum Arzt, zum Sport und die Verhinderungspflege durch Ersatzpersonen auch stundenweise finanzieren können.
Wie aus Kreisen der SPD-Fraktion verlautet, werden im parlamentarischen Verfahren noch Änderungen des Gesetzentwurfs angestrebt, darunter auch der Schutz von Pflegeleistungen wie etwa der Verhinderungspflege. Richtig so.
Steuermittel für die Schonung von Vermögen
Heikel ist die Frage, inwieweit eigenes Einkommen und Vermögen der Pflegebedürftigen eingesetzt werden sollen, wenn es zum Heimaufenthalt kommt. Die SPD fordert mehr Zuschüsse zu den steigenden Eigenanteilen der Heimbewohner:innen. Laut einem Gutachten des Instituts für Wirtschaftsforschung wäre aber mehr als die Hälfte der Rentnerhaushalte in der Lage, die Eigenanteile im Falle des Heimaufenthaltes finanziell zu stemmen, sogar ohne dass dafür eine eigene Immobilie verwertet werden muss.
Es ist also richtig, wenn die jetzt eingesetzte Pflegestrukturkommission höhere Zuschüsse zu den Heimkosten von der Einkommens- und Vermögenslage der Pflegebedürftigen abhängig machen will. Wobei der Sturz in die Sozialhilfe verhindert und die Vermögen nicht noch stärker geschützt werden sollen als bisher ohnehin schon.
Pensionierte Beamte werden im Falle eines Heimaufenthaltes derzeit per Beamtenrecht extra abgesichert, aus Steuermitteln, um deren Vermögen zu schonen. Das könnte man hinterfragen. Wohlhabende, die ihr Vermögen für die Erb:innen sichern wollen, können dies durch eine früh abgeschlossene private Pflegezusatzversicherung tun.
Dass Ausgaben begrenzt werden müssen, ist ernüchternd, aber in der Pflegeversicherung nicht zu vermeiden. Eine Diskussion, wo im System noch am ehesten gespart werden könnte und wo überhaupt nicht, ist angesagt und sollte nicht von vornherein tabuisiert werden, auch nicht aus linker Perspektive. Etwas Pragmatik schadet auch den Gerechtigkeitsdebatten nicht.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://hellgatenyc.com/the-weird-wild-r.title: The Weird, Wild Races We're Watching Tomorrow
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-weird-wild-r.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-weird-wild-r.text:
Did you know there's an election Tuesday? The Hell Gate podcast will be LIVE on our YouTube channel starting at 9 p.m., and we'll be bringing you the type of pipe-cleaner, construction-paper-based analysis you will NOT find anywhere else.
As you await our livestream, please peruse our election-adjacent content: Hell Gate Interviews Governor Kathy Hochul, Our Crash Course on New York City's Ballot Proposals, Hell Gate chats with Clairializa, Who the Fuck is Bruce Blakeman? and A Visit to Battleground Southern Brooklyn. Last week, we had elections-knower Michael Lange on the pod to talk about many things, including what these midterms mean for Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
New York is hardly a swing state, but it's still taken center stage in this year's midterms. A Hudson Valley congressional seat is one of Democrats' best chances for a pick-up, and a North Country seat has become surprisingly competitive. In a year so grim for Republicans that they could lose a Senate seat in Texas, Vice President J.D. Vance is weirdly coming to New York to rally with an absolute car wreck of a Republican congressional candidate. If Democrats take back the House and Senate, leadership of both chambers could fall to two New Yorkers. And while he's not on the ballot, Mayor Zohran Mamdani is looming just as large in this election as President Donald Trump is.
New Yorkers are clearly following this year's elections. Early voting turnout is way up. Kathy Hochul received a kind-of warm welcome in Dimes Square on Friday. Voter registration data released by the state Board of Elections showed that tens of thousands of people have registered to vote since February, most of them unaffiliated with a political party, as City & State reported.
All statewide offices are on the ballot. In New York City, Democrats are working to flip four Brooklyn state legislative seats, and there's a rare swingy vacant Assembly seat in the Rockaways. The election is nigh. The popcorn is out. Here are some of the things we're watching for on Tuesday:
How does Governor Kathy Hochul fare against Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman?
Many underestimated Kathy Hochul, but she has been a surprisingly durable governor. Since the was thrust into power in 2021, she's found her footing, bringing the Legislature to heel, forming a partnership with New York City's juggernaut mayor, and holding her own against President Donald Trump. She's led the way on a national stage with social media regulations, banning cell phones from schools, and pausing data center development.
Still, Hochul is having to answer for an affordability crisis that is pushing people out of the state as the economy seems to be on the brink of transformation. She's facing Bruce Blakeman, the Republican Nassau county executive who claims he can dramatically reduce taxes and energy bills. Blakeman, now 71, has had a patchy career in politics. He bounced around local office in Nassau in the '90s, then lost reelection to the county legislature following deeply unpopular tax hikes in 1999. Blakeman has made several attempts at higher office, running unsuccessfully for state comptroller, New York City mayor, U.S. Senate and for Congress. He did a stint at the Port Authority and then was appointed to the Hempstead Town Council in 2015. So far, his career has culminated with his capture of Nassau's previously Democratic county executive post in 2021.
Then came the theatrical MAGA turn: Sometime around 2024, as Donald Trump was running to take back the presidency, Blakeman got really on board, embracing an anti-trans, anti-immigrant, crime-fighting ideology. In March of that year, he memorably held Trump's umbrella for him while Trump addressed reporters outside the funeral of an NYPD officer. Blakeman ran for county executive on lowering taxes in Nassau, but he found more success charging into the culture wars when he banned trans women from playing sports with cis women in county facilities in July of that year. (A legal challenge to that law is ongoing.) A couple months later, he tried to gather a group of 75 dudes with gun permits to form an armed civilian group that he insisted was NOT a militia. He has raised eyebrows by hosting campaign-style events with Trump in county facilities or using county resources. He directed local police to cooperate with ICE and then called it the "one of the saddest days of my life as county executive" when a new state law forced him to end that partnership.
Blakeman has touted achievements in getting Nassau County on solid fiscal footing, but his decisions to use pandemic federal funds and opioid settlement funds to balance the budget were controversial. He has not managed to lower property taxes so far as county executive, and he's opted to freeze property tax rolls multiple years in a row. That approach has drawn a state audit and accusations that it puts the burden on individuals to contest their now extremely outdated property tax assessments.
This is Hochul's second reelection fight, and she's already saying she'll seek another term in 2030. Polling this year has been all over the place, but most surveys now show Hochul with a lead that at least hits the low double digits.
What's up with fundraising? Hochul has a huge, huge fundraising advantage, which is all the more notable because she opted out of the state's brand-new public matching funds program. She's also gotten a boost from outside spenders, including former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg. Blakeman has opted into the state's matching funds program, messily, and he's benefited from the largesse of Madison Square Garden billionaire James Dolan.
Hochul Yankee Candle Recipe: Aroma of toasted plain English muffin, the beery sweat of a Buffalo Bills bar, baby powder
Blakeman Yankee Candle Recipe: Notes of gunsmoke, Debra Messing's conditioner, the chemical smell of newly printed T-shirts for these "Gen-Z" dancers

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Life mirrors art: the story of Yayoi Kusama
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alex Wang
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
When Yayoi Kusama died in Tokyo on 14 August, aged 97, she left behind a legacy almost unparalleled in contemporary art. The Japanese artist, who arrived in New York in 1958 as an outsider—female, Asian and largely unknown—eventually became one of the most recognisable artists on the planet. Her dots and pumpkins migrated from canvases and sculptures onto handbags and shopfronts; her Infinity Mirror Rooms generated queues around museums and millions of selfies.
Yet Kusama’s visibility has, when it comes to the structures that once excluded her, remained extraordinary.
“Kusama’s global success has had enormous symbolic force,” says Izumi Nakajima, an art historian specialising in feminism and post-war Japanese art. “Yet the exceptional success of an individual woman artist and a structural transformation in the gendered and geographical asymmetries of the art world operate on different registers.” A canon, Nakajima adds, can accommodate “a small number of monumental women artists while continuing to marginalise a far larger number of women”.
That distinction complicates the familiar story of Kusama as a trailblazer for women and Asian artists. Japan in the 1950s and early 60s, Nakajima says, had a substantial cohort of women pursuing experimental practices, including Atsuko Tanaka and Hideko Fukushima. To project Kusama’s present fame backwards risks producing a history in which she appears uniquely radical from the outset. Kusama’s departure from Japan in 1957 was crucial: while Japan’s high-growth era increasingly reorganised women’s lives around domesticity, she pursued her career abroad, relentlessly making both her art and herself visible through exhibitions, photographs, fashion, happenings and the media.
Is fame the same as success?
For the Tokyo- and Vienna-based feminist and queer publishing and research collective Multiple Spirits, the transformation since Kusama’s early career is nevertheless real. Compared with a global art world then dominated overwhelmingly by white men, opportunities to encounter artists from different backgrounds have unquestionably expanded, the collective says. But it questions whether Kusama’s trajectory should still function as a model of “success” when the criteria by which success is measured remain largely inherited from that same art world. “Values and measures different from those shaped by a white male-centred art world are still insufficient,” the collective says.
Nor does Nakajima see Kusama fitting comfortably into another role frequently assigned to her: that of the feminist icon. Rather than treating feminism as “an attribute or categorical designation”, Nakajima argues, it is more productive to use it as a critical method through which to read her work. Kusama’s repetition, sexuality, self-representation and negotiation of the body all invite feminist interpretation. But unlike strands of feminist art that rejected Modernism’s claims to autonomy and universality, Kusama repeatedly resisted being circumscribed as either a “woman” or a “Japanese” artist. “She sought to occupy the position of the universal artistic subject that Modernism had imagined,” Nakajima says.
The Multiple Spirits collective similarly notes a gap between Kusama’s international reception and her popular image at home. In Japan, it says, she is less commonly understood as a feminist icon than as the creator of colourful polka-dotted paintings and installations. The politics of her 1960s happenings—their anti-war messages and calls for sexual liberation—have received comparatively less attention. Rather than reducing Kusama to an individual “feminist” or “queer” identity, the collective argues that these radical practices need to be reconsidered within the social and cultural conditions that produced them.
Journey to global cultural brand
Another paradox lies in Kusama’s transformation from avant-garde provocateur to global cultural brand. In 1966, she appeared uninvited at the Venice Biennale with Narcissus Garden, offering mirrored spheres for sale beneath a sign declaring “Your Narcissism for Sale”. Decades later, the mirrors themselves became among contemporary art’s most coveted attractions. Visitors queue for hours to spend seconds inside an Infinity Mirror Room, phone in hand, while collaborations with Louis Vuitton turned her dots into a globally recognisable luxury motif. Critics have consequently cast Kusama as both a precursor of the immersive “artainment” economy and one of its most successful brands.
For Hidenori Ota, the founder of the gallery Ota Fine Arts and Kusama’s longtime representative in Japan, the artist’s embrace of visibility cannot be separated from the struggle to make herself heard. “I imagine that, in order to deliver a voice that otherwise could not reach people, she first needed to make her own presence larger,” he says. Having directly experienced war, Ota suggests, Kusama sought a language capable of reaching a mass audience, repeatedly returning to the word “love” as a vehicle for criticism.
Kusama’s popularity also made mental illness unusually visible within mainstream contemporary art. She voluntarily lived at a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo from 1977 onward, working for decades at a nearby studio. While frequently connecting her compulsive repetition and artistic production to hallucinations and psychological distress, she generally eschewed disability advocacy. Narratives around Kusama have drawn criticism for reproducing the familiar trope of the “mad genius” who triumphs over adversity, while doing relatively little to address disability, psychiatric experience or accessibility. Nakajima similarly warns against narratives that link women’s creativity to illness, trauma and psychological compulsion: such frameworks, she says, have historically helped women artists gain recognition while simultaneously restricting how their practices are understood.
Perhaps the most troubling asterisk in Kusama’s legacy relates to her descriptions of Black people in her 2002 autobiography, Infinity Net. In the original Japanese edition, she blamed Black residents and unhoused people for the decline of her New York neighbourhood. That, along with other denigrating lines, was omitted from the 2011 English translation. When the comments received renewed attention ahead of her 2023 exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Kusama said she “deeply regret[ted] using hurtful and offensive language” and apologised for the pain she had caused.
A symbol of inclusion
The episode sits uneasily beside the universalist language of love that characterised Kusama’s later public persona. Asked how it should shape her legacy, Ota says: “Rather than simply viewing her through that label of ‘racist’, [her words] should be examined in relation to the social conditions and historical context of the time.” He adds that it requires further debate and study. The controversy nevertheless underscores the limits of transforming a complex historical figure into an uncomplicated symbol of inclusion.
Ota is likewise sceptical of attributing subsequent changes in Asia’s art world to a single artist. “Rather than Kusama changing things herself, I think the larger shifts of the era—particularly the social and economic rise of Asia—were more significant,” he says. “She moved in step with those larger changes.”
The Multiple Spirits collective flags how, in Japan and beyond, as shrinking cultural budgets require museums to pursue larger audiences and alternative funding sources, Kusama shows became reliable for producing economic results. But her visibility has not particularly helped other marginalised artists. “We cannot entrust structural change in the art world to the success story of a minority artist,” the collective says. What matters instead are less spectacular changes: improving working conditions and accessibility, using inclusive language, protecting freedom of expression and connecting such efforts across institutions.
Kusama entered a Western, male-dominated art world and ultimately became bigger than almost any artist within it. But “exceptional success and structural inequality can coexist”, Nakajima observes. Kusama changed who could occupy the centre of contemporary art, but not the nature of that centre.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Ilhan Omar: “Trump Has an Unhealthy and Creepy Obsession With Me”
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
In the predawn hours of October 12, Department of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents raided the home of US Representative Ilhan Omar, DFL-Minnesota. The raid was reportedly part of a criminal fraud investigation that was focused on decades-old immigration and citizenship paperwork that was filed by Omar’s father when she was a child. Omar, an outspoken progressive, is a refugee from Somalia who came to the United States at age 12. She has been the target of attacks by Trump, his Republican allies, and right-wing media for the better part of a decade. She denied any wrongdoing and decried the raid as “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
That sentiment was echoed by former president Barack Obama, along with many other prominent Democrats and defenders of civil liberties. For his part, Trump claimed he had nothing to do with the raid. Yet, on the same day that it occurred, the president ripped into Omar as “totally crooked personally” and “a terrible person.” He also endorsed Minnesota Republican US Senate nominee Michele Tafoya, who is mounting a high-stakes challenge to DFL candidate Peggy Flanagan in Tuesday’s midterm election. With Republican prospects fading in Senate battleground states such as North Carolina and Georgia, Tafoya’s bid was on Trump’s radar to such an extent that, just hours after the raid on Omar’s home, he was telling Minnesotans, “You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who’s a very respected person.”
The Nation recently asked Omar to discuss the raid and the politics surrounding it. Here’s what she had to say.
—John Nichols
John Nichols:  There was an immediate show of support from your constituents after the raid. You can’t be too worried about your own reelection prospects. But do you think that the president and his allies are trying to stir up anti-immigrant and anti-Somali sentiment in the broader context of the midterms?
Ilhan Omar: Absolutely. This is political, and it’s a deliberate attempt to distract the American people from the failures of this administration. Republicans don’t want to talk about the soaring cost of living, the Epstein files, the war in Iran, Trump’s shady diesel deal with Russia, or a healthcare system that is spiraling out of control. So instead, Trump sends DHS to raid my home. This is what authoritarianism looks like: weaponizing the federal government against anyone he sees as an opponent, scapegoating immigrant communities, and using racism and fear to divide us. He is reaching for the same tired playbook because he knows his party is in trouble. Trump thinks he can turn our neighbors against one another to win an election. I believe the American people are better than that.
JN: Why do you think the president and so many Republicans are obsessed with you?
IO: Trump has an unhealthy and creepy obsession with me. I represent everything Trump and today’s Republican Party seem to despise. I’m a woman, an immigrant, a refugee, a Muslim woman who wears a hijab, and someone who refuses to be intimidated into silence. I know who I am and why I do this work.
The Republican Party has chosen to serve billionaires and powerful corporations over working people. They know that our vision of healthcare for everyone, an economy that works for working families, and a country where everyone can live with dignity is popular with the American people. So they resort to racism, Islamophobia, conspiracy theories, and lies. They want to make me the story because they don’t want to answer for their own failures. But I will not let their hatred define me, and I will not let it distract me from the people I came to Congress to serve.
JN: Many Minnesotans have complained about being targeted by the administration—with last winter’s Operation Metro Surge, and with all the focus on you. Why do you think this is happening?
IO: Trump has said that this is political retribution. I believe Minnesota is a target because we represent everything his politics of division cannot understand. We are a community that chooses solidarity over fear and care over cruelty. We welcome immigrants and refugees. We don’t just welcome them into our neighborhoods—we send them to Congress. When our neighbors are threatened, we show up, even in below-zero temperatures. We deliver meals, give children rides to school, check on one another, and organize mutual aid. We understand that when one family is hurting, our whole community has a responsibility to help. I have seen that love firsthand in the outpouring of support from my constituents. In moments when this administration tries to make people feel afraid and alone, Minnesotans have reminded me what this country can be at its best. Their courage and compassion mean more to me than I can put into words.
That is what Trump cannot stand. He wants us to believe that our differences make us weaker, that some people belong here more than others, and that fear is the only way to lead. Minnesota proves otherwise. Our strength comes from looking out for one another, recognizing our shared humanity, and refusing to abandon our neighbors. The antidote to authoritarianism is community. It is love. It is solidarity. It is the belief that every person deserves dignity and that none of us are free until all of us are free. Those are Minnesota’s values. Those are American values. And no raid, no threat, and no amount of hatred will take them away from us.
JN: You have often spoken about your patriotism and your pride at being an American. How does the raid—and the president’s very personal attacks on you—make you feel about your country and the people who are currently leading it? Do you think Trump is out of touch with American values and ideals?
IO: Trump’s behavior echoes some of the darkest chapters in our nation’s history. But I believe deeply in the promise of this country because generations of Americans have fought, sacrificed, and organized to make it a more just and equal place. That’s why I ran for office.
My family and I have endured death threats, relentless harassment, and years of personal attacks from this president. It has been painful, but it has never shaken my love for this country or my belief in its people. Trump may be out of touch with our values, but I know the best of America is found in people who stand up for one another, refuse to give up, and keep fighting for a country that lives up to its promise. I will never stop fighting for an America where everyone can see a doctor, afford a safe home, and put food on the table.
JN: What can Congress do to hold Trump and DHS to account?
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
IO: Congress has a constitutional duty to stand up to this abuse of power. We must defend our rights under the Speech and Debate Clause [outlined in Article I, Section 6, Clause 1 of the United States Constitution] and make clear that no president gets to use the power of the executive branch to intimidate or target members of Congress for political reasons.
This is bigger than party. It is about defending our democracy and protecting the independence of Congress. When we allow one branch of government to intimidate another, we weaken the very foundations of our republic.
[House Speaker] Mike Johnson has failed to meet this moment. But I promise you this—when Democrats retake the majority in November, we will stand up, hold this administration accountable, and defend the institution and the constitutional rights that every member of Congress is sworn to uphold.
JN: President Obama offered a powerful statement in your defense. It is notable that he was also a target of Trump’s conspiracy theories and a questioning of his citizenship. Were you struck by that?
IO: President Obama knows the world of right-wing conspiracies better than anyone. In many ways, the conspiracy world I find myself in was created around him. That is why he can so clearly see the purpose and contradictions of the lies being told about me. He knows that no amount of evidence or facts will ever be enough for these trolls, because they are not after the truth. The conspiracy itself is what drives them. It meant so much to me to know that President Obama sees this for what it is and was willing to speak out.

Por Jeff Xiong*
Em 19 de outubro de 2026, o Departamento de Segurança Interna dos EUA ordenou que as agências civis federais removessem o DeepSeek de seus sistemas, indo além dos próprios produtos da empresa: tudo o que tiver sido construído com sua tecnologia também deve ser eliminado. O critério é a origem da tecnologia, e vale para todas as agências civis do governo federal.
Vinte e quatro horas depois, em 20 de outubro, DeepSeek anunciou ter aberto integralmente o código do DeepInfer, o framework interno de inferência por trás da oferta de seus modelos de baixo custo, junto com o codec, componente de codificação que garante que uma instalação própria funcione igual ao serviço oficial. Assim, comunidades de todo o mundo podem rodar o modelo de forma tão barata quanto a própria empresa. Profissionais do setor reagiram espantados, pois a empresa havia “dado de presente ao mundo, de graça, sua máquina de imprimir dinheiro”.
No mesmo dia, Chen Deli, pesquisador sênior da DeepSeek, escreveu no X: “Código aberto contra código fechado, luz contra trevas. Uma batalha decisiva entre dois futuros, dois destinos para a humanidade. Por quanto tempo quiserem lutar, nós lutaremos, até conquistarmos a vitória completa.” O South China Morning Post e a Bloomberg repercutiram a publicação. A frase tem mais de setenta anos: Mao Zedong a pronunciou em 7 de fevereiro de 1953, na sessão de encerramento da Conferência Consultiva Política do Povo Chinês, no terceiro ano da Guerra da Coreia, a guerra que o bloco imperialista levou até a fronteira da China socialista recém fundada, na tentativa de estrangulá-la.
Para ler corretamente a batalha atual, vamos olhar primeiro para as trevas. O plano sombrio está escrito nos próprios documentos dos monopolistas. Sam Altman, diretor-executivo da OpenAI, afirmou que a superinteligência “é possível… em alguns milhares de dias”. A carta de princípios de sua empresa define a inteligência artificial geral como sistemas que “superam os humanos na maior parte do trabalho economicamente valioso”. Quem chegar primeiro será dono da inteligência avançada e, com ela, da direção da ciência e do conhecimento — e a mais ninguém será permitido chegar.
O conteúdo desse plano foi revelado pelo próprio Altman: sem infraestrutura suficiente, escreveu ele, a IA “será um recurso muito limitado, pelo qual se travarão guerras e que se tornará sobretudo uma ferramenta para os ricos”. Um produto de luxo para usuários, um armamento para Estados. Os dados são a outra metade do esquema: a vida social é extraída para treinar os modelos, e os modelos prontos são vendidos de volta às sociedades das quais foram tirados.
Os balanços mostram quanto custa o esquema. As contas auditadas da OpenAI de 2025, verificadas pelo Financial Times, registram US$ 13,07 bilhões de receita contra US$ 34 bilhões em custos e despesas, um prejuízo operacional de US$ 20,92 bilhões e um prejuízo líquido de US$ 38,53 bilhões, quase oito vezes o do ano anterior. Os responsáveis por essas contas reconhecem o que está acontecendo. “Estamos numa fase em que os investidores, como um todo, estão excessivamente empolgados com a IA? Minha opinião é que sim”, disse Altman sobre o mercado; Bezos, numa conferência de tecnologia em Turim, chamou isso de “uma espécie de bolha industrial”.
Prejuízos desse tamanho deixam de ser privados. O financiamento da IA migrou do fluxo de caixa operacional para o mercado da dívida, por meio da emissão de títulos, com cerca de US$ 3 trilhões em compromissos fora do balanço. Em maio de 2026 o Conselho de Estabilidade Financeira (FSB) alertou que uma correção brusca “poderia levar a perdas de crédito consideráveis”. Dirigentes do banco central dos EUA começaram a se perguntar se o ecossistema da IA é “grande demais para quebrar”. O índice P/L de Shiller, que mede se as ações estão caras em relação aos lucros, passou de 40 pela primeira vez desde o estouro da bolha das pontocom; o KOSPI, da Coreia do Sul, arrastado pela venda das ações de memória para IA, caiu 44% em quarenta dias. A onda de choque já atravessou fronteiras.
A exclusão se cristalizou em política. A lista de países atendidos pela OpenAI deixa de fora Cuba, Irã, a República Popular Democrática da Coreia, Síria e Rússia. O uso fora da lista, adverte a empresa, pode resultar em bloqueio de conta. A ordem que abriu este artigo é a mesma lógica levada à máquina do Estado: agências federais expurgando de seus sistemas um modelo e todos os produtos construídos com ele. O que esse projeto defende não é a segurança, mas o monopólio. Ele ataca um ecossistema que coloca ferramentas poderosas nas mãos de todo mundo.
Ainda assim, a luz já está rompendo as trevas, e seu avanço é de conhecimento público. Em janeiro de 2025, a DeepSeek publicou o R1, com seus pesos sob a licença MIT, livres para uso comercial, modificação e destilação. O aplicativo chegou ao primeiro lugar em 140 mercados em dezoito dias, e a Nvidia, no pânico que se seguiu, perdeu US$ 589 bilhões em valor de mercado num único pregão, a maior perda em um dia da história do mercado estadunidense. Pesos, diferentemente de serviços, podem ser copiados por qualquer pessoa no planeta.
Em 13 de agosto de 2026, a empresa abriu o código do DeepSeek Harness sob a licença MIT, um ambiente de execução de agentes construído sobre o lema “tudo é um plugin”: modelo, ferramentas, sessões, armazenamento, agendamento e interface são peças intercambiáveis. Em poucas horas, desenvolvedores deram 33 mil estrelas para o DeepSeek Harness no GitHub, 169 mil em uma semana. Em setembro, a empresa lançou seis componentes centrais para os chips Ascend, da Huawei, cada um equivalente a uma de suas ferramentas para Nvidia. Com apoio incondicional da Huawei, as duas empresas desenvolveram juntas um supernó de 128 chips. Assim, o chip de treinamento deixou de ser refém de um único fornecedor. Em outubro veio o DeepInfer, o sistema de produção por trás da oferta de baixo custo da empresa, que foi entregue por inteiro e é compatível tanto com Nvidia quanto com Ascend. A DeepSeek não está sozinha nessa história: Zhipu, Kimi e StepFun lançaram seus principais modelos com pesos abertos.
A adoção veio rápido. No OpenRouter, plataforma que agrega o tráfego de modelos de desenvolvedores do mundo todo, os modelos chineses responderam por 57% a 67% dos tokens na semana de 14 de setembro, frente a 6% a 13% em fevereiro, segundo os números da própria plataforma. Entre empresas dos 82 países que o OpenRouter classifica como Sul Global, a fatia é ainda maior: mais de dois terços dos tokens do Sul hoje rodam em modelos chineses. Essa tendência chega ao próprio Império. Um relatório da Comissão de Revisão Econômica e de Segurança EUA-China ao Congresso cita a estimativa de um sócio de fundo de capital de risco do Vale do Silício segundo a qual 80% das startups estadunidenses constroem seus produtos sobre modelos de base chineses. Até o Airbnb usa o Qwen, da Alibaba, nos chats de atendimento ao cliente.
A tecnologia é aberta, mas sua finalidade não fica entregue ao mercado: o Estado a orienta para o bem-estar do povo, e não para o lucro do capital. O Conselho de Estado da China, em suas Orientações de 2025 sobre a ação “IA+”, compromete o programa com “garantir que todo o povo partilhe das conquistas do desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial”, fixa metas de adoção de mais de 70% para terminais e agentes inteligentes até 2027 e de 90% até 2030, e acrescenta uma cláusula sobre ajudar os países do Sul Global a desenvolver capacidades e “superar o fosso global da inteligência”. A abertura é o meio; o compartilhamento é o fim declarado.
Esse espírito pode ser visto na realidade concreta. Em povoados do interior da China, vans-clínicas equipadas com diagnóstico assistido por IA percorrem mensalmente as estradas montanhosas até povoados sem médico residente. A consulta, do exame à receita, acontece dentro do veículo. Agricultores fazem cursos intensivos curtos de anotação de dados para treinamento de modelos e de uso de IA, e saem com certificados profissionais emitidos pelas autoridades do trabalho. Nos canteiros de obras, robôs assumiram as tarefas mais perigosas de soldagem e acabamento, e os trabalhadores que antes as executavam agora operam e treinam as máquinas.
Ao passo que a adoção da IA se espalha, a governança se afirma. Na China, nenhum serviço de IA generativa pode chegar legalmente ao público antes de passar por uma avaliação de segurança e ser registrado junto à Administração do Ciberespaço da China. Até 31 de agosto de 2026 o cadastro público reunia 1.112 serviços e 731 aplicações. O registro não é a única forma de fiscalização. Nas campanhas “Qinglang” contra o uso indevido da IA, os órgãos reguladores identificaram e tomaram medidas contra mais de 14 mil produtos de IA irregulares, como aplicativos, miniprogramas e agentes. Mais de seis milhões de itens de conteúdo ilegal foram removidos e, em abril, o órgão regulador citou publicamente o Jianying (versão chinesa do CapCut) por violações de rotulagem. A resposta da população aparece nas pesquisas: entre os 26 países pesquisados pela Ipsos, 83% dos entrevistados chineses dizem que os benefícios da IA superam os danos, contra 39% nos Estados Unidos. Os benefícios chegam até as pessoas e os riscos tem responsáveis identificados que respondem por eles.
Voltemos à frase de Chen Deli. Os combatentes não são dois países, mas duas formas de organizar a inteligência. Os pesos abertos dos modelos são decisivos para a decisão de que lado estará a maior parte do mundo: qualquer governo, cooperativa, escola ou empresa pode baixar os pesos, implantá-los em suas próprias máquinas e adaptá-los à sua própria língua e às suas próprias leis. A equipe do DeepSeek Harness diz o mesmo sem palavras de ordem: quer que mais empresas e organizações do mundo todo implantem seus modelos e lucrem com isso.
Esta coluna começou, há um ano, com uma pergunta feita por Tica Moreno: a inteligência artificial pode servir ao povo? Um ano depois, a meu ver, a pergunta começou a encontrar sua resposta: pesos, frameworks, chips e sistemas de inferência que qualquer um pode tomar para si, ganharam uma batalha e estão abertos a todos. Há mais de setenta anos, quando Mao Zedong disse “por quanto tempo quiserem lutar, nós lutaremos”, o “nós” era uma nação sob bloqueio. Hoje esse “nós” é maior do que o laboratório de Hangzhou que provocou a ordem dos Estados Unidos de eliminação de seu sistema: é cada movimento, cooperativa, escola e aldeia que se recusa a aceitar o cercamento da inteligência. Por quanto tempo quiserem lutar, nós lutaremos, até conquistarmos a vitória completa.
*Jeff Xiong é secretário-geral do Fórum Acadêmico do Sul Global e pesquisador do Instituto Tricontinental de Pesquisa Social.

Opportunities in November 2026
Residencies, fellowships, grants, and open calls from Baton Rouge Gallery, Columbia University, MFA Houston, the Nelson Atkins Museum of Art, and more in our monthly list of opportunities for artists, writers, and art workers.
Hyperallergic’s monthly Opportunities Listings provide a resource to artists, art workers, and creatives looking for funding and community support to further their work.
Subscribe to receive this list of opportunities in your inbox each month. Sign up here!
Awards & Grants
Asian Cultural Council – 2027 Fellowships & Grants
ACC provides artists, arts professionals, and scholars with support for research and cultural exchange between Asia, the US, and within Asia. Read more on Hyperallergic.
Deadline: November 16, 2026 | asianculturalcouncil.org
Lower Manhattan Cultural Council — Manhattan Arts Grants
Manhattan-based individual artists, collectives, and non-profit organizations working across all artistic disciplines, backgrounds, and neighborhoods are invited to apply for project and/or unrestricted grant support.
Deadline: November 12, 2026 | lmcc.net/apply
Queens Arts Fund — Arts Access Grant and the New Work Grants
The Arts Access Grant and the New Work Grant, as part of the Queens Arts Fund, are currently accepting applications through NYFA. These programs are supported through increased city-funded grants for artists through the NYC Department of Cultural Affairs.
Deadline: November 17, 2026 | nyfa.org
Open Calls
Baton Rouge Gallery, Center for Contemporary Art — Surreal Salon 19 Open Call
The annual exhibition celebrating the pop-surrealist/lowbrow movement will share the work of over 60 artists who are hand-picked by juror Lauren YS. $2,000+ in prizes and a Best in Show feature in Beautiful Bizarre Magazine. $35 application fee
Deadline: November 7, 2027 | wearecreativewest.org
Turchin Center for the Visual Arts — Appalachian Mountain Photography Competition Exhibition
Staring at a Glimpse invites artwork that explores haunting in its broadest sense, encouraging work that considers the visible and invisible forces shaping communities and personal histories. Both single- and series-image submissions are permitted. $15 - $20 application fee
Deadline: November 19, 2026 | tcva.appstate.edu
Residencies & Fellowships
Nelson Atkins Museum of Art — Research Fellow, Missouri Remembers Project
In this 12-month fellowship, the selected candidate will conduct original research, write accessible and engaging scholarly content, organize research data and digital assets, coordinate image permissions, and work with Museum colleagues and partners across Missouri.
Deadline: December 18, 2026 | nelson-atkins.org
Museum of Fine Arts, Houston — Core Residency Program
The Core Residency Program awards residencies to exceptional, highly motivated visual artists and critical writers committed to developing a sustainable practice. $12 application fee
Deadline: January 8, 2027 | mfah.org/core
Triangle Arts Association — 2027-2028 Open Call for Residency
Triangle is a residency program based in Brooklyn, New York, that focuses on process, ideas, and building community. In addition to 3-month studio residencies, the program also provides a 3-day intensive focused on the theme “The Fourth Wall.” $10 application processing fee applies
Deadline: December 15, 2026 | www.triangleartsnyc.org
Smack Mellon — Artist Studio
From Sept. 2027 to Aug. 2028, the Artist Studio provides emerging artists with a private studio, shared production facilities, studio visits and open studios, and a fellowship (funding dependent).
Deadline: Dec 1, 2026 | smackmellon.org
Job Opportunities
Columbia University, School of the Arts — Assistant Professor/Associate Professor of Visual Arts (tenure-track)
Candidates must have demonstrated the capacity for creative work and the accompanying pedagogy qualifying them for future nomination to tenure. All disciplines will be considered. Assistant Professor: $108-$115,000, Associate Professor: $115-$135,000
Review of applications: January 10, 2027 | Link to apply

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/eu-china-cap.title: The EU Fears China’s Power Over Private Capital
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/eu-china-cap.author: Alexandra Gerasimcikova
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/eu-china-cap.text:
The EU Fears China’s Power Over Private Capital
Emmanuel Macron celebrated a new EU deal to reduce Chinese car imports as a blow against “unfair competition.” What really troubles European leaders is that China has successfully disciplined its capitalists — something Europe is unwilling to attempt.
To the joy of French and German leaders, the European Union has reached an agreement with Beijing to help alleviate the bloc’s €360 billion trade deficit in goods with China. French President Emmanuel Macron celebrated the deal reached in October, which aims to reduce Chinese hybrid car imports and improve market access for some European products, as a way of protecting Europe from “unfair competition.” Further measures to rebalance EU-China trade are being discussed.
To be sure, China’s exports are a challenge for Europe’s struggling industries in more ways than one. Its industrial giants are increasingly struggling to sustain exorbitant profits and dominate in its traditional markets, including China, where consumers are now increasingly turning to cheaper Chinese products.
Volkswagen’s historical restructuring is a case in point. Rather than increasing investment in research and development to produce smaller, cheaper electric cars, Volkswagen continued milking its old business model, distributing €20 billion to shareholders over the past three years. Now, with profit falling by 9.5 percent to €3.5 billion in the second quarter of 2026, the carmaker has abandoned its collective agreements with unions and announced plans for four factory closures in Germany along with one hundred thousand job cuts globally. All the while, Volkswagen aims to increase its operating profit margin from around 4 percent to whopping 8–10 percent by 2030, citing investors’ return expectations.
But fearmongering over China’s trade surplus with the EU and its supposedly “unfair” subsidies tends to obscure Europe’s discomfort with China’s political economy.
Take German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for example, who says China “deliberately combines its market-driven dynamism with state intervention, overcapacity, aggressive pricing, an undervalued currency, and heavily subsidized exports.” Amid Merz’s accusations of unfair competition lies the real problem: China’s system entails a level of political intervention in the economy that European leaders are unwilling to enforce on capital at home.
State-Owned Enterprises
The first place to look when trying to understand China’s system is the foundational role of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in its economy. Since opening up its economy to private capital and global markets from 1978 onward, China has maintained a strong network of SOEs. While their share in industrial production decreased over the past decades, they comprise 62 percent of total SOE assets worldwide. Europe follows with a mere 14 percent, after decades of privatization substantially reduced public ownership.
The strength of SOEs lies in their ability to operate beyond profitability as the central objective. That does not mean they are unprofitable, but they can prioritize long-term and capital-intensive investments where returns are low and uncertain.
With leadership appointed by the Communist Party of China (CPC), SOEs are central to China’s industrial strategy and form what is called the “lifeblood of the national economy” in sectors like energy, transportation, and finance. They also support employment stability by maintaining jobs during economic downturns instead of carrying out mass layoffs, which has an anchoring effect on employment in associated industries. In addition, SOEs train a large number of engineers who later move into private manufacturing and technology firms. According to China’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council (SASAC), SOEs account for more than 70 percent of assets in strategically important sectors.
This makes SOEs a powerful industrial policy tool — especially when they include giants such as China’s State Grid Corporation, the world’s third-largest company by revenue, which delivers an essential economic input: electricity. Thanks to robust public investments into transmission and generation guided by political objectives rather than just profitability, China has achieved the world’s highest electrification rate. In parallel, it has established global leadership in clean technologies, producing renewable energy that increasingly powers its industrial development. After focusing on coal-intensive growth of manufacturing and heavy industry, China now has a major advantage in scaling up electricity-hungry sectors such as AI and robotics, the next realms of global “competitiveness.”
The Asian electrostate stands in a stark contrast to Europe’s reliance on private investment and market profitability to drive the rollout of renewable power. Europe has the capacity to expand its lending to a public renewable electricity system, for example through its European Investment Bank and the European Central Bank. But conservative interpretations of these institutions’ mandates, coupled with fears of “crowding out” private capital, have denied the public sector a more active role in decarbonization. Meanwhile, fossil fuel companies’ interests continue to shape the European energy market.
The problem is that the EU’s green transition plan, the Green Deal, was designed from the outset to make the transition profitable for private capital rather than to plan long-term, strategic investment. When that failed to materialize at the desired scale, green policies have been increasingly rolled back across the bloc. This is evident from the EU’s current deregulation agenda aimed at “cutting red tape” for businesses — which in practice means dismantling workers’ rights and environmental protections.
As a result, European industrial electricity prices are twice as high as those in the United States — and 50 percent higher than in China. Its electrification rate has been rather stagnant over the past decade, matched unsurprisingly by a slow progress in electric mobility and the decarbonization of industries such as steel. Worse, some European industries are even rejecting subsidies for green investments for lack of profitability.
Public-Private Economy
The second major difference is the relationship between the public and private sectors in China and the EU.
In China, public and private companies don’t simply operate in parallel. Deeply connected through industrial clusters, they can share the benefits of SOEs’ political mandates and their access to cheap financing from public banks. Private companies are part and parcel of the country’s socialist market economy. According to figures cited by Xi Jinping in 2018, the private economy accounted for 60 percent of GDP and provided over 80 percent of urban employment.
At the same time, the state maintains a considerable degree of control over private capital. Market access remains restricted in some sectors, such as finance, telecommunications, or health care. Recently, China has also launched a historic tax recovery campaign on its companies. One of its largest agricultural conglomerates, for example, should reportedly repay a sum amounting to 120 percent of its 2025 profits.
Unthinkable in today’s Western economies, many Chinese private companies, especially large ones, have CPC units within their structures that help align business with party priorities and national objectives. They date back to 1994, when company law introduced the ambition to establish the CPC units to serve as a “fighting fortress in the non-public economy.” They appear to be concentrated in sectors where SOEs are more present, ranging from manufacturing and finance to real estate and high tech.
Private companies are linked to SOEs through industrial clusters and special economic zones, created in 1980 as test sites for markets with private and foreign capital. With significant state support, these zones bring together public and private resources to reap the benefits of integrated supply chains, joint research institutions, and skilled workers. SOEs also build supporting infrastructure — electricity networks or high-speed rail interconnections — which increases their chances to grow economies of scale and lower production costs. Today the government continues to embrace this model as a way to develop strategic clusters beyond manufacturing of the 2000s toward high-tech development zones.
One example is the Greater Bay Area, a city cluster that includes Shenzhen, China’s first special economic zone launched in 1980 and now home to companies such as consumer electronics giant Huawei and carmaker BYD. In 2017, national and provincial governments of Guangdong, Macao, and Hong Kong launched a development plan to transform the region from a traditional export-oriented and low-cost manufacturing area into a global innovation and technology hub, including ambitions to provide good living standards and ecological conservation. While still in development, the Greater Bay Area has become a key site for electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, and humanoid robotics. According to Professor Cai Huajie of Fujian Normal University, the area’s total economic output reached 14.79 trillion yuan (around $2.21 trillion) in 2024, placing it close to that of the New York area, the world’s largest metropolitan economy.
State Subsidies With a Plan
When CATL — now one of the world’s leading battery manufacturers — opened in Ningde in 2011, provincial and local authorities helped develop a supply chain of component manufacturers to support its business, which now includes over ninety companies. In turn, CATL helped create one of the world’s leading battery manufacturing hubs that has shaped the city’s economy.
State subsidies and protectionist measures shielding domestic battery production from foreign competition surely played a role in CATL’s rise. But unlike Western governments that are reluctant to use subsidies as a strategic and time-bound tool within a long-term industrial plan, China adjusts them as industries mature. In 2018, China lifted its foreign equity cap on manufacturers of new energy vehicles, and those produced by foreign enterprises gradually became eligible for the same consumer subsidies as domestic models. Subsidies were scaled back, and national purchase subsidies for consumers were phased out at the end of 2022. CATL invested further into research and development to adapt to the less protective environment. When demand for electric vehicles slowed in 2023, CATL cut battery prices to help automakers boost sales and secure its market share.
Naturally, the state has a much bigger stake in this mixed economy. This also means that the private sector’s production and sales are in effect included in a form of public planning that goes beyond “market signals” — particularly in sectors where China competes with foreign companies.
For instance, following the slow rise of companies such as BYD, the government launched the “Ten Cities, Thousand Vehicles” pilot project in 2009 to introduce at least one thousand electric vehicles annually into the public transport system of ten cities. BYD, now the world’s largest electric vehicle manufacturer by sales, was one of the electric bus suppliers for the project. In Shenzhen, this project helped the city achieve 100 percent fleet electrification by 2017.
This approach is now extended to robotics. The Robot+ application plan, developed by sixteen governmental agencies and the Ministry of Industry and Information in 2023, promotes the innovative use of robots in manufacturing, health care, eldercare, and other sectors. China’s 2025 AI+ plan similarly supports adoption of artificial intelligence by SOEs for aviation fatigue detection, health monitoring, operations of the State Grid’s power lines, and other uses.
Financing and Shared Investment Funds
The benefits of China’s public-private ecosystem are also evident when it comes to financing. China’s robust public banking system and its cheap loans are one part of the story. The other is equity: in China, companies in which the public sector holds over a quarter of the shares make up almost half of market capitalization. Across the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), this level is just 2 percent.
But both public and private capital are actively used for equity investment. China has created thousands of government guidance funds to pool finance from governments, public banks, and public and private companies. These funds provide long-term, patient capital but also an avenue to generate returns while sharing high investment risks. One of the largest such funds is the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund to help China achieve self-sufficiency in semiconductors.
Compared to Europe’s de-risking model, consisting mostly of loans and guarantees, the scale of public sector equity ownership is striking. According to OECD data, China’s public sector held around $3.5 trillion in listed equities in 2023, 79 percent of which was owned by national and local governments. Europe’s public sector held $1.3 trillion, with around half of it owned by governments. In the United States, the figure was $1.6 trillion, and most of the listed equity belonged to public pension funds and foreign-owned sovereign wealth funds.
Far from increasing joint and strategic public spending, the EU is heading in the opposite direction. As negotiations are underway on its next multiyear budget for 2028–34, several countries, including Germany, demand radical cuts in the spirit of austerity. These could reduce the budget’s real value by 10 percent compared with the current one. Yet as the Green Deal retreats, military spending — not investment in a productive economy — is growing dangerously.
What Does This Mean for Europe?
Learning from the successes of China’s “socialism with market characteristics” doesn’t mean that Europe should imitate China’s industrial policies and try to win the race for global market dominance. The massive scale of production and resource use that such competition would require is bound to have a range of destructive consequences for workers and the planet.
Europe’s current leaders are already showing what this race would look like. After returning from China, Merz advised that, instead of work-life balance, “we simply have to do a little more now.” Workers are increasingly squeezed as working hours are pushed up across Europe, along with austerity cuts to pensions, unemployment, and public services. But as Mariana Mazzucato has demonstrated in her study of Europe’s three hundred largest publicly listed nonfinancial corporations: labor costs aren’t the problem in the European economy. It’s the failure to reinvest corporate profits, an electricity system not fit for decarbonization, and a lack of public ownership.
The wave of mass strikes and protests across Europe over collapsing school systems, housing shortages, and the intolerable cost of living is a predictable consequence of the EU’s misguided approach. Workers, young and old, demand socially necessary investments that the pursuit of “competitiveness” simply can’t deliver.
Instead of sacrificing collective bargaining achievements for which the working class struggled for centuries, Europe should think beyond “Made in Europe” protectionism and start nurturing its industries — above all by reining in big capital and directing it into productive investments. With this strategic approach, it can also tap into opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation with China on technologies necessary for a low-carbon economy.
Cracks are emerging in the current obsession with competitiveness amid collapsing public investment. The Left can take this moment to campaign for a socialized economy based on public ownership, workers’ decision-making, and people’s real needs — not dividends, export markets, or the production of utterly unnecessary products such as AI-powered kettles or flying cars. Here, China’s political economy can provide some useful lessons, though Europe must create its own path.

The Whitney Museum of American Art has appointed Nolan Jimbo as Arnhold Associate Curator. He begins his new role organizing exhibitions, public programs, and publications on November 16.
Jimbo comes to the Whitney from the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago (MCA), where he served as an assistant curator with a focus on Asian diasporic artists and abstraction. While in Chicago, Jimbo organized solo exhibitions of the work of Gregory Bae and Mike Cloud, as well as Kenzi Shiokava’s first institutional solo show. He also contributed to the group exhibitions “Dancing the Revolution: From Dancehall to Reggaetón” (2026) and “Forecast Form: Art in the Caribbean Diaspora, 1990s–Today” (2022).
Jimbo also worked as co-director of the MCA DNA Research Initiative, a multiyear program that commissioned interdisciplinary scholarship, digital content, and public programs focused on the museum’s collection and archives.
“Nolan is a star among a new generation of curators with fresh perspectives on art both past and present,” Scott Rothkopf, Alice Pratt Brown Director of the Whitney Museum of American Art, said in a press release. “His work moves fluidly between exhibitions, performance, and scholarship, and his expertise in Asian diasporic artists will add to new narratives in American art. We are thrilled to welcome him to the Whitney.”
Before the MCA, Jimbo held curatorial positions at the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art (MASS MoCA), where he organized “Close to You” (2021), a group exhibition focused on kinship, and the Dallas Museum of Art, where he produced a mural commission by Nicolas Party in 2016.
Jimbo replaces Rujeko Hockley, who co-curated the 2019 Whitney Biennial, among other exhibtions.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/texa.title: Warnings About ICE at the Polls Risk Their Own Kind of Voter Suppression
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/texa.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/texa.text:
Anxiety over ICE at the polls is a double-edged sword for the Trump administration: There’s the fear that federal immigration agents will illegally descend on voters, and there’s the threat that by boosting awareness of that fear, activists and journalists will help the federal government carry out the work of voter intimidation.
“Even just rumors of [ICE at the polls] are going to spread fear. That’s not what we want,” said Daniela Padilla, deputy director at Texas for All, a statewide coalition of organizations working on democracy and justice issues. “Even your reporting around, ‘We’re watching for ICE at the polls’ — it could scare voters.”
In Texas, a 40 percent Latino state where a longtime Republican grip on power now finds itself in question, there are real concerns that Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents could pop up in targeted communities to make people afraid to go out and vote on Tuesday. But while the possibility of election interference has been discussed as one of several “big ticket items” of this year’s midterms, Padilla said, “the biggest threat that we face in Texas this year is voter suppression.”
That suppression can take many forms. In Tarrant County, for example, where local officials closed 92 polling locations, reports from early voting indicated some election officials wrongly turned away eligible voters. More than fearing ICE would actually approach the polls, Padilla and several organizers working on election integrity and voting rights in Texas told The Intercept they were worried that journalists amplifying the Trump administration’s stated plans to “surround the polls” with ICE and federal agents could function as an inadvertent form of voter suppression.
Federal and state law prohibits federal immigration agents from being inside polling sites and bar any form of voter intimidation. Those laws haven’t stopped the Trump administration and its allies from threatening to deploy ICE and military personnel around the country during elections. In August, the Department of Justice announced that it planned to send at least 1,000 federal monitors to oversee midterm voting, prompting multiple states to assert they would not let them inside polling locations. As states like Maine prepared to respond to the federal presence at the polls, the DOJ claimed to Newsweek it “never said” it would send federal law enforcement to the polls.
“The Trump administration has been spreading fear for months, refusing to say that they will not send ICE to the polls,” said Emily French, policy director at Common Cause Texas. “I think that the main function of this discussion around ICE at the polls from the Trump administration is scaring people into staying home on Election Day.”
According to Brianna Brown, executive director of the Texas Organizing Project, disinformation efforts are a common voter-suppression tactic in Texas. “So we’re trying to reassure people it’s safe to vote,” she said.
Texas is home to one of the most dramatic potential Senate upsets in the country, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico leading in the polls over the state’s scandal-plagued Republican attorney general Ken Paxton in a race that could see Texas end up with a Democratic senator for the first time since the ’90s. And the 32 million-person state has enough voter suppression strategies even without ICE in the picture, Brown said, pointing to a 2021 bill that banned drive-through voting, weakened protections for disabled voters, and gave more power to poll watchers appointed on behalf of a candidate or political party.
“Texas is just like a perfect storm,” Brown said.
When ICE showed up at a polling site in San Antonio in May — marking the first known case of ICE at the polls in the country during this year’s primaries — the county sheriff kicked the agents out. Even then, it did not appear that the federal agents were targeting someone in the process of voting; they had arrived at the scene shortly after state police, with whom they work closely, pulled someone over in the polling site’s parking lot.
That day, staff at the Texas Organizing Project and a group of civil and voting rights organizations working as part of the Texas Election Protection coalition helped coordinate outreach to the local sheriff to get ICE removed from the site.
The state coalition is part of a nationwide effort to protect this year’s elections from interference — federal or otherwise. In Texas, the Lawyers’ Committee and several other groups including the Barbara Jordan Leadership Institute, Common Cause Texas, and the Texas Civil Rights Project have been training people to help make sure voters know their rights on Election Day and that they report any instances of voter intimidation — whether an eligible voter is wrongly turned away or someone spots ICE — to a national hotline.
“We want to inform people, but we don’t want to scare them from coming to the polls,” said Khanay Turner-Osborne, executive director of the Barber Jordan Leadership Institute. She said she hasn’t heard much concern about ICE showing up around polling sites in Tarrant County, where she’s based and where people can vote at any polling site in the county. But still, for voters in hotspots of ICE activity and other forms of voter suppression, the group has told them to consider voting at a different eligible site, she said.
The group wants to help people prepare, Turner-Osborne said. “But I don’t want it to be in a way that deters people from voting.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘Mariko Mori anticipated the zeitgeist’: curator Alexandra Monroe on her new show and how Japan's art scene has changed
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Andrew Maerkle
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The US curator Alexandra Munroe has three decades of experience working closely with Japanese institutions, going back to her landmark survey Japanese Art after 1945: Scream Against the Sky at the Yokohama Museum of Art in 1994. Now she is back in the country as the co-curator of the current Mariko Mori retrospective at the Mori Art Museum in Tokyo. The show is a collaboration with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, where she is a senior curator at large, and has been co-curated with the Mori Art Museum’s director Mami Kataoka.
The Art Newspaper: How has Japan’s museum ecology changed over the years?
Alexandra Munroe: It’s changed enormously. The Yokohama Museum of Art opened in 1989, anticipating the museum boom of the 1990s when municipalities and prefectures across Japan were opening new institutions with extraordinary buildings designed by architects like Fumihiko Maki, Arata Isozaki and others.
Although there were important precursors like the Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura, established in 1951, and the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, established in 1952, there was remarkably little concerted historical understanding of Modern and contemporary Japanese art and its role in global art history. Around the early 1990s, curators and scholars were piecing together how such art had evolved under the umbrella of post-war society—defeat in the Second World War, reconstruction, Americanisation—as well as through the contributions of Japanese artists abroad like Yoko Ono, Yayoi Kusama and On Kawara. The new museums contributed to the tremendous growth of the field, both within Japan and internationally.
Successive institutions have built on that legacy. It’s been gratifying to see the Mori Art Museum develop into a global museum under the trailblazing leadership of Mami Kataoka. The recent Sou Fujimoto exhibition was one of the greatest architectural shows I’ve ever seen, while the solo shows of Louise Bourgeois, Ai Weiwei and Lee Bul, going back 20 years now, are among the most influential for those artists staged anywhere in the world.
All of this has been aided by the simultaneous transformation of the gallery scene, with a proliferation of experimental galleries since 1994, not to mention international galleries representing Japanese artists or movements like Gutai, Mono-ha and Neo-Pop. I also appreciate the role that Benesse Art Site Naoshima has played, through the vision of patron Soichiro Fukutake, in the emergence of Japan as a contemporary art superpower. Only a few hundred people attended the opening of Benesse House Museum in 1992. Now events like the Setouchi Triennale draw millions to the islands when the home population is a few thousand. And Benesse’s commissioning programme has given artists like Yukinori Yanagi, Rei Naito and Shinro Ohtake a platform for staging their most ambitious works.
Recent decades have seen a remarkable expansion of museums in China and Korea, Southeast Asia and the Gulf. At the same time, institutions around the world are facing new challenges with austerity measures and a withdrawal of public support for art. What lessons can Japan offer other art scenes?
I have great admiration—and some envy—for the public funding of Japanese art museums. The Japanese model of collecting regionally yet within an international context is something to emulate. There’s also something to be said for collections focusing on artists whose histories were shaped by the places where they grew up and, in some cases, ran away from. The Nagoya City Art Museum has extraordinary holdings of On Kawara’s works, including rare early reportage pieces, even though he left the region in his teens. The Ashiya City Museum of Art and History’s collection of Gutai is unparalleled in the world. And the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, under the guidance of curators like Kuroda Raiji, has sought to map and reimagine artistic exchanges in Asia.
I commend all the brilliant scholarship that has emerged out of these enterprises.
That said, in recent years Japan has retreated from its post-war identification as an international country. One motivation for doing the Mori show is to stimulate a revival in collaborations that can help bring the work done in Japan into international circulation.
Collaborations between Japanese and international institutions typically take the form of touring shows, whereas intensive co-productions are rare. How did the collaboration between the Guggenheim and the Mori Art Museum come about?
It’s called synergy! In the summer of 2024 both Mami Kataoka and I had begun talking to Mariko Mori about staging a retrospective and we combined forces. Mariko rose to meteoric stardom in the 1990s for Cyborg (1994-95), the first of her series of photomurals inserting herself as a cyborg, and later a Buddhist-inflected deity, into digitally rendered settings. That interest in technology subsequently found form in complex multisensory environments like Wave UFO (1999-2002), the first artwork to incorporate brainwave biofeedback.
I was interested in reappraising Mariko’s work in the current context of technology-based art, specifically digital technologies. Technology is not an obstacle to humanism for her, but a means of envisioning a new kind of humanism that allows for higher states of consciousness. At the same time, Mariko’s engagement with [pre-historic Japanese] Jōmon culture, alternative belief systems and the afterlife resonates with Indigenous and First Nations artists incorporating Indigenous knowledge into critiques of Western epistemes of modernity and linear time.
For her part, Mami has a longstanding interest in art that addresses spirituality in the modern era, which opens up a critique of the dominant trends of contemporary art as established by market forces and Western institutions, so I think Mariko’s work felt urgent to that curatorial research and practice.
It’s a creative partnership.
Yes. Collaboration is integral to Guggenheim programmes like the Asian Art Initiative and the UBS MAP Global Art Initiative. We have consistently partnered with museums, curators and artists across Asia to help us collectively think through the larger argument of global art history and how to present exhibitions that map histories and ideas beyond the Eurocentric canon. The collaboration with the Mori is a direct outcome of that, and I’d say it’s a direct outcome of the Mori’s profoundly international outlook as well.
A compelling retrospective does not just look back but also shows how the artist was ahead of their time. In what ways have we finally caught up with Mariko Mori?
Mariko’s work resonates with the writings of the contemporary philosopher Yuk Hui, who argues for a holistic understanding of technology grounded in Eastern thought and cosmologies, or “cosmotechnics”, as opposed to its bifurcation in modern Western traditions. Mariko anticipated that zeitgeist as a Japanese woman artist who conducted deep research into schools of thought like Pure Land Buddhism and Jōmon cosmology alongside contemporary sciences of the mind.
These are areas of enormous interest to artists now. Look at LuYang, a young Chinese artist who is a serious practitioner of Tantric Buddhism and uses game engines to illustrate themes of transmigration of the soul, multiple selves and the world as an illusion. The Korean new media artist Ayoung Kim also looks up to Mariko for unabashedly drawing parallels between art and technology as ways to “recalibrate our reality”, as Ayoung told me.
I think there will be an enthusiastic response to Mariko’s work from younger artists who are interested in storytelling and altered states of mind, artists who are seeking to break free of the lingering hang-ups of Western art, and anyone looking to just get away to another world.
• Mariko Mori: All That Shines, Mori Art Museum, 31 October-28 March 2027
