https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-officers.title: NYPD officers shoot man after exchange of gunfire outside Bronx deli, police say
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-officers.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-officers.text:
NYPD officers shot a man in the Bronx on Monday afternoon after he fired at them, police said.
The shooting occurred around 3:20 p.m. near Bainbridge Avenue and East 194th Street in the Bronx, police said. The NYPD advised the public to avoid the area near 2657 Bainbridge Ave. and expect road closures and delays.
Police said Victor Soto, 49, had been involved in a dispute with several people inside Sammy Gourmet Deli, where he pulled out a firearm and pointed it at people inside, causing them to duck for cover.
The man then left the deli and began walking northbound with the gun in his hand, slamming it against the deli's glass window, according to police.
The NYPD said two officers arrived at the scene and ordered the man to drop the gun. Police said he ignored their commands and instead pointed the firearm directly at the officers.
This led to "an exchange of gunfire between the officers and the subject," according to NYPD Assistant Chief Aneudy Castillo, who spoke at a news conference Monday evening.
"As the subject is discharging his weapon, he is continuing northbound and firing behind him in broad daylight with civilians in the area," Castillo said.
Officers shot the man and took him into custody, police said. Soto was hospitalized in stable condition and is expected to survive, according to Castillo.
Attorney information for Soto was not immediately available.
Castillo said the incident was captured on police body cameras and surveillance cameras both inside and outside the deli. He said police also relied on eyewitness accounts in describing what happened.
The NYPD's Force Investigation Division is reviewing the shooting.

https://hyperallergic.com/a-midterm-elec.title: A Midterm Election Guide for Artists and Arts Workers
https://hyperallergic.com/a-midterm-elec.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/a-midterm-elec.text:
A Midterm Election Guide for Artists and Arts Workers
Issues touching on arts funding, censorship, AI regulation, and more are at stake for the country’s cultural sectors across key Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races.
Midterms are tomorrow, marking the first nationwide election since President Donald Trump started his second term in the Oval Office. In the wake of Trump’s financial and ideological crackdowns on Smithsonian, unapproved pet projects around the US Capitol, devastation to cultural landscapes through border construction, and dozens of other policies targeting history and heritage, many will be lining up at the polls with arts and culture policies on their minds.
Because Congress ultimately decides appropriations for federal arts entities, such as the National Endowment for the Arts, control of the House and Senate is incredibly important for the cultural sector. (Republicans currently have narrow majorities in both chambers.) From artists running for Congress, like Claire Valdez in New York and musician Bobby Pulido in Texas, to longtime culture advocates like Angie Nixon in the Senate race, we zeroed in on some of the key campaigns to watch in the United States if you care about artistic freedom, affordability for artists, and cultural funding.
We've organized this guide into three sections: Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races. Click through each section below.
Rebecca Schiffman and Lisa Yin Zhang also contributed to this guide.
Senate Races
Michigan
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by an average of five points in one of this election cycle’s most-anticipated races. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and the former head of the Detroit and Wayne County health departments, has been subject to repeated racism and culture war tirades over his Muslim faith and criticism of Israel by Rogers and President Trump throughout his campaign. Rogers, a former FBI agent and United States Representative, was endorsed by Trump in July 2025 and has received major funding from pro-Israel lobbying groups during this election cycle.
Here’s what you should know.
- At the center of Abdul El-Sayed’s platform is “Medicare for All,” which he co-authored a book guide on with Micah Johnson in 2021. This is particularly relevant for artists, among whom only 84% have access to health insurance, according to a 2023–25 survey by the National Opinion Research Center. El-Sayed also believes “unions are one of the most important bulwarks for the dignity of work in a moment when AI is coming for a lot of that.” He has been a member of the National Writers Union, the SEIU (Service Employees International Union), the AFT (American Federation of Teachers), and the Michigan-founded UAW (United Auto Workers), which represents workers at museums including Manhattan’s Museum of Modern Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
- Mike Rogers has routinely aligned with President Trump on key issues. Encore, a local Michigan performing arts news outlet, notes that “his congressional majority is the one that proposed zeroing out the federal arts education funding,” making his contrast with El-Sayed’s across-the-board pro-educational funding initiatives “not subtle.” Also in opposition to his Democratic opponent, Rogers has fiercely fought Medicare for All proposals and has consistently battled against UAW in Congress.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Meu futuro não cabe em uma barraca’: atos contra especulação imobiliária em Portugal crescem apesar da repressão
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Telesur
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Longe de apaziguar o descontentamento popular, a intervenção violenta da Polícia de Segurança Pública (PSP) nas primeiras horas da segunda-feira (2), em Lisboa e no Porto, alimentou a indignação pública contra a crise habitacional em Portugal.
A repressão brutal nas primeiras horas da manhã deixou quase 100 feridos e 13 presos por “desobediência”. Esses casos começaram a ser avaliados pelo sistema judiciário, enquanto movimentos sociais convocavam vigílias de solidariedade.
Centenas de pessoas estavam desde domingo (1º) na icônica Praça do Rossio, na capital, e em locais de protesto no Porto. Elas instalaram acampamentos e exigiam a retirada imediata da controversa proposta do governo para a lei de aluguel, que elimina os tetos de preços e facilita despejos em massa.
O novo encontro noturno, que transcorreu em grande parte de forma pacífica, com assembleias populares e eventos culturais, teve um momento de tensão após a explosão de um rojão e a subsequente perseguição de um indivíduo por manifestantes que o identificaram erroneamente como um agente infiltrado.
Os manifestantes, entoando slogans como “Meu futuro não cabe em uma barraca”, exigem a revogação da lei, o congelamento dos aluguéis, o fim dos despejos e demolições e um aumento substancial na oferta de moradias sociais. Eles também questionam o impacto do turismo de massa na valorização imobiliária em seus bairros.
As manifestações massivas em Lisboa e em outras cidades portuguesas são uma resposta a uma explosão de descontentamento social causada por uma grave crise habitacional e pelo aumento generalizado do custo de vida, uma situação agravada pelas recentes reformas promovidas pelo governo do primeiro-ministro Luís Montenegro.
Como principal método de luta, diversos grupos de cidadãos ocuparam espaços públicos importantes, como a Praça do Rossio, na capital, instalando acampamentos urbanos que desafiaram repetidamente as ordens de despejo forçado.
Esses protestos, que contaram com o apoio ativo de partidos portugueses de esquerda, como o Bloco de Esquerda e o Partido Comunista Português, foram estrategicamente intensificados em frente à Assembleia da República para coincidir com o debate sobre os orçamentos do Estado, procurando pressionar os legisladores a abandonar as políticas de austeridade e a enfrentar a emergência social que priva a população de habitação digna.

Dutch art historian, critic, and curator Rudolf “Rudi” Fuchs died in Amsterdam on October 25 at the age of eighty-four. A former director of the Stedelijk Museum and one of the Netherlands’ most influential museum leaders, Fuchs was an early proponent of placing works of different periods and styles in conversation with one another. Refreshingly novel in the 1970s, the curatorial approach frequently earned him pushback from traditionalists. “To me, the combination was powerful and exciting, he said years later. “That’s why I did it—so that I, and the public, could see things from a fresh perspective.”
“[Fuchs] was not simply a museum director or a curator,” wrote Belgian artist Jan Fabre on social media. “He was a passionate observer, a storyteller, a man who understood that art must remain alive, unpredictable and free.”
Rudi Fuchs was born in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, on April 28, 1942. From 1967 to 1975, he studied art history at Leiden University, concurrently producing critical art essays, beginning in the late ’60s. In 1975, at the age of thirty-two, he was named director of Eindhoven’s Van Abbemuseum, becoming the youngest person ever to occupy the role. He immediately established himself as a collection-shaping force—at a time when contemporary American art held sway in the continent’s museums, he instead focused on acquiring contemporary European art, especially that from Germany, Austria, and Italy.
In 1982, Fuchs was named artistic director of Documenta 7 in Kassel, becoming the first—and, to date, only—Dutch person to lead the quinquennial. Featuring just a single video—Dara Birnbaum’s PM Magazine, 1982—and abounding with sculpture and paintings, including those by Georg Baselitz, Joseph Beuys, Daniel Buren, and Keith Haring, the exhibition was marked by controversies including boycotts, claims of censorship, and cronyism.
The show split critics, with one lauding it as a “palace of pleasure” and others deriding it as too apolitical or too Western-centric. “To its detriment, the angry, the thoughtful, and the serious are juxtaposed with many trivial young artists, betraying a lack of attention on Documenta’s part,” wrote Annelie Pohlen in Artforum that year, while Edit DeAk, in the same publication, lamented that the exhibition “wasn’t about art.” Fuchs was unconcerned. “My attitude is that artworks touch one another and deal with one another, just as people do on the street,” he said later.
In 1984, Fuchs accepted the role of director of the Castello di Rivoli in Turin, which he held until 1991. In 1987, while still at the Turin institution, he was named director of the Hague’s Gemeentemuseum, known for its massive, heterogenous collection of art, and especially for its trove of Mondrians, the largest in the world. His stint there, ending in 1993, was not entirely successful, as he left the museum roughly 4 million guilders (about $5.8 million in 2026) in the hole. He would later acknowledge that he had “no talent for administrative affairs.”
In 1993, Fuchs was named director of the Stedelijk Museum. While there, he continued his practice of eschewing wall labels, and of showing unlike works in complementary pairings, as in the series “Couplets,” which exhibited historical works from the collection alongside contemporary pieces. In yet another prescient move, this one predicting today’s appetite for starry guest curators, he often reached beyond the art world in asking people to organize the museum’s exhibitions, notably inviting Queen Beatrix to do so on one occasion.
“There are all kinds of influences: the new youth culture, Internet, new countries entering the discussion—New Zealand, Australia, China,” he told Robert Leonard in 1998, explaining his directorial philosophy. “And you can’t say to China; ‘This modern art thing is ours, is West European, is North American.’ . . .The solidity and the authority of the traditional canon is failing. It’s coming apart like an old ship, creaking and starting to leak, and the mast falling down,” he continued. “It’s a good time to start the new contemporary art.”
The Stedelijk became mired in financial woes, in part brought about by an over-ambitious expansion plan, and Fuchs departed in 2003, embarking on a career as a teacher and writer. He returned to the Stedelijk as a guest curator in 2016, when the museum mounted an exhibition, titled “Excitement,” highlighting his curatorial accomplishments there, at the Van Abbemuseum, and the Gemeentemuseum.
“Fuchs brought a clear, uncompromising vision to Amsterdam, rooted in a fundamental belief in the autonomy of the artwork and the direct encounter between the viewer and the art,” said Rein Wolfs, the current director of the Stedelijk in a statement. “Through his acquisitions, presentations, and publications, Rudi made a significant contribution to the understanding of art; everything he did served as an encouragement to really look.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Russia’s security service detains teen over alleged terror plot targeting Moscow museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sophia Kishkovsky
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Russia’s FSB security service has detained a teenager on charges of threatening Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve via TikTok after an unusual warning from US officials of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” on 31 October. The alert was posted on the website of the US embassy in Moscow and social media. Der Spiegel reported that German citizens in Russia had received a similar warning.
On 1 November, the FSB distributed a video, published on sites such as Tass, the official state news agency, showing an unidentified young man being detained, footage of a knife, camouflage and neo-Nazi content on his phone, and his confession to posting “propaganda of Nazism” on his TikTok page. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee posted the same footage to its YouTube channel.
The US issued a similar alert several days before an attack that killed at least 149 people in March 2024 during a concert at Crocus City Hall in Moscow. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack; before it occurred, Russian President Vladimir Putin denounced the warnings as “outright blackmail”.
In a change reflecting US President Donald Trump’s cooperation with Russia, the FSB in a statement on 1 November, posted on the agency’s website, credited “US law enforcement agencies” for warning of an impending attack at Tsaritsyno: “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”
The FSB statement added that “in the interest of public safety, planned cultural events at the museum-reserve have been cancelled, and security measures in the surrounding area have been stepped up”. The museum is typically closed on Mondays, while the surrounding park, known for its rolling hills, fountains and wooded paths, is open daily. Russian media reported that the park reopened on Sunday.
The FSB’s statement claims the detained minor had posted images on TikTok “showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, cap, eyewear and headset—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon” as well as “photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, accompanied by the caption: ‘I found a place’”.
The complex, which was originally intended as a summer residence for Catherine the Great in the 18th century, is consistently ranked as one of Moscow’s most visited tourist sites. Tsaritsyno’s website states that over 7 million people visit the museum and park in southern Moscow annually. The Grand Palace, its centrepiece, is known for its neo-Gothic design by the architect Matvey Kazakov, which remained unfinished after Catherine’s death. Many other buildings on the grounds were designed by Kazakov’s teacher, Vasily Bazhenov, Catherine’s court architect, who was initially commissioned to design the palace before falling out with the Empress.
Some preservationists denounced the glitzy completion of the palace, inaugurated in 2007 with Putin present. It was carried out under Moscow’s mayor at the time, Yury Luzhkov, who was known for monumental construction projects. Although some attempts have been made to show contemporary art at Tsaritsyno, its exhibitions are primarily focused on the tsars and historic Russian folk crafts.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Public Hospital Leaders Warn of ‘Crisis’ from Federal Medicaid Restrictions
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Trenton Daniel, Healthbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Healthbeat. Sign up for their public health newsletters at healthbeat.org/newsletters.
Leaders from New York City’s public hospital system anticipate a crisis of coverage as federal healthcare policies force hundreds of thousands residents to lose their Medicaid plans.
Drs. Ted Long and Jonathan Jiménez of NYC Health + Hospitals offered a preview this week at a City Council oversight hearing of the turbulence the NYC Care program could see as Medicaid work requirements take effect Jan. 1. Overseen by NYC Health + Hospitals, the nation’s largest public healthcare system, NYC Care is a healthcare program for low-income New Yorkers and will assume the role of last resort for residents who lose their Medicaid or insurance coverage.
“This will be a crisis,” Long, senior vice president and chief medical officer for clinical services and population health at Health + Hospitals, said at Wednesday’s hearing. “We’re going to move heaven and earth to do as much preparation as we can.”
New York City public hospital leaders say they are increasing staffing for NYC Care, ramping up outreach, and connecting with influencers to prepare for an influx of patients because of federal health policy changes. Health + Hospitals officials declined to say more about the influencers, including if they are being compensated.
Former Mayor Bill de Blasio launched NYC Care in the Bronx in 2019, and it later expanded to all five boroughs. It guarantees low-cost and no-cost services to New Yorkers who do not qualify or cannot afford health insurance based on federal guidelines, which includes undocumented immigrants who are excluded from Medicaid and other public programs. The aim of NYC Care is to connect uninsured New Yorkers to a primary care physician before their health worsens and they end up in the emergency department.
NYC Care members pay on a sliding scale, and there are no premiums, deductibles, or co-pays. More than 90% of enrollees receive an appointment with a primary care provider at one of the Health + Hospitals locations within two weeks of enrollment, Long said.
After primary care, speciality services include cardiology, rheumatology, orthopedics, podiatry, mental health and substance abuse services.
NYC Care enrollment peaked at more than 143,000 in 2024, but enrollment numbers have since dropped. As of Oct. 23, enrollment stood at 125,766, Long said Wednesday.
Long and others at NYC Care attribute the overall drop to aging participants switching to Medicaid. The latest Mayor’s Management Report said Health + Hospitals had heard anecdotally that local immigrants are becoming increasingly reluctant to share their personal information with government agencies.
The city’s public hospital system has already seen disruption brought on by federal policy changes. On July 1, 450,000 New Yorkers lost coverage through the Essential Plan after the state narrowed insurance eligibility for some of its low-income members. The Essential Plan offers a low-cost insurance plan to New Yorkers who earn too much to qualify for Medicaid but may struggle to afford private plans sold through the state health insurance marketplace.
As of Aug. 30, 41% of the members who lost Essential Plan coverage on July 1 had not enrolled in another plan through the state marketplace, according to the state Health Department, potentially leaving some without insurance. A Health Department spokesperson said Wednesday those numbers haven’t changed.
On Wednesday, Queens Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers asked if NYC Care had seen an increase in the number of enrollees because of the elimination of the Essential Plan tier that covered New Yorkers making up to 250% of the federal poverty line.
“Thousands of them — on the level of thousands went into NYC Care,” Long said. “This gave us a lot of clues about what doing a good job is and how we can, you know, get ready for the Medicaid transition.”
Officials declined to provide a specific number.
Long said the program could take in as many as 20,000 new patients. Its annual budget is $100 million.
To learn more about the program, New Yorkers are urged to call 1-646-NYC-Care (646-692-2273).
Trenton Daniel is a reporter covering public health in New York for Healthbeat. Contact Trenton at tdaniel@healthbeat.org or on the messaging app Signal at trentondaniel.88.

D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités.

                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application

                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The False Promise of Bob Woodward
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Richard Kreitner
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The False Promise of Bob Woodward
He’s always been known as an intrepid journalist. But critics in The Nation, throughout decades, identified ways he held important stories for his own gain.
The False Promise of Bob Woodward
He’s always been known as an intrepid journalist. But critics in “The Nation,” throughout decades, identified ways he held important stories for his own gain.
“Sometimes people have a vision of themselves that just doesn’t fit with reality,” Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward writes in his new memoir, Secret. For example, he does not feel the public’s understanding of him as “‘all business’ and cold” is quite right. But the problem is deeper than that. Woodward has always presented himself as a fearless and committed truth-teller, intent on getting to “the center of what was really going on.” Repeatedly, however, Woodward’s books, purporting to bring readers into the inner operations of the US government, have obscured more than they revealed.
Decades of reviews in The Nation of Woodward’s books show the consistent flaws and oversights that have marked the journalist’s work, not least a habitual reliance on the tropes and trivialities of inside-the-Beltway access-mongering. Jefferson Morley spotted the tendency early, reviewing Woodward’s 1987 book, Veil: The Secret Wars of the C.I.A., 1980-1987, which largely focused on Reagan’s CIA director, William Casey. “Woodward has not so much misreported his story as misinterpreted it,” Morley argued. Training his attention on minute “power struggles” between top officials, Woodward “tends to neglect the more fundamental and important news,” such as the Agency’s support for the contras in Nicaragua, which became international news while Woodward was reporting his book. Instead of telling readers about what the US government was actually up to—including the crimes that high officials were committing—the journalist focused on petty personal squabbles: “Because there was not much dispute among Woodward’s high-level sources about routine C.I.A. support for contra operations, he had no controversy to report on. No high-level controversy, no story.”
The excerpt of Woodward’s new memoir that recently ran in The New Yorker purports to recount a time when he courageously chose to publish the unvarnished truth about infighting within the George H.W. Bush administration, at the cost of losing a close friend who had been his source for the story. But Morley’s review highlights a consistent thread throughout Woodward’s career: His closeness to sources has often won out over a commitment to printing the truth. “Woodward probably has more access to top government officials than any other Washington reporter,” Morley noted. “But access always—always—has a price. Veil confirms that the more access a reporter has, the higher price he or she pays.” Indeed, Woodward himself acknowledged that he did not have the time to pursue the contras story because he was busy talking to Casey for the project that turned into Veil.
Reviewers have often pointed to the glaring lack of background information in Woodward’s supposedly immersive political narratives. Assessing 1991’s The Commanders, framed as an unparalleled glimpse into the (first) Bush administration’s deliberations on the eve of the (first) invasion of Iraq, Jon Wiener observed that “the book’s fatal flaw is that it contains virtually nothing about the political context in which Bush made up his mind in favor of war”— for instance, that his decision to invade was motivated by a sluggish economy and slumping poll numbers ahead of an important midterm election.
But Wiener identified an even worse problem with Woodward’s book, one that would keep cropping up throughout the journalist’s career: his tendency to keep a lid on important stories until the moment was right for him. In the run-up to the first Gulf War, it would have been useful for the public to know that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff was opposed to an invasion. Wiener asked, “What did Woodward know and when did he know it?… Why did that information become Woodward’s private property, which Simon and Schuster would sell to us months later for $24.95? The information Woodward possessed would have been a powerful weapon for the antiwar movement…. Woodward has privatized the news.”
As the Reagan era segued seamlessly into the reign of Clinton, Nation critics objected more strenuously to Woodward’s customary tricks and tics. Reviewing The Agenda, in 1994—a “work of intensive stenography,” about the early years of the Clinton administration—Christopher Hitchens wrote, “The portentous vacancy of neoliberal argot has met its chronicler in one who takes it seriously.”
Woodward’s next book was The Choice, a nearly 500-age tome about the 1996 election, which happened to be published months before that election. Republican challenger Bob Dole “cooperated readily” with the author, as Lynn Phillips wrote in her Nation review, while neither President Clinton nor first lady Hillary Clinton agreed to do so, an imbalance that Woodward never quite managed to rectify, as Phillips wrote: “And when a reporter gets so close to his candidates that he speaks from inside their mouths (Bob Dole, c’est moi!), his reportorial glasses fog up.”
Woodward’s glasses were especially foggy in the early years of this century. His 2003 book Bush at War, about the months after the September 11 attacks, was appraised in The Nation by Washington editor David Corn: “Woodward stuck with what has become in recent years his standard MO: Approach each power player and say, ‘All the other power players are telling me their side of the story, so you should do so as well.’ Woodward then weaves the various self-serving versions—supplied, of course, on background—into a quasi-official chronicle, with little overt sourcing.” While his Watergate investigations “excavated a story the big shots didn’t want public,” Woodward’s later work related only “what the powerful do want known.”
And so on, through the Obama, Trump, and Biden years, and into our own abysmal present. Most recently, in 2025, Matthew Duss, executive vice president at the Center for International Policy, assessed Woodward’s book, War, about the Biden administration’s handling of conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine. As Duss wrote, “Woodward consistently fails to interrogate any of what he is told, choosing instead to simply record and relay it and allow his readers to assemble the picture as they wish, as if the real journalistic feat was just getting the decision-makers and insiders to talk to him in the first place.”
Despite the self-serving accounts in his memoir, Woodward remains, as he has long been, a conduit for largely meaningless internecine battles among elites, a glorified stenographer haplessly doing the bidding of the powerful even while he presents himself as a heroic crusader for the vitality of the Fourth Estate. It’s a vision of himself that doesn’t fit with reality, even if Woodward’s first-draft accounts of history have done all too much to shape it.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-early-vot.title: NYC early voting dips compared to 2025, but spikes in majority-Black districts
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-early-vot.author: Brigid Bergin, Joe Hong
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-early-vot.text:
The Mamdani bump did not extend into 2026.
A year ago, a record number of New Yorkers turned out for early voting, fueled by an uptick in young and first-time voters energized by Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor.
This year, the numbers tell a different story. Early voting in New York City dipped by about 13% compared to last year’s surge. The drop was due to lackluster turnout among early voters between the ages of 18 and 24, since 15,000 fewer young people showed up to vote early.
Analysts say the numbers bode well for Democrats, who have voted early at seven times the rate of Republicans in New York City. Early-voter turnout among Democrats dropped by 3% from last year, but turnout among Republicans dipped even more with a 15% decline.
Gov. Kathy Hochul, who’s hoping to fend off a challenge from Republican Bruce Blakeman, has campaigned aggressively throughout the five boroughs, particularly over the nine days of early voting, making multiple appearances with Mamdani to try to animate the electorate that sent him to office. But some of the drops in the city’s early voting turnout were in parts of the city where Mamdani overperformed last year.
Neighborhoods in Brooklyn that are considered part of the Commie Corridor saw the biggest drops in voter turnout. Assembly District 53, which includes East Williamsburg and Bushwick, saw a decline of 34% drop in early voter turnout
“ No one is Mamdani,” said Fordham political scientist Christina Greer. “He has a certain level of populism, like a Donald Trump, that people come out for the individual.”
Districts that saw the biggest increases in voter turnout compared to last year were largely Black majority districts, in keeping with a national trend that’s seen higher rates of Black early voter turnout across the country.
Analysts say the turnout should serve as a reminder that even as the Democratic Party expands its tent, Black voters remain a crucial constituency.
“ Black voters tend to be a stronghold for the Democratic Party and will continue to be that even with the rise of the DSA,” Brooklyn-based Democratic strategist Lupe Todd-Medina said. “ I'm not gonna be surprised to see some lines out the door because there are still those that want to vote on Election Day.”
Todd-Medina, who worked for Hochul’s 2022 campaign and Lieutenant Governor candidate Adrienne Adams’s mayoral campaign last year, said Black voters are energized to come out to the polls for people like Adams, state Attorney General Letitia James and in parts of Central Brooklyn, to re-elect Rep. Hakeem Jeffries.
Jeffries could become the first Black Speaker of the House and the first Speaker from New York City if Democrats win majority control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
Turnout in Assembly District 58 in Central Brooklyn, which overlaps with Jeffries’ congressional district, had the largest increase in early voting, with a 60% increase compared to 2025. The district spans the neighborhoods of East Flatbush, Canarsie and Brownsville. The district population is nearly 80% Black, according to census data analysis by the CUNY Mapping Service at the City University of New York's Graduate Center.
Southeast Queens is home to a concentration of Black voters who are also disproportionately Democratic voters. Districts there turned out in lower numbers last year but saw increases in voter turnout so far in this election.
Assembly District 29 in Queens saw an increase of over 47% in early voting compared to last year. The district includes neighborhoods like Jamaica, Hollis and Springfield Gardens. The neighboring Assembly District 31 also saw one of the steepest increases in turnout, with a 40% increase. The district contains the Queens neighborhoods of Far Rockaway, South Ozone Park and Rosedale.
Overall turnout was also up among older voters. The number of voters 55 and older increased by 14% compared to last year. Voters 75 and older saw an increase of 23%.
Overall, early voting turnout is up in the state and citywide compared to four years ago, as voters continue to acclimate to a system that was first introduced in 2019. Early voting turnout statewide increased from 1.2 million to two million compared to 2022, and in the city from more than 432,600 voters to 690,000.
Last year’s surge in early votes continued into Election Day, with New York City seeing the highest turnout for a municipal election in more than five decades.
Greer said the Mamdani effect helped catapult democratic socialist and left-leaning candidates who were aligned with him ideologically in the June primary. The mayor was an ardent supporter of Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander, who are all expected to win their congressional races on Tuesday.
However, Greer said it may be harder to motivate voters on the left who see Hochul as too moderate, despite Mamdani’s endorsement.
“ There's a certain special sauce that Mamdani has that Hochul doesn't, and he's doing his part as a good Democrat to sort of say, ‘Listen, we're not the same ideologically, we do have some differences, but, you know, I endorse this woman because she's exponentially better than the alternative.’”

https://hyperallergic.com/10-art-books-t.title: 10 Art Books to Curl Up With This November
https://hyperallergic.com/10-art-books-t.author: Hyperallergic
https://hyperallergic.com/10-art-books-t.text:
10 Art Books to Curl Up With This November
Celia Paul’s latest essay collection from Venice, Salman Toor’s painted worlds, the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg, a new Roy Lichtenstein catalog for old fans, and more.
The publishing industry is already preparing for spring, but we're still stuck on all the delights and challenges of this fall's slate of art books. Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara recommends an exploration of Marxist revolutionary Rosa Luxemburg's secret garden of pressed plants, an art form in its own right; critic Natalie Weis sinks into painter Celia Paul's kinetic prose. Catalogs on Salman Toor, Roy Lichtenstein, and more to discover below. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor
Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, edited by Alex Da Corte and Meg Onli | Whitney Museum of American Art, November 3
In this publication, the Whitney frames its Roy Lichtenstein show as a “radical” picture as “never before,” made up of a “novel” selection that is “genuinely new” to an audience “newer than ever” (emphasis the museum’s). But the catalog, inspired by the composition notebooks the artist kept to gather inspirational clippings, doesn’t feel academic or overstuffed, and includes beautiful plates — in other words, it’s easy, clean, and classic, all the reasons we’ve always loved Lichtenstein. —Lisa Yin Zhang
Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice by Celia Paul | New York Review Books, November 17
Celia Paul writes much like she paints, excavating shimmering insights from familiar subjects, in prose that is as haunting and luminous as her portraits. In this memoir, she uses a Venetian residency to examine her relationship with her deceased husband, mother, and first lover (the unnamed Lucian Freud). Grief, guilt, death, and desire stalk the artist through the city’s narrow corridors; once more, Paul seeks self-knowledge through art, literature, and the act of painting. —Natalie Weis
Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond by Arlene Dávila | Duke University Press, October 13
Arlene Dávila begins where most mainstream criticism of Latinx art ends: by challenging the term itself. The professor and curator’s ninth book continues her decades-long critiques of perfunctory “Latinx representation” through shrewd essays on indie filmmakers, fashion designers, and artists — such as Edra Soto and Ela Troyano — who refuse the tropes imposed on their work and often operate outside of the Los Angeles and New York bubbles. Her insights are a reminder to question the narratives that “make Latinx culture palatable for mainstream culture,” to always dig deeper. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pa.title: Pace CEO Marc Glimcher Responds to Reports of Financial Losses, Says Gallery Will Open New Location in Europe
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pa.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pa.text:
Pace Gallery’s CEO Marc Glimcher is looking ahead and washing over the headlines over the last week regarding the gallery’s financial accounts.
“We’re all off the bottom, we just had a record art fair at Art Basel Paris, and we’ve had sellout shows of primarily young artists—everything is turning,” he told ARTnews in a phone interview on Monday, noting that the business is already back in the black and will open a new location in Europe “fairly soon.”
Pace Gallery has been shifting its real estate portfolio recently. Back in June, Pace’s London property was put on the market, with the gallery saying it was seeking a “less corporate” space in the British capital, while in September, Pace announced it was seeking tenants for part of its Chelsea headquarters. Glimcher reiterated that London remains a “great market.” He added, “London is working very well. We are never going to close in London.”
He said that many galleries use the city as an international hub where “a lot of work gets done managing Asian and European units. It’s a great place to have headquarters and it carries a lot of weight the way New York does.”
Glimcher hinted that he already has “a couple of amazing choices” for Pace’s next London property, The gallery is currently situated on Hanover Square, taking up 8,600 square feet. The gallery will be “about the same size, and we’re going to a more prime location that fits the model we’ve been working on,” said Glimcher, contending that the business has “done a lot of internal reengineering of the way the companies work together” and that the success of its arms in Berlin and Japan have been “very instructive” to the overall strategy of the business.
Pace Gallery published its 2024 accounts last week with Companies House, the British government’s business register. The filing was 10 months late and recorded a turnover of $67.7 million in 2024, a 35.5 percent drop from 2023, which cashed in $105 million. A pre-tax loss of $2,429 was recorded for 2024 compared to a $6.8 million profit for 2023. (The mega-gallery’s UK registered company, The Pace Gallery Limited, serves as the umbrella company for its operations in Europe and Asia, excluding Tokyo as well as the US.)
Shortly after that, Pace Gallery’s 2025 accounts were published, with turnover dipping 2.6 percent to $65.9 million. “We did a balance sheet shift, which appears to be a loss because we’re changing around the way we invest money and take money from other units and let the money flow through each unit independently,” said Glimcher. “We’re in a process of keeping those units a little more autonomous and self-sufficient, to do that, you have to shift the balance sheet.”
In June, the gallery laid off 50 staffers and dropped 50 artists from its roster, including Keith Coventry, TeamLab, John Gerrard, and Glenn Kaino. (Pace now represents a total of 85 artists.) But now that the dust has settled, Glimcher said the gallery is ready for new life.
“We’re always adding artists and the artists that left the roster were artists [who] we were really not working with,” he said. “There were areas that we were really not engaged with, it wasn’t benefiting them or us. They were not artists that we had a super active engagement with. It’s just about focusing your efforts to do less better than doing more not as well.”
Glimcher said that all galleries have been making changes of late and—at least, for Pace—new strategies are starting topaying off.
“We have had an extremely profitable year already in Los Angeles. The things we’ve done are already bearing fruit, and they’re bearing fruit because the market has substantially changed,” he said. “What we’re doing in London, when we have the space and announce it, it’s going to make a lot of sense to everybody.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Irã propõe reabrir Estreito de Ormuz em dois dias e retomar negociações com EUA
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Opera Mundi
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governo do Irã afirmou nesta segunda-feira (02) que pode reabrir o Estreito de Ormuz em até dois dias e retomar as negociações com os Estados Unidos, desde que Washington aceite as condições apresentadas por Teerã. A proposta é uma versão reduzida de um plano de sete etapas apresentado em setembro e está sendo discutida por canais diplomáticos com a participação de Catar e Paquistão.
Em entrevista à agência estatal iraniana Irna, o ministro das Relações Exteriores, Abbas Araghchi, afirmou que as conversas com os mediadores são intensas. “Se os Estados Unidos aceitarem nossas condições, o Estreito de Ormuz será reaberto e as negociações serão retomadas”, disse.
A proposta foi detalhada pelo porta-voz da chancelaria, Esmaeil Baghaei. Ele afirmou que o plano pode ser implementado em dois dias, mas que a reabertura da passagem marítima depende do atendimento prévio das exigências iranianas. “O Estreito de Ormuz não pode ser reaberto enquanto o bloqueio não terminar e as demandas do Irã não forem atendidas”, afirmou, de acordo com a Tasnim.
Entre as principais exigências iranianas estão o encerramento das operações militares em todas as frentes, o fim do bloqueio naval dos Estados Unidos aos portos iranianos, o descongelamento de ativos do Irã mantidos no exterior e a suspensão das sanções contra o setor petrolífero do país.
Araghchi também mencionou a necessidade de estabelecer, em acordo com Omã, uma nova rota de trânsito pelo estreito, além de reduzir a presença de tropas estadunidenses na região e suspender sanções impostas desde agosto.
Até esta segunda-feira, não havia confirmação de que os Estados Unidos tivessem aceitado as condições iranianas. O presidente estadunidense, Donald Trump havia rejeitado a proposta de sete etapas apresentada em setembro. Na última semana, o governo iraniano passou a considerar de forma pública uma nova ação militar dos EUA, apesar da continuidade dos contatos diplomáticos.
Plano de sete etapas
A proposta atual deriva de um plano de sete etapas apresentado por Teerã em setembro. Na versão inicial, o cronograma previa a reabertura do estreito no sexto dia e a retomada das negociações no sétimo. Após consultas com representantes do Catar e do Paquistão, o governo iraniano afirma ter reduzido o prazo para dois dias.
As tratativas ocorrem por meio de intermediários, principalmente Catar e Paquistão. O vice-ministro das Relações Exteriores iraniano, Kazem Gharibabadi, esteve em Doha para facilitar a troca de mensagens com Washington. Uma delegação iraniana deixou o Catar no domingo, após conversas com representantes cataris. Segundo autoridade ouvida pela Reuters, uma minuta de proposta está circulando e uma nova reunião ainda poderá ser realizada.
O porta-voz Baghaei confirmou que as mensagens entre os dois governos continuam sendo transmitidas por mediadores. Ele também disse que a proposta de sete etapas, agora condensada, permanece como base das conversas.
Teerã defende que as condições relacionadas ao bloqueio, às sanções e à segurança sejam atendidas antes da retomada das negociações sobre o programa nuclear iraniano. Washington quer que a questão nuclear esteja incluída nas conversas desde o início. Segundo a Reuters, o governo iraniano também rejeitou a possibilidade de transferir para outro país seu estoque de urânio altamente enriquecido.

Participating exhibitors at Art Basel Paris are demanding compensation for the fair closing two days early on October 23 due to security concerns over planned protests the next day. The fair was scheduled to take place from October 23-25 with VIP previews occurring in the days leading up.
As per Artnet News, the Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA), an industry group representing over a quarter of the exhibitors, wrote an open letter on October 28 with their demands addressed to Karim Crippa, director of Art Basel Paris. In the letter, which was reviewed by Artnet News, CPGA wrote: “The decision to close the fair was made by Art Basel Paris, and by Art Basel Paris alone.”
The letter described the decision as one that caused “profound incomprehension,” among dealers and other exhibitors. This cost them two days of business, which, as per the dealers, warranted “fair compensation.”
Although many dealers suspected that the fair would be closed on Saturday, the decision to remain shut on Sunday came as a surprise. Dealers also told ARTnews that they were informed of the closure at 3:30 p.m. on Thursday. As a result, they had little time to decide whether to pack up or hold tight until things calmed down in Paris.
The letter added that other fairs such as Design Miami Paris, AKAA, and Offscreen stayed open on Sunday. Signed by CGPA president, Philippe Charpentier (co-founder of the Paris gallery Mor Charpentier) the letter featured the signatures of 14 other dealers, including Michel Rein, Christophe Gaillard, Nathalie Obadia, Jocelyn Wolff, and Magda Danysz.
Additionally, CGPA also noted in the letter that it had a more collaborative relationship with Art Basel Paris’s earlier management. CGPA later told Artnet News that Christopher Miles from France’s Ministry of Culture is organizing a meeting to discuss the demands between Art Basel Paris, CGPA, and GrandPalaisRmn, which operates the Grand Palais, the fair’s venue.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Objects reinstalled at Museo Nacional de Colombia following removal by right-wing government
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Mercedes Ezquiaga
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Bogotá’s Museo Nacional de Colombia has reinstalled the 63 objects previously taken down from its permanent galleries over claims of “political indoctrination”. The move followed a court order that reversed the national government's removal of the items on 15 October.
On the evening of 28 October, César Enrique Osorio Ortiz—a judge at Bogotá’s 24th Family Court—ordered Colombia’s cultural ministry and the museum to return the works to their original locations within 48 hours. The ministry complied with the order on Friday (30 October).
The decision came in response to a constitutional-rights case filed by cultural groups and political opponents who had accused the government of the country's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella of censorship. The judge also ordered both institutions not to remove works based on their content or the views they express.
Among the removed pieces were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo, a pen made from a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 peace agreement between the state and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.
The removals came amid calls by De la Espriella for a “cultural war” and a “direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture”, an offensive that affected the country’s main museum.
The government’s decision sparked a series of protests during which hundreds of people gathered outside the museum, as well as a joint statement by six museums expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of their professional autonomy. The signatories included the Modern art museums of Bogotá, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellín and Tolima, as well as the Museo Rayo.
Marielsa Castro Vizcarra, the chief curator of the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (which signed the joint statement), tells The Art Newspaper that the cultural sector responded quickly, from street protests to the statement and the involvement of the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art. Castro described the incident as “a precedent we need to take into account” and “an authoritarian way of spreading fear”.
According to the judge's ruling, the artefacts had been removed “without a documented curatorial justification” in a decision that “disregarded the constitutional protection of cultural expressions”. The court did not rule out future changes to the exhibitions, provided they are properly justified and not based on the authorities’ objections to the works’ content.
“No government owns our history!” wrote Gabriel Becerra, a left-wing lawmaker behind the constitutional-rights case, in a post on X welcoming the court’s decision.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Admin Intervenes on Eviction, a First Use of New Deed Fraud Law
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
For the first time, Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration used a new law to intervene on behalf of a Brooklyn family facing eviction they say is because of deed fraud.
But the move may not have worked.
A city lawyer filed papers Friday to try to prevent the impending eviction of a family in order to examine a possible underlying case of deed fraud or theft related to the historic Crown Heights brownstone where they live.
But a Brooklyn housing court judge declined to grant the stay, writing in a filing that two courts had already litigated the deed theft allegations.
An eviction could take place as soon as this week. The City Law Department is evaluating next steps, according to spokesperson Nick Paolucci.
The family, including Helen “Queen Afua” Robinson and her grown children Sherease and Ali Torain, have been fighting to keep their home for over a decade. They alleged their late grandmother Ida Robinson, who purchased the home with her husband in 1968, was a victim of deed theft.
“After all this time, I was hoping for something totally different and unfortunately this happened,” said Sherease Torain on Sunday evening from her stoop, where over 30 locals gathered to speak about the situation and plan to stop a possible eviction by physically blocking the home.
“It really breaks my heart that I started this in my 30s, now I’m in my 40s , and I’m not too far away from my 50s,” she continued. “This is what it does to you — it steals time and that’s something you can never get back.”
The ongoing saga has played out across multiple lawsuits over the years, as the family tried to reclaim the property deed and the current recorded owner of the home attempted to kick them out. In the past, local tenant organizers have kept watch over the stoop to prevent previous eviction attempts — and at one point, helped the family re-enter the home after the owner changed the locks.
New Law to Halt Eviction
The Friday filing marked the first time city lawyers had intervened in court to halt an eviction related to possible deed theft under a state law. In 2023, state lawmakers had updated the law to allow for government entities to motion for a stay — to prevent eviction — in order to investigate matters where deed theft or fraud may have taken place.
Philip Schaffroth, the chief of detectives at the Office of the New York City Sheriff supported the request for a stay, as the city Department of Finance’s Bureau of Investigation looks into a claim of deed fraud. The Mayor’s Office of Deed Theft Prevention referred the case to the finance agency’s investigators in September, Schaffroth wrote in court documents.
He said the investigation would include a records review, interviews of the parties involved and subpoenaing bank records.
The law states that if a government motions for a stay, the court “shall issue a stay” of the proceeding in the face of an ongoing investigation. But a Housing Court judge, Javier Ortiz, did grant the request
“Any new investigation constitutes futility of process with an inevitable and obvious conclusion,” Ortiz wrote.
Edward Mostoller, director of the Homeowner and Consumer Debt Advocacy Project at the City Bar Justice Center who is not involved in the proceedings, said he was “surprised” by the judge’s decision to not grant the stay.
“Like with many newly instituted legal protections for consumers and homeowners, it will take efforts to educate our courts to promote greater awareness and a more uniform (and proper) interpretation of these new laws,” Mostoller wrote in an email.
Disputed Deed
The dispute over the deed stems from a deal Ida Robinson appears to have made in 2015. Property records show she sold the home to an LLC, which transferred the property to another LLC and then to Menachem Gurevitch, who is the owner according to current property records.
Robinson and her family became tenants in the home. They have alleged in court documents that the deed was forged. Gurevitch, who is associated with the companies Mandy Management and Netz Capital Management, moved to sue the family for eviction, but they have continued living in the home.
Gurevitch and his lawyer did not respond to an emailed request for comment and in a brief call, Gurevitch’s attorney Pamela Smith declined to comment. In court papers, they have denied the family’s allegations. In a letter to the court after the city filed its paperwork, Gurevitch’s attorneys called the move “an eleventh hour ploy” to delay eviction.
Previously, both the New York Attorney General’s office and Brooklyn District Attorney’s office have investigated the matter regarding the brownstone. Neither office brought criminal charges.
Deed theft happens when the title to a home is stolen without the homeowner’s approval or knowledge. It can involve forgery, fraud or other tricks. A lawyer who examined the case in 2022 — whom Attorney General Letitia James referred to the family — determined the situation could be a “foreclosure rescue scam,” a scheme where an entity claims to help a property owner who is behind on their mortgage but exploits them instead.
Deed theft has been an ongoing issue in New York City, especially in gentrifying Black and brown communities where home values have skyrocketed. Elderly people have long been targets for predatory real estate schemes.
Deed theft burst into the national spotlight in the spring when Councilmember Chi Ossé was arrested while protesting an eviction of a family at a Bedford-Stuyvesant brownstone, about a mile north of the Crown Heights home at the center of the Robinson’s fight.
Ossé — along with Inez and Charles Barron, both former members of City Council and the state Assembly — appeared at the stoop of the Crown Heights home Sunday evening.
Editor’s note: This article previously stated that Ida Robinson had once fallen behind on her mortgage. It has been updated and corrected.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Lula’s Victory! Bolsonaro’s Defeat! What’s Next for Brazil?
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: James N. Green
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Lula’s Victory! Bolsonaro’s Defeat! What’s Next for Brazil?
A leading Brazil scholar predicts that Trump will continue to meddle in Brazilian politics.
On October 25, Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a momentous, come-from-behind victory over the candidate of authoritarianism, Flávio Bolsonaro. The dramatic electoral outcome has generated a wave of hope in Brazil and beyond; Lula’s win is widely perceived as a rebuke to the march of ultraconservative forces throughout Latin America and to the Trump administration’s flagrant attempts to bolster Bolsonaro and assert US control over Brazil’s political and economic future. Referencing US interference, Lula declared in his acceptance speech that his victory demonstrates that “this country does not accept being anybody’s backyard.”
Flávio is the 45-year-old son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup to stay in power when he lost the presidency to Lula four years ago. Like his father, Flávio has refused to concede his loss. Under investigation for corruption and money laundering, this week he fled Brazil and, on Trump’s order, was allowed free passage into the United States. Hoping for US support to install him in power, Bolsonaro promptly declared himself “president-elect” of Brazil, even though he lost the election by over 4 million votes. The mainstream Brazilian media has accused Bolsonaro of “coup-mongering.”
To understand the implications of these dramatic events, The Nation placed a call to one of the leading international experts on Brazil, Brown University professor emeritus James Green, in São Paulo. This, with a bit of editing for clarity, is what he told us.
—Peter Kornbluh
The Nation:  Lula’s win is being heralded as historic. How do you interpret this unexpected and extraordinary victory for the first Brazilian to be elected president for a fourth time?
James Green: It is historic. I think it solidifies Lula as the greatest politician in Brazilian history. But there are reasons for this historic victory.
It is important to note that the first round of voting on October 4 took place amid one of the biggest corruption scandals in Brazilian history—the discovery that the head of a major bank, Banco Master, was bribing numerous Brazilians in the political world, including members of the Supreme Court. [Bolsonaro himself has been implicated in this scandal.] This caused tremendous distraction from the electoral process, and Lula’s campaign was quite lackluster; consequently, he lost the first round of voting by 1.9 points to Bolsonaro, leading to the runoff election on October 25.
After the October 4 vote, Lula’s campaign was in shock for a day, and then they turned it around. In less than three weeks, they did three key things to win the final election runoff.
The first was to carry out massive demonstrations in all the major cities of the country—huge, big demonstrations. This created a feeling of energy and community, and the possibility of winning with massive numbers of people in the streets.
The second was building a very effective social-media campaign. A pro-Lula congressman, André Janones, who is a very energetic and dynamic person, transformed his WhatsApp channel into a “Lula’s Army” website, which quickly garnered 10 million followers. This allowed the campaign to reach out through the Internet and to circumvent the algorithms that Meta was using to favor Bolsonaro’s campaign. For the first time, the left dominated the right on social media.
And the third initiative started spontaneously but then became a key part of Lula’s electoral campaign: asking supporters to draw up a list of friends and relatives whom they could convince to flip their vote or just get out and vote. The campaign targeted 16- to 18-year-olds, who can vote but don’t, as well as people over 70 who are not required by law to vote. There were wonderful videos on social media of people bringing their grandmothers to the polls, wearing their red Workers’ Party shirts and voting, of course, for Lula. This campaign helped bring 4 million people who had not voted in the first round to the polls for the runoff. And Lula won by about 4.5 percent, or about 4.5 million votes.
The night he won, there was just a huge, amazing celebration. It was as if Brazil had won the World Cup! It was that amazing.
TN: As you know, the defeated candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to concede and then fled into exile in the United States with the help of the Trump administration. (President Trump personally ordered that Bolsonaro be given “a pass” so he could enter the country.) As soon as he arrived in Miami, Bolsonaro cried “electoral fraud” and declared that he was the “president-elect” of Brazil—Brazil’s true “leader.” What do these political machinations mean for the aftermath of the election?
JG: It is still too early to know what Trump’s plan is with Flávio Bolsonaro, but I think Marco Rubio is interested in creating an exile government to pressure and weaken Lula’s administration. I imagine that they will impose more sanctions against Brazil, including on members of the government—performative sanctions against Brazil and some actual economic sanctions on the country.
But it is all going to backfire. There is a tremendously strong nationalist sentiment in the country. People are really questioning Bolsonaro’s commitment to Brazil since he refused to concede the election results and left the country. And because of the mass mobilization around the elections, I think there will be a lot of energy around mobilizing against any serious US measures to punish Brazil for this situation.
That said, Trump’s plan appears to consist of applying pressure from the United States, creating an alleged exile government in the United States, and also pushing the new Brazilian Congress, in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party now has a majority, to pressure Lula’s government—including efforts to impeach him. So it is going to be a very rough time for the new Lula administration. There is going to be tremendous pressure from the far right against it.
TN: Trump tried to put his thumb on the Brazilian election and engineer a victory for Bolsonaro. What, in your opinion, has motivated him to take such a keen interventionist interest in Brazil?
JG: The answer to that question lies in the Trump administration’s broader strategic plan for Latin America. Trump wants to return to a neocolonial time when there are spheres of influence and Latin America clearly belongs to the United States. He wants to put Latin America—Central and South America and the Caribbean—under the thumb of the United States again, reassert the Monroe Doctrine and US hegemony in the region.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
That means controlling the economies of Latin America to provide markets and materials to the United States. And in Brazil’s case, also guaranteeing US access to rare earth minerals, which Trump has fixated on controlling. Brazil has the second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals in the world. Trump wants that. And Flávio Bolsonaro offered that to him.
There is also the issue of Cuba. At the end of the day, I think the big goal of both Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio is to destabilize and bring down the Cuban government. One of the major countries in Latin America that has maintained diplomatic relations and an open and friendly relationship with Cuba has been Brazil.
TN: Lula’s reelection has generated attention all over the world. Beyond Brazil’s borders, what are the regional and global implications of this very important victory over Bolsonaro?
JG: After a period of time when left-oriented, social-democratic governments were elected to power, there has been a counterwave of the far right throughout the region. And that has demoralized the Latin American left, leaving it weakened and disunited.
Now Brazil offers an inspiration. There is a possibility that Brazil could mark the beginning of a new dynamic, a counterswing away from the far right that now dominates countries like Argentina, Chile, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia. Lula’s victory, I think, will inspire others to stay in the fight for social justice and equality, environmental protection, etc., rather than being demoralized about the future. That is an element of this dynamic that will be important.
