https://gothamist.com/news/washington-sq.title: Washington Square Park snowball thrower gets community service for pelting NYPD
https://gothamist.com/news/washington-sq.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/washington-sq.text:
An influencer accused of criminal assault for pelting an officer with a snowball during a viral Washington Square Park snowball fight earlier this year will have his case dismissed for community service.
Manhattan prosecutors on Friday agreed to toss the charges against Gusmane Coulibaly, 28 — AKA “Diaper Man” — if he completes 20 hours of community service for the Parks Department.
The plea deal marks the end of a chapter in the snowball-gate saga. The social media-fueled showdown between a rowdy crowd and police officers sparked a broader debate about Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s approach to public safety. Mamdani downplayed the incident as “a snowball fight,” while NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch called the incident “disgraceful” and “criminal.”
Even Gov. Kathy Hochul weighed in, saying it was “never acceptable to throw anything at a police officer, full stop.”
The NYPD put out wanted photos for four men in connection with the snowball fight following a historic blizzard that dumped 20 inches of snow on the city. Officers arrested Coulibaly a few days later.
Prosecutors in Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office declined to pursue assault charges, instead charging Coulibaly with misdemeanor obstructing government administration and a harassment violation.
Both charges will be dismissed if Coulibaly completes the community service hours. In a prepared statement to the court Friday, prosecutors said, “We believe this disposition is appropriate and consistent with this defendant’s conduct that day.”
Police union officials disagreed.
“We’re not surprised that we’re getting weak justice in this case, because DA Alvin Bragg and Mayor Mamdani made sure of that from the beginning,” Hendry said in a statement. “By downplaying this attack on police officers, the mayor and DA gave this individual a free pass to keep causing chaos on our streets.”
Hendry had appeared at Coulibaly’s arraignment in February, alongside about a dozen uniformed officers.
A second suspect, 18-year-old Eric Wilson, was arrested in March after turning himself in. Wilson pleaded guilty to non-criminal harassment charges in April in exchange for community service, according to the Manhattan DA’s Office.
Coulibaly has continued to have run-ins with police since the snowball fight.
Police arrested Coulibaly on Oct. 8 for allegedly attempting to rob a street vendor in East Harlem. Officers accused Coulibaly of lifting his shirt “to reveal the handle of a firearm in his waistband,” court records show. Coulibaly has pleaded not guilty.
In a video posted to his “Diaper Man” Instagram page on Oct. 22, Coulibaly appears to be arrested by NYPD officers after driving an e-scooter on a sidewalk.
“Took the cops on a lil troll run,” the caption reads.
Coulibaly did not respond to an inquiry. His attorney declined to comment.

https://hyperallergic.com/10-art-shows-t.title: 10 Art Shows to See in Upstate New York This November
https://hyperallergic.com/10-art-shows-t.author: Taliesin Thomas
https://hyperallergic.com/10-art-shows-t.text:
10 Art Shows to See in Upstate New York This November
Julia Whitney Barnes’s organic paradise, Emily Nomer’s mystical geometric paintings, Maria Molteni’s conversations with the divine, and more
As autumn unfolds across the East Coast, people around the United States are visiting the polls. May we strip the monsters of power and steer this nation out of its ghoulish ambiance and toward soulful care, not continued scare. In step with the changing times, a robust round of exhibitions in Upstate New York invites you to experience the treats of the season. At Ipso Facto Gallery in Hudson, artists explore creative modalities for surviving the technological hellscape of contemporary life, while Public Private Gallery presents outrageous sculptural works by legendary artists Judy Pfaff and Michael David. Ann Street Gallery features dynamic works by the three artists chosen for their 2026 Emerging Artist Fellowship, and Tyte Gallery showcases a series of lush botanical works on paper by Julia Whitney Barnes. Geometrically inspired paintings by Emily Nomer at Gallery 40 yield bright mystical visions, while a group show at Yellow Studio Arts Center celebrates the commonplace as muse. To all those who fear these hellish times, no more tricks! We conjure our determination and perseverance in the face of ghastly evil!
The TV Glow Sees Me
Ipso Facto Gallery, 362 ½ Warren Street, Hudson, New York
Through November 22
Remember life before the internet and obsessive screen time? The TV Glow Sees Me presents the work of five artists who consider how to find themselves amid the “technological hellscape of rapid expansion,” as curator Hannah Studnick puts it in the press release. Featuring mixed-media artworks that reflect a digital culture overflowing with miscellaneous mayhem, Jesse Morsberger’s painting “Up Late” (2026) is a faithful embodiment of our current society: A boy sits alone in a dark room facing the eerie glow of an empty screen. In a crimson-hued scene by Mina Watanabe DeVore, “Look Up” (2026), two youthful figures take a selfie in a graffiti-laden bathroom reminiscent of the legendary Manhattan music club CBGB. Other highlights include Jackson Daughety’s “Where is MrBeast When You Need Him” (2023), a gestural abstract work on stitched canvas, and Allyson Packer’s “Subtropolis 02” (2025), a mash-up sculptural work that includes an LED tube behind a sublimation print in which braces-heavy mouths above a car smash into an unknown object in a bizarre vision that defies explanation.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/le.title: Cosmic Leonora Carrington Painting Reemerges at Auction After 70 Years
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/le.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/le.text:
In a dreamy development for the fall auction season, another Surrealist standout has resurfaced on the market. After seven decades out of public view, Leonora Carrington’s Fil d’Or (1953) will appear at Heritage Auctions in New York on November 10, with an estimate of $250,000–$350,000.
Its title translates from the French to “gold thread,” a term traditionally referring to the delicate metal wire used to ornament luxury textiles. The cosmic bird Carrington depicts appears to be composed of intersecting threads, all emanating from a single source: the golden galaxy pulsing in place of a heart.
She employed a technique developed by her former partner, the artist Max Ernst, known as grattage, in which layers of fresh paint are scraped with a blade or spatula. The process exposes unexpected shapes and patterns through texture, creating an impression of spontaneous motion, as though the picture were realizing itself.
“By choosing this title, Leonora Carrington shifts focus away from the obvious. Instead, she redirects the viewer’s awareness to consider coexisting, alternative meanings—in this case, her meaning—by experimenting with how we emotionally respond to different thoughts,” Heritage Auctions wrote in its citation. “Ultimately, Fil d’Or demonstrates that words hold multiple meanings, explores how others perceive them, and questions whether they are truly understood at all.”
Carrington created Fil d’Or in Mexico, to which she fled after the outbreak of World War II in Europe. There, she formed a swift friendship with fellow refugees, including the Surrealist painter Remedios Varos and photographer Kati Horna, over alchemy, the occult, and esoteric symbolism.
Carrington died in Mexico City in 2011, at the age of 94. Although she achieved success in her lifetime as both a visual artist and a writer, female Surrealists have experienced an unprecedented surge in market interest over the past decade, thanks in part to Cecilia Alemani’s 2022 Venice Biennale, titled after Carrington’s book The Milk of Dreams. The market reached a high point in 2024, when Carrington’s 1945 painting Les Distractions de Dagobert sold for $28.5 million at Sotheby’s, setting an auction record for the artist. The sale easily surpassed her previous auction record of $3.2 million, set in 2022.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Janones vai à Argentina para reunião com Cristina Kirchner e grava vídeo no canal ‘Exército do Peronismo’
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O deputado federal André Janones (Rede-MG) esteve na Argentina nesta segunda-feira (2) para se reunir com a ex-presidenta argentina Christina Kichner e com o ex-ministro da Fazenda e ex-candidato peronista à Presidência, Sergio Massa, em um encontro voltado para o alinhamento de estratégias de mobilização digital.
Atualmente em prisão domiciliar, Kichner trava uma disputa jurídica para recuperar seus direitos políticos, apontando ser vítima de uma condenação irregular. Ela afirmou que pretende disputar a presidência de novo, caso tenha sucesso em reverter a inabilitação perpétua para exercer cargos públicos imposta pela Justiça.
Massa, que acabou derrotado por Javier Milei na corrida presidencial de 2023, pretende construir o caminho para também se apresentar novamente como uma alternativa da frente peronista nas eleições de outubro de 2027. Para chegar lá, ele enfrenta uma disputa interna dentro da oposição com Axel Kicillof, atual governador da província de Buenos Aires, que também busca a candidatura ao comando do país.
Selando a aliança, o deputado gravou um vídeo em espanhol para o canal “Ejercito del Peronismo”, que conta com 70 mil seguidores no WhatsApp e 19,7 mil no Instagram. “Vocês vão fazer parte da história da Argentina. Creiam nisso e sigam o exército”, diz Janones em espanhol na gravação. “É possível vencer. Espero que a vitória do presidente Lula inspire a todos os argentinos a dizer: nós podemos derrotar a extrema direita.”
As reuniões na Argentina contam também com os publicitários brasileiros Chico Kertesz e Rafael Marroquim, ex-sócios do ministro da Secretaria de Comunicação Social, Sidônio Palmeira, e que atuaram na campanha de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. O objetivo é analisar formas de replicar no ecossistema político argentino a tática de redes sociais implementada no Brasil, considerada fundamental na vitória petista. As informações são da colunista Mônica Bergamo, da Folha de S.Paulo.
A eficácia do modelo digital articulado por Janones é evidenciada por um estudo da empresa de pesquisa Ipse Global, divulgado pelo Brasil de Fato. A análise comparou a atuação do canal de WhatsApp “Exército de Lula” com o grupo de oposição “Tropa do Flávio”, apontando ampla vantagem da mobilização governista em velocidade, proatividade e escala de integrantes.
Enquanto a comunidade articulada por Janones ultrapassou a marca de 10,5 milhões de participantes, o grupo adversário encerrou o período eleitoral com 2 milhões de membros. O tempo de reação também registrou disparidades significativas: a média de resposta para o cumprimento de missões digitais no canal petista ficou em 3,4 minutos, contra 13 horas e 17 minutos do grupo de oposição. Em termos de velocidade máxima de engajamento, hashtags lançadas pelo “Exército de Lula” chegaram às redes sociais em apenas 19 segundos, ao passo que a resposta mais rápida do lado oposto demandou 24 minutos.
De acordo com Leonardo Magalhães, diretor-executivo da Ipse Global, a diferença técnica esteve na metodologia adotada pelos articuladores. Enquanto a liderança adversária concentrou a emissão de mensagens de forma centralizada e com apelo publicitário tradicional, Janones capacitou a militância por meio de tutoriais, incentivando que os próprios usuários produzissem e distribuíssem conteúdos de forma descentralizada. Para cada internauta ativo no grupo de oposição, cerca de 35 apoiadores se mobilizavam no canal governista.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘Another way of engaging the city’: centrepiece of Art Week Tokyo sends visitors to venues across the capital
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alex Wang
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
AWT Focus launched in 2023 as Art Week Tokyo’s centrepiece exhibition platform. Last year it took place at the Okura Museum of Art, where Adam Szymczyk brought together more than 50 artists for What Is Real? For 2026, the format is being radically reconfigured. In collaboration with Curated by, the Vienna gallery festival, Art Week Tokyo has invited curators to organise ten exhibitions across ten participating galleries and art spaces around the city.
The shift brings AWT Focus closer to the structure of Art Week Tokyo itself. Unlike an art fair, the annual event has no central venue: its network of museums and galleries is dispersed across the metropolis, with free shuttle buses connecting participating venues during the week. Running from 4 to 8 November, this year’s fifth full edition will bring together a record 56 museums and galleries.
“From the start Art Week Tokyo was conceived of as an event that would evolve in dynamic response to the city,” says Atsuko Ninagawa, the event’s co-founder and director. The multi-venue AWT Focus, she says, offers “another way of engaging the city and its diverse audiences”. Rather than organising the programme around a single curatorial proposition, “the idea is to bring multiple worldviews to Japan”.
Those worldviews take varied forms. Among the ten projects are Polish curator Maria Brewińska’s presentation of Japan-born, Poland-based artist Koji Kamoji at Take Ninagawa gallery; Ekow Eshun’s presentation of British-Sierra Leonean artist Julianknxx at the Space Un arts and culture venue; and New York-based curator Augusto Arbizo’s intergenerational exploration of painting at Yutaka Kikutake Gallery. Elsewhere, curators Greg Dvorak and Kenji Ono draw on the contrasting post-war histories of eastern and western Tokyo for the latest edition of the recurring exhibition series The Constitution of Japan, at Mujin-to Production, with a second site at Aoyama | Meguro.
The city becomes part of the show
For Multiple Spirits, the feminist collective founded by Mai Endo and Mika Maruyama, the dispersed format allows the character of the city itself to enter the programme. “Even within the same city of Tokyo, each place and space has a completely different face,” the collective says. “The location, surrounding environment and flow of people differ from venue to venue”, allowing each exhibition to take shape in relation to its surroundings. The collective also sees potential in moving away from a single curatorial voice towards a more open structure in which “different perspectives by many practitioners” can co-exist.
Multiple Spirits’s exhibition at Waitingroom, Patchwork of Ruffled Wings, draws together zines, textiles and other works through what the collective calls a “vine-like archive”, connecting “girls’ culture, queer culture, artistic movements, underground culture and social movements”. Rather than arranging these histories into a linear genealogy, Multiple Spirits is interested in how cultures are interrupted, inherited or grafted onto others, and how they are shaped by changing social conditions, taboos and forms of resistance. Art Week Tokyo, it suggests, can itself become a site where people with different backgrounds and practices meet, allowing different perspectives to connect while retaining their complexity.
The collective’s own history also complicates any simple division between the “local” and the “international”. Multiple Spirits was founded in Austria and continues to work between Vienna and Tokyo, collaborating with people across national, racial, ethnic and gender backgrounds. Through AWT Focus, the collective hopes to show that the Tokyo art scene encompasses “alternative and diverse activities” that extend beyond any single urban context and are connected through multiple networks.
Looking at Tokyo from elsewhere
For the Seoul-based curator Jaemin Shin, meanwhile, working with Tokyo-based artist and poet Natsumi Aoyagi offers another way of reading the city. Shin first worked with Aoyagi for the 2025 exhibition Patchwork! at the WilloW in Seoul. Her AWT Focus exhibition, Possible Words, Possible World, at Misa Shin Gallery, brings together two multimedia installations concerned with systems of recording and ownership.
One takes Tokyo Bay’s artificial islands—territories whose histories begin with administrative records such as land registries—as its point of departure; the other reimagines relationships beyond ownership and Japan’s family-registration system.
Shin sees parallels between the systems of registration and record-keeping, and patriarchal structures in Japan and Korea. But Aoyagi’s work has also altered her perception of the Japanese capital. “Looking at Tokyo through her work, I stopped seeing just a rigid megacity,” Shin says. Instead, she came to see it as “not a singular structure, but one with fluid and fragile boundaries”.
For Shin, the new AWT Focus format creates further opportunities for such readings. An outside curator can translate culturally specific ideas into different contexts, she says, creating new connections, while the dispersed format enables a more intimate engagement with particular parts of the city. Rather than simply presenting artworks, she says, an exhibition can connect to specific urban and social sectors in Tokyo, shifting the curatorial gesture towards “actively inhabiting the city” through artworks and ideas.
For Eshun, who returns to Art Week Tokyo after participating last year, the new structure also creates opportunities for exchange among curators. “Part of the goal for me, in travelling internationally to events like Art Week Tokyo, is to discover how different curators are working and thinking and making exhibitions,” he says. “It’s a great opportunity to meet and talk and build new relationships.”
His exhibition How Much Light Must I Consume? will be Julianknxx’s first in Japan. The artist’s practice spans geographies and diasporic histories, while the central work draws on oral traditions from Comoros, the small island nation near Mozambique. Eshun resists predicting what connections those histories might generate in Tokyo. “All successful art is predicated on discovery, on unknowing, on the revelation of unanticipated connection,” he says. “The hope is that it sparks new ways of seeing and imagining.”
Building networks beyond the week
Art Week Tokyo’s organisers are also looking beyond the encounters generated during a single week in November. Previous editions have recorded rising audiences: overall attendance increased by 33% between 2022 and 2023 and by another 15% in 2024, while international VIP participation has also grown sharply.
Ninagawa argues that the event has helped build networks and visibility that participating institutions and galleries can continue to develop independently. Internationally, she believes Art Week Tokyo has helped “rebrand” a Japanese art scene that had been overlooked in global discourse. Overseas visitors who once came to Tokyo primarily interested in the city as a tourist destination, she says, are increasingly arriving specifically to learn about Japanese artists and art history—and going on to develop projects from those encounters.
Eshun offers a more personal account of that process. Tokyo’s art world may appear smaller than those of some other global centres, he says, “but it runs deep”. He describes himself as still mapping its “paths and roads and streams and tributaries”, with Art Week Tokyo helping him “find my way and keep exploring”.
That metaphor feels particularly apt this year. Until now, travelling across Tokyo was primarily how visitors moved between Art Week Tokyo’s participating institutions. With the new AWT Focus, movement through the city is no longer simply a means of reaching its exhibitions; it has become part of the curatorial proposition itself.
The ten projects in this year’s AWT Focus
The Quiet
Curator: AugUsto Arbizo
Venue: Yutaka Kikutake Gallery
Augusto Arbizo assembles works by six Japanese and international artists into an intergenerational conversation on painting practices that offer a space for quiet concentration amid the frenetic visual culture of the city.
Erika Verzutti: Portrait of Sculpture
Curator: Julie Boukobza
Venue: Misako & Rosen
Artist Erika Verzutti and curator Julie Boukobza extend their collaboration for this exhibition of monoprints, which builds on a show of sculptures the two produced for a room at the Hôtel Balzac, Paris, in 2025.
The Constitution of Japan 2026
Curators: Greg Dvorak & Kenji Ono
Venue: Mujin-to Production
Curators Greg Dvorak and Kenji Ono take charge of the fourth edition of this recurring exhibition using art to reread the Constitution of Japan. This year’s edition includes works by video artist Fuyuhiko Takata, multimedia duo MES and more.
Nobuko Tsuchiya: Ace of Hearts
Curator: Martin Clark
Venue: SCAI The Bathhouse
Martin Clark, the director of London’s Camden Art Centre, oversees a new site-specific project by Nobuko Tsuchiya, a UK-based Japanese artist known for her sculptural assemblages of found objects that play on the enigmatic and the familiar.
Mary Weatherford: Komorebi
Curator: Jeremy Strick
Venue: Shibunkaku
Veteran US museum director Jeremy Strick presents the first exhibition in Japan of leading Los Angeles-based painter Mary Weatherford, with a focus on recent works on paper accompanied by one of her signature neon paintings.
Natsumi Aoyagi: Possible Words, Possible World
Curator: Jaemin Shin
Venue: Misa Shin Gallery
Korean independent curator Jaemin Shin guides this solo project by emerging artist Natsumi Aoyagi, whose multimedia installations juxtapose poems, moving images, AI-generated imagery, recorded sound and fiction. The resulting works generate multilayered meanings shaped by a speculative imagination.
Julianknxx: How Much Light Must I Consume?
Curator: Ekow Eshun
Venue: Space Un
London-based artist Julianknxx addresses the history of Africa and its diasporas through poetry, performance, film, music and sculpture. The artist’s first exhibition in Japan, curated by Ekow Eshun, will feature multimedia works inspired by salt as well as a series of special choral performances.
Koji Kamoji: Everyday Life
Curator: Maria Brewińska
Venue: Take Ninagawa
Koji Kamoji left his native Japan for Poland in 1959 and went on to become a key figure in the Polish avant-garde art scene. Warsaw-based curator Maria Brewińska has worked closely with the 91-year-old artist to develop an exhibition reflecting on the connection between art and survival.
Patchwork of Ruffled Wings
Curators: Multiple Spirits
Venue: Waitingroom
The queer feminist collective Multiple Spirits uses its eponymous zine as a base for producing artworks, exhibitions and other activities. Patchwork of Ruffled Wings explores the concept of the “vine-like archive” through the presentation of printed matter, textiles and other works by Japanese and international artists.
Taro Masushio and Sophie Nys
Curator: Olivier Mignon
Venue: XYZ collective
Olivier Mignon, the founding director of Keijiban in Kanazawa, juxtaposes works by two artists at XYZ collective. New York-based photographer Taro Masushio addresses themes of queer embodiment and the politics of the gaze, while Brussels-based sculptor Sophie Nys investigates the relationship between language and objects.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: CUNY Students Won on Investment Disclosure. Now They’re Demanding Divestment.
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Ana Agudelo
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
CUNY Students Won on Investment Disclosure. Now They’re Demanding Divestment.
The records reveal that the public university was invested in companies—including Lockheed Martin, Caterpillar, and Elbit—that are linked to Israeli military operations in Gaza.
After battling for two years to obtain the City University of New York’s (CUNY) investment records, student divestment activists won a big victory on September 9. A Supreme Court decision ruled in favor of the students, who argued that under New York’s Freedom of Information Law, the university could no longer withhold its records from the public.
Despite the ruling, CUNY, which operates 26 colleges across all five boroughs of New York City, has failed to disclose the full cache of materials students have requested, including purchase order histories for the 30 companies whose financial ties to CUNY organizers sought to investigate. Of these, the university only provided records for two—the American technology companies Dell and IBM. Through these holdings, organizers were looking to identify the university’s financial ties to companies they believed profited from Israeli military actions.
Since 2024, CUNY4Palestine, an organization of CUNY students and workers, has been the force behind calls for the university to disclose investments in companies that are connected to Israeli military operations in Gaza. Across all 26 schools, CUNY4Palestine has organized divestment efforts for years, connecting this investment campaign to broader demands for institutional change.
The newly released forms reveal that from 2020 until 2025, CUNY was invested in companies, including Boeing, Raytheon, Lockheed Martin, Elbit Systems, and Caterpillar, that have provided Israel with weapons and military equipment used in its decimation of Gaza. CUNY also held stock in mass detention and surveillance companies such as Palantir, Geo Group, and CoreCivic.
For many students, the newly released information raises another question: What should CUNY do now?
A draft resolution, a collaboration by Hunter College’s student government and Hunter SJP members, demands that CUNY “immediately divest from these harmful holdings” and instead “adopt an ethical investment policy.”
For many students, the university has failed to uphold its mission as a university “for the whole people of New York.” They believe the university has profited from genocide, displacement, and incarceration, which stands at odds with the values and goals of the larger CUNY community.
“Students have become passive actors in mass violence without their knowledge” by paying tuition that may find its way into the university’s invested fund, said one Hunter SJP member, who asked to remain anonymous for safety reasons. “CUNY is merely a facade of a public institution that instead perpetuates harms to the very communities it claims to serve.”
Corinna Mullin, an adjunct professor in the political science and economics department at John Jay College and Brooklyn College and a member of CUNY4Palestine, said the fight goes beyond CUNY’s investment practices.
“We have always linked divestment—as we did in the encampment—to broader systemic change at CUNY: cops off campus, demilitarization, a fully funded CUNY with free tuition, fair contracts for CUNY workers, and solidarity with the Palestinian liberation struggle,” Mullin said. The group has also advocated to keep Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) away from CUNY campuses.
For Mullin, the disclosure of CUNY’s investments marks a new stage in the group’s organizing efforts.
Mullin participated in the Gaza Solidarity Encampment at Columbia University in 2024. In 2025, four Brooklyn College adjunct professors, including Mullin, were removed from their positions due to ongoing support for Pro-Palestinian protests and movements. Three have since been reinstated; Mullin continues to advocate for the last member to regain their post.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Mullin said that one of the organization’s mantras, borrowed from the Black feminist movement, is “None of us is free until all of us are free.”
Many of these student- and faculty-run organizations share one goal: to hold the university accountable and to ensure its representatives accurately reflect the people who make up the university community.
CUNY is known for the wide undergraduate racial and ethnic representation of its student body. For Mullin and other members of CUNY4Palestine, campuses should represent the larger New York City community.
“Now that we’ve won disclosure, we’re building a broad coalition because we recognize that CUNY investments are connected not only to settler colonialism and genocide in Palestine,” Mullin said, “but also to the US imperialist war machine and to repression at home.”
“We want a university run by and for its students, workers, and community members,” she said.
To some CUNY professors, the disclosure story is significant not just for what the records reveal but also for what the university’s refusal to release them says about the school and its true priorities.
Anthony Alessandrini is a professor of Middle Eastern Studies at the CUNY Graduate Center and chair of the Professional Staff Congress’s Academic Freedom Committee. The committee is dedicated to protecting CUNY faculty and staff and ensuring freedom throughout the university.
Alessandrini explained that faculty members have tried to defend students’ right to organize long before this phase of the divestment movement started. He traces CUNY’s Palestine solidarity organizing to a 2013 Brooklyn College panel on the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions.
For decades,“the message being given to students [has been], we’re here to teach you critical thinking, we want you to question things, we want you to look and analyze things, but not your own university,” Alessandrini said.
He also points out that the university’s refusal to disclose these records is part of a broader pattern of restricting academic freedom and student activism, not only at CUNY but also in schools worldwide. Alessandrini looked to France, where high school students and teachers are leading protests over poor educational facilities and staff shortages. For him, these demonstrations highlight the importance of holding educational institutions accountable.
He said the university’s response to student protests and its treatment of workers involved in the movement also raises questions about its role as a public institution.
“If you’re arresting your students, if you’re refusing to disclose your investments to students, if you’re firing workers for being against genocide,” Alessandrini said, “you’re not a functioning university.”

https://gothamist.com/news/buzzer-beater.title: Buzzer beater? MTA vows to turn this SoHo pit into a basketball court in 30 days.
https://gothamist.com/news/buzzer-beater.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/buzzer-beater.text:
A Downtown Manhattan basketball court that’s been in MTA construction purgatory for four years is set to reopen at the end of November, according to transit officials.
The refreshed Grand Canal Court at Sixth Avenue will feature new benches, a water fountain, upgraded lighting and fencing. The courts were ripped up in 2022 so workers could build a new substation that provides electricity to trains.
The MTA said in a December 2022 statement that the project would be complete by the end of 2024. Signage at the site states the project should have been done by April 2026.
Now, the MTA and parks department say the project will actually be done by the end of November — though making that deadline may require a buzzer beater.
The site was abuzz with activity Thursday. Crews were still working in pits below the street shored up with timber. The site has not yet been paved and none of the new amenities — or the basketball court and hoops — have been installed.
“We look forward to welcoming the community back to Grand Canal Court with an upgraded space for New Yorkers to come together, stay active and enjoy the game,” Alberto Roldan, the parks department borough commissioner, wrote in a statement.
The budget for the project was $45 million in 2014, but now it's nearly doubled to $83.7 million, according to MTA records. The agency blamed a host of issues for the increase, including unforeseen utility work.
The worksite is surrounded by litter, and straphangers must squeeze through a narrow passage to reach the Canal Street subway station entrance at Sixth Avenue.
John Underwood, 68, a retired city worker who has walked by the site for decades, was skeptical it would reopen soon.
“It might open in a year or two,” he said. “I had even forgotten it was a basketball court.”
The wedge-shaped parkland was created by Sixth Avenue’s southern extension in the 1930s, said Andrew Berman, executive director of local civic group Village Preservation.
“These little oddly shaped lots along Sixth Avenue have been surprisingly popular and resilient recreational spaces over the years,” he said.
Not everyone wants the basketball court back. An online petition to replace it with a dog run has 2,200 signatures.
Berman compared the shifting demands to bocce courts in Manhattan giving way to ballfields and playgrounds. “Sometimes longtime uses disappear,” he said.
Herb Tam, an organizer with the Chinatown Basketball Club, remembered teenagers spilling from the Canal Street station and nearby schools to play ball at the park.
Tam said a closed park changes the feel of the whole block. “When you have live parks, the whole neighborhood around the park feels safer, he said.
“I can’t imagine our court closing for even, like, a month… let alone how long the courts over at Canal and Sixth Avenue have been closed,” he said.
“If I was one of the regulars, I probably would’ve found other places to play already.”

https://hyperallergic.com/barbara-takena.title: Barbara Takenaga’s ‘Awestruck’
https://hyperallergic.com/barbara-takena.author: Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art
https://hyperallergic.com/barbara-takena.text:
Barbara Takenaga’s ‘Awestruck’
At Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, 40 paintings invite viewers into an exhibition where scale, pattern, and perception are explored and celebrated.
On view at Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art in Kansas City through April 11, 2027, Barbara Takenaga: Awestruck presents the artist’s first comprehensive survey in nearly a decade. Bringing together 40 works spanning her career since the early 2000s, the exhibition reveals the many approaches to abstraction that have shaped Takenaga’s practice. The exhibition is organized by Jessica May, Ph.D., Executive Director, Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, and Tae Edell, Independent Curator.
The exhibition examines Barbara Takenaga’s intricate compositions through four thematic sections: an emphasis on process, a masterful confusion of scale, an embrace of illusion, and reverent nods to art history. Together, these strategies work to upend the viewer’s expectations, engaging imagination and stoking curiosity for more.
"My paintings are often seen as abstract, but with implied narratives:  natural phenomena, imagined landscapes, microscopic or cosmic views. Cross sections of minerals or aerial maps of land or Big Bang explosions. There is a labor-intensive aspect to the work, with an aim to reconcile random, chance elements with structure and order. I’m enormously pleased to have this rare opportunity to look back at work from the past 25  years."
—Barbara Takenaga
Featuring works from institutional and private collections across the nation, this exhibition includes paintings up to her most recent, revealing Takenaga’s continued push to further her approach across increasingly expanding canvases, opening new paths within her ongoing exploration of abstraction.
Learn more and plan your visit at kemperart.org.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ea.title: New Eames Museum in California Funded in Part by Trump Appointee
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ea.author: Andy Battaglia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ea.text:
A new museum devoted to design legends Charles and Ray Eames in the Bay Area of Northern California received more than $25 million in initial funding from Joe Gebbia, an Airbnb cofounder who is currently a Tesla board member and previously worked with Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), according to a report by SFGATE.
“Gebbia is an unexpected benefactor behind the museum in Marin County,” the publication wrote, after citing the $25-million figure from the North Bay Business Journal. “After co-founding Airbnb in San Francisco in 2007, which helped him to eventually earn over $9 billion, Gebbia turned to politics and joined DOGE last year. President Donald Trump later tapped Gebbia to become the chief design officer of the United States and redesign government websites. In response to Gebbia’s political affairs, Airbnb began distancing itself from one of its co-founders.”
The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity is slated to take over the former campus of the Birkenstock shoe company, with a building design by the Swiss architecture firm Herzog & de Meuron and landscape design by Field Operations, the firm behind New York’s High Line park.
Gebbia’s support of the nonprofit represents a considerable chunk. The Eames Institute raised over $165 million in contributions from 2021 through 2024, anchored by Gebbia’s $25 million.
Asked about Gebbia’s connection to the planned museum—with his $25 million making up a significant portion of the $165 million raised between 2021 and 2024, Eames Institute president and CEO John Cary told SFGATE that donors have no outside influence. “Joe’s views are his own and do not reflect the Eames Institute,” he said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Se 40% dos judeus concordassem com Estado palestino, haveria paz’, diz presidente da Fepal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
As eleições em Israel ficaram marcadas pela colocação em xeque do poder do primeiro-ministro Benjamin Netanyahu e um avanço no número de cadeiras do partido de representação palestina, que conseguiu 19 das 120 cadeiras do Knesset. No entanto, apesar do avanço da oposição, ainda não há maioria para retirar Netanyahu do poder, e isso dependerá de alianças. Um dos grandes obstáculos para uma coalizão forte é que, mesmo entre os partidos de oposição, o sionismo é maioria. Embora com algumas diferenças de atuação, com exceção dos partidos árabes, essencialmente, as outras legendas até aceitam negociar a formação de um Estado Palestino, mas que se mantenha subjugado a Israel. Ou seja, rejeitam a autodeterminação do povo palestino.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Ualid Rabah, presidente da Federação Árabe Palestina (Fepal), afirma que, para compreender o cenário político atual e a formação do novo parlamento, é preciso identificar o voto judaico e o não judaico, que seria o voto passível de ser considerado de esquerda. “O voto não judaico é o voto palestino dos que permaneceram naquela região depois da limpeza étnica de 1948. Das 19 cadeiras não sionistas, as duas listas foram feitas pelo voto árabe. A população originária palestina representa de 21% a 23%”, afirma.
Rabah reforça que, mesmo com as 19 cadeiras, o parlamento, “em maior ou menor grau, considera que o Estado palestino não deve existir, concordando com a ocupação da Cisjordânia e da construção de colonatos, mantendo o bloqueio e apoiando o genocídio em Gaza”.
Além disso, o especialista explica que, mesmo os partidos não sionistas, são obrigados a concordar com a exigência de que Israel seja um Estado exclusivamente judeu para poderem ter cadeiras no parlamento. “Apenas pessoas de fé judaica têm autodeterminação”, critica.
Outra importante provocação trazida por Ualid Rabah é que, para ter maioria, o bloco não sionista deveria ter 42 cadeiras. “Ou seja, se 40% dos judeus em Israel concordassem de que pelo menos deveria haver um Estado Palestino em parte do território tomado, haveria paz”, ressalta. “Israel é o único estado da história moderna em que 100% da sua população judaica adere a alguma coisa parecida com o nazismo. E ela não é”, continua.
Estados Unidos, o país aliado de primeira hora de Israel, também vive eleições de meio de mandato que poderão reconfigurar a força no Parlamento e um possível crescimento da oposição a Donald Trump, que, por sua vez, depende da manutenção de poder de Netanyahu para seguir tendo alguma influência no Oriente Médio. “Trump depende de uma guinada mais extremista na política externa. Está quase certo que perderá a maioria na Câmara e talvez no Senado. Então ele partiria para uma política externa mais agressiva para se legitimar”, avalia, ao destacar que este é o momento em que há maior iminência de uma Terceira Guerra Mundial.
“Existe a possibilidade de um ataque nuclear ao Irã. E é isso que tem feito com que Trump tenha dificuldades de conseguir um apoio resoluto de seus aliados petromonárquicos do Golfo, especialmente os Emirados Árabes. O ataque nuclear traria consequências para toda aquela região, inclusive contaminando aquíferos”, afirma.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Architect Kae Ito creates a modular ‘secret garden’ for Art Week Tokyo's bar
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Azby Brown
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Since its inception in 2022, the pop-up AWT Bar has become one of the most appreciated hubs of Art Week Tokyo. This year, the architect Kae Ito has been commissioned for the spatial design. Ito opened her independent firm Office Itokae in 2025 after ten years at the Pritzker Prize-winning firm Sanaa / Kazuyo Sejima & Associates in Tokyo, where she worked on notable projects like the Better Co-Being pavilion for Expo 2025 Osaka, the Inujima Landscape Project and myriad exhibition designs in Japan and abroad.
Her AWT Bar, titled Kuru Kuru, she says, is intended to evoke a “secret garden”. Ingenious openwork structures of stainless steel and acrylic are distributed throughout the space, their placement guided by a geometric design on the floor. Multimedia elements by the artist Nile Koetting further enliven the space.
Ito recently spent time in Mongolia investigating ger, the traditional nomadic homes of the region, which are designed to be easily folded up and moved. Like those, Kuru Kuru is made of modular, collapsible elements, composed of rings and semi-circles, with a simple locking mechanism to render them stable. Colour-coded acrylic hemispheres have flat upper surfaces that form seats, tables or counters. These exquisitely fabricated units call to mind orreries or models of atoms. An aluminium-covered wall with circular service openings reinforces the science-lab vibe. Ito says, “I’m hoping [the bar] encourages people to have a happy time, eating and drinking with other visitors.”
Chef Ryuichi Yokomizo’s orchestration of the culinary experience at the AWT Bar is a sophisticated inversion of expectations. Following nine years at the Michelin-starred Joël Robuchon restaurant in Tokyo’s Ebisu district, the 30-year-old chef was asked to helm La & Le in Aoyama, which opened in March this year. For Art Week Tokyo, he is presenting two canapés: a gâteau of duck rillettes and pain d’épices, and a tarte tatin-inspired sablé.
These pleasantly deceiving creations display a beautiful autumnal colour palette, and reward the diner’s attention. The beautifully constructed savoury option layers duck rillettes over dark pain d’épices, finished with foie
gras mousse, a paper-thin slice of apple, caramelised walnuts and delicate sprigs of micro amaranth. The tarte reimagines the classic tarte tatin, layering deeply caramelised apple over a sablé Breton base, topped with a quenelle of calvados-infused buttercream and artfully placed micro celery. Each masquerades as its opposite: the savoury rillettes appear at first glance to be a dessert, while the sweet tarte appears savoury.
“I’m deeply interested in the element of surprise in cuisine,” Yokomizo says. “My theme for Art Week Tokyo, Entre, centres on the Japanese ideas of tsunagu—to connect—and aida—the space between,” he says. “Like art, cuisine changes with one’s point of view. I hope to show how simply changing the angle of approach can transform eating into an entirely different experience. I believe that sharing good food and drink in this way can foster deeper communication.”
The artist-devised cocktails on offer are similarly inventive. Mariko Mori’s All That Shinesuses luminous kuzumochi spheres, tapioca balls and rose caviar to evoke “the invisible ripples that are sent out into the world as our souls interact”. For Part-Time Job, Yoshihiro Suda reached back into his past as an illustrator for cider and whisky brands to make a cocktail as bittersweet as his memories. Natsumi Aoyagi’s sudsy Caipirinha de Cinco Sabões (Caipirinha of Five Soaps) is accompanied by a fable that alludes to the drink’s historical rural Brazilian roots. Combining uniquely ambitious design, cuisine and cocktails, the AWT Bar promises an unforgettable multisensory experience.
• AWT Bar, Art Week Tokyo, 4-8 November

https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-school-p.title: NYC's school PTA fundraising gap is growing, mirroring broader racial disparities
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-school-p.author: Joe Hong
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-school-p.text:
Parent teacher associations may conjure images of read-a-thons and fun runs, where grandparents and relatives pledge to pay their grade schooler for every page they read or lap they jog. And of course, there’s the iconic PTA bake sale.
But in New York City, PTA fundraising efforts vary from hawking homemade muffins and pastries for a few hundred dollars to running sophisticated, self-sustaining nonprofits that operate like small businesses and take in millions in revenue.
P.S. 29 in Cobble Hill, Brooklyn, raised about $2 million in donations and revenue, more than any other school last year, according to data from the Department of Education. In second place was P.S. 158 on Manhattan's Upper East Side, which raised $1.7 million. Both schools enroll between 600 and 700 students. New Explorations into Science, Technology & Math, a K-12 school on the Lower East Side, which enrolls about 1,600 students, came in third, raising $1.4 million.
Each school in the city is required to have a parent association. In total, they reported nearly $70 million in revenue and savings in the 2024-25 academic year, which helped their schools pay for beneficial after-school enrichment programs, field trips, support staff and in some cases even building maintenance.
“We find evidence that PTA money above and beyond any public resources actually do boost achievement in reading and math,” said Brittany Murray, an education professor at Davidson College who researches PTAs. “But it tends to help those that are more affluent.”
PTAs in many of the city’s low-income neighborhoods are far less flush with cash, with some parent groups reporting donations of just a few hundred dollars or nothing at all. A comparison with demographic data reveals sharp racial disparities in which students benefit the most from parent fundraising that have only grown since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Last year, schools serving more white students outraised those that primarily serve Black children 5-to-1.
The findings come as the Mamdani administration is under increased pressure to address segregation and inequality in the city’s education system.
On the whole, PTA funds ultimately made up a small amount compared to the city education department's overall $41 billion budget. And the city makes an effort to offset the detrimental effects of poverty on education by providing other sources of money for schools in underprivileged neighborhoods.
Nicole Brownstein, a spokesperson for New York City Public Schools, pointed to the city’s Fair Student Funding formula, which channels more money to schools with large concentrations of poverty, students with disabilities and English learners. The city also provides money for these schools to expand arts education.
“We recognize that funding capacity reflects differences in community resources and fundraising capacity – that is why we are consistently working to strengthen our Fair Student Funding formula, meeting schools and students where they are,” she said.
But experts in education policy say even that additional money is not enough, and that while PTA fundraising is a lifeline for many schools, the wide gaps in fundraising can worsen inequality and are yet another symptom of a segregated school system that has come under fresh scrutiny since the start of the school year. Last month, New York Times journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones detailed her daughter’s experience with inequality and segregation in the city’s school system, renewing calls to address long-standing disparities.
“When you have places that are highly economically segregated and racially segregated, then you're gonna see vast differences in the schools that can fundraise,” said Murray. “It exacerbates inequality.”
Anita Baier, a PTA president at P.S. 8 in Brooklyn Heights, said PTAs do more than fundraising. She said they play an essential role in planning events for families and connecting parents within the community But she said much of their work is unfortunately focused on raising money to pay for necessities the city does not provide, like after-school programs and support staff.
“Not only do we need more funding, we need predictable and adequate funding year over year so parents are not always having to be on alert and step up to plug these gaps,” Baier said.
Racial and geographic disparities
The five boroughs are home to more than 1,200 parent associations. And yet just 15 PTAs accounted for a third of the $70 million raised and saved by parent associations last year. Those in Manhattan had the highest average revenues last year, over $200,000. But the top funded parent groups were scattered across both Manhattan and parts of Brooklyn.
Gothamist used PTA financial data and student demographic data from the Department of Education to calculate how much a typical student, depending on their race, benefits from PTA fundraising. The average white student in the 2024-25 school year benefited from$254 in PTA money. For the average Black student, the amount was just $46.30. Of the 15 schools that raised more than $1 million, only two have Black enrollment above 4%.
Take P.S. 8 in Brooklyn Heights, where 69% of enrollment was white and 3% was Black over the course of the last school year. Only 1-in-8 students at the elementary school came from low-income households, compared to a citywide average of nearly 3-in-4 students. The school raised $1.3 million and ended the year with $844,000 in the bank after expenses.
At the top earning school, P.S. 29 in Cobble Hill, 69% of grade schoolers were white. According to the education department’s data, the school had just six Black students, and 13% of pupils overall came from low-income households. Out of the $2 million the school raised in total, it ended the 2024-25 year with over $1.1 million after expenses.
Contrast that with P.S. 399 in Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighborhood, where 66% of students are Black, and P.S. 43 in the Bronx’s Mott Haven neighborhood, where 78% of students are Latino. Over 95% of students at both schools come from low-income households, among the highest concentrations of poverty in the city. Their PTAs each raised less than $1,000 last year.
None of the parents at the school’s parent association, or those at several other low-fundraising PTAs, responded to requests for interviews.
Claire Mackevicius, an education professor at the University of Oregon who researches parent teacher associations across the country, said affluent parents are often blamed for those wide fundraising disparities. But she said they’re merely plugging holes in school systems that are struggling to provide enrichment programs, pay for tutoring and keep class sizes down.
“ I want to be clear that sort of onus and burden is not on the committed and hardworking volunteers in the PTA organization itself,” Mackevicius said. “Our public schools are underfunded, full stop.”
She said the chasm between rich and poor PTAs is instead a reflection of broader disparities, and that elected officials and policymakers have grown complacent about inequality and segregation in schools. By some measures, school segregation in the city has worsened since the 1990s, with students of color more likely today to be attending a school with fewer white students.
Murray, the Davidson College professor, said segregation has worsened in part because New York City’s parents can choose to send their children to middle and high schools outside of their neighborhoods. And a PTA that raises more money is another factor that makes certain schools more attractive than others in the eyes of some parents.
“It's this kind of circular problem,” she said. “It’s really hard to disentangle the segregation piece and the school choice piece.”
How PTAs spend
The Department of Education’s rules for PTAs, known as Regulation A-660, allow parent fundraising to support a variety of personnel and services at schools. PTAs can pay for specialized, supplemental teachers who rotate into different classrooms throughout the school day, or staff who work during after-school or weekend programs. This includes academic support like tutoring or homework help, as well as enrichment and extracurricular activities, such as science and math clubs or art classes.
After-school programs are a big component of what some PTAs provide, and some parent associations hire a staff member to oversee those services. That might mean managing a contract with a company that provides art, music or dance lessons.
What PTAs can’t do is cover classroom teachers for core subjects like math, science, English and history.
New York City Public Schools does not collect and publish detailed data on how PTAs spend their money. But a review of some tax filings show that many of the PTAs that raise hundreds of thousands of dollars each year generate revenues by collecting fees from families attending after-school programs. Most of those revenues typically go back into staffing those programs.
According to tax filings for P.S. 8’s PTA, the organization spent $526,000 in 2024-25 on its after-school program, including $146,000 for the program’s staff salaries. Other costs included paying third-party vendors who come with their own staff and curriculum, according to PTA Co-President Amélie Walker-Yung. The fees collected from families for after-school and extracurricular programs and clubs amounted to $991,000.
Walker-Yung said the after-school program regularly changes its offerings based on what parents and students want. Clubs and activities range from chess and STEM-based programs to drama, dance and sports. She said her son is currently taking a comic-book drawing class.
Gothamist’s analysis found a $200 difference on average in how white students benefit from PTA fundraising compared to Black students.
“ It doesn't sound like much,” Murray said, but it can be spent in “highly impactful” ways. A field trip or an after-school program that fosters an interest in science or technology can pay off in the long run, she said.
“ When you accumulate that across the whole school, that can make a big difference,” she said. “Whether it's supplies, whether it's grants for teachers, whether it's field trips, that goes a long way across a school building.”
Her research shows that the PTAs that raise enough money to afford additional programs and activities are most likely to be in white, affluent neighborhoods.
P.S. 29’s PTA in Cobble Hill spent $1.6 million on its after-school program, which included $700,000 for staff. Additional money went to staff training, supplies and insurance. The program in turn raised $1.5 million in fees, according to tax filings. Some of the instructors in the after-school classes are also classroom teachers at the school. The PTA also covers training for teachers in the program.
After-school offerings at P.S. 29 change periodically, said Kasey Noziska, one of the school’s PTA presidents. Students have taken classes in cooking, fashion design and understanding the stock market. Parents pay from $25 to over $100 per session, depending on whether the class needs extra materials or equipment, which is a bargain compared to private school programs in the area. Noziska said the PTA offers financial assistance for families who can’t afford it.
In addition to academic and artistic enrichment, the after-school programs fulfill a more basic parental necessity: childcare.
“It started because there was a huge need for childcare after school, and there weren’t many affordable options,” said Noziska. “And there wasn’t a real diversity of options catering to children’s interests.”
For schools without PTA-funded after-school programs, the city operates 900 free programs across the five boroughs.
PTA tax filings for some schools include more detail than others: P.S. 158’s PTA on the Upper East Side spent $39,000 on a fifth grade trip and $10,600 on the school yearbook. Records also show the PTA supported a “photo day” to the tune of $5,900.
Other PTA tax filings are more vague. Take Stuyvesant High School, the highly selective high school that integration advocates criticized for admitting just three Black students this school year. Its PTA provided $841,253 in grants to the school for “additional funding for various departments, educational & extracurricular programs” while also earning $32,000 in “investment income.” What those investments were are not detailed in the association’s tax forms and PTA leaders at Stuyvesant High did not respond to emailed questions about either of these amounts.
PTA funding vs. public funding
Hannah-Jones’ New York Times magazine article about her family’s experiences with school segregation and disparate educational outcomes in Brooklyn has reignited calls to fix what advocates say is a broken system.
Education policy experts have urged Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who campaigned on expanding free childcare, to propose a more robust plan for addressing systemic inequality and increasing funding for the city’s public schools.
PTA fundraising dollars make up a fraction of the overall amount of money received from local, state and federal sources. On average, the city already spends roughly $35,000 each year per student, according to education department data, far more than other large school districts, with the bulk of that funding coming from city coffers. It’s an increase of about 34% from pre-COVID 19 pandemic levels. Nearly 40% of that budget is spent on K through 12 education. Another third or so goes to employee benefits and pensions, along with debt payments.
The Department of Education gives each school the same amount per pupil, but then adds supplemental funding that depends on a student’s grade level, academic need and household income.
At P.S. 29 in Brooklyn, where the PTA raised $2,886 per student during the last school year, the school received about $17,000 per pupil in public funding.
But at P.S. 307, the elementary school where Hannah-Jones enrolled her daughter in 2014, the funding sources are essentially flipped. It received $42,000 in public, per-pupil funding in 2024-25. The school’s student body is 46% Black, 35% Latino and 10% white. About 85% of students come from low-income households. The school’s PTA did not report any fundraising income in 2024-25.
And at P.S. 44 in the Bronx, the PTA raised just $332 in total last year, less than $2 per pupil. It was among the lowest of PTAs that reported at least some income. A third of the students are Black, 67% are Latino and nearly all students come from low-income households. The school received $35,000 in per pupil funding from the city, state and federal governments.
Both P.S. 307 and P.S. 44 benefit from additional city funding that goes to schools serving more students from low-income households. They also get additional federal dollars, known as Title I money, allocated to schools serving high-poverty communities. The funding is designed to pay for extra teachers, additional curriculum and after-school tutoring to help counteract the ways poverty can prevent students from doing well in school.
Some parents at high-fundraising PTAs say differences in public spending make PTA fundraising necessary to provide critical parts of a “well-rounded education.”
“We’re not a Title I school, so we get significantly less money from DOE,” said Noziska at P.S. 29. “There are a lot of things necessary for our children, like arts, that DOE does not provide enough for us to fund.”
But Murray, the Davidson College professor, urged caution when drawing comparisons between PTA fundraising for schools in more affluent neighborhoods and extra city and federal support for schools in low-income neighborhoods designed to level the playing field.
“I don’t think that takes into account just how much it costs to educate a student that is poor,” she said. “Money matters, especially for students with the greatest needs.”
