https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Eleições nos EUA podem limitar poder de Trump e influenciar ofensiva contra o Brasil
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Rodrigo Chagas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Os Estados Unidos vão às urnas na próxima terça-feira (3) para definir o controle do Congresso durante os dois últimos anos do governo de Donald Trump, do Partido Republicano. A disputa acontece em um cenário de baixa popularidade do presidente, aumento do custo de vida e desgaste provocado pela guerra contra o Irã. Uma eventual vitória do Partido Democrata poderá limitar a atuação do governo estadunidense, inclusive nas medidas adotadas contra o Brasil após a reeleição de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).
Os republicanos controlam atualmente a Câmara dos Representantes, com 218 deputados contra 214 democratas, e o Senado, com 53 das 100 cadeiras. Para conquistar a maioria em qualquer uma das casas, os democratas precisam de um ganho líquido de quatro assentos. As eleições realizadas na metade do mandato presidencial, renovarão todas as 435 cadeiras da Câmara e 35 das 100 que compõem o Senado, além de definir governos estaduais e cargos locais.
Uma pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos divulgada na segunda-feira (26) apontou que 47% dos eleitores registrados pretendiam votar nos democratas, contra 36% nos republicanos. A aprovação de Trump ficou em 32%, próxima do menor patamar de seus dois mandatos. A preferência nacional pelos partidos, porém, não determina diretamente a distribuição das cadeiras, decididas em disputas estaduais e distritais.
Para Zoe Alexandra, diretora de notícias do BreakThrough News, a queda de popularidade de Trump tornou-se um dos principais argumentos das campanhas democratas, que apresentam a disputa como uma avaliação popular do governo.
“Se os democratas conseguirem uma maioria nas duas casas, será um golpe duro para Trump e para o MAGA”, afirma Alexandra, em entrevista ao Brasil de Fato, em referência ao movimento Make America Great Again (Faça a América Grande de Novo, em inglês), que reúne parte importante da base política do presidente.
Stephanie Weatherbee, da coordenação da Secretaria da Assembleia Internacional dos Povos (AIP), observa que o partido que ocupa a Presidência costuma enfrentar dificuldades nas eleições de meio de mandato, especialmente quando há insatisfação com a economia.
“Surpreendentemente, a margem de vitória dos democratas não é tão grande. Seria de esperar que, dada a aprovação tão baixa de Trump, a diferença entre os que favorecem os republicanos e os democratas fosse maior em favor dos democratas”, afirma.
O que pode mudar para o Brasil?
Uma nova maioria na Câmara ou no Senado poderia ampliar a fiscalização parlamentar sobre as medidas adotadas pelo governo Trump contra o Brasil, especialmente as tarifas comerciais, as sanções contra autoridades brasileiras e o envolvimento estadunidense nas disputas políticas do país.
O governo Trump utilizou instrumentos comerciais e diplomáticos para pressionar o Brasil desde 2025, justificando as medidas como resposta ao processo judicial que condenou Jair Bolsonaro por tentativa de golpe de Estado e às decisões da Justiça brasileira sobre a atuação das plataformas digitais. Também manifestou apoio à família Bolsonaro durante a eleição presidencial deste ano.
A tensão voltou a crescer após a vitória de Lula sobre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), no último domingo (25). Trump questionou a lisura do resultado, sem apresentar provas de irregularidades, e autorizou a entrada do senador e de sua família nos Estados Unidos. Flávio chegou a Miami na quarta-feira (28), depois de deixar o Brasil pela Argentina, apesar de uma determinação judicial para entregar seus passaportes.
A contestação do resultado brasileiro contrasta com as avaliações das missões internacionais que acompanharam a votação. A Organização dos Estados Americanos (OEA) divulgou relatório preliminar sobre o segundo turno em 27 de outubro, enquanto o Centro Carter também acompanhou o processo eleitoral.
O reconhecimento internacional do pleito é considerado pela diplomacia brasileira um elemento de fortalecimento da posição de Lula diante das pressões externas.
Democratas pressionam Trump
A acolhida de Flávio por Trump provocou reações de parlamentares democratas. Um grupo de 25 deputados enviou uma carta ao secretário de Estado, Marco Rubio, cobrando explicações sobre a concessão de vistos à família Bolsonaro e a eventual participação de autoridades estadunidenses na saída do senador do Brasil.
Os congressistas querem saber se o Departamento de Estado tinha conhecimento das investigações contra Flávio e da ordem judicial brasileira, além de questionarem o possível uso de recursos diplomáticos para facilitar sua viagem. Também pedem esclarecimentos sobre eventuais contatos com autoridades da Argentina e do Equador, países por onde o senador passou antes de chegar aos EUA.
Um relatório do Serviço de Pesquisa do Congresso dos Estados Unidos, atualizado também na quinta-feira, aponta que o Legislativo pode fiscalizar a utilização de sanções, tarifas, vistos e recursos de assistência externa pelo Executivo. Os parlamentares também podem propor restrições legais e orçamentárias a determinadas medidas.
O documento registra que o Senado aprovou, em outubro de 2025, uma resolução para encerrar a emergência nacional declarada por Trump em relação ao Brasil. A proposta ainda depende de tramitação na Câmara e enfrenta a possibilidade de veto presidencial.
As mudanças no Congresso poderiam, portanto, abrir novas frentes de pressão sobre a Casa Branca. Isso não significa que os democratas conseguiriam reverter automaticamente as sanções ou obrigar Trump a reconhecer o resultado eleitoral brasileiro.
Fontes ouvidas pelo Brasil de Fato no Itamaraty indicam que uma eventual maioria democrata em pelo menos uma das casas do Congresso poderá favorecer o Brasil, especialmente nas relações com as grandes plataformas digitais e nas negociações ambientais.
A avaliação nos bastidores do Itamaraty é de que a reeleição de Lula fortaleceu a posição diplomática do Brasil, permitindo preservar a estratégia adotada durante o tarifaço de 2025, quando Brasília manteve as negociações comerciais mesmo diante das sanções impostas pelo governo Trump.
A acolhida a Flávio ocorre em um contexto de endurecimento das operações do Serviço de Imigração e Controle de Alfândegas (ICE), responsável por prisões e deportações de imigrantes. A agência registrou quase 51 mil prisões em agosto, um recorde pelo terceiro mês consecutivo.
O próprio Alexandre Ramagem, ex-chefe de inteligência do governo Bolsonaro e foragido da justiça brasileira, foi preso pelo ICE, mas solto dias depois.
Para Zoe Alexandra, a autorização de entrada concedida ao senador brasileiro evidencia o tratamento diferenciado dado a aliados políticos de Trump, enquanto milhares de imigrantes enfrentam detenções e deportações. “É outro exemplo desse privilégio das elites e do desprezo pelo povo”, afirma.
Guerra e custo de vida pressionam Trump
A economia é uma das principais preocupações dos eleitores estadunidenses. Na pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos de outubro, 73% dos entrevistados avaliaram que o custo de vida estava seguindo na direção errada.
A guerra iniciada pelos Estados Unidos e por Israel contra o Irã, no fim de fevereiro, agravou as pressões sobre os preços da energia. Segundo estimativa do Pentágono obtida pela Associated Press, o conflito já teria custado US$ 47,1 bilhões ao país, sem contar com os prejuízos provocados pelos ataques iranianos a instalações militares estadunidenses.
Weatherbee alerta que o conflito também contraria as expectativas de parte dos eleitores que apoiaram Trump por suas promessas de reduzir os custos domésticos e evitar novos envolvimentos militares.
“Há uma insatisfação muito grande, inclusive dentro de uma parte da base do Partido Republicano, a parte que é mais de baixa renda, sobre o efeito da guerra e sobre a falta de políticas para reduzir a inflação e o custo do combustível e dos alimentos”, explica.
Os preços dos seguros de saúde, dos serviços médicos e dos medicamentos também aparecem entre as preocupações apontadas pela pesquisadora. Segundo ela, o descontentamento nessas áreas atinge os dois partidos, mas tende a pesar especialmente sobre os republicanos por controlarem a Presidência e o Congresso.
Alexandra relaciona a deterioração da economia à estratégia militar do governo estadunidense, mas destaca que a insatisfação com a política externa não começou com a guerra contra o Irã. As mobilizações contra o financiamento militar a Israel durante o genocídio palestino já haviam ampliado o debate sobre o envolvimento dos Estados Unidos em conflitos internacionais.
“Antes se dizia que o eleitor estadunidense não se importava com a política externa como tema das eleições. Hoje é um tema muito importante”, afirma.
A jornalista também cita as operações contra a Venezuela e o aumento da presença militar estadunidense na América Latina. Na avaliação dela, cresce a percepção de que as intervenções estrangeiras podem agravar crises migratórias que o próprio governo Trump utiliza para justificar sua política de deportações.
“Dizem que precisam deportar todas essas pessoas, mas, ao mesmo tempo, vão desestabilizar o continente para que haja mais fluxo migratório”, resume.
Até onde os democratas podem mudar os EUA?
Uma vitória democrata na Câmara permitiria ampliar investigações parlamentares, convocar integrantes do governo e exercer maior influência sobre a aprovação do orçamento. O controle do Senado também daria ao partido instrumentos para bloquear nomeações de autoridades, incluindo integrantes do Judiciário federal.
Trump manteria o poder de veto sobre projetos aprovados pelo Congresso, além de importantes atribuições executivas nas áreas de política externa, imigração e segurança nacional. Para derrubar um veto presidencial, seria necessária uma maioria de dois terços nas duas casas.
A guerra contra o Irã é um exemplo dessas limitações. Parlamentares podem tentar restringir o emprego das Forças Armadas por meio de resoluções baseadas na legislação sobre poderes de guerra, mas enfrentam obstáculos políticos e jurídicos para impor limites ao Executivo.
Weatherbee lembra que a utilização desse mecanismo dependeria não apenas de uma maioria democrata, mas também da capacidade de reunir apoio suficiente para superar um eventual veto presidencial. Uma diferença pequena de cadeiras entre os partidos tornaria essa tarefa particularmente difícil.
“É difícil imaginar que, se os democratas tiverem uma maioria pequena, conseguiriam pôr fim à guerra no Irã”, afirma.
A pesquisadora também lembra que o Partido Democrata sustentou o financiamento militar a Israel durante o governo de Joe Biden, inclusive nos momentos mais críticos da ofensiva israelense contra a população palestina.
Zoe Alexandra aponta dificuldades semelhantes para eventuais mudanças na política migratória. O Congresso já aprovou recursos expressivos para ampliar a estrutura federal de fiscalização, detenção e deportação, com verbas previstas para exercícios fiscais futuros. A mudança da maioria legislativa não eliminaria automaticamente esses recursos nem as atribuições do Executivo.
“Os democratas estão dizendo que podem retomar as duas casas e fazer mudanças reais. Mas, quando tiveram esse poder no passado, não fizeram isso”, critica.
Weatherbee destaca, ainda, a influência do financiamento empresarial sobre as decisões dos dois partidos. Ela cita como exemplo os setores farmacêutico e de seguros privados de saúde, cujas contribuições eleitorais tendem a dificultar a aprovação de políticas contrárias aos interesses dessas empresas.
Segundo levantamento divulgado pela Reuters, a publicidade política nos Estados Unidos já havia movimentado aproximadamente US$ 3,8 bilhões até outubro. O empresário Elon Musk destinou, sozinho, cerca de US$ 366 milhões ao apoio a candidatos republicanos, conforme registros de financiamento eleitoral.
A esquerda democrata
A disputa pelo futuro do Partido Democrata também passa pelo avanço de candidaturas vinculadas ao Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), organização que defende a ampliação dos direitos sociais, o fortalecimento dos sindicatos e o enfrentamento do poder econômico das grandes corporações. O grupo apoia 131 candidatos nas eleições de novembro, dos quais dez disputam vagas na Câmara dos Representantes.
Nas eleições primárias, candidaturas socialistas derrotaram parlamentares democratas tradicionais, como Melat Kiros, de 29 anos, que venceu Diana DeGette, deputada há quase três décadas pelo Colorado. Em Nova York, Darializa Avila Chevalier derrotou Adriano Espaillat, enquanto Claire Valdez conquistou a indicação democrata para uma cadeira aberta. Há expectativa de crescimento na atual representação, que tem duas cadeiras na Câmara.
Stephanie Weatherbee considera que essa disputa revela uma dificuldade dos democratas em enfrentar o avanço da extrema direita. “É importante notar que os democratas, tanto nesta eleição como em outras, estão mais focados em minimizar a força potencial de candidatos mais progressistas, de esquerda, como os candidatos do DSA, do que em minimizar o crescimento da extrema direita”, afirma.
A pesquisadora também chama atenção para os obstáculos à participação eleitoral, como as leis que exigem documentos específicos de identificação para votar e o gerrymandering, prática de manipulação dos limites dos distritos eleitorais para favorecer determinados partidos.
Em 24 estados, os eleitores precisam apresentar documentos com fotografia, exigência que, segundo organizações de defesa dos direitos eleitorais, pode dificultar a participação de pessoas pobres e integrantes de minorias.
Segundo ela, os republicanos promoveram essas mudanças ao longo de décadas, enquanto os democratas não organizaram uma resistência suficientemente consistente. As regras podem prejudicar desproporcionalmente a representação de comunidades negras, latinas e de baixa renda, dependendo de sua aplicação em cada estado.
“Esse processo é muito antigo, vem acontecendo ao longo dos últimos 20 anos e esse é o caráter verdadeiramente antidemocrático dessa eleição”, conclui.

https://gothamist.com/news/child-dies-in.title: Child dies in raging Upstate New York measles outbreak
https://gothamist.com/news/child-dies-in.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/child-dies-in.text:
A child in Lewis County has died from the measles, marking the first death from the disease in New York state in 30 years, state health officials announced.
State and county health officials did not offer additional details about the child who died. In a joint statement, they called for privacy for the child’s family.
The death comes as the highly contagious disease continues to spread through undervaccinated communities upstate in an outbreak that prompted Gov. Kathy Hochul to declare a state disaster emergency last month.
“I am heartbroken to learn that a child in Lewis County has died after contracting measles,” Hochul said in a statement Monday evening. “As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through.”
The measles is a highly contagious disease that typically brings on symptoms such as a runny nose, watery eyes and a fever before a rash emerges several days later, according to the state health department.
In New York, there have been 178 confirmed cases of the measles this year through Oct. 24, with most cases recorded since August, according to the state Department of Health. All but eight of those who got sick were outside of New York City.
Health officials in Otsego and Seneca counties, which have been affected by the outbreak, told Gothamist the true toll is likely much higher than the official count shows, however.
Outbreaks of the disease are also raging across the country, including in neighboring Pennsylvania. Nearly 5,000 cases of the measles have been confirmed nationwide this year as of Oct. 30, the highest number since 1991, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
New York state health officials said they have offered to assist Lewis County with community outreach and vaccination efforts, “both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak.”
Hochul’s disaster emergency order also allowed more types of health care workers to administer vaccines and conduct measles testing.
But some people in areas affected by the outbreak remain resistant to vaccination, according to healthcare workers and county health officials upstate.
People with ties to Amish communities in New York say they are among those most affected by the outbreak, though state and county health officials have declined to say which groups are bearing the biggest burden.
The outbreak comes as some Amish New Yorkers are seeking to add a religious exemption to the state’s school vaccine mandate.
Nationally, cases of the measles are rising as childhood vaccination against the disease declines, according to the CDC.
Hochul called out the Trump administration following the Lewis County measles death, saying the fatality is a “devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
President Donald Trump and his administration have called in recent months for children to be immunized against fewer diseases. Although the CDC continues to recommend vaccination against the measles, Trump has suggested the measles, mumps and rubella shot should be split up into three separate vaccines.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.title: Israel political deadlock leaves Netanyahu’s future hanging in the balance
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Israel political deadlock leaves Netanyahu’s future hanging in the balance
With neither bloc near a majority, Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties hold the key to Israel’s next government.
Israel’s election results are due to be certified on Wednesday, but with both leading blocs falling short of a parliamentary majority, negotiations remain deadlocked.
As things stand, the right-wing coalition of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured 53 seats in the October 27 vote, while the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot had 48. A majority requires 61 seats in the 120-strong Knesset. The 19 remaining seats went to the two Arab-led lists – the Joint List and Ra’am, or the United Arab List.
Netanyahu’s camp has been accused of seeking to delegitimise the results after launching a series of largely discounted claims that the vote for the Arab parties, which scored their best-ever electoral performance, had been manipulated by foreign interference.
Despite their historic showing that was boosted by an unprecedented surge in voter turnout, the two Arab-led lists remain politically isolated. And while there have been indications that they would be prepared to support, or at least not oppose, an Eisenkot-led government, their backing remains contentious within the opposition – a broad and increasingly fractious alliance that also includes parties led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, left-winger Yair Golan and right-winger Avigdor Lieberman.
After a meeting on Tuesday, the main opposition leaders issued a statement announcing that they were preparing to “act immediately” to replace Netanyahu’s governing coalition “with a national emergency government and translate the clear parliamentary majority in the Knesset into action”. Yet, the statement did not specify how they would reach the majority that would ultimately depend on them allying with either the Arab-led lists or two ultra-Orthodox parties, which have historically supported Netanyahu in return for shielding some of their members from military service.
“Essentially, we’re both on track to a government, and nowhere near being able to form one,” Israeli pollster Mitchell Barak told Al Jazeera.
‘Not clear who’s talking to who’
Though informal negotiations are widely reported to have begun, official talks on establishing a governing coalition will start only after the results are certified on Wednesday. Netanyahu’s Likud party has already mooted refusing to recognise the results, citing its continuing claims of irregularities in the Arab vote. Those allegations have been investigated and discounted by police, while a separate probe by the internal security service, the Shin Bet, remains ongoing.
Once the results are certified, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with all the parties to determine which member of the Knesset, not necessarily a party leader, is best placed to form a government.
Herzog, who lost to Netanyahu after an especially bitter contest in 2015, has found himself in the unusual position of having to decide who should be given the first opportunity to form a government, while simultaneously considering the prime minister’s longstanding request for a pardon in his ongoing corruption trial.
One of Herzog’s options is to ask the Arab parties to recommend Eisenkot. If selected, the leader of the centrist Yashar party will initially have 28 days to assemble a coalition, a period that can be extended by 14 days. Should he fail, Herzog can then invite another candidate to try.
For his part, Netanyahu on Monday argued that Likud’s first-place finish, with 27 seats, gave him a mandate to lead the next government. “We aim to form a broad government with our partners and with any other party that wishes to join, provided they do not support terrorism,” he said.
Still, it is unlikely he will be able to command a majority without entering an alliance with the Arab parties that he has consistently vilified, or a large-scale wave of defections from the opposition.
Whatever the state of the negotiations, the new Knesset is due to be sworn in on November 10.
Barak said coordination within the opposition appeared minimal, while personal animosities between Netanyahu and Herzog further complicated already fraught negotiations.
“It’s really not clear who’s talking to who,” he added.
“Earlier this week, they named [Bennett’s running mate] Lapid as their choice of speaker, which was apparently news to both Eisenkot and Bennett. Equally, Netanyahu now has to appeal to his political rival, Herzog, both to be given the responsibility of forming a government and to be pardoned before any conviction,” Barak continued.
“All the while, he’s claiming that the Arab parties cannot be considered legitimate partners in government, which makes it almost impossible for anyone to form a coalition with them.”
Clear as mud
However, the extent to which the efforts to delegitimise the Arab parties may succeed remains uncertain. Ra’am served as a central plank of the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021–22, the first time an independent Arab party had formally joined an Israeli government, with public pressure to do so again growing.
Over the weekend, thousands rallied in Tel Aviv calling upon Eisenkot to make a deal with the Arab parties that reflected the overwhelming number of votes cast against Netanyahu’s governing coalition. However, following the meeting between the opposition leaders on Tuesday, sources within the Joint List told Al Jazeera they were not expecting to be invited to support the bloc anytime soon.
Instead, speculation has turned to the possibility of one of the two ultra-Orthodox parties – Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), and particularly the latter – defecting to the opposition and backing Eisenkot.
Neither Shas nor UTJ have had straightforward relationships with Netanyahu’s governing coalition. In fact, it was the withdrawal of their parliamentary support in May, following what they saw as the coalition’s failure to pass a draft law exempting some of their ultra-Orthodox members from military service, that fundamentally weakened its majority in parliament.
“There are rumours that the Ashkenazi [Jews, who make up the bulk of the UTJ membership] are ready to break with Netanyahu and go to Eisenkot,” political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera.
“I am sceptical, but even that would still leave them short of an overall majority, so they would still need support from one of the Arab parties, even if that is Ra’am supporting them from outside a formal coalition,” he said of the parliamentary arithmetic.
Spoilers
Hanging over all, however, are developments tied to Israel’s deep and longstanding alliance with the United States.
Barak said the entire government-formation process risked being disrupted by the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, which could weaken Israel’s foremost ally, President Donald Trump, or be overtaken entirely by renewed war with Iran.
Netanyahu, particularly, went to pains during the election campaign to stress his relationship with Trump, whose Republican Party faces a tough race to keep hold of Congress.
Equally, both Trump’s rhetoric as well as the renewed build-up of US forces in the region may all signal the beginning of renewed conflict with Israel’s regional nemesis, Iran.
“Netanyahu cannot form a coalition,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera. “It’s a numbers game, and he just doesn’t have the numbers – no amount of talking and planning can change that, but an emergency could, and in Israel, there’s no more popular an emergency than one involving Iran.”
In such an instance, he speculated that the incumbent could ask the opposition to fall in behind him, but that would raise the possibility of a former captain dictating war policy to former generals.
“There’s also the possibility that, however you want to define it, Israel has a successful war against Iran. That leads to a surge in popularity for Netanyahu when negotiations on a coalition resume, or [him] calling unnecessary, fresh elections,” said Mekelberg.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dereglemen.title: Les bonnes affaires de Tony Blair : comment l’ex-premier ministre britannique veut réformer l’UE au profit des États-Unis
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dereglemen.author: Lina Sankari
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dereglemen.text:
L’ancien premier ministre travailliste britannique garde une influence considérable grâce à son institut. Il propose une thérapie de choc pour l’Union européenne qui vise, au nom de la puissance, à y rétablir l’influence de Londres, au profit des États-Unis.
Tony Blair n’a plus de mandat, mais il a des idées. Et quelques leviers pour les imposer. Premier ministre travailliste britannique entre 1997 et 2007, il reste pour beaucoup le symbole de l’aplaventrisme depuis l’intervention militaire britannique en Irak en 2003, aux côtés de George W. Bush.
À l’époque, la « relation spéciale » avec Washington présentait un intérêt manifeste pour le locataire du 10, Downing Street en ce qu’elle lui permettait de garder ses distances avec Bruxelles. Mieux, il n’a cessé de plaider pour l’élargissement de l’Union européenne (UE) pour mieux affaiblir certains membres historiques récalcitrants à l’atlantisme, dont Paris.
Puis en 2004, il voit dans l’accueil de dix pays de l’Est au sein du cercle européen une manière de reléguer la Russie au rang de puissance de second ordre : « Nous nous réjouissons en effet de cette étape historique qui mettra un terme aux divisions artificielles de la guerre froide », écrit-il dans une tribune intitulée « Mon Europe », publiée par Le Monde.
Depuis, le Brexit est passé par là et l’influence du Royaume-Uni sur les affaires du Vieux Continent a perdu de sa superbe. Mais Tony Blair n’a visiblement pas renoncé à la sienne. C’est aujourd’hui...

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Former High Museum of Art executive sentenced to 12 months in prison for embezzlement
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Matthew Terrell
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Brady Lum, a former chief operating officer at Atlanta's High Museum of Art, was sentenced to 12 months in federal prison on Monday (2 November) for embezzling more than $600,000 from the institution. The sentencing comes as the High celebrates its centennial and its parent organisation, the Woodruff Arts Center, conducts a major corporate fundraising campaign.
Federal prosecutors said Lum diverted museum funds to pay for personal purchases, including guitars, music lessons and woodworking equipment. He concealed the expenditures through falsified invoices, reimbursement requests and accounting adjustments. The scheme began in September 2019, less than nine months after Lum joined the museum, and continued until its discovery in November 2025.
Lum paid full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High and voluntarily paid approximately $500,000 more to cover costs the museum incurred while uncovering and investigating his criminal activity.
During Monday's hearing, US District judge Michael L. Brown focused extensively on the deterrent purpose of sentencing. Although Brown said he did not believe Lum was likely to reoffend, he emphasised the court's responsibility to discourage similar financial crimes by others in positions of trust.
The judge acknowledged similarities between his own professional and socioeconomic background and Lum's, discussing how sentencing structures have historically been shaped by educated, professionally successful individuals whose circumstances resemble those of many white-collar defendants.
Brown also considered Lum's prompt restitution after the misconduct was discovered, distinguishing between voluntarily returning stolen funds before detection and repaying them after being caught. The latter, he indicated, carried less weight in assessing accountability.
Lum addressed the court and apologised for his conduct, expressing regret for disappointing his family and community. The gallery appeared to consist largely of relatives, friends and supporters of Lum.
Contacted for comment following Monday's sentencing, a spokesperson for the Woodruff provided the following statement: "We respect the court’s decision and remain focused on fulfilling our mission, responsibly managing our resources and connecting deeply with the audience we serve."
Both the Woodruff and the High declined to provide substantive information about financial safeguards introduced following Lum's misconduct, or whether they intend to publish a remediation plan addressing financial controls, governance reforms and oversight procedures.

Brady Lum, the former chief operating officer of Atlanta‘s High Museum of Art, has been sentenced to one year in federal prison for stealing more than $600,000 from the institution. He previously pleaded guilty to the charges in July. Before his sentencing, Lum paid full restitution to the museum and reimbursed $500,000 of its legal and investigative fees.
The disgraced former COO joined the High Museum in January of 2019 and resigned in December of 2025. He started to siphon money from the institution in September of 2019, and continued until the discovery of fraud in November of 2025. He used doctored invoices and used his power to approve transactions for personal purchases, and used accounting adjustments to spread his expenses across multiple cost centers. He utilized the money he embezzled to purchase high end guitars, music lessons, and woodworking equipment. The Justice Department found that Lum had received more than seven hundred reimbursements from the museum, most of them under $1,000.
U.S. District Judge Michael L. Brown sentenced Lum to one year in prison, followed by one year of supervised release. Lum took a plea deal, which involved paying full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High Museum. “We expect leaders of one of our communities’ historic institutions to serve as stewards, not loot it,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta, in a press release from the US District Attorney’s Office of Northern Georgia. “Brady Lum manipulated internal processes to steal hundreds of thousands of dollars. The FBI is committed to uncovering and stopping this kind of greed and fraud.”

https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.title: New York City SNAP Participants Will Get Extra Funds for Fresh Produce in 2027
https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.text:
Share This Article
The city is expanding its Health Bucks program, which matches every $2 a SNAP participant spends on fruit and vegetables at farmers markets and other select vendors. The change comes as inflation and rising food costs has more households struggling.
With food costs on the rise, the city is expanding a program that offers low-income New Yorkers extra money to spend on local produce, the Mamdani administration announced Thursday.
Starting in January, participants in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP or food stamps, will have greater spending power under the city’s Health Bucks program, which matches every $2 they spend at farmers markets and farm stands with coupons they can use to purchase additional fruits and vegetables.
The city is raising the daily Health Bucks cap from $10 to $14, meaning SNAP participants can qualify for an extra $4 a day for fresh produce at more than 100 locations across the city—what officials say will offer a boost to both households’ budgets and local farmers.
“Every day, New Yorkers walk into a store hoping prices haven’t gone up again,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement announcing the change. “As food insecurity rises, far too many families are forced to skip the fruits and vegetables.”
From 2021 to 2024, the number of city residents at risk of food insecurity—meaning their households sometimes or often struggled to afford food—increased by 18 percent, from 2.2 million to 2.6 million, according to Health Department data released last month.
For certain demographic groups, the numbers were even starker: some 59 percent of Latino and 50 percent of Black New Yorkers were at risk of being food insecure in 2024, the same report found, compared to 40 percent of the city’s population overall. Food insecure households were more likely to forgo fresh produce, the report found.
The city says it expects to distribute nearly $2.3 million in Health Bucks benefits next year with the expanded matching cap.
The change comes as inflation and rising food costs have more SNAP households stretching their monthly dollars to make ends meet. A recent Urban Institute analysis found that for many counties across the country, maximum SNAP benefits fall far below the average cost of a “modestly priced” meal in that area.
In Manhattan, for example, that average meal is approximately $6.07—109 percent more than the $2.90 per meal that a maximum SNAP benefit covers, the analysis found, one of the largest gaps in the country.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Americans go to the polls in referendum on Trump’s agenda
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Chris Hippensteel and Lucy Campbell (now); Yohannes Lowe (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
What is being decided in the midterms and why do they matter?
David Smith
The US Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and theSenate. Both must approve federal legislation before it can become law and both play important roles in overseeing the executive branch.
The House is elected every two years, meaning all 435 voting seats are contested at every congressional election. The Senate has 100 members serving staggered six-year terms, so roughly a third of its seats are up for election every two years.
This year’s ballot includes:
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives. Republicans are defending a narrow majority, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.
35 seats in the Senate. Thirty-three seats are up in regular elections, along with two special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the remainder of terms that were vacated early. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need to gain four seats to secure a majority.
39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.
Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.
The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.
The midterms have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.
Speaking to reporters after casting his ballot in Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers denounced what he called “vicious” Democratic attacks on Haley Stevens, the former Democratic primary candidate who abandoned her party to endorse him in the eleventh hour before the midterms.
“Obviously I’m disappointed in how vicious they’ve been,” Rogers told reporters assembled in a parking lot “But I think that speaks to who the modern Democrat party is.”
Rogers continued: “Here’s somebody who said ‘I voted Democrat all the way down the list, except for one person who I think is too extreme for our state.’ That’s country over party. They ought to celebrate her courage and encourage her to continue being a Democrat rather than trying to throw her out of the party.”
“I’ve never seen such viciousness online.”
Stevens, the erstwhile challenger of Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, broke with her party to endorse Rogers over the weekend, after a renewed public break with El-Sayed over an issue that fiercely divided them in their primary race: US support for Israel.
The line to vote at Burbank Early Childhood School in Columbus, Ohio grew long as hundreds of people filed into the polling site to vote throughout the morning.
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, voted at the site alongside his wife, Apoorva Ramaswamy. He said before entering the school:
At the start of this day, if I have one suggestion to those who are deciding how to vote today, vote for the person who can actually make your life better. Vote for the person who you believe in your heart of hearts is actually going to make your family’s life better.
This election, especially for the role of governor, comes down to who’s going to allow your family to live a better life.
He added, “Our work begins tomorrow morning”.
After filing into the building, Ramaswamy and his wife stood in line with other voters.
Some voters experienced minor issues as they tried to cast their ballot. “My voting machine didn’t work, and I was standing next to Ramaswamy and thought that was kind of ironic,” said Andrea, a Columbus native.
Several other voters turned around when they saw the line. “I’ll try again in the afternoon,” said John Pearson.
On election day, Georgia resident Bunny Calloway tells our colleague George Chidi about her hopes for AI regulation and expresses concerns about misinformation and the possibility of people not honoring the outcome of the midterm results.
Two days of torrential downpours gave way to a brighter morning in south Florida, where voters took advantage of the brief respite to show up at soggy polling stations in what officials said were encouraging numbers.
At Ramblewood elementary school in the Fort Lauderdale suburb of Coral Springs, Curt Tiefenbrun, president of the local Democratic club and a water district candidate, dodged an early shower to greet a “receptive” line of voters when the polls opened at 7am.
“We had a pretty good turnout this morning before everybody had to go to work. They’re very enthusiastic as they accept our voter guide, and we’ve seen a lot of Democrats come out. We’re really happy with that,” he said.
Sunday it rained for hours and people were coming out to vote. All of us were standing out there wearing our ponchos, handing out guides. It was fun to see everybody come out and really participate.
Florida election officials released early voting figures on Tuesday showing registered Republicans in the state returned over 250,000 more ballots than Democrats - 1.49 million to 1.21m. Democrats are hoping in-person turnout on Tuesday, together with support from hundreds of thousands of independent voters and Republicans disillusioned with their party, will help them overcome the deficit.
Tiefenbrun said Democratic turnout in early voting was “extremely encouraging” compared to what he saw in 2024 and 2022. “We’re hoping we can stay above the fray, so to speak, on this final day, election day,” he said.
Polls are set to begin opening in Alaska, which is hosting the competitive Senate race between Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola, his Democratic challenger.
The race has been complicated by revelations that Peltola’s campaign allegedly recruited another man named Dan Sullivan to join the race, hoping to peel ballots away from the incumbent. While the tactic wasn’t clearly illegal, it’s prompted calls from the Trump administration to toss out the results if Sullivan doesn’t win out, and to investigate Peltola’s campaign for potential criminal violations.
A federal judge recently denied a Department of Justice request to block the race’s certification, and the state of Alaska – itself investigating Peltola – assured the court that ballots were designed to minimize confusion. But we’ll learn over the coming days just how many votes the imposter Sullivan will receive – and if it’s enough to sway the outcome of a crucial contest.
Trump tells Fox he'll slash aid to Israel by end of this year
In an interview with Fox & Friends this morning, in which he made a meandering final pitch to Americans voting in the 2026 midterm election, Trump said that he had agreed with Benjamin Netanyahu to cut off $4 billion of US military aid to Israel.”
“Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal,” Trump said. “We give Isreal $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping. And they’re fine with it, because, you know, they’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it. And we won’t be paying anymore to Israel.”
Trump said that the deal came at the insistence of Netanyahu, whose political future is in doubt following an Israeli election that failed to deliver the longtime prime minister a clear majority.
US ties to Israel, the country’s conduct in Gaza, and the conflict with Iran have become major issues in the 2026 midterm election.
‘Call me senator after tomorrow’: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed mocks Trump in final rally – video
Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, mocked Donald Trump and rallied supporters alongside senator Elizabeth Warren in Detroit, in a final push for votes before Tuesday’s midterm elections. Progressive El-Sayed is seeking to hold an open seat for Democrats against Republican Mike Rogers, who received a last-minute endorsement from Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens.
A leading abortion rights group has endorsed Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate for Maine, while attacking the record of his Republican opponent, Senator Susan Collins.
Mini Timmaraju, president of the advocacy group Reproductive Freedom for All, hailed Jackson - who was formerly an opponent of abortion - for “evolving” on the issue at a last-minute canvassing event in Scarborough. At the same time, she attacked Collins for trying to depict herself as “pro-choice”, saying she had voted to confirm the conservative US Supreme Court justice, Samuel Alito, who was the author of the 2022 court ruling that overturned the historic Roe versus Wade decision that guaranteed the right to an abortion. Jackson has repeatedly criticised Collins’ 2018 vote to confirm another conservative justice, Brett Kavanaugh, who subsequently voted to overturn Roe v Wade.
Timmaraju said Jackson’s election was vital to counteract a Trump administration plan to be “hand-off on abortion post-midterms” that she said would make it easer to dismantle state protections.
“We know the Trump administration has plans for a few weeks from now to reverse on abortion, to make it harder to get,” she said. “If we do not put Troy Jackson in the Senate, we won’t have that protection in Maine, where so many Mainers get access to abortion through the mail, through Telehealth.
“There are so many ways to ban abortion, by going around the states, and that is what the Trump administration is extremely interested in.”
Doug Emerson, a self-described activist, parked his car, festooned with slogans protesting the Trump administration’s policies, outside the office of Senator Susan Collins in Portland, Maine’s biggest city.
Emerson said he wanted to bring the attention of Maine voters to what he described as Collins’ tacit collusion with Donald Trump’s most extreme actions, despite her image as a moderate, independent-minded Republican cultivated over five terms as the state’s senator.
“We can’t change things unless we alter the demographics of the current Congress,” said Emerson. “I’m not sure Mainers are paying close enough attention.”
Astronauts For America, an alliance of more than 100 former Nasa explorers, has written an election day open letter to US voters reminding them of the importance of their vote in defending constitutional principles against threats to democracy.
“Federal authority is not a license for any president or federal agency to take over state election administration,” the letter, also signed by ther non-partisan, pro-democracy groups National Security Leaders for America and Leadership Now, said.
“Regardless of political party or personal beliefs, every American should be able to trust that elections are conducted according to the law, every lawful vote is counted, and the results are determined through established legal procedures - not political pressure or the arbitrary exercise of power.”
Astronauts For America, which includes astronauts from almost every generation of US spaceflight from Apollo to the space shuttle, recently completed a nationwide tour of college campuses urging young and first-time voters to ensure their voices are heard.

https://taz.de/Jugendliches-Trinken/!622.title: Jugendliches Trinken: Enthält Alkohol
https://taz.de/Jugendliches-Trinken/!622.author: Jan-Paul Koopmann
https://taz.de/Jugendliches-Trinken/!622.text:
Jugendliches Trinken: Enthält Alkohol
Ob Alkopops oder gleich Schnaps: beim Trinken, weiß unser Kolumnist, geht es immer auch um ein Stück Identität.
I m hiesigen Supermarkt stehen seit Anfang Oktober zwei mannshoch beladene Paletten Korn-Cola in Dosen. Das Gros ist noch eingeschweißt, und obwohl allein ich schon zwei- oder dreimal beinahe zugegriffen hätte, werden es einfach nicht weniger. Wundern tut mich das nicht, etwas trübsinnig stimmt es mich aber doch. Noch während ich das schreibe, wird mir klar, dass ich gleich noch mal losfahren werde, um mir ein Gebinde des mutmaßlich widerwärtigen Getränks zu kaufen, bevor es im November dann ausgelistet und für immer vergessen wird.
Ich will das nicht an die große Glocke hängen, an dieser Stelle aber auch nicht verschweigen, dass ich mit einigem Recht als Erfinder dieses Produkts gelten muss. Nein, nicht Korn-Cola, sondern ganz spezifisch eben die fertige Mische in Dosen. Als Anfang des Jahrtausends nämlich die Alkopop-Debatte losging – die Älteren werden sich erinnern –, da habe ich öffentlich und vor Zeug:innen gesagt: „Man füllt ja auch nicht Korn-Cola in Dosen und glaubt, dass es dann jemand kauft.“ Aber wie man so sagt: Der Prophet zählt wenig im eigenen Land – und das gilt nirgends so sehr wie hier oben im Nordwesten, wo eben der Korn herkommt und die Sturköpfigkeit.
Vielleicht aber muss man Auswärtigen doch erst einmal erklären, was überhaupt das Problem an der Sache ist. Korn-Cola ist nämlich nicht einfach eine Unappetitlichkeit unter vielen, nicht irgendein preisgünstiges Adoleszenzschmiermittel, sondern ein Stück Identität – das man im Zuge der Menschwerdung ab 20 so eilig wie nachdrücklich hinter sich zu lassen versucht.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Vorher aber ging es rund. Bei Schützen- und Feuerwehrfesten war Korn-Cola die logische Folge von Bier, manchmal flankiert vom weltbürgerlicheren Wodka-O. Den karibische Nächte versprechenden Bacardi gab es in reicheren Nachbargemeinden, aber auch da erst später. Korn mit Cola bekömmlich zu machen, war ein Trick, die Reife und Kantigkeit der Erwachsenen immerhin zu simulieren. Immerhin sich selbst gegenüber. Und nicht irgendwelche Erwachsenen, sondern diesen besonderen Menschenschlag, der (egal, wo man ihn traf) immer knietief im Torf zu stecken schien, mit Pfeife im Mund und einer ausgefransten Rolle Seil am Gürtel. Eine Idee von Vater, wie wir ihn (zum Glück) alle nicht hatten.
Mein echter Vater trank nie Korn, aber jedes zweite Jahr kaufte er doch welchen. Um die Runde wieder voll zu kriegen. Denn seit wir damals vom echten Land in die Siedlung zogen, bekam er jedes Jahr vier Flaschen zum Geburtstag: von jedem Nachbarn eine, und zwar das gute Zeug in der Tonflasche. Eine machte er auf und verteilte die Hälfte direkt an der Tür unter den Schenkenden. So behielt er drei volle Flaschen über, für die Geburtstage von drei der vier Nachbarn. Und für den Besuch an der Tür im nächsten Jahr hatte man noch die angebrochene Flasche vom letzten Jahr.
Durchbrochen wurde diese Geschenkökonomie erst viele Jahre später, als mein Freund Ronald und ich die Geschenke meines Vaters eines Abends heimlich austranken. Mit Cola natürlich. Und diese Zeit ist es auch, von der hier zwar aus guten Gründen wenig die Rede sein soll, die einem aber im doppelten Sinne wieder hochkommt, wenn man nun vor diesem Dosenberg im Supermarkt steht. Das alles ist lange her, und früher war trotz anders lautender Gerüchte nicht alles besser. Man weiß das und beginnt doch zu zweifeln.
„Das Leben wird in gewissem Sinne gefahrloser“, schrieb Norbert Elias 1939 in „Über den Prozess der Zivilisation“ – „aber auch affekt- oder lustloser“. Und ebendarum ist es dann doch auch fast ein bisschen schade, dass kein Mensch diese Dosen kauft.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Fies 2: inscrições para vagas remanescentes terminam nesta terça
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Daniella Almeida
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O prazo de inscrição para as vagas remanescentes do Fundo de Financiamento Estudantil (Fies), referentes ao segundo semestre de 2026, termina nesta terça-feira (3). Os estudantes interessados podem se inscrever exclusivamente pelo Portal Único de Acesso ao Ensino Superior. Para isso, é preciso fazer login pela conta da plataforma Gov.br.
O programa oferece financiamento para estudantes que desejam cursar o ensino superior em faculdades privadas bem avaliadas pelo Ministério da Educação (MEC). O Fies cobre as mensalidades do curso e permite que o estudante pague, com condições facilitadas, o valor financiado após a conclusão da graduação.
Nesta edição, as vagas remanescentes são destinadas exclusivamente à contratação do financiamento no segundo semestre letivo deste ano, sem possibilidade de extensão do prazo.
Uma das etapas do processo seletivo vai verificar se os candidatos pré-selecionados têm condições de acompanhar as atividades acadêmicas e concluir o semestre com aproveitamento suficiente.
Quem pode participar
Para participar, é necessário ter feito o Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) a partir de 2010, com média igual ou superior a 450 pontos nas cinco provas de conhecimentos e nota acima de zero na redação. O estudante não pode ter participado do exame como treineiro.
O candidato também precisa ter renda familiar mensal bruta por pessoa de até três salários mínimos, de acordo com o edital.
Na parte acadêmica, o candidato pré-selecionado deve ter condições de cumprir a frequência mínima exigida pela instituição privada de ensino superior neste segundo semestre letivo de 2026.
Vagas
Ao todo, são 50 mil vagas distribuídas pelo país. O edital reserva 50% dessas vagas remanescentes a candidatos com renda familiar mensal por pessoa de até meio salário mínimo e inscrição atualizada no Cadastro Único para Programas Sociais do governo federal (CadÚnico). Para essa verificação, serão consideradas as informações cadastrais atualizadas até 8 de outubro de 2026.
Os estudantes pré-selecionados nessa modalidade poderão solicitar financiamento de até 100% dos encargos educacionais, conforme as regras do programa.
O resultado da chamada única está previsto para 16 de novembro.
