https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.title: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.author: Cengiz Yar
https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.text:
Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.
The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues.
The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.
Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?
In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks. Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided. The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding.
The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”
My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster.
When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.
While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously.
Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it.
Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning?
In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.
Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year.
But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso flooding.
There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.
I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.
Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle.

https://www.equator.org/articles/speak-t.title: Speak the Wind
https://www.equator.org/articles/speak-t.author: Hoda Afshar
https://www.equator.org/articles/speak-t.text:
Speak the Wind
Hoda Afshar
08.04.2026Photo Essay
The wind, it is said, can possess a person.
In the islands of the Strait of Hormuz, off the southern coast of Iran, a distinctive local culture has emerged as the result of many centuries of cultural and economic exchange. Its traces are seen not only in the material culture of these islands but also in the customs and beliefs of their inhabitants.
Central to these is a belief in the existence of winds that may bring misfortune, principally in the form of illness, and a corresponding ritual in which a hereditary cult leader speaks with the wind in one of many local tongues to negotiate its exit.
Wider beliefs about these winds permeate the culture but are seldom openly discussed – perhaps out of fear that language might manifest the invisible.
While their exact origins are unclear, the existence of similar beliefs and practices in many African countries suggests that the cult may have been brought to the south of Iran from southeast Africa through the Arab slave trade – an account that agrees with that of many locals who hold that the winds themselves travel from Ethiopia.
For locals and visitors, too, these beliefs resonate with the surreal landscape of the islands – a topography marked by strange valleys and statue-like mountains that have been carved by the wind over many millennia.
This project documents the history of these winds and the traces they have left on these islands and their inhabitants – a visible record of the invisible seen through the eye of the imagination.

https://gothamist.com/news/a-typo-a-miss.title: A typo. A missing screw. These are the small snags keeping NYC families in shelters.
https://gothamist.com/news/a-typo-a-miss.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/a-typo-a-miss.text:
Roxy Shweky’s job is to make sure New York City apartments pass their inspections. Once they do, families living in city shelters can use housing vouchers to move into them.
Shweky works for the housing nonprofit Anthos Home, acting as a liaison between the landlord, tenant and the city.
During a recent tour of a Brooklyn apartment that had already failed twice, she showed an inspector the smoke detector that needed to be moved closer to the bedroom and the electrical outlet that needed grounding. Then he noticed a tiny detail on a kitchen window frame. On a metal bracket where there should be two screws, there was only one.
The apartment failed again. Shweky would need the landlord to make the fix before the apartment could get the OK for a family to move in.
“We all care deeply about households moving into quality, safe, dignified housing,” said Chris Mann, vice president of public policy and strategy for WIN, the city’s largest provider of family homeless shelters and supportive housing.
“But the complexity doesn't need to be this way.”
New York City’s cityFHEPS housing vouchers are a lifeline for people trying to leave the homeless shelter system. But getting city approval for a voucher can be a serpentine process — where one wrong move can mean starting over.
Housing advocates said even the smallest issue — like a burned out light bulb during an apartment inspection or a typo on a form — can delay a family moving out of a shelter and into an apartment by weeks. The pitfalls can happen at nearly every step of the process: from the moment a household applies for rental assistance, to finding an available unit, to the nearly 70-100 pages of paperwork and forms the city requires before giving a final OK.
“ We're talking about people's lives,” Mann said. “Every day in shelter is a day too long for a family.”
Housing advocates said the municipal voucher program is unnecessarily convoluted, trapping New Yorkers who desperately need a place to live in shelters for too long.
The Mamdani administration has announced a series of changes to speed up the process and said it’s already cut down the number of days it takes an application to be reviewed.
Nicholas Jacobelli, a spokesperson for the Department of Social Services, which administers the vouchers, said the administration has “taken numerous steps to cut the red tape required for New Yorkers to move out of shelter and into stable housing. We continue to test new mechanisms to further expedite these processes with the goal of housing New Yorkers more quickly.”
He said the city reduced how often applications from shelter residents are returned from 94% to 58% and cut down the number of times an application is returned prior to its approval by more than half. City officials also launched a new pilot to make move-ins for shelter residents into housing much faster by working directly with landlords.
But nonprofit groups and shelter providers said there’s still more to fix, and the stakes are high: A record number of New Yorkers are residing in city shelters every night as the rate of available apartments remains historically low.
Several bills introduced by City Council members aim to streamline parts of the system, like requiring city officials to approve or deny voucher applications within 15 days. The city said it now takes an average of 24 days to approve or deny an application, down from 28 days in the past. Applications are usually returned over missing, incorrect or incomplete forms, according to the Department of Social Services.
Jackie Mallon, chief operating officer for Anthos Home, a nonprofit focused on getting shelter residents into housing quickly, describes a process reminiscent of the board game Chutes and Ladders.
“There are a lot of points in the process where you could be stuck, have to go back to the beginning and start all over, and it's frustrating and difficult,” Mallon said. “It's just incredibly hard to do it on your own.”
Erin Dalton, the social services department's commissioner, said during a recent city council hearing the agency needed to balance making inspections faster while making sure the apartments taxpayers are subsidizing are safe.
She said once a person is found eligible for a voucher, it takes an average of nearly 8 months, or 236 days, for a family to move into a unit. City officials said the dearth of affordable housing and the city’s 1.4% of empty apartments can make the search process longer.
About 14,200 people are currently in shelter who have been found eligible for a voucher and are authorized to look for an apartment, city officials said.
Growth and savings
The CityFHEPS voucher program is one of the largest municipal voucher programs in the country.
More than 74,000 households rely on the program that’s expanded due to high demand. Recipients pay no more than 30% of their income toward rent. The city covers the rest.
With federal cut backs to rental assistance programs and only modest state rental aid, the vouchers are the primary way New Yorkers are able to leave the city’s homeless shelters.
But even as the city is pushing reforms, some efforts have backfired. Earlier this year, the Mamdani administration announced it would make the $1.2 billion program more efficient and save $500 million by cutting back how much it pays brokers and landlords.
In April, officials began checking to make sure the city wasn’t overpaying rents — an initiative that resulted in even more delays.
The new review process meant what used to take two days began taking an average of 53 days, according to Jade Vasquez, director of policy and research at WIN.
“ You don't want to overpay city dollars to landlords that are overcharging. But the process just seems very burdensome,” Vasquez said.
In September, the city moved the new rent review requirement to after a tenant moves into the unit to avoid further delays. But the change only applies to rent stabilized units. Market-rate units continue to experience move-in delays, providers said.
“It's like a half of a solution,” Vasquez said.
Repeat inspections
Housing advocates said inspections can be the most onerous part, setting back move-ins by months over issues that are often minor. Inspections are done by nonprofit partners, with the harder ones conducted by the Department of Social Services — and based on a strict checklist.
“Water temperature has to be between 120F and 128F. If it's too low, it won't pass. If it's too high, it won't pass,” said Shweky, housing unit readiness and repairs specialist at Anthos Home.
According to the Department of Social Services, 44% of inspections it conducts fail, with the top causes due to water temperature, electrical outlet deficiencies, missing or unlabeled apartment numbers, window guard and bracket violations or fridge and freezer temperature failures.
“ The porridge has to be exactly the right temperature for it all to magically be ready,” said Laura Lazarus, cofounder and CEO of Anthos Home.
Landlord and developer Iser Shepherd said the process can take so long that units are sitting vacant for months.
“Everyone gets frustrated. The tenant wants to know, the management wants to know. The landlord's getting furious like, ‘I'm not getting any response. Let me get another tenant,’” he said.
“Landlords, they want to accept vouchers. They just want to have a way that 's easy to do.”
City officials said they piloted a fast track inspection process that will expand next year.
Reams of paperwork
After a person is found eligible for a voucher, finds an apartment, gets the unit approved by the city and collects all necessary paperwork, everything is submitted to the city in a package.
The complete application includes forms like the last 30 days of income for everyone in the household over 18 years old, a letter from the homeless shelter, a checklist for the unit’s conditions, and a lease agreement. All of it can number as many as 100 pages.
Mann said a typo on the paperwork sent to the city — such as the apartment written as both 1A and A1 — can mean rejection, and having to resubmit everything again.
And if along the process, an applicant’s income changes by more than $125 a month, then they have to resubmit their pay stubs to the city so they can recalculate the budget.
Mario Vega, program director of operations for Anthos Home said since many applicants are hourly workers, just a couple work shifts can trigger the lengthy process
“I can't imagine a participant being able to do any of this without the support of their shelter worker or … us.”
Social services officials said homeless shelters are budgeted to have one housing specialist that can help with housing applications for every 40 residents, though not all shelters have one. Officials said all shelter staff should know how to navigate the housing voucher process.
Three case managers
Kelvin Wallace, 65, spent 11 months in a homeless shelter as he scrambled to figure out how to move out with a housing voucher. He said he worked with three different case managers in that time.
“I had to submit my application [on] at least three different occasions with three different case managers,” he said.
The challenge for him was figuring out whether he was even eligible for a voucher and being able to see the status of his application.
“ You have to reset each and every time,” a case manager changes, he said. Wallace said his case was ultimately referred to Anthos Home which helped him get an apartment in four months.
“I feel comfortable that I'm here. I'm on solid ground,” he said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
Ukrainian president meets Germany’s Merz in Berlin as chancellor says Russia is yet to engage seriously in peace efforts.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he hopes upcoming United States-mediated talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi will lead to a three-way meeting of leaders that includes Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking in Berlin on Tuesday alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Zelenskyy said the adviser-level talks, set for November 10 and 11 , were part of a broader diplomatic push to end the war.
“We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
Asked about the Abu Dhabi talks, Merz said it was “important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement”.
“I do not see that happening so far,” the chancellor said.
Zelenskyy’s visit to Berlin was not announced in advance for security reasons.
On landing, he said on X that diplomatic coordination, strengthening air defences and supporting Ukraine’s energy sector would top the agenda.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff announced the new round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US on Monday. He said the discussions would focus on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace”.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that a Russian delegation would attend, led as before by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported.
Europe seeks a seat at the table
The build-up to next week’s talks follows one of the most notable displays of cooperation between the warring sides since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Last week, human rights ombudsmen from Russia and Ukraine oversaw a local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in a mission brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Putin and Zelenskyy have had no direct contact since the invasion, and their representatives have held only a handful of rounds of talks.
Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane, reporting from Berlin, said there was a clear sense from Zelenskyy and Merz that the Abu Dhabi meeting “is a step forward, and there was an element of positivity about it”.
He said one journalist raised an important issue, saying “Europe and Ukraine are supposedly in lockstep with each other”, before asking, “why then are the Europeans not going to be in Abu Dhabi in those talks?”
“There was not much of a reply there, but it’s clearly an issue, a thorny issue, perhaps, certainly for the Europeans,” Kane said.
European governments have insisted on being involved in the negotiations but are unlikely to be at the table in Abu Dhabi.
Instead, US envoys are due to meet representatives from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, NATO and the European Union in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe’s post-war security architecture.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs an additional 70 billion euros ($77.5bn) from European countries next year.
Kane said successive German governments had pledged their full support to Ukraine, financing its efforts to fend off Russian attacks and supplying weapons and ammunition.
But he said Merz knows that “the financial aspect of helping Ukraine has become a real issue, given that the economy here and in other European countries is particularly threatened right now”.
“The cost of living in this country for many voters has become a serious issue,” Kane said.
He added that parties opposed to funding Ukraine, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Die Linke, were “prospering in the polls and in elections”.
Several summits are planned before year-end
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin may hold three-way talks on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 and 19 .
Around the same time, the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of about 35 countries backing Ukraine, is due to meet in Berlin.
The Group of 20 (G20) summit follows in Florida from December 13 to 15 , where it remains unclear whether Putin will attend for the first time since the invasion.

La France insoumise place la santé au cœur de son projet pour 2027. Son plan, dévoilé en exclusivité par l’Humanité, entend réduire les inégalités d’accès aux soins et limiter la place des intérêts privés, avec une question centrale : comment soigner tout le monde ?
C’est un invariable des enquêtes d’opinion : les années passent et la santé figure systématiquement parmi les premières préoccupations des Français. Hormis les sympathisants LR, tous les électorats placent, d’après un sondage Toluna Harris Interactive publié fin septembre, cette thématique dans leurs cinq priorités de l’élection présidentielle.
« C’est le sujet numéro un, avance même le député LFI Hadrien Clouet, qui a coordonné le programme de Jean-Luc Mélenchon avec sa collègue Clémence Guetté. https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.text:
Israeli prison guards ‘shot prominent Palestinian detainees nine times’
Israeli prison guards shot and wounded prominent Palestinian detainee Hassan Salameh nine times last month, his fiancee and a prisoners' rights group have said.
The assault on Salameh, 55, came after National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir stormed his cell and filmed himself threatening to kill him.
The Palestinian Prisoners’ Society (PPS), which monitors the conditions of Palestinian detainees, said it received information about the assault following a visit to Salameh by a lawyer on Monday.
Information provided to the group and Salameh’s fiancee, Ghufran Zamel, indicated that he had been severely beaten and shot nine times.
The type of ammunition used and the precise circumstances of the shooting remain unclear.

Israeli prison guards have recently stepped up the use of rubber-coated bullets against prisoners, firing at them from close range inside their cells.
The practice has caused severe injuries and potentially irreversible harm, according to rights groups.
PPS said Israeli restrictions on prison visits had prevented the lawyer from obtaining further details.
“This has raised serious concerns about the prisoner's fate and underscores the urgent need to disclose the circumstances of the incident and guarantee his physical safety,” the group said.
Zamel told local media that Salameh was beaten before Ben Gvir's visit and after he left. An Israeli force stormed the cell, subjecting him to a severe beating, including blows to the face, before firing nine bullets at him.
Three days after the assault, Salameh was taken to have his injuries photographed. He was then returned to his cell without medical treatment and given only painkillers, despite the injuries he had sustained, Zamel said.
According to Zamel, Monday's visit by the lawyer confirmed that Salameh was still suffering from the effects of the assault and remained in poor health. He appeared visibly exhausted.
PPS said the attack came amid what it described as a campaign targeting prominent Palestinian prisoners, which goes “beyond repression and punishment” and places their lives at risk.
“Prisoner leaders are facing various forms of physical and psychological torture, systematic crackdowns and public threats to kill them made by Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir,” the group said.
“The continuation of these policies, alongside restrictions on visits and the absence of independent oversight, paves the way for further violations and deprives prisoners of even the most basic protection.”
Escalating abuse
Born in the Khan Younis refugee camp in southern Gaza in 1971, Salameh became involved in Palestinian resistance against the Israeli occupation after the outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987.
He later became a leading figure in the armed wing of Hamas, the al-Qassam Brigades. In 1996, Israel convicted him of orchestrating several bombings that killed and wounded scores of Israelis.
Salameh said the attacks were carried out in response to Israel's assassination of Hamas bombmaker Yahya Ayyash earlier that year.
He was sentenced to 48 life terms and has spent a total of 14 years in solitary confinement since his imprisonment 30 years ago.
In September, Ben Gvir posted a video showing himself in Salameh’s cell, surrounded by security guards, as he told him that he wanted to "execute" him.
The minister also vowed to ensure prisoners such as Salameh were "put to death" if he became defence minister.
Palestinian prisoners, particularly prominent figures such as Salameh, have long faced abuse by Israeli prison authorities.
However, reports of abuse have escalated since the Gaza war and genocide began in October 2023. Several rights groups have accused Israeli prison authorities of widespread torture, physical assaults, sexual violence, starvation, medical neglect and humiliation of prisoners since then.
Last month, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel said they had collected 21 testimonies documenting what they described as a “dangerous practice” of prison guards firing rubber-coated bullets at prisoners from close range.
In one incident, an Israeli prison guard seriously wounded a Palestinian prisoner by firing rubber-coated bullets at his testicle. His right testicle was “completely crushed” and had to be surgically removed.
