https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Why Mary Cassatt was more than just a painter of the 'modern Madonna'
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Annabel Keenan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
As the centennial of the death of Mary Cassatt (1844-1926) brings renewed attention to the US-born Impressionist, a new publication challenges the image of her as a sentimental painter of mothers and daughters. In Cassatt Reconsidered, Mary G. Morton uses her expertise as a curator and head of French paintings at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, to examine how the art world shaped Cassatt’s reputation, and posits a broader view of her within radical French Modernism.
The book coincides with major exhibitions on Cassatt, including at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris (until 31 January 2027), the Art Institute of Chicago (until 3 January 2027) and the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut (7 November-14 February 2027). Looking closely at the artist’s work and framing her within the experience of women in a modern Paris, Morton shows why Cassatt deserves another look.
The Art Newspaper: What prompted your reassessment?
Mary G. Morton: I thought I knew enough about Cassatt until a 2014 exhibition at the National Gallery on Cassatt’s artistic pas de deux with Degas emphasising their radical technical experimentation. A few years later, an encounter with the PhD candidate Nicole Georgopulos transformed Woman with Sunflower (1905) in my mind from a generic mother and child image to a complex realist allegory, a kind of feminist manifesto responding to and supporting the contemporary suffrage movement. The public recognises Cassatt’s name but associates her with images of maternity. There is so much more to her art, to her story.
How did the art market contribute to the narrowing of Cassatt’s reputation?
Her dealer essentially marketed her as a painter of motherhood, the painter of the “modern Madonna”, hiring critics to write about her in this vein. And while he had success selling her work, the strategy did not serve her well in art historiography. Another dynamic is the burgeoning field of American art history in the 20th century, when Cassatt became an asset to curators as an Impressionist. In most major US museums, her work hangs with US artists, depriving her of the aesthetic context in radical French Modernism. She looks loud, garish, awkward, whereas if you put her with Degas, Renoir and Morisot, she fits in.
What would you like museums, scholars and the public to see differently about Cassatt?
It would be great if Cassatt could exit the limited box she has been put into. Cassatt was the most successful avant-garde artist of the 19th century to represent the lived experience of women in modern urban Paris. She created a fresh visual vocabulary for women’s interests and concerns, refusing the oppressive social norms of her class and producing an extraordinary body of work. Cassatt brings us women’s side of the story.
The primary aim of this book is to provoke readers who might be familiar with Cassatt as a misty-eyed painter of mothers and children to look again. My hope is that the book compels people into museums to find Cassatt’s art and experience what I have: brilliantly expressive, innovative objects that relay a unique vision of humanity and of women’s lives as they were lived more than 100 years ago.
• Mary G. Morton, Cassatt Reconsidered, Getty Publications, 208pp, $35 (hb)

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Christian voters in Washington state divided by common religion: ‘I don’t think the US is God’s kingdom on Earth’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lok Darjee
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A few days before the Fourth of July, Ron Peterson, the 38-year-old pastor of Longview United Pentecostal church, stood beneath a large white tent in a parking lot in Longview, Washington.
Surrounded by church members selling fireworks for a fundraiser, Peterson remembered watching area residents rally after an industrial accident at the local paper mill killed 11 people in May. “We can all come together,” he said. “There’s not going to be sections in heaven.”
At least two-thirds of his church members are Latino, Asian, Black or of multiracial backgrounds, according to Peterson. His congregation reflects a racial diversity that complicates the political image of evangelical Christians, who are largely (but not all) white, overwhelmingly backed Donald Trump in 2024 and tend to support his hardline immigration agenda.
But in this corner of southern Washington, even among churchgoers, there’s also a diversity of opinion about the role of religion in politics.
Peterson grew up poor in an Oregon household he describes as more New Age than Christian and works full time in sales while pastoring. He sees church as a place where people in his community – including families dealing with addiction or other crises – can come for support and succor.
He also holds views that place him squarely in the country’s culture wars. He believes that people like him – white Christian heterosexual men – have become targets.
“People need someone to blame,” he continued. “I think the ire is towards white Christian males. Now, they want to call them white Christian nationalists. But being white and Christian is actually, if you’re truly a Christian, a wonderful thing for society.”
He recounted being called into a meeting with human resources after singing a Christian hymn at work.
“I sang His Eye Is on the Sparrow. And because it said, ‘Jesus is my portion,’ I had to have a meeting with HR. Someone got offended,” he said. The Guardian could not independently verify his account.
He contrasted that experience with what he sees as greater tolerance for sexually explicit music. “So you can sing about sleeping with a bunch of women. [But] I can’t say Jesus?’
Peterson gives Trump high marks even as he criticizes the president’s lack of fiscal discipline. Peterson said, “From the standpoint of righteousness, he’s done more to help the country than any president, maybe ever.” But he argued the president was not a true fiscal conservative and that “from the standpoint of fiscal responsibility, I think he’s probably done worse than almost any president.”
For Peterson, Trump’s shortcomings appear to matter less than his willingness to advance causes important to the pastor’s faith. Asked about Trump’s felony conviction in the New York business-records case, the jury that found him liable for sexually abusing the writer E Jean Carroll, and his infidelity, Peterson brought it back to the supreme court – the justices Trump appointed, whose 2022 Dobbs decision overturned Roe v Wade. “Allowing the supreme court to hear Roe versus Wade again, I think that was very important,” he said, before acknowledging that his judgment ultimately “comes back down to my faith”.
‘Politically religious’
Religion has always been a factor in American life, and evangelicals have made the Christian right into a political powerhouse. Here in Longview, faith has featured in the neck-and-neck contest for Washington’s third congressional district. The Democratic incumbent, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, faces Republican John Braun in one of the nation’s most-watched House races. Both candidates have drawn on religion to connect with voters; Braun has defended expressions of religious and conservative speech on college campuses, and Gluesenkamp Perez, whose father served as an evangelical pastor, attends a Capitol Hill Bible study and has discussed sometimes feeling that her Christianity has embarrassed her Democratic party colleagues.
But a common faith does not mean common political stances. As Daniel HoSang, a Yale University professor who studies race and conservative political movements, put it, “For some, the idea of America as a Christian nation means protecting their freedom to practice their faith in a country they believe was founded on Christian values.”
For others, it means something more far-reaching – and potentially dangerous: a country where Christianity occupies a privileged position in government and public life, at the expense of people of other faiths. “If it’s a Christian country founded by Christians for Christians, that then authorizes discriminatory treatment against members of other religions,” he said.
In the nearby city of Battle Ground, I met 41-year-old dietitian Laura Oltmann at a new Italian pastry shop, where she expressed concern about religion’s growing influence in local politics and the treatment of immigrants under Trump’s administration.
The Ridgefield resident and registered independent grew up in a conservative Christian family where religion was often presented in strict terms of right and wrong. She studies the Bible, listens to morning devotionals on her way to work, and attends a small church near Battle Ground. The congregation, which she estimated has between 100 and 150 members, meets in a school, where worshippers unpack equipment each week before putting it away again. Oltmann said she felt called to mentor others and teach the Bible.
But she’s grown uncomfortable with what she views as the increasingly exclusionary bent of the Republican party and the idea that being Christian meant holding a particular set of political beliefs.
“I don’t really like that we’re conflating being Christian with being politically religious. Those are different things,” she said.
She also openly rejects the idea that the United States has a special claim to Christianity; in the Christian nationalism that Peterson referenced, proponents believe that the country was divinely chosen by God and founded to promote Christian values. “I don’t believe that America is, like, God’s kingdom on Earth,” she said.
That tension is particularly evident in her views on abortion. She does not believe it can be reduced to a simple political choice. She supported Gluesenkamp Perez in 2024 despite the congresswoman’s support for abortion rights.
“That’s definitely been a difficult conflict for me personally,” she said. “But I also feel that there’s just something about the power of choice and for a woman to be able to make that decision with her doctor.” Oltmann, who says it’s time for a female president, questioned the consistency of opposing abortion while resisting government programs that support children and families.
“You’re gonna be anti-abortion, but you’re not gonna support children’s programs, children’s nutrition, children’s schooling, the things that they need to function,” she said. “Are we taking a stand on these children’s lives, but not their growth and development? You know, that has to be both. As someone who follows Christ, how can I tell people that I don’t think they should feed kids, you know?”
Oltmann’s ballot-box decisions sometimes revolve around the compassionate politics she wants. “We need a leader who not only can lead and make decisions and communicate well, but can have empathy and see the problems,” she said. “Like, we don’t need a dictator.”
As a healthcare professional, Oltmann has been troubled by Trump’s immigration crackdown. “At one point, there was a concern that there was gonna be ... ICE coming into the hospital,” she said.
For her, the issue went beyond immigration policy. It was about how people should be treated, regardless of their status.
“I want people to be able to feel safe, to have access to healthcare. And to be able to thrive in their communities. And if you’re living in fear, how can you function?”
Oltmann ultimately voted for Gluesenkamp Perez because the congresswoman strikes her as “pretty middle of the road”, the same place she puts herself.
And “to be honest, the person she was running against [before] came across this very Christian nationalist, and that scares me more than probably anything”, she said.
That was Joe Kent, the Republican who lost to Gluesenkamp Perez twice and later served as director of the National Counterterrorism Center. During the 2022 campaign, CNN and other outlets reported that Kent had ties to white nationalists, including an interview with a Nazi sympathizer. Kent has denied the characterization and has distanced himself from extremists. He could not be reached for comment.
However, according to Oregon Public Broadcasting, Kent appeared on The Battle Ground Project, the Christian localism podcast co-hosted by the area pastor CR Wiley and an executive at the local electronic-equipment company, Maddox Industrial Transformer.
According to Frederick Clarkson, a research analyst who studies Christian nationalist movements for Political Research Associates, Christian localism emphasizes building influence within smaller communities, where religious groups may have greater opportunities to shape local institutions, businesses and government.
“It’s easier to get theocratic control, the fewer [the] people in the territory [that proponents] are trying to control,” he said.
An April investigation by Oregon Public Broadcasting found that Camden Spiller, Maddox Industrial’s co-owner and chief executive, was connected to more than a dozen corporations that purchased over 30 properties in Battle Ground in six years.
Spiller has described his Christian faith as one motivation for investing in the community. In an opinion essay, he cited a passage from the biblical book of Jeremiah: “Seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you.”
Some residents welcomed the investments as a revival of the city’s downtown. But others worry about religious influence on politics or the concentration of so many local businesses in the hands of a few. Spiller and his brother also own the city’s newspaper, among other interests.
Battle Ground’s mayor, Eric Overholser, also works at Spiller’s company. On 1 June this year, Overholser read two proclamations supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and another recognizing the federal designation of antifa as a domestic terror organization. Two weeks later, Overholser signed a proclamation celebrating nuclear and traditional families, defining them as a husband, wife and children.
Spiller is also financing a new chapel for First Presbyterian church of Battle Ground, where he also serves on the board. The church’s pastor, Wiley, has longstanding ties to Doug Wilson, a self-described Christian nationalist who has built a network of churches, schools and other institutions around his religious vision based in Moscow, Idaho. Wilson has advocated banning abortion and incorporating Christian religious principles into American law. Wilson’s publishing house, Canon Press, has published several books by Wiley.
The Guardian contacted Spiller and Wiley with detailed questions about their possible involvement in Christian localism but received no response by publication time.
Clarkson warned that efforts to establish religious authority through local institutions could pose a longer-term threat to democratic governance, although he cautioned against overstating the movement’s influence. “It’s important to understand the severity of their ideas without exaggerating their immediate consequence,” he said.
The greater concern, Clarkson argued, was what could happen if one interpretation of Christianity gains the power to govern people who do not share its beliefs.
“To the extent that it grows in influence and becomes synonymous with Christianity, to whatever degree, that’s a threat to democracy in the United States,” he said.

https://taz.de/Umweltpolitik-der-Tuerkei.title: Umweltpolitik der Türkei: Schlechtes Klima, schlechte Luft
https://taz.de/Umweltpolitik-der-Tuerkei.author: Jürgen Gottschlich
https://taz.de/Umweltpolitik-der-Tuerkei.text:
Umweltpolitik der Türkei: Schlechtes Klima, schlechte Luft
Nächste Woche beginnt in Antalya die Weltklimakonferenz. Die türkische Regierung will sich positiv präsentieren. Dabei hat sie viel Nachholbedarf.
Durch Nejla Işıks Heimat fressen sich riesige Bagger: Der Braunkohletagebau hat schon Wohnhäuser, große Teile des Akbelen-Walds und Olivenhaine in und um den Ort İkizköy in der südwestlichen Türkei geschluckt. Viele von Işıks NachbarInnen mussten umziehen. Die Mittvierzigerin ist das Gesicht der Bewegung gegen den Abbau klimaschädlicher Kohle in der Region geworden. Im November wird ihr Protest sie 380 Kilometer weit in die Mittelmeermetropole Antalya führen: Dort beginnt am kommenden Montag die Weltklimakonferenz. Umweltaktivist*innen planen einen Alternativen Klimagipfel.
Sie wollen den Blick der Weltöffentlichkeit darauf lenken, dass die Gastgeberin Türkei in ökologischer Hinsicht viel Nachholbedarf hat. Im Akbelen-Wald stand über Jahre ein landesweit bekanntes Protestcamp, von dem aus sich UmweltschützerInnen aus der gesamten Türkei jahrelang den Braunkohlebaggern entgegenstellten. Mit massiver Gewalt wurde das Camp vor drei Jahren geräumt und das Waldstück abgeholzt. Jetzt laufen Gerichtsverfahren gegen die Enteignung weiterer Olivenhaine. Wie der Widerstand gegen den Braunkohleabbau weitergehen kann, soll nun auf der alternativen Klimakonferenz diskutiert werden.
Die Kohle ist nicht das einzige Problemfeld der türkischen Klimapolitik: Beispielsweise gehört die größte Mülldeponie Istanbuls zu den schlimmsten Methanemittenten der Welt. Aus Lecks entweichen stündlich 7,4 Tonnen des hochwirksamen Treibhausgases, zeigen Berechnungen von US-ForscherInnen der Universität von Kalifornien in Los Angeles auf Basis von Satellitendaten.
Demnach entspricht der Klimaeffekt durch das Methan pro Stunde dem, den 1,5 Millionen SUV im selben Zeitraum hätten. Die zweitgrößte Deponie der 18-Millionen-Einwohner-Metropole bringt es immerhin auch noch stündlich auf 4 Tonnen Methan. Die Mülldeponien der anderen türkischen Großstädte wie Ankara, Izmir und auch Antalya haben ebenfalls immense Methan-Emissionen.
Dreckige Luft wegen fossiler Energie
Sie entstehen, weil die mit Lehmschichten abgedichteten Müllberge Lecks haben, durch die das Methan entweicht. Dabei wäre das Problem relativ leicht lösbar. Einmal könnte man dafür sorgen, dass Speisereste, durch deren Gärungsprozess das Methangas entsteht, auf anderen speziellen Deponien verarbeitet werden, was in anderen Ländern längst Praxis ist. Oder man fängt das Methan noch auf der Deponie auf und nutzt es für die Wärmegewinnung. Das ist technisch machbar, wird in der Türkei aber nur unzulänglich versucht.
Die anhaltende Kohleverbrennung, die großen Rohölraffinerien, die zahlreichen Zementfabriken und der dichte Autoverkehr in den Metropolen heizen nicht nur die Klimakrise an, sie sorgen auch für gefährliche Luft. Eine jüngst veröffentlichte Studie der internationalen Plattform für das Recht auf saubere Luft zeigt, dass die hohe Luftverschmutzung für jährlich 26.500 Tote verantwortlich ist und das Land rund 55 Milliarden US-Dollar jährlich kostet. Das ist das Zweieinhalbfache des Budgets des Gesundheitsministeriums.
Zu den ökologischen und gesundheitlichen Aspekten kommt hinzu, dass die Türkei Öl und Gas zum allergrößten Teil teuer importieren muss. Der Londoner Energie-Thinktank Ember empfiehlt der Türkei deshalb dringend, den Einsatz von Elektrizität im Energiemix zu erhöhen. Tatsächlich will die türkische Regierung diese Frage sogar auf der Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya zum Thema machen. Sie schlägt ein globales Ziel vor, den Anteil von Strom am Endenergieverbrauch von aktuell 20 bis 23 Prozent bis 2035 auf 35 Prozent zu erhöhen.
Hilfreich für das Klima ist das aber vor allem dann, wenn der Strom aus erneuerbaren Energien gewonnen wird. In der Türkei ist das bei rund 44 Prozent des Stroms der Fall. Vor allem gemessen am Potenzial, das die Türkei wetterbedingt hat, ist das immer noch sehr wenig.
Energiewende spät begonnen
Das Land ist sehr spät in die Produktion von Strom aus Windenergie und noch später in Solarenergie eingestiegen. Lange Jahre kam der erneuerbare Strom allein von Wasserkraftwerken, die in Staudämmen verbaut wurden. Noch heute liefert Hydropower den größten Anteil an erneuerbarem Strom.
Das Problem bei dem Ausbau der Wind- und Solarenergie ist, dass die türkische Regierung dabei sehr zentralistisch vorgeht. Flächen für Windparks werden von der Regierung festgelegt, ohne mit den Kommunen vor Ort zu kommunizieren. Bauern erfahren oftmals nur auf dem Liegenschaftsamt, dass ihre Felder plötzlich für Windkraftanlagen vorgesehen sind. Das erhöht die Akzeptanz für Windräder natürlich nicht, auch weil die Entschädigungssummen nicht dem tatsächlichen Wert der Flächen entsprechen.
Bei Solaranlagen ist es ähnlich. Die Türkei setzt bislang ausschließlich auf große flächenintensive Solaranlagen und behindert Photovoltaik-Anlagen auf dem eigenen Dach eher, statt sie zu fördern. Es gibt nicht nur keine Förderung, die Genehmigung und Einspeisung in das öffentliche Netz ist kompliziert und bringt finanziell nichts. Deswegen sieht man auf den Dächern, wenn überhaupt, nur kleine Warmwasseranlagen und keine Solarpaneele.
Hinzu kommt, dass die Regierung aus politischen Gründen an der Verfeuerung von Kohle festhält, ja sogar Kohle noch importiert, statt die Nutzung zu reduzieren. Sie steckt auch Geld in den Bau von Atomkraftwerken, statt Wind und Sonnenenergie massiv zu fördern. Bei der Diskussion um den schnellen Ausstieg aus den fossilen Energien dürfte die Türkei bei der Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya deshalb eher auf der Bremse stehen – auch als Gastgeberin.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Mundo vive o ‘parto doloroso’ de uma nova ordem, diz estrategista iraniano em entrevista exclusiva ao BdF
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Marco Fernandes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Na semana passada, a exportação de petróleo pelo estreito de Ormuz caiu para 8,7 milhões de barris por dia, metade do nível de antes da guerra, segundo a consultoria Kpler. O diesel chegou a US$ 220 o barril no atacado, mais que o dobro de antes do conflito no Oriente Médio, e as cinco maiores petroleiras ocidentais somaram mais de US$ 50 bilhões de lucro no terceiro trimestre. Para Seyed Mostafa Khoshcheshm, é a prova do que ele chama de a arma mais poderosa do Irã. “É uma arma milhões de vezes mais forte que a bomba atômica”, disse ao Brasil de Fato. “Com uma bomba atômica, você atinge um país uma vez. Com o estreito de Ormuz, você atinge o planeta inteiro, repetidamente.”
Na primeira parte desta entrevista, o estrategista iraniano falou da nova rodada da guerra que se espera. Agora, ele vai do estreito à ordem mundial. Dessa década de guerras, prevê, não sairá nenhuma superpotência, mas quatro grandes potências — China, Índia, Rússia e Irã —, todas no Brics e na Organização para Cooperação de Xangai.
Khoshcheshm não acredita que essa transição se decida só com mísseis. Derrotados pelo Irã, diz, os Estados Unidos “não terão a menor condição de enfrentar a China” e vão apostar na guerra híbrida, inclusive biológica. “Depois do Irã, será a China. Acredito que, em 2027, veremos a disseminação de vírus como a COVID.” A disputa seguinte, avisa, é a da inteligência artificial, que dividirá o mundo entre “senhores e escravos”. As monarquias do Golfo que escolheram o campo estadunidense já a perderam, e seus data centers, diz, “serão os próximos” na terceira rodada da guerra.
Confira a segunda parte da entrevista exclusiva para o Brasil de Fato.
Brasil de Fato: Em um artigo na The Atlantic, Robert Kagan, um dos principais pensadores neoconservadores, escreveu que os Estados Unidos sofreram a pior derrota estratégica da sua história e que o Irã vai emergir como a principal potência regional. Ainda falta a terceira rodada, mas como será o Irã como potência regional, a relação com os países árabes, o futuro dos Estados Unidos na região? O Irã pode se tornar uma potência global?
Seyed Mostafa Khoshcheshm: O mundo está numa transição de poder da civilização ocidental para o Oriente há mais de uma década, até intelectuais estadunidenses e europeus afirmam isso. Para mim, a década de 2020 é a deste “parto doloroso”, e haverá cada vez mais guerras. Quem tem o poder, o império ocidental liderado pelos Estados Unidos, não o larga facilmente. Haverá guerras e atritos, sobretudo com as potências emergentes: Rússia, China e Irã. Por isso, acredito que veremos alguma forma de guerra contra a China em 2027 ou 2028.
Os chineses já dizem isso. Estão se preparando.
Se os Estados Unidos forem derrotados pelo Irã, eles não terão a menor condição de enfrentar a China. Vão recorrer mais à guerra híbrida, que será completamente diferente. Vão recorrer à guerra biológica, a diferentes tipos de guerra ao lado da militar. Até nuclear. Seja como for, eles estão resistindo, como os europeus contra a Rússia.
Acredito que, em 2027, veremos a disseminação de vírus como a COVID. Os Estados Unidos não vão largar o poder tão facilmente. Trump pode gostar de Putin, mas existe um deep state que ele não controla. Eles não vão deixar a Rússia vencer tudo tão facilmente. Se não conseguirem pela via militar, farão isso com armas biológicas. Na China, o mesmo. No próprio Irã, o mesmo. Conheço os estadunidenses, a guerra híbrida deles, as intenções do Estado profundo e o seu comportamento. O padrão me diz que, quando se sentirem sem esperança e derrotados, vão soltar a guerra assimétrica, as novas formas de guerra, incluindo essa, e os ataques cibernéticos vão se intensificar.
Até na ciberguerra é assim. Antes de 2010, antes do Stuxnet [vírus de computador atribuído aos Estados Unidos e a Israel, que sabotou centrífugas do programa nuclear iraniano], o mundo vivia num ambiente de ameaças à segurança, com roubo de informação industrial e coisas do tipo. O Stuxnet transformou isso numa guerra cibernética entre Estados. Desde então, todos os grandes atores aumentam essa capacidade e investem nela de formas desconhecidas. A inteligência artificial é a nova versão de tudo: ciberguerra, guerra híbrida, em diferentes aspectos.
Se o mundo não estivesse numa transição de poder, com guerras como esta, o mundo do futuro, para mim, já não seria o do petróleo ou dos combustíveis fósseis. Seria o da inteligência artificial, com duas categorias: os senhores e os escravos, ou seja, quem possui o software e o hardware de IA, e o resto. Uma das principais disputas entre o Ocidente e o Oriente hoje é quem será o senhor da IA no futuro. Os campos estão se formando. A Arábia Saudita e os Emirados, entre os países árabes do Golfo Pérsico, decidiram entrar no campo estadunidense.
E uma das coisas que esses países árabes do Golfo Pérsico já perderam é a IA, porque dependiam demais dos Estados Unidos. Até agora falamos de duas guerras; a terceira ainda não aconteceu. Os data centers serão os próximos, na terceira. É uma das coisas que eles e Israel vão perder. Isso é muito importante.
Se Biden estivesse no poder, os Estados Unidos seriam mais duros com Putin.
Sem dúvida. Com Trump é diferente, ele joga demais no campo de Putin.
Mas não seria um cálculo estratégico? Gente do círculo de Trump dizia, antes mesmo da eleição, que a guerra contra a Rússia era um erro, porque a Rússia não é o principal adversário. Ele estaria encerrando essa guerra para se concentrar na China.
Não há dúvida de que o Irã é o principal inimigo ideológico dos Estados Unidos, e a China é o inimigo econômico. Mas nem tudo se controla: às vezes as guerras simplesmente estouram. Ou a Rússia percebe, por exemplo, que uma ameaça iminente está surgindo. Talvez tenham feito os cálculos: se fizermos isso, não haverá guerra contra nós; vamos enfraquecê-los agora, antes que seja tarde demais. Porque eles não entrariam numa guerra total, como no caso da Crimeia.
Depois de uma década de guerras, não sobrará nenhuma superpotência: a capacidade de todos estará desgastada. Mas o poder estará no Oriente. A nova ordem mundial que vai surgir no horizonte, provavelmente depois de 2030 ou 2032, será definida por coalizões regionais e internacionais como o Brics e a Organização para Cooperação de Xangai, que equivalem ao G7, à Otan e à OCDE do Ocidente. A Conferência de Segurança de Munique [fórum anual sobre segurança internacional, na Alemanha] já ocupou o centro do palco; hoje sua rival, a de São Petersburgo, ganha importância e prestígio. Não haverá superpotências, mas esses agrupamentos vão definir a nova ordem.
A maioria dos pensadores acredita que haverá quatro grandes potências, não superpotências: China, Índia, Rússia e Irã. Se ficarem juntas, podem começar algo novo no mundo. Se brigarem entre si, haverá uma confusão no mundo inteiro.
Interessante pensar que as quatro são membros do Brics e da Organização de Xangai.
Sim. Há grandes diferenças entre a China e a Índia, mas as duas estão no Brics porque perceberam isso. Agora, por que o Irã estaria entre elas? Economicamente, não se compara às outras três. Militarmente, a China e, sobretudo, a Rússia estão muito à frente. A razão é o que torna o Irã único: o Eixo da Resistência [aliança regional liderada pelo Irã, com o Hezbollah libanês, o Ansarullah iemenita, milícias iraquianas e grupos palestinos], em terra e no mar.
Em terra, é um mercado de 400 milhões a 500 milhões de pessoas na região mais estratégica do mundo, o coração do mundo: a Ásia Ocidental, com as reservas de energia, os minerais, as civilizações antigas, as religiões, ligando o norte ao sul e o leste ao oeste. Nos próximos dez ou 20 anos, quem quiser fazer negócios ou impor uma nova ordem mundial ou regional terá de trabalhar com o Irã por causa desse Eixo da Resistência que resistiu ao teste do tempo.
O mar é ainda mais importante. Há cinco estreitos e canais estratégicos no mundo, como o do Panamá, de Suez, Malaca, Ormuz e Bab al-Mandab. Eles importam porque a maior parte do comércio mundial e dos deslocamentos militares passa pelo mar, e esses atalhos mudam o tempo, o custo, o seguro e o risco. Nem os Estados Unidos, nem a China, nem a Rússia, nem a Índia, nem a Alemanha e nem a França controlam esses cinco. Em Malaca, acredito que, se estourar uma guerra, não será por Taiwan, mas pelo controle do estreito. Quem controla Malaca controla os mercados e as economias do Sudeste Asiático.
Por isso os Estados Unidos avançam tão rápido nas Filipinas. Tinham cinco bases, agora têm nove. Um dos primeiros decretos de Bongbong Marcos [Ferdinand Marcos Jr., presidente das Filipinas desde 2022] depois de eleito foi dar mais quatro bases aos estadunidenses.
Exatamente. E o Irã controla Ormuz, por onde passa um terço da energia do mundo. Mesmo quando não houver mais uma superpotência chamada Estados Unidos, os chineses vão precisar do petróleo que passa por ali, então vão precisar do Irã. O outro é Bab al-Mandab, sob controle do Ansarullah [o movimento houthi, que governa o norte do Iêmen], no Iêmen, que faz parte do Eixo da Resistência. Bab al-Mandab, o mar Vermelho e o canal de Suez funcionam como um cano: o que entra por um lado sai pelo outro. Depois que o Ansarullah fechou Bab al-Mandab na guerra que começou com o Dilúvio de Al-Aqsa [a ofensiva do Hamas contra Israel em 7 de outubro de 2023], o Egito publicou três relatórios em um ano dizendo que tinha perdido 60% da receita do canal e do tráfego marítimo. Ou seja, o Irã, à frente do Eixo da Resistência, controla pelo menos dois estreitos e meio.
Isso me mostrou, há anos, que os Estados Unidos acabariam entrando em guerra com o Irã, além de todas as outras razões, como Israel. Eles não podem aceitar isso enquanto escalam a tensão com a China em Malaca e com o Panamá por causa dos operadores chineses no canal. Não vão deixar você em paz, vão vir lutar. O Irã será uma das grandes potências se mantiver o controle sobre essas rotas, e até agora o Irã e o Ansarullah provaram que conseguem. O mundo precisa de vocês hoje e vai precisar amanhã. Todas as economias foram atingidas pelo fechamento de Ormuz, e, mesmo que o estreito reabrisse hoje, as economias do mundo calculam mais dois anos de petróleo caro. Veremos dias econômicos ainda piores nos próximos meses.
Li uma carta de Ali Akbar Velayati [ex-chanceler iraniano (1981-1997) e conselheiro do Líder Supremo para assuntos internacionais desde então] a Mojtaba Khamenei, propondo um polo islâmico centrado no Irã, ao lado dos aliados estratégicos Rússia e China, e acompanhado de países “autenticamente não alinhados”, como África do Sul, Brasil e Cuba. Em abril, ele chamou isso de “terceiro polo” do mundo. O senhor compartilha essa visão? Há lugar para a América Latina e a África?
Minha visão é um pouco diferente. Acredito que, à medida que China, Rússia, Irã e até Índia ganharem mais poder no formato do Brics, mais países vão aderir. À medida que o dólar perder valor e participação no mercado mundial, mais países vão se sentir livres para fazer o que quiserem, inclusive os latino-americanos. Vão estreitar laços econômicos e políticos com esses países, dependendo das políticas futuras da Índia, e vão entrar no Brics.
Mas isso não acontecerá nos próximos anos. Depois de uma década de choques e guerras, todos estarão fracos, e haverá desordem no mundo. Então surgirão coalizões regionais: a América Latina vai formar a sua, porque tem interesses e ameaças em comum. Ao mesmo tempo, o Brics e a Organização de Xangai vão ganhar importância, porque haverá um vácuo de poder, e parte do mundo estará livre do jugo do Ocidente. O mundo vai precisar de uma nova ordem, mas não vai aceitar uma como a do pós-Segunda Guerra, a ordem ocidental, com as categorias de senhores e escravos. Todos terão uma parte maior, ainda que haja essas quatro grandes potências como porta-bandeiras.
E a relação com os países árabes?
O Irã quer muito promover a unidade entre os muçulmanos e quer ser amigo dessas nações, porque tem uma prioridade: derrotar o inimigo principal, Israel e Estados Unidos. Não quer atritos. Acreditamos que “dividir para reinar” sempre foi a política britânica. Eles nos dividiram, fragmentaram a Umma, a comunidade do povo islâmico, para além das fronteiras nacionais.
Mas isso não acontece da noite para o dia, há etapas. No caso dos países árabes do Golfo Pérsico, a primeira é vencer esta guerra e manter o controle de Ormuz, que o Irã sempre teve. Esse será o instrumento para redefinir as relações geopolíticas, estratégicas e de vizinhança, porque é uma arma milhões de vezes mais forte que a bomba atômica. Com uma bomba atômica, você atinge um país uma vez. Com o estreito de Ormuz, você atinge o planeta inteiro, repetidamente. Desde a Segunda Guerra Mundial, ninguém conseguiu mexer tanto nos juros dos títulos estadunidenses, no preço do petróleo e na inflação dos Estados Unidos.
O Irã não vai usar essa arma para colonizar esses países, mas para corrigir as relações com eles. O que isso significa? Os Estados Unidos são um inimigo que atacou o Irã usando o território desses países como plataforma de lançamento. Então não deve haver bases estadunidenses ali. Israel coopera estreitamente com os Emirados e com outros, até com os sauditas. O Irã quer Israel fora. Depois que eles mostrarem que não representam ameaça, haverá relações em pé de igualdade, saudáveis, porque temos ameaças e inimigos em comum.
Como saber que será assim? No governo do presidente Raisi, o chanceler Amir-Abdollahian lançou um plano de diálogo e fórum de segurança regional com os países árabes: os seis do Golfo, mais o Irã e o Iraque, o chamado “seis mais dois”. A ideia era garantir a segurança uns dos outros sem países de fora da região. O Irã já tinha dado esses primeiros passos antes da guerra. Ele quer reparar os laços com os países árabes, mas só depois que eles abandonarem Israel e os Estados Unidos e deixarem de permitir que o Mossad, a CIA e outros ataquem o Irã. Não se pode lutar contra todos para sempre. Temos um objetivo claro e um plano claro para o futuro.
Vocês se preparam para isso há décadas, né?
Há décadas nos preparamos para esta guerra e para o estreito de Ormuz, porque sabíamos que um dia ia acontecer, mais cedo ou mais tarde. Se não agora, nos próximos 20 anos.
O orçamento do Pentágono é 100 vezes maior que o orçamento militar do Irã. Pela lógica terrena, militar e econômica, eles deveriam ter derrotado o Irã nos primeiros dias. Por que não conseguiram? Todos estão surpresos, e não é só por causa da guerra assimétrica que praticamos. A força nem sempre faz o direito.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.title: Politische Kampagnen | Wahlbeeinflussung nach Staatsräson
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.author: Matthias Monroy
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.text:
- Kommentare
- Politische Kampagnen
Wahlbeeinflussung nach Staatsräson
Russland werden politische Kampagnen angelastet, aber zu Israel schweigt die Regierung. Inzwischen manipulieren aber auch Merz, Rhein und Steinmeier.
Wenn es auch nur den leisen Verdacht einer staatlichen Wahlbeeinflussung durch Russland gibt, lesen wir davon in einschlägigen Investigativmedien, die ihre Informationen in »Hintergrundgesprächen« von der Bundesregierung erhalten. Auch vor den Landtagswahlen am 20. September gab es eine solche staatlich gesteuerte Kampagne in sozialen Medien. Kolportiert wurde das rechte Narrativ eines »großen Austauschs« der Bevölkerung, eines der antiislamischen Videos hatte 1,5 Millionen Aufrufe. Haben Sie davon etwas in Investigativmedien gelesen? Wir auch nicht. Das mag daran liegen, dass laut ausländischen Medien mutmaßlich israelische Stellen dahinter stecken – da wird dann in Deutschland aus Gründen der »Staatsräson« lieber zur Wahlbeeinflussung geschwiegen.
Inzwischen versuchen sogar hochrangige einheimische Politiker, die Wahlen in ihrem Sinne umzubiegen – auch hier mit Blick auf Israel. Am 7. Oktober forderte Friedrich Merz SPD und Grüne auf, mit angeblich antisemitischen »Linksradikalen« keine Koalitionsverhandlungen zu führen und sich lieber der CDU zuzuwenden. Regierungsmitglieder dürfen ihre staatliche Autorität aber nicht für den parteipolitischen Wettbewerb einsetzen, urteilte schon das Bundesverfassungsgericht. Merz missachtet dieses Neutralitätsgebot vorsätzlich, genauso wie Hessens Ministerpräsident Boris Rhein, der am Montag bei der Eröffnung der Jüdischen Akademie in Frankfurt behauptete, die Linkspartei werde in Berlin »nicht trotz, sondern wegen ihres Antisemitismus« gewählt.
Man mag solchen anti-demokratischen Machtmissbrauch von CDU-Politikern inzwischen für normal halten. Aber selbst bei Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier fielen in Frankfurt alle Schranken, als er erklärte, Antisemitismus dürfe nirgendwo in Deutschland Einfluss auf die Regierungsarbeit bekommen – erkennbar adressiert an die laufenden Berliner Koalitionsverhandlungen.
Wer nur ein bisschen beieinander ist, durchschaut die Kampagne und weiß, dass die Linkspartei nicht antisemitisch ist. Viel eher sind es Merz, Rhein und Steinmeier, wenn sie Jüdinnen und Juden pauschal mit Israel gleichsetzen. Der Kanzler bezeichnete die jüdischen Deutschen bei einer Wahlkampfveranstaltung am 17. September sogar – aus Versehen oder aus Dummheit? – als »Ausländer«.
Es wird Zeit, dass die Linke endlich in Berlin regiert. Im Moment sieht es allerdings so aus, dass die SPD von der politisch motivierten CDU-Kampagne sturmreif geschossen und damit eine Koalition verhindert wird. Am Ende sind es dann nur noch Linke, die die Demokratie verteidigen – jedenfalls nicht die Parteien, die das Wort im Namen tragen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malm-rooney-.title: Let Andreas Malm Speak
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malm-rooney-.author: Chris Saltmarsh
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malm-rooney-.text:
Let Andreas Malm Speak
Britain has banned climate scholar and left-wing activist Andreas Malm from visiting the country. Following the ban on Hasan Piker, it points to an alarming repression of pro-Palestine speech in Britain.
Andreas Malm’s work has been among the most important of any scholar in any academic field over the past decade. His theoretical and strategic contributions have led developments in our understanding of the climate crisis’s basis in capitalism and fed debates about how to respond.
Yet last week, Britain’s Home Office banned Malm from entering the country, on the grounds that his “presence in the UK is not considered to be conducive to the public good.”
Malm had been due to visit London to speak alongside Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori at a Tribune magazine event, attend the academic conference Historical Materialism, and be interviewed by BBC Radio 4.
No specific reason was given for the ban. But it seems that the government’s decision is due to Malm’s principled opposition to the proscription of the direct-action network Palestine Action, officially labeled a “terrorist organization.” The move came a fortnight after publisher Faber & Faber announced that it would withdraw Sally Rooney’s novels from the UK market due to her support for Palestine Action, which means she is unable to collect revenue in the country. She too had fallen victim to the government’s silencing of free speech on Palestine, and to measures widely condemned by leading authors, artists, and public figures.
In June, American left-wingers Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur had already been banned from entering the UK.
The decision by Andy Burnham’s government to ban Malm represents a further attack on the Marxist left. It denies ordinary citizens the opportunity to hear from someone who speaks and writes so clearly about the imminence of climate catastrophe, the horrors of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and their entanglement.
It is surely no coincidence that these are the two areas in which Burnham’s government is failing resoundingly.
The ban on Malm comes in the same month that Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea despite the Labour Party’s 2024 manifesto commitment to issue no new licenses for oil and gas.
It also comes just a few weeks after Burnham insisted that Labour could not work with Green councilors who failed to renounce their party’s policy holding that “Zionism is racism.” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s recent emotive denunciation of Israel’s ethnic cleansing and settler violence does not do enough to stop the material support that the British state continues to provide to the genocide.
Malm is not an extremist from whom the British public needs protecting. His work is resolutely in the Marxist tradition but is cited widely by scholars across disciplines and spanning the political spectrum.
The Destruction of the Earth
Malm’s contributions are many. His seminal 2016 work, Fossil Capital, is perhaps the most important theoretical account of the historical entanglement of fossil fuel production in capitalism. The Progress of This Storm stakes out a clear position in ecological Marxist debates, asserting the need for human agency in confronting the crises we face. In the early 2020s, Corona, Climate, Chronic Emergency and How to Blow Up a Pipeline elaborated on this with essential contributions to debates on climate strategy following the insurgency of Extinction Rebellion and school climate strikes. Coauthored with Wim Carton, Overshoot and The Long Heat then offered masterful accounts of the ideological and technological bases of the march toward climate catastrophe.
More recently, Malm’s impassioned 2025 work, The Destruction of Palestine Is the Destruction of the Earth, places Israel’s genocide in Palestine in its proper historical setting, locating it in the context of British empire and enduring expansion of the fossil economy.
Malm, like Rooney, is no terrorist. In fact, it is the power of his ideas and the clarity of his expression that make him particularly dangerous for the British government. It clearly fears that Malm — like Rooney, Palestine Action, and Just Stop Oil (JSO) — will expose their inexcusable negligence on the most consequential questions of our time.
This episode raises a sobering question not just for the Marxist left, but for anyone in Britain committed to freedom of speech and political expression, and anyone who might expect to publicly criticize any government failing to act on genocide and climate collapse in the coming years: If Burnham’s government is prepared to ban Malm from entering the country, how many of its own citizens would it gladly deprive of their political freedoms if it had the opportunity?
This is an instructive moment. The only real difference between Burnham’s Labour and his predecessor Keir Starmer’s rule lies in the world of vibes and affect. Burnham says he identifies with ordinary people’s problems, names neoliberalism as an enemy, and shares your cultural tastes, perhaps evoking some combination of hope, nostalgia, and northern English pride.
But his government shares with Starmer’s an inability to confront the precipitous decline in living standards, an enthusiasm for growing the destructive defense and AI industries, and ongoing material support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
It leaves untouched the massive intensification of state repression of peaceful protest introduced under the last Tory government (in response to Extinction Rebellion and JSO), which was extended to Palestine Action by Starmer’s government.
Even worse than Starmer’s, Burnham’s government has abandoned Labour’s hard-won commitment to stop new fossil fuel production in the North Sea.
Each of these positions undermines the medium- to long-term viability of human civilization as we know it. The banning of Malm is an insight into how ostensibly center-left governments will deal with political dissent as they fail to address the crises in the years to come.
The Marxist left, within and outside the UK, is not only a legitimate political tradition that must be protected from repression on principle. It is the political tradition offering the strongest insights and most vibrant debate on the nature of the crises we face and how to overcome them. Its repression is an assault on everyone.
We should express our solidarity with Andreas Malm and Sally Rooney. But this situation also raises wider demands: for the de-proscription of Palestine Action and the repealing of anti-protest legislation. And, more materially, for an end to the UK’s practical support for Israel’s genocide in Palestine and to fossil fuel production in the North Sea.
Each of these claims are basic expressions of humanity and should be uncontroversial to state out loud in Britain today. It is the moral responsibility of anybody in the public sphere to express them. Burnham’s government rejects them all, and for this deserves our unrelenting opposition.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/hi.title: Pace’s Marc Glimcher Responds to Reported Financial Loss, High Museum of Art Former COO Sentenced to Prison for Embezzlement, and More: Morning Links for November 3, 2026
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/hi.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/hi.text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.
Good Morning!
- Pace CEO Marc Glimcher responded to ARTnews about reports of financial losses and the gallery’s direction.
- Brady Lum, former COO of the High Museum of Art has been sentenced to one year in federal prison.
- For the first time, lawmakers in Italy are examining a new bill to facilitate the restitution of art and cultural items looted between 1933 and 1945.
The Headlines
KEEP UP THE PACE. Pace CEO Marc Glimcher responded to ARTnews about reports of financial losses and the gallery’s direction. “Everything is turning,” Glimcher said over the phone, noting a “record” Art Basel Paris last month, “sellout shows” helping business get back in the black and a new location expansion in Europe coming “fairly soon.” Last week, Pace published its accounts with Companies House, showing significant losses in turnover for 2024 and 2025. Glimcher said: “We did a balance sheet shift, which appears to be a loss because we’re changing around the way we invest money and take money from other units and let the money flow through each unit independently.” He added that the 50 artists dropped by the gallery in June “were not artists that we had a super active engagement with,” and “it wasn’t benefiting them or us.” He is also working on moving into a new space in London, to be decided. “When we have the space and announce it, it’s going to make a lot of sense to everybody,” he said.
DOING TIME. The High Museum of Art’s former COO, Brady Lum, has been sentenced to one year in federal prison, followed by one year of supervised release, for embezzling over $600,000 from the museum by tampering with invoices and approving personal purchases, announced Georgia’s United States Attorney’s Office. “Lum brazenly pilfered hundreds of thousands of dollars from a beloved civic institution to pay for his high-end guitars and other personal items,” said US Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “His appalling breach of trust damaged not only the High Museum but also the larger art community,” he added. Lum served as Atlanta’s High Museum of Art COO from January 2, 2019, to December 9, 2025. He has paid back the full, stolen $607,688 to the museum, plus another $500,000 to cover costs the museum spent to uncover his own crime.
The Digest
Lawmakers in Italy are examining a new bill to create a committee that will research provenance and facilitate the restitution of art and cultural items pillaged by Nazis and Italian police between 1933 and 1945. [The Art Newspaper]
A city council in New South Wales will not exhibit Phil Buehler’s “Wall of Tears” installation memorializing the names of children killed in Gaza, due to cited safety concerns. [The Guardian]
In an interview pegged to a new limited-edition collaboration with watchmaker Hublot, Jeff Koons said: “I never think about price. I know I’m associated with very valuable things, but it’s not something I think about. I believe in the value that things have for humanity, in a conceptual way. In the knowledge and care they reflect.” [El País]
Despite turmoil at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, its prestigious annual Kennedy Center Honors celebration for lifetime achievement is pressing forward, awarding the likes of pop singer Paul Anka, playwright David Mamet, actor Andy Garcia, and country singer Barbara Mandrell. [The New York Times]
An unknown, intimate drawing by Duncan Grant of Vanessa Bell, the English artist and sister of Virginia Woolf, was discovered amid research for Tate Britain’s forthcoming show on Bell and Grant. [FAD Magazine]
The Kicker
ART WANTED, DEAD OR ALIVE. Thanks to an inventive “WANTED” campaignby the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans in France, aimed at tracking down hundreds of WWII-era looted artworks, one painting has just been found, reports Le Journal des Arts. The stolen painting by Dutch artist Willem Cornelisz Duyster, titled Le Buveur, was located at an auction house in Switzerland and is expected to be restituted to the museum shortly. Its owner purchased the painting in the 1990s, agreed to hand over the artwork, and said they had not known of its problematic provenance. In June 1940, Nazis attacked the city of Orléans, burning an annex of its fine arts museum, known as the Musée Paul Fourché, which was subsequently almost entirely ransacked, likely by people on both sides of the conflict. Some 350 paintings from Europe, dating back to the 16th century, were lost.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Kamala Harris Has Her Eye on Today’s Gubernatorial Races
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Kamala Harris Has Her Eye on Today’s Gubernatorial Races
The former vice president reminds The Nation that, even if government is divided in DC, “a governor, as the chief executive of a state, can actually make things happen.”
Today’s midterms will mark the end of one election cycle and the beginning of another. As soon as the votes from 2026 are counted, the 2028 presidential race will take center stage. But that’s just a formality.
For all intents and purposes, the 2028 contest began during the course of the midterm campaign. Several dozen prospective contenders for the Democratic nomination hit the midterm trail to boost their national profiles—campaigning in states across the country and positioning themselves as allies of the candidates who could flip control of Congress and check President Trump in the last two years of his term.
Most of these 2028 hopefuls zeroed in on Senate races, which grabbed the spotlight in final weeks of the 2026 campaign. Nobody doubts the importance of these contests, whether in Michigan, which saw a chaotic close to the race between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Trump Republican Mike Rogers, or in Texas, where Democratic James Talarico could become the first Democratic senator from the state in more than three decades.
But the front-runner in several surveys that tested the strength of 2026 Democratic presidential prospects has placed an emphasis on today’s gubernatorial races, which will define the direction of states across the country.
That prospect is former vice president Kamala Harris, who, in a national Harvard-Harris poll released one week ago, garnered 34 percent support among likely Democratic presidential primary and voters—16 points ahead of the second-place finisher, California Governor Gavin Newsom. It was the same story in two other polls that were released in October—one for the Financial Times and one by the Echelon Insights firm—both of which gave the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee a clear lead.
Harris—whose 75,017,613 vote total in 2024 was the highest in history for any candidate except for the Republican who narrowly beat her that year, Donald Trump (77,302,580), and for the Democrat with whom she served as vice president, Joe Biden (81,283,501) in 2020—told The Nation that she has not decided whether to mount a new bid for the presidency. That’s a genuine response, as is Harris’s insistence that the top factor in making that decision will be her family. But she has little doubt that she could do the job, as someone with significant White House experience who recalls that she has “spent a lot of time with foreign leaders, thinking about America’s responsibility and role globally, as well as our responsibility as a government to our own people.”
To a greater extent than many prominent political figures, Harris thinks about the duties of executives—in Washington and in statehouses across the country. So while Harris made plenty of 2026 campaign appearances with Senate candidates—including El-Sayed in Michigan, late-surging Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff—she also focused on some of the 36 gubernatorial races that will be decided today.
For Democrats, the chance to win control of statehouses is especially important. Even if they secure majorities in the House and Senate, they will still have to operate with divided government at the federal level—given that Trump is still in the White House. Democratic governors and legislatures can move far more immediately and far more effectively to address economic concerns, expand access to healthcare, invest in education, regulate data centers and artificial intelligence, and protect the rights of women and the LGBTQ+ community. They can also defend democracy by moving to address gerrymandering and to defend against voter suppression in the run-up to the 2028 election.
This understanding led Harris to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in the days before the midterm election, where she campaigned with David Crowley, the Milwaukee County Executive who this year is the Democratic nominee to replace outgoing Democratic Governor Tony Evers.
Harris appeared on October 26 with Crowley—who’s in a tight race with MAGA Republican US Representative Tom Tiffany—at a packed Democratic campaign headquarters in a neighborhood on Milwaukee’s northwest side and then at a huge “Women for Crowley” event in a downtown hotel. As always, Harris came prepared, with plenty of insights regarding the Democrat she was supporting and plenty to digs at the Republican he was opposing. And the crowds loved it.
Harris has her share of critics, and there are certainly Democrats who would rather she sit out the 2028 race. But her fans are ardent, and they have been out in force this fall as she hit the trail on behalf of Democratic candidates from Michigan to Mississippi to New Hampshire and Georgia. That was certainly the case in Milwaukee, where Harris was greeted by enthusiastic crowds of Democrats who held cameras aloft, waved posters, and cheered her every remark.
“She’s a huge mentor of mine,” declared Crowley.
For her part, Harris was effusive in her praise of the candidate, whom she described to The Nation as someone who is “in it for all the right reasons.”
“He is a true public servant,” she said of Crowley, who grew up in a Milwaukee neighborhood that is one of the poorest in the country. “He has had the experience of being hungry and knowing that you can’t assume that the very basic needs that you have will be fulfilled—without the government playing its part to help those in need, at a time when they need it most.”
In the closing days of a campaign where candidates on both sides of the partisan aisle are talking about affordability, Harris recognized Crowley’s authenticity.
“It’s not lip service. It is a lived experience for him—in a way that he sees the pain that people are experiencing right now. There’s a whole lot of pain right now. It is about affordability of the basic needs that people have. And that pain is compounded with a real legitimate belief [on the part of so many Americans] that their needs are unimportant, as compared to the powerful and the rich.”
Crowley, she said, “gets it. He understands what the priority should be.”

Crowley is one of eight Black gubernatorial candidates who are running in states across the country today. Five of them are Democrats: Maryland Governor Wes Moore, who is seeking reelection, and former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, state Attorney General Aaron Ford in Nevada, state Representative Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina, and Crowley. Three are Republicans: US Representative Byron Donalds in Florida, US Representative John James in Michigan, and state Representative Lisa Demuth in Minnesota.
“The eight Black nominees in governor’s races this year are seeking to force change that has been slow in coming, long after the ends of slavery and the Jim Crow era,” noted CNN. “While some carry favorable odds and others are long shots, taken together, they represent a record number of candidates in one cycle.”
Harris, the first Black person to serve as vice president and the first Black woman to be nominated for president, simply said, “It’s about time.”
She has campaigned not just with Crowley but with Ford and Lance Bottoms too—all three of whom would make history if they’re elected as the first Black governors of their states. “I am a witness to her grace and her greatness as a leader,” said Harris when she traveled to Georgia to appear with Bottoms. “Georgia has Keisha Lance Bottoms who will be the first Black woman governor in the history of the United States.” With Ford in Las Vegas, she urged Black voters to “honor the ancestors” by electing the attorney general as the first Black governor of Nevada and the first Black governor of a state located west of the Mississippi River.
While Harris made reference in campaign stops with the gubernatorial candidates to the civil rights era and to contemporary struggles for justice, she also spoke with fervor about the economic pain and chaos created by the Trump administration, which she describes as “the most callous, corrupt, and incompetent presidential administration we’ve ever experienced.” At every turn, she spoke of the candidates she has endorsed as uniquely qualified. And she reminded people of the power of governors to get things done.
“I was campaigning for Aaron Ford, and he’s been attorney general for two terms. So he knows the state, he knows it from the perspective of fighting for consumers, law enforcement, and all that,” she explained to The Nation. “I think there’s an obvious point, which is that a governor, as the chief executive of a state, can actually make things happen—and these really outstanding candidates want to make things happen in their state.”
