Ashes to Pistachios
Golan Haji
Translated from Arabic by Robin Moger
06.02.2026Translation
Introduction by Robin Moger
I first encountered Golan Haji in 2021, when the Egyptian magazine Al-Manassa published a short piece by him, an extract from a book-in-progress about the life of Kheir Eddin al-Assadi, a twentieth-century Aleppan scholar, bibliomaniac, antiquarian and surrealist poet, the author of something called The Comparative Encyclopedia of Aleppo (seven volumes with entries on 20,000 words, divided into the city’s “55 arts of speech”).
“Each city is cities,” Haji wrote. “And, occasionally, the writer is a battalion. What is better able than language to incorporate every possible human thing? Life, like words, is governed by the rules of grammar and composition. The word is a journey that does not end, a myth lived daily; in everything one sees a symbol and a truth. By reading the world as a text written with breath, al-Assadi was Sufi. He built his city in a book, breathed its spirit into the pages and, gathering from speech the scattered fragments of the living and the dead, of men both neglected and famed, he encompassed the world’s chaos in the chaos of the alphabet.”
The more I read of Haji’s work, the more this piece returns to me. Al-Assadi’s “vast library”, which “occupied a whole floor”, finds its counterpart in the encyclopaedic clutter of Haji’s mind. And like al-Assadi, he too is a traveler, though with a broader compass: he crosses the borders of both country and language. “I live in a moving, linguistic in-between, as if in no language,” he has said.
Haji is a Syrian Kurd who writes in Arabic – “a second language” – and translates into it from French and English. He was born in 1977 in Amuda in north-eastern Syria and now lives in Saint-Denis in France. He has published five collections of poetry, most recently The Word Rejected (2023), and is even more prolific in prose. In any case, his essays are impossible to extricate from his poetry. Both share a density of reference to sources across the vast sweep of the Arabic tradition and through to contemporary literature in English, French and Farsi; both tease out the ramifying meanings of words with repeated passes of etymology’s comb. As one of Haji’s champions, the poet Fady Joudah, has observed: “He writes his essays as if a poet is writing a memoir, but ends up with a journey through the soul of the world/the word.” Though many of his poems and essays can be found in translation, most notably by Marilyn Hacker, his only English book is A Tree Whose Name I Don’t Know (2017), a selection of 61 poems translated in collaboration with Stephen Watts.
The text below is a lightly edited extract from a chapter of The Wandering Kurd, a volume that is itself a compilation of unfinished books on a breathtaking range of subjects. Haji’s memoirs of a Kurdish childhood branch into etymology and language games, nature writing and political history; his extensive recent art criticism, with its attention to imagery and process, finds echoes in his travelogues, which run through Damascus and Beirut, Berlin and Nantes, en route to Saint-Denis; essays on Syria’s present horrors decry the external censorship that has been imposed on local cultural production, and are studded with the most generous and enlightening references. A piece that begins with Andalusian flower poetry passes through the tenth-century Levant and William Carlos Williams.
The Wandering Kurd, which is seeking an English publisher, opens with two telling epigraphs. The first is an Aleppan proverb recorded by al-Assadi: “Four were created for corruption: the rat, the locust, the Bedouin, and the Kurd.” The second is an extract from the 331st of The Thousand And One Nights (Haji reminds us that in this great work, Kurds feature principally as “a mendacious rabble”). When a judge accuses a Kurd of stealing a man’s knapsack, he responds: “Your Honour, all know this sack of mine and know what it contains – its castles and forts, cranes and lions, the men who play chess and their boards; its mare and two foals, its stallion and two steeds, and its two long lances; there is a lion and two rabbits, a town and two hamlets, a whore and a pair of sly pimps, a sissy and two bottoms, one sightless man and two most perspicacious, a lame man and two limping, a priest and two deacons, a bishop and a brace of monks, a judge and two witnesses – and all will bear witness that the sack, this knapsack, is mine.”
All Haji’s writing comes out of that knapsack.
On 13 November 1960, the Shahrazad burned down, claiming the lives of 283 children. The mud-brick cinema in Amuda was showing an Egyptian film at the time (dark crimes and romance: The Midnight Ghost) chosen by management over a biopic about Djamila Bouhired – the profits would have been sent to support the revolution of a million martyrs in Algeria. The ancient projector, which had been playing films all Sunday long, now overheated. A spark leapt from the magic box and brushed a sackcloth drape, igniting it. Running through the straw and planks of the flooring, the fire caught on the bamboo chairs and mud-brick benches.
The auditorium was packed with students from two primary schools, Al-Ghazali and Al-Mutanabbi. Those who jumped through the only window to escape the flames tumbled down the well immediately outside; others, piling through the narrow exit, sealed it tight; the rest suffocated and were scorched.
The smell drifted through the late afternoon air to the surrounding villages, whose residents, seeing the black smoke climbing up, readied carts and wagons and rushed down to the town’s southern district. They knew the firemen would only get there once it was too late. Between the cinema and the hospital, surrounded by mosques, they lost their way.
They were cursing Gamal Abdel Nasser. These were the days of the union between “the sisters”, Egypt and Syria, and they were convinced that the man who had forbidden Kurds from rearing their goats had now given orders to smother their progeny in the cradle. It was said that the fire was the God of their ancestors, immolating children for their fathers’ sins. “Ibrahim, father of the Kurds,” a crowd of women from Malali and Mashayekh cried out. “Why won’t your Lord make His fire cool and harmless for my son, too?” And maybe that, too, was why some of the wounded, mummified in their bandages, later passed away. Even in their prayers, the villagers clung to their polytheism, invoking others alongside Him – so God had withheld autumn’s blessing, kept it trapped in heaven.
It rained that day, but only once death’s business was done, the black water flowing past the houses like a clown’s tears. People started calling Amuda Cinema Town.
The screening room was as black as the base of the wheat-boiling pots at autumn’s end. A calligrapher (also a bodybuilder) slipped inside to scrape the sticky soot off the walls, collecting it like powdered charcoal in a big bowl. He would use the residue to paint kaabas on the whitewashed rectangles by people’s front doors, beside the words that greet pilgrims returned from Mecca: “A blessed hajj / and a praiseworthy effort: / Who visits my tomb must pray for my soul”. The same soot was sometimes mixed with mother’s milk and pricked into tattoos of wings on newborns’ ankles, to help them escape the dangers that lay ahead.
Even though it happened many years before I was born, consigned to police files marked “no perpetrator”, we all knew of the fire. It was the reason why I was always frightened by the white flecks that spat and danced on the edge of the screen as the reel ran on. To this day, the first thing I do in any cinema auditorium, before the show begins, is make sure I know where the emergency exits are.
My friend Nuh used to borrow copies of Cinema Life from his teacher. He’d page through issue after issue, sitting up for hours each night, hunched over a copy in the mudafa, the guest annex that had become his study after his father’s death, sipping cold tea. He savoured imagined scenes from the films he read about, whose stills he’d see reproduced, but which he had never seen in motion. And the more his imagination worked, the more he fell into them, loved them like he was part of the cast. He started to wonder – half-fearful, half-thrilled – that he might leaf a page one day to find himself on screen; to discover that, unbeknown to him, he’d played a bit-part in some film.
Nuh considered keeping the dead company, projecting not Cinema Paradiso but Oblomov onto that sacred screen, the wailing wall within our little town’s cemetery. His thoughts were of the corpses interred in the Tombs of the Black Angels, our name for the mass graves in which those burned children were buried when it proved impossible to identify them.
Aboul Nanaat would join us for the sessions where we discussed films we’d never seen. His passion was for book titles, and he knew a vast number of them off by heart. He would finger through catalogue cards in school libraries and the cultural centre’s archives, pore over the Babtain Encyclopaedia of Modern Poetry, skim the listings of new releases in the Lebanese press and issues of The Arab – but I can’t recall him having ever read a book. To him, titles mattered more than content: they were the distillate, the key. What need was there to run flailing into a novel’s ocean of blather, to force down a dense textbook or work of criticism that only pretended to gravity and depth? Why batter through a mountain of paper only to find yourself back where you began, unable to remember a word past its title? To Aboul Nanaat, the only true book – or the only perfect book – was the Quran, because it was memorised word by word.
Poets from neighbouring villages would seek him out to suggest a title for their self-published collections, something unique, but as far as I know he never gave them what they asked for. Instead, he offered those poetry-loving Bedouin long and tangled phrases, or single-letter interrogatives and imperatives – Ma, Qi, Ra, ‘Aa (What? Protect! See! Be aware!), or letter games: for instance, raa‘i, meaning shepherd, was the ‘ayn el-‘aql (the “eye of the mind”, or the summit of reason) because its root letters Ra and Ayn might separately stand for ru’ya and wa‘iy, meaning vision and awareness, which is to say, basr and basira, or sight and perception.
Whenever our conversations grew heated, Aboul Nanaat liked to respond with titles of these books he’d never read, answers that were epigrammatic, obscure, shorn of explanation. If we were roaring with laughter, he’d mutter, “there is no strength or power save in God,” then announce, “Laughter and Disaster”, the name of a collection by Bandar Abdel Hamid. Unpicking the riddles wasn’t always easy. Who was ever going to know, or remember, the author of The Sorrows of the Green Moon, or Love and Theology, or Behind the Mirage? We had no chance of matching his obsessively acquired knowledge.
He had his own system of classification. For instance, he would describe Syrian poetry as two parties struggling for power: the Ministry of Prose and the Union of Meter. The first was headed by Antun Maqdisi at the Ministry of Culture, which published many Syrian and Arab prose poets; the leader of the second was Ali Uqla Arsan, who ran the Pan-Arabist Arab Writers’ Union, a stronghold of metrical poetry. Arsan’s comrades – or fellow warriors, if we consider the word to be a weapon (and Ba‘athists, like communists, most certainly believed that it was) – had embellished his past. As a boy, they would claim, he had learned to scale the minaret of his village mosque in the countryside around Deraa, and this was why he was such a deft opportunist: climbing ladders was no problem.
From time to time we would be joined in Nuh’s annex by another young man we called Sculptor. He was good with his hands, and had written, in Kurdish – a banned language that he’d had to teach himself – a lengthy elegy with a title to match: “My share of the misfortune: the imagined fates of the children who died”. He lived right next to the cinema, which over the years had transformed from a site of holocaust to a little garden with a statue, the “memorial” that was now the focus of Sculptor’s attention and his scathing commentary: “That’s not how you memorialise something! Where’s Bavé Behmed, who saved the kids? Why did that government artist Mahmoud Jelal only sculpt three children? Why have they got the Algerian flag up and not the Amazigh flag, when it’s the Amazigh who are persecuted like us Kurds? If it was up to me, I’d have a statue of Joan of Arc standing calmly amid the flames, or of the dragon being slain.”
Sometimes we’d meet there, hopping the garden fence as the gate was usually locked and gathering around the backfilled mouth of the well that had swallowed the children who leapt from the window. We would recite elegies we’d written, or observe long and silent vigils that were only broken when one of us posed a question in the form a single word, to which someone else would muster a curt and cryptic response:
“Cigarette?”
“White regret burned down by the unemployed boy.”
“Sisyphus?”
“Beetle hoists a dung ball in its antlers and scales a hill filled with graves.”
We loved to sit in the shade of the pines and listen to the wind. The straight trunks whitewashed from their roots up reminded us of the white boots worn by Turkish soldiers. In the branches we had hung dozens of tiny cradles, woven from the orangey pine bark. Each bore the name of a child who’d perished here, written out in sunlight and burned black beneath a magnifying glass.
The Sculptor would argue with everyone about the garden. “Knowledge is relative,” he’d always say; in answer to Aboul Nanaat’s questions: “There’s no need to treat everything like a competition… ” He would ask if we knew the name of Maradona’s barber, or of the midwife who delivered Isaac Newton, or the number of mules around whose necks Mela Mustafa Barzani hung lanterns then sent on ahead to trigger ambushes in the Qandil mountains. Or how many matches it took Mazlum Doğan to set himself alight in Diyarbakır Prison.
He’d made a little scale model of the Colosseum, its smooth stones collected from brooks that ran down the foothills of the Taurus mountains and the springs of Serê Kaniyê. There were coloured pebbles you could chew on, soft as erasers. He also went collecting in the bodies of his forefathers and uncles, which were veritable quarries; the unspoken agonies held in men’s innards petrifying with the passing years like the pearls that oysters shape impossibly slowly in the sea’s dark depths. He explained: “The smaller the pebble, the sharper the suffering and the louder the cry, the same as the troubles that find us in reality. The petty things take you out of yourself; you blaspheme and swear for the smallest reason. As when a swallow shits overhead and the good omen runs down your glasses, or you stain your shirt just as you’re getting ready to go out, or you loosen a screw with the tip of a knife. Disaster, on the other hand, freezes you, strikes you dumb; you might even act as though nothing’s going on.”
He liked to mock the word “project” and the reality show The Million’s Poet, in which people competed to be crowned the best poet in the Arab world: “They must have stolen the idea from Amuda”. Nevertheless, he began a project of his own, in honour of his mother: “The Million Pebbles”. It was to a be a “vast” work of art, incorporating parts of her body: he had already embedded her gallstones into the base of the model. She had insisted on seeing the wound after they’d removed her stone and the stitches; the great scar beneath her right breast, reflected in the mirror at home, had startled her: “Who cut this big black grin over my liver? Did they think they were giving me a smile for life?”
In the model Colosseum, the Roman arena of death became a little dish for treasures, like her ashtrays decorated with shells. She would drop the family teeth into it – the grandchildren’s milk teeth, the grandfathers’ false sets, wisdom teeth – along with her own gallstones and kidney stones and urinary sand, then put it back behind a white curtain embroidered with flowers, from which hung a kohl pot, a little mirror, and pockets to hold scissors and a needle.
We walked together on the endless plains, reciting the old poets. We trod the boundary lines between fields and waded through wheat until our trousers turned patchwork, blotched with green. The lucky one got to hold a china box we called “the plumb line of innocence”. It held milk teeth. When you shook it on those still spring afternoons, amid poppies in bright sunshine, its rattle was the music that accompanied the recital of a young poet seated on the ground beneath the sky.
But the Kurds’ spring is bloody; their March is a month of joys and disaster. On the night of 24 March 1993, another great fire at the Hasakah Central Prison consumed (among others) 25 Kurdish inmates. The following morning, still unaware of the event, I had propped my motorbike by the bakery on the west side of the town, and was securing it when I heard a scream. At first, I thought nothing of it; I imagined one of Sculptor’s relatives clutching at his side, mouth gaping, caught short by renal colic. You would sometimes catch sight of them in the distance, flipping in agony down a hillside, the cylinders of their bodies rolling like gas bottles, maybe accompanied by their donkeys: tipped on their back, hooves lifted to the heavens.
I stopped to listen, and heard something like a cry for help or a complaint. I followed the sound. It was the metal-turner Felemez, surrounded by neighbours. His dark blue overalls were spattered with engine oil. He was out of control, shaking his blackened fists at the sky and raving, having heard the news that his brother had burned to death in Hasakah: “A smoker! A hash smoker! Kerosene! Insect powder! Blankets!”
We walked up in the fields later that day. There was no poetry spoken. As we were getting ready to leave, Sculptor said: “Blood becomes dust and water. Just like our neighbour, Youssef the tailor, who stitched blue overalls with green thread, Napoleon was colourblind, too. He carried his massacres on into spring because to him the blood flowed green, indistinguishable from the fresh green grass. The French are poets by nature; a nation of envious, jealous poets. This is why they bombed our town in 1936 after the massacre of the Christians, the year my mother was born. They burned the livestock and they burned the wheat fields before the harvest could be brought in, but they never went near the brothel and the slaughterhouse, which were built by a Frenchman.”
Six high school students together; we hadn’t discussed it beforehand. We loosened the ears of the Ba‘ath flag – untied those four flapping corners – and let it flutter down into a puddle of rainwater. Then we hurried from the scene of our petty desecration. The key was to get away quickly, away from the crowds of potential witnesses who lined both sides of the main road outside party headquarters. I didn’t even look back to watch the Ba‘ath colours being smeared with mud, trampled under the feet of people leaving the Evacuation Day celebrations, its polyester sheen being pricked with embers from roadside torches. The next morning, after we saluted the flag and chanted party slogans on the basketball court, the school principal thrashed his cane to splinters over my bloodied, outstretched palms. He had selected it from a pile of dry branches that came from the pine trees towering over the east end of the courtyard.
I was suspended from Al-Ma’arri High for a week, but my family didn’t realise it. Every morning, I would get ready for school as though nothing was out of the ordinary and then, dressed in my paramilitary-style uniform, head off to the plains. There was always the nagging thought that a Turkish soldier might mistake this little figure for a conscript, wandering alone through the open expanse, holding a book, a crust of bread and a lump of salty white cheese sprinkled with poppy seeds, and with a Russian-made telescope tucked beneath his jacket – to spy on the Taurus mountains. A goods train might pass through, the cattle’s tearful eyes visible though slots in the sides of the carriages. A herd of sullen mules might be descending the lower slopes towards fields sown with watermelon. I had with me a selection of poems by Mani the Mad, which had caught my eye at the Hurriya Bookshop, where it was clipped to a clothes’ line with a pair of pegs.
The locals were offended by the ugliness of the muezzins’ voices. In The Book of Songs, al-Isfahani tells how Mani the Mad once heard a call to prayer that upset him so much that, scrambling up to the top of his tower, he “took the muezzin by the beard and gave his bald spot such a slap it seemed his head must fly off”. The construction of a huge, multistorey religious school was underway in Amuda, each of its four minarets overlooking a different street. On the wall that ran down Malali Street, it read: “Mosque for sale”. Outside its gate, drunks lifted up little bags of cigarette butts and ashes, demanding Sheikh Abeed give his blessing. The sheikh was known to have a green hand: a touch would turn the ashes to pistachios.
Before me the plains run into the distance, where the National Water Company office stands: the only building in this direction, with its little courtyard of pines. Over the years, storm winds have clipped their heads off, lightning has split them. One or two sway in a soft breeze; the rest don’t move. A riddle that perplexes me: a double gate held shut by a rusted assemblage of lock and chain.
I jump down from the fence, shielded by the trees from the possibility of a carelessly aimed warning shot. White feathers: soft, caught like little sails on the grass in the shade. A slender leaf twirls propeller-like in its fall. I pick it up and clamp it between nose and lip to give myself a thin pimp’s moustache. In a patch of sun, a Sharq beer bottle glitters greenly on a bed of dry pine needles, wrapped in a faint steam that rises from the rough dirt. Teenagers run wild in this courtyard after evening falls, their drunkenness taken to its pitch when the April breeze comes through and the moon is full. They down little bottles of lightly scented gin and lemon that they keep tucked at their waist; the Yazidis sneak hits of the lettuce proscribed by their faith. I don’t partake.
And I jump back out. I lean against the south-facing wall, where someone’s scrawled “fareeq saher al-kora”: the football wizard’s team. The hollow of the “a” at the end of kora has been painted in to look like an Adidas ball. The sun hides, a light wind springs up, and shadows speckle my body; light dresses me in a dead leopard’s still-warm hide. Overhead, bronzed and heavy with cones, dead branches hang next to living boughs on the same tree. The needles are dusty green. I love how they feel, like when I leave the barber’s and sweep my palm over the clipped brush at the base of my skull. Above the stacked twigs and branches are layers of cloud, each sliding in a different direction. “It’s because the wind runs down invisible lanes,” I tell myself: “It twists and turns, runs into itself.”
The clouds move faster in the morning. They drift away and their sumptuous white turns grey. The heavier clouds, plump as naked monarchs or stickers of putti on the cover of a school book bound in blue card, drift west to Serê Kaniyê. They are brighter, lower, slower. On their white shelves, I stack a library of the mind: the books I haven’t read, or haven’t had the time to read, or to read again. The points of my elbows and my shoulders rest against the wall, and I raise my head. The boughs branch like the blood vessels over my grandmother’s brain, which I saw in a VHS recording of the catheterisation. They are the veins of the air, as seen in the ground’s snapshot of the tree with the sky behind, or maybe a white cloud, like the backdrop in an ID photo.
I think to myself that I’ll stay here until these peeling trunks are blushing in the evening light. Sheltering from the April sun, I cover my head with Mani’s poems. The children of Hazdeh will be passing soon, filing on foot from the Salim al-Sayyid High School to their village. I had just heard one shouting – “On high!” – and the cockerels had crowed a pious reply: “qul qul qul qul qul qul… ” Say say say say say… Say, in the name of your Lord. A phrase never completed. As though the echo is a vast boulder rolling across the fields, I track it with my eyes. And do not see it.
In the distance, amid the fields’ green, is a Nissan pickup. Orange, tiny, the cargo bed shivers like a tit’s tail. This is an Electricity and Communications Company vehicle. It usually lives in the garage beneath the post office known as the Eiffel Tower, but now it’s heading to Umm al-Rabie, the village of the al-Ghamr Bedouin. Whenever called out for repairs, the pickup is driven by Bashir Hazouke, the communist engineer whose quick-tempered outbursts cause his blood sugar to spike. Having to drive out here means he’s probably feeling that way.
This is bee-eater season. Are they ever eaten? Like when the girl feeds her lover grilled bee-eater in that song by Gulistan Perwer? They move and stop in small flocks, and their green feathers blend with the grass of Tell Mozan, whose knoll lies still as Sinbad’s sleeping whale, deaf to the Nowruz fireworks, a campfire kindled on its back. The flocking bee-eaters wheel slowly. Tiny wings. Breasts iridescent in sunlight. A beauty the beekeepers loathe. No sooner as their soft call is heard and the birds are spied on the phone lines strung over the barley, there is the echo of gunshots. It’s the hunter. Instead of the bee-eaters, he hits the lines on which they perch.
The phones of Umm al-Rabie go cold.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Do sports stars have the right to free speech?
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Do sports stars have the right to free speech?
The Mbappe controversy demonstrates how market power in sport is being used to enforce conformity.
French football superstar Kylian Mbappe recently landed in trouble over a meme. Discussing an image that apparently superimposed his face on Mao Zedong’s, he referred to the late Chinese leader as someone he thought was a dictator, without naming Mao.
The offhand remark became an international controversy. Chinese sponsors withdrew their support. State television suspended La Liga broadcasts. Apologies followed from Mbappe and his club, Real Madrid, while the league expressed regret over the offence caused.
Mbappe was riffing on one of the running jokes about his outsized influence over his clubs and teammates. He was not delivering a considered assessment of Chinese history. Yet the response turned a passing remark into a test of respect for an entire nation.
Mbappe is not the first athlete to discover how quickly political sensitivities become instruments of discipline. A decade ago, American football star Colin Kaepernick knelt during the United States national anthem to protest systemic racism and police killings of Black people, and was effectively frozen out of the National Football League.
In May, after Spanish footballer Lamine Yamal waved a Palestinian flag during Barcelona’s title celebrations, Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, accused him of inciting hatred and demanded that the club distance itself from the gesture.
Kaepernick and Yamal made deliberate statements. Mbappe made a joke. Yet the distinction offered the latter little protection. An athlete need not deliberately enter politics to discover how tightly his speech is policed.
Mbappe’s extraordinary visibility gives him influence and makes him commercially valuable. But the commercial relationships that make him valuable also hand others the means to discipline him.
The logic is an old one. In ancient Greece, victorious athletes could receive substantial rewards from their cities, including money, meals at public expense and civic honours. Sporting success could open a path to political influence, and their achievements brought prestige to the communities that claimed them.
But the claim could become possessive. According to the ancient Greek geographer and writer Pausanias, the runner Astylus, originally associated with Croton, later proclaimed himself a Syracusan when competing at the Olympic Games. His former compatriots responded by pulling down his statue and converting his house into a prison.
Today, sporting institutions make similar claims on the people whose achievements they celebrate. The athlete represents the nation, embodies the club, carries the sponsor’s values. Each relationship becomes a reason to keep an inconvenient thought to oneself. As Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho put it, “Often the best thing you can do is keep your mouth shut, because there’s danger in so many things you say or comment on.”
When a single remark threatens access to a market, the club and the league acquire a financial interest in treating it as misconduct, and the pressure to recant can be extreme. When a state broadcaster suspends an entire league, it punishes thousands of players, staff and viewers who had nothing to do with the remark, effectively holding them hostage to one man’s apology. That is market power being used to enforce conformity.
This is where the contradictions of celebrity become especially apparent. Sporting businesses sell courage, authenticity and individual character. They encourage audiences to identify with the person behind the performance. But the expression of that character becomes a problem when it threatens another part of the business.
The athlete is invited to be themselves, subject to approval.
Further, audiences add their own pressure. We increasingly expect sports stars to address moral and political questions, and we judge their silence as well as their speech. Fame does carry obligations. But athletic excellence does not confer political wisdom, and prominence is not a qualification. If we want courage from athletes, we must also confront the institutions that make courage professionally dangerous.
Mbappe’s case is revealing precisely because he was not taking a heroic stand. The freedom to speak cannot depend on an athlete being historically knowledgeable, perfectly articulate or deliberately brave. It must leave room for an uncertain remark and a foolish joke, as well as a carefully planned protest.
However, it is clear that freedom does not confer immunity from critique. Fans can disagree loudly, and athletes should answer for objectionable speech. But the test should be whether a remark harms people, not whether it embarrasses a state or threatens a balance sheet.
The supposed neutrality of sport helps to hide these demands for conformity. Flags, anthems and governments’ pursuit of prestige already fill sporting spectacles with political meaning. Athletes’ independent expression, on the other hand, attracts demands for silence when it disrupts those authorised messages.
Yet though bringing honour to a community, a champion’s achievement does not give that community ownership over them. Clubs can purchase sporting services. Sponsors can purchase advertising. Neither transaction entitles anyone to dictate an athlete’s convictions.
If sporting institutions insist on selling us the person behind the performance, they must accept that the person has a voice of their own.

Le journaliste, écrivain et documentariste réalise son premier long métrage de fiction. Une famille française, porté par un financement participatif, raconte la Seine-Saint-Denis, celle où il vit, loin des clichés.
Du gros matos envahit le petit trois-pièces. Une quinzaine de personnes s’affairent, courent dans tous les sens. « Ça va ? Tu veux un thé ? » Nadir Dendoune passe une tête. En repasse une autre cinq minutes plus tard. « Un café ? » On lui sourit. « Non, non. Toujours rien ! » Il s’excuse. Assure qu’à la pause déjeuner, il sera plus tranquille. Assise à table, face à un imposant buffet, l’actrice Hiam Abbass attend le coup d’envoi. Nadir se marre. « Ça tombe bien que l’Huma soit là, on va tourner la scène où Djamila, le personnage principal, se sert du journal pour éplucher des carottes. »

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.title: How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.author: Lubna Masarwa
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.text:
How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians
A day before the Israeli elections, I was walking through a well-heeled, leafy neighbourhood in West Jerusalem, five minutes from President Issac Herzog’s official residence.
I was on my way to interview an expert on Palestinian citizens of Israel, who were expected to vote in large numbers for the first time.
Three children - they could not have been more than seven or eight - jumped off the slides in a playground and ran towards me.
One of them asked whom I was going to vote for. A funny question, I thought, coming from kids.
I told them I would vote for the Joint List. The leader of the group asked, “What is the Joint List? Is it Bibi?” I said no, without explaining that it was an Arab bloc of parties.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The kid said: “So you’re not voting for Netanyahu?”
I said no. He spat at me, and the other two gave me the middle finger.
They must have thought I was a Jew defecting from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp. I wondered what they would have done if they knew I was Palestinian.
Kids spitting at a middle-aged woman didn’t seem to bother any of the passersby.
To liberal Zionists, this election was a debate about the boundaries of Israeli democracy, and whether it could include us as Arabs.
Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians
But the more I think about it, something far deeper is going on than mere hatred of a minority group, deeply entrenched though that is. The reaction to 7 October merely brought it out into the open.
Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians, and calling openly for more occupation, expulsion and deportation.
Palestinians who live in the city have to hold their breath if they want to live with this reality. They have no right to complain against another sticker calling on them to be killed or expelled.
It’s not just in every debate in this election campaign. You can hear it in small conversations in the street: “We will not sit with the Arabs.”
All the discussion is about how to build coalitions without the votes of the Arabs.
Palestinians vote for survival
Three Israeli political parties ran on platforms that openly support the deportation, displacement and expulsion of Palestinians - even those with Israeli citizenship.
Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister and head of the Religious Zionism party, has made “Judaising” the Galilee and Negev regions of Israel, where many Palestinians citizens live, a key feature of his election campaign.
All of this was orchestrated by the person who by rights should be Israel’s outgoing prime minister, Netanyahu, but who continues as its caretaker.
Haaretz analysed Netanyahu’s social media activity on election day. Every second post by the prime minister was against Arabs, laying the groundwork for claims about the integrity of the vote.
The response of Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up a fifth of the population, was immediate. They flocked to the polls, gaining an unheard-of 19 seats, and became the third-largest parliamentary bloc after Likud and Yashar.
Those who had boycotted elections for their entire lives went to vote for the first time.
This was not some sudden revelation. Every Palestinian understood that they were only part of Israel as window dressing, to make it look democratic, but with no meaningful ability to change their lives. In the past, just over half of them voted.
The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself
But this time, it was different.
The Palestinians of Israel know that what happened in Gaza, and is continuing to happen in the occupied West Bank, could happen to them too.
Israel committed genocide and got away with it. This vote is a survival vote; an expressed, very existential fear.
Palestinian sociologist Ameer Fakhoury told Middle East Eye: “The moment your existence becomes the central concern, the very meaning of citizenship changes. A citizen, in the substantive sense, should not have to engage in politics simply to avoid death.
“This is not how citizenship is supposed to function. When survival becomes the dominant motivation, the boundaries of ordinary political participation collapse. The symbolic and substantive meaning of citizenship is fundamentally undermined.”
Such a result in a “normal” democratic country would have ended with the opposition winning.
But not in Israel. Netanyahu’s initial loss became an orgy, a festival of racism against Palestinians.
No good or bad Arabs
Channel 12 News reported that on election day and its aftermath, there was a 400 percent rise in racist discourse against Arabs on social media, as Arabs were accused of stealing the elections.
Ayala Hasson, the veteran journalist of Israel’s public broadcaster, Kan 11, claimed, without any proof, that some of the 19 newly elected Knesset members from the Palestinian-led parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, “transferred money to Hamas”.
Hasson, a pro-Netanyahu journalist, also questioned the integrity of the elections, saying that Palestinian voters received envelopes with money as part of an illegal voter mobilisation campaign.
It doesn’t really matter what your politics are. The fact that you are an Arab is proof enough of your guilt.
Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has openly adopted a Zionist agenda by acknowledging the Jewish state and calling for national service.
He received the same treatment. This means that even Palestinians who strip themselves of their national identity cannot be part of a political system designed for Jews only.
The same thing happened to Lucy Aharish, an Arab journalist married to an Israeli Jew who served as a combat soldier in the reserves during the genocide in Gaza.
Aharish was savaged by prominent figures in Likud.
Itzik Bonzel, a Likud candidate, posted on Facebook: “You can walk around our streets as much as you like, but merely living among us does not make you Israeli in any way, and you will never be part of us, nor part of the people of Israel.”
Aharish is an opponent of the Palestinian national cause. Bonzel said she was “a foreign body, without any real roots in this land, and you will never be an Israeli”, concluding with a threat: “Know your place.”
Arabs in Israel can no longer ignore the fact that for large groups in Israel, possibly now the majority, there are no good or bad Arabs. It matters not who goes over to their side.
For them, Palestinians are illegitimate and should be expelled from the Jewish state.
The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself - and this should not be ignored by the Palestinian leadership.
I was asked in an interview with a Canadian radio station whether I thought Palestinians would vote again in future elections. Did this result inspire them?
For a moment I was taken aback by the stupidity of this question.
“I am not inspired, I am terrified,” I replied.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: The story behind Grant Wood’s American Gothic and what made it go viral
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Grant Wood’s painting American Gothic (1930)—the realist depiction of an austere rural man and woman posed stiffly before a modest white house with a gothic-styled window—has seeped into the public consciousness on a par with Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa and Edvard Munch’s The Scream. “I never stopped watching the ways American Gothic has transitioned into the iconic ‘couple with the pitchfork’ over the past six decades,” says the US art historian Wanda Corn, whose new book The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon delves into the cultural history of the painting.
Over the decades, Corn says she accumulated an “immense archive of reimagined couples” and her publication “sheds critical light on the cultural forces that transformed an image with humble roots into a global icon whose reach and charisma extend far beyond the world of art”, according to the publisher, Princeton University Press.
Grant Wood today is seen as a far more complicated and tragic figure than he presented and for many years was understood to be Wanda Corn
Corn, professor emerita of art history at Stanford University, outlines in detail how Wood picked his sitters: his 30-year-old sister, Nan Wood Graham, and his 62-year-old dentist, Byron McKeeby. “The two men shared a sense of humour, often chuckling over their ‘bridge for a bridge’ exchange; the dentist had provided the artist with a dental bridge and Wood paid him with a painting of a Paris bridge,” Corn writes.
Crucially the image has been misconstrued over the decades, with viewers interpreting the couple as married when in reality the pair represented a father and his daughter, according to the artist’s sister. “In Wood’s mind, the two people in front of the house represented a father and his aging daughter—a spinster—living in small-town America,” writes Corn. Wood and his closed circle described it this way repeatedly, she adds.
“Yet when the painting went out into the world, not one person saw the couple as a parent and child, nor did they see them as from a small town … this is one of the best examples in the history of art of how an artist’s intentions in a work can differ from the public’s reception of a painting.”
The person who corrected Corn about this widespread misconception was Wood Graham herself. “I too thought it represented a married couple,” Corn says. She explains that when she was photographed as the pitchfork couple with her husband in the 1970s, for a feminist work called Joe and Wanda Corn, Holiday Card (1975) by Keith M. Jones Sr, she was “under the assumption that [Wood’s sitters] were a married couple. But when I went to see [Wood Graham], I talked about them as a couple and she said in no uncertain terms: ‘They’re not a couple. It’s a father and daughter.’”
The image, and Wood’s achievements as an Iowa-based artist, were consistently lambasted and dismissed though. Early art historical texts initially ignored him, such as A History of Art (1962) by H.W. Janson, which only included the work in its seventh edition published in 2006. Corn’s survey of such texts establishes, she says, “how passive-aggressive the coverage of American Gothic was in this literature”.
The critical reaction to a Wood show Corn curated in 1983 was also brutal. “A writer of a Wall Street Journal article in May 1983 … labelled it the ‘Great Grant Wood Redemption Campaign’ and quoted the reaction of a well-known art dealer in town: ‘Flush it down the drain. It’s just cornball, provincial, nationalistic propaganda and it has nothing to do with art!’”
Corn’s 1983 exhibition of Wood’s work, Grant Wood: The Regionalist Vision, which launched at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, toured to other venues such as the Minneapolis Institute of Art (Yale University Press published an accompanying book). “The last landing of the exhibition was in San Francisco [at the de Young museum], and what better place to launch the first gay Gothic [work] on the walls of a major museum than in San Francisco,” she says, referring to the 1983 front cover of the gay magazine Frontiers that was included in the show.
Sexuality under scrutiny
The author unpicks the thorny issue of Wood’s sexuality, which has come under the microscope in recent years. “The upshot is that Wood today is seen as a far more complicated and tragic figure than he presented and for many years was understood to be,” she writes, acknowledging that two art historians, Tripp Evans and Sue Taylor, have contributed the most to recent psychosexual interpretations of Wood’s life and “the uncovering of his homosexuality”.
“I can see his struggles constantly,” Corn says. “But on the other hand, I also know people who found him just boundless fun to be with, lovable and endlessly creative, not dark and gloomy … we have to get a more balanced view [of him].”
How American Gothic came to be assimilated into the art history canon, across high and low popular culture is also explored through a wide variety of images including Obama Gothic (2012) by Mario Piperni, which shows Michelle and Barack Obama in front of the White House as the pitchfork couple, and Barry Kite’s photocollage Gothic Wave (2010) that draws on Hokusai’s famous 19th-century woodblock print.
“I actually could not have written the book I wrote now back then [in 1983] because I didn’t have the raw data,” Corn says. “I didn’t have this notion of the episodic uses of [the image] for everyday transient events and political events. I didn’t have any sense of what the computer was going to do to the image: the way it was going to translate it but also just make it a resource anybody could tap into.”
• Wanda Corn, The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon, Princeton University Press, 312pp, $49.95/£42 (hb)

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Judge orders Iowa to permit Satanic Temple holiday event at state capitol
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A federal judge ordered state officials in Iowa on Monday to permit a local Satanic Temple organization to hold a holiday event in the rotunda of the state capitol after years of denying the group’s application.
The religious organization and Iowa Republican state officials have been in a legal battle over the group’s applications to hold a holiday event at the state capitol in recent years.
Republicans in Iowa, who currently control the governorship and majorities in the state house and senate, have cited the capitol building’s policies prohibiting gratuitous violence and obscene displays as justification for denying the applications.
According to the office of the attorney general, Brenna Bird, state Republicans intend to appeal the federal judge’s decision.
The Satanic Temple and Iowa chapter leader filed a lawsuit in August, alleging discrimination from former and current state officials.
Chief District Judge Stephanie M Rose stated in her court order that the group was likely to succeed on its free speech claim and ordered the current director of the Iowa department of administrative services to approve the holiday event application within seven days.
The Satanic Temple (TST), which was founded in Salem, Massachusetts, in 2013, characterizes itself as a “non-theistic religious organization” that advocates for secularism and emphasizes separation from the Church of Satan founded in 1966.
The Satanic Temple argues it does not believe in Satan, rather arguing it uses Satan as a symbol to protest against religious authoritarianism.
“Satan is a symbol of the Eternal Rebel in opposition to arbitrary authority, forever defending personal sovereignty even in the face of insurmountable odds,” the Satanic Temple’s website states. It adds: “Satanists adhere to the principles of individual sovereignty and the rejection of tyrannical authority.”
In December 2023, the group had a religious holiday display in the Iowa state capitol, but it was vandalized by a Christian military veteran. The Turning Point founder, Charlie Kirk, pledged $10,000 to the accused vandal’s legal defense. The following year, the Satanic Temple’s application for a holiday display and event was denied.
“State officials have made it clear that they denied TST permission to hold events in the Capitol rotunda because they disagreed with their religious viewpoint,” said Shefali Aurora, ACLU of Iowa staff attorney, in a statement on the court order. “It is a foundational principle that the government cannot restrict speech in this way, favor one religion over another, or discriminate against religious groups because they don’t agree with them.”
The group said its proposed holiday event would include costumes of the European folklore character Krampus, caroling, coloring for children and ornament making. In its denial of the application, state officials cited sticks included in the costumes that could be used as weapons and policies meant to protect children who might be present in the public space.
Judge Rose wrote that the state officials’ arguments did not justify the denials, noting the argument that the character Krampus might scare children was “not a permissible basis for excluding speech” and the argument about the sticks included with the costumes “cannot justify denying the entire event”.
The Iowa department of administrative services and the Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, have not yet commented on the court order.
In 2023, Governor Reynolds stated in response to the group’s holiday display at the state capitol, “like many Iowans, I find the Satanic Temple’s display in the Capitol absolutely objectionable. In a free society, the best response to objectionable speech is more speech, and I encourage all those of faith to join me today in praying over the Capitol and recognizing the nativity scene that will be on display – the true reason for the season.”

https://taz.de/Ukraine-unter-massivem-Be.title: Ukraine unter massivem Beschuss: Kältetod mit Ansage
https://taz.de/Ukraine-unter-massivem-Be.author: Julia Surkowa
https://taz.de/Ukraine-unter-massivem-Be.text:
Ukraine unter massivem Beschuss: Kältetod mit Ansage
Russland greift in der Ukraine gezielt und verstärkt zivile Infrastruktur an – und zwar landesweit. Bereits jetzt kommt es zu massiven Stromausfällen.
Aljona Towbuch deckt die Risse in den Wänden ihrer Wohnung mit Plastikfolie und Sperrholzplatten ab. Anfang Herbst beschädigte eine russische Rakete ihr Haus in Boryspil, einer Stadt in der Nähe der ukrainischen Hauptstadt Kyjiw. Jetzt, da die erste Kälte eingesetzt hat und es zu Stromausfällen kommt, werden die Wände in der beschädigten Wohnung feucht und setzen Schimmel an.
„Hier kann man nicht mehr leben. Wir haben diese Wohnung gekauft, von der wir unser ganzes Leben lang geträumt hatten. Kurz darauf fiel mein Mann an der Front. Zwei Monate später zerstörten die Russen unser Haus“, erzählt die 38-Jährige, die ein schwarzes Tuch als Zeichen der Trauer trägt und an diesem Tag auch noch ein paar Sachen mitnehmen will.
Die technische Begutachtung des Hauses dauere noch an, doch sie habe ihr Zuhause höchstwahrscheinlich für immer verloren, sagt Aljona. Durch die ständigen Stromausfälle sowie die russischen Angriffe auf Kyjiw und die Umgebung, die in diesem Herbst zugenommen haben, wird auch ihre Situation immer schwieriger.
Am Montag hatte der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj vor der Vorbereitung eines neuen massiven Angriffs auf die Energie- und Logistikinfrastruktur gewarnt. Bereits in der darauffolgenden Nacht führte Russland einen kombinierten Angriff auf die Ukraine durch. „In Charkiw haben die Russen direkt ein städtisches Krankenhaus getroffen. 73 Menschen wurden verletzt, die kardiologische Abteilung wurde beschädigt“, schrieb Selenskyj am Dienstagmorgen auf seinem Telegram-Kanal.
Angriff auf Hospiz
In der Ortschaft Komyschuwacha, in der Region Saporischschja, sind nach den Angriffen am Dienstag bislang 33 Tote zu beklagen, über 50 Menschen werden noch unter Trümmern vermutet. „Mein Beileid gilt den Angehörigen und Hinterbliebenen. Die Rettungsarbeiten dauern an, soweit es die Sicherheitslage zulässt – denn es besteht die Gefahr erneuter russischer Angriffe – so hinterhältig, wie sie eben immer vorgehen“, teilte der Präsident mit. Auch die Stadt Dnipro war betroffen. Der Bürgermeister Borys Filatow postete Bilder von einem Hospiz, auf denen zwei zerstörte Krankenzimmer zu sehen sind.
Am Dienstagmorgen teilte das ukrainische Energieunternehmen DTEK mit, dass drei seiner Wärmekraftwerke die Stromerzeugung eingestellt hätten. „Infolge mehrerer Angriffswellen kam es zu großflächigen Zerstörungen und erheblichen Schäden an der Ausrüstung und Infrastruktur der Anlagen. Die Kraftwerke haben die Stromerzeugung eingestellt“, heißt es in einer Mitteilung des Unternehmens.
Aus Sicherheitsgründen gibt DTEK den Standort der beschädigten Anlagen nicht preis. Gleichzeitig bekommen die Einwohner Kyjiws und der Region Kyjiw die Folgen der angespannten Lage im Energiesystem schon jetzt zu spüren. Die Stromversorgung erfolgt nach festen Zeitplänen, in einigen Stadtteilen Kyjiws ist Strom nur für wenige Stunden am Tag verfügbar.
Die Situation ist derzeit noch nicht kritisch, doch die Rettungskräfte in Kyjiw sind darauf vorbereitet, mobile Hilfsstationen einzurichten, falls die Stromversorgung für mehrere Tage ausfallen sollte. „Wir haben das im vergangenen Winter durchgespielt. Sollte der Strom für drei Tage ausfallen, sind wir darauf vorbereitet, Anlaufstellen einzurichten, wo man Telefone aufladen kann. In Kyjiw gibt es Gebäude, in denen alles vom Strom abhängt: die Heizung, die Wasserversorgung und die Zubereitung von Mahlzeiten. Für die dort lebenden Menschen muss es einen Ort geben, an dem sie heißen Tee trinken und sich aufwärmen können“, sagt Pawel Petrow, ein Vertreter des Kiewer Katastrophenschutzdienstes (DSNS). Derzeit habe es jedoch keinen Sinn, solche Einrichtungen präventiv einzurichten.
Wirtschaftsleistung geht zurück
Laut Militärexperten hätten die Russen ihre Angriffstaktik grundlegend geändert. Während im Sommer noch die Mehrheit der Ziele militärischer Natur gewesen sei, seien in den vergangenen Monaten zunehmend wirtschaftliche Einrichtungen und zivile Infrastruktur angegriffen worden.
„Sie nehmen Lebensmitteleinzelhändler, die Pharmabranche, Tankstellen und Verkehrswege ins Visier. Inzwischen sind 60 Prozent der Ziele ziviler Natur, 40 Prozent militärischer. Dieser Trend wird bis zum Frühjahr 2027 anhalten, solange das kalte Wetter andauert. Die Hauptziele in diesem Winter bleiben Brücken, die Energieinfrastruktur sowie Fahrzeuge auf Schienenwegen“, erklärt der Militäranalyst und ehemalige Mitarbeiter des Geheimdienstes SPU, Iwan Stupak.
„Kyjiw liegt 200 Kilometer von der Grenze entfernt. Die Russen können nicht physisch hierhergelangen, also zerstören sie die zivile Infrastruktur und die Wirtschaft. Wir erleben leider zum ersten Mal seit Jahren einen Rückgang der ukrainischen Wirtschaftsleistung“, sagt Stupak.
Er weist darauf hin, dass die Nationalbank der Ukraine ihre Prognose für die wirtschaftliche Entwicklung verändert habe – aufgrund der verstärkten russischen Angriffe auf Industrie, Energieversorgung und Logistik. „Die Nationalbank der Ukraine (NBU) hat ihre Prognose für die Entwicklung des realen BIP im Jahr 2026 nach unten korrigiert – auf –0,4 Prozent. Den größten Einfluss auf die Verschlechterung der Prognose hatten die Folgen des verstärkten Beschusses. Sein negativer Beitrag zum BIP wird auf 1,9 Prozentpunkte geschätzt“, erklärte NBU-Chef Andrij Pyschnyj am 29. Oktober bei einem Briefing in Kyjiw.
Aljona Towbuch, die um ihren Mann trauert, verfolgt die Nachrichten nicht. Doch sie und ihre Familie spürten, dass sich die Lage jeden Tag verschlechtert. Derzeit leben Aljona und ihre Tochter bei Verwandten. In deren Wohnung wird der Strom täglich für fast 12 Stunden abgeschaltet.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Casa Astral seleciona 12 artesãs periféricas para capacitação gratuita em projetos culturais
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Fátima Pereira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Artesãs que moram em comunidades periféricas do Recife podem se inscrever, até o dia 5 de novembro, na formação gratuita “Artesanato é Cultura, Sonhos Virando Realidade”, promovida pelo Ponto de Cultura Casa Astral. A iniciativa vai selecionar 12 mulheres para um percurso de capacitação em elaboração de projetos culturais, com quatro encontros presenciais entre os dias 10 e 19 de novembro, das 14h às 18h, na sede do Instituto Casa Astral, no bairro de Poço da Panela, Zona Norte da capital pernambucana. Cada participante selecionada receberá uma bolsa-incentivo de R$ 750.
A proposta é oferecer ferramentas para que as artesãs possam transformar seus conhecimentos e práticas em projetos culturais, ampliando as possibilidades de participação em editais públicos e de desenvolvimento de iniciativas com impacto artístico e social.
Além das atividades coletivas, a formação prevê três mentorias individuais para cada participante. O recebimento da bolsa está condicionado à presença em, pelo menos, 75% das atividades previstas.
A seleção também estabelece medidas para ampliar a participação de grupos historicamente marginalizados. Do total de vagas, 50% serão destinadas a mulheres pretas ou pardas, 20% a pessoas LGBTQIAPN+ e 10% a mulheres com 60 anos ou mais. Também haverá uma vaga reservada para artesã com deficiência (PcD). A programação contará com intérprete de Língua Brasileira de Sinais (Libras).
“O objetivo é fortalecer a autoestima e instrumentalizar as artesãs das nossas periferias para que elas consigam ampliar o acesso a editais públicos e transformar seus saberes em projetos de impacto social e artístico”, destaca Guida Gomes, presidenta do Ponto de Cultura Casa Astral e uma das facilitadoras da formação.
Podem participar mulheres cisgênero, trans e travestis, com idade a partir de 18 anos, que tenham atuação comprovada no artesanato e residam em áreas periféricas do Recife. As inscrições são gratuitas e podem ser feitas por meio de formulário eletrônico ou presencialmente, mediante agendamento, na sede do Instituto Casa Astral.
O resultado final da seleção será divulgado em 8 de novembro. O projeto conta com incentivo do Sistema de Incentivo à Cultura (SIC), da Fundação de Cultura da Cidade do Recife, da Secretaria de Cultura e da Prefeitura do Recife.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.title: Verhandlungen IG Metall | Das ist eine Kampfansage
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.author: Stephan Krull
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.text:
- Kommentare
- Verhandlungen IG Metall
Das ist eine Kampfansage
Der IG Metall geht es im Tarifkampf um die Abwehr von Lohnsenkungen und Arbeitszeitverlängerung für 3,7 Millionen Beschäftigte. Ein Kommentar.
Es ist, wenn überhaupt, ein vergiftetes Angebot, mit dem die Unternehmensseite in die zweite Tarifrunde in der Metall- und Elektroindustrie startete: 1,3 Prozent Lohnerhöhung ab Juli 2028, nach 20 Monaten ohne Lohnerhöhung. Bei einer Laufzeit von 26 Monaten sind das 0,6 Prozent pro Jahr. Zugleich gibt es eine Inflation von drei Prozent, einen Produktivitätszuwachs von 1,5 Prozent, außerordentliche Gewinne in der Luft- und Raumfahrt, Elektro- und Medizintechnik und der Rüstungsindustrie. Selbst die Autoindustrie verzeichnet Gewinne, wenn auch geringer ausgewiesen.
In Betrieben, denen es nach Buchhaltung der Unternehmen gut geht, wollen sie im Juli 2028 eine Einmalzahlung bis zu 800 Euro gewähren. Sie verlangen Maßnahmen zur Senkung der Krankheitskosten und Abweichungen vom Flächentarif in Betrieben, die nach eigenen Berechnungen geringe Gewinne ausweisen.
Alles zusammen ist eine Verhöhnung, die von der IG Metall zurecht als Kampfansage anstelle eines Angebots bewertet wird. Die Belegschaften in über 2.000 Betrieben haben seit dem 1. November mit dem Streikauftakt von Dresden bis Köln, von Flensburg bis München starke Zeichen gesetzt und gezeigt, dass sie zusammen und hinter der Gewerkschaft stehen. Die Erwartung der Mitglieder der IG Metall: die Abwärtsspirale beim Lohn angesichts der Preisentwicklung stoppen, das Leben wieder bezahlbar machen und den Abbau von Arbeitsplätzen in der Industrie zu beenden.
Die Gewerkschaft wäre auch aus eigenem Interesse gut beraten, das naheliegendste Mittel zur Sicherung von Arbeitsplätzen, die Forderung nach Arbeitszeitverkürzung, zu stellen. Mehr Lohn sichert Kaufkraft und Binnennachfrage, die Vier-Tage-Woche sichert Arbeitsplätze.
»Ein Streik ist mehr wert als tausend Schulungen«, sagte einst Willi Bleicher, der legendäre Bezirksleiter der IG Metall aus Baden-Württemberg. Das gilt, wenn der Streik erfolgreich ist; das gilt auch, sollte der Kampf verloren werden. Eine Lohnerhöhung unterhalb von Inflationsrate und Produktivitätsentwicklung und kein Ende des Personalabbaus wären jedenfalls eine Enttäuschung.
Die Kampfbereitschaft der Arbeiterinnen und Arbeiter ist so hoch wie die Erwartungen. Allein werden sie diese Klassenauseinandersetzung aber nicht für sich entscheiden. Mit praktischer Unterstützung der DGB-Gewerkschaften, der Sozialverbände und der Linken, mit einer umfassenden Mobilisierung und Solidarität sollte dieser Kampf gewonnen werden.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sarayu Bongale
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
I Am a UMich Student From Texas. Choosing Where to Vote Was Impossible.
Despite Michigan being a battleground for one of the most contentious midterm races this cycle, I couldn’t help but feel a draw to my native Texas.
These days at the University of Michigan, it is virtually impossible to walk through central campus without being reminded of the midterms. Blue and red tables line the walkways, and student organizers will literally chase you down to offer their spiel about which candidate deserves your vote.
It is not uncommon for professors to invite student organizations to give voter registration and election information presentations before class starts. As early voting began in Ann Arbor, on-campus voter hubs frequented classrooms to help Michigan-registered students cast their ballots. Even as I open my laptop and scroll through social media, advertisements for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers flash across my screen.
The visibility of the midterm elections in purple Michigan has been a striking contrast to my first 18 years growing up in solidly red Texas. There, I seldom encountered campaign advertisements and often questioned whether casting a ballot had any effect on electoral outcomes. But in Michigan, there is no doubt about it: Every vote matters.
University of Michigan student Britta Pingree, president of Turn Up Turnout, a nonpartisan organization that promotes civic engagement, said she has seen more political messaging and student advocacy during this “big election.”
“It definitely does seem like an energetic and important time,” Pingree said. “Students are aware of candidates and the specific offices that they’re voting for. They are knowledgeable about the ballot proposals that are available on the Ann Arbor and Michigan ballot.”
Despite Michigan’s being a battleground for one of the most contentious midterm races this cycle, I couldn’t help but feel drawn to my native Texas. The result of the tight race between Texas Senate candidates James Talarico and Ken Paxton may well be a litmus test for whether Democrats can make gains in red states.
Medha Kristipati, a student of government at the University of Texas at Austin, said she has noticed greater political engagement among students in recent years.
“I definitely do think people are more invested in politics now than when I was a child in Texas,” Kristipati said.
At the relatively liberal UT Austin, Kristipati has particularly noticed Democratic campaign outreach surrounding the Texas elections. She told me there’s an energetic effort to flip Texas blue—and that there’s a real sense that this might be possible.
“People are really pushing to make that happen.”
Experiencing these two political environments has led me to reconsider what makes voting feel meaningful. Although Michigan is a swing state where individual votes can carry significant weight, my connection to Texas shapes my decision to vote there instead. Having spent most of my life in Texas, I feel a personal responsibility to contribute to the state’s future, especially as it appears to be on the precipice of significant change.
Rather than viewing the state’s political leanings as a reason to disengage, the possibility of flipping Texas further encourages me to vote there and help shape a different political future for the place I call home.
