How Gaza Broke the Art World
David Velasco
22.12.2025Essay
There are lines as I arrive at the Neue Nationalgalerie – long ones, snaking across the vast concrete plaza from which the museum, a squat glass pavilion, protrudes. On the façade, in bright neon scrawl, is the title of Nan Goldin’s show: This Will Not End Well. I landed in Berlin a few hours ago. It’s late on a Friday, November 2024. I meet up with Nikki Columbus, a friend from New York who is writing a piece about the night for The Nation, and we scout the perimeter, looking for familiar faces. We try our luck at the entrance. The museum’s director, Klaus Biesenbach, is outside. He shouts my name and grabs my shoulder, then waves us in.
Six large temporary pavilions swathed in black curtains are scattered in the sparse atrium. Each pavilion houses one of Nan’s penetrating videos or slideshows: early masterpieces like The Ballad of Sexual Dependency and The Other Side, plus more recent works like Sirens, an elegy to addiction. The show’s proposition is that Nan, one of our greatest living artists in any medium, merits recognition, specifically, as a filmmaker. The slideshows are not films in a traditional sense; mostly they are magnetic pictures of magnetic people drawn from the artist’s life, alchemists who have wrung beauty from desolation. The images are composed and ordered according to her singular sensibility, alert to pacing – dactyls of resemblance, resemblance, difference – and fastened together with music you might put on a mixtape to a lover: Marianne Faithfull, John Kelly, Rosalind Hunt. I think about how art is more or less a talent for putting one right wrong thing next to another to make something new, and how Nan knows this better than anyone.
I stake a spot in front of a stage near the museum’s entrance. I know what’s about to happen. Everyone does. It’s why we came. Klaus arrives and nervously asks where Nan is. A crowd collects in front of the platform – mostly young bodies in black clothes. She finally shows up, 20 minutes to eight, garnet curls, black tuxedo, trailed by a minder. The air crackles. Klaus stumbles as he walks to the lectern.
“Good evening. Good evening. My name is Klaus Biesenbach, and I’m the director of the Neue Nationalgalerie, and I’m really honoured that you’re all here tonight. I wish… I had a camera, I’d photograph you, it’s very beautiful. Thank you, thank you.”
The crowd is unmoved.
He continues: “As you might have heard, [Nan and I] decided to disagree. We decided to agree to disagree – you see, that was a Freudian… Um, I treasure the freedom of expression here and now in Berlin in 2024, to allow the Nationalgalerie to be such a place that you can do that. That sounds great, but I mean it.”
Nan ascends to the podium. I feel the holy tingle through my arms.
“I’m starting with a period of silence, in honour of the dead,” she begins. “Please put your phones away and join me.”
My mind runs a familiar montage – horror, depression, boredom, anger, helplessness. Here we are, for what it’s worth, feeling these things together.
“Why did I feel I have to talk tonight?” Nan asks. “This is my lifetime retrospective, but there is nothing in it from the past year, and that’s missing. The museum has kept its promise to allow me to talk, and I thank them. But they claim that my activism and my art are separate, even though that has never been the case. The last year has been Palestine and Lebanon for me. Since October 7th, I have found it hard to breathe. I feel the catastrophe in my body, but it’s not in this show.”
Germany has been consumed by a moral panic over antisemitism, and expressions of solidarity with Palestine have been demonised by the custodians of the state’s “memory culture”. Nan speaks of the more than 180 cancellations of pro-Palestine artists and teachers in Germany, the need for diverse strategies of resistance and cooperation inside the movement. She speaks of Islamophobia and the weaponisation of antisemitism, the consensus over the term “genocide” among members of the UN, even the pope. She speaks of the horror of watching the land grabs and domicide, the murders live-streamed to our phones.
“Antizionism has nothing to do with antisemitism.” Nan permits a smile as the crowd erupts in applause. “What I see in Gaza reminds me of the pogroms that my grandparents escaped. Never again means never again for everyone.” A bigger smile as the crowd cheers, and she pats her chest. A large black banner reading “ARMS EMBARGO NOW” unfurls behind her.
“The more of us there are, the more of us there are.”
Nan passes Klaus as they trade places on the platform. Neither acknowledges the other.
“As I mentioned in my introduction earlier,” Klaus begins, but his words are overwhelmed by the crowd’s chants of “Free, Free Palestine!” “As I mentioned in my introduction earlier,” he tries again, “I disagree with your opinion. Still, I stand for your right to express yourself freely.” A group outside, visible through the Mies van der Rohe building’s glazed façade, pulls open a large banner behind him: “STAATSRÄSON IST GENOZID”, referring to Germany’s official policy – its “reason of state” – of unflinching support for Israel. Museum staff arrange their bodies in a comical attempt to block the sign while Klaus pushes on, eventually conceding to the chants emerging from the canopy of keffiyehs and Palestinian flags.
He will return later, when the crowds have dispersed, with a puzzling speech describing how he turned 20 in Israel, how he met Nan in 1992, how he was a caregiver for Susan Sontag in 2004, how Susan taught him to “be unafraid”.
I think it takes a certain blinkered arrogance for a museum director to give a rebuttal to an artist’s remarks at their opening – an unprecedented act, as far as I know. I’m not sure this is the fearlessness Sontag had in mind. It is perverse for the person representing the state institution to claim that he, and not the artist speaking truth to power, is modelling courage. Or for him to describe Nan’s fury at the genocide in Gaza, and her call for introspection and action, as “opinion” – as if this might be dismissed as simple disagreement.
There are people who will go on to claim that the audience is silencing or even “censoring” Klaus by shouting him down, but I think that Klaus is not speaking so much as parroting the senescent propaganda of Staatsräson, the version of history that floats undisturbed through the technocratic ventilation systems, a malevolent spirit seeking new host bodies. I am aware on some level that Klaus has also done something unique and acted as an institutional buffer so that Nan could speak at all, so that the show could go on. I am aware that the protesters’ shouts are an incantation against the spell of the state.
Nan and I and a few friends slip away and take an elevator down to an empty loading dock behind the museum.
“How was it?” she asks, her voice trembling as she offers me a cigarette. “I hate talking in public.” She lights hers, takes a drag. “I usually don’t show up. You know that?”
“You’re a hero, Nan.”
“Oh man,” she says, dragging again. “I’m going to be in a lot of trouble after this one.”
I was in Berlin because Nan asked me to be there. She asked me to be there, I think, because I understand something about the shape of the situation. She had been preparing her remarks for weeks, and this is not the kind of thing you do alone. I’ve found myself in trouble alongside Nan before, trying to change things that seem impossible to change until you do, and I feel bonded to her. It’s strange enough to be a screen for others’ projections, which we are all the time in daily life. It is stranger still to know the queasy feeling of exposure that comes when you’re briefly shot into the vertiginous penumbra of history.
From October 2005 until October 2023, I worked at Artforum, the glossy, monthly scripture of contemporary art. For many, the magazine was the North Star of criticism – a peerless instrument of canonisation. For an artist, landing the cover was a consecration. People collected them: a row of the magazine’s totemic spines on a bookshelf signalled sophistication. (An Artforum on Edward Cullen’s Barcelona couch in the movie Twilight quickly establishes his urbanity.) I was editor-in-chief for the last six of those years, and during that time I witnessed history’s quickening: a #MeToo scandal at the magazine that resulted in the resignation of a disgraced publisher; protests at the Whitney Museum that provoked a rare surrender of a board member; the global standstill of Covid-19; the flash of white consciousness around Black oppression in the summer of 2020; Israel’s assault on Gaza during the Unity uprising in May of 2021; Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022. A sympathetic friend dubbed me the “crisis editor”. I took for granted that Artforum’s project was imbricated with the politics of the left, and ran the magazine on that basis; as a result, I sometimes heard people call it “Wokeforum”.
The fact that I refer to Artforum’s “project” at all reveals the grandiosity that is one of the art world’s key features, the soil for its spectacular financialisation – its unparalleled ability to transform radicalism into capital. This grandiosity was inflected in much of the bright and lofty material that we published. The stakes were high; we believed we were writing history, and we often were. Compared with my predecessors, my tenure as editor-in-chief was marked by a greater appetite for protest, for using our position to intensify pressure on institutions, to force real structural change. In some ways, this was a continuation of strategies of protest and institutional critique among artists we admired, from Adrian Piper and Hans Haacke to Andrea Fraser. But as time went on, our targets were becoming clearer, our tactics more refined.
I thought I knew how to move within the contradictions. I was not fired when I published, in my first issue as editor, the portfolio that launched Nan’s campaign targeting the Sackler family – prominent art-world patrons whose names were inscribed at the Metropolitan Museum, the Louvre and the Guggenheim – for their role in the opioid crisis. I was not fired when I commissioned “The Tear Gas Biennial”, a fiery polemic that cinched the departure of Warren Kanders, CEO of the weapons manufacturer Safariland, as vice-chairman of the Whitney Museum’s board. I was not fired in June 2020 when I posted calls on Artforum’s social media channels to donate to bail funds and defund the police.
There has been plenty of controversy in Artforum’s history. In 1974, the artist Lynda Benglis presented an ad featuring herself nude and holding a double dildo between her legs, a gesture that inspired a split in the editorial department and the subsequent founding of the journal October. A decade later, Thomas McEvilley’s article “Doctor Lawyer Indian Chief”, a searing critique of the “Primitivism” show at the Museum of Modern Art, occasioned an impassioned back-and-forth between the curators and the critic about art history’s colonial underpinnings, instigating a new phase of critical discourse. (As one of the magazine’s publishers was fond of telling me, we didn’t report the news, we were the news.) Controversy, the invigorating expression of oppositional positions, telegraphs health. We were modernists, after all. Risk and dissent were our sun and moon. Editors didn’t just survive controversies; they made their names with them. We knew that conflict is the engine of that eternal hysteria called “relevance”. As far as I know, prior editors left when they got bored or ran out of things to say. I was the ninth editor in the magazine’s 60-plus-year history, and the first to be fired for something I did. It is no surprise that this something concerned Palestine.
On 19 October 2023, I authorise the publication of an open letter from culture workers in support of Palestinian liberation and a ceasefire in Gaza. Twelve days have passed since Palestinians broke through the heavily fortified border walls surrounding the Gaza Strip, killing around 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping 251. Already, more than 3,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s retaliation.
I am in Paris for the opening of a major art fair, and I have spent the past week-and-a-half reaching out to contributors I hoped could rise to the occasion. I am experiencing profound alienation. In the art world you become accustomed to cognitive dissonance, but I am running up against my limits. At the fair, everything is proceeding as normal – invitations to dinners and parties, the rich swapping stories and resources. Almost no one speaks about Gaza. Those who do mostly take Zionist sympathies for granted: of course your passion is for the murdered and kidnapped Israelis, of course you condemn Hamas.
The letter is drafted by a group of anonymous individuals who decide not to take these sympathies for granted. When a colleague shares it with me, it feels obvious that the magazine should respond with solidarity instead of analysis. It feels obvious that we should do so quickly. We know that we are in one of those strange and extraordinary periods when collective action has more purchase. My colleague asks if they can use my name when approaching Nan about signing the letter, and I say yes, and sign it as well. In no time at all, the group collects some 8,000 signatures – many of whom are major artists and contributors to the magazine – which they cap just prior to publication.
As I am negotiating the letter, a missile hits a courtyard of al-Ahli Arab Hospital in Gaza City, killing hundreds of people who were sheltering there. Later we will find it quaint to recall that, at the time, Israel claimed that a failed Palestinian rocket launch caused the explosion, and that most newspapers take the word of the “most moral army in the world”. In the months to come, Israel will kill tens of thousands of Palestinians and demolish nearly all the hospitals in the Gaza Strip. We will find it hard to imagine a time when anyone could believe that Israel wouldn’t target civilians and hospitals. We will find it hard to imagine that, at the time of the letter’s publication, the principal objection was that it focused on Palestinian suffering, and that it refused to invoke or condemn Hamas.
Shortly after we publish the letter, all hell breaks loose. My phone, once a conduit for benign distractions, acquires the menacing nimbus of a grenade. In the car from Newark airport, I take a call from the head publicist of Penske Media, the company that acquired Artforum a year earlier, who implores me to do something acknowledging “the other side”. Our Instagram post about the letter becomes a flashpoint, generating more than 15,000 likes in a handful of hours – far more than any other post in our history. The comments feed is flooded with emojis of Palestinian flags, but also accusations of antisemitism and calls to unsubscribe. In an unprecedented move, the publishers go above the heads of the editorial department and take down the Instagram post. They remove the letter itself from the magazine’s homepage and briefly make it invisible in the search function, so that to find it you need a direct link. Shortly afterwards, they stop responding to my messages.
We begin to receive texts and emails from artists and curators asking to have their names removed from the list of signatories. There are some predictable figures – major artists with less experience in activism – as well as a few sad surprises. Some explain that they can’t be associated with anything that doesn’t explicitly condemn Hamas; others say they’re afraid for their jobs and careers. Each lost name is another chink in the armour of collective action. Some have the dignity to write to me directly; others employ expensive art PR teams. (“_____’s name is apparently still on the signatory list. He is asking that his name be removed immediately.”)
Some collectors are calling up individual artists who signed, threatening to sell off their works or stonewall exhibitions by refusing to lend to museums. Gallerists tell me and my artist friends that patrons are threatening not to fund exhibitions or buy work from anyone who signed. Messages from a WhatsApp group of Zionist collectors and gallerists called “Art World for Israel” are leaked, revealing an organised strategy of intimidation targeting artists who signed the letter. There seems to be a particularly vindictive ire toward the Jewish artists who spoke up to support the Palestinian cause – Goldin, Tai Shani, Candice Breitz, Nicole Eisenman. Museum board members pressure institutional leaders to distance themselves from the letter and raise the idea of deaccessioning works of Palestinian artists. A team of dealers and collectors writes a counter-letter, which is signed by artists such as Marina Abramović and Richard Prince, and publishes it in full-page ads in The New York Times, Le Monde and The Wall Street Journal. I have never seen anything like this. If this is the response, then the letter must really matter.
On the day that I am fired, I am offered a choice. It’s a little before noon on 26 October when I meet with Jay Penske, the youthful CEO of Penske Media. We are at the company’s New York headquarters, an airless sepulchre of corporate banality in a prewar office building on Fifth Avenue. Jay is friendly as we speak, a practised inquisitor. “You have good friends,” he says with some amusement, referring to a letter, composed by the filmmaker Laura Poitras and signed by some big names, petitioning to keep me on board.
He asks me to walk him through my decision, which I do, carefully. I tell him that I felt, and still feel, that the magazine needed to respond to the moment. I had consulted the editorial staff and had reached out to contributors. No one felt they had the authority to write about 7 October and its aftermath. I had watched the agile responses of several magazines that I trusted, and the clumsy nonresponses of nearly every other publication. I contemplated various savvy “art world” takes, all of which seemed specious. In Paris, one of our contributors brought the letter to my attention, and I told them we would publish it, which, as editor-in-chief, is literally my prerogative. I did this swiftly, in consultation with the web team and our international reviews editor, who were entirely on board.
Jay asks me why I signed the letter, and I explain that we’re not a newspaper, but a leftist art publication. People should know where we stand on genocide, and why not? What kind of interest are we protecting? He tells me about the tricky situation the publishers are in. We’ve all been spammed with threatening calls and emails, many from people we’ve never heard of. (“The artists and other persons whose names appear as signatories and supporters of this shameless letter have no soul in their hearts,” preaches Gil Brandes from Tel Aviv.) The art dealer Marianne Boesky writes a letter: “This is appalling to me as a Jew and I need Artforum to remove all Boesky ads from Artforum’s platforms immediately.” I am told that the Chanel Culture Fund has demanded that we stop the presses in order to pull their ad from our November issue. (We didn’t comply.) The gallery Lévy Gorvy Dayan has written a rebuttal, which I agree to publish online because it seems worth having a public record of the surreal moral universe it represents.
I am aware that much of the sentiment is divided by class: the letters’ signatories are mostly artists, the letters’ detractors are mostly their dealers and collectors. This is not a new rift in the art world, but Palestine seems to have deepened it beyond repair. Jay tells me that the magazine’s publishers are putting together a statement, and he asks me to write something describing my missteps, something I could post on Artforum’s website and to my personal Instagram. “And if I say no?” I ask. “Hopefully it won’t come to that,” he tells me.
I walk downtown to clear my head. What can I say? I don’t like the barely veiled threat, and I’m not sorry. Two weeks earlier, I cringed watching Samira Nasr, the editor of Harper’s Bazaar, post an apology for an Instagram story stating that Israel cutting off Gazans’ access to water and power “is the most inhuman thing I’ve seen in my life”. To me it’s simple: my job is to position the magazine correctly in the current of history. We have done the right thing.
My phone rings. It’s Jay. He sounds panicked. “Someone has tipped off The New York Times,” he says. “We need to accelerate your statement.”
“I can’t produce something on this timeline,” I reply.
“I’m very disappointed to hear that,” he says. “I had really hoped this would work out.” He hangs up.
A colleague at the magazine calls next. “Are you really going to throw everything away?” he asks. “Over this?”
“I’m not the one doing the throwing,” I say.
“The letter wasn’t even a success,” he says. “Look, it’s divided the art world.”
“I think we have different ideas of success.”
That night, at 7:39 PM, I am at home when I receive an email from one of the two publishers with the subject line “Your Employment”. The phrasing is evasive, but the message is clear: “Dear David, I was disheartened to learn that you did not respond to Jay this afternoon, we are therefore assuming that you have decided to leave your role.” I start to respond that I most definitely have not “decided to leave my role”. A minute later, the magazine’s website posts a statement from the publishers saying that the letter’s publication “was not consistent with Artforum’s editorial process”. Few people know “editorial process” better than I do – the “process”, after all, ended at my door. The sudden invention of phantom procedures is one of the more despicable attempts to disguise my firing as a matter of protocol rather than politics.
My termination is immediate; there is no settlement. I will be paid through the week and no more. It is 18 years to the day since I began at the magazine. Later that night, The New York Times publishes a story about my firing, kicking off another media storm. Nearly a third of the Artforum editorial staff resigns and 700 writers sign on to a boycott of the magazine. More editors will follow in the coming weeks. In every way that counts, the magazine as we knew it is over. The era of Vichy Artforum begins.
Of course, I’m not alone. Shortly after my firing, Jazmine Hughes, a prominent contributor to The New York Times Magazine, is forced to resign after signing an open letter condemning the genocide. Gabriella Karefa-Johnson, a Black editor-at-large at Vogue, resigns after an Instagram post condemning Israel as an apartheid state. Michael Eisen, the editor-in-chief of eLife, a prominent science journal, is let go for retweeting a satirical article from The Onion: “Dying Gazans Criticized for Not Using Last Words to Condemn Hamas”. The actress Melissa Barrera is fired from Scream 7, Susan Sarandon is dropped from her agency for speaking at a rally, and CAA agent Maha Dakhil apologises and endures a Stalinesque “re-education” after reposting an image stating, simply, “You’re currently learning who supports genocide.” Two years later, the fever of this repressive moment will largely be forgotten.
Billionaire donors run “doxxing trucks” around campuses featuring faces of people who protested Israel’s assault, and state officials study lists generated by the Canary Mission, a ghoulish conclave that targets student activists. The presidents of major universities are called before congress to testify. Their limp acts of contrition fail to satisfy the establishment’s thirst for blood, and Harvard’s Claudine Gay and the University of Pennsylvania’s M. Elizabeth Magill resign. We’ve been quick to label all this “McCarthyism”, but in truth, the fallout, which outrages the popular conscience, signals a vaster and more insidious repression.
The crackdown is international: across Europe, there are whispers and then headlines about artists, writers and curators losing residencies, sales and even jobs. An awards ceremony at the Frankfurt Book Fair for the Palestinian author Adania Shibli is cancelled in the weeks following 7 October. The city of Bremen and other sponsors of the Hannah Arendt Prize withdraw their support when its recipient, the Russian-American writer M. Gessen, publishes an essay in The New Yorker comparing Gaza to the Jewish ghettoes of Nazi-occupied Europe. Friends in Berlin in particular report an atmosphere of absolute censorship and policing, and across Germany, foreign nationals are threatened with deportation for showing solidarity with Palestine. The stealth punishments are perhaps the most pernicious: the jobs not offered, the sales not made. They contribute to an ambient fear that persists in people’s minds. The resulting silence is the only sign of its efficacy.
I don’t know why I thought we were an exception. Maybe because sometimes we were. Artforum, for many years, was about as leftist as an elite publication could get. We really did play a role in holding weapons manufacturers and the engineers of the opioid crisis to account. We really did give jobs and bylines to some singular and brilliant people. We really were a brainy refuge of weird glamour married to principle, and sometimes I wonder if mine is the last generation to grow up thinking of the art world as a place for ungovernable outsiders and talented eccentrics, which doesn’t hear the word ‘art’ and think immediately of commerce.
For me, and for many of my friends, art once seemed to offer a kind of promise. I grew up poor, brown and queer in Oregon, but I was still privileged enough to make it to a fancy college, where I looked for ways to orient myself amid unfamiliar codes of inclusion and exclusion. A young gay friend – an artist who made careful, exquisite paintings and sculptures, and whose ambition eventually yielded to his anarchic politics – exposed me to Portland’s small but vivid art scene. Here you could open a gallery or independent-minded bookstore, encourage strange and talented people to pursue their passions, and invite revolutionary thought into your life. I began to consider art a home for ideas and rebellion, a way to be yourself outside the stultifying halls of academia.
Those were the years when I encountered Adrian Piper, the Black conceptual artist who made politically incisive work with heart, who in 1970 withdrew a piece from the New York Cultural Center to protest against the US invasion of Cambodia, and in the early 1980s taught “funk lessons” to college students to exorcise xenophobia. I read the words of artists like David Wojnarowicz, who enraged senators with his scathing communiques about our genocidal indifference to AIDS. I learned about Felix Gonzalez-Torres, the sentimental minimalist who, in 1988, made a work called “Forbidden Colors”: four solid-colour paintings – red, black, green and white – installed side by side, evoking the Palestinian flag. (At the time, the colours were banned from being displayed together in the occupied territories.)
In New York, I fell in love with an artist who showed me Nan Goldin’s honest depictions of beautiful, untamed people who we believed shared our DNA. I learned to write about art to impress him, and in 2005 I landed a job as an editorial assistant on Artforum’s website. I discovered a fortunate alchemy: qualities that were liabilities in my early life could be transformed into clout through the magic of identity politics. My leftist orientations were tolerated and sometimes even rewarded. I was paid for my ideas, and flown to faraway places to write about biennials with themes inspired by Marx, Fanon and Aimé Césaire. I pictured cracks in the corridors of power.
I’m not yet cynical enough to think that the cracks were simply illusions. In the wake of what quickly came to be known as the “Artforum letter”, some of us were surprised to find that we were being asked to sacrifice something. For years we had been signing petitions for all kinds of social causes, calls for liberation – feminism, queer rights, climate justice, abolition – that were often taken up by the institutions that housed us. Until 2025, nearly every museum had a gay pride celebration. When George Floyd was murdered in May 2020, a parade of museums frantically marshalled committees of sacrificial minorities, staged unctuous exhibitions and asserted their commitments to “diversity, equity, and inclusion”.
Palestine is different. Even with broad public support, no major museum has taken up the genocide in Gaza. No large institution I know of has put on an exhibition about Palestinian artists or Palestinian lives. Instead, the opposite: in June 2025, the Whitney Museum “suspended” its 57-year-old Independent Study Program after some of its members dared to host a performance critical of Israel. The art world, with all its progressive scaffolding and humanist ornamentation, practically designed to celebrate and aestheticise every rebellion, couldn’t metabolise Palestine. It still can’t.
It’s October 2025, nearly a year after Nan’s “scandal” at the Neue Nationalgalerie, and she is in Milan to celebrate the penultimate stop of her retrospective at the Pirelli HangarBicocca, an old manufacturing plant retrofitted into a vast exhibition space. The chilly claustrophobia of the Berlin show is replaced with a warm sense of possibility. In the streets, more than a million Italians are striking in solidarity with the people of Gaza and the Global Sumud Flotilla. A tentative ceasefire is on the horizon, and Nan meets supporters everywhere she goes.
She has spent the past year making the most of every available platform. In July, during the opening of the prestigious Rencontres d’Arles photography festival, she and the writer Édouard Louis spoke about Palestine activism in front of 2,500 well-heeled attendees in an ancient Roman amphitheatre. The Milan version of This Will Not End Well includes a brutal montage called Gaza: Notes on a Genocide 2023-2025, a “work in progress” comprising unsparing footage from friends and journalists of explosions, starvation and forced displacement.
Nan’s persistence has won her many fans, but it has come with a cost. “Personally, my career tanked,” she told Mahmoud Khalil in an interview with Dazed in September. “My market tanked from one day to the next because of my support of Palestine.” The German press responded to her speech with universal savagery. The conservative daily Die Welt called it “undoubtedly the saddest, most undignified, and most shameful moment in the 56-year history of the Neue Nationalgalerie”, and Klaus Biesenbach told Der Spiegel the night was a “horror”, and the artist’s words were “hard to bear”. “I never thought Nan would be so cold,” he said.
The past two years have given the lie to any wisdom that the art world constitutes the progressive avant-garde. I can count acts of bravery from less-visible artists, but a fog of silence continues to dominate the field: few expressions of solidarity forthcoming from institutions, and too few artists willing to speak out via social media, much less their own work. What do we make of this depressing amalgam of fear and apathy? How many will it take to break the art world’s attitude of mute acquiescence?
I am struck by the fact that major celebrities seem more likely than major contemporary artists to publicly express support for the Palestinian cause. The musician Lorde lights the stage at Madison Square Garden in red, white and green. The actress Jennifer Lawrence tells reporters: “What’s happening is no less than a genocide and it’s unacceptable”. Joaquin Phoenix, Olivia Coleman and thousands more sign a boycott of Israeli film groups “implicated in genocide”. Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem make regular statements, and Hannah Einbinder shouts “Free Palestine” as she accepts her Emmy. These are not simply symbolic gestures, but meaningful demonstrations of solidarity.
“The more of us there are, the more of us there are,” Nan said at the end of her speech. She understands that we pierce repression with a surplus of reparative and disruptive actions. More voices, more collective, louder, riskier. She understands that we make change not through holding ideologically correct or coherent beliefs, but through an uneven accretion of strategic and local decisions. Not everyone has to make the same choices. Certainly not everyone has to agree. But we all have to act.
I have spent the past two years on unofficial hiatus from the official art world. Its ceremonial sound and fury feel remote to me. Speculation has been hollowing art out for decades, and we might simply have passed a threshold where price is the only measure of worth. But I’m alert enough to know that the era of unbridled conspicuous consumption might be ending. The proverbial bubble has burst. Collectors are disposing of their minions and concierges. Galleries are closing, or having less lavish parties. Artists at every level are feeling the burn. It’s only appropriate, now that the uneasy truce between the market and its playthings has been scuttled. Brute reality tore the mast from the boat.
None of this is “complicated”, as the boilerplate from strategic wafflers would have you believe. As I write this, dim leaders celebrate the supposed end to this “war”. Those who couldn’t admit to a genocide now begin to speak of it in the past tense. We’re roughly 11 weeks into a supposed ceasefire, which Israel breaks daily with routine barbarism. As I write this, IDF soldiers continue their enduring project of annexation and extermination in the West Bank. A politics of wilful ignorance and escalating stupidity keeps the killing machines going. The writing can’t keep pace. Every minute there’s another atrocity tidily packaged as a sedate number in a headline. At least 70,000 Palestinians have been murdered, but these are the underreported official counts. Around 30 percent of these have been children, with an estimated average of 28 children killed each day since October 2023. More than 98 percent of Gaza’s cropland has been damaged or made inaccessible, or both. It’s increasingly hard to hold in mind the scale of devastation. It’s increasingly hard to care about the fate of an art world narcotised by money and self-regard. We had a chance to at least try and make a difference. We had a chance to not sell ourselves out. We had a chance, and we blew it. This did not end well, and still we can choose to begin again, tilting – collectively, contingently – toward the pitch of liberation.

https://gothamist.com/news/ballot-proble.title: Ballot problems in Westchester: Lawler v. Conley race results could be delayed
https://gothamist.com/news/ballot-proble.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/ballot-proble.text:
Voting on Election Day hit an early snag in Westchester County Tuesday as issues with voting machines were reported throughout the county, according to a statement from the county’s Board of Elections.
The board in statement initially said a paper thickness problem prevented the devices from accepting ballots. In a subsequent statement it removed mention of the paper issue. Voters' ballots will be counted, the board said, but delays may occur.
Westchester is ground zero for the marquee congressional race between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and Democratic challenger Cait Conley.
The agency strongly suggested that voters remain in line and cast their ballots in spite of the technical difficulties. They said once ballots are filled out, they will be placed in emergency ballot bags, which will be secured and monitored by poll workers.
The ballots will be counted later in a way consistent with election procedures, the statement said. The statement said every eligible vote will be counted despite the snafu.
Aside from Congress, Westchester County, just north of New York City, could be a critical swing county in a number of races, including the gubernatorial election.
Lawler tweeted about the issues Tuesday morning, encouraging his supporters to remain in line.
“Every ballot will be counted,” he wrote. “Stay on line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting.”
His challenger, Cait Conley, similarly encouraged voters to stay at the polls and said the issue was being handled and resolved in a bipartisan way.
“The Polls are open and operational, and every vote cast will be counted. Please stay in line and have your voice heard as they work to resolve the issue,” she said on social media.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.title: Syria says it foiled Hezbollah plot to target Homs oil refinery
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Syria says it foiled Hezbollah plot to target Homs oil refinery
Hezbollah denies the Syrian accusations, reiterating that it does not have any presence on Syrian territory.
Syrian security forces have said they foiled a plot to target the Homs oil refinery in central Syria, arresting a cell affiliated with Lebanon’s Hezbollah armed group.
Syria’s General Intelligence Service (GIS) said on X that “the preemptive security operation” was carried out in cooperation with the country’s Internal Security Forces.
It identified two arrested individuals with their initials – M S and B Sh – but did not elaborate on the time or the location of the operation, “which resulted in the seizure of explosive devices in their possession that had been prepared to execute the plot”.
Hezbollah denied the Syrian accusations in a statement, reiterating that it does not have any presence on Syrian territory and is not involved in “any activity that undermines the security and stability of Syria”.
Hezbollah fought alongside former President Bashar al-Assad’s forces during Syria’s nearly 14-year civil war, but relations with Damascus have deteriorated sharply since his overthrow in 2024.
Syrian authorities have accused Hezbollah of involvement in a series of alleged plots, including planned assassinations, rocket attacks and arms smuggling.
The Homs refinery is one of Syria’s two oil refineries, along with the Baniyas refinery, and plays a key role in securing petroleum products.
ISIL cell
In a similar operation, the GIS said on Sunday that they arrested two members of a suspected ISIL (ISIS) cell in the governorate of Deir Az Zor.
Sunday’s statement added that investigations “showed the detainees’ involvement in carrying out a series of assassinations in the province, the latest of which targeted defence ministry member Ibrahim al-Jassem with a gunshot near the al-Rashid mosque in the city of Mayadin”.
The operation led to the seizure of weapons and ammunition found in the cell’s hideout, the security forces said, adding that authorities were continuing investigations of “the terrorists to uncover their links in preparation for bringing them to justice”.
On September 27, the security forces said they had arrested four members of an ISIL cell involved in planning and carrying out several attacks in different parts of the country.
On September 30, the Syrian Electricity Company said the Deir Ali, Nasiriya and Tishreen power stations had gone out of service after an explosion on a gas line at the Tishreen station in the Damascus countryside, which cut off the gas supply needed to run them.
On October 15, the Syrian Petroleum Company said the pipeline carrying petroleum products from Baniyas to Homs was damaged near the village of Hadida in western Homs countryside, causing a fuel leak, state media reported, in the latest in a series of attacks on Syria’s energy infrastructure.
Last month, Syria’s security forces foiled a plot to target a police patrol in Damascus countryside, saying that an ISIL cell was preparing to carry out the attack, Syrian state television reported. They said the group was responsible for explosions and assassinations in Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Homs.
Damascus joined the US-led international coalition against ISIL last November, which was formed in 2014 and has carried out operations against the group in Syria and Iraq.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-isra.title: « L’heure est venue de dire la vérité sur l’occupation » : Ayelet Kroizer devient porte-parole de l’ONG Breaking the Silence
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-isra.author: Hayet Kechit
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-isra.text:
Révulsée par son éphémère expérience au sein du service de presse de l’armée israélienne, Ayelet Kroizer vient d’être nommée porte-parole de l’ONG « Breaking the Silence ». Avec l’intention revendiquée de rompre la chape de plomb entourant les exactions dans les territoires occupés.
« L’heure est venue de dire la vérité sur l’occupation. » C’est par ces mots que l’ONG israélienne Breaking The silence a souhaité la bienvenue sur X à sa nouvelle porte-parole Ayelet Kroizer. Une recrue qui a valeur de symbole retentissant pour l’organisation créée en 2004, dont la mission est de « briser le silence » pesant autour des soldats israéliens de retour à la vie civile.
Et pour cause, le parcours et la liberté de parole revendiquée par la jeune femme née dans un environnement ultra-orthodoxe, révulsée par son éphémère expérience en tant que porte-parole de l’armée israélienne, tranchent au sein d’une société acquise aux discours déshumanisants frappant les Palestiniens. Ayelet Kroizer, qui explique n’avoir « jamais été douée pour (se) taire face aux injustices », a en effet long à en dire.
« Exposée à la réalité en Cisjordanie et à Gaza »
« Au sein du service de presse de Tsahal, j’ai été exposée à la réalité en Cisjordanie et à Gaza, et à la manière dont Tsahal choisit de présenter cette réalité au public », raconte, sur son compte X, celle qui a vu de l’intérieur la fabrique du mensonge.
Les exemples, concrets, cités par la jeune femme font écho aux voix qui dénoncent depuis trois ans l’instrumentalisation de l’attaque terroriste du 7-octobre pour justifier le génocide en cours : « J’ai vu comment le mot » terroriste « est accolé même à des Palestiniens innocents », a encore dénoncé Ayelet Kroizer, qui exhorte : « Si vous avez servi pendant la guerre, ne vous taisez pas non plus. »
Pour une information libre sur la Palestine
Nous avons été l’un des premiers médias français à défendre le droit des Palestiniens à disposer d’un État viable dans le respect des résolutions de l’ONU. Et nous avons inlassablement défendu la paix au Proche-Orient. Aidez-nous à continuer de vous informer sur ce qui se passe là-bas. Grâce à vos dons.
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: UK Supreme Court to hear landmark appeal over Palestine Action ban
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Katherine Hearst
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
UK Supreme Court to hear landmark appeal over Palestine Action ban
The British government will defend its decision to ban Palestine Action at the UK Supreme Court, in a landmark case that continues to test the boundaries of British counterterror legislation, freedom of speech and the right to protest.
The appeal, which begins on Wednesday and is expected to last two days, comes amid mounting civil unrest and police crackdowns across Britain in relation to the ban on Palestine Action.
A portion of the proceedings will be heard in secret because of the national security nature of the evidence.
Over the weekend, police arrested hundreds of demonstrators outside the US Embassy in London and Edinburgh for holding placards that read “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
Since the government banned Palestine Action in 2025, the six-word statement has become a rallying cry and led to 4,000 people facing arrest under Britain’s Terrorism Act, including human rights lawyers, elderly activists and holocaust survivors.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: A new book looks at how Marcel Duchamp’s ‘impossible’ love for the sculptor Maria Martins changed his work
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Tara Anne Dalbow
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Glacial, calculated, distant, sly: these are among the adjectives used to describe the “godfather of conceptual art” Marcel Duchamp (1887-1968). In the opening chapter of Impossible, a monograph by the prominent Duchamp scholar Francis M. Naumann, the artist appears as a (mostly) reticent introvert. But over the course of 192 richly illustrated pages, that familiar, spectral figure becomes flesh and blood: tender, wistful, even romantic. Duchamp falls in love.
Naumann’s account of the French-American artist’s relationship with the Brazilian sculptor Maria Martins (1894-1973) unfolds through a series of speculative scenes that draw, at times uneasily, on the conventions of the romance novel, interwoven with formal analysis that demonstrates reciprocal artistic influence. The author’s nearly five decades of writing on Duchamp, along with the rigorous notes and chronology included at the back of the volume, help temper any initial scepticism about the balance between projection and documentation. From Duchamp and Martins’s first meeting in March 1943 until their respective deaths five years apart, Naumann argues that the two sustained a profound emotional connection, even if the most intense—and presumably physical—phase of their relationship lasted less than a decade. Despite Duchamp’s evident longing, Martins never left her three children or her husband, a Brazilian ambassador to the US.
What first attracted the two artists intellectually to one another is not fully known. But from early on, Duchamp was no longer indifferent, at least where Martins was concerned. Asked to design an announcement for an exhibition at Julien Levy Gallery in December 1943, he placed a cupid figure atop a chessboard depicting an endgame problem with no way to win. “There is no solution,” the artist had famously said, “because there is no problem”. Now, however, there was a problem. Despite a previous marriage and a long-term relationship with the American artist Mary Reynolds, Duchamp had never been in love before. At this point, 26 years had passed since he made Fountain and 20 since he had declared The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even (The Large Glass) definitively unfinished. It was the problem of Martins, Naumann suggests, that reanimated Duchamp’s interest in making—shifting the affair from a biographical register into a lens through which to view Duchamp’s late work.
Intimate exchange
As the relationship develops, Naumann focuses on the lovers’ sculptures, exchanged or produced in parallel, as a metonym for the physical encounters he is otherwise obliged to omit. There is Paysage fautif (faulty landscape), an intimate piece made with his own seminal fluid on plastic and backed with black satin, that Duchamp gave to Martins in 1946. And then her cast bronze The Impossible, III (at the Museum of Modern Art in New York) from the same year, in which two creatures, their heads ringed in tendrils, reach toward one another in a gesture that is at once an embrace and a devouring. Martins was, Naumann writes, “unquestionably referring to the impossibility of her relationship with Duchamp”. The goddess figures borrowed from Brazilian folklore that populated her second show at the Valentine Gallery in New York became increasingly abstract and psychologically charged as her career progressed, perhaps reflecting Duchamp’s own preference for the cerebral over the real, the concept over the image.
There is then no shortage of confusion surrounding Duchamp’s final work, Étant donnés: 1º La chute d’eau, 2º Le gaz d’éclairage (Given: 1. the waterfall, 2. the illuminating gas, 1946-66). Why, after decades of apparent withdrawal, would the celebrated Modernist devote 20 years to a highly illusionistic installation of a nude woman posed in a landscape that recalls Gustave Courbet’s The Origin of the World (1866)—the very tradition of “retinal art” he had long disavowed? Naumann’s retelling, which frames the work as the culmination of their coupling, is in this sense instructive. Martins emerges not merely as muse or model but as collaborator. She lends her body to be cast, but also choreographs its position, advises on process and technique. There is no precedent in Duchamp’s oeuvre for the imagery, yet echoes of Martins’s prints and sculptures persist in both the figure and the vegetal setting. Even after she returned to Brazil and their contact waned, Duchamp retained, through work on the diorama, a means of beholding her body and sustaining their artistic tête-à-tête.
Interspersed passages from Duchamp’s letters to Martins reveal the force of his affections, rendering it difficult to regard Étant donnés as anything other than an act of devotion, however strange or disconcerting it may appear from the outside. The florid sentiments strain against the claim that it is just another one of his jokes. “At heart, my little one, I am profoundly sad, for I can see all our days passing rapidly and fading away,” he writes. And elsewhere: “I feel totally lost now that we are cut off from each other… This isolation hurts.” Reproduced in one of the final chapters is a notebook page with the words “Please do not throw this on the floor” typed above a hand-drawn heart, filled in with red crayon, and scrawled below it: “that is for Maria”.
Martins’s voice silent
Although Martins’s letters to Duchamp are not available to the public, it is said that she kept a photograph of him in her studio, and another on her charm bracelet, alongside a lock of his hair—observations that complicate Naumann’s repeated casting of her as a “femme fatale” who “did whatever she needed to get a man to fall in love with her”. The absence of her subjectivity on the page creates an asymmetry that the text acknowledges yet cannot quite overcome. What she truly made of Duchamp—of his work, their relationship—remains largely unknown.
After her husband’s death in 1965, Martins returned to New York and visited Duchamp, who was by then married to Alexina “Teeny” Duchamp. As Naumann notes, it is possible that he signed and dated Étant donnés then and there, unable to complete it until finally, at long last, they were together again.
• Impossible: The Love Affair between Marcel Duchamp & Maria Martins, and the Artwork It Inspired, by Francis M. Naumann, published by Abbeville Press, 192pp, illustrated, $30 (hb), 31 March

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Justice department funds research into gender dysphoria and violent crime in latest anti-trans effort
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Abené Clayton
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US Department of Justice is funding research aimed at exploring whether there is a link between gender dysphoria and violent crime.
Last month, the National Institute of Justice (NIJ), the research arm of the justice department, said it would grant up to $1m for studies into the frequency and type of violence committed by people who have been diagnosed and treated for gender dysphoria.
The notice comes as the Trump administration has aggressively sought to curtail the rights of transgender people in the US, limiting their access to healthcare and identification documents with their correct gender identity on them. It also comes more than a year after the administration has cut funding to research into hate-fueled and extremist violence.
The Trump administration has repeatedly sought to falsely portray transgender people as more likely to commit extremist violence, said Wendy Via, the co-founder and CEO of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism (GPAHE). By doing this, the administration diverts attention from violence driven by far-right extremist ideologies such as the “great replacement” theory, which several high-profile shooters have cited in their manifestos, she added.
“What the administration is doing is very dangerous,” Via said.
Experts and LGBTQ+ advocates call these attempts to link trans people and violence “pseudoscience”, because they depart from a growing body of academic literature showing that it is impossible to link a single characteristic, such as race, political affiliation or gender, as the prime reason for violence. Instead, researchers say the most common thread between most high-profile attackers is not their identity, but their views, which often include racism, homophobia, misogyny and nihilism.
That has not stopped public speculation around the role gender identity plays in violence.
After conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot and killed in September 2025, rightwing influencers argued that the suspected shooter was motivated in part by what they call “transgender ideology”, a term often used by those on the right to falsely suggest that being trans is a political ideology, not an identity.
The idea that being trans or that being an ally to trans people represents a dangerous political ideology was included in a White House counter-terrorism report this year. Part of its counter-terrorism approach is to address leftwing violence and “transgender ideologies”.
The vast majority of mass shootings in the US have been carried out by cisgender people, although transgender and non-binary people have committed some mass shootings, including ones at Annunciation Catholic school in Minneapolis, Club Q in Colorado Springs, and Tumbler Ridge elementary school in British Columbia in Canada. In these cases, transgender shooters shared characteristics of modern high-profile mass shooters, such as idolizing other killers and online radicalization.
“We don’t know exactly why a person decides to commit mass violence, because they’ve all had things in their lives that have led them to it,” Via said. “Being trans or being straight likely doesn’t have anything to do with it.”
The NIJ’s new funding priorities will shift attention away from the dangers posed by far-right extremists and toward trans people, said Zane McNeill, a staff attorney with Lawyers for Good Government.
“I see it as a part of this larger apparatus to distract from who’s propagating the violence,” McNeill said. “It’s also about weaponizing funding decisions. They’ve been undermining projects while diverting taxpayer dollars for far-right pseudoscience.”
The NIJ is not the only part of the government trying to find links between transgender people and violence. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently published the report, Where the Clinic Meets the Movement: Does Gender Ideology Arm Left-Wing Authoritarian Psychology?
The report was commissioned by HHS and authored by researchers from Rutgers University, the Manhattan Institute and the Network Contagion Research Institute. It’s based on a survey of about 1,200 adults in the US and suggests that people who receive or support gender-affirming care are more likely to support political violence.
Last month, McNeill sent a letter to HHS requesting several corrections to the report, and argued that it violated the agency’s own guidelines. McNeill and other researchers are trying to obtain access to the survey data so they can offer their own analysis.
“This research is so flawed that it should not be published,” McNeill said. “It’s obvious that it’s extremely biased.”
The NIJ and the institutions affiliated with the HHS report did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
In a statement to the Guardian, HHS press secretary Grace Davis Jamison said that the department’s report will help the government better understand how “political radicalization develops”.
“The findings should be evaluated based on the evidence, and under the Trump administration, HHS will not shy away from asking important questions to protect the health and safety of the American people,” she said.

Kommunalwahlen in Südafrika: Kap der falschen Hoffnung
Südafrikas „Regenbogennation“ sollte allen einen Platz bieten. Doch seit Monaten hetzen Nationalisten wieder gegen Migrant:innen auch jetzt vor den Kommunalwahlen. Einblicke aus Kapstadt.
L inda Muwalos Augen huschen unter ihrem Tarnfleckhut nach rechts und links. Dann beugt sich die Marktfrau etwas vor. Sie spricht leise, fast flüsternd: „Ich kann nicht nach Hause gehen. Ich habe vier Kinder, wir brauchen das Geld.“
Muwalo ist Ausländerin. Sie kam vor zehn Jahren aus dem bitterarmen Malawi nach Südafrika, nach Bellville, einem Vorort von Kapstadt. Hier verkauft die 37-Jährige Tomaten, Orangen, Okraschoten und afrikanische Heilkräuter an Menschen mit wenig Geld. Ein bescheidenes Geschäft, von dem eine ganze Familie abhängt.
Lange stand Linda Muwalo mit ihren Waren auf den guten Plätzen am Eingang des Marktes. Dann begannen die Anfeindungen. „Concerned citizens“, besorgte Bürger, verjagten Muwalo und andere Händler:innen. Nun breitet die Ostafrikanerin ihre Tüten mit Gemüse und Grünzeug ein Stück abseits auf dem Gehsteig aus. Über ihr steht ein fleckiger Pavillon. Darunter sucht sie mit befreundeten Verkäuferinnen aus Malawi und Somalia Schutz vor der Oktobersonne. „Geht nach Hause!“ Diesen Satz, sagt Muwalo, hören die Frauen mehrmals am Tag. Es genüge, als Ausländerin erkannt zu werden. „Wenn sie damit nur aufhören könnten.“
Im Frühjahr begannen in Bellville ausländerfeindliche Proteste. Rund 300 Südafrikaner:innen zogen singend durch das Viertel, Baseballschläger und Stöcke in den Händen. Auf ihren T-Shirts stand der Name ihrer Bewegung: „March and March“. Sie greift einerseits den Zulu-Nationalismus des früheren Präsidenten Jacob Zuma auf. Andererseits ist sie anschlussfähig an eine Organisation rechter, weißer Afrikaaner.
An der Spitze marschierte Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, Radiomoderatorin und Anführerin der Proteste. “Ja, wir spalten“, sagte sie damals einem Fernsehteam. „Wir spalten uns ab von Leuten, die längst das Land hätten verlassen müssen.“
Kurz zuvor war in den sozialen Medien behauptet worden, ein aktuelles Grundsatzurteil des Verfassungsgerichts garantiere Asylsuchenden automatisch den Aufenthalt – Fake News, die sich wie ein Lauffeuer verbreiteten.
Ob jemand wie Linda Muwalo völlig legal in Südafrika lebt, scheint für March and March keine Rolle zu spielen. Für Ngobese-Zuma, ihre Bewegung und die radikalen Parteien, die auf dieser Protestwelle reiten, hat Zugehörigkeit nichts mit dem Gesetz zu tun. Und nicht so viel mit der Wirklichkeit. Nach offiziellen Zahlen leben nur 2,4 bis 3,3 Millionen Migrant:innen in Südafrika. Das sind 4 bis 5 Prozent der Bevölkerung. Und sie sind wichtig für die Wirtschaft, sagen Expert:innen.
Im Juni standen die Leute von March and March vor den Läden von Somaliern, Pakistani und Simbabwerinnen. Sie wollten die Geschäftsleute zwingen, ihre Läden zu schließen. Auf informelle Händlerinnen wie Linda Muwalo warfen sie Obstkisten, um sie von ihren Stammplätzen zu vertreiben. Im August floss dann Blut auf das Pflaster des Marktes von Bellville.
Die Stöcke, Symbol des Nationalismus der Zulu, der größten Volksgruppe Südafrikas, blieben nicht länger bloße Drohgebärde. Sie wurden zu Waffen. Die Protestierenden griffen die ausländischen Händler:innen damit an, traten auf Menschen ein und plünderten Geschäfte. „Ich hatte solche Angst“, sagt Linda Muwalo, die zumindest körperlich unverletzt blieb. Der Polizei sei es schwergefallen, die Gewalt unter Kontrolle zu bringen, sagt Muwalo. Trotz Tränengas und Blendgranaten. Im September und Oktober gab es ganz ähnliche Szenen, hier und andernorts im Land. March and March wollte vor Südafrikas Lokalwahlen am 4. November Druck aufbauen.
Die Republik an Afrikas Südspitze kennt solche Ausschreitungen. Schon 2008 starben bei ausländerfeindlichen Angriffen mehr als 60 Menschen. Zehntausende wurden vertrieben. Danach flammten die Proteste immer wieder auf. Neu an der jüngsten Welle sind ihr Organisationsgrad und ihre geografische Reichweite. Der Hass entlädt sich nicht mehr nur in der Provinz Gauteng rund um Johannesburg. Er erfasst das ganze Land. Und er zeigt Wirkung.
Seit Juni haben mehr als 160.000 Ausländer:innen Südafrika verlassen. Viele meldeten sich freiwillig, um sich in staatlich organisierten Bussen deportieren zu lassen. Simbabwe, Nigeria und Ghana leiteten schließlich selbst Maßnahmen ein, um ihre Staatsbürger:innen zurückzuholen. Auch Muwalos Mann machte sich auf den Weg zurück nach Malawi. Mit den vier Kindern legte er 3.000 Kilometer zurück. Linda Muwalo blieb. Die Familie braucht die paar Rand, die sie hier auf dem Markt verdient.
Nicht alle schafften es rechtzeitig fort. Im Sommer machte Nigeria die südafrikanischen Behörden für den Tod zweier seiner Staatsbürger verantwortlich. Ende Oktober schlugen rund 50 Randalierer in der Ostküstenstadt Durban einen Ausländer tot.
In Kapstadt fallen die Proteste kleiner aus als in Johannesburg und Durban. Doch auch hier im Süden kann die Gewalt tödlich enden. Bashiru Isak, ein Ghanaer und Vater von drei Kindern, wurde hier während der Proteste im Sommer erschossen. Ausgerechnet hier. In einer Stadt, deren politische Führung nicht müde wird, sich vom Rest des Landes zu distanzieren.
An der Voortrekker Road, nur ein paar Schritte entfernt vom Markt in Bellville, steht Hausnummer 177: ein ockerfarbener Klinkerbau aus den neunziger Jahren, die Außenstelle des südafrikanischen Innenministeriums. Vor dem Eingang warten rund 50 Menschen in einer Schlange. Weiße Rentner, die ihre Reisepässe abholen, indische Südafrikanerinnen, Coloureds und Schwarze, die Geburts- oder Heiratsurkunden brauchen. Und Ausländer:innen, die ihre Aufenthaltspapiere erneuern wollen.
Dorel Clansia ist 22 Jahre alt und stammt aus dem Kongo. „Ein Land, das Ausländer anzieht, ist gesegnet“, sagt er. 2016 kam er nach Südafrika, zum Studieren, eigentlich. Dann starb sein Vater, das Geld aus dem Kongo blieb aus. Das Studium war nicht mehr zu bezahlen. Clansia begann, Autoreifen zu flicken. Heute verdient er damit genug, um seine Freundin zu unterstützen, eine Coloured-Südafrikanerin, und für die gemeinsame kleine Tochter zu sorgen.
„Es gibt genug Männer, die ihre Kinder im Stich lassen“, sagt Clansia. Er werde nicht gehen. Er werde sich um seine Tochter kümmern. Sie sei schließlich eine „richtige“ Südafrikanerin.
Clansia ist groß gewachsen, er trägt Shorts und ein graues T-Shirt. Sein Englisch hat einen leichten französischen Akzent. „Wir sind keine Kriminellen, wir arbeiten, wir zahlen Steuern“, sagt er. „Wir sind alle Afrikaner.“ Die Südafrikaner, die im Kongo lebten, würden nicht so schlecht behandelt.
Dass March and March gegen Menschen wie ihn mobilmacht, während weiße deutsche, niederländische und andere Ausländer:innen in Südafrika weitgehend unbehelligt bleiben, hält er für keinen Zufall. Die Bewegung werde die Weißen nicht antasten, glaubt Clansia. Warum? „Weil sie Geld haben und ins Land bringen. Was die nicht sehen: Schwarze investieren auch hier.“
Die Schlange vor dem Amt rückt langsam vor. Clansia wartet darauf, seinen Aufenthaltstitel verlängern zu lassen. Eine Plastikkarte, die darüber mitentscheidet, ob er bleiben darf, wo er sich ein Leben aufgebaut hat. „Die Regierung ist so etwas wie unser Vater“, sagt Clansia. „Sie bestimmt, wer gehen muss und wer nicht.“ Doch zu dieser Macht gehört auch eine Verantwortung. Clansias Stimme wird fester. Von einem Mob werde er sich nicht vertreiben lassen. „Die Regierung muss viel entschiedener eingreifen“, sagt er.
Doch ausgerechnet jetzt, kurz vor den Wahlen, hält sich die Politik auffällig zurück. Die Kandidat:innen und Abgeordneten wagen kaum, March and March in die Schranken zu weisen. Noch seltener sind öffentliche Gesten der Solidarität mit den Ausländer:innen, die angegriffen, bedroht und von ihren Arbeitsplätzen vertrieben werden. Zu groß scheint die Furcht, sich gegen das zu stellen, was die Parteien als den „Willen des Volkes“ vermuten.
Dabei geht es bei diesen Kommunalwahlen doch um mehr als Sitze in den Kommunalräten und Rathäusern oder um Themen wie eine funktionierende Infrastruktur. Es geht um den Charakter der südafrikanischen Gesellschaft – und die Zukunft einer noch jungen Demokratie.
Schon die Lokalwahlen 2021 waren ein Schlüsselmoment für das freie Südafrika. Die Vorherrschaft des African National Congress (ANC), einst Befreiungsbewegung gegen die Apartheid und Partei Nelson Mandelas, schwand erstmals deutlich. Koalitionen wurden notwendig in Südafrikas 257 Kommunen, 2024 schließlich auch auf nationaler Ebene.
Der neue politische Wettbewerb könnte dem ANC helfen, Korruption und Chaos in den eigenen Reihen in den Griff zu bekommen. Dass in sechs der acht Metropolregionen, dass sogar in der ANC-Hochburg Johannesburg die weiß geprägte, wirtschaftsliberale Democratic Alliance (DA) die anstehenden Lokalwahlen gewinnen könnte, erhöht den politischen Druck enorm. Und dann sind da ja noch die Proteste.
In Kapstadt regiert die DA schon seit 20 Jahren und rühmt sich ihrer Infrastrukturprojekte. „Cape Town works“ – Kapstadt funktioniert, lautet die Devise auch in diesem Wahlkampf. Als ließe sich die Kapmetropole vom Rest des Landes trennen. Als wäre das, was jenseits der luxuriösen Villen an der Sonnenseite des Tafelbergs geschieht, nicht Teil Kapstadts. Etwa die Welle der Gewalt gegen Taxifahrer in den Townships Delft, Gugulethu, Khayelitsha und Bonteheuwel. Drei Tote, sechs Verletzte allein in den Tagen vor der Wahl. Und dann die ausländerfeindliche Gewalt in Bellville und andernorts in der Stadt.
Zwischen den riesigen Wellblechsiedlungen und den Stränden der Schönen und Reichen im vornehmen Clifton liegt das Viertel Bokaap mit den bunten Häuschen, den Moscheen und Schwulenbars – und natürlich Kapstadts schattige Altstadt. Afrikanische Marktstände zwängen sich hier zwischen Kolonialbauten und gotische Kirchen. Handwerker, Hipster und alte Kap-Malaiinnen streifen durch die Straßen, Letztere mit Kopftuch und ohne Schuhe. Reinigungstrupps, ganz in Gelb, marschieren mit Besen in der Hand. Private Sicherheitsfirmen kontrollieren im Auftrag der Stadt die Einkaufsstraßen. Cape Town works.
Vom achten Stock eines Hochhauses an der Church Street aus liegt Kapstadt Paula Assubuji zu Füßen. Von hier oben, über den Dächern der Stadt, betrachtet die Ökonomin ein Land, in dem sich die politischen Fronten neu sortieren. Assubuji leitet das Auslandsbüro der grünennahen Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung in Kapstadt. Die zierliche Frau mit den Locken beobachtet, wie sich der Hass auf afrikanische Einwanderer:innen zu einer politischen Kraft entwickelt hat.
„Vor diesen Wahlen hat die afrophobe Bewegung richtig Fahrt aufgenommen“, sagt sie. Dass March and March und andere Gruppen so gut organisiert seien, lasse auf finanzielle Unterstützung schließen. Woher das Geld komme, sei unklar. Möglich sei, dass ausländische Regierungen ein Interesse daran hätten, Südafrika zu destabilisieren. Viele im Land spekulieren, ob nicht US-Präsident Donald Trump seine Finger im Spiel haben könnte, der Südafrikas Regierung verachtet. Er hatte immer wieder behauptet, in Südafrika finde ein „Genozid“ an weißen Südafrikanern statt und sie würden ohne Entschädigung ihres Landes beraubt. Auch Israel vermuten manche als Akteur im Hintergrund, weil Südafrika das Land vor dem Internationalen Gerichtshof verklagt hat, in Gaza einen Völkermord zu begehen. Nachweise für all das gibt es nicht.
Im Inland sieht Assubuji Verbindungen zum politischen Umfeld der Partei uMkhonto weSizwe, kurz MK, des früheren Präsidenten Jacob Zuma. Zuma habe die Zulu, seine eigene Volksgruppe, stets politisch bevorzugt; March and March knüpfe daran an. Auch Afriforum, eine rechte Organisation, die vor allem weiße Afrikaaner vertritt, suche die Nähe zur Bewegung.
Denn für politische Außenseiter können die Proteste zur Bühne werden: Wer gegen Ausländer mobilisiert, schafft es in die Nachrichten – und hofft, bei den Kommunalwahlen Stimmen dazuzugewinnen. Gegen Ausländer:innen können Weiße wie Schwarze Nationalist:innen mit Gewinn hetzen. Und auch die Coloureds, in deren Stammbäumen sich Europäer:innen, Kapsklavinnen und indigene Khoi-San finden, haben hier in der Provinz Westkap eine ausländerfeindliche Kleinpartei: die Patriotic Alliance.
„Das ist nicht weniger als eine direkte Attacke auf die südafrikanische Verfassung von 1996“, sagt Paula Assubuji. Die sollte nach dem Ende der Apartheid den Gegenentwurf zu einem Staat bilden, der Menschen nach ihrer Hautfarbe sortierte: eine demokratische Ordnung, in der unterschiedliche Bevölkerungsgruppen gleichberechtigt zusammenleben.
Doch ausgerechnet die „Regierung der nationalen Einheit“ unter ANC-Präsident Cyril Ramaphosa habe den afrophoben Protesten Raum verschafft, sagt Paula Assubuji. Zwar habe Ramaphosa die Gewalt verurteilt. Zugleich aber habe sich seine Regierung von der Stimmung auf der Straße treiben lassen.
Kommunalwahlen in Südafrika
Am Mittwoch, 4. November, werden in Südafrika die Kommunalvertretungen neu gewählt. 10.526 Sitze stehen in 4.488 Wahlkreisen zur Wahl, von den Bürgermeisterposten der Millionenstädte bis zu den Dorfräten.
Bei den vergangenen Kommunalwahlen 2021 war die ehemalige Befreiungsbewegung ANC (African National Congress), die Südafrika seit 1994 regiert, erstmals unter 50 Prozent gerutscht und bei rund 45 Prozent gelandet. Sie regiert seitdem nur noch vier der acht Großstadträume und büßte zahlreiche Gemeinden ein. Die Parlamentswahl 2024 bestätigte den ANC-Abwärtstrend. Dieses Jahr ist die große Frage, ob die ANC-Wählerbasis weiter erodiert.
Besonders deutlich werde das beim Innenministerium, sagt Assubuji. „Das ist eigentlich eine chaotische Institution. Aber in dem Moment, in dem es um Abschiebungen ging, funktionierte sie.“ Als Ramaphosa Vertreter von March and March in Pretoria zu Gesprächen empfing, habe er sie zusätzlich aufgewertet. Aus einer Bewegung, die Menschen einschüchtert, sei damit auch ein Gesprächspartner der Regierung geworden.
Die Democratic Alliance gibt sich gemäßigter. Zumindest auf den ersten Blick. Die Partei, die in Pretoria mitregiert und Kapstadt regiert, präsentiert sich gern als farbenblinde Verfechterin effizienter Verwaltung. Sie bemüht sich, nicht mit den offen ausländerfeindlichen Gruppen in einen Topf geworfen zu werden. Doch auch sie wolle Härte demonstrieren, sagt Assubuji – vor allem gegenüber wohlhabenden Ausländer:innen.
Im Wahlkampf ließ sich Kapstadts DA-Bürgermeister Geordin Hill-Lewis dabei filmen, wie er in bürgerlichen Vierteln Westafrikaner in teuren Autos anhielt und ihre Papiere kontrollierte. Die Inszenierung zielte auf einen Verdacht: Wer sich solche Wagen leisten kann, so die Botschaft, müsse sein Geld illegal verdient haben. Ein anderer DA-Kandidat ging noch weiter. Für seine sozialen Medien organisierte er auf eigene Faust eine nächtliche Razzia bei schwarzen Männern, die in einem ärmlichen Verschlag übernachteten. “Sprecht ihr Afrikaans?“, brüllte er sie an. Die Frage sollte offenbar klären, ob es sich bei den Männern um Südafrikaner handelte. Auch Armut ist wohl erst legitim, wenn sie die Richtigen trifft.
Assubuji hebt resigniert beide Hände. „Die DA singt dasselbe afrophobe Lied wie die anderen Parteien“, sagt sie. „Es unterscheidet sich nur in der Tonart.“ Dabei steht Südafrika vor Aufgaben, die sich nicht mit krassen Videos und Ausländerhass lösen lassen.
Der ANC müsse sich grundlegend erneuern, sagt Assubuji. Der Verweis auf die eigene Rolle im Befreiungskampf habe sich abgenutzt. „Zu sagen: 'Ich war während der Apartheid ein Freiheitskämpfer’, reicht nicht mehr.“ Für die Menschen gehe es bei den Wahlen heute vor allem um Konkretes: um Strom, der zuverlässig fließt, um sauberes Trinkwasser, um Straßen, die instand gehalten werden. Um Steuergeld, das nicht veruntreut werden darf.
Doch auch die DA, die ihre Kapstädter Erfolge bei diesen Themen auf die anderen Metropolen im Land übertragen will, könne sich nicht allein auf funktionierende Infrastruktur berufen, sagt die Grüne Paula Assubuji. Auch in einer Analyse des Südafrikabüros der konservativen Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung heißt es, dass sich in Kapstadt hinter den Touristenpfaden und den sauberen Straßen eine Stadt verbirgt, die geprägt sei „von extremer Ungleichheit, Wohnungsmangel, Bandengewalt, räumlicher Apartheid und zunehmend erbitterten Auseinandersetzungen darüber, wer von ihrem Erfolg profitiert.“
Wo der Wettbewerb um Wohnraum und ein Einkommen immer härter wird, sind Ausländer:innen schnell zu Sündenböcken gemacht, sagt wiederum die Soziologin und Aktivistin Vainola Makan aus Bellville. Makan setzt sich mit ihrem Verein Ubuntu für den gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt in ihrem Viertel ein – und auch für die Ausländer:innen. „Wir Nichtweiße haben in der Zeit der Apartheid viel von der Menschenfeindlichkeit internalisiert“, sagt Makan, „das bekommen nun die afrikanischen Ausländer:innen zu spüren.“
Und die dürfen bei den Lokalwahlen nicht mitmachen. Sie können sich nicht wehren. Oder etwa doch?
Die Hauswände um den Markt in Bellville, an dessen Rand die Malawierin Linda Muwalo und ihre somalischen Freundinnen Tomaten und Orangen verkaufen, haben Graffiti-Künstler:innen gestaltet. Auf einer Mauer läuft eine Herde von Elefanten, kleine und große, in Violett, Rot, Orange, Gelb, Grün und Blau. Das Bild soll die Regenbogennation symbolisieren, zu der sich die Republik Südafrika nach dem Ende der Apartheid ausgerufen hat.
„Eines Tages werden wir uns mit der so hochgepriesenen Verfassung auseinandersetzen und überlegen müssen, wie wir uns vor ihren verheerenden Auswirkungen schützen können“, schimpfte die afrophobe Anführerin Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma kürzlich auf ihrem Facebook-Account. Der Anlass: Der Verein der Somalier:innen in Südafrika hat zusammen mit südafrikanischen Anwält:innen des Legal Resources Centres im Namen von 20 informellen Händler:innen aus Bellville Klage eingereicht. Gegen Ngobese-Zumas ausländerfeindliche Bürgerwehr – und gegen die Stadt Kapstadt.
Die Händler:innen möchten, dass das Hohe Gericht der Provinz Westkap das Unterlassen wirksamer Sicherheitsmaßnahmen seitens der Stadt und Polizei für verfassungswidrig erklärt. Die Behörden sollen einen „detaillierten, abgestimmten Plan“ zum Schutz der Händler:innen vorlegen. Ein Urteil gibt es noch nicht, die Stadt reagierte aber schon mit dem Versprechen, die Situation in Bellville genau zu beobachten und die Sicherheitsmaßnahmen gegebenenfalls auszuweiten. Und Polizeisprecher Ndakhe Gwala sagte, seine Behörde habe „einen Notfallplan mit zusätzlichen Einsätzen in der Hinterhand, um ein erneutes Auftreten solcher Gewalt zu verhindern“.
In Durban ist die Polizei inzwischen selbst vor Gericht gezogen, um ein Demoverbot um den Wahltag herum zu erwirken. Während der Wahl und der Auszählung der Stimmen sind dort March-and-March-Proteste nur noch zwischen 9.00 Uhr und 15.00 Uhr gestattet – und nur ohne Waffen und Gesten der Einschüchterung.
„Wir haben keine Sonderwünsche“, sagt Linda Muwalo in Kapstadt. Sie und die anderen ausländischen Händler:innen auf dem Markt von Bellville wollen sich schlicht wieder sicher fühlen. Sie haben gültige Verkaufslizenzen. Und Vertrauen in eine Verfassung, in deren Präambel es heißt: „Wir glauben daran, dass Südafrika all jenen gehört, die darin leben – vereint in unserer Vielfalt.“
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Sociedade civil não pode permitir continuidade das bets’, diz Lula em dia de audiência no STF
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) convocou a população a acompanhar a audiência pública sobre as bets que o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) realiza nesta terça-feira (3). Em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais, Lula criticou a composição do debate conduzido pelo ministro Luiz Fux e pediu mobilização contra a volta das apostas on-line.
“É importante que a sociedade civil acompanhe, porque me parece que tem mais gente participando que interessa que as bets continuem funcionando do que as pessoas que são contra as bets”, afirmou o presidente. “É importante que a sociedade civil participe para que haja justiça na decisão”, completou.
Lula também defendeu os resultados da proibição, em vigor desde a edição da Medida Provisória (MP) 1.394/2026, em setembro. “Vocês sabem que as coisas começaram a melhorar muito depois que as bets fecharam”, disse.
O presidente atacou os interesses econômicos por trás da tentativa de retomada do setor. “Poucas pessoas querem que as bets continuem, sobretudo aqueles que querem continuar ganhando dinheiro às custas da violência, às custas do sofrimento das pessoas pobres que, na perspectiva de ficar rico, jogam o que não têm”, criticou. “A sociedade civil não pode permitir a continuidade das bets. Por isso, eu conto com vocês”, concluiu.
Na legenda da publicação, Lula reforçou o chamado. “É hora de ocupar esse debate, pressionar e deixar claro: a proteção do povo brasileiro precisa estar em primeiro lugar”, escreveu.
Maioria contra a proibição
A crítica do presidente se apoia na lista de expositores definida por Fux, relator das ações que pedem a derrubada da MP. Dos 34 participantes, ao menos 22 já se posicionaram publicamente contra a proibição. A manhã inteira da audiência foi reservada a clubes de futebol e entidades esportivas.
A Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) contestou a composição original e pediu a ampliação da lista. Fux acabou incluindo os ministérios da Saúde e da Justiça e Segurança Pública e a Associação Brasileira de Supermercados (Abras). A Abras atribui ao fim das bets o aumento do consumo de alimentos no país. Segundo a entidade, a alta foi de 6,5% na primeira quinzena de outubro em relação ao mesmo período de 2025.
A defesa da medida também aparece nas pesquisas. Levantamento Atlas/Bloomberg mostrou que 75% dos brasileiros apoiam a proibição das apostas on-line. Outro estudo calculou que os custos sociais das bets equivalem a quase R$ 4 para cada R$ 1 arrecadado pelo governo.
A audiência não define o futuro das bets. Ela serve para reunir subsídios ao relator, que ainda vai analisar o pedido de suspensão da MP. No Congresso, a comissão mista que analisa o texto não havia sido instalada até a última sexta-feira (30).
