https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mckinney-det.text:
Another Detroit Socialist Is Heading to Congress
Donavan McKinney, a Democratic Socialists of America–endorsed candidate for the US House in Detroit, is set to win his general election today. Jacobin spoke to him before Election Day about why he’s running and what he hopes to accomplish in office.
- Interview by
- Sara Wexler
In 2018, the election of two democratic socialists to the House of Representatives marked the beginning of a new political era. The socialist freshmen, both endorsed by the recently reinvigorated Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), were Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from New York City and Rashida Tlaib, representing Michigan’s Twelfth Congressional District in Detroit.
Eight years later, DSA boasts more than 120,000 members and politicians in elected offices across the country. And after a wave of Democratic primary victories earlier this year, democratic socialists are set to significantly grow their foothold in Congress in today’s general election.
Among the likely socialist victors is Donavan McKinney, who is expected to win easily in Michigan’s deep-blue Thirteenth District in Detroit and join Tlaib in representing the Motor City in the House. Jacobin spoke to him about why he’s running and how growing up working class in Detroit shaped his politics.
- Sara Wexler Why are you running for Congress?
- Donavan McKinney I’m running to bring the urgency that this moment demands. Right now, I represent the poorest state house district in Michigan: $14,000 is the median income. If you divide that up by twelve months, that’s a little over $1,200 a month. And the average rents in our neighborhoods, if you’re lucky, start at $1,300. So that’s all your money down the drain, and you’ve got to worry about the increase in the price of gas and groceries, and insurance costs, whether it’s health insurance or auto insurance. We have some of the highest auto insurance rates in the country. Then childcare costs as well and so many day-to-day expenses. I’m running to represent one of the five poorest congressional districts in the country. What I’m going through on the state level is the same thing. [Being in Congress will mean representing] bigger communities, a lot more people. However, it’s the same narrative — the same story: “I just don’t have enough resources to make ends meet.” So for me, this is about meeting the moment, getting people in these positions who are going to put working families first and put our district first.
- Sara Wexler Can you tell me about your campaign platform? What priorities are you running on?
- Donavan McKinney Universal childcare, Medicare for All, and getting big corporate money out of politics. First, I talk about universal childcare a lot as a state legislator. I coled the movement for Pre-K for all. We have pretty much universal pre-K in Michigan now because of our advocacy and the advocacy of many others. We want to expand that to childcare across the board; we’ll take the fight to Washington, DC, for universal childcare. For my wife and I, that’s the biggest expense in our day-to-day lives, because we have three beautiful children — two boys, four and two, and a baby girl who just turned one. We pay more for childcare for one of our children than we do for our whole mortgage. And you’ve got to think about how impoverished my district is. If we’re living paycheck to paycheck off of childcare alone, I don’t know how everybody else is getting through it. Second, Medicare for All: I’m a big believer because of my mom and what she had to go through. When I was an undergrad at the University of Michigan, I got a call from my mom panicking because she was rushed to the hospital emergency room and they had to do emergency brain surgery. She comes to find out that she had brain tumors growing. And at the time, the only way she could get health care was through her employer; she was working at the time, but her employer didn’t offer it. So she was uninsured. And they did the emergency surgery, but guess what? She got that big six-figure bill for that procedure, and she didn’t have any way to pay it. They put her on a payment plan, but I had to go work three jobs at the time while I was a full-time student to make sure that she got the care she needed. By the grace of God, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) kicked in not too long after that, and she was able to afford health care. But I’m a big believer in Medicare for All, because she had preexisting conditions. Whether you have a preexisting condition or not, you deserve health care. That’s why I’m a big proponent of Medicare for All. There [are so many problems] when it comes to ACA premiums, as well as my seniors on fixed incomes, rubbing pennies together to try to figure out if they should have food on their table for the day or pay more out of pocket for their doctor’s visits and skyrocketing costs when it comes to lifesaving prescription drugs. The third thing I talked about is getting money out of politics. I’ve led that initiative here at the state level. I’ve introduced that legislation two times since I’ve been in office, in back-to-back terms. Each term, we got more and more people. I think the first term we had fewer than ten people sign on. This time around, when we introduced it last year in the state legislature, I think we had thirty or forty people sign on. Now, if you look at every Democrat who’s running for state legislative office here in Michigan, they signed on to the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics initiative. We couldn’t get a hearing in the state house. So organizations and people on the ground decided to take back our power over legislation and create a ballot initiative. They collected six hundred thousand signatures across the state, and that initiative will be on the November 3 ballot. I’m excited about it, because it targets monopoly utility companies, our public utilities, as well as our insurance companies — health insurance companies and auto insurance — which give a lot of money to state legislators to really bend the needle toward them instead of working people. I’m looking to do the same thing federally, to sign onto the legislation of Congresswoman Summer Lee and Senator Bernie Sanders, which gets rid of all that dark super PAC money, as well as to overturn Citizens United. Those are my big three pillars.
- Sara Wexler You grew up working class in Detroit. Can you tell me a bit about your background and how that shaped your politics?
- Donavan McKinney I was born and grew up in Detroit, raised with my mom, my grandmother, and my younger brother. We moved thirteen times across the city; I spent the vast majority of my life in northeast Detroit, which I now represent in the state legislature. And if the general election goes well, I’ll be representing it in the halls of Congress. Like I said, we moved thirteen times. We stayed in cars, shelters, sometimes out in the street. We didn’t know where our next meal was going to come from, but there was no shortage of love and prayers that got us through those tough times. I remember what my grandmother told me growing up. She told me two things that I still live by today. Number one is count your blessings, because you woke up this morning when a lot of people didn’t. You have a roof over your head, clothes on your back, food on your table, and — we live in Detroit, the Motor City — a car to drive. Because our transit system isn’t that good yet, but we’re working on it; that’s something we’re going to take to DC to work on. But you’re able-bodied, you’ve got your mental health, you’ve got your faculties, things we take for granted day in and day out. Number two, she always used to say, “In life, there will always be people better off than you. There will always be people worse off than you, but never fight the urge to give.” And I put that quote on my first piece of literature when I first ran for state representative ten years ago, back in 2016 when I was just a bushy-tailed kid coming out of college, just trying to figure out life. I still live by those two principles today — they’re my North Star. That’s why I’m so passionate about working people and about the service, because that’s what’s forgotten in politics. [I like to say], politics is about the service of the people and bringing humanity and love and leading with your heart back into the politics, which [currently] is so divisive. There’s a lot of hatred, a lot of negativity, and we try to lead with love.
- Sara Wexler It seems like when you were growing up, people’s needs weren’t being met, and the affordability crisis was worsening, regardless of whether Democrats or Republicans were in power. What do you make of this?
- Donavan McKinney A lot of people I’ve talked to view the Democrats and the Republicans very similarly when it comes to economics. I do believe that the Democratic Party is the party of the people. I have seen the Democrats do a lot more than the Republicans in terms of [helping the] working class. But I’m a big believer in the Scripture. Scripture talks about how you can’t serve two masters. What is happening, especially now, is that the Dems are serving the corporate oligarchs, same as the Republicans. You’re either going to have to do what’s best and serve the interests of working people, or you’re going to serve the interests of just a few and increase the wealth of those who are taking advantage of regular working people. For me, we follow what we preach. That’s what people want to see. They want to see receipts. So look at our campaign: we ran a campaign that was people powered. We didn’t take a cent of corporate PAC money or AIPAC [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] money. A lot of our money came from individual people across our district, across our state, across our country, who believe in a different style of politics. Leading up to the primary, our average donation on ActBlue was around $30 or $32, something like that — tens of thousands of people just donating to a vision. I’m forever grateful for it, because we were outspent. My opponent [in the primary], the current congressman, had his own wealth. He made his money off of pharmaceuticals, and so he had his own money to put in. But he also took money from ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] contractors and AIPAC as well as other corporate PACs, crypto, all of that — DTE, our monopoly utility — and just lying on our name, putting a lot of ads out. I’m very grateful, by the grace of God, that people were really waking up and realizing, “You know what? Donovan is better for the job.” We’re bringing a message that resonates with people and brings folks together.
- Sara Wexler Before running for office, you worked for Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Healthcare Michigan, which is the state’s largest health care union. How has your experience with labor organizing informed your politics?
- Donavan McKinney I tell this story a lot about my grandfather. My grandfather passed away late last year during the campaign cycle. I’m trying to not be emotional, because the man taught me a lot. When I was a kid, he used to bring me to the union meetings a lot. He worked at Ford Motor Company in the Detroit metro region and was part of the United Auto Workers (UAW) for forty-two years. One of the most interesting things about my grandfather is that during those forty-two years, he never missed a day of work. I asked him at his retirement party some years ago, “Granddad, how did you do it?” He told me one thing that stood out, which was that he took pride in what he was doing. He knew that, with his bare hands, he was helping change a life or a family’s life. But more important, he knew that not only the union had his back, but that Ford Motor Company had his back. But fast-forward to the year 2026, that work that he had and that salary that he made — that dollar isn’t stretching as far. And these corporations have gotten greedier. Take, for instance, what happened at the Poletown plant in my district, which is on the border of Detroit and Hamtramck. It’s a General Motors factory plant. It’s nicknamed “Factory Zero.” It was the first factory in America, and the first factory in America to be net zero. It was really green, really environmentally friendly and forward-thinking around that. Earlier this year, they cut over a thousand jobs, all union jobs. They cut everybody’s jobs, and then, just a few months later, replaced them with robots. I talk about it in the union halls a lot; I talk about how much it’s bullsh–t and how, at the end of the day, nobody has our back but working people ourselves. We need to start electing folks with the right type of mindset and, more importantly, with the lived experience that [leads them to prioritize working people] over these greedy corporations.
- Sara Wexler That leads nicely into my next question. You’re running as a democratic socialist. What does that mean to you?
- Donavan McKinney I define politics as the redistribution of resources. That’s it; it’s black and white. If you’re in these positions of power and influence, if you’re not trying to figure out ways to bring home as many resources as possible back to your communities and the people you represent, then I need you to get up out of here. That’s what led me to run for Congress in the first place, because I felt like our current congressman wasn’t meeting the moment. We’re going to be able to pick up the phone and do constituent service work, because I understand what it’s like being on the phone trying to get somebody to answer to help when you’re in dire need. My current congressman is known for not picking up the phone, not doing the real constituent work of the job. Half the battle is showing up. The other half is trying to figure out resources to improve the quality of life of the people you represent. So in terms of democratic socialism, I’m a big believer in Dr Martin Luther King’s teachings. And Tupac [Shakur] said it best: “They got money for wars but can’t feed the poor.” You’re telling me we’re spending money for a war that nobody wants — a billion dollars a day in Iran. And you’re also telling me that, with H.R. 1 [the One Big Beautiful Bill Act], the Republican trifecta cut health care and food assistance for the most vulnerable populations across our country. And I thought Republicans didn’t believe in red tape: I thought they believed in slim government and lean government and achieving efficiency in government. But they want to hurt people in order to give a tax break to the wealthiest top 1-percent earners of our country. They’re telling people, “We want you to get recertified every six months for your health care. But we DOGEd government, and we know that you’re not going to get recertified in time because we don’t have the caseworkers to certify you in the right amount of time. Because of the savings we’re going to have on the back end from folks not being able to recertify, we’re going to give a tax break to the ultrawealthy.” That’s not the America I want to live in; that’s not the America people in my community want to live in, or anyone who I know wants to live in. It’s up to us Democrats to level the playing field and right the ship, so to speak. I’m going to push hard as hell and advocate for the poor folks in my communities. A lot of my community is struggling and they’re looking for somebody that’s going to fight for them, and that’s my job.
- Sara Wexler As you mentioned, you were able to oust the incumbent Democrat in your primary. I’m wondering what role different organizations, DSA for instance, have played in your campaign.
- Donavan McKinney I was quoted earlier in the campaign, and I said, “We’re building the biggest and baddest coalition in the country,” which is true. I’ve even had members of Congress call me because they’re like, “Yo, how did you do this?” We have some of the most established folks and even the most conservative Democrats endorsing our campaign, as well as all-the-way-to-the-left DSA types endorsing our campaign. I don’t know if it was just because of me or also because of how bad the incumbent was, but it’s because we’re speaking values. We’re leading with our heart, and we’re following what we’re preaching. We brought together faith leaders, elected officials from the federal, state, county, and local levels, community block club leaders, and unions. I was told I was the only nonincumbent the AFL-CIO endorsed on the federal level when it came to the Democratic primary. So we had the unions; we had groups like Justice Democrats and DSA and so many other great folks coming together and realizing that we deserve better. That was our campaign message: We deserve better. I’m so grateful because I couldn’t have done it without this coalition. I couldn’t have done it without people coming together and realizing that their voices matter and that they have the power to make a difference in our politics and change the trajectory of our country. We’re going to continue that movement as we get sworn in in January. It’s the inside-outside strategy that Dr King talked about. You need people on the outside agitating, advocating, but you also need people on the inside who are willing to listen, willing to really put those words to paper and move legislation very swiftly in this moment, with the urgency that it demands.

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: Philippe Jaenada, lauréat du prix Goncourt avec « l’Inconnue du quai de Javel »
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Sophie Joubert
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Après le Médicis hier, remis à Philippe Vasset, Flammarion fait un doublé prestigieux avec un roman qui mêle l’enquête et l’autofiction. Une belle consécration pour un auteur très aimé du public, dont les livres se vendent bien en librairie. Le Renaudot revient à François-Henri Désérable pour le Palais, un livre sur le monde du vin.
Le Goncourt 2026, c’est un peu comme le foot (masculin) dans les années 1990, quand l’Allemagne écrasait systématiquement les autres équipes. Cette année, le suspense était limité, les quatre finalistes (Yannick Haenel, Philippe Jaenada, Clémentine Mélois et Sylvain Prudhomme) étant publiés dans des maisons appartenant au groupe Madrigall, propriété de la famille Gallimard. Même si on peut noter la disqualification des maisons du groupe Hachette (Fayard, Grasset, Stock…), propriété de Vincent Bolloré, une telle monochromie en dit long sur la concentration qui ronge le monde de l’édition.
Cela étant posé, la consécration de Philippe Jaenada, dont l’Inconnue du quai de Javel se vend bien en librairie (17 000 exemplaires les trois premières semaines), est une bonne nouvelle. Même si on avait un faible pour Sylvain...

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120363.title: Russland | Kreml gegen Kommunisten
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120363.author: Ewgeniy Kasakow
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120363.text:
- Politik
- Russland
Kreml gegen Kommunisten
Die KPRF gilt als domestizierte Oppositionspartei. Jetzt geht der Staat mit neuer Härte gegen die verbliebenen kritischen Stimmen in ihren Reihen vor.
Noch immer ist Russlands Kommunistische Partei (KPRF) mit ihren gut 160.000 Mitgliedern fester Bestandteil der Politik des Landes. Bei der Parlamentswahl im September konnte die KPRF trotz erheblicher Verluste den zweiten Platz verteidigen. Und das, obwohl die Partei fast komplett auf Regierungslinie ist. Von Beginn an unterstützen die Kommunisten den Ukraine-Krieg, Gennadij Sjuganow, seit 1993 ZK-Vorsitzender, nimmt gegenüber Präsident Wladimir Putin eine geradezu demonstrativ servile Haltung ein.
Und dennoch bleibt die KPRF ein Ort für oppositionelle Meinungen. Denen scheint der Kreml nun den Krieg erklärt zu haben. Noch im August wurde mit Nikolai Bondarenko einer der bekanntesten Politiker wegen der »Verbreitung extremistischer Symbolik« angeklagt. In seinem Regionalverband im Saratow vermied Bondarenko Kriegsrhetorik und rückte dafür soziale Themen in den Vordergrund. Sein Videoblog ist landesweit bekannt. Zur Wahl durfte er trotzdem nicht antreten, weil er angeblich ein Foto des liberalen Oppositionellen Alexei Nawalny in sozialen Medien gepostet haben soll. Da half nicht einmal die Intervention von Sjuganows Stellvertreter und potenziellem Nachfolger Jurij Afonin.
Plattform für verschiedene Oppositionelle
Vor einem Monat zeigte sich zudem, dass die KPRF nach wie vor viele oppositionelle Kräfte anzieht, die in ihr die einzig legale Plattform für ihre Arbeit sehen. »Nieder mit dem Zaren!« (Gemeint ist Präsident Wladimir Putin, Anm. d. Red.) und »Nein zum Krieg« skandierten Aktivisten, Linke und sogar Jabloko-Anhänger auf einer genehmigten Kundgebung gegen die Fälschungen bei der Dumawahl in Moskau. 60 Menschen wurden festgenommen. Auch in anderen Städten meldeten KPRF-Mitglieder Demonstrationen an. Sie werden nun von den Behörden verfolgt. In Ischewsk wurde Dmitrij Morosow, der sich als »demokratischer Sozialist« bezeichnet, wegen Drogenbesitz verhaftet und dabei offensichtlich schwer misshandelt. Obwohl kein Mitglied, unterhält er Kontakte zum kritischen Teil der Partei.
In der Republik Komi geriet der regionale Parteichef und frühere Duma-Abgeordnete Oleg Michailow ins Visier der Behörden. Am 21. Oktober wurde er an einem Moskauer Flughafen wegen »öffentlicher Rechtfertigung von Terrorismus« verhaftet. Michailow wird ein Post aus dem Jahr 2024 zur Last gelegt, in dem er seine Solidarität mit dem sozialistischen Wissenschaftler Boris Kagarlitzki ausdrückt. Kagarlitzki sitzt seit 2023 wegen »Aufruf zum Terrorismus« in Haft. Der Soziologe hatte den russischen Einmarsch in die Ukraine verurteilt.
Gegen den nationalistischen Mainstream
Michailow nahm sich in der Vergangenheit einige Freiheiten heraus. So verließ er bei allen Abstimmungen zu Kriegsgesetzen in der Duma den Saal. Seine diesjährige Wahlkampagne führte er unter dem Slogan »Frieden für die Welt, Steuergelder zurück in die Republik«. Wie ein ehemaliger ehrenamtlicher Mitarbeiter gegenüber »nd« erzählt, unterhielt Michailow nicht nur gute Kontakte zu den sozialen Bewegungen in seinem Wahlbezirk, er unterstützte auch die Umwelt-Proteste gegen eine geplante Müllverbrennungsanlage in Schies in der Nachbarregion Archangelsk.
Während sich die KPRF auf föderaler Ebene positiv zu russischen Nationalismus äußert, unterstützten Michailow und seine Regionalorganisation die nationale Bewegung der finno-ugrischen Komi. In der nach ihnen zu Sowjetzeiten benannten Republik stellen sie heute nur noch weniger als 23 Prozent der Bevölkerung. Michailow setzte sich für das Recht ein, Komi als Sprache im Regionalparlament zu verwenden und an Schulen wieder zum Pflichtfach zu machen.
Solidarität von linientreuen Kommunisten
Jewgenij Stupin, der zwischen 2019 und 2024 für die KPRF in der Moskauer Stadtduma saß und inzwischen aus der Partei ausgeschlossen wurde, erklärt gegenüber »nd«, die neue Repressionswelle wolle durch Einschüchterung mögliche negative Reaktionen auf die Wahlfälschungen verhindern. »Leider muss man sagen, dass das funktioniert. In Ischewsk gelang es zwar, die Erlaubnis für eine Demonstration zu bekommen, doch nach der Verhaftung von Morosow fand diese nicht mehr statt.«
Mittlerweile haben sich selbst KPRF-Politiker, die für verschärfte Repressionen eintreten, wie die Duma-Abgeordnete Nina Ostanina, mit Michailow solidarisiert. Für den Kreml könnte die Disziplinierung der Kommunisten so durchaus nach hinten losgehen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says US will end military aid to Israel by the end of this year
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.
In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, Trump said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it.”
“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.
Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”
During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.
Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as Foreign Military Financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.
Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, where US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. He would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.
A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.
Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president JD Vance has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”
During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

https://taz.de/CDU-in-der-Krise/!6227059.title: CDU in der Krise: Dem Ärger Luft gemacht – und nun?
https://taz.de/CDU-in-der-Krise/!6227059.author: Anna Lehmann
https://taz.de/CDU-in-der-Krise/!6227059.text:
CDU in der Krise: Dem Ärger Luft gemacht – und nun?
Zwei Tage lang haben rund 160 CDU-Kreisvorsitzende der Parteiführung die schlechte Stimmung an der Basis geschildert. Was davon nimmt Merz mit?
Seit vier Jahren ist Friedrich Merz Vorsitzender der CDU, doch zwischen ihm und seiner Partei kriselt es gewaltig. Ehemalige glühende Anhänger seien enttäuscht, berichtet etwa die Vorsitzende des Kreisverbandes Frankfurt (Oder) Desirée Schrade im Gespräch mit dem Journalisten Paul Ronzheimer in dessen gleichnamigem Podcast. Sie spüre eine richtige Zerrissenheit in der CDU. Und der Rückhalt in der Gesellschaft schwindet. In Brandenburg gelinge es nicht mehr, als reine CDU-Kandidatin ein gutes Ergebnis zu erzielen, und „wir finden kaum noch jemand, der für uns an die Info-Stände geht“. Es gebe Parteiaustritte in Größenordnungen.
So hatte Schrade das auch am Montag dem Parteivorsitzenden und Kanzler Merz geschildert, der sie und die rund 330 CDU-Kreisvorsitzenden zwei Tage lang zur Aussprache in die Berliner Parteizentrale eingeladen hatte. Etwa die Hälfe der Ehrenamtlichen war der Einladung gefolgt.
Eine von ihnen war Serap Güler, erste weibliche Vorsitzende des fast 4.000 Mitglieder zählenden Kreisverbandes Köln. Gülers Arbeitsort ist Berlin, sie ist auch Staatsministerin im Auswärtigen Amt. Sie habe eine offene und kritische Debatte erlebt, viele hätten die Gelegenheit gehabt, „mal Luft abzulassen“, berichtet sie der taz. „Das war wichtig, auch über die Unzufriedenheit zu sprechen und damit Gehör beim Kanzler zu finden.“ Das müsse jetzt fortgesetzt werden. Dazu gehöre auch, stärker mit der Basis zu kommunizieren und die Politik der Bundesregierung besser zu erklären und einzuordnen. Sie plädiert dafür, solche offenen und kritischen Aussprachen regelmäßig zu führen. „Das täte beiden Seiten gut.“
Schrade aus Frankfurt (Oder) fordert, die CDU müsse sich auch breiter aufstellen. Eine Forderung, die Güler vom Arbeitnehmerflügel, CDA, unterstützt. „Wenn wir sagen, wir müssen uns breiter aufstellen, dann gehören dazu aber auch mehr Frauen in führenden Positionen.“ Bei der Aussprache in Berlin und unter den Kreisvorsitzenden generell seien die weiblichen Vertreter klar in der Minderheit gewesen.
Zum ersten Mal eine Bundespräsidentin
Merz griff die fehlende Repräsentanz von Frauen zumindest in einem Punkt auf. Auf der Konferenz hatte er sich am Montagabend darauf festgelegt, dass eine Frau zum ersten Mal das höchste Staatsamt der Bundesrepublik bekleiden soll. Die CDU hat das Vorschlagsrecht für die oder den Bundespräsidentin/en, der oder die im Februar neu gewählt wird. „Ich werde der Partei eine gemeinsame Kandidatin vorschlagen, eine Kandidatin der politischen Mitte. Ich bin festgelegt in der Frage, dass es eine Frau werden muss“, sagte Merz nach Angaben der Deutschen Presse-Agentur.
CDU-Generalsekretärin Franziska Hoppermann sagte, die Entscheidung liege bei den Parteigremien voraussichtlich Anfang kommender Woche. Jetzt würden noch Gespräche geführt, die erforderlich seien. Inhaltlich sagte die CDU-Generalsekretärin, in diesen polarisierten Zeiten wäre es gut, wenn jemand im höchsten Staatsamt sei, der mit „Herzenswärme und Bodenständigkeit auf die Menschen zugehen kann“ und zugleich politische Erfahrung mitbringe. Die CSU hat bereits die bayerische Landtagspräsidentin Ilse Aigner vorgeschlagen, die SPD unterstützt diesen Vorschlag.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iran-.title: Iran says US ceasefire proposal 'insufficient' as strikes are reported on Qeshm Island
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iran-.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iran-.text:
Iran says US ceasefire proposal 'insufficient' as strikes are reported on Qeshm Island
Iran cast doubt on the chances of a deal with the US on Tuesday, after the US carried out air strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, with the fate of last-minute negotiations between the two sides uncertain.
The air strikes, which occurred late on Monday, came after US President Donald Trump said he did not plan to attack Iran after the midterm elections and voiced hope for a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said an agreement could be reached and that the government was “authorised” to renew a truce.
However, on Tuesday, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, rejected an offer passed to Tehran from Qatari negotiators.
“America’s response to the demands of the Iranian nation was insufficient. They must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened,” he said on X.
Last-minute negotiations to avert what officials and analysts in the region say could be a return to full-scale war took place against the backdrop of US air strikes on Qeshm Island, a strategic place that Iran has used as it attempts to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz.

The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the strikes on Qeshm, said the US was deliberately keeping the attacks quiet to reduce the risk of escalation. One US official described the strikes as “defensive” in the report.
According to the report, in one exchange, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired a surface-to-air missile at a US warplane, which fired back in self-defence. Another strike occurred after the US intercepted a missile fired from Qeshm at a commercial vessel.
Iran also said it downed a US MQ-9 Reaper drone and two Lucas drones near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the ball was in Washington's court after Tehran had delivered what he described as a "strong and rational response” to the proposal conveyed by Qatar.
"The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit," Qalibaf said.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Tehran has a seven-step proposal for a diplomatic solution that could be implemented in two days.
The plan would call for the US to end its blockade on Iranian ports, Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz waterway, a US waiver on Iranian oil sales, the cancellation of new sanctions on Iran, and then talks on the nuclear file.
The US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire in the spring and then signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding to advance talks, but it was never implemented. The talks collapsed in part over the US’s reluctance to agree to Iran controlling traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.

https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-spend-.title: How to spend $20M in East Williamsburg? A discussion begins.
https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-spend-.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-spend-.text:
The East Williamsburg section of Brooklyn is wrestling with an enviable question: How to spend a $20 million grant from Albany?
Last summer, the neighborhood won the money through the governor’s Downtown Revitalization Initiative, which funds capital projects to spur economic development in commercial corridors.
Community members and organizations have been asked to submit project proposals to help decide how the money is spent. Applications close on Wednesday. Those close to the initiative say it’s a tricky question in a community with so many divergent needs.
The neighborhood has become a destination for wealthy families looking to raise their children, and young people seeking a version of the cool, creative Williamsburg that its namesake to the west once was. East Williamsburg is also home to generations of residents who have managed to stay, mostly in rent-regulated and tenant-protected sites.
City leaders in charge of allocating the grant funding are trying to identify projects that will serve the entire community, not just those who patron the new fancy restaurants and night clubs.
“Navigating the demands of the neighborhood … is really challenging,” said Francesca Fernandez Bruce, the president of the Grand Street Business Improvement District and leader on the project. “It’s a hard line to walk in terms of balancing and making sure that everything is inclusive.”
Bruce said neglected infrastructure and aging public spaces are a concern, especially when residents can shop online instead. Low foot traffic was the paramount issue merchants said they were concerned about in a neighborhood needs assessment published this spring.
“East Williamsburg is a really great example of a community that has in many ways been underserved for a really long time, both from a design and a financial perspective,” Bruce said.
Tree canopy and open green space in the neighborhood is some of the smallest in the city, according to a report published alongside the request for proposals. Summers are desolate, she said, and winters are dark.
“ At 4 p.m. in the wintertime you can't really walk down [the street] because cause there's no sidewalk lighting,” Bruce said. “People don't feel safe to go shopping, and that hurts our mom and pops.”
But, she said, a few simple fixes could make a big difference.
Theresa Middleton, now 53, said she agrees.
Middletown said she has lived in the same apartment in East Williamsburg since she was a child. The rent stabilized unit was passed down by her parents.
She said it’s the only reason she can still afford to live in the neighborhood.
“I wouldn't be able to pay it, between light, gas,” Middleton said. “It's hard nowadays, especially with the cost of everything, trying to make ends meet.”
With all the new wealth in the neighborhood, she said she’s surprised that there’s not more open places for people to just hang out. She hopes the new grant funding can change that.
“It’s peaceful,” she said. “It's a good place to raise a family. There is a future there. There really is.”
A neighborhood identity crisis
The neighborhood’s own name makes some New Yorkers scratch their heads.
Alberto Valentin, who leads the Graham Street BID, told Gothamist that local lore is that East Williamsburg’s name was popularized by developers trying to take advantage of Williamsburg’s brand – which, before it became one of the most costly places to live in the city, was a hot spot for artists and hipsters.
If it’s true, the developer’s trick worked. More than a decade later, the neighborhood has clearly gone through what Valentin calls the “g-word” – otherwise known as gentrification.
Bistros with no available reservations in sight, wine bars and luxury towers are now plentiful. The average one-bedroom apartment in the neighborhood, according to Rent Hop, an apartment rental website, is about $4,700 a month.
Farther east, the area is industrial, where warehouse clubs, some cramming in thousands of sweaty bodies at a time, are peppered among powerplants and manufacturing facilities.
Leah Archibald, the executive director of Evergreen Exchange, a nonprofit that represents the industrial and manufacturing community, said that “all the cool stuff migrated east,” after “Williamsburg proper” became home to luxury chains like Chanel and Hermès.
But, East Williamsburg, too, has become whiter, more affluent and more expensive to live, according to data published along with Downtown Revitalization Initiative’s request for proposals.
As of 2024, the number of non-white residents of East Williamsburg have declined since 2010, according to the report. The neighborhood's median household income rose 50% over the same period, to more than $82,000 — higher than the average for Brooklynites.
But there are still pockets of people living in poverty, said Antonio Reynoso, the Brooklyn borough president, and gentrification may have already maximized their displacement.
There are about six public housing developments in the same general area, he said, and “no one from those housing developments is going anywhere.”
The key, he said, will be to make the area inhabitable for the different demographics who now call the neighborhood home.
“ People assume that because of the gentrification, that there are no more poor people,” Reynoso said.
East Williamsburg, Reynoso said, is now lined with fancy bars and restaurants for what he calls “ a very specific demographic that has a lot of expendable cash.”
But the thousands who live in public housing or tenant protected units don’t necessarily benefit from that kind of development, he said.
The changes, Reynoso said, “are not supporting the longer term residents in the neighborhood.”
He said he hopes an influx in money for neighborhood improvements will change the script.
“ We feel like we can build an environment that is both fruitful and economically prosperous, while not forgetting that we have a large population of poor people that still need services as well,” Reynoso said.
The $20 million question
So how’s the money going to be spent?
“That’s the $20 million question,” Bruce said. The wish list for potential neighborhood improvements to East Williamsburg is long.
The planning committee Downtown Revitalization Initiative will ultimately decide from the project proposals that community members have thrown in the ring – and a consultant will help tweak the projects to make sure they are feasible.
Bruce and Reynoso said they’re particularly interested in projects that improve public space: efforts like adding more green space and better lighting, outdoor dining areas, turning cul de sacs into small parks, and sprucing up the existing parks with more trees, better benches, dog runs and lending libraries.
Only so much can be done with the money, Reynoso said, but he said he hopes the grant will open the floodgates for additional investment.
“ I expect the city to be big-time partners with us for this,” Reynoso said. “ I expect that at least $40 million to come down on this project once it's all said and done.”
As for Middleton, she said that the hopes from longstanding community members are simple.
“People just want to live decent and comfortable,” Middleton said. “They don't want that stress … Should I pay my rent, my light, or put food on the table for my children? They just want to be in peace and live. That's, that's all we hear.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Governo Lula quer aprovar PEC da Segurança Pública sem incluir redução da maioridade penal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governo Lula vai trabalhar para aprovar a Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública sem incluir a redução da maioridade penal. A orientação foi anunciada nesta terça-feira (3) pelo ministro da Secretaria de Relações Institucionais (SRI), José Guimarães, horas antes da votação no plenário do Senado, marcada para as 16h.
“A posição do governo, depois de avaliar todas as possibilidades, é que nós vamos votar a PEC tal como veio da Câmara dos Deputados”, afirmou Guimarães a jornalistas no Palácio do Planalto. O ministro disse que o governo não se opõe a discutir a maioridade penal, mas defende que o tema tramite em outra proposta. “Separa e trata em outro projeto. Essa discussão está posta no governo, mas não dá para misturar”, declarou.
A posição foi fechada em reunião de líderes governistas no Planalto, convocada para alinhar a base antes da votação. Segundo Guimarães, a emenda alternativa apresentada pelo líder do PT no Senado, Camilo Santana (CE), que reduziria a maioridade para 16 anos apenas em crimes hediondos, será retirada. “O governo está unido e coeso nessa posição”, garantiu o ministro.
‘Jabuti’ na PEC
A estratégia do Planalto é evitar que a PEC volte à Câmara. Se o Senado alterar o texto aprovado pelos deputados, os trechos modificados precisam passar por nova análise, o que atrasaria a promulgação. A PEC é considerada pelo governo etapa necessária para a criação do Ministério da Segurança Pública, promessa de campanha de Lula.
“Trazer o debate da maioridade penal para o âmbito dessa PEC é o que a gente chama de corpo estranho à PEC. Não que não seja um debate que precise ser feito, mas não no âmbito de uma PEC da Segurança, que é algo muito mais estruturante do sistema”, argumentou a líder do governo no Senado, Teresa Leitão (PT-PE).
Para barrar as mudanças, o relator da PEC, senador Rogério Carvalho (PT-SE), vai rejeitar as emendas sobre o tema. “O relator Rogério Carvalho vai emitir o seguinte despacho: os temas relativos à redução da maioridade penal tramitarão em PEC autônoma e serão despachados para a proposta que já está sendo debatida na Câmara dos Deputados e que tem calendário próprio para apreciação”, explicou o líder do governo no Congresso, Randolfe Rodrigues (PT-AP).
A saída apontada pelo governo é a comissão especial instalada na Câmara em julho para discutir a maioridade penal. O colegiado deve apresentar relatório até o início de dezembro.
Oposição insiste
A oposição, porém, não recuou. Depois de reunião de líderes com o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), o líder da oposição, Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), confirmou que vai manter o destaque. “Vamos manter o destaque, porque é de interesse de quase 80% da população brasileira. Espero ter votos”, disse.
A emenda de Marinho reduz a maioridade penal de 18 para 16 anos como regra geral e para 14 anos em crimes hediondos, tortura, tráfico de drogas, terrorismo e participação em organizações criminosas. Para entrar na PEC, o texto precisaria de ao menos 49 votos, três quintos do Senado, em cada um dos dois turnos. O governo afirma ter votos suficientes para derrubá-la.
O impasse já havia levado Alcolumbre a retirar a PEC da pauta em 15 de outubro, às vésperas do segundo turno. A redução da maioridade ganhou força na campanha, quando Flávio Bolsonaro apresentou proposta sobre o tema. A emenda de Camilo, articulada como resposta, dividiu a bancada petista e enfrentou resistência na base social da esquerda. Na época, o PT chegou a desistir de inserir a redução no texto. Lula declarou depois ser favorável à redução em crimes hediondos, mas defendeu que o assunto fosse tratado separadamente.
Aprovada pela Câmara em março, a PEC prevê a integração entre União, estados, Distrito Federal e municípios no combate ao crime organizado. O texto inclui o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (Susp) na Constituição, amplia as atribuições da Polícia Federal e da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) e endurece as regras para líderes e integrantes de facções e milícias.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Italy set to create restitution panel for Nazi-looted art
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Italy’s parliament is considering legislation that would, for the first time, establish a formal process for restituting art and cultural property seized by the Nazis and Italian authorities from victims of racial persecution during the Holocaust era.
Introduced by a lawmaker from Brothers of Italy, the party led by the country’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni, the proposal has been hailed by as “an act of civilisation” by representatives of heirs of those whose property was stolen, and would bring Italy in line with Germany, Austria, France, the Netherlands, the UK and Switzerland, the latest European country to establish its own restitution mechanisms.
The bill grants the government powers to establish a five-member committee to examine the provenance of works that were confiscated, looted or sold under duress as a result of racial persecution between 1933 and 1945. The committee would assess individual cases and issue decisions on restitution to the original owners, their heirs or—if no living heirs are identified—the broader Jewish community in Italy.
If enacted, the bill, which is currently being examined by the lower house’s culture committee, would give the government six months to establish the restitution system.
“Introducing this bill does not merely mean finally bringing Italy into line with the highest international standards... but means, first and foremost, fulfilling a historic duty,” Federico Mollicone, a key Meloni ally who introduced the bill in March, tells The Art Newspaper.
“We are not merely talking about property claims, but about restoring human dignity, memory and the fundamental principles of our constitution,” says Mollicone, who is the president of the culture commission in Italy’s lower house of parliament.
Seized works in state museums
State-sponsored looting, confiscation and forced sale of Jewish-owned art and cultural heritage became increasingly commonplace following the fascist dictator Benito Mussolini’s 1938 introduction of racial laws that prohibited Jewish books, excluded Jews from public office and introduced limits on Jewish property ownership. The dispossessions increased from 1943, when Italian and occupying German Nazi forces began arresting and deporting Jews to concentration camps.
Some of the seized works subsequently entered the collections of Italian museums, where four publicly known disputed works are currently displayed, according to Katharina Hüls-Valenti, an expert in provenance research at Parma University. They include Edouard Manet’s Portrait de M. Arnaud à cheval (1875), which Hüls-Valenti says was sold under duress in 1935 by its owners, the family of German painter Max Liebermann, and donated to the Galleria d’Arte Moderna in Milan in 1958. Hüls-Valenti says that Liebermann’s heirs had sought restitution but had encountered resistance from the museum.
Asked to respond to those allegations, Paola Zatti, a curator at the Galleria d’Arte Moderna, said in a statement to The Art Newspaper: “The painting was sold by Liebermann’s wife in 1935 (incidentally, to a Jewish antiques dealer), but there is no evidence that she was forced to do so.”
Zatti added that, in accord with a lawyer representing Liebermann’s heirs in Germany, the museum had agreed to display a label explaining the work’s ownership history. The text, Zatti said, “clearly highlights the tragic moment when the work was sold by its Jewish owners” and helps visitors appreciate the “circumstances under which [the work] left Germany”.
Another painting, Cristo portacroce (around 1508-09) by Girolamo da Romano, was requisitioned by France’s pro-Nazi Vichy government in 1941 from the family of Federico Gentili di Giuseppe, an Italian Jewish businessman and art collector living in Paris. It was auctioned to a private collector and then bought by Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera museum in 1998. Following a request by the heirs, US authorities seized the work while it was on loan to a Florida museum in 2011.
The real number of Holocaust-era seizures currently held by museums, Hüls-Valenti suggests, could be closer to dozens. “We really don’t know for sure,” she says. “Better research is required.”
Italy endorsed the 1998 Washington Principles, which established guidelines for the restitution of Nazi-looted art. A 2001 enquiry led by Tina Anselmi, a former Italian government minister, found evidence of systematic expropriation from Jews. It found evidence of 7,847 seizure warrants issued up to April 1945 for property including houses and land, businesses, bank deposits, insurance policies, jewellery, paintings and furniture.
Despite the report’s findings, Italy, a global leader in securing the restitution of its own national heritage, has been slower than other European countries to seek justice for dispossessed Jews. France created a commission for restitutions and compensation in 1999. The UK established the Spoliation Advisory Panel in 2000 to evaluate claims to works held by British national institutions.
Delay due to several factors
“Italy is obviously a central country in the world of art... and yet on this issue of the Holocaust restitution it had barely scratched the surface in addressing it,” says Gideon Taylor, the president of World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO).
Experts point to various reasons for the delay in Italy’s response, including a national reluctance to confront the country’s fascist past, insufficient political will to prioritise the restitution of Jewish-owned cultural heritage, and a lack of transparency about provenance in museums. They say poor cataloguing has contributed to an assumption that few works would be affected by a law.
Complicating matters, Italian law recognises works held in Italian museums as inalienable parts of the national heritage. The bill addresses this hurdle by indicating that the final restitution decision would automatically remove the work from the public domain. Further, restituted works would no longer be subject to the protections of Italy’s heritage code, meaning they could permanently leave the country. The bill also indicates that existing statutes of limitations would not prevent restitutions.
The commission would accept claims from legitimate owners, their descendants or heirs, and the Union of Italian Jewish Communities (UCEI) or individual Jewish communities. It would include a member nominated by Italy’s art police and have to rule within 180 days of a claim. The bill is intended to help heirs seeking restitution from both public and private collections.
Italy’s parliament adopted the bill following the submission of a report evaluating the country’s restitutions record commissioned by the WJRO and written by the lawyer Lorenzo Casini, a former chief of staff at the culture ministry who now heads a public research institution in Lucca. It was written with the support of six leading experts, including Hüls-Valenti, the Parma professor.
“Museums don’t necessarily hide their works, but there isn’t full understanding of just how important transparency is and how helpful it would be for all these works to come to light,” Casini says. “Besides addressing the tragic wounds left by looting and filling the legislative gap in Italy, the law is specifically designed to bring those artworks to light.”
Speaking to parliament’s culture commission in June, Casini praised the bill but suggested areas for improvement, proposing widening the commission’s remit from art to other cultural heritage—including manuscripts, books, archives and ceremonial objects—and advising that the commission and researchers would require additional funds to carry out their work.
“The next step could hopefully be to seek funding once the law has been passed,” Casini tells The Art Newspaper.
Federico Mollicone says lawmakers will “ensure” the culture ministry’s upcoming funding plans include “adequate resources to support research projects on provenance, the digitisation of archives, and the training of dedicated experts”. He highlights culture minister Alessandro Giuli’s “strong commitment to this issue”.
He also predicts the bill will have a smooth passage into law, noting that there is “wide political consensus” on redressing injustices from racial persecution. Brothers of Italy has roots in the post-fascist parties that rose from the ashes of the Second World War.
“Our goal is to complete the parliamentary review and pass the bill in the coming months,” Mollicone says. “We want to bring this historic reform to a successful conclusion within this legislative session.” A general election is due to take place before the end of next year, with analysts suggesting it may be brought forward to the spring.
Paolo Gnignati, UCEI’s head of legal affairs, says the bill’s arrival in parliament is significant. “The regulations on restitution are something that can be meaningful to specific individuals because they have financial and personal implications,” he says. “But they are also, fundamentally, an act of civilisation.”

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.title: Gewerkschaften | Tarifabschluss im Einzelhandel: Kaum mehr als der Mindestlohn
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.author: Christian Lelek
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120362.text:
- Berlin
- Gewerkschaften
Tarifabschluss im Einzelhandel: Kaum mehr als der Mindestlohn
Gewerkschaft und Einzelhandelsverband haben um Centbeträge gestritten. Die spürbaren Effekte des neuen Tarifvertrags dürften sich in Grenzen halten.
Nun ist es auch in Berlin und Brandenburg unter Dach und Fach. Die Beschäftigten im Einzelhandel bekommen mehr Geld. Am Montagabend gaben der Handelsverband und die Gewerkschaft Verdi eine Einigung in den Tarifverhandlungen bekannt.
Die Löhne steigen stufenweise um fünf Prozent. In Berlin gibt es rückwirkend ab 1. September drei Prozent mehr Gehalt, ab dem 1. Juli 2027 weitere zwei Prozent. Der neue Tarifvertrag läuft 25 Monate bis zum 30. Juni 2028. In Brandenburg verschiebt sich der gesamte Zeitraum um einen Monat nach hinten.
»Mit den Abschlüssen für Berlin und Brandenburg schaffen wir für die Unternehmen in beiden Tarifgebieten verlässliche Rahmenbedingungen. Die Belastungen sind erheblich, zugleich erhalten unsere Unternehmen die notwendige Planungssicherheit für die kommenden zwei Jahre«, erklärt Nils Busch-Petersen, Hauptgeschäftsführer des Handelsverbandes Berlin-Brandenburg (HBB).
Die Tarifparteien vereinbarten darüber hinaus eine Anpassung der »Entgeltuntergrenze«. Wer im Geltungsbereich des Tarifvertrags arbeitet, soll demnach in Berlin ab September dieses Jahr (in Brandenburg ab Oktober) nicht weniger als 14,20 Euro pro Stunde verdienen. Damit liegt der Tarifabschluss 30 Cent über dem derzeitigen gesetzlichen Mindestlohn. Im Januar 2027 wird dieser Wert in beiden Bundesländern mit dem gesetzlichen Mindestlohn auf 14,60 Euro steigen, ab Juni 2027 in Berlin (ab Juli in Brandenburg) dann noch mal auf 14,90 Euro. Für ein halbes Jahr ist dann also die tarifliche Entgeltuntergrenze auf dem Niveau des gesetzlichen Mindestlohns.
»Besonders wichtig war uns, dass auch die Kolleg*innen in den untersten Entgeltgruppen echte Tariferhöhungen bekommen und nicht lediglich durch die Anhebung des gesetzlichen Mindestlohns mehr Geld haben«, erklärte Verdi-Verhandlungsführerin Conny Weißbach. Ausgerechnet um die niedrigsten Entgelte sei bis zuletzt am härtesten gerungen worden. Dabei garantiert der Abschluss in den ersten fünf beziehungsweise sechs Monaten im Jahr 2027 lediglich ein Einkommen auf Mindestlohnniveau.
Es ist allerdings gut möglich, dass ab 2028 die Untergrenze des Tariflohns unter dem gesetzlichen Mindestlohn liegt. Die Mindestlohnkommission wird im Laufe des kommenden Jahres über eine Anpassung entscheiden.
In anderen Branchen gibt es deutlich höhere Branchenmindestlöhne. Derzeit liegt der Branchenmindestlohn im Elektrohandwerk beispielsweise bei 14,93 Euro, für Gerüstbauer*innen bei 14,35 Euro pro Stunde, für Pflegehilfskräfte bei 16,10 Euro und für Beschäftigte in der Gebäudereinigung bei 18,40 Euro.
Branchenmindestlöhne gelten auch für Unternehmen einer Branche, die nicht Mitglied im Arbeitgeberverband sind. Sie sind also allgemeinverbindlich. Die Tarifverträge, die der HBB und Verdi miteinander verhandeln, gelten hingegen nicht für alle Beschäftigten im Einzelhandel. Etliche auch namhafte Unternehmen wie Galeria, das Kadewe und Thalia haben sich in den vergangenen Jahren aus der Tarifbindung gelöst. Ihre Beschäftigten streikten in der Runde dennoch zum Teil mit, um zu erreichen, dass die Arbeitgeber den Tarifvertrag wieder anwenden.
Vereinbarungen wurden auch über die Ausbildungsvergütung getroffen. Ab September 2026 soll sie im ersten Lehrjahr auf monatlich 1100 Euro steigen, im zweiten Lehrjahr auf 1210 Euro und im dritten Lehrjahr auf 1340 Euro. Ab September 2027 sollen die Auszubildenden dann 1120 Euro, 1230 Euro beziehungsweise 1380 Euro bekommen.
Der HBB hatte zu Beginn der Tarifrunde von einer beispiellosen Lage für Unternehmen in der Region gesprochen. »So eine nachhaltige und intensive Krise hat es in den letzten Jahrzehnten nicht gegeben«, hatte Busch-Petersen »nd« gesagt. Die Kauf- und Konsumlaune sei immer noch nicht auf dem Niveau der Vor-Corona-Jahre. Auch auf das anstehende Weihnachtsgeschäft blicken die Einzelhändler*innen mit Sorge.
Angesichts der äußerst widrigen Bedingungen für die Gewerkschaft lobt Verdi-Sekretärin Weißbach ihre Mitglieder. Der Tarifabschluss sei das Ergebnis des entschlossenen Einsatzes der Beschäftigten. »Ohne Streiks wäre dies nicht möglich gewesen«, sagte Weißbach.
Für die Gewerkschaften sind die Auseinandersetzungen schwierig, da nur vergleichsweise wenige Beschäftigte Mitglied sind. Die Anzahl der Teilzeitbeschäftigten lag 2023 im Einzelhandel, Minijobs eingeschlossen, bei 64 Prozent. 66 Prozent der Beschäftigten sind Frauen.
Mit den Abschlüssen in Berlin und Brandenburg endet die bundesweite Tarifrunde. Zuerst hatten sich Arbeitgeber und Gewerkschaft Ende August in Nordrhein-Westfalen geeinigt. Dieser Pilotabschluss wurde dann in den übrigen Ländern und nun zuletzt auch in Berlin und Brandenburg übernommen.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: ‘The nipple touch of doom’: what is sad nipple syndrome and what causes it?
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Ivana Rihter
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
Some say it feels like a sudden burst of anguish; others liken it more to homesickness. The sudden onset of a sinking, upsetting feeling due to nipple stimulation is anecdotally known as Sad Nipple Syndrome (SNS), and for Sandra, it can be triggered by something as commonplace as putting on a shirt.
“I was probably a child when I first noticed: ‘Why does touching my nipple make me sad?’” says the 28-year-old. The sensation seemed to happen at random, and without the words to describe it, she kept it a secret. It wasn’t until college that she worked up the courage to Google it. “I realized I wasn’t crazy,” she says.
There are many others like Sandra (who, for privacy, has asked to use a pseudonym). Breastfeeding mothers, queer lovers and cis men alike have all sought an explanation for this phenomenon.
What is Sad Nipple Syndrome (SNS)?
Sad Nipple Syndrome is often discovered in private. People describe it as a sudden dysphoria (a profound state of unhappiness or uneasiness) that follows nipple stimulation. It is often resolved within a couple of minutes, but can cause confusion and disruption.
I spoke to four people who experience SNS, and each described similar negative feelings. Sandra described it as “dread, a nostalgic sadness or the feeling of a bad memory”. Salma Zaky, a New York-based comedian who has talked about her SNS on stage, says she can “tell if a woman has gone through it – they’ll light up or clap”. Zaky likens it to a mix of homesickness or nostalgia.
For Sandra, the most common trigger is a light, unexpected touch when changing clothes or towel drying. Its intensity can vary depending on the circumstances. For instance, if she triggers the feeling on her own with light touch, “the negative feelings tend to persist for more than just a few seconds,” says Sandra. If there is sustained friction with her clothing, she sometimes feels “deep grief”.
Their sentiments are echoed in thousands of online posts asking whether anyone else experiences the “nipple touch of doom”. In the absence of a formal clinical diagnosis, most people’s understanding of Sad Nipple Syndrome has come from word of mouth or chatter online.
“Reddit was helpful in just being like: ‘Oh, I’m not an insane person,” says Zaky. “Other people feel this too.”
What do scientists think is happening in SNS?
SNS is not an official medical diagnosis, and scientific research remains in short supply. That said, awareness is growing, even among researchers and medical practitioners.
As with many conditions that primarily affect women’s intimate or hormonal experiences, there is not much medical curiosity, funding or research. “While there is no explanation yet, we can assume that the hormone oxytocin is somehow involved, since nipple stimulation leads to its release,” says Dr Vladimír Kraus, PhD, Department of Gynaecology and Obstetrics at Pavol Jozef Šafárik University.
Oxytocin is often referred to as the “love hormone”. Largely responsible for bonding and increased emotional connectivity, it is triggered by physical touch like hugging, massage or sex, and also after uterine contractions during childbirth or breastfeeding. When it comes to its role in SNS, Kraus theorizes that “some subtle changes may cause the [oxytocin signaling pathway] to go haywire and [could] be responsible for the surprisingly prompt and very negative feeling experienced”.
There are no SNS-specific studies, but there are two more well-studied conditions that are similar enough to help us understand it. The first is dysphoric milk ejection reflex, or D-MER, which occurs during breastfeeding. It is an emotional response to the milk letdown, the moment where milk starts flowing out of the milk duct. People commonly describe the sudden rush of emotion as homesickness, sadness, loss of hope, worthlessness, shame and guilt, according to Alia Macrina Heise, an international board-certified lactation consultant and an expert on D-MER in Naples, New York. “It is disruptive to the duration of lactation and to the mother’s experience of breastfeeding and bonding,” she says.
SNS and D-MER present identically, and are also similar to post-coital dysphoria, says Heise. While SNS and D-MER are focused on nipple stimulation, the negative feelings people experience with post-coital dysphoria occur after the hormonal spike of orgasm. Anyone who has one of these conditions “will describe the embodied emotional sensations basically exactly the same way, even though the cause and the trigger is different”, says Heise.
The prevailing theory is that these three conditions involve a “hormonal cocktail inside the body”, says Heise.
The two most relevant hormones are prolactin and dopamine. This cocktail Heise refers to affects every human in a multitude of ways. “Prolactin and dopamine have a known relationship inside the human body – male, female, breastfeeding, not breastfeeding, in sexual arousal, in orgasm,” says Heise. Prolactin also contributes to weight control, immunoregulation, stress adaptation and maternal behavior.
Meanwhile, dopamine drives the brain’s reward system, playing a key role in movement, pleasure, desire, motivation and thinking. “Dopamine is often called prolactin’s gatekeeper,” explains Heise. In order for prolactin to flow into the body, dopamine has to allow prolactin through in order to complete one of its many jobs.
It’s possible that what happens in SNS, D-MER and post-coital dysphoria has to do with the way prolactin and dopamine go about their daily duties. One possible explanation is “inappropriate dopamine activity”, says Heise, who first heard a colleague mention SNS in the 2000s. “With dopamine being a mood stabilizer, that inappropriate activity is causing a mood destabilization that lasts for a very short amount of time.”
There is a growing body of research focused on D-MER, but to truly understand these conditions, we need more specialized studies. Without a clearer picture, sufferers are left feeling alone and “crazy”. Even if they work up the courage to ask their doctor about it, most medical professionals don’t have enough experience with these conditions to recommend treatment.
Techniques for reducing the severity of symptoms are mostly experimental. “One of the tricks that we’ve found helps the most by also targeting the dopamine system is cold therapy,” says Heise, who’s worked with thousands of breastfeeding mothers with D-MER. “Mothers drinking ice water or putting cold wraps around the back of their neck and cooling down their face and mouth receptors before letdown significantly eases the symptoms because it increases prolactin levels.” But whether this trick works for people with SNS is unknown.
How does SNS affect people?
Unexplained physical phenomena can be confusing and distressing, especially when they involve intimate body parts. The impact of SNS goes beyond the brief sensations, to shame and confusion over what they might mean.
Without formal answers from the medical community, many have developed theories about the causes, including forgotten sexual trauma, questions about one’s sexuality and marital doubts. These unfounded explanations can do real harm.
Kraus says SNS has rarely come up in his practice, but those who experience it often feel concerned “about their mental state or fear that they don’t like their partner or sex”.
As with all sexual preferences or personal boundaries, clear communication is key, experts say. It may also feel challenging or personal for partners of people who experience SNS.
“This isn’t about you, and it isn’t rejection,” says Dr Jennifer Lincoln, a board-certified OB-GYN and author in Portland, Oregon. “Talk about it outside the bedroom, agree on a signal to pause or change what’s happening, and let the person with the reaction lead.”
It can be tricky to bring up something you might not even know the name for, feel ashamed of or confused by. But talking about it can be helpful.
“Even just naming [Sad Nipple Syndrome] helps a lot, because many people think they’re going crazy – or with D-MER, that they are a bad mother,” says Lincoln. Similarly, shame can arise when SNS leads to negative experiences during sex and intimacy.
“I just avoid any nipple stuff during sex now, and it’s completely fine,” says Zaky.
“It pretty much has not impacted my sex life at all,” says Sandra. “I think the hardest part was simply feeling like a weird freak, and having a reaction that can’t be explained.”
Ivana Rihter is a writer in Chicago whose work has appeared in Vogue, Vanity Fair, Slate, Nylon and more

https://taz.de/Max-Slevogt-als-Illustrat.title: Max Slevogt als Illustrator in Berlin: Nicht zuletzt ein Kräftemessen
https://taz.de/Max-Slevogt-als-Illustrat.author: Katrin Bettina Müller
https://taz.de/Max-Slevogt-als-Illustrat.text:
Max Slevogt als Illustrator in Berlin: Nicht zuletzt ein Kräftemessen
In der Liebermann-Villa in Berlin wird Max Slevogt als Illustrator vorgestellt. Bruno Cassirer war sein Verleger, der ihn forderte und förderte.
Autsch. Das tut weh. Der Mann in Frack und Zylinder hat die Schere angesetzt am langen Schwanz des gehörnten Faun, der bockig nach vorne zieht. Diese Szene entwarf Max Slevogt als Werbeanzeige für die erste Ausgabe der Zeitschrift „Kunst und Künstler“, die der Verleger Bruno Cassirer 1902 gegründet hatte. Das Tauziehen am langen Schwanz habe sich dabei, so erklärt es die Kuratorin Viktoria Bernadette Krieger, auf einen Konflikt zwischen Verleger und Künstler bezogen: Der Künstler wollte gerne immer ein wenig mehr Platz auf der Seite, als der Verleger und Mappengestalter für angemessen hielt.
Dem produktiven, aber nicht immer spannungsfreien Verhältnis von Max Slevogt als Illustrator und Bruno Cassirer als Verleger ist eine Sonderausstellung in der Liebermann-Villa am Wannsee gewidmet. An mehr als 51 Illustrations- und Mappenwerken arbeiteten sie zusammen, seit Slevogt 1901 nach Berlin gekommen war. Max Liebermann hatte den Malerfreund aus München für die Secession in Berlin gewonnen; der Galerist Paul Cassirer hatte ihm einen guten Vertrag angeboten, dessen Vetter Bruno Cassirer war als Verleger an ihm interessiert.
Ein Forschungsprojekt zum Nachlass von Max Slevogt (1872–1932), unter anderem vom Landesmuseum Mainz und dem Saarlandmuseum, hat die Korrespondenz zwischen Slevogt und seinem Verleger untersucht. Darauf beruht die Ausstellung in der Villa Liebermann: Sie skizziert Slevogt als durchaus eigenwilligen und kapriziösen Menschen, den der Verleger immer wieder mahnen und motivieren musste.
Die Ausstellung
„Auf zu neuen Werken! Max Slevogt, Bruno Cassirer und Max Liebermann“: Liebermann-Villa am Wannsee, bis 18. Januar 2027
Slevogt liebte Dramatik, Witz und das Skurrile. Bei Ali Baba wurde der Kopf eines Enthaupteten auf einer Platte, über den beschwingt mit Messer und Tambourin eine Figur tanzt, zur Titelvignette. Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten sitzen in einer Tuschzeichnung schwer beschäftigt am Tisch, der Hund leckt den Teller aus, der Esel hantiert mit Besteck, die Katze steht auf den Hinterbeinen, um gründlich an den Rest im Topf zu kommen.
Von Bruno Cassirer ist ein fotografisches Porträt zu sehen, das ihn auf der Trabrennbahn zeigt. Er war auch erfolgreich als Importeur amerikanischer Pferde und hatte eine eigene Zucht. Slevogts Skizzenbücher belegen sein großes Interesse an Tierstudien, Pferden, Affen, Katzen. Das Spontane und Flüchtige, mit dem die Impressionisten die Malfläche aufbrachen, fand hier ein ideales Motiv.
Sozialgeschichte der Kunst
Die ausgestellten Grafiken, für die man seine Lesebrille dabeihaben sollte, so fein ist oft der Strich, so klein die Formate, werden um wenige Gemälde ergänzt, etwa einem Porträt, das Liebermann von Slevogt gemalt hat in warmen Rottönen.
Auch Liebermann arbeitete mit Bruno Cassirer, er illustrierte etwa Goethes Novelle „Der Mann von fünfzig Jahren“. Der wird, verliebt in die Freundin seines Sohnes, von neuer Eitelkeit gepackt und arbeitet hart an seiner Verjüngung. Eine durchaus ironische Geschichte, die Liebermann intim mit Interieurs aus seinem Haus und Modellen der Familie in fein gestrichelten Zeichnungen besetzte.
Die Ausstellung „Auf zu neuen Werken“ ermöglicht so einen, wenn auch nicht umfangreichen, Blick auf die grafischen Arbeiten von Slevogt und Liebermann. Mit der Zusammenarbeit von Verleger und Künstler schlägt sie zudem ein weiteres Kapitel der Sozialgeschichte der Kunst und der Produktionsbedingungen der klassischen Moderne auf, das wesentlich zu deren Erfolg beigetragen hat.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht.
